column36: Understanding the generation and protective functions of broadly-neutralizing humoral immune responses against influenza A virus
column37: Influenza virus is one of the top ten leading causes of death in Canada, and remains one of the gravest threats to global public health due to its propensity to cause pandemics. To combat seasonal influenza epidemics, massive annual vaccination programs are carried out at tremendous expense to the healthcare system. The ability of influenza virus to cause seasonal epidemics is conferred by its capacity to rapidly evolve in order to escape pre-existing immunity. This in turn necessitates that influenza virus vaccines be reformulated on a nearly annual basis. Frequently, the strains of influenza virus that actually circulate do not perfectly resemble the strains included in the vaccine. Due to the exquisitely strain-specific immunity that current vaccines elicit, vaccine efficacy can suffer substantially when imperfect matches occur. More importantly, current vaccines offer little to no protection against the emergence of a novel influenza virus pandemic. Therefore, there is a tremendous need to develop new influenza virus vaccines capable of inducing broad and long-lasting protection. The recent discovery of broadly-neutralizing antibodies that bind to the stalk domain of hemagglutinin has raised the hope that development of a "universal" influenza virus vaccine may be within reach. While many studies have addressed how these antibodies function in isolation, little is known about the way that broadly-neutralizing antibodies are generated and function in the context of the polyclonal responses that are naturally elicited by vaccination and infection. Our studies will define the mechanisms that govern the generation and function of broadly-neutralizing antibodies in the context of the polyclonal response to infection and vaccination. The knowledge gained from these studies will be used to advance the development of "universal" influenza virus vaccines and therapeutics which have the potential to substantially reduce the global burden of influenza-related illnesses

column36: Targeting endothelial KCa channels in vascular dysfunction.
column37: Patients with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) have a 2-4 greater risk of experiencing cardiovascular disease, such as atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease, hypertension and stroke. An early event in the development of T2D is injury to the vascular endothelium, a monolayer of cells lining the lumen of blood vessels that is critical for controlling vessel diameter and ultimately blood pressure. Injury or dysfunction of the endothelium directly contributes to the onset and severity of cardiovascular disease and it is now recognized that preventing or reversing endothelial dysfunction should improve the health of T2D patients. Using both human and rodent tissues, we have recently reported that membrane proteins (i.e. K+ selective ion channels) in vascular endothelium play a critical role in the regulation of blood vessel diameter by controlling vascular smooth muscle contraction. Moreover, manipulation of these ion channels with a novel class of drugs reverses the dysfunction of the vascular endothelium associated with T2D. In the accompanying research proposal, we will pursue these observations in order to identify the cellular defects preventing the normal activity of endothelial K+ channels and how a drug-like activator of these channels can improve vascular function in diseased blood vessels and tissues obtained from T2D rodent models and human patients. Our experiments will incorporate biochemical and functional measurements of key biological events in single endothelial cells, small arteries, intact beating hearts and whole animals that will provide critical information about T2D-associated injury to blood vessels. These proposed studies will reveal important, new insights into the cellular defects contributing to endothelial dysfunction in T2D patients and how manipulating key proteins in the vascular endothelium may lead to potential new therapeutic strategies to reverse disease-related vascular dysfunction and debilitating cardiovascular complications.

column36: New approaches to evaluating frailty in solid organ transplantation
column37: Solid organ transplantation is a life-saving treatment for people with organ failure, but organ donors and recipients must be chosen carefully since transplants are risky and donor organs are so scarce. In recent years, transplant programs have been accepting older donors and recipients with more chronic health problems. It is possible that some of these patients are frail - in other words, their bodies are less able to withstand stress - and this may lead to poor outcomes after transplantation. We do not know how best to measure frailty in organ transplant candidates and recipients. Without appropriate tools to measure frailty, we do not know if frail patients get as much benefit from transplantation as non-frail individuals, or how to help frail patients with organ failure have longer and better lives before and after transplantation though exercise or other treatments. We also do not know whether organs from frail people can safely be used for transplantation. The objective of this study is to develop and test the usefulness of a new tool to measure frailty in donors and candidates for heart, lung, kidney or liver transplantation. We will determine whether frailty is associated with worse health outcomes before and after transplantation. The results of this study will help transplant programs better predict benefit from organ transplantation, will improve our understanding of the aging process and how it is affected by transplantation, and may lead to strategies to reduce frailty and improve the medical care of individuals with advanced organ failure.

column36: Slit-Robo Signalling in Atherogenesis
column37: Heart disease and stroke are the leading causes of major illness and death in the Western world and result from atherosclerosis, which occurs when blood vessels become inflamed and narrowed. Progressive narrowing occurs when white blood cells from the bloodstream and muscle cells from the outer vessel wall migrate into the inner layer of the blood vessel where they cause injury. White blood cells also engulf lipid that is present, causing them to release harmful chemicals that worsen atherosclerosis. In heart attack and stroke, blood vessels supplying the heart and brain become critically narrowed and blocked by blood clot formation. Clot formation itself worsens inflammation in the blood vessel wall, fuelling the entire process. At the cellular level, each event described above contributes to atherosclerosis. Traditional therapies and preventative strategies focus on targeting individual events or on lowering blood levels of lipids. These strategies have been largely unsuccessful. Recent work from our laboratory suggests that Slit2, a molecule originally described in the developing brain, can potentially block recruitment of white blood cells, and blood clot formation. Our recent studies further suggest that Slit2 can prevent uptake of lipids by white blood cells. Indeed, Slit2 is not a synthetic medication, but rather, a molecule normally produced by blood vessel cells in the body, whose levels fall when vessel injury has occurred. We will use a combination of cutting-edge biochemical, molecular, and cell biology techniques to define how Slit2 prevents blood vessel injury in atherosclerosis. We will use animal models of atherosclerosis to test Slit2's ability to prevent blood vessel damage in the living organism. By understanding the molecular details, these studies will allow development of completely new strategies for preventing and minimizing the damage from heart attack and stroke.

column36: A new approach to studying retention: following the professional journey of midwives in Canada
column37: Midwifery as a regulated, licensed profession, is a new addition to our health care system. It has proven to bring many benefits to women and their newborns and is much less costly than physician provided maternity care. At the same time there has been a significant reduction in the number of doctors providing maternity services, so we are facing a significant shortfall in women's health care delivery in Canada. Midwifery is part of the solution to address this critical gap. The number of births in Canada continues to grow, but the numbers of trained maternity health care providers, especially midwives are not keeping up. This is due in large part to an alarmingly high attrition rate among midwifery trainees (close to 25%) and working midwives (20% in some provinces). Retention of health care professionals is critical for Canadian policy makers and governments. To make the changes that will retain workers and sustain our health care system requires the type of research we propose in this grant. The goal of this research proposal is to examine the workforce trends of Canadian midwives in order to improve retention. We need to understand the workplace experiences of Canadian midwives from their initiation to the profession in university, up to and including 10+ years in actual practice. Our study will be a pan-Canadian on-going survey following the students at the seven national midwifery schools as well as all practicing midwives at important steps in their careers. It will allow us to understand how different stages impact the available workforce and to understand how these women maintain their work-life balance while managing their career and personal life. Our research will recommend policy changes that will ultimately increase the number of working midwives and provide improved maternity care to Canadian women.

column36: Characterization of novel effectors that contribute to the fine-tuning of the antiviral cellular response following virus infection
column37: In response to viral infection, infected cells defend themselves by activating several families of cellular proteins known as transcription factors. These proteins have a role of messenger within the infected cells and will dictate if a particular gene will be used (induced) or not. Of these transcription factors, proteins named or called IRF3 and IRF7 play a key role as once turned-on or activated, they are responsible for the induction of genes with antiviral activities (known to impede pathogens' survival in the host). The latter are potent antiviral agents and powerful immunological modulators and understanding the cellular mechanisms by which infected cells produce these antiviral agents is required to identify novel cellular targets for future antiviral therapies. Discoveries in this particular field of research have demonstrated the essential roles of enzymes controlling the activity of IRF3 and IRF7. Notably, proteins called TBK1 and TRAF3 were shown to be of paramount importance in the establishment of an anti-viral defense system. Studies have demonstrated that cells infected with viruses are equipped with sensors that detect in incoming pathogens and relay this information to TRAF3, which is required for the activation of TBK1. Once activated, TBK1 is in turn responsible for the activation of IRF3 and IRF7. This type of regulation is referred as an activating signaling cascade, which control the induction of genes with antiviral activities. Albeit these important discoveries, how TRAF3, TBK1 and other "yet to discover key players" orchestrate and fine-tuned the antiviral cellular response is still largely unknown. Our endeavor in understanding the roles of TRAF3 and TBK1 in antiviral immunity as allowed us to discover other proteins with antiviral activity, namely TFG and mTOR. The propose research program will thus verify the implication of these proteins, which we believe to be essential effectors essential to fine-tune the antiviral cellular response.

column36: Menin and osteoblast function
column37: Osteoporosis is characterized by low bone mass and deterioration of bone tissue. This silent disease progresses without symptoms and leads to bone fragility and increased risk of fractures, particularly of the hip, spine and wrist. According to Osteoporosis Canada fractures from osteoporosis are more common than heart attack, stroke and breast cancer combined. As people age, one in three women and one in five men will suffer from an osteoporotic fracture. Eighty percent of hip fractures are related to osteoporosis and result in death in 20% of cases, and disability in 50% of the survivors. The annual healthcare cost of treating osteoporosis and the fractures it causes has been estimated to be almost two billion dollars in Canada alone. Maintenance of bone mass and function depends upon the balance between bone breakdown and formation. Osteoclasts resorb (breakdown) bone and importantly osteoblasts build bone. Learning more about the functions of bone cells is required to identify new drug targets that may be beneficial for treatment of osteoporosis. We have been studying a protein called menin and found in tissue culture models that it is important for the generation and differentiation of the bone building cell - the osteoblast. We have now generated mouse models in which the level of menin is altered in mature osteoblasts. Lack of menin leads to reduced bone mass and abnormal bone structure in adult mice, whereas overexpression of menin leads to increased bone mass. Further studies are proposed to determine the key molecular signaling pathways that menin interacts with in the osteoblast. In addition, further mouse models that we have already generated in which menin expression is altered at earlier times in the life of the osteoblast - in progenitor stem cells and immature osteoblasts - will be investigated. This knowledge will be used to identify new drugs for improved treatment of bone diseases like osteoporosis.

column36: Co-targeting parathyroid-hormone related protein (PTHrP) signaling and osteoclast activation to counter breast cancer metastasis to bone
column37: Skeletal metastases appear as complications in up to 70% of breast cancer patients. Once bone tumors are established, they are usually incurable. In advanced cases, the skeleton often bears the major tumor burden, causing considerable suffering and morbidity due to hypercalcemia, pathological fractures, cord compression and intractable pain. The current therapies against skeletal invasion use anti-resorptive agents such as bisphosphonates, but these compounds are not curative and new targets must be identified in the fight against bone metastases. Breast tumors and other types of cancer are composed of two main populations of cancer cells. The bulk of a tumor is composed of cells with limited proliferation capacity that are sensitive to conventional anti-cancer therapies. There is also a small population of long-lived cancer stem cells (CSCs) that are resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy. A notoriously difficult-to-treat cancer is the CSC-driven triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). TNBCs have very poor prognosis because they currently lack effective therapies. Traditional cancer therapies can effectively de-bulk tumors but fail to produce long-term remissions and prevent metastases, possibly due to their inability to eliminate CSCs. Our laboratory has identified a novel target known as the parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), previously implicated in the development of bone metastases, but which has never before been associated with CSCs or TNBC. We have produced an anti-PTHrP antibody that blocks PTHrP action and is highly-efficient against breast cancer growth and metastases. Our preliminary studies suggest that PTHrP is very likely a driving force behind CSC proliferation and dissemination to distant organs. Our goal is to attack this resistant breast cancer cell population within bone with our novel blocking monoclonal antibodies against PTHrP, in combination with approved bone targeting bisphosphonates, to eradicate skeletal metastases.

column36: A Genetic Model for Neurofibromatosis Type II
column37: Neurofibromatosis Type II (NF2) is a crippling cancer, mostly of the nervous system. The chance of developing NF2 depends on the genes you inherit. For example, NF2 patients are often born only one functional copy the NF2 gene instead of two. If that functional copy was mutated, tumours may repeatedly develop in the brain and spinal cord. The NF2 gene encodes a protein named Merlin. Merlin acts as a tumour suppressor, a name for proteins that instruct cells not to divide. This activity may be related to a second function for Merlin: it helps cells to "stick together," which is crucial for forming various organs within our bodies. Our laboratory is determining why Merlin is found in almost all cells of the human body, but mutations in the NF2 gene mostly induce cancer in just the brain and spinal cord. Other researchers that study the Merlin protein mostly work with isolated human cells for simplicity, but that approach makes it more difficult to determine how Merlin causes cells to adhere to one another to form tissues like the brain. Animal models such as mice would be vastly preferable for tissue studies, but they are more difficult to work with than isolated cells. At the crossroads between cells and mice is the commonly studied laboratory animal Drosophila or the fruit fly. The fly brain is a reduced version of the human brain, with the same types of cells acting in the same ways. Using flies, we have shown that Merlin needs to work with other proteins to perform its tumour suppressor and cell-adhesive functions. Notably, some of these other proteins are found only in brain cells. We plan to determine how these proteins assist Merlin activity in the fly brain. We already know that related forms of these proteins are found in the human brain. Our goal is to understand how these proteins function with Merlin to control how cells grow and stick together in the nervous system. Our results will aid the development of improved diagnosis and therapies for NF2 tumours.

column36: Obesity and nutritional programming of the paternal sperm epigenome: effects on offspring development and health
column37: The impact of diet and body condition on the father's reproductive health and that of his offspring has been relatively under-explored and under-emphasized. Over the past two decades male fertility is declining as measured by lowered sperm counts, increased DNA damage in sperm and rising rates of testicular cancer. Other factors contributing to increasing male infertility are the increase in chronic diseases that are widespread including, obesity, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders. While we know each of these factors can negatively impact sperm counts and quality, what is even more alarming is the emerging evidence from the field of epigenetics which suggests these factors are not limited to just damaging male fertility, but may passed on to influence the health of children and perhaps even grandchildren. So how does sperm transmit information concerning diet and body condition across generations? It involves a biochemical set of information that is hereditary just like DNA, but sits on top, or within the DNA and controls whether a gene is turned active or not. The overall research question we address is: Does a father's diet and body mass index predispose his offspring to chronic disease or developmental defects and how is this information related to the sperm epigenome? The mechanisms underlying transmission of environmental memory from parents to offspring is far from understood. In prior studies we demonstrated that a folate deficient diet altered the sperm epigenome and that these changes were associated to genes implicated in development and chronic disease. In humans fast food diets, obesity and its metabolic sequelae are known to alter folate metabolism. Using data from murine models and human samples collected from a fertility clinic we will determine how folate and body mass affects the sperm epigenome, its association with markers of chronic disease and the consequences for offspring.

column36: Defining the mechanisms and therapeutic potential of ShcA-mediated angiogenesis and metabolism that fuel breast tumorigenesis
column37: Cancer cells grow uncontrollably and are unresponsive to the checkpoints that restrain the growth of normal cells. In order to support such rapid proliferation, cancer cells must substantially increase their ability to acquire nutrients and oxygen by generating a new blood supply (neo-vascularization) and also to generate the energy (ATP) for cancer cells to divide. Our research focuses on a particular class of proteins, called receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), which substantially increase the ability of cancer cells to recruit a new vasculature and generate ATP. Adaptor proteins bridge these RTKs to downstream effector pathways, which are critical for their biological function. Our research has shown that one adaptor protein, called ShcA, is a central hub downstream of many RTKs to fuel breast tumor growth. We have generated extensive data to show that breast cancer cells with high ShcA activity substantially increase breast tumor vascularization and ATP production, leading to increased tumor growth. Herein, we will address the molecular mechanisms by which ShcA regulates tumor vascularization, energy production and cell proliferation, each of which contribute to tumor aggressiveness. The advent of targeted therapies have revolutionized clinical management of breast cancer patients. Despite the availability of a plethora of such therapies, the remaining challenge is to choose the treatment that has the best chance of success to manage the disease in advanced breast cancer patients. Our data suggests that the activation status of ShcA can alter the sensitivity of breast tumors to pharmacological inhibitors targeting pathways that promote tumor vascularization, ATP production and cell growth. We will examine whether measurement of the ShcA activation status of breast tumors can serve as a predictive biomarker to determine whether the tumor is more likely to be more sensitive to one type of therapy over another. This is the cornerstone of personalized medicine.

column36: Stress and Obesity: the Ghrelin connection

column37: Common conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes compromise kidney functions leading to kidney disease and failure. The number of Canadians living with or are at risk of developing kidney disease is estimated to be 2 million. Although progress has been made in understanding how kidney disease develops, there are still large gaps in our knowledge. The role of highly specialized kidney cells, the tubular epithelium in disease generation is now increasingly recognized. Chemicals released by immune cells or the epithelium itself alter epithelial function and initiate harmful responses. Importantly, the intactness of the cell architecture, the so called cytoskeleton, is vital for normal functions, and its disruption is an early step in many diseases. The objective of this proposal is to investigate how the chemical named Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) alters tubular cell functions and causes injury in the kidney. We will focus on the cellular molecules called RhoA and their regulator GEF-H1, as these have central roles in many cell functions. They are regulated by harmful stimuli, but the details of the ensuing events are not well known. Therefore, we will use various biochemical, cell biological and fluorescent microscopic techniques in kidney tubule cell lines to study these molecules. We will also test our findings in animal models of kidney diseases. These studies will provide new information about the mechanisms of chronic kidney disease, with the hope of finding novel targets for designing drugs for these currently untreatable conditions.

column36: Cesarean section: impact on infant gut microbiota, childhood obesity and allergic disease
column37: The World Health Organization recommends that the rate of Cesarean section (CS) should be no higher than 15% and that infants should not be fed anything other than breast milk for the first 6 months. Currently in Canada, 27% of births are by CS, up from 18% in the mid 1990s. Also, only 14% of Canadian infants are strictly breastfed for the first six months of life and less so if they are born by CS. The consequences of decision-making around birth method and infant feeding should not be underestimated. Beyond risks to the mother and infant at the time of delivery, long term health effects are associated with CS birth, including allergy, asthma and overweight. Breastfeeding provides health benefits to the child by reducing the risk of these conditions. It is thought that health outcomes related to CS and breastfeeding may be due to changes in the bacteria living in the intestinal tract, called the gut microbiota. This community of beneficial bacteria evolves in response to the bacterial environment of the infant. Normally, the first exposure to microbes is the bacteria encountered in the birth canal. In a CS-delivered infant, exposures come from the mother's skin and hospital environment. Antibiotic treatment to prevent infection in CS may also affect the development of infant gut microbiota. A clearer understanding is needed of how the gut microbiota is affected by birth method and early feeding, and how these changes affect the health of the child later in life. The main goal of our research in 3,300 healthy Canadian infants is to understand long term child health outcomes arising from changes in the development of the infant gut microbiota in response to CS delivery. A secondary goal is to determine how other factors, like breastfeeding and antibiotic use, alter the effects of CS on the infant gut microbiota. This will help parents and physicians make more informed decisions about birth method and infant feeding.

column36: Microtubule dynamics and age-related aneuploidy in mammalian oocytes
column37: At fertilisation a new individual is created by the fusion of the sperm and the egg, each of which contributes half of the genetic material (chromosomes) for the offspring. However, for reasons that are very poorly understood, the development of the egg is error-prone, such that unfertilised eggs frequently possess the wrong number of chromosomes. This is particularly the case as women get older. These chromosomally abnormal ('aneuploid') eggs are the cause of developmental conditions such as Down's, are a leading cause of miscarriage, and are the leading reason for age-related infertility. We will investigate the cause of aneuploidy in eggs, particularly focussing on the spindle, the part of the cell responsible for ensuring that chromosomes are correctly divided between cells (called chromosome segregation) during the final cell division which occurs as part of egg development. Using state-of-the-art microscopy we will compare spindles in eggs from old mice and young mice, to determine precisely why the spindle in the developing egg from older mothers is more prone to chromosome segregation errors. Our preliminary data suggest that the kinesin-13s family of proteins, which are important for correct chromosomes segregation in many cells, may be defective in old eggs. We will test the role of kinesin-13s in developing eggs, and establish which of these proteins are the most important for preventing chromosome segregation-errors. Moreover, in collaboration with clinical colleagues, we will perform some of the first such studies in human eggs, and determine whether kinesin-13s are important for preventing aneuploidy. Our experiments will provide key information as to why developing eggs are likely to mis-segregate chromosomes, particularly in older mothers, and thus will help explain why pregnancy establishment becomes more difficult as women become older.

column37: Bullying in schools is a severe problem in many countries. In Canada between 20% and 25% of girls and boys are bullied by peers at some point during their school years. Little is known, however, about how chronic peer victimization during the school years may affect later mental health in young adulthood. Understanding this association is crucial, because mental health problems during young adulthood have profound implications for the quality of later life. It is also critical to identify the bio-physiological mechanisms through which peer victimization gets "under the skull, skin and cells" and leads to mental health problems in young adult women and men. By accounting for the role of genetic influences, this design is ideal for understanding the influence of adverse environmental experiences on health. Together with the previously collected data, the proposed research will provide unique insights into the long-term effect of peer victimization and offer empirically-based resources for health professionals concerned with promoting a healthy transition to adulthood for female and male victims of school bullying.

column36: Fundamental processes impacting Campylobacter jejuni pathogenesis
column37: Campylobacter jejuni (Cj) is the leading cause of bacterial food poisoning in the developed world. Yet, its mechanisms of pathogenesis remain mysterious. Through screening and selection, we have identified means by which this pathogen is so successful. One is its shape. Cj is helical/corkscrew in morphology, and this abets its ability to burrow into the mucosa of both susceptible and commensal hosts. We have, for the first time, identified gene products involved in the cell envelope (peptidoglycan; PG) required for this shape, and logical candidates for further study. Using a rounded genetics and biochemical approach, we will perform gene deletion studies, protein localization, exploration of newly identified factors, investigation of how these factors interact with each other to control helicity, and studies of PG factors involved in the natural shape-change processes of cell division and coccoid formation as the bacteria age. Also through genetic screens, we identified and defined the Cj hyperosmotic stress response. Surprisingly, this revealed significant heterogeneity within wild type Cj 'clones', at a frequency significantly outweighing standard single nucleotide polymorphism and phase-variation. This type of heterogeneity may be what underlies the ability of Cj to infect and survive in so many diverse environments despite fragile growth requirements. We are investigating the role of purine metabolism in this process, exploring a novel regulator, and identifying and characterizing new hypervariable genes. We are excited to continue studies linking this variability with our bacterial cell shape findings, which also yield heterogeneity in a wild type population. Ultimately, we hope that the combination of traditional microbiology, genetics, and biochemistry, together with newer next-gen approaches, will finally provide insight into how and why Cj is such an important human pathogen, and clues to its eradication.

column37: All of our genes are arranged on large pieces of DNA called chromosomes. The chromosomes are huge molecules that must undergo multiple levels of compaction to fit into the cell. At the same time, the genes characteristic of that cell type must remain accessible for activation. In a stem cell the chromosomes are loosely packaged and many genes are poised for activation. When the stem cell commits to becoming a specific cell type (eg. neuron) it must tightly package and silence those genes that are not required and fully activate those genes that will be turned on. To manage this process cells have developed a complex series of proteins to control the structure of chromosomes and the regulation of genes. When this process is defective, cells cannot divide, differentiate or initiate gene expression effectively. Indeed, recent work has shown that mutations in chromosome regulating proteins cause a variety of human diseases, including developmental disorders with severe intellectual disability and numerous types of cancer. The main aim of this research is to delineate the roles of two closely related chromosome organizing proteins, Snf2h and Snf2l that appear to have complementary roles on neural stem cell function during brain development. Defining this fundamental process is critical for us to understand how a stem cell commits to a specific cell fate and how it maintains an organized chromosome. A thorough understanding of these processes is a prerequisite to determining how these complex disorders develop, progress, and for engineering novel treatment strategies.

column37: A central idea in immunology is that an infection must stimulate the immune system to make special cells called memory T cells. We also plan to examine whether there is a role for autophagy in controlling memory responses to human vaccines. column37: In a normal cell, growth and proliferation is regulated by signals that come from the surrounding tissue and neighboring cells. Signals from outside are interpreted by protein receptors that span the limiting membrane of the cell (half inside and half outside). A signal received outside is transmitted inside by the receptor which then passes the signal on to molecules in the cell that control cell behavior. Once a receptor molecule is activated it is quickly pulled inside the cell where it is destroyed and the signal is terminated. This is process called receptor down regulation. In some cancers, this control mechanism is lost, and the receptor stays at the surface of the cell, and continues to send signals. As a result the cell continuously divides, or migrates and invades surrounding tissue inappropriately. The focus of this proposal is a molecule called Numb that controls the down regulation of receptors. There is evidence that the function of the Numb molecule is lost or altered in human breast lung and ovarian tumors. We hypothesize that these changes in the Numb molecule disrupts the normal down regulation of receptors causing tumor growth and metastasis. In this proposal we will use biochemical, cell biology, and animal model studies to: 1. Investigate what causes the altered forms of Numb observed in cancer cells. 2. To determine how changes in normal Numb activity affects the growth and survival of human breast cancer cells. This information will allow us to evaluate whether changes in the Numb molecule occurs in tumors that have a failure of receptor down regulation. This is could impact cancer treatment as new cancer drugs specifically target cell receptors in an effort to shut them off. In addition, it will also give us specific information on how Numb becomes altered in human cancer, and whether restoration of normal Numb activity is useful and potentially achievable therapeutic goal.

column37: The kidney is an important physiological "filter" that allows us to eliminate all waste products, while retaining vital components. One vital molecule is bicarbonate, which we must retain to compensate for the acid produced while processing food. The kidney anion exchanger 1 (kAE1), which exchanges chloride for bicarbonate, is of particular importance for bicarbonate reabsorption. Some individuals with mutated bicarbonate transporter kAE1 are unable to properly retain bicarbonate in their kidneys, thus bicarbonate is expelled instead of reabsorbed. The result of our studies will be relevant to the growing population of patients with kidney stones as well as hypertensive Canadians, a condition that affects more than a third of North American adults. To reach these goals, we will use an animal model mimicking the pathology seen in these patients, complemented with in vitro analyses to dissect these mechanisms at the cellular level. This study will provide a greater understanding of why not all, but only some persons with BD show brain changes and memory impairment. column36: B cell intrinsic mechanisms of germinal center reaction
column37: Germinal center (GC) is a small lymphoid structure in spleen and lymph nodes. Under normal circumstance, GC reaction can generate differentiated B lymphocytes called memory B cells and plasma cells, the latter produce antibodies that are responsible for neutralization and elimination of various viral and bacterial pathogens. However, abnormal GC reaction may lead to immune deficiency, autoimmune diseases, and even GC-derived B lymphomas that compose the majority of B cell tumors. During pathogen infection the incoming pathogens first activate B cells through B cell antigen receptors (BCR), The activated B cells then migrate to GC where they may proliferate multiple rounds, modify their antibody coding genes, and differentiate into either plasma or memory B cells. While it has become clear that coordination between B cells and other immune cells appears to be essential for GC reaction, molecular mechanisms that control B cell differentiation inside a GC remain not entirely clear. We found that Cbl proteins, a group of similar protein modifiers, play a critical role in GC reaction. We showed that Cbl proteins deficiency disrupts GC formation at multiple stages and severely impaired antibody production. We also identified that the impairment is caused by several defects, including loss of coordination between B and other immune cells and alteration of B cell function to produce high affinity antibodies (termed affinity maturation). In addition, Cbl deficient mice develop high incidence of lymphomas after immunization, indicating that they may function as tumor suppressors. The current proposal aims at understanding how Cbl proteins regulate GC reaction and antibody affinity maturation, and elucidate how Cbl deficiency contributes to B lymphoma genesis. Completion of this project will not only bring new insight in our understanding of GC reaction but also provide clues in the prevention and treatment of various immune system disorders.

column36: Compensatory role of the motor cortex in the recovery of locomotion after spinal cord injury
column37: In Canada, about 86,000 people live with a spinal cord injury (SCI), and more than 4,300 new cases arise every year. For SCI individuals, limitations in sensorimotor activities such as walking and posture severely affect their quality of life. In most cases, patients have an incomplete injury that spares some connections between the brain, which initiates movements, and the spinal circuits, which generate them. This places brain structures with partial connectivity to the spinal cord in a particularly favorable position to compensate for the lost function. Specifically, the motor cortex offers significant and unappreciated opportunities for recovery of walking and is a potential target for treatments. My main goal is study the role of the motor cortex in the recovery of locomotion after incomplete SCI. We will use a well-established rat model of SCI in which hindlimb locomotion is progressively re-expressed over five weeks. While this short time course does not mimic recovery in humans, it facilitates exploration of the underlying biological mechanisms. By combining innovative paradigms to manipulate cortical activity with behavioral, electrophysiological and neuroanatomical techniques, we will study the mechanisms by which the cortex affects the spinal circuits that generate stepping after SCI. We will then tap into these mechanisms to foster and enhance recovery of walking by testing cortical stimulation protocols. Our experiments will provide a comprehensive examination of the role of the motor cortex and the mechanisms through which it influences locomotor recovery after SCI. This proposal has the potential to expand our knowledge on the neural basis of recovery after SCI. Activity-based neurorehabilitation and brain stimulation protocols can be developed to harness cortical activity that may catalyze functional recovery, e.g. walking and posture, following SCI.

column36: Mechanisms of therapeutic efficacy of deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting more than 100,000 Canadians and more than 5 million people worldwide. Clinically, it is characterized by a progression of motor symptoms that include slowness of movement, rigidity, tremor and postural instability. The main pathological feature involves a progressive loss of brain neurons containing the neurotransmitter dopamine. The dopamine precursor (L-DOPA) is the most effective pharmacotherapy for PD, but adverse effects hamper its chronic use. Within 5-10 years of L-DOPA treatment, most patients begin to experience motor complications including abnormal involuntary movements that can be more debilitating than the disease itself. These patients can be proposed surgery that consists in the permanent implantation of stimulation electrodes. Despite its long history of improving the quality of life and motor symptoms in over half of the patients, the mechanisms by which deep brain stimulation (DBS) produces its therapeutic effects remain unclear. In addition, DBS is associated with a variety of adverse effects including acute or chronic neurological and neuropsychological complications. To further improve the effectiveness of DBS treatment for PD patients, while reducing its side-effects, our research project aims at generating insights into the underlying mechanisms of DBS using behavioural, neuroanatomical and biochemical studies in parkinsonian monkeys.

column36: Cell biology of an evolutionarily conserved ciliary compartment essential for cellular signalling
column37: Cilia are cellular 'antenna' that enable many essential physiological and developmental processes. For example, motile cilia clear respiratory airways of debris and allow sperm movement. Sensory (non-motile) cilia protrude from the cells of most organs and perform vital roles in capturing and transmitting environmental signals-such as photoreception (vision) and olfaction (smell). Defects in cilia, as for example seen in patients affected with Joubert syndrome, Meckel syndrome and Nephronophthisis, result in a spectrum of ailments, including impaired vision, kidney dysfunction, skeletal anomalies and brain malformations. Our goal is to elucidate how a complex structure at the base of cilia, termed 'transition zone', is formed and carries out its function as a barrier or 'gate' that controls the molecular composition of cilia. The aim of the research is to provide new fundamental biological insights and to increase our understanding of the links between cilia and disease. To achieve our objective, we propose using innovative approaches to uncover and analyse novel components of the gate. Multiple complementary strategies will be used to help define the molecular organisation of transition zone components, and to probe the molecular functions of the gate. The studies will involve the use of the nematode C. elegans, a powerful, genetically-manipulable model system. This organism allows us to take advantage of cutting-edge resources and experimental tools not readily available for researchers using vertebrate/mammalian systems. Lastly, collaborations with human geneticists will facilitate our discovery and analysis of novel disease genes associated with cilia defects (ciliopathies). Together, our findings will help us make significant strides towards understanding fundamental mechanisms of cilium formation and function-seen as increasingly relevant to human health and disease.

column36: Sensory processing and plasticity at peripheral arterial chemoreceptors
column37: In the neck region near major arteries, 'receptor' cells in tiny organs help maintain blood chemicals at particular levels via the control of breathing. These 'receptor' cells sense blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity, and send electrical signals to the brain that help correct any major disturbances. Abnormalities in this reflex pathway can have fatal consequences. For example, changes in 'receptor' cell properties are associated with clinical conditions such as obstructive lung disease (COPD), sleep apnea (where breathing stops periodically), hypertension, and congestive heart failure. These conditions are associated with fluctuations in blood oxygen levels, which can lead to hyper-activity in the reflex pathway, compromising blood pressure regulation and heart function. Our investigations aim to understand how these 'receptor' cells work, how they communicate with the brain, and how their properties change in disease states. To simplify the system, in one approach we isolate these 'receptor' cells from rats and grow them in tissue culture dishes alone, or with the nerve cells that contact them in the animal. Recent studies have shown that these rat 'receptor' cells behave similarly to those in humans. We grow the cells in an incubator under different oxygen levels, thereby mimicking the environment experienced in disease conditions. Also, we can expose live animals (rats) to environments where oxygen levels can be varied in precise patterns, so as to mimic the above clinical conditions. We can then apply various techniques (e.g. recording of electrical activity, imaging, molecular biology) to help understand how the 'receptor' cells communicate with nerve cells, and how their properties change in different oxygen environments. This understanding will help in the design of new drugs to target and correct abnormalities that arise in the aforementioned clinical conditions.

column36: IGFBP7 - A Novel Biomarker, and a Clue to the Pathophysiology of Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction?
column37: Heart failure, or progressive deterioration of heart function to supply blood to the rest of the body, affects 1 in 5 Canadians, and accounts for over 100,000 deaths a year in Canada. It is the most costly medical condition. While the traditional form of heart failure is accompanied by an enlarged heart (so called systolic heart failure), a new form of heart failure which is accompanied by a small stiff heart (so called diastolic heart failure) is the new cardiovascular epidemic. It occurs in older patients, associated with diabetes and hypertension. Most concerning is the fact that to date, we don't yet have a good diagnostic tool, nor effective therapies for the condition. To address this problem, our team recently identified a novel molecule that can be detected in blood that appears to be a specific marker for diastolic heart failure. In addition, it appears to predict risk of progression and bad outcome in this condition, and has been replicated by at least 2 other teams. The molecule is called IGFBP7 (Insulin Growth Factor Binding Protein 7). Its function in heart disease is entirely unknown. Interestingly, IGFBP7 appears to accelerate aging, and may lead to the changes in the heart we find in diastolic heart failure. We would like to find out if this is indeed the case. We want to (1) check if risk factors for heart failure accelerate the aging process in the cells that make up the heart chamber; (2) see if IGFBP7 produced in this process will lead to the heart failure process, and whether the different heart cell types will enhance each other in response. We also want to (3) find out if we blocked this molecule's presence in the heart, whether it would benefit the patient. There is thus an opportunity that our research is opening new windows in this enigmatic disease, and potentially can change the lives of patients affected by this condition.

column36: The role of PCL2/PRC2 in hematopoietic stem cells and leukemia
column37: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is one of the deadliest types of cancers. Thirty to forty percent of AML patients younger than 60 years of age are long-term survivors, while only 10-15% of patients over 60 years of age are long-term survivors. The standard treatment has not changed in over 30 years, which is why survival rates have not improved during this period. The exception to this dismal news is that some targeted therapies have been developed to specific molecular causes of AML. Patients with these types of AML have responded well to drugs that are specific to these mutations. Unfortunately, in about half of the AML patients, mutations associated with their AML have not been identified. We have recently identified a protein called PCL2 that regulates the expression of many other proteins, including many that are involved in cancer. PCL2 expression is lost in 40% of AML patients. Our preliminary data suggest that PCL2 is important in controlling cell growth and inducing mutated cells to die, processes that prevent cancer development. Thus, we believe that PCL2 could be a target for new chemotherapeutic drugs to treat patients in a targeted manner. However, to pursue this strategy, we need to understand the function of PCL2 in normal blood stem cells and AML cells. In this study, we will analyze the function of PCL2. We will turn off the expression of PCL2 in both normal blood stem cells and AML cells. We will determine how the loss of expression of PCL2/PRC2 proteins changes the molecular networks that regulate cell behaviour including growth and death of blood stem cells and AML cells. Knowing the function of PCL2 may help us to induce AML cells to die.

column36: Kinematics and Muscle Activation of the Cervical Spine During Impending Head First Impacts in Motor Vehicle Rollovers
column37: Vehicular rollovers are a significant source of major injuries. Specifically, rollovers can cause neck injury, through head-first impact when an occupant "dives" into the roof during roof to ground impact. Rollover neck injury mechanisms are poorly understood and although cadaver studies have been used to study rollovers, they lack muscles and because rollovers take several seconds to develop, muscles are important to the spine posture during rollovers. We plan to study spine posture and neck muscles in human volunteers during simulated rollovers. We have developed techniques previously to record neck posture with x-ray movies and neck muscle activation with electromyography (small needles that are inserted into the various neck muscles to record their electrical activity). We will modify this rig so that it moves similarly to a vehicle during a rollover and use the same x-ray and electromyography techniques to study the volunteers necks during our experiments. This information will allow us to validate existing computational models of the neck during rollovers and we can use it to develop new seatbelts, roof panels and other novel safety devices to prevent these injuries from happening as frequently as they do now.

column36: Close encounters of a Natural Killer kind: Understanding how NK cells protect against HIV infection.
column37: Some people remain HIV uninfected despite multiple exposures to this virus. The term HIV exposed seronegative (HESN) has been used to describe such individuals. By comparing HESN to HIV susceptible subjects we previously identified two genotypes coding for variants of Natural Killer (NK) cell receptors (NKR) and their ligands (the molecules recognized by NKR) that were associated with protection from HIV infection. NK cells are part of the innate arm of the immune system, which means that they are primed and ready to kill HIV infected cells, and secrete factors with anti-HIV activity. As such they have the kind of functional profile needed to act early to prevent the establishment of HIV infection. In this project we will continue our examination of how NK cells and autologous HIV infected cells (i.e. cells from the same person) interact to stimulate NK cells for anti-HIV activity. We will investigate the NKR profile of the NK cell subsets activated by autologous HIV infected cells, what ligands for NKR are induced by HIV infection and what stage of the HIV life cycle NK cell inhibit. We will also explore the potential and limitations of an NK cell function that links the innate and adaptive arms of the immune response. This function, if better understood, may be exploited to trigger protective immunity in a vaccine setting.

column37: Glioblastoma (GBM), a lethal cancer, is very heterogeneous, containing mixtures of different cell types. column36: Targeting TAZ and YAP: a new approach to anti-fibrotic therapy in the kidney
column37: Scarring is a major cause of chronic organ failure, accounting for up to 50% of all deaths in the developed world. In the kidney, scarring is the final common pathway of damage activated by nearly all forms of chronic kidney disease. If left unchecked, kidney scarring can lead to kidney failure, an increasingly common, costly, and life-threatening condition requiring dialysis or kidney transplantation for survival. Unfortunately, no safe and effective anti-scarring treatments exist. Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) is the main stimulus for scar production. Drugs that block TGF-beta are not widely used as anti-scarring agents because TGF-beta not only promotes scarring, but also controls many other important non-scarring functions in the body. Following injury and especially with scarring, organs become stiffer. Recent studies have demonstrated that fibroblasts, the main source of scar tissue in the kidney, can sense this increased stiffness, and react by augmenting their responsiveness to TGF-beta. We have identified two proteins named TAZ and YAP which play a critical role in regulating stiffness-dependent fibroblast scarring responses. TAZ and YAP are activated when fibroblasts are grown on a stiff surface reminiscent of an injured, fibrotic kidney, and inactivated when fibroblasts are grown on a soft, healthy kidney-like surface. We have shown that active TAZ and YAP may promote fibroblast scarring responses to TGF-beta, and that inactivation of these proteins seems to block these scarring responses. The proposed studies will explore how TAZ and YAP are activated by kidney stiffening, how they promote TGF-beta-induced fibroblast scarring responses, and using specialized gene-modification strategies will test whether loss of TAZ and/or YAP can prevent kidney scarring in animal models of chronic kidney injury. Ultimately these studies aim to identify new safe and specific anti-scarring agents for the treatment of patients with chronic kidney disease.

column36: Mapping the microcircuits of attention in the primate brain
column37: The human brain has a limited capacity to process the overwhelming amount of information entering the senses at a given time. The mechanism of attention overcomes this limitation by selecting signals relevant to behavior for further processing, while filtering out irrelevant signals. Deficits of attention are core symptoms of mental disorders such as ADHD, Autism and Schizophrenia. For example, children with ADHD cannot effectively focus attention on specific people or objects but instead attend to every salient item in the environment. This diverts cognitive resources from important information and causes learning disabilities, complicates social interactions, and impairs memory. Our incomplete knowledge of how attention is implemented in the brain is a central obstacle to the treatment of these deficits. The long-term goal of my research is to unravel the mechanisms of selective attention in the primate brain, as well as how failures in such mechanisms can cause disorders of attention in humans. We have demonstrated that attention modulates brain activity amplifying signals that are important and suppressing unimportant ones. We have further demonstrated that the lateral prefrontal cortex, a specialized region of the primate brain, plays a fundamental role in this process. Importantly, evidence from imaging studies in humans indicates that the same area is dysfunctional in patients with mental disorders characterized by deficits of attention (e.g., ADHD, Autism, and Schizophrenia). Such a dysfunction may originate from abnormal connectivity patterns within the area that affect the way brain cells interact with one another to process information. The research proposed here will first explore how neurons in the lateral prefrontal cortex interact to implement the function of attention. Second, we will manipulate such interactions using drugs and brain stimulation techniques to produce different attentional states that resemble the one in affected individuals.

column36: Mechanisms of Protective Immunity in Ovarian Cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer is a challenging disease with unacceptably high mortality. Despite this, about 30% of patients "beat the odds" and live for many years after treatment. Why do some patients do so well? In the past decade, it has become well established that some ovarian cancer patients mount strong immune responses against their tumor. Tumors from such patients are densely packed with killer T cells, a type of white blood cell that fights viral and bacterial infections, as well as cancer. Importantly, patients with large numbers of killer T cells in their tumor have markedly higher survival rates. This is a very promising finding, as it shows that the immune system can have a profound influence on survival from ovarian cancer. With better understanding of the immune response, it will be possible to design new treatments such as vaccines that enhance tumor immunity and increase patient survival. However, to do this intelligently, we need to better understand how the immune response works. Although killer T cells are important for fighting tumors, they do not work alone. We recently showed that tumors containing both T cells and B cells are associated with even higher survival rates than seen with T cells alone. In this study, we will investigate the mechanisms by which T cells and B cells work together to promote tumor immunity. We will pay particular attention to how the immune system adapts to changes in the tumor during standard treatment and progression. We envision our work will lead to a major re-think about cancer immunotherapy: instead of simply trying to activate killer T cells, we also need to find effective ways to activate their team mates, the B cells. With better understanding of how T cells and B cells fight cancer, we can design new forms of treatment that enhance the patient's natural defences.

column36: Investigating Host Defense of the Lung Microvasculature By Patrolling Sentry Neutrophils In Vivo
column37: The lung directly contacts the environment via a huge collection of air-filled sacs called alveoli. The disadvantage of this interaction is the constant exposure of the host airways to airborne pathogens. As well, the lung alveoli are richly supplied with blood, which results in a massive surface area of blood vessels in close proximity to potential pathogen portals of entry. Certainly, microbial pathogens can penetrate from the lung alveoli into the circulation and rapidly disseminate to other vascular beds and tissues. Bacteremia, or bacteria that has entered the blood stream, has important clinical implications as affected patients require longer courses of intravenous antibiotics, longer hospital stays and have higher mortality rates. Being at the forefront of pathogen interactions, the lung plays a critical role in containing pathogens before they spread, however it remains unclear if, and how, the lung deals with microbes that breakthrough the barrier and make it to the blood circulation. The overarching hypothesis of this grant proposal is that pre-positioned lung neutrophils in the blood vessels act as vascular sentries by performing surveillance and capture of any blood-borne bacteria. We are utilizing state-of-the-art microscopy for intravital lung imaging, which allows for greater cellular and molecular resolution of pulmonary intravascular immunity, in live animals, in real time. Understanding the role that lung neutrophils play in protecting us from harmful pathogen entry into the blood will allow rational therapeutic design to enhance this process in severely infected humans.

column37: Epilepsy is one of the most common and severe neurological conditions, characterized by frequent seizures due to abnormal excessive electrical activity in the brain. Although many drugs are currently available for the management of epileptic seizures, a surprisingly large number patients fail to respond to these treatments. As many as 30% of patients with epilepsy are refractory to current treatments, and many others suffer significant side effects from these drugs. Also, many of the drugs used to treat epilepsy are decades (or even centuries) old. Taken together, these observations suggest that new approaches are needed. A principal reason for the unmet need in seizure therapy that many existing drugs are redundant - they act on similar ion targets in the brain. However, genetic studies have identified dozens of proteins in the brain that may regulate electrical activity and seizures. Our study will focus on a recently introduced anti-epileptic drug named retigabine (also known as Ezogabine, Trobalt, or Potiga). This drug was approved for use in Canada in 2012, and is unique because it is the only anti-epileptic drug that targets a class of protein called voltage-gated potassium channels in the brain. These voltage-gated channels alter their activity when the drug binds, helping to suppress seizures. Our study applies several cutting edge approaches to study the specific chemical forces that allow retigabine to interact with its target, and to unravel the changes in protein function that take place after retigabine binds. Since retigabine is the first drug of its class that has been developed to treat epilepsy, we anticipate that our research project will identify changes that can be made to improve the potency and effectiveness of the drug.

column37: Diabetes mellitus is a growing epidemic that is associated with a number of severe cardiovascular complications that ultimately result in death in as many as 65% of diabetic patients. Included amongst these are cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (which results in an inability to properly regulate heart rate) and atrial fibrillation (the most common cardiac arrhythmia). Our objective is to determine how and why abnormal heart rate regulation occurs in diabetic patients. We also aim to determine the mechanistic basis for atrial fibrillation in diabetes. Although often attributed to damage to the nerves innervating the sinoatrial node, our work demonstrates that improper regulation of heart rate in diabetes is also associated with abnormal sinoatrial node function, independently of the nerves. This represents an important new way of looking at cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy. We have also uncovered novel insight into how atrial fibrillation occurs in the diabetic heart. This involves alterations in the muscle cells of the atria as well as the presence of scar tissue in the atria. Our proposed studies will greatly advance our understanding of abnormal heart rate regulation and the occurrence of atrial fibrillation in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. This will be accomplished using a range of powerful experimental approaches in intact diabetic mice, as well as in isolated hearts and isolated cells from the sinoatrial node and the atria. My laboratory is one of only a handful worldwide that can study the sinoatrial node in mice, which uniquely positions us carry out these highly important studies. We are also highly experienced in studies of atrial fibrillation. The ultimate goal of our work is to identify new therapeutic targets for the treatment of cardiovascular disease in diabetics.

column36: Computation and theory to predict structures and mechanisms for protein misfolding in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
column37: As we age, we begin to face an onslaught of threats to our health that evolution has not protected us against. Many of these include degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Lou Gehrig's disease or ALS. It is up to us to design strategies for slowing, stopping, or reversing the progression of these currently incurable diseases. To do this involves understanding the causes of the disease, which are due fundamentally to proteins behaving badly. Here we will investigate the molecular origins of how proteins malfunction in ALS, a neurodegenerative disease, to elucidate at the atomic level what may be going wrong in the cell. Malfunction often involves proteins that have misfolded, and as a consequence have aggregated together. Misfolding may be exacerbated by oxidative damage to proteins, which generally occurs as a natural consequence of aging. Most cases of ALS strike sporadically, with no known hereditary link, with the likelihood increasing as we age. What goes wrong in the cell? We will focus on how oxidative damage may be a cause of sporadic ALS. We will investigate how oxidative damage may destabilize proteins and render them susceptible to misfolding. We have previously developed a computational method that is capable of predicting how long a patient will live once diagnosed with ALS, given they have an inherited form of the disease. We propose here to extend our computational method to the much more prevalent sporadic form of the disease, by investigating the role of oxidative damage in the aging brain. We have previously developed a novel computational method that allows misfolded protein to be specifically targeted. Developing and applying our methods to describe the mechanisms and consequences of protein misfolding in ALS will allow us to rationally predict critical protein targets that may stop the progression of this currently fatal, misfolding-related degenerative disease.

column36: Mechanisms of dendritic integration and plasticity in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons
column37: Over a century ago, Santiago Ramon y Cajal postulated the law of dynamic polarization according to which dendrites represent a receiving apparatus of the neuron specialized in integrating and processing the vast majority of synaptic inputs. Since then, the large structural diversity of dendritic arbors in different types of neurons has captivated the imagination of scientists. In addition to morphological complexity, dendrites exhibit a highly complex functional organization. They are endowed with multiple ion conductances, which are able to control the integration and propagation of local and global dendritic signals in a highly dynamic manner. Two types of signals are generated in dendrites: electrical and chemical. Both can be highly compartmentalized within individual dendritic branches and synaptic specializations, providing a means for the highly selective integration and modification of incoming information. However, despite the tremendous progress in dendrites research, we still do not understand the nature of computations performed by neuronal dendrites and, more importantly, their relevance to the operation of a particular neuron within its local circuitry. Here, we will use a combination of optophysiological, optogenetic and computational tools in brain slices and in behaving animals in vivo to determine the relationship between the distribution of dendritic conductances and the function of dendrites in a genetically defined population of cortical inhibitory interneurons that play a crucial role in the generation of brain rhythms and are affected in epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism. We will establish the rules of dendritic integration and the role of dendritic computations in the operation of interneurons during behavior in animals navigating in virtual environment. The results of the study will be important to connect the computations performed by single neurons to the operation of its local network, and higher-level brain function and malfunction.

column37: Cerebral blood flow (CBF) is highly regulated by carbon dioxide and oxygen in the arterial blood. This process becomes impaired with cerebrovascular disease processes and by aging. This approach will allow us to study the interactions between the cerebral circulation and cognitive function, and may provide powerful diagnostic tools to help identify those individuals at risk of dementia. This work may have a positive impact in helping delay or prevent the onset of disabilities due to diseases like AD and dementia.

column36: Structure, dynamics and function of non-membranous organelles
column37: If you ask most biomedical researchers how molecules are organized in the cell to do specific tasks they'd likely resort to the metaphor of a factory. As in the components of a factory, the molecules that do the work in cells, like robots and humans on an assembly line, are logically arranged in time and space to perform their roles in a complex process. This description has served as a helpful and meaningful metaphor for biochemical machinery. But what if you were told that sometimes molecules are organized in the cell the way that people and airplanes are organized at an airport? Recently, such molecular organizations have been discovered in cells and they may serve a number of important cellular functions and underlie neurological diseases, including Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases and ALS, among others. Molecules in the discovered structures are arranged like oil droplets in water; loosely organized and exchanging rapidly with the cell. How many such structures, called non-membrane organelles (or NMO), could exist in the cell and what are their functions? What happens if NMOs are disrupted? These are the questions we address in this proposal. The central aim of our proposal is to create a compendium of NMOs in a model of the eukaryotic cell; the bakers yeasts. Yeast is an ideal model because it shares many genes with humans, notably those that are most primordial and those become dysfunctional with age and in diseases such as cancers, and neurodegeneration. We have shown how certain types of cell regulation including gene function and spatial organization of large cell structures depend on NMOs. The compositions of NMOs are surprisingly rich in protein molecules that when mutated, are known to underlie neurodegeneration. We hope to define how these mutant proteins cause dysfunction, perhaps by disrupting the normal functions of NMOs, and what kinds of strategies could re-stabilize them.

column37: Our intestines host a community of bacteria that rival contemporary industrial nations in terms of population density, diversity, and output. column36: Role of mitochondrial cholesterol homeostasis in brain energy metabolism and neuronal function
column37: The brain is the most cholesterol-rich organ in the human body, and contains nearly a quarter of total body cholesterol. Cholesterol serves to insulate nerve cells to ensure rapid transmission of signals, and it is present in high levels in nerve cells themselves. Changes in the distribution of cholesterol in the brain and within nerve cells have negative consequences for nerve cell function, and they have been observed in many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease and a rare genetic disorder called Niemann-Pick Type C (NPC) disease. NPC disease is known for severe defects in cholesterol metabolism, which lead to loss of nerve cells, to increasing loss of brain function, and ultimately to death of the patient. Our previous work has shown that one of the different ways how cholesterol might negatively affect nerve cells is by changing energy metabolism in the brain. In NPC disease, cholesterol levels were higher than normal in parts of the cell called mitochondria, which are responsible for generating much of the energy used by nerve cells. This increase in mitochondrial cholesterol can cause defects in mitochondrial energy production; however, we do not know yet, how cholesterol causes this effect, and under what conditions these effects become more pronounced. With our research, we want to find out how mitochondrial cholesterol affects energy production in neurons, what the consequences are for nerve cell function, and whether defects in nerve cells could be improved through addition of energy substrates or special nutrients.

column37: Under normal conditions, cells require signals from their surroundings in order to grow, to move, or just to survive. Finally, we will characterize the expression of RET in prostate and colon cancers, where perineural invasion is linked with poor outcomes, to see if RET plays a role in this process. column36: The role of DEPTOR in Energy Balance Regulation
column37: Obesity is a major public health issue leading to major costs emerging from the treatment of cardiovascular, metabolic (type 2 diabetes) and respiratory diseases. Obesity is characterized by an imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure, which is incidentally in agreement with the latin root of obesity "obedere", meaning "to eat in excess". Its activity is reduced by fasting and induced by refeeding, whereas anorectic signals such as leptin, insulin and ghrelin require mTORC1 activity to exert their inhibitory effects on feeding. Recently, we have identified DEP-domain containing mTOR-interacting protein (DEPTOR) as a key modulator of hypothalamic mTORC1. We have evidence that DEPTOR may be sensitive to variations in energy stores and therefore could play a significant role in the regulation of energy balance. Whether DEPTOR could affect the metabolic profile of the obese by modulating mTOR activity has never been tested. This research proposal aims to investigate the role DEPTOR in the regulation of energy balance using molecular approaches, genetically-engineered mice and advanced molecular imaging methodologies.

column36: Systematic characterization of the Hsp70-regulated proteostasis network
column37: Proteins are major macromolecules of the cell that have incredibly versatile functions. Some are enzymes, others transport molecules inside the cell or in the bloodstream, yet others make sure our immune system stays alert. But to be able do so, each protein needs to adopt its unique shape that determines its function. Starting as a linear chain, proteins fold into intricate shapes like cellular origami. But when this process goes awry, the result can be a disease like Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease or even cancer. Because protein folding is such a fundamental process for all living organisms, cells have evolved special machines (themselves also proteins) whose function is to make sure proteins fold correctly. These proteins are aptly called chaperones. In this project, we will study how these chaperones can associate with thousands of diverse proteins but, at the same time, provide unique support to each of them. In particular, we will characterize how so-called co-chaperones, which constantly regulate the function of chaperones, provide specificity to the chaperone machinery inside the cell. We will systematically identify the proteins that each co-chaperone associates with, and use this knowledge to understand how drugs in clinical use affect these associations. The results from this study will help researchers to understand the chaperone/co-cochaperone network in unprecedented detail, biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies to understand how their drugs affect cells, and, ultimately, patients to benefit from more specific and more potent drugs against diverse diseases.

column37: Sensory neurons relay information between our body, spinal cord and brain via peripheral nerves. column36: How does rapid drug delivery promote compulsive drug use?
column37: Addiction is the most common psychiatric disorder of our era. It accounts for 12% of deaths worldwide, and costs Canadians nearly $40 billion per year. In spite of much research, medications approved for drug addiction are lacking. This is in part because preclinical tests are typically conducted in animals that take drugs, but that do not show addiction-like traits. Animals that simply take drugs are not necessarily 'addicted'. The reliance on such animals to study addiction might have misled us regarding the neurobiology of addiction. With CIHR funding, we have refined a new model whereby rats taking rapid intravenous cocaine injections show excessive motivation to obtain the drug, whereas rats taking slower injections do not. Thus, by varying the speed of drug delivery, we have in our hands a powerful model whereby two groups of rats take cocaine, but only one group shows an addiction phenotype. Studying these two groups represents a unique window of opportunity to hone in on a fundamental question; what is the difference between a drug-taking brain and a drug-addicted brain? Based largely on studies using animals that self-administer drugs, it has been suggested that addiction might involve a hyperactive orbitofrontal cortex (a brain area involved in the evaluation of rewards) and changes in the activity of two molecules in the downstream dorsal striatum (a brain area involved in the pursuit of rewards). These molecules are the neurotrophin BDNF and the neurotransmitter glutamate. But are these changes truly linked to addiction, or are they simply a consequence of taking drugs? Here I propose to use our unique model to address this. In essence, we will use variation in the speed of drug injection as a tool to parse the neurobiology of addiction from the neurobiology of mere drug taking. This is certain to better our understanding of how addiction evolves, and how it might be treated.

column36: Endosomal control of autophagy in colorectal cancer
column37: Cancer is the first cause of death in Canada. Colorectal cancers are among the most common and lethal malignancies. This cancer has a poor prognosis in advanced stages due to its resistance to conventional therapies. Cancer cells have developed means to resist to treatments and one of them is called autophagy. Autophagy is the process by which cells degrade and recycle their own constituents. Importantly, autophagy is induced by the lack of nutrients, and cancer cells often grow in environments lacking proper blood supply.
