column36: The NEUROlogically-impaired extubation Timing Trial (NEURO-ETT)
column37: Thousands of patients suffer severe brain injuries every year, from causes such as trauma, stroke, and infection. Many of them will have impaired consciousness and therefore be unable to keep food or mouth secretions from entering their lungs (called aspiration). To protect against aspiration, these patients require artificial respiration and intubation with a temporary breathing tube inserted through the mouth into the lungs. After the early phases of illness, doctors can use a test called a spontaneous breathing trial to assess when artificial respiration can be discontinued. Many patients with severe brain injury, however, pass this test yet still have impaired consciousness and an ongoing risk for aspiration. Unfortunately, little evidence exists to guide decisions about when to remove the breathing tube in these patients. There are different approaches that are commonly used in this situation. One approach involves simply discontinuing artificial respiration and removing the breathing tube, accepting that aspiration may still occur but reducing the potential for harm associated with prolonged artificial respiration. The other treatment is to perform a tracheostomy. A tracheostomy involves neck surgery to insert a new tube directly into the trachea, replacing the temporary breathing tube. The usual clinical practice is often just to keep the patient on artificial respiration for longer in the hope that the patient will wake up before removing the tube, or performing a tracheostomy if they don't wake up. Each strategy has risks and benefits, and uncertainty about the best approach often leads to prolonged use of the temporary breathing tube. This randomized controlled trial will test whether removing the temporary breathing tube as soon as possible after the patient passes a spontaneous breathing trial leads to better patient outcomes compared to performing a tracheostomy, or to the usual approach of waiting longer.

column37: Diseases of the cardiovascular system, such as coronary heart disease and stroke due to atherosclerosis, are known to start in the cells that line blood vessels, the vascular endothelium. This research laboratory has a long-term interest in understanding how endothelial genes are regulated in health and disease. We argue that we need to understand how genes are expressed in the endothelial cells of the body and how these pathways become abnormal in disease. What makes an endothelial gene turn off in diseased human blood vessels? Classically the nucleus has been viewed as the key regulator of gene expression, yet all cells have the same DNA. Why do endothelial cells express only certain genes in healthy tissue? In disease many of these genes turn off. How does the nucleus get affected? These processes are chromosome-based or chromatin-based, and are also called epigenetic processes. What we inherit from our parents, or what one cell passes on to two cells when it divides, represents the "nature" side of the equation. These processes are influenced by the environment. Whatever our cells sense in their external world interacts with genetic material in the nucleus to influence gene expression. We are among the first to study these concepts in the cardiovascular sciences. We believe that the principles we uncover in endothelial cells will teach us about blood vessel gene regulation in general. Our understanding of these newer concepts offers the hope of innovative approaches to preventing and treating the underlying problem in diseased blood vessels of patients. We anticipate findings that will provide important new insight into how genes are turned on and off in disease.

column36: The Pathophysiological Role of Adrenergic Antibodies in Postural Tachycardia Syndrome
column37: Postural Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is a chronically disabling disorder of autonomic nervous system function ("dysautonomia") with cardiovascular dysregulation, yet their causes remain largely unexplained. POTS is characterized by an excessive increase in heart rate on standing, and characteristic symptoms on standing that are relieved by lying down, including palpitation, chest pains, tremulousness, blurred vision and mental clouding. POTS affects up to 0.33% of the population, mainly women of childbearing age. Patients have very poor health-related quality of life (comparable to heart failure). The mainstay of pharmacological therapy for POTS includes Beta-blockers (e.g. propranolol) to control the excessive heart rate, and midodrine, a vasoconstrictor. It has long been suspected that POTS may be an autoimmune disease, but this has been hard to prove. We recently found that the blood of some POTS patients has antibody activity against "adrenaline receptors" that regulate heart rate and blood vessel tone. This is a newly discovered pathophysiological mechanism in POTS that could explain the symptoms in this disorder. We propose a series of translational studies with the ultimate goal of personalized medical treatment for POTS patients. We will build on the preliminary work and assess the physiological significance of these antibodies in POTS patients. By using pharmacological drug "probes", we will determine if these antibodies affect POTS patients' responses to commonly used drugs. These innovative aims could bring an antibody guided, personalized medicine approach to the management of POTS patients. We will also test "proof of the concept" that clearing these antibodies will reverse the pathophysiology in ("cure") POTS patients. Taken together, these highly innovative translational studies could create novel treatments for patients with POTS.

column36: Structural Biology of DNA Damage-Dependent PARPs
column37: The DNA that composes our genetic information is susceptible to damage that must be repaired in order to maintain the integrity of the genome and the health of an organism. Correspondingly, cells have extensive DNA repair mechanisms that detect and correct the damage that arises from environmental agents such as ultraviolet radiation and through normal cellular processes such as DNA replication. Several human deficiencies in DNA repair are associated with genomic instability and cellular transformations that can lead to cancer, thus underscoring the need to understand at a detailed molecular level the mechanisms of DNA repair. Our research focuses on a family of proteins called poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases, or PARPs. Several PARP family members are integral to the DNA damage response, where they detect damage and facilitate repair. PARP inhibitors are under clinical development to treat various cancers. An exciting aspect of PARP inhibition is the ability to selectively target cancer cells with known DNA repair deficiencies (e.g. BRCA1/2 deficient cancers). Our research group uses a structural biology approach to study how the PARP proteins recognize DNA breaks and how binding to these breaks turns on their catalytic activity to coordinate DNA repair. In particular, we use x-ray crystallography and other structural biology techniques to obtain detailed three-dimensional structures of PARPs that allow us to understand their function and mechanism at the molecular level. We further use cell biological and biochemical analysis to advance our understanding of PARP contribution to DNA repair, and to identify novel ways of inhibiting PARPs for cancer treatment.

column36: Sensori-motor integration in trigeminal circuits of the masticatory central pattern generator
column37: Repetitive movements like walking, breathing and chewing insure vital functions and are produced by more primitive areas of the brain. Although these movements are executed with a high level of automaticity, as all movements, they need to be constantly adjusted to the conditions of the outside world. How would we know otherwise if we are walking on a slippery surface and need to adjust our gate? Information from the outside world reaches the brain through our senses, but little is known about the mechanisms and circuits that enable interaction between sensory inputs and motor commands. To achieve their tasks in any brain circuit, neurons need to communicate to one another using an electrical language which pattern constitutes their code for communication. A circuit that programs a repetitive movement needs to generate a rhythmic activity pattern. In this proposal, we examine how a nervous circuit in the brainstem generates the rhythmic motor command for chewing and how sensory inputs change the pattern of this command. In addition to neurons, we also consider astrocytes in the circuit that we examine. Astrocytes, another sort of cell in the brain are traditionally considered to play only a support role for neurons, but our recent findings show that they play a key role in shaping the pattern of electrical activity of neurons. Here we propose to examine how sensory information arriving to the brainstem interacts with astrocytes and modulates their behavior. This should help understand how sensory information can drive movement. Because these mechanisms are not unique to the circuit responsible for chewing, but are shared by other circuits that generate rhythmic movements, we believe that they may help devising strategies to restore movements after injuries. More importantly, we think that they may help understand what goes wrong in pathologies like Parkinson's or epilepsy, where similar mechanisms are involved and generate an uncontrolled rhythmic activity.

column36: Mechanisms of GnRH action
column37: Human fertility depends on the coordinated activities of many organs in the body. These organs communicate with each other via chemical messengers called hormones. In general, hormones produced by one organ travel via the bloodstream to control the function of other organs. In the case of the reproductive system, the brain synthesizes and secretes gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which controls production and release of two other hormones, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), by the pituitary gland. The pituitary sits at the base of the brain and secretes FSH and LH into the bloodstream following GnRH binding to its receptor on specific pituitary cells. If we think of GnRH as a key, then its receptor serves as the lock in to which this key uniquely fits. Once secreted, FSH and LH act on the ovaries in women and the testicles in men to control the production of eggs and sperm as well as the synthesis of steroid hormones like estrogen and testosterone. These steroids then feedback to the brain to control their own production by inhibiting GnRH secretion. Though we have a general understanding of where and how each of these hormones acts, fundamental questions remain unanswered. In this application, we address three general questions about how GnRH functions. First, does GnRH activate common or distinct pathways in pituitary cells to stimulate the synthesis and secretion of FSH and LH? Second, do pituitary cells make a protein that helps GnRH preferentially stimulate LH? Finally, does the GnRH receptor have unique features that enables it to preferentially control LH versus FSH synthesis? The answers to these questions will not only advance our knowledge of the hormonal control of reproduction, but will also identify novel causes and treatments for human infertility and other disorders of the reproductive system, including polycystic ovarian syndrome.

column36: Regulation of a neuronal synaptic pathway in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders
column37: Development of accurate connections between nerve cells is a prerequisite for proper brain development and function. These connections, known as synapses, are the fundamental units of communication and information processing in the brain. Synapse organizing proteins trigger formation of nerve cell connections and are important for various aspects of synaptic function. Variations in the genes that encode major synapse organizing proteins predispose individuals to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders including to autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia and mental retardation. Although a number of synapse organizing proteins have been discovered, how they are regulated in synapse development and function is poorly understood. We have discovered a biochemical switch that controls the activity of an important synapse organizing protein family. This switch acts through an important binding partner which has been shown to be important for normal synapse development. We propose to explore, both in cultured nerve cells and in a mouse brain circuit, how synapses develop and function when this switch is differentially regulated. The second aim will explore the molecular processes underlying development of synapses as well as how these molecular factors control the cellular mechanisms of learning. The third aim will explore how these processes can be regulated to correct impaired synaptic function in disease. We propose to use a combination of mouse molecular genetics, fluorescence imaging, biochemistry, electron microscopy and electrophysiology to determine how altered biochemical signaling affects brain wiring, synaptic composition, structure, and function. The study of how synapse organizing proteins are regulated will expand our understanding of the molecular basis of cognitive disorders, which we expect will help identify amenable targets to design rational drug treatments.

column37: Endothelial cells (ECs) are intimately involved in angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels from preexisting ones. The opening of intercellular contacts between ECs initiates the angiogenic process and detachment of ECs allows them to migrate to form a vascular network in an area deprived of oxygen. The overall objective of our research program is to understand intracellular signaling events in ECs that control vascular development and angiogenesis. We will investigate if intercellular contacts control the effects induced by factors that act on ECs to promote angiogenesis. We will also determine if NO acts directly on a protein localized at cell-cell contact points, beta-catenin, to alter its function. A better understanding of the molecular events that control angiogenesis will help in the development of novel therapeutic approaches where the formation of new vessels is central to disease progression such as in ischemic tissues and vascular retinopathies.

column37: Antipsychotic medications are used extensively for treatment of schizophrenia and other psychiatric disorders. One of the most debilitating side effect is antipsychotic-induced weight gain (AIWG) which can result in obesity and related medical conditions (e.g. diabetes and cardiovascular diseases) leading to a high risk for premature death. In addition, patients who are obese will create substantial additional costs to the health care system. Our main goal is to develop a genetic risk model to predict AIWG. In addition, the clinical utility of the model will be investigated in a large sample of antipsychotic-treated patients. These represent important steps towards clinical application of genetics of AIWG. In summary, a better understanding of genetic risk factors for AIWG may help clarify the biological mechanisms and help the clinician choose the best medication for an individual patient. In addition, it may provide novel targets for future drug discovery. This increased standard of care through individualized treatment will also help to reduce health care costs and therefore be beneficial for Canadian patients and the health care system.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are common among people with autoimmune diseases with arthritic symptoms. People affected by rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) have a greater risk of early subclinical atherosclerotic disease due to accelerated development of atheromatous plaques. Elevated levels of platelet-derived microparticles are associated with many diseases state including RA and SLE. Since ATX can bind to activated platelets we monitored the presence of platelet-derived microparticles positive for ATX and discovered a new class of microparticles abundant in plasma from SLE patients but not from healthy individuals, the ATX-associated microparticles was identified. According to our hypothesis microparticles serve as a vehicle to transport ATX into the vascular wall, thereby disseminating inflammation within the vascular tissue. The main goal of the research proposal is to characterize and study the role of these microparticles-associated ATX in RA and SLE. The abundance of these microparticles might correlate with development of atherosclerosis and may become useful clinical marker for increased risk of CVD in arthritis.

column37: Background: The cardiac electricity-generating protein, named "HERG", is important for normal heart rhythm. A reduction in the amount of HERG protein disturbs heart rhythm and causes sudden death. Diseased conditions such as insufficient blood supply to the heart muscle (ischemic heart disease) is a common cause of irregular heartbeat and sudden death. Presently, it is not well understood how ischemic heart disease causes irregular heartbeat. Objectives: We aim to establish (1) that a special region of the HERG senses a reduced level of potassium in the blood to cause HERG to break down. (2) that this same region of HERG is easily broken down by biological molecules (named enzymes) released from heart cells as a result of insufficient blood supply. (3) a novel strategy using small synthetic molecules (peptides) to protect HERG and prevent sudden death in patients suffering from ischemic heart disease. Description of the research project: We have obtained evidence showing that a special region of HERG plays an important role in breaking down HERG in the heart when the blood potassium level is low or when blood supply to the heart muscle is insufficient. Ischemic heart disease increases the abundance of enzymes that selectively break down HERG. We will study which enzymes released from heart cells break down HERG. We will use cultured cells as well as heart cells from rats and rabbits. We will also make a rabbit model that mimics human ischemic heart disease. Importantly, we will design synthetic HERG-binding molecules to shield the special region and thereby protect HERG against breakdown. Significance: Ischemic heart disease is the leading disease in our society, and it causes irregular heartbeat and sudden death. The proposed research can potentially lead to novel drugs for treating irregular heartbeat and preventing sudden death in patients with ischemic heart disease.

Such cues are prominently used in the developing embryo, for example, to instruct a progenitor cell to keep dividing to increase the size of an organ, or to make a cell stick to another to build a tissue, or to connect a neuron with its synaptic partner. Such individual signals and their receptors on the surface of cells have been identified, as have been the relay pathways that transmit those signal from the receptor to other compartments inside the cell or neuron. What is also unclear is how pathways activated by different signals might work together to integrate the information about the extracellular environment. To answer this question, we are proposing to work in the developing nervous system, to understand the how signals from two very different families of secreted molecules are integrated. We also discovered that when ephrin and netrin are presented simultaneously, nerves develop in a very different manner compared when each signal is presented alone. We propose to examine how this happens in neurons made from neuronal stem cells in vitro, using biochemical fractionation and protein complex formation measurement. Ephrin and netrin signals have been implicated in many diseases such as cancer and neurodegeneration. In the long term, once we understand ephrin-netrin signal integration, we would search for drugs that might boost or disrupt it.

This supports a role for the NKR-P1:Clr interactions in fighting cancer and infectious disease. However, malignant cancer cells and viral pathogens can evolve ways to subvert this immunity and become pathogenic. In addition, there are stimulatory NKR-P1 receptors that recognize abnormal proteins and directly activate NK cells ("induced-self"). We propose to advance our understanding of innate immunity by studying how these cells develop, how their function supports our immune defenses in fighting cancer and infection, and how pathogens can evade this immune recognition. This knowledge could lead to therapies in cancer treatment and control of infectious disease.

column36: Cerebral cortical neural mechanisms of motor and non-motor decisions.
column37: The world constantly bombards us with sensory inputs about many possible motor actions. Imagine walking along a breakfast buffet table. Sometimes, the input is clear and the action is obvious - you see a glass of orange juice, reach to it and put it on your tray. Other times, the situation is uncertain or even conflicting - you see pancakes and waffles and like both; which should you take? The 1st aim of this proposal is to study how premotor and prefrontal cortical areas use conflicting sensory inputs about different actions to select one action to make, using neural recordings in non-human primates that perform conditional motor tasks. We do not respond slavishly to every sensory input. Instead, voluntary behaviour is flexible and often involves arbitrary stimulus-response (SR) rules that we learn by experience. Normal interactions with the world involve selective and often conditional context-dependent responses to only some stimuli, such as the sequences of arm and leg movements elicited by green, yellow and red traffic lights while driving to work. The 2nd aim is to study how neurons in those cortical areas apply arbitrary SR rules to control action. Failure to impose rule-based control on behaviour leads to problems for both the individual and society, including impulsive, inappropriate and even criminal behaviour. We also often use rules to assess the "rightness" or "wrongness" of observed events. We know we should stop when the light is red, so when we see someone drive through an intersection on a red light, we know that what they did was wrong. column36: Mechanisms of RNA Degradation by Autophagy
column37: Mutations in genes that activate a waste recycling program in cells, called autophagy, or "self-eating" are one cause of cancer and are implicated in neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). When autophagy is inhibited, excess waste consisting of damaged or old cellular components accumulates. In most cases we don't understand which specific type of cellular waste accumulates and causes disease when autophagy is inhibited. Our lab has been at the forefront of research on a new class of molecules degraded by autophagy called RNA. RNA is one of four major types of substrates in cells and is required for genes in our DNA to build cellular components and allow them to respond to their environment. Early studies had shown that autophagy degraded large amounts of RNA when cells were stressed, as in infection or disease. Now, our results demonstrate that autophagy uses an unusual mechanism to mark large clusters of RNA for degradation by autophagy. Fascinatingly, these RNA clusters are a defining feature of ALS that is believed to cause progressive motor neuron death and paralysis in this disease. Strikingly, genetic mapping studies suggest that mutations in genes that cause either inappropriate formation of RNA clusters or block their elimination by autophagy may cause ALS. We will investigate the surprising mechanisms underlying the ability of autophagy to recognize and degrade these RNA clusters in cellular and mouse models of ALS. Using mouse models, we will test whether autophagy-activating drugs used in patients to treat other diseases, could be an effective new treatment for ALS. This research therefore aims to understand a novel and fundamental process involved in ALS and help devise new means to treat this devastating disease.

column36: Exploitation of host ubiquitination pathways by pathogenic E. coli
column37: Pathogenic E. coli strains cause life-threatening diseases manifesting by recent outbreaks in Canada and worldwide. column36: Understanding a novel molecular mechanism controlling structural development of neurons
column37: About 200-300 newborn infants in Canada are affected by stroke each year. There are very limited treatment options and currently no pharmacological interventions. If we block these pores, or remove Pannexin 1 altogether, the cells extend processes called neurites, structures that are critical for rewiring of connections. The primary goal of this research is to bridge key gaps in knowledge of the role of these proteins in creating structural changes in brain cells. Successful outcomes of this work will ultimately lay the groundwork for the development of novel therapeutics that could be used to improve health outcomes in patients affected by acquired brain disorders such as stroke and cerebral palsy.

In every eukaryotic cell, including humans, genes are housed within a spherical, membrane-enclosed compartment, termed the nucleus. The membrane shell that surrounds the genome is termed the nuclear envelope (NE). In recent years it has become clear that the NE organizes chromatin and participants in defining how certain genes are controlled. We have shown that structures present in the NE can grab on to genes and, like puppeteers, they can alter their structure and, in this way, control whether a specific set of associated genes are turned on or off. Using state-of-the-art techniques, we are investigating how the interactions of genes with the NE are regulated and identifying the signals that control these events. As the NE is highly conserved in structure and function in eukaryotes as diverse as humans and yeast, these studies can be conducted in a yeast model system where powerful genetic and biochemical approaches can be used to investigate NE/chromatin interactions. It is clear that defects in NE proteins lead to diseases including heart abnormalities and cancer. Understanding their functions in nuclear organization will provide us with a critical understanding of the underlying causes of these diseases and provide an avenue for eventual rational intervention.

column37: Under healthy conditions, our bodies carry trillions of bacteria. These bacteria usually have a positive effect on the development and function of our immune systems. The question we want to answer is how do bacteria go from living on our bodies without causing disease to becoming lethal microbes. Understanding how this happens may hold the key to new ways of treating infections and inflammatory, immune-mediated diseases like multiple sclerosis and diabetes and preventing transplant rejection. Our team is tackling this question by studying the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. This microbe is carried by more than 25 per cent of healthy individuals without causing serious infections. We propose here to delineate the whole gene program and the steps that turn it on and off. In doing so, we will have a target to develop new drugs that modulate inflammation and immune function.

column36: Investigating the regulation of lymphocyte function by metabolic reprogramming
column37: T lymphocytes, or T cells, are the "soldiers" of the immune system; they function primarily at the front lines of infection to identify and clear infected cells or eliminate pathogens and protect the host from infection. The ability of T cells to successfully respond to an infection depends on the T cell having enough energy and building blocks to complete the task. To meet these demands T cells display fundamental changes in their metabolism - the biochemical processes cells use to generate energy - to allow them to grow and divide and ultimately defeat foreign invaders. Our previous work has established that T cell function is very sensitive to changes in their metabolism. As T cells differentiate during an immune response they move from lymphoid organs to sites of infection or inflammation, where oxygen, nutrients, and growth factors may become limiting. Our hypothesis is that T cells actively adapt their metabolism during immune responses to maintain their function and promote immunity to pathogens. This proposal uses in vitro and in vivo experimental systems to study how cellular metabolism influences T cell function to ensure proper immune function. Ultimately we would like to determine whether manipulating T cell metabolism could be a suitable therapeutic avenue for the treatment of inflammation, autoimmune disease, or transplant rejection.

column37: Heart disease is a condition where the arteries nourishing the heart become too narrow. A common procedure to treat heart disease is to implant stents to reopen the blood vessels. Over 50 000 coronary artery interventions are performed in Canada each year. To reduce the risks of complications such as sudden heart failure years later, a normal cell lining should be re-established on the stent surface. The endothelial cells that cover our healthy blood vessels secrete molecules that inhibit blood clotting and vessel narrowing. To restore this cell lining, the stents can be coated with antibodies that capture endothelial progenitor cells from the blood stream. These cells can generate large numbers of endothelial cells in vitro. Studies have shown that stents that capture the circulating progenitor cells become covered by endothelial cells. However, this did not improve the performance of the stents. We hypothesize that this is due to the lack of a natural microenvironment to help cell growth and maturation. More mature endothelial cells should produce higher amounts of the molecules that inhibit blood vessel obstruction. We therefore propose to engineer stents that mimic the normal endothelial cell environment. To do so, we will coat the stents with combinations of molecules involved in endothelial cell adhesion, growth and maturation. We will also use stents that slowly dissolve over time. These stents would provide the transient support needed to reopen the vessel and recruit cells with regenerative potential. The use of biodegradable materials will avoid leaving a foreign body behind once the stents have served their purpose. These engineered materials could help restore a normal vasculature at the implant site. The stents developed during this project could help patients suffering from heart disease live without the constant fear of a recurrent heart failure or other complications.

column37: Nearly every cell in our bodies contains our full genetic blueprint (DNA), but each cell uses only a small part of the blueprint to direct its function. For example, immune cells are specialized to fight infection and brain cells to process information. During development, cells receive instructions about which part of the blueprint (which genes) to use. They organize their genetic material so that parts that will be used are easy to access, while parts that aren't needed are stashed away. Thus different cells have the same genome organized in different ways. This genome organization is carried out by proteins that associate with DNA. Together, these proteins and the DNA form a structure called chromatin. Each time a cell divides, it duplicates the chromatin organization so that the same parts of the genome are used by the two new cells. We are studying how chromatin structure can be duplicated in one step in cell division called mitosis. Mitosis is the process that ensures that each new cell receives one full copy of the DNA. In mitosis, chromatin is reorganized so that each of the multiple long threads of DNA in cells (called chromosomes) condenses into a rod-like structure. These rods line up in the middle of the cell and are distributed evenly to opposite sides of the cell. Immediately after mitosis, the genome is reorganized to its cell type specific state. column37: Psychiatric disorders represent a major public health problem, accruing enormous socioeconomic costs. The available treatments remain largely insufficient. column36: Methods for the economic evaluation of personalized medicine: a case study in advanced colorectal cancer
column37: Personalized medicine -- the tailoring of care based on individual characteristics -- has grown rapidly in recent years, particularly for cancer treatment. There is significant variability within cancer types, and with tumour testing many new therapies can be targeted to the patients most likely to respond to the drug. However, the cost of these drugs and of the testing required is a significant obstacle to their use. A challenge facing health care systems is how to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of personalized therapies. Data from clinical trials can be limited, and may not reflect how the drug is used in practice. The real-world effectiveness and costs of a drug can be evaluated using comparative effectiveness research methods, using data from patients being treated with the drug in real clinical settings. However, these methods have a limited ability to account for variability between patients, and in the case of personalized medicines understanding this variability is essential to understanding the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the drug. This project will look at analytic methods to compare the benefits and costs of personalized medicine, using data on advanced colorectal cancer treatment as a case study. Two drugs, cetuximab and panitumumab, targeted to colorectal cancer patients with a specific gene, were adopted in British Columbia in 2009. This study will use real-world data for patients treated for advanced colorectal cancer at the BC Cancer Agency to calculate the cost-effectiveness of these two drugs, and compare conventional evaluation methods to methods that account for the personalized nature of this therapy. These research methods can be used to generate better evidence for policy decisions around personalized medicines, ultimately improving health at the individual and population levels while using scarce healthcare resources more efficiently

column36: Primary Healthcare Research and Integration to Improve Health System Efficiency (PRIIME)
column37: The primary care system in Newfoundland & Labrador today looks much the same as it did 20 years ago, but the need for more comprehensive care among the residents of NL has been steadily increasing. With the commitment of key decision-makers across NL, PRIIME has an opportunity to support major changes to the primary care system that will provide better care for patients from birth to death, particularly complex patients whose needs haven't always been met. The Network's leadership is dedicated to finding new ways to care for patients in community-based primary care while making efficient use of limited resources. PRIIME will look at changes to primary care that have worked in other parts of Canada, such as care teams that include doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other allied health practitioners working together to support their complex patients. The goal is to build a sustainable system of community-based primary health care in a way that will meet the needs and improve the health of Newfoundlanders and Labradorians.

column36: A research program on the pathogenesis, treatment and prevention of respiratory and herpes viruses
column37: Infections caused by respiratory viruses and herpes viruses are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality among Canadians. For instance, influenza viruses affect 1 of 6 Canadians each winter and cause approximately 30 000 hospitalizations and 3 000 deaths annually. In addition, the incidence of genital herpes has increased by 30% over the past 20 years. In the next 7 years, Dr Guy Boivin proposes an ambitious research program to better understand these viral diseases using relevant laboratory and animal models and to develop/evaluate novel therapeutic and preventive approaches. To this end, his group has defined 3 research themes and assembled a multi-disciplinary team of collaborators including enzymologist, immunologist, pathologist, physicist and specialist in genomics/proteomics. The first theme of this program consists in studying the virulence and transmissibility of respiratory and herpes viruses. The second theme involves the characterization of antiviral drug resistance mechanisms as well as the development of innovative antiviral and immune-based therapeutic strategies. The third theme consists in developing/improving a series of vaccines based on new routes of immunization (mucosal, intradermal), powerful adjuvants and recombinant attenuated viral strains. The research program of Dr Boivin will be significant at many levels for the Canadian population. First, his work on drug-resistant viruses and development of new antivirals and immunomodulatory compounds will result in improved health care towards patients with respiratory and herpes virus infections. Also, his research on new vaccines and viral transmission could have a major impact on public health policies and pandemic preparedness.

column36: The role of the immune system in obesity related insulin resistance and metabolic disease
column37: Obesity is associated with a metabolic syndrome characterized by high fat and sugar in the blood, and is linked to type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. Obesity associated metabolic disease is a major health concern, affecting more than 20% of Canadian adults, with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes alone affecting at least 10 million Canadians, and costing our healthcare system more than $10 billion. Despite this burden on Canadians, the underlying mechanisms of disease are poorly understood. The Winer lab and others have shown that low levels of inflammation lies at the core of metabolic disease. When people become obese, inflammation blocks the body's ability to respond well to insulin, called insulin resistance (prediabetes), and this process leads to high blood fatty acids and sugar, triggering type 2 diabetes and liver disease. The Winer lab has identified inflammation in the fat surrounding internal organs as a major cause of insulin resistance. In particular, fatty tissues in obese mice and people contain high amounts of white blood cells, including T and B cells that cause inflammation. These cells produce inflammatory molecules called cytokines, which cause insulin resistance. The identification of immune cells in fat controlling metabolic disease is considered as one of the "breakthroughs of the decade" in metabolic research. The goal of the research program is to build on this work, and investigate how the immune system drives insulin resistance in fat and in other organs like the liver and gut. The lab will also understand how insulin affects immune system function. The program will utilize the latest in high resolution and robotic equipment, mouse models, and metabolic assessment, with aim to translate findings in humans. This program may lead to new ways to prevent, diagnose, and treat diabetes. Moreover, it is only through study of the immune system will vaccines with the ability to prevent diabetes altogether become a future reality.

column37: In the absence of treatment, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which has already killed more than 34 million people worldwide. By using small molecules we were able to uncover parts of Env and showed that under certain conditions infected cells can be easily eliminated. The proposed research program will put us a step closer towards HIV eradication by extending these observations and generating better molecules to expose vulnerable parts of Env. Information generated by my research program will also be valuable in the current worldwide efforts aimed at developing an HIV-1 vaccine.

column36: Inherited susceptibility to cancer: from gene discovery to mechanisms to clinical applications
column37: Cancer is a common disease which is typically the result of genetic changes that lead to aberrant growth and behaviour of affected cells, which then produce tumours which can spread throughout the body. Some individuals are at higher risk for cancer because of a family history of the disease. In these families, critical genetic alterations are inherited from one generation to the next in cancer predisposition genes. A better understanding of these predisposing genetic changes is not only useful to help the individuals who are mutation carriers, but it also improves our general understanding of how cancers develop in everyone else in the population by better understanding which genes are involved and how. The work performed in our laboratory for the past 20 years has focused on the study of inherited cancers in high risk families. This work led us to identify a number of new cancer susceptibility genes where genetic alterations can cause disease. In addition, we have also identified very specific changes, referred to as founder mutations, which are observed at higher frequency in our local Quebec populations. There are several reasons to continue this important work. 1) The discovery of novel cancer susceptibility genes / mutations provides at risk patients with surveillance and prevention options for their cancers. This can improve the odds for patients to survive their cancer and can also improve their psychological well-being by giving them a measure of control over their disease. 2) The establishment of population-specific screening panels provides cost effective avenues for genetic screening tailored to local populations, making screening more financially accessible to the health care system providing this service locally. 3) Identification of mutations can allow physicians to choose more effective treatment options for some cancers by using targeted treatments based on the molecular profile of the patients and the tumours they harbour.

column36: Harnessing chemical biology to control pathogenic bacteria and regulate the gut microbiota
column37: Bacteria have the ability to either harm or help us. Harm comes from pathogenic bacteria that can cause infections. Help comes from beneficial bacteria, such as those that live in the human gut, that help to digest food and prevent infection. To eliminate harmful bacteria and promote the growth of beneficial bacteria, we must first study the underlying chemistry and biology that controls their growth and function. The proposed research program will study bacterial chemistry and biology in two ways: 1) we are developing new antibiotics against bacteria that cause infections; and 2) we are studying the biochemical pathways that enable beneficial bacteria to survive in the human gut. A brief summary of both components is provided below. The first part of the proposed research program aims to develop antibiotics to treat bacterial infections. Antibiotics are chemicals that specifically kill bacteria. Since the discovery of antibiotics, these chemicals have become essential medicines to prevent and cure infections. A key challenge for using antibiotics, however, is the emergence of drug-resistance, where bacteria acquire the ability to survive despite the presence of the antibiotic. We are developing new antibiotics to treat antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The second part of the proposed research program aims to understand how certain bacteria survive in the human gut. Babies are born with a sterile gut, and gradually acquire a complex community of bacteria through interaction with the environment. These gut bacteria help digest food and prevent infections by pathogenic bacteria. Many diseases are caused by 'microbial imbalance,' where the composition of bacteria and other microorganisms in the gut deviates from normal. We will investigate how the underlying chemistry and biology enable certain bacterial species to survive in the human gut. This knowledge could ultimately enable the development of probiotic and nutritional supplements to prevent and treat disease.

column36: Enteric neural and glial control of gastrointestinal function in health and inflammatory disease.
column37: The function of your digestive system is key to good health. During digestion food moves from the stomach to the small intestine, where absorption of nutrients occurs, and finally to the colon for elimination. Movement of food through the intestines requires precise control. Not only does the gut move and digest food, but while doing so it must protect the rest of the body from ingested pathogens and from the microbes that live in its lumen. These microbes are essential for health, but must remain in the intestine or they can cause harm. Thus the gut has a dual role: digestion and defense. Digestion and defense are sufficiently complex that a "brain" is required to regulate and control them. This brain in the gut is called the enteric nervous system (ENS). The ENS is composed of nerves and specialized cells called enteric glial cells. Enteric glial cells were originally thought to be passive support cells, but through my research we know that nerves and glial cells actively communicate with each other by releasing chemical messengers. This bi-directional nerve-glial communication is important for the ENS to control the movement of food through the gut and for defense. Alterations in chemical communication in the ENS appears to be responsible for many of the symptoms of gastrointestinal disease. The vision of my research program is to discover new ways to alleviate the symptoms of gut disorders through studies of enteric nerve-glial communication. column37: The current proposal is founded on the discovery of a new approach for the treatment of autoimmune disease (occurring when the white blood cells of our immune system mistakenly recognize and attack natural components of our own tissues). Traditionally, vaccines have been used to expand white blood cells affording protection against viruses, bacteria or cancer, or to delete white blood cells causing autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes (T1D) and multiple sclerosis (MS). We have developed a new type of 'vaccine' based on nanotechnology (using particles thousands of times smaller than the size of normal white blood cell) that can stop anti-self immune responses by selectively expanding what we call 'autoregulatory' white blood cells. These 'autoregulatory' white blood cells put the brakes on the disease-causing autoimmune attack, by inhibiting the activation of all the disease-causing white blood cells, resulting in their complete suppression. As a result, these nanomedicines can blunt highly complex autoimmune responses in mice, including T1D, MS, primary biliary cirrhosis and arthritis, without causing generalized suppression of the immune system. Importantly, we have established that human disease-relevant nanomedicines can effectively trigger the expansion of human autoregulatory white blood cells in 'humanized' mice (mice carrying white blood cells from patients), indicating that this approach is applicable to humans. Here, we will dissect the cellular origin of the disease-suppressor cell type triggered by our nanomedicines, as well as the mechanisms and the downstream cellular targets through which it suppresses disease. Furthermore, we will use mice 'humanized' with white blood cells from T1D patients to select the corresponding drug candidates for clinical development. We anticipate that these studies will open new lines of inquiry in immunity and autoimmunity and will propel a promising new therapeutic avenue for autoimmunity to the clinic.

Abnormal (higher/lower) activities of these enzymes can result in severe biological disorders, and hence PCs are prime targets for therapy in a number of human diseases. We are world leaders in understanding the role of PCs in pathologies, including cardiovascular diseases resulting from high levels of the bad cholesterol (low density lipoprotein, LDL), cancer, viral infections, brain dysfunctions such as in Alzheimer's disease and those resulting in increased anxiety and depression. Our research program will focus on the biology of two of the PCs that we discovered, namely PCSK9 and PC7. 1-PCSK9 regulates the levels of LDL in the blood. Hence, too much of this enzyme results in high levels of cholesterol that are associated with coronary heart disease, heart attacks and stroke. Resulting in large part from our pioneering work on this protein, new injectable treatments using antibodies to block PCSK9 have been developed and shown in early clinical tests to lower LDL by as much as 60% in high-risk patients. However, this approach has some limitations and our own research suggests that serious long-term effects could result from a general blockade of PCSK9. Our goal is to fully describe the molecular mechanisms through which PCSK9 acts and to use this knowledge to develop more effective and better-targeted drugs against PCSK9. 2-The engineered PC7 inactivation in mice results in much reduced anxiety, depression and emotional fear. In humans, lower PC7 levels are also associated with a more efficient iron metabolism, higher levels of the good cholesterol high density lipoprotein (HDL) and lower levels of the bad triglycerides. We will study the biology of PC7 in mice and humans and develop PC7 inhibitors that should find new therapeutic clinical applications for the above indications.

Cognitive deficits can easily be tested with simple eye movement tasks. For example, we have long known that people who suffer from schizophrenia show telltale eye movements under certain conditions. Told to look away from a flash of light, they are unable to resist the automatic urge to glance at the stimulus. Subjects without the disorder can override the impulse. In my research program, we will train monkeys to perform these simple, yet powerful eye movement tasks to find drugs that have effects on brain activity and task performance. We will focus on drugs that act on muscarinic acetylcholine receptors which have been proposed as a novel way to treat cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. We will record the activity of individual brain cells in different areas in trained monkeys, manipulate their activity through the application of drugs that act on different muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and measure brain-wide changes in activity and communication using functional imaging techniques. My goal is to understand the role of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in cognition from the level of single brain cells to the communication in the entire brain. By understanding how brain areas interact and how certain drugs can improve cognitive processes, we hope to identify drugs that will improve the cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.

Lessons learned in rural Saskatchewan will be shared with policy makers and research partners to spread the use of the toolkit to other rural areas in Canada. Research partners in Australia and Europe will help to spread the use of the RaDAR Toolkit outside of Canada. The ultimate goal of this research is to improve the quality of life of older adults with dementia and their caregivers living in rural areas. column36: Transcriptional control of hematopoiesis, immune cell differentiation and leukemia
column37: Circulating in the blood is a myriad of cells with different functions that are critical for our health, including red blood cells that carry oxygen, platelets that help to stop bleeding and immune cells that fight off infections and cancers. These circulating blood cells are not immortal, but rather are constantly being renewed by a continuous repetition of the process that led to their initial specialization. In this complex process, banks of genes are turned on and off in precursor cells to "steer" their differentiation toward one specialized cell type or another. This occurs primarily through the action of proteins called transcription factors, which reside in the cell nucleus and can regulate the activity of thousands of genes simultaneously. Not surprisingly, mistakes sometimes occur in this complex process and can lead to a number of very serious diseases. My own research has focused on identifying the critical components in normal blood cell differentiation and in characterizing the molecular defects that lead, in particular, to bleeding disorders and blood-borne cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma. Over 20 years ago, I co-discovered two transcription factors (Gfi1 and Gfi1b) and was the first to determine the role of Gfi1 in blood diseases including leukemia. More recently, I discovered the role of another transcription factor and co-factor of Gfi1, called Miz-1, in blood cell formation and leukemia. My goal is to understand how key blood formation processes are controlled on a molecular level and how deficiencies in these processes that lead to diseases can be fixed. Over the next few years, we will bring together clinical expertise and the most advanced biomedical research techniques to address two blood cancers: acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) as well as inherited platelet disorders (IPD) that lead to blood clotting problems.

column36: Thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self
column37: Self/nonself discrimination by T lymphocytes is a fundamental requirement of life in vertebrates and is implicated in most fatal diseases in humans. Indeed, i) nonself recognition is essential for elimination of microbes and cancer cells, while ii) immune responses against self antigens cause classic autoimmune diseases (e.g., type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis) and are instrumental in chronic inflammatory diseases, hypertension and atherosclerosis. T lymphocytes learn how to distinguish self from nonself in the thymus. Importantly, the thymus ages more rapidly than all other organs, and by the age of 45 y, 75% of the thymus is lost in humans. Thymus senescence decreases the ability to recognize new antigens and responsiveness to vaccines, and increases the risk of infection, cancer and autoimmune diseases in ageing people. Hence, it is a sobering thought that our understanding of the molecular composition of the immune self is very rudimentary and that we do not understand the mechanisms of thymic involution. Accordingly, the two main themes of my research program are thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self. My specific objectives are i) to discover the molecular composition of the immune self, ii) to uncover how the immune self is perturbed in cancer cells, iii) to understand the rules governing T lymphocyte education in the thymus, and iv) to find a strategy to rejuvenate the thymus. Answers to these questions will be instrumental in i) treating thymus atrophy, the most common cause of immune deficiency in humans, ii) understanding the molecular bases of self-tolerance and enabling molecular evidence-based treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, and iii) discovering cancer-specific antigens that can be used as personalized vaccines for cancer treatment.

column37: Stroke and Parkinson's disease are devastating neurological disorders with devastating personal, social, and economic consequences. This may be related to the fact that conventional MRI visualizes only some of the lesions and damage seen by pathologists in brain slices. Ultra-high magnetic field MRI systems have the potential to be more sensitive to the microscopic changes in tissue properties that occur as MS begins and progresses. MRI machines at such magnetic field strengths are undergoing approvals for clinical diagnostic use. Using a 7 Tesla (140,000 times the earth's magnetic field) human MRI system, we will develop MRI techniques that can characterize MS in patients on a microscopic scale. This could lead to earlier diagnosis of MS, and therefore the ability to intervene sooner with drug treatments. Earlier intervention results in better patient outcomes and lower treatment costs

column36: Canadian Program for Monitoring Overuse in Injury Care

column36: Molecular and Genetic basis of heart development and disease
column37: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects 1-5% of the population and represents the largest class of birth defects. It is the leading cause of death in infants during the first year of life. It is also an independent risk factor for premature onset of adult cardiovascular disease including degenerative valve disease, myocardial infarction and sudden death. It is well established that CHD is a heritable trait, i.e. it 'runs in the family'. However, its transmission does not follow simple Mendelian inheritance and is influenced by other genetic as well as environmental factors. Despite great advances over the past decade, the genes responsible for the majority of human CHD remain unknown. A better understanding of the genes required for normal heart development will immensely advance our understanding and detection of CHD. It will also improve care for individuals with CHD and help prevent cardiovascular complications. During the past decade, our lab has proudly contributed to this area thru our discovery and characterization of several genes essential for normal heart development such as GATA4 and GATA5. Alterations in these genes are associated with several types of human CHD, including bicuspid aortic valve, atrial and ventricular septal defects as well as rhythm abnormalities. Using our unique tools and animal models of human disease, we wish to pursue our studies aimed at understanding the genetics of normal and abnormal heart development. We will also use our animal models to gain a better understanding of how cardiac birth defects make the heart more vulnerable to other cardiovascular problems. Such knowledge will help design therapies for prevention and treatment that are presently unavailable. The results of our research will continue to impact diagnosis and care of individuals with heart disease or with a family history of the disease.

column36: A Rapid Analytics Platform for Influenza Vaccine Evaluation and Translational Research
column37: Influenza remains a major cause of death and illness in Canada and globally. "Seasonal" flu vaccines remain the mainstay of flu control, but their field effectiveness, especially among the sick and elderly who need them the most, is questionable. Newer expensive vaccines with limited data have mushroomed raising the cost and complexity of vaccine programs. Our challenge is to design effective & sustainable strategies of continually and comprehensively evaluating conventional and novel flu vaccines and understanding their complex interactions with viral, host & environmental factors. I envision a safe and effective societal response to both seasonal epidemics and& pandemics. To this end, I propose to further develop our rapid analytics platform built on a continually updated comprehensive data warehouse and use it to address knowledge gaps, guide decision-making and develop new vaccine research methods. column36: Wearable technology to assist with hand and finger function

column36: The biology and clinical significance of the tumour microenvironment in B cell lymphomas
column37: Lymphoid cancers are the fifth most frequent cancer in humans, affect patients of all ages, and despite generally effective treatments, a significant number of patients still die of their disease. Our studies will be very important for physicians and patients as our research will develop clinical tests that provide information about the individual prognosis of lymphoma patient and will help developing new drugs and personalized treatments. column36: Tuberculosis: From Genomics to Control
column37: As a doctor and a scientist, I ask why many people are exposed to the bacterium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but only a minority develop the disease tuberculosis (TB). To understand these variable outcomes, I have established CIHR-funded programs of research that study the spread of this bacterium (epidemiology) and the fundamental biology of the disease (looking from both the perspective of the bacterium and that of the human host). The present application brings together three themes of TB research that share conceptual and methodologic synergies. In molecular epidemiology work (theme 1), our group makes a DNA 'fingerprint' of bacteria to track chains of transmission. This information, integrated with Public Health data, will define better ways to intervene with antibiotics in settings with drug sensitive and multidrug resistant settings. In bacteria-based studies (theme 2), our group compares the bacteria that causes TB with related bacteria that live in the environment and do not cause a contagious disease. These studies will uncover bacterial targets to neutralize in a new vaccine. In host-based studies (theme 3), our group studies how a part of the immune system, called innate immunity, recognizes Mycobacterium tuberculosis and how this translates into effective control of the infection. These studies will define host responses to be enhanced by a new vaccine. Together, these studies, carried out at the level of human populations and within a laboratory setting, will identify critical bacterial- and human-determinants of disease. I am one of very few TB researchers in the world who has the necessary training and a track record of success to lead this combination of studies. The information gained will drive the best application of existing antibiotics, to better control TB, and inform the development of a new vaccine, to eliminate TB.

column36: Insomnia: Research Innovations to Optimize Treatment Outcome in Primary Care
column37: Sleep problems are among the most common health complaints, with insomnia affecting 20% of adults at least occasionally and 10% on a chronic basis. Insomnia is characterized by difficulties initiating or maintaining sleep associated with distress and impairments of daytime functioning. Chronic insomnia produces significant psychological (increased risks of depression), physical (increased risk of hypertension), and economic burdens (reduced productivity and increased absenteeism). Despite some recent progress in insomnia research, there are still some major gaps in understanding and treating this sleep disorder. First, little is known about its risk factors and long-term consequences. Secondly, although chronic sleep disturbances are often associated with co-existing medical and psychiatric conditions, the specific role of psychological and biological factors in insomnia is still poorly understood. Thirdly, despite its high prevalence, insomnia often remains untreated and when treatment is initiated, it is usually limited to prescribed or over-the-counter drugs. Long-term use of sleep medications is often problematic due to their adverse effects and risks of tolerance and dependency. Behavioural therapies for insomnia are effective and well accepted by patients, yet they are not readily available and are infrequently used in practice. The main objectives of this research proposal are to: a) document the natural history, risk factors, and long-term health consequences of insomnia; b) develop more efficient and cost-effective therapies; and c) examine how we can make these interventions more accessible to those who need it (i.e., patients and health care practitioners). This research program is likely to have practical implications by producing new knowledge that will improve our understanding of insomnia and how best to treat it in clinical practice, hence reducing the individual and societal burden of this important public health problem.

column36: The pancreatic islet in human health and diabetes
column37: I am a world-leading expert on the insulin producing pancreatic islets of Langerhans. My group combines this with molecular, imaging, and cell physiological approaches to study: biochemical connections linking cellular metabolism with insulin secretion; the organization of insulin release at the cell membrane; and processes that underlie insulin secretory dysfunction in human T2D islets and animal models of diabetes. My lab is making important inroads in these areas, leading to a better understanding of insulin secretory function in health and diabetes. This work is informing drug development and testing through partnerships with industry, and providing new insights into how secretory dysfunction in T2D may be reversed.

column36: Immune Regulation during Chronic Disease
column37: Persistent viral infections are a global health concern, with over 500 million people infected with HIV and hepatitis B and C viruses. Specifically, we will investigate three possible approaches; 1) Improve the penetration of blood clotting agents to wounds using delivery vehicles that can move against blood flow, which otherwise washes away factors that promote clotting, 2) Increase the ability of platelets to induce clotting, as these cell are first-wave responders that naturally help blood clot, and 3) Increase the strength by which blood clots adhere to injured blood vessels. Each strategy is based on biochemical insights and drug delivery techniques that my lab has already developed, and the research program will focus on applying these techniques to understanding and treating severe bleeding. My lab is uniquely poised to address this issue due to our extensive experience in both blood biochemistry and biomedical engineering, as well as the extensive support we have received from clinicians and the industry, which will allow us to translate laboratory findings into the clinic. The short-term goal of this program is to identify limiting factors that prevent the successful treatment of severe bleeding with current therapeutics, and then use these insights to develop novel technologies that enhance blood clotting. In the long-term, this program will lead to new clinical tools for treating severe bleeding, and has the potential to reduce death and related complications from uncontrolled bleeding in Canada and abroad.

column36: Chromosome instability and synthetic lethality in yeast and cancer
column37: Effective cancer therapy exploits specific biological differences between cancer cells and normal cells. Cancer cells often have defects that reduce the efficiency of chromosome transmission. Indeed, mutations in cancer cells that cause chromosome instability (CIN) are now widely recognized to be an important driver in cancer initiation and progression. These CIN mutations also represent tumour specific genetic vulnerabilities that could be exploited in developing new cancer treatments. Because the same building blocks are used to construct organisms as diverse as yeast, worms, and humans, "model organisms" provide powerful experimental tools for investigating the mechanistic basis of disease and for developing potential therapeutic interventions. The goals of our work are to understand the mechanisms of chromosome transmission at the levels of genes, pathways, and networks using yeast and the nematode worm as models, and to directly relate our studies to cancer and the development of new cancer therapies. Using yeast genetic techniques, in particular, global synthetic lethality analysis, we will identify yeast genes, and the corresponding human gene counterparts, that define potential therapeutic targets for selective killing of cancer cells relative to normal cells. We will use yeast to rapidly test millions of possible combinations of tumour-associated defects, drug targets, and chemotherapeutic agents to identify effective combinations, and will prioritize them for further testing in tumour cell cultures. The results of our proposed research will provide a basic understanding of the mechanisms of normal chromosome transmission, and of the corresponding defects associated with cancer pathology. Our results will also lead to the identification of new drug targets and will enable the identification of new small molecule inhibitors and combination therapies that could be used for the selective killing of cancer cells in patients.

column36: Molecular regulation of muscle stem cell function in regenerative myogenesis
column37: I am interested in understanding the mechanisms that control stem cell function and applying this knowledge to improve health. Our studies are focused on muscle stem cells and how they function in the growth and repair of skeletal muscle. The research is critical for developing novel treatments for many muscle-wasting diseases, for example Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). Our studies have already transformed our understanding of the mechanisms that control muscle stem cell function and have led to the development of a protein called Wnt7a as a novel therapy. Second, we will define the mechanisms that regulate the division of muscle stem cells as this is a central control point that governs regeneration efficiency. We will investigate these control mechanisms with the longer-term goal of identifying targets and hence drugs that could be used to stimulate muscle stem cell function. Third, we will map the regulatory networks of proteins called transcription factors that control the expression of genes in muscle stem cells from healthy versus diseased tissue. This information is key to understanding how these stem cells function. Finally, we will identify new drugs capable of stimulating muscle stems cells to enhance muscle regeneration. In parallel, we will validate our findings on human muscle stem cells to transition our therapeutic strategies into the clinic. In conclusion, the research will advance our knowledge of stem cell function and lead to novel treatments for diseases involving wasting of skeletal muscle. Importantly, this work will improve the health of patients, and also benefit the families and care givers that are affected by these devastating diseases.

column36: Bridging the Gap in Paediatric Traumatic Brain Injury: Environmental, biological and clinical markers associated with preschool concussion and TBI
column37: Concussions and other traumatic brain injuries are a frequent cause of death and disability in youth, and children under the age of 6 are at particularly high risk. Older children with brain injuries often suffer serious mental, psychological, social, and behaviour problems. Even mild injuries have the potential to cause lasting problems in children because of subtle changes in how the brain works. Recently, international teams have been working to better understand the course of recovery in children with concussion or brain injury; however, children under 6 have generally been excluded from this research. This is extremely problematic because of the high prevalence of brain injuries in toddlers and preschoolers and because they are particularly vulnerable to the effects of brain injury. Indeed, injury to the brain disrupts normal development and critically affects acquisition of new knowledge and skills. Currently, we know very little about the consequence of brain injuries in young children, or what initial signs and symptoms might help us predict development in later years. This research program will investigate the functioning of young children after they sustain brain injuries and determine how we can predict their outcomes. We will also determine whether functional problems are associated with changes in the integrity of the brain or particular genetic predispositions. The results will help us to better understand how problems develop after brain injuries in the youngest and most vulnerable age group. In turn, these findings will lead to the development of clear guidelines for doctors and health practitioners to follow when treating young children after a concussion or brain injury. We will also be able to quickly identify preschoolers who are at-risk for problems after brain injury and provide them and their families with the resources needed to prevent problems before they occur and to foster their development and quality of life.

Via these strategies, this research will identify the gene variants that cause and influence outcome of two prototypical autoimmune diseases and elucidate the mechanistic pathways that link such variants to disease. column36: Evolutionary approaches to treat and evade antibiotic resistant pathogenic bacteria
column37: Bacterial infections are major threats to human health. In the last century, antibiotics have served as our arsenals to fight bacterial infections. However, unfortunately, bacteria have since evolved resistance against virtually all known antibiotics, in several cases only a few years after a new antibiotic was introduced. We therefore urgently need to develop novel strategies if we are to prevent the spread of antibiotic resistance, and to discover sustainable antibiotic reagents (i.e. for which resistance cannot easily evolve). I envision that I will lead the field to pioneer new antibiotic strategies to improve our healthcare system by employing "evolutionary approaches" to predict and prevent the evolution of antibiotic resistance. First, I will establish a platform to examine evolutionary potential and limit of antibiotic resistance using experimental evolution in the laboratory. Second, using laboratory evolution and engineering, I will generate novel anti-virulence reagents, e.g. enzymes to degrade cell-to-cell signaling molecules and therefore inhibit biofilm formation. Targeting such molecules is a potentially sustainable antibiotic strategy as it is unlikely that bacteria can easily evolve resistance. My research program will create powerful new approaches and tools to combat multi-drug resistant pathogenic bacteria. My strong expertise in laboratory evolution and engineering, and established collaborations with structural biologists, microbiologists and computational biologists will enable me to effectively tackle this challenge. My CIHR Foundation program will lead us to the development of novel antibiotic strategies and reagents to battle against antibiotic-resistant pathogenic bacteria.

column36: Towards new therapeutics through manipulation of glyco-enzymes
column37: The surfaces of every cell in the human body are coated with specific sugars. These play several roles, principally providing a way for the cell to interact with other cells and their components. Invading bacteria and viruses also use these sugars as an entry point, thus an understanding of these interactions and of how the specific sugars are built and degraded, can lead to new therapeutics. An example is the influenza virus drug Tamiflu, which blocks the critical viral enzyme that cuts a sugar off our cell surfaces and allows the virus to spread. Our recent research has shown that some of the enzymes used by disease-causing bacteria and parasites in order to infect human cells are unlike any enzymes present in human cells. This allows us to design and synthesize new classes of drug to either specifically block these enzymes, as with Tamiflu, or to liberate toxins specifically within the invader. Using such approaches, in collaboration with microbiologists, we shall develop new strategies for treatment of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, as well as the parasites that cause Chagas disease in South America. In a second part of our work we shall use enzymes to modify these cell surface sugars for a variety of applications. In one case we use enzymes to cut specific sugars off the surface of red blood cells, thereby changing their blood type from A or B (or AB) to the "universal donor" Type O. Using an approach that mimics the process of natural evolution, but accelerates it, we shall engineer these enzymes to speed them up for clinical use. This work should greatly improve our supply of blood for transfusions. In a second case we shall use enzymes to improve the performance of increasingly important protein-based drugs such as antibodies and growth factors. Most such proteins have sugars on their surface that play important roles. We shall engineer enzymes to add sugars in a highly controlled manner, yielding drugs of improved performance.

column36: Discovery and engineering of ice-binding proteins for health applications.
column37: Some organisms resist freezing to below -30 C, but quickly die if ice forms in the body. Other organisms actively promote freezing at -2 C and can tolerate freezing and thawing with minimal damage. My CIHR-funded research program has discovered ice-binding proteins that control these processes. They include antifreeze proteins that stop the growth of ice and protect animals and their organs, tissues and cells from freezing; as well as ice recrystallization inhibitors used by freeze-tolerant organisms to lessen the damage that occurs on freezing and thawing. Here we will apply these ice-binding proteins to cool organs well below 0 C so that they can be kept for longer and hence increase the supply of organs for transplant. We will also use these proteins to improve the recovery of frozen blood and stem cells for transfusions. In addition, we will engineer improvements to the ice-binding proteins that will give them greater activity and potency for these human health applications.

column36: Beyond Structured Administrative Data (BEST DATA)
column37: To monitor how our health care system functions, researchers use data routinely collected through public services, such as bills from physician visits, hospital discharge information, and social data from non-health services. Analyzing these records allows us to examine factors that influence the health of Canadians and how we use public services. Until now, researchers have performed these analyses using structured data (such as spreadsheets) that can be easily plugged into statistical programs. However, with the development of new analysis techniques, there is great potential to conduct more in-depth research using unstructured data, such as clinical notes from electronic medical records (EMR). Big data analytics can be used to analyze free text (i.e. natural language). This proposal will employ these new techniques to analyze free text in the health and social data at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy (MCHP). Big data analytics will allow us to answer broader research questions that will help to improve clinical practice. For example, Canadians sometimes receive unnecessary medications (antibiotics), and undergo unnecessary tests like back x-rays. By developing the tools to analyze clinician's notes (free text) in EMRs, we can examine why these events occur and better understand the role of patients in decision making. Using the extensive person-level data available at MCHP, we will follow patient exposure to antibiotics over time while considering travel history and other contributing factors. Thus, the inclusion of free text analysis adds an additional dimension to our understanding of antibiotic resistance and will help to curb this growing problem. This research will advance the science of population level data analysis to a new level, adding depth to the research questions we can answer, and supporting the development of evidence-based policy.
