column36: Neurovascular and neuroimmune interplay in retinal vasculopathies
column37: Loss of eyesight is the most feared ailment in North America after cancer. The part of the eye that senses visuals scenes and transmits them to the brain is a structure rich in nerve cells and blood vessels called the retina. This structure is biochemically part of the brain. In debilitating diseases of the retina such as the sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity and age-related macular degeneration, the degeneration of blood vessels precipitates loss of nerve cell function. These retinopathies are the leading causes blindness in the industrial world and account for over 25 million cases of compromised vision in North America. The degeneration of blood vessels in the retina prevents nutrient and oxygen delivery and leads to a constellation of biochemical changes that deregulate cellular function. While the body attempts to repair and restore blood vessels, there are a number of yet unknown factors that hinder reparative vessel growth and consequently aggravate the loss of nerve cell function. Current treatment paradigms are largely inefficient and focus on destroying diseased blood vessels instead of repairing those that provide oxygen and essential nutrients. An attractive alternative approach would be to regenerate functional vessels into zones of the retina where vessels were damaged. In this proposal we outline a therapeutic strategy that would restore healthy blood vessels to the retina in retinopathies. This approach will help design new medications and be achieved by molecularly altering the response of retinal nerve cells to vascular injury.

column36: Targeting the dynamics and genomics of clonal evolution in cancer patients
column37: Cancers evolve over time and the gene mutations driving them can change. A major bottleneck in the treatment of epithelial cancers is a lack of diverse therapeutic / treatment options. This is especially relevant in cancer, as tumours are able to evolve/adapt to "escape" from single-agent treatment (similar to what occurs in antibiotic-resistant bacteria, where a combination of drugs is required to treat the infection); breast cancers often develop drug resistance so that their tumors recur, and mutational evolution likely underlies this event. It is critical to identify new options/approaches to target tumours that have become drug-resistant, as a result of mutational evolution. We know that clonal complexity - the so called "cellular superbug" phenomenon, is associated with instability in the tumour's genetic sequence (driven by the inability of DNA to repair itself). We hypothesize that specific sections of the genome, with unique DNA structures may be targetable through directed approaches, and plan to explore novel approaches that target structural vulnerabilities within the human genome. By combining chemical genomics of DNA targeting with genetic technologies to uncover conditional genetic interactions and methods for measuring clonal structure, we expect to derive a completely new mechanistic approach to targeting genomically unstable epithelial cancers. Our studies have the potential to answer specific questions about how breast cancer arises, progresses, and becomes resistant to treatment. These findings will have a global impact within the cancer research community, allowing the design of improved and more effective therapies. In short, the practical application of cancer cell genetics will become a reality in the clinic -- representing a significant step forward in direct translational benefits for patients.

column36: Epigenetic Approaches to Enhance Cancer Immunotherapy and to Target Cancer Initiating Cells
column37: The premise of Cancer Immunotherapy is to stimulate the patient's immune system to attack the tumour cells. Recent progress in cancer immunotherapy protocols has led to a transformation in the treatment of several types of solid tumours. However, the majority of Colorectal Cancer (CRC) patients do not respond to immunotherapy, suggesting the need to combine immunotherapies with other anti-tumour strategies. Unfortunately, chemotherapy - the mainstay of cancer treatment for over 40 years - is immunosuppressive and not suitable for combination with immunotherapy. On the other hand, the new class of therapeutics called epigenetic therapies hold great potential for enhancing anti-tumour immune response and for use in combination with immunotherapy. We have found that DNA demethylating drugs can activate immunogenic signals in cancer cells, specifically those that engage the interferon and antiviral pathways. We will investigate how this process happens and how it can be used to increase the tumour cell immunogenicity and to improve the immune response against the tumour. Another major barrier in effectively treating CRC arises from the emergence of resistance to current standard of care. The source of therapeutic resistance is due to a rare group of cells within the tumour called cancer-initiating cells (CICs, also known as cancer stem cells) that are responsible for the continued tumour self-renewal. These CICs are highly resistant to chemo- and radiation therapy. Evidence from mouse models of cancer and human clinical trials indicates anti-cancer therapies select for and increase the number of CICs in tumours, which explain why tumours tend to be more resistant following the initial rounds of therapy. We have found that DNA demethylating agents can target colorectal CICs. We will explore a strategy of targeting CICs using epigenetic therapy and how it can be used to avoid tumour recurrence with the ultimate aim of curing this disease.

column37: Many hormones and transmitters have their biological effects by modulating the activity of receptors located at the surface of cells. Among these, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR) represent the largest family of protein involved in transferring information from the outside to the inside of the cells. With more than 800 members, GPCR control many distinct physiological functions such as neurotransmission, cardiac contraction, vascular tone, endocrine secretion, metabolism, etc.... As a consequence, they represent privileged targets for the development of drugs for many distinct clinical indications. It is estimated that more than 30% of the current prescription drugs act through GPCR. Yet, only a limited fraction of the therapeutic potential of GPCR has been exploited to date. Many receptors with important roles have not yet been targeted and new developments in molecular pharmacology and structural biology offer new opportunities for the development of drugs with greater therapeutic efficacies and less undesirable effects. In particular, new tools allowing to unravel their structures and to monitor their signaling activities with unprecedented sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution open the perspective of developing new drugs based on an intimate understanding of their mode of action at the molecular level. Therefore, the present proposal aims at further understanding the molecular mechanisms controlling GPCR activity, with the intention of identifying novel processes that could be pharmacologically targeted for therapeutic purposes. The studies proposed also include the search for new chemical entities that will serve as tools to better probe receptor functions and could represent interesting lead candidates for the development of new drugs classes for unmet clinical needs.

column36: Vaccination & screening for control sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and STI-related cancers
column37: Sexually transmitted infections (STI) are a major public health concern among Canadians. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common STI, so much so that 3/4 people will get this infection at least once. This is concerning because certain HPV types cause cervical, anal, and oral cancers. Rates of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis have risen for more than a decade. HIV infections continue and the effects of STIs are worse among people living with HIV. STIs are more commonly diagnosed among gay men with HIV than the general population. Women and men with HIV are many times more likely to get a cancer caused by HPV compared to people without HIV. Our vision is to gather the highest quality evidence to help Canadians choose the best vaccination & screening strategies to prevent and control STIs and STI-related cancers among Canadians at risk, especially those living with HIV. The newest HPV vaccines could prevent 90% of cancers caused by these viruses and are effective and safe, including in people with HIV. The negative consequences of STIs can be largely avoided by testing more often and getting treated right away. This not only improves patient health but prevents passing on the infection to partners. Screening for early signs of cancers caused by HPV, such as Pap tests for women, can ensure proper follow-up to prevent cancer development. Solutions will specifically address communities that may be harder to reach due to stigma and poverty. First, we will find out why people do or do not get vaccinated or tested for STIs and cancers caused by HPV. Next we will test new ways to offer vaccination & screening to see which are most effective and practical. Finally, we will follow our progress over the long term to ensure that chosen strategies protect the health of Canadians for years to come. Globally, 1 million people acquire an STI each day. Thus lessons learned may also assist international efforts to end STI epidemics, complications & deaths.

column36: Developmental Pathways to Health and Disease: Fetal Programming and Protection
column37: My research program integrates discovery, translational and clinical research with a goal of optimizing fetal health and preventing the negative life-long consequences of early adversity. It is predicted that chronic diseases/disorders will account for 50% of global disease burden by 2030, costing $47 trillion. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) system that regulates cortisol (the primary stress hormone) can drive a number of these chronic disorders. We have determined that adverse fetal environments (including maternal/fetal stress and certain therapeutic drug treatments) can program life-long function of the HPA axis, which can predispose individuals to disease in later life. We found that transporter proteins (first discovered in cancer cells) are present in the placenta and fetal brain, where they prevent entry of a wide range of substances including maternal stress hormones, anticancer, anti-HIV and pesticides into the fetus and its brain. We also discovered that pregnancy complications (i.e. infection) change levels of these proteins, decreasing fetal protection. Utilizing a multidisciplinary approach, my team will determine the mechanisms by which adverse fetal environments program life-long susceptibility to endocrine (HPA axis) and behavioural disorders; develop tools to help identify individuals at risk; and create interventions that reduce the burden of chronic disease in individuals that experienced early adversity. We will also determine the regulation of the key transporter proteins that protect the fetus in normal and abnormal pregnancies. Harnessing this new knowledge will provide opportunity for innovative new therapeutic approaches for the fetus and mother and improve health in the next generation. column36: Living Kidney Donation: Improving Safety, Access, and Outcomes
column37: Kidney Failure: Kidney failure is a serious health condition that affects more than 40,000 Canadians. The best treatment for kidney failure is a new kidney by transplantation. Unfortunately, patients with kidney failure often wait years to receive a new kidney. Many patients die while they are waiting. Living Kidney Donation: It is safe for a living person who is healthy to donate one of their kidneys. Family and friends of patients who need a kidney often volunteer to donate one of their kidneys. With advances in transplantation, the donor and recipient do not have to be related or be of the same gender, race, or age. Canada and other countries are looking for ways to safely increase living kidney donation. Barriers to Living Kidney Donation: Unfortunately, many patients who would benefit from a kidney transplant do not receive one. There are many reasons for this. Doctors do not always talk to their patients about transplantation. Patients are often uncomfortable discussing living kidney donation with family and friends. Many people do not realize that it is safe to donate a kidney; some are told they are too old to donate despite new research showing it is safe if they are healthy. As well, donor evaluation often takes a year to complete (when it should only take 3 months). A long evaluation process has negative consequences for both donors and recipients. Safely Increasing Living Kidney Donation: My research team is working with living kidney donors and transplant programs to develop and test solutions to overcome barriers to living kidney donation. As well, we are studying a large group of living kidney donors over many decades to confirm long-term safety. Information from our studies will enable more patients with kidney failure to safely receive transplants, and will help candidates make informed decisions about becoming living kidney donors.

column37: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most serious intestinal disease among newborn babies, mostly those who are born prematurely. We do not completely understand what causes NEC, or why it becomes more serious in some newborns. To improve the outlook for babies with NEC, help their families, and reduce costs to the health care system, we need to find out why and how babies develop NEC, and test new ways to treat it. I have dedicated my scientific and clinical career to advancing pediatric surgery, focusing on caring for babies with NEC - and have developed promising new ways to treat it. My leadership in the surgical and NEC fields led to my active recruitment to Canada. My research here will improve the health of babies with NEC. I will establish and lead a program that will produce exciting new basic science discoveries, and will test new approaches to heal babies with NEC in the clinic. This research will deliver new and improved treatments for NEC, helping babies survive and thrive, and easing the burden of NEC on families and the health care system.

column36: New Resources for Chemical Genomics and Metabolomics in Biomedicine
column37: Small molecule compounds such as drugs, nutrients and pollutants affect our health in many ways. Nutrients are needed to sustain life, drugs are needed to cure us of illnesses, while pollutants can kill us. Millions of these compounds exist. The complete collection of these compounds is called the "metabolome" -- derived from the word metabolite (a substance produced by metabolism). The study of how the metabolome affects us is called metabolomics. While metabolomics is a relatively new field, scientists have been collecting detailed information about metabolites for ~100 years. Unfortunately, most of this data is scattered in millions of textbooks and journal articles. The lack of centralized databases or electronic resources for metabolomics means that we still know very little about the chemical universe around us. We don't know how many metabolites there are, we struggle to identify or measure them, we don't know where they come from, we can't tell if they are good or bad and we rarely know how they act on our cells or modify our genes. My long-term research goal is to develop the resources needed to address these problems. Using advanced methods in information technology and analytical chemistry, my lab has created a number of databases and software tools that are helping to answer some of these questions. Our plan is to greatly improve these resources by using the latest techniques in artificial intelligence. By using computers to automatically identify and harvest vast amounts of data from the literature and learn from that data, it should be possible to develop far better resources that will allow us to better characterize, predict and exploit the chemical universe around us. This work will not only revolutionize metabolomics, it will greatly accelerate the discovery of new drugs, identify the underlying chemical causes of diseases, enable improved diagnostics and help predict those at risk of developing diseases such as cancer, heart disease and diabetes.

column36: Families Overcoming Risks and Building Opportunities for Well-being (FORBOW): Early Intervention Targets Psychopathological Antecedents to Pre-empt Severe Mental Illness in Youth at Risk
column37: Severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression, tends to develop in late adolescence. Once the illness is established, available treatments cannot cure it. Early intervention before the illness develops may avoid years of suffering and disability. Families Overcoming Risks and Building Opportunities for Well-being (FORBOW) tests a novel type of pre-emptive early intervention that aims to prevent severe mental illness. In addition to youth from the general population, we include children of parents with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression, who are themselves at high risk of developing a mental illness. This risk is increased further among those who show antecedent symptoms like mood lability, anxiety and unusual sensory experiences. We focus on assessing these symptoms as well as using genetic tests to identify individuals who may benefit most from pre-emptive early interventions. In those aged 9-17 who have one or more antecedent symptom, we test the Skills for Wellness (SWELL) intervention, which helps young people learn skills that not only address their present problems, but also equip them to deal with future challenges. Half of the eligible youth are randomly selected to be offered the SWELL intervention. We monitor all participants annually to assess their health and development. We test the effects of the intervention by comparing those who were offered SWELL against those who were not offered the intervention. We also want to find out whether a genetic test may help select individuals who are most likely to benefit from the intervention. Our vision is to provide timely personalized interventions to maximize the benefits for mental health of the next generation.

column36: Multimodal strategy to identify novel diagnostic and therapeutic targets in lung and pancreatic cancer
column37: My research program focuses on lung and pancreatic cancer, the first and fourth most common cause of cancer deaths among Canadians. These two cancers account for 16% of new cancer cases in Canada in 2015, but disproportionately account for 33% of all cancer deaths. Currently, only 16% and 5% of lung and pancreatic cancer patients are expected to survive beyond 5 years. During the last decade, major advances in the treatment of lung cancer have been achieved through the discovery of genetic changes that transform airway lining cells into cancer cells. Mutations in cancer causing genes result in increased activation of their cell growth/survival pathways, to which the cancer cells become dependent on. New drugs developed to shut down the activities of these mutated genes cause dramatic tumor shrinkage in high percentage of patients whose tumor harbor the target mutations. This personalized cancer treatment strategy has generated tremendous excitement in oncology, even though the numbers of patients who may benefit from these new drugs remains a small proportion of lung cancer patients in Canada. However, a similar initial success has not been achieved for pancreatic cancer patients. Due to the complexity of cancer genetic and biology, our understanding of critical cellular and molecular pathways driving cancer cell growth and spread is still superficial, and drug response and resistance mechanisms remain to be explored. During the last few years, my laboratory has identified novel genes that play such important roles. We have also developed new experimental models and resources to investigate their biology and clinical relevance. The goals of my Foundation program are to gain greater understanding on how these novel genes drive the malignancy of lung or pancreatic cancers, and to develop new agents targeting some of these genes for improving the diagnosis and treatment of these two deadly cancers.

column37: Confidence in Canada's health care and public health systems has been eroded by evidence of the country's declining performance across a range of measures of healthcare delivery and population health. Ultimately this proposal offers a promising way to effectively improve population health and efficiently use health resources to optimize health system synergy and population impact.

column36: Transforming chronic kidney disease care:A personalized, patient-centered approach
column37: Approximately 1 in 10 adults have chronic kidney disease (CKD), a condition that is associated with poor health outcomes and poor quality of life. Patients with earlier stages of CKD are cared for by family doctors, while those with more severe disease are cared for by nephrologists in special clinics. Not all of these patients, however, receive appropriate treatment. This is known as a risk-treatment paradox; a mismatch between a patient's risk profile, and the treatment they actually receive. There is also a focus on care that reflects provider, rather than patient, goals. The potential risk-treatment paradox and lack of patient engagement suggests our current approach to CKD care is not optimal. I am a physician with expertise in clinical research in CKD. I hold a Research Chair, have 351 publications, and have received over $16 million in funding as lead investigator. My research has influenced international practice guidelines for CKD, thereby shaping clinical practice, and has led to changes in health policy in Alberta. My research program has been directly informed by patients, and I have integrated patients into all aspects of my work. The goal for my research program is to improve CKD care using a personalized and patient-centered approach. Over the next 7 years I will: 1) test use of a risk prediction tool in primary and nephrology care to identify a patient's risk to guide care and referral; and 2) develop, implement and test tools that are tailored for patients and their families, to help them manage their kidney disease and be active partners in the decision making related to their care. My program of research will address key priorities for improving care identified by CKD patients , care providers and decision makers. I aim to reinvent CKD care to make it personalized and patient-centered, to ultimately improve outcomes, enhance the patient experience and provide economic benefits through cost savings for the health system.

column36: Discovery and characterization of alternative splicing regulatory networks with critical roles in development and disease
column37: We have shown that almost all human genes encode multiple protein products through a process known as alternative splicing. Each gene is transcribed into an RNA copy that contains coding and non-coding segments. RNA splicing joins the coding segments into a contiguous messenger RNA that can be translated into a functional protein product. Alternative splicing occurs when the coding segments are spliced in different combinations such that a single gene can produce multiple RNA and protein products. This process greatly diversifies the regulatory and functional capacity of genes, resulting in biological complexity. Alternative splicing is frequently disrupted by mutations that cause or contribute to human diseases and disorders. Moreover, some disease mutations can affect entire programs of alternative splicing by targeting the factors that regulate this process. However, we currently know nothing about the specific functions of most individual protein variants generated by alternative splicing, nor how these variants, when mis-regulated, contribute to human diseases. These questions represent key challenges for future biomedical research and form the main goals of this proposal. We will draw on our world-leading expertise in the areas of alternative splicing, functional genomics, and proteomics, to provide the first large-scale map of splice variant function in the context of both normal physiology and human disease. We will systematically dissect the regulatory pathways that control functionally important and disease-associated splicing events. Finally, we will use information generated by our project to develop new therapeutic strategies for correcting altered splicing programs that underlie human diseases and disorders, focusing on autism. Our research will yield unprecedented new insight into the multitasking functions of our genes, and it will further facilitate the development of a new generation of splicing-directed therapeutics.

column36: The Molecular Mechanisms that Regulate Immunological 'Exhaustion' in Chronic conditions
column37: A certain immune cell type, killer T cells play an important role in controlling chronic infections such as HIV and cancer. However, these cells become dysfunctional and unable to eliminate infected cells and tumor cells in the course of chronic infections and cancer. My research focuses on better understanding why these killer T cells become dysfunctional and how we can restore their functionality. I will be developing novel immunotherapy approaches to use person's immune system to fight back chronic infections and cancer. Unfortunately, until recently, most cancer immunotherapies did not work for most patients, or caused severe side effects, and almost all failed. The dream of a successful cancer immunotherapy only came to life in the last few years. Science, one of the top scientific magazines named this new approach 'breakthrough of the year' for 2013. This breakthrough approach targets a way to re-start the immune system, using immune checkpoints' inhibitors. These immune checkpoints' inhibitors jump-start a patient's immune system to recognize and kill infected cells and tumors. They are game-changers for chronic infections and cancer. Using immune checkpoints' inhibitor therapy is revolutionizing cancer treatment by manipulating a person's immune system to fight their infected cells and cancer cells. I will perform a wide range of experiments to understand how T killer cells become dysfunctional in order to develop novel immunotherapy drugs. I will identify and make novel immunotherapy approaches to target these immune checkpoints to allow killer T cells to stay protective and kill infected cells and cancer cells.

column36: Childhood Aggression: A New Developmental Approach to Its Study and Treatment
column37: Antisocial behaviour problems, such as aggression against people and property, bullying, and violence, are widespread among children and adolescents. The long-term outcomes of antisocial behaviour pose major health burdens on the individuals, their families, and the Canadian society. Thus, understanding the underlying biological, emotional, and clinical risk and protective factors for antisocial behaviour is of critical significance. The proposed program of research will investigate the role of emotions, such as rage, empathy, and guilt, as well as their biological correlates, in the development of aggression. We hypothesize that these emotions may have divergent effects, with high levels of guilt and empathy preventing antisocial behaviour, while exaggerated levels of rage increasing antisocial behaviour. Specifically, this program of research will examine if children with elevated levels of antisocial behaviour differ in their emotional, physiological, and electrophysiological responses to conflicts about rules and obligations, compared to normally developed children. Given the recognition that emotions and underlying biological processes play an influential role in how children resolve conflicts with peers and adults, the proposed program of research will provide timely knowledge on the role of biological and emotional processes in antisocial behaviour. This information about child socioemotional development will be used to develop new, early intervention strategies (e.g., targeting emotions and awareness of physiological arousal) for treating antisocial behaviour in children.

column37: I have been a senior scientist in both basic scientific and clinical research for over 25 years. Due to numerous achievements and publications, my laboratory is now recognized as a leader in both fields with major national and global impact. The main focus of my research program has been to develop an understanding of how lipid (fat) metabolism is regulated in diabetic states. Obesity and diabetes are major risk factors for heart disease, and have been increasing at an alarming rate in both children and adults. These conditions are associated with intestinal dysfunction and an overproduction of harmful fat particles (called "chylomicrons"), greatly increasing the risk of heart disease. The critical importance of the intestine in diabetes is now widely recognized as intestinal bypass surgery can rapidly cure type 2 diabetes and normalize blood sugar in diabetic patients. My research program has been investigating how dietary fat absorption and generation of fat particles by the intestine is regulated and altered in diabetic states. We have identified important hormones in the gut and brain that can regulate dietary fat uptake, and have shown that the balance of these hormones is disrupted in diabetic states. Understanding the factors that control dietary fat uptake by the gut may lead to direct benefits in management of lipid disorders in obesity and diabetes. Most of our research in this area has been performed using a hamster model of pre-diabetes, but our findings have recently been confirmed in adult human studies. Now, due to the growing number of children and adolescents with obesity and type 2 diabetes, we plan to investigate the levels of intestinal lipids and gut hormones in the pediatric population. First, we will determine the normal levels of these factors in healthy children of different ages and sexes. Then we will investigate how these levels change in children attending pediatric obesity and diabetes clinics at the Hospital for Sick Children.

column36: Neuron-Glia interactions in brain disease
column37: The goal of my research is to prevent neuronal death and brain impairment that occurs following stroke and during neurodegeneration. My work in the past has shown that the preservation of a healthy brain requires communication between the nerve cells and the surrounding cells termed glia, such as astrocytes and microglia. My research will show how glia respond to brain diseases and traumatic damage and how they aid in recovery. The major cause of patient mortality after stroke or brain injury is brain swelling called brain edema. We have found a new pathway allowing chloride to enter nerve cells that leads to increased water entry into neurons. We will determine how to block chloride entry and brain swelling in nerve cells and we will investigate the contributions of glia to the control of chloride entry into neurons and brain swelling. The goal is to discover the triggers that cause brain swelling and how therapeutic compounds could block brain edema to reduce brain damage and patient mortality. One type of glia, called microglia are the immune cells of the brain and respond to infections and to damage by repairing surrounding tissue and removing debris. Sometimes however microglia can themselves cause damage and brain impairment. We will determine the factors that cause microglia to switch from protecting the brain to releasing factors to cause damage or impair brain function. This will guide us in developing drugs to prevent microglia-induced damage. The brain is the most metabolically active region of the body and requires a constant supply of oxygen and glucose (sugar) via the blood via processes regulated by astrocytes, another glial cell. Experiments will be undertaken to carefully determine the conditions under which astrocytes regulate neuronal activity and cerebral blood flow in normal brains and in conditions of neurodegeneration such as Alzheimer's. This work will guide the development of new therapies to maintain brain health.

column36: Mapping the resting brain: A new frontier for studying neurovascular physiology and age-related brain diseases
column37: Aging, often accompanied by brain and cognitive decline, is an enormous challenge for the Canadian health system. In the past decade, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized the study of the aging brain. However, tasks or invasive challenges have traditionally been required to assess brain function. Resting-state brain mapping, which came on the scene two decades ago, does not require tasks or challenges, is particularly well suited to the elderly and patients, and has revealed age- and disease-related brain-network changes. However, despite heavy worldwide investment in resting-state fMRI, the resulting data are difficult to interpret and limited in utility. My research is dedicated to achieving a fundamental biological understanding of resting fMRI data, and to expanding current resting brain mapping techniques into a family of patient-friendly methods that provide useful assessments of brain health. Such techniques, which do not yet exist, will be important for healthy aging, as well as dementia and late-life depression. My work will lead to a paradigm shift in the global effort for large-scale information gathering in order to understand aging, eventually leading to the identification of viable therapeutic targets against Alzheimer's disease and other age-related brain diseases.

column36: FROM PROTEOLYTIC NETWORKS TO HUMAN BIOLOGY AND DISEASE: Protease regulation of signal transduction in chronic inflammatory diseases
column37: Chronic inflammatory diseases like periodontitis, arthritis and lupus affect 82% of Canadians and for the 1/2000 Canadians with immunodeficiencies, untreatable infections are imminent threats as drug resistance rises. These diseases commonly involve loss of disease-fighting defense proteins. I discovered that defense proteins are lost after they are cut by white blood cell immune proteases. In immunodeficiencies, inherited genetic defects reduce defense proteins in white blood cells. These crucial discoveries were possible by my innovative and highly advanced techniques known as degradomics. Degradomics is a method of uniquely identifying the cut ends of proteins by selectively purifying them from the rest of the protein. As cuts are formed only during active disease, these segments are highly valuable as disease markers to develop new clinical tests. By detecting and treating earlier, inflammatory diseases are easier to manage before disease worsens, and thus reduce long-term disability. Also, as part of the international Human Proteome Project consortium, I am using degradomics to identify the natural ends of all human proteins. This will allow us to characterize the functions of normal vs. diseased proteins and hence reveal new disease mechanisms. I will now use degradomics to generate clinically relevant knowledge on how proteases damage disease-fighting defense systems in human inflammatory and immunodeficiency diseases. I will obtain human tissues discarded in treatment, e.g. inflamed gum from wisdom teeth extractions, and study white blood cells from patients. As defense proteins are alike in many diseases, my results will be broadly applicable. This knowledge will translate to develop new drugs to combat inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. From identifying cut protein ends in these diseases, I will reveal the damaging proteases that can be targeted with new drugs to improve health of Canadians and thereby ensuring sustainable health care costs.

column36: Design for Better Health: User-Centred Design and Evaluation of Interactive Media for Health Education, Communication and Decision-Making
column37: This research is about helping people make decisions about their health. I want to help people make decisions that (1) are informed by the best available medical evidence and (2) reflect what matters to the person or people affected by the decision. This can be hard to do. One reason it's hard is that it can be difficult to make sense of medical statistics. The statistics may not be very clear, people may not feel confident interpreting statistics, and different ways of presenting statistics feel different. For example, being told you have a 1% chance of having a side effect can feel different than being told you have a 99% chance of everything being fine. Doctors and other health care professionals are influenced by different ways of presenting statistics, too. Even when people understand the statistics, it can still be hard to deal with tradeoffs. Many health decisions require people to choose between competing priorities. For example, people may have to choose between maximizing their quality of life or their length of life. I have figured out ways to address these challenges by designing interactive web applications that help people better understand complicated statistics, sort out what matters to them in tradeoffs, and make decisions by putting medical evidence together with what's important to them. However, there is still work to do. In this research project, I aim to develop new web and mobile tools to help more people make their best health decisions. My team includes patients, doctors, nurses, and others to make sure I take everyone's ideas into account. I will use advanced testing methods to make sure that the tools I develop are helpful and easy to use. Once I am confident that they help people, I will implement my tools in patient portals connected to electronic health records. This will help people across Canada get the information and tools they need to make the best possible health decisions for themselves and their families.

column36: Using artificial pancreas closed-loop systems for the treatment of type 1 diabetes
column37: In healthy individuals, blood sugar levels are tightly controlled by 2 hormones: insulin and glucagon. Secretion of insulin, a vital hormone to reduce blood sugar, is lost in type 1 diabetes (T1D). Thus, patients with T1D are treated by insulin therapy using multiple daily injections or insulin pump. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is frequent in T1D individuals and can lead to malaise, convulsions and death. In case of hypoglycemia, patients might need glucagon, a key hormone to raise blood glucose. Our team has developed a wearable artificial pancreas (WAP) that regulates sugar levels for patients with T1D. The WAP is composed of three components: continuous glucose sensor (to measure blood sugar changes), infusion pumps (to provide insulin with or without glucagon) and an intelligent dosing method that links the sensor with the pump to implement dose changes with the pump based on the blood sugar fluctuations. Two configurations of the WAP have been developed: one that infuses insulin and another that infuses insulin and glucagon. column37: One of the major ways that normal cells can get sick is when their fuel's supply to demand balance is disrupted. column36: Using the eye movement system to study brain function and dysfunction
column37: One of the most pressing challenges in neuroscience is to understand how human perception, memory, and action, become dysfunctional with neurological and psychiatric disease. We use eye movements, and pupil dilation systems to study intact and impaired sensory, motor, and cognitive processes, employing behavioural testing, neuroimaging, neurophysiology and computational modeling. Our approach has the potential to revolutionize not only our understanding of the brain, but also the diagnosis and rehabilitation of patients with brain disorders and development of animal models for therapeutic drug testing. We study non-human primates (NHPs) and compare recordings from single neurons in crucial regions of the cerebral cortex and brainstem to determine how active vision is both coordinated and controlled. NHPs have similar sensory, motor, and cognitive systems as humans, thus the knowledge gained from detailed neurophysiological and behavioural experiments can be used to search for behavioural biomarkers in neurological and psychiatric patient groups. Knowledge gained from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now guiding a reverse translational effort: we are using our knowledge of patient pathology to generate and study a form of AD in NHPs. Because there has been great difficulty translating therapies that work in rodents to the specific human disease condition, shifting to NHPs with a brain similar to humans is crucial. In AD there is a build-up of toxic molecules in the brain called amyloid-beta oligomers (ABOs). We have shown that injection of these ABOs into the NHP brain leads to similar brain pathology as found in AD patients. We are now examining if there are changes in behaviour and cognition, and if so, how therapeutics can prevent or reverse those changes. The expected outcome of the proposed studies is the identification of a strategy that could slow AD progression and/or interrupt the onset of AD.

column36: Discrete dynamic complexes and phase-separated states of disordered proteins in neurobiology
column37: Proteins are the molecular machines that perform most biological functions. Some proteins have stable structure but others, called intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), are highly flexible. Disorder is very abundant in brain proteins, particularly those associated with neurological diseases, as flexibility is advantageous for protein interactions, which are essential for regulating key biological processes. We have pioneered studies of disordered proteins and their interactions, leading the development of methodology to study them and defining a new paradigm for protein binding that relies on dynamic interactions. Our studies of disordered proteins have been published in major journals (including Nature, Molecular Cell, PNAS, EMBO) and have led to 164 invitations to speak at conferences and universities, as well as 32 invitations to write review articles. Our work has changed the way proteins interactions are viewed, including those between two, multiple or even huge numbers of protein molecules, which can come together in a process called phase-separation to form liquid droplets involved in organizing the cell. Brain function is poorly understood and there are no effective drugs for major neurological disorders, such as autism, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. The previously dominant static view of protein binding has hindered progress and we propose that our perspective focusing on the role of dynamic interactions of disordered proteins will fundamentally change the understanding of brain function. We will apply our considerable expertise and powerful methods to key disordered proteins involved in brain function and their interactions. We hypothesize that loss of regulation and rigidification of dynamic complexes of these disordered proteins leads to pathology in the brain. We will test this hypothesis and glean information to enable novel therapeutics for a variety of neurological diseases.

column36: Lipid nanomedicines for health and disease
column37: Current drugs suffer from two major limitations. First, they go everywhere in the body and only a small proportion arrives at a disease site such as a cancerous tumour. This results in toxic "side effects" due the effects of the drug on healthy tissue, as well as limited potency. Second, most drugs used today are "small molecules" that are small enough to penetrate into cells in the body to affect disease. The ability to use larger "genetic" drugs based on RNA and DNA to enable genetic therapies would have revolutionary consequences. Such drugs use natural regulatory processes in the body to treat disease leading to new potential treatments for most human diseases. The goal of this project is to develop "smart" nanomedicines that target small molecule drugs more accurately to disease sites and that enable genetic drugs to be used as therapeutics. These smart nanomedicines consist of the drug encapsulated into a nanoparticle that is administered by intravenous injection. These nanoparticles have dimensions of 100 nm or less, approximately 100 times smaller than a cell in the body. They are therefore able to permeate through most tissues and can be readily accumulated by most cells in the body. Specific goals of the project are to: 1) Development of triggered release lipid nanoparticle (LNP) systems to release therapeutic concentrations of small molecule drugs at sites of disease; 2) Development of LNP systems to extend applications of genetic drugs to extra-hepatic tissues; 3) Development of LNP systems containing genetic drugs that are not immunogenic; 4) Demonstrate efficacy of LNP systems in animal models of osteoporosis, diabetes, inflammation, neurological disorders, prostate cancer and leukemia. This research program builds on a strong record in drug development, as well as a well-established interdisciplinary network of collaborators in academia and industry.

column36: When Treatments Harm: Building Better Systems and Enhancing Research Capacity to Reduce Adverse Drug Events
column37: Medications have transformed the lives of Canadians who suffer from painful or debilitating illnesses. However, medications may also cause harm. As medication use rises, so does the incidence of adverse drug events-harmful and unintended events related to medication use. Today, adverse drug events cause 1.7M annual emergency department visits in Canada, and are a leading cause of hospital admissions. Identifying and treating patients with adverse drug events is not easy. Healthcare providers often unknowingly re-expose patients to medications that previously caused harm. This is because we misdiagnose 40% of adverse drug events, and lack effective ways of communicating information about these events between care providers even after the diagnosis is made. For example: "I saw a diabetic who was discharged from hospital recently, where he was admitted for hypoglycemia [low blood sugar] due to glyburide [a blood sugar lowering drug]. The physician asked him to stop the glyburide, and gave him a prescription for gliclazide, a drug with a lower risk of causing hypoglycemia. But the patient presented here comatose with an even lower blood sugar. When I looked at the patient's blister pack I discovered that both glyburide and gliclazide had been dispensed. The patient had been given a discharge prescription for gliclazide, but no note was made to discontinue glyburide, and neither the GP [general practitioner] nor the community pharmacist were aware of what had happened." Hospital pharmacist, 2012. To address this gap, I aim to develop, evaluate and implement innovative solutions to help healthcare providers diagnose and treat patients with adverse drug events, and prevent harmful re-exposure. My team plans to create the first adverse drug event surveillance program in Canada, improve the quality of data on adverse drug event outcomes, and create a new resource for health professionals to study safer prescribing, optimize medication use and improve health outcomes.

column36: Evaluating and Understanding the Impact of Tobacco Control Policies of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control in a Rapidly Changing Global Tobacco Market: The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation Project
column37: This century, 1 billion people will die from tobacco use. The 2003 WHO treaty, the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) obligates 180 countries (90% of the world's population) to implement policies to reduce global tobacco use. If fully implemented, the FCTC would be the greatest disease prevention initiative in history. But FCTC implementation has been slow, weakened by tobacco industry influence. The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation (ITC) Project is a global research program addressing the urgent need for strong evidence about FCTC policy impact by (1) evaluating FCTC policies, (2) understanding determinants of tobacco use vs. quitting, (3) identifying differences in global FCTC policy impact. The ITC research team of >100 tobacco control experts has conducted cutting edge evaluation studies of FCTC policies in 22 countries, home to >70% of the world's tobacco users. ITC has consistently reported evidence used globally to strengthen tobacco policies that improve population health (www.itcproject.org). Since its start 13 years ago, ITC data have been used to strengthen tobacco control policies in many countries, including Canada. We propose to continue this global project by: 1) continuing our rigorous evaluation of FCTC policies, focusing on regions where the tobacco industry is increasing its attention (e.g., Asia, Africa, Middle East); 2) expand ITC to evaluate new leading-edge policies (e.g., plain packaging, additive bans), 3) conduct the first-ever international cohort study of e-cigarettes to answer critical questions about their impact on tobacco use; and 4) strengthen dissemination efforts to bring our evidence to governments to support stronger tobacco control globally. ITC has advanced science, improved population health initiatives, and built strong collaborations with governments and health communities globally. We will strengthen our efforts to use science to combat the world's leading preventable cause of death and disease.

column36: Development epidemiology: identifying evidence-based interventions for improving population health and promoting health equity
column37: There is abundant evidence that social conditions impact health. However, our ability to improve population health and reduce health inequalities is limited: we do not yet understand well enough how public policies and programs can be used to influence these social determinants of health. Rigorously assessing the impact of interventions, from national policies to smaller-scale programs, has become an active area of inquiry in social sciences such as economics, but less so in epidemiology. This research program will fill this gap by systematically identifying and evaluating evidence-based interventions that can improve population health and promote health equity in a global context. Countries are constantly designing and implementing policies and programs. By systematically grouping countries together and carefully analyzing comparable similarities or differences in implementation and outcomes, we can achieve a far better understanding of what public policies and programs really make a difference to the health of individuals. As the world moves towards the new Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in 2015, there is as a new set of targets to meet that will improve health and reduce health inequality worldwide, and an outstanding window of opportunity to generate new evidence to meet them. This program focuses particularly on policies related to socioeconomic status, health services, public health, and the environment, and identifies the effects on the health-related SDGs of different policy variations across nations (Aim 1); within nations that have substantial policy variation at the provincial or state level (Aim 2); and in terms of their cost-effectiveness (Aim 3). The program will develop partnerships with policymakers, non-governmental organizations, and intergovernmental institutions to develop relevant research questions and ensure that research results inform the development of effective policies and programs on the ground.

column37: The brain is the most energy 'expensive' tissue in nature, thus requiring a massive and complex blood supply that is precisely regulated across space and time. Even when examined on a small scale, different types of brain cells and small blood vessels are highly intertwined and connected, making the brain-blood-interface difficult to understand on a foundational level. My research program uses advanced fluorescence microscopes, lasers and genetic tools to both observe and control the activity of specific types of brain cells in intact animal models. Our objective is to gain insight into how the brain coordinates brain activity with the delivery of brain fuel via the blood supply so that the brain's need for energy is properly met. This is important because numerous neurological conditions including stroke, migraine, dementia and others, are associated with a mismatch between the supply and demand of brain energy. Our objectives are to learn the cellular mechanisms by which brain activity and the delivery of brain blood are matched, and then test how these mechanisms go awry in models of disease. The novel research questions and state-of-the-art experimental approaches we employ will allow us to discover the exact communication pathways utilized by specific cells, as well as understand how to manipulate these cascades using small molecule therapies to ameliorate various brain dysfunctions. Our central aim is to make important scientific advances in this area to ultimately aid the human condition.

column36: Structures and Functions of Megaenzymes
column37: Very many clinically-used therapeutics are produced naturally by earth's flora and fauna. They are often made in microbes by huge enzymes called nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) and polyketide synthases (PKSs). Examples include daptomycin, used against MRSA superbugs; viomycin, used to treat multidrug-resistant tuberculosis; actinomycin D, used to fight cancers like Wilms tumor; cyclosporin, which was widely used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants and can also inhibit the hepatitis C virus; and penicillin. A frequent target of natural compounds is another megaenzyme, the ribosome. The ribosome makes proteins in all cells. Inhibiting the ribosome in bacterial cells can kill bacteria and cure infections. The goal of this research is to expand our knowledge of how megaenzymes make important natural drugs and how megaenzyme-made drugs act on the ribosome. Using biochemistry and biophysics, we will analyze NRPSs and PKSs and capture 3D pictures of them at different points in the process of making natural products. We will also capture 3D pictures of natural products bound to and inhibiting the ribosome. This enables us to answer a range of questions, elucidating the details of how building blocks are chemically assembled into the antibiotics, explaining the large rearrangements NRPSs need to perform to create drugs and revealing new ways that natural drugs work against the ribosome. Megaenzymes hold a vast potential to produce new drugs. Because NRPSs and PKSs are divided into segments, with each segment adding one building block to the drug, we can alter the order of segments and the specific types of segment to produce variants of the drug product. For some drugs, we will visualize what each building block is doing to the ribosome. Our studies can help us learn how best to rearrange NRPS segments to make millions of new compounds, to better kill antibiotic resistant bacteria and also to fight other challenges to human health like viruses and cancer.

column36: Neural circuits underlying aberrant motivated behaviour
column37: The rising rate of obesity poses the biggest challenge to our health care system, such that obesity is complicated with many other comorbidities. Prevention of obesity and its comorbities is likely the best strategy to reduce health care costs and improve health. This is difficult in a society where easily accessible, inexpensive, highly palatable and caloric foods are abundant; we are forced to temper our 'heightened motivation' and engage our 'willpower' to prevent us from eating beyond satiety. The ventral tegmental area, and its inputs and outputs, engages individuals in motivated behaviour whereas the orbitofrontal cortex functions to assess the current value of rewards and updates our actions based on these values and underlies 'willpower'. Thus a research strategy of understanding how these circuits are impacted with obesity provides a unique opportunity to really understand why we overeat. I have the unique expertise to address this problem as we employ techniques that can address changes at the synaptic, circuitry and behavioral level in lean and obese animals.

column36: Dynamic Imaging of the Musculoskeletal System: From Cells to Humans
column37: The focus of this program is the development and application of quantitative 3D imaging systems for applications related to musculoskeletal disease. Bone and joint conditions (including arthritis, osteoporosis, and trauma) cause morbidity, disability and huge economic impact, affecting over 11 million Canadians and costing the Canadian economy over $30B annually. Research findings from this program will have an impact on the development of novel therapies for musculoskeletal disease, mobilized through collaborations with clinical Program Experts. Our studies will help to answer important questions, such as: Why do some tissues (like cartilage) degrade in damaged joints? How does the mechanical micro-environment within skeletal tissues influence remodeling? column37: Social participation is critical to promote health, prevent disabilities and foster health equity in older adults and society but is restricted for approximately half of older Canadians. column36: Imaging neural circuit dynamics in the awake developing brain: Identifying origins of neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: The primary goal of my research is to understand how brain circuits form during early development and how mutations and errors give rise to dysfunctional circuits that underlie common neurodevelopmental disorders such as Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) and Epilepsy. The distinctive feature of our research approach is the development of multi-disciplinary and highly innovative imaging tools that combine electrophysiology, genetics and technology development in microscope design to see brain neural network activity and growth. In addition to the development of these tools, I also developed a leading model of vertebrate brain circuit formation by taking advantage of the unique development features of the albino Xenopus tadpole. Specifically, the external development and transparency of the embryos allows us to directly image brain circuit formation in live animals. Another example of our novel approach involves labeling individual brain neurons using single-cell electroporation, a technique I invented to tag neurons and control their gene expression so that we can image 3D growth in real time using ultrafast microscopes constructed in my lab. Our research has demonstrated that neural activity in response to external stimuli guides neuronal growth and connectivity in a manner that allows for self-organization and optimization in processing the input encountered during development. Our findings on brain circuit formation have provided important insight into the origins of ASD where a large proportion of associated gene mutations disrupt the function of synaptic proteins. We also created single-cell models of ASD to express mutant genes in order to test alterations in growth, synapse formation and encoding. In parallel, we study Epilepsy to test whether seizures hijack activity-driven growth events. Once we understand how normal and dysfunctional brain circuits are formed, we will develop and evaluate new interventions for preventative and corrective treatments.

column36: Application of antibody internalization domain to improve the efficacy and safety of Antibody Drug Conjugates
column37: Recent revolution in anti-cancer therapy utilizes the antibody's power to target cancer cells with chemotoxins. This approach of conjugating toxin to antibody (ADC= antibody drug conjugates) with specific affinity to cancer cells have dramatically improved both the safety and efficacy of the treatment. The most notable recent success is Kadcyla which combines DM1 toxin with anti-HER2 antibody to treat breast cancer. A critical factor in developing a successful ADC is an antibody's ability to internalize itself once it binds to the target cancer cell's biomarkers (receptors). However, many cancer cell specific receptors do not internalize efficiently enough to advance into clinical development. iProgen has developed a peptide domain that can be engineered into an antibody and dramatically boost the antibody's internalization efficiency on target cancer cell. Now, we are testing these candidates in conventional cell line xenograft models. While such cancer cell line models have merits for cancer research, the cell lines used do not adequately predict efficacy of anticancer drugs in the clinic. Drs. Wang at the Living Tumor Lab (www.livingtumorlab.com) has established next-generation patient-derived cancer models, which more closely resemble a patient's cancer than the existing standard cancer models. Such models provide valuable tools for further testing our drug candidates. We want to see whether the ADC improvement in efficacy seen on cell line can translate into in improvement in efficacy and or safety in the respective animal model testing. We are also interested in testing new ADC targets that have either failed to advance in clinic or that have largely been ignored by the pharmaceutical industry largely due to the poor internalization property of the antibody-receptor complex.

column37: The rising incidence of non-communicable diseases (NCD), including diabetes, hypertension and obesity, remains one of the greatest challenges to global health. The incidence of NCD in pregnancy mirrors this global pattern, and has a major impact on short- and long-term maternal and infant health, including preterm birth, fetal growth restriction and perinatal mortality, as well as predisposition of the infant to future obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Unfortunately, information regarding the optimal management of pregnancies complicated by NCD is lacking. Studies on the management of these pregnancies requires large-scale collaborative efforts to identify risk factors for adverse outcomes and to evaluate the impact of interventions on maternal and neonatal outcome in pregnancies complicated by NCD. Our aim is to establish a multi-disciplinary research team that will utilize a unique infrastructure of an existing obstetrical research network to improve maternal and neonatal health in pregnancies complicated by NCD. The Southern Ontario Obstetric Network (SOON) is a unique, recently established, network of 9 academic and 11 non-academic hospitals that account for over 60,000 births per year, and is committed to sharing resources, data and knowledge to create best practices/guidelines and conduct research. We plan to use this platform in order to conduct a series of studies that will address the following questions: 1) Assess the impact of NCD on preterm birth and maternal and neonatal health; 2) Identify risk factors for preterm birth and adverse pregnancy outcome in pregnancies complicated by NCD, 3) Identify knowledge gaps and variation in care of pregnancies complicated by NCD; and 4) Explore the ability of medical and educational interventions to improve maternal and neonatal outcome in pregnancies complicated by NCD.

column37: Canada, like most developed nations, is in the midst of an obesity epidemic: one in four adults is currently classified as obese, with this number expected to increase to one in three in the next two decades. In London Ontario, 45% of births are by overweight or obese mothers, posing significant management challenges for obstetrical providers. Pregnant women with obesity have a 2 to 3-fold increase in pregnancy complications related to preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. In addition, the obstetrician has significant difficulties in obtaining and interpreting results from routine tests that screen for pregnancy complications and work well in the pregnancy without obesity. Through their Collaborative Obesity in Pregnancy Research Team, Drs. de Vrijer and Eastabrook, early and mid-career Maternal-Fetal Medicine clinician-researchers, propose to develop new tools to address the unique needs of the obese pregnant woman in prevention of adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preeclampsia, and fetal growth restriction. The proposal will target the mother's cardiovascular and metabolic health and the effect of the associated chronic stress effect on the placenta and fetus, using novel technologies such as MRI (IDEAL and BOLD), assessment of metabolic stressors (metabolomics), placental response to stress (autophagy) and maternal blood vessel stiffness (pulse wave analysis). Support is sought for the Collaborative Obesity in Pregnancy Research Team, which includes well established clinical and basic scientist collaborators, to build the administrative, educational and research infrastructure to make this group successful in knowledge translation and future grant applications. This group has found excellent mentorship in Drs. Han and Lala, renowned clinical and basic science researchers (respectively) and will be supported by the University of Western Ontario, the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology and Western's Children's Health Research Institute.

column37: La naissance prematuree, c'est-a-dire qui survient avant 37 semaines de grossesse, touche environ 1 naissance sur 10. C'est une cause importante de deces des nouveau-nes. La prematurite a un impact important pour les couts de la societe et pour les familles. Il y a deux causes principales de prematurite : celle dite 'spontanee', par exemple un travail pre-terme, et celle dite ' medicalement induite', par exemple quand le travail est provoque pour une pression arterielle elevee et grave pour la mere et son bebe (une condition nommee pre-eclampsie). Notre projet d'equipe est axe sur la prematurite. Nous voulons mieux comprendre ses causes et pouvoir proposer des traitements adaptes aux patientes dans le but de prevenir l'accouchement pre-terme et les consequences parfois graves pour le nouveau-ne. Notre equipe est composee de trois cliniciens-chercheurs qui seront guides durant toute la duree du projet par deux mentors tres experimentes dans le domaine de la prematurite. L'equipe de recherche inclut aussi des experts indispensables pour repondre aux questions qui seront etudiees et pour transmettre les conclusions aux medecins et aux patientes. Il y a trois projets principaux proposes et les questions portent sur 1) une approche de traitement (pessaire et progesterone) pour prevenir la prematurite, 2) l'evaluation d'un test urinaire (podocine) pour predire la pre-eclampsie, et 3) la validation d'une methode pour mieux classer les differentes causes de la prematurite et evaluer leur impact sur la sante du nouveau-ne. Ces projets sur la prematurite se derouleront dans trois centres de soins et de recherche situe au Quebec (villes de Sherbrooke, Montreal et Quebec). Il y a un total de pres de 14 000 naissances/an dans ces 3 centres. Ce grand nombre permettra a notre equipe de pouvoir repondre plus rapidement aux questions sur la prematurite et ameliorer les soins aux patientes suivies durant leur grossesse.

column37: More than 5 million Canadians have the chronic interrelated diseases of obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) and their incidence in the population are rapidly increasing. Obesity is an important risk factor for developing NAFLD and T2D which contribute to the development of liver cancer and heart disease. Therefore, designing new ways to treat or prevent T2D and NAFLD are important. Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is an organ which has long been known to exist in rodents and infants but remarkably only in the last 5 years has been discovered in adult humans. BAT has the unique capability, compared to any other organ in the body, to burn large amounts of sugar and fat and effectively dissipate this energy as heat due to the presence of unique protein called uncoupling protein 1. Thus BAT is frequently characterized as the body's furnace. The activation of BAT in rodents has been shown to reverse obesity, T2D and NAFLD. In addition recent studies have shown that by exposing humans to cold you can increase BAT activity and lower blood sugar levels suggesting that increasing BAT activity may represent a viable therapy for treating T2D. Unfortunately, in individuals with obesity or T2D the ability to switch on BAT is compromised. Determining why BAT activity is reduced and identifying new ways to switch it on has generated world-wide scientific and clinical excitement around developing a new therapy for obesity, NAFLD and T2D and is the focus of the current proposal. In this proposal we will conduct studies in cells, mice and humans to examine how agricultural and food processing practices may regulate BAT metabolic activity directly or indirectly by altering the billions of bacteria that reside within our gastrointestinal tract. These studies will help us develop new strategies to enhance BAT activity that may be effective for treating and preventing obesity, NAFLD and T2D.

column36: The diet-microbiota-gut axis in pediatric IBD
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) describes a group of chronic conditions of the digestive system whose hallmark is unrelenting inflammation of the lining of the intestines. Crohn's disease (CD) and Ulcerative colitis (UC) are the two main subtypes of IBD. There are no cures for IBD and the ultimate cause also remains unknown. Accurate early diagnosis and effective treatments are important in reducing suffering and complications. The identification as to why these diseases develop may lead to ideas and ways about how to prevent and treat them. For instance, how the bacteria (microbiota) normally work together in our intestines is believed to play an important role in keeping us healthy but its disruption can lead to IBD. It is well accepted that the gut microbiota plays a crucial role in breaking down the food we eat into important nutrients that are essential for human health. In addition, what we eat is also known to affect which bacteria are present in our intestines and what they do. Based on this knowledge, we propose to assess the contribution of diet in the development and unrelenting continuation of the inflammation that defines IBD. This research program will investigate the complex interactions among diet, the gut microbiota and the host and provide information that may be important for personalized dietary and microbiota changes needed to keep people with IBD healthy. We propose to characterize the impact of the diet on the activities of intestinal bacteria to understand whether and how specific diet components or food consumption habits may lead to IBD and contribute to the ongoing inflammation or reasons why current treatments fail in some children. This study will generate the information required for the development of methods to improve bacterial activities in our intestine as treatment for IBD patients. This research will have important implications for the quality of life of people with IBD everywhere.

Hence, research that strives to understand the brain differences of people who engage in repeated aggression could lead to new treatment tools and violence prevention strategies. column36: Research Advancement through Cohort Cataloguing and Harmonization (ReACH)
column37: More and more Canadians are affected by chronic diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive lung disease, diabetes and mental illnesses. Many of these conditions have their origins in early life (conception, pregnancy, infancy and childhood) and a number of very good Canadian pregnancy and birth cohort studies have been implemented to explore hypotheses related to such Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD). However, there is general agreement that the research community could get more out of existing cohort resources. In addition, cohort investigators recognize that individual studies often do not have the statistical power, specific data items, or appropriate design needed to fully support the current and upcoming needs of cutting-edge research. For example, even the largest and best-designed cohorts can often only generate enough participants to detect the most important relative risks, investigate relatively common health and social issues, and provide limited potential to explore how environments interact with genetic factors to influence health. To address these issues and speed up discovery, more and more stakeholders are calling for a shift in the manner we conduct our science. Enabling timely access to research data and samples, increasing potential to share and integrate data across cohorts and promoting a multidisciplinary and collaborative approach to research are major assets of this new path. The ReACH initiative (Research Advancement through Cohort Cataloguing and Harmonization) responds to this demand by providing resources (comprehensive web-based catalogue and harmonization platform) to the Canadian research community to optimize the use of existing Canadian cohort data and samples, and leverage national and international DOHaD research collaborations.

column37: 40% of Canadians suffer from gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms of abdominal pain and a change in bowel habit. The commonest causes for these symptoms are inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (affecting 0.5 million) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) (affecting 6 million). Canada has the highest rates in the world for these diseases and they cost the health care system $7.7 billion per year. IBS can occur at any age and IBD typically first presents in teenagers and young adults but then lasts life long as there is no known cure. IBD patients often need powerful drugs to suppress the immune system and sometimes surgery to remove part of the bowel. Mental health issues such as anxiety and depression affect IBS and IBD sufferers more than normal. The cause of these disorders is unknown and it is unclear why they are connected to mental health problems. We are now are beginning to understand the role our gut bacteria play in GI and mental health. Our intestines would occupy the area of a football field if stretched outside our body. This vast area is teeming with bacteria that outnumber our own body cells 100:1 and yet the intestines also have to stay permeable so that we can absorb the nutrients that we eat. It is astonishing that we are not ill all the time and we stay healthy because most of our immune system is focused on our GI tract. This is a delicate balancing act and disease may arise because the equilibrium between our gut bacteria and our immune system is disturbed. This concept has been proven in animal experiments that show IBS, IBD, and psychiatric disorders can be linked to changes in gut bacteria. We have developed a network of researchers across Canada that will study the gut bacteria and diet of IBD and IBS sufferers compared to those that are healthy. We will use this information to develop changes in diet, probiotics, fecal transplants or antibiotics to improve IBD, IBS and mental health. With this network we can start to IMAGINE a cure for these diseases.

column36: SPOR Network in Diabetes and its Related Complications
column37: Individuals with diabetes fear suffering from blindness, limb amputations, kidney and heart failure, and low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). These complications are influenced by genetic risk, life-style, sex/gender, socioeconomic and cultural (e.g., Indigenous) status, geography (rural) and co-morbid disease (e.g., arthritis). Patients and non-researcher health professionals have joined our SPOR Network to redefine methods for earliest diagnosis and treatments that will transform the health outcomes for all with diabetes. We will design a smart-phone app, Risk Calculator, to aid patients and healthcare providers in their shared decision-making about care paths customized to address unique risk. By linking clinical information with other biological factors (genetics, medical imaging of affected organs), we will identify why some individuals have higher risk than others for complications. This knowledge will guide our development of diagnostic and therapeutic interventions to be applied before clinical signs of complications appear. To achieve best glucose control and prevent hypoglycemia we will develop and test innovative external artificial pancreas therapies in conjunction with smart-phone apps to monitor glucose control, physical activity and other modulators. We will evaluate novel diagnostic tests and therapies discovered by our scientists for diabetic heart, kidney, eye and nerve disease, along with user-friendly web-based tools to assess lifestyle (diet, physical activity) and effectiveness of personalized behaviour-modifying interventions. By aligning biomedical, clinical, population health and health services research and education with what matters most to patients we will bridge the knowledge translation gap with real impact on chronic disease outcomes.
