column36: Listening, Learning, Leading: Canadians Seeking Solutions and Innovations to Overcome Chronic Kidney Disease (Can-SOLVE CKD)
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects nearly 4 million Canadians, particularly Indigenous peoples, children and the elderly, and patients with CKD have a quality of life similar to those with advanced cancer. Treating people with CKD and kidney failure is very expensive, costing the health system nearly $50 billion per year in Canada. Kidney disease is very common in people with diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, and kidney disease increases the risk of dying in such patients by two to eight-fold. The Canadians Seeking Solutions and Innovations to Overcome Chronic Kidney Disease (Can-SOLVE CKD) Network is a national partnership centered around patients and involving all key stakeholder groups: patients, caregivers, health practitioners, policy-makers, and researchers. Our Network will create new national core infrastructure that can support research, knowledge translation and training for years to come. Over the last three years, we have worked with patients with CKD and policy-makers to determine their top research priorities. We then developed a research program around these projects, which focus on three themes: Theme 1: Identify Kidney Disease Earlier and Support Those at Highest Risk of Negative Outcomes; Theme 2: Define Best Treatments to Improve Outcomes and Quality of Life; and Theme 3: Define the Optimal Ways to Deliver Patient-centered Care in the 21st Century. Over the next 5 years, our research program will find and test new discoveries. Evidence will be translated into practice and care to benefit patients. We will build capacity among junior scientists in patient-oriented research, and will also educate patients and policy-makers about this type of research. Our vision is that by 2020, every Canadian with, or at high risk for, chronic kidney disease will receive the best recommended care, experience optimal outcomes and have the chance to participate in studies of novel therapies, regardless of age, sex, gender, location or ethnicity.

column36: Grossesses adolescentes au Nunavik: quels sont les facteurs de risque?
column37: Au Nunavik, les jeunes femmes agees entre 14 et 19 ans ont 3,6 fois plus de grossesses qu'au Quebec. Au Canada, le pourcentage de jeunes ages de 15-16 ans ayant des relations sexuelles etait de 4% en 2002 et de 6% en 2010. Les facteurs de risque associes aux grossesses adolescentes sont : l'activite sexuelle precoce, l'inutilisation de contraceptifs, les echecs scolaires, la consommation de substances et les caracteristiques familiales. Plusieurs efforts de prevention regionale au Nunavik ont echoue dans la reduction des taux de grossesses adolescentes. Cette problematique s'inscrit dans les priorites de la Regie Regionale de la Sante et des Services Sociaux au Nunavik (RRSSSN) en matiere de sante mentale et sexuelle, et cadre egalement dans les annonces de priorites des IRSC. Dans l'optique de repondre a ce besoin, cette etude propose de comprendre les differences hommes-femmes dans les facteurs influencant la survenue des grossesses adolescentes. Les resultats contribueront a definir le role des facteurs sociaux, culturels, economiques et psychologiques des grossesses adolescentes chez les hommes et les femmes Inuit du Nunavik, et permettront ultimement d'envisager des strategies plus efficaces pour reduire les risques de grossesses adolescentes. Cette etude permettra egalement de mieux adapter les outils de promotion en sante sexuelle et ainsi contribuera significativement a l'effort actuel de prevention des infections transmises sexuellement et par le sang (ITSS) chez les jeunes adultes.

column36: Antipsychotic medication prescription in a Canadian offender population: A longitudinal analysis of drug safety and effectiveness
column37: Severe mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are vastly overrepresented among offender populations worldwide. Treatment with antipsychotic medication is the cornerstone of therapy for these conditions. However, adherence to these medications is a well-established challenge, complicated by often severe side effects. Previous research has found that antipsychotic medications are heavily prescribed while prisoners are in custody, but that their ongoing use is frequently disrupted during the transition from custody to community settings. Low adherence leads to an increased risk of relapse and repeat involvement with the justice system. Clinical trials of clozapine - often known as the gold standard of therapy - and long acting injectable antipsychotic drugs have shown particular promise for improving outcomes. However both are under-utilized. The proposed study is the first of its kind to investigate the impact of clozapine and long acting injectable antipsychotics in a very large sample (>250,000) of offenders. The study is supported by the School of Social Welfare at the University of California Berkeley - one of the world's leading centres investigating the interface of serious mental illness and crime. Data will be drawn from a large database created in the province British Columbia (BC), Canada, which links comprehensive justice and pharmaceutical details for the entire population of BC. These administrative data will be supplemented with clinical details drawn from hospital charts in California. This research is expected to produce findings that guide improvements in the safety and effectiveness of treatments using antipsychotic medication for mentally ill offenders. Findings may also extend to opportunities for improved prescription practice among non-offenders with severe mental disorder.

column36: Pannexin 1 in swelling-induced neuronal death
column37: Brain swelling is a major cause of mortality following insults such as stroke and traumatic brain injury. This condition is often caused by an underlying swelling of neurons in the brain, leading to cell death. We currently have limited capacity to replace these neurons, and therefore must devise strategies to reduce the swelling-induced cell death. Recent evidence suggests that an ion channel protein, called Panx1, is involved in this process. Ion channels act essentially as conduits between cells and the external environment. These proteins pass important signalling molecules to co-ordinate cellular responses, such as cell growth, movement, or death. In this project, I will test whether Panx1 conduits promote cell death following neuronal swelling. I will also examine the mechanisms through which Panx1 channels are activated during neuronal swelling. Early experiments indicate that harmful molecules known as reactive oxygen species, which are created within swollen cells, might play a role in this Panx1 activation and neuron death. Reactive oxygen species cause damage to all cellular components, including proteins. Therefore I will also examine whether these molecules activate Panx1 conduits by modifying parts of the protein structure. This work contributes to unraveling the complex and still largely unknown mechanisms underlying neuronal swelling and death, and will guide future studies on therapeutic interventions for brain edema and neuronal death.

column36: Treatment of paediatric anxiety disorders using reconsolidation update mechanisms: implications of executive functioning
column37: Paediatric anxiety disorders are frequent, can be extremely impairing and may lead to increased risks for adult anxiety disorders. Exposure-based therapies (including cognitive behavioural therapy [CBT]) are the first-line treatment for paediatric anxiety disorders. However, some children do not adequately benefit from treatment, and some experience a relapse of symptoms following treatment cessation. There is clearly scope to enhance the efficacy and durability of exposure therapy in paediatric anxiety disorders. The reconsolidation update mechanism suggests that following initial encoding, a memory is stored, but does not necessarily remain stable. When the memory is reactivated, it becomes labile and sensitive to change for a window of time. New information presented during this window can disrupt the reconsolidation of this memory, updating the original memory trace with new information. Augmentation of the fear memory may improve the maintenance of treatment gains following exposure therapy, because the memory can be modified and replaced with a less anxiety-evoking one. Besides, deficits of executive functioning, that is, the cognitive functions allowing for goal achievement such as planning, inhibition, and cognitive flexibility, have been extensively reported in anxious individuals, and have been associated with treatment response. Moreover, enhancement of executive functioning has been observed after successful CBT. The present study aims to test the hypothesis that incorporating reconsolidation update mechanisms to exposure-based therapy will improve treatment response in anxious youths aged 9-17 years old. We will also investigate executive functioning in our sample and potential contributions to treatment response. Our results will contribute to ameliorate exposure-based therapy protocols, will allow identifying the most at-risk youth, and may lead to the development of better targeted interventions.

column36: Elucidating the circuit-level anatomic and molecular mechanisms that mediate locomotion in neuroprosthetic rehabilitation after spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury is a devastating disease that affects individuals physically, emotionally, and economically. Currently, there is no cure for spinal cord injury. However, promising research in our laboratory has demonstrated the ability to restore voluntary motor control after severe spinal cord injury via spared nervous system circuits with a strategy termed neuroprosthetic rehabilitation: a combination of immediate motor control with electrochemical spinal cord stimulation and subsequent neuroplasticity developed with long-term training regimens. Despite these positive results, how this strategy enables control centers above the injury to use formed connections with spinal circuits below the level of injury to mediate locomotion remains unknown. The aim of this project is to elucidate the circuit-level mechanisms that mediate this process by anatomically understanding the residual connections below the level of injury then determining the functional contribution of these pathways to motor control after injury both in the short-term and in the long-term after neuroplasticity has occurred. This understanding will help with the future design of interventions that target the identified neural circuits as well as provide a stronger basis on which these interventions, including neuroprosthetic rehabilitation, can be translated into human trials to help individuals with spinal cord injury.

column36: Examining the role of bystanders and laypeople to prevent and address opioid overdose and other health emergencies: a mixed methods study
column37: Opioid overdose is now the leading cause of accidental death in North America, causing more fatalities than motor vehicle collisions. One approach to address this epidemic is to teach laypeople to identify overdose and give first aid, including calling 911 and giving naloxone, an opioid reversal agent. From its origins in public health settings, this intervention is expanding into Canadian emergency departments, hospitals and clinics. But little is known about how well this intervention works in clinical settings. This research program will explore the role and effectiveness of this intervention. First, a feasibility study will assess brief overdose training and naloxone distribution increases rates of satisfactory bystander resuscitation performance in a high-fidelity simulated opioid overdose. We hypothesize that simple training can equip laypeople to deliver essential life-saving interventions in an opioid overdose. Second, we will complete the first Canadian analysis of out-of-hospital near deaths associated with drug toxicity. Understanding the epidemiology, patterns of care, and prognosis in drug-related OHCA are prerequisites for improving the prehospital management of these patients. Third, we will conduct a systematic review of the effects of engaging laypeople in the delivery of emergency care in vulnerable and underserviced populations. This research will lay the foundation for effective overdose prevention programs in clinical settings, and deepen our understanding of the role of laypeople in the delivery of essential emergency healthcare interventions.

column37: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) describes a collection of squamous cell cancers (SCC) arising in the head and neck region. HNSCC is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to the fact that treatment options for patients with late-stage metastatic disease are limited to radiation and chemotherapy. New and effective therapies are urgently needed to help improve the lives of individuals with HNSCC. Development of novel therapeutic options relies on understanding the mechanisms that contribute to progression of HNSCC. Recent evidence indicates that interactions between tumor cells and cells of the immune system, including antibody-producing cells (B cells) and cells with direct and specific killing function (T cells), may play a role in the development of HNSCC. For example, our previous studies revealed that antibodies secreted from B cells promote the development of SCC in mouse models. In addition, it is now known that the presence of molecules that suppress the killing activity of T cells have been associated with tumor progression. The studies proposed here use mouse models of SCC as tools to study HNSCC. We will examine the hypothesis that new therapeutic approaches that target the tumor-promoting properties of B cells and also inhibit T cell suppression can improve chemotherapy responses and reduce tumor burden. Results from our research may reveal novel therapeutic targets for treatment of HNSCC. Importantly this pre-clinical modeling is being performed alongside a phase 2 proof-of-concept clinical trial evaluating whether therapeutic targeting of both B and T cell pathways slows tumor progression in patients with advanced HNSCC. We anticipate that data generated from these studies will be crucial for identifying biomarkers that stratify patients based on their likelihood to respond to therapy and will guide clinical trials by aiding the ability of clinicians to monitor disease progression, regression and/or remission.

column36: Supporting evidence-informed public health decision making in breast cancer prevention
column37: The purpose of this project is to investigate ways in which to best support the use of high quality research evidence on cancer prevention into decision making, policies and programs for cancer prevention within various public health organizations across Canada. Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada. Despite continued advances in early detection and treatment, prevention of cancer is the best way to reduce the number of cancer diagnoses and deaths due to cancer. There are many ways for individuals to reduce their cancer risk, such as physical activity, healthy eating and avoiding tobacco and alcohol, however this knowledge has not been well-translated into programs within the public health system in Canada. Through enrolment of public health professionals from various organizations across Canada, we will implement various knowledge translation strategies (tailored email messaging, educational webinars, and social media) to increase the uptake of high-quality research evidence on cancer prevention. We will evaluate which tools were most effective, and resulted in the greatest uptake of research evidence in policies and program decision making.

column36: Social Inequalities in Children's Mental Health and Development: A study of longitudinal birth cohort data from France, Denmark and Canada.
column37: Children exposed to early socioeconomic adversity have a high risk of experiencing psychological difficulties immediately and long-term. The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) model postulates negative perinatal (0-18 months) exposures have lasting consequences on development irrespective of later occurrences. Other theories place importance on the accumulation of risk and protective factors across childhood. At least two key questions on the consequences of early socio-economic adversity on child mental health remain unclear: 1) the nature and timing of the relationship between early socioeconomic adversity and later mental health and 2) factors that may provide resilience to certain children faced by early adversity. This project will test whether the perinatal period is a critical sensitive period where socioeconomic adversity durably affects brain and behavioural development. It will compare different measures of socioeconomic adversity (ex: parent income, occupation) as well as the relative importance of adversity during the childhood vs. gestational periods. Finally, it will examine whether institutional supports, such as access to day-care, may help children with an adverse start overcome the odds. High-quality, longitudinal birth cohort data from France (EDEN study, 2002 children), Denmark (DNBC study, 100 000 children) and Canada (QLSCD study, 2120 children) will be analyzed, and results will be compared across the three settings. Results will be of interest to researchers and policy makers. They will help clarify which indicators of early socioeconomic adversity are related to later development; identify sensitive periods in which family-support interventions are important; and pinpoint protective factors which should be promoted to upturn the consequences of early adversity. We hope to make an important contribution to the science aimed at promoting healthy child development and preventing the intergenerational transmission of poverty.

column36: Mismatch repair and its role in cancer predisposition
column37: Just like the spell checker in Word, cells have "spell checkers" of their own when copying their genome to ensure proper fidelity in the DNA. The spell checker that I study is called mismatch repair, which is composed of four proteins encoded by the genes MSH2, MSH6, MLH1 and PMS2. These proteins function together to correct incorrectly paired or mismatched DNA. When mismatch repair is defective, mutations like "spelling mistakes" occur in the DNA and accumulate with each cell division, paving the way to cancer. Individuals who have inherited a mutation in one of their two copies of a mismatch repair gene are at high risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancer - cancers that often arise in adults. When an individual inherits mutations in both copies of a mismatch repair gene, a more severe condition results leading to extremely high levels of mutations, causing a heightened risk of brain, blood, colon, and other cancers - which arise early in life; as children. Moreover, many tumor types eventually suffer defects in mismatch repair. Such defects are linked with tolerance to widely-used chemotherapeutic agents, and can lead to futile treatments and tumor relapse. I will be using human cell lines with inherited mutations in mismatch repair genes to study the molecular mechanisms that initiate cancer development. Specifically, I would like to understand how mismatch repair deficient cells further incapacitate their "spell checker" function allowing them to progress towards tumour development. Understanding these pathways may lead to new cancer prevention therapies to halt DNA damage and cancer progression as well as targeted therapies for mismatch repair deficient tumours.

column37: Maternal obesity and/or excess gestational weight gain are primary risk factors for childhood obesity and metabolic compromise, perpetuating a feed forward cycle of chronic disease risk for future generations. In this program we ask, how is it that exposure to an obesogenic environment in utero gives rise to children that are destined to become obese, and what are the signalling pathways? Excess adipose is associated with chronic inflammation, which has been implicated in many chronic diseases such as diabetes. It is also associated with significant changes in gut health; where changes in the composition of intestinal bacterial communities are associated with inflammation in metabolic tissues. We hypothesize that similarly, during pregnancy, excess adiposity changes the bacterial populations in a mothers gut and that these changes could cause placental inflammation modifying placental and/or fetal development, predisposing offspring to obesity and chronic disease. In this integrative multidisciplinary program we will evaluate basic biological pathways that regulate gut health and immunity in pregnancy, and whether these pathways are impaired in pregnancies characterized by excess adiposity. We will use both animal models to understand molecular mechanisms and human studies to investigate relationships between adiposity, pregnancy weight gain and the maternal gut bacteria to uncover novel pathways that mediate the early origins of childhood obesity. We will take our data, and translate it into an informative community-based, fully-developed, intervention program to support diet and lifestyle improvements in women before and during pregnancy, with a special focus on high risk populations.

column37: Suicide is the second leading cause of death among 15-24 year olds across Canada, and 10-20% of youth are affected by some kind of mental illness. However, it is estimated that only one in every five children in need of mental health services actually receives such services. Indigenous Cree youth face additional challenges to accessing services due to their remote setting. The Cree also face a legacy of colonial persecution, which has disconnected them from traditional healing methods and culturally relevant forms of support. A pan-Canadian initiative is currently underway to improve access to mental health services across the country, and the Cree community of Mistissini has been selected as one of the sites where new strategies will be developed and tested. This represents a unique opportunity to evaluate new mental health strategies as they are being rolled out. It also means there is a crucial need for youth input to ensure that these strategies address their needs and concerns. My research aims to generate a better understanding of how Cree youth think about mental illness, the reasons they decide to access or avoid mental health services, and their reactions as new strategies are taking place. I will work with Cree youth as equals throughout the research process, empowering them to think critically about the mental health challenges and resources in their community. In addition to informing the ways that mental health services can best engage youth in the Cree community, the research will generate recommendations for scaling up youth-friendly services in other communities throughout the country. By approaching the issue of mental health service access from the youth perspective, I aim to generate innovative solutions to mental health challenges that will alleviate suffering in the Cree community and beyond.

column36: Deciphering the metabolic signatures of the metabolic syndrome (MetS) in young children
column37: Babies who are born with a high amount of body fat carry this excess fat through childhood. Children who are obese often have excess abdominal fat, high blood sugar, elevated cholesterol and blood pressure, which increases their risk of diabetes and heart disease as adults. When these are present together, it is called the "Metabolic Syndrome". These risk factors may begin to develop early in life and are influenced by both "nature" (e.g. genetics) and "nurture" (e.g. a mother's diet during pregnancy, childhood diet, and physical activity). Measurement of dietary intake using questionnaires have some limitations and new biological measures have greater specificity to reflect dietary intake. We have brought together 4 multi-ethnic Canadian cohorts of pregnant mothers and their babies. The goal of our research program is to uncover markers in the blood of the pregnant mother, and child (from birth through 5 years), that reflect dietary intake and can forecast a child's likelihood of developing the "Metabolic Syndrome", a strong risk state for future diabetes and heart disease. We anticipate that these findings will strengthen the scientific evidence underpinning dietary guidelines for pregnancy and early childhood. It will also provide novel data to guide future research, and have direct relevance for clinical practice, and public health policy aimed at the prevention of heart and lung disease, and their risk factors in early life.

column36: How the early environment interacts with prenatal adversity and genetic susceptibility to moderate the risk for anxious and depressive disorders from infancy to early adolescence - the moderating effect of maternal care and the mediating effect of temperament
column37: The precocious and chronic course of depression makes it the disease with the leading cause of disability, an effect marked by a 2-fold difference in the rate for girls and women as of early adolescence. The pace of reduction in the prevalence of anxious and depressive disorders has failed to keep up with those of other chronic disorders. Arguably what is missing is not a list of risk factors, but rather a precise knowledge of how factors interact to predict those at higher risk. Findings associating prenatal experience and psychopathology provide interesting directions. Differences by gender in the response to stress are well document in early emotional development but evidence is needed in older children and adults. Genetic differences in susceptibility to prenatal events are also important. Finally, the early environment as seen in early maternal care might be a significant positive or negative influence on the effect of prenatal, gender and genetic risk. For cost-effective interventions to exploit the higher neuroplasticity in children, such a complex developmental approach is needed to identify those at risk. This is more poignant given the availability effective individual and family interventions. We will examine these important questions by means of a collaboration of 4 prolific international longitudinal cohorts, in Canada (Maternal Adversity, Vulnerability and Neurodevelopment), the United Kingdom (Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children), the Netherlands (Generation-Rotterdam) and Singapore (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Health Outcomes). With samples of 590-15,290 subjects with comparable data on prenatal exposure, genotype, early mother-child interactions and temperament as well as anxious and depressive psychopathology, we will develop a complex model of prediction of anxious and depressive psychopathology in early adolescence which would support efforts for prevention and early identification and intervention of this chronic disorder.

column36: Programmatic research to understand how modifiable environmental factors interact with the genome in the development of asthma.
column37: Lungs are for life, and we don't think about them much. Yet even small babies and children can have serious lung diseases, like asthma. In fact, asthma is the most common long-term illness that starts in very early life, and if it starts in childhood, it is a life-long problem. In asthma, the breathing passages (airways) become red, swollen and "twitchy" so they sometimes go into spasm, making it very hard to breathe. Asthma has no cure. Even if they feel fine, people with asthma still have the disease and it can flare up at any time. In Canada, about 1 in 3 people has asthma. It isn't clear why only some people get asthma, but we think it is probably due to a combination of environmental and genetic (inherited) factors. Our goal is to understand environmental and genetic factors that cause asthma in children. We will use samples and data from a large Canadian study, where the mothers and babies were assessed in pregnancy, at birth and up to age 5 years. We will determine effects of 4 carefully-chosen environmental factors predicted to be related to asthma in children: traffic pollution and the amount of green space in neighborhoods; types of bacteria living in our intestines; stress families experience during pregnancy and in the early life of a baby; and breastfeeding. We hope to gain new understanding to create better tools to predict who will get asthma and find ways to prevent asthma from developing in the first place.

column36: Determining the genetic and environmental factors associated with metabolic phenotypes across Canada
column37: The Canadian Partnership for Tomorrow Project (CPTP) is the product of $150+ million dollar investment to create a first class infrastructure to support health research internationally. It is Canada's largest population cohort with detailed data on 300,000+ adults, and a vast collection of biospecimens. The leaders of CPTP have teamed-up with scientists from a range of disciplines from air pollution science to genetics and endocrinology to enable a deeper understanding of how air pollution and the surroundings where people live interact with genes to influence cardiometabolic health. The program capitalizes on existing data and resources to address highly relevant questions for public health authorities, researchers, and health practitioners. The focus is on metabolic syndrome (MetS), a cluster of medical conditions that are common in aging adults, including: obesity, hypertension, high cholesterol, high blood sugar, and insulin resistance. Because people with MetS are more likely to develop diabetes and cardiovascular disease, this disorder represents a substantial burden on healthcare systems. MetS results from the interaction of many genes, lifestyle and the environment, including air pollution, but these mechanisms are not well understood. The activities of this program are: (1) To quantify the effect of air pollution and built environment on MetS; (2) to study the effect of air pollution on molecular changes in DNA that regulate gene activity, and to determine if these changes are associated with MetS; (3) to map differences in the DNA code that regulate the expression of genes, and see if their effect are modified by environmental factors. There are no studies on the genetic and environmental risk factors of MetS at this scale in terms of size, richness of health and genomic data. Neither is there any program that has the infrastructure to return and share data with researchers to facilitate discovery; making this an invaluable return on investment.

column36: Gene and environment effects on lung health and risk for chronic respiratory disease, asthma & COPD
column37: Chronic lung diseases such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are very common illnesses in Canada and around the world. Nearly 1 in 3 Canadians will be diagnosed with asthma in their lifetime. These diseases affect how well you can breathe, cause people to get sick and end up in hospital and even shortens their lives. We, along with other scientists, believe that the air we breathe, the things we eat and the colds we get can cause injury to the lungs of infants and children. These injuries over time can cause breathing problems such as asthma. But not everybody reacts in the same way to these exposures; and some exposures actually make your lungs even stronger. Our team of researchers will study a group of babies that have been followed since birth, whose families have filled out lots of questions about what they eat, breathe and how often they get sick. These kids and their families have also done breathing tests that measure how well their lungs are doing. From studying all of this information, we believe we can discover what things each person can do to improve their lungs and prevent them from getting chronic breathing problems, making Canada the healthiest place to live.

column36: Using bacteria-phage interaction networks as a metric for stability in the human microbiome
column37: This research proposes to combine two recent and remarkable advances: the first, the advent of powerful tools to study bacteria that reside in the human body, and the second, the recent discovery of an amazing bacterial adaptive immune system against phages, viruses that infect bacteria. Organisms that call the human body home, collectively called the human microbiome, have been linked to many serious health effects such as cancer and gastrointestinal disorders. Studies of the human microbiome have documented high variation in the types and abundances of organisms, making it difficult to determine what it means to have a healthy microbiome. I propose to develop a metric of microbiome health by studying the interactions between phages and bacteria in the human microbiome. The ongoing war between bacteria and phages has powerful effects on microbiomes, and previous work to study interactions has relied on difficult experiments limited by the fact that most microorganisms cannot be grown in a laboratory at all. I will use a pervasive bacterial immune system that records a "memory" of phage infections to construct bacteria-phage interaction networks using publicly available genetic data, overcoming the constraints of direct experiments. I will then analyze these networks for patterns that remain consistent across many individuals to develop a better understanding of the features of healthy microbiomes. This research will shed light on important unknowns about the consistency of microbiomes across many individuals, an essential milestone in the quest to understand the microbial communities that impact humans.

column36: Why is sexual communication challenging for couples? Understanding the consequences of sexual versus nonsexual communication
column37: Couples in romantic relationships may avoid engaging in critical sexual discussions because they view them as threatening to their relationship. Studies show that partners speak more tentatively to each other during sexual (as compared to nonsexual) discussions, perhaps in an attempt to reduce conflict that can arise from sexual conversations (Rehman et al., in prep). As concealing one's emotions requires mental effort, sexual communication may be mentally taxing for couples (Richards & Gross, 1999). The first goal of my doctoral dissertation is to examine whether sexual discussions are more mentally draining for couples than nonsexual discussions. Second, I explore whether sexual communication can be made less challenging for couples using a technique called cognitive reappraisal, defined here as changing one's beliefs about a concept by highlighting its benefits. In Study 1, I will examine the cognitive costs of sexual versus nonsexual discussions. Couples will be randomly assigned to discuss a sexual issue or a nonsexual issue and then complete a cognitive task. I expect that couples who discuss a sexual issue will perform worse on the task than those who discuss a nonsexual issue. In Study 2, I will examine whether cognitive reappraisal can be used to make sexual discussions less mentally challenging for couples. Couples randomly assigned to a reappraisal condition will read about the benefits of sexual communication, while those assigned to a control condition will read about the benefits of a healthy relationship. All couples will then discuss a sexual issue and complete a cognitive task. I expect that couples in the reappraisal group will perform better on the cognitive task than those in the control group. This research seeks to clarify and resolve issues that interfere with vital sexual discussions between partners. As open sexual communication fosters intimacy, this research aims to improve the quality of romantic relationships for Canadian couples.

column36: Le sexisme sur le web, un espace de reconduction des inegalites de genre
column37: Les espaces de discussion se multiplient sur le web. Les debats les plus virulents laissent parfois place a des commentaires discriminatoires, sexistes, racistes et haineux. Dans la derniere annee, les denonciations du sexisme sur le web ont marque la blogosphere quebecoise. L'anonymat relatif du web permet d'exacerber les prejuges puisqu'il n'y a pas de responsabilite immediate pour les positions tenues ou de systeme de filtrage des commentaires. Tous les jours, des femmes quebecoises y recoivent des commentaires haineux associes a leur genre, leur identite sexuelle, leur origine. Le web quebecois offre neanmoins des safe space comme lieux de ressourcement pour les militantes feministes qui luttent contre le cybersexisme. Comment s'incarne la violence faite aux femmes dans le cyberespace? Comment la violence faite aux femmes faconne-t-elle les rapports de domination dans le cyberespace? Comment la violence faite aux femmes propagee dans le cyberespace se distingue-t-elle de celle qui s'exprime sur d'autres medias? Une telle recherche s'impose en originalite dans un contexte ou la cyberviolence a l'egard des femmes est encore un phenomene relativement nouveau. Depuis quelques annees seulement, notamment depuis l'avenement du plus grand reseau social qu'est Facebook, les rapports sociaux de sexe se produisent egalement dans le cyberespace.Sujet d'actualite qui alimente les debats, c'est aussi une question fondamentale qui doit faire l'objet d'une analyse plus systematique. Or, pour le moment, cet enjeu important n'a pas ete particulierement aborde au sein du monde universitaire.

column36: "Talk the talk but can you walk the walk?" The role of inter-group dialogue programs in mobilizing young adults for peace
column37: Policy makers, researchers and activists argue that civil society is vital determinant of peace. There is limited understanding however of how do people in conflict-ridden societies mobilize for the peacebuilding effort. Farther, number of studies found that in countries characterized by intractable conflicts civil society participation in peacebuilding is actually declining. In my dissertation project I seek to examine the effectiveness and utility of efforts at the grassroots level to promote conflict resolution and peace building. A tool often applied by civil society for grass-roots-level peace building is inter-group dialogue programs. I use the Israeli-Palestinian inter-group dialogue programs as study case to examine whether participation in such projects mobilizes university students from conflicting groups to actively engage in civil society. The study examines diverse sample of programs to accommodate variability in contents, duration and structure. The research design combines quantitative methods, longitudinal survey, and qualitative methods, interviews and participant observation, to provide a thorough and comprehensive account of the various factors contributing to the success or failure of grassroots programs in mobilizing civil society activism. Insights obtained by the research can contribute to reconciliation and peacebuilding efforts among groups in protracted asymmetrical conflicts, as well as groups engaged in latent or nonviolent conflict. Canada is a multi-cultural and diverse society, it can therefore profit from lessons on initiatives that mobilize young citizens to meaningful civic engagement and effective approaches to conflict resolution. Systematic examination of mobilization as an indicator of individual change is a methodological contribution to ongoing scholarly discourse regarding the assessment measures of programs aimed to create social change.

column36: Thinking with trees to see the forest: Huayruro and the lived experience of deforestation in San Martin, Peru
column37: Without a radical rethinking of our relationship to forests, conservation efforts will be unable to address the rapid disappearance of the world's forests. This is important not only because of species loss, but because of the reality of climate change and a warming world. In Peru, forest loss causes 33% of national carbon dioxide emissions (MINAM 2014b). In the Amazon basin, and in Peru in particular, the largest cause of deforestation is the expanding agricultural frontier. The Peruvian Andean Amazon region of San Martin consistently has the highest rate of forest loss in the country, despite also having the greatest biological diversity. This anthropological research looks at peoples' lived experiences of deforestation by focusing on Amazonian peoples' use of the tree "huayruro" (Ormosia coccinea, Ormosia sunkei). The hardwood tree is used in construction, and its vibrant red and black seeds are used both in souvenirs and as a powerful good luck talisman. Artisans who use the seed to make jewelry note that it is no longer as readily found in the forests as before. Amazonian peoples, the Kichwa-Lamista and Awajun in particular, recognize each tree and plant as having a spirit and as being an individual. For them, knowledge comes from nature - primarily through ingestion of strong medicinal plants. How do these histories of intimate engagement with forests, and recognition of the animacy and power of plants, translate into ordinary interactions with a non-medicinal tree species? Why is the huayruro considered to be powerful for people living in the Upper Mayo and Lower Huallaga watersheds? And how can Amazonian peoples' use of this tree as both a timber and a non-timber product help us understand the lived reality of deforestation?

column36: The Michif language continuum: Supporting language vitality in Metis communities of Manitoba and Saskatchewan through language documentation and sociolinguistic study
column37: The Michif language continuum presents a fascinating linguistic case. A truly mixed language, Michif incorporates Canadian French nouns and Cree verbs, with some lexical borrowings from other indigenous languages such as Ojibwe and Dene. French Michif, a variety of Michif, has a Canadian French foundation with significant Cree influences. The origin of how the Michif languages came to be is still not well known and there are now approximately 650 speakers left in Canada. As Michif is disappearing, steps towards revitalization need to be taken: these include efforts to document the language from remaining speakers to study language variation and assessments of speakers' attitudes towards their language. The goal of this research project will be to address these steps and explore the following questions: how important is the Michif language to the identity of the Metis people of Canada and how crucial is its preservation to the well-being and prosperity of its communities? The project will be a collaborative project with community members and speakers of Michif in Manitoba and Saskatchewan Metis communities and an opportunity to be attentive to their needs. It will also explore social and economic issues that impact language perceptions, transmission and vitality. As well, it will consider accounts of the origin of French Michif and Michif, which is still not well understood. Among the many contributions that can be made by the study of Linguistics, none is more important than the preservation and promotion of endangered languages, such as Michif. After all, a language is the voice of a culture and a people. I believe that valorization of a language is a means of giving importance to the history and the stories that it tells, to a way of thinking and a way of life. The uniqueness and richness of the Michif language and culture are one of the jewels of Western Canada's heritage and identity. To see it preserved and revitalized would benefit everyone.

column36: Therapeutic interventions to impact lung inflammatory responses induced by exposure to environmental pollutants
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a term that encompasses a number of diseases such as chronic bronchitis & emphysema, is a progressive inflammatory condition of the lungs predominantly caused by inhalation of ambient pollutants such as cigarette smoke and air pollution. COPD is a worldwide public health problem that has been projected to be the 3rd leading cause of death and 5th leading cause of disability by 2020 worldwide. Recent epidemiological studies have shown that subjects with COPD and asthma taking statins to control high blood cholesterol suffer fewer exacerbations of their lung disease. We have shown that in animal studies, statins reduce lung inflammation caused by exposure to ambient urban air pollutants. Statins are known to have anti-inflammatory properties, and we suspect that these qualities are responsible for the beneficial effect in subjects with inflammatory lung diseases. Here we propose to directly test the effect of these medications on lung inflammation in subjects with COPD. We will target the lung macrophage, one of the pivotal cells in the lung responsible for processing and clearing the inhaled toxins and particles from the lung. We will use novel state-of-the-art technology to explore the effects of statins on lung inflammation in COPD and specifically on lung macrophages. In addition, it has recently been shown that the lung has its own microbiome (bacterial flora) and several studies have shown that this microbiome is closely linked to the inflammatory response in the lung. Here we will also investigate the impact of statin treatment on the lung microbiome of subjects with COPD. New treatments for COPD are urgently needed and these studies will test statin treatment as a new therapeutic approach to impact lung inflammatory pathways in COPD.

column36: Leukodystrophy: A Translational Research Program
column37: Leukodystrophies are a group of rare genetic diseases affecting previously healthy children and leading to progressive disabilities and death over months to years. Unfortunately, no curative treatment is available. It is estimated that 30-50% of patients remain without a precise diagnosis despite multiple tests. The first step to discover a treatment is to understand the causes of the diseases and therefore, to identify the causal genes. Leukodystrophies are characterized by abnormal white matter (myelin) of the brain. Myelin is responsible for the insulation of brain cells (neurons), allowing fast electric conduction in the nervous system. Leukodystrophies are classified as hypomyelinating (lack of myelin formation) and non-hypomyelinating (abnormal myelin maintenance) based on features seen in brain scans. My research program focuses on hypomyelinating leukodystrophies, and more specifically on one disorder called POLR3-related or 4H leukodystrophy. Children with this disease develop progressive difficulties to walk, talk, swallow and see (myopia). 4H is caused by mutations in 3 genes that are important for survival of the cells. Using 4H as my primary disease of interest, my comprehensive research program aims at describing these diseases, including their evolution over time and their impact on patients and their families, finding causal genes and explaining how mutations lead to disease (pathophysiology) in order to improve medical care for the patients and families, find new treatments and prepare for the upcoming clinical trials.

column36: The influence of neurogenetics and stressful experience on emotionally-biased attention and learning
column37: Individuals vary hugely in the aspects of the world they perceive and remember: Some filter their environments through rose coloured glasses to perceive sources of pleasure, while others are overly tuned to signs of threat. Such affective biases in attention are distorted in emotional disorders such as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) as well as in addiction. It has been estimated that mental health disorders, including PTSD, anxiety, depression, and addiction disorders are the second leading cause of disability and premature death in Canada, costing the Canadian Health Care system ~$51 million annually. Given such costs, focused research on individual differences influencing neural circuitry and behaviours that contribute to such symptoms is essential. Yet much remains to be learned about neural mechanisms underlying such biases, and the factors that influence their potential for change. This study will investigate how common variations in genes that influence the activity of neurochemicals, or brain chemicals that influence how the brain functions, influence such biases, and how these can go awry in major depression and PTSD. Understanding these patterns will allow us to better predict why certain individuals may be more vulnerable to emotional disorders and addiction than others in the face of life's stresses. It will also help us to determine how different people may respond to specific treatments differently, where what helps one person harms another, to aid in developing individually tailored treatments.

This paradigm is useful in the study of uncommon diseases. An example of an uncommon disease is scleroderma. SSc is a disease that can affect the skin, joints and lungs. There is no cure. The leading cause of death for Canadians with SSc is high pressure in the lungs called pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Lung transplant may help those with end-stage lung disease. We will develop innovative research methods for all researchers who study uncommon diseases.

column36: Role of Embryonic-Derived Cardiac Macrophages in Tissue Repair
column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death not only in Canada, but worldwide. After heart tissue is injured, immune cells become activated and are both required to repair injured tissue, but also can themselves cause tissue damage. It was unclear how immune cells could possess such opposing roles. Our new work has revealed that prior to birth, primitive immune cells called macrophages enter the heart and remain there into adulthood. These primitive macrophages help experimental animals heal after heart tissue injury. In contrast, macrophages that arise in adults also can enter the heart after injury and promote tissue damage. Over the next 5 years our lab will investigate how these different immune cells are related to heart disease in animals and humans in order to improve the ability of heart tissue to repair itself after injury.

column36: Towards the use of Epigenetic Therapy as a Primer for Cancer Immunotherapy
column37: The main premise of Cancer Immunotherapy is to stimulate the patient's immune system to attack the malignant tumour cells. Recent progress in cancer immunotherapy protocols has led to exciting clinical results in several types of solid tumours. However, for some cancer types, such as Colorectal Cancer and Ovarian Cancer, the majority of patients do not respond to this type of anti-cancer approach, suggesting the need to combine immunotherapies with other anti-tumour strategies. Unfortunately, chemotherapy - the mainstay of cancer treatment for over 40 years - is immunosuppressive and not suitable for combination with immunotherapy. On the other hand, the new class of therapeutics called epigenetic therapies hold great potential for enhancing anti-tumour immune response and for potential use in combination with immunotherapy. We have found that DNA demethylating drugs can activate immunogenic signals in cancer cells, such as those that engage the interferon and antiviral pathways. We will investigate how this process happens and how it can be used to increase the tumour cell immunogenicity and to improve the immune response against the tumour. We will also evaluate new epigenetic therapeutic strategies that can improve the efficacy of anti-tumour immunotherapy.

column36: Targeting Epigenetic Mechanisms in Prostate Cancer
column37: Prostate Cancer (PCa) is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men in Canada. Although cure can be accomplished when the cancer is detected at its early stages, there is currently no curative treatment when the cancer has metastasized, a phenomenon that is accompanied by the appearance of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). The major clinical challenges in PCa are thus the lack of biomarkers that can distinguish early stage, indonent from more aggressive forms of PCa, and the lack of effective treatment for the CRPC. PCa is one the most heritable disease, and more than one hundred genetic variants have been found to increase the risk of PCa -cumulatively explaining 33% of the familial risk for PCa. Understanding of how the genetic variants predispose PCa provides opportunities to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. A few of the risk genetic variants affect genes that translate into protein, but the majority of them don't. About 1.5% of the human genome encodes protein-coding genes, and about 70% encodes genes that do not translate into protein, which are named as noncoding RNAs. Noncoding RNAs function through epigenetic regulation. Unlike genetics that is irreversible, epigenetics can be reversed by various approaches. Through computational analysis, we have identified sixty noncoding RNAs affected by more than half of the genetic variants in PCa. We propose to further investigate how these genetic variants affect noncoding RNAs, and through what epigenetic mechanisms these noncoding RNAs promote PCa development and progression. Finally, we will target these epigenetic mechanisms to improve the treatment of PCa. By revealing the functional nature of specific genetic variants our proposed research may identify specific genetic and lncRNA biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This will favor personalized/precision medicine where therapies are tailored to the unique genetic identity of each patient.

column36: Image-based evaluation of orthopaedic devices and surgical procedures
column37: New orthopaedic implants are routinely introduced by device manufacturers, and are implanted in over 100,000 Canadians per year. Yet a recent study found no benefit from the introduction of any new implant design over a five-year period, with a third of those devices performing worse than the ones they replaced. This has led to device recalls, thousands of revision surgeries, and multi-billion dollar lawsuits. Even with well functioning devices, one in five knee replacement patients are dissatisfied with the procedure, for reasons that are indeterminate with currently available tools. There is a clear need to better identify appropriate targets for innovation, and properly select the patients who could benefit from that innovation. I have developed new techniques to measure hip and knee implant wear using high resolution CT scanning (micro-CT) for preclinical imaging, and video x-rays (fluoroscopy) for clinical imaging. Over the next five years, I will build on this experience, expanding my research to include upper extremity joints and implementing sensor technology alongside these advanced x-ray imaging techniques. The goal will be to measure domains that limit implant performance and patient outcomes, including implant wear, joint instability, and patient activity. Imaging tools will be shared with collaborating researchers at other institutions, and knowledge surrounding specific devices and surgical techniques will be provided to surgeons.

column36: Investigating pathogenesis of blood-borne infections among people who use illicit drugs
column37: The substantial toll from the intertwined epidemics of addiction to illicit drugs and infection with viruses like HIV and hepatitis C remains a leading public health concern in Canada. People addicted to illicit drugs, especially those who use them via intravenous injection, suffer high levels of preventable morbidity and mortality from a variety of causes. Although much research to date has focused on interventions to prevent new cases of HIV and HCV, the determinants of access and adherence to treatment for these infections remain poorly investigated. Understanding ways to optimize treatment outcomes among drug users is becoming increasingly important, especially in light of new efforts to eliminate new cases of HIV through improved testing and care, such as the United Nations' recently announced 90-90-90 initiative, based on the Treatment-as-Prevention (TasP) approach. Over the next five years, my goal is to continue to develop my programme of rigorous and consequential research that contributes to efforts to reduce the extremely elevated rates of morbidity, mortality and associated healthcare costs among people addicted to illicit drugs. The objectives of my research programme are to identify contextual barriers to optimal HIV care; map areas of elevated levels of uncontrolled HIV infection and investigate their causes; evaluate new efforts to improve HIV/AIDS treatment outcomes, like harm reduction-based services; and evaluate knowledge and attitudes towards new treatments for hepatitis C virus infection. I will address these objectives using data from the ACCESS study, my ongoing prospective cohort study of approximately 900 HIV-positive people who use illicit drugs living in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. My strong research foundation includes an appointment as an assistant professor at the University of British Columbia and a research scientist at the BC Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS.

column36: The Development of Novel Therapeutic and Preventative Strategies for Kidney Stone Disease
column37: This research will prevent urinary tract infections in patients with ureteral stents, as the attachment of bacteria to these tubes is a common cause for hospital acquired infections. Ureteral stents are commonly used by a urologic surgeon in the treatment of kidney stones or other issues causing the ureter to become blocked. Urinary devices account for >80% of hospital acquired infections which are difficult to treat. In addition to increased mortality, these complications add millions of extra health care costs. Currently, antibiotics are our only method of attempting to deal with these infections, but they do not work well due to bacteria forming large communities on the surface of these devices, called biofilms, that can not be penetrated by antibiotics, therefore making them highly resistant. The project included in this application is based on the latest breakthroughs by the Lange, Straus, Kizhakkedathu, and Hancock laboratories at UBC on the development of a novel universal method to coat these devices with novel short broad spectrum anti-bioflim peptides (ABPs) designed to prevent proteins and other components from urine as well as bacteria from attaching to the surface of ureteral stents, thereby decreasing the number of infections caused by these devices. We anticipate that the technologies developed will help the more than 3 million Canadians who need urological intervention each year. The project will establish a strong collaboration among natural science, and medicine, and provide unique HQP training opportunities. The novel anti-infection coatings will also provide a general method for preventing infections associated with other medical devices.

column36: Maximizing Independence through the Use of Assistive Technology
column37: Within the next 25 years, the number of Canadians over the age of 65 will double. This, coupled with an anticipated rise in lifestyle diseases (e.g. diabetes), will cause disability rates to increase dramatically. Assistive technology refers to any device that is used to maintain or improve the functional capabilities of people with disabilities. In light of increasing demands on care providers and the health-care system, assistive technology is crucial to maintain and to maximize the health of Canada's ageing population. Over the next five years, I will continue my program of research in the area of assistive technology, whose goals are to: (1) improve how existing devices are used, (2) evaluate how assistive technology devices are currently used and improve how outcomes are measured, and (3) help create novel devices to meet users' needs better. As an independent investigator, I am carrying out five projects. 1) I am conducting an experiment to evaluate the effect of scooter skills training on users. 2) I am exploring the experiences of individuals ageing with spinal cord injury (SCI) and those who sustain a SCI later in life. 3) I am developing a mobile platform to enable individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) to learn disease self-management skills. 4) I am leading a project to improve social participation among individuals with mobility impairments. 5) I am identifying novel assistive technology solutions to help informal caregivers of older adults. Ultimately, my research will enable assistive technology users to be more independent, which will improve their quality of life and decrease reliance on informal and formal caregivers and the health-care system.

column36: Leaving the Familiar Behind: Predictors of Friendship Formation and Social Integration in New Communities
column37: Social connections and social support networks are essential for physical and mental health. In fact, how long people live is better predicted by the quality of their social relationships and how well they are integrated in their community, than it is by how much they smoke and drink, or whether they are obese. Loneliness, on the other hand, is strongly associated with negative health outcomes including depression, poor sleep quality, more hospital and doctor visits, and compromised immune system functioning. My research investigates the processes involved in successful social interactions with strangers, friendship formation, and social integration. I focus on questions including: What motivates people to seek social contact, and why do some people have a harder time making friends than others? How do people cope successfully with social stress and social setbacks? How do people develop a larger sense of belonging when they move to a new community? These are timely topics, given that North American cultures are characterized by high rates of immigration and residential mobility. Specifically, I will examine whether and how genetic variants, psychological beliefs about oneself and others, and specific behaviours such as eye contact and mimicry, influence the outcome of social interactions. I will also investigate the long-term consequences of neurobiology, beliefs, and behaviour on the social integration outcomes of people moving to a new community. Moving to a new community can be highly stressful, and successfully establishing a new social support network during this transition has substantial long-term effects on health. Indeed, social support is one of the most important buffers against the detrimental effects of stress. In the long term, I plan to use the findings of this research to identify people who are likely to experience difficulty transitioning into new environments and to develop strategies for promoting healthy coping and socialization.

column36: Molecular And Cellular Mechanisms Leading To Pancreatic Cancer Heterogeneity
column37: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the fourth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. This cancer has been called a "silent killer" because it often does not cause symptoms until very late stages of the disease. At this point, treatment options are limited because the tumor is very resistant to chemotherapy and surgery is often not an option. There are, however, documented cases of patients responding exceptionally well to therapy. This variable therapeutic response emphasizes that there are differences between tumors, which is also known as heterogeneity. Pancreatic cancer heterogeneity has also been observed through differential expression of genes between tumors, but it is unclear what molecular or cellular mechanisms underlie the development of this variability. To improve disease outcomes, we need to better understand what causes this heterogeneity so that we can identify diagnostic tools to robustly identify tumor subtypes. If we can identify tumor subtypes, we can then develop effective treatments against those subsets. To begin to understand heterogeneity, we will use animal models to manipulate characteristics underlying tumor initiation and examine their impact on tumor heterogeneity. Briefly, we will examine whether combinations of different initiating cell types or gene mutations result in differences in tumor appearance, gene expression, or the type of additional mutations present in the tumor. We will then determine whether key differences identified in our models identify subsets of human tumors with distinct clinical outcomes. These studies will expand our understanding of factors underlying the development of tumor heterogeneity and also provide preclinical models to test novel therapeutic strategies potentially revealed by our studies. The knowledge generated by this research will aid identification of molecular markers that can reproducibly identify human PDAC subtypes with distinct therapeutic responses and clinical outcomes.

column36: Understanding the contribution of long chain omega-3 balance in brain health
column37: The brain develops until approximately 6 years of age, and is the tissue with the highest lipid concentration, after adipose tissues. Between the ages of 20 and 100, the brain undergoes physiological changes with the loss of nearly 20% of its weight - mostly in lipids. The brain is especially rich in long-chain fatty acids such as docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and arachidonic acid (ARA). Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) intake seems to be efficient in animal studies to promote neurodevelopment and prevent onset of cognitive decline but there is controversy towards this strategy in humans. My hypothesis is that DHA plays a role in human brain functions and cognition but this is conditional to DHA efficacy. In this program, we will investigate three conditions which we have found to alter DHA efficacy: aging, the presence of the APOE4 allele (most important genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease), and diabetic pregnancy. From this new starting point, I aim to answer these questions: what are the conditions needed to achieve efficacy, by which means could DHA supplementation benefit human brain function, does it necessarily involve cerebrovascular health? For this, we will complete our current randomized control trial (300 participants), we will test whether there are breakdown in the cerebrovascular system of APOE4 mice during aging, we will test the relation between DHA supplementation and cerebral oxygenation and vascular functions in humans and we will evaluate DHA transfer to the fetus during diabetic pregnancies and evaluate whether this is linked with neurodevelopment evaluated by electroencephalography. This program focuses on two of the most vulnerable populations suffering from brain diseases - the babies and the elderly - with the ultimate goal of promoting brain health throughout the entire life span.

column36: Prevent metastatic disease by characterizing and targeting postoperative immunosuppression
column37: Surgery is one of the most important steps in curative cancer treatment. Most patients with solid tumors have an operation to remove the tumor, but for many patients the cancer will come back, often spreading to distant organs. My research and that of others has shown that surgery increases the spread of cancer to distant sites by weakening the immune system. Despite this, patients do not get immune boosting treatment to prevent cancer spread. My research is focused on understanding how immune cells are involved in the spread of tumor cells after surgery so that more effective and less toxic treatments can be given to patients around the time of their operation. In this proposal, I will study how surgery increases the amount of suppressor cells in the body, how suppressor cells impair natural killer immune cells, how natural killer cells are weakened following surgery and how novel immunotherapies can target these immune cells and prevent cancer recurrence in order to improve cancer survival.

column36: Integrating innovative interventions promoting social participation to foster health in aging Canadians
column37: Social participation, which involves activities that meet fundamental needs for interactions and self-actualization, is seriously challenged in aging and a major intervention target. Although included in health orientations, few social participation interventions are implemented in Canada. Our recent research demonstrated the feasibility and positive impact of clinical interventions in increasing seniors' functional autonomy, social participation and quality of life. However, to reach a substantial number of seniors, population interventions are also needed. Over the next five years, we will continue to develop, implement and evaluate clinical and population interventions targeting the social participation of older adults. Specifically, we will evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of two clinical interventions with older adults from pilot communities: the Personalized citizen assistance for social participation (APIC; Obj.1) and the Lifestyle Redesign(R) (Obj.2), in helping community organizations and clinicians target social participation. In parallel, one population intervention, the Index of Social Participation Potential (IPPS), will be developed, implemented and evaluated (Obj.3) to guide municipal stakeholders in identifying policies, services and structures that best foster social participation among seniors. Development of the IPPS will be enriched by exploring how age-friendly key components foster positive health, social participation and health equity of aging adults across Canada (Obj.4). These innovations, i.e. APIC, Lifestyle Redesign(R) and IPPS, will be optimized and integrated in one multicomponent intervention, implemented and evaluated in other communities (Obj.5). Our preliminary results suggest that this multicomponent intervention will foster social participation in aging. Since most chronic diseases can be prevented or delayed by an active lifestyle, our results point to one of the most promising avenues to live longer and better.

column36: Developmental Coordination Disorder: Integrating Brain Imaging and Rehabilitation to Improve Outcomes
column37: Developmental coordination disorder (DCD) is a common condition that affects 5-6% of school-aged children, or 1-2 children in every Canadian classroom. Children with DCD find it hard to learn motor skills and perform everyday activities, such as getting dressed, tying shoelaces, using a fork and knife, printing, riding a bicycle, or playing sports. Children with DCD often feel lonely, depressed or anxious, and may have low self-esteem and problems with peers. They also tend to avoid physical and social activities, which further affects their friendships. DCD is a life-long condition that affects school performance, vocational choices, and leisure activities. Up to 50% of children with DCD will also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which further compounds the difficulties that these children face in daily life. We do not know what causes DCD, but we think there are differences in brain development and brain function in children with DCD compared to typical children. Our previous studies have shown that children with DCD use different brain areas to perform and learn motor skills compared to typically-developing children. Having a better understanding of other brain differences will help to explain why children with DCD struggle to learn motor skills. We can then determine if we can change the brain and improve motor skills through rehabilitation. In this study, we will use MRI to compare images of children's brains to accomplish two goals: (1) determine how the brain differs in children with DCD and children with DCD+ADHD compared to typically-developing children; (2) determine if rehabilitation can change the brain and improve motor function of children with DCD+/-ADHD. This study is the first of its kind and will advance our understanding of DCD and hopefully improve outcomes of affected children. Findings will provide evidence for current treatment approaches or offer insight into developing alternate interventions.

column36: Developing Adequate Protein and Energy Recommendations for the Prevention and Treatment of Sarcopenia in Cancer
column37: Two out of five Canadians will develop cancer in their lifetimes. People with cancer lose significant amounts of muscle mass due to the disease itself or its treatment. Low muscle mass, also termed sarcopenia is a common and important factor leading to worse outcomes to those with cancer. These include physical disability, frailty, extended hospitalization, infectious complications, poorer quality of life, cancer progression and shorter survival. Eating an adequate amount of protein and energy is essential to sustain muscle mass but our current nutritional recommendations are not specific to people with cancer, and have not been developed based on scientific evidence. This research will be the first to study the energy and protein needs of people with cancer and to determine the efficacy of different protein and energy ratio diets for halting and correcting cancer-associated muscle loss and its related health consequences. The outcomes of this research have immediate implication for people with cancer. By improving principles of optimal nutrition intervention to counteract sarcopenia, we will improve well-being and survival, ultimately reducing the burden on Canada's health care system.

column36: Respiratory Evaluation Sciences Program (RESP): Innovations in analytic approaches to improve efficiency in respiratory care
column37: Chronic respiratory diseases, in particular asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), are among the leading causes of death and disability, and contribute to our raising health care costs. column36: Novel health informatics solutions for improving the management of nursing resources and patient safety in acute care hospitals
column37: Adverse events (AEs) occur in 2.9% to 16.6% of all acute care hospitalizations and are responsible for 44,000 to 98,000 deaths each year. Moreover, it is estimated that 30% to 58% of all AEs are preventable. Recent studies suggest that understaffing and certain nurse staffing policies, such as the use of less qualified nursing staff and of overtime hours to meet peak staffing demands, could significantly contribute to the occurrence of preventable AEs. However, there is scant evidence-based information to guide nursing managers in defining the optimal numbers and mixes of nursing staff that are required to minimize the risk of AE. To meet this need, longitudinal studies are required to systematically examine the relationship between various nurse staffing policies and the occurrence of AEs, as well as to define safe staffing policies. Until recently, the detailed data required to conduct such an investigation were not easily accessible. With the advent of electronic health records and the digital capture of nurse staffing data, there is now an exciting opportunity to optimize the management of nursing resources in acute care hospitals. The goal of this program of research is to determine if: a) nurse staffing policies are associated with an increased risk of AEs, b) the risk of AEs in relationship to nurse staffing policies is modified by the complexity of patient requirements and, c) optimal nurse staffing thresholds can be established by level of patient complexity. An important prerequisite to answer these important questions in the management of nursing staff in acute care hospitals is to have access to accurate measures of AE occurrence. For this reason, a fourth objective of this program of research is to pursue the development and the validation of such measures.

column36: The Molecular Mechanisms that Regulate Immunological 'Exhaustion' in Chronic conditions
column37: A certain immune cell type, killer T cells, play an important role in controlling chronic infections such as HIV and cancer. My group has discovered that certain killer T cells are genetically different in a very small percentage of people with HIV. These people have natural immunity that prevents disease progression to AIDS. The killer T cells continue to function at a high level and destroy HIV infected cells to ensure that the virus cannot reproduce to the extent of full blown AIDS. However, in most of people these cells become dysfunctional and unable to eliminate infected cells and tumor cells in the course of chronic infections and cancer. My research focuses on better understanding why these killer T cells become dysfunctional and how we can restore their functionality. I will be developing novel immunotherapy approaches to use person's immune system to fight back chronic infections and cancer. Until recently, most cancer immunotherapies did not work for most patients, or caused severe side effects. The dream of a successful cancer immunotherapy only came to life in the last few years. Science, one of the top scientific magazines named this new approach 'breakthrough of the year' for 2013. This breakthrough approach targets a way to re-start the immune system, using immune checkpoints' inhibitors. These immune checkpoints' inhibitors jump-start a patient's immune system to recognize and kill infected cells and tumors. They are game-changers for chronic infections and cancer. Using immune checkpoints' inhibitor therapy is revolutionizing cancer treatment by manipulating a person's immune system to fight their infected cells and cancer cells. I aim to understand how killer T cells become dysfunctional in the context of HIV and cancer in order to develop novel immunotherapy drugs. I will identify and develop novel immunotherapy approaches to target these immune checkpoints to allow killer T cells to stay protective and kill infected cells and cancer cells.
