column36: Understanding the generation and protective functions of broadly-neutralizing humoral immune responses against influenza A virus
column37: Influenza virus is one of the top ten leading causes of death in Canada, and remains one of the gravest threats to global public health due to its propensity to cause pandemics. To combat seasonal influenza epidemics, massive annual vaccination programs are carried out at tremendous expense to the healthcare system. The ability of influenza virus to cause seasonal epidemics is conferred by its capacity to rapidly evolve in order to escape pre-existing immunity. This in turn necessitates that influenza virus vaccines be reformulated on a nearly annual basis. Frequently, the strains of influenza virus that actually circulate do not perfectly resemble the strains included in the vaccine. Due to the exquisitely strain-specific immunity that current vaccines elicit, vaccine efficacy can suffer substantially when imperfect matches occur. More importantly, current vaccines offer little to no protection against the emergence of a novel influenza virus pandemic. Therefore, there is a tremendous need to develop new influenza virus vaccines capable of inducing broad and long-lasting protection. The recent discovery of broadly-neutralizing antibodies that bind to the stalk domain of hemagglutinin has raised the hope that development of a "universal" influenza virus vaccine may be within reach. While many studies have addressed how these antibodies function in isolation, little is known about the way that broadly-neutralizing antibodies are generated and function in the context of the polyclonal responses that are naturally elicited by vaccination and infection. Our studies will define the mechanisms that govern the generation and function of broadly-neutralizing antibodies in the context of the polyclonal response to infection and vaccination. The knowledge gained from these studies will be used to advance the development of "universal" influenza virus vaccines and therapeutics which have the potential to substantially reduce the global burden of influenza-related illnesses.

Changes in gene regulation often underlie the mechanism of genetic disorders and cancer. These changes can arise from variation in genomic DNA sequence. They can also come from alterations in epigenomic properties, such as DNA methylation, chromatin packaging, histone modifications, or 3D chromosome conformation. New sequencing technology reveals a forest of genomic and epigenomic variation, but we are hindered by insufficient understanding of the variation's consequences. As a result, we can apply these data to diagnosis or personalized drug therapy only in limited cases. My research program addresses this gap in knowledge to understand interactions between genome, epigenome, and phenotype in human cancers. My program applies a systematic framework to create and validate predictive models of (1) how genetic variants cause epigenomic changes, and (2) the effect of epigenomic changes on gene regulation and phenotype. First, we start with data from collaborators or public resources, using cancer cell lines and cancer patient primary tissue. Second, we develop machine learning models of how a genomic or epigenomic input leads to an epigenomic or phenotypic output. Third, we perturb input data and predict changes in output. Fourth, we validate predictions with targeted experiments. Our research will yield better understanding of the impact of epigenomic changes in cancer. It will also deliver new software and annotations to help biologists and clinicians assess changes in the noncoding sequence and epigenome of cancer patients.

column36: Cell surface signaling microdomains in heath and disease
column37: Tumours are made up of cells that can be recognized by doctors and scientists by several changes they exhibit compared to normal cells. Some of these changes involve alteration in the abundance and function of a family of proteins called receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) within tumour cells. These changes in the function of RTKs are required for tumours to grow and spread in the body. Obtaining a better understanding of how a cell controls RTKs (and related proteins) has the potential to provide new ways to treat tumours and prevent cancer spreading. One member of the RTK family of particular interest is named Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). Much has been learned about how EGFR functions to control the behaviour and growth of cells, mostly by identifying the other proteins in a cell required for EGFR to do this. However, much like knowing the name of dancers does not tell us much about the dance that they will perform, we need to know more than the identify of proteins that work with EGFR to control cell growth and spread: we need to understand their choreography. In molecular terms, we need to understand the organization of EGFR and other key proteins in space and time. We have recently discovered that EGFR signals must be organized in structures called clathrin-coated signaling microdomains to control cell growth and movement. Using advanced microscopy that allow us to 'see' the movement of EGFR and other key proteins (dancers), we aim to understand how these clathrin-coated signaling microdomains work in normal cells and how they are disrupted in cancer cells. Understanding how these structures control the "dance" of EGFR required to dictate cell growth and movement has the potential to allow the development of new therapies aimed at changing the "beat" to control how RTKs drive tumour growth and spreading. Hence, our research aims to help uncover novel strategies to treat certain types of cancer that are difficult to treat with existing therapies.

column36: Preventing Injecting by Modifying Existing Responses (PRIMER)
column37: Injection drug use remains a primary source of HIV transmission globally, and people who inject drugs (PWID) have been shown to play a key role in the initiation of others into injecting. However, no interventions to prevent injecting initiation are proven effective. Importantly, ongoing exposure to injecting increases the risk that street youth and other 'at-risk' populations might initiate injecting, and data suggest that the majority of non-injectors are initiated into injecting by PWID. Reducing the exposure of street youth to injecting is therefore likely to reduce their risk of initiation into injection. This multicountry, mixed methods project will therefore investigate whether a range of interventions and factors that influence injecting among PWID (opioid substitution therapy, supervised injection facilities, stable housing, incarceration environments, public injecting, and gender) may also influence the risk that they initiate others into injecting. This study will seek to: 1) determine how often PWID initiate others into injecting; 2) assess factors potentially influencing the risk that PWID initiate others into injecting; 3) investigate drug scene roles (i.e., drug dealer) that increase the risk that PWID might initiate others into injecting; and 4) test the impact of an existing structural or biomedical intervention on the risk that PWID will initiate others into injecting. To accomplish this, we will conduct a multi-site study of 3,050 PWID across North America and France employing quantitative and qualitative data from five separate ongoing observational studies of PWID (San Diego, STAHR; Tijuana, El Cuete; Vancouver, VIDUS/ARYS; Toronto, HHiT, Bordeaux/Marseille/Paris, COSINUS). This project is the first study to investigate structural approaches to reducing HIV risk by preventing injecting initiation. This novel approach addresses a major gap in HIV prevention programming.

column36: Stiffness as a novel biomarker and therapeutic target for kidney fibrosis
column37: Scarring is a major cause of organ failure, accounting for up to 50% of all deaths in the developed world. In the kidney, scarring is the final common pathway of damage activated by nearly all forms of chronic kidney disease. If left unchecked, kidney scarring can lead to kidney failure, an increasingly common, costly, and life-threatening condition requiring dialysis or kidney transplantation for survival. Unfortunately, clinicians have no safe and effective ways to diagnose or treat kidney scarring currently. Following injury and especially with scarring, organs stiffen. My lab has been working on ways to take advantage of this knowledge to better diagnose and treat kidney scarring, to identify those patients at highest risk for kidney failure and to treat these individuals with new anti-scarring treatments. In the first set of studies described in this application, we will take advantage of our discovery: (1) that fibroblasts, the main producers of kidney scar tissue, can sense stiffening after injury, and (2) that this stiffening makes them more sensitive to pro-scarring stimuli. We will explore how fibroblasts sense kidney stiffening, to develop new treatments that block the ability of fibroblasts to recognize that stiffening is occurring, and therefore that shut off the scarring process. In the second set of studies, we will take advantage of our recent development of new MRI techniques that can image the stiffness of a kidney without needles or surgery. Our goal is to test: (1) whether MRI measures of kidney stiffness are accurate, (2) whether they correlate with kidney scar measurements as determined by gold standard analysis of kidney biopsies, and (3) whether they predict if kidney function will decline. Given the importance of scarring to kidney disease, our expectation is that these studies, through improving the care of kidney scarring, will ultimately improve the lives of patients with kidney disease.

column37: Mothers have been crucial to infant survival and well-being through time, yet now they are minimally involved in critical care settings. Whereas much of the past neonatal research examined what was provided to families, this research seeks to identify what parents can contribute to optimizing their child's outcomes. In sum, health outcomes of Canadians and the efficiency of health systems will be improved as a result of this research.

column36: Impairments of cortical GABAergic interneurons in epilepsy
column37: Epileptic encephalopathies (EE) are severe childhood-onset epilepsies with developmental delay or intellectual deficiency. These disorders were of unknown etiology up to recently. The advent of next-generation sequencing has revolutionized our ability to identify the cause of EE in many patients and to discover new candidate EE genes in most of the other patients. My work focuses on the identification of the genetic causes of EE and on the discovery of new candidate genes using whole-genome sequencing in a large cohort of children with unexplained EE. Furthermore, I have developed means to selectively repress or mutate these new genes of interest in developing mouse brain cells. This will enable me to study the role of these new candidate genes on neuronal development and function. I am particularly interested in the roles of these genes on the generation, migration, maturation and synaptic function of cortical GABAergic interneurons, the inhibitory cells of the cortex. Indeed, my recent work has demonstrated that altered development or function of cortical interneurons leads to severe epilepsy in mice, reminiscent of that seen in patients with EE. My preliminary results on some of the new candidate genes I identified in children with EE suggest that these genes are indeed fundamental regulators of interneurons migration or function. My work should therefore widen our understanding of the molecular etiology underlying EE and of the cellular and network mechanisms causing the disease. A better understanding of these mechanisms will be critical to our ability to develop new and better-targeted therapies for children with EE and to improve these children's long-term neurological outcome. This personalized medicine approach will undoubtedly improve care for children with EE and their families.

column36: Improving Outcomes in Frail Older Adults with Cardiovascular Disease
column37: The aging population has redefined the field of heart disease from single-system disease-oriented care to multi-faceted patient-oriented care. Frailty is a syndrome seen mainly in older adults that is central to the patient-oriented care model as it reflects the individual patient's reserves and resiliency to stressful events such as surgery. My research has shown that frail patients suffer a 3-fold increase in death, complications, and poor recovery of physical function after heart surgery and other invasive heart procedures. However, existing tools to measure frailty are limited by low specificity in hospitalized patients and ambiguity about their actionable ramifications - this is a critical barrier that has stifled the advancement of treatment strategies. The solution that I am proposing is to use a different marker to measure frailty, one that has the potential to be treated in clinical practice, namely - sarcopenia. Sarcopenia, "the biological substrate of frailty", is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Various criteria exist to define it, some using special scales and others using bone density scanners, but these have not been adequately assessed in patients with heart disease who may have issues such as fluid retention that can cause inaccurate measurements. Thus, I will compare the accuracy and prognostic value of various criteria to determine how we should optimally diagnose sarcopenia in patients with heart disease. Then, I will identify patients who are referred for heart surgery and have low muscle mass and strength (sarcopenia) to test a targeted treatment - a specialized protein supplement beverage - which was designed to stimulate muscle building in older adults, and, I hypothesize, will improve their recovery of physical function and other outcomes after the heart surgery procedure.

column36: alpha-cell glucagon secretion: regulated exocytosis, dysregulation & rescue of type-1 diabetes
column37: In the pancreas, alpha-cells release glucagon (which causes blood sugar to go up) and beta-cells release insulin (which causes blood sugar to go down). In type-1 diabetes, beta-cells are destroyed by inflammation. Glucagon release however also does not work properly, which can cause life-threatening low blood sugar after insulin injections. No treatment has been developed to regulate glucagon secretion. Dr. Herbert Gaisano is examining pancreatic alpha-cells to: 1) determine how glucagon is normally released which is surprisingly unclear, 2) why glucagon is not released properly in type-1 diabetes, and then 3) determine if there are ways to fix this process. To do this, his laboratory has devised unprecedented imaging technologies to visualize alpha-cell glucagon secretion as dispersed single cells, and also alpha-cells within the intact pancreas in health and in type-1 diabetes. In diabetes, alpha-cells are profoundly influenced by lack of secretion from neighboring beta-cells (destroyed) and excess secretion from delta-cells (somatostatin that inhibits alpha- and beta-cells). Knowing precisely how neighboring islet cells normally communicate with each other, and become unneighbourly to alpha-cells in diabetes will reveal new paradigms in treating diabetes.

column37: Most pharmacological principles used in psychiatry have been discovered by serendipity in the 1950s and 60s. column37: Memory formation requires the production of new proteins that modify connections (synapses) between neurons in the brain. The overall goal of this project is to define specific protein synthesis mechanisms that determine where, when, and how specific mRNAs are translated into protein at synapses to support their plasticity and utilize these mechanisms to alleviate cognitive deficits in diseases such as AD. To achieve this goal, we will study a pathway we uncovered involving the molecule Fragile X Related Protein 1 (FXR1P). The FXR1P pathway is unique in its ability to selectively restrain the synthesis and activity-dependent delivery of the glutamate receptor subunit GluA2 to synapses in order to control synaptic plasticity and memory formation. Our Objectives are to: 1) Demonstrate how FXR1P regulates structural/functional plasticity of individual synapses, and 2) Determine how regulation of FXR1P and GluA2 can be used to mitigate synaptic deficits and memory impairments in AD models. This research will reveal new concepts regarding the healthy and diseased brain, and potentially identify a strategy for improving memory loss and rescuing the lost potential of individuals with cognitive impairments.

column37: My research will be driven by my diverse training in economics and population and public health to conduct research in women's reproductive health using the large population-based datasets that already exist in British Columbia, Canada. column37: Rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease are chronic conditions that affect all ages. Both conditions are caused by the body's immune system attacking healthy cells in different parts of the body. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the joints, resulting in joint swelling, pain, and difficulty moving. In Crohn's disease, the gastrointestinal tract or intestines are affected, resulting in pain, diarrhea and weight loss. Both conditions have a large impact on patients' quality of life. There is no cure for either disease, but fortunately many treatment options are available for both. Choosing the right treatment for the right patient requires an understanding of what is important to people living with these conditions. Some treatments may work better but have potential side effects. Some medications are taken as pills and others as injections at home or infusions through a vein in a clinic. Currently, treatment recommendations for both conditions are made primarily based on research evidence alone. In this program of research, we will perform multiple studies to understand how treatment decisions can be best aligned with research evidence and patient's unique disease characteristics and preferences. This will include studies in which we personalize estimates of benefits and side effects for a patient based on his or her disease characteristics, and patient surveys to determine what is most important to patients when choosing between these treatments. We will use this information to determine which treatments treatment patients would prefer, which will help inform patient-centered treatment recommendations and decision tools. We will also conduct surveys in doctors to determine if they have different views about what is important to patients. The ultimate goal of this research program is to help doctors and patients choose treatments that best match current research evidence and patients' preferences.

The proposed project associated with this application intends on working with a research team composed of Indigenous and allied scholars and service providers to develop a stress-reducing intervention grounded in Indigenous culture. Using the RE-AIM framework, we will also evaluate the intervention for an additional 3 months after the study is completed in order to assess its feasibility and utility in a real world setting. column36: Optimizing the delivery of HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis with Text Messaging Services and Nursing Support
column37: HIV Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is an HIV prevention modality where uninfected persons take 28 days of antiretroviral medications (ARVs) shortly after an HIV exposure to minimize the risk of acquiring HIV. PEP is highly efficacious and is considered the standard of care on medical and ethical grounds. Unfortunately, implementation challenges have limited its clinical and public health impact in Canada. At present, access to PEP is inconsistent and the quality of care varies nationwide. We seek to address two major issues with PEP delivery: First, retention in care after nPEP initiation is a major challenge as only 50% of our patients complete follow-up at the required 3-4 month time point. Mobile phone-based text messaging may offer a simple, innovative solution to address this problem. The 'WelTel' text messaging platform has proven been to improve health outcomes in prior randomized controlled trials but has never been studied in nPEP. Second, the costs associated with nPEP are high, in part because care is usually provided by specialist physicians. However, nPEP patients could readily be followed by trained nurses, since it is administered according to strict protocols and because most patients are healthy. Nurses in public health clinics are ideally suited to this role, being experienced with sexual health and available in health units nationwide.. We propose a pragmatic randomized controlled trial using a 2x2 factorial design to determine whether the proportion of nPEP patients that successfully complete follow-up: a) is higher among those receiving mobile phone-based text messaging support via WelTel than among those receiving standard care; and b) is non-inferior among those receiving care from a sexual health clinic nurse compared to those receiving hospital-based physician care. Our data will provide important information on how to strengthen retention in care and reduce costs to the healthcare system for PEP delivery.

column36: Assessment, applied health and health policy research to improve health outcomes in northern Indigenous populations
column37: In northern Indigenous populations, rates of chronic disease have risen sharply in recent decades due to a combination of rapid acculturation to Western lifestyle and economic development that lags behind that of other Canadians. My research program conducts ongoing assessment, intervention, health policy research with the goal of reducing chronic disease in northern populations. Assessment research examines how patterns of child growth and nutrition are changing; Canadian Inuit children are no longer shorter than southern populations, for example, and if they continue to grow at the current rate, they will be the tallest generation of Inuit ever to live in Canada. Adult bodies are also changing in response to their environments. Younger Inuit no longer consume a large portion of their diet in the form of fish and marine mammals, a fact which may lead to increased risk of diabetes and heart disease in the coming years. It is important to monitor these changes in growth and dietary patterns in order to provide health promotion and treatment programs tailored to the particular needs of the Inuit population. Interventions are already underway in many northern communities. My research evaluates whether programs to promote healthy lifestyles, including school-based games and young harvester training programs, are doing a good job of exposing children and youth to the healthful benefits of traditional Inuit practices. Early results show that these programs are producing positive effects that go beyond increasing physical activity and exposing children to a wide range of nutritious, healthy, traditional foods. Participating in culturally-derived activities is increasing Inuit children's confidence and self-esteem, promoting responsibility and sharing behaviour, and increasing ties between family and community members. Children are becoming valued carriers of positive health messages, a fact that underscores the importance of investing in child and youth development.

column36: Transforming Inequities: Community-Based Health Equity Research with Indigenous Populations
column37: There is considerable evidence that significant health inequities exist for Indigenous peoples when compared to majority populations, including greater presence of disease, lower health outcomes, and barriers to healthcare access due to cultural tensions between Indigenous cultural knowledge and biomedicine. In collaboration with Indigenous individuals, communities, and organizations in Canada and Belize, this 5-year program of research will move beyond descriptions of health inequity to build evidence based knowledge of health and social equity interventions that address priority needs for (1) Indigenous peoples living with HIV/AIDS in Saskatoon and Winnipeg, (2) Q'eqchi' Indigenous healers and Maya populations in Belize, and (3) Indigenous youth living in urban contexts of Saskatoon, Winnipeg, and Halifax. This program of research will close the gaps of current inequities by working authentically alongside Indigenous community partners to address priority needs and concerns that have emerged in each context. Together, these projects can significantly advance our understanding of community-based and collaborative health initiatives that improve social equity and wellness among Indigenous populations.

column36: From genetic diversity to genomic instability: in vivo characterization of the deubiquitinase OTUB1 in B-cells
column37: Our DNA carries the information required for the growth/maintenance of life. Problematically, environmental agents or pollutants can jeopardize its integrity and generate DNA lesions. If not repaired, these lesions can lead to mutations and the development of cancer and immunodeficiencies. We are particularly interested in one type of DNA lesions, called DNA double-strand break (DSB). DSB is a highly dangerous DNA lesion with unexpectedly beneficial applications. B-cells use DSBs during an infection to produce high affinity antibodies that eliminate the intruders. This process, named antibody diversification, carries however the risk of deleterious chromosomal rearrangements that favor the development of malignancies, including lymphoma, leukemia and multiple myeloma. Thus, it is imperative that we fully understand how DSBs are regulated to elicit a functional immune response while preserving DNA integrity and limiting cancer development. Ubiquitin, a small regulatory protein, plays a major role in DSB signaling/repair. Several ubiquitylation events catalyzed by E3 ubiquitin ligases take place during the DSB response and have been implicated in antibody diversification. However, less is known about the importance of deubiquitylation events, the process of cleavage of ubiquitin, in B-cells. We are particularly interested in a specific deubiquitinase named OTUB1, which has been previously linked to the DSB response. We are currently characterizing the role of OTUB1 in B-cell biology and the emergence of B-cell malignancies in vivo using an Otub1 knockout mouse model. Understanding OTUB1 functions in vivo will provide insight into B cell biology and carcinogenesis. It may also provide a rationale for the development of therapeutic approaches targeting OTUB1. This work will have broader implication for immunology and cancer biology due to the central role of DSB repair in these fields

column36: Single gene mutations in the nematode C. elegans: working towards a mutation in all 20,000 genes.
column37: Our goal in this project is to continue providing researchers with deleterious mutations in genes in the small model nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. We will focus on a target list of genes that includes genes with human counterparts (homologs) as well as nematode specific genes. The former group of genes is of practical importance in human health and disease as C. elegans offers a suitable model to efficiently determine the function of a novel gene at the cellular and intercellular level. The latter group of genes are important to target because various nematodes are parasites of humans, livestock and crop plants. Determining the function of genes specific to nematodes could offer the pharmaceutical industry new targets to effectively kill parasitic nematodes with little or no side-effects on the host. Many biochemical pathways are conserved between the nematode and humans and genes within the nematode can often be functionally replaced by their human homologs. In many cases these genes when dysfunctional within humans lead to inherited diseases, susceptibility to cancers or other health related problems. Understanding the basic biological function of these genes in the nematode will have direct benefits for medical diagnosis and treatment in humans. On a broader level, the availability of thousands of gene knockouts in C. elegans will provide a powerful resource to study a range of basic problems in developmental biology. The impact of this project will be to open up new avenues of discovery on gene function. The C. elegans Gene Knockout Facility at the University of British Columbia is part of an International Consortium and is recognized worldwide as a leader for C. elegans genetics and genomic studies. The mutant strains we provide are a priceless resource, and because nematodes can be frozen these mutant strains are a permanent resource. This will be a significant and enduring legacy of Canadian science.

column36: Understanding how cells sense the "stress" of virus particle entry following membrane perturbation.
column37: Cells respond to a virus infection by inducing a set of proteins that function to block virus replication and spread. Much is known about how cells recognize the accumulation of specific virus components within a cell. We previously discovered that in response to all enveloped viruses, cells can also recognize the general entry process, following disruption of the cell membrane. We identified an essential cellular factor, IRF3, that is activated and induces a non-specific anti-viral response that protects the cell against diverse viruses, by targeting conserved viral processes. IRF3 is emerging as a key player in recognizing and responding to many types of cellular stress, suggesting that entry of virus particles is likely sensed as a host stress response. Here, we propose to understand how the virus entry process activates this stress response, and identify key events and pathways. Findings will enable the development of novel, generic antiviral therapies capable of protecting against new, emerging viruses. Moreover, as IRF3 is implicated in a myriad of seemingly unrelated diseases, understanding its activation and function is of clinical importance.

column36: Synapse formation, synaptic plasticity and neurodegeneration: The role of MEN1 gene and its products
column37: Defining the fundamental mechanisms that underlie precise neuronal assembly during development and regeneration are critical not only for understanding all brain functions, but also for various developmental (e.g. Autism spectrum) and neurodegenerative disorders (e.g. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's etc.) that are met in clinical practice. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is one of the most common and debilitating neurodegenerative disorders globally, and the situation will only worsen with an aging population producing an unsustainable burden on our healthcare systems. Our understanding of the fundamental mechanisms underlying AD neuropathology remains however poor, and the treatment regimes are restricted to short-term symptom management at best. We have made a surprising finding implicating neurotrophic factors and the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene in the regulation of expression and synaptic maintenance of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR), which regulate many aspects of learning and memory. A dramatic loss of cholinergic synaptic connections and transmission in the hippocampus is one of the most important neuropathological hallmarks of AD. Moreover, cholinergic synaptic activity is known to regulate the expression of neurotrophic factors (NTF) and their reduced expression in hippocampus is commonly observed in AD. Using mouse models and human brain tissue, we will test a novel hypothesis that a deficit in neurotrophic factor-dependent expression of MEN1 underlies nAChR dysfunction in AD. We will seek to determine how MEN1 gene function underlies the regulation of nAChR expression during NTF-dependent synapse formation and synaptic plasticity, and whether its perturbation generates cognitive and neuropathological hallmarks of AD. We anticipate that our novel and exciting findings will lead to transformative insights into synaptic mechanisms of AD - at a resolution never achieved before, and identify new pathways as putative targets for therapeutic intervention.

column36: Structural and Functional Changes in the Retina and Optic Nerve in Experimental Glaucoma
column37: Optic nerve diseases such as glaucoma lead to visual disability and blindness, and are a significant health concern. Specific neural damage occurs as a loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), specialised neurons that carry visual messages from the eye to the brain. Clinical methods to diagnose and monitor glaucoma attempt to estimate how many RGCs are damaged, however, up to date they cannot provide an accurate estimate. Experimental animal models allow us to understand the mechanisms of disease and how to better monitor and treat patients. However, also in experimental models scientists are unable to directly measure cellular changes and how they affect visual function. In this project we will use novel imaging methods in living animals that have experimental glaucoma. These imaging methods allow us to calculate the density of RGCs in the same animal as the experimental glaucoma progresses. They will also allow us to examine individual RGCs and how their shape and processes change. Finally, we will measure the function of these cells with a technique called electroretinography. Because we will be able to perform these tasks repeatedly in the animal over time, it will allow us to plot the time course of how experimental glaucoma affects RGCs. This research has direct value towards guiding clinicians in how to monitor glaucoma in patients.

column36: Limits to growth: Intrinsic molecular 'brakes' to peripheral neuronal regeneration
column37: Peripheral nerves are the essential connections between the brain, spinal cord and body. Without them, there is no movement or sensation. Injuries and disease of peripheral nerves are very common. Unfortunately nerves regenerate slowly and incompletely, if at all. There are no specific interventions to improve regeneration of nerves. The Zochodne laboratory has discovered that a series of molecules, earlier studied in tumours, when suppressed can activate improved growth in peripheral nerves. Peripheral nerves contain these molecules, and they appear to 'brake' or restrain robust regrowth after injury. Relaxing these brakes using inhibitor agents or blocking them, an approach known as siRNA, enhances growth in experimental nerve injury of rats and mice. In this proposal, the PI plans to study whether growth in peripheral nerves can be improved with combinations of these molecules and with related molecules. Several new molecules with similar actions will also be studied. The plans involve analysis of growth in single adult neurons, nerve regrowth at early timepoints and longer term models of regeneration. The overall approach is to find new regeneration solutions that may be translated into therapy for persons with nerve injury or disease.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of intervertebral disc degeneration and pain
column37: Back pain arising from intervertebral disc degeneration (IVD) is the second most common medical condition in North America and worldwide. Intervertebral disc degeneration has a major negative impact on the quality of life, and in the United States alone, accounted for an estimated cost of up to 238 billion dollars in 2013. Despite the prevalence, little is known about the molecular mechanisms leading to intervertebral disc degeneration and its associated pain. As there are no conservative treatment options available, patients presenting with advanced stages of the disease require invasive surgery to relieve pain. It is well known that the matrix properties change as a result of degeneration, however, it is less clear how this is initiated and how it could be prevented. Previous work: Our previous work has demonstrated that degenerating and painful human IVDs release increased levels of factors that can affect nerve growth and induce pain. We have established that injury to human IVDs can initiate the factors associated with degeneration and back pain. We have also demonstrated an increase in toll-like receptor expression as a result of injury. Proposed study: We propose to evaluate if Toll-Like Receptor expression and signalling is directly associated with intervertebral disc degeneration and the development of chronic pain. We will evaluate if matrix fragments called "alarmins" promote expression and activation of Toll-Like Receptors. Finally we aim to evaluate if drugs targeting Toll-Like Receptors will halt the progression of degeneration and pain. Significance to Human Health: An expanded knowledge of the aetiology and pathogenesis of intervertebral disc degeneration will lead to improved therapeutic interventions and ultimately decrease pain and improve the quality of life of patients living with intervertebral disc degeneration

column36: Exploring the role of the Hippo pathway in lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the most common cancer, killing 1.6 million people each year worldwide. Despite major progress in our understanding of the causes of lung cancer, over 85% of lung cancer patients still die within 5 years after diagnosis. This is due to lack of effective drugs or even "druggable" targets, or development of resistance to drugs after initial treatment, which results in spread of lung cancer cells to other parts of the bodies (metastasis). Therefore, there is an urgent need to determine what changes in the cell cause lung cancer spread and drug resistance, and find druggable targets. We and others recently discovered that certain changes in a number of genes which work together as a team, named "Hippo", are critical for the development and spread of lung cancers and their resistance to therapeutic drugs, suggesting that Hippo may be a good target for lung cancer. However, exactly how Hippo works in these processes is not completely known, and there are at present no drugs that can directly target Hippo for lung cancer therapy. Using state-of-the-art technologies, in this study we will fully decode the secret of Hippo-induced lung cancer formation, spreading, and drug resistance and finally develop novel Hippo-targeted drugs in preclinical lung cancer models. We will also combine Hippo-targeted therapies with other therapies (chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy) to test whether they potentiate one another's effect upon drug resistance or metastasis of cancers that are the most difficult to treat. Our research findings will not only establish Hippo as a druggable target for lung cancer, but also leads to effective therapeutic strategies for successful treatment of lung cancer.

column36: Dissecting the molecular mechanisms of Semaphorin/Plexin signaling in synapse map formation
column37: Human nervous system consists of billions of neurons and each neuron is connected by a special interface called synapse. Neurons transmit signal through synapses to process information. It is therefore important to place synapses in the right place with their genuine partner cells. Synapses formed at the abnormal site will transmit signal to the improper cells, which causes malfunction of the neural network and is believed to cause various neurological disorders that affect higher order of brain function such as motor coordination, memory and thinking. My research goal is to understand the mechanisms that ensures precise synapse patterning in the nervous system. For this purpose, we use the nervous system of round worm, Caenorhabditis elegans, as an experimental model. C. elegans has a simple nervous system consists of 302 neurons, much less than that of a human (over 1 billion). Nevertheless, C. elegans employs almost the same machineries as mammals to build its nervous system. Therefore, knowledge obtained from our research using C. elegans will be directly applicable to human nervous system. Using C. elegans, we will study how precise synapse pattern is formed and how it is affected when we disrupt the function of genes which are believed to be misregulated in several neurological disorders including schizophrenia and Alzheimer's diseases. Using state-of-the-art microscope combined with genetic and biochemical analyses, we will uncover the mechanism of fine neuronal map formation toward our ultimate goal which is to find possible drug target to cure patients with neurological diseases.

column36: Testing existing and new therapeutic interventions in a novel animal model of acute Spot Positive intracranial hemorrhage
column37: There is no effective treatment for bleeding into the brain or ICH. While we cannot do anything about the initial ICH, expansion of a bleed is the most important cause of bad outcome in ICH. We first described the Spot Sign which, when seen in ICH, strongly predicts expansion. We developed clinical trials (that are ongoing) selecting patients for treatment with drugs that stop bleeding based on the presence or absence of the Spot sign. There is evidence now however to suggest that this approach is flawed as the Spot sign represents varying rates of ICH expansion rather than an all-or-none situation. In other words, some Spot positive bleeding may be so quick that no medical treatment will be effective while others so slow that no treatment is needed because no meaningful expansion will occur. The problem is that current studies will not tell us what rates of bleeding are responsive to existing medicines and will likely fail because we did not consider the rate of bleeding. We have therefore developed a unique animal model that most closely mimics the Spot positive bleeding that occurs in humans. By aiming ultrasound beams from outside the head to specific brain regions we are able to damage the walls of small vessels causing them to rupture. By controlling the power of the ultrasound delivered we can adjust the rate of bleeding by targeting different vessel sizes. We propose using this model to test existing (medicines) and new (new medicines, using ultrasound to stop bleeding and surgical) ways to minimize expansion of bleeds based on the rate of bleeding associated with Spot positive bleeds. Once the ranges of bleeding rates responsive to our proposed medicines and novel treatments are established we can test these in humans using existing imaging sequences that measure rates of bleeding. By selecting patients based on these measures we can tailor treatment to the particular rate of bleeding ensuring better outcomes, less dependency and lower cost to society

column36: Structural composition and regulation of electrical synapses in the CNS
column37: Numerous neurotransmitters are used by nerve cells in the brain to communicate with each other at chemical synapses. However, over the past 15 years, surprising discoveries by us and others have shown that another mode of neuronal communication mediated by electrical synapses is also prevalent in the mammalian central nervous system. These synapses are critical for information processing related to cognitive, sensory and motor functions of the brain. Such synapses are formed by structures called gap junctions that are located at close appositions between neurons, and are composed of the gap junction-forming protein connexin36 as well as a growing list of accessory proteins. Our work shows that these structures are complex, with many protein components supporting their assembly, maintenance and neurotransmission functions. Identification of those components and their functions is essential for understanding the normal operation of electrical synapses and how their malfunction could contribute to brain disorders. With our past and more recent discoveries of some of their key protein components (ZO-1, MUPP1, AF6, cingulin, N-cadherin, nectin-1, alpha-catenins and beta-catenin, SynGAP1), we aim to determine how these proteins are organized and regulate electrical synapses. Our finding of the protein SynGAP1 at these synapses is particularly intriguing, because it is already known to be important for regulating communication at chemical synapses and may be equally important at electrical synapses. Further, mutations in the gene coding for this protein were recently found to cause significant intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy in people. We expect that our work will reveal entirely new concepts on cellular mechanisms that govern the activities of electrical synapses, which will ultimately be important for considerations of how these synapses could potentially malfunction and contribute to neurological disorders.

column37: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) causes the devastating lung disease tuberculosis (TB). Nearly two million people die from TB annually. Mtb infects and grows inside macrophages, a type of white blood cell, present in the lungs of patients. With the increasing prevalence of multidrug and extensively drug resistant tuberculosis in multiple countries, there is a pressing need for new approaches to combat TB. column37: The retina is a light-sensitive layer of cells lining the back of the eye that help us to see. When babies are born too early, the blood vessels on the retina are not fully developed. Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is the name for the improper growth of the blood vessels on the retina of the eye in a premature infant. Up to 90% of babies born before 31 weeks (a term baby is considered at 37 weeks) will develop some form of ROP. Complications of ROP can include nearsightedness, eye misalignment, and, in severe cases, blindness. Specialized immune cells called macrophages have oxygen tension sensing capacity and can produce a broad array of substance capable of stimulating blood vessel formation. The accumulation of macrophages in low oxygen areas contributes to the improper blood vessel growth observed in the injured retina. Our studies have shown that microparticles (very small vesicles are microscopic in size) generated from human lymphocyte T cells (immune cells that help body fight against infection), significantly limit the disorganized growth of blood vessels seen in ROP. We are therefore interested in investigating the hypothesis that these microparticles exert their beneficial effects in the retina in part by regulating the activity of macrophages. We propose to dissect the impact of microparticles on macrophages function and on the growth of retinal blood vessels using an animal model that reproduces the disorganized growth of retinal blood vessels seen in ROP. Data generated from this proposal could elucidate new cellular communication pathways that microparticles interact with macrophages. The molecular mechanisms of action of these microparticles may be transferred to other diseases associated with abnormal retinal blood vessel growth, including ROP, diabetic retinopathy (caused by complications of diabetes), and age-related macular degeneration of the retina (a major cause of blindness and visual impairment in people over the age of 50 years).

column37: The circadian timing system generates biological rhythms in physiology and behaviour that are synchronized with the environment. Disruptions to the circadian system, caused by either genetic or environmental factors, have been implicated in the pathology of many human diseases including cancer, diabetes and obesity, cardiovascular disease, and neuropsychiatric disorders. Biol., 2008; Krupp et al., Neuron, 2013). Using this system our future research will seek to understand how temporal information from both the internal and external environment is integrated to produce coherent circadian rhythms in cellular physiology, and how rhythms in physiology are coordinated within cells and across tissues and organ systems. Given the high degree of conservation between the circadian system of Drosophila and that of mammals we anticipate that our findings will translate to humans and increase our understanding of the circadian processes that contribute to human health.

column37: Over the last decade impressive advances have been made in our understanding of spinal cord injury (SCI) and identification of possible therapies. One of the success stories in treatment of spinal cord injury has been the adoption of active locomotor-based rehabilitation. A consensus has emerged that part of the recovery is due to activity-driven reorganization of spinal circuits. These spinal circuits are essential for producing many motor behaviors including walking. Despite the success of these programs, patients do plateau in their recovery over time, and indeed activity-dependent rehabilitation does not work for some patients. We show that centres within the brain that contain orexin are particularly effective in activating locomotor activity. This raises the possibility that stimulation of these orexin centres could facilitate locomotion in patients with movement disorders.

column37: This proposal focuses on a new treatment for Alzheimer's disease using a drug that blocks the activity of a glutamate receptor in the brain, called mGlu5, which is now extensively implicated in contributing to the cause of Alzheimer's disease, the most prevalent neurodegenerative illness in older adults. Our goal is to understand the mechanism by which mGlu5 contributes to Alzheimer's pathology and to repurpose the mGlu5 antagonist CTEP for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

column37: Malaria is one of the greatest threats to human health today. Globally, there are approximately 200 million cases per year, resulting in approximately 600,000 deaths, the majority of which are small children. Malaria is caused by a microscopic parasite transmitted from mosquitoes to human hosts. Once inside the host, the parasite invades red blood cells to consume nutrients from the host in order to develop and multiply. The treatment, control, and eradication of malaria have long been impeded by the ability of the parasite to rapidly develop resistance to antimalarial drugs. Therefore, it is imperative to develop new drugs that act through molecular mechanisms distinct from existing drugs to control the disease and combat the spread of drug resistance. Due to the complex biochemical interactions between the drug, parasite, and human host, identification of the molecular target of potential antimalarial drugs is an enormous challenge requiring years of intense research. An emerging approach for identifying the molecular target of antimalarials is to sequence the genome of parasites that have developed drug resistance in order to identify the responsible genetic mutations. This project aims to develop a new technology to isolate these drug-resistant parasites in order to sequence their genome to rapidly identify the molecular target of antimalarial drugs. This work leverages a recent discovery made by our research team that found all antimalarial drugs dramatically reduce the deformability of infected red blood cells, which aids the clearance of the infected cells from the host. Using this characteristic, our technology will separate infected red blood cells based on mechanical deformability in order to isolate cells drug-resistant parasites from those containing drug-sensitive parasites. Once separated, we will then sequence the genome of mutated parasites in order to identify the molecular target of potential antimalarial drugs.

column36: Characterization of the proteostasis decline upon aging
column37: Aging is a complex process characterized by a progressive decline of the ability of tissues to retain their functional integrity. At the cellular level, aging has been associated to a reduced capacity to maintain the integrity of the proteome (which is the ensemble of proteins present in the cell). This decline has been associated to the accumulation and aggregation (i.e., clumping) of several proteins in age-related pathologies like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's and prion diseases. In this project, we will specifically identify which proteins become misshapen and tend to clump in brain tissues of aging mice. Our hypothesis is that clumping proteins share similar characteristics that make them more susceptible. We will employ a computational approach to identify these features and thereby rationalize why the identified proteins are more affected upon aging. This study will lead to unique and novel fundamental knowledge that could potentially reveal how proteostasis (i.e., maintenance of a balanced proteome) is affected upon aging, and provide a first glimpse of how the cell landscape is affected when things "start to go wrong". With the current ageing society, it becomes critical that we address this knowledge gap, and identify biomarkers related to cellular aging. These age-related biomarkers could be used in the future to guide studies aiming at delaying cellular aging and stop the progression of age-related diseases.

column36: The roles of WT1 in fibrosis development
column37: Loss of tissue or organ function due to abnormal scarring, also called fibrosis, contributes to about 40% of all deaths in the Western world. Once fibrosis has commenced, none of the available treatments consistently prevent its progression or recurrence. To design more effective treatments, we need to gain a better understanding of this disease process and to identify the events that cause normal tissue and organ repair to deviate toward fibrosis. The focus of this application is a gene called WT1. This gene is well known for its roles in promoting cancers. Increased activity of this gene has been recently noted in non-cancerous fibroses of the lung, liver, heart and hand. We have found that molecules secreted by the immune system potently induce the activity of WT1 and we hypothesize that chronic exposure to these molecules induces sustained WT1 activity, disrupts normal tissue repair and enhances fibrosis development. Rather than testing this hypothesis in animals that do not normally develop fibrosis, we will take the novel approach of "bioengineering" the fibrotic process in our laboratory using cells derived from human tissues. This approach allows us to use genetically identical cells from the same patients before and after fibrosis development. As members of the Roth|McFarlane Hand and Upper Limb Centre, the largest specialist surgical unit of its kind in Canada, we have direct access to the tissues we need to maintain these models. The aims of this project are to determine if increased WT1 activity 1)Disrupts tissue repair processes, and 2)Enhances fibrosis progression. If increased WT1 activity induces fibrosis, there is real potential to target it with treatments and prevent fibrosis. Treatments that target WT1 in cancers have already been proven to be safe and clinical trials of these treatments are currently underway. This project will determine if it is feasible to cross-purpose these treatments to prevent tissue and organ fibrosis.

column37: Electrical activity commonly exists in our body. It transfers information through nerve and activates our muscles. So there are cells that are sensitive to electricity and are responsive to electrical stimulation. Based on this, we have been studying how to use electricity to change cell activities in order to help the repair of wound. Instead of using metals to conduct electricity, we use conductive polymers. Conductive polymers are manmade organic materials that allow electricity to pass. The advantages of using conductive polymers but metals are that polymers are more like natural tissues such as in softness and elasticity. Polymers also do not get corrosion that may produce metal ions toxic to cells. Organic materials can also be degraded. In previous years we have successfully produced three categories of conductive polymers, the composite with biodegradable polymers and the composites with biostable or biodegradable textiles. We grow human cells on such polymers and then connect electricity to the polymers. In such a way the cells are exposed to electricity. We found that under some types of electrical stimulation, human cells become more active, growth faster, move faster, and produce chemicals and proteins that accelerate the repair of wound. We have presented our results in about 30 scientific articles and many scientific conferences, which makes our group the international leader in this research field. In the next five years, we will expand our research to look at the mechanisms about how electricity affects cells, and to develop protocols to find out how the electrically activated cells can heal the wound in animals. We will use our electrical stimulation model to study the interactions between the cells that made up our skin and blood vessel. Our project combines material science, electrical engineering and biosciences, providing an excellent environment to train students.

column37: Thousands of dental and orthopedic implants are placed each year to address the ravages of bone degenerative diseases such as osteoporosis, osteoarthristis, osteonecrosis and periodontal disease. column36: Therapeutic strategies for improvement of airway epithelial repair by targeting CFTR defect and bacterial infection in cystic fibrosis patients
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF), the most common genetic disease among Caucasians, is due to mutations in the gene coding for a protein called CFTR. Although CF affects many organs, the progressive lung damage due to bacterial infections remains the first cause of mortality in CF patients. Several years ago, we thus decided to devote our efforts to identify novel therapeutic strategies to promote lung repair in CF patients. We first discovered that the capability of airways to repair after injury is less efficient in CF patients than in healthy subjects, due to both the CFTR dysfunction and the presence of infections. Our work also unveiled that CFTR rescue with new compounds called correctors significantly enhances airway repair, but this CFTR rescue and repair improvement are dampened by bacteria. Importantly, we have new data supporting that lung repair could be improved by targeting products released by bacteria and using combinations of CFTR modulators. Using both airway cells and bacteria collected from CF patients, our aim is now to dissect the mechanisms whereby CFTR and infection regulate epithelial repair. Then, we will precisely define the bacterial products responsible for the deleterious effect of infection on airway repair and CFTR rescue. Finally, our aim is to evaluate the most effective strategy, with CFTR modulators and compounds interfering with bacteria, to reach the highest level of CFTR rescue and CF airway repair improvement, despite the presence of infection. column36: Regulation of muscle satellite cell self-renewal and differentiation by CCAAT/Enhancer Binding Protein beta: Implications in disease pathogenesis.
column37: Skeletal muscle has a remarkable ability to repair itself after injury or exercise, a feature that can be attributed to resident stem cells called satellite cells. After injury, satellite cells begin to divide to produce daughter cells. Of these, the majority will mature into myocytes that can fuse to one another or to damaged muscle fibers to initiate repair. The remaining daughter cells remain as satellite cells, ensuring that the muscle retains its capacity to repair over the lifespan of the organism. Understanding, on a molecular level, what makes a cell decide to mature or to remain a stem cell can help understand how disease arises in muscle and can help us develop better stem cell-based therapies. My laboratory has discovered that the protein C/EBPbeta regulates entry into myogenesis, promotes stem cell marker expression, and is necessary for maintaining the satellite cell population. In the absence of C/EBPbeta, satellite cells precociously differentiate and don't self-renew, resulting in bigger muscle fibers and a smaller stem cell population that cannot support muscle repair long term. In healthy muscle, C/EBPbeta can be found in satellite cells but once these cells become activated to repair muscle, C/EBPbeta levels drop but reappear at the late stages of new fiber formation. C/EBPbeta is misexpressed in skeletal muscle in cachexia and during aging where muscle wasting occurs. While we know that C/EBPbeta is important to prevent satellite cell maturation, it is unclear how C/EBPbeta regulates self-renewal or what its function is in new myofibers. The proposal will concentrate on answering these questions with the ultimate goal of understanding how C/EBPbeta contributes to muscle disease, and how this can be converted into novel therapies for muscle wasting.

column36: Epigenetic Mechanisms in Chronic Pain
column37: The Canadian Pain Society estimates that one in five Canadians suffer from chronic pain, costing up to $60 billion a year in health care and lost productivity. Despite enormous efforts, significant advances in pain management continue to be elusive. One reason that chronic pain is resistant to treatment is that it is associated with long term biological changes that are difficult to reverse, including pathological changes in gene expression in the brain. Very little is known about how pain-related changes in gene expression are regulated. We hypothesize that they are controlled by chemical changes to the genes referred to as epigenetic modifications. Epigenetic changes can occur in response to the environment or to injury and act as a memory, altering gene expression for decades. We have previously demonstrated that chronic pain results in widespread epigenetic changes in the brain. In this study we propose to use a rodent model of chronic pain to determine the role of epigenetically-regulated genes in chronic pain and if we can target these mechanisms for the treatment of chronic pain. The research team represents a partnership between pain researchers and epigenetic experts coming together to study chronic pain in a new way. Improved understanding of the role of epigenomic modulation in chronic pain could have significant impact on the quality of life for millions of individuals currently suffering from chronic pain.

column36: Using C.elegans to identify drugs that target a metabolic pathway that is essential for parasitic helminths but absent from humans
column37: Parasitic Helminths (PHs) are major human pathogens. They include the giant roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides as well as whipworms and hookworms. PHs infect over 2 billion people worldwide causing tens of thousands of deaths per year and widespread sickness. PHs are thus a major global health problem and, while there are a few available drugs, resistance is rapidly emerging and there is therefore a great need for new drugs. How can we treat PHs? To do this effectively, we must kill the infecting PH without harming the human host. This means that we need to exploit crucial differences in the biology of humans and PHs. One key possibility lies in the way that humans and PHs make energy. For much of their life cycle, PHs make energy in the same way that humans do. However, when PHs are inside the human body, there is little oxygen available for them - under these conditions, they make energy using an unusual pathway, the FR/RQ pathway, that is completely absent from humans. Drugs that block FR/RQ would thus be ideal anti-PH treatments. No such drugs exist since almost all the simple living systems in which drug screens are done (e.g. yeast, mammalian cells) do not have FR/RQ and so one cannot find FR/RQ inhibitors in these models. The nematode worm C.elegans is different - it has an intact FR/RQ pathway and is easy to grow and study in the lab. We have established conditions in which we can rapidly assay FR/RQ activity in C.elegans. We have also built a novel drug screening pipeline which allows us to screen thousands of drugs per day to find drugs that block FR/RQ. We are therefore in a unique position to attack this major health problem. Our goals are: (1) find which genes are required for FR/RQ and understand how the FR/RQ pathway is regulated. (2) To screen for drugs that inhibit FR/RQ. These are potentially powerful and specific anti-PH drugs. Together, these will be major advances in the treatment of this massive global health challe

column36: Driving disease: Molecular mechanisms of apicomplexan parasite motility
column37: Parasitic infections pose a major threat to global human health. Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium falciparum, the causative agents of toxoplasmosis and severe malaria, respectively, are particularly important due to their widespread distribution and disease outcomes. Toxoplasmosis is highly prevalent in the developed world and is a leading cause of food-borne illness related deaths in the United States. Toxoplasma infections can lead to a variety of disease outcomes and, if congenitally transmitted, can result in abortion, neonatal death and fetal abnormalities. Children that survive prenatal infection are likely to suffer significantly reduced quality of life with neurological deficiencies such as mental retardation. Nearly 3.4 billion people live in at risk zones for malaria resulting in more than 200 million clinical cases and half a million deaths per year, 85% of which are young children. Given the clear impact of these parasitic diseases on human health and the current challenges in effectively controlling them, novel treatments are desperately needed. To establish infection and cause disease, these parasites must invade the individual cells of a host. To accomplish this, they rely on a sophisticated motility system driven by a unique molecular "motor". However, very little is known about the inner workings of this motor and thus the overall process of parasite motility is poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we will use cutting edge biophysical and biochemical techniques to dissect the motor complex. These studies will provide crucial insight into how these globally devastating pathogens invade host cells, which we will, in turn, leverage to identify novel targeted therapies.

column36: The structural basis of plasmid segregation by bacterial actins
column37: In addition to their chromosomes, bacteria possess small pieces of DNA called plasmids. Plasmids play a vital role in human health and disease because they encode genes for antibiotic resistance, virulence machinery, pathways to digest unusual substances and synthesize toxins. Since plasmids are small, they often get transferred between bacterial cells and thus contribute to the ever-growing problems of antibiotic resistance, infection and disease, nutrient indigestion, and food poisoning. Since plasmids are advantageous in a bacterial population, bacteria have evolved systems to ensure their proper segregation into daughter cells. With this project we focus on plasmid segregation systems driven by bacterial actin, a distant relative of the cytoskeletal filament actin of eukaryotic cells. As in higher organisms, plasmid segregation in bacteria is highly orchestrated process. To understand the molecular mechanism that drives plasmid segregation, we will integrate cutting-edge structural and biochemical approaches aimed at bridging single molecules to macromolecular assemblies in the cell. Understanding how the machinery of plasmid segregation works at the molecular level and within the cell will provide opportunities to effectively disrupt the process in drug-resistant pathogenic bacteria.

column36: Restoring useful function to complete and permanently denervated skeletal muscles
column37: Skeletal muscles regulating movements such as walking, hand grasping, breathing and swallowing are controlled by cells in the nervous system called motoneurons. Motoneurons controlling individual muscles often die after a spinal cord injury. Motoneuron death causes the affected muscles to become paralyzed because they are permanently disconnected from the nervous system. There is currently no known way to restore meaningful function to these muscles. However, previous studies from my lab showed that muscles can be genetically modified to express a light activated protein known as channelrhodopsin 2 (ChR2). Muscles expressing ChR2 contract when exposed to bright light even when there are completely disconnected from the nervous system. Here we propose that this technology can be further advanced to restore function to paralyzed muscles without the use to genetic manipulation. For example, paralyzed skeletal muscles will be injected with muscle stem cells that were forced to express ChR2 using viral technology. We propose that the muscles stem cells will become incorporated with the paralyzed muscles causing them to express ChR2. Once they express ChR2, the targeted skeletal muscles can be controlled in a meaningful way with small light emitting diodes (LEDs). We believe these studies will lay the foundation for using this new technology to restore meaningful movement such as hand grasping, or breathing, to individuals whose hand muscles or diaphragm were permanently paralyzed due to motor neuron death after a spinal cord injury.

column36: Investigating the role of eIF2beta in translation reprogramming in cancer
column37: mRNA translation is a process during which proteins are synthesized by translation machinery based on the information stored in messenger RNAs (mRNAs). Abnormal mRNA translation is common in cancer. Alterations in mRNA translation provide proteins necessary for neoplastic transformation (a process during which normal cells become malignant), as well as tumor progression and dissemination. However, understanding of the role of translation in cancer remains incomplete. This hampers development of therapeutic strategies to target translation machinery in cancer. The mammalian/mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is considered to be the major pathway that controls mRNA translation in response to changes in the cellular environment. mTOR function is elevated in the vast majority of cancers. Through CIHR funded research, we demonstrated that mTOR together with CK2, another regulatory cellular protein implicated in numerous malignancies, activates the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2) by phosphorylating its eIF2B subunit. eIF2 is a pivotal translation regulator that has a crucial role to deliver the very first transfer RNA carrying amino acid methionine (initiator tRNA) during the initiation step of translation. Activation of eIF2 constitutes a previously unrecognized way of how mTOR may stimulate mRNA translation. Persistent eIF2B phosphorylation leads to increased protein synthesis, proliferation (increase in cell number) and neoplastic growth, which are all characteristics of cancer cells. Based on these findings, we propose to establish the role of eIF2B phosphorylation in inducing changes in mRNA translation that favor production of cancer-promoting proteins. Considering that the changes in translation, mTOR and/or CK2 signaling are commonly detected in the vast majority of cancers, we expect our findings to yield new strategies to target translational machinery in malignant tumors.

column36: Pre-Existing Immunity Prior to Heparin Exposure Increases Susceptibility for Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
column37: Platelets are small cells in the blood that help control bleeding. Heparin is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) used in major surgeries, such as heart surgery, and to manage heart attacks and strokes. Patients receiving heparin may have an allergic-type reaction called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Patients with HIT have low platelets (thrombocytopenia) and can develop severe clotting (gelling of blood so it no longer flows) causing loss of limbs, heart attacks, stroke and even death. So this drug (heparin), which usually helps patients, can actually cause more strokes and heart attacks in some people. HIT is a serious problem because it causes catastrophic effects in patients. The problem starts because some people develop attack proteins (antibodies) when they are given heparin. Some of these dangerous HIT antibodies attack platelets. However, other antibodies look the same but do not attack platelets. Testing if people have HIT is a major problem because most tests cannot tell the difference between the dangerous antibodies and the antibodies that do not cause HIT. Our first goal will be to find ways to determine ahead of time who will react to heparin and who will not. If we know that a patient will react to heparin, then the doctor can avoid its use. Our second goal is to understand why some patients develop HIT while others do not. We will study specific cells in patients to see if there is a change during HIT compared to the ones that do not have HIT during major heart surgery. Our group has the knowledge and the equipment to carry out all planned experiments. We are a HIT testing centre for many hospitals across Canada and we are located in an area that specializes in both heart- and blood-diseases providing us with ongoing access to patients with HIT. Once we understand why some patients get HIT and others do not, we will be able to provide better tests and better patient care while avoiding the disease.

column36: Modeling connexin-linked disease
column37: It is a general requirement for normal tissue function that adjacent cells communicate directly with each other through special channels called gap junctions. The goal of our research is to investigate and uncover novel mechanisms that contribute to atherosclerosis and heart disease in the hopes of developing more effective prevention and therapeutic strategies.

column36: HIV antiretroviral exposure in early pregnancy - assessing the impact on progesterone mediated decidual development and function.
column37: It is now recommended that all HIV-positive (HIV+) women take HIV medications during their pregnancy. In Canada, most HIV+ women begin HIV medications before they become pregnant or early in pregnancy. Taking HIV medications reduces the risk of HIV transmission to the baby to almost zero. However, these medications have side effects: they have been associated with a higher risk of having a miscarriage, a preterm birth, and a low birth weight baby. We don't fully understand how HIV medications cause these side effects, or which HIV medications have the fewest side effects when taken during pregnancy. Our lab discovered that some HIV medications cause the levels of progesterone, the "pregnancy hormone", to decrease in HIV+ pregnant women. Progesterone is very important in maintaining pregnancy by helping form the placenta, an organ shared by the mother and the fetus. In particular, the maternal side of the placenta, called the decidua, relies on progesterone to form properly. If progesterone levels are lowered by HIV medications, the decidua may not form properly, possibly affecting the success of the pregnancy. To examine this possibility, we will investigate how different HIV medications affect the formation and function of the decidua. We will use a test-tube model and an experimental model of pregnancy to test how HIV medications affect the growth of blood vessels in the decidua, an important developmental process to ensure that enough maternal blood is available to provide oxygen and food to the fetus. We will also use advanced imaging techniques to compare decidua blood vessels in HIV+ pregnant women on HIV medications with those from uninfected women. Finally, we will test whether supplementing with progesterone will reverse the effects of HIV medications on the decidua. Our findings will inform the selection of safer HIV medications to use in pregnancy and help identify therapies to use in combination with HIV medications to improve pregnancy outcome.

column36: Obesity, Diabetes & Eating Disorders: The role of Calcium Signaling and the Calcium Transporter, NCKX4
column37: Obesity and eating disorders are known to lead to pathological changes in metabolism, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and are significant and growing health problems in western societies with a very high burden on individual health and the health care system (http://www.cdc.gov/obesity/data/facts.html). Despite intensive investigation and steady advances in our knowledge about the ways in which appetite and eating are regulated by the brain, we still do not fully understand how these behaviours are controlled, nor why and how this control can go wrong and then lead to disease. Consequently, there are currently very few effective treatment methods. Further study and new insights are necessary to combat this escalating health problem. The objective of this proposal is to investigate detailed cellular mechanisms that underlie a central and essential pathway in the brain - the melanocortin pathway - that controls eating behavior. Our proposal takes advantage of very recent discoveries in my laboratory that suggest a completely new way in which the melanocortin pathway works inside cells of a particular region in the brain, called the hypothalamus. We have shown that when a special protein that transports calcium out of brain cells, NCKX4, is not working in mice, those animals eat much less and weigh less. We have also shown that this is because the receptor protein, MC4R, that starts signaling in the melanocortin pathway, uses calcium to work. With these new ideas as a starting point, we will test exactly where and how the melanocortin pathway works. The experiments proposed here will lead to an in-depth understanding of the cellular signals that control feeding behavior, satiety and obesity. This information will be critical in understanding normal feeding behaviour and the events that underlie its dys-regulation. This information has the potential to lead toward the development of novel, much needed, therapeutic agents for eating disorders.
