column36: Fetal Origin of Endocrine Dysfunction: The Plasticizer Model
column37: Reduced testosterone has been linked to obesity, cardiovascular diseases, erectile dysfunction and infertility. Adrenal dysfunction can lead to changes in blood pressure. Phthalate esters are used as plasticizers to add softness and flexibility to polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plastics, used for a wide variety of products, including personal care products, toys, food wrappings, medical devices, and building and household products. DEHP is the most commonly used phthalate in industry. Because it is not covalently bound to the PVC polymer, it leaches into the environment and comes into contact with humans mainly through dermal exposure, oral ingestion, and inhalation. Active metabolites of DEHP are found in humans of all ages, from fetus to adulthood, and have been shown to decrease fetal testosterone production in animals. In men, there is an inverse correlation between DEHP metabolites and circulating androgen levels. In rats, fetal DEHP exposure results in reduced circulating testosterone and aldosterone levels in the adult offspring, affecting blood pressure and adipose tissue function. Recently, a new plasticizer DINCH has been introduced to replace DEHP in medical devices, toys and food packaging. Based upon preliminary data we hypothesize that in utero exposure to low doses of DEHP as well as DINCH leads to changes in testicular and adrenal function in the adult offspring, and that the altered endocrine physiology results in increased vulnerability to additional exposures to drugs and pollutants. We propose to determine the endocrine and metabolic changes occurring in adult males following in utero exposure to relevant doses of plasticizers, and to identify the mechanisms underlying long-term effects on androgen and adrenal steroids. It is critical to determine whether plasticizer exposure could be a risk factor in the origin of reproductive and metabolic disorders and identify targets for the potential pharmacological reversal of their detrimental effects.

column36: Regulation of steroid hormone biosynthesis
column37: Steroid hormones are critical for the maintenance of the organism's homeostasis, adaptability to the environment, developmental and reproductive functions. Changes in the rate of steroid formation in response to genetic defects, metabolic disorders, and/or drug or environmental exposures can result in life-altering diseases. Reduced testosterone has been linked to infertility, erectile dysfunction, obesity, osteoporosis and cardiovascular diseases. Adrenal cortisol synthesis is involved in stress-response and adaptation; changes in adrenal aldosterone production can lead to changes in blood pressure and thus cardiovascular diseases. Adrenocortical tumors produce excessive amounts of cortisol, and androgen and ovarian tumors produce androgen and estrogen, all leading to endocrine disorders and potentially to pathological conditions. Changes in circulating steroids in peripheral tissues and brain have been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders. The adrenals, gonads and placenta form steroids from cholesterol. The steroids exert their functions throughout the body. Other tissues, including brain, adipose, prostate, and skin can also form steroids that fulfill local needs. For over 50 years, steroid levels have been as indicators used to diagnose various diseases, e.g. Cushing's syndrome, Addison's disease, congential adrenal hypeplasia, hypogonadism, precocious puberty, etc, and steroids have served as drugs for the treatment of endocrine, reproductive and metabolic disorders. These conditions span from early development to aging. Despite the widespread use, and abuse, of steroids, there are major gaps in our knowledge of the mechanisms regulating their production, and the effects of hormones and drugs on their synthesis and function. The goal of this project is to understand the mechanisms underlying steroid hormone biosynthesis and regulation, and thus pave the way for the development of novel pharmacological strategies to control steroid formation.

column36: The International HIV Adaptation Collaborative: harnessing host and viral genetic data globally for HIV-1 vaccine design
column37: Ending the HIV-1 pandemic will require effective vaccine(s). To date however, no HIV-1 vaccine candidate that has reached advanced clinical testing has been able to elicit protective cellular immune responses. Improved T-cell immunogen designs capable of overcoming HIV-1's extensive capacity for mutation, genetic diversification and adaptation to host populations are thus urgently needed. Vaccine concepts guided by analysis of large-scale human/viral datasets represent a promising novel approach. Towards this goal, we have assembled a global team of computational, molecular and clinical biologists with expertise in HIV-1 adaptation, viral fitness, and vaccine discovery and who lead unique HIV-1 cohorts globally. The fundamental premise of our proposal is that large-scale, integrated analyses of host genetic, HIV-1 genetic and HIV-1 functional data can inform the design of novel HIV-1 T-cell vaccine immunogens for both prophylactic HIV-1 vaccines (to protect people against infection) as well as "personalized" immunotherapeutic approaches (to eliminate HIV-1 from those already infected). Importantly, our proposal features both basic and translational aims. Specifically, it seeks to extend our signature evolution/function- guided approaches to elucidate pathways of immunodeficiency virus adaptation within human populations and across species barriers with the goal of identifying universal versus host/viral context-specific HIV-1 epitopes for vaccine inclusion. It also describes how we will apply existing knowledge of HIV-1 adaptation to design - and test - personalized vaccines for HIV cure. We believe that results have the potential to significantly advance HIV-1 vaccine and cure research.

column36: A dopamine receptor complex mediates susceptibility to depression with enhanced effect in females
column37: Depression is highly prevalent, occurring in up to 7% of adults with 3 fold higher incidence in women during their reproductive years and postpartum. column36: Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes of Prenatal Stress
column37: Prenatal stress is suggested to be a primary cause of adverse pregnancy outcomes. We hypothesize that adverse consequences of prenatal stress (both generational stress and multiple stresses) can be passed on through generations to lead to poor pregnancy outcomes, especially preterm birth, and adverse developmental trajectories in the offspring. Using three distinct rat models of prenatal stress and state-of-the-art immunological, behavioural and epigenetic assessments, we will (1) study effects due of generational stress (transgenerational and multiple generational) and two-hit stress to mothers and fathers and correlate to adverse pregnancy and newborn developmental outcomes; (2) study both paternal and maternal transmission of stress to offspring and (3) study mitigating effects of enriched environments and inflammatory receptor antagonists. This work is expected to lead to the development of an animal model of transgenerational programming of pregnancy outcomes and associated biomarkers. We will identify mechanisms including how the brain translates stress to alter pregnancy health and identify markers of prenatal stress that translate to future human studies as early biomarkers of risk assessment. Further, we will determine if environmental enrichment and drug treatment are able to reverse preterm birth risk and improve maternal and newborn long-term health outcomes. Our goal is to develop new treatments that promote healthy futures for our children and next generations.

column36: Anti-CD11d immunotherapy for CNS trauma
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) are catastrophic, giving rise to lifelong disabilities. While the primary causes of SCI and TBI may differ, they both trigger robust acute inflammatory reactions that negatively impact recovery and may lead to the development of long-term chronic inflammation and further loss of neurological function. Neuroinflammation is driven by nervous system-specific processes and compounded by the recruitment of blood-dervied pro-inflammatory cells to the lesion site. The priority of any treatment strategy must be to minimize damage to the neurons not affected by the initial trauma. The need for a neuroprotective therapy for acute brain and spinal trauma is clearly unmet. The Spinal Cord Injury Team's (SCIT) research at the Robarts Research Institute has focused on developing an anti-inflammatory neuroprotective treatment for SCI and TBI. This anti-inflammatory strategy uses an antibody to CD11d to block blood-derived pro-inflammatory cells from entering into the spinal or brain lesion. CD11d participates in the mechanism that allows blood cells to migrate into spine and brain lesions. This reduces the overall inflammation in the lesion, protects against the loss of additional neurons and increases the overall rate of neurological recovery. Our goal is to advance the CD11d antibody strategy for use in human SCI or TBI clinical trials. We now have available five candidate CD11d antibodies with anti-inflammatory activity in rats that bind to CD11d on the surface of human blood cells. To progress toward human treatment, we will determine which of these candidate antibodies promotes the best neurological recovery and prevents human blood-derived pro-inflammatory cell infiltration into a CNS lesion in appropriate rodent models. Based on these results the best CD11d antibody will be selected for a Phase I Clinical Trial in either SCI or TBI.

column36: The collaborative ideal in Canadian healthcare delivery: Its rise, practice and future
column37: Collaboration is widely touted as a solution to healthcare's challenges, from fatal errors to escalating costs. Canadian governments, institutions of higher education and hospitals have acted on this rhetoric, and invested time, money and personnel resources to improve collaborative practice. Decades after the initial calls to improve care delivery through collaboration, the literature connecting these investments with positive patient care outcomes remains exceedingly sparse and inconclusive. We know that failures of collaboration and communication often harm patients, but educating providers for collaborative practice has proven to be very difficult, and rarely leads to improved patient care. The goal of this project is to draw on historical and social scientific evidence to transform how we teach healthcare professionals to collaborate. In contrast with the pre-existing literature, we see collaboration as a social construction: an idea that was championed by individuals and organizations who successfully integrated it into education and policy. This new framing will help us reach two related aims. First, it will make the development of the idea of collaboration visible through a historical case study. Second, it will allow us to document the impact of the rise of collaboration as a solution on current patient care practices. Providers will be interviewed about their views on collaborative healthcare delivery, on how collaboration has changed practices in their work environments, and on how education for collaboration could be improved. They will also be observed as they work, to help identify the factors that facilitate teamwork. By engaging healthcare professionals and leaders at every step of our project, we will ensure that we maximize the reach and impact of this project. This grant will thus help us prepare the next generation of healthcare professionals for collaboration through evidence-based education.

column36: Prohibitin: a circulating mitokine involved in the Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Syndrome.
column37: Patients with pulmonary hypertension (PHT; high blood pressure in the lungs) have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. These cells proliferate like cancer cells and create an obstruction of the vessels, making it difficult for the blood to go through. Their right chamber of the heart fails as it has to pump against increased pressure, causing many symptoms like shortness of breath, poor exercise capacity, and eventually death. They also have evidence of inflammation in their blood, similar to patients suffering from infections. Although we know that this inflammation is detrimental to the blood vessels and the heart, we do not know its cause in PHT. Finally, evidence of insulin resistance has been found in patients with PHT like in diabetic patients, and again without known cause. All these organs have something in common: they display the same abnormal way to produce energy (metabolism). We therefore hypothesized that factors circulating in the whole body could be responsible for this overall aberrant metabolism seen in organs otherwise unconnected. We were particularly interested in Prohibitin (PHB), a circulating factor that has been found increased in the serum of patients with cancer, another disease with multi-organ metabolism abnormalities. We propose to study the role of circulating PHB in PHT. We will determine 1) whether PHB levels are increased in the blood of humans and animal models of PHT; 2) the potential of PHB to change arterial cells' metabolism, proliferation and survival, and to induce PHT in animals; 4) the mechanisms by which circulating PHB acts; 5) whether the inhibition of these mechanisms improve PHT in human cells and animals. If this is proven to be true in humans, it will have a tremendous impact on our knowledge regarding how PHT starts and progresses and may reveal new ways to treat the disease.

column36: Lymphatic vessel function in atherosclerosis
column37: High blood cholesterol is an important risk factor of cardiovascular disease such as atherosclerosis. High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is called ''good cholesterol'' because it transports cholesterol away from tissues, such as the blood vessel walls, carrying cholesterol through the blood circulation for eventual excretion into intestines. Unfortunately, the clinical outcomes aiming at increasing levels of circulating HDL (or "good cholesterol") have not been as successful as expected, suggesting that raising HDL may not lead to an increased cholesterol clearance capacity or prevention of coronary heart disease. Expressed differently, more cargo ships (cholesterol transporter) leaving from the harbour docks (blood vessel wall), have not led to more merchandise delivered (cholesterol clearance). Thus, a better understanding of the cholesterol clearance process has become necessary to efficiently modulate the progression of atherosclerosis. In this regard, we provided unprecedented insight into the path that cholesterol trapped in peripheral tissues takes during cholesterol mobilization for eventual excretion (Martel, JCI 2013). We demonstrated that cholesterol (merchandise) gets out of tissues (harbour docks) and reaches the bloodstream (sea) by first entering so-called lymphatic vessels (canals). As the lymphatic system - lymph, from Latin lympha, meaning water - generally governs the transport of macromolecules from the tissues to the blood and, accordingly, peripheral lymph contains cholesterol transporters (HDL), a role in cholesterol transport seemed logical. Therefore, we view that improvement of the delivery efficiency would rely on enhancing the navigation conditions, instead of the number of cargo ships per se. The main objective of our emerging research team aims to understand the mechanisms connecting abnormal lymphatic function and atherosclerosis progression, to ultimately lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets.

column36: Development of drug combinations in acute myeloid leukemia
column37: Treatments in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) consist of standard chemotherapy which has been unchanged in the last 30 years and showed limited therapeutic benefits for the majority of patients. Moreover, long-term resistance to these drugs is the main cause of relapse in patients. Recent studies on the evolution of tumour cells suggest that, although the failure of single-agent therapies is almost inevitable, combination of therapies might effectively cure many cancers. However, the mechanism of action of most anticancer drugs is poorly characterized, which makes the rational design of combination therapies extremely challenging. Moreover, due to the large number of possible drug combinations, it is not feasible to test them all experimentally. There is therefore a dire for innovative computational approaches to better explore the large space of drug combinations with the aim to direct in vitro and in vivo testing of the most promising therapeutic strategies. In this project, we propose to address this issue by leveraging large amounts of pharmacogenomic data measuring how drugs affect cancer cells in order to identify efficient drug combinations in AML. We will develop an innovative computational pipeline to explore the large number of possible combinations of thousands of drugs, and to build companion tests predictive of their response in individual patients. We will validate our most promising candidates in the laboratory to test their therapeutic potential in AML cells in a dish and in mouse models. Upon successful validation, our novel therapeutic strategies and associated companion tests will also allow to avoid overtreatment and unnecessary toxicity by selecting the best drug combinations for each individual AML patient. Since we will enrich our drug combinations for FDA-approved drugs in our discovery pipeline, this will allow repurposing of existing drugs and will provide a mechanism to rapidly translate the results of our project to the clinic.

column36: Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Approaches to Stargardt Macular Degeneration
column37: Inherited retinal degenerative diseases are a heterogeneous group of disorders that are a major cause of blindness in Canada and the developed world. They are typically characterized by progressive loss in vision resulting from mutations in genes encoding proteins essential for the survival of rod and cone photoreceptor cells. Stargardt macular degeneration (STGD1) linked to mutations in the membrane transporter ABCA4 is the most common monogenic inherited retinal degenerative disease. Affected individuals typically experience loss in central vision in their first decade of life often progressing to total blindness in later years. Mutations in ABCA4 are also associated with other severe retinal diseases including retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration. My lab has shown that ABCA4 functions in the removal of vitamin A derivatives known as retinoids that are produced as part of the visual process. Disease-associated mutations cause a loss in the ability of ABCA4 to remove retinoids. As a result toxic retinoid compounds accumulate causing photoreceptor cell death and a loss in vision. The goal of this research is to further understand the molecular structure and function of ABCA4 and determine how mutations in this protein cause a loss in vision. This information together with our expertise in retinal degenerative diseases will be used to design and develop novel pharmaceutical agents (drugs) as promising treatments for STGD1. This research will increase our knowledge of the visual system and retinal degenerative diseases and lead to therapeutic treatments that will improve the health care and quality of life of individuals with STGD1 and related diseases, and reduce their economic burden on society. Our research program will also train graduate students and postdocs for future careers in basic science and translational medicine and produce new intellectual property and commercialization that will benefit Canada.

column36: Metabolic role of arylacetamide deacetylase (AADAC)
column37: Obesity is a serious health problem in Canada. Obesity is often accompanied by increased fat deposition in liver and intestine (and other cells and organs), which consequently leads to decreased action of a hormone called insulin. When insulin does not work well in liver and intestine, these organs increase production of particles that carry "bad" cholesterol in blood and cause heart disease and stroke. The amount of fat in liver and intestine is determined by fat production, fat breakdown (process called lipolysis) and fat export out of these organs. Lipolysis is carried out by proteins called lipases. We are researching one of these lipases called arylacetamide deacetylase (AADAC), which is present only in liver and small intestine. We are proposing experiments that will show that AADAC decreases fat levels in liver and intestine and therefore also the production of particles carrying "bad" cholesterol. AADAC might also metabolize certain drugs, including flutamide. column36: Characterization and cytoskeletal regulation of nucleocytoplasmic traffic and expression of mechanosensitive transcription factors. Relevance to organ fibrosis.
column37: Organ fibrosis or progressive scarring of vital organs such as kidney, lung liver and heart is a failed healing attempt in response to chronic injury. Fibrosis is the final common pathway leading to organ failure in many common diseases including diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerosis and substance abuse. It is a striking but lesser known fact that fibrosis is a major component of mortality, being responsible for 45% of all deaths in the Western World. Despite its paramount medical importance, fibrosis has no cure; currently there are no means to stop or reverse the disease process and the only temporary hope is organ replacement therapy. It is therefore critically important to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the initiation and progression of organ fibrosis. Fibrosis-associated changes are brought about by altered gene expression in various cells. This is due to chemical and mechanical injury-induced activation of transcription factors. These factors need to travel to the cell's nucleus where they turn on target genes. However we do not understand how this process happens and how it can be inhibited or exploited to lessen fibrosis. Our previous work shows that cellular stress induces robust remodeling of the cell's skeleton (cytoskeleton), which may be a key regulator of the nuclear traffic of transcription factors. Therefore, the overall aim of my research is to understand the molecular and cell biological mechanisms underlying the general and cytoskeletal regulation of fibrosis-inducing transcription factors. We will use this knowledge to develop new antifibrotic molecular therapies, such as antifibrotic viruses to halt or reverse fibrosis. To achieve these goals we will create a new molecular toolkit to study and alter the traffic of transcription factors. In summary, these studies will provide fundamental insight into a new area of cell biology, and use the acquired knowledge to combat a common, currently incurable disease.

column36: Impact of chronic infections on hematopoietic stem cell function
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), or blood forming cells, are found in the adult bone marrow, where they are essential for the continuous generation of circulating blood cells, including the cells of the immune system. Their function is normally tightly regulated, and the different types of blood cells are being produced in balanced quantities. In a situation of stress, such as an acute infection, HSCs become activated and they will multiply and change the proportions of the different blood cells being produced with the goal to better respond to the infection and eliminate the infectious agent. Once the infection is resolved, the HSCs will go back to their normal, dormant state. However, it is not known what happens to the HSCs when the infectious agent cannot be eliminated. Some chronic infections lead to bone marrow failure, or the loss of new blood cell production, which can be fatal. There is very little information on how this happens or how it could be prevented. The goal of our research therefore is to better understand how HSCs react during chronic infections using two well-established mouse models. We also propose that the infectious agents (virus or parasite) may actually use the HSCs to escape the immune response by inducing the HSCs to produce one type of blood cell over another. After the completion of our studies we expect to have sufficient new information to identify new targets to treat and hopefully cure chronic viral or parasitic infections.

column37: The insula is one of the least understood brain areas. This is mostly due to its deep location, which makes it less accessible than other structures. column37: Our ultimate goal is to contribute to the development of a drug treatment for the long-term cognitive impairments caused by traumatic brain injury (TBI). column36: Structural and functional investigation of arrhythmia-associated mutations in calmodulin
column37: Cardiac arrhythmias are life-threatening conditions whereby the heart beats irregularly and blood flow to the brain can be temporarily restricted. This can lead to fainting or, in worse cases, to sudden death. Knowing which type of arrhythmia someone has is absolutely key to adjust the lifestyle appropriately and to receive the proper treatment. Many arrhythmias have a clear genetic cause, and typically certain genes are linked to very specific types of arrhythmia. We know that mutations in specific genes can lead to cardiac mutations, but in most cases we don't know how. We simply know that 'somehow a mutation in gene X or Y triggers this or that particular arrhythmia'. In this project, we wish to solve this problem, by investigating the direct mechanisms of individual mutations. In particular, we will investigate several mutations in a gene known as 'CALM'. These mutations have been found in various patients worldwide that have cardiac arrhythmias. Surprisingly, depending on the exact mutation within the CALM gene, the arrhythmia is different. We wish to pinpoint exactly how each mutation works, and how it affects the electrical properties of the heart. Almost every gene in our DNA forms a code to make protein. Ultimately, it is the protein, and not the gene, that plays the actual role in our bodies. A mutation in a gene thus leads to a slightly different protein, which could then result in differences large enough to cause a serious disorder. One problem is that proteins are so small that they are hard to visualize via regular microscopy. We therefore use a highly advanced technique, known as 'X-ray crystallography', whereby we can easily see differences smaller than a 10-billionth of a meter. Here we will compare normal and diseased forms of the protein encoded by the CALM gene. This will yield important insights into the exact mechanism of the disease.

column37: A hallmark of Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the deposition of amyloid plaques composed of beta-amyloid peptide in the brain. The goal of this project is to understand a new neuronal system that secretes beta-amyloid called lysosomal secretion. Beta-amyloid is produced by the cleavage of the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) by secretase enzymes. Recently we have shown that these cleavages may occur in a compartment called the lysosome. Although lysosomes are normally viewed as digestive organelles, many cells use lysosomes to secrete specialized contents, including the thyroid, lung, liver, platelets, T-cells, eosinophils, and neurotophils. We have data that shows that neuronal lysosomes contain Beta-amyloid and they are capable of secreting. We will demonstrate lysosomal secretion using a special microscopy technique called Total Internal Reflection Microscopy (TIRFM), which allows us to look at structures very close to the cell membrane (100-200 nanometers). We load cells with fluorescent dyes and use are use this microscope to create videos of lysosomes secreting their contents. We will demonstrate that this process occurs in human neurons. We will then examine several of the regulatory proteins that control this process in non-neuronal cells. Finaly we will demonstrate that beta-amyloid is secreted from lysosomes. Because many other intracellular protein aggregates are also secreted like beta amyloid, this mechanism will likely be broadly applicable across neurodegenerative diseases. An understanding of these processes will aid in the design of therapeutic strategies for AD and neurodegenerative disease.

column37: During pregnancy, disruption of the supply of oxygen to the baby is a common cause of injury and death. Early delivery is a treatment option, but this must be weighed against the risks of premature birth such as infection and poor organ development. The goal of this project is to develop highly specific and potent inhibitors for viral deubiquitinases. Using protein engineering technology, we propose to make ubiquitin mimics that will associate tightly with these enzymes in a manner that inhibits function. We will validate their inhibitory function in mammalian cells using established biological assays. Additional structural analyses of critical contacts that mediate specificity and affinity will further aid the development of chemical inhibitors as drugs. In conclusion, this work will generate invaluable tools to understand and modulate activity of pathogenic deubiquitinases and will open new routes to effective antiviral therapy.

column36: Deciphering breast cancer HER2-negativity with regard to HER2-targeted therapy
column37: Breast cancer is the type of cancer with the highest incidence, and it represents the second cause of death in women. Several biomarkers such as hormone receptor status expressed in the breast tumors could predict to a certain level the aggressiveness and potential of development into invasive cancer. The Human Epidermal Growth Factor 2, HER2, is a prognostic marker of clinical outcome in breast cancer. High expression of HER2 occurs in 20-25% of breast tumors and has been associated with a more aggressive clinical behavior. Anti-HER2 agents are administered only to patients with HER2-positive (HER2+) breast tumors. Therefore, patients with HER2-negative (HER2-) breast tumors receive no personalized treatments. These women have higher rate of recurrence, and when this happens a change in HER2 status is often observed (i.e. HER2- at primary diagnosis to HER2+ at breast recurrence). Such tumors could therefore benefit from anti-HER2 treatments at time of diagnosis, which currently are not provided for a primary HER2- tumor. This study will establish a breast cancer gene signature that will identify women in whom an anti-HER2 treatment in prevention (i.e. at breast cancer diagnosis) would be beneficial to prevent a breast cancer recurrence. Through lack of better options, these patients are currently treated with aggressive chemotherapeutic agents only. We can thus expect our research to have an impact not only on the incidence of breast cancer recurrence and prognosis, but on response to treatment as well, hence impacting greatly on their quality of life.

column36: The relationship between iNKT cells & the microbiota in the control of intestinal inflammation
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) likely result from deregulated immune responses to the indigenous microorganisms that reside within the intestine, collectively termed the microbiota, in genetically susceptible hosts. The intestine contains a large number of different immune cells that have the delicate task of fighting off pathogens while "keeping the peace" with the resident microbes. Of these immune cells, T cells are central to maintaining the status quo, and deregulated T cell responses are believed to be at the core of IBD. This past decade has revealed the importance of the microbiota in health and disease, and how it influences the immune system, including the function of different types of T cells. Invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells are a type of T cells that can regulate immune responses during numerous diseases such as cancer, autoimmunity and inflammation. Specifically, iNKT cells play protective or deleterious functions in animal models of Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), respectively. Moreover iNKT cell defects have been found in CD patients. These cells are particularly well equipped to recognize microbes and therefore protect from pathogens. However, their interaction with the commensal microbiota remains elusive. Our previous research has shown that mice deficient in iNKT cells have an altered and pro-inflammatory microbiota. This research project will build on these findings to explore how iNKT cells and the microbiota influence each other, and the impact of this bidirectional relationship on the establishment of intestinal inflammation. Identification of these mechanisms may lead to new therapeutic strategies targeting iNKT cells for the treatment of IBD.

column37: Childbirth is a major risk factor for pelvic floor muscle (PFM) trauma. In one third of women, stretching of the PFM will result in an avulsion injury (i.e. disconnection of the muscle from its insertion points on the pubic symphysis). Recent advances in imaging have led to the discovery of this previously unknown major injury and further research now enables its diagnosis with readily available techniques. Avulsion injury has alarming consequences because it has been associated with a higher rate of stress urinary incontinence (SUI) in the postpartum period as well as the long-term development of other major urogynecological conditions such as pelvic organ prolapse and anal incontinence. Women with avulsion are not only confronted by severe symptoms with significant related impacts on physical activities, overall well-being and quality of life, but they also present a higher rate of surgical failures. Moreover, it is still unknown whether the most recommended first-line treatment for SUI -PFM physiotherapy- is effective in women with this major trauma. Until now, only a pilot study conducted by our team supports the rationale and the efficacy of physiotherapy for improving PFM function in women with avulsion, despite their major muscle injury. The proposed study aims to further investigate the efficacy of physiotherapy for SUI in this sub-population with major obstetrical injuries. Women with an avulsion injury will be randomized either to receive physiotherapy or to be in a waiting-list control group for which treatment will be available after a 9-month follow-up. The current proposal addresses the urgent need to evaluate whether or not women with an avulsion -a prevalent and debilitating long-term condition- could benefit from physiotherapy treatment as a first-line intervention. It will enable women with avulsion to be directed to appropriate treatment options and, if proven effective, PFM physiotherapy could be proposed as a cost-effective first-line treatment.

column36: Functional investigation of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex in neuronal development and function.
column37: Recent technical innovations in the field of genomics have lead to rapid discovery of many mutations associated with human disease. For neurodevelopmental disorders like Intellectual Disability (ID), there are now over 700 known causative genes. Stemming from this tsunami of new information is an increased need to understand the function of these genes in a relevant biological context. Among the 700+ known ID genes, there are several biological processes that are over-represented. This includes chromatin modifiers and epigenetic regualtors, which affect gene expression through biochemical modifications that do not directly alter the DNA sequence. My lab is focused on understanding the role of chromatin regulation in neurons. This project focuses on a specific chromatin remodeling complex, known as SWI/SNF, which is one of the most overrepresented complexes in ID. My lab has initiated a systematic analysis of SWI/SNF components in regulation of learning and memory in Drosophila. The high evolutionary conservation of this complex allows us to use flies to investigate the role of all 15 SWI/SNF subunits in neuron development and function. Our initial studies have identified a role for SWI/SNF subunits in development of specific brain regions that are required for memory. The main aims of this project are: (1) To investigate whether SWI/SNF complexes also play a role post-development, in adult-specific processes involved in learning and memory. (2) To identify SWI/SNF target genes that are important in the regulation of learning and memory. We use a multidisciplinary approach that combines spatiotemporal genetic manipulation, with high-throughput behaviour and cell-type specific genomics. These studies will begin to elucidate the role of the SWI/SNF complex in regulation of neuron development and function. This is a critical starting point toward understanding the human neurodevelopmental disorders associated with mutations in genes encoding SWI/SNF complex members.

column37: Recognizing the critical importance of children's environment to their lifelong health and development, the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child's (CRC) reporting system is intended to help State Parties to identify and correct weaknesses and deficits in government service that impact children. Canada, though one of the driving forces behind the CRC, has consistently fallen short of the desired level of compliance with and reporting on CRC. While reporting difficulties might be explained by Canada's federal structure, it is also possible that inadequate reports reflect inadequate compliance. A comprehensive monitoring tool can facilitate the compliance and reporting. This project is intended to help to align Canadian internal processes with our international obligations and commitments to the CRC, by creating a monitoring and accountability tool. In addition to providing a fully contextualised database available to different levels of government and researchers, GC would address consistent weaknesses in Canadian CRC reporting. Ultimately it will provide credible evidence to evaluate existing government service delivery against international standards and to guide the development of more effective policies and procedures. We have demonstrated the usefulness of the concept and created international interest in both the ECRI and the possibility of a tool like GC. We intend to build on this to create GC, a fully digitized, bilingual tool for all children in Canada, paying particular attention to our Indigenous children.

column36: Transgender youth in clinical care: A pan-Canadian cohort study of medical, social and family outcomes
column37: Recent media reports have increased awareness of medical interventions to delay puberty and alter physical sex characteristics to align with inner gender identity. As a result, youth whose gender identity does not match the gender they were assigned at birth have been increasingly referred to pediatric clinics that provide this type of care. Rapidly increasing numbers of referrals to nine clinics that provide such treatment in Canada reflect international trends. This project will study 300 youth (puberty to age 16 at enrolment) who have been referred to these nine clinics for puberty suppression and/or hormone therapy for gender identity issues, as well as their parents/caregivers. As a result, we will know much more about the youth who are referred for gender issues and their families, including their previous care, gender identities, family dynamics, social stressors, and factors that affect their health and well-being. We will understand more about medical and mental health outcomes for youth undergoing puberty suppression and other medical interventions, and identify factors that may result in better outcomes, for example age at which treatment is started, type of treatment, or level of parental support. We will also learn about treatment side effects. We will know more about gender and sex development among these youth, and how their physical, mental and social health develops. In addition, we will study how family functioning and parent/caregiver's well-being may change over time. We expect our study will result in changes to medical care, social services, and youth and family decision-making.

column36: Multimorbidity in Children and Youth Across the LIFEcourse (MY LIFE)
column37: Nearly 15% of youth less than 18 years of age are affected by both a physical and mental health problem, a situation known as 'multimorbidity'. This combination of problems can lead to compromised life quality, hardship for families, and considerable burden on the healthcare system. However, given the normal challenges of childhood and adolescence and stress of having a chronic physical condition managing multimorbidity in youth is difficult, but critical. We will determine how and why some youth develop multimorbidity, while others do not, because this knowledge is essential for establishing interventions to improve outcomes. Building on our successful feasibility study, we will document the course of mental health symptoms over time, as well as identify individual, family, and community predictors of mental disorder among 504 youth with chronic physical conditions. We will also examine whether the effects of these predictors are amplified or act through other psychosocial and biological variables such as poverty or physical activity. Furthermore, we will assess the extent to which multimorbidity increases the amount or alters patterns of psychiatric services usage among youth. We will enroll youth aged 2-17 years with a variety of chronic physical conditions (e.g., asthma, diabetes, epilepsy) receiving outpatient care at McMaster Children's Hospital and follow them for 24 months. We will also enroll a subset of age-matched healthy sibling controls. We will use provincial health care data to confirm psychiatric diagnoses and service use. Advanced statistical modeling will be used to estimate trajectories of health outcomes. With rare exceptions, previous studies were cross-sectional and none examined the extent to which youth multimorbidity impacts the amount of psychiatric services youth access. Preventing youth multimorbidity is essential to improve youth trajectories, strengthen families, and in turn, improve care and reduce costs.

column37: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a severe, life threatening reaction that occurs upon exposure during surgery to certain anesthetics. column36: The role of anillin in modulating the cytoskeleton of dividing and differentiated cells
column37: Cells adopt different shapes to efficiently carry out specific functions. Cell shape changes are caused by rearranging internal networks of proteins collectively called the cytoskeleton. When the cytoskeleton adopts the wrong shape at the wrong time the cell cannot carry out its function. One important example in human disease is that disruption of the cytoskeleton disrupts cell division and can lead to tumors. Other cytoskeleton rearrangements are required for cell migration, important for metastasis, and the production of cilia, the cell's antennae which are needed for correct kidney function. Therefore understanding how the cytoskeleton is dynamically reorganized at the molecular level will provide new platforms for drug discovery and therapeutics to treat diseases such as cancer and ciliopathies. Our proposal focuses on the protein anillin that binds to and regulates the cytoskeleton. As anillin interacts with many cellular factors, we propose that anillin accepts different incoming cellular signals and translates them into changes in the cytoskeleton. We have discovered a new mechanism whereby anillin regulates the formation of new cytoskeletal elements during cell division. We propose to determine how this new process regulates cell shape changes during cell division and determine if this mechanism operates in other cell shape changes during cell migration. We have also made a new and exciting discovery that anillin is required for making cilia. When cilia are disrupted the cell cannot function and, especially in the kidney, this leads to disease. Mutations in anillin are linked to kidney disease and we will determine how anillin role in making cilia. We expect our studies to identify new regulatory mechanisms that control cell shape during cell division, cell migration and ciliogenesis. This information will be important for the development of new therapeutic strategies in human disease, in particular cancer.

column37: Over the last 50 years, multiple chronic diseases have seen a dramatic rise in frequency in childhood. They include type 1 diabetes (T1D), type 2 diabetes (T2D), inflammatory bowel diseases and asthma. These diseases share a common feature - they involve the immune system. This system normally functions to protect the body from pathogenic organisms. In diabetes, excessive immune responses towards normal cells that drive tissue inflammation and damage. The recent increase in frequency of these diseases likely reflect dynamic changes in our environment, including our diet, physical activity, hygiene, and use of antibiotics in agriculture and medicine. We aim to understand how microbiome disturbances control diabetes development. We will analyze fecal bacteria from children with high T1D or T2D risk to identify how they elicit inflammation. The children's bacteria will be transferred into mice to determine if they cause inflammation and diabetes. We will study the effects of the bacterial products on insulin production and function. With integrated studies in humans, mice and isolated cells, we will identify the interaction between the microbiome, metabolism and immunity during diabetes progression. Because the intestinal microbiome can be changed with diet, medications or probiotics, identification of bacterial products can reveal new therapies to prevent or delay both the forms of diabetes that afflict so many persons in Canada and abroad.

column36: Imaging Tools for Quick and Appropriate Triage of Stroke Patients
column37: Stroke, mainly caused by a blood clot blocking a brain artery, is the leading cause of morbidity in the developed world. Removing the clot quickly saves at-risk brain tissue, improving the patient's chance of a good outcome. A current clinical method for removing blood clots is giving a drug that dissolves clot (clot-buster); however, this method only works 15-25% of the time for larger clots, and may cause bleeding into the brain in some patients. A more recent method of clot removal is to pull it out mechanically using a catheter inserted through an artery in the groin. This technique has a much higher success rate, but is only available at large hospitals and requires a talented surgeon. This procedure is therefore not available in community hospitals. When treating a patient with stroke, a community physician therefore needs to know if the clot in the patient's brain blood vessel dissolves quickly with the clot-busting drug or will the patient need to be sent to a larger hospital where the clot could be pulled out with a catheter? The community physician has to make decisions on treatment and transfer fast as every minute counts with stroke treatment. On the other hand, decisions have to be appropriate and correct, as otherwise some patients may be harmed while others who do not need the catheter-based procedure may be transferred unnecessarily to the bigger hospital. Moreover, the community physician sees a small number of patients with stroke each year and therefore lacks expertise in interpreting brain scans and making these decisions. To address this gap in expertise between large hospitals and community hospitals, we propose to develop an automated imaging-based triaging decision support tool that can help community physicians make clinical decisions on triage of patients with acute ischemic stroke at any time of the day or night quickly and correctly. We will automate many important imaging concepts we have developed until now for this purpose.

Fc-FcR interactions can activate FcR+ innate immune cells and induce anti-viral activity. Which FcR an Ab Fc region binds and the strength of the binding interaction depends on the Ab immunoglobulin class, the amino acid sequence of the Fc domain and the composition of added sugars (i.e. Fc biophysical features). These Fc features in turn determine which innate immune cells are activated for functions that can kill or clear pathogens (i.e. function). The pattern of HIV-specific Ab Fc functions and features differs in recipients of protective versus non protective HIV vaccines. Remarkably, the rare subset of HIV infected individuals, known as Elite Controllers (ECs) have patterns of Fc functions and features that differ from those seen in progressors suggesting that Ab dependent anti-HIV activity can control HIV. The proposal will investigate this hypothesis by considering the degree of HIV control as measured by HIV viral load (VL) and cellular HIV reservoir size and how these correlate with Fc dependent parameters. HIV+ ECs and those starting treatment in acute infection (AT) can achieve similarly low HIV viral loads and HIV reservoirs unlike those left untreated or who start treatment late in infection. But AT loose HIV control when treatment is stopped. We will investigate whether and which patterns of HIV-specific Ab Fc parameters distinguish EC from AT. The goal will be to better understand the link between Ab dependent activity and HIV control. The field of Ab therapeutics is developing ways to deliver and engineer Abs having desirable characteristics for particular disease outcomes. The information learned from this project will characterize the Ab Fc parameters that support HIV control thus potentially providing a benchmark for therapeutic Ab design for control of HIV infection.

column36: Identifying integrative biomarkers of risk and resilience to childhood psychopathology
column37: Mental disorders constitute the largest contributor to the global burden of disease as measured using the disability-adjusted life years index. The most common mental disorders, including major depression and conduct disorders show a peak age of onset in later childhood and adolescence thus derailing the quality of life and productivity of individuals over entire lifetimes. However, by identifying at risk children at an early age we have an opportunity to intervene and prevent many of such mental disorders. The challenge is in effectively identifying truly vulnerable children to be able to intervene in a timely manner. Current programs for identifying at risk children are constructed on evidence linking early life adversity, such as poverty or birth outcomes, and the risk for mental illness. These factors predict mental illness at the level of the population, but are inefficient at the level of the individual due to the considerable variability in outcomes: many children born early, small, or into poverty are healthy and productive. The goal of this project is to identify robust and predictive biological and psychological measurements that help to predict which children are at risk early on. In particular, by assaying molecular markers that capture the biological mechanisms associated with specific psychiatric outcomes, we will identify factors that differentiate those who do and do not succumb to childhood mental illness given the same set of known early life risk factors. This study will thus inform targeted, and personalized interventions aimed at both reducing the severity of onset of these disorders and the negative outcomes that accompany them, such as suicide and substance abuse.

column36: Elucidation of the molecular mechanisms governing currently untargeted RAS effector pathways towards novel therapeutic approaches for the most refractory human cancers
column37: Cancers are driven by abnormal changes to the genetic material of various cell types in the human body. These changes frequently result in the production of mutated proteins, or an overproduction of proteins, leading to unregulated cell growth. The protein RAS has long been recognized as a key driver of human cancers with fully 30% having mutations in RAS genes, and significantly more showing high activity of associated pathways. RAS has thus been a vitally important target for drug development, but efforts have so far proven unsuccessful. Indeed, a lack of effective therapies for RAS-driven cancers is the major reason why lung, colon, and pancreatic cancers remain the most refractory to available treatments. Improved technological approaches, however, should allow a better understanding of mutant RAS and its associated proteins, and have massively revitalized interest in developing RAS-targeted therapeutics. I have developed new methods to study RAS function, and its connections with other proteins in cells. Targeting such associations is finally proving effective in treating some cancers, yet important relationships between RAS and some partners remain completely unstudied. This includes proteins that regulate the ability of cells to move, linked to metastasis, and proteins that lead to self-directed cell death, which I believe could be exploited as a novel cancer therapy. I use leading-edge techniques such as NMR spectroscopy and X-Ray crystallography to gain insight to the structure of proteins at a molecular level, and complement these data with studies in human cells to observe how mutations lead to cellular transformation. I propose to identify and characterize new therapeutic targets in the RAS pathway, and these efforts will be complemented by the drug discovery capabilities at IRIC. These studies are highly significance to many patients, particularly those with currently untreatable cancers such as pancreatic adenocarcinomas and lung NSCLCs.

Early prognostic markers may be useful to identify patients at high risk of losing their transplants so they may undergo more intensive therapy and avoid minimization/withdrawal of their anti-rejection medications. This trial is the first of its kind to evaluate the impact of an early rejection marker on transplant outcomes. These new urine tests may be used to personalize medicine and improve patient and transplant outcomes. Finally, strategies that improve transplant outcomes may result in long-term health care savings.

column36: The impact of perturbations in T cell migration on the spatio-temporal dynamics of CD4 T cell homeostasis and effector cell differentiation
column37: In our global society, many of us travel to and from work, fly between cities, or even set up residence somewhere new. Along the way, we might bump into others, exchange information, and learn new things that inform our behaviour. Hence, what we learn during our travels can have a dramatic impact on our lives. T lymphocytes have a similarly cosmopolitan lifestyle within the body. The job of T cells in the immune system - to detect and stop the replication of a pathogen or cancer cell as quickly as possible - makes it essential for them to commute continuously between the blood and secondary lymphoid organs. Within lymphoid organs, T cells make critical interactions with other cells that dictate their function and fate. During infections, such interactions can license them to enter tissues and even set up residence there, protecting from reinfection. To understand the implications of the jet-setting behaviour of T cells on their function, we use advanced microscopy to track their movements within tissues in real time. This approach enables us to investigate a number of important questions. How do the interactions T cells make with other cells keep them alive? Why do pathogens or gene defects that prevent migration lead paradoxically both to severe immune deficiencies and to immune-mediated disease? In the long-term, answers to these questions will contribute to the design of better therapies for immunological diseases, such as allergy and autoimmunity, and allow us to harness the function of T cells to improve our ability to treat or prevent infections, from Ebola virus to HIV and beyond.

column36: The Influence of Acute Bouts of Aerobic Exercise on Neuroplasticity and Motor Learning after Stroke
column37: Recovery from stroke is most often incomplete and requires large amounts of practice that are expensive and often not feasible. Because of this it is important to develop new ways to speed learning after stroke. One approach that is promising is to prepare or "prime" the brain for learning by pairing exercise with skilled practice of movement tasks. Past work showed that pairing single sessions of exercise with skilled motor practice enhances learning. Our work demonstrated that the short bout of exercise primes or prepares the brain for learning by lessening inhibition which then facilitates brain plasticity. However this intervention has only been tested in healthy controls. Further, at this time we have only tested single sessions that pair a short bout of priming exercise with skilled practice. As such we do not know what the effect of multiple sessions that pair priming exercise with skilled practice would be on motor learning. The present study is designed to test the effects of priming exercise on motor learning as an intervention that is designed to enhance motor learning after stroke. This is important as such an intervention could be used to enhance the effects of rehabilitation after stroke. In total we will test two main aims: 1)We will determine if the effect of priming exercise is to lessen inhibition in the brain after stroke. 2)We will deliver repeated sessions of priming exercise paired with skilled motor practice to see if compared to a group who rests before motor practice, the exercise group shows greater learning. Our data will illustrate a new way by which learning could be enhanced after stroke. Exercise could easily be incorporated into rehabilitation settings. As such our findings can be rapidly translated to the clinical setting to promote the recovery of Canadians with stroke.

column36: Evolution of evidence-based practice: evaluating the contribution of individual and contextual factors to optimize patient care
column37: There is strong research evidence on the effectiveness of rehabilitation (i.e. occupational therapy (OT) and physical therapy (PTs)) interventions for improving important outcomes such as morbidity, mortality and quality of life in individuals with high burden conditions such as low back pain, stroke and cancer. The process by which clinicians apply results from research to make decisions in their daily practice is referred to as evidence-based practice (EBP). Unfortunately, the application of research results in clinical practice is critically lacking in these professions. Though academic rehabilitation programs in Canada are designed to promote competence in EBP, the EBP outcomes at graduation (what new graduates "look like") and over time (whether EBP declines, improves, or remains the same) as well as the factors that influence clinicians' use of EBP following graduation and over time are poorly understood. The goal of this research is to understand how individual (e.g. knowledge, attitudes, confidence, behaviours) and contextual factors (e.g. resources) impact EBP, and how these change from graduation to clinical practice and over time. Using questionnaires targeting EBP (attitudes, knowledge, confidence and behaviours) as well as interviews and focus groups with groups of clinicians, this research will follow new graduates (class of 2016) from professional OT and PT Master's programs across Canada for the first 3 years post-graduation to measure and understand changes in EBP. This research is vital for designing curricula that better prepare graduates for the evolving clinical contexts, for designing organizational supports to stem any decline in EBP, and for informing continuing professional development programs aimed at maintaining clinical competence, ensuring that clinicians are offering state of the art evidence-based services.

column36: Challenges to the vulnerable child in the transitions from preschool to grade school in a pregnancy cohort
column37: How is it that 10-15% of school children end up with mental health problems? We know that most of these children showed early signs in preschool, and many risk factors were evident in the perinatal period. Some suggest that the challenges of having to rapidly adapt to a more structured and demanding environment such as formal school will be very stressful for vulnerable children, depending on the support they will receive from family and school environments. Further, a mismatch between child and environment could not only worsen symptoms to the status of disorders, but also spill over into additional problems. We will now follow the children, families and schools yearly for four years, before, during and after the transition. We will carefully and more intensely assess cortisol, a stress hormone, in a subsample. Because several of the children we follow will be developing childhood mental health problems, this is a very time-sensitive project that needs to be done now as they enter this important transition phase.

column36: Role of inflammation in experimental post-traumatic epilepsy
column37: Severe traumatic brain injury leads to epilepsy in up to 50% of survivors. There are medications used to treat seizures after epilepsy has started, but none to prevent the development of epilepsy in the first place. Inflammation is a biological process initiated by the body's immune system after brain injury to try and protect from ongoing harm. However, inflammation can also have detrimental effects and is a significant mediator of ongoing secondary injury, which occurs as an indirect result of brain trauma. Secondary injury, including inflammation, has been implicated in the development of post-traumatic epilepsy. Our hypothesis is that inflammation after traumatic brain injury is necessary for the development of post-traumatic epilepsy, and can be modulated to prevent epilepsy from developing later on. In order to demonstrate a causal role, the proposed studies will measure inflammation after experimental brain injury and look for the later development of epilepsy in the same individuals, which has not been previously done. This will also determine whether the inflammatory response to brain injury can predict the later development of post-traumatic epilepsy. We will also use drugs to increase the amount of inflammation at the time of brain injury, to show this leads to increased rates of epilepsy later on and to determine which inflammatory mediators are involved. Other studies will use medication to decrease the amount of inflammation after injury to try and prevent epilepsy. The proposed projects will determine whether people with severe traumatic brain injury may benefit from acute anti-inflammatory treatment in order to prevent the development of epilepsy. This could have a huge impact not just for post-traumatic epilepsy, but also more broadly within the field of epilepsy, as it would represent a significant change from currently available treatment options for patients at risk of developing epilepsy.

column36: Improving Periphery Lung Cancer Detection by Endoscopic Laser Raman Spectroscopy
column37: Early detection is crucial to increasing the survival rate of lung cancer and reduces the cost of treatment. If lung cancer can be detected early in the pre-invasive stage, the 5-year survival is >90%. However, with conventional diagnostic techniques, lung cancer is generally asymptomatic until it has reached an advanced stage, when the treatment outcome is poor. In the past decade, great progresses have been made for improving central airway lung cancer detection due to the development of new optical technologies for endoscopy. However, these optical technologies have not been applied to the detection of periphery lung cancers due to technical challenges. Periphery lung lesions are usually spotted by X-ray computed tomography (CT) as nodules on the images. Then radial ultrasound imaging (under bronchoscopy/virtual CT guidance) plus biopsy are conducted to determine if a nodule is malignant or benign. column36: Promoting neurovascular recovery following focal ischemic stroke
column37: In the healthy brain, neurons, glia, and vessels work in concert so that blood flow adjusts in proportion to the level of neuronal activity. In stroke, a blockage of a major artery results in a sharp decline in blood flow, damaging the neurons and inducing sudden paralysis, impaired speech, and/or loss of vision. If the blood clot is dissolved rapidly, a complete recovery is possible. However, because the currently available treatments are safe and effective only when applied rapidly following the stroke onset, only ~10% of patients receive them; most suffer significant disabilities, and up to a third are institutionalized. Uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes needed for full recovery of brain function is a major factor preventing the development of more widely applicable therapies. It has become clear that recovery is strongly affected by changes that occur in the neurons, glia and blood vessels in the peri-infarct zone, the impaired, but potentially salvageable brain region surrounding the site of stroke. Using advanced imaging in live rats, we will track the function of peri-infarct neurons, glia, and vessels in the weeks following stroke. We will treat the animals with specific drugs, delivered directly to the perilesional tissue, to raise the activity of the surviving neurons while providing them with increased metabolic support, so as to bolster the remapping of lost function to these neurons. We will develop these interventions first in the young rats and then tailor them to the middle-aged rats suffering from metabolic syndrome (e.g. high cholesterol, diabetes) that are common in humans and known to impede stroke recovery. These experiments will establish the ways by which brain functioning can be affected in the chronic stage of stroke so as to improve recovery. The insights obtained will spur the development of new treatments that are effective in the chronic stage following stroke and thus stand to benefit the vast majority of patients.

column36: Cannabis smoking and psychotic experiences in adolescents: A longitudinal brain Imaging study
column37: Cannabis smoking increases the risk for psychosis. Although the effects are small at the population level, growing evidence indicates that they are large in those with premorbid vulnerabilities and those who initiate cannabis use in early adolescence. What remain unclear are the biological mechanisms involved. Important clues are provided by the core characteristics of schizophrenia. Indeed, schizophrenia is associated with aberrant emotion processing, a disturbed sense of self and deficits in working memory. In schizophrenia patients and young adults at risk for psychosis, functional imaging studies show that the neural pathways underlying these functions are impaired. Notably, cannabis smoking impairs these brain networks, indicating that there is a significant overlap between the neural effects of cannabis and the pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Despite this, no functional imaging study has examined the neural effects of cannabis smoking in psychosis-prone adolescents. Here, we propose to perform a 3-year longitudinal neuroimaging study examining the neural effects of cannabis smoking in psychosis-prone adolescents using tasks assessing emotional processing, self-reflection and executive function. We hypothesize that "at risk" adolescents will have impairments in the targeted neural pathways, which will be further impaired by the growth in cannabis use during adolescence. The project will be embedded in an ongoing 5-year clinical study involving 3850 adolescents, providing the unique opportunity to recruit an uncommon though vulnerable group of teenagers. The current study will shed new light on the mechanisms underlying the cannabis-psychosis association. Such inquiry is of the utmost importance given that cannabis use is highly prevalent in Canada and schizophrenia is one of the top 10 causes of disability. With the ongoing debate on cannabis legalization, the study of teenagers experiencing cannabis-related signs of clinical deterioration is timely.

column36: Contribution of circulating microRNAs to the etiology of vascular disease
column37: Heart diseases (including atherosclerosis) are a major cause of death and debilitation in Canada. Atherosclerosis results from blocked blood flow to the heart muscle due to the thickening of the vessel wall by the growth of a plaque, which mostly contains inflammatory white blood cells. During the early stages of disease, the cells lining blood vessels (endothelial cells) send signals to inflammatory cells in the blood to enter the wall of the blood vessel. In advanced stages plaques can burst, resulting in heart attack or stroke. It would benefit patients if we had a better way to diagnose heart disease at early stages and if we could determine the best treatment for a particular patient. This may be achieved by measuring biomarkers, which indicate aspects of the disease that are not easily seen by a doctor. It has been found that small nucleic acids known as microRNAs are found in the blood and the level of particular microRNAs may be useful as biomarkers for heart disease. We have found that endothelial cells secrete microRNAs into the blood, which can be taken up by inflammatory white blood cells. This microRNA uptake decreases the ability of monocytes to enter the vessel wall and produce plaques. Our proposal will test whether this communication between endothelial cells and inflammatory cells is disrupted during the development of heart disease. We will also measure differences in the types of microRNAs that are transferred between these cells during disease. While certain types of microRNAs are beneficial in health, the microRNAs present during heart disease may have damaging effects and actually promote atherosclerosis. Finally, we will develop methods to deliver helpful microRNAs to inflammatory cells to prevent these cells from forming an atherosclerotic plaque. Our studies will provide important new insight into the diagnosis and treatment of heart disease.

column36: Novel mediators of thioredoxin-interacting protein in diabetes complications.
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a common disease affecting 5-10% of Canadians and is associated with complications such blindness, kidney failure and nerve damage. While chronic exposure of tissues to high glucose (HG) is known to be the cause, the cellular and molecular changes are not completely understood. There is no effective treatment for these complications. Our laboratory has discovered that a protein called thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP) is markedly increased by HG and mice which lack TXNIP are protected from developing diabetic nephropathy (DN). We believe that this way TXNIP contributes to DN is by inhibiting thioredoxin (trx), a cellular component that functions as an oxidoreductase which protects proteins from being altered by processes called nitrosylation and oxidation stimulated by HG. One target protein is an enzyme, glyceraldehyde phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) which regulates glucose metabolism. HG alters its activity from an active enzyme to injure cells. Thus, TXNIP would block Trx from maintaining GAPDH in its normal state to promote cell damage. These studies are designed to prove the key role of modified GAPDH in mediating DN and that TxNIP is critical in regulating this action by its inhibition of Trx. These novel findings would lead to new approaches to treatment and prevention of diabetes complications.

column36: Predicting the impact of mutations in intrinsically disordered regions
column37: Current "personalized medicine" projects are identifying all the mutations in every patient, and we need to know which of those mutations are likely to cause diseases. About 1/5 of known disease mutations occur in enigmatic protein regions known as intrinsically disordered regions. When we discover new mutations in disordered regions, we currently can't tell which are harmful (drivers of disease) and which ones are benign (bystanders). Evolutionary analysis can point to biological function because functional sequences are preferentially preserved during evolution. If mutations in disordered regions disrupt features of disordered regions that have been preserved over evolutionary time, we predict that these are more likely to affect function and cause disease. Based on this principle, we propose to develop new bioinformatics to better predict the impact of mutations in disordered regions. To understand why disrupting the conserved features is harmful, we will test the impact of engineered mutations in yeast cells, because they are simpler and easier to study than human cells. In the end, we hope to develop better methods to predict the impact of mutations in disordered regions, and also understand why the mutations in these regions lead to disease.

column36: Elucidating the role of the V-ATPase "a" subunit in targeting and function: a novel therapeutic target for bone-loss pathologies and cancer
column37: Many essential 'housekeeping' functions in the body require acid to be pumped across the membranes of cells and tissues. Acid is pumped into lysosomes, cellular recycling bins that break down old cell components into reusable building blocks, and it is pumped into urine to rid the body of the excess produced during physical activity. Bone repair requires that specialized cells (osteoclasts) secrete acid to dissolve the bone surface prior to its being replaced by new bone. In all these cases, variants of one ubiquitous acid pump, known as V-ATPase, perform the job. Genetic mutations that impair V-ATPase activity are known to cause diseases, such as cutis laxa (wrinkly skin disease), renal tubular acidosis (too much acid in the body), and osteopetrosis (heavy, brittle bones). In contrast, abnormal increases in V-ATPase activity can also lead to diseases, such as osteoporosis (thin, fragile bones) and inflammatory arthritis (eroded joints). In tumours, V-ATPases can acidify and degrade the surrounding tissue, helping cancer cells to detach and spread to other parts of the body. Our goal is to investigate aspects of V-ATPase structure and function that are still poorly understood: the structures and organization of its protein constituents, the variations that cause it to be sent to different locations within cells of the body, factors that control its activity to match its location, and how genetic mutations in V-ATPase genes cause disease. Understanding these factors will reveal new strategies to manipulate the V-ATPase acid pump activity in a manner that is required to alleviate disease. These strategies will enable specific targeting of bone cell or cancer cell V-ATPases without affecting the acid pumps that are engaged in vital housekeeping functions. Specific targeting is a crucial requirement for developing new drugs for the prevention of bone loss in osteoporosis and inflammatory arthritis, or the spread of cancer, without causing serious side effects.

column36: Interfering with HIV persistence in CD4+ T cells during antiretroviral therapy
column37: HIV/AIDS continues to impact the health of millions of people worldwide. Advances in the treatment of HIV infection have dramatically reduced the death rate from AIDS and improved the quality of life of many HIV-infected patients. Despite this unquestioned success, effective therapy does not eradicate HIV and requires life-long adherence. In addition, the possible long-term toxicity associated with antiretroviral therapy (ART), resistance, stigma and cost all contribute to the necessity of finding a cure. In infected individuals taking ART, HIV persists in a small number of cells that can survive for the lifetime of the infected host. This pool of persistently infected cells, usually referred as the "reservoir for HIV infection", is the main barrier to HIV eradication. The overarching goal of this project is to develop therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing the size of the reservoir, with the ultimate objective of finding a cure for HIV infection. Multiple gaps still exist in our understanding of the basic mechanisms involved in the maintenance of the HIV reservoir. We propose to identify the cells in which HIV persists in the blood and tissues (such as the gut) of HIV-infected individuals taking ART. We will isolate the cells carrying HIV from these anatomical reservoirs. This will allow us to characterize the mechanisms by which HIV is able to persist in these cells. We will then test the ability of several drugs at interfering with HIV persistence in these cells and identify combinations that will lead to the death of the reservoir cells. Our goal is to identify a combination of drugs that can eliminate all latently infected cells in HIV-infected individuals. The results from these studies will constitute the basis for the design of a clinical trial aimed at eradicating HIV.

column36: Preclinical approach to improve testing of immuno-oncology combination therapies for early or late stage metastatic disease
column37: The proposed Project Scheme has two major complementary aims. One is designed to leverage what is the most promising development in cancer therapy since the discovery of chemotherapy: the impact of new drugs which harness the body's immune system ability to fight cancer. The other is to develop improved mouse cancer models to better predict the clinical impact of immune therapy drugs when used in combination with other selected therapies to treat early or late stage distant metastatic disease. These other therapies are antiangiogenic drugs which target a tumor's blood supply, or chemotherapy given in a less toxic, continuous low dose ('metronomic') manner. The overall rationale is twofold. First, while the clinical impact of new immune therapies is remarkable, only a minor subset of patients (eg. 10-15%) derive dramatic benefits. So strategies are needed to improve these figures, e.g. to combine immunotherapy drugs creating 'cocktails' with different anti-cancer drugs - especially those where there is a sound underlying rationale. Second, initial assessment of new therapies is almost always done in mice - usually by treating localized 'primary' tumors - an approach historically poor in predicting what later happens in patients with distant metastatic disease. Dr. Kerbel's lab instead has focused on the development of postsurgical models of metastatic disease of different cancers to model "adjuvant" antiangiogenic drug or chemotherapy treatment of either early stage or advanced metastatic disease. His results have helped contribute to the initiation of phase II and III clinical trials, a number of which have now shown positive results. However, the models - which have been distributed to numerous investigators around the world - involve growth of human tumors in immune suppressed mice. This does not allow testing of immune therapy. So the next step is to develop a similar resource using immune competent mice for studying promising combination based immunotherapies.
