column36: Accuracy and generalizability of using automated methods for identifying adverse events from electronic health record data
column37: Adverse events (AEs) are injuries caused by medical management rather than by the underlying condition of the patient. AEs are estimated to occur in 2.9% to 16.6% of all acute care hospitalizations, and studies have suggested that 30% to 58% of all AEs are preventable. Preventable AEs are a leading cause of death, resulting in 44,000 to 98,000 deaths each year. AEs are also very costly, with total annual costs estimated to range between USD $17 and $29 billion. For these reasons, preventing AEs is a high priority in acute care hospitals worldwide. An important requirement to evaluate the success of preventive measures is to have access to accurate, timely and efficient methods for monitoring AE rates. Moreover, with the growing emphasis on benchmarking and public reporting of AE data, these methods must also allow for valid inter-institutional comparisons. However, at present, there are no such methods. With the advent of electronic health records (EHR), and the development of automated methods for encoding and classifying EHR data, there is an exciting opportunity to identify potentially better methods of AE detection and monitoring. Taking advantage of this new opportunity, the objective of this research project is to assess the accuracy and the generalizability of using automated methods for detecting three of the most common AEs affecting hospitalized patients: 1) hospital-acquired pneumonia, 2) ventilator-associated events and, 3) central line-associated bloodstream infection. It is expected that this research project will result in more accurate and efficient measures of AEs. These measures could be used to assess the incidence rates of AEs, evaluate the success of interventions aimed at improving patient safety, and track progresses in patient safety through time. Lastly, automation has a strong potential to standardize AE monitoring, both within and across institutions, which is an important prerequisite to valid public reporting of AE data and benchmarking.

column36: A Randomized Trial of Regional Radiotherapy in Luminal A Breast Cancer
column37: Studies have shown that radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional nodes following mastectomy and radiotherapy to regional nodes after breast conserving surgery reduces the risk of recurrence and breast cancer mortality in women with node positive breast cancer. While these benefits are important, it is recognized that there is a large group of patients with node positive breast cancer who are unlikely to recur or benefit from radiotherapy. Biomarkers are increasingly used to identify breast cancers that are likely to recur or respond to treatment. The luminal A breast cancer subtype has a low risk of recurrence and is less likely to respond to chemotherapy. Recent evidence from MA.20 a randomized trial of radiotherapy to the regional nodes supports that such cancers were less likely to respond to radiotherapy. This suggests that regional radiotherapy may not be necessary in patients with node positive luminal A breast cancer. The objective of this study is to determine if radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional lymph nodes following mastectomy or radiotherapy to the regional nodes following breast conserving surgery can be safely omitted in women with 1-3 positive axillary lymph nodes and luminal A cancer. An international multicentre randomized trial will be performed. Patients treated by mastectomy will be randomized to radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional nodes or not. Patients treated by breast conserving surgery will be randomized to radiotherapy to regional nodes or not. Radiation following surgery is associated with significant short-term and long-term side effects. The luminal A subtype of breast cancer accounts for up to 40% of patients with node positive breast cancer. If regional radiotherapy could be avoided in this group of patients it would have substantial benefits not only for women with breast cancer and their families, but the health care system at large.

column36: Regulation of TGF-beta action in chondrocytes: signaling via ALK1 versus ALK5 pathways
column37: Arthritis refers to several related conditions that affect joints, causing pain, inflammation and swelling. Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and occurs when there is damage in and around the joints, which the body cannot repair. Currently there is no cure for OA and its progression significantly affects an individual's quality of life. OA affects nearly 4.6 million Canadians and is expected to increase to about 7.5 million by 2036. Despite much research effort, the causes and factors involved in OA are not fully understood. Transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta is a protein made in many tissues of the body and there is ample evidence to indicate that its abnormal action in cartilage is involved in the OA disease process. Our research has shown that TGF-beta can have both beneficial and harmful effects on cartilage cells (chondrocytes) depending on the type of "receptor" it uses. In particular, we have shown that TGF-beta will promote healthy cartilage by acting through one type of chondrocytes receptor (known as ALK5) but gives rise to OA-like features when acting through another receptor (ALK1). We have also shown that certain molecules such as TGF-beta co-receptors can influence whether TGF-beta acts through ALK5 or ALK1 receptor. Thus we will examine the role of two co-receptors called endoglin and CD109 in regulating the activity of ALK5 and ALK1. Our goal will be to unravel the mechanism involved in the abnormal action of TGF-beta in chondrocytes and to manipulate the activity of proteins (such as ALK1 and co-receptors) to regulate TGF-beta action, in order to promote cartilage repair. The experiments will be performed using cell and animal models of OA. We expect that findings from the proposed research may lead to the development of innovative therapeutic strategies for the treatment of this debilitating disease.

column36: Caracterisation et representations de l'accessibilite physique aux jeux de hasard et d'argent au Quebec: un outil pour la prise de decision et la creation d'environnements favorables.
column37: La pratique des jeux de hasard et d'argent peut engendrer des problemes de sante pour les joueurs et leurs proches. Au Quebec, plusieurs recherches ont demontre que l'offre de jeu etait plus importante dans les quartiers defavorises et que cela contribuait a generer un environnement moins favorable a la sante de la population. Officiellement, aucun critere sanitaire n'est pris en compte pour configurer l'offre de jeu au Quebec. Dans ce contexte, un portrait a jour et une analyse de l'accessibilite physique au jeu au Quebec sont necessaires afin de soutenir la creation d'environnements favorables a la sante des populations. La presente etude a ete concue pour repondre a ce besoin de connaissances. Ce projet vise a : 1-Realiser une revue de litterature mettant a jour les connaissances sur l'influence des milieux de vie sur la sante et sur les liens entre les environnements de jeu, la defavorisation et les prejudices lies au jeu. 2-Dresser un portrait de l'accessibilite physique de l'offre de jeu au Quebec qui rende compte des niveaux de defavorisation et des impacts du jeu par secteur geographique. La realisation d'une cartographie et son analyse seront les methodes utilisees pour y parvenir. 3-Realiser des entrevues aupres de joueurs pour comprendre comment l'offre de jeu presente dans leur milieu de vie agit sur leur parcours et habitudes de jeu. 4-Elaborer des recommandations et valider leur pertinence et leur faisabilite aupres d'experts et de decideurs des domaines concernes. Les resultats fourniront des indicateurs indispensables a la prise de decision sur le deploiement de l'offre de jeu et la creation d'environnements plus favorables a la sante. En matiere de prevention, les resultats permettront d'identifier des zones geographiques sensibles au Quebec et d'y developper des initiatives preventives mieux adaptees. La specification des declencheurs de jeu est aussi susceptible d'orienter les interventions dans les services de traitement du jeu problematique

column36: Characterization of the TGFbeta microRNAome - implications for new biomarkers and therapeutic targets in human cancer
column37: Proteins are synthesized as a result of gene expression and play a critical role in maintaining normal cell function. When expression of proteins is deregulated, diseases such as cancer can arise. We focus on the action of microRNAs (miRNAs), which are micromolecules naturally synthesized by the body and capable of regulating the production of a large proportion of proteins. MicroRNAs are interesting because given the nature of their structure, they are easy to synthesize in a laboratory setting and non-toxic to cells, hence offer a valuable therapeutic option. TGFB is a growth factor capable of promoting or inhibiting critical miRNAs. Indeed, we found that when we expose a cell to TGFB, the expression of these miRNAs changes, and that as a consequence, the expression pattern of proteins within the cell will also change. Interestingly, TGFB can prevent the formation of tumors in healthy cells and early cancers, and promote metastasis (i.e. cancer dissemination) in more advanced cancer cases. With our current research, we want to identify the miRNAs that are regulated by TGFB, and investigate how modulating their expression affects tumor suppression and progression. With our newly acquired knowledge, we will determine if the abundance of our identified miRNAs is of relevance in differentiating between normal versus tumor tissue and between different types of tumors, and if they can be an indication of prognosis or response to treatment. Furthermore, we will investigate their ability to refrain tumor development, growth, and dissemination in live organisms.

column36: Functions of the pulvinar in normal vision: role in transthalamic cortico-cortical communication
column37: It is generally considered that the visual images that we are seeing are analysed by a number of areas of the cortex, leading to a coherent perception of the world. This dogma has been challenged in recent years. There is now evidence that subcortical structures located in the thalamus are also involved in the complex processing yielding the perception of the visual world. My laboratory explores the possibility that neurons in the largest thalamic nucleus, the pulvinar, contribute to our capacity to analyse and interpret the various components of our visual environment, in close relation with cortical areas. This work is important not only to understand how our brain can perceive and interpret an image (yielding to an appropriate action) but also to understand pathologies in which communication between the cortex and the thalamus is altered, such as in schizophrenia.

column36: The dopaminergic ultradian oscillator and psychopathology
column37: Sleep and wake follows a 24hr rhythm, which is controlled by an internal timing system, the circadian clock. However, our daily life is also influenced by rhythms of arousal which cycle approximately every 4 hours. We have now identified the timer that generates these rhythms and it critically relies on the brain chemical dopamine, which is known to promote arousal. We found that increasing brain dopamine levels in mice can drastically lengthens the timing of a single arousal cycle and, intriguingly, the resulting patterns of rest:activity appear strikingly similar to the abnormal sleep:wake behaviour observed in individuals suffering from bipolar disorder or schizophrenia. We now wish to confirm that these sleep/wake abnormalities are indeed due to an imbalance of the dopamine clock we have discovered. We will do this by creating novel mouse models based on gene mutations that have strong links to these psychiatric conditions. We further plan to perform experiments aimed at uncovering the precise brain location of this timer as well as the mechanism of rhythm generation. The proposed studies will improve our understanding of this new biological clock but may also inform the underlying causes of mental illness, thereby paving the way for novel strategies of disease identification, prevention, and treatment.

column36: Resolution of inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity in DLBCL using mass cytometry
column37: Recent work has shown that patients with cancer often have tumors that are composed of several different types of cancer cells, each with a slightly different set of genetic mutations. This variability, or "heterogeneity", means that successful therapy must target not just one, but perhaps several different cancers at the same time. As well, there is renewed appreciation for the importance of the patient's own immune system in defeating cancer, and some therapies are even focused at reawakening the patient's immune cells to attack the cancer. Thus, cancer can no longer be regarded simply as an overgrowth of one particular type of cell, but may better be considered as a complex ecosystem with multiple interconnected and constantly evolving parts. In order to diagnose cancer more accurately and to treat it more effectively, it is important that we understand the full complexity of the tumor ecosystem. We propose here to use a cutting-edge technology called mass cytometry , or "CyTOF", to examine patients' tumors one cell at a time in order to get an ultra high definition, widescreen picture of the problem at hand. We will also use the most up-to-date genomics tools to understand which genes are mutated in which cells and how those cells are functioning abnormally. We will use this information to develop a new, cost-effective, same-day test that can be provided to each and every patient and will help doctors to better understand what sort of tumor is present, if and how well the patient's immune system is responding, and what the best treatment options may be.

column36: Brain imaging biomarkers of recovery from sport concussion
column37: Concussions are a growing health concern, with over 4 million occurring annually in sport and recreation in North America. These injuries are associated with a variety of impairments in thinking (confusion, feeling "slow"), emotion (anger, depression) and physical function (dizziness, nausea). Currently, medical clearance (a "clean bill of health") is based on resolution of symptoms and performance on tests measuring thinking ability. These assessments do not directly measure the severity of brain injury. This is a significant concern, as athletes are at risk for significantly worse outcomes if they are re-injured before brain recovery is complete. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a versatile tool that can measure aspects of brain anatomy, function and blood flow. However at present, it has seen limited use in medical assessment of concussion. In this research project, we propose to use advanced MRI techniques to scan university athletes with and without concussion. For concussed athletes, we will perform scanning at key time-points in the recovery process, including while symptomatic (<7 days), time of medical clearance, and 1 month after clearance. This will enable us to visualize brain changes in concussed athletes, and to determine if the brain has recovered or is still healing at the time of medical clearance to return to play. This research will provide novel information about the brain's recovery from injury. It may be used to develop safer guidelines for concussion management, and in the future, will lay the groundwork to develop better measures of brain health and recovery.

column36: Adult neurogenesis and delay-based decision making
column37: We are continually faced with choices and must consider the benefits associated with making one particular choice over another. However, we do not always choose the most beneficial option if the payout is very hard to obtain or if we are unsure about its availability. Another cost to consider is the time required to benefit from our actions. Often is it advantageous to forego something that immediately satisfying and wait for something better. For example, despite the short-term pleasure of consuming junk food, we may instead opt for healthy food knowing that the long-term benefits will be greater. Many disorders, such as schizophrenia, depression, drug addiction and Alzheimer's disease are associated with impulsive preference for immediate rewards. We are interested in the possibility that newborn neurons that are added to the adult brain could reduce impulsivity and promote preference for delayed, advantageous rewards. New neurons are continually added to the brain of all animals, including humans. They are largely added to the hippocampus, and they contribute to hippocampal functions in memory but their exact role remains unclear. Current evidence indicates that the hippocampus is important for mentally recreating past experiences and for creating mental representations of possible future experiences. The hippocampus may reduce impulsivity by enabling individuals to envision possible future experiences and choose the behaviors that lead to long-term beneficial outcomes. However, a role for new neurons in impulsivity has never been investigated. To test this role for new neurons we will block neurogenesis in rats and assess their ability to choose a large delayed reward over a small immediate reward. We will also examine how learning to choose delayed rewards activates circuits of new neurons, to see if their functions are different from older neurons. These findings will be important for developing new treatments for disorders of impulsive decision-making.

column36: The Longitudinal Course of Intracortical Myelination and Cognitive Function in Bipolar Disorder
column37: Bipolar disorder is a mental illness that severely hampers healthy living and work productivity and affects more than 2% of the Canadian population - or more than half a million people. It is associated with episodes of depression (e.g. low mood, sadness) and mania (e.g. agitation, impulsive behavior), interspersed with periods of relative symptom relief between depressive and manic episodes. But even when their mood symptoms are absent or minimal, 60% of individuals with bipolar disorder show problems with attention, concentration and memory (also called "cognitive dysfunction"). This means that the majority of sufferers are chronically impaired. However, the exact causes of these brain deficits in bipolar disorder are unknown and there are no proven treatments for cognitive dysfunction in this population. We seek to investigate for the first time whether a loss of a specific substance, called myelin, in the outer part of the brain (the cerebral cortex) accounts for poor brain function in bipolar disorder. To that end, we will combine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine myelin with clinical testing to assess brain function in 100 individuals with bipolar disorder and 100 individuals who have no mental illness. They will be recruited at five sites across Canada and followed for two years. Our project will probe the link between myelin loss and poor brain function, which could suggest an important mechanism to improve brain function in those with bipolar disorder. In turn, this could guide new interventions to ameliorate their difficulties with thinking, concentration and memory.

column36: A novel in-vivo mechanical marker of early changes in post-traumatic osteoarthritis
column37: Rationale: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is one of the most common and debilitating injuries to the knee and many injured patients go on to develop post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA). Abnormal knee motions and joint biology changes after ACL injury likely disrupt the structural integrity of cartilage reducing its load bearing capacity. Such weakened cartilage may be at an increased risk of mechanical wear during activities of daily living and experience significant and progressive cartilage loss. Critically, there are no accurate clinical diagnostics sensitive to early PTOA changes. This gap prohibits optimal prevention of longitudinal cartilage degradation. Goal: We propose to address the unmet need for a novel "mechanical marker" that will use dynamic imaging techniques to assess the mechanics of the knee with respect to the structural and compositional changes of the knee joint cartilages at the very early stages after injury, and potentially identify those at high risk of OA following knee injury. Approach: In this project we will compare ACL injured participants with age, sex and activity matched healthy individuals. Using state-of-the-art non-invasive, in-vivo biomechanical and imaging approaches, for the first time, groups will be compared using information of cartilage load-bearing capacity (i.e. mechanical marker), regional cartilage thickness changes, knee joint soft tissue structure and composition, dynamic knee joint movements, joint morphology change and knee function. Follow up assessment of ACL injured individuals and healthy controls will provide the means to identify how these measures interact and clarify the mechanisms of early PTOA progression. Outcomes: This unique project will address the burden of OA by informing research on clinical OA diagnostics and clinical practice, enabling monitoring of the effects of interventions on patient outcomes, and advancing a novel diagnostic tool for early PTOA assessment.

column36: Neuraminidase 1 as a trigger of immune thrombocytopenia: using animal models to understand pathophysiology of the disease and develop novel therapies.
column37: This project concerns thrombocytopenia, a disease of blood coagulation caused by low counts of blood cells called platelets or thrombocytes. Some individuals with thrombocytopenia may experience external bleeding such as nosebleeds, and/or bleeding gums. A person with this disease may also complain of fatigue and general weakness with or without accompanying blood loss. The immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is caused by production of antibodies against platelet proteins causing capture of platelets by white blood cells, macrophages. One of the factors triggering ITP is the presence on the surface of platelets and white blood cells of enzymes called neuraminidases. These enzymes remove a negatively charged sugar, sialic acid from different proteins. By removing sialic acid neuraminidases change properties of proteins and the way in which they interact with each other. We propose to study genetically modified mice that do not have neuraminidase 1 (Neu1) in macrophages and platelets and test if these animals can develop ITP. We also propose to study how Neu1 triggers ITP if we can use this link to stop or reduce progression of this disease in human patients.

column36: Circuit computations of the cortical system for spatial cognition and memory
column37: Many psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases including Dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, and Schizophrenia are characterized by reduced size, metabolic activity, and physiology of hippocampal brain circuits and result in severe memory impairments. These disorders and diseases cause far-reaching negative personal and economic burdens on individuals and their caregivers. Efforts are therefore needed to understand the fundamental principles of how the hippocampal memory systems works in order to guide efforts to restore its function in disease. The set of research aims in this Project Scheme Grant will use state-of-the-art technologies to monitor and control brain activity in freely behaving animals to identify how neuronal circuits in mammalian memory system function. Two key aspects of memory which are often impaired in disease include the ability to recall the location and temporal order of events in our lives. The aims of this grant focus on how the brain's memory system generates representations of space and time in the brain. Animals will perform various behaviors during these recordings, from simple foraging behavior to solving spatial memory tasks. For each experiment, we will use a transgenic mouse and viral strategy to selectively express photo-activated of non endogenous ligand-activated channels in select neuronal populations (i.e. cell type, or specific circuit projection). This allows my laboratory to control these circuits during neuronal recordings and behavior, which will allow us to determine functional role of each circuit in the memory system. This overall strategy of identifying which neuronal populations underlie the processes of memory encoding has great potential to guide new directions in the search for therapies for diseases that affect the brain's memory system.

column36: Participatory Risk Communication: Indigenous Youth-Generated Messages for Community Health Promotion
column37: Communicating about health risks is very important in helping people to understand the risks and make informed decisions on health behaviours. However, health risk communications with Indigenous peoples often have limited success. This is primarily because these communications are usually 'one-way' messages from government or other health agencies that are not suitable or meaningful for Indigenous peoples. Recent research with Indigenous youth on tobacco use, food security and physical activity has shown us that messages developed and delivered by these youth seem to be more trusted and effective for communities in providing information, changing behaviours and promoting healthy lifestyle choices. Communities and researchers will work together in a participatory manner to identify relevant health risk issues, determine how the youth will be engaged in message development, and decide how the value of the messages and the message development process will be measured. column36: Toward a better understanding of the impact of vascular health on Alzheimer's disease pathology and clinical expression
column37: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, affecting nearly 50% of Canadians over 80 years of age. With the aging of the population, the prevalence of dementia is expected to increase dramatically, generating major social and economic costs. Currently, Alzheimer's disease has no known cure, and by the time a person meets the clinical diagnosis for Alzheimer's disease, brain and cognitive changes related to the disease are already probably irreversible. It is therefore essential to find ways to delay, slow down, or even prevent this devastating disease. Amyloid and tau are the pathological hallmarks of the disease. Vascular risk factors (i.e. hypertension, dyslipidemia and diabetes) are well known risk factors for Alzheimer' disease in addition of being risk factors for vascular brain injuries, which also increase the likelihood of dementia. The advent of amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) imaging now allows for assessing the interplay between vascular risk factors and Alzheimer's pathology in-vivo. Amyloid PET imaging has helped establish that vascular risk factors can increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease via pathways that directly related to amyloid pathology. The current research proposal will explore mechanisms by which vascular factors may increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease. More specifically we propose a series of experiments to explore mechanisms by which genetic (e.g. ApoE and other genes related to both Alzheimer's disease and vascular health) and lifestyle risk factors (e.g. hypertension and diet) may impact brain change and memory deficits. This study will be conducted in cognitively normal and mildly impaired individuals with a family history of Alzheimer's disease. The overall goal is to identify new preventive strategies that may delay the onset of Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: etiology involving troponin mutations
column37: Familial hypertrophy cardiomyopathy (FHC) is a congenital heart disease which causes the walls of the heart to thicken (hypertrophy) and disrupts the organization of the heart's contractile machinery. Even though numerous genetic defects (mutations) have been associated with FHC, the underlying cause is not understood. As a result of this disease the heart restructures itself not just on a gross level that can be seen by echocardiography but also on a microscopic level, often resulting in irregularities in contraction and electrical disturbances (arrhythmias). As a consequence of these events premature sudden cardiac deaths (SCD) are a common outcome of FHC. The first objective is to address a possible mechanism for FHC. We will explore one of the major hypotheses as to the cause of FHC by making mutations in the molecules (troponin C) which sense the signal (calcium concentration inside the heart cells) that serves as the coupling between cardiac excitation (as seen on an ECG) and contraction. We believe that mutations in the troponin complex which is made up of three protein including troponin C which are associated FHC alter the manner in which molecule interacts with calcium and we will test this hypothesis. We will address the idea that sudden cardiac death in patients with FHC is due to factors which increase the risk for SCD and precede the development of hypertrophy. The work will be undertaken at many different levels of organization from a detailed structural analysis of the thin filament which houses the troponin molecule, all the way to comprehensive studies on possible changes in the structure and function of the heart that occur as a result of the mutations engineered into this molecule. We believe that because sudden cardiac death is often the first symptom of abnormality for these individuals, it is critical to understanding the underlying cause of this disease.

column36: Team Approach to Polypharmacy Evaluation and Reduction (TAPER)
column37: Multi-morbidity is the most common condition affecting older adults. As a result seniors in most countries now take around 7 medications daily. Death and illness rates from drug side effects in seniors are as high as those from many chronic diseases and affect falls, thinking, nutrition, fatigue and mobility. Taking 5 or more drugs ('polypharmacy') results in adverse drug effects requiring medical care affect in 13% of Canadian seniors: 1/3 are thought preventable. These are costly to those individuals, and costly to health systems. Canada's health care system lacks a systematic approach to minimizing these negative effects in routine care. We trialed a systematic method of patient centred reduction in medication burden in 70 seniors. This was safe, and the results suggested improvement in health and quality of life. We also tested the effect of discontinuation of single drugs in patients using over a long period to assess benefits and side effects and reviewed methods for asking patients with multiple conditions about their overall priorities for use of drug treatments, finding few tools that help incorporate these into research and clinical care. This program of research will develop these complimentary themes of generation of research evidence around drug discontinuation, and integration of patients' priorities for care. These will be drawn together in a new preventive framework for clinical care, aiming to minimize the harms of treatments in polypharmacy by patient centred discontinuation ('deprescribing'). We will test this intervention in large trials across Canada, assessing the important effects on patients and the healthcare system and will be using insights from patient's and prescriber's experiences of the process of drug discontinuation to provide tools for both. Our aim is to embed reduction of medication burden through medication review and 'deprescribing' as part of regular preventive care in older adults.

column36: Studies on novel immune-surveillance mechanisms underlying cancer elimination
column37: Cancer is a devastating disease and is the number one killer in Canada. The immune system is the body's primary defence against cancer and is tasked with the elimination of tumour cells. During the emergence of cancerous cells, they can undergo mutations altering their genetic code and enabling the cells to divide rapidly. These cells form the primary tumour that grows in one location of the body and can be medically treated. However, newly formed tumour cells may acquire further mutations that mask them from the immune system. This immunoevasive phenotype allows them to covertly enter the blood and lymph vessels and travel to distant organs. This type of cancer is classified as metastatic upon the successful colonization of these alternative sites in the body. Metastatic cancer is considered the final stage of the disease, and survival of patients with this form of cancer is significantly reduced due to the difficulty of treatment. Recently, researchers have discovered methods that can predict the turning point in cancer where the disease moves from the primary to the metastatic form; by examining the gene mutations that are present in the patient's tumour cells. We have conducted studies on metastatic tumours and have identified a key gene that is involved in metastatic progression. This gene controls the recruitment and activation of a newly described type of white blood cell and our data implies that this novel cell type plays an unidentified role in immunity to cancer cells. This observation has been validated in prostate and kidney cancer patients. Through the use of mouse studies, we will further validate the ability of this gene and the new type of white blood cells it induces, to reduce tumour burden and prevent metastasis. These novel and exciting discoveries will be explored as entirely new immunotherapies for cancer patients and could prevent metastasis.

column36: Transfusion in traumatic brain injury (TSiTBI Trial)
column37: The incidence of anemia (a decrease in the quantity or quality of red blood cells) is frequent among critically ill patients. Because red blood cells, through the molecules of hemoglobin, are oxygen carriers, a decrease in the availability of oxygen to the different organs is often to fear. In patients with traumatic brain injury, mechanisms regulating oxygen delivery to the brain are affected by the injury. The development of anemia may thus potentially worsen lesions to the brain and blood transfusion may correct anemia. However, clinicians are currently restricting the use of blood transfusion in traumatic brain injury making inferences with non brain-injured populations. Few evidence-based data help clinicians treating patients with traumatic brain injury to determine what minimal red blood cell levels (hemoglobin levels) can be tolerated before a blood transfusion is required. This project aims to conduct a pan-canadian multicenter clinical trial to compare a liberal transfusion strategy (transfusion when the red blood cell levels are not too low with the objective to keep it high) to a restrictive transfusion strategy (transfusion when red blood cell levels are low with the objective to keep it low). We believe that liberal transfusion strategy will allow better oxygen delivery to the brain, prevent secondary cerebral lesions and will improve long-term outcomes. This project is part of a vast research program aiming to identify when and under what circumstances should we give red blood cells following traumatic brain injury.

column37: Adolescence is a sensitive period for engagement in health-risk behaviors (e.g., substance use, physical inactivity, poor nutrition, risky sexual activity), which can have life-long repercussions. This project assesses the prominent Dual Systems model of adolescent brain development, which suggests that adolescent sensitivity to health-risk behaviors is due to the asynchrony between an early maturing reward-seeking system (likely due to puberty) and a slower maturing impulse control system. Research in this area is limited by reliance on cross-sectional designs, short-term effects, small samples, and a focus on only one or two aspects of development. Participants will include 600 boys and girls (ages 8-13 at Year 1) who will be followed for 5 years. Participants will complete an annual self-report survey and a three-year lab component. This project will provide 1) an integrated investigation of the development of youth health-risk behaviors, 2) evidence-based support (or lack of support) for the Dual Systems Model of adolescent brain development and its implications for youth vulnerabilities and opportunities, 3) annual updates of precipitating factors that impact on on health-risk behaviors and brain reactivity over time that are best to target in prevention/intervention programs, such as activities that enhance impulse control and positive lifestyle choices, and 4) a timely and widespread application of findings given the strong team of researchers, partners, and integrated knowledge translation strategies.

column36: New statistical methods for cohort studies of adverse effects of medications
column37: The number of medications available to treat various health problems increases steadily. Most new drugs help improve patients' health, their quality of life and life expectancy, but some may have important unintended side effects while other may be less effective than existing, often less expensive, 'older' medications. Thus, an accurate assessment and comparison of the safety and effectiveness of alternative medications has become one of the primary objectives for both public health agencies and patients' organizations. Accordingly, considerable resources are invested in research attempting to link data on the use of specific medications with both intended and unintended health outcomes. In Canada, such research endeavors are largely facilitated by the existence, in several provinces, of large, administrative databases that contain complete information on both health outcomes and prescriptions received by individual subjects. However, to draw scientifically valid and rigorous conclusions from the analyses of population-based studies of drug safety or effectiveness, we have to address several methodological challenges. For example, patients prescribed a new drug may be more likely to have a more advanced disease and additional risk factors than those not given any drug or prescribed a less expensive older drug. If not accounted for, such differences in the characteristics of drug users may lead to biased results and incorrect conclusions. In addition, differences in the treatment duration and dose of drugs used by different patients, possibly due to treatment non-adherence, may also affect the accuracy of the results. We propose several new statistical methods that will address the above challenges and will permit more accurate assessments of the safety and effectiveness of different drugs used by Canadians. Our new methods may also help designing more rational treatment regimens, to maximize health benefits while reducing the risks of serious adverse events.

column36: Characterization of the genes and gene regulatory mechanisms that control motor neuron stability and neurotransmission in a Drosophila model.
column37: How neurons maintain structural and physiological stability of synapses (contact points) is poorly understood, even though synaptic degeneration is an established hallmark of most neurological disorders. An important clue has come from work in the fruit fly, Drosophila, which revealed that bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) secreted from muscle activate BMP signaling in motor neurons. Loss of BMP signaling (or BMP regulated gene expression) in motor neurons severely destabilizes synaptic morphology and reduces neurotransmission. Follow up work confirmed that BMPs play the same role in mammalian motor neurons, and disrupted BMP signaling has become implicated in motor neuron diseases such as ALS. It is now clear that BMP signaling controls a battery of novel genes required for morphological and physiological stability of motor neuron synapses (and other synapses) from Drosophila to humans. Most of these genes have not been identified. Our preliminary data has taken the first important step by identifying all BMP regulated genes in fly neurons (by RNAseq). With these in hand, this project can now address two, important knowledge gaps: 1) How does BMP signaling control those genes' expression? We will determine which transcription factors, resident in motor neurons, enable the BMP pathway to control gene expression in motor neurons. 2) What is the function of those genes? We will determine the function of ~100 of these novel genes that we postulate play novel conserved roles in synaptic stability of morphology and neurotransmission in humans. We address these questions in Drosophila. The mechanisms under examination are extremely well conserved from Drosophila to humans, and Drosophila offers the only genetic toolset able to complete these goals in 5 years. As this project will reveal how a novel gene network is regulated and deployed to control synaptic stability, our work will revolutionize our ability to combat synaptic degeneration in neurological disorder

column37: Babies born with a genetic deletion (missing piece of DNA) on one of the pair of chromosomes 22 are known to be at high risk of having birth defects and, later on, learning difficulties and schizophrenia. Families, healthcare providers, and researchers want to anticipate and ultimately prevent the most disabling outcomes. This will enable us to identify and interpret other genetic changes, both new and inherited, that make it more (or less) likely for individuals with the deletion to develop specific features that affect lifelong outcome. To start, we will compare those with and without schizophrenia. Some new genetic changes may cluster together in the genome. We will examine whether these clusters are associated with poor outcomes, and/or with the occurrence of the deletion event itself in the family. The results promise to help identify factors that shape important outcomes in individuals with this deletion, so that we can intervene early and help to prevent major disabilities. This study will also advance our understanding of common diseases like schizophrenia, and of the many genetic conditions that are similar to this specific genetic deletion.

column36: Epigenetic Signatures of Successful Aging
column37: Aging is a complex process that involves a host of physiological changes. Approximately 25% of the variation in human lifespan is attributed to genetics, with the remainder proposed as being associated with life style or environmental exposure. Epigenetics is the study of how experiences can "get under the skin" by acting as a mediator between environmental influences and genetics. DNA methylation is the most well studied epigenetic mark, and has the potential to influence how certain genes are turned on or off in association with environmental or life styles exposures, such as stress or smoking. We aim to assess DNA methylation in the longevity population of Costa Rica, the Nicoya Peninsula, to characterize an epigenetic blueprint of healthy aging. Our preliminary pilot study results suggest that age-related DNA methylation trends are different in high longevity populations when compared to individuals from adjacent control regions. We propose to expand our sample size in Nicoya, and investigate two other longevity populations: Sardinia, Italy and Ikaria Greece. We then propose to compare these findings with the DNA methylation profiles of Canadians from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. The characterization of biological aging will not only aid in understanding the etiology of age-related disease but will contribute to eventually extending the number of healthy and mobile years Canadians spend in old age.

column36: Individual differences in autobiographical memory: cognitive, behavioural, and neural correlates and their relationship to aging
column37: The notion that people differ with respect to memory abilities is accepted in the general public. Recently, people with extreme profiles of memory abilities have been discovered. Individuals with highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM) have an uncanny ability to access details from personal past events regardless of the nature or importance of the event. Individuals with severely deficient autobiographical memory (SDAM) have normal learning and memory for factual information, but do not recollect details of personal events at all. These extreme memory syndromes may reflect the ends of a normal continuum of memory abilities that would be expected based on introspection and comparison with others. Yet when studying memory, researchers calculate averages across groups of people, ignoring such individual differences. In this research, we will contrast groups of individuals with HSAM and SDAM to better understand the nature of their memory function. We will test specific hypotheses regarding memory abilities and their relationship to brain structure and function that will shed light on the entire range of memory ability, not just the extremes. We will also examine how individual differences in autobiographical memory play out with aging. Memory impairment is among the commonest cognitive complaints in aging and is considered a cardinal sign of neurodegenerative disease, such as Alzheimer's disease. Yet no one has examined how such complaints and abilities relate to individual differences in autobiographical memory. It may be that individuals with high or low autobiographical memory abilities have differential susceptibility to aging and neurodegenerative effects. This research will contribute to the creation of new memory assessment tools that will be important to diagnosis and intervention in individuals with memory changes due to aging or age-related disorders.

column36: Refugee integration and long-term health outcomes in Canada
column37: Canada provides protection to refugees from overseas through two different programs. In one, the government selects and supports refugees for the first year of settlement: government assisted refugees (GARs). In the other, support is provided by volunteer groups: private sponsored refugees (PSRs). Private sponsorship is unique to Canada but is of increasing interest internationally. Yet, despite resettling a third of refugees as PSRs, there is little research comparing GAR and PSR effectiveness in supporting the integration of refugees into society. Resettled refugees have poorer health than host populations. Studies show that social integration affects wellness but we do not have much research examining how the experiences of settlement and integration contribute to the long-term health of refugees. Refugees face unique challenges prior to migration, including exposure to trauma, prolonged uncertainty, hazardous living conditions, and disrupted education trajectories. In the short-term, security, less hazardous living conditions, and access to health services result in improvements in resettled refugees' health. However, research with other immigrant groups in Canada shows that in the long term, health and well-being are affected by newcomers' sense of inclusion, respect and belonging in their new country. column36: Unraveling the Mechanism of Action of the Adiponectin Receptor Pathways in a Humanized in vitro Model of Carotid Plaque Instability
column37: Every 10 minutes a Canadian has a stroke, which kills ~14,000 Canadians yearly. Strokes are mainly caused by fatty deposit build-ups (plaques) in the arteries of the neck, which can break-off and travel to the brain. It is important to find out early when a plaque becomes dangerous (ready to break off). However, we only know for sure if a plaque is dangerous when it is removed by surgery and checked under a microscope. Often this is too late as the patient may already have had a stroke. Thus, research should focus on understanding why some plaques become dangerous, while others remain harmless. Current knowledge: 1) Some cells in plaques, called macrophages, can make the plaque more dangerous. Macrophages come from cells in the blood called monocytes. When monocytes enter the plaque, they transform into macrophages. 2) Adiponectin is a substance in the body that may protect our arteries from developing dangerous plaques. To work, it is like a key that must attach to its lock. This lock is the receptors found on monocytes and macrophages. Unknowns: 1) Do people with dangerous and harmless plaques have differences in the adiponectin receptors on their monocytes and macrophages? 2) Do differences in receptors make the plaques more dangerous? We will include patients going for surgery to remove the plaques from their neck arteries. We will examine adiponectin receptors on monocytes and macrophages of people with dangerous and harmless plaques. We believe that in people with dangerous plaques the receptors on the monocytes and macrophages will not work properly. We will use advanced lab techniques to determine if: 1) faulty receptors lead to dangerous plaques, and 2) we can fix these receptors. Our study will clarify the role of adiponectin receptors in the development of dangerous plaques. In the future, we may find treatments that can fix the receptors and turn the plaques from dangerous to harmless. Ultimately, this could prevent strokes and save many lives!

column36: Telomere instability transforms differentiated stem cells into teratomas: implications for aging and disease
column37: Stem cells are the progenitor cell populations that give rise to all tissues in our body, and are responsible for the stable propagation of our genomes into the next generation. In response to external and internal cues, stem cells commit to specific cell lineages in a process termed cell differentiation. In this proposal, we show that critically eroded and damaged chromosome ends (telomeres) allow differentiated, non-dividing stem cells to revert back to a proliferative state and permit the formation of stem cell tumors called teratomas. We will test the implications of this inappropriate rewiring of cell fate in age-associated disease. In this proposal we will: 1) Develop tools that enable us to characterize the unstably differentiated cells and the tumors that they form in mice. 2) We will assess the incidence of these inappropriately dividing cells in mouse tissues during aging. We will test whether their presence correlates with tissue dysfunction, and whether this dysfunction is reversible upon repair of damaged telomeres. 3) We will employ genetic techniques to selectively cull these inappropriately dividing cells in older animals, to determine if their removal ameliorates age-associated disease and tissue decline. In summary, we believe we have uncovered a mechanism that may be an extremely important means by which cellular aging leads to tissue aging and cancer development. We have developed genetic tools in our laboratory that will enable us to test whether critically eroded telomeres, and their ability to promote the inappropriate proliferation of differentiated cells, results in the persistence of abnormal cell types in old animals and tissues, and whether the removal of these cells improves animal health. These studies may have wide-ranging implications for our understanding of the aging process, and how to influence it to our advantage.

column36: Identification of the immunologic basis for production of pathogenic autoantibodies in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
column37: The immune system plays an important role in discriminating between molecules that are foreign, such as those in bacteria and viruses, and molecules that are normal parts of the body (self). Foreign molecules are attacked while self-molecules are normally left unharmed. We believe that Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (lupus) results from defects in the immune system that lead to abnormal activation of cells that react to self-molecules, resulting in production of autoantibodies that attack the body's organs. In the immune system two classes of cells, T and B cells, act in concert to mount an immune response. In many strains of mice that develop lupus, B cell functional abnormalities play a central role in the pathogenesis of disease. In our previous work, we found several B cell functional abnormalities in human lupus, consistent with this possibility. In addition, we found that lupus patients had increased proportions of B cells in their blood that had features suggesting that they were specific for self-molecules. These blood changes result in part from the presence of inflammatory molecules in the blood of lupus patients that alter B cell function. However genetic factors are also proposed to play an important role in the development of lupus, and a number of genes that promote lupus are predicted to alter B cell function. In this grant we will examine how genetic factors and pro-inflammatory molecules perturb B cell function to promote production of autoantibodies. This will be done by examining genetically manipulated mice with changes that mimic those seen with lupus genes and mice with high levels of the pro-inflammatory factors similar to those seen in lupus patients. We will also investigate the impact of these changes and factors on human B cell function. Identification of the underlying causes for the altered B cell function and production of autoantibodies in lupus will allow us to develop better therapies for this condition.

column37: Translation is an essential biological process by which cells produce proteins from the information encoded in their genes. A gene that ribosomes read is made of a molecule called "mRNA". One misunderstood way by which mRNAs stimulate their own translation is mRNA circularization, a process by which the two ends of the mRNA join one another. Not all mRNAs circularize at the same rate; there is a set of conditions that make mRNA circularization more likely, for example the presence of a so-called "poly(A) tail" at the end of the mRNA. There is a correlation between translation stimulation and cancer progression, and some studies have shown that conditions that favor mRNA circularization, for example excess production of a poly(A) tail, also favor cancer progression. I propose to use smFRET, a biophysical technique, to characterize mRNA circularization dynamics. smFRET will be ideal to this study because it will inform on the exact dynamics of single molecules of mRNA at a time. I will be able to observe the behavior of individual mRNAs on a microscope and develop a model for mRNA circularization under a variety of conditions. This study will help understand how mRNA circularization stimulates translation at the molecular level, which will help understanding one mechanism for cancer progression and may help design anti-cancer therapeutics.

column37: In Canada, mental illness and suicide among First Nations youth are occurring at an alarming rate, one that is sadly on the rise. To fully understand suicide among this group we must recognize the damaging consequences of historical and political practices including: colonization, discrimination, and marginalization. In the Canadian population, mental health literacy, the knowledge, beliefs and abilities that support the prevention and management of mental health issues, has been identified as a central component of suicide prevention. Unfortunately current definitions of mental health literacy, and programs aimed at increasing it, fail to consider essential First Nations cultural, historical and contextual differences that are critical to successful programs. A better understanding of mental health literacy among First Nations youth is therefore essential to the design, implementation, and evaluation of programs aimed at preventing suicide in this group. The objective of this study is to develop a theory of First Nations youth mental health literacy grounded in their experiences and perspectives. We will investigate the culturally and contextually distinct knowledge, beliefs and abilities of First Nations youth that support the prevention and management of mental illness. The data generated through this study will be used to inform the design and evaluation of programs aimed at preventing First Nations youth suicide and the development of culturally relevant health promotion practice. The research plan involves: 1) partnering with two First Nations in Southern Alberta who are participating in a theatre-based suicide prevention program; 2) collecting data in the form of stories shared by the youth during the theatre program and 3) interviewing the youth participants, their family members and local service providers to explore broadly the social and cultural contexts in which First Nations youth experience both mental illness and wellness.

column36: Allocentric vs. Egocentric Neglect in Stroke Patients: The Impact on Functional Recovery and Outcomes.
column37: Background & Objective: Hemispatial neglect is defined as a failure to attend to the contralesional side of space in patients who have suffered a stroke. In other words, neglect causes an individual to behave as if one side of sensory space (the side opposite to the hemisphere of their stroke) is nonexistent. Neglect can be divided into two subtypes; Egocentric neglect results in inattention to stimuli presented on one side of the body, while allocentric neglect is shown by inattention to elements on one side of individual objects. Few studies have reached agreement on the assessment, frequency, or prognosis of neglect as they relate to these subtypes. Furthermore, there is no existing research that has investigated potential differences in recovery rate and functional outcome between patients with either allocentric or egocentric neglect. It is the goal of this research to shed light on these important issues. Method: Stroke patients with neglect symptoms will be administered full neuropsychological assessment batteries to assess cognitive functioning and functional independence in daily living. Neglect subtype will be assessed using previously validated tests in conjunction with novel eye-tracking technology. Follow-up testing will be conducted 6 months post-stroke, with primary outcome variables including persistence of neglect symptoms and functional independence level. Correlational analyses will be conducted to examine whether neglect subtype can predict prognosis and functional outcome for stroke patients. Implications: Investigating the assessment, frequency, and functional outcome implications of the subtypes of neglect is a vital step toward improving our understanding of this common and debilitating condition. This study will provide novel information as to how allocentric and egocentric neglect might differentially impact patients' recovery and ultimate quality of life, with the potential to inform improved rehabilitative treatment planning for patients.

column36: Development and evaluation of a decision support tool to guide theory-informed knowledge translation practice in health care
column37: Efforts to change behaviour, practice or policy in health care can be challenging. One approach known to improve the likelihood for success is to apply appropriate theories when designing and evaluating knowledge translation (KT) interventions. Compared to models and frameworks, theories uniquely attempt to explain how and why certain results are achieved and identify 'active ingredients' influencing implementation success. Despite this, evidence suggests that theories are used infrequently in KT practice and support tools are needed to help address this challenge. The objectives of this research are to systematically identify all existing KT theories, and use the findings to develop and test an online tool to guide researchers and front-line implementers (i.e. individuals working on or supporting KT activities in health care organisations) through the process of selecting and applying appropriate theory to inform their KT activities. Phase 1 will include a systematic scoping review to identify all existing KT theories. Phase 2 will involve focus groups and interviews with end-users of the tool to determine their specific needs. We will use the needs of the end-users (Phase 2 results) and the volume and content of Phase 1 results to determine the focus for the tool; specifically, it could focus on theories addressing the entire implementation process or on theories for one or more sub-processes such as scalability and sustainability of interventions. Phase 3 will evaluate the usability of the tool and Phase 4 will consist of a pilot randomized trial to further test the acceptability of the tool. This research is unique because it will be the first comprehensive review of all KT theories, and will result in the creating and testing of a tool to support the use of KT science to inform KT practice. The tool has the potential to benefit the health care system by helping users develop better strategies and achieve more success when implementing evidence into practice.

column36: Cognitive Processes Underlying Increased Vulnerability to Stress
column37: Two individuals face the same potentially stressful situation. One individual reacts to the situation by releasing stress hormones (e.g. cortisol) while the other individual stays calm and do not produce these hormones. The chronic activation of the physiological stress response in the first individual may lead to physical and psychological problems in the long run, while no impact will be observed in the second individual. For the last three decades, scientific research on human stress has tried to understand the various mechanisms underlying the important inter-individual differences in reactivity to stress, and to determine which factors can significantly increase reactivity to stress in some individuals. We now know that factors such as sex, age, genes, and poverty can lead to increased reactivity to stress in humans. Although these factors are noteworthy, most are essentially unmodifiable. Interestingly, the majority of studies now show that exposure to early adversity is a significant predictor of increased vulnerability to stress in adulthood. The goal of my PhD projects is to test whether some cognitive processes (notably mind wandering and attentional biases) known to be sensitive to early adversities can predict increased reactivity to stress in adult humans. If I can show that cognitive processes sensitive to early adversity are significant predictors of increased vulnerability to stress in humans, I will then offer potential avenues for treatment. Indeed, cognitive processing is amenable to change through guided cognitive interventions and consequently positive results on my PhD could open the door to new forms of cognitive therapy for stressed individuals of all ages.

column37: All drugs have side effects, which can and do cause serious harm to many Canadians. Ensuring the safety of new drugs, to minimize drug-induced hospitalizations and deaths, is a critical function undertaken by Health Canada. To improve Canada's ability to monitor the safety of drugs the federal government in 2011 provided funding to create a large team of leading Canadian drug safety researchers and applied this expertise to large databases in seven provinces. Is isotretinoin for severe acne increasing the number of newborn infants with abnormalities? Do new treatments for diabetes cause cancer of the pancreas and damage to the heart? Having established one of the world's largest drug safety networks, we are proposing continuation of funding for a further five years to continue monitoring the safety of new drugs being introduced onto the Canadian market. Having learned how to use the network we will improve engagement with a broader range of stakeholders as well as increase productivity, efficiency and timeliness of the work. CNODES will continue to develop new statistical methods in drug research and will also study 'real world' benefits to determine whether new drugs deliver on the promises made by their manufacturers. Our proposal also outlines plans for training the next generation of Canadian drug safety and effectiveness researchers, ensuring maximal benefit to Canadians from this investment of research funds.

column36: IL-33: an orchestrator of the brain tumor microenvironment
column37: Gliomas affect approximately 2800 Canadians yearly, the majority being aggressive, high-grade glioblastomas with dismal prognosis. Although there has been progress in the treatment of GBM as a result of a treatment regimen that combines maximum surgical resection with radiotherapy and concurrent and adjuvant chemotherapy, five-year survival rates are only a mere 10%. Thus the current therapies can be considered palliative at best. This need is further emphasized based on a recent study from the United States demonstrating that brain and CNS tumors represent the number one cancer for years of potential life lost of adults, highlighting the major societal impact of this disease. This proposal focuses on the brain environment and how it impacts brain tumor progression. For several decades, therapeutic approaches have focused almost entirely on the cancer cells. While this strategy has led to a better understanding of the disease, advances in the clinic for patients with brain tumours remains disappointing despite the development of molecularly targeted drugs and survival is still measured in months. While there are a large number of potential contributing factors for clinical failure including tumor heterogeneity, and lack of effective drug delivery across the blood-brain-barrier, we propose that the unique microenvironment for which the glioma cells reside within the brain is a major contributor to the complexity and challenges of treating this disease. The tumor microenvironment consists of cells, soluble factors, signaling molecules and extracellular matrix that can be co-opted by the cancer cells to fuel tumor growth as well as contribute to therapeutic resistance. This proposal is in line with the emerging shift in therapeutic emphasis from the glioma cells that contain numerous genetic mutations to one of modulating and/or targeting the normal cellular environment to suppress tumor growth and prolong overall survival of glioma patients.

column37: With more than 80% of Canada's population living in urban areas and the urbanized proportion of the global population growing dramatically, there is an urgent need to learn how to design and modify cities to improve, not degrade, population health. This will enable studies looking at how these factors affect health, from birth to old age. We will also be able to map, over time, where and how conditions are changing, and how that increases or decreases the risk of health impacts. Our Consortium includes many leading researchers in Canada, and our specific aims by the end of the first five years are to have: -Completed the linkage of the above exposure metrics to individuals in multiple cohorts. -Filled priority gaps in the environmental data identified by environmental health researchers and knowledge users and delivered the existing and new data and methods to the platform. -Worked closely with environmental epidemiologists (CANUE members and others) to generate new knowledge on the association between features of the urban/suburban environment and health outcomes, emphasizing analyses that consider multiple exposures and their interactions.

column37: Canadian Institutes for Health Research (CIHR) in Canada has funded a Canadian Consortium on Neurodegeneration in Aging (CCNA: www.ccna-ccnv.ca) to become the major vehicle to coordinate and strengthen Canadian research on dementia (including Alzheimer Disease and other neurodegenerative diseases). The CCNA overall objectives are, through its teams, to carry out transformative research that advances understanding of the biology, natural history, clinical presentation and management of these serious conditions, resulting in new and better treatment of these diseases. In this proposal, a team of scientists from across Canada are coming together to leverage three sets of studies and databases in order to carry out "big data" analyses to provide new insights into dementia and search for better treatments and better understanding of dementia risk factors. These studies are the COMPASS-ND study of the CCNA, a 20 year population study of aging in Canada called CLSA, (the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging), and a rich administrative database called interRAI, or MDS RAI, which assesses individuals in home care and nursing homes. We will focus on building the infrastructure for longitudinal studies which track the trajectory of dementia in these three datasets, building normal comparison groups, developing algorithms for delineating cognitive decline in the CLSA, and assess the ethical questions involved in big research on dementia. A major goal will be to position these Canadian studies to work together with international groups, particularly in areas such as genomics, where thousands of individuals must be pooled together to get novel insights. The team will be administered by the current CCNA administrative structure at the Lady Davis Institute at McGill University, and will lay the groundwork for "big data studies in dementia" over the coming decade.

column36: RETRAC2: Research on Commercial Tobacco Reduction in Aboriginal Communities
column37: The overall purpose of this project (RETRAC2) is to contribute to knowledge about commercial tobacco control interventions that aim to prevent chronic lung diseases in Aboriginal communities in Canada. We will determine the effectiveness of tailored and evidence informed community-developed strategies in reducing commercial tobacco use and assess the implementation factors that contribute to their success. In Canada, First Nations (on and off-reserve), Inuit and Metis Peoples have remarkably high rates of commercial tobacco use and associate chronic lung and other diseases compared to non-Aboriginal groups. RETRAC2 builds on a previous study (RETRAC1), where 7 Aboriginal communities conducted research to understand their community's contexts of tobacco use and develop tailored community commercial tobacco reduction strategies. RETRAC1 included a systematic review of literature and studied Aboriginal communities around the world that had success in reducing commercial tobacco use. RETRAC2 provides opportunity for the 7 RETRAC1 communities to implement and evaluate their interventions and for 6 new Aboriginal communities to conduct community-based research, develop and begin to implement their own commercial tobacco reduction strategies. Developmental evaluation research on implementation factors and successes in these varied contexts will provide rich learning for scaling up the RETRAC approach for routine implementation in Ontario and beyond. Successful reduction of commercial tobacco use in Aboriginal communities will begin to address a historic crisis that is one result of contact /colonization. It is vital to close the very large gap in the relative health burden experienced by Aboriginal as compared to non-Aboriginal people in Canada. Participation in the GACD network will both contribute to RETRAC2 and facilitate dissemination of knowledge gained to prevention of chronic lung disease work in LMICs and amongst vulnerable population in HICs.

column36: Examining the impact of tobacco pricing and packaging strategies on tobacco use and equity in middle-income countries
column37: Tobacco use causes more than 6 million deaths per year worldwide, a number that is expected to rise to more than 8 million by 2030, and most of which will be occurring in low- and middle-income countries. Smoking is the leading cause of lung disease: smoking causes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (including emphysema and chronic bronchitis) and most cases of lung cancer; smokers are about 12 times more likely to die from COPD than nonsmokers and 25 times more likely to develop lung cancer. We will study the impact of tobacco prices on smoking onset, smoking cessation, and tobacco consumption in Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, South Africa, and Vietnam. The effects of both tax and retail price will be further analyzed according to their effect by socioeconomic status, sex, and age with simulations to determine the ultimate impacts on tax revenue, tobacco use, and health outcomes. Additionally, the impact of cigarette packaging, including plain packaging, and major recent country-specific policy changes will be analyzed. There is overwhelming evidence that higher cigarette prices reduce tobacco use with greater reductions among young people and those from more socioeconomically disadvantaged groups. The tobacco industry, however, asserts that tobacco taxes harm vulnerable populations and lead to increased consumption of illicit cigarettes and that packaging policies are ineffective. Evidence generated by this research will be used to address these claims with the aim of influencing tax policy and tobacco product labeling practices in low- and middle-income countries with the goal of ultimately preventing ill health and deaths caused by tobacco consumption.

column36: Sino-Canada HeLTI: A Multifaceted Community-Family-Mother-Child Intervention Study for the Prevention of Childhood Obesity
column37: The epidemics of obesity and metabolic syndrome related disorders are a major public health concern. Increasing evidence points to the role of early life adverse factors in the developmental origins of the vulnerability to such metabolic disorders. Reducing the risk of overweight and obesity (OWO) from early life stages will produce substantial benefits to decrease population burdens of metabolic diseases. However, current intervention measures remain insufficient to halt the increasing OWO epidemics. Building on our strengths in large birth cohort studies, clinical trials and studies on developmental programming of metabolic disorders, our transdisciplinary Sino-Canadian team will conduct a community-based multi-centre cluster-randomized controlled trial to test the effect of an evidence-based and multi-faceted early life-course community-family-mother-child interventions package incorporated into the routine pre-conception, prenatal and child care systems on childhood OWO rates in 1-6 years old children in China. A total of 48 community health centers linked to 3 distinct regional large obstetric care hospitals will be randomized into the intervention or control (routine care) group. We will explore the mechanisms (microbiome, epigenetics, micro RNAs) that may underline the development of OWO, and the impacts of the intervention. The research program will for the first time evaluate an integrated intervention package from pre-conception and early pregnancy into childhood on OWO rates. The findings will produce a scalable community-based intervention package that may be recommended for implementation at regional and national-level to reduce the risk of OWO and metabolic syndrome related disorders in China.

column37: Vulnerable populations include people who are, or at risk of, becoming homeless, marginalized because of their social status, immigrant status, age, or other defining features, and living with more than one illness requiring significant health care. They often "fall through the cracks" in preventive and on-going health care management resorting to emergency room care when they get sick. As the Embedded Clinical Researcher (ECR) Dr. Tracey Rickards will connect research, clinical reality, and community to show how collaboration in an urban community health centre can improve health outcomes for vulnerable populations and try to decrease health care costs. The focus of research is: adequate housing to achieve stable health for vulnerable populations, nurses impact on health outcomes to decrease health care costs, outreach care for the most vulnerable clients, and evaluation of the Nurse Practitioner role in New Brunswick. These priority goals will drive the ECR while building a strong culture of research at the Fredericton Downtown Community Health Centre (FDCHC). Dr. Rickards is an RN with clinical and research expertise and a keen interest in vulnerable populations. She is an Assistant Professor at UNB, worked as a nurse for 30 years, and has been involved with the FDCHC for over a decade. As the ECR, Dr. Rickards will mentor novice nurses and researchers/teams, as well as examine how full scope of practice for both nurses and Nurse Practitioners can impact the health practices of vulnerable populations and decrease visits to emergency rooms and how interdisciplinary collaboration can support positive preventive health care experiences. The results will give clear direction for effective use of resources for governments and institutions as health care costs continue to increase. In this four-year CIHR funded project, Dr. Rickards will develop clinically relevant research and a strong research team within the FDCHC who will do transformative and innovative research.

column36: Maternal Obesity in Atlantic Canada: Implementing evidence into clinical practice
column37: Obesity is a serious global health problem. Nearly 60.6% of Canadian adults are overweight or obese, with rates having doubled in some parts of Canada in just two decades1. Atlantic Canada has among the highest rates of obesity in Canada2. More specifically, as demonstrated in the Canadian Maternity Experiences Survey, women in Nova Scotia have the highest average prepregnancy body mass index3. Associated with obesity are a number of important safety and financial implications for health care professionals and the health system2. Our health care system is also struggling to manage and provide proper care for the rising numbers of pregnant patients living with obesity who are frequently affected by a number of comorbidities4. There are serious health and safety risks to health care workers associated with lifting and moving obese patients, including back and soft tissue injuries. In an effort to improve the health of these childbearing women in Nova Scotia, our goal in this research project is to implement and evaluate two clinical practice initiatives, a clinical practice guideline and a best practice model, that provide evidence-based recommendations for the care of women that are obese prior to and during their labour and birth. Initiatives to change the behaviour of health care professional and to enhance the health of consumers are influenced by a variety of issues. In order to be successful, we will need to understand more about the setting. That is, the area where both prenatal and labour and delivery care is provided to women. We will also need to work with all health care providers employed in these settings to make sure that the strategy we will use to bring about change is the best for everyone. Through this study, we will begin to not only improve the surveillance of management of this population, but also identify ways to improve education, practice, policy, and research in the area of management for obese women giving birth in Nova Scotia.
