column37: Each year, more than 10,000 Canadian children will suffer post-concussion syndrome, which includes long term problems with thinking, headaches, sleep disturbances, depression, social withdrawal, poor quality of life, and lost time at school. When children experience post-concussion, then there is increasing demand on families, schools, and health care organizations. Unfortunately, we understand very little about the causes of post-concussion syndrome and even less about what we can do to treat it. My mission is to enhance children's functioning, outcome, and quality of life following concussion (or mild traumatic brain injury). The focus of this embedded clinician research program over the next four years is on the children who have post-concussion syndrome; about 10-15% of those who get a concussion. My goals are to: (1) improve our ability to diagnose concussion in youth and determine who will have poor outcome; (2) better understand post-concussion syndrome from biological, psychological, and social viewpoints; (3) determine whether there are long-term effects for youth who sustain concussions; and (4) study new treatment interventions that can reduce symptoms, speed up recovery, or even prevent the post-concussion syndrome. As a clinician within Alberta Health Services and practicing at Alberta Children's Hospital, I am fully embedded with a province-wide health system and am in a unique position to have my clinical research improve quality of care. I am the director of neuropsychology services for this hospital, I meet with hospital management about policy, care, and innovation on a regular basis to dictate strategies for psychology, I am a co-investigator with several members who sit on a provincially based concussion clinical pathways task force, and I have also established several local, national, and international collaborations. Through these avenues I will implement new clinical care pathways and change how care is provide to youth every year.

column36: Transitions in Care: Improving Outcomes for Cardiac Patients
column37: Transitions in care occur when patients move from a hospital to home or another site of care. Another critical transition in heart care is when heart attack patients seek care at a hospital. Such transitions are known to be a time of heightened risk for all patients, and cardiac patients are no exception. These risks may be related to insufficient information being provided to the patient and family, inadequate planning for follow-up care, or patients' or caregivers' lack of required knowledge and skill to manage the transition. Poor transitions can lead to more emergency department visits and hospital admissions, as well as unnecessary suffering. My program of research, based at St. Paul's Hospital's Heart Centre and the UBC School of Nursing, aims to address some of the critical transition points in cardiac care, focusing on patients with unique and underappreciated needs. Overcoming ethnicity-based barriers to seeking and receiving care for heart attacks (of great importance, as timely treatment is crucial for success), improving access to depression care for affected heart patients, and enhancing understanding of, and adherence to, discharge instructions are some of the issues I will tackle, which are all united around the common theme of transition. The Heart Centre at St. Paul's Hospital is a centre of excellence for heart care and the only centre in BC to provide the full spectrum of care This includes prevention and reversal, diagnostic tests and the full range of treatments, including surgery, angioplasty, transplants and rehabilitation. UBC School of Nursing is a research-intensive school that boasts many world-renowned faculty members. With current appointments that straddle the clinical and academic settings, I am ideally positioned to identify relevant questions arising from practice, lead key studies to address these questions, and efficiently translate findings into practice. The embedded clinician-researcher award will allow me to achieve these aims.

column36: Journey out of Intensive Care: Reengineering Return to the Community
column37: When patients are transferred from one care setting to another there is a high risk of error. The discharge of patients from the intensive care unit (ICU) is an example of a high-risk transfer. These are the sickest and most complex patients. For the past four years I have led a team of professionals and interested citizens to re-design the transition of care for patients discharged from intensive care. We are making good progress, but have stumbled upon an unexpected and important observation that we believe needs to be urgently addressed. Patients are being discharged directly from the ICU to the community! Traditionally, discharge from the ICU has been a two-step process; transition to a 'regular' hospital ward for a period of care, rehabilitation and assessment, and then return to the community (e.g., home). However, because of growing demands on our healthcare system, patients are being discharged directly from the ICU to the community. In 2014, 1 in 10 adult ICU patients in Alberta were directly discharged to the community! This new approach offers potential advantages (e.g., could be more efficient) and disadvantage (e.g., might not be as safe), but we don't know because it has not been studied. In direct response to this challenge, I propose to expand my team's work to re-design the transition of care for patients discharged from intensive care and develop an evidence-informed 'ICU discharge tool kit' that supports all patients - those who receive care on a hospital ward before leaving hospital and those that return directly to the community. This tool kit will be similar to the World Health Organization's Surgical Safety Checklist, and will be designed to ensure that the right patient is discharged at the right time to the right setting with the right care plan.

column37: Kidney Failure: Kidney failure is a serious health condition that affects more than 40,000 Canadians. The best treatment for kidney failure is a new kidney by transplantation. Unfortunately, patients with kidney failure often wait years to receive a new kidney. Many patients die while they are waiting. Living Kidney Donation: It is safe for a living person who is healthy to donate one of their kidneys. Family and friends of patients who need a kidney often volunteer to donate one of their kidneys. With advances in transplantation, the donor and recipient do not have to be related or be of the same gender, race, or age. Canada and other countries are looking for ways to safely increase living kidney donation. Barriers to Living Kidney Donation: Unfortunately, many patients who would benefit from a kidney transplant do not receive one. There are many reasons for this. Doctors do not always talk to their patients about transplantation. Patients are often uncomfortable discussing living kidney donation with family and friends. Many people do not realize that it is safe to donate a kidney; some are told they are too old to donate despite new research showing it is safe if they are healthy. As well, donor evaluation often takes a year to complete (when it should only take 3 months). A long evaluation process has negative consequences for both donors and recipients. Safely Increasing Living Kidney Donation: My research team is working with living kidney donors and transplant programs to develop and test solutions to overcome barriers to living kidney donation. As well, we are studying a large group of living kidney donors over many decades to confirm long-term safety. Information from our studies will enable more patients with kidney failure to safely receive transplants, and will help candidates make informed decisions about becoming living kidney donors.

column36: Characterizing care transitions for complex populations using patient-centred episodes of care and evaluating solution-focused targeted interventions
column37: Transitions from one sector of the health care system to another are the most dangerous and vulnerable periods for patients and caregivers. Therefore, improving transitions and related experiences is a major focus of quality improvement in most health jurisdictions within Ontario, Canada and globally. Because transitions involve care across different providers, it is essential to use a patient perspective and measure individuals' transitions over time. Further, in order to improve transitions of care, it is necessary to understand the contextual factors surrounding transitions throughout transitions of care. Addressing this important health system issue, in partnership with Health Quality Ontario, this research program aims to: (1) characterize trajectories for complex populations through patient-centred episodes of care using administrative health data; (2) understand patient, caregiver, provider and decision-maker experiences for health system performance improvement using qualitative methods; and (3) identify and evaluate quality improvement interventions to optimize transitions in care for complex populations. Given rising health care costs, it is increasingly important to provide efficient value-based health care that is needs driven for specific populations across the continuum of care. Working with Health Quality Ontario, this innovative research will inform opportunities for system improvement for targeted intervention, such as the creation of potential payment bundling options for care episodes among different complex populations. In understanding trajectories for persons with complex needs, transformational models of care can be co-created with patients and providers to encompass the entire anticipated expected trajectory of care for optimal service delivery and outcomes.

column37: Certaines personnes atteintes de maladies chroniques ont egalement des problemes psychologiques et/ou sociaux qui augmentent leurs besoins face au systeme de sante. Pour une petite proportion de ces personnes, les services offerts ne repondent pas adequatement a leurs besoins et elles consultent tres souvent a l'urgence et dans d'autres services de sante sans necessairement obtenir les services dont elles auraient besoin. La gestion de cas est une intervention qui pourrait les aider tout en ameliorant l'utilisation des services. Cependant, il est necessaire de bien identifier la clientele qui pourraient beneficier le plus d'une intervention de gestion de cas. Ce programme de recherche, developpe en partenariat avec la Direction de l'organisation des services de premiere ligne integres du Ministere de la sante et des services sociaux du Quebec, avec les Centres de sante et de services sociaux du Saguenay-lac-St-Jean et de l'Estrie, vise a mieux identifier les patients atteints de maladies chroniques a risque d'une grande utilisation des services de sante pour leur offrir une intervention de gestion de cas qui pourra mieux repondre a leurs besoins. En plus de produire de nouvelles connaissances scientifiques qui pourront etre utiles dans d'autres contextes au Quebec, au Canada et a l'international, ce programme de recherche aura plusieurs retombees directes sur le systeme de soins. Des changements seront apportes dans des programmes de gestion de cas deja existants pour ameliorer l'experience de soins des patients et l'utilisation des ressources. Les decideurs et le Ministere seront mieux informes pour planifier l'organisation des services pour cette clientele et un outil clinique sera integre au dossier clinique informatise pour identifier plus rapidement des patients qui devraient recevoir des soins mieux adaptes a leurs besoins.

column36: Addressing Transitions in Care: An Indigenous-based, Integrated Care Pathway for Opioid Dependence in Pregnancy in Northwestern Ontario
column37: Opioid use affects up to thirty percent of pregnancies in Northwestern Ontario. Accessing appropriate care during pregnancy and after birth can be overwhelming especially for women with substance use issues living in rural and remote communities. There is little support for the women as she and her infant transition through the health and social service systems. First Nations women have the additional layer of complexity in that they also have to navigate both federal and provincial healthcare systems. Furthermore, practitioners and programs in Northwestern Ontario often work in isolation with little inter-sectoral and inter-organizational communication. There are no consensus guidelines for the management of opioid addiction in pregnancy and no standardization of treatment protocols across the region. This leads to wide variation in the care of pregnant women with opioid dependence. The objective of this program of research is to improve the care of substance using pregnant women and their infants by addressing transitions in care. First, evidenced-based standards of care for the management of pregnant women with substance use issues who live in rural and remote areas will be developed. Next, an Indigenous-based, integrated care pathway will be developed, implemented and assessed in terms of its impact on health service provision and quality of care for opioid dependent pregnant and parenting Aboriginal women and their children. Finallay, the role and interplay of tele-obstetrics, tele-mental health and tele-addictions along with web-based tools in the management of substance using pregnant and parenting women will be investigated. The development of a regional, integrated care pathway for substance-using women in pregnancy and while parenting will be the first of its kind in Canada.

column36: Four Year Embedded Clinician Researcher Program
column37: I will be an embedded clinician researcher at Health Quality Ontario (HQO), the provincial advisor on the quality of healthcare in Ontario. I will work together with leaders and staff at HQO to develop a set of quality measures that assess how good the care is for people admitted to hospital and discharged home. Research has demonstrated that the care people receive when transitioning out of hospital is often fragmented and puts them at risk of developing complications. Yet, we currently do not have good ways of measuring and reporting on this care. Measuring the quality of care is a necessary step for improvement. Our research program will begin by asking members of the public what they think are the most important aspects of care for people transitioning from hospital to home. We will also look at what existing research says can be done to improve this care. We will use the feedback and research findings to develop a "Quality Standard" that outlines what good care looks like when people are discharged home from hospital. The Quality Standard will include 5 to 15 concise, specific recommendations. Each recommendation will be accompanied by a set of measures that can help organizations assess whether they are providing excellent care. Once we develop the measures, we will assess whether it is feasible for HQO to collect and report some of them systematically for hospitals, primary care practices, and home care organizations in Ontario. We will consider which of these measures should be reported directly to the public, which should be reported to organizations privately, and which would be most useful to spur local improvements in care. We will then conduct a large research study to evaluate the impact of having HQO i) publicly report measures and ii) prioritize measures for local quality improvement. We will assess whether these changes result in improvements to the quality of care for people discharged from hospital to home.

column37: Each year in Canada, nearly 500 000 community-dwelling seniors sustain injuries that are not fatal but that limit their mobility and daily activities. The vast majority of these seniors seek medical care in Emergency Departments (EDs) and two-thirds are discharged back home with various minor injuries. Evidence generated by the Canadian Emergency Team Initiative (CETI), has shown that these minor injuries can trigger a downward spiral of functional decline (in mobility and daily activities) in 16% of seniors who are still independent at the time of their injury. Moreover, these injuries unmask early signs of impairments as well as a pre-frail/frail status. As there are no ED management guidelines designed to prevent these injured seniors from losing their mobility and function, they deteriorate within 6 months post-ED discharge. This is unfortunate as there is compelling evidence of the effectiveness of community-based mobility interventions in improving frailty & function. Such interventions include fall prevention & exercise programs, which are available across all Canadian communities. In that context, identification of seniors at risk of functional decline is crucial in EDs to implement effective interventions. The CETI has validated a Clinical Decision Rule (CETI-CDR) to screen & orient seniors at high, moderate & low risk of decline to appropriate post-ED follow-ups. We thus propose the new CEDeComS intervention that combines CETI-CDR screening with rapid linkage to mobility programs in the community, directly from the ED. The main objective of this study is to assess the effectiveness of the new CEDeComS intervention on reducing functional decline in seniors presenting to the ED with minor injuries. The study builds on the formation of new ED-community partnerships that will improve the care continnum to help these seniors remaining independent.

column36: Four Year Embedded Clinician Researcher Program - Improving Care Transitions between the Hospital and Community for Youth with Obesity
column37: Youth obesity is one of the most serious public health challenges of the 21st century. A number of tertiary care centres in Canada offer structured pediatric weight management clinics. Although these programs are effective, dropout is substantial, availability is limited, and access to this specialized care is difficult. These programs do not typically employ a patient- and family-centred approach that incorporates family expectations and perspectives about treatment which contributes to high dropout rates. Therefore, novel care models should be designed with patient-and family-centred services that improve care transitions between the community and hospital-based weight management clinics where youth can be supported with longitudinal integrated weight management strategies. The proposed research program demonstrates originality, relevance, and responsiveness to the diverse local community by identifying and addressing existing gaps along the continuum of care for obese youth. Through novel research methods including social network analysis and experience-based co-design, we will describe the current state of the local health system for obese youth, highlight opportunities for collaboration between healthcare providers and community-based organizations such as public schools, public health agencies, and community centres, and co-design with patients and families a future state community care model that improves care transitions for obese youth between a hospital-based weight management clinic and the community. A culminating research project will bring patients, families, healthcare providers, and community-based organization members together in a learning collaborative to further develop this prototype care model. The proposed research program will foster the development of an interdisciplinary cadre of future health services researchers and translate youth obesity research findings to improve access to specialized care and promote service integration.

column37: Significant oral health disparities exist in Canada. Increasing access to early oral health care for vulnerable groups of children is critical in order to curb the incidence of ECC. My clinical background, research training and life experiences along with my research focus are perfectly aligned with this CIHR opportunity as it relates to the oral health of vulnerable populations. Since good oral health during early childhood sets the foundation for a lifetime of optimal dental and total health, my proposed program of research aims to improve access to oral health care for young children at-risk for ECC and improve oral health care delivery for children requiring dental surgery to treat their ECC. column36: Supporting the creation of a LEARNing INteGrated health system to mobilize context-adapted knowledge with a Wiki platform to Improve the transitions of frail Seniors from emergency Departments to the cOMmunity: the LEARNING WISDOM program
column37: Elderly patients discharged from emergency departments are often repeatedly readmitted, lose functioning capacity, and increase caregivers' burden of care. Care becomes fragmented, discontinuous, and costly. In addition, Quebec's Bill 10 has merged healthcare institutions but has not yet integrated their information, human resources or care management systems, resulting in further fragmentation of care. However, using proven (evidence-based) strategies can improve transition for the elderly. The Acute Care for Elders Program at Mount Sinai applied innovative strategies (interventions) which reduced lengths of hospital stay, reduced readmissions, increased patient satisfaction, and saved over $6 million in 2014. Strategies included providing transition coaches, follow-up calls and using discharge order sets and patient self-care guides (knowledge tools). Successful programs often remain an exception, however, because technical challenges and different organizational cultures make adapting them to other contexts difficult. Our WikiTrauma open-source collaborative database and Wiki 101 training program are designed so that a program can be adapted by the people affected (knowledge users) and then applied (implemented) locally. The "Wiki-suite" was successfully used in adapting trauma care, and now managers and clinicians want to apply it to geriatrics. This proposal will use the Wiki-suite to adapt and apply the Acute Care for Elders Program, specifically its care transitions component, in four hospitals in the Chaudieres-Appalaches region (CISSS CA) of Quebec. We will assess the impact of using the Wiki-suite to adapt and apply the ACE Program by asking managers, clinicians and patients about its effects on patient empowerment, health outcomes, and costs. We will also explore how the Wiki-suite works in terms of behavior and organizational change to gain insight into using it to adapt any successful program to any local context (scale up).

column37: Despite the surge of interest in using Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in brain science, the biological mechanisms underlying it is poorly understood. column36: Patterns of Resilience Among Youth in Contexts of Petrochemical Production and Consumption in the Global North and Global South
column37: Both oil and gas production and the process of consumption (as it relates to climate change) have large impacts, both positive and negative, on social, economic and environmental systems that affect young people's mental health and overall wellbeing. To better understand these complex relationships at both ends of the carbon cycle, a multidisciplinary and multisectoral team of researchers and community and industry partners in two communities in Canada (Drayton Valley in Alberta, Cambridge Bay in Nunavut) and two communities in South Africa (Dunoon in the Western Cape, Secunda in Mpumalanga) will study the resilience of young people and the systems with which they interact. Unique among studies of resilience, this project will carry out case studies that examine at the same time the biological and psychological resilience of young people, family and community resilience, and the resilience of environmental systems as they interact over a period of several years. The research uses a transformative sequential mixed methods design to facilitate data collection across multiple human and ecological systems. We expect that a systemic understanding of how oil and gas industries affect the multiple social and physical determinants of youth health can increase the potentially positive impacts of extraction industries (e.g., employment, community cohesion) while mitigating the negative consequences of oil and gas production (e.g., finding better ways to help youth deal with family stressors, social disruptions, pollution and forced migration). Simply put, we want to learn how young people adapt across the carbon cycle and use what we learn about their patterns of resilience to improve the lives of all youth. To do this research, we will provide training for 50 graduate students and 5 postdocs, and we will engage youth themselves as citizen scientists and co-researchers. Our findings will inform socially and environmentally sound government policies and industry practices.

column36: Gut Metabotypes as Biomarkers for Nutrition and Health
column37: During the last decades, nutritional science and biomedicine have made a tremendous progress in the development of modern molecular and cellular research technologies resulting in the awareness that health is a condition of homeostasis not only of our different eukaryontic cells but also of the millions of microorganisms living in symbiosis on (e. g. skin) or within (e. g. gut) our human body. The aim of the consortium is to identify an indicator of that homeostasis as a biomarker for nutrition and health. The overall goal is to identify biopatterns of gut microbiome metabolites in human serum that are indicative for a symbiotic homeostasis of humans and microbes indicating a healthy nutrition and human health in general. To this end we will: (1) identify beneficial gut microbiota indicating healthy nutrition patterns in several human cohorts (FoCus, TOMORROW, FoCus re-call, PopGen). (2) detect specific metabolites and/or metabolite profiles in the human serum by advanced Metabolomics and Lipidomics which are related to the identified healthy microbiota type. (3) combine the data into a nutrition - microbiome - serum metabolite axis which is indicative for a healthy nutrition and/or human health in general. With our approach, we are extending the biomarker research on the human gut microbiome, which is heavily influenced by diet and therefore might be more suitable as a biomarker for nutrition and health compared to serum proteins. Also, we are not focusing on one certain bacterium (like on one certain serum protein) but on biopatterns of metabolites of microbiome populations indicating a symbiotic homeostasis of humans and microbes as a marker for health.

column36: The Built Environment and Active Transportation Safety in Children and Youth
column37: The Convention on the Rights of the Child states that "...children have the right to the highest attainable level of health and the right to a safe environment, free from injury and violence." Active transportation (AT), such as walking and biking, is a healthy way for children to explore their environment and develop independence. However, children can be injured while walking and biking and these injuries can be severe when children are hit by motor vehicles. Many Canadian cities make changes to the built environment (e.g., traffic calming features, separated bike lanes) to try and keep people safe. There is some research on how effective these changes are in preventing adult pedestrians and bicyclists from getting hurt, but very little research has been done to show how safe various environments are for children and youth. We propose a research program to study how features of the built environment affect whether kids walk or bike to school and whether or not certain built environment features increase or decrease their likelihood of getting hurt. Our program is unique because we are partnering with injury prevention professionals, provincial governments, environmental organizations and traffic safety professionals who are in a position to help us better understand what features of traffic environments are dangerous or safe. Our research will be very useful in making walking and biking much safer for children and youth.

column37: How our cities are designed, including roads, houses, and neighourhoods influences how much physical activity people get. The design of our cities can also influence how much people participate in social activities and how good they feel about the where they live. As a society we spend very large amounts of money on building infrastructure for cities. For example, our federal government recently pledged $12 billion toward public transportation and sustainable development projects in Canadian cities in the next 2 years. The goals of our research project are to measure how designing healthy cities can influence physical activity and how much people participate in social activities. Another goal is to use and design tools, like mobile phone based apps, to measure how and where people move in their cities. Our team will evaluate four new infrastructure designs in four different Canadian cities. First, the Arbutus Greenway, a 9 km rail corridor that will become a continuous walking and cycling path in Vancouver, BC. Second, #Biketoria, a bicycle network plan in Victoria, BC, that will build a 5.4 km grid of protected cycle tracks downtown and a 24 km network across the city. Third, Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), a 22 km transit system along three major roadways in Saskatoon, SK. Last, the Montreal Community 2016-2020 sustainability plan, which includes urban form interventions, including traffic calming measures, transportation infrastructure and greening. Our team will also develop and refine smartphone apps to measure how people move through cities. These tools will include apps to measure physical activity and apps for interactive mapping of where people move in a city. Our team includes researchers who are experts in public health, geography, and urban planning. Our team also has the urban planners who are implementing the new infrastructure designs in each city.

column36: Climate Change and Indigenous Food System, Food Security, and Food Safety (Climate Change IFS3)
column37: A changing climate will affect food through a range of effects on agriculture, livestock, water systems, and wildlife, which have implications for food security, foodborne disease, and malnutrition. Indigenous populations who rely on the environment for livelihoods are considered highly sensitive to these impacts. The Climate Change and Indigenous Food System, Food Security, & Food Safety (Climate Change IFS3) research program addresses a significant deficit in understanding the food-related health (agri-health) dimensions of climate change among Indigenous populations globally. The research program has created a multinational intersectoral team to characterize the vulnerability and resilience of Indigenous food systems to climate change to inform, enhance, and expand climate change adaptation interventions and adaptation planning. The program responds to needs identified by communities, public health units, Indigenous organizations, governments, and the United Nations through ongoing partnerships with Inuit (Canada), Batwa (Uganda), and Shawi (Peru) populations. Working within these regions, the program has 3 research pillars: 1) Community-driven environment and health surveillance, 2) Projecting climate change impacts on agri-health outcomes, and 3) Developing place-based adaptation pathways. Within the foci of food and climate, we will examine how culturally defined gender roles and age impact vulnerability and resilience, and highlight the importance of Indigenous Knowledge. Comparative analysis is an explicit goal and is built into program design through the use of consistent methodologies across regions. Our participatory, community-based approach will offer best practice guidance for other initiatives, will create community and scientific leaders with expertise in Indigenous agri-health and climate change, and demonstrate the importance of Indigenous Knowledge for adaptation, seeking to empower communities to manage the agri-health effects of climate change.

column36: Multisectoral Urban Systems for health and Equity in Canadian cities
column37: At the end of the 19th century, confronted by epidemics of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis or gastroenteritis, public health authorities began collaborating with municipalities to improve urban environments. Major works were undertaken to install drains and eliminate unhealthy housing, notably by prohibiting dwelling units in basements and windowless rooms. These efforts were very successful as infectious disease rates decreased and did so well before the advent of antibiotics. Initially in developed countries and now in developing nations, there have been major increases in chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and several cancers. At the beginning of the 21st century, to counter these threats to population health, Public Health Departments have forged new alliances with major Canadian cities. Together, they are working to create environments that foster the supply of healthy and affordable food, enhance active transportation, and reduce the risks of bad housing conditions. Our research program aims to study these cross-sector partnerships, which involve collaborations between health practitioners, municipalities, representatives from civil society, housing authorities, and actors from other sectors. We will study partnerships aimed at transforming built environments to increase the availability of fruit and vegetables, promote public transport and physical activity, and improve availability of affordable housing. We will also look into how these partnerships take into account social and gender inequalities and pay special attention to children and youth. To carry out these studies and make comparisons, we will rely on the active participation of the Directors of the Public Health Organizations in Montreal, Saskatoon, Toronto, and Vancouver. Ultimately, we will identify the factors that lead to success in forward-looking initiatives aimed at preventing the new epidemics of chronic diseases.

column36: DERIVE: DEvelopment of Riboflavin biomarkers to relate dietary sources with status, gene-nutrient Interactions and Validated health Effects in adult cohorts
column37: Riboflavin, or vitamin B2, plays a crucial role in human development and health across the lifespan. Recently, an increase in riboflavin intake was suggested to having a blood pressure reducing effect. In most countries, there is little or no knowledge about the riboflavin nutritional status of the population due to the lack of convenient blood indicators and assessment tools. Dietary records are the sole source of information for most countries; however these do not reflect the biochemical status of the population which is a better indicator of health effects related to suboptimal riboflavin intake. In this international and multidisciplinary project, we aim to develop accessible blood indicators for riboflavin status assessment and identify which most sensitively reflect dietary intakes and food sources of riboflavin in Irish and Canadian adults. We will also demonstrate an important health effect of riboflavin by investigating its role in modulating blood pressure via a novel gene-nutrient interactive effect. In summary, suboptimal riboflavin status may be more widespread than is generally recognized across the developed world, because of the reliance on dietary data only in nutrition surveys, without blood indicator evidence. This project will address this gap by developing accessible riboflavin blood indicators for use in population surveys globally, and by demonstrating important functional, gene-nutrient and health effects of optimal riboflavin status in Canadian, Irish and UK cohorts.

column37: Cancer is the leading cause of mortality in Canada representing 30% of all deaths. One in 2.2 (2.4) men (women) will get cancer and ~1 in 3.5 (4.1) will die from it, incurring $124 billion in direct cost in the USA in 2010. Chemo- and radiation therapies (with surgery) are frequently used as treatments for cancer. They function by overwhelming the DNA repair machinery causing excessive DNA damage, resulting in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. While the prognosis for certain cancer types (breast) has improved, it is because of a better understanding of the molecular machineries that drive these cancers and availability of more specialized therapies. Epigenetics is one of the expanding fields of research that holds great potential for therapeutic intervention. Inhibitors of protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs) and other epigenetic enzymes represent the next generation of cancer therapeutics. Signalling pathways that feed to RNA binding proteins are also highly sought after therapeutic targets. By funding this Foundation Program, it will ensure that the mechanisms of these therapeutics are defined, thereby facilitating the generation of better inhibitors for improved cancer treatment. The overall program goal of this foundation grant, is to improve patient care by identifying and validating novel drug targets for cancer. Our proposed program will advance our knowledge of the multifunctional nature of PRMTs and RNA binding proteins such that efficient inhibitors can be improved for effective cancer therapy.

column36: Individual Differences in Pain Sensitivity: Genetic and Environmental Factors in Mice and Humans
column37: Chronic pain is the most prevalent human health problem, affecting 15-25% of the population at any one time (and 50% over a lifetime), and costing the Canadian economy $6B in direct costs per year and up to $60B per year in total costs. Chronic pain, perhaps more than any other common disorder, is associated with robust individual differences in susceptibility, sensitivity, and response to treatment. Heritability studies performed in humans and in mice suggest that somewhat less than half of this variability is genetic in nature, and thus a complete understanding will require the elucidation of both genetic and non-genetic factors. My laboratory has been devoted to the identification of these factors-in both mice and humans-for the last two decades. The laboratory will be working on the following experimental themes over the next few years, with appropriate collaborators from across Canada and worldwide: -Genetic studies of pain. -Sex differences in the modulation of pain by the immune system. -Social modulation of pain in mice and humans. -Development and characterization of novel measurement strategies for pain in mice. This research is expected to identify and characterize multiple causes of pain variability: genes, sex-dependent brain circuitry, social factors, and interactions between them. Building on proven success with translation, this information should prove invaluable to pain researchers everywhere, and lead to clinical advancements in the management of pain.

column36: Fundamentals on Telomere and Telomerase Functions
column37: One could compare our genome to a large library that contains numerous shelves, each with an extraordinary large number of books. The combined information contained in all the books represents our genetic information and is required to make us who we are. In this paraphrase, the bookshelves represent our chromosomes. Due to the heavy use of the books and because the whole library, including the shelves, need to be duplicated each time a cell divides, there is continued wear and tear on the terminal bookends on the shelves. Without continued upkeep and repair, the bookends will eventually become dysfunctional, causing books to fall off the shelves and get lost. The telomeres and the telomerase enzyme that we study are, respectively, the bookends and the maintenance operator for the bookends. In real life, it is essential to ensure the integrity of the ends of our chromosomes. The telomerase enzyme is composed of several subunits; two of which, one protein and one RNA molecule are required for the enzyme to work in a minimalistic test-tube system. Inadequate supply of any of the components, causing instability of the chromosomes, is associated with aging and human disease, foremost cancer, but also dyskeratosis congenita (DKC) and other congenital disorders now called telomeropathies. Using a simple but powerful model system, we propose to investigate the biology of telomeres and the telomerase enzyme. In particular, we plan to identify all the components, learn more about how they interact, are regulated and localized. Most importantly, we will determine when and how telomerase operates at its most important location, namely on telomeres. Given that telomere and telomerase function and regulation are highly conserved across many species, from yeast to humans, our studies will provide critical clues and input into how telomere biology could be exploited for the benefit of human health.

column37: Lung tuberculosis (TB) is a leading infectious cause of morbidity and mortality in the developing countries and parts of developed countries including Canada despite decades-long use of BCG vaccine and antibiotics. Built upon our past success, our current program aims to decipher the immune mechanisms underlying the failure of host defense to effectively control TB and apply new knowledge to developing the most robust vaccination strategies to combat it by using innovative approaches. column36: Addressing the health impacts of socioeconomic marginalization among people who use illicit drugs
column37: Socioeconomic marginalization (SEM) is a key driver of drug use and drug-related harm, resulting in excess morbidity and mortality among people who use drugs and a significant social and economic burden in Canada and internationally. However, key dimensions of SEM and their health impacts are not fully understood and interventions that address drug use and related harm by targeting SEM are urgently needed. Further, research has shown that there is a strong link between understanding how SEM impacts individual outcomes and the generation of evidence-based strategies to reduce health inequity. My proposed program builds on my previous research in this field, and includes an established network of local, national and international collaborators, a growing training platform, and an integrated knowledge translation (iKT) strategy. My overall goal is to reduce drug use and related harm through effective interventions that address SEM among people who use illicit drugs. Using linked observational, intervention and randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluation studies, the specific objectives of my CIHR Foundation program are to: 1) Conduct observational research that identifies elements of SEM to be targeted via social and structural interventions; 2) Implement social and structural RCTs that test public health solutions targeting SEM; and 3) Evaluate how social and structural drivers of SEM affect addictions RCT recruitment, retention and experiences from local and comparative national perspectives. Through qualitative, quantitative, experimental and mixed-methods approaches, this work will yield a robust evidence base for strategies to reduce drug use and drug-related harm driven by SEM. Parallel iKT initiatives will promote the integration of public health objectives into social and welfare policy, thereby reducing the human and health system costs of SEM among people who use drugs.

column36: Mechanisms of peptide hormone action: metabolic and therapeutic implications
column37: The Drucker lab studies the mechanism of action of gut hormones, principally glucagon, the glucagon-like peptides (GLP-1 and GLP-2) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP). The lab explores how these hormones work to control food intake, nutrient absorption, body weight, and inflammation, improving glucose and fat metabolism. There has been remarkable progress in translating our basic science into new therapies now widely used for the treatment of human disease. Notably, GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists are now approved for treatment of both obesity and diabetes and GLP-2 is used for the treatment of intestinal failure. We continue to make new discoveries that should enable development of next generation medications with improved efficacy and tolerability, Our studies of glucagon will enable understanding how glucagon simultaneously controls glucose metabolism and energy expenditure with an emphasis on determining the contribution of direct glucagon action s in fat tissue. Related studies with GIP will identify how GIP controls nutrient flux in fat depots, with implications for energy storage and weight loss. We propose to determine whether GLP-1 from the distal gut controls improvements in intestinal permeability and reduction of inflammation. Our analyses of GLP-2 will identify key cellular sites within the gut that are essential for transducing the physiological actions of GLP-2 that control mucosal integrity and nutrient absorption. Proposed studies of DPP-4 will determine the importance of key tissues and mechanisms linking DPP4 to control of blood lipids. Our research program will use mouse genetics and experimental models of inflammation, diabetes, obesity, liver and intestinal disease, to delineate mechanisms of hormone action that may be of direct clinical relevance. Collectively, this research program will address critical questions to advance our understanding of the translational biology and therapeutic potential of gut hormone action

column36: Targeting neuronal and glial signaling in chronic pain
column37: Chronic pain has been labelled the silent health crisis, afflicting hundreds of millions of people worldwide. Chronic pain causes more disability than cancer and heart disease, and the monetary cost of treatment and lost productivity around the globe is hundreds of billions of dollars annually. My group has pioneered a new understanding of the underlying causes of chronic pain as being due to abnormalities in a number of molecules, cells and circuits in the pain system in the spinal cord. Our goal is to develop novel, effective, safe therapies for chronic pain, individualized to the person who is suffering. We will do this by taking advantage of our recent discoveries illustrating the roles of genes, gender and molecular pathways in producing chronic pain. We will focus on developing molecules which inhibit the abnormal functioning of receptors and molecules we have implicated in causing pain. An important experimental approach will be to test these inhibitory molecules in human neurons and microglia, derived by using skin cells from individual patients with chronic pain. Altogether, we anticipate engineering entirely new classes of safe and effective medications for chronic pain.

column36: Developing new therapeutic strategies for AML (Acute Myeloid Leukemia)
column37: Aggressive induction chemotherapy produces complete remission in ~70% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but most ultimately relapse, at least in part, due to the persistence of dormant stem cells that are resistant to standard chemotherapy. Thus, there is an urgent need for better makers that predict response to chemotherapy and new treatments that more effectively kill the leukemia stem cells. Previously we discovered that AML cells and stem cells have abnormal mitochondria function and a unique the energy produced by these organelles. In addition, blocking protein breakdown in the mitochondria by targeting the mitochondrial enzyme ClpP killed AML cells but not normal cells. In this research program, we will investigate the biology of ClpP. We will determine the substrates of ClpP and its role in the mitochondria. We will also test ClpP inhibitors and activators as potential new therapies for AML. As part of this project, we will work with our industry collaborators to develop new drugs that target mitochondrial pathways. Most chemotherapy drugs act by killing the cancer cells. Another strategy is to cause the cancer cells to differentiate into more mature and functional cells. In project 2, we will investigate how mitochondrial pathways influence AML differentiation and stemness. Finally, in project 3, we will identify new genetic subgroups of high risk AML and define new therapeutic strategies for these patients.

column36: Molecular and cellular biology of T regulatory cells
column37: The goal of my research is to understand how our immune system regulates itself and to use this information to develop new ways to treat patients with immune-related diseases, such as autoimmunity or transplant rejection. A healthy immune system must strike a balance between attacking infectious or dangerous substances while not reacting to our own cells and tissues. This delicate balancing act is called immune tolerance. Both autoimmune diseases and transplant complications are caused by disrupted immune tolerance. At present, immunosuppressive drugs are our only treatment for these conditions. Yet these drugs suppress all immune responses, putting patients at risk of infection and cancer, often without controlling their disease. We need to find better ways to prevent harmful immune responses. I am an expert is the study of a type of white blood cell called T regulatory cells, or Tregs, which coordinate immune responses and maintain immune tolerance. My work has defined how Tregs develop and function, and led to clinical trials to test use of Tregs as a cell therapy in transplantation and autoimmunity. I developed methods to monitor the presence of Tregs in blood and tissues, allowing more precise measurement of immune tolerance. If used as a treatment, Tregs could control pathological immune responses without altering healthy immune balance. Towards this aim, the next stage of my research has 3 goals, to: 1) create "designer" Tregs that are engineered to be active only in the presence of a transplant and test their ability to prevent transplant rejection and preserve normal immunity; 2) design new ways to alter Tregs so their function is tailored to specific disease contexts; and 3) identify biological pathways that regulate Tregs, so that they can be targeted for new treatment options. My research will enable new Treg-based therapies to prevent and treat the many chronic diseases that are caused by a failure of immune tolerance.

column36: The growing biomedical significance of intracellular membrane trafficking
column37: All human cells, including cancer cells and nerve cells in the brain are highly compartmentalized, and proteins move between the compartments in small membrane bound transport carriers. This process called membrane trafficking controls the levels of proteins and allows the proteins to function at their proper cellular location. Membrane trafficking is highly regulated and alterations in proteins that control membrane trafficking are a feature of many human diseases including neurological disorders and cancer. We have identified exciting new links between a family of proteins that regulate membrane trafficking with cancer and neurological disease. The studies described in this program will provide new insight into the fundamental mechanisms of membrane trafficking and how alterations in this process lead to disease.

column36: The Lived Brain: Whole body effects on women's brain health
column37: Canada leads the world in gender and health research policy. The applicant, building on more than 2 decades' leadership in women's health research, education, policy, and outreach, will advance Canada's leadership position by developing the Wilfred and Joyce Posluns Chair in Women's Brain Health into an internationally-recognized focal point for significant advances in research and recognition of the importance of women's brain health. The initiative will be guided by three principles: (i) Sex & gender: Biological differences (sex) and social position (gender) both affect brain health, requiring integrated projects; (ii) Brain, body, culture: The brain is not autonomous; it responds to and integrates other body processes, sensitive in turn to the outside world, including to changes induced by cultural (gendered) practices; (iii) Life Process: Brain health, especially in aging, is a result of accumulating life-long processes involving diverse interacting factors. Using these principles, the Chair will implement integrated programs of research, mentoring, education and knowledge translation (KT). Brain-imaging, neuropsychological testing, and qualitative interviews of women post-oophorectomy will elucidate the importance of estrogens for women's brain health, building on other projects on women's brain health in the Einstein lab. Mentoring and education will involve graduate and undergraduate research training, yearly graduate research awards, a student-run conference on women's brain health, and lecturing on women's health. KT will involve community advisory groups, community fora, partners and advisors to disseminate research results through national and international channels. An arts-based initiative will include an exhibition of women's poetry, body maps, and artists' representations of women's brain health. Through these activities, the Chair will promote the importance of women's brain health in scientific, professional and public communities.

column36: Functional Protein Dynamics in Health and Disease
column37: Protein molecules play critical roles in cellular function and they catalyze many of the biochemical reactions that are necessary for life. The three-dimensional shapes of these molecules are necessary for guiding proper function and they can change with time due to interactions with other molecules, during the process of carrying out specific functions, or simply the result of random fluctuations. Although very detailed static pictures of protein molecules have been produced using traditional biophysical tools, macromolecular function and misfunction is, in many cases, intimately coupled to flexibility; knowledge of molecular motions therefore becomes critical. Thus, static pictures of proteins that have been generated to date often do not completely explain results from functional biological assays, nor do they necessarily illuminate the path for engineering new functions or for rational drug design. The goal of this research is to develop new Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy based techniques for studying motional processes in proteins and for relating these to function and to apply the methodology to important protein systems that are implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration and amyloidosis. The insights obtained will augment the structure-function paradigm that has dominated our understanding of how proteins work to include the important role of molecular dynamics. They will inform how function can be manipulated by changing how parts of proteins move in relation to each other and provide clues about how to design, in a rational manner, new classes of drug molecules. Advances that are made in the laboratory will be translated into potential drugs through collaborations with leading medicinal chemists and clinician scientists.

column36: Aging in Place in First Nations Communities: A community-based approach to supporting older Indigenous people with dementia.
column37: First Nations (FN) populations in Canada are rapidly aging. Rates of dementia are reported to be 34% higher than the non-Aboriginal population and rising more quickly [1]. Chronic diseases are epidemic in FN communities whereby the number of individuals aged 55-64 reporting three or more chronic conditions is 3.5 times higher than non-First Nations people [2] and 45% of the 65+ population report fair/poor health with 69% having activity limitations [2]. Thus, onset of frailty occurs at a much younger age and the burden of morbidity among older Indigenous persons with dementia results in substantial caregiver burden. Diverse community contexts, complex relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians, and continued colonial policies governing access to services, all present significant challenges to empowering communities [3]. The purpose of this proposal is to engage local integrated Knowledge Translation (iKT) teams to develop, evaluate and implement care models that empower caregivers and communities to support people living with multiple chronic conditions (MCC) and cognitive decline including dementia. Our goal is to address the unmet needs of Indigenous persons living with or at risk for dementia, and to support their families and communities to reduce caregiver burden. The goal is to build a legacy through partnership with FN communities to empower and support research-based, community-identified strategies that combine Indigenous practices with Western technologies to support aging in place in FN communities.

column36: Improving Outcomes for Preterm Infants and their Families: A Canadian Collaborative Network
column37: Being born too soon, or "preterm", is a life changing, stressful and emotional experience for families. Preterm babies require support for the development of all organs and any disturbances in such development or processes can have life-long consequences for the baby and their family. In Canada, every year 25,000-30,000 babies are born preterm. In order to improve outcomes of women who experience preterm labor, babies who deliver at preterm gestation and families affected by the birth of a preterm baby, we are proposing a Pan-Canadian Network, which will bring together researchers, doctors, nurses, and families from coast-to-coast to prevent and manage the consequences of preterm birth. Over the next 5 years, we aim to improve the delivery of care to extremely preterm infants during the antenatal, perinatal, and postnatal periods, and to increase the rate of survival without morbidity from 47% to 61%. The Network will work with families and parents who have undergone such experiences to understand what matters most to parents and where further research is needed. The Network will build a national database for the ongoing collection of maternal and infant characteristics related to preterm birth, so that we can understand who is at risk of preterm birth and what can be done to improve outcomes for babies born preterm. We will investigate the impact of some promising interventions via this Network and improve the transmission of knowledge of activities that can lead to better care and improvements for infants, families and societies at large.

column36: Regulation of postsynaptic expression and function of ionotropic neurotransmitter receptors
column37: Normal function of the brain depends on tightly regulated communication between neurons. The neurons communicate with one another through junction sites called synapses via "synaptic transmission". During this process, neurotransmitter molecules are released from presynaptic neurons and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic neurons. Deregulated synaptic transmission is believed to be at the root of many brain diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, epilepsy, and stroke. I believe that by better understanding the mechanisms controlling the efficacy of the synaptic transmission among neurons there is the potential to identify targets and thereby to create better therapeutics for these brain disorders. Theoretically, the strength of synaptic transmission can be regulated by altering either the presynaptic neurotransmitter release or the responsiveness of postsynaptic neurotransmitter receptor. Research in our laboratory has focused on the regulatory mechanisms which determine the responsiveness of postsynaptic ionotropic receptors. Strong evidence accumulated from our work and other labs suggest that both function and number of these receptors may be rapidly altered. These rapid changes may be responsible for the pathogenesis of many brain disorders. Currently, we are proposing experiments to investigate how rapid changes in the function and number of postsynaptic receptors, therefore synaptic transmission strength, is regulated. The main objective of our research is to identify molecular processes underlying the regulation of the efficacy of synaptic transmission. Through these fundamental investigations we aim to identify new therapeutic targets and develop new drugs to treat brain disease. Since inter-neuronal communication is a pivotal component of brain function and the alteration of this process underlies many disorders, our proposed studies can be expected to lead to better treatment for these diseases

column36: Alternatives to antibiotics: New strategies for treating multi-drug resistant infections
column37: Antibiotics are the most successful medical intervention in human history. They are critical for preventing and treating life-threatening infections. A lack of effective antibiotics would lead to difficulties with major surgeries, chemotherapy, transplantations, and early-term births; even minor injuries could become infected and deadly. Thus the relentless and concerning increase in multi-drug resistance to antibiotics in the face of a inadequate pipeline for new antibiotics has caused great concern for public health officials and the general public. Indeed, in Sept 2016, all 193 member countries of the United Nations declared antimicrobial resistance "the biggest threat to modern medicine". Here we will investigate the mechanisms of adaptive, multiple-antibiotic resistance in the important pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, one of the most difficult to treat bacterial "Superbugs" in our society. Adaptive resistance is a feature of specific bacterial "lifestyles" that are triggered during growth in patients; we will investigate the mechanisms of such resistance in the context of growth circumstances that occur during infections. To tackle adaptive and acquired resistance and provide new therapies that address the poor success of modern antibiotic discovery, we will then develop three alternatives to antibiotics: 1) Novel anti-biofilm peptides to treat adaptive multiple-antibiotic resistance due to the growth of bacteria on body surfaces as multicellular colonies termed biofilms (representing two thirds of all hospital infections); 2) Peptides that enhance the anti-infection properties of the immune system; and 3) Compounds that will reverse the inability of the immune system to respond to pathogens in patients with sepsis (causes 8% of all deaths worldwide). A feature of these strategies is that they will assist in making available antibiotics work better. Our research will move our discoveries to clinical testing during the funding period.

column36: Leveraging Essential Genes and Genetic Networks to Cripple Human Fungal Pathogens
column37: The impact of fungal pathogens on human health is devastating. They infect billions of people around the globe, and kill more than 1.5 million each year. The most vulnerable are people with reduced immune function, such as those with HIV or those undergoing immune suppressing treatments for cancer or organ transplants. One of the leading fungal pathogens of humans is Candida albicans. It kills ~40% of people suffering from bloodstream infections. Treating these infections is extremely difficult, as fungi are closely related to humans and there are very few drugs that kill the fungus but not the host. With the emergence of drug resistance, it is now critical to develop new therapeutic strategies. To address this important clinical need, it is critical to uncover the genes and genetic networks that are required for the pathogen to survive and cause disease. We are one of the first academic labs to obtain a powerful resource that will allow us to test the function of almost every gene in the C. albicans genome. Through collaboration with a pharmaceutical company, we now have access to the largest library of C. albicans mutants, which enables genetic depletion of ~40% of genes in the genome. We will use sophisticated computational approaches to predict essential genes, and will expand this resource to cover them all. This resource provides an unprecedented opportunity to identify which genes are essential for the pathogen, and to determine their molecular function and interactions. We will use this platform to characterize the impact of reducing the dosage of each gene on growth, cellular physiology, and traits associated with the capacity to cause disease. We will perform state-of-the-art screens to identify new molecules that target essential genes, and will evaluate their therapeutic potential. This research will reveal new approaches to cripple the pathogen, and enable development of novel therapeutic strategies to improve clinical outcome for millions of people.

column36: Exercise and Depression: Moving from Efficacy to Effectiveness
column37: Physical inactivity is a health risk factor and a burden on Canadian public health. While inactivity is of concern at a population level, it is even more troubling for individuals with mental illness such as depression. One of the most effective non-pharmacological interventions for mental illness is engagement in exercise. As a timely response to new clinical guidelines and national mental health strategies, the proposed research program will be unique internationally in developing, assessing, and evaluating exercise interventions and initiatives aimed at alleviating depression across the lifespan. Three primary inter-related projects will develop an exercise intervention tool-kit for use by mental health practitioners in collaboration with their patients, and test several novel approaches to delivering exercise interventions to individuals with depression including referral to structured and supervised exercise and the development of a mobile app-based intervention to increase physical activity in adults with depression. My research will provide a blueprint to individuals and healthcare providers for innovative, sustainable, and feasible physical activity strategies that can reduce the burden of depression.

column36: Mutation, cell context, and the pathogenesis of ovarian cancer
column37: Each year in Canada, 2800 women are diagnosed with ovarian cancer and 1750 die from this disease. I study common forms of ovarian cancer, namely endometrioid, clear cell, and high-grade serous ovarian cancers, and also rarer ovarian cancers, such as small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type. This latter cancer is extremely lethal and tragically affects young women. My overarching goal of my research is to decrease death and suffering from ovarian cancer, through improving the way they are diagnosed, prevented, and treated. I hope to achieve this through pursuing three distinct aims. The first is to identify tools that can be used to improve sensitivity and specificity of diagnosis. The second is to study the precursors of cancer, such as endometriosis, to better understand the process of cancer development. This understanding will hopefully allow easier identification of women who are at increased risk of developing ovarian cancers and can most benefit from screening and prevention strategies. Thirdly, I plan to perform experiments, both in cells and animal models that are accurate representations of ovarian cancer, to understand how the combination of genetic mutation, cell environment, and the environment surrounding the cell combine together to drive tumour formation. This understanding can help us develop new treatments for disease. These treatments can similarly be tested for efficacy in the same model systems, which is work I am currently undertaking to study a new class of drugs that could benefit women with small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type. In summary, I hope to be able to generate new tools for diagnosing, managing, and treating ovarian cancer though the work described in my research program.

column37: Projections indicate that by 2050 drug resistant bacteria will kill more people than will cancer. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is one of many emerging new bacterial infections arising from drug resistance. These NCEs are designed to target a specific biosynthetic pathway found in Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria and mycobacteria thereby making it an attractive target for the development of a broad-spectrum anti-infective. Local and national collaborators have been identified to facilitate development of the most promising candidate molecules synthesized.

column36: Investigation of a new approach for treatment of deprivation-induced vision impairment
column37: Brain regions that support visual perception complete their development early in postnatal life when visual experience informs the proper development of neurons and their connections. Disruption of normal visual experience during this formative postnatal period, as can happen with cataracts, refractive errors or misaligned eyes, alters the development of neural connections and can result in the leading cause of vision impairment in children called amblyopia. We have recently demonstrated fast and complete recovery from amblyopia in kittens reared in complete darkness for 10 days. Our preliminary investigation of the molecular changes underlying this recovery suggests that darkness reverses the accumulation of proteins called 'molecular brakes' that attenuate the capacity for neural plasticity and recovery. We have also recently observed a similar remarkable recovery from amblyopia following temporary binocular retinal inactivation. Successful treatment of amblyopia with darkness or retinal inactivation represents a potential breakthrough in visual health research. Experiments in this proposal will provide a better understanding of the optimal treatment parameters for both treatments, and will investigate potential mechanisms engaged to enable recovery. We will address key issues important for the translation of these treatments to human benefit, including examination of the time window within which they promote recovery, the consequences of different lengths of treatment, and the importance of post-treatment binocular vision. We further propose to provide a more thorough mechanistic understanding of the molecular events that enhance neural plasticity and promote visual recovery, with focus on a collection of proteins known to restrict the capacity for neural modification. The overarching goal of this proposal is build up to a proof of principle study on a clinical population of human amblyopes.

column36: Optogenetic visualization and manipulation of neural activity
column37: Life on the earth's surface is bathed in the white light of the Sun. This light provides energy to support life through photosynthesis, but life on earth has evolved to harness light in a myriad of other critical ways. For example, receptors in our eyes respond to certain wavelengths of light, such as those reflected from the corals of a tropical reef. The receptors send electrical signals to our brain that we perceive as colour. We are harnessing light as a research tool to understand how our nervous systems work. Light-based tools will advance our understanding of many nervous system disorders, such as neurodegenerative diseases, brain damage from stroke, and chronic pain. Biologists can now borrow natural systems that interact with light and transplant them in mice and other organisms that serve as models of human disease. These transplanted systems are called "optogenetic tools," and they have revolutionized our ability to visualize and manipulate biology in live animals. They have a particularly big impact in neuroscience. Optogenetic tools now help neuroscientists to watch the electrical signals from thousands of individual neurons in a model animal's brain. They also let researchers effectively write a memory into a mouse brain using light - a capability that was in the realm of science fiction until just a few years ago. Knowledge that we gain from these studies in animals with optogenetic tools can be applied to treating nervous system disorders in humans. My research program develops new optogenetic tools for neuroscience research. My speciality is borrowing the proteins that give coral their colour and altering them to create innovative research tools. One theme of my research is equipping neuroscientists to visualize the chemical communication between neurons of the brain that increases or decreases neuron activity. Another theme is creating more subtle and specific methods to activate key biochemical processes in neurons with light.

column36: Iron acquisition and storage mechanisms in Staphylococcus aureus pathogenesis
column37: Iron is an essential nutrient that is required for the survival and growth of all living organisms. This is no less important for disease-causing bacteria. In order to acquire sufficient iron to meet their needs, many bacteria have highly efficient systems to acquire iron. These infections range from mild (minor wound infections and carbuncles, for example) to more serious (endocarditis, osteomyelitis, arthritis, septicaemia, and toxic shock syndrome, for example). S. aureus is also the most common source of hospital-acquired infections and is frequently found as the cause of surgical wound and foreign implantation device infections. However, efforts to control this bacterium with antibiotics are becoming increasingly difficult due to its ability to acquire resistance to many different antibiotics. Our research is centred around identifying the mechanisms that this bacterium uses to acquire iron in defining how this bacterium responds to iron limitation during infection of a vertebrate host. Ultimately, our goal is to take advantage of our knowledge of the iron response in S. aureus to be able to find new avenues of treating infections caused by this bacterium. Our studies will provide novel information for how serious human pathogens, like S. aureus, can obtain iron and thereby cause serious infections. It is envisioned that uncovering these essential processes will lead to the rational design of successful next-generation drugs and therapeutic strategies to treat patients suffering from S. aureus infection.

column36: Optogenetic identification of the role of specific neurotransmitter receptor signaling in epileptogenesis
column37: Our goal is to control the changes in brain excitability that follow a precipitating event and lead to mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE); this process is known as epileptogenesis. To this end, we will employ an animal model in which spontaneous seizures start to recur around 5-10 days after a status epilepticus (SE) induced by i.p. injection of pilocarpine; a similar, but more prolonged, seizure-free latent period also occurs in MTLE patients. Previous studies suggest that in rodents the appearance of spontaneous seizures following SE results from the sustained inhibitory control of interneuron excitability that in turn leads to disinhibition of principal glutamatergic cells. Therefore, we hypothesize that the dynamic changes in GABA type A receptor-mediated inhibition occurring in the limbic system after SE can be delayed (and perhaps arrested) by direct or indirect optogenetic stimulation of interneurons, implemented shortly after SE. This hypothesis will be tested by using in vivo EEG recordings along with optogenetic activation of specific types of neurons in the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex of transgenic mice for up to 14 days after the initial pilocarpine-induced SE. Specifically, we will establish whether: (i) optogenetic direct activation of parvalbumin-positive interneurons in the hippocampus can delay the appearance of the first spontaneous seizure that marks the beginning of the epileptic condition; and (ii) optogenetic activation of CamKII-positive principal (glutamatergic) cells in the entorhinal cortex (which in turn project to the hippocampus activating principal cells and different types of local interneurons) can alter the length of the latent period in a way similar or opposite to what observed with optogenetic activation of parvalbumin-positive interneurons. Data obtained from mice undergoing these two protocols will be compared with those seen in animals implanted with the optogenetic device but not stimulated.

column36: Pre-Clinical Translation of Circadian Biology to Benefit Treatment of Heart Disease
column37: Body processes in mammals cycle with a 24-hour day-night (circadian or diurnal) rhythm, which is controlled by molecular clocks in the brain and other tissues such as the heart. Our cardiovascular system appears to follow a day-night rhythm as well. For example, heart rate and blood pressure are highest during the day when we are awake and lowest at night during sleep. Heart disease also exhibits a rhythm, as heart attacks and sudden cardiac death are more likely to occur in the morning than at night. In earlier and preliminary studies we used murine heart disease models and showed that the circadian mechanism underlies time of day variations in the genes and proteins in the heart, cardiac structure and function, and pathophysiologic responses to disease. Several of our high impact murine experimental studies reveal clear translational potential for applying circadian biology to benefit treatment of heart disease. 1) Timing drug therapies to the body's physiologic and molecular rhythms can improve drug efficacy and benefit outcome of heart disease. 2) Minimizing circadian rhythm disruption in the first few days of critical illness can improve healing - this especially has implications for intensive care units and multi-bedded wards where daily rhythms are disturbed. Here we intend to pursue the insights gained from our most promising circadian rhythms research studies, and apply them to the treatment of clinically relevant myocardial ischemia-reperfusion (mI/R, heart attack). We will demonstrate efficacy and uncover the direct role of the circadian mechanisms in rodent mI/R models, followed by vital testing in our new pre-clinical centre with state-of-the-art imaging relevant to humans (echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging). Reconsidering how we practice medicine, by translational application of circadian biology to clinical cardiology (and medicine in general), is a fundamental new approach to understanding and treating heart disease.
