column36: Determining the pathways, components and functional niches that define specialized ribosomes.
column37: Ribosomes are the cellular protein synthesis machinery, and highly conserved from bacteria to humans. They are complex molecular machines made up of four ribosomal ribonucleic acids (rRNAs) and 80 ribosomal proteins. Until recently it was believed that ribosomes are the exact same in every single cell within an organism, from a liver cell to a neuron. However, recent studies showed that there exists a small pool of 'specialized' ribosomes that can be found either in specific cells or tissues, such as testis or oocytes, and which appear to be involved in the biosynthesis of very specific proteins. Moreover, genetic mutations in components of ribosomes, resulted in highly specific diseases affecting the blood, skeleton or cancer predisposition, and established themselves often during early development, suggesting that these components, and 'specialized' ribosomes, may have an important role. While some of the differences between 'normal' and 'specialized' ribosomes have been uncovered, the proteins they are to synthesize as well as how specialized ribosomes are produced and fine-tuned themselves have not. Ribosome biogenesis, the process of making ribosomes, involves the coordinated function of over 200 proteins, and understanding the mechanisms that define making and function of specialized ribosomes will be of great importance to understand human development and disease on a molecular level. The main aim of the proposed research is to determine the events that distinguish different populations of ribosomes and their activity within different cell and tissue types. This will allow us to gain insight into how specialized ribosomes, and mutations within them, can affect the development of certain diseases as well as the fate of cells and organs during human development as a whole.

column36: Distinct regulation of T cell fate and memory via differentially IL-2- and IL-7-activated mTORC1-KIF13A-M6PR axis and AMPK-FOXO-Eomes pathway
column37: CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) provide major protection against infection and cancer. Upon infection, CTLs undergo a three-phase developmental program, wherein they first rapidly proliferate in the expansion phase and differentiate into effectors that kill infected cells. Then, the majority (~90-95%) of CTLs die by apoptosis in the contraction phase, and the remaining surviving cells (~5-10%) become long-term memory CTLs in the memory phase. However, what mechanism determines CTL die or survival remains unresolved. Since the goal of vaccination is to prevent diseases by immunological memory, a detailed understanding of the molecular basis for CTL fate and memory is critical to vaccine design. T cell-surface mannose-6-phosphate receptor (M6PR) is a multifunctional receptor that can uptake cytolytic molecule called granzyme-B (GzmB), leading to T cell death. We demonstrated that CTLs with low M6PR -expression (M6PRlow-CTLs) survived because GzmB could not bind to and kill these M6PRlow-CTLs. We also demonstrated that interleukin (IL)-7 cytokine was able to down-regulate CTL M6PR-expression, thus leading to M6PRlow-CTL surviving the contraction phase and becoming memory CTLs. In this project, we will elucidate the molecular mechanisms or pathways regulating T cell fate and memory in IL-7-stimulated CTLs. Therefore, we can incorporate our findings in rational vaccine design to develop potent vaccines with less contraction, but enhanced CTL memory and in new drug development for infectious and cancer diseases.

column37: Obesity is defined as the excessive accumulation of white adipose tissue (WAT) and is an important risk factor for the development of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. Recent studies indicate that the adipocyte population that composes WAT is very dynamic and that a good proportion of adipocytes are renewed every year. This indicates that adipose cells are constantly dying and being replaced by new adipocytes, which opens a possible therapeutic window to regulate WAT mass. The mechanisms regulating the early steps leading to the recruitment of new fat cells from progenitors are unknown. Recently, we have discovered a protein that plays an important role in the development of adipocytes in vitro. This protein, named V-set and transmembrane domain-containing 2A (VSTM2A), is expressed and secreted by committed preadipocytes. Experiments performed in cell culture showed that VSTM2A depletion blocks adipogenesis, whereas its overexpression induces this process. The proposed research project has as its major objective to define the mechanism of action of VSTM2A and its role in regulating WAT development and expansion in vivo. Improving the understanding of the mechanisms regulating WAT formation is important as this could lead to the development of new therapeutic avenues to modulate WAT size, distribution and function and to reduce the negative consequences of obesity.

column36: PET and SPECT Probes for the Diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease Targeting Cholinesterase Activity
column37: Cholinesterases are enzymes involved in the breakdown of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter, important in brain cell communication, that is reduced in Alzheimer's disease (AD). AD is marked by loss of memory and deposition of abnormal proteins toxic to brain cells that form abnormal structures called amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. The ability to detect the presence of structures in the living brain could facilitate early diagnosis of the disease. In AD brains, plaques and tangles contain the enzyme butyrylcholinesterase, the presence of which could provide an opportunity for early detection of AD. Therefore, we are developing radiolabelled compounds that bind to butyrylcholinesterase for detection of AD plaques and tangles in the living brain, using PET or SPECT imaging techniques. We have synthesized such compounds with radioactive iodine incorporated into their structures. Our preliminary experiments with these radioactive tracers have shown that they are indeed taken up in abnormally located butyrylcholinesterase "hot spots" in a mouse model of AD. Furthermore, we have been able to visualize abnormal deposits, typical of disease, in donated human AD brain tissue. With this significant advance, we now propose to extend this work, based on these lead imaging compounds, to identify related compounds with even greater ability to detect butyrylcholinesterase associated with plaques and tangles in the AD brain. It is anticipated that butyrylcholinesterase imaging agents will permit early detection of AD signs in the living human brain with non-invasive diagnostic scanning that may lead to development of effective new treatment for AD.

column36: Microbial Biofilms: Molecular mechanisms to therapeutics
column37: Bacteria typically live as collections of cells attached to a moist surface surrounded by a slimy coating. This mode of growth is called a biofilm and is beneficial to bacteria because the self-produced slimy coating protects them from antibiotics and our immune system, and provides a perfect environment for them to evolve and acquire antibiotic resistance. This protection and the bacteria's ability to grow on a large range of different types of moist surfaces, including human cells, make biofilms a major medical problem. Biofilms are responsible for ~80% of all infections in the body. This includes infections of the inner ear, urinary tract and pulmonary system, and those associated with contaminated medical devices such as catheters, heart valves and prosthetic joints. The failure of current antibiotics to clear biofilm infections results in serious health complications for patients and highlights the urgent need for effective new therapies to treat these often-fatal infections. A critical component of the protective biofilm coating are long chains of sugars units. Biofilms cannot form if the bacteria are unable to produce these sugar chains or when the chemical composition of the sugars is altered. Our goal is to understand how the bacteria make these sugar chains and to use this knowledge to develop novel anti-biofilm therapeutics. Our goal is to develop two types of therapeutics: the first would be used to prevent biofilm formation and hence eliminate the life-threatening complications that frequently occur; while the second would be used to treat and clear biofilms, thus improving health outcomes for individuals suffering from chronic infections.

column36: Identifying and Evaluating New Environmental Risk Factors for Cancer, Cardiovascular, and Neurological Diseases through Innovative Approaches to Population-Based Exposure Assessment
column37: Environmental exposures have an important impact on public health. Specifically, outdoor fine particulate air pollution is known to contribute to cancer and heart disease and emerging evidence suggests a possible association with brain illnesses including dementia. However, we still know surprisingly little about how the specific sources and components of particulate air pollution ultimately impact population-health. New approaches to exposure assessment are needed to address this crucial knowledge gap. These approaches must incorporate emerging technologies and new chemical assays and must be scalable to large populations to take advantage of population-based cohorts available in Canada. Moreover, this evidence must be integrated and communicated in a manner that is accessible to the general population to affect change not only through regulatory decision making but also through individual-level behavioural changes. Our research program will address these issues in a number of important ways. The first theme will focus on developing new exposure models for airborne pollutants in metropolitan areas. One example includes combustion-related nanoparticles that have been shown to reach the brain and may contribute to neurological illnesses. The second theme will apply these new models to population-based cohorts to evaluate population health risks. The third theme will focus on panel studies of local environmental health issues that can inform policy interventions. One example includes evaluating the impact of air pollution from residential wood burning on children's health. The fourth component will integrate knowledge across program areas to provide direct dissemination of results to government stakeholders and the public. Our vision is to identify and evaluate new environmental risk factors for chronic diseases to decrease the burden of illness associated with environmental contaminants originating from human activities and climate change.

column36: Pathogenic Strategies of the Lyme Disease Spirochete
column37: Lyme disease is an emerging infectious disease caused by a spiral-shaped bacterium (Borrelia burgdorferi) that is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tick. Incidence of the disease is increasing, triggered in part by global warming. The disease can result in a wide variety of symptoms, mimicking other medical conditions, often making diagnosis difficult. The focus of this project is to investigate two important strategies used by B. burgdorferi to mount a successful infection. 1) Antigenic variation. This is a process by which the pathogen continually changes the sequence of the major component of the outer coat that is recognized by antibodies. The outcome is a continual wardrobe change for the pathogen that keeps it one step ahead of host recognition resulting in persistent infection. Antigenic variation occurs by continual DNA rearrangements in the gene for the major surface protein, VlsE. We will study this process in detail using next generation sequencing. We will also study the DNA regions involved in the rearrangement process and the protein molecules that promote the DNA rearrangements. 2) Vascular transmigration. The reason why B. burgdorferi can cause such a large number of different symptoms is because the organism disseminates through the circulatory system and can exit the vasculature in virtually any part of the body. The result is varying symptoms depending upon where B. burgdorferi exits the bloodstream. The process of vascular transmigration is mediated by interactions between B. burgdorferi and endothelial cells lining small blood vessels. We will investigate these interactions and the changes they cause in blood vessels that allow B. burgdorferi to exit. We will also study the proteins and signaling pathways involved and the molecular changes occurring to the endothelial layer that unlock the door for escape. Details uncovered on these important processes may be useful for future development of clinical interventions.

column36: Human gene expression regulatory mechanisms
column37: Most mutations in human DNA that cause disease are not in sequences that code for protein but rather in regulatory sequences that determine whether particular proteins, or parts of proteins, are made. These regulatory sequences are recognized by about 1600 regulatory proteins called transcription factors. We are studying a large family of more than 700 transcription factors known as the zinc finger proteins. We have unexpectedly discovered that the zinc finger proteins almost always recognize RNA as well as DNA and propose to identify the sequences that they recognize. This will enable better understanding of human disease and help us to better predict both what diseases might occur and how best to treat those diseases. We are also studying several proteins in which mutations cause three devastating and fatal neurodegenerative diseases, spinal muscular atrophy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; also as known as Lou Gehrig's disease) and fronto-temporal dementia, as well as another protein important for the growth of many kinds of cancer cells. We propose to determine how the zinc finger proteins control the splicing together of RNA fragments to form contiguous segments that code for protein, as well as how the zinc finger proteins, the neurodegeneration proteins, and the cancer-promoting protein determine where RNA polymerase II, the enzyme that reads human genes, stops at the ends of genes. We will also try to identify chemicals that prevent RNA polymerase II from stopping and might be developed into new kinds of anti-cancer drugs.

column36: Characterizing Arm Recovery in People with Severe Stroke (CARPSS)
column37: Every year, over 50,000 new strokes are reported in Canada. Recent advances in acute care have increased the likelihood of surviving a large stroke and have resulted in up to 30% of all stroke survivors living with severe upper limb disability. Stroke survivors with severe arm disability have the poorest prognosis, lowest health related quality of life, incur the greatest costs to the healthcare system and receive the least amount of intensive rehabilitation. While some people with severe disability show little recovery, others attain a substantial amount of functional recovery. This highlights a need to be able to identify people with severe upper limb disability who have the most potential to show recovery. Additionally, there is currently poor understanding of what an individual with stroke considers to be meaningful recovery. Thus, the main aims of the proposed research are to: 1) track individuals with severe upper limb disability across the first year post stroke to determine which factors best predict recovery of function, 2) establish a definition of meaningful recovery using data from stroke survivors themselves in combination with clinical and brain based measures, and 3) test a novel algorithm that predicts the degree of functional recovery. Determining reasons why someone with severe upper limb impairment achieves meaningful recovery after stroke is an important question; this information will help to develop novel interventions for the growing and under-served group of people living with severe upper limb disability. Also, understanding how recovery occurs in people with severe arm impairment will enable the appropriate delivery of individualized rehabilitation interventions and better outcomes for Canadians with stroke.

column36: Structural Biology of Tankyrase Activity and Regulation in Cell Signaling
column37: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) create the posttranslational modification poly(ADP- ribose) to regulate a wide variety of cellular programs, such as DNA damage repair, gene transcription, cell death signaling, and metabolism. The PARP superfamily has 17 members with a diverse set of regulatory domains attached to the conserved catalytic domain that creates the ADP-ribose modification. A more detailed understanding of the specific biological pathways regulated by PARPs has emerged recently. However, there remain fundamental gaps in our knowledge of how the catalytic activities of the different PARP family members are regulated, and this limits our understanding of how several important cellular programs are regulated by ADP-ribosylation. Tankyrase is a PARP enzyme that is involved in a number of cellular pathways, including telomere maintenance, glucose homeostasis, Wnt signaling, mitotic progression, and RNA processing. How tankyrase selects cellular target proteins for modification is poorly understood, in part due to limited structural information, and in part due to a paucity of biochemical analysis. Based on our preliminary structural and biochemical work, the proposed studies will provide important advances in our understanding of how tankyrase selects and modifies target proteins. Several PARP enzymes, including tankyrase, are the targets of small-molecule inhibitors used for the treatment of cancer. Current PARP inhibitors lack isozyme specificity and are therefore limited in their ability to serve as specific biological probes of PARP function. The proposed studies will build toward a mechanistic understanding of tankyrase activity and regulation that will contribute to the design of tankyrase-specific inhibitors as chemical probes, and potentially as new anti-cancer compounds.

column37: Asthma is characterized by excessive constriction of the airways and inflammation in the lung. Ten percent of people in the world suffer from asthma and the prevalence increases by 50% every decade. Currently there is no cure for asthma; the available treatments only control the symptoms. Traditional drugs target two aspects of the disease; inflammation and airway constriction. Fatal asthma-attacks usually result from failed response of airway muscle to relaxant drugs. The fact that muscle relaxants and anti-inflammatory drugs do not cure asthma suggests that they are not targeting the root cause of asthma. Recent research in our laboratory has revealed a new drug target that may be related to the root cause of asthma. We have found that the stiffness of the relaxed airway muscle contributes to the overall stiffness of the airways, and is partially responsible for the reduced airway distensibility found in asthmatic patients. Interestingly the muscle stiffness does not respond to the traditional muscle relaxants, which is effective only on activated muscles. We found that a new class of drugs targeting the structural integrity of airway muscle cells is effective in reducing the cell stiffness, and in the presence of mechanical stretches similar to those experienced by the muscle in a breathing lung, the relaxant effect of the drugs on airway muscle is synergistically enhanced. In this application we propose to identify new drug targets that "soften" the airway muscle cells, making them more responsive to mechanical stretches imposed by breathing, which further softens the cells, leading to improved airway distensibility and dilation. The goal of our research is to provide a better alternative for treating asthma.

This research will yield the crucial first steps in developing lower-cost and efficacious Internet interventions for people suffering from depression who also drink in a hazardous fashion - promoting the widespread availability of care for those in need.

column36: Sustaining evidence-based chronic disease management
column37: Canada is a nation of pilot projects, with a lot of resources spent on implementation but failure to address sustainability. We then need to develop a strategy to implement early mobilisation in hospitals, this is called a knowledge translation (KT) intervention. If the KT interventions are effective, how do we then sustain (or adapt) them across hospitals? Despite a successful KT intervention implementation, there is a tendency to return to old practices after implementation activities end and attention is focused on the next clinical intervention. Thus, failure to sustain implementation has implications for cost and patient care and diminishes trust and support for future implementation. column37: Up to 80% of schizophrenic patients show disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms. column36: Regenerative biomaterials in vascularized tissue engineering
column37: Our goal is to create new medical devices to address unmet needs in medicine. The materials that are used to build current devices provoke a scar which prevents their integration with the host. This is a fundamental challenge to tissue engineering in which tissue constructs are created to act as "spare body parts" to replace diseased tissues and organs. Such constructs require blood vessels in order to supply the tissue with oxygen and enable tissue survival and integration. We have pioneered two approaches to forming the needed blood vessels. In one method ("modular tissue engineering") collagen gel pieces are coated with endothelial cells, the cells that line blood vessels. However, vessel formation is slow and the resulting vessels are imperfect. Here we address the barriers (low oxygen, inflammation) to successful vessel formation in order to accelerate this process. We are using this approach to enable under the skin delivery of pancreatic islets to resolve the issues with this promising treatment for the 1% of Canadians who live with insulin dependent (type 1) diabetes. We have also discovered that materials that incorporate methacrylic acid cause blood vessels to grow once the material is implanted. This vascular regenerating effect is unique among biomaterials. Unfortunately we don't understand why we are getting blood vessels (instead of the conventional "scar" response), although we have some clues as to the origins of this seemingly "magical" effect. We propose to deepen our understanding of the magic by using a method that analyses the critical means by which cells respond to changes in their environment (here our unique biomaterial). We expect these results will help us design better materials and better devices for use in diabetes (e.g., better glucose sensors) and in other situations which are as yet precluded by the limitations of existing materials.

column36: Optimizing cardiac energy metabolism to treat heart disease
column37: The very high energy demands of the heart are met by continous metabolism of sugars, fatty acids, ketones and amino acids. Normally, there is a balance between the use of these fuels. However, in clinical conditions such as heart failure, myocardial ischemia (i.e. such as following a heart attack), obesity or diabetes, energy production in the heart switches towards an excessive use of fatty acids. This excessive use of fatty acids causes the heart to be less efficient at using energy, which can compromise heart function. Our research has shown that a major contributor to this excessive use of fatty acids is due to changes in the levels of a molecule called malonyl CoA within the heart muscle, and due to an increase in a process caused post-translational acetylation. The studies proposed in this grant application will determine the cellular mechanisms responsible for how malonyl CoA levels and acetylation are regulated in the heart, and how alterations in these processes alters fatty acid use by the heart. We will also determine if preventing the switch from sugar to fatty acid metabolism, can be used as a therapeutic strategy to protect the heart in heart failure or following myocardial ischemia. We will also examine the molecular mechanisms responsible for the maturation of cardiac fatty acid oxidation following birth, and what impact congenital heart defects (that are seen in approximately 2% of infants) has on this maturation of energy metabolism. These experimental studies will be translated into clinical studies in which energy metabolism is optimized to improve heart function in patients with heart failure. Understanding how energy metabolism is regulated in heart should lead to the development of therapies that optimize energy use by the heart and decrease the severity of heart disease.

column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) remains a global health challenge. Despite the significant advances made over the past decades with respect to our understanding of how HIV causes AIDS, the hope for a definitive cure has been frustrated by the seemingly endless propensity of HIV to subvert host defenses and to persist in long-lived viral reservoirs (VR) that cannot be eliminated by current antiretroviral therapies (ART). While ART have dramatically improved the prognosis for infected individuals, they are not curative because of the persistence of VRs. HIV eludes host immune defenses and establishes VRs in part because it encodes a set of small accessory proteins, whose function is to overcome various types of antiviral immune response. My Team discovered and characterized two of the six accessory proteins encoded by HIV and we are world leaders in understanding the role of these virulence factors in HIV transmission, pathogenesis and persistence. Given their crucial roles in overcoming host defense mechanisms, these accessory proteins are attractive targets for the design of HIV cure strategies aimed at eradicating persistent HIV infection. Our research program will focus primarily on two of the accessory proteins encoded by HIV-1, namely Viral protein U (Vpu) and Viral Protein R (Vpr), to unravel the full spectrum of their activities and better define their functions in HIV persistence, to elucidate how they operate at the molecular and cellular levels and to identify new areas of their biology that are applicable to therapeutic intervention. This work will uncover viral and host targets for HIV persistence reversal and provide new insights that will inform and guide HIV cure strategies. While conducting these studies, our dynamic and forward-looking training and mentoring program will provide trainees with a conceptually and technically deep experience and skills that are sought by employers in academia, government and the private sector

column36: Innate immunity and its disruption by microbial and genetic factors
column37: Approximately 1/150 Canadians have Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IBD) like Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis. These diseases devastate affected individuals and their families, and significantly burden our health care system. IBD are caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors, including how our bodies interact with bacteria. Genetic studies link IBD to innate immunity. Innate immunity encompasses the tissue and cellular defenses that protect us from infection. Innate immunity allows us to co-exist with the many 'good' bacteria in our guts, and to kill the 'bad' bacteria that we encounter. The factors that regulate innate immunity and its alterations in IBD are not clear. Our research will examine innate immunity in three ways. First, we will study a critical component of innate immunity that is linked to IBD, called autophagy. Autophagy is a process that delivers cellular contents to specialized compartments called lysosomes, where they are broken down. This process protects our cells during stressful conditions like bacterial infections. We will build 'maps' of how the autophagy machinery interacts with other cellular components under normal conditions, and how it changes in IBD. Second, we will study how two bad bacteria, Salmonella and Listeria, hide inside our cells during infection. These bacteria use toxins that disrupt our innate immune defenses, and can teach us how innate immunity is regulated. Third, we will study genes linked to IBD, and ask how they change autophagy and other innate immune defenses. Our studies will advance scientific understanding of how innate immunity controls our interactions with bacteria, and will provide knowledge that can be used to develop new ways to treat IBD.

column36: Neighbourhood Design and Physical Activity: Generating Evidence to Inform Healthy Public Policies
column37: Creating health supportive environments has the potential to improve population-level health, including increasing physical activity participation in Canadian adults. Moreover, there is a lack of evidence on the economic value of creating physical activity-supportive neighbourhood environments. Building on my previous research, I will lead a research program that will deliver rigorous causal and economic evidence in a form that can be used by policymakers to create better built environments that support health for all individuals regardless of their socioeconomic circumstances or life-stage. This research will incorporate natural experimentation with mixed methods and economic analyses, and will advance previous research on neighbourhood design and physical activity by using recent technological advances in physical activity and built environment assessment. column36: Mechanisms underlying vulnerability of selective neuronal circuits following early life seizures
column37: One of the most frequent problems in the neonate is the occurrence of lack of oxygen for a short time in the uterus (prenatal period) or during birth (perinatal period). A lack or reduction of oxygen during birth, or birth asphyxia, can often result in lifelong neurological consequences such as learning problems, lower IQ and increased vulnerability for disorders such as cerebral palsy (a disorder of movement and posture), epilepsy or schizophrenia. This problem occurs in approximately 1-6/1000 live births and despite many years of research, there are no available drug therapies to protect brain neurons from ongoing damage once birth asphyxia has occurred. We propose to use new, cutting-edge techniques, which have been recently made available in the neuroscience field to study the cellular and molecular mechanisms that link birth asphyxia to the occurrence of lifelong neurological problems. The neocortex, the outer region of the brain, is composed by two main types of neurons (specialized brain cells): excitatory and inhibitory neurons, that produce glutamate and gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), respectively, as neurotransmitters (a chemical that facilitate communications between brain cells). GABAergic cells are very important for the regulation of brain function and excitability. This group of cells displays a stunning diversity of shapes, functions and ability to change following environmental stimuli. Our hypothesis is that birth asphyxia alters the development of specific types of GABAergic cells. We further hypothesize that these differential effects are in part responsible for the lifelong neurological consequences in adults that experienced birth asphyxia. We propose to study the molecular mechanisms that lead to specific GABAergic cell deficits following birth asphyxia using transgenic mouse models.

column36: Optimizing Combination Strategies for GPNMB-expressing Triple Negative Breast Cancers
column37: BACKGROUND: Breast cancer can be sub-divided into distinct molecular subtypes, including triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), which is associated with the poorest patient outcomes. However the precise molecular mechanisms by which GPNMB induces these effects are largely unknown. Interestingly, we have shown that GPNMB is most highly expressed in TNBC. CDX-011 is a GPNMB-targeted antibody-drug conjugate that has shown robust clinical activity in late-stage clinical trials for breast cancer. We will also devise effective combination therapy strategies involving CDX-011 that may increase the efficacy of current therapies used to treat TNBC. The research proposed in this application will produce the necessary data to support clinical trials to test such therapeutic combinations.

column36: Cellular and molecular characterization of T cell development for immune-reconstitution
column37: The proposed research focuses on blood cell development, and, in particular, on how a subset of white blood cells, known as T lymphocytes, are generated. T cells are important effectors and master regulators of the immune system, which protects us from cancer and infectious diseases. The thymus is where T cells are generated from progenitor cells that arrive from the bone marrow. The overall research program direction is also guided by our recent work showing that transplanting in vitro-generated human progenitor T cells along with bone marrow stem cells into immunodeficient mice results in a dramatic increase in the ability of stem cell-derived cells to give rise to new T cells in the host thymus. This is an important discovery given that stem cell transplants in humans typically fail to regenerate new T cells. The proposed work will ensure that we continue to make important fundamental discoveries as to how Notch signals induce and regulate T cell development, improve upon on how to employ those insights for the generation of human T cells from stem cells, and enable us apply our advances to realize important cell-based immune-reconstitution and immune-therapeutic clinical applications.

column36: Targeting Interferon-beta in leukemia immunotherapy
column37: Dr. Spaner is trying to develop methods to improve the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy. Chemotherapy is the main form of treatment for cancer but cannot cure most types of cancer. Immunotherapy is another form of treatment that tries to stimulate cells of the body's immune system, called T cells, to kill cancer cells. Unfortunately, cancers may become resistant to T cells in the same way they learn to resist chemotherapy. This resistance is due largely to cytokines and other factors that are associated with cancer and suppress the immune system. A drug called Ibrutinib, which is used currently to treat blood cancer patients reduces production of these immunosuppressive factors and helps T cells kill cancer cells. Unfortunately, cancer cells are still able to survive in the presence of Ibrutinib. Dr. Spaner's group has found that Ibrutinib causes the production of a cytokine called Interferon-beta that can continue to suppress the immune system. In this project, Dr. Spaner will try to learn more about how Interferon-beta suppresses T cells and if using drugs that prevent interferon-beta from acting on cancer cells together with Ibrutinib can be a safe and effective way to improve immunotherapy. He will study cancer cells from patients with Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), the most common leukemia in Canada, as it is easy to obtain large numbers of cancer cells for experiments, unlike most other cancers. The results of this project are expected to justify using Ibrutinib and Interferon-signaling inhibitors to treat CLL. This approach is expected to increase cure rates with immunotherapy in CLL and also many other forms of cancer.

column37: Intracranial aneurysm (IA) is a common cerebrovascular disorder that can lead to sudden and unpredictable severe complications with devastating consequences for the patients and their families, and implicate huge costs for the health system of Canada. Genetic predisposition has been considered as one of the most significant risk factors for IA based several independent studies. Previous epidemiological studies have shown that certain isolated populations, such as Inuits, are particularly at high risk to develop IA. Over the past 10 years, we have identified 50 individuals with definite brain aneurysm belonging to 25 families from 8 different villages in Nunavik. We have also collected a second cohort of French Canadian people diagnosed with IA, originating from Quebec City. Within this cohort, we have identified and collected 80 families with IA (total of 144 affected individuals and 180 unaffected first-degree relatives). A cohort of 500 sex- and age-matched control individuals has been collected as well. Genetic studies using next generation sequencing was undertaken in order to characterize the specific genetic vulnerability to IA in both Inuits and French Canadians. These two populations, in which founder effect has been well documented, offer advantages for gene mapping of heritable disorders by reducing both the genetic and the environmental heterogeneity. The pathogenecity of genetic DNA variations, identified through next generation sequencing analyses, will be biologically validated using our unique in vitro tissue-engineered patient-derived vascular and microvascular models. We expect to identify and validate a number of genes conferring susceptibility to IA, and to gain insight into the mutational mechanisms and pathogenic pathways of this disease. Also, this approach could provide unique tools to identify "at risk" patients, which would be able to be followed in a timely fashion, allowing the prevention of the devastating outcome of aneurysm rupture.

column36: BRCA1 therapy for heart failure
column37: Heart failure (HF) occurs when the heart is damaged and unable to pump blood normally resulting in reduced oxygen and nutrient supply to the rest of the body. It is typically caused by a progressive increase in dying or dead heart cells resulting in loss of heart muscle function. We previously showed that the breast cancer gene BRCA1 has an important role in maintaining heart cell survival. In this study, we will examine in various established HF models the therapeutic potential of directed BRCA1 gene delivery to the heart to reduce and/or slow down heart cell death thereby improving heart muscle function and increasing overall survival.

column36: A clinical decision support tool for diagnostic imaging use for low back pain
column37: Objective: To develop a tool to help doctors make appropriate decisions about the need for diagnostic imaging for patients with low back pain. Rationale: Low back pain is one of the most common and disabling health problems in Canada and the world. In most cases, low back pain resolves without requiring diagnostic imaging (x-ray) and with little treatment. Yet, diagnostic imaging is frequently used for low back pain contrary to recommendations from clinical guidelines. This is despite evidence that diagnostic imaging is of limited value in most cases - exposing patients to unnecessary radiation, increasing health services use and worsening patient outcomes. Currently, no clinical decision support tool is available. Clinical guidelines describe 'red flags' - characteristics of serious cause low back pain such as fracture, or cancer - where diagnostic imaging may be appropriate. However, few studies have evaluated these red flags, contributing to inconsistent recommendations across guidelines. A clinical decision support tool will improve the delivery of appropriate clinical care, and create opportunities for improved patient outcomes and reduced healthcare costs. Methods: Our study population will be patients presenting to five Canadian emergency departments with low back pain, assessed at their emergency department visit, then 3 and 12-months afterwards. We will develop a statistical model to determine which low back pain patients should or should not receive diagnostic imaging. We will then work with clinicians and hospital administrators to convert the statistical model into an easy to use clinical decision support tool. The tool will enable quick and accurate assessment of the need for diagnostic imaging for low back pain. Team: Our team brings extensive expertise in clinical tool development, low back pain research, the clinical management of back pain patients, and implementation science. We regularly consult with a diverse group of Low Back Pain Advisors.

column36: Targeting sleep to optimize brain recovery and slow neurodegeneration
column37: Breakthrough discoveries in rodents have revealed that sleep is crucial for generating neurons, strengthening synapses, and clearing brain waste products. Considering the high prevalence of sleep disorders in the general population, it is now urgent to assess how these new discoveries translate to the human brain. The Foundation grant will allow me to determine whether and how sleep could be a target for slowing down neurodegeneration and optimizing recovery after brain damage in humans. I will achieve this goal by studying 2 clinical populations with vulnerable brain health and sleep disorders: older individuals with obstructive sleep apnea and younger patients with traumatic brain injury. Obstructive sleep affects 20% of individuals after the age of 65. It produces hundreds of awakenings per night and chronic intermittent hypoxia. Sleep apnea impacts brain structure and function in older individuals. How sleep apnea affects long-term brain health with age and whether sleep apnea treatment can slow down neurodegeneration are topical questions. Traumatic brain injury affects mostly young adults and is the main cause of disability in that population. It destroys brain structures and connexions that need regeneration. We found that patients have severe sleep disturbances while they are hospitalized. We need to test whether sleep disturbances inhibit recovery and identify causes of acute sleep disturbances that we could use as a target for treatment. In the next 5 years, I will identify patients with sleep apnea at risk of neurodegeneration. I will produce new evidence regarding the neurodegenerative profile of treated vs. untreated patients. I will identify causes of sleep disturbances occurring after traumatic brain injury and characterize the link between sleep disturbances and brain recovery. My research program has the potential to transform and improve clinical care protocols by including sleep management among treatment priorities.

column36: Non-coding RNA in diabetic kidney disease
column37: Kidney disease caused by diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure in Canada. Currently, the main treatments to stop kidney disease from getting worse in diabetes are medications that lower blood sugar levels and medications that lower blood pressure levels. Although these medications are helpful, they are only partly effective and we need new treatments. RNAs are small molecules that are present in all cells. It has been known for several decades that RNAs pass the genetic code from the DNA in our genes to make proteins, the workhorses of our cells. DNA carries the code for RNA and RNA carries the code for protein. More recently it has come to be appreciated that a large amount of our DNA makes RNA that does not carry a code to make proteins. These RNA molecules are called non-coding RNAs and they can be classified according to their length: long or short. Although long non-coding RNAs do not code for proteins they do have important roles in cells, like helping to turn genes on or off, acting as scaffolds or helping other RNA molecules to make proteins. Long non-coding RNAs often go wrong in disease but their contribution to the development of diabetic kidney disease is essentially unknown. Through our earlier work, we have discovered that the amount of a particular long non-coding RNA, called HOTAIR, is increased in diabetic kidney disease and that blocking its actions helps protect special kidney cells, called podocytes, from damage caused by high sugar levels. In this project, we will conduct a series of experiments to explore the role of HOTAIR in the development of diabetic kidney disease and to determine whether blocking HOTAIR can protect against kidney damage. These studies will provide important new information about the previously underappreciated actions of non-coding RNA in diabetic kidney disease, with long non-coding RNA blocking therapy being a plausible new treatment for the condition.

column36: Combined cancer therapy with NKT cell activation and oncolytic viruses
column37: Ovarian and pancreatic cancers are deadly diseases that do not respond well to existing treatments. The development of new therapies to target these, and other cancers, is urgently needed. One promising approach is to boost the power of the immune system to target cancer cells. The immune system is a natural defense network made up of special cells and proteins in the blood and tissues. This system normally works to detect and kill abnormal or damaged cells. However, abnormal cells sometimes gain advantages that allow them to avoid or overwhelm the immune system, resulting in the generation of harmful tumors. Dr. Johnston's team studies a group of immune cells called natural killer T (NKT) cells. These cells can be stimulated to enhance detection and killing of cancer cells. However, it is likely that combining NKT cell activation with other therapies will result in even better tumor clearance. In this project, Dr. Johnston will examine whether viruses that selectively infect and kill cancer cells can be used in combination with NKT cell activation therapies to boost the immune system and target ovarian and pancreatic cancers. This work could lead to new treatments that target these lethal cancers.

column36: Role of HMG CoA reductase protective and risk variants in the pathophysiology and treatment of sporadic Alzheimer's disease
column37: The brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) begin several years before the onset of cognitive changes; there is currently no prevention and no cure for the disease. This proposed study will use resources from the Centre for Studies in the Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease and the Douglas-Bell Brain Bank in Montreal to examine the neurobiology and the mode of action of a series of novel genetic variants in a gene called HMG CoA reductase, which were found to either accelerate or slow down the progression of the disease in the years prior to diagnosis. This gene which is either protective or detrimental, depending on its genetic make-up, regulates cholesterol production in the brain. It was also was shown to alter specific biomarkers of disease progression which are known to directly impact memory performance in humans. The novel information to be obtained via this research program is bound to be very significant at many levels: It will allow scientists a) to determine whether these variants are specific to AD pathology or, if they can be used as more general indicators of unhealthy/healthy brain aging; b) to develop, on an individualized basis, a number of genetic and biochemical predictors of disease protection and finally c) to validate what could be a novel therapeutic target for the treatment or the delay of the common form of AD.

column36: The intertwined biology, pathobiology and translational implications of factor VIII and von Willebrand factor.
column37: The two most common inherited bleeding disorders, von Willebrand disease (VWD) and hemophilia A (HA), are the result of deficiencies and/or dysfunction of two critical proteins in the human blood clotting system - von Willebrand factor (VWF) and factor VIII (FVIII). These two proteins circulate together in the blood and regulate key stages in the development of a normal blood clot. We will continue studies that have been ongoing in our group for the past 25 years aimed at understanding basic and translational aspects of VWF and FVIII. Although most of the proposed studies employ molecular and animal model strategies, there are obvious connections to clinical care that have the potential to enhance the quality of life of VWD and HA patients. The research program encompasses three interrelated themes exploring the normal and pathologic biology of VWF and FVIII. First, we will conduct studies to better understand the genetic basis, structure and function of VWF. We will use genetic approaches to determine the basis for the 35% of type 1 VWD patients in whom mutations in the VWF gene have not been identified, and will investigate whether the VWF propeptide has an independent clotting function. The second area of focus will evaluate risk factors for the development of an adverse immune response to FVIII therapy in HA, a complication of treatment in ~30% of these patients. We will determine the influence of VWF on FVIII immunity, and will explore the role of the host gut microbiome as a risk factor for FVIII antibody development. In the final phase of this proposal, we will conduct two complementary series of experiments that address the safety and efficacy of gene therapy approaches for the treatment of HA. Using our unique canine hemophilia resource, we will first determine the vector integration patterns following long-term adeno-associated viral vector gene transfer, and will then compare these outcomes with a novel foamy viral vector-based approach.

column36: Novel Approaches Directed to Prevention and Treatment of Huntington Disease
column37: Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited brain disease that affects approximately 1 in 7300 people in the Western world. HD is caused by a mutation in one copy of the HTT gene, which produces a toxic mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. This mutant protein disrupts many vital cellular functions and is ultimately responsible for the brain cell death associated with HD. There is no treatment for this disease. We propose targeting different steps of the disease process, including suppression of the mutant HTT gene, increasing clearance of the mutant protein, and inhibiting its toxic effects to advance complementary therapies for treating HD. One therapeutic strategy to prevent production of mHTT is to silence (or turn off) the mutant HTT gene using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeted to genetic variations found in mutant HTT. Our goal is to develop multiple ASO drugs targeting the most common genetic variations in HD patients, maximizing the number that could be treated through gene silencing of mutant HTT. ASOs are unable to enter the brain when delivered in the blood and must be injected directly into the fluid that bathes the brain. This procedure is invasive, and ASOs delivered this way do not reach all susceptible areas of the brain. Therefore, we are developing new non-invasive ways to enhance delivery of ASOs to the brain. Another strategy is to reduce levels of mHTT protein by increasing its degradation in the cell through a process called autophagy. Autophagy is abnormally reduced in HD which may be due to altered protein modifications of mHTT. We will target specific mechanisms that could increase clearance of mHTT from the cell and reduce its toxicity. Our final therapeutic strategy is to target pathways that are disrupted by the presence of toxic mHTT. We are investigating the effect of modifying molecular components of these pathways using small molecules to promote protection and survival of brain cells, and in the long run improve patient outcomes.

column36: Seeking Molecular Signatures for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
column37: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a unique cancer of the head & neck region, wherein most diagnosed patients are relatively young (peak incidence between 40-45 years) and have advanced disease; the 5-year overall survival rate of such patients is a dismal 65%. These patients typically die from the distant spread of their cancer, known as distant metastasis. Currently, we do not have any clinically useful biomarkers to distinguish patients who will develop metastasis versus those who will not. Furthermore, we do not understand why some patients respond to treatment yet others do not. Our group recently identified a potential "molecular signature", based on the analyses of biological molecules called "micro-RNAs" that are produced by the tumor. The signature is capable of predicting which patients will develop distant metastasis. The objectives of this proposal are to: 1. Validate the molecular signature on a separate group of NPC samples to confirm its clinical applicability; 2. Incorporate other types of biological molecules (DNA, mRNA) into the molecular signature to identify their usefulness; 3. Discover the underlying mechanisms by which the molecular signature works; and 4. Evaluate the utility of blood-related molecular signatures as a way to assess NPC aggressiveness. At the completion of these proposed studies, we will have developed the most informative molecular signature in terms of predicting metastasis for NPC patients and evaluated the underlying biology. This molecular signature may then be used to aid in the clinical management of future patients; patients who will experience metastasis may be treated with more aggressive therapies, while those who will not relapse may be spared the side-effects of harsher treatments. All the generated data will be shared with the medical community. Ultimately, this project will advance our goal of personalized cancer therapy for NPC patients, which will have significant national and global impact.

column36: In vivo regulation of stem cell division and self-renewal
column37: The human body is composed of billions of cells that largely have specialized properties, allowing them to sustain the normal function of the organs and tissues where they reside. Among these, stem cells are unique in that their divisions are important to regenerate the various tissues of our organs. Stem cells must divide in a way that enables tissue regeneration without loss of the stem cell pool, a process known as self-renewal. Proper regulation of stem cell division and self-renewal must be tightly controlled, because defects in these process can have deleterious consequences to an organ's function and thus be a primary cause of disease. For instance, stem cell division without self-renewal can lead to the atrophy of an organ or tissue, and thus compromise its function, while stimulating uncontrolled proliferation in stem cells can result in cancer. Understanding the fundamental aspects of stem cell division in an in vivo context is therefore crucial to identify the critical steps that govern their properties and devise novel strategies to exert control over their self-renewal. The objective of this project is to study how stem cells divide in vivo and understand what molecules control this process. I tackle this problem using a small nematode worm as experimental model, allowing me to use various methods that are not feasible in humans. The stem cells of this nematode worm divide very much like human cells and use essentially the same building blocks to go through the process, and therefore our findings in this model organism will greatly inform on human stem cells. As such, they help to guide the experimental design of approaches aimed at the development of novel therapeutics for cell proliferation-based diseases in humans.

column36: Protease-activated receptor (PAR)-2: A novel effector of mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel diseases
column37: The inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, affect over 200,000 Canadians. These are lifelong, debilitating conditions that have no clear cause, no cure, and which have significant costs to the health care system and patient quality of life. For unknown reasons, Canada has the highest incidence of IBD in the world. Unfortunately, current therapies are costly, ineffective for some patients, and can have serious side effects. We need to understand the underlying causes of IBD so that we can develop better treatments and, ultimately, find a cure. Our research team is studying the epithelium, the layer of cells that lines the intestinal wall and which provides an important barrier between the trillions of bacteria in the intestinal lumen and the immune system of the intestine. Over-activation of the immune system by gut bacteria plays an important role in IBD. We know that the epithelial barrier breaks down in IBD, and we think this may be an important contributor to these diseases. We hypothesize that a specific type of protein receptor on epithelial cells, protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2), may play a role in the resolution of the inflammatory response and speed healing. In this proposal, we have set three aims to test our hypothesis. First, we are going to measure the enzymes that activate PAR2 in IBD tissue. We will then see if they act through PAR2 to turn on genes that control the healing process. Second, we are going to use new cell culture methods in epithelial cells derived from mouse intestine and intestinal biopsies from consenting IBD patients to determine how PAR2 alters epithelial cell behaviour, especially cell migration, to speed healing. Third, we are going to test these PAR2-mediated effects in mouse models of disease, to see if they are appropriate targets for therapy. Ultimately, our proposed research will identify avenues for the development of new treatments for IBD.

column36: Beyond the Exome: Decoding the Next Frontier of the Rare Disease Genome
column37: Around 7000 rare genetic diseases (RDs) affect more than 1 million Canadians, most of them children. When considered together, RDs are a common cause of disability, early mortality, and healthcare costs. Over the past several years my research program has efficiently examined the protein-coding portion of the genome (~1%) to understand the cause of many RDs; however, as many as 60% of patients remain undiagnosed after this analysis. These patients often undergo a diagnostic journey involving multiple specialist consultations, imaging studies, invasive investigations, and other laboratory and genetic tests; a slow (5 to 30 years for 25%) process referred to as the diagnostic odyssey. These families are faced with significant uncertainty surrounding treatment, prognosis and the chances of future children or other family members also being affected. The goal of my research is to understand the genetic cause of unsolved RDs to end the diagnostic journey for as many Canadians with RD as possible. Given the rarity of all of the diseases we study, my program will help design and employ international RD patient data-sharing so that we, and indeed all RD scientists, can readily identify families with the same disease and changes in the same gene to prove causality. To look more broadly, my program will use the latest and most comprehensive technologies to examine a person's entire genome to identify the genetic cause of unsolved RDs. Finally, my program will develop new tests to determine whether a given genetic change has an impact on protein function. The outputs of my RD research program will lead to new insights into human biology in health and disease, develop novel diagnostic tools and tailor management to improve the care for Canadians with RDs, while enhancing global synergy, thereby ensuring continuing Canadian leadership in this realm.

column36: Enhancing Mitochondrial Integrity to Promote Brain Regeneration and Repair
column37: It was always believed that the adult brains cannot regenerate damaged brain tissue and that brain cells (neurons) must last throughout life. Recently, it was found that the adult brain contains active stem cells and progenitor cells, which have the capacity to regenerate new neurons. A major challenge is that most neural stem cells lie dormant in the adult brain and their numbers decline with age. It is therefore essential to identify new strategies to activate and expand the adult stem cell population. Defects in mitochondria, the energy producing powerhouse of the cells, is associated with neurodegenerative diseases. The impact of mitochondrial impairment in adult stem and progenitor cells in the adult brain remains unknown. Our preliminary data shows that adult stem and progenitor cells are highly sensitive to changes in mitochondrial dynamics and loss of mitochondrial function causes a severe impairment in the development of new neurons in the adult brain. In these studies we will manipulate mitochondrial dynamics in an effort to prevent the decline of adult neurogenesis in the aging brain or in neurodegeneration. The overall goal is develop new treatment strategies by which to regenerate damaged brain tissue.

column36: Regulation of hippocampal network and memory by inhibitory interneuron synaptic plasticity
column37: GABAergic interneurons are the major inhibitory cells in the brain and they play a crucial role in controlling the excitability of projection cells in neuronal networks. They are multiple types of inhibitory interneurons which regulate neuronal activity in distinct ways. They are essential for normal brain function and are implicated in many CNS disorders, including epilepsy, autism, Rett syndrome, anxiety disorder, Tourette syndrome, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. However the specific role of the different types of inhibitory interneurons has been difficult to elucidate because of the large diversity of these cells. The hippocampus is an excellent model system to determine the role of inhibitory interneurons in cortical networks because of its highly ordered, well-defined anatomical architecture and its known function in learning and memory. We take advantage of new transgenic mice and molecular biological approaches that allow cell-specific manipulations in certain subtypes of interneurons. We build on our previous work and carry out a comprehensive study of the function of a specific class of GABA interneurons that provide dendritic inhibition and regulate hippocampal network plasticity underlying memory consolidation. Identifying and elucidating such network contributions of identified interneurons shed new light on the inhibitory control of neuronal networks in the brain at the molecular, cellular, network and system levels. These are necessary first steps in developing new approaches to tackle the important health problems associated with CNS disorders implicating memory deficits and GABAergic interneurons.

column36: Identifying translational regions underlying synaptic plasticity
column37: The connections between neurons are called synapses. Changing the strength of synapses is important for neural development, neural homeostasis, and memory formation. These forms of synaptic plasticity are partly mediated by the local synthesis of proteins encoded for by messenger RNAs (mRNAs) that are specifically localized near synapses. This local synthesis is activated by specific signals. An important finding is that different signals activate local translation of distinct proteins. The subset of mRNAs regulated by a specific signal is called a translational 'regulon'. The goal of this application is to both define the 'regulons' important for synaptic plasticity and the mechanisms by which signals can activate these 'regulons'. The regulation of local translation is an important target for neurodevelopment disorders and neurodegenerative diseases and thus a better fundamental understanding of these processes has important health implications.

column36: Targeting GABA-A receptors to mitigate postanesthetic cognitive deficits
column37: General anesthetics are an essential component of modern medical care. Each year, millions of patients undergo anesthesia worldwide. Despite their widespread use, general anesthetics are inherently unsafe and their molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. Such lack of knowledge has stalled the discovery of safer anesthetics and the development of treatments for their adverse effects. Our research program addresses three questions that have perplexed scientists for over a century: How do anesthetics depress brain function? What are their adverse effects? How can such adverse effects be treated? We discovered a mechanism and potential treatments for a major adverse effect: persistent postanesthetic cognitive deficits. The results are important because many patients experience long-term cognitive deficits and delirium after anesthesia and surgery. Such cognitive deficits are associated with poor long-term outcomes, increased mortality, and higher healthcare costs. The causes are unknown, and no effective treatments are available. We showed that anesthetics target both astrocytes (the most abundant support cells in the brain) and neurons. Activation of anesthetic-sensitive sensors in astrocytes may cause both the desired, acute memory-blocking effects of anesthetics and the undesired, persistent cognitive deficits. Anesthetics stimulate astrocytes to release soluble factors. These factors modify the function of neurons, which causes persistent cognitive deficits that last long after the anesthetics have been eliminated. We will determine how astrocyte-neuron crosstalk causes both the desired and undesired effects of anesthetics. We will also develop new treatments based on our patented drugs and other newly discovered compounds. Overall, this research program will advance our understanding of anesthetic mechanisms and will allow the development of new treatments to ensure that patients don't simply survive anesthesia but thrive in the postoperative period.

column36: Role for metabotropic glutamate receptors in Huntington's disease
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a devastating autosomal dominant inherited neurodegenerative disorder that is characterized by progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric impairments. A polyglutamine (CAG) expansion/repeat at the amino-terminus of the huntingtin protein is the cause of HD, and the length of this repeat is inversely correlated with the age of disease onset and directly correlates with the severity of disease symptoms. However, the underlying mechanism(s) responsible for mutant huntingtin pathogenicity remain largely unknown. Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain and is essential for a wide variety of physiological processes, such as integrative brain functions and neuronal cell development. We have preliminary data to show that antagonism of metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) with a mGluR5-selective inhibitor significantly improves locomotor behaviour and reduces huntingtin aggregates in a zQ175 knock-in mouse model of HD. We also have evidence that a process termed autophagy can be active by blocking mGluR5 signaling with CTEP and may contribute to a reduction in huntingtin protein aggregation. In addition, we have identified optineurin, a regulatory of autophagy as a mGluR5 regulatory protein. Therefore, this application will focus on the following three specific aims: 1) To repurpose mGluR5 antagonists for the treatment of HD and 2) To determine how mGluR5 antagonism alters a GPCR regulated autophagy pathway in HD mice and genetic deletion of optineurin alters HD disease progression. The proposed experiments will guide both the validation and repurposing of mGluR5 selective antagonists to treat HD. In addition, the proposed experiments will allow us to examine the role autophagy in HD, as well as help determine whether huntingtin aggregates are contributory to the HD disease process.

column36: Role of Postsynaptic Density Proteins in Dopamine Receptor Function and Crosstalk
column37: Dopamine is an important chemical of the brain. Dopamine communicates with the exterior of nerve cells by attaching to specialized group of proteins called D1, D2, D3, D4 and D5 receptors to unlock signals inside the cells. A crosstalk exists between the dopamine D1 receptor and another type of receptor that attaches to glutamate, which also a key brain chemical. Abnormal dopamine and glutamate receptors have been implicated in mental illnesses. Our research has identified a novel partner of the dopamine D1 receptor called synaptic-associated protein 102 or SAP102. SAP102 attaches to a part of the D1 receptor located in the interior of cells. As SAP102 has been previously shown to also attach to glutamate receptors, we hypothesize that SAP102 is important in the cross-talk between dopamine and glutamate receptors. The present research project will test how SAP102 facilitates the crosstalk between dopamine D1 and glutamate receptors. We will also study the role of SAP102 is involved in the control of brain functions by the D1 receptor such as movement, learning and memory using mice. These functions are abnormal in human brain illnesses such as Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder. To do our research, we will use cultured cells, mouse brain slices, mouse behavior testing, electrophysiology, microscopy and biochemical assays to identify the SAP102 mechanisms controlling the crosstalk between D1 and glutamate receptors. It is hoped that our research will improve our knowledge of the crosstalk between the SAP102, the D1 receptor and the glutamate receptor in normal and diseased brains. We believe that our research will help developing novel drugs that target specifically the cross-talk between these three proteins to restore normal dopamine and glutamate function in individuals suffering from mental illnesses such as Parkinson's disease and schizophrenia.

column36: The impact of sex, menopausal status and +APOE4 risk for Alzheimer's Disease on the neural correlates of episodic memory in healthy middle aged adults.
column37: Our ability to encode, store and retrieve past experience in rich contextual details (episodic memory) declines with age and can be an early sign of Alzheimer's disease (AD).Our previous fMRI research showed that context memory tasks are more sensitive than recognition memory tasks at detecting early signs of episodic memory decline with healthy aging. Indeed, we found declines in the ability to recollect the contextual detail of past events were apparent by midlife and were associated with changes in prefrontal cortex (PFC) and ventral visual cortex function. Importantly, midlife is a time of transition from pre/peri-menopause to menopause in MA females and is associated with decreased endogenous estrogen levels, which can negatively impact memory. In our prior work, 70-80% of our MA samples were females. As such it is not clear if our prior findings generalize across the sexes and what aspects of our previous results may have be driven by the menopausal status of females. Moreover, given that there are more females diagnosed with AD compared to males, after controlling for sex differences in life expectancy, it is also important to explore if known risk factors for AD, i.e. having and apolipoprotein E e4 allele (+APOE4), differentially impacts females vs. males at midlife. The goal of the current study is to extend our prior work on midlife brain aging and episodic memory and investigate how biological sex, menopausal status, and +APOE4 status impacts the neural correlates of episodic memory in MA using functional and structural magnetic resonance imaging methods. This work is significant because our results will help determine if +APOE4 impacts memory and brain structure/function in females > males by midlife, and if this effect interacts with female menopausal status. This data will ultimately help refine our ability to identify adults at risk of developing AD at an age when intervention may be most beneficial

column37: Dr. Mona Loutfy is recognized as a national and international leader in the area of women, reproductive health, and HIV. Dr. Loutfy has worked as an ally to Indigenous researchers and leaders for a decade and is committed to continuing this work by contributing to strength-based and culturally-grounded research with Indigenous women. column36: Impact of transitioning to secondary schools on health behaviours associated with obesity and academic related outcomes: A socio-ecological perspective
column37: In developed countries, including Canada, rates of being overweight and obese in children have increased substantially. Lack of physical activity, too much sedentary time, and poor dietary habits all contribute to unhealthy weight trajectories. Adolescence is a period when many unhealthy behaviours emerge or escalate. Most notably, we and others find that these problems are exacerbated during the transition from elementary to secondary school. Our goal is to examine factors that influence adolescents' physical activity, sedentary time and dietary habits as they transition from elementary to secondary school. We will use qualitative and quantitative methods (interviews, surveys & direct measures) to determine changes that occur in the school, household and social settings during this transition to identify how they influence adolescent health behaviours. We will also determine if health behaviours relate to academic performance. First, we will collect health and related data in grades 7 and 8 (before/after the transition to a new school) from 736 students/parents from 49 schools in BC. We will assess health behaviours (physical activity, sedentary time & dietary intake) and school (access, availability, opportunity, environmental context), household (modeling, access & availability, parenting practices & styles, family environment), and social (modeling, co-participation, norms) influences. Then, to better understand and interpret data from questionnaires and direct measures, we will interview 40 student/parent pairs before and after the transition. Our findings will provide new insights into how school, household and social environments contribute to health behaviour during the transition to secondary school. In future, our data can be used to develop targeted programs to address these factors and encourage more positive behaviours at adolescence. Ultimately, we aim to alter the current trajectory towards increased health risk among Canada's youth.

column36: Promoting Brain Health to Prevent Dementia: Roles of Covert Vascular Brain Injury and Cognitive Reserve in Age-Related Cognitive Decline
column37: Dementia is Canada's largest, and growing, public health problem, affecting more than 500,000 Canadians and costing more than either cardiovascular disease or cancer. There is encouraging evidence that, for persons of a given age, the risk for dementia has decreased somewhat. Other scientists have proposed that this is because people's brains are healthier (that is, that they have more cognitive reserve) or that they are less like to get silent strokes (small strokes seen on brain scans in people at risk for cognitive decline), but without proof. Meanwhile, the risk for Alzheimer's disease has probably not changed, and it remains incurable. My Foundation program is designed to identify the factors that promote healthier brain aging and lower risk of silent strokes, and to explore new ways of diagnosing and monitoring symptomatic patients. My background in neurology, epidemiology, and neuroimaging has prepared me well for this work. At the University of Calgary I have established one of the world's largest brain MRI analysis centres. Leading a national team of Program Experts, I will examine risk for stroke and cognitive decline in persons recruited from the community in two studies (with 9,700 and 1,500 participants) all of whom have had a brain MRI. We will repeat the brain MRI in six years in 1,500 to see who has had new silent strokes or excessive brain tissue loss (i.e., atrophy). We will look at many potential protective factors including education, occupation, income, diet, physical activity, social activities, and stress levels. In another study I will examine markers of disease-related brain changes in persons with Alzheimer's disease and a related blood vessel condition called cerebral amyloid angiopathy. These studies will point to effective strategies to promote brain health and to diagnose and monitor symptomatic patients.

column36: Targeting the Mammalian Mitochondrial Interactome to Dissect Macromolecular Assemblies and Pathways in Health and Disease
column37: Mitochondria (mt) generate the majority of a cell's energy supply, which is consumed by neurons in the brain to execute diverse cellular functions. Beyond its essential role, defects in mitochondrial protein (MP) function can cause or contribute to neurodegenerative disorders (NDs), for which no effective long-term cure currently exists. This is likely owing to the central involvement of MPs in a myriad of interconnected essential functions in neurons, including the quality control (QC) systems that support cellular homeostasis by maintaining healthy mt for proper neuronal function and integrity. However, impairment in QC during energy demands causes accumulation of damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria, resulting in neuronal death. Despite detailed mechanistic investigations of individual MPs, our understanding of the relationship between how all human MPs globally function and interact together at the level of complexes and cellular pathways still remains incomplete. Emerging evidence suggests that QC systems play a key role in the development of Parkinson's disease (PD), and potentially influences mt homeostasis and neuronal death. While this presents an avenue for therapeutic development, the intricate network of interacting MPs in complexes/pathways is not yet fully understood, hindering progress. My proposal aims at addressing the aforesaid gaps by drawing on our recent advances in proteomic and genetic platforms to provide the first high-resolution view on the molecular organization and mechanistic operation of human MP assemblies, and to uncover the pathway-level relationships for genes encoding the components of QC machineries linked to PD. This work will yield molecular models for new binding partners in mt processes, provide valuable data resources for the community, facilitate discovery of potential new therapeutic targets for NDs, and inspire further research into novel treatments for sustainable health care.
