column36: Porphyrin Nanomedicine for Cancer Imaging and Therapy
column37: Despite decades of research, applying cancer nanomedicine for patient care still faces many challenges including inefficient nanoparticle delivery to tumours, safety concerns associated with inorganic nanomaterials, the diverse architecture of tumours, and over-complexity in nanoparticle design. In 2011, we discovered first-in-class organic nanoparticles, termed porphysomes, with the ability to address these limitations. They are non-toxic, being made from lipid (i.e., fat) and natural pigment porphyrins (i.e., chlorophyll in plants and heme in blood). Furthermore, they are simple in design, yet can exhibit multifunctional imaging and therapeutic properties, stemming from a single porphyrin-lipid building block. These diverse properties include the ability to bind metals, and transform locally delivered light energy into heat, sound waves or chemicals toxic to cancer cells. In this Foundation Project, we will build upon porphysomes' inherent multifunctionality to expand knowledge and address key issues in cancer nanomedicine, phototherapy, and drug delivery through the creation of a new generation of porphyrin biomaterials: 1) porphyrin microbubbles and biomimetic porphyrin nanoparticles able to effectively target brain tumour therapy beyond the blood-brain barrier; 2) porphyrin nanoparticles that harness the immune system to enhance lung cancer therapy; 3) stimuli-responsive porphyrin nanoparticles that improves phototherapy efficacy and safety; 4) nanoparticles made of expanded porphyrin molecules with the ability to bind metals for nuclear and radiation medicine. The clinical translation of these materials will be facilitated via our fifth Program pillar, which establishes clinical safety and efficacy of prototypical porphysome. Ultimately, the outcome of this program will be the development of clinically relevant materials that realize the potential of cancer nanomedicine in improving current cancer therapy regimens.

column36: Improving health equity for LGBTQ youth in Canada and globally: Addressing the role of families and culture
column37: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, Two Spirit and queer (LGBTQ) adolescents face persistent health gaps compared to their straight and cisgender peers in Canada and globally. Is it getting better? Our Stigma and Resilience Among Vulnerable Youth Centre at UBC has developed leading evidence to answer this question: some health gaps are narrowing, but only for some LGBTQ youth (mostly gay boys) and these trends are not yet documented for rural or ethnoculturally diverse LGBTQ youth. Likewise, families are important sources of support for adolescents, but trends show parental support for LGBTQ youth is not improving. Interventions are needed to help all families better support their LGBTQ youth, and to reach youth and families in rural areas. Our Vision: to reduce stigma, foster resilience, and improve health equity for LGBTQ youth in Canada and throughout the world. Our 7-year program of research has 4 primary aims: 1) to track trends in health and health disparities for LGBTQ youth from diverse ethnocultural groups in Canada, Europe, and New Zealand; 2) to identify how families reject or support LGBTQ youth in different cultural groups in these same regions, and examine the link between family support and LGBTQ youth health; 3) develop and test new culturally-relevant on-line and smartphone-based interventions to build parental support and lower family rejection of LGBTQ youth; and 4) develop & test similar technology-based health promotion interventions for diverse and rural LGBTQ youth. Our participatory mixed-methods approaches will use population-based surveys, on-line focus groups, longitudinal research methods, and pilot tests of on-line and text message interventions. With our team of experts from Canada, the USA, New Zealand, and Europe, we will identify culturally-specific knowledge to improve clinical care of LGBTQ youth and families, and create new, culturally relevant family and youth interventions, to narrow the health gaps for LGBTQ youth.

column37: Over half of Canadians are overweight or obese. Obesity leads to higher levels of blood insulin and glucose. These are features of prediabetes, which leads to type 2 diabetes. Diabetes has serious consequences to our health and economy. Even prediabetes contributes to over 2 million annual deaths worldwide. Existing treatments help control blood sugar usually by increasing insulin. However, existing treatments focus on glucose, but do not address the root cause of prediabetes progression during obesity. Higher insulin can accelerate obesity and promote "insulin resistance". The discovery of insulin has saved many lives by controlling blood sugar. Now we need to stop the progression of prediabetes. After every meal or snack containing sugars, insulin is secreted and then cleared from the blood. Obesity slows clearance of insulin, exposing the body to more insulin. This can add up over time to further worsen obesity and prediabetes. Drugs that change insulin clearance all the time (not just after a meal) have failed and we still do not have good weight loss drugs that change eating behaviour or the body's ability to burn more energy. It is very important to discover ways to reduce the repeated exposure of the body to prolonged insulin after each meal. A key problem was that we did not understand enough about what changes insulin levels after eating. My lab discovered that bacteria in the gut produce factors that can lower insulin. The trillions of bacteria in our gut are an untapped source of new drugs. My lab has already found one part of bacteria that makes insulin work better. The next step is finding out how bacteria are sensed by the immune system to alter insulin. This research will combine unique resources across Canada to find out which parts of bacteria can be used to stop or slow prediabetes. This research may lead to new ways to target insulin and the development of prediabetes, which are different from the current drugs that focus on blood glucose.

column36: Origins, Consequences and Outcomes of Neuroprogression in First Episode Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is an illness that causes a high degree of personal disability, caregiver burden, and societal impact. Despite the advances in medical, psychological and social aspects of care in the last 60 years, less than 1 in 7 people with schizophrenia achieve paid employment. Existing treatments have a good effect on reducing 'positive' symptoms of schizophrenia (hearing voices, having false beliefs), but currently, there are no treatments to reduce the 'negative' (reduced motivation, interests, and activity) and 'cognitive' symptoms that are central to the persistent disability seen in many patients. We lack understanding of what brain processes, when affected, produce these resistant symptoms. One promising area is to look at the process of continuous loss of brain tissue that occurs in this illness. Patients who have poor outcomes have a higher rate of brain tissue loss; abnormalities in brain's innate defense mechanisms against infection may contribute to continued tissue loss. We now have very sophisticated brain-imaging facilities that allow us to study this over the course of illness using the magnetic field. As these brain scans are non-invasive and do not involve harmful radiation, we can repeat them multiple times. We propose to study patients experiencing the first episode of schizophrenia and follow them up over 1 year to assess the course of change in brain tissue and symptoms. The objective of this study is to develop an insight on the triggers of tissue loss and how it eventually leads to a poor outcome, enabling us to discover treatments to reverse this process. There are several protective treatments that can prevent brain tissue damage, but we must first identify the right patients to treat. Treating intractable cognitive, negative and persistent positive symptoms could potentially result in a reversal of functional deterioration to an appreciable extent and promote patients' journey towards recovery from this debilitating illness.

column36: Behavioural, neuroimaging, and connectome studies of the medial temporal lobe in healthy and epileptic brains
column37: The medial temporal lobe (MTL) is a brain network that plays an important role in memory, spatial navigation, and social cognition. Pathology of this region has been observed in several neurological conditions, including temporal lobe epilepsy, the most common drug-resistant epilepsy in adults. In addition to seizures, epileptic patients often present with difficulties in memory and emotional wellbeing, likely due to damage to the MTL. Many patients undergo surgery to treat the seizures. However, some may show further memory deficits and emotional problems after the operation, which may ultimately impact their quality of life. This research program is centered on assessing whether these problems can be understood through a comprehensive evaluation of the anatomy and wiring of the different elements in the MTL. We will integrate high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging of MTL microstructure, function, and connectivity, and relate these markers with memory and emotion regulation scores obtained in behavioral studies. By studying epileptic patients before and after surgery, we can evaluate consequences of temporal lobe resection on brain networks mediating these cognitive and affective skills. column36: Nouveau paradigme de traitement optimise par corset de la scoliose idiopathique de l'adolescent
column37: La scoliose est une deformation de la colonne vertebrale affectant 2-4% des adolescents. Le traitement par corset est le seul traitement conservateur efficace pour limiter la progression de la deformation. C'est un traitement difficile pour les jeunes (inconfort, atteinte de l'image de soi, limitation des activites) qui doivent porter cette orthese rigide 20 a 23 hres/jr durant toute la croissance. L'efficacite du traitement est reliee au temps de port du corset. Toutefois, il existe un probleme inquietant de participation au traitement car en moyenne, le corset n'est porte que 12 hres/jr. Cette non-participation du patient a porter son corset mene assurement a l'echec du traitement. Les objectifs de ce projet sont de mieux cibler les sujets a traiter; offrir un corset plus efficace pour corriger la deformation; developper un questionnaire de mesure de qualite de vie et de confort du corset et mettre en place une equipe d'intervenants pour encourager une meilleure adhesion au traitement. Notre equipe travaillera a changer radicalement le traitement par corset en selectionnant mieux les candidats a traiter en evaluant le risque de progression de leur scoliose afin d'eviter de porter un corset inutilement, et en offrant un corset plus efficace pour les patients qui sont a risque de progression. Nous analyserons aussi les resultats du questionnaire pour verifier sa capacite a informer le personnel sur les raisons du refus au traitement et nous interviendrons aupres du patient non-adherent selon ses besoins. Cette nouvelle approche ameliorera la correction apportee par le corset afin d'amener un meilleur taux de succes au traitement qu'obtenu precedemment. Notre nouveau corset devrait etre plus confortable, mieux tolere et donc apprecie des patients. Finalement, l'equipe transmettra les outils developpes dans ce programme afin que les technologies et les interventions demontrees efficaces soient disponibles pour tous les patients dans les centres specialises.

column36: Ubiquitination of histone H2B in B cell immunobiology and cancer
column37: The immune system plays a major role in protecting humans from bacteria, viruses, and toxins (known as antigens). One of the ways that the immune system accomplishes this is by producing antibodies that bind to and neutralize these antigens. Antibodies are small molecules made by B cells. Each B cell makes only one type of antibody which will bind to only one antigen. By changing the antibody stalk, the properties of the antibody are changed. For example, IgM antibodies can be changed to IgG antibodies which can be used by macrophages to engulf bacteria that are coated by these antibodies, or to IgA antibodies that can be secreted into mucosal tissue and can neutralize pathogens in the lung or the gut. Changing the antibody class is accomplished by the class switch recombination process, and the key enzyme that initiates this process is called AID. Much still needs to be investigated about how class switch recombination is accomplished in B cells and the enzymes that are involved. We have recently identified novel genes that function in class switch recombination, namely RNF20, RNF40, and USP22, and propose to investigate how these genes function in this process using cell lines. Our current work suggests it functions by repairing DNA breaks that occur in B cells. We have also made mice where we can specifically delete USP22 in any tissue of our choice. We will specifically delete USP22 in B cells to determine whether B cell development and class switch recombination require USP22. Hence, our proposed work will allow us to determine how an effective antibody response is generated. Since enzymes involved in DNA repair are typically found to suppress tumor development, and because AID and the class switch recombination process are linked to the development of lymphomas, we will also test whether USP22 is critical for the development of lymphomas and colon cancer.

column36: Novel therapy for Hyperkalemic Periodic Paralysis (HyperKPP)
column37: Hyperkalemic Periodic Paralysis (HyperKPP) is a neuromuscular disease that is characterized by periods of myotonia weakness and paralysis. Few treatment options are available to patients suffering of HyperKPP, and in many cases they lose efficacy over time. Using a HyperKPP mouse model, we first found that HyperKPP muscles are weaker than normal; i.e., they generate less force. Then, we found that activating two proteins in the cell membrane, an ion transporter and one ion channel, can provide a novel therapy that fully restores force development back to normal levels. There is also evidence that the activity of two of these proteins can be increased using a drug that activates protein kinase A (PKA). This is advantageous because a single drug can be used to activate PKA instead of two drugs, reducing the extent of side effects. More importantly, it is proposed to test the efficacy of three already Federal Drug Administration (FDA) approved drugs that are used to treat various diseases via an activation of protein kinase A. In a first series of experiments, we will determine in vitro how effective each of three drugs is at increasing force generation in HyperKPP muscles toward that of normal muscles. In a second series of experiments, we will treat HyperKPP mice with the most effective drug to determine how effective they are at improving force generation over long period of time; i.e., to make sure they do not lose effectiveness over time. If successful, the ultimate aim will be to initiate clinical trials.

column36: Cortical and basal ganglia mechanisms in movement disorders
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the commonest neurodegenerative diseases. It is due to dysfunction of parts the brain known as the basal ganglia and the cortex, and different parts of the brain are abnormally connected to each other. Theme 1 of the research program will use several state of the art techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging, magnetoencephalography and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to determine how the connections in the brain are altered in PD. We will develop novel treatment to normalize these connections. Theme 2 will define the inhibitory functions of the basal ganglia that are particularly relevant to impulse control disorder and gait disturbance in PD. Electrical activities of the basal ganglia will be directly recorded from deep brain stimulation (DBS) electrodes implanted in the basal ganglia and with stimulation applied at selected times during inhibition tasks to define the role of the basal ganglia in inhibitory functions. Theme 3 will promote changes in the brain by combining a surface magnetic brain stimulation technique (TMS) with DBS, and will test this approach as a novel treatment for PD. Theme 4 will determine how electrical activities in deep brain structures are related to different clinical states of PD patients. We will use this information to develop new DBS systems that will automatically adjust stimulation parameters depending on the clinical status to produce the optimal stimulation effects. This will lead to new and improved DBS treatment for PD. The program will be conducted by the Program Leader with a group of Program Experts who are established investigators with diverse expertise. It provides an excellent training environment for future researchers. The findings will advance our knowledge of PD, and lead to improved treatment for PD patients.

column37: At present, there are 4.6 million Canadians living with the pain of arthritis for which there are inadequate drug treatments. We hypothesise that PAR activation can lead to nerve damage and consequently arthritis pain. In this project, we plan to identify the enzymes responsible for joint nerve injury and pain. We will also test drugs that block PARs to see if we can protect joint nerves from further damage and uncover a new way of alleviating arthritis pain.

column36: Improving Transition of Care and Outcomes of Cardiovascular Disease Using an Innovative Big Data Approach
column37: Heart disease continues to pose a significant burden on healthcare systems in Canada and around the world. Each year, more than 600,000 patients present to the emergency department for chest pain assessment, more than 80,000 patients are hospitalized with a heart attack, and more than 60,000 patients undergo coronary angioplasty to treat heart blockages in Canada. Although there have been significant advancements in the prevention and management of heart disease, patients continue to be at risk for serious events. For example, heart attack patients have a ~10% chance of dying and ~40% chance of being readmitted to the hospital in the first year after their initial events. Emerging data suggest many adverse events occur because the care during transitions of patients from hospital to home, or from the emergency department, is suboptimal. This proposal consists of a series of innovative, large-scale projects that will close the gap in the quality of care received by heart disease patients during care transitions. We will examine how to measure care properly, assess the current level of care, and understand what the drivers of these deficiencies are. Next, we will create tools to help patients and clinicians in order to improve the quality of care. Lastly, we will create a Learning Health System so that we can align the priorities of patients, clinicians and policy makers. The ultimate goal of this research program is to build capacity and sustainability to continue to improve the care and outcomes patients with heart disease.

column36: Identification and Characterization of Human Hematopoietic and Leukemia Stem Cells and Elucidation of their Role in Regenerative Medicine and Disease
column37: Blood is the most regenerative human tissue with a trillion cells produced daily. The dozen mature cell types that compose adult blood originate from rare hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Only HSCs have the capacity to give rise to other HSCs while regenerating the entire blood system. When the mechanisms controlling normal blood development go awry, it can lead to leukemia, a form of blood cancer. Our lab was the first to show that acute leukemias possess a hierarchical structure similar to that of normal blood development. We discovered that cancer stem cells (CSCs) are at the apex of this hierarchy and possess the ability to self-renew and produce all of the cells of the tumour. CSCs are responsible not only for initiating and maintaining acute leukemias, but also for therapy resistance and recurrence of disease after treatment. Through CIHR's Foundation Program, we will identify and study the molecular mechanisms underpinning the unique properties of HSCs and CSCs, especially those that enable CSCs to resist treatment and cause relapse. Our research findings will lay the foundation for the development of new methods to enhance HSCs from cord blood, making them more amenable for transplantation. HSC transplantation is an effective treatment for many diseases; however, two thirds of patients who require a transplant cannot receive it because they lack a matched donor. Findings from our Foundation program will also lead to the development of new prognostic and predictive biomarkers for leukemia and identify new therapeutic targets to eliminate leukemia CSCs while sparing normal HSCs. Although most adults with acute leukemia (B-ALL and AML) respond initially to conventional therapy, 50-75% of patients experience a relapse and >60% of adult patients succumb to their disease. We will work with our clinical and industry partners to ensure that our research findings are translated to improve the health of Canadians.

column36: The predictive values of novel metabolic markers for early knee osteoarthritis changes
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis, affecting about 10% of the world's population aged 60 years or older. It is the major source of joint pain and disability, and imposes substantial socioeconomic burden on society with a cost estimate between 1.0% and 2.5% of gross domestic product. Presently, available treatment is entirely directed at controlling the pain associated with OA with joint replacement for end-stage disease. This is unlikely to change in next few years, reinforcing the relevance of targeted interventions at early stage of the disease or even before the development of symptoms. As a result, clinicians have a challenging task of identifying those at highest risk of developing severe OA in a timely manner. However, the prediction of OA risk is still in its infancy. Using a metabolite profiling method, we identified seven novel metabolic markers that are related to knee OA with greater power to discriminate OA patients from controls than any other biomarkers identified so far. Given that OA manifests first as abnormal joint tissue metabolism before any structural changes can be detected, these novel metabolic markers would have great potential for early diagnosis of OA. We therefore propose to examine the predictive values of these novel metabolic markers for knee OA early changes in well-established longitudinal cohorts. The results will provide a better understanding of how these novel metabolic markers predict early OA diagnosis and OA worsening. These novel metabolites could also be potential novel targets for drug development for OA.

column36: Regional specificity of aortic aneurym: Cell specific function of disintegrin and metalloprotease-17 (ADAM17) in thoracic versus abdominal aortic aneurysm
column37: Aortic aneurysm (focal dilation of the aorta) is a serious vascular disease and a great health concern with fatal or devastating outcomes. Aorta is the largest artery in the body which carries the blood from the heart to the rest of the body. In aortic aneurysm, an area of the aorta becomes enlarged (bulges out). The wall of the aorta loses its elastic property (like an old rubber band) and unable to squeeze the blood along (forward) to different body parts/organs. When an old rubber band is subjected to high pressure (blood pumped from the heart), it can snap (i.e. aortic rupture) which results in a large amount of blood loss which can often result in death (if in the chest), or lower body paralysis (if in abdominal area). So far, there have been no treatment for this devastating disease. ADAM17 is a an enzyme located in the cells withing the aortic wall. It can clip membrane-bound molecules and release them initiating (or inhibiting) their activity. ADAM17 is increased in the aortic wall during aneurysm formation, but it is unknown whether it contributes to disease progression, or if it is simply a by-stander. In addition, it could have different functions in the thoracic versus the abdominal aorta. Our lab is among the few labs (world-wide) that has developed models of aortic aneurysm (in thoracic and in abdominal aorta, independent from atherosclerosis). We will use genetically modified mice that with cell-specific ADAM17-deficiency (in smooth muscle cell or endothelial cells) and models of thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm to determine the role of ADAM17 (in different cell types in the aorta) in aortic aneurysm formation and progression. We will use aorta specimens from patients with aortic aneurysm to confirm our findings from our mouse models. The findings from this study will reveal novel function of ADAM17 in aortic aneurysm which can also be beneficial for patients with other aneurysms (e.g. brain aneurysm & stroke).

column36: Oncohistones in Cancer
column37: Histones package our genetic information (DNA) and regulate all processes needed for a cell to grow or differentiate. There are several changes in the histone tail that act in concert with other factors (epi-genome) to govern gene activity states and the overall function of our genetic identity. Indeed, the epigenome is like the symphony of our cells, the partition that makes sense of the musical notes (DNA). Therefore, aberrant histone and chromatin modifications disrupt these normal cellular processes leading to the development of cancer. Our ground-breaking discovery of mutations in these histone genes (oncohistones as we named them with mutations at three specific residues in the histone 3 tails) in deadly brain cancers in children has linked human normal development and what we now know are epigenetic-driven cancers. We also recently uncovered oncohistones in other bone or muscle cancers, leukemia and head an neck cancers. We aim in this program to understand how this new mechanism of cancer promotes aberrant growth, identify targets amenable to therapy, provide relevant models to test the effects of these therapies prior to rapidly translating them by using our collaborative network to clinical trials at the bedside. Ultimately, if successful, our program will positively change the bleak outcome of oncohistone-associated cancers.

column37: It is estimated that 27,000 Canadians are survivors of preterm birth, many reaching adulthood and afflicted with chronic lung diseases related to prematurity. Since the fetal lung develops more slowly than other organs, preterm babies often have difficulty breathing and require additional oxygen, causing further injury. Up to 40% of extremely premature infants suffer from bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), a lung disease which incurs significant healthcare costs, second only to asthma among childhood illnesses. Furthermore, BPD is associated with chronic lung diseases later in life such as asthma that result in frequent visits to the hospital and can be fatal. Although there is currently no cure, newer therapies are offering hope that BPD can be treated or even reversed if detected early enough. However, conventional diagnostic tests often look normal in early BPD and cannot be used reliably to determine if a treatment is required or whether it is working. There is a need for better tools to detect and diagnose early BPD in order to develop better treatments and determine those infants that stand to benefit from existing therapies. In this proposal, we will use Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to detect early BPD and response to treatment. MRI can pinpoint how well the lung is working without the need for radiation, making it safe and potentially useful for assessment of BPD in premature infants. We will test our approaches in newborn animals (rats and rabbits) with lung lesions that mimic human BPD to determine how and when to best detect and treat early disease. Animals grow quickly compared to children and will allow us to study BPD early and throughout the life span and investigate treatments that could be used in humans in future. The development of MRI as an effective tool for animal models of BPD will enable translation of these findings to the clinic for improved acute care of the lungs of premature infants and reduced chronic health consequences due to BPD.

column37: The gene expression program of a cell defines its identity, i.e. it tells us, and the cell itself, who it is, what is its role and how to play it in complex organisms like ours. We study mechanisms for the control of gene expression and their misregulation in disease. The blueprint for this control is in our DNA and changes in this blueprint result in mutations. Both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms orchestrate the complex development of a functional human and their deregulation cause diseases. We use a hormone-coding gene of the pituitary gland as our model system and throughout the years we have discovered new regulators and new mechanisms that account for normal processes but also disease states. We have thus predicted a form of hormone deficiency that is lethal to neonates, explained it and provided a treatment that fully recovers the lethal outcome of this condition. The new frontier in the field is the epigenetic level of regulation and we are exploring this with state-of-the-art high-throughput massive DNA sequencing technologies. We also identified mechanisms involved in development of the pituitary tumors that cause Cushing disease. This disease is particularly deleterious because of excessive uncontrolled hormone production leading to hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, and metabolic disruption. We have partly explained the resistance to hormone feedback that characterises these tumors and we now seek to determine how cell growth is deregulated in order to develop novel treatment approaches.

column37: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of arteries and remains the principal cause of death in our society despite effective cholesterol-lowering therapies. Atherosclerosis develops silently for decades before causing heart attacks and strokes. My research focuses on cells and genes that participate in atherosclerosis. Currently, there are no therapies targeting cells in the artery wall to inhibit the formation and progression of atherosclerosis. This is the first step in the formation of atherosclerosis, and is followed by other white blood cells entering the artery and becoming foam cells. Recently, we discovered a novel protective mechanism by which up to half of DCs in the normal artery exit into the bloodstream in response to inflammatory stimulus or exposure to bacteria. However, engulfed lipid blocks DC exit. Our goal is to elucidate the mechanisms underlying DC exit from the normal arteries so that we can determine the changes that shut off this process in foam cells. This is an important endeavor since we believe that in the future we can overcome these inhibitory mechanisms so that accumulated lipid can be removed from the artery wall by exiting lipid-loaded foam cells. This could become a unique approach to reduce both the lipid burden and foam cells. In atherosclerotic lesions, the number of foam cells increases with time in part due to cell division. Moreover, after DC exit their numbers recover within a day because remaining cells divide. Thus, therapeutic strategies that promote foam cell exit from aorta must also target molecules that promote cell division.

column37: Regenerative medicine (RM) offers an opportunity to address the root causes of chronic diseases, which typically result from the breakdown of tissues maintained by stem cells (SC). These simulations allow us to connect the genetic coding inside SC to the environment that influences SC growth. These simulations will one day dramatically shorten the time it takes to develop new therapies for degenerative diseases. Second, we are rewiring the genetic code in, and the environment around, SC to understand the key requirements of SC-based tissue development and to increase the quantity and quality of SC-derived cells produced. Third, with our partners, we are moving promising discoveries towards the clinic using advanced models of disease, with a focus on testing specialized blood cells as blood cancer and autoimmune disease therapeutics. column36: Structural Biology of Calcium-Dependent Cellular Processes in Health and Disease
column37: As the most abundant mineral in the body, calcium has long been recognized as vital to the formation and maintenance of living systems. Bones, where calcium is stored in the solid state, continuously release ions or salts of this mineral (i.e., Ca2+) into the body, and this soluble form of calcium plays a central role as a messenger within cells. We call this the biological calcium signal. However, too much Ca2+ (or too much calcium signal) is detrimental to cells, and uncontrolled calcium levels in our body are life-threatening. In cancer, the calcium signal is largely deregulated for the advantage of cancer cell growth. In order to understand how normal and cancer cells produce and respond to calcium signals, we will investigate the molecular details of the calcium-dependent cellular processes that we think are most relevant to cancer. In this proposal, we attempt to answer key questions: (i) how is the calcium signal generated and how does it become deregulated in cancer?; (ii) how does the calcium signal influence other signaling circuits that drive the growth and proliferation of cancer cells?; and (iii) how does the calcium signal affect the proper cell adhesion of normal cells, and contribute to metastatic properties of cancer cells? Part of this program is also relevant to immunodeficiency, as genetic defects (mutations) in the calcium signal generators we study (called STIM/ORAI) cause severe combined immune disease or SCID. The proposed program will contribute to a better understanding of how cancer cells use the calcium signal circuits to promote their survival and growth, as well as how immune cells battle infectious agents in the human body. Deeper understanding of the calcium signal transduction system will provide new clues for novel therapeutic strategies to treat patients with immunodeficiency and cancer.

column36: Mechanisms Coordinating Polo Kinase Activity and Localization in Cell Division
column37: Cancer is the excessive division of cells in the body. To duplicate, cells must separate two identical sets of chromosomes during mitosis and divide correctly. This process requires the coordinated activities of several proteins that have been conserved between species during evolution. The Polo kinase protein (Plk1) is necessary for cell division by interacting with and modifying other proteins. Several types of cancer cells become addicted to elevated Polo activity. Thus, if Polo is inhibited partially, cancer cells die while healthy cells can still live and divide. Efforts have been deployed to obtain molecules capable of blocking the catalytic activity of Polo. Some of them are in clinical trials for the treatment of various cancers and have given promising results. However, the toxicity and side effects of these drugs limit their use. Our goal is to gain new knowledge of how Polo functions and how the cell responds to interference with Polo. This information will help design more effective and less toxic therapies targeting Polo in cancers. Recent findings by us and others have indicated the existence of previously unrecognized levels of regulation of Polo. The proposed research will build on these discoveries to uncover the precise molecular mechanisms controlling Polo activity in space and time during cell division so that it can fulfill its functions. For this part of the project, we will use the fruit fly Drosophila as a model system allowing a powerful combination of approaches. The new knowledge will provide basis to efforts in the development of compounds that interfere with specific aspects of Polo functions to kill cancer cells but not healthy cells. We will also use the new CRISPR technology to search for genes that become essential in the presence of low doses of Polo inhibitors in human cells. This information will direct the development of combinatorial therapies simultaneously targeting Polo and synergic mechanisms in cancer cells.

column36: Heterogeneity through space and time drive the clinical behaviour of childhood medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Medulloblastoma is really made up of four diseases, of which two types, Group 3 and Group 4, account for the majority of cases, as well as the majority of children who are dying of their disease. The main tumor 'lump' in the cerebellum is called the 'primary tumor'. The primary tumor can spread (metastasize) to cover other regions of the surface of the brain and spinal cord. The most damaging therapies for children with Group 3 and Group 4 medulloblastoma (radiation) are necessary to treat the metastases. The dream of curing cancer through precision medicine has entailed sequencing cancer genomes to identify tumor specific mutations, which could in turn be targeted by pathway specific drugs that are lethal to the tumor but harmless to a child's normal cells. While this model is showing early success for some adult cancers, it holds limited promise for treatment of medulloblastoma; recent results from our lab have shown that most medulloblastomas harbor few of these tumor specific mutations and that the tumours differ greatly both across a given 'lump' and between the primary tumor and the metastases. Instead, medulloblastomas appear to be driven by large deletions or insertions of genes. We now also know that some of these differences are seen regularly in medulloblastomas and the metastases and this makes them an excellent choice for the development of targeted therapy. We have begun developing new tools, and aim to use these tools to study these differences which occur in the tumours and between the primary tumor and the metastases-we strongly believe this is the best, and perhaps the only way to improve survival for children with medulloblastoma.

column37: Dependence receptors are cell surface receptors that determine cell fate dependent on the availability of their extracellular ligand, called Netrin-1 (NET1). We focus on the structure and function of NET1 and how it orchestrates its unique interactions with individual dependence receptors, such as UNC5 and DCC. Most remarkably, if the NET1-dependence receptor complex is interrupted- a programmed cell death is triggered. However, to date it is not known how NET1 orchestrates on a molecular level this complex set of signals. We aim to perform an integrated structural biology approach, combining protein X-ray crystallography in conjunction with SAXS, AUC/DLS/SEC-MALS and in-depth biochemical and functional assays. When combined, these tools create a detailed molecular understanding of how NET1 acts on its receptors, and how the activated receptors together work to influence the cell physiology. This research proposal aims to define the molecular basis of NET1-UNC5 and NET1-UNC5-DCC complex interactions and to unravel the structural basis for relevant signaling pathways. In these studies we will seek to develop new therapeutic targets with the overall goal to interrupt NET1-mediated dependence receptor complexes and thereby causing apoptosis in tumor cells.

column36: Cell volume regulatory mechanisms in oocytes and preimplantation embryos and their role in development and embryo health
column37: Early embryos are extremely sensitive to conditions that disturb their cells' size. This implied that regulation of cell size is critical to early embryo development. We previously found, using the mouse as our model, that early embryos have a unique mechanism for maintaining cell size that relies on accumulation of high levels of the amino acid glycine inside embryonic cells. Glycine is needed to replace some of the salts that the embryos, like other cells, routinely take up to quickly correct deviations from their preferred size. We also found that cell size regulation first arises in the egg, beginning when they are ovulated from the ovary. We do not know how the glycine mechanism is turned on at ovulation or how these processes are regulated in eggs and embryos. We also have little information about the effects of disruptions of these normal processes on the health of later embryos and the resulting offspring. In this project, using the mouse model, we will determine how the egg switches on the mechanism that uses glycine. Finally, we will find how disruptions of the unique cell size-regulatory mechanisms in eggs and embryos affect the health of offspring. Increasingly, infertile couples (more than 15% of couples in Canada) are treated by assisted reproduction technologies (ART) that include in vitro fertilization (IVF) and the extended culture of eggs and embryos outside the woman's body. Fertility preservation for cancer patients similarly relies on ART. In addition to important knowledge about eggs and embryos, our project will potentially lead to better understanding of what can go wrong during ART and effects on the health of the children that are born, and lead to safer ART techniques.

Naturally occurring bacterial machineries, called tailocins, are closely related to phage tails and can be used to kill bacteria in a highly specific manner. We are developing methods to engineer these tailocins to kill any desired bacterial strain. These engineered tailocins will be used to manipulate the human microbiome to alleviate disease conditions, such as Crohn's Disease. Tailocins also have the potential to treat antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections.

I carried out a modifier screen in a mouse model for Rett syndrome, a neurological disorder, which uncovered missing pathway members, revealed new genetic interactions, and pinpointed new drug targets. The modifiers revealed unexpected facets of Rett syndrome, which has changed the health management of Rett patients and suggested therapies. Using unparalleled resources in Canada for mouse work and human genome sequencing, we will collaborate with a multi-disciplinary team of outstanding researchers in the areas of neuroscience, epigenetics, imaging, genome editing and sequencing to 1) understand additional modifiers that provide surprising disease insight; 2) make sure our findings are relevant to humans and other neurological conditions, 3) determine how the modifiers alter the phenotype of people carrying Rett mutations, and 4) inform treatment strategies. Greatly improved health in Rett mice that carry modifiers from two pathways suggests that combination therapy will confer amazing improvement. Outcome-predicting biomarkers, identified through our studies, will be employed as we inform strategies for clinical trials with our company ArRETT. Our approach is paradigm-shifting, because it illustrates the power of unbiased modifier screens to discover therapeutic targets, providing proof-of-principle for a modifier approach to be considered for other rare disorders, which currently have no treatment options. The knowledge will impact the health of Canadians by broadly informing clinical outcome of neurological disorders, reducing the financial burden on the health care system.

column36: Synaptic alterations underlying major brain disorders.
column37: BROAD GOALS The overarching theme of this research is to establish the molecular mechanisms by which synaptic transmission is modulated in the CNS and how errors in this process contribute to major brain disorders. We will focus on the process known as long-term depression (LTD), which we will study at synapses within the rodent hippocampus. BACKGROUND Information is stored in the brain via a process known as synaptic plasticity. The two most extensively studied forms of synaptic plasticity are long-term potentiation (LTP) and LTD. Increasing evidence suggests that errors in these processes may cause or contribute to many of the most severe neurological and psychiatric disorders. Our working hypothesis is that the cognitive deficits that are associated with these disorders are due, at least in part, to an exaggerated LTD process. It is now believed that LTD is a normal physiological process that is necessary for synaptic development and for learning and memory throughout the life-span. LTD involves the weakening of synaptic transmission and can lead to physiological synaptic elimination (pruning). We believe that LTD is normally tightly regulated but that in numerous brain disorders this regulation breaks down, due to environmental and or genetic causes. Aggressive LTD may explain the initial cognitive deficits and synapse loss. RESEARCH AIMS 1. Discover the key missing components in the process of hippocampal synaptic plasticity, with a focus on LTD. 2. Determine how hippocampal synaptic plasticity, in particular LTD, becomes altered in rodent models of neurodegenerative, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. 3. Identify new drug targets and develop new compounds with novel actions on synaptic plasticity, as part of the process to develop better treatments for major brain disorders.

column36: Mitochondria are a critical regulator of enteric epithelial-bacteria interaction
column37: The bacteria that colonize the human intestine are a critical determinant of health and susceptibility to disease such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and neurological disorders. The epithelial lining of the gut is the primary point of contact with these bacteria and hence knowing how the epithelium acts as a barrier to exclude the entry of bacteria into the body and how the epithelial cells respond when bacteria penetrate them or cross the epithelial barrier is central to health and well-being. Mitochondria are the cells' power-station, generating the energy needed for the cell to function and are generally described as a discrete organelle - both positions are overly simplified: mitochondria form a complex, dynamic network that remodels by the controlled processes of fission and fusion, and they produce signaling molecules (mainly reactive oxygen species) that direct many cellular events. We showed that epithelial cells with deranged mitochondrial activity have reduced barrier function and actually internalize bacteria: both events have implications for health and disease management. Loss of epithelial barrier function could precipitate local inflammation and potentially sepsis, and bacteria inside the epithelial cells are likely a threat requiring mobilization of immune activity that could result in tissue damage. There is surprisingly little information on how mitochondrial function regulates epithelial-bacteria interaction and how bacterial pathogens or pro-inflammatory signals regulate mitochondrial form and function, particularly fusion and fission: the latter promoting cell death which would contribute to loss of epithelial barrier function. We have developed a novel study with leading edge technologies to precisely examine how mitochondria mould the epithelial-bacterial relationship in the gut. With this knowledge we will be better positioned to advance approaches to maintain digestive health and treat (or cure) gut problems such as IBD.

column36: Investigating Mechanisms for Synapse and Circuit Dynamics using the C. elegans Model
column37: A human brain consists of numerous neurons that communicate with each other. Abnormal communications, caused by inabilities to form structural connections, send or receive signals, or control signal intensity, lead to neurological disorders. Using a small animal model called C. elegans, whose nervous system contains only a few hundred neurons, we have discovered new genes that are critical for either the structural development, or activity tuning of neuronal communication. Through collaboration with other biologists, human geneticists, and neurologists, we have demonstrated that not only do these genes function similarly in other animals, human mutations that cause their functional anomalies lead to neurological disorders. Here we continue to use the C. elegans model to uncover genes and pathways that are critical for brain development and function. A specific question that we aim to address is how development impacts function. Like all animals, we continue to grow after birth. The ability for animals, humans included, to sense signals from the environment, and select and execute meaning motor responses is essential for the viability of both individuals and the specie. This ability, called sensorimotor function, is governed by a nervous system that changes structure and property after birth. How does a nervous system coordinate growth and functionality? We will address this question through comparing the structure and function of neural circuits during development. Applying already acquired insights, we have established C. elegans models for several human neurological disorders, whose cognitive and functional defects have fundamental developmental origins. By applying similar interrogations to these models, our studies will not only shed light on fundamental mechanisms that define the dynamic changes of the nervous systems, but also address the physiological and developmental origins of neurological disorders.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of antibody-mediated QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias
column37: Autoimmune disease affects more than 20 million people in North America. Autoantibodies such as anti-Ro52 are present not only in autoimmune disease patients but also in 0.6-2.7% of the general population. In addition, monoclonal antibody drugs such as rituximab are a fast growing area of drug development with a multi-billion market. Emerging clinical evidence suggests that certain antibodies (e.g. anti-Ro52 and rituximab) can cause a heart electrical disorder called long QT syndrome, and cardiac arrhythmias. The rhythmic heartbeat is controlled by specialized proteins in the cell membrane called ion channels. Among them the potassium channel "hERG" is the common target for various medical conditions. Dysfunction of hERG is the primary cause of medical condition-induced long QT syndrome. We hypothesize that certain antibodies (e.g. anti-Ro52, rituximab) damage hERG function and thus cause long QT syndrome. Our project has three aims. 1. We will determine whether and which specific antibodies impair hERG function in hERG-expressing cell lines as well as in heart cells isolated from neonatal rats. 2. We will perform detailed investigation on how hERG function is impaired by antibodies using state-of-the-art biomedical techniques in hERG-expressing cell culture systems. We will also investigate novel strategies to prevent antibody-mediated impairment of hERG channels. 3. We will induce specific antibodies in a live rabbit model via immunization and verify the idea that the induced antibodies disturb the heart rhythm. We will investigate how to prevent antibody-mediated heart rhythm disturbances using biological and pharmacological approaches. This project reveals a novel cellular pathway that underlies antibody-mediated heart rhythm disturbance, and explores novel means for its prevention and treatment. The novel information will also be important for pharmaceutical companies to develop safer drugs to avoid antibody-drug-induced heart rhythm disorders.

column36: Innovative biomechanical and molecular strategies to fight fibrosis
column37: Different precursor cells are activated to rapidly repair injured tissues. Examples for injury are skin trauma or burn wounds, infarct or chronic overload of the heart, lung epithelium damage, liver infection or alcohol abuse, and kidney damage because of high blood pressure. The activated cells are called myofibroblasts (MFs) because they secrete fibrous collagen matrix ("fibro") that is contracted ("myo") into mechanically stabilizing scar tissue. Although MFs are essential to restoring mechanical integrity of damaged tissue, they never truly regenerate organs and scar formation comes at the cost of reduced organ function. Worse, MF deregulation leads to excessive tissue and organ scarring - a condition called fibrosis. Fibrosis contributes to ~45% of deaths in industrialized nations by causing malfunction and failure of vital organs, such as heart, liver, kidney, lung, and vasculature. Fibrosis promotes tumor progression in the stroma reaction, leads to implant failure in foreign body responses, jeopardizes mesenchymal stem cell therapies by turning stem cells into scar cells and disfigures skin. MFs are key pharmaceutical targets but anti-MF therapies have not yet been translated to clinical treatments of fibrosis. Identifying the joint mechanical and biochemical regulators of MFs, which are incompletely understood, will be essential to promote healing with intervention therapies. Our unrivalled, state-of-the-art research will provide new insights into understanding disease progression, establish novel markers for wound healing therapies, enable the production of innovative technology for use in mechanobiology cell studies, and develop industry-standard drug screening devices. New drug targets, screening tools, biomarker and treatment strategies have tremendous commercial potential/value and will improve the quality of life of fibrosis patients in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) starts with a long "silent" phase during which the disease is present in the brain, but symptoms are minimal. This may explain why up to 200 medications to treat the disease have failed in the last 30 years, as all of them have been introduced "late", missing this early silent phase. Understanding what is happening in the brain during this phase of the disease, and predicting which mildly impaired individuals will progress to AD is crucial to our development of cures. This early period may represent a critical time for pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions intended to halt the progression of the disease or to mitigate symptoms. Many older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or with a subjective complaint decline (SCD) stand in this early stage of the disease. Thus, studying these individuals might provide the precursor markers of AD. This program proposes to identify their brain and clinical symptoms using advanced neuroimaging and cognitive techniques. We have previously found hyperactivation during that stage, i.e., greater brain activation than healthy older adults. We want to better understand this phenomenon, as it may provide insight into how the brain attempts to counteract the effects of neurodegeneration. We will test the hypothesis that hyperactivation is due to intense compensatory neuroplastic processes. We will also follow subjects longitudinally to see if a combination of functional imaging and other measures can accurately predict who will progress to dementia. Finally, we will assess if cognitive training programs can increase neuroplastic compensatory processes during that early phase of AD and identify the optimal program and dose and the type of training that is most adapted to different individuals. If successful, this program will allow for an earlier diagnosis of AD and develop novel approaches to non-pharmacological prevention strategies for older Canadians who are at risk of cognitive decline.

column36: Mechanism for high fat diet-induced activation of MCH neurons and its role in obesity
column37: Obesity is a major health problem worldwide, as it increases the risk for cardiovascular diseases, type II diabetes, certain cancers etc. The main cause of obesity is excess intake of high-calorie food and sedentary lifestyle. As the brain controls food intake and energy expenditure, in particular a region called the hypothalamus, it is important to understand how high fat food affects the hypothalamus to promote weight gain. It has become clear that high fat diet (HFD) induces inflammation of the hypothalamus. Importantly, this inflammation causes excess food intake and obesity. However, how hypothalamic inflammation affects body weight regulation remains poorly understood. One key cell population in the hypothalamus is melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) neurons that promote food intake. Our preliminary study using rodent models suggests that a certain inflammatory mediator (prostaglandin E2; PGE2) is induced by HFD and activates MCH neurons. This results in more food intake and weight gain. Aim 1: We will elucidate the effect of HFD on PGE2 production in the hypothalamus. This will be the first study to investigate the role of hypothalamic PGE2 in diet-induced obesity. Aim 2: Cellular mechanisms underlying HFD-induced changes in MCH neurons will be investigated, with a focus on PGE2 signaling. Aim 3: We will test whether blocking PGE2 signaling in MCH neurons can alleviate diet-induced obesity. The proposed study will explain why HFD-induced inflammation induces obesity. Given the prevalence and impact of obesity on our health and society, it is important to determine the consequences of diet-induced hypothalamic inflammation and discover novel therapeutic targets for obesity.

column36: Ultrasound detection of placental pathology based on hemodynamic pulse wave reflection
column37: The "after-birth" or placenta, connects the developing baby to the inside of the mother's womb to supply it with nourishment and oxygen to stay healthy and grow into a full-term healthy baby. This "placental insufficiency" disease can be difficult for doctors to recognize and as such developing babies are lost to stillbirth. Doctors use ultrasound "scans" to follow baby size and Doppler ultrasound to measure blood flow in the umbilical cord arteries, that connect the developing baby and its placenta. The problem with these Doppler ultrasound scans is that they are not accurate enough to find all babies at risk of stillbirth from placental disease. If we can improve Doppler scans in pregnancy, we can plan the delivery of at risk pregnancies to avoid stillbirth, and when the tests are normal we can let the pregnancy continue normally until natural birth. Our plan for this work is to use pregnant mice where we can reliably produce different types of placental problems and evaluate how the test results change. column36: Neuronal correlates for body-centered and world-centered representations of spatial self-motion
column37: Whether running to catch a ball or turning to reach for a coffee cup, our ability to interact with the environment depends critically on knowing our motion and orientation in space. As we move, the brain combines multiple sensory signals to compute estimates of our motion that we use to maintain balance, navigate, plan actions and maintain clear visual perception. This poses a challenge because different types of motion estimates are required for different tasks. For example, to keep our eyes on target as we move requires estimates of our head motion along axes centered in the head. However, when running to catch a ball, tasks such as estimating our heading direction, maintaining balance as we run, and reaching accurately to grasp the ball require estimates of the axes along which the body is moving and their orientation with respect to gravity. Because no individual sensor provides such estimates they must be computed by transforming and combining information from multiple sensory sources. The aim of this work is to investigate how brain circuits transform and combine multisensory signals (vestibular, proprioceptive) to compute the types of motion estimates that are essential for tasks such as postural control, spatial navigation and voluntary reaching. Despite the importance of these estimates for the majority of tasks we perform every day, our understanding of how and where they are computed and the nature of the motion representations encoded remains rudimentary. Spatial disorientation, balance and dizziness disorders are particularly common in the elderly for whom the result is often loss of balance and falls resulting in significant injury or even death. By providing a better understanding of how the brain computes and uses self-motion estimates for tasks such as navigation, postural control, and goal-directed action it is hoped that this research will lead to improved diagnostic tools and rehabilitative strategies to counteract these debilitating problems.

column36: Regulation of vascular homeostasis and development of vascular diseases: Role of a small GTP-binding protein
column37: The development of cardiovascular diseases such as hypertension, atherosclerosis and heart failure has often been associated with impaired function of cell surface proteins named receptors. These are the targets of more than 50% of all drugs sold today. Blocking the activation of the receptor often results in important sides effects. Therefore, the identification of new intracellular pharmacological targets will allow us to design more effective and specific drugs to treat cardiovascular diseases. For the last 12 years, we have engaged in the study of an intracellular protein that is activated by hormone stimulation. We have shown that this protein named ARF6 is a central regulator of several cellular responses misregulated in cardiovascular diseases. Our findings indicate that this protein could be an interesting new drug target. We propose here to further study its function in cells of the vasculature in order to further demonstrate its key role in responses altered in pathology. In this project, our main goal is to study the function of ARF6 in vascular smooth muscle cells. These constitute the main body of cells in arteries and are responsible for the contractile response. Our main hypothesis is that the intracellular protein ARF6 is a key regulator of the most important vasoactive substance. It is therefore fundamental to delineate and understand the role of ARF6 as a future drug targets in order to minimize adverse effects of newly designed drugs. The first objective of our research project is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which ARF6 regulates the most important cellular responses that are altered in disease. These are complete change of phenotypic features that leads to increase growth, motility and free radicals. Next, we propose to engineer new animal models to study the ARF6 gene in vivo. We will be able to study these animals and understand the role our protein of interest plays in normal physiology but also in disease.

column36: Regulation of antiviral responses by Ras/MEK
column37: Oncolytic viruses are engineered or naturally occurring viruses that replicate in cancer cells, but not in normal cells. They have become a focus of attention for cancer therapy in recent years as clinical studies have shown them to be quite promising. However, the biochemical mechanisms of their tumor selectivity still remain to be studied. In this proposal, we will investigate how one of the oncogenic cell signaling pathways, Ras/MEK, promotes the replication of certain oncolytic viruses in cancer cells. We will investigate how the Ras/MEK pathway inhibits function of interferon regulatory factor (IRF)-1, which is known to block viral replication, resulting in efficient replication of oncolytic viruses in cancer cells. Our study will provide a novel insight into the molecular mechanisms of viral oncolysis as well as the future development of new oncolytic viruses with improved efficacy and safety in treating cancer.

column36: Role of factor XIII-A and plasma fibronectin in etiology of obesity and type 2 diabetes.
column37: Obese fat tissue shows abnormal accumulation of connective tissue components which is a hallmark of fibrosis. Fibrosis of fat tissue limits normal fat storage and fat tissue expansion in obesity and leads to inflammation, increased circulating fat and its accumulation to liver and other tissues. This abnormal fat accumulation pattern is tightly linked to development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Objective of this research proposal is to understand factors that may limit healthy tissue expansion. It focuses on a newly discovered obesity-linked gene, F13A1 (Factor XIIIA transglutaminase) and the how it may contribute to adipose tissue fibrosis and metabolic problems. Our results from cell culture studies suggest that Factor XIIIA normally regulates accumulation of a liver-derived protein fibronectin to fat tissue to increase fat cell numbers. However, plasma fibronectin in fat tissue can also limit cell growth in size and lipid storage and contribute to tissue fibrosis. Our animal studies show that mice that are lacking Factor XIIIA gene do not develop insulin resistance on a high fat diet. Results from lean and obese humans suggest that FXIIIA levels are increased in obesity associate with unhealthy metabolism and signs of pre-diabetes. The project involves a full examination of weight gain, fat tissue function and development of insulin resistance in two mouse models that lack either plasma fibronectin or FXIIIA. We will also investigate if defects in F13A1 gene exist in obese humans and if altered function is linked to unhealthy metabolism. Our work will allow us to better understand the mechanisms how type 2 diabetes develops in obesity. This will open possibilities to create therapeutics that can change the levels and activity of Factor XIIIA and plasma fibronectin in adipose tissue to allow its normal function.

column36: HB-EGF as a central regulator of pancreatic beta-cell proliferation.
column37: One in 10 adults will have diabetes by 2040. The numbers of beta cells in pancreatic islets is insufficient in individuals with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Hence, one therapeutic strategy consists of finding ways to increase beta-cell mass either prior to islet transplantation in type 1 diabetes or in individuals at risk for type 2 diabetes. We have identified a molecular pathway centered on the growth factor HB-EGF that is a potent mediator of beta-cell proliferation. The goal of this research is to determine whether this pathway can be harnessed to expand beta-cell mass. We will pursue three specific objectives. The first objective will be to understand how the HB-EGF pathway contributes to the regulation of beta-cell proliferation. The second objective will be to dissect the action of molecules that negatively affect the HB-EGF pathway. The third objective will be to examine its role in beta cells under physiological (pregnancy) and pathological (high-fat diet) metabolic stress conditions. To complete this study we will make use of the expertise existing in our lab after more than 15 years of beta-cell research as well as specialized platforms in the institute. This project will further our understanding of the control of beta-cell proliferation and open novel avenues for diabetes therapy.

column36: The impact of host-pathogen interactions on cell-mediated immunity
column37: Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) is critical for control of many globally relevant infections and diseases such as hepatitis C virus, HIV and cancers. Approaches aimed at understanding and enhancing CMI will have a profound impact on improving our health. However, we currently do not fully understand how these cells function, which have prevented researchers from successfully harnessing the therapeutic potential of CMI. A specialized immune cell that plays an essential role in CMI by killing infected and cancerous cells are CD8 T cells. These cells protect us from infection, but they can also cause disease such as autoimmunity if they are not properly regulated. Our laboratory studies how the environment impacts CD8 T cell function. Our previous results have shown that cytokines (small proteins produced following infection) can influence regulatory pathways by changing how a CD8 T cell functions. New data being generated in our laboratory suggest that certain pathogens can take advantage of these regulatory pathways to weaken CD8 T cell function and establish chronic infection within the host. We propose studies centered on understanding how pathogens can alter the biology of CD8 T cells thus providing us with the knowledge of which pathways can be targeted for therapeutic intervention. These therapeutic targets would aim to reduce the function of CD8 T cells in a situation where they cause disease (e.g. autoimmunity or transplant rejection) and increase their function in a situation where they do not function properly (e.g. chronic infection or cancer). The data being generated in our laboratory will also help develop novel vaccination approaches. CMI is our defense against invading pathogens and debilitating diseases. Increasing our understanding of how the immune system works will provide insight into how to effectively control and eliminate infections and devastating diseases such as HIV, multiple sclerosis and cancers.

column36: Identifying new therapeutic opportunities by elucidating the physical protein complexes and pathways driving invasion in malaria parasites
column37: Malaria causes devastation and misery worldwide responsible for the deaths of 500,000 every year. Despite its terrifying impact, few drugs are available and resistance is emerging. New therapeutics are urgently needed. To lay the foundation for drug discovery programs, global initiatives have revealed thousands of proteins that help the Plasmodium parasite (the etiological agent of malaria) infect its human host. The challenge is to identify those that play the most important roles in infection and may therefore be targeted for therapeutic intervention. Proteins do not work in isolation; instead they form components of highly complex molecular machineries such as protein complexes or biochemical pathways. Understanding how the proteins are organized within the context of these machines allows the identification of those that play the most critical roles. Here we propose a sophisticated biochemical separation strategy to build a global roadmap that describes how parasite proteins work together as molecular machines to allow the parasite to invade host cells and disseminate to other hosts. Through pilot funding from CIHR, we have already constructed a draft map for a related parasite Toxoplasma - providing a wealth of novel information on the processes that allow these parasites to infect and cause disease. Over the next five years, we will capitalize on this initial investment to construct high quality roadmaps for Plasmodium. Exploiting these maps, we will identify parasite proteins that are essential for infection. Working with colleagues at the forefront of drug development, our findings will translate directly into drug screening pipelines that attempt to identify novel anti-parasitic therapeutics.

column36: Understanding bacterial ribosome biogenesis to enable antimicrobial discovery
column37: Emergence of antibiotic resistance among organisms responsible for infectious disease has outpaced new antibiotic development posing a serious health problem in Canada and globally. Significant efforts must be focused on developing new antibiotics if we are to avoid the return to a pre-antibiotic era of healthcare, when infection control did not exist - people at the mercy of microbes, the elderly dying from pneumonia, more children dying in infancy and treatments such as heart surgery or chemotherapy no longer possible. This proposal focuses on the assembly process of the bacterial ribosome. Ribosomes are essential enzymes for all bacteria, including major pathogens for humans. They are complex molecular nanomachines made up of over 50 components that synthesize all proteins in the cell. Their assembly pathway has tremendous potential but that has not been explored as a target for antimicrobials. We propose to determine the function of three essential proteins RbgA, YphC and YsxC, which precise molecular functions in the maturation of the ribosome remain to be elucidated. We will use an electron microscope to directly image these proteins to gain insights into how they work and how they interact with assembling ribosomal particles. Recent advances in electron microscope instrumentation provide an opportunity to see these structures at high resolution. Our work promises to give an unprecedented view of this essential bacterial enzyme. In addition, RbgA is widely distributed and homologs are found also in eukaryotes (including humans). Therefore, the proposed work will inform on ribosome assembly not only in bacteria but also in humans. Importantly, recent work has highlighted the importance of defective ribosome assembly in the development of blood cancers. Thus our work may also have relevance for development of cancer treatments.

column36: Defining the Roles of the Overgrowth Syndrome Genes NSD1, Setd2 and EZH2 in Shaping the Epigenome and Transcriptome in Early Embryonic Development
column37: Human overgrowth disorders such as Sotos syndrome are characterized by pre- and postnatal increased growth, intellectual disability and facial anomalies. These diseases result from mutations in genes that encode enzymes that turn off other genes by changing the structure of DNA. These genes include NSD1, most frequently mutated in Sotos Syndrome patients, and SETD2. Both encoded enzymes chemically modify a specific amino acid on a specific protein associated with DNA called histone H3. Other patients with overgrowth syndromes have mutations in the gene Dnmt3a, which encodes an enzyme that chemically modifies the DNA itself. Interestingly, the modifications of histone H3 influences the activity of the protein that modifies the DNA, as well as that of another protein, EZH2, which chemically modifies histone H3.The ezh2 gene is mutated in the related overgrowth disorder called Weaver Syndrome. These observations suggest "cross-talk" between these enzymes and in turn the genes they regulate. However, a systematic study of the consequences of disrupting these regulatory proteins has not been conducted. Here, using the mouse as a model system, we will study the interplay between these enzymes and the marks they deposit, by mutating these "overgrowth syndrome genes" in the mouse and studying the consequences of such mutations in the early mouse embryo, where these genes are first active. This "genome-wide" study, using state-of-the-art sequencing technology and mouse genetics, will lead to a better understanding of the molecular basis of several human overgrowth syndromes including Sotos and Weaver, potentially leading to new avenues for treatment of these diseases.

column36: Evaluating the Potential of ACE Inhibitors in Alzheimer's Disease
column37: AD is the most common cause of dementia in the aging population for which there is no cure. Recently, studies have reported a significant reduction in the incidence of AD among some subjects taking ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs). Both ACE (Angiotensin Converting Enzyme) and the Angiotensin Receptor (AR) are part of the renin-angiotensin system known to regulate blood pressure. Why ACE inhibitors & ARBs are beneficial in AD and why some patients benefit from the drug while others do not, is completely unknown although studies have demonstrated that it is unrelated to effects on blood pressure. What is clear is that unraveling the mechanisms of action of ACE inhibitors & ARBs would provide insight into which patients could benefit from these drugs and have immediate impact on the treatment of this devastating disease. Drosophila has proven to be an excellent model system to study neurodegenerative diseases. The short life span of flies coupled with powerful genetic approaches has made it possible to generate models of disease that faithfully recapitulate many features observed in patients. Once a model has been generated it can also be used to rapidly evaluate the effectiveness of various drugs. We have established several models of AD in Drosophila and shown that these flies exhibit progressive neurodegeneration and defects in synaptic plasticity and memory. We have also shown that ACE inhibitors & ARBs can suppress many of these defects. Our goal is to take advantage of these fly models to: 1) Evaluate the therapeutic potential of these drugs; and, 2) Determine how these drugs work by identifying their molecular and cellular targets. Altogether, these studies will determine the mechanism by which ACE inhibitors and ARBs are effective in AD and which patients are most likely to benefit from this novel therapy.

column36: Acute Lung Injury - Directions from Therapeutic Hypercapnia
column37: Patients with injured lungs usually require admission to intensive care. If they require mechanical ventilation to help with their breathing, their mortality is high - about 40%. Carbon dioxide (CO2) is commonly elevated in such patients. We discovered that deliberately raising CO2 in experimental settings can protect against injury (but in some circumstances it can cause harm). Because of the mixed effects -but strong potential for benefit- understanding the molecular mechanisms of protection might enable enable patients to receive selective therapy (i.e. likely to help, unlikely to cause harm). We have recently discovered two distinct mechanisms (i.e., molecular pathways), one termed 'sheddase', which is inhibited by CO2; the other termed vitamin E transporter protein, which is induced by CO2. Because CO2 exerts much of its benefit via either of these mechanisms, in this proposal we outline how exploiting each of these 'pathways' will likely enable the design of 'individualized' therapy for critically ill patients with injured lungs.
