column36: Assessing the site and mechanism of Parkinson's disease initiation in vivo
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is an age-related movement disorder whose familiar features of tremor and rigidity result from the loss of neurons in characteristic regions of the brain. There is a growing body of evidence that these symptoms are preceded by other abnormalities that may arise decades before the movement issues become obvious. Notable amongst these abnormalities are a diminished sense of smell and persistent constipation, which are attributable to a loss of function of neurons in the nose and gut respectively. It has been postulated that PD is actually initiated at these sites by the exposure of neurons to some environmental agent (viruses or pesticides, for example) which promotes misfolding of a critical protein in susceptible individuals. The misfolded protein (alpha synuclein) may aggregate and spread from one neuron to another and act as a template to promote the misfolding of additional molecules of alpha synuclein. Over the course of decades the misfolding problem may reach the brain, having traversed neuronal connections from the distant sites of disease initiation. If true, this mechanism would provide a large window of opportunity for interventions to delay or eliminate the disease. We propose to test the hypothesis using a mouse line that we have created specifically for this purpose. We have engineered this line such that the aggregation of the misfolded protein generates a fluorescent signal that can be detected by microscopy. We will use known genetic or environmental triggers to initiate the process, and determine where in the gut or nasal lining the fluorescence is first detected. We will follow the fluorescent signal over time and determine if there is spread to the brain. We will also use clinical samples to determine whether the forms of misfolded alpha synuclein that are present in subtypes of human neurodegenerative disease initiate spread in our mouse model.

column36: Role and therapeutic potential of RGS16 in pancreatic beta cells.
column37: One in 10 adults will have diabetes by 2040. Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is by far the predominant form and affects more than 3M Canadians. The root to addressing this major public health challenge will be the identification of the major, druggable molecular players, a prerequisite to the design of more effective therapeutic strategies. The secretion of insulin from the beta cell in pancreatic islets is deficient in individuals with T2D. Hence, one therapeutic strategy consists of finding ways to increase functional beta-cell mass in T2D. We have identified a protein known to play a role in modulating signals inside the cell in other tissues, called RGS16, as a regulator of insulin secretion and beta-cell proliferation. The goal of this research is to elucidate the role and evaluate the benefits of targeting RGS16 in beta cells for the treatment of T2D. We will pursue three specific objectives. The first objective will be to ascertain the mechanism of RGS16 action in the regulation of insulin secretion and beta-cell proliferation. The second objective will be to examine its role in beta cells under physiological (pregnancy) and pathological (high-fat diet) metabolic stress conditions. The third objective will be to assess whether targeting RGS16 to increase its activity in the beta cell is a potential therapeutic strategy for the treatment of T2D. To complete this study we will make use of the expertise existing in our lab after more than 30 years of beta-cell research as well as specialist platforms in the institute. This project will further our understanding of the control of insulin secretion and beta-cell proliferation and open novel avenues for T2D therapy.

column36: Multilayer Hybrid Biomaterial for Treatment of Diabetic Foot Ulcers
column37: The risk of toe or foot amputation in infected wounds is 20 times higher for diabetic people. Diabetics also have a 66% greater chance to die within the first year following amputation. In Canada, the cost of treating diabetic foot ulcers will be $7.6 billion by 2024, and it will take the lives of hundreds of thousands of Canadians. Diabetic foot ulcers are difficult to treat because of infection, inflammation and poor wound healing. Current therapies do not treat all 3 of these problems at the same time. In this project, we will develop a new treatment for diabetic foot ulcers that will simultaneously kill bacteria, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. We have designed nanosilver that can eliminate infection and reduce inflammation, but is safe for human cells. The nanosilver formulation will be directly sprayed onto the wound as a thin layer. This will then be covered by a gel made of collagen containing small skin columns. The skin columns are taken from healthy areas of the patient's body. The skin column and gel mixture will promote wound healing and skin regeneration. This therapy has the potential to reduce the amputation rate in patients with diabetic foot ulcers, thus greatly improving the quality of life of diabetics in Canada and abroad.

column36: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of Natural Killer cell-mediated vascular remodeling in pulmonary arterial hypertension
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a fatal disease that preferentially targets young women in their 30s and 40s. PAH involves a loss of blood vessels in the lung. This loss leads to increased stress on the right side of the heart and eventual death due to heart failure. Although there is a well-appreciated link between PAH and immune disorders, there is currently little understanding of how changes in the immune system lead to disease in the lung vasculature. Our previous research has shown that particular immune cells, known as Natural Killer (NK) cells, are impaired in PAH patients and animal models of disease. We have also found that genetically modified mice lacking either NK cells or a specific molecule on the surface of NK cells both develop PAH. The current project will use these mouse models, as well as NK cells from PAH patients, to determine exactly how NK cell impairment contributes to disease. This work will focus on identifying the proteins that NK cells use to regulate blood vessel structure in health and disease. Recent studies have also shown that NK cells in humans are diverse. The specific subsets of NK cells that regulate blood vessels will also be identified. Despite the approval of several new treatments, the the annual mortality rate of PAH remains high (~15%), in-line with that of stage 3 breast cancer. This poor survival is linked to the fact that available therapies primarily treat the symptoms of PAH and do not address the underlying factors driving disease progression. Such treatments are also extremely expensive, placing a large burden on the Canadian health care system. The proposed work will help to clarify the role of NK cells in PAH, with the goal of developing new treatments for this devastating disease.

column36: Advancing Mental Health Care by Improving the Delivery of Therapist-guided, Internet-delivered Cognitive Behavioural Therapy in Clinical Practice
column37: Depression and anxiety are prevalent and disabling conditions that often go untreated. Internet-delivered Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (ICBT) is a relatively new approach to treatment that is a convenient way for patients to access care. ICBT is highly standardized and involves patients reviewing weekly lessons over the Internet. Patients also receive brief weekly support from a therapist via secure emails or phone calls. Past research shows that ~75% of patients complete ICBT and report large symptom improvements. Although these results are very promising, research also suggests that ICBT could potentially be improved by being more personalized in terms of treatment duration and amount of therapist contact, especially for clients with more severe symptoms. We will conduct three studies to evaluate personalized ICBT. The first trial will involve therapists who work in a clinic that specializes in ICBT. Over 18 months, we will randomize 440 patients with depression and/or anxiety to either receive standardized (5 lessons completed in 8 weeks; weekly therapist contact) or personalized ICBT (5 lessons; personalized duration and therapist contact). In the second study, 440 patients will be treated by therapists working in five community mental health clinics in Saskatchewan. We will compare outcomes of 220 patients treated with standardized ICBT in one year to outcomes of 220 patients treated with personalized ICBT the following year. In both trials, we will compare patients who receive personalized and standardized ICBT on outcome measures, intervention usage, satisfaction measures and costs. In the third study, we will interview therapists and managers to learn about strengths and challenges of delivering personalized ICBT. The research will ultimately advance how ICBT is used in clinical practice and is expected to lead to improvements in mental health outcomes and mental health care delivery.

column36: Osteocalcin-driven metabolic changes in osteogenesis imperfecta
column37: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) is an inherited disorder in which the gene for a key structural molecule in bone (type I collagen) is mutated, resulting in brittle bones that fracture easily. Our clinical studies have shown that children with OI, even with the mildest forms, have slow growth and low muscle mass, which to date remain largely unexplained and untreated. It has been recently discovered that bone cells produce a hormone osteocalcin that can affect energy balance in the whole body. We hypothesize that since OI patients have abnormal activity of bone cells, their osteocalcin levels may be affected. In fact, in experimental OI in mice with mutation in collagen type I, we observed a 2-fold increase in osteocalcin. Since such change in hormonal status can affect the function of the whole body, we propose to examine how OI mice produce and utilize energy and how these differences may affect bone and muscle function as well as overall growth. We will also examine if children with severe OI have differences in their metabolism and body temperature compared to control population. A better understanding of the systemic consequences of collagen type I mutations obtained in this study will help to address compromised growth and low muscle mass in OI patients and to improve the care of children with OI.

column36: Tumour Acidification Treatment: Optimization using pH-Weighted MRI
column37: Cancer remains the leading cause of death in Canada and more effective treatments are needed. There are many different types of cancer, but cancer cells share hallmark physiological features that can be exploited to selectively induce cell death. For example, aggressive cancer cells produce energy from sugar differently than normal cells, generating a high concentration of acidic metabolites. But cancer cells have developed ways to remove these acidic metabolites, making them alkaline. Drugs that acidify the cancer cells can induce cell death. Many drugs already approved for use in humans may acidify cancer cells. We have preliminary data showing that three such examples work in a mouse model of aggressive brain cancer. Combining drugs is expected to produce an even greater effect that could provide a new treatment approach. In the past, optimizing such a treatment paradigm was difficult because there was not a good method available to measure the acidity of the tumour. However we have developed a method to measure tumour cell acidity using magnetic resonance imaging. As a result we have a method that could be used to effectively optimize this new treatment approach. The overall goal is to optimize acidification treatment in the most aggressive type of brain cancer. We will show that show that making the cancer cells acidic will reduce tumour size and the more acidic we make them, the more effective the treatment. We will show that combining drugs that affect different cell mechanisms will be more effective than using only one drug. And we will show that feeding the cancer sugar along with the drugs will also lead to a greater reduction in tumour size. All this work will be completed in several different animal models of brain cancer. Optimization of tumour acidification treatment could provide a new approach to control the growth of the most aggressive and fatal brain cancer.

column36: Regulation of receptor mobility and spatial organization: Key factors in B cell activation
column37: Activated B cells make antibodies that protect against infection. However, people with autoimmune diseases make antibodies that attack parts of their own body. Hence the ability to modulate B cell activation has significant implications for health and disease. Each B cell has B cell receptor (BCR) proteins on its surface that determine what molecule it responds to (i.e. the antigen). Binding of antigen to the BCR triggers intracellular signals that cause B cell activation and antibody production. However even in the absence of antigen, the BCR continually generates a low-level of antigen-independent "tonic" signaling. The strength of this tonic BCR signaling determines whether a B cell is in a resting, partially activated (primed), or activated state prior to encountering antigen. We showed that bacterial components drive B cells into a primed state in which they are more sensitive to antigen and need less to become activated. Understanding how B cells become primed in this way may help us design better vaccines. Conversely, B cells from autoimmune patients are hyperactive and may require little or no antigen to become activated and make damaging antibodies. Reverting these cells to a resting state could prevent autoimmunity. Our project builds on new ideas about how BCR signaling is controlled by the movement and organization of the BCR within the cell membrane. To signal, BCRs must form clusters with each other, interact with other membrane proteins that organize signaling machinery, and move away from negative regulators. New advances in microscopy have allowed us to visualize the movement and clustering of the BCR in the membrane, as well as its interactions with positive and negative regulators. Our goal is to elucidate how BCR mobility, organization, and interactions are controlled, and how this determines the strength of tonic BCR signaling. This may suggest new ways to modulate B cell activation in order to improve vaccines and prevent autoimmunity.

column36: Analysis of the Anabolic Activity of Hormones Regulating Skeletal Metabolism
column37: One of the most common causes of disability and death during aging is metabolic bone disease, which includes osteoporosis, bone disease due to cancer, hyperparathyroidism, and osteomalacia. We are studying three major hormones, parathyroid hormone (PTH), PTH related peptide (PTHrP), and vitamin D which regulate normal bone metabolism, but can also contribute to the development and progression of metabolic bone disease. Calcium itself can act as a hormone by interacting with a calcium sensing receptor (CaSR), which has been identified in several tissues including parathyroid (which produces PTH), kidney and bone. Activation of CaSR can lower PTH and CaSR activators, called calcimimetics have been developed to control hyperparathyroidism. Although continuously high levels of blood PTH, as occur in hyperparathyroidism, can destroy (resorb) bone (producing "catabolic" effects), in contrast, intermittent PTH administration forms bone (an "anabolic" effect) and is therefore used in osteoporosis therapy. Vitamin D has also been reported to have both anabolic and catabolic effects on bone but the precise mechanism is also unclear. Wnt is a growth factor which is a potent stimulator of bone formation, and can be inhibited by a bone-derived protein called sclerostin. Our goal is to understand how PTH, PTHrP and vitamin D exert their anabolic effects on bone. We will use genetically modified mouse models to examine the ways PTH and PTHrP act to form bone, determine if CaSR activation can influence the anabolic effects of PTH on bone, and determine if vitamin D stimulates bone by interacting with sclerostin. These studies should improve our understanding of how these hormones influence bone, and how to develop improved anabolic therapies for important diseases of the skeleton.

column36: Determining the role of histone modifications in mediating transcriptional consistency in beta-cells and in diabetes pathogenesis
column37: During the development of type 2 diabetes immune cell induced inflammation and metabolic stress induce insulin secreting beta-cells to lose their normal functionality. In part this is because the beta-cells have reduced levels or critical genes that help maintain them as fully functional cells. Restoring the levels of these critical genes can restore beta-cell functionality and is a possible therapeutic approach to treating type 2 diabetes. Despite this the mechanisms by which the levels of these factors become reduced in beta-cells during T2D progression is not clear. Our recent data shows that the structure of the chromatin around these genes plays a key role in regulating their expression, which dictates the levels they are present in in the cell. Specifically, we have found a unique type of modification that can occur to the chromatin can help reduce the variability of a genes expression in different cells, as genes with these modifications have reduced cell to cell variability than genes that do not have it. However, we find that in patients with T2D genes with these modifications become just as variably expressed as genes without these modifications. This not only results in an overall reduction in the levels of these genes in the beta-cells of T2D patients, but also means that some beta-cells exist in these patients with much lower levels than the average. We believe these cells become highly dysfunctional, and are a critical component of how T2D progresses. In this work we intend to determine how age and T2D increase transcriptional variability in beta-cells in both mouse models and in humans. We will assess whether these factors directly affect the chromatin modifications we believe control gene expression variability, and generate mouse models to understand the role these modifications play in maintaining normal gene expression. This work stands to generate significant novel insight into T2D progression, and may implicate novel therapeutic approaches.

column36: Dissecting NF1 signaling in melanoma
column37: Unlike the majority of cancers where the rate of newly diagnosed cases and deaths are declining, melanoma rates have been increasing significantly in both men and women. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in Canada, and in 2015, melanoma was responsible for 70% of skin cancer-related deaths. Much progress has been made in the development of treatment options for melanoma patients based on basic science discoveries. For example, from focused gene sequencing studies, we know melanoma is caused by mutations in two genes, BRAF and NRAS, that lead to uncontrolled growth of melanocytes in about 70% of patients. These findings led to the development of targeted therapies, so-called "smart drugs", designed against BRAF and targeting NRAS in an indirect way. Unfortunately, many patients that are given these "smart drugs" eventually develop resistance. Furthermore, targeted therapy options for patients that lack BRAF and NRAS mutations are limited. In contrast, other immune-based therapy that harness the power of a patient's immune system have shown incredible clinical utility for melanoma patients. However, over 50% of melanoma patients do not have durable long-term responses to immune therapy. It is still unclear why some patients respond to immune therapy and why others do not. With the advent of next generation sequencing technology, we recently gained the ability to sequence all genes in many melanoma patient samples. Our studies revealed half of patients that lack mutations in BRAF and NRAS possess mutations in a gene called NF1. However, it is still unclear how we can use this information in the clinic to treat patients. Our preliminary work suggests that NF1 regulates components of the immune system that may have implications for immune therapy response. The goal of this project is to understand how NF1 promotes melanoma and modulates the response to immune therapy, as well as to develop novel therapeutic strategies to treat this melanoma subtype.

column36: Does Mechanopluripotency Enhance the Derivation and Expansion of Naive Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells?
column37: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer huge potential for regenerative medicine. Being pluripotent, they can be differentiated to any cell or tissue in the body. Pluripotency is one component of stemness; the other is the ability to self-renew. In order to meet the anticipated demand for high quality iPSCs, we have been developing bioprocesses for expanding them as aggregates in computer controlled vessels called stirred suspension bioreactors (imagine a smaller version of an upright washing machine). Recently we made international headlines when we demonstrated that we could generate mouse iPSCs 1000-fold more efficiently in bioreactors compared to static culture. Our research has led us to the discovery of a new phenomenon, mechanopluripotency, wherein mechanical forces caused by bioreactor stirring promote pluripotency. In this project, we plan to study if mechanopluripotency occurs in human iPSCs and if it can be used to improve and standardize hiPSC expansion culture. Our study focuses on the newly characterize naive hiPSCs, which more closely resemble their mouse counterpart. We will determine if mechanopluripotency operates in naive hiPSCs and by what mechanism. We will determine if mechanopluripotency allows hiPSC expansion without a requirement for pluripotency maintenance factors and chemical inhibitors. This move will not only lower iPSC expansion costs, it will also increase cell quality since inhibitors are suspected to have negative consequences on quality. Finally, we will determine if mechanopluripotency allows the efficient derivation of hiPSCs in bioreactors, a goal which has previously eluded us.

column36: Molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern the development of cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM)
column37: Cerebral Cavernous Malformations (CCM, also referred to as Cavernous Angiomas) are dilations that form mainly in the blood vessels of the brain. CCM are surprisingly common, with roughly 0.5% (1 in 200) of the population having at least one such lesion. CCM result in leaky vessels that can lead to symptoms ranging from a mild headache to seizure and even hemorrhagic stroke. A CCM diagnosis can only be achieved at present via detailed MRI, something a patient would not have until the symptoms have become very severe. The only "treatment" available at present is surgical removal of CCM, however in severe cases lesions are either not accessible to surgery or they are too numerous to remove. Because CCM are diagnosed late, we do not understand how they first arise and then develop to full-blown leaky lesions. This knowledge is critical to designing therapies that can prevent worsening or new development of CCM in patients or people from at-risk families. To address this, we will use complementary approaches in roundworm (C. elegans) and vertebrate (zebrafish) animal models to dissect the events that lead to CCM. C. elegans is a genetic powerhouse, which has been used to discover many genetic pathways that regulate human development and disease, notably cancer. Zebrafish have a brain vasculature much like our own, and as their embryos are transparent, we can use microscopy to watch the vasculature at high resolution as disease develops in real time. Using C. elegans and zebrafish, we will uncover the key players in CCM disease progression, identify what goes wrong in vascular cells in CCM, and examine the ability of different interventions to stop CCM onset and progression. This will lay the foundation for future clinical work aimed at preventing severe neurological damage in patients suffering from CCM.

column36: Reactivation of occult hepadnaviral infection and hepatitis in the woodchuck model of hepatitis B
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) belongs to the most deadly human microbes. It causes life-threatening liver diseases, such as chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis and liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). More than 2 billion people (~1/3 of global population) show evidence of HBV infection, while 240-370 million have symptomatic chronic hepatitis B of which up to one million die annually. In Canada, ~270,000 individuals have chronic hepatitis B. We discovered that, in addition to symptomatic infection, HBV in humans and woodchuck hepatitis virus (WHV) in woodchucks cause asymptomatic (occult) chronic infection that can also culminate in development of HCC. This occult infection under certain conditions, like immunosuppression or anti-cancer therapy, can reactivate and cause sever hepatitis, liver failure and death. The mechanisms of this reactivation are unknown. Because HBV infects only humans and higher primates and the caused liver disease cannot be studied in cultured cells, the use of an appropriate animal model is essential. We developed a unique research facility at Memorial University in which woodchucks susceptible to WHV infection are studied. We also devised models of occult HBV infection in woodchucks. In this study, we want to reactivate occult infection in woodchucks by commonly used drugs, such as dexamethasone (corticosteroid) and a drug against rheumatoid arthritis and B cell lymphoma. We want to identify factors that predispose to development of severe hepatitis in occult infection and molecular mechanisms involved. By doing so, we can learn how to predict if reactivation may occur and what to do to prevent it. Also, the preclinical model for testing of new drugs for their HBV reactivation abilities will be established. In addition, we will learn about mechanisms of reactivation of other silent (latent) viral infections which complicate current treatments.

column36: Improving Clinical Decision Making for Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects 1 in 10 Canadian adults, and can lead to kidney failure requiring dialysis. In most cases, CKD remains stable, and can be safely managed by a family doctor. However, for some patients, it can progress quickly and needs specialist care. In 2011, we developed an equation that accurately identifies patients at the highest risk of progression. We are now proposing national studies that will test how our equation can be integrated in patient care. First, we want family doctors to use the equation to talk to their patients about their risk of kidney failure and how to reduce it. Doctors will use the equation to determine whether a patient needs to see a kidney specialist or not. Second, we want kidney specialists to use the equation to plan for dialysis or transplantation, but only for patients at the highest risk of kidney failure. These studies will help ensure patients are involved in making health care decisions with their doctor and will help provide clinical care specific to each patient. In the next 5 years, these studies will transform care for CKD in Canada and beyond our borders.

column36: Predicting the onset of bipolar disorder: A longitudinal high-risk study
column37: Bipolar disorder is a severe psychiatric illness that runs in families and onsets in adolescence - a critical time of brain and emotional development. Bipolar disorder is likely the result of a number of susceptibility genes triggered by exposure to multiple social, psychological, and biological risk factors. This proposal builds on prior funded research and requests funds to study the most promising risk factors that may be amenable to treatment in adolescent and young adult high-risk offspring of parents confirmed to have bipolar disorder over a 5-year period. At the end of this study, we will be able to develop a predictive model - a first of its kind - that will estimate the likelihood and timing of illness in individuals with variable sets of risk factors. This information will improve identification of individuals at familial risk who are most likely to develop mood disorders and advance the development of specific innovative preventative and early intervention approaches. Ultimately, this work will result in a major leap forward in understanding genetically-mediated causal pathways leading to bipolar disorder and help to change the trajectory of this illness through informing strategies to prevent onset and progression.

column36: Small nucleolar RNAs as regulators of gene expression
column37: Small RNAs form several large families of biomolecules emerging as essential regulators of fundamental cellular processes. While miRNAs, a large family of cytoplasmic small RNAs regulating transcript stability on widespread levels, have been extensively characterized, nuclear small RNAs are also emerging as fundamental regulators performing varied roles. The conserved family of small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a group of such nuclear small RNAs. SnoRNAs have been well-characterized as guiding the chemical modification of ribosomal RNAs, an important step in ribosome biogenesis and ultimately in protein synthesis. However, over the past 5 years, many independent reports have identified specific snoRNAs as involved in diverse other functions ranging from the maturation of pre-messenger RNAs to the response to stress in the cytoplasm. By analysis of deep-sequencing datasets of small RNAs of several human cell lines, we identified groups of snoRNAs differing in terms of their protein binding preferences and terminal sequences, suggesting they could play different regulatory roles in the cell. In light of these recent findings, we propose to characterise specific families and subgroups of small RNAs and to define their role in the regulation of essential nuclear processes, using computational and experimental methods. Many small RNAs display significantly deregulated expression in cancer and a subset have been shown to play an important role in cancer development and maintenance. column37: Bariatric (weight loss) surgery is the most effective treatment for extreme obesity, but surgery does not treat underlying psychological and behavioural issues. Objective: This study will examine if adding a convenient and accessible psychotherapy by phone one year after surgery will lead to increased weight loss two years after surgery. Primary Hypothesis: Relative to the Control group (who will get routine care), the group of individuals who get psychotherapy will have lower weights 2 years after surgery. Secondary Hypotheses: Relative to the Control group, the psychotherapy group will report significantly less maladaptive eating behaviours and medical burden, and significantly greater quality of life. Method: Participants recruited from the Bariatric Surgery Programs at Toronto Western Hospital and Humber River Hospital will be randomly assigned to 1 of 2 groups: 1) Control (Usual Standard of Care) or 2) Tele-CBT (a 7-session telephone-based cognitive behavioural therapy [a type of "talk therapy"] intervention focused on developing coping skills to improve maladaptive thoughts, emotions, and eating behaviours, specifically designed for bariatric surgery patients, delivered 1 year post-surgery). They will have their weight measured and will complete measures of eating behaviour and quality of life prior to the intervention, and again at several time points extending to 2 years post-surgery. Implications: If Tele-CBT is found to improve bariatric surgery outcomes, it could become the standard of care in Canadian bariatric surgery programs and beyond, and be routinely offered to patients who cannot feasibly attend CBT sessions due to physical or practical barriers.

column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) affect 1 in 150 Canadians, one of the highest incidences worldwide. Our working hypotheses are that (i) moderate UV exposure produces molecules that act to reinforce immune signaling by the AhR in peripheral organs, and (ii) that AhR signaling induced by cutaneous UV exposure influences the microbial composition of the intestine. column37: Women who had gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) during pregnancy are at high risk of future type 2 diabetes, which can be prevented with lifestyle programs that improve diet and physical activity. column36: Activation of Pyruvate Kinase M2 as a Novel Therapy for Chemotherapy-Induced Cardiotoxicity
column37: Chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity (CIC) is a very common complication of many anti-cancer agents and although cancer therapies maybe suppressing tumor growth, these patients begin to develop heart failure. Therefore, a better understanding of the signalling pathways involved in CIC are desperately needed, as there are currently no therapies that prevent the onset of this condition and most patients eventually die of either cancer or heart failure. One of the challenges in designing appropriate therapies to prevent CIC is selectively protecting the heart without preventing the benefits of cancer therapies against tumors. An intriguing difference between the heart and the tumor environments are the levels of oxygen (the molecule we breathe and required for life). The heart is present in an area of high oxygen levels, while the tumor can survive in areas of low oxygen. Therefore, screening for oxygen-sensitive proteins that may be induced by CIC agents in the heart may provide targetable therapies that are selective to the heart, without interfering with the anti-cancer effects of promising cancer therapies in the tumor. We have identified a candidate oxygen-sensitive protein called pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) that is induced in the heart by CIC agents. Intriguingly, drugs that activate PKM2 has previously been shown to suppress tumor growth, however, PKM2 function in the heart remains elusive. We show that activating PKM2 in the heart, where oxygen levels are high protects against CIC, but maintains and in some cases even enhances cancer therapy-mediated regression of the tumor, where oxygen levels are low. The therapeutic implications of this project may provide drug discovery platforms that could directly prevent CIC, which are desperately needed, but may also be applicable to other metabolic pathologies, including other forms of heart failure, cancer and diabetes.

column36: Mechanism of Ribosomal RNA Gene Silencing and Its Roles in Pluripotency and Cancer
column37: Building the cell's protein factories is a complex job involving many hundreds of components and takes up much of a cell's efforts to grow. For cancers to grow, they must find ways to make more of these protein factories than surrounding normal tissues. So, if we could find ways to limit the manufacture the protein factories, known as ribosomes, we could control cancer. In fact, we have recently demonstrated that targeting the genes that make the RNAs of the ribosome kills cancer cells while leaving normal cells untouched. Several "tumour suppressor" proteins prevent cancer by doing just this. For example, the ARF and TP53 tumour suppressors are very important in limiting ribosome production and either or both are inactivated in 80% of cancers. We recently discovered that highly proliferative cancer cells show an unusual "epigenetic silencing" of the Ribosomal RNA genes. Epigenetic silencing is one means by which genes are selectively inactivated to establish different tissues such as skin, bone, blood, intestine, etc. We found that silencing of the Ribosomal RNA genes is lost in some cancer cells and closely resembles the situation in the embryonic stem cells that will create all the different tissues of the body. We discovered some years ago that the ARF tumour suppressor regulates a protein called TTF1. This protein is known to determine epigenetic silencing of the Ribosomal RNA genes. We hypothesize that the changes in ribosomal RNA gene silencing may allow pre-cancerous cells to grow rapidly, but more importantly cause the type of chromosome rearrangements that lead to full-blown cancer. Our lab. is trying to understand how this happens in the hope of discovering novel and more effective ways of treating cancer.

column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common genetic disorder affecting children and young adults in Canada. While life expectancy for CF patients has improved in recent decades, recurrent and persistent infections are major causes of lung function decline that ultimately lead to death. New treatments are becoming available that can slow the long term rate of decline in lung function. However, conventional breathing tests often look normal in young patients with early CF lung disease and cannot be used reliably to determine if the treatment is working. Therefore, the medical community needs tests that can better assess the lungs of young CF patients, especially to follow the effects of treatment. A picture taken of the lungs, or medical imaging test, would allow doctors to see and properly treat the lungs of children with CF at an early stage, before disease is severe. X-ray imaging is one such approach but is generally not able to measure the effects of CF treatments and also involves unwanted radiation, a particular concern for repeated scans in younger patients. In this proposal, we will investigate a novel magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique called xenon-MRI (Xe-MRI). Xe-MRI provides clear pictures inside of the lungs and involves no radiation so can be used repeatedly in children. Xe-MRI has been used successfully to diagnose several lung diseases but has not yet been investigated for monitoring lung disease treatment in children with CF. We will test the ability of Xe-MRI to detect improvements following treatment of early CF lung disease, not demonstrated by conventional breathing tests. By showing that Xe-MRI is useful for detecting and following the treatment of early CF lung disease, this test could also be used for the development of new improved treatments for children with CF in future. Furthermore, this test would likely also be useful for assessing other lung diseases such as asthma.

column36: Targeting molecular scaffolds for the treatment of obesity and metabolic disease
column37: As a risk factor for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, obesity has been steadily increasing in society at alarming rates. Approximately 25% of Canadians are either over-weight or obese. Anti-obesity therapies have varying degrees of effectiveness, but no therapies actually target fat cells, which are key in the development of obesity. Fat cells, or adipocytes, grow through a complicated roadmap of signals that need precise direction. It is currently not known what are the proteins in fat cells that direct these signals needed for fat cell growth, but specialized proteins called molecular scaffolds could be the key players. One type of molecular scaffolds are 14-3-3 proteins, which we previously found to control the growth of fat cells in mice. We previously studied one member of 14-3-3 proteins, 14-3-3zeta, and mice that were genetically modified to have no 14-3-3zeta in all cells had less fat than normal mice. When mice were made to have more 14-3-3zeta in every cell, they actually gained more weight when fed food high in fat. It has been found that fat samples from obese individuals have higher levels of 14-3-3zeta. Combined with our mouse data, this raises the question of whether having more 14-3-3zeta in fat cells is enough to promote the development of obesity. Therefore, the aim of this proposal is to see if 14-3-3zeta can be a suitable target in the fat cell for treating obesity. This will be tested in mice that do not have 14-3-3zeta in their fat cells and to see if this protects them from developing obesity. Studies will also try to understand what 14-3-3zeta does in a fat cell and also if new drugs can be developed to block the actions of 14-3-3zeta in fat cells. Collectively, these studies will examine if 14-3-3zeta can be a suitable drug target to treat obesity, which continues to grow at alarming rates throughout the world.

column36: Discovery, validation, and pre-clinical development of novel strategies to prevent anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.
column37: Background: A staggering 42% of childhood cancer patients develop disabling/life-threatening adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Anthracyclines are widely used for the treatment of ~70% of adult and childhood cancers. However, anthracyclines cause serious heart damage in 5-16% of patients, resulting in death or life-long disability. Currently prevention is limited to reducing the dose of anthracyclines or using a second drug to protect the heart, dexrazoxane. However, dose reduction reduces anti-cancer effectiveness and dexrazoxane is restricted to adult patients with advanced cancer receiving high anthracycline doses, and dexrazoxane is not approved for use in pediatric patients due to risks of secondary cancers. Our goal is to prevent anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We identified that the RARG gene is related to anthracycline-cardiotoxicity in a large children's cancer study (Nat Gen, 2015). Building upon these findings, we will pursue two prevention strategies: 1. Develop a novel cardioprotectant that disrupts the RARG pathway. We will screen a panel of targeted drugs in a human cardiac cells, followed by evaluation in well-established animal models of anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We have now demonstrated proof-of-principle for 2 drugs exhibiting up to 95% cardioprotection in cultured cardiac cells and these were more effective than dexrazoxane. 2. Identify new genetic risk factors to pre-emptively identify patients at higher risk of anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We have collected DNA from a large group of adult patients for high-throughput genomic analyses. We will combine pediatric and adult studies to improve the study. Validated factors will be incorporated into a predictive test and explored as additional candidates for strategy #1. Expected Outcomes: A new safe and effective anthracycline-cardioprotectant will be primed for clinical evaluation in patients. New genetic risk factors will be transitioned to a clinical testing program.

column36: Mechanisms of insulin resistance in podocytes and diabetic nephropathy
column37: Clinically evident kidney failure eventually develops in patients with type 1 (T1D) and type 2 (T2D) diabetes, and continues to progress despite receiving intensified glycemic control and renal protective drugs. Moreover, up to now, we have only a diffuse understanding of why some diabetic patients develop nephropathy whereas other patients never progress to dialysis. Elevated glucose and saturated fat (FFA) levels may cause local factor changes affecting podocyte survival, an important vascular cell in kidney, which are not easily reversed. I made a very interesting finding on a potential target called SHP-1 that is elevated with high glucose concentrations in diabetic kidney of rodent animals. SHP-1 is a member of the protein tyrosine phosphatase family that downregulates the activity of important growth factors such as insulin, VEGF and nephrin, which are crucial for podocyte survival and function. Interestingly, insulin resistance caused by FFA is triggered by the activation of the protein kinase C (PKC)-alpha. Thus, unwanted abnormalities of renal podocyte function causing insulin resistance in T1D and T2D can be regulated by the activation of two independent pathways: SHP-1 and PKC-alpha. The aim of the present proposal will characterize and explore the role of SHP-1 and PKC-alpha activation producing biological abnormalities such as podocyte death and insulin resistance. To accomplish this aim, we will use several methods to specifically manipulate the protein expression level of SHP-1 and PKC-alpha in podocyte cell line and evaluate their impact on insulin and nephrin actions. Moreover, I will use genetically modified tissue specific mice of SHP-1 to characterize its cellular mechanisms implicated in diabetic nephropathy using a T1D and T2D mouse models. We believe that this proposal will help us better understand the mechanisms underlying renal cell dysfunction related to kidney failure in T1D and T2D.

column36: Neural circuitry for detection of texture boundaries
column37: Our rich and effortless perception of the complex mixtures of objects and surfaces comprising our everyday world is one of the most remarkable achievements of the human brain. A key early step in the required neural processing is separation of the retinal image into regions corresponding to distinct surfaces of different objects. In natural images we can effortlessly perform such "figure-ground segmentation" of borders defined by differences in a variety of local image properties, for example differences in luminance, colour, contrast, or texture. This segmentation process necessarily precedes higher-level visual functions such as object recognition, and is fundamentally important to normal visual perception. Analysis of complex visual patterns begins in the early visual cortex, areas V1 and V2. The responses of single neurons in these cortical areas are highly specific, or "tuned", to particular kinds of visual stimuli. An understanding of the nature of stimulus selectivity of these neurons forms a critical basis of our current understanding of human visual perception. This research program has three specific objectives: to evaluate and extend our recently discovered model of the neural circuitry for detecting luminance and texture boundaries in early visual cortex; to explore whether there might be two different kinds of such neural processing; and to examine the relationship to detection of colour boundaries. The outcomes of this work will yield fundamental, health-related knowledge that may facilitate the future design of diagnostic tests and therapies for visual disorders.

column36: Microparticles in Diabetes
column37: People with diabetes are far more likely to suffer a heart attack than nondiabetics. Diabetes causes changes to the blood vessels and this is believed to responsible for the increased risk of heart attacks and stroke. This project seeks to expand our understanding of how diabetes causes damage to the blood vessels. Microparticles are tiny pieces of cells that are released from dying cells in the body. Recently it has been found that the levels of microparticles in the blood are increased significantly in diabetes. Increased microparticles can predict a risk of a heart attack or death due to heart problems. The goal of this project is to determine how microparticles are formed in diabetes and how they may cause damage to blood vessels. We anticipate that by understanding the proteins carried by microparticles and the signaling that microparticles activate in diabetes we will be able to develop new drug treatments that can be used to reduce risk of heart and kidney problems in diabetes.

column36: Mitigating Illness and Raising Wellness at the Human-Dog Interface in Northern Canada
column37: Dogs have been an integral part of the physical, social and cultural environment of Inuit and First nations but also can be a source of health risks in contemporary Northern communities. Attacks, bites, injuries, sometimes death, and the transmission of deadly rabies and probably other microbes are part of the reality in Northern communities. All these dog-related health issues are exacerbated by the lack of, or limited access to, veterinary services, the presence of free-roaming dogs and dog overpopulation, which remain chronic issues in Northern communities. The project's ultimate goal is to improve the health and wellness of Inuit, Naskapi, Cree and Westerners living in Northern Canada by mitigating dog-associated health risks and by supporting the role of dogs on wellness in these Northern communities. The Inuit, Naskapi, Cree and Western knowledges and perspectives on health and dogs will be mobilized during the course of the project as they are essential in contributing to a comprehensive understanding of the health effects at the human-dogs interface in the Northern communities and to inform the most successful sustainable interventions to protect human health and support human wellness. The primary project outcome is the reduction of the dog-related threats to human health and wellbeing in the North (i.e., attacks, bites, potential rabies case management, death), as well as supporting the positive dog-related health and cultural roles following the implementation of community-based, sustainable solutions during the course of the project.

column36: Functional organization of the human brain for colour and form vision: from LGN to extrastriate cortex.
column37: The understanding of human colour vision is a challenge that has interested scientists for over 300 years. The core of the problem is to understand how the spectral differences across the visual scene in the physical world are translated by the brain into the neural signals that represent the wide array of colours that we see in our perceptual world; in other words, how the human brain sees in colour. It is well known that there are two major subdivisions in the human visual system. The dorsal pathway is dedicated to visual guidance of our actions and motion through the visual world, whereas the ventral pathway encodes what we see in terms of the shapes and objects in the visual scene. In this proposal I investigate the role of the ventral pathway in the encoding of form and colour. I aim to identify which pathways and brain areas are used to encode colour as compared to the achromatic (black & white) components of the visual image, and how colour, form and shape analyses are combined within the brain. The research uses the latest techniques, including fMRI of the human brain and brain stimulation (TMS), to identify how the brain regions and pathways are functionally organized to deconstruct the visual image and then reform it into global percepts, enabling us to see the coloured version of the visual world that we so easily take for granted.

column36: Efficacy and Safety of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in patients with mild vascular cognitive impairment
column37: Despite promising leads, to date clinical trials of medications to halt or reverse dementia have failed. Consequently, treatment interventions for dementia are now focusing on those with cognitive problems who are at high risk of progressing, to intervene before there is irreversible damage to the brain. Cognitive problems are common in patients with heart disease and those who experience cognitive difficulties are more likely to develop dementia. While exercise can help many people maintain cognition, many people do not achieve cognitive benefits. Our research has provided the first evidence that oxidative stress may limit the benefits of exercise on brain function and cognition. Recent research suggests that reducing oxidative damage in the brain may possibly be an effective way to prevent the brain changes that lead to the cognitive deficits and functional impairment in dementia. N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a widely available and safe supplement, has powerful antioxidant effects, which may be beneficial to boost cognition. This study will test whether the antioxidant supplement NAC is safe and effective to improve cognition in patients with heart disease who show early memory problems, known as vascular cognitive impairment-no dementia (VCIND). In the current study, patients will be randomized to NAC supplements or placebo orally for 24 weeks while participating in a supervised exercise program. Standardized neuropsychological testing will be used to compare cognitive performance between the placebo and NAC groups. We will use new techniques to accurately measure the amount of oxidative stress damage in blood and evaluate whether the treatment is more efficacious in individuals with certain brain characteristics on MRI scans. If positive, these results will be important for the design of a longer term trial to investigate whether NAC can delay the onset of dementia.

column36: Sleep and circadian rhythms in men and women
column37: Women are up to twice as likely to suffer from insomnia as men. For a similar sleep schedule, we find that young adult women's circadian clock causes them to fall asleep and wake up earlier than men. These results in naturally cycling women are helping us understand why women are more likely than men to wake up earlier in the morning and feel tired after a night's sleep. After menopause, the risk of sleep disturbances increases substantially and affect 25-50% of women. Yet, almost nothing is known about the changes that occur with the circadian system regulating sleep and waking during menopause. In the present study, we propose to recruit postmenopausal women, aged 45 and older. From this group, 14 will be healthy sleepers and 14 will suffer from chronic insomnia. Each participant will be studied twice in time isolation for 3 consecutive days. During each visit, they will undergo a special procedure of multiple naps designed to test how their circadian clock controls sleep, waking, and mood. Saliva samples will be collected in order to assess internal biological time by measuring their content in the hormones cortisol and melatonin. Sleep will be recorded during naps and performance will be tested during waking episodes. Results will be compared between healthy sleepers and insomniacs in order to clarify how the circadian clock and melatonin affect sleep and waking in postmenopausal women. The present study will help understand the role the circadian system plays in the greater female susceptibility to sleep-wake disturbances. Future studies will pursue similar questions in men.

column36: Hippo Regulation of Hepatocyte Identity and Function
column37: The term "liver disease" comprises over 100 types of disorders. However, the most common form of chronic liver disease is Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD), which affects an estimated 30-46% of the population in the US. In Canada, over 2,000 deaths per year are due to liver disease and a further 1,700 deaths from liver cancer. As in the US, obesity is the leading cause of liver disease, with over-exposure to common chemicals or medications and viral infections such as hepatitis, being major contributors. Regardless of the initiating factor, chronic liver disease can cause permanent liver damage and scarring that will progress to cirrhosis, poor liver function and eventually may advance to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Currently, there is no cure for cirrhosis. Treatment focuses on slowing progression and minimizing complications, such as portal hypertension. When it is no longer possible to manage the complications, a liver transplant is required, but demand for transplants far exceeds available donor tissue. Recent advances in the differentiation of human pluripotent cells (hPSCs) into hepatocytes has excited researchers by providing a potential source of cells for liver transplants, drug testing and bioartificial liver devices. However, current methods of growing liver from hPSCs do not yet result in fully functional cells. Thus, methods to improve donor tissue expansion or the derivation of liver tissue from hPSCs require a better understanding of the factors that promote and maintain liver cells proliferation and differentiation. Our reserach will focus on how cells communicate and regulate the expression of genes in the liver. Using mouse as a model system, we will study how the different cell types in the liver are made and allow the liver to grow.

column36: Regulation of DNA double-strand break repair pathways in multiple myeloma
column37: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is the second most common hematological malignancy in Canada. Due to its heterogeneity, a large portion of patients affected by MM is refractory to or relapses from first line therapies, including the proteasome inhibitor (PI) Bortezomib. Therefore, it becomes crucial to better understand the pathobiology of MM and the resistance mechanisms of this malignancy. MM are characterized by recurrent chromosomal aberrations and aneuploidy. These features have been correlated with dysregulation of the DNA damage repair pathways. However, little is known about the exact mechanisms driving genomic instability in MM. We are particularly interested in one type of DNA damage, called DNA double-strand break (DSB). DSB is a highly dangerous DNA lesion that can result, if improperly repaired, in deleterious chromosomal rearrangements characteristics of MM. We are currently characterizing the major two DSB repair pathways, classical non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination, in different MM cell lines. Our goal is to determine at what level these pathways are dysregulated, thereby contributing to the heterogeneity and aggressiveness of MM. Understanding DSB repair pathways in MM will provide targets for the treatment of this pathology. It may also provide novel biomarkers to predict the risk of relapse/refractory MM.

column36: tRNA synthesis as a target of Ras signaling in the control of cell and tissue growth
column37: Understanding how cells grow and divide is a fundamental question in biology. During animal development the proper regulation of cell growth is essential for controlling organ and organism size. While in cancer, deregulated cell growth is often an early event in tumor formation. The processes that control growth are remarkably similar across different species. For example, in both humans and fruit flies similar genes regulate growth and mutations in these genes often lead to cancer. These similarities allow us to use the fruit fly as a simple, yet powerful genetic system to study what genes and molecules controls growth. We made the striking discovery that overproduction of a single molecule, called transfer RNA, can accelerate growth and increase body size in fruit flies. Transfer RNA plays a critical role in the synthesis all of the proteins and enzymes in a cell, including those essential for growth. Our goal in this grant is to understand how the production of tRNA is controlled and how increase in the production of transfer RNA can drive growth. Abnormal production of transfer RNA is often seen in cancer cells, therefore our work in fruit flies may provide clues to help us understand the runaway growth that makes this disease so devastating.

column36: Roles of the PRP19 complex in the Maintenance of Genome Stability
column37: Our cells are constantly subjected to stress that can damage their genetic material and cause mutations. Mutations can lead to the development of diseases such as cancer. To prevent the occurrence of deleterious mutations, our cells harbour signaling pathways that detect the DNA structures associated with damage and protect our genomes from degradation. Cancer cells often have defects in these protective pathways and are thus more sensitive to stress and accumulate mutations more readily than healthy cells. This is leveraged by doctors to destroy tumors through the use of chemo- and radio-therapy which cause unsustainable levels of damage to the genetic material of cancer cells. In an effort to identify novel therapeutic targets that could help in the fight against cancer, we have recently identified many new proteins that can recognize the structures found at broken regions of the genome. Amongst these factors, PRP19 is particularly important for the resistance to chemotherapeutic drugs and irradiation which tells us that PRP19 helps cells repair their DNA. PRP19 works by modifying other proteins in the cell such as RPA, an essential guardian of our genome. Our work will help us understand how the modification of RPA and other proteins by PRP19 and additional PRP19-like proteins called ubiquitin ligases allows our cells to protect their DNA. We will thus examine how PRP19 works with other proteins to remove the toxic DNA lesions that may appear when cells replicate their genetic material. This new information will improve our understanding of the complex pathways that protect our DNA and guide us in the elaboration of novel strategies that will improve the efficiency of current anti-cancer treatments.

column36: Translational studies into human colon motor dysfunction
column37: Colonic motility disorders, ranging from Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) to chronic constipation and pseudo-obstruction, impose a heavy personal and economic burden affecting 7 million Canadians, with a health care cost of >$8 billion /year and >$8 billion/year in lost productivity. Children with chronic constipation experience depression and stunted education. Treatments are often not beneficial because we do not have a complete understanding of how motility is controlled and we do not know what is actually wrong with the colon of patients because we do not measure it. I propose inherently translational studies aimed at understanding mechanisms underlying colonic dysmotility, generating novel therapeutic approaches. My first aim is to understand the mechanisms by which the colon creates normal or abnormal motility with a focus on the critical role of interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC), the pacemaker cells of the gut that orchestrate most motor patterns. I am internationally recognized as a leader in this field and ICC abnormalities are the most common pathology finding in constipation. My second aim is to measure and understand motility dysfunction in patients, using 84-sensor high-resolution manometry. Parallel animal and human studies will allow me to identify optimal stimuli to be used in the assessment so that I can translate abnormal responses to stimuli into causes of dysmotility. My third aim is to understand pathophysiology. In animal models, and in patients through mucosal biopsies, I will reveal relationships between abnormal motility, abnormal bacterial composition and abnormal microbe-derived metabolites. As outcome I will obtain optimal diagnostic testing of colonic dysmotility in patients, a better understanding of the underlying pathophysiology to allow for better management of each patient to increase health-related quality of life. Elucidation of the nature of the dysmotility will allow the development of new treatments and reduce hospital costs.

column36: Imaging of cerebral vascular adaptation following traumatic brain injury
column37: The blood vessels that supply the brain with oxygen and nutrients form a complex and highly organized network whose proper functioning is essential for our survival. Disease or injury to the brain may damage this network and disrupt the transport of blood and the mechanisms that regulate how much oxygen and nutrients are delivered. As the brain recovers from injury, new blood vessels are added, others are removed, and existing blood vessels may change in dimensions or even move. How these changes occur is poorly understood yet is thought to be essential to recovering healthy brain function. The goal of this project is to understand this adaptation process for the purpose of developing better methods to monitor and promote recovery following brain injury. Our research strategy is to use experimental mice that receive an injury to the part of the brain that is responsible for controlling movement. Advanced 3D optical microscopy methods will be used to directly observe the changing blood vessel network following injury. Magnetic resonance imaging will be used to assess how blood is being distributed within the brain and the capacity of the brain to elevate blood flow when needed. A subset of the mice will undertake voluntary exercise to evaluate whether this improves recovery. We will use these observations to identify beneficial patterns of blood vessel remodelling following traumatic brain injury and to assess when and if exercise can be used to promote recovery. Finally, we will evaluate a new ultrasound diagnostic technique in the mice to monitor changes in how blood is supplied. Together these findings could lead both to better methods to promote recovery following brain injury and to new diagnostic methods that could be used clinically to monitor the progress of treatment.

column36: The Notch signalling pathway: a master regulator of CD8+ T cell differentiation
column37: The immune system of an individual is devoted to figth infectious agents. This is achieved by white blood cells that patrol the organism to eliminate pathogens. T cells, a type of white blood cells, are the central player allowing to mount an efficient immune response. These T cells recognize specifically the foreign materials via a cell surface receptor, the T cell receptor (TCR). This recognition allows for the expansion and differentiation of T cells that are specific to the infectious agent. The differentiation of T cells is crucial to allow them to acquire the ability to eliminate the infectious agent. After pathogen clearance, most of the differentiated T cells will die to reset the system. A few of these T cells will survive as long-lived memory T cells. We have recently shown that the evolutionary conserved Notch signalling pathway controls the generation of T cells endowed with the ability to control the infectious agents. In this proposal, we will determine the molecular mechanisms by which Notch signalling controls T cell differentiation during an immune response.

column36: Efficacy of cognitive behavioural and skills training therapy of adolescents with ADHD
column37: Attention Deficit/ Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common childhood psychiatric condition,which often persists into adolescence. In adolescence ADHD is associated with poor academic, social, and emotional functioning, other psychiatric problems, substance abuse, and antisocial behaviour. Although medication effectively reduces symptoms such as hyperactivity and inattention, it does not directly address academic, social, emotional, and behavioural problems. Overcoming these would require building skills in organization, time management, problem solving, emotional modulation, stress management and interpersonal rapport. Yet, psychosocial treatments targeting such skills in adolescents with ADHD have been little studied and are scarce in the community. The proposed study will evaluate cognitive behavioural and skills training therapy (CBT+S) for adolescents with ADHD. Adolescents will be randomly assigned to 14 sessions of either manualized group CBT+S or manualized supportive group therapy (SGT, control condition). An additional treatment-as-usual group will be evaluated to control for repeated measurements. CBT+S will focus on skill acquisition in common problem areas for adolescents with ADHD, such as organization and time management, distractibility, impulsivity, and social skills. A coach will call each participant twice a week to help practice the learned skills. Parallel groups will be provided for parents of CBT+S and SGT participants focusing on education, support and sharing experiences. If CBT+S proves to benefit adolescents with ADHD, it can be made widely available to these adolescents in the community. This would help them improve their academic, social, and emotional functioning and ultimately their long term outcomes.

column36: Genetic mosaicism in human development
column37: A growth restricted fetus is more likely to be born premature or with birth defects and is at increased risk for adverse neonatal, childhood and adult health outcomes. Poor growth is most often linked to a placenta that does not deliver oxygen and nutrients efficiently tot eh developing baby. One cause of poor placenta function, present in ~10% of pregnancies with pathologically small babies, is a chromosome (genetic) abnormality found in the placenta that is not present in the baby. This is referred to as confined placental mosaicism. In the past only large chromosome errors could be tested for in the placenta, but with advances in diagnostic technologies, smaller genetic changes can now be detected. These likely also account for a portion of small babies. Our goal is to determine the incidence of genetic abnormalities confined to the placenta and how often they explain why a baby is born too small. This genetic data is also important for interpreting prenatal testing; increasingly, prenatal testing is done by analyzing cell-free DNA derived from the placenta that circulates in maternal blood. Our goal is to fill the major gap in knowledge concerning the incidence and impact of placental mosaicism on fetal growth and development.

column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death globally and in Canada, where it kills more people than breast, prostate, colorectal and pancreatic cancers combined. This proposal aims to uncover how the tumor suppressor P53 works at molecular level and when it is important in the evolution of a fully malignant metastatic cell - both of which are paramount to discovering new and effective cancer treatments. Genetically modified mouse models (GEMM) are presently the gold standard for whole organism cancer modeling. We will make use of our novel GEMMs of human lung cancer where we can control the site, the number and the timing of specific genetic events. column37: A major problem for people with diabetes is the loss of insulin-producing beta-cells in the pancreas. Repopulating beta-cells requires a thorough analysis of the factors that regulate their growth and maintain their function. One important cell type near by the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas is the pancreatic star-like cell (PaSC). PaSCs required maintain pancreatic structure and exocrine function is well-studied, whether it has effects on the beta-cell is unknown. We carried out a preliminary study of these cells in the human fetal pancreas and found that the PaSCs proliferate rapidly and show changes in gene and protein expression during development. In contrast, in the adult pancreas, PaSCs were found to be activated following pancreatic organ injury and to be involved in repair of the damaged tissue. In the diabetic mouse pancreas, there was activation of the PaSCs within beta-cell clusters. These pilot studies indicate that PaSCs likely have a role in the pancreas during development and following injury or the onset of diabetes. Because our understanding of the precise roles of PaSCs in the developing human pancreas and in the experimental (pancreatic injury, diabetes) models remains limited, our present objectives are threefold: (1) to characterize the functional role of PaSCs in regulating beta-cell growth in the developing human pancreas; 2) to examine whether activated PaSCs are required during beta-cell regeneration in the pancreatic injury model; and 3) to determine if over-activated PaSCs are involved in development of beta-cell dysfunction in the diabetic model. These studies will enable us to help ensure the development of more successful protocols for generating and maintaining insulin-producing cells for the treatment of diabetes.

column36: Therapeutic targeting of immune-inflammation pathway via IL23-IL17 axis in Endometriosis
column37: Endometriosis, characterized by growth of endometrial lining outside of the uterus, is the most prevalent global cause for hysterectomy, infertility and pelvic pain. It affects 6-10% of reproductive age women and 35-50% in women with pelvic pain/unexplained infertility. Despite its staggering economic impact ($1.8 Billion/year Canada; $22 Billion/year USA), endometriosis remains misdiagnosed, misunderstood and ineffectively treated. Diagnosis relies on invasive laparoscopy procedure to visualise lesions. Current treatments transiently alleviate but do not cure endometriosis. Growth of endometriotic lesions depend on abnormally levels of estrogen combined with pronounced inflammatory environment in the peritoneal cavity. Indeed, we provided striking evidence that endometriotic lesions are major regulators and promoters of inflammation. From our preliminary data and published papers, IL23-IL17 axis emerged as a major pathway in regulation of pain and inflammation. However mechanisms and molecular drivers of IL23-IL17 axis that modulate inflammation and pain in endometriosis is unidentified. Using endometriosis patient samples, cell lines and our established mouse models, we will: 1) Determine the basis for endometriosis associated immune dysfunction and how it contributes to susceptibility and progression of endometriosis.2) Identify and validate immune-inflammatory mediators (e.g., IL-17/IL-23 axis) contributing to the pathogenesis of endometriosis and for their diagnostic/therapeutic potential. 3) Conduct pre-clinical evaluation of IL-23-IL17 axis for therapeutic targeting in mouse model of endometriosis. Our research will provide novel insights into how complex immune networks are involved in the pathogenesis of endometriosis and deliver real-life solutions for improved diagnosis and better management of endometriosis patients.

column36: Mechanisms underlying schizophrenia
column37: Clinical Issue: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a debilitating mental disorder affecting young adults. SZ symptoms include early social isolation, cognitive decline prior to episodes of auditory hallucinations, false beliefs and associated anxiety and depression. Current treatments targeting the dopaminergic system remedy psychosis but not other schizophrenia symptoms. The goal is to identify therapeutic targets dysregulated early in the disease process to provide better outcomes for SZ. We have recently discovered a new mouse model of SZ in which the phosphatase enzyme PTP1B is hyperactive in the brain. We also found that in two other commonly used experimentally induced mouse models of SZ this enzyme activity is increased in the affected brain regions. Our previous work showed that hyperactivity of this enzyme disrupts the function of important glutamate receptors on neurons. This can lead to malfunction of dopaminergic circuitry and cause psychosis in humans. Moreover, we reported that hyperactivity of this enzyme also impairs the production of one of the body's own cannabis-like substances (endogenous cannabinoid). Since cannabinoids control how much neurotransmitters are released from neurons, this would further lead to aberrant neuronal activity. Dysregulated levels of cannabinoids in the serum and the cerebrospinal fluid are observed in SZ patients. Our hypothesis is that elevated PTP1B activity is the central mechanism that accounts for functional deficits in the SZ brain. We will test whether targeting this enzyme with a selective inhibitor called Trodusquemine will ameliorate SZ symptoms in two preclinical mouse models. Significance: In Canada, about 1% of the population (~350,000) has SZ. Successful validation of targeting PTP1B to improve SZ in preclinical mouse models can rapidly move to clinical trials since Trodusquemine has already undergone phase 1 clinical trials to treat obesity.

column36: A Good Start Matters: Do supportive childcare centre environments, policies and practices enhance physical activity?
column37: The early years of life are critical to establishing healthy behaviours. Sadly, the majority of preschool age children are not meeting both Canadian physical activity and screen time guidelines and have poor motor skills. Childcare centres are important settings as more than half of children attend childcare and spend a large proportion of their days and weeks there. To meet these research goals, we will conduct province-wide surveys assessing the policies, practices and environments of licensed childcare providers before and after implementation of the province-wide communication and capacity-building interventions are initiated. We will also interview childcare providers in all regions of BC to gain more in-depth understanding of the factors that influence implementation of the AP Standards. In a sub-set of centres, we will also measure children's physical activity, sedentary behaviour and motor skill competencies. The findings will inform future policies and enhance our understanding of how policy action supported by communication and capacity-building strategies influences the environment of childcare centres.

column36: Ultrasound based pedicle screw navigation: an intraoperative image guidance system without radiation exposure
column37: Each year more than 28,000 Canadians are treated surgically for lower back pain. Many of these cases require instrumentation with pedicle screws, which requires some form of X-ray imaging like fluoroscopy or intra-operative CT thus exposing patients and operating room personnel to significant amounts of harmful radiation. This project will adapt and clinically test a new intra-operative ultrasound-based navigation system that is an inexpensive, radiation-free alternative to intra-operative X-ray imaging. This novel technology allows for precise identification of the bony surface of the vertebrae without exposing the spine by merging the pre-operative CT and intra-operative ultrasound images. Such 3D renditions of the spine improve patient-to-image registration facilitating image-guided spine surgery. The novel system will be validated as a safe, accurate, and novel method for intraoperative guidance to perform instrumented lumbar spinal fusion and decompressions. The immediate benefits of this system compared to current standard intraoperative X-ray-based imaging technology are: 1) Elimination of all intraoperative radiation exposure to patient and operating room personnel 2) Real-time navigation at every level of the spine with intuitive visualization. 3) Increased accessibility (in terms of lower costs, smaller footprint, less cumbersome) of navigated spine surgery for all surgeons. 4) Decreased operating room time and thus decreased morbidity of spine surgery. 5) Improved accuracy of navigation through better registration. 6) Decreased numbers of malpositioned screws and consequently, reduced numbers of revision surgeries. And finally, 7) unlimited levels of fusion may be performed with the novel navigation method. This is of particular importance in scoliosis cases where current technology only captures 5 to 6 segments at a time and dose constraints limits the number of X-ray based images.
