column36: MRI parenchymal enhancement and risk of breast cancer: A population-based study of women screened in the Ontario Breast Screening Program
column37: The Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP) High-Risk Screening Program includes women between the ages of 30 and 69 years who have a very high risk of breast cancer. As part of this program, women undergo breast screening every year with both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and mammogram. Because of their very high risk, these women are also frequently considered for preventive surgeries (e.g., having their breasts and/or ovaries removed). While potentially reducing a woman's risk of breast cancer, these surgeries can seriously impact their quality of life. New markers of breast cancer risk that can identify the women who would benefit the most from these interventions are needed. This will help provide personalized recommendations for both breast cancer prevention and screening. Mammograms generate an image of the breast where fat appears white and breast tissue appears dark. The amount of breast tissue a woman has is called mammographic density (MD). Having high MD is known to strongly increase a woman's risk of breast cancer. This relationship is well known in average-risk women but it is not known if it is also true for high-risk women. Another characteristic of the breast that might tell us about a woman's risk of breast cancer is seen on MRI and is called background parenchymal enhancement (BPE). Small studies have shown that having high BPE may increase a woman's risk of getting breast cancer. Dr. Brooks and her research team will examine the relationship between MD and BPE and risk of breast cancer in women being screened in the OBSP High-Risk Program. This study will be the first to look at the relationship between BPE in an established screening program. This study will provide us with information that will better determine a woman's risk of getting breast cancer, helping to guide recommendations for breast cancer screening and preventive interventions. This could significantly impact how high-risk women are screened and treated in the future.

column36: Developmental origins of childhood obesity: tracking the causal epigenetic changes programming adiposity in children
column37: Obesity now affects up to 1 in 5 children in Canada. Obese children are more likely to stay obese as adults and this has profound impacts on their long-term health. Indeed, obesity increases risk to develop diabetes and heart diseases among many other diseases. Events during pregnancy are suspected to play a role in 'programming' whether a child develops obesity, but we still do not know much about the mechanisms involved. Scientific and medical observations strongly suggest that "epigenetic" factors are important. The term epigenetics refers to chemical modifications of the genes that act as a change in the software reading the genetic information (hardware). Maternal conditions - such as diabetes in pregnancy - influence the environment in which the foetus develops. The environment of the foetus in the womb can affect the epigenetic marks with profound effects on the reading and expression of the genetic information throughout life. Such long-term changes involving genes implicated in weight control will have an impact on the risk to develop obesity and related chronic diseases. For this reason, the so-called epigenetic mechanisms have a real potential to explain why some unfavourable environment within the womb affecting foetal development during pregnancy may predispose newborns to develop obesity early in their life as well as diabetes and heart disease later on. Our primary objective is to identify epigenetic marks observed at birth that predict which child will become obese. Then, we will determine which specific pregnancy events, whether maternal obesity or diabetes during pregnancy, cause these epigenetic changes. Finally, the impact of these epigenetic changes on gene expression levels will be assessed. Our study will help to understand the biological mechanisms linking epigenetic events occurring during pregnancy and the increased risk for children to develop obesity.

Poor blood flow (ischemia), inflammation and fibrosis are profound in these diseases, generating an environment that prevents muscle repair. New strategies must improve this environment to impact the lives of patients. A promising approach that is believed may improve the muscle environment uses vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to improve blood flow. However, contrary to this approach, our group has now demonstrated in a preclinical mouse model of DMD that delivery of VEGF is not sufficient to reduce ischemia, and in fact increases muscle inflammation and fibrosis! Our hypothesis is that the vasculature in DMD is abnormal. Thus, our overarching objective is to rescue abnormal vasculature in DMD by administering a factor that stabilizes it, Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1). These data will allow us to critically identify a window of opportunity to intervene with delivery of Ang-1 as a therapeutic. 2. To provide laboratory-based proof of concept in DMD mice for the administration of Ang-1 to improve muscle repair. 3. To develop a novel, targeted Ang-1 delivery approach that will allow for the precise regulation of Ang-1 delivery that will be essential for future clinical use in patients. Significance: Without an approach to improve the muscle environment, and prevent/reduce ischemia/inflammation/fibrosis, it is unlikely that the benefits of therapeutics for muscle regenerative disorders can ever be fully realized. Our vascular-targeted strategy will reduce medical costs, prolong ambulation and longevity, and improve quality of life for patients not only affected by muscle degeneration, but perhaps by any vascular defect.

column36: The role of RhoA/mDia1 pathway in salt-sensitive hypertension
column37: Hypertension is the prevalent treatable risk factor contributing to cardiovascular diseases, which remain the most common cause of death in industrialized countries taking the lives of over one million people every year in the U.S. alone. In Canada, over 20% of adults are diagnosed with hypertension, and an estimated 9 in 10 people who live an average lifespan will develop the condition in their lifetime. Excessive dietary salt intake is strongly correlated with cardiovascular diseases such as myocardial infarction and stroke, and is regarded as a major contributing factor to hypertension. While the link between salt and hypertension is well established, the mechanisms by which high salt intake leads to increased blood pressure remain unclear. Consumption of salt in a meal increases the levels of salt (sodium) in the blood, causing activation of specialized brain cells that release a hormone called vasopressin. Vasopressin leads to retention of water in the kidney in order to decrease blood sodium levels back to normal. Vasopressin also affects blood vessels causing them to constrict. These effects of vasopressin can lead to the elevation of blood pressure. Our hypothesis is that chronic exposure to excessive amounts of salt causes a hyperactivation of vasopressin-secreting brain cells. These cells have a specialized cellular skeleton that determine their shape (just like the shape of the body is determined by its skeleton). This cellular skeleton becomes denser and stiffer when the cells are chronically exposed to high salt levels. As a result, the cells become overly activated and secrete excessive amounts of vasopressin, leading to a sustained blood pressure increase and hypertension. We propose to study the mechanisms by which high salt causes the modification of cellular skeleton in the brain cells thereby leading to hypertension.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an incurable, severely debilitating disease with suboptimal therapy and no cure. Canada has the highest incidence of MS in the world with 291 cases per 100,000 people. MS is most commonly diagnosed in young adults and patients suffer progressive and irreversible damage to the brain. The root causes and risk factors for MS are still unknown. As such, current therapies are limited to treating symptoms, rather than the root cause. Other incurable diseases that lead to progressive loss of quality of life, and death, include the occupational respiratory diseases; which are caused by breathing in toxic materials such as asbestos and silica. These diseases commonly affect our firefighters, miners and military personnel. MS and occupational respiratory diseases are caused by chronic inflammation of the brain and lung respectively. Although the brain and lung have very different functions in the body, they share some common features during inflammation. One common feature is that the inflammatory protein IL-1 is made by cells locally and leads to excessive inflammation and tissue damage. It is well known that if we limit IL-1, we can protect from MS and occupational respiratory diseases; but we don't fully understand how and why IL-1 is made. We have exciting new evidence to suggest that a recently found digestive protein in immune cells triggers the release of IL-1 in both the brain and lung. Mice that don't have this protein are protected from experimental models of MS and respiratory disease caused by silica. Interestingly, this protein was recently identified by other scientists as being a possible risk factor for MS. Our research will determine how this protein brings about IL-1 release and inflammation in the brain and lung. This will allow scientists and doctors to better understand how chronic inflammation develops and potentially formulate new strategies to treat diseases such as MS and occupational respiratory disease.

column37: The ability to walk outdoors is key to participating in the community. Walking outside the home is a universally accessible form of physical activity with multiple health benefits. Practice walking across roads, slopes and curbs, while talking, and dealing with crowds and traffic, is safe and feasible and can improve confidence and walking ability. Walking outdoors in nature appears to improve mental health more than walking indoors. Despite these health benefits, the majority of older Canadians infrequently walk outside. Barriers include fear, physical disability, inappropriate footwear and walking aids, challenging physical environments, such as uneven pavement, and poor weather. The best strategy for getting people to walk outdoors regularly is unknown. In this study, older adults who have difficulty walking outdoors will participate in either a 1-day workshop and 3-month outdoor walking program or the workshop and receive weekly reminders for 3 months. At the workshop, participants will learn about appropriate footwear, walking aids, equipment, and goal setting, and practice skills to increase outdoor walking. In the outdoor walking program, groups of 9 participants will meet for one hour, twice a week, to practice increasingly challenging activities in parks and built environments. The effect of the workshop and outdoor walking program compared to the workshop plus reminders on improving outdoor walking activity, physical activity, participation, and health-related quality of life, will be evaluated. Each participant will complete four evaluations: before the intervention and 3, 5, and 12 months later. We will interview select people at 6 and 12 months to ask their opinions of what worked and didn't work. Increasing outdoor walking is expected to improve health and well-being, and help people live independently in the community for longer.

column36: Targeting brain inflammation and its resolution. Omega-3 fatty acids, omega-6 fatty acids or both?
column37: Neurodegenerative diseases are a relatively broad class of neurological disorders, however, recent evidence suggests that dietary n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), commonly found in fish, may be of benefit in preventing or treating these diseases, including Alzheimer's Disease. One common link between neurodegenerative disorders is that they have a neuroinflammatory component. It is well established that n-3 PUFA are anti-inflammatory in the periphery, but whether or not they are also anti-inflammatory within the brain is unknown. It is thought that one way omega-3 might be beneficial in the brain is by interfering with omega-6 fatty acid metabolism. We have developed diets that can lower or increase omega-6s. By combining these approaches we will be able figure out if it is the omega-3s, the omega-6s or both. This is very important as, currently, diets are very high in omega-6 fatty acids and, thus, there is a lot of room to decrease them. The objective of the current proposal is to test if n-3 PUFA are anti-inflammatory within the mouse brain and to evaluate the mechanisms by which they accomplish this. We have established a mouse model of neuroinflammation to test this hypothesis and our preliminary results strongly suggest that docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is protective against neuroinflammation. Having a better understanding whether increasing omega-3 fatty acids and or decreasing omega-6 fatty acids can protect us from the neuroinflammation associated with Alzheimer's disease could lead to new therapies for prevention.

column36: Role of the Type 2 Ryanodine Receptor in Familial Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia and a huge burden on health care globally. Despite worldwide efforts, all clinical trials on AD to date have failed. These disappointing findings demonstrate that our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of AD is far from complete, and that novel and effective treatments for AD are urgently needed. It is thought that the accumulation of amyloid-B (AB) in the brain is a primary driver of AD. However, an unresolved question is what causes the accumulation of AB. An increasing body of evidence indicates that alterations in intracellular Ca handling occur in AD long before the appearance of AB plaques. We recently discovered that genetically suppressing the activity of ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2) dramatically reduces AB level and blocks memory impairment in a mouse model of AD. This exciting finding indicates that RyR2 plays a major role in AD pathogenesis. The goals of this project are to determine RyR2's contributions to AD pathogenesis and to develop novel RyR2-targeted treatments for AD. To achieve these goals, we will determine the role of RyR2 in AB accumulation, neuron loss, and memory impairment in AD mice. We will define how genetically suppressing or enhancing RyR2 activity affects Ca regulation in AD neurons. Further, we will establish if pharmacological RyR2 inhibition suppresses AD pathology. We have developed the necessary tools and obtained key preliminary data demonstrating the feasibility of our approaches. We expect to reveal for the first time direct evidence that RyR2 plays a major role in AD pathology. We also expect to reveal novel insights into the molecular mechanism underlying abnormal Ca regulation in AD and identify the first RyR2-targeted potential treatment for AD. These proposed studies will advance health-related knowledge and improve health outcomes by uncovering novel fundamental mechanisms and developing novel treatments for AD.

column36: Health service redesign in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside: A linked, observational cohort design for comprehensive evaluation
column37: Every year, one in five Canadians experiences a mental health or addiction problem, with an estimated cost of $51 billion annually. While such patients commonly have multiple health and social service needs, Canada's healthcare sectors typically run in silos, posing immense challenges to continuity of care. In 2017, following years of consultation with patients, local care providers and provincial stakeholders, Vancouver Coastal Health (VCH) will embark upon a comprehensive redesign of health services delivered within the city's impoverished downtown Eastside (DTES) neighbourhood. Over the next 5 years, the DTES Second Generation Strategy (2GS) will roll out coordinated policy changes aimed to integrate over 50 different service to provide better-coordinated care. Our study uniquely offers the best possible empirical basis to assess the impact of DTES-2G. Using cutting-edge econometric and epidemiological techniques, we propose a multidimensional health services research platform focusing on access to care, quality of health care delivery, and costs during the implementation of the DTES-2GS. Data will come from long-running observational cohort studies of >3000 people who use drugs in Vancouver that is linked to various health administrative data. As healthcare quality itself is multidimensional, we consider measures of unmet need for health services, clinical outcomes, patient-reported outcome measures, measures of clinical process and health system responsiveness. Finally, we will measure expenditure related to the redesign to help identify the optimal allocation of available resources for DTES-2GS. Working closely with VCH staff and local groups, our findings will inform DTES-2GS policy change as the systemic redesign occurs, while also providing relevant evidence for other urban jurisdictions contending with similar problems in Canada and beyond.

column37: Neurocristopathies form a specific group of rare genetic diseases that result from problems with neural crest cells - a specific type of stem cells that migrate extensively from the neural tube (the central nervous system primordium) during embryogenesis. Such characteristics allow neural crest cells to colonize several regions of the developing embryo and generate a wide array of cell types such as peripheral neurons and glia, pigment cells, craniofacial bone cells as well as specific cell subsets of the heart, inner ear and thymus. Because of the large number of neural crest cell derivatives, distinct structures/cell types (isolated or in combination) are affected in each neurocristopathy. The most important issue in this research field is that the underlying genetic cause and associated pathogenic mechanism of most cases of neurocristopathy are poorly understood. To address this problem, we use the mouse as a model organism and take advantage of the state-of-the-art methods of genomic modifications and analyses. Such studies are complemented by more classical techniques of molecular and cellular biology. Importantly, through established collaborations with researchers working in a clinical setting, we also validate our findings in children affected by the studied neurocristopathy. Notably, this work allowed us to identify a new gene for which the mutation can cause CHARGE syndrome - a neurocristopathy with a very complex clinical presentation and which can be fatal for many young children. The main objective of the current project is to understand the function of this new gene (Fam172a) in both normal and pathological conditions. This work is expected to significantly improve the way children suffering from CHARGE syndrome - as well as their families - are currently being taken care of.

column36: Tau: a novel target to prevent early neuronal dysfunction and death in glaucoma.
column37: Sight is essential for humans to gather critical information about their surroundings. The fear of going blind has been reported to be more powerful than that of having cancer or heart disease. Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness, affecting >60 million people worldwide. There is no cure for glaucoma and current therapies are inadequate. Loss of vision in glaucoma results from the death of retinal ganglion cells, the neurons that convey visual information from the retina to the brain. High intraocular pressure is the most significant risk factor for developing the disease, but the mechanisms by which ocular hypertension damages retinal ganglion cells are unknown. A major roadblock towards developing effective therapeutics for glaucoma is that very little is known about the early pathological alterations that lead to retinal ganglion cell dysfunction and death. Our recent work has identified a new and intriguing role for tau, a microtubule binding protein implicated in Alzheimer's disease, in ganglion cell neurodegeneration. We showed that tau undergoes substantial alterations early in glaucoma including abnormal phosphorylation, aggregation and missorting. In this application, we will determine the role of tau in the earliest pathological changes in glaucoma, namely retinal ganglion cell dendrite retraction and anterograde axonal transport impairment. This project is unique and timely because it will provide new insight into the molecular mechanisms that govern glaucoma pathogenesis, and it will serve as a springboard to identify new therapeutic targets and potential diagnostic tools for this blinding disease.

column36: Elucidating the role of alpha 11 integrin in mediating cardiac fibroblast-extracellular matrix interactions in health and disease
column37: When the heart is damaged, the body responds by laying down scar tissue. In the early stages, this is a good thing and helps to keep the heart pumping. After some time though, the scar tissue causes the heart to stiffen and it becomes more and more difficult for the heart to both pump, and fill up, with blood. The cells which produce the scar tissue are called fibroblasts, and they "talk" to the scar tissue so that they put the right amount down in the right place. However, this process often goes wrong, and that can cause the heart to fail even sooner. The proteins which help the cardiac fibroblasts "talk" to the scar tissue are called integrins. Our group has identified an integrin, which we don't know much about. It is called the "alpha 11 integrin". Research by our team has shown that when this integrin is missing, the hearts become stiff and the cells look small and thin. This research project will study how this protein "talks" to scar tissue, and what role it plays in the normal heart, and after the heart suffers damage. Given the fact that about 45% of all deaths in the world occur as a result of chronic scar tissue formation, it is vital that we understand exactly how scar tissues and cells work, so that we can one day develop new treatments to stop people dying not only of heart disease, but also other diseases where scar tissue is a problem such as liver disease, lung disease and kidney disease!

column36: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy: Seizure induced brainstem hypoxia
column37: People with epilepsy often die suddenly and unexpectedly. In fact they are 27 times more likely to do so compared with the general population. This unfortunate occurrence is called Sudden Unexpected Death in EPilepsy (SUDEP) and it is the leading cause of death in persons with epilepsy. SUDEP most often occurs where an individual with a history of epilepsy is found dead with evidence of a prior seizure. From the few studies on patients in a hospital setting, that would have died if not for medical intervention; we know that SUDEP is ultimately caused by failure to breathe either during a seizure or very soon after a seizure ends followed quickly by heart failure. What we don't know is what causes the failure to breathe. My laboratory has recently discovered a period of severely low oxygen levels (hypoxia) during and following a seizure. The hypoxia is found only in brain regions involved in the seizure and is severe enough to cause behavioural dysfunction. I hypothesize that SUDEP occurs when seizures invade the breathing centers in the brainstem and local tissue oxygen falls below a critical level impairing the function of those areas which leads to breathing failure and death. We will first determine the relationship between seizure activity and local oxygen levels in brain breathing centers on breathing behaviour. To do this we will use an implantable device that continuously measures the absolute levels of oxygen in awake behaving mice. We will next determine more drugs that can prevent seizure-induced hypoxia. We have previously identified two kinds of drugs that prevent the seizure-induced blood vessel constriction and low oxygen levels. We will use these to determine the effect of preventing the seizure-induced hypoxic period on mouse breathing and survival. We believe that SUDEP is preventable and that the knowledge generated by these proposed studies will ultimately save lives.

column36: Long QT syndrome in Northern British Columbia: Gene-gene interaction, life course differences, and implications for safe management
column37: Usually rare, LQTS is a treatable hereditary heart rhythm condition, which if unrecognized may cause sudden cardiac death. Northern BC First Nations likely have the highest rate in the world, 15 times higher than expected. For over 10 years, our team has partnered with the Gitxsan Community to understand the effect of the common KCNQ1 gene mutation, identifying more than 140 carriers, and enrolling more than 800 community participants. We have learned that other genetic factors can increase risk, and certain times in life may have higher risk than others. Our data suggests young women of childbearing years have the highest risk for sudden death. However, children over a year of age may be spared from the fatal effects until they reach adulthood. Treatment with beta blockers is used in all ages to prevent risk of sudden cardiac death. The problem is that this standard treatment to reduce risk may have the side effect of predisposing to low blood sugar, especially in young children. Furthermore, another genetic factor common in the population (CPT1A P479L) may also increase risk of low blood sugar. A third risk factor is the KCNQ1 mutation causing LQTS can also lead to increased insulin secretion in the pancreas, further risking low blood sugar. Four children in Northern BC have now presented with severe episodes of low blood sugar, all with LQTS and CPT1A P479L, while on treatment with beta-blockers. This emerging information has implications for safe management of infants and children with LQTS in Northern BC. Priority attention will be focused on infancy, childhood, pregnancy, and for all women of childbearing years for 1) risk of cardiac event 2) evidence of treatment complication resulting in potentially damaging low blood sugar. We will also focus on children to explore their lived experiences with the condition and its management. Information from this study will provide evidence for the development of effective and acceptable management strategies.

column36: Genetic mechanisms of arterial calcification
column37: Calcification of the heart's (coronary) arteries occurs as a result of atherosclerosis and increases the risk of dying. Normally, the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the artery wall release calcium but also produce specialized proteins that bind to calcium and prevent calcification of the arteries by promoting calcium removal by macrophages. Coronary artery calcification (CAC) is heritable and common genetic variants on chromosome 9 (at 9p21.3) increase the susceptibility to atherosclerosis and accelerate CAC through an unknown mechanism. We compared human arterial SMCs with 0, 1 or 2 copies of the 9p21.3 risk variants and found that the most differently expressed gene is statherin, a tiny protein known to block calcification in the saliva but not previously tied to this function in SMCs. SMCs with 2 copies of the risk variants expressed almost no statherin, were susceptible to calcification in culture, and could be rescued from calcification by over-expressed statherin. Importantly, we detect statherin in the blood and find lower levels in patients with atherosclerosis and CAC. Our hypothesis is that loss of statherin is the reason 9p21.3 risk variants accelerate CAC. We propose 3 Aims: 1) We will confirm in patients with coronary artery disease that coronary calcification is tied to lower active (phosphorylated ) or higher inactive (dephosphorylated) plasma levels of statherin. 2) We will determine how statherin affects calcium crystal uptake and inflammation of macrophages. 3) We will use a transgenic mouse expressing an active form of human statherin to reverse arterial calcification caused by atherosclerosis or by a genetic defect. Significance: 75% of the world population carries the 9p21.3 risk variants. Therapy targeting statherin to block progression of arterial calcification could reduce mortality in many people.

column37: Preeclampsia is a serious and prevalent disease of pregnancy. In this project, we will determine how aberrant activity of these uterine immune cells leads to placental dysfunction and affects fetal health. We will also examine whether the absence of these immune cells can improve placental and fetal health. Collectively, this project will test the applicability of targeting uterine immune cells to improve placental development, and will form a foundation by which we can decrease or prevent the incidence of preeclampsia.

column36: CD200 dysregulation in asthma: potential for therapy?
column37: Our lungs are relentlessly bombarded by foreign particles and must continually work hard to discriminate between dangerous and harmless ones. Considering the volume of allergen-filled air inhaled every day, the prevalence of inflammation and lung diseases is surprisingly low. Nonetheless, the incidence of asthma has increased alarmingly over the last two decades. There are over 235 millions of asthmatics around the world and its prevalence is around 10% in Canada. Asthma has become an important cause of mortality, decreases the quality of life, and its ensuing health care costs continue to increase every year. Recently, a molecule found at the surface of our cells called CD200 was shown to be involved in the control of inflammation. Our preliminary data show that allergen exposure increases CD200 expression on macrophages, cells located in the lung. Interestingly, no increase of CD200 on these cells was observed in allergic asthmatic animals. Since these macrophages are the most numerous immune cells in the respiratory system and their primary role is to stop unnecessary inflammatory responses, our data therefore suggests that increasing CD200 may contribute to reduce lung inflammation. To investigate whether CD200 is important in protecting against asthma pathogenesis, we treated allergic asthmatic animals with a synthetic CD200 prior to allergen challenge. column36: Developing a framework for the ethical design and conduct of pragmatic trials to improve the quality and value of health care systems and practices
column37: The randomized controlled trial is the gold standard method for evaluating medical interventions. However, the majority of trials are conducted under laboratory-like conditions, which limits their applicability to the real-world clinical setting. There is therefore an urgent need for so-called pragmatic randomized controlled trials, which are undertaken in the routine clinical setting. Pragmatic trials can provide patients, doctors and policymakers with more reliable information as to which treatments and strategies are best for patients. But whilst ethical guidelines exist to protect participants in research -their applicability for pragmatic trials is not straightforward. This has led to confusion, where some trials have been carried out with inadequate protections, and in others, strict enforcement of current guidelines have posed unnecessary obstacles, undermining scientific quality and impeding improvements in the quality of healthcare. Our goal is to clarify this situation by developing novel ethics guidance to help researchers and research ethics committees conduct and review pragmatic trials. Questions addressed will include: Should pragmatic trials comparing accepted and routinely available medical treatments be classified as research and therefore receive extra scrutiny or should they be considered within the scope of usual medical care (as some have suggested) and fall under the rules of the doctor-patient relationship? Do patients always need to be informed about pragmatic trials and be required to provide informed consent? What information about risks and benefits should be disclosed to patients? We will answer these and other questions through extensive analysis of ethics documents and national and international regulations. We will also build a database of completed trials and examine practices; survey researchers, research ethics committees and patients; organize a consensus meeting to generate guidance; and disseminate our work to stakeholders.

column37: Approximately one in two Canadians will develop cancer during their lifetime. However, cancer treatments have changed little in the last 30 years. The recent success stories of GLEEVEC and similar drugs has generated considerable interest in generating more inhibitors that work in the same way, although they sometimes lack specificity and tumours can become resistant to them. An alternative approach that is gaining momentum is to target cancer cells specifically while they are dividing, causing cancer-specific cell death as a result of massive chromosome segregation errors. This approach would be not only more effective, but would considerably decrease side-effects as lower doses of each drug would be required, and would decrease the chance of acquiring resistance, when used in combination therapy. With this mind, my lab is interested in investigating how this approach could be used to target molecules involved in cell division, a process that is invariably disrupted in cancer. We are studying the mechanisms of how the key proteins that guard the integrity of the cell division process are deregulated in cancer cells and how they can be potentially targeted to specifically kill cancer cells and not the healthy neighboring tissue. Our work thus focuses on the basic biology of cancer, but we are also screening for drugs that target some of the proteins we are studying with the ultimate aim of developing new cancer therapeutics. Our research in the basic biology of cancer is therefore directly leading to new advances in the science behind cancer development and translating to tangible benefits for the Canadian public.

column37: The flow of blood in uninjured vessels and the rapid conversion to an insoluble clot following injury are essential for maintaining life. Conversely, inappropriate clot formation (thrombosis) in intact blood vessels causes heart attacks and stroke. Drugs that prevent blood clotting are frequently employed to treat patients at risk of such diseases. However all of the currently used drugs either increase the risk of bleeding in patients or are ineffective in certain populations. New drugs that prevent thrombosis but do not increase the risk of bleeding are needed for better patient management. Blood cells called platelets are important initiators of thrombosis. It is believed that blocking platelet function by inhibiting sensors on the surface of these cells is a strategy for preventing thrombosis without increasing the risk of bleeding. We have identified a new drug (RAG8) that acts on one such platelet surface sensor called PAR4. By blocking PAR4 with RAG8 we prevent very specific cellular events to disrupt the formation of large disease causing clots, without affecting the formation of smaller platelet aggregates. This should reduce the risk of bleeding in patients taking this drug. In this project we aim to better understand how PAR4 works and test the ability of RAG8 to prevent heart disease in a mouse model that mimics human disease. Two groups of mice, one with RAG8 and another with an inactive drug, will be monitored over time and the development of heart disease in the two groups of animals will be studied. We will also use blood isolated from healthy human volunteers and study the effect of RAG8 on releasing factors that lead to the formation of large clots. Combined these studies will generate data that will help advance this drug to human clinical studies and give us a clear understanding of mechanisms that contribute to formation of heart diseases and stroke causing blood clots.

column37: For the Mi'kmaq of Pictou Landing First Nation (PLFN), the estuary adjacent to our community, known as A'se'k (and now known in English as Boat Harbour), and the surrounding landscape have provided us with the foods, medicines, transportation, shelter, and tools we have needed to survive and thrive since time immemorial. But for 50 years, a nearby mill has been piping its effluent directly into the waters of A'se'k and pumping its particulate matter out the stacks into the prevailing winds, which directly target PLFN. Concerned about our children's health, the Pictou Landing Native Women's Group (PLNWG) mobilized in 2010 to undertake community-based participatory health research. We were concerned for our community's physical, mental, emotional and spiritual health in relation to the industrial pollution. Bringing academics in, our team has worked together since then to implement a Two-Eyed Seeing approach to research the women's question: "Are we getting sick from Boat Harbour?" To date we have been researching the mill's health impacts using a number of Indigenous and western research methods to meet this goal. Throughout, we have been documenting our journey by collecting film footage for the production of a documentary film. Now we want to share our novel health-related knowledge vis-a-vis a documentary film about our integrative research. Using the film as a catalyst, we want to investigate how university-based and community-based researchers across disciplines, professions, and sectors can begin to conceptualize a Two-Eyed Seeing approach in their own research in the spirit of healing and reconciliation in Indigenous health. Our overarching goal for this Project is to foster a Two-Eyed Seeing approach across the four health pillars at CIHR that will ultimately translate into improved Indigenous health knowledge, services, and outcomes in Canada, and move us all towards reconciliation and healing for a shared future.

column36: Deciphering the signalling cascades controlling cell-cell fusion
column37: Cell-cell fusion is a regulated cellular process, occurring only in a few cell types, which is essential for development. During embryogenesis, the most frequent type of cell fusion is myoblast fusion, which joins the membranes of two different muscle cells to form a small muscle fibre. This process is repeated thousands of times until the muscle fibre reaches its correct size. Abnormal cell fusion is also a feature of muscle diseases, such as Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophy. However, signalling cascades controlling cell fusion remain largely undefined. Therefore, the objective of this project is to uncover the mechanisms underlying cell fusion has it is not only important for basic biology, but will also contribute the knowledge essential for its manipulation in therapeutic settings, such as promoting regeneration in muscle diseases. Genetic studies in the fruit fly revealed the identity of some genes controlling fusion. Interestingly, the majority of them are involved in controlling the actin cytoskeleton, which is a structure that defines the cell's shape. We are expert in studying cytoskeletal dynamics. The conserved proteins governing cell fusion in vertebrates remained unknown until we discovered Dock1 as the first protein essential for myoblast fusion in mice. We next uncovered a signalling pathway essential for fusion composed of a receptor called Bai3, a signalling molecule called Elmo that binds Dock1, and their target Rac1. Here, we propose to characterize the mechanisms that ensure controlled activation of Bai3 at the right time for myoblast fusion to take place. Next, we outline experiments that will define the role of Elmo in myoblast fusion in muscle development and regeneration. Finally, we identified a protein that is selected by Rac1 to induce cell fusion. We found that this protein is tightly linked to a number of proteins involved in helping cells define their direction in a tissue, and we will determine how Tanc1 orchestrates cell fusion.

column37: With the discovery and use of the first antibiotics during the 1930's, the mortality or morbidity associated with infectious diseases have considerably decreased. However, over the years the use, abuse and misuse of antibiotics have selected for "superbugs" resistant to a wide spectrum of, and in some cases all known antimicrobial drugs. Multidrug resistant bacteria cause untreatable and hard-to-treat infections associated with high mortality rates and increased healthcare costs. Because microorganisms are increasingly resistant to antibiotics, and the pipeline of discovery and development of new antibiotics is slowly drying out, the World is now facing the risk of returning to a pre-antibiotic era, when even the most common infection was potentially fatal. It is now recognized that the emergence and propagation of "superbugs" are largely fueled by exchanges of genetic material (DNA) between microorganisms. The most potent mechanism of transmission of DNA between two bacterial cells is called conjugation. During conjugation, a multidrug resistant donor cell injects parts of its genome into a sensitive recipient cell and converts it into a multidrug resistant "superbug". The goal of our research project is to characterize key elements of the "syringe" and "needle" used by the donor cell to promote the injection of its DNA into the recipient cell. Understanding the molecular aspects of the mechanism promoting the exchange of antibiotic resistance genes will provide us with new targets for the rational design of new drugs aimed at blocking gene transfers to curb antibiotic resistance transmission between microorganisms causing infectious diseases in human and animals.

column36: Diet, physiological dysregulation, and aging: understanding longitudinal links through trajectory analysis
column37: It may seem obvious that what we eat affects how we age, but how diet might affect underlying aging processes remains largely unknown. In light of recent studies showing that vitamin supplements are mostly not helpful and may even be harmful, it is increasingly clear that molecule-by-molecule approaches to guiding nutrition are insufficient. How then can nutritional guidance for older adults be more precise than simply "eat well"? There is very little scientific understanding of how nutrition affects the physiology of aging, in part because the cellular and molecular links are complex and the fundamental mechanisms of aging remain controversial. Addressing this problem is not simple. We need to (1) find appropriate ways to simplify and accurately measure the complexity of what people eat, and of how our bodies age; (2) use data sets that permit us to see how one affects the other within aging individuals over many years; and (3) use sophisticated analytical approaches that let us examine how both nutrition and underlying biology change with age, and how each of these changing systems affects the other as it changes. Our team has this broad expertise, and we will use NuAge, the only cohort study in the world with sufficiently detailed data on both nutrition and biomarkers during aging to tackle these questions. Innovative and validated analytical methods will identify key signals from complex data on nutrition and aging biology, and then assess how these trajectories interact during an individual's lifetime. Our preliminary results have already identified dietary changes that appear to slow aging. The results of our study will (a) help establish how nutrition impacts biological aging processes; and (b) allow us to develop dietary strategies for aging adults exhibiting specific biological aging signatures, measurable through biomarker profiles.

column36: Understanding the Plasma Membrane as a Barrier to Drug Accumulation and Nutrient Absorption
column37: We have recently made an exciting discovery that impacts our understanding of how the plasma membrane (the membrane that encapsulates a cell) of animal cells interacts with molecules in the environment, including nutrients and drugs. For our studies, we use a nematode worm, called C. elegans, to better understand animal biology. For over 40 years, the study of this worm has lead to many discoveries that directly impact our understanding of human biology. In animals, the plasma membrane (PM) is composed of four different fat-like molecules called lipids. One of these lipids, called sphingomyelin (SM), is made by a SM biosynthetic pathway. Through our investigation of how chemicals interact with the worm, we discovered that the activity of this pathway is a key determinant of how molecules interact with the PM. When the SM pathway operates normally, large fat-loving molecules are able to associate with the PM, and smaller molecules are unable to pass through the PM. When the SM pathway is defective, the fat-loving molecules cannot associate with the PM, and smaller molecules can pass through the PM barrier. These observations impact our understanding of how drugs and fat-like nutrients get absorbed by cells. In AIMs 1 and 2 of this proposal, we describe our experiments to investigate this process in detail. One of the enzymes that we think operates in the SM biosynthetic pathway is called PGP-14. Evidence suggests that PGP-14 provides the SM pathway with a precursor, called phosphatidylcholine (PC), for SM synthesis. The human version of PGP-14 is called ABCB4, which provides PCs in the liver so that the body can absorb fats. When ABCB4 doesn't work, children develop an incurable liver disease called PFIC3 and require a liver transplant to survive. In AIM3 of this grant, we use PGP-14 worm mutants as a tool to find drugs that will make up for the lack of PGP-14/ABCB4 biochemical activity in the hopes of providing a cure for children suffering from PFIC3.

column36: Sweet and Stiff: How diabetes activates YAP and TAZ to trigger kidney fibrosis
column37: Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure in Canada. Although significant treatment advances have been made, many patients with diabetes still develop significant kidney injury, ultimately progressing to kidney failure. One of the main reasons why diabetic kidney disease still progresses is that scarring, a critical cause of kidney injury in diabetes, remains poorly understood and thus not well treated. Historically, researchers have focused on chemical triggers of scarring such as high blood sugar levels. As scarring develops, however, the kidney also progressively stiffens. We recently found that this kidney stiffening is an important mechanical trigger for further scarring. How cells respond to diabetes-induced chemical and mechanical stimuli to cause kidney scarring has so far remained a mystery. We and others have recently found that: (1) YAP and TAZ are two important proteins that respond to high sugar (chemical) and kidney stiffness (mechanical) injury stimuli, and (2) YAP and TAZ are important drivers of kidney scarring. In this proposal, we will test whether cells use YAP and TAZ as final common injury sensors to trigger kidney scarring in diabetes, and examine how YAP and TAZ use high sugar and kidney stiffness stimuli to activate scar production. These studies will provide important insights into how kidney scarring begins early in diabetes, and progresses at later stages. Early in diabetes, sugar levels are increased but the kidney is soft because it is not yet scarred. We hypothesize that YAP and TAZ are activated only by high blood sugar in this setting. Later, sugar levels remain increased, but because the kidney has now become scarred, it has stiffened. At this stage, YAP and TAZ are activated both by high sugar levels and the stiffened kidney. Most importantly, if successful, these studies will establish anti-YAP and TAZ treatments as a way to effectively treat both the early and late stages of diabetic kidney disease.

column36: Peptide-based Inhibitors of Bacterial Drug Efflux Pumps
column37: Multidrug resistant bacteria are becoming increasingly widespread, creating an urgent societal need for improved infection treatment and control. A major mechanism of multidrug resistance in bacteria involves protein 'pumps' that remove antibiotics by rapidly pumping the drugs out. These proteins are embedded in the membranes that encircle the bacteria, where they must assemble into unique 3-dimensional structures to produce the pathways ("holes") in the membranes through which the antibiotic molecules are excreted. In research to-date, our laboratory has learned key details as to how one such pump performs its drug pumping action. Using this information, we designed, synthesized, and tested novel peptide (small protein) molecules, and showed that they significantly block ("inhibit") the protein's pumping activity by penetrating the bacterial membrane and interacting with it in a specific manner that disables its pumping mechanism - thus trapping the antibiotics inside the bacterial cell and restoring the drug's intended bacterial killing action. As well, we have recently discovered that this pump works by a virtually identical mechanism in most of the common infectious bacteria. Now, the top priorities of our proposed project are to improve the structures and antibacterial activity of these peptide-based molecules to produce new broad-spectrum agents that will be highly active against a wide range of bacteria. We also propose to extend the approach to inhibit another major drug pumping protein. Our best molecules can be used not only directly to kill bacteria, but also in combination therapies with existing antibiotics to improve treatments, such as for cystic fibrosis, and as additives to decontaminating chemicals to create powerful "double action" antibacterial solutions. In the longer range, our research will generate a novel class of peptide inhibitors for clinical use as a strategy for overcoming a major source of bacterial resistance.

column36: Modulation of Adolescent TBI via the Orexin System, Sleep, and Glymphatic Function
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is one of the most under-addressed and expensive pediatric health problems in Canada. Mild TBIs account for the majority of these brain injuries and incur national costs well above $3 billion/year. Adolescence is a particularly vulnerable time for mild TBI, and in particular repetitive mild TBI (RmTBI). Despite the fact that adolescents demonstrate heightened sensitivity to mild TBI, and are at increased risk for RmTBI, adolescence is a scarcely studied population within this context. A recently discovered waste clearance system for the brain, the glymphatic system, has been linked to functional recovery from brain injury and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. This waste clearance system is much more effective during sleep, essentially disengaging while the individual is awake. Given that 70% of patients with mild TBI report sleep disturbances and adolescents are significantly more likely to be sleep deprived, we hypothesized that RmTBI in adolescence impairs sleep and glymphatic system function, resulting in increased risk for short and long-term neurological consequences. Using a clinically relevant animal model of mild TBI, this project proposes to 1) explore the short- and long-term neurological outcomes associated with RmTBI in adolescents using behavioural, epigenetic, and MRI techniques; 2) determine how RmTBI in adolescence disrupts circadian rhythms, sleep and the glymphatic system; and 3) remediate pathology associated with adolescent RmTBI with a pharmacological agent that improves sleep and targets the glymphatic system. We believe this project will capitalize on exciting and novel innovative mechanisms like the glymphatic system and sleep to vastly improve our understanding of RmTBI in the adolescent brain. Pharmacological treatment of the RmTBI with a sleep-promoting agent will provide mechanistic insight into mTBI pathology and provide new therapeutics for treatment of RmTBI in adolescents

column37: Despite major advances in the past three decades, HIV-1 infection remains a major health problem, with a total of 36.9 million infected people worldwide and 2 million new infections in 2014. In Canada, new infections continue to occur among young men having sex with men as well as within the First Nations communities. Current antiretroviral therapies (ART) are highly efficient in controlling HIV replication. However, viral eradication is not achieved and ART interruptions are followed by rapid viral rebounds. The cost of life-long ART together with drug toxicity and resistance, as well as stigma, justifies the need for an HIV cure. Accordingly, the focus of this translational research proposal is to generate knowledge for the rational design of new cell-specific therapies to reduce HIV persistence and boost immune restoration. The T helper 17 (Th17) cells represent a subset of CD4+ T-cells that play a critical role in the immunity against pathogens at barrier surfaces. Studies by our group and others provided solid evidence that Th17 cells fuel HIV infection and viral reservoir persistence during ART. Briefly, i) Th17 cells are preferential infection targets and their virus-induced depletion from mucosal sites causes non-AIDS co-morbidities; ii) Th17 cells express drug efflux pumps that may render the intracellular concentrations of ART suboptimal; and iii) a fraction of Th17 cells are long-lived and harbor replication-competent HIV reservoir. This project builds on our unique expertise in the identification of molecular mechanisms governing HIV replication in Th17 cells. Specifically, our studies will explore the role of the biological clock within Th17 cells as an "Achilles heel" that could be targeted by specific drugs to prevent HIV infection and the subsequent viral reservoir reactivation. This will contribute to the ultimate goal of HIV eradication in the ART era. The feasibility of our studies is ensured by our team of experts.

In addition, we will seek to establish whether these drugs are able to ameliorate disease in the conditions that overlap with MTM. If successful, we will have identified novel therapies suitable for translation to patients with MTM, and will have established for the first time the prospect of pan-therapy for a broader range of severe childhood neurogenetic conditions.

column36: Understanding the neurobiology of memory retrieval
column37: Over the last few decades, neuroscientists have tried to better understand the different phases of memory. Researchers now know more about the mechanisms involved in the learning and storage of memories. However, very little is known about remembering. Even though people suffering from conditions such as Alzheimer's disease or amnesia have difficulties remembering, a lot less effort has been made to study this memory phase because it was traditionally believed to be only an automatic process. column36: Cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying sex-related differences in atrial fibrillation
column37: Cardiac arrhythmias are electrical disturbances that can prevent the heart from working properly. Death resulting from cardiac arrhythmias is one of the leading causes of mortality in most Western societies. Electrical activity in the heart is regulated in part by ion channels. Changes in ion channels can alter cardiac electrical patterns and synchronicity. Sex-related differences in susceptibility to cardiac arrhythmia exist. For instance, men have a higher prevalence of atrial fibrillation (AF) than women. The basis of these sex differences is far from being understood. AF is characterized by very rapid and disorganized electrical impulse. It is the most common arrhythmia in the population and is a significant source of cardiovascular complication and mortality. Currently, the therapeutic options for the treatment of AF have limited effectiveness and adverse effects can often be encountered. In order to develop an improved therapeutic approach for AF, there is a critical need for a detailed understanding of the mechanisms responsible for the higher male susceptibility to this arrhythmia. This information would not only provide valuable insight onto how and why men are more at risk of developing AF than women, but it would also lay foundation for enhanced and sex-specific therapies for the disease. Accordingly, the primary objective of this proposal will be to identify the basic mechanisms responsible for the higher prevalence of AF in men. These studies will be realized using combination of electrophysiological and biochemical techniques while using mouse and human tissues. This work will help to better understand sex-related differences in the pathogenesis of AF. Ultimately, understanding the mechanism responsible for sex differences in cardiac arrhythmias may help to develop improved strategies for the prevention and the management of cardiac arrhythmias in both men and women.

column37: Infections with flaviviruses constitute a major global public health concern worldwide. Notably, Dengue virus (DENV) causes the most prevalent mosquito-borne viral disease with estimated 400 million infections per year. Ultimately, this project may pave the way to the identification novel drug target for therapeutic treatments of both Dengue and Zika fevers and associated complications.

column36: Probing Hippocampus function in primates using virtual reality. Implications for the study of memory deficits in humans.
column37: The Hippocampus is a brain structure that plays a fundamental role on memory formation. It is one of the most profoundly and early affected brain regions in patients with Alzheimer Disease, other dementias, and Schizophrenia, all characterized by profound memory and cognitive deficits. However, our knowledge of Hippocampus function and mechanisms of memory formation in humans remains superficial. Addressing this issue is fundamental in order to advance our understanding of many brain diseases. Two main theories have dominated the field of hippocampus research over the last decades: a) that the Hippocampus plays a fundamental role in spatial navigation, pioneered by studies in rodents, and b) that the Hippocampus plays a fundamental role in the formation of associative memories, pioneered by studies in humans and non-human primates. In the proposed experiments I will use non-human primates navigating in virtual environments to answer fundamental questions about the role of the primate Hippocampus in memory and cognition. First, we test the hypothesis that the Hippocampus possesses a cognitive map of spatial and non-spatial variables that encode associative memories. Second, we will test two different hypothesis of the role of rhythmic oscillations and eye movements in memory formation in the Hippocampus. Finally, we will manipulate neural activity in different parts of the Hippocampal network and determine the effect of the procedure on memory formation. We will use a novel combination of electrophysiological recordings, optogenetics activation/inactivation of neural activity and behavioral measurements of eye movements and performance in non-human primates performing complex navigation tasks in virtual reality environments. The results will be relevant for advancing our basic knowledge of Hippocampal function, searching for the causes of core symptoms of mental disease and for generating interventions to ameliorate and/or prevent such symptoms.

column36: NETs in complement-mediated TMA
column37: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a disease, in which blood clots block small blood vessels. Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a form of TMA, caused by defects in the immune system that affects the kidneys. Available treatments are dialysis or kidney transplants, but even transplantation is not a guaranteed cure, because the disease can recur in the graft. aHUS eventually leads to clot formation in multiple organs and death. We need new treatment approaches for aHUS, which will require a better understanding of how this disease develops. Factors that predispose to the development of aHUS include genetic mutations that interfere with the normal function of the immune complement system (50%). The commonest factors that trigger aHUS are infections (>60%). How these "predispositions" and "triggers" combine to produce aHUS is not well understood. We also do not understand the cause for this disease in the rest of the patients. Our new idea is that a type of immune blood cells, called neutrophils, is altered in these patients. Neutrophils can form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). These toxic traps, akin to fishnets, can damage the inner lining of the blood vessels and promote blood clot formation. Our goal is to understand the combined effect of NETs and complement in triggering and worsening aHUS. These studies are important, as current treatments that are directed to stop complement problems are way too expensive for most patients. We also propose to identify new genetic mutations to improve the diagnosis of aHUS and treatment options. Our research group has a longstanding interest in understanding what controls the actions of complement and NETs, pioneering treatments for aHUS, and identifying disease-associated mutations. This project holds great promise for advancing the understanding of aHUS and of other diseases involving the immune system and blood clots. We have all reagents, patient groups and expertise to successfully complete these studies.

column37: Celiac Disease (CD) is a complex intestinal inflammatory disorder induced by dietary gluten, which development is controlled by a combination of environmental and genetic risk factors. CD is highly prevalent in North America with around 1% of the Canadian population affected by the disease. The only effective treatment currently available for CD is a lifelong gluten free diet (GFD), yet persistent symptoms and intestinal tissue damage are commonplace among celiac patients that adhere to a GFD. Thus, there is an urgent need for non-dietary therapies that improve patient health and alleviate the social and personal constraints associated with following a GFD. The development of new therapies has however proven challenging because of our incomplete understanding of the mechanisms underlying CD pathogenesis. It is well recognized that T lymphocytes play a central role in CD by causing tissue destruction, however, B lymphocytes - specialized cells involved in the secretion of antibodies and autoantibodies - are also likely very important. Indeed, autoantibodies against the enzyme tissue transglutaminase are produced in CD and their titers have been shown to correlate with intestinal damage. Here we propose to study the contribution of intestinal B cell responses to the pathogenesis of CD and to evaluate in vivo the biological role of autoantibodies in a mouse model of CD that recapitulates all the main features observed in CD patients. We will capitalize on the use of our unique mouse model together with human serum samples to decipher the contribution of B cells to CD immunopathogenesis and to characterize the impact of autoantibodies on the development and/or exacerbation of the disease. In addition of a considerable gain of knowledge on the immunopathogenesis of CD, our work may lead to the identification of novel targets that might guide novel therapeutic strategies.

column37: We perceive the world through our five senses. A central questions of neuroscience is how nervous systems integrate information from multiple sensory modalities to make such decisions. column36: Using C.elegans to learn to predict the personal severity of mutant phenotypes
column37: Why do people have different risks of getting specific diseases? In part, the answer lies in their genes. We know hundreds of mutations that cause genetic diseases e.g. inheriting mutant forms of the CFTR gene causes cystic fibrosis. However, even in well-known examples, the situation is complex - two people inheriting the exact same mutation can have very different severity of symptoms. At present we do not understand the basic mechanisms underlying this. Our goal in this project is to use the powerful genetic tools available in the nematode worm C. elegans to examine systematically why the same mutation can have different effects on different individuals. We will compare how changing each of ~1400 genes affects 10 different worm strains - these 10 strains are as different as 10 different people. This study will yield the first view of the effect of genetic variation on mutant phenotypes in any species and will tell us how to predict this. We already measured the mutant phenotypes of ~1400 genes in 2 worm isolates in a pilot study. We found that ~20% of genes had different mutant phenotypes in this pair of worm isolates showing that genetic differences between individuals often have a major effect on mutant phenotypes. Crucially, we find that we can predict some of these differences in severity, a major step - this study yielded two high profile publications. We now propose to extend this study to 10 worms - comparing 2 worms was just a start. This will give us much more power to investigate the causes of the differences in severity of mutant phenotypes. It will also give us a large enough dataset to begin to build models that will predict the severity of a mutant phenotype in any individual. Ultimately, uncovering the basic principles that govern why the same mutation can have such different disease outcomes in different people will have a key impact on our understanding of genetic disorders in humans.

column37: While combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) has significantly reduced HIV-1 morbidity and mortality, cART is not a cure. This is because HIV is capable of persisting in a dormant or "latent" state in a small number of cells throughout the body. These cells, called "HIV reservoirs", can become re-activated at a later time to produce infectious virus; thus, cART must be maintained for life. Towards the goal of achieving durable HIV remission (or the ultimate goal of a complete cure), two opposing strategies have been proposed: reservoir elimination and reservoir containment. The former involves the use of latency reversal agents (LRAs) to "activate" HIV reservoirs, after which they can be eliminated naturally or therapeutically - whereas the latter involves the use of pro-latency agents (PLAs) to permanently maintain HIV reservoirs in a dormant state. However, the few LRAs and PLAs that have been discovered and tested to date have shown only limited clinical success. Thus, discovery of new agents and combinations are urgently needed. Natural products are a rich source of distinct chemical compounds. We screened >400 unique compounds derived from marine natural products and African traditional medicines and have identified 7 new compounds with LRA activity and 2 with PLA activity in vitro. Initial mechanistic studies suggest that at least 3 of these compound classes target HIV reservoirs by processes distinct from those of existing agents, suggesting their potential to synergize with existing therapies. In this project, we propose to assess these compounds' toxicities, their abilities to target HIV reservoirs from patient-derived cells, and to elucidate their mechanisms of action. We also propose to identify compound analogues with improved therapeutic potential. The results of this research will increase our knowledge of HIV reservoirs and have the potential to identify new therapeutic strategies to cure HIV.

By quantifying these stress molecules early on, we hypothesize that we can predict the severity of atherosclerosis in the individual patient non-invasively with medical imaging. Furthermore, we will investigate antioxidants that have been shown to outperform nature's best agent: vitamin E. The success of this proposal will result in a novel medical imaging agent and a novel therapeutic that could both see rapid clinical application and begin to improve the cardiovascular health of Canadians.

column36: Identification and testing of novel inhibitors of pathological eye angiogenesis
column37: In disorders causing blindness, such as retinopathy of prematurity, diabetic retinopathy, and age-related macular degeneration (AMD), sprouting of new blood vessels (angiogenesis/neovascularization) that mainly occurs in the embryo leads to death of the nerve cells of the retina. These neovascular disorders place a substantial burden on patients and the health care system. AMD alone affects approx. 100,000 Canadians over the age of 50, while diabetic retinopathy is the most common cause of blindness in people under 65. Understanding the molecular basis of these diseases is the best hope for developing new medications to tackle them. Nerve cells in the retina require nutrients and oxygen provided by two distinct vessel beds: retinal vessels that support the optic nerve cells of the inner retina, and the choroid vessels that sustain the light-capturing photoreceptors of the outer eye. In neovascular eye disorders, the existing vessels sprout and new, leaky vessels extend within the vessels beds. The leakage leads to swelling in the eye that disrupts the nutrient and oxygen supply, and vision loss occurs as retinal cells degenerate. Current approaches to block new blood vessels from forming are not effective in all patients and they may have serious side-effects. We urgently need an effective way to prevent these faulty new blood vessels from forming, without affecting the health of retinal nerve cells or the normal blood vessels. This proposal addresses this gap by providing fundamental knowledge of a novel mechanism to prevent new blood vessels forming in the eye. We have identified a mechanism that normally controls eye vessel growth in the embryo that is implicated in pathological blood vessel growth in the adult eye. In this project we will define these mechanisms of normal and pathological eye blood vessel formation, informing the development of new treatments for neovascular eye disorders.

column36: Ontario's Opioid Drug Observatory: Leveraging the Narcotics Monitoring System to inform and evaluate provincial drug policy.
column37: The use of prescription opioids has increased markedly in recent years, and Canada is now the second leading consumer of opioids per capita in the world. This has been associated with a dramatic rise in rates of dependence, addiction, and overdose death involving these drugs. This public health crisis has becoming a priority for provincial and national governments, and population-based research in this field has been an important tool for policymakers developing strategies to address this growing threat to public health. Historically, most research has been limited to government-reimbursed prescriptions. However, because most Canadians do not receive government-funded drug coverage, large gaps remain in our understanding of opioid prescribing and its consequences. The introduction in 2012 of Ontario's Narcotic Monitoring System (NMS), which captures all opioid prescriptions in Ontario regardless of payer, offers a novel opportunity to explore opioid prescribing in a truly population-based fashion. Through linkage of this dataset to a broad repository of health care data, we will describe provincial patterns of opioid prescribing, evaluate the real-world impact of existing programs, quantify indicators of inappropriate prescribing and misuse, identify populations at highest risk of overdose and death, and inform policies likely to impact on this crisis. All work will be overseen by a steering committee comprised of patients, researchers and policy-makers to ensure broad relevance, uptake and dissemination. As Canadian decision-makers struggle to develop evidence-based policies to address the growing national opioid crisis, this work will provide a picture of the current state of the opioid epidemic in Ontario and potential areas for change. This research will generate evidence to help inform and evaluate prescribing policies that will have broad implications for public health.

column36: Identifying genes and regulatory pathways that control sex differences in lipid storage using Drosophila as a model.
column37: In Canada, >10 million people are affected by metabolic diseases associated with excess fat storage (e.g. cardiovascular disease, obesity). Approximately 40% more men suffer from diseases of fat storage than women and drugs used to treat abnormal fat metabolism often work better in one sex (e.g. fenofibrates); yet, knowledge of how men and women differ in fat storage is incomplete. While lifestyle and sex hormones contribute to sex differences in fat storage, therapies based on lifestyle changes are difficult to maintain, and sex hormone therapy has undesirable side effects in both sexes. The next step forward in developing better treatments for abnormal fat storage is to identify the genes that control fat storage in each sex. Targeted therapies will reduce the burden and cost of diseases associated with fat storage (currently >$20bn). My research is at the forefront of discovering genes that drive sex differences in fat storage using fruit flies as an innovative model. Importantly, the genes that regulate fat storage are the same in flies and humans, and our work has shown that sex differences in fat storage faithfully reproduce male-female differences in mammals. Thus the genes involved in sex differences in fat storage we identify in flies will advance our understanding of this problem in mammals. Our use of flies has allowed excellent progress in 18 months: we identified fat storage genes that are regulated differently between the sexes. We hypothesize that this regulation explains why the sexes differ in fat storage. The goal of our project is to discover which of these genes is essential for fat storage in each sex, and to understand how these genes are regulated differently in males and females. We will advance health-related knowledge by identifying a pool of genes that control sex differences in fat storage, providing an essential starting point for researchers to develop new therapies for tackling metabolic disease that will work in men and women.

column36: Stromal Gene Expression Predicts And May Drive Metastasis in Prostate Cancer
column37: Men with low to intermediate risk prostate cancer (PCa) face vexing decisions regarding treatment. The tumour can remain indolent and will not impact the patient within his lifetime, or it can progress to become life threatening (metastatic tumour). A holy grail of PCa research is the identification of prognostic biomarkers, which are biological factors that are associated with the disease outcomes, that can be used to improve patient risk stratification at time of diagnosis and guide treatment decisions. We have created patient-derived PCa tumour mouse models with different metastatic potential that fully recapitulate the transition of a patient tumour from indolence to metastasis. In an effort to identify the mechanisms that drive the growth of a metastatic tumour in these models, we have identified a rich source of prognostic biomarkers in the mouse stroma, which is the tissue supporting tumour growth. We have been able to identify a group of 93 genes only active in the mouse stroma associated with metastasis. We called this group of genes the Stromal Metastatic Signature or SMS. In collaboration with GenomeDx Biosciences, a Vancouver-based company, we confirmed our preliminary observations; that the SMS is strongly prognostic for predicting metastasis in human tumour. The purpose of this very innovative proposal is to seek funding first to further validate the SMS using additional large human tumour cohorts, second to improve the SMS prognostic value by integrating existing tumour-based signatures, and finally to test the hypothesis that the stromal compartment drives metastasis using a novel therapeutic agent developed in our research centre. This very innovative project represents a unique opportunity to apply novel and exciting research findings to the advancement of an important health issue.

column36: Harm reduction: Public health reasoning in law and public policy in relation to morally controversial behaviours
column37: This project tracks, theorizes and evaluates an emerging trend in law and public policy to seek workable agreements in areas associated with moral controversy through the frame of harm reduction. Harm reduction refers to policies, practices or interventions designed to minimize negative health and social consequences associated with a given behaviour, without requiring its cessation and without moral condemnation. It has its origins in grassroots movements and public health. Recently, an expanding range of actors have begun to integrate harm reduction approaches into law and policy in areas ranging from drug use, abortion, physician-assisted dying, and sex work, among others. This project will probe the ethical foundations of harm reduction in these new contexts and consider how this growing reliance on harm reduction can be a way for law and policy to meaningfully address social determinants of health.

column36: Chromatin-Binding Factor MYSM1 in B Lymphocyte Development
column37: B cells are the key component of our immune system, and are responsible for antibody production in response to infections. B cells are continuously produced in our bone marrow throughout life from a small population of hematopoietic stem cells. Disruptions in B cell development can lead to life-threatening disorders including immunodeficiencies and leukemias. Recently we and others identified MYSM1 as an essential protein for normal B cell production in both mice and humans. MYSM1 is a DNA binding protein that regulates gene activity during the process of B cell differentiation from stem cells. In this work we propose to identify the genes regulated by MYSM1 and characterize the mechanisms of MYSM1 activity during B cell differentiation. The role of MYSM1 in B cell cancers, including leukemias and lymphomas, will also be addressed, using mouse as a model. The work is expected to advance our understanding of B cells, and the biology of the bone marrow and the immune system. In the long-term this may lead to a better understanding and management of diseases involving B cell dysfunction.
