column36: Dissecting early and progressive leukemogenic impairments in the hematopoietic hierarchy and function using pre-leukemic inherited bone marrow failure syndromes as human disease models
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a blood cancer with a bleak outlook despite treatment with intensive chemotherapy and bone marrow (BM) transplant. Tools for early detection and prevention are desperately needed. Yet, it is unknown how AML evolves because patients is generally not tested before they become ill. The purpose of this study is to decipher how BM progresses from a non-leukemic state to leukemia, while discovering BM defects in patients with high leukemia risk, namely, inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFSs). Fanconi anemia (FA) and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) are IBMFSs that start with deficient formation of blood cells in the BM during childhood and progress to pre-leukemia (early signs of cancer), which, if untreated, culminate in AML. Patients with FA and SDS die from either low blood counts (causing infections and bleeding) or leukemia or from the treatments' side effects. Since patients with FA and SDS annually undergo BM testing to check if they develop leukemia, samples for research can be obtained from consenting patients before, during pre-leukemia and overt leukemia. Such samples provide a unique opportunity to study how leukemia develops and identify early changes in BM that indicate treatment. In this study we will analyze BM cells from patients with SDS and FA at three stages: no-leukemia, pre-leukemia and leukemia. We will identify BM cells that grow fast (like leukemia cells), discover genetic mutations that indicate early leukemia and determine why early leukemic cells grow in excess. Last, we will use specially prepared cells from IBMFS patients called pluripotent stem cells as a model to insert mutations that we identify and study which mutations turn the cells leukemic. The results of our study can be used for early detection and prevention of leukemia in IBMFSs, and for discovery of drugs that correct the early damage. The principles learned will likely apply to other cancers, though the specific defects may vary.

column37: Effective treatments for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) usually emphasize a behavioural approach called Exposure and Response Prevention. In this treatment, patients are encouraged to face their fears repeatedly and for extended periods of time, with the help and support of a caring therapist. Although this is an approach that has been shown to work, many patients find the treatment to be difficult; some even refuse the treatment, or drop out before improvements are seen. We have been working to develop an alternate approach which is just as effective as Exposure and Response Prevention, but which we think will be much more acceptable to those who seek help for their OCD. column36: Quantitative electroencephalography in rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep: an early marker of cholinergic neurodegeneration in mild cognitive impairment
column37: The prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia is increasing at a rapid pace. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent cause of dementia. The Alzheimer Society of Canada states that 747,000 Canadians had AD in 2011 and that the current estimated costs of dementia for Canada is around $33 billion annually. The degenerative process leading to AD is believed to start decades before the onset of dementia. This long and progressive period is called mild cognitive impairment (MCI) but not all individuals with MCI will develop AD. The identification of earlier markers to detect which MCI individuals will progress to AD is urgently needed for the development and assessment of preventive and therapeutic strategies. Up to now, promising markers measuring brain activity have been identified in awake patients. We propose that rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep is a more sensitive state than wakefulness to detect early neurodegeneration in MCI patients. Indeed, during REM sleep, the activity of the acetylcholine system, which is affected early in MCI, is not masked by other systems that are active during wakefulness. The goal of this project is to predict, in individuals with MCI, those who will develop AD three years later by studying REM sleep characteristics. We will also validate that REM sleep is linked to the integrity of the cholinergic system using brain imaging. If our hypotheses are confirmed, REM sleep characteristics have the potential to become a reliable non-invasive and low-cost tool to help identify MCI individuals at high risk of progressing to AD and test the efficacy of preventive treatments.

column36: Next Generation Antithrombotics: Safer Inhibitors for Thrombosis that Targets Procoagulant Polyanions
column37: Thrombosis- clotting of the blood in blood vessels- is the leading cause of death in Canada and in the Developed society. Blood clot formation in arteries (blood supply vessels) is a major cause of majority of heart attacks and stroke. Blood clot in veins (venous thromboembolism (VTE)) is the third leading cause of death in world after heart attacks and stroke, and is one of the leading cause of death in patients with cancer. Current treatment of these diseases includes the use of drugs which can prevent platelet (a type of blood cell) activation and aggregation, and the use of anticoagulants (blood thinners). However, none of these therapies are perfect due to inherent bleeding side effects associated. Importantly, none of these treatments target the fundamental cause of pathological thrombosis in veins and arteries. Recent studies discovered that biomolecules such as polyphosphate released by platelets and extracellular nucleic acids released by the damaged or activated cells in the blood vessels initiate blood coagulation and cause pathological thrombosis. Thus, in this proposal we are developing novel molecules that can directly neutralize the activity of these potent thrombus generating polyanionic biomolecules by selectively binding them and forming a complex thereby preventing the thrombus formation. This novel drug molecules will also have no or minimal bleeding side effects unlike the current drugs used in the management of thrombosis. This research is based on a recent discovery of a patented novel class of dendritic polymeric inhibitors in our laboratory. This novel therapeutic approach will change the way clinicians treat the patients suffering from blood clot problems and will save the lives of millions of people, and improve their quality of life.

column36: ULK1 (most upstream autophagy inducer) as a potential therapeutic target in Osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and major cause of disability worldwide. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms by which OA can be prevented or treated remains to be determined. Cartilage is the most critical tissue in our joint that is destroyed during OA. Cartilage consists of only one type of specialized cells called chondrocytes and during ageing these cells tend to die faster resulting in destruction of the cartilage and joint tissues. In order to stop cartilage destruction, it's essential to identify key biological processes that can increase the survival of chondrocytes in the cartilage. Our studies using animal models and human OA cartilage samples have identified such biological process of cell survival called autophagy. During ageing and OA, this process does not function very well i.e. this process is weaker resulting in decreased cell protection and increased cell death. The central factor that controls autophagy in the cartilage is unknown. Our studies suggest that a biological factor called ULK1 is a central factor that controls autophagy and maintains chondrocyte survival as well as controls destructive activity within the cartilage. Based on our preliminary data, our hypothesis is that during OA, ULK1 function decreases and as the result autophagy decreases resulting in greater cell death and cartilage destruction. Thus delivering ULK1 in joints will increase chondrocyte survival and halt further cartilage degeneration. To prove this hypothesis, we have generated mice in which ULK1 is specifically absent only in the cartilage, allowing us to specifically identify the role of ULK1 in OA disease process. Furthermore we have also created a method of delivering ULK1 in knee joint of mouse OA model to see if ULK1 therapy can stop chondrocyte death and stop cartilage destruction. Data obtained from this study has the potential to show that ULK1 therapy can be used to stop cartilage destruction and halt OA disease.

column36: Defining the maternal legacy: Does mode of delivery impact the role of the maternal vaginal microbiome in predicting the infant gut microbiome?
column37: The role of bacterial communities throughout the body in health and disease is being widely studied. Preliminary research shows a possible link between delivery type (vaginal or caesarean delivery) and the bacterial communities found in the gut in early infancy. In Canada 1 in 4 women have a caesarean delivery and there is some evidence of increased risk of conditions such as asthma, celiac disease, and allergies in caesarean-born infants. To date no cause for this increased risk has been identified. Some researchers have proposed that this potential transfer of maternal vaginal bacteria may be prevented by a caesarean delivery. This may result in altering the establishment of the infant's own bacterial community. However a clear link between delivery type and the infant's bacterial community has not been established. As a result of this idea the practice of "vaginal seeding" has emerged, where a newborn delivered via caesarean section is swabbed with the mother's vaginal secretions to transfer the mother's vaginal bacteria to the infant, mimicking what the infant would have been exposed to during vaginal birth. However the benefits of "vaginal seeding" have not been evaluated and the safety of this practice has not been proven despite it coming into clinical use. The goal of our study will be to determine if the maternal bacterial community is actually transferred to the infant during delivery and if the different types of deliveries alter this transfer. This study will use advanced gene-based methods to profile the bacterial communities present in women who deliver vaginally or via caesarean section and connect these to the infant gut bacterial community in the first 3 months of life. This research will lead to a deeper understanding of the potential role of the maternal bacterial community on the infant gut bacterial community.

column36: Regulation and function of chondroitin sulfate glycosaminoglycans in urologic cancers
column37: Many proteins expressed by cancer cells are modified with carbohydrate chains. The human placenta and cancer cells express a common type of carbohydrate chain on their cell surface proteins called chondroitin sulfate (CS). The presence of a CS carbohydrate on cancer cells has allowed us to take advantage of an evolutionarily optimized protein called VAR2CSA from the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Malarial VAR2CSA binds to distinct CS chains, which are normally only present in the placenta. However, we have recently discovered that VAR2CSA also binds a similar placental-like CS structure broadly present in human cancer. Based on this, we have developed a protein-based technology that can detect and target cancer via their carbohydrate signature. Placenta and cancer has many features in common such as rapid growth, the ability to invade adjacent tissue, and an elaborate formation of blood vessels to feed the tissue. It is therefore tempting to speculate that tumors re-express placental-type CS to accommodate these important cellular processes. In this project we will elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind CS reconfigurations in human prostate and bladder cancer, and establish the role of these CS modifications in tumor cell growth and survival. Our work will provide new insight into the regulation and function of cancer-associated carbohydrates, essential for developing effective therapeutic strategies targeting human cancer.

column36: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Study III (LAAOS III)
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common heart rhythm disorder that causes one out of six strokes. Prevention of strokes in AF is achieved through the use of blood thinners such as coumadin. Although blood thinners are effective, they are limited by the risk of serious bleeding, by physician and patient unwillingness to use, and by noncompliance and discontinuation. The left atrial appendage is a structure on the upper chamber of the heart that is the most common source of stroke in patients with AF. This structure is easily accessible for removal during open heart surgery, and has been a target of interest for stroke prevention. However, there is currently no definitive evidence that removing it prevents strokes. The LAAOS III trial randomly (like the flip of a coin) assigns patients with AF undergoing heart surgery for other reasons to have their left atrial appendage closed or not closed. These patients will be treated in the usual manner except for this small procedure which has been shown to be quite safe. Having successfully recruited 2300 participants into the trial supported by multiple seed and bridge grants, we now seek full funding to complete recruitment to the full 4,700 participants required to know if left atrial appendage closure works. The LAAOS III trial will determine if closing the left atrial appendage can reduce stroke and other complications in addition to usual therapy. A positive study will change the way heart surgery is performed on patients with AF and result in a large reduction in the number of strokes in Canada. Further, it will promote further research into this approach that could be applied beyond AF patients undergoing heart surgery.

column36: Opposite roles of MYCN and YAP in cancer initiation
column37: Retinoblastoma is a rare childhood cancer of the eye. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a common and very lethal adult tumor caused by smoking. It kills more people than any other cancer. These cancers have much in common, including frequent loss of the RB tumor suppressor gene. Dissecting other shared features that drive these cancers will illuminate new strategies to prevent and treat both diseases. Retinoblastoma arises from cone photoreceptors in the embryonic retina, the cells we use to detect colour. They are hypersensitive to RB loss because they have naturally high levels of MYC, a pro-cancer protein. Why do they need such a dangerous protein? We discovered that MYC is potent at forcing cells to become cones. Cones make other pro-cancer proteins, so by driving this cell fate, MYC inadvertently facilitates tumor formation. Remarkably, we find that MYC also promotes formation of the lung cells that give rise to SCLC. MYC regulates gene expression, so we will identify the targets it controls that promote formation of the tumor-prone cell types in retina and lung. In related work, we discovered that the YAP protein blocks retinoblastoma and SCLC. This is also surprising, because in many other tumor types YAP drives cancer. Our data suggests that YAP impairs retinoblastoma by inhibiting cone formation (and so MYC production). Here, we will examine more closely whether YAP does this in the embryonic human retina, and whether it also blocks the formation of the cells that give rise to SCLC in the lung. YAP is switched off in retinoblastoma and SCLC, so reactivating this gene could be a potent new therapy. To test this idea we will ask if inducing YAP blocks SCLC progression in the mouse lung. If it does, this result would justify extensive efforts to identify drugs that reactivate the silent YAP gene in RB-deficient cancers. SCLC treatment has changed little in decades, but our insights offer hope for new therapies.

column37: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6) is a devastating genetic disease that leads to progressive motor impairment (called ataxia) and cerebellar degeneration. This work will result in important findings that could directly contribute to new treatments for a currently untreatable disease. Furthermore, since several other forms of ataxia, as well as aging, have common changes in the cerebellum, our findings may have broader impact on other degenerative diseases as well.

We will also assess the effect of these 2 treatment options several other outcomes. These include the effect on complications like stroke, time in an intensive care unit and hospital and on quality of life. It isn't clear right now when doctors should be treating low blood levels to improve patient outcomes. This study will provide the answer to this common and important question. column37: In Canada, the proportion of older adults is expected to surpass the proportion of children under age 15 as early as 2017 and will exceed 30% by the year 2050. Still, older adults are among the most sedentary Canadians - 85% fail to meet PA guidelines. This reality is a call to action. This provides a unique opportunity to conduct research into program effectiveness and factors that influence implementation. Therefore our overall research goals are to assess: 1) whether CTM increases PA and increases social connectedness of older adults (Part 1 - Impact evaluation), and 2) factors that help or hinder implementation of CTM across BC (Part 2 - Implementation evaluation). We build upon a history of collaboration among a core team of junior and more senior health researchers who have expertise working with older adults, physical activity and translating research findings into action. column37: The main damage done by most cancer cells results from invasion and metastasis. For this to occur, cancer cells have to leave the primary tumor and move to other tissues. Cells in our body do typically not leave their home tissue when healthy; in order for that to happen cancer cells have to change the properties of the glue that cells use to stick to their neighbors. Dr. Tepass' laboratory identifies and analyzes the components of this molecular glue that mediates adhesion between cells. The glue molecule cadherin has been shown to be broadly relevant for normal tissue development and cancer progression. Cadherin function critically depends on several other molecules including a-catenin, the focus of this study. Cadherin and a-catenin localize at the cell membrane of epithelial cells, preventing those cells from leaving the epithelium to form metastases. This is of particular significance as app. 85% of all forms of cancer derive from epithelial cells and are called carcinomas. The maintenance of epithelial tissue integrity, to which cadherin and a-catenin make major contributions, plays a pivotal role in the prevention of metastatic development in carcinomas. We use the fruit fly Drosophila as a stand-in for humans to investigate how cadherin and a-catenin govern cell behaviour. The main work in the Tepass laboratory focuses on a-catenin, which links cadherin to the cytoskeleton of the cells, an interaction that is essential for cadherin function and currently only poorly understood. Insights into how cadherin and a-catenin work normally is expected to inform us about the role of these factors in cancer, and ultimately will help develop better tools for cancer diagnosis and treatment.

column36: A novel BAFopathy syndrome: Functional genetics using human stem cells and gene editing technologies
column37: Certain molecular complexes are required for brain cells to mature properly. In mammals including humans, a complex called BAF is known to be essential for brain development. BAF is made up of several subunits, some of which are already associated with childhood brain disorders including intellectual disability and disorders on the autism spectrum. BAF functions to bind to DNA and to turn genes on and off. We previously performed genome sequencing on a family with two children with the same severe neurodevelopmental disorder and identified mutations in ACTL6B, a gene which makes a protein that is a subunit of the BAF complex and which has never been associated with disease before. We have identified four unrelated cases with mutations in this gene and with a similar clinical profile, strongly suggesting that mutations in this gene cause disease. Using the index case, we have made stem cells from skin, and turned these skin cells into brain cells, and have done the same in healthy controls. We have performed whole genome gene expression analysis and mapped the binding sites of the BAF complex using similar technology. We have also made isogenic control cells with CRISPR/Cas9 technology where we have repaired the patient mutation and deleted the gene itself, two ways to generate excellent comparison data for rare diseases. In this proposal, we plan to make stem cells from all patients with an ACTL6B mutation, to assess gene expression and BAF binding to DNA at multiple neurodevelopmental timepoints, and to compare human data with mouse knock-in data, where we will generate mice with the patient mutations. This project will do functional genetics of a newly discovered neurodevelopmental disorder and provide new insight into the role of a necessary complex for human brain development.

column36: Neurophysiological biomarkers of insomnia treatment response: towards personalized therapeutic approaches in chronic insomnia
column37: Insomnia is a frequent problem in the general population and is associated with physical and mental health problems. It is still difficult to treat insomnia. Indeed, sleeping pills have side effects and tend to lose efficacy over time in many people with insomnia. Psychological treatment for insomnia - called cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-I) - is effective in a majority of people with insomnia, even in the long term, but requires access to qualified therapists. In addition, up to 40% people will still have insomnia symptoms after treatment. In order to provide the treatment option that is the most likely to work for each specific person, it is important to be able to predict which individuals will respond better to CBT-I. Brain electrical signals measured with electroencephalography (EEG) during sleep (particularly a type of brain signal called sleep spindle) tend to vary from one person to another, but remain stable from one night to the other in a specific person; for this reason, they are considered as a 'trait', i.e. a fingerprint characterizing a specific individual. Some of our preliminary work shows that insomniacs with less sleep spindles tend to benefit less from CBT-I treatment. This means that sleep spindle could be used to predict if people will be likely to have their sleep improved after CBT-I before it is used. In this project, we now wish to confirm these results on a larger group of insomniacs, using more detailed measures of sleep spindles. We also wish to define reference values of sleep spindles - adjusted for age and sex - that will allow identifying insomniacs likely to respond to CBT-I. The findings from this research will allow evaluating if a brain electrical measure such as spindles can be used to predict the efficacy of the recommended first-line treatment option for insomnia, and can thus be used as a tool to guide which treatment to recommend in a specific person.

column36: Timing Deficits in Developmental Coordination Disorder: Understanding the Role of Auditory-Motor Interactions and Implications for Therapies
column37: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) affects 5-6% of school-aged children and is characterized by difficulties in activities of daily living. These children are of normal intelligence but show slow and inaccurate gross and/or fine motor movements. Without intervention, the deficits continue into adulthood in the majority of cases. This population is at high risk to develop anxiety, depression, and obesity; these children are at generally increased risk for physical and mental health problems because DCD affects children's ability to interact socially. One of the core deficits in DCD is poor motor timing. Rhythms and timing are fundamental to biological organisms. In humans, breathing, heart beats, walking, and perceiving speech and music rely on the ability to extract timing regularities in auditory signals and/or to produce regular movements. Remediation treatments for DCD have focused on movement therapies. However, recent work from our group and others on understanding how time and rhythm information is processed in the brain shows that the perception of auditory rhythms is accomplished through interactions between auditory and motor (movement) areas of the brain. Simply hearing an auditory rhythm sets up oscillatory brain rhythms we can measure with electroencephalography (EEG) involving both auditory and motor regions. Thus, we hypothesized, and pilot data corroborated, that children with DCD also show timing deficits in the perception of sounds. The research program aims to (1) understand these auditory perceptual deficits in DCD from both a brain and behavioural perspective and (2) investigate benefits of adding auditory rhythmic cuing to existing movement-training therapies to improve outcomes. The research is significant in furthering our understanding of sensorimotor timing deficits underlying DCD and applying this knowledge to improve treatment programs.

column36: Development of small molecule modulators of Ras signaling
column37: Activating mutations in Ras genes are among the leading drivers in human cancer. The prevalence of Ras genetic lesions is especially high in pancreatic (>90%), colorectal (50%), and lung (30%) cancers. We propose herein a two-pronged strategy to develop small molecule modulators that will block Ras activity in human cancer cells and therefore provide drug candidates for several deadly cancers. We recently identified a series of chemical inhibitors by high-throughput screening with an assay detecting the interaction of Ras with its effector RAF. These molecules were found to inhibit oncogenic signaling and proliferation in Ras-mutant cancer cell lines. We now need mechanistic characterization of these compounds in order to further optimize them and improve their effectiveness. More specifically, we will confirm the binding of these compounds to Ras-ERK pathway components and we will assess their selectivity by biophysical, biochemical and genetic approaches. In a second approach, we will develop compounds mimicking a synthetic protein, named NS1 that binds to Ras with high-affinity. NS1 was recently developed by our collaborators and was shown to block oncogenic signaling and the proliferation of cancer cells (Spencer-Smith et al. Nat. Chem. Biol.). We will exploit this privileged information to rationally design and synthesize Ras inhibitors. The NS1 crystal structure with Ras will be used as a template for computer-assisted molecular modeling. Mimicking protein-protein interactions with small molecules has historically been challenging. We therefore propose to synthesize larger molecules, named macrocyclic peptides, designed to interact over an extended surface while retaining drug-like properties. The two aims of this proposal represent innovative strategies to inhibit Ras function in human tumors. It can be expected that compounds emerging from these approaches will form the ground of effective treatments for many common cancers bearing activating Ras mutations.

column36: Accelerating vascularization and blood perfusion for cell transplantation and myocardial regeneration
column37: Blockage of heart blood vessels (also known as heart attack) causes death of heart muscle cells and small blood vessels. This leads to scar formation that interferes with normal heart function and causes heart failure. The heart muscle cells cannot self-regenerate and one of the possible treatments for regeneration of the heart muscle is the transplantation of heart muscle cells obtained from the patient's own stem cells. Stem cells have that ability to differentiate into any cell type in the body, including the heart muscle cells. However, studies have shown that implanted cells do not survive, in part due to lack of oxygen and nutrients. This happens because the blood vessels are absent in the affected area. Here, we propose to test a new strategy to promote the survival of the heart muscle cells transplanted into hearts that are affected by heart attack. This innovative strategy involves the use of ready-made small vessels obtained from fat tissue to re-establish the blood flow and promote the delivery of nutrients and oxygen to the muscle cells we transplant. These ready-made vessels have the unique ability to connect with host vessels and start carrying blood within the first few days post implantation. We will inject human muscle cells obtained from stem cells with ready-made small vessels from fat tissue into the heart of rats that were surgically submitted to heart attack. We will investigate how this will improve the survival of transplanted heart muscle cells and the heart's ability to pump blood efficiently. This work may provide new therapeutic avenues to treat heart disease and could improve the quality of life of patients suffering from heart attack and heart failure in the future.

column36: Tumor suppressor mechanisms of SOCS proteins in hepatocellular carcinoma
column37: The liver carries out many vital functions such as metabolism of dietary nutrients, storage of vitamins and iron, synthesis of blood proteins and formation of bile. Besides, the liver purifies blood to prevent toxic substances from reaching other vital organs. Hepatocytes, which are the main cell type in the liver, detoxify and eliminate toxic substances that enter blood. During this process, hepatocytes may get injured and undergo death, which prompts adjacent normal cells to proliferate regenerate a functional liver mass. However, repeated/persistent assaults (e.g., alcohol abuse, hepatitis virus infection) induce chronic inflammation and liver 'fibrosis', leading to 'cirrhosis' - characterized by replacement of loss of liver tissue with fibrous tissue, resulting in reduced liver functions. In livers with cirrhosis, hepatocytes undergo recurrent proliferation to restore liver functions. This causes the formation of liver nodules, within which cells accumulate genetic lesions and may become cancerous. While liver failure caused by cirrhosis ranks among the top 10 causes of death in the western world, liver cancer remains the 3rd leading cause of cancer death. Understanding the molecular basis of abnormal hepatocyte proliferation following liver injury is essential to develop more efficient treatments for liver cancer. The key mediators of hepatocyte proliferation are cytokines and growth factors. Normally, their actions are tightly controlled by diverse mechanisms, one of which is mediated by the 'Suppressor Of Cytokine Signaling' (SOCS) family of proteins. The genes coding for SOCS1 and SOCS3 proteins are frequently inactivated in liver cancer biopsies, indicating that they play important roles in preventing hepatocytes from becoming cancerous. Our goal is to understand how these SOCS proteins function in the liver using mouse models of liver cancer so that this knowledge could be used to develop rational strategies to treat liver cancer.

column36: Role of activated astrocytes in APP metabolism and its functional implications in Alzheimer's disease pathology
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a brain disease characterized by a gradual loss of memory, followed by deterioration of other cognitive functions such as language, calculation and judgment. The pathological features associated with AD brains include the loss of nerve cells in selected regions along with abnormal deposits of certain molecules such as amyloid-beta (Ab) peptide and tau protein in structures called as plaques and tangles, respectively. The plaques are usually surrounded by activated immune-related cells called astrocytes and microglia. There is evidence that increase levels of Ab peptides may initiate the loss of nerve cells and subsequent development of AD pathology. Although Ab peptides are generated mostly in nerve cells of the brain, it is reported that activated astrocytes located around the plaques accumulate high levels of Ab. Since astrocytes under normal conditions do not generate Ab peptides, it is of clinical relevance to determine the origin of Ab in activated astrocytes and its role in the development and propagation of AD pathology. In a series of experiments, we will establish whether activation of astrocytes can lead to increased production and/or decreased removal of Ab which can subsequently influence loss of neurons. Additionally, we will establish whether activation of astrocytes by Ab peptide can enhance the secretion of small vesicles called exosomes containing Ab peptides which can influence the development/ propagation of AD pathology. Results from this study will highlight the origin and significance of Ab peptides in activated astrocytes and their role in the development/propagation of AD pathology.

column36: Real-time imaging and co-transcriptional probing of riboswitch regulatory mechanisms
column37: The Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) and the Functional Annotation Of Mouse (FANTOM) consortiums reported that there are far more transcripts than initially anticipated. Surprisingly, it turned out that coding transcripts represent only <3% of the total genome, whereas the majority of other transcripts have no coding potential. The existence of the large number of noncoding transcripts has been disregarded as junk DNA and transcript noises for some time, but increasing evidence suggests that a significant part of such noncoding transcripts are in fact functionally active RNA molecules. Importantly, the biological function of noncoding RNAs is thus primarily determined by their structure and their interactions with protein partners. Among these non-coding RNAs are riboswitches, which are structured elements typically found in the 5' untranslated regions of mRNAs. Riboswitches regulate gene expression by altering their structure upon binding to small cellular metabolites. Similarly to the majority of non-coding RNAs, very little information is known regarding how the structure of riboswitches is used to modulate genetic expression. As a result, it is imperative to employ novel high-resolution methods to characterize RNA structures under conditions closer to the in vivo context, most preferably allowing to study the structure of nascent transcripts. A major goal of our research is to unravel the molecular mechanisms by which riboswitches perform ligand binding during their transcription (i.e., co-transcriptionally) to control gene expression. Our research could be used to design novel general antimicrobial drugs based on riboswitch ligand analogs, which would be selectively toxic to bacteria carrying these RNAs. The knowledge obtained from this research will also be generally applicable to study more complex systems, such as long non-coding RNAs associated to cardiovascular diseases and several types of cancer.

These three proteins are indispensible for fertilization, as mice lacking in CD9, Juno or Izumo1 are healthy but infertile. Here, we propose a series of integrated, multidisciplinary approaches designed to unravel the role of Izumo1, Juno and CD9 in sperm-egg fusion. These studies will bring us one step closer to the development of non-hormonal contraceptives and fertility treatments.

column36: Molecular Therapeutic Targeting of Malignant Gliomas
column37: Malignant gliomas are highly aggressive cancers with a survival expectancy of less than 2 years despite surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Over the past 30 years, limited progress has been made in treating this aggressive cancer despite our increased understanding of the molecular genetics and basic biology of these tumours. Accordingly, new treatment strategies are desperately needed. Malignant gliomas are comprised of a central glioma core (GC) of cancer cells which are rapidly dividing to increase the size of the tumour mass. Intrinsic resistance mechanisms of these cancer cells in the GC prevent chemotherapy and radiation therapy from being effective. In addition, malignant gliomas are characterized by highly invasive cells which are not rapidly dividing but are capable of migrating a considerable distance away from the central core in a zone of infiltration (ZOI). These invading glioma cells are somewhat protected by an intact blood brain barrier (BBB) which prevents chemotherapy from effectively reaching the ZOI. In this proposal, we will use novel therapies based on our recent studies to treat the rapidly dividing glioma cells in the GC. We will focus on metabolically reprogramming glioma cells in the GC to reduce their proliferation, and to inhibit glioma cells from following pro-survival pathways in response to cellular stresses such as hypoxia, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. In addition, we will target the invading glioma cells in the ZOI using novel inhibitors of cell invasion, and magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound to break down the BBB around the GC to facilitate contact of these inhibitors with the invading glioma cells. We expect that simultaneous precision targeting of the GC and ZOI with potent drugs and advanced delivery strategies will provide therapeutic and survival benefit to patients suffering from this lethal cancer.

column36: The role of circ-Dnmt1 in cardiac remodeling and senescence
column37: Cardiac diseases are the leading cause of death in developed countries. Over time, as hearts age or become senescent, adverse remodelling that is initially beneficial, progressively leads to reduced cardiac functioning. Our research aims to understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie this remodeling and repair. Circular RNAs are closed continuous loops of RNA that were recently detected in eukaryotic cells, and may affect cell physiology through a variety of mechanisms. Our work revealed that the circular RNA circ-Dnmt1 is tightly associated with senescent or aged heart. We thus hypothesize that circular RNAs may regulate cell aging and tissue repair by binding to protein regulators of cardiac senescence. To test our hypothesis, we will modify cardiac fibroblasts so that they express more of the circular RNAs in question. We can also use the reverse approach to silence circular RNA expression, and observe the changes in function. Using these two approaches, in conjunction with standard experimental models, we can better understand the function of circular RNAs in cardiac senescence. There are two unique aspects to our proposed study. Firstly, we are among the first to produce a stable expression construct allowing long-term studies of the circular RNAs. The second unique approach is our inhibitor system that is designed to block the function of individual circular RNAs in both cell and animal models. These allow us to specifically study individual circular RNAs, and better understand any causal relationships. Our proposed experiments will help us explore the regulatory roles of circular RNAs in both cardiac aging and other cellular repair contexts. The agents developed may be used as tools in understanding the role of circular RNAs in heart development, aging, disease-associated injury and tissue regeneration. With these approaches, we hope to design therapies to intervene against the adverse remodeling associated with age-related heart disease.

column36: Copper Drug Complexes: Development of a novel class of drugs with significant potential for treatment of platinum insensitive cancers
column37: One strategy that Dr. Bally has been using to develop drug candidates for use in treating cancer involves repurposing drugs utilized for the treatment of diseases other than cancer; illnesses such as malaria, fungal infections or even alcoholism. He wants to repurpose these drugs for use in patients with cancer because they have unusual and unexpected ways of affecting cancer cell growth and survival. Further these drugs are very active in cancer cells that are resistant (insensitive) to one of the most commonly used drugs available to oncologist- cisplatin. Sadly, the useful form of these approved drugs is often water insoluble and cannot be injected into patients. Dr. Bally's team has solved this problem for many such drugs by synthesizing them inside small (100 times smaller than a red blood cell) spherical structure prepared from lipids. These structures are called liposomes ("lipid bodies"). Liposomes with entrapped drugs have been used successfully to improve the therapeutic effects of cancer drugs, but in the current research the liposomes are enabling the creation of the active drug inside the spherical structure in a manner which keeps the drug in solution; in a form that can be administered to patients. This research program will characterize and develop selected versions of these drugs for use in the treatment of cancers that are resistant or insensitive to cisplatin.

column36: A transgenic mouse model of multiple sclerosis offers new ways to identify mechanisms of progression and novel therapies
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory disease of the brain leading to paralysis, that mostly affects young adults. The majority of patients will present with a relapsing-remitting (RRMS) form of the disease in which the occurrence of symptoms (relapses) is followed by periods of partial or complete recovery (remission). In primary progressive MS (10-15%), which affects mainly men, there is a steady worsening of neurological function without intermittent recovery. Affecting more than 100, 000 Canadians, women 2-3 times more often than men, research into the exact cause and disease mechanism of MS is essential to find an effective treatment. Current treatments can temper, but not cure RRMS and no therapy is available to treat the progressive disease. The current and common mouse models for MS lack some essential disease features i.e. gender differences, spontaneous disease development, progressive disease phase and involvement of various inflammatory cells, making them inadequate to study this disease in vivo. Our goal is therefore to use a new mouse model, named the TCR1640 model, that thoroughly reflects the clinical features of MS to fully elucidate the exact disease mechanisms, that are so distinctive for MS, and to find novel specific therapeutic targets for every disease phase. We will first investigate the relationship between gender and disease development. Next, we will elucidate how different disease phases occur (relapse and progressive) and resolve (remission) from an immunological and neurological point of view. Finally, we will use this mouse model to test new therapeutic strategies for all types of MS. After this, we can look forward to implement these in MS patients. Therefore, using a mouse model that clinically and immunologically reflects human MS disease is essential to shed light on disease development, gender differences and on the untreatable progressive disease phase to find an effective treatment for all disease courses.

column36: Getting Ready for Vision Therapy in Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders
column37: Our goal is to identify therapies for a group of genetic diseases, the Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders (PBD). Progressive retinal degeneration leading to blindness is one of the major, untreatable handicaps in this condition and correcting vision would vastly improve the quality of life of these individuals. PBD are due to mutations in PEX genes, whose protein products are required to assemble peroxisomes- intracellular organelles vital for complex fat metabolism. Most persons with PBD have a common mutation in the PEX1 gene, that encodes a misfolded protein, PEX1-G843D, with significant residual function. These children and adults have a condition characterized by progressive tissue damage due to ongoing peroxisome dysfunction over time. Importantly, there is a window of opportunity to intervene and halt this progression. We have now identified two promising drugs (approved for other purposes) that recover peroxisome function in patient cell lines by acting as 'chaperones' to improve PEX1-G843D function. We also have a mouse model with the equivalent mutation that has a retinal degeneration similar to patients. A recent pilot study showed that our candidate drugs recovered retinal functions in the mice by electroretinogram studies. In this project, we will study the murine retinal disease to determine the best time points to intervene for therapy and accurate clinical endpoints to measure response. Expanding our patient cohort, we will also carefully study and compare the human retinal disease to ensure we can translate this therapy to patients. If successful, this will be the first targeted therapy for PBD and address a devastating feature, blindness. The information we gather on the course and pathophysiology of the disease, will also enable and accelerate all future, independent avenues for correction of the retinal disease in PBD. Finally, we expect that these chaperone drugs will also be able to treat other body systems involved in this disease.

column36: What is the cause of chromosome segregation error in the mammalian preimplantation embryo?
column37: The health of the newly fertilised embryo is an important determinant of fertility. One problem commonly experienced by women undergoing fertility treatments is that the early embryo has cells with the wrong number of chromosomes - termed 'aneuploid' cells. Embryos with aneuploid cells are considered unlikely to give rise to a healthy baby. Indeed, many clinics use the presence of aneuploid cells to discard bad-quality embryos rather than transfer them back to the patient. The presence of aneuploid cells in the early embryo indicates that errors have taken place during chromosome segregation - the process of sharing the chromosomes between the daughter cells at the time of cell division. However, despite the clear importance in human fertility, the cause of these chromosome segregation errors in early embryos is unknown. Our laboratory specialises in the use of state-of-the-art imaging approaches to observe and investigate the process of chromosome segregation, and we have developed an assortment of techniques for observing these processes in embryos. Here we will perform some of the first examinations of how chromosome segregation works in the early mammalian embryo, and try to understand why this process goes wrong so often. Most of our experiments will use mouse embryos, with some experiments using human embryos that can no longer be used for treatments. This work will shed light upon the causes of chromosome mis-segregation in the embryo, helping to explain the problems experienced by many fertility patients, and we hope that our experiments will directly lead to improved methods for selecting embryos for transfer to patients in the clinic.

column36: The role of TRPV1 receptors in the pathogenesis of febrile seizures- links to respiration and inflammation
column37: Febrile seizures are the most common seizure disorder to affect children who are at a high risk of developing intractable epilepsy. The mechanisms of febrile seizures are unknown which has limited the development of prophylactic treatments. There is strong evidence supporting that febrile seizures occur when children have fever-induced increases in breathing associated with an infection that leads to respiratory alkalosis and subsequent decreased seizure thresholds. Indeed, shifts in acid-base balance are well recognized to alter brain function such that alkalosis leads to hyperexcitability and decreased seizure thresholds, and acidosis producing the opposite effect. Given this link between fever, respiration and febrile seizures, it is important to determine the precise mechanisms by which fever leads to increases in breathing and subsequent respiratory alkalosis. Transient receptor potential vanilloid type 1 receptors (TRPV1) are heat sensitive receptors that play an important role in thermoregulation and responses to inflammation. Importantly, TRPV1 has been localized in the vagus nerve which is a key driver of the fever-induced increases in breathing linked to respiratory alkalosis. The overall goal of this proposal is to test, in an inflammation-based model of febrile seizures established in my laboratory, the link between TRPV1, inflammation and fever-induced increases in breathing accounting for respiratory alkalosis and consequent increased risk of febrile seizures. The results of this study will provide a molecular target upon which, currently unavailable, prophylactic treatments for febrile seizures can be developed and made available for use in clinical practice.

column37: With the increase in antibiotic resistance, the treatment of certain strains of tuberculosis (TB) is becoming more challenging. TB caused 1.4 million deaths in 2014 making it the single most deadly bacterial infection worldwide. Multidrug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is a condition afflicting an estimated 480 000 globally, and is defined as TB that is resistant to the primary antibiotics used to fight the disease. MDR-TB is treated using different combinations of alternative antibiotics. What is not known is which types of patients respond better to which combinations of antibiotics, and which patient characteristics are most closely related to successful treatment. In order to use statistics to answer this question, a large amount of data is needed. Previous studies (with limited numbers of patients sharing their data) did not have enough information for investigators to unravel the relationships between patient characteristics and the probability of curing the disease. The objectives of our study are to 1) Learn which patient characteristics affect treatment success for different combinations of antibiotics, and 2) Design treatment strategies to maximize the success of treatment for MDR-TB. Our team has previously performed a large review of existing studies and has combined all available data into a much larger dataset. This dataset will allow us to investigate which patient characteristics (such as age, sex and antibiotic resistance) can help predict the success of specific treatments. We will use this information to statistically construct patient-specific treatment guidelines, which will ideally be used by doctors to treat their patients.

column36: Molecular Rules in Brain Cell Microcircuits in Health and Disease
column37: Maintaining the balance between excitation and inhibition is a fundamental attribute of brain function that is necessary for information processing and higher functions, such as affect and cognition. The maintenance of this balance occurs through the constant fine-tuning of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission on multiple time scales, from milliseconds to weeks and months. Much has been learned about short-term functional adaptations (seconds to hours) at the cell contact level; however how the different cell types of brain microcircuits synchronize their functions on longer time-scales (weeks to months) to maintain optimal function, while allowing plasticity, is less well-known. Our data suggest a predominant role for inhibitory cells in mediating adaptive changes during brain aging. We and others show similar inhibitory changes, albeit out of synchrony or exaggerated, in the context of depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Hence we predict that (1) changes in gene function, specifically in inhibitory neurons, maintain long-term adaptations during life-long brain aging, and that (2) changes in the same cell-dependent gene programs occur in several brain disorders. Using molecular biology and computational methods, we will test this hypothesis directly in the human post-mortem brain, using samples from midlife and older subjects. Similar approaches will be used in rodent models to investigate mechanisms and conservation of processes across species. We will then determine the extent of changes in the same cells and pathways in the context of diseases, using human samples from bipolar depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's patients. This novel dimensional approach across species, lifespan and brain disorders has the potential to reveal the molecular mechanisms and rules that govern long-term homeostatic processes across the main cell types of brain cell microcircuits in health and brain diseases.

column36: Dissecting the hematopoietic hierarchy and function using inherited human disease models of hematopoietic stem cell/progenitor loss
column37: The bone marrow (BM) makes millions of blood cells every day via a complex multistep process. White blood cells fight infections, platelets prevent bleeding and red cells deliver oxygen; all are crucial to sustain life. Reduced blood formation is a common problem caused by infections, toxins, cancer treatment or genetic conditions. Current treatments include blood transfusions, BM stimulants or BM transplants. Unfortunately, these treatments frequently cause serious side effects or are ineffective. Developing better treatments requires deep understanding of how the BM forms blood cells. Our understanding of blood cell formation has been advanced. Yet, most studies used animals such as mice that have significant limitations due to major differences between mouse and human BM cells. Inherited BM failure syndromes (IBMFSs) are rare genetic diseases in which one or more types of BM blood-producing cells are impaired, leading to infections, bleeding and heart failure. The study of IBMFSs can not only help develop cures for these patients, but also help understand how the human BM normally works and overcome the critical limitations of animal research. The goal of our study is to advance our understanding of how the human BM functions, while deciphering why blood cell formation is disrupted in IBMFS patients. We will analyze patients' BM and identify cells that are reduced in number. To determine why the affected BM cells are reduced, we will determine the type of genes that are activated or inactivated in these cells, the cells' growth properties and ability to survive various stresses. Last, we will use specially-prepared cells from IBMFS patients called pluripotent stem cells as a model to correct the blood defects. Our study will close critical gaps in our understanding of how human blood cells are formed. This information is crucial for developing effective and safe ways to improve blood formation in various conditions including IBMFSs, infections and cancers.

column36: The Role of Kidney Injury Molecule-1 in Renal Transplantation
column37: Kidney transplantation is the ideal treatment for patients with end-stage kidney disease. Despite better drugs to suppress the immune system, however, the long-term survival of the transplants remains suboptimal. Damage of the kidney due to the lack of blood flow during organ procurement and cold storage before transplantation (ischemia-reperfusion injury, or IRI) is believed to be a major contributor to the limited lifespan of transplants. The tissue injury is further compounded by rejection episodes in the transplanted kidney. There is also growing evidence to suggest that IRI may interact with immune factors worsening graft injury. Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1) is a protein produced by native and donor kidneys following injury. Using mice genetically engineered to be deficient in KIM-1, we previously showed that KIM-1 protects the native kidneys of mice from tissue damage and kidney dysfunction following IRI. Paradoxically, however, KIM-1 can also promote chronic kidney disease and scarring. Whether KIM-1 protects or is harmful in transplanted kidneys is unknown. In this project, we will use a mouse model of transplantation to help determine if KIM-1 in the transplanted kidney can protect it from tissue damage from IRI as well as from acute rejection, or whether KIM-1 leads to long-term scarring and premature graft loss. We will also test the therapeutic potential of a new molecule called AIM, which we have shown can protect native kidneys from the damaging effects of IRI via a KIM-1 dependent pathway, in improving the lifespan of transplanted organs. The findings from our proposed studies will advance our understanding of why transplanted kidneys fail prematurely, and help us to develop new potential treatments to prolong their lifespan.

column36: Cocaine Addiction: Epigenetic Studies in Living and Postmortem Brain
column37: The overarching goal of this research is to understand how interactions between inherited genes and early drug use can affect vulnerability to addictions. Genes determine how fast or slow or accurately particular proteins are produced, thereby affecting all aspects of our biology. Drug use can alter the expression level of genes leading to long-lasting changes in brain and behavior. Until recently, it has not been possible to study these "epigenetic" effects in much detail. Now, thanks to two major advances, we will conduct the following studies. First, we will use a recently developed brain imaging technique (PET with the tracer, [11C]Martinostat) to measure, in people and research animals, the effects of cocaine use on "HDACs," a class of enzymes that affects gene expression. Second, we will use new gene editing techniques to experimentally induce HDAC changes and measure the effects on gene expression and cocaine use in laboratory animals. Third, the gene expression changes seen in the research animals will serve as targets to investigate in postmortem brain tissue donated from people who had struggled with cocaine addiction. We are starting with the study of addictions because understanding better the causes of addiction could help us develop effective treatment and prevention strategies. And the need for new treatments is urgent. Substance use is associated with economic costs greater than all other psychiatric disorders combined, and the present research is expected to identify critical genes, enzymes, and brain pathways that could serve as important therapeutic targets. If the strategy is successful, the same approach can and will be applied to other problems.

column37: Microtubules (MTs) are protein polymers that form a cable-like network of transport super-highway to move important cargoes around inside a cell. One of these cargoes is our chromosomes, the genetic material that makes us what we are. It turns out that these cables need to grow and shrink all the time to perform their functions such as capturing and transporting chromosomes, especially when cells are dividing. A clinically proven strategy to stop cancer cell proliferation is to perturb the growing and shrinking dynamics of MT polymers. In fact, MT-targeting drugs are among the most successful chemotherapeutic agents currently used in the clinics. However, their success is hindered by adverse side effects and the development of drug resistance in cancer patients. To address these shortcomings, we propose to further exploit this proven approach through an alternative route - by targeting the protein enzymes that control the MT polymers. Using a high-throughput screening approach, our lab has already identified chemical agents that modulate these MT modifying enzymes. Importantly, these agents exert a potent growth suppressive effect on cancer cells, but seem to spare non-cancer cells. However, the precise molecular mechanism how these molecules work is still not known. In the proposed project, we aim to use modern cutting-edge technologies to understand the following: 1) How these chemical agents affect the MT-regulating enzymes at the molecular level; 2) how this in turn affects cancer cell proliferation; and 3) how to improve the specificity and efficacy of this new class of potential chemotherapeutics. Our ultimate goal is to validate this new strategy in order to develop the next generation anti-cancer drugs.

column37: Human papillomaviruses (HPV) infect undifferentiated stem cells of our skin. Others and I have shown that HPV disrupts this response in OPCs but it remains largely unclear how the virus controls this phenomenon. To understand how different cellular backgrounds impact the response of HPV+ OPCs to anti-cancer treatment, we aim to identify the landscape of genes that promote resistance in these cancer cells by using a CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing approach. Finally, as different types of viral genome integration are detected in OPCs, we also plan to investigate how they affect the response of OPCs to treatments. Globally, our findings will define how the virus impacts the biology of OPCs and how it is affecting their response to chemoradiation treatments. Furthermore, our unbiased approach to identify genes that promote resistance to treatment is likely to provide therapeutic targets that can be exploited to treat HPV+ OPC patients that resist current therapies. Finally, our project has the potential to reveal new biomarkers to measure the responsiveness of HPV+ OPCs to treatments.

column36: On the road to promoting mobility and health after driving cessation among older adults
column37: Mobility is a broad concept that can be understood as the ability to move oneself within environments that include one's residence and neighbourhood. For many older adults, mobility outside the home is primarily achieved through driving a motor vehicle. Driving affords independence, forms a central part of identity, and has been associated with high quality of life. Older adults who have ceased driving describe a void in their lives after driving. Driving cessation among older adults is associated with poor health as well as increased risk of institutionalization and mortality. The research on driving cessation has been focused on the negative health impacts of non-driving with little emphasis on mobility impacts or variables that protect against negative health outcomes. It is now necessary to shift the focus to understanding and supporting older adults who are no longer safe to drive and to reframe this issue in terms of mobility. Our main objectives are: 1) confirm the associations and better understand the temporal relationship between driving cessation and health related outcomes in a large Canadian sample; and 2) identify individual- and contextual-level factors that moderate the relationship between driving status and health-related outcomes among older adults. Participants will be derived from the Candrive project, a large prospective cohort study of older drivers that collected a host of variables over a 7-year period. Additional measures related to the individual and their environment will be administered to consenting participants already enrolled in the Candrive study. This study will follow individuals for an additional 4 years in order to observe more cases of driving cessation. This study will identify factors that promote health among older adults after driving cessation and will be used to develop interventions and policies to facilitate a healthy transition to non-driving.

column36: The 'Phi-Nong' Project: Development and Pilot Testing of a Culturally Adapted, High-impact HIV Preventive Intervention with Young Men who have Sex with Men and Transgender Women in Chonburi Province, Thailand
column37: In Thailand, as in Canada and globally, young men who have sex with men (YMSM) and young transgender women (YTGW) are at high risk for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). In Bangkok, MSM have 100 times higher rates of HIV than the general population, with YMSM (16-21 years-old) at even higher risk than older MSM-among the highest rates of new HIV infections in the world. Despite this, YMSM and YTGW are largely excluded from existing Thai HIV outreach efforts: these primarily target older MSM and TGW at gay bars and clubs, with a minimum age of entry of 20-years-old. Additionally, many YMSM and YTGW do not publicly identify as gay or TGW, and do not feel comfortable using HIV services delivered by gay or TGW community-based organizations (CBOs). This convergence of high HIV risk, lack of access to HIV prevention programs, and lack of evidence to support interventions tailored for these populations, is a public health emergency. The goal of this innovative project is to culturally adapt and evaluate an evidence-based HIV prevention program with YMSM and YTGW in Thailand. We will work with YMSM, YTGW, a Community Advisory Committee, local CBOs and service providers to build on a peer outreach model with demonstrated effectiveness in reducing HIV risk among YMSM in North America, by culturally adapting (such as matching slightly older with younger YMSM and YTGW, more appropriate in Thai culture than same-age peers) and testing the model in Thailand. column36: Optimizing the Curative Treatment for High Risk Prostate Cancer: Combining Advanced Imaging, Trans-perineal Mapping Biopsies, and Dual Air Kerma Strength LDR Brachytherapy Implants to Minimize Radiation Dose to Normal Tissues
column37: Radiotherapy plus hormonal treatment is the recommended form of treatment for men with high risk prostate cancer. An increase in the delivered treatment dose has been shown to improve treatment success rates in these patients. The downside, however, is increased treatment side-effects. The ASCENDE-RT trial, a recent multi-center randomized trial at the BC Cancer Agency, shows that men treated with external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) followed by low-dose-rate prostate brachytherapy (LDR-PB) boost had better treatment results compared to conventional dose-escalated EBRT (DE-EBRT). Though, worse side-effects, mostly in the form of urethral strictures, were also observed. LDR-PB is particularly well suited to target tumors of the prostate. However, since determining the tumor location cannot be reliably done (and, therefore, is usually not done) the extra-dose is given to a majority of the prostate gland. By identifying tumor locations and focusing higher treatment doses to these areas and a lower dose to healthy tissue (i.e. 'focal LDR-PB boost') we expect less treatment side-effects in men with high-risk prostate cancer. We propose to develop and evaluate a new alternative for treatment of high-risk prostate cancer which involves: 1- Template-guided, trans-perineal mapping biopsy (TTMB) for accurate tumor localization. 2- Multi-modal, multi-parametric imaging (MRI, ultrasound, and PET/CT) for patient selection and follow-up. 3- Novel dual-source based focal LDR-PB for improved targeting of the tumor. Cancer maps created from multi-modal, multi-parametric imaging will ultimately be used to guide or replace TTMB for patient selection, treatment planning and follow-up. We expect the proposed approach to provide a treatment alternative with fewer adverse effects for approximately 15-20% of men with high-risk PCa.

column36: Haploinsufficient loss of ESCRT components as new drivers of cancer
column37: Receptors located at the surface of the cell integrate the extracellular environment towards cellular functions such as cell survival, proliferation and migration. To efficiently control extracellular signals, cell surface receptor levels and turnover is tightly regulated. This process is orchestrated by the Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery, composed of several cellular proteins. Importantly, ESCRT components are essential for the attenuation of the cell surface signalling. Impairment in ESCRT function leads to receptor stabilization, persistent signalling, and cancer promotion. During cancer progression, some genes that prevent tumor development are inactivated and are called tumor suppressors. The identification and characterization of these tumor suppressors is essential to develop new cancer therapies. Our previous work identified HD-PTP, a new member of the ESCRT complex, as a novel tumor suppressor. Indeed, inactivation of HD-PTP in mice leads to development of lung cancer and lymphoma. Interestingly, we have shown that UBAP1 and Endofin, two novel ESCRT components and HD-PTP binding partners, share HD-PTP functions. Therefore, we hypothesize that HD-PTP and its binding partners (UBAP1 and Endofin) exert tumor suppressor functions. This research project aims to characterize the physiological function of HD-PTP/UBAP1/Endofin-containing novel ESCRT complex and to determine their role in tumor development. Moreover, since ESCRTs play a central role in a wide range of signaling pathways activated downstream of numerous cell surface receptors this project might have significant implications in the development of new therapeutic strategies that would be applicable to a wide range of cancers.

column36: Targeting novel acid stress resistance mechanisms in cancer cell metabolism
column37: In all cancer cells, a series of fundamental metabolic changes occur that enable growth and spread of tumours throughout the body. Hence, these metabolic changes are important potential therapeutic targets in the treatment of cancer. An important metabolic change that occurs, called the Warburg effect, is related to how cancer cells generate cellular energy to feed their growth and survival. A consequence of the Warburg effect is accumulation of damaging intracellular acid, and cancer cells must have systems in place to counter acid accumulation. The only known system involves turning on acid pumps to pump the acid out of the cell into the surrounding tumour environment, and drugs are currently being developed against this limited set of targets. Using a discovery-based approach we have identified over thirty new potential targets of acid stress in cancer cells. The objective of this grant proposal is to validate roles for these targets in growth and survival of cancer cells and to test them as potential therapeutic targets using animal tumour models. Identifying additional systems that cancer cells use to survive acid stress will provide insight and facilitate novel approaches in the treatment of cancer, and will potentially lead to development of new classes of anti-cancer drugs.

column36: Making I-SPARX fly in Nunavut
column37: Inuit youth in Northern Canada face extreme adversities, leading to concerning mental health needs, and the highest adolescent suicide rates in the world. Despite their increased risk, remote Northern communities are often without resources for early prevention and intervention programs. A strong focus needs to be placed on creating intervention tools that will be accessible in Northern communities. Furthermore, little prevention or intervention research has been conducted with Inuit adolescents who are at risk for depression in Nunavut. The extent, severity and idiosyncrasies of Inuit adolescent depression need to be studied, and suitably tailored interventions evaluated. Cultural relevance, with regard to Inuit and adolescent culture, should be paramount in the selection of approaches. Making I-SPARX fly in Nunavut strives to enhance resiliency and increase mattering by empowering youth who are at risk for depression with skills to foster their own mental health and positively contributing to the collective welfare of their communities. This project evaluates a holistic, multi-generational intervention that brings together cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), emotion regulation support (ER), culture identity and community processes to foster resilience. Included in the intervention is the use of an award-winning computer program, SPARX which uses CBT and ER skills to teach the user how to cope with negative thoughts and feelings. The proposed intervention will be anchored in the youth-driven design of an Inuit version of SPARX (I-SPARX), supported by Elders. This design will aim to integrate the six integral principles of Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit. Additionally, youth will take on activities that engage their communities in the dissemination and practice of I-SPARX teachings. SPARX- once adapted to Inuit culture and with Nunavut youth making the program their own - may become a useful tool for both Nunavut youth at-risk for depression and for those working with them.

column37: Stem cell transplantation to prevent amputation in patients with critical limb ischemia (CLI) is under intense investigation. However, new blood vessel formation requires contributions from at least 3 distinct cell lineages; endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) that represent the building blocks of vessels, hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPC) that stimulate vessel growth, and mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) that form vessel-wrapping cells called pericytes. Understanding how these cells can be used to form new blood vessels remains the key to translating the potential of stem cells into a curative cellular therapy for CLI. Using readily available human umbilical cord blood (UCB) samples, we have pioneered the selection and expansion of HPC, EPC and MSC lineages to generate the large cell numbers required for regenerative therapies in humans. Importantly, each subset retained complementary vessel building functions after expansion. HPC abundantly secreted protein signals that accelerated the recovery of blood flow after implantation into the ischemic limbs of mice. EPC spontaneously formed tube networks in lab cultures and integrated into vessels after transplantation. MSC demonstrated vessel-wrapping function and improved vessel stability. Despite these promising findings, donor cell survival was limited after direct injection into the ischemic limb and improved delivery methods are required to prolong benefit. By combining expertise in stem cell biology with advanced bioengineering, we aim to develop an effective treatment for CLI using UCB-derived progenitor cells delivered within implantable, 3-D bioscaffolds derived from human adipose (fat) tissue. We hypothesize that co-delivery of UCB-derived progenitor cell subsets within cell-supportive 3-D bioscaffolds will improve donor cell survival and function to permit stable human blood vessel formation. These studies will provide proof-of-concept for the development of novel cell therapies for the treatment of CLI.

column36: Exploring structure-function relationships between dietary fibre and the gut microbiome: Towards predicting and personalizing nutritional strategies.
column37: Being overweight significantly increases risk for numerous diseases that have been linked to the microbial populations that inhabit our gastrointestinal tract. The exact role of the gut microbiota in human health appears to depend partially on diet. A diet high in fat can trigger inflammation when harmful molecules are produced by gut bacteria and taken up into the body. On the other hand, gut bacteria can ferment dietary fibre to produce short-chain fatty acids, molecules that have anti-inflammatory properties. However, we do not yet understand all the consequences of microbial fibre fermentation in the gut to healthy functioning of an individual. We also do not know how individual differences in types of bacteria that compose each person's gut microbial community influence how we can ferment different chemical types of dietary fibre. With such knowledge at hand, it would be possible to adjust an individual's diet based on the configuration of the microbes in our digestive tract. We propose to systematically investigate the interactions between fiber chemistry, the genetic make-up of the gut microbiota, and metabolic and immunological measures of health in overweight and mildly obese people. We will also look for links between different types of dietary fibre and the composition and function of each person's gut microbiota. This will allow us to test whether microbiome patterns in individuals predict the effects of the fibre. To achieve this, we will begin with an exploratory nutritional trial that compares the effects of three types of fermentable dietary fibre with the effects of non-fermentable cellulose. We will measure how fibre type and microbiota composition and function affect specific health outcomes such as reduced inflammation. This new knowledge can be used to improve dietary strategies for preventing obesity, develop strategies to modulate a person's gut microbiota for better health outcomes, and lay groundwork for personalized human nutrition.

column36: The population health and healthcare burden of poor dietary patterns and potential strategies for reducing mortality, morbidity and healthcare use in Canada
column37: Chronic diseases are major causes of reduced quality of life, increased hospitalization, and premature death. Poor diet is a common preventable risk factor and likely plays a significant role in morbidity and premature death in Canada. This project will describe dietary patterns of Canadians and how these patterns have changed over time. The study will also calculate the impact of unhealthy dietary patterns on chronic diseases (cardiovascular diseases), death and healthcare use. The health and healthcare benefits of strategies to improve dietary patterns will also be examined. Culturally-relevant dietary patterns will be "reverse engineered" to examine how to reduce health and healthcare burden and inequalities among Canadians. This study will use the nutrition focused Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) 2004, and the forthcoming 2015 cycle. The CCHS 2004 is unique worldwide; it is the largest population-based dietary survey linked to health and health care outcomes. These data allow very detailed assessment of health and social outcomes. Robust population health policy models will be created to support evidence-based nutrition policy for reducing the burden of poor dietary patterns. Policy actors will be involved in model development to ensure that models address questions of real-world policy relevance. Health calculators (risk-assessment tools) will be created from the policy models. These calculators can be used by individual Canadians and their clinicians to increase awareness of health risks from poor dietary patterns. This project will provide the first evidence on dietary patterns and health and healthcare outcomes at the national population level, an essential component for development of nutritional guidelines and policies. The models and supporting data linkages will create a lasting infrastructure and will position Canada as a world leader in population health assessment of nutrition policy.

column37: Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH) is a disease characterized by aberrant mineralization of soft connective tissues in the spine. Importantly, the cause of DISH is unknown and there are no specific treatments. Our proposed studies promise to provide breakthrough insights into the etiology of DISH, and will permit the development and preclinical testing of novel therapeutics to prevent or delay the progression of this debilitating disorder. These studies may also generate important information on related disorders of spine calcification, such as ossification of the posterior spinal longitudinal ligament (OPLL).
