column37: Patients who are critically ill in the Intensive Care Unit, especially those who need breathing machines, can develop ulcerations in the stomach that bleed. To prevent bleeding, most critically ill patients around the world receive a daily drug called pantoprazole that suppresses acid production. However, today, compared to decades ago, patients appear less likely to develop gastrointestinal bleeding, perhaps due to earlier feeding, modern medicine and better resuscitation. Studies of acid suppression are old and of poor quality such that their results are being questioned. There are also harms associated with acid suppressing drugs, including lung infections (pneumonia) and bowel infections (Clostridium difficile). Therefore, it is difficult to know whether pantoprazole does decrease stomach bleeding these days, or whether the dangers of lung and bowel infections are actually more common and serious. Whether the harms are worth the benefits, and whether the benefits are worth the costs, will be determined by an economic analysis to inform patients, families, clinicians, and healthcare systems globally.

column37: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) ensure the lifelong production of all essential blood cells in the organism, and transplantation of these cells is used for the treatment of certain types of cancer of the blood system. Our group has recently optimized a proteomics approach that allows the identification of markers at the surface of cells. This method will be used to identify specific HSC markers, with the goal of improving HSC purification from heterogeneous CB samples and develop novel strategies for their expansion. Ultimately, our findings should help optimise HSCT and provide a better prognosis to patients affected by acute myeloid leukemia and other blood diseases.

column36: Symptom screening and early palliative care in patients with advanced cancer: a randomized trial
column37: Palliative care is defined as care by a team of specialists that increases quality of life (QOL) for patients with a life-threatening illness. Four large randomized controlled trials showed that when patients with advanced cancer were referred early to specialized palliative care teams, they had improved QOL and greater satisfaction with their cancer care. Although it is known that patients with the most severe physical and psychological symptoms have the greatest need for palliative care, these patients are often not referred to palliative care teams. Therefore, it has been suggested that there should be a triage system to identify patients who have the greatest need. Our research team has developed a system that identifies patients with high symptom burden in order to offer them access to the palliative care team. This system, which uses information patients already report about their symptoms at each oncology clinic appointment, is called STEP (Symptom screening with Targeted Early Palliative care). We propose to run a trial at Princess Margaret Cancer Centre and Kingston General Hospital comparing STEP with regular symptom screening in oncology clinics. Patients are eligible to participate if they have advanced cancer and a life expectancy of at least 6 months. Consenting patients will be assigned randomly (by chance) either to receive STEP or to follow routine symptom screening. Patients in both groups complete symptom screening on computers in the waiting room of oncology clinics. For patients in the STEP group, if one or more of their symptom ratings are higher than the defined cut-off, a nurse will be alerted to call them to offer an appointment in the palliative care clinic for assessment and follow-up. All patients will complete questionnaires measuring outcomes of QOL, depression, symptom control and satisfaction with care at recruitment, 2, 4 and 6 months. We will measure the impact of STEP on these outcomes, compared to screening alone.

Despite the significant health burden associated with stimulant use, there are currently few evidence-based treatments for stimulant use disorders (SUD) and little attention has been paid to the integration of these interventions across healthcare and recovery systems. Recent advancements in psycho-social interventions (e.g., contingency management) have shown promise in the treatment of SUD, and several pharmacotherapies (e.g., dexamphetamine, cannabinoids) are being explored. However, there has been a lack of research into the acceptability and feasibility of prospective treatment interventions among stimulant-using populations, and the preparedness of healthcare and recovery systems to implement these interventions. Building upon our extensive experience in examining contextual influences on the health of adult persons who use drugs (PWUD) and drug-using street-involved youth (SY), this project aims to: (1) examine social, structural, and environmental influences on the implementation and effectiveness of current strategies for the management of SUD among PWUD and SY; (2) examine the acceptability and feasibility of prospective pharmacotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of SUD among PWUD and SY; and, (3) explore individual and contextual influences on readiness to adopt prospective pharmacotherapeutic interventions and evidence-based practices for the management of SUD across the health system. This study will be nested within the research and training infrastructure of the BC Centre for Substance Use, and will leverage the relationships of this centre to translate findings into improvements in health planning and systems in relation to stimulant use.

column36: An "Inducible" Gene Therapy for Glaucoma: A Novel Approach to Prevent Loss of Vision
column37: Glaucoma is considered the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. The increased intraocular pressure (IOP) has been established as the main risk factor for the development of glaucoma. Unfortunately, currently approved therapies for glaucoma that target IOP are unable to prevent the detrimental course of the disease, raising the need for novel treatments that can prevent or stop the progression in glaucoma. A family of enzymes that degrade proteins, called proteases, are activated in glaucoma. Abnormal activation of these proteases in glaucoma can cause inflammation by releasing harmful molecules in the eye. Recently, we have developed a special protein that replaces those in the cell so that instead of harmful factors, special therapeutic factors are released. The long term goal of this novel and first-in-class strategy is to have the retinal cells release the special, therapeutic proteins during the first signs of glaucomatous damage in the eye. Our proposed "inducible" therapeutics will be positioned in retinal cells in advance of disease, and will work as needed to reduce the negative systemic and off-target effects frequently associated with current therapies for eye diseases. column36: Augmented Renal Denervation for the Prevention of Cardiac Arrhythmias.
column37: Heart rhythm disorders (HRD) are the most common cause of sudden death following a heart attack. High sympathetic nerve activity (SNA) is known to cause HRDs. Inhibition of SNA may be an effective preventive treatment for HRDs. Renal denervation (RDN) is a relatively new medical procedure performed to de-activate nerves along large blood vessels at the kidneys. Originally developed to treat high blood pressure, RDN was found in recent studies to also reduce irregular heartbeats. Our preliminary study demonstrated that RDN reduced spontaneous HRDs following a heart attack. However, the clinical use of RDN was halted on the basis of inconclusive results regarding the true benefits of this treatment, with its failure in clinical trials attributed to methodological concerns and the regeneration of renal nerves, as well as the inadequacies of the currently available technology for the RDN procedure. The lack of tools to monitor nerve activity during the nerve de-activating procedure is particularly glaring. New accessories are needed to improve the technology before RDN can be defined for therapeutic use. RDN has thus far been delivered blindly, without the means to verify if therapy has truly been delivered at the nerves and if SNA has been impacted. It is important to understand how adequate deactivation of nerves can be assessed and the mechanisms by which RDN may reduce HRDs following a heart attack. Recently, we have developed a specialized catheter to measure renal nerve activity during the RDN procedure. In this proposal, in an in-vivo pig model of heart attack, we aim to explore the effects of heart attack on renal SNA and the long-term effects of repeated RDN on cardiac arrhythmias. We will also demonstrate how our novel catheter can be deployed to address the glaring need for nerve monitoring and improve the RDN procedure for future clinical use.

column36: Genetic Insights to the Causes of Cerebral Palsy
column37: Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common cause of physical handicap in children. CP describes a group of diseases that affect the brain in early life. We are now starting to understand that our genetic code plays an important role in causing CP. Genetic testing is not done routinely for all children with CP. To change practice, we need more proof that genetic testing brings important information to a lot of families with CP, and how this information affects families. We will invite 200 children and their parents participating in the Canadian CP Registry (CCPR), living in the Greater Montreal and Toronto areas, Calgary and Edmonton, to give a blood sample. From their blood, we will read all of their genetic information, using a method that has been used in many other genetic disorders but has never been used before in CP research. We will look for genetic mutations that are present in the child but not seen in their parents. We will also ask families to complete two questionnaires to see how they feel about this testing, and if it makes a difference to their lives. We will see if the effect of genetic testing on families is different by type of CP and also by parent characteristics. With a more complete understanding of the genetic causes of CP, doctors will be able to identify CP earlier, have better ways of preventing CP, develop new therapies and better understand the causes of CP. Also, with more information on the impact of genetic testing on the family, doctors will be better able to support families after they get their test results, decrease the family's level of stress and have a patient-centered approach to care.

column36: Brain oxidative stress and disability progression in multiple sclerosis
column37: The cause of chronic progression in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains a mystery. One cause, which is suspected by many experts, is so-called oxidative stress. This refers to the generation of abnormally increased amounts of highly reactive molecules that oxidize many other molecules and damage cells, particularly nerve cells, leading to their premature death. Cells have intrinsic mechanisms in place to deactivate/detoxify these highly reactive molecules. One of these, and perhaps the most important, is to produce the anti-oxidant molecule, glutathione (GSH). It is now possible to measure the amount of GSH in the brain of living subjects by implementing special sequences on MRI scanners to perform magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) that is specifically designed to measure GSH. For this project, we propose to use one such special sequence to measure GSH in the brain of patients with MS. This will allow us to answer a number of important questions related to the role of oxidative stress in driving disease progression in MS, and also allow us to calculate the number of patients that would be required to use this technique to assess the ability of drugs to treat oxidative stress.

column36: The great escape: Improving the activity of chemotherapeutics delivered by antibody-drug conjugates with integrated endosome escape and nuclear-directional trafficking control capabilies
column37: The image of the 'therapeutic missile' commonly used to present targeted drug delivery agents emphasizes precision, control, and efficiency. For the next evolution of cancer treatment, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are a great representative of this concept. ADCs home to tumor cells with exquisite precision and control. However, upon landing on tumor cells, ADCs lose their precision, control, and efficiency for effectively delivering and accumulating the drugs inside the cell. ADCs travel in an intracellular route that is controlled by the cancer cell that transports ADC back outside the cell or respond in ways that kick the delivered drugs out. Without the drugs reaching effective cellular concentrations, cancer cells are able to resist and survive and patients soon relapse and die. We will develop ADCs that take control of their intracellular travel by incorporating our new Canadian technology (ACCUM) that mimics how viruses travel inside the cell. ACCUM attaches easily to ADCs enabling them to take control of their travel, which consists of a more efficient route to deliver their drugs. The result is that ACCUM-empowered ADCs are able to deliver their drugs with better efficiency inside target cancer cells than current ADCs. The increased accumulation has resulted in more effective cancer cell killing. The goal of this project is to further mature this technology for use in patients with invasive bladder cancer (IBC) - a worldwide problem without any life saving medications. We performed a clinical study and discovered a target (IL-5Ra) for IBC and developed rodent models that mimics the growth of human IL-5Ra-IBC. The research experiments designed in this proposal are to optimize conditions for clinical translation by optimizing ACCUM-ADC formulation and IBC cell killing. We will then determine the tumor killing effectiveness in our rodent models. This research will place Canada in an ADC leadership role and provide effective treatment for IBC.

column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) - commonly referred to as chronic bronchitis or emphysema - is a progressive and debilitating disorder of the lungs. In most cases, it is caused by long-term exposure of susceptible individuals to tobacco smoke. Typically, COPD is characterised by persistent inflammation of the lungs leading to difficulty in breathing and, ultimately, premature death. An acute attack of COPD, known as an exacerbation, describes a rapid worsening of a patient's disease above normal day-to-day variability. Such attacks can be life threatening, are one of the leading cause of hospitalizations in North America and have a detrimental impact on ease of breathing and quality of life. Treatment of COPD is limited and mortality remains high. However, it is known that patients with COPD who experience exacerbations derive benefit from a class of drugs collectively known as LABAs. It is believed by many investigators that LABAs protect against exacerbations by opening the airway passages. However, recent research from our laboratory suggests that the beneficial effects of LABAs may also be due to their ability to switch-on a variety of genes in the lungs that, together, suppress inflammation, improve breathing and reduce the severity of attacks. To test this idea, we will explore the biology of candidate genes switched-on by LABAs using lung cells from normal healthy subjects and smoking individuals with COPD. We will also conduct a clinical study to measure the effect of a LABA on gene expression changes in the lungs of patients with COPD to confirm results obtained with isolated cells. We believe this research is important because acute attacks of COPD are associated with a considerable risk of death. The work proposed here should improve our understanding of how LABAs benefit patients with COPD and identify novel genes that could be exploited therapeutically.

column37: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has emerged as a less invasive option for relieving symptoms and prolonging life in high-risk older adults with severe aortic stenosis. I will now transition from measuring frailty to treating frailty in order to improve outcomes. The home-based intervention has a high potential for sustainable clinical implementation due to its accessibility, low cost, promotion of self-care behaviors, and a track record of safety and efficacy in geriatric patients. column37: About six million Canadians are now at the age of 65 or older. For these people, their age is inevitably a major risk factor for contracting cardiovascular diseases. One well-recognized vascular hallmark in aging subjects is the stiffening of arteries, and it has been regarded as a predictor for future cardiovascular events. Four objectives have been set forth to devise and apply this technology to vascular aging investigations: 1) Design a suite of robust computing algorithms for VAST-MAP; 2) Calibrate the experimental efficacy of VAST-MAP by conducting laboratory experiments; 3) Assess the practical effectiveness of VAST-MAP by applying it to young and aged human subjects; 4) Pursue the first application of VAST-MAP in vascular aging intervention studies. The key expected outcome of this project is that a new imaging tool (VAST-MAP) for local arterial stiffness quantification will become available for use in vascular aging research. This will pave way for the development of new diagnostic routines to complement the existing risk scoring system for prediction of future cardiovascular events.

column37: Scar formation following injury to skin is a common, unwanted outcome of the wound healing process. Clinically, scars can range from fine lines to expansive, disfiguring hypertrophic or keloid scars. In spite of these advances, no effective therapy to predictably prevent scar formation exists today. Intriguingly, studies from several laboratories using rodent models have indicated significantly faster wound healing in oral mucosa than in skin. Our findings using a validated pig model have provided the first systematical evidence that oral mucosal wound healing also results in significantly reduced scar formation as compared to skin wounds. In this preclinical study, we will develop novel bioengineered skin substitutes carrying oral mucosal fibroblasts to test whether they can be used to promote wound healing and prevent scar formation in skin using the pig model. column36: Lung Transplantation using Hepatitis C Positive Donors to Hepatitis C Negative Recipients: A Safety Trial
column37: Lung transplantation is a life-saving intervention for people with end-stage lung disease. However, the overall success of lung transplantation is currently hindered by a shortage of available donor organs. Thus, new sources of lungs are in great need. Currently, a large proportion of donors have infectious diseases such as the Hepatitis C virus (HCV). Despite otherwise good quality organs, lungs from HCV donors cannot be used due to exceedingly high risk (>90%) of transmission to the transplant recipient. Previous reports have shown poor survival of recipients when this practice was applied. The emergence of new direct-acting antiviral drugs suggests a high chance of cure for HCV; nevertheless this has never been evaluated in the context of lung transplantation. The current research study will investigate the safety of using HCV+ donors to lung transplant recipients. If this proves to be successful, a large source of new donors will become available for patients with lung failure.

column36: Investigating Pharmacogenetic Mechanisms of Doxorubicin-Induced Cardiotoxicty in Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Cardiomyocytes
column37: Many anti-cancer drugs cause side effects that damage the heart. Doxorubicin is one of the most commonly used anti-cancer drugs and is used to treat breast cancer, lymphoma, and many childhood cancers. However, up to 26% of patients who receive this drug experience cardiotoxicity, which can lead to heart failure, heart transplantation, and death. Currently, we lack the ability to predict which specific patients are at risk of this adverse drug reaction, and we have no effective methods to prevent it. The goal of this study is to investigate the function of specific genes that have been associated with doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity. By understanding if these genes directly impact the response to doxorubicin, and what biological mechanisms are involved, we could potentially use these genes as genetic tests to predict which patients are most likely to develop cardiotoxicity from this drug. We will study the role of these genes in heart cells generated from human stem cells. My lab has recently described a new way of studying doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity using such stem cell - derived heart cells. We will introduce the specific gene variants of interest using a state-of-the-art gene editing technology called CRISPR. We will compare heart cells with or without these gene variants to determine how they respond to doxorubicin. We will also isolate stem cells from the blood of patients that have suffered from doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity, turn these stem cells into heart cells, and study how they respond to the drug, in the presence or absence of the specific gene variants. If we can identify the patients at highest risk of drug-induced heart damage, we could take steps to prevent or mitigate this devastating adverse drug reaction. Ultimately these efforts will result in safer and more effective drugs and will allow Canadians to stay healthier and experience fewer side effects.

column36: Supporting the creation of a LEARNing INteGrated health system to mobilize context-adapted knowledge with a Wiki platform to Improve the transitions of frail Seniors from from hospitals and emergency Departments to the cOMmunity: the LEARNING WISDOM Phase II scale-up project
column37: Elderly patients do not always receive the best care to help them return home after being discharged from the hospital. The connections between the hospital and community-care settings are often inadequate. As a result, elderly patients may be repeatedly readmitted to the hospital and their capacity to function may decrease. Caregivers may feel more burdened by the increasing care for their elderly loved ones. As well, healthcare costs increase. Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto developed the Acute Care for Elders (ACE) program to improve healthcare for the elderly. By using innovative strategies such as transition coaches, follow-up calls and patient self-care guides, the ACE program reduced lengths of hospital stay and readmissions for elderly patients, increased patient satisfaction, and saved the healthcare system over $6 million in 2014. In 2016, the Centre integre en sante et en services sociaux de Chaudiere-Appalaches (CISSS CA) received funding from the Canadian Foundation for Healthcare Improvement and support from Mount Sinai experts to implement the ACE Program in one hospital in the CISSS CA with a focus on improving transitions between hospital and the community for the elderly. The goal of this research project is to implement the ACE Program in three other hospitals within the CISSS CA, using a "Wiki-suite" to help adapt and apply the ACE Program to each hospital. The Wiki-suite is an open-source collaborative database of knowledge tools and a training program which help clinicians share information and improve patient care. Our research project will evaluate how the ACE program implemented and improved care transitions for the elderly at these hospitals. We will also evaluate how the Wiki-suite helped adapt and apply the ACE program in participating hospitals.

column36: Rational optimization of CFTR modulators and assessment of predictive potential of novel cystic fibrosis (CF) airway epithelial models for clinical outcome
column37: The cystic fibrosis (CF) protein (CFTR) resides at the cell surface and ensures normal water and ion composition of the liquid that lines the airway. CF mutations impair CFTR function and the composition of the airway surface liquid layer. This leads to lung infection and uncontrolled inflammation, the primary cause of premature death in CF. Robust correction of these defects has been achieved for only 9 rare mutations, by ivacaftor, representing a small subset of >2000 mutations, corresponding to ~5% of the CF patient population. The recently approved FDA drug combination of lumacaftor and ivacaftor (Orkambi) targets the most common mutation with variable clinical benefit: 50% of patients gained >5% (FEV1) lung function, while the others showed no or only very modest benefit, indicating a substantial variability of responsiveness. Importantly, the drug susceptibility of most other CFTR mutations, which may be correctable, is still unexplored. To overcome the limited efficacy of the available drugs, there is unmet need for authentic and validated model systems for preclinical investigations. We will implement novel "primary" cell based models derived from noninvasively collected nasal epithelial cells. Based on our preliminary data, this model will maintain patient specific hallmarks of airways cells expressing rare CF mutations. To complement this approach, we will generate 60 of the rare mutations in respiratory epithelial cell lines and use these models for testing approved drugs and optimizing novel combinations of investigational CF drugs in functional and biochemical assays. Promising combinations will be validated in human airway cells and their effect will be compared to their clinical benefit to identify mutation and patient specific treatment protocols.

column36: Genetic Determinants of Individualized Islet Responses to Dietary Macronutrients
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) impacts more than 3 million Canadians and 385 million people worldwide. Obesity, which increases the risk of T2D, has also reached epidemic proportions, impacting ~30% of the population. Despite numerous treatment options many obese and/or T2D patients suffer from a decreased quality of life. Defects in the insulin-secreting beta cells are critical for the development of obesity/T2D. Elevated fasting insulin (hyperinsulinemia) is a pre-requisite for the development of obesity. Interestingly, obesity and its complications can be prevented in mice that are genetically protected from diet-induced hyperinsulinemia, suggesting that a reduction in insulin levels is beneficial to the metabolic health of an individual with obesity/T2D . While glucose is the main driver of acute insulin release, other dietary macronutrients can also potentiate insulin secretion. However, insulin release in response to these macronutrients is different between individuals. This could explain why 'low-carb' diets that aim to keep insulin levels low are only effective in a subset of the population. Thus, the goal of our study is to understand these variations, and identify pathways that determine the sensitivity of individuals to various macronutrients. We will characterize human islet functional responses to dietary macronutrients by measuring insulin release. The responses will be compared to the unique genetic profile of the donor. Multi-scale modelling will used to predict obesity and diabetes risk. We will also use glucose-responsive insulin producing cells (that have been generated from human embryonic stem cells) as a controlled cell model system to identify the molecular mechanisms that influence insulin secretion in response to nutrients. The proposed final outcome will be the development of a model that will allow us to predict, based on a person's genetics, whether they will be an insulin hypersecretor in response to any macronutrient.

column36: Gonococcal subversion of classical neutrophil functions
column37: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ngo) is a bacterial pathogen that causes more than 100 million cases of the sexually-transmitted disease gonorrhea in the world each year. In addition to the copious male urethral or female endocervical discharge that are the hallmark of gonorrhea, Ngo infections can progress to cause scarring of the reproductive tract, chronic pelvic pain and dangerous ectopic pregnancies in women, or blindness of children born to infected mothers. Critically, Ngo has recently attained 'superbug' status because it has acquired resistance to all clinically relevant oral and injectable antibiotics, making the threat of untreatable gonorrhea a looming reality. This has led to a global urgency to develop new strategies to halt the spread of Ngo and/or to treat established infections caused by this dangerous microbe. It is clear that the damage associated with Ngo infection is caused by an overzealous response of a single type of white blood cell, known as the neutrophil. What is disconcerting is that the neutrophil is the immune system's most potent bacterial-killing immune cell type, yet the massive numbers of neutrophils that enter Ngo-infected tissues are not capable of clearing the infection. Moreover, the neutrophil response is clear evidence that the immune system has been alerted to the presence of a dangerous bacterial intruder, yet it does not develop an effective immune 'memory' response that would otherwise protect against subsequent infections. Notably, recent work has revealed that different types of neutrophils exist, with functions ranging from the promotion of inflammation to the suppression of effective immune responses. This paradigm-shifting finding clearly contradicts the classical belief that all neutrophils are the same. column36: Mechanisms controlling estrogen receptor alpha expression and activity in breast tumorigenesis
column37: Breast cancer is a prevalent world-wide disease but its manifestations are heterogeneous, necessitating treatment regimen adapted to the main tumor subtypes currently identified. Two thirds of tumors overexpress the estrogen receptor alpha (ER) compared to normal tissues and are candidates for targeted treatments that block estrogen signaling. These tumors are associated with the best prognosis. Estrogen receptor-negative tumors on the other hand are not sensitive to these treatments and, for a significant proportion of them, can be treated only with chemotherapy. Further, ER-positive tumors can become resistant during tumor progression. Thus, understanding why some tumors gain or lose expression and/or activity of this important therapeutic target is crucial to improving the appropriate classification and treatment of this disease. To address this question, the applicants have initiated large-scale screens in breast cancer cell lines that express ER. Through suppression of expression of each individual gene in the genome, they have identified candidate proteins that are thought to modulate the expression and/or activity of ER using a surrogate assay that measures the activity of this protein. In this application, they will use a recent and sensitive technology for modulation of gene expression called CRISPR-Cas9 to validate current candidates and identify new ones. In addition, candidate ER regulators identified in current and future screens will be characterized for their capacity to modulate ER expression and/or activity. Finally, whether defects in these ER regulators arise during breast tumorigenesis will be investigated using archived breast tumor samples, and the impact of these proteins on the tumorigenic properties of breast cancer cells and their response to ER-targeted treatments will be investigated in cell line and animal models.

column36: Probing biased recognition of flu hemagglutinin by precursors of broadly neutralizing antibodies to the HA stem
column37: Influenza virus remains a serious threat to public health. Superior vaccines would be desirable that confer immunity against a broader diversity of flu strains, especially given the pandemic-causing potential of flu. Influenza vaccines stimulate our immune system to produce antibodies that help to protect against viral infection. For reasons that are not fully clear, broadly reactive antibodies (brAbs) can be elicited in some individuals by seasonal vaccination, as evidenced by the occasional recovery of such antibodies from select individuals. Developing a vaccine formulation that purposely is able to elicit such brAbs would constitute a significant advance. Understanding how the development of such brAbs is best triggered and promoted would likely help to inform new vaccine design strategies. The brAbs that we focus on in this project target a fairly invariant area on the flu protein hemagglutinin (HA), which is functionally important and displayed abundantly on the surface of the virus. Studies show that brAbs to this region originate from just a few antibody genes, suggesting that brAbs deriving from the same gene share a particular bias in how they initial recognize HA and that they may evolve along similar genetic pathways to turn into brAbs. This project will determine if early versions of potential brAbs indeed share common features in their development towards broad recognition of flu HAs and investigate if HAs from certain flu strains are preferentially bound by early versions of such antibodies. To probe these questions thoroughly, we will use novel genetically engineered animals with capacity to produce human-like antibodies, thus providing a surrogate readout system for antibody responses in humans. We expect the results of our work to further the development of better flu vaccines with capacity to evoke antibodies that offer broader protection than those produced by current seasonal vaccines.

column36: An examination of forebrain circuit activity that promotes hedonic reactions to palatable food consumption
column37: Approximately 10% of Canadian adults will experience major depression at some point in their lives. One of the core symptoms of this psychiatric disorder is a pronounce absence of pleasure in most activities. This research proposal seeks to identify neural circuit activity that promotes the sensation of pleasure. We focus on one very specific cause of pleasure, the consumption of highly palatable food. The pleasure derived from eating, at least as measured by positive facial reactions in rodents, can be driven by mu opioid receptor signaling in a particular forebrain area: the rostral nucleus accumbens shell. In humans, neural activity in this region correlates with the pleasures of food, sex, addictive drugs, music, and art. Mu opioid receptor signaling here is believed to alter the balance of activity between different types of output neurons, but the details and mechanisms of this effect are unknown. The principal aim of this grant is to identify in rodents how positive facial reactions to food consumption arise from mu opioid receptor signaling in the nucleus accumbens. We will use a combination of tools to record and manipulate specific cell types and circuits to identify what specific balance of activity in this area is the cause of mu opioid receptor-induced positive facial reactions to feeding. We will also try to enhance positive feeding reactions in an enduring manner through long lasting circuit manipulations. A better understanding of this particular source of hedonic reactions will provide a framework for a more general understanding the neural underpinnings of pleasure. Insights gained from these kinds of circuit analyses have already been used in the development of highly specific therapeutic interventions designed to improve the lives of patients afflicted by mental illness.

column36: Predicting outcomes for Canadians receiving home care: An examination of home care delivery and impact
column37: Supporting older Canadians through home care is a health policy priority in Canada. However, there are still significant gaps in access to care and quality of services that are provided. As a result, those who receive home care sometimes experience undesirable and potentially preventable health outcomes, such as hospital stays, emergency room visits, early entry to nursing homes, or even death. Part of the challenge is the underfunding of home care; this is why the Canadian government had recently promised to invest $3 billion dollars in enhancing the care provided in this setting. An equal part of the challenge is a lack of evidence in what types of care people need and how much care is required to reduce adverse outcomes. This grant will use rich population-level data for those who are receiving home care to, first, describe the needs of home care recipients (e.g., disease and disabilities). We will also aim to explain the differences in the level and types of home care services provided in Ontario, and across several provinces in Canada. Finally, we will use statistical techniques to identify the mix (i.e., personal support workers, nursing) and intensity (i.e., hours per week) of services that may be required prevent unwanted outcomes for different types of home care users - paying special attention to people are are frail and may be nearing the end of life. We will build tools that will map out and predict how we can prevent these undesirable outcomes. The tools will be designed for patients, their family and caregivers to inform care planning, but could also be used by health care planners and policy makers to improve care for the entire population. Our goal is to generate knowledge and tools to inform current and new investments for home care, and can support interventions to improve care for Canadians, especially those who are frail and may be nearing the end of life.

column36: Stimulating Functional Networks to Enhance Stroke Recovery
column37: Currently ~400,000 Canadians live with the after effects of stroke and stroke is the number one cause of disability. Despite often not having a full recovery from stroke, most people will have a remarkable improvement in function in the absence of any therapy. The problem is that this only occurs in the first few months after a stroke. This fact suggests that the brain has the ability to temporarily heal itself "naturally" through repairing and rebuilding connections between the cells in the brain called neurons. During recovery from a stroke regions of the brain reorganizing on their own. This suggests that we can enhance stroke recovery by stimulating new, active group of neurons. New treatments are being tested in patients that aim to strengthen the formation of new sets of neurons by stimulating the brain. These treatments appear promising yet only some patients get better. One reason why stimulation therapy may not always work is that we do not know which particular neurons need to be stimulated. This project will identify which neurons reorganize naturally during recovery and test if stimulating these neurons can improve recovery. Our work will be performed in animal models of strokes since there is no non-surgical method that allows us to manipulate or visualize individual neurons after a stroke in humans. We will determine which specific neurons participate in recovery from stroke and identify the timeline of brain reorganization following stroke. We are well suited to accomplish this task using special mice that allow us to 1) label and visualize individual neurons to see what neurons are active at any given time and 2) stimulate neurons in a live animal that is performing a behavior task. Thus, this fundamental study will not only shed light on the underlying mechanisms of stroke recovery, but also allow us to design better treatments for stroke recovery, so survivors will struggle less with disability and enjoy a better quality of life.

column36: Viral Control of Autophagy to Reprogram the Host Cell Secretome
column37: Viruses are incredible tools that teach us how our cells work. In my lab, we study the virus, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). This virus causes a rare skin cancer called Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). My lab is interested in how this virus changes cells that comprise blood vessels, called endothelial cells, to make them secrete proteins that are called inflammatory cytokines, that promote the cancer KS. I have discovered that KSHV targets granules called processing bodies (PBs) that play an important role in controlling inflammatory cytokine production (Corcoran et al. 2015 PLoS Path. 11:e1004597). My lab now has exciting new evidence that connects the disappearance of PBs to the process of autophagy, which literally means 'self-eating'. Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism that permits cells to survive the stress of starvation by promoting the degradation and recycling of a variety of cellular structures, thereby providing essential cellular building blocks and energy for survival. Autophagy has also been shown to regulate inflammatory cytokine production; however how this occurs is not clear in most cases. My compelling preliminary evidence connects autophagy increases with the disassembly of PBs and increased inflammatory cytokine production. This is the first evidence suggesting the coordinated regulation of autophagy and PBs controls inflammation in our cells. Impact and Significance: My lab has made a fundamental discovery about how inflammatory cytokine expression is regulated. Inflammatory cytokines are aberrantly produced in many disorders in addition to KS, such as rheumatoid arthritis and many other cancers. Increasing our knowledge of how autophagy and PBs are functionally linked will help develop new treatments to limit inflammation in many situations.

column36: Mobilizing a land-based culturally appropriate active living intervention among Indigenous youth
column37: The benefits of physical activity (PA) are far-reaching, and individuals with high PA have better mental, physical and emotional health. However, our population is more inactive than ever and to tackle this health issue it is important to act early, especially in populations that are most vulnerable. In Canada, one of the most marginalized groups is Indigenous youth. Even though they are Canada's fastest growing group, Indigenous youth have poorer health outcomes than others. As PA's benefits are numerous, we propose to develop sustainable ways to improve PA in Indigenous youth and thus, ultimately increase their chances of leading a healthy life. The answer lies in adopting culturally appropriate ways to integrate to PA into the daily lives of Indigenous youth. We have devised an intervention that is not only culturally appropriate, but also novel. In our 5 year intervention we will invite youth from our partnering communities to spend 5 days/year at a tipi camp. In this tipi camp we will teach youth to take advantage of living on the land, and combine this approach with introducing them to active arts-based theatre games. We have done a similar tipi camp in the past and observed that being in the tipi camp improved not only their PA, but also their mental health and overall wellbeing. After the tipi camp we will follow up with active arts-based programs through the schools of these youth. We will assess their PA and overall wellbeing in three different seasons every year throughout the intervention period. We aim to demonstrate that this novel intervention will allow Indigenous youth to lead a healthier, active life. We believe that if we generate evidence that establishes the importance of culturally appropriate active living, it will change the current state of affairs, where Indigenous youth are left to fend for themselves. We ultimately aim to show that this is an effective and economical approach to address a wide range of health issues in Indigenous youth.

column36: Lipid homeostasis regulation by brain glucagon signalling
column37: Background: A key feature of diabetes and obesity is an abnormal level of fats ("lipids") in the blood. High blood levels of lipids made by the liver increase the risk of damaging bodily systems that serve to maintain our metabolism. Thus, it is important to discover and understand mechanisms that affect how lipid production and balance is controlled by our bodies and work towards the goal of lowering lipid levels in the blood, to reduce the risks of health problems associated with an imbalance in metabolism. Objective: Our research aims to unveil novel actions of glucagon, in the brain, that alters whole-body balance of lipid levels. Research project: We will test how glucagon, a hormone made and found in the body, is used by the brain to control liver lipid production, and consequently lipid levels in the blood. We will assess the action of glucagon in the brain under normal conditions and in obesity (from high calorie feeding) and in diabetes. We hypothesize that the brain, by specific pathways controlled by this hormone, alters lipid production and output by the liver. Hence, glucagon action in the brain will affect blood lipid levels. We hypothesize that nutrient excess impairs glucagon's action in the brain, which contributes to an over-production of lipids by the liver. Hence, targeting this defect will help restore blood lipid levels in conditions of obesity and diabetes. Impact: Insights gained from the proposed research will reveal new pathways and mechanisms to regulate blood lipid levels. The research will advance our current understanding of how glucagon affects lipid metabolism, not just by its known effects on tissues like the liver, but also by its novel actions in the brain. These findings will reveal putative new targets, which can help lower blood lipid levels in diabetes and obesity, and thus improve the quality of life of people affected by these conditions. This also helps to reduce the collateral effects on health care and spending.

column36: Improving treatment efficacy: A randomized controlled trial of the combined used of intranasal oxytocin and cognitive behavioral therapy for the treatment of major depressive disorder
column37: Major depressive disorder (MD) is recurrent, debilitating, and, to some extent, a chronic disorder, despite the many advances in treatment. Although both drug and psychological treatments are considered to be efficacious in the short-term treatment of MD, at least one third of patients do not respond to treatment. One strategy to improve treatment efficacy is to use of some form of antidepressant augmentation which refers to adding an additional medication or psychological procedure (i.e. such as adjunct "mindfulness" meditation) to augment the therapeutic efficacy of a traditional treatment. We are currently completing a pilot study where patients receive intranasal oxytocin as an adjunct to psychotherapy for MD. Oxytocin is a hormone found in the body and brain that is important in reproductive functions (for example, lactation), and has recently been shown to promote positive social behaviors, such as trust. Preliminary analyses of 16 patients indicate evidence of improved clinical outcomes in those receiving adjunct oxytocin administration. In this application, we are proposing to conduct a randomized clinical trial that attempts to augment the therapeutic effect of psychotherapy for MD using intranasal oxytocin. Building on our pilot study where we used a therapy focused on interpersonal relations, we intend to assess the efficacy of intranasal oxytocin augmentation in a larger sample using a different form of psychotherapy: cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). In addition to testing clinical outcomes, part of the project will focus on understanding how oxytocin improves psychotherapy outcomes (does it improve the relationship between the therapist and patient?), and whether some people may benefit from this dual treatment more than others (does oxytocin augmentation benefit patients with poor interpersonal functioning or adverse childhood experiences?). The novel study has the potential to improve the use of psychotherapy in treating patients with MD.

column36: Transcriptional Regulatory Networks in Embryonic and Neural Stem Cells
column37: Pluripotent stem cells have the potential to become any cell type in an adult organism including nerve cells. SOX2 is a critical gene in stem cells and is also required for normal brain development and nerve cell regeneration. Mutations outside the SOX2 gene, in specialized DNA sequences called enhancers, can influence when and where the SOX2 gene is turned on in the brain. This aberrant expression of SOX2 can lead to neurodegeneration, epilepsy and, in severe cases, infant death due to brain malformation. Our research team recently discovered new enhancer sequences that turn on the SOX2 gene in stem cells and showed that these sequences influence the production of nerve cell precursors from stem cells. Our current proposal will determine the sequences that are important for the function of these regulatory elements and find new genes which, like SOX2, are critical for nerve cell regeneration. Furthermore, we will identify additional enhancers that regulate the expression of genes in the stem cell compartment of the brain and determine how these enhancers are epigenetically modified during brain development and with ageing. This will allow us to better understand why some people develop neurodegenerative diseases that include epilepsy, multiple sclerosis and Huntington's disease and improve disease diagnosis and treatment using precision medicine approaches.

column37: Recently, an important new class of molecules influencing cell behavior was discovered: the microRNAs. About one thousand of these little nucleic acid regulators are at work in human cells, and they have been implicated in almost every biological process, but also in numerous diseases including cancer. MicroRNAs act as repressors of genes by directly binding to a portion of the messengers of genes (mRNAs), termed the 3 prime untranslated region (3'UTR). MicroRNAs interact with RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and 3'UTRs to finely tune the expression of genes. Better understanding how microRNA interact with mRNAs and with RBPs will allow to discern on the biologically important microRNA-binding sites in the genome from weak or non-functional ones. Hence, this project offers much promise in grasping the impact of microRNAs and RBPs in important biological processes, and their roles in diseases.

column36: Improving social inclusion for Canadians with dementia and carers through sharing dance
column37: People with dementia and their carers experience barriers to meaningful social inclusion across a range of settings. Addressing these issues requires the development and evaluation of accessible, non-stigmatizing and affordable interventions that facilitate social inclusion in the home, communities and institutional settings across urban and rural Canada. A growing body of research suggests that arts-based health interventions can improve the lives of people with dementia and their carers; however, little is known about how these programs might address social inclusion specifically. The proposed research focuses on the potential of an innovative arts-based intervention, the National Ballet School of Canada's Sharing Dance for Seniors Program, to improve the social inclusion of people living with dementia and their carers. What is unique about the Sharing Dance Program is its emphasis on making dance accessible through in-person (live), on-line (live-streamed) and blended (in-person and live-streamed) dance outreach engagement sessions. The research will examine the experiences of people living with dementia and their carers participating in the program as well as assess the effectiveness of the multi-modal delivery of the program and the challenges of expanding and sustaining the program. The study will involve pilot studies of Sharing Dance for Seniors in Peterborough, Ontario and Brandon, Manitoba featuring in-depth observations and weekly diaries with program participants as well as focus groups and interviews with program participants, coordinators, instructors and volunteers. Ultimately, the research seeks to improve social inclusion for people with dementia and their carers where they live.

column36: A comparative policy analysis of programs to support people with dementia and co-existing complex needs and their caregivers
column37: Health care systems in Canada and around the world face the challenge of meeting the needs of people living with dementia and their unpaid caregivers. Many people with dementia have additional health needs, like pain related to Arthritis, which can be very complex to manage. This puts a lot of strain on caregivers who help people living with dementia at home. Understanding how health care systems can support people with dementia and complex needs, and the unpaid caregivers who help them, is an important tasks for health researchers and health policymakers. In this research project we will compare programs to support people with dementia and complex needs, and their unpaid caregivers in 5 jurisdictions: Newfoundland & Labrador, Ontario, British Columbia, Vermont, and New York State. We will draw on a collaboration between researchers and policymakers, called a "North American Observatory of Health Systems and Policies", to support the improvement of health care systems across North America. By comparing these 5 jurisdictions and bringing researchers, policymakers, health care providers and unpaid caregivers together, this project will help to improve and develop programs to support people with dementia and complex needs, and their unpaid caregivers.

column36: Moving With and Tuning In: A participatory mixed methods study to foster social inclusion of individuals with dementia and their carers
column37: One of the most insidious consequences of dementia is the rupture of relationships, which occurs both between the individual with dementia and his/her primary caregiver (the dyad), and between the dyad and other members of society. As a result, both members of the dyad suffer from a loss of personhood, and are likely to experience social exclusion. In this research program, we examine the effect of two interventions - Moving-With and Tuning-In - on perceptions of personhood and social inclusion/exclusion. We will first identify and characterize social situations and places where individuals with dementia and their primary caregivers have exceptional experiences of social inclusion and exclusion. We will then facilitate in ten Moving-With sessions, where dyads will be guided by a dance therapist in an embodied, partnered experience. Video and physiological data will be recorded, and used with retrospective interviews to 1) identify the active ingredients in the Moving-With intervention and 2) to train a physiological-based emotional classifier for individuals with dementia. Finally, we will use the trained emotion classifiers to sonify the physiological signals of individuals with dementia. This technology (Tuning-In), will be tested in three settings: 1) home; 2) places of identified social exclusion; and 3) institutions who have indicated their willingness to develop more inclusive practices. We will use physiological signal analysis and qualitative methods to characterize the effects of Tuning-In on experiences of social inclusion/exclusion for the dyad. Upon completion of this project, we expect to have developed and assessed two interventions that can be scaled up, created training manuals and online videos of best practices for each intervention, and used our understanding of the transformations in personhood to inform policy and recommendations for participatory research in the context of dementia care.

column36: Improving Quality of Living and Dying for People with Advanced Dementia and Their Caregivers
column37: People who are living with dementia are one of society's most frail and socially excluded populations of older adults, especially those with advanced dementia (i.e., moderate and late-stage). As dementia progresses, the likelihood of placement in residential care (e.g., long term care, supportive housing) or hospital-based care is high , seriously limiting participation in the wider community. Within these settings, too, the social isolation of residents with advanced dementia is pronounced; those with advanced dementia often have little to no social interaction outside of basic care activities . Efforts to support social inclusion in dementia should encompass the full course of the disease. This proposed study will evaluate a new program called Namaste Care, that aims to promote social inclusion and quality of life for older adults and their family carers, by engaging them in meaningful activities together. We expect that by participating in Namaste Care, people with dementia will feel more socially engaged, have better quality of life, and their family members will report less stress, and improved family visits.

column36: Cardiac repair: A balancing act between cardiomyocyte cell cycle arrest and proliferation.
column37: Heart failure affects a growing number of Canadians. Quality of life and prognosis for this group of patients is poor with more than $1 billion of the annual health budget being spent to treat these people. This health problem is growing in epidemic proportions placing an ever increasing burden on the health care system. There are currently no means available to directly target this disease. As such, it is very important to find new ways to treat patients with heart failure. The root of the problem lies in knowing that cells within the heart cannot divide in adults. As a result, heart cells cannot restore themselves to allow the heart function to return to normal once it has been damaged. We feel that this area of research is both of critical clinical importance and holds great scientific merit. Our interest is in identifying 1) the factors which prevent the loss of heart cells at the time of injury, such as after a heart attack and 2) the factors that may allow heart cells to multiply and provide the sick heart with the potential to "repair" itself. What is fascinating is the ability of heart cells to grow and multiply for a short period of time after birth to accommodate the rapid growth of the individual through the early stages of life. However, there are a series of roadblocks that are put in place that prevent further growth after this initial burst. We have been able to identify a family of factors that are linked to control of growth and regeneration/repair in heart cells and we think that it is a tight control of these factors that may provide the ability of heart cells to overcome the roadblocks that stop them from multiplying. We are excited by the experimental evidence that we have obtained thus far, showing that this is indeed the case. Therefore, our research proposal outlines a series of experiments that will allow us to prove this and expands our knowledge to states of normal growth and proliferation that happen shortly after birth.

column36: Targeting the cardiac troponin complex to enhance the understanding, diagnosis, and treatment of heart disease
column37: In heart muscle cells, the protein troponin complex is the molecular switch that turns contraction on and off with each heartbeat. Troponin is important to the health of Canadians in the following ways: 1) Genetic diseases are caused by DNA mutations that change the structure of a particular protein. The heritable cardiomyopathies are common genetic disorders (about 1:500) affecting heart muscle proteins like troponin, increasing the risk of heart failure and sudden cardiac death. We are studying how the function of troponin is regulated in the healthy heart, and how it becomes dysregulated by mutations. This will allow us to develop drugs to correct the problem. 2) We are designing troponin-specific drugs to correct the effect of mutations that cause the heritable cardiomyopathies. This would improve heart muscle function and restore normal muscle growth, preventing the development of heart failure. We anticipate that these drugs could also be used to treat heart failure caused by other conditions. 3) When the heart is damaged, troponin leaks into the bloodstream, where it can be detected by blood tests used by physicians to diagnose heart damage. In a heart attack, not only is troponin released, but it is also partially digested by enzymes. Right now, conventional blood tests do not distinguish between intact troponin and digested troponin. We are developing a blood test to make this distinction, which will provide more useful information about the cause of heart damage in order to guide treatment. Understanding troponin will help doctors to better diagnose and treat heart disease, which affect over a million Canadians every year.

column36: Function of circular RNA in prostate cancer development and progression
column37: Prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in men in western countries. While patients with low-risk and intermediate-risk tumours can be subjected to active surveillance, surgery or radiotherapy, patients with advanced disease need more intensive treatment. Despite the use of stringent clinical criteria to place patients into tight clinical prognostic groups, a large proportion of patients still fail precision treatment due to local resistance and or systemic spread. In addition, there is still no cure for metastatic prostate cancer that has spread out of prostate. Therefore, additional prognostic and predictive factors as well as improved treatment strategies are in great need for the management of prostate cancer. We have identified more than a hundred circular RNAs that may drive prostate cancer development and progression. As circular RNAs are resistant to endonuclease digestion and are thus more stable in bloodstream, they have the potential to serve as non-invasive biomarker using liquid biopsy. Our research will bring together expertise in basic cancer research and clinical oncology to implement all our findings into clinical application to improve cure and personalize the care of cancer patients.

column36: Developing a Framework for Wastewater Reuse in Canada: Using Quantitative Microbial Risk Assessment, Risk Communication, and Community Engagement for Evaluating Water-Fit-For-Purpose Reuse
column37: Drinking water treatment and sanitary waste management are considered the most important environmental public health achievements for infectious disease prevention. However, population growth, loss of environmental services and climate change are forcing communities to explore opportunities that treat municipal wastewater to allow its safe return for community uses or harvest rain/stormwater for various non-drinking water uses (all referred to here as wastewater reuse). There are also multiple synergies when wastewater reuse is considered within a broader, one-water approach that provides economic opportunities for society to reduce water service costs, provide resiliency to floods/droughts and promotes public health improvements while meeting future water demands. While wastewater reuse has been accepted in various arid, warm regions (including Arizona, California, Israel & Australia), Canada's cold climate poses uncharacterized challenges to wastewater treatment (e.g. sudden cold-water snowmelt events reducing treatment efficacy) and therefore uncertainty in the potential risks to human health posed by the recovered water. There is also a lack of international agreement on reuse guidelines/regulations that are protective of human health. Lastly, informed citizens are increasingly aware of new disease-causing agents produced by modern societies (e.g., antibiotic-resistant bacteria and respiratory pathogens that grow in distributed waters such as Legionella) and seek to engage in decision-making for new water services. Hence, water reuse strategies require an understanding of the public's perceptions and receptivity to wastewater reuse as well as technical understanding of how to control key hazards - major elements of the proposed participatory water reuse framework to engender trust in government and utilities to provide safe reuse water that communities seek to have in an equitable way to address Canada's $90 billion water service infrastructure deficit.

column36: The ECHO Network (Environment, Community, Health Observatory): Strengthening intersectoral capacity to understand and respond to health impacts of resource development
column37: Health is influenced by resource development through interrelated socioeconomic, ecological, cultural, and political pathways, which demand upstream, intersectoral responses. These relationships are especially important in Canada, where the economy remains tightly coupled with the development of natural resources and where the rate and scale of social and environmental change occurring in resource-rich regions is fueling debate regarding health impacts, especially for rural, remote and Indigenous communities. Our project, titled "The ECHO Network (Environment, Community, Health Observatory): Strengthening intersectoral capacity to understand and respond to health impacts of resource development", aims to: (1) make evidence-based recommendations on the form and function of a cross-jurisdictional ECHO that will foster understanding of the complex dynamics of resource development and health, and; (2) trial and evaluate intersectoral strategies to address the cumulative determinants of health that interact over time and space, targeting actions and responses that cannot be achieved by the health sector alone. The ECHO Network team has several key features: (1) our research team is informed by experienced health, environmental and social science researchers; (2) the research program is also anchored in four regional cases (New Brunswick, Alberta, British Columbia and Northern BC). In each regional case, knowledge-users have identified decision-support needs or issues that demand a better integration of environment, community and health impacts. The ECHO will provide a platform of integrative tools and processes that connect people to a network of information, practices and people in order to develop a shared perspective and more effective responses to the cumulative impacts of resource development. The research will involve four components, each linked to specific objectives, mentorship and capacity building processes over five years.

column36: Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals: Towards Responsible Replacements
column37: As part of our everyday lives we are exposed to a wide variety of chemicals derived from consumer products, such as foam, electronic equipment and plastics, that enter our food and drinking water. Most of these chemicals are present at very low concentrations. However, even low doses of substances that disrupt the body's own hormones, known as endocrine-disrupting compounds (EDCs), can exert important biological effects during critical windows of susceptibility. In the past decade governments across the world have regulated the production, uses and importation of specific flame retardants, plasticizers, and food packaging materials that have been shown to act as endocrine disruptors. The consequence is that alternative chemicals are needed to fill market "gaps". However, there is often little information on the extent to which we are exposed to these replacements or on their health impacts. Our research will focus first on determining the extent to which our food, drinking water and breast milk contain the chemicals that have emerged as replacements for polybrominated diphenyl ether flame retardants, phthalates and bisphenol A. We will then determine if these new alternatives are safer than the substances that they have replaced. We will investigate the effectiveness of various food preparation procedures and water purification strategies to decrease exposure and thus prevent possible adverse health effects associated with alternatives that are deemed to be hazardous. Finally, we will analyze international regulations/regulatory processes related to the assessment of alternatives/replacements, with a focus on Canada, US, Europe and South Africa. Our goal is to transform the knowledge that is acquired during this team grant into international policy objectives and legal standards.

column36: A SHARED Future: Achieving Strength, Health, and Autonomy through Renewable Energy Developments for the Future
column37: Our research program will focus on bringing forward stories of reconciliation and healing in an innovative context: intersectoral partnerships in renewable energy development. Our research goal is to bring to light new and restored understandings of integrative health. Indigenous peoples have adapted to local environments for millennia. Place-based knowledge systems, embedded in and communicated through language (especially stories), situate Indigenous peoples in a deep understanding of the interconnectedness and interdependence with the natural world. While the link between a healthy natural world and healthy people is only beginning to be detailed and modeled in dominant (Western) scientific discourse, it has been known, embodied, and taught through stories in Indigenous contexts for hundreds of generations. We are created from four energies - Earth, Water, Fire, and Air - and without these, we cease to exist. And now, the defining issue of our times is anthropogenic climate change. It is Mother Earth's response to our misguided attempts to colonize her. Climate change is a real-world 'wicked' problem that requires horizontal and vertical intersectoral and multi-jurisdictional responses from local to international scales. But these responses cannot come from the stories of Western science alone. We need to put them together with other stories to help us acknowledge, understand, and most importantly, reconcile the damage we have done. Our research premise: Renewable energy development could be a platform for putting reconciliation at the heart of decision-making and implementation. We will examine how Indigenous knowledge systems - as applied to intersectoral partnerships for renewable energy development - have the potential to lead us towards new and restored understandings for integrative health by reconciling and healing our relations with each other as well as the land, air, and water around us.

column36: A systems approach for enhancing perinatal care regionalization
column37: Canadians benefit from an excellent perinatal health care system. However, some problems persist as evidenced by disparities in illness and death among mothers and babies, and unfavourable international comparisons. Thus, rates of serious illness/death among mothers and babies vary significantly by region, socio-economic status, rural vs urban residence, Aboriginal status and other factors. The single biggest challenge confronting the perinatal health care system in Canada relates to regionalization of perinatal care i.e., receipt of the appropriate level of care based on the risks faced by the mother/baby. This problem is highlighted by maternity services in rural regions of Canada - the closure of small hospitals has resulted in the need for low-risk pregnant women to travel long distances for childbirth. Problems also exist in high volume/intensity regions such as the Greater Toronto Area where inadequate tertiary capacity dictates that high-risk women deliver in non-tertiary settings. Other challenges include those due to geography, climate, emergency transport, organizational issues, and the absence of evaluation and monitoring of regionalization. We propose to use a systems approach for evaluating the structure, processes and outcomes of regionalized perinatal care. Such a critical analysis will assess perinatal care regionalization in terms of hospital services, care provision in rural and remote communities and emergency transport. We will also use mapping of travel times from maternal residence to hospital and other novel techniques to rationalize the delivery of maternity/newborn care services. The results of this critical analysis will be used to formulate recommendations in collaboration with provincial/territorial Perinatal Care Programs and Ministries of Health. Implementation of recommendations will also be a carried out in close collaboration with provincial/territorial stakeholders.

column36: UCAN CAN-DU: Canada-Netherlands Personalized Medicine Network in Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatic Disease
column37: Arthritis is a common chronic disabling diseases of childhood. Many children with arthritis will continue to have arthritis as adults. New medications called biologic therapies are now available to treat arthritis. These target key biologic molecules that cause inflammation. Biologic therapies, while very effective in treating arthritis in children, may have serious side effects including infections and potentially cancers, and are very expensive and doctors don't know, which one to choose for which child. In this unique Canadian-Dutch Research Network, we will develop tests that enable us to learn about the biology of each child's arthritis and be able to predict when and which biologic therapy to start and when to stop. We will improve the health of each child by selecting the right, effective treatment and prevent medication side effects. This approach will result in a dramatic reduction in health care burden for patients, families and society. A better understanding of the biology of disease will also lead to better therapies and ultimately a cure for arthritis. One of the many advantages of studying diseases in children is that we will learn about the underlying biology without the complicating influences of aging, environmental exposures and lifestyle choices that affect adults. Lessons learned in childhood arthritis will be shared with physicians worldwide through strategic partnerships with decision-makers throughout the world and also by building a state-of-the-art electronic Health platform to share information with physicians, patients and their families in real-time. Our interdisciplinary research team will partner with patients, family members and policy-makers. We expect the results will rapidly lead to improved care for children with arthritis as it will help ensure that biologic therapies are used in the safest and most beneficial and cost-effective way, directly improving the health and quality of life of affected children and their families.

column36: Engineering Pulmonary Valve Tissue for Pediatric Patients with Tetralogy of Fallot
column37: Children born with congenital heart diseases, such as tetralogy of Fallot, often have defective heart valves. For example, in tetralogy of Fallot, the pulmonary artery and valve are narrowed. Surgeons can enlarge the artery and add a valve leaflet by using a patch made from pericardial tissue from around the heart or a synthetic fabric. While this provides temporary relief to the infant or child, the repair materials cannot grow with the patient and are prone to scarring and calcification, leading to a lifetime of reoperations and clinical interventions for the patient. Here, we propose to use principles of heart valve tissue engineering to produce sheets of living valve leaflet tissue that can be used as an alternative repair material. The sheets will be made from stem cells from the infant's own umbilical cord grown on a polyurethane mesh, which will eventually dissolve away in the body to harmless byproducts, leaving behind a living valve leaflet produced by the stem cells. To kickstart tissue production, we will first grow the valve tissue in bioreactors that exercise the tissue to improve its strength and flexibility. Most engineered valve tissue fails by scarring, so to prevent this, we will inject nanoparticles loaded with an anti-scarring drug into the tissue prior to implantation. We will test this novel replacement tissue in pigs to assess whether the material is durable, does not scar, and remains functional in the body. Over the next three years, our interdisciplinary team of material scientists, heart valve experts, and cardiac surgeons will train next-generation engineers, scientists, and surgeons and will collaborate with our partners at SickKids Hospital and Tissue Regeneration Therapuetics to translate this novel concept in congenital heart defect repair towards practice, significant improvement in the current standard of care, and economic impact through commercialization.

column36: Innovation in Pediatric Clinical Trials
column37: Clinical trials use real patients under carefully controlled situations to measure how well a medication works and how safe it is. Knowledge gained from trials helps doctors choose which medicines to prescribe. Clinical trials for children are difficult to do, because they get sick less often than adults, and parents are understandably protective and reluctant to enroll their kids in a trial. Also, many hospitals need to be involved to study enough patients, which is expensive to coordinate. As a result, doctors don't have enough solid evidence for prescribing medicines to kids, which means a lot of guesswork. We are using new methods of study design to see if they will make clinical trials in children easier and better. We will create resources for trial design, management and analysis that can be used by researchers across Canada to make clinical trials for children easier, less expensive and more informative. These resources will be known as KIDSCAN, a Canadian effort for safe drugs in kids. We will be testing these new methods and resources in 4 clinical trials conducted in 6 pediatric emergency departments across 4 provinces. The medical conditions and treatments to test were chosen by researchers in pediatric emergency medicine because they are common, and include breathing problems, stomach upset, and pain from an injury or procedure. We will use statistical methods that will determine what information already exists that a trial can build on, and what information we might still need in order to change what doctors decide to do. As well, we will use centralized systems and services to conduct the trials and manage the data. To determine if these new methods and resources were successful we will look at the cost of the trial, the quality of the evidence generated, and the changes in procedures used in the pediatric ED. We hope to show that these new methods and resources will mean doctors will have more and better information on which to base their decisions.
