column36: Using the Skin Immune System to Induce Systemic Tolerance
column37: In autoimmune disease, the immune system that is designed to prevent infection and cancer attacks the healthy body. There are over 60 types of autoimmune disease - examples include type 1 diabetes and inflammatory bowel disease. Autoimmune disease is a significant economic and psycho-social burden and an enormous challenge clinically, as treatment is symptomatic but not yet curative. One promising solution is immunomodulation, whereby the immune system is "reprogrammed" to suppress unwanted inflammation. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are potent contributors in suppressing inflammation and can directly restrain inflammation in a manner that targets specific antigens, or molecules that are causative to inflammatory disease. Human skin is particularly rich in Tregs. I propose to harness the skin immune system to direct immunosuppressive Treg responses using a technique called topical immunomodulation. My doctoral thesis will examine how to 1) expand skin Treg populations, 2) assess their function in targeted immunosuppression, and 3) re-home skin Treg into organs affected by inflammation. I will investigate the capacity of ultraviolet B radiation, topical corticosteroid and topical vitamin D in expanding functional Treg. Topical vitamin A will be examined for its potential in re-homing immunosuppressive Tregs into intestinal tissue. I will use mouse models of allergic contact dermatitis, type 1 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease to test the effectiveness of these topical immunomodulatory strategies in treating or curing inflammation in mice. In humans, my doctoral work will test whether topical corticosteroid and/or vitamin D ointments can expand functional Treg in the skin and blood of people with nickel or pollen allergies. The findings of my doctoral work will contribute critically essential knowledge for the development of clinically effective therapy for patients with autoimmune disease and related inflammatory disorders.

column36: DDX11 as a potential synthetic lethal target for cancer therapeutics in cells with cohesion mutations
column37: Cancer is an individualized disease - each patient's tumor is a unique combination of genetic changes that drive its development. Recent advances in DNA sequencing of individual tumors have enabled scientists to identify the specific genetic changes (mutations) that are driving the tumor growth, and offer the promise of personalized treatments based on these changes. Unfortunately, our ability to identify the specific genetic changes of a tumor far exceeds our ability to make use of this knowledge therapeutically, as most of the genetic changes do not currently have targeted treatments. A large percentage of brain and bladder tumors contain mutations in cohesin (a protein complex important for accurate division of genetic material) but no drug has been developed yet to target this genetic vulnerability. Research performed in our lab has previously identified two potential therapeutic targets (FEN1 and DDX11) for treatment of tumors containing mutations in cohesin. We have also previously identified chemical inhibitors of FEN1 activity which are currently in pre-clinical trials. My research focuses on the second target identified - DDX11. My goal is to develop DDX11 as a therapeutic target using a similar approach to the one used to develop FEN1 inhibitors. I aim to demonstrate that targeting DDX11 can selectively kill cancer cells that have mutations in cohesin. In addition, I intend to identify drugs capable of inhibiting DDX11 activity and to test these on a range of cancer-derived cells. This research will provide new treatments for tumors that previously did not have therapeutic options. Personalized cancer therapy is being adopted on the frontlines of cancer treatment and has been successful in treating cancers that have resisted conventional treatment. My research is driving the development of a new class of drugs that can contribute to the potential of personalized cancer therapy.

column36: Understanding human biology and disease through tissue-specific protein-protein interaction networks
column37: In many inherited diseases, a mutation present in virtually every cell in the body causes dysfunction in only one or a few tissues or organs. For example, in Huntington's disease, a mutation to the huntingtin gene causes a neurodegenerative syndrome originating in the brain, while sparing most other organs, despite the fact that the mutated protein is expressed in many different types of cells. To understand why this is the case, it is important to realize that genes (and their protein products) do not operate in isolation. Rather, proteins accomplish normal cellular tasks by interacting with other proteins. The protein-protein interactions within a cell form a large and complex network. Mapping this network of interactions-known as the interactome-is essential to understanding both how proteins interact with one another to accomplish biological functions in healthy organisms, and how these interactions are disrupted in disease. However, studies that have mapped the interactome in humans or model organisms have rarely taken into account tissue or cell type. Recent developments in mass spectrometry have made it possible to map the interactome in individual tissues. This new data has the potential to significantly improve our understanding of human biology in general, and of disease more specifically. I propose to conduct computational analyses to reveal how cells separate interactions required for tissue-specific functions from interactions that occur in all cells. I will identify cellular pathways underlying tissue-specific pathologies in hereditary diseases. Finally, I will identify the protein-protein interactions disrupted by genetic mutations associated with inherited diseases in each tissue affected by the disease, to identify molecular mechanisms for many hereditary diseases and new targets for therapy. The analysis proposed here promises to leverage a unique new dataset to develop insights into human biology and the mechanisms underlying human disease.

column36: Early injecting careers: Implications for health, HIV risk behaviours and clinical care
column37: Injection drug use among youth is a significant public health concern that is associated with severe harms among youth including, fatal drug overdose, violence, and risk of HIV and Hepatitis C (HCV) incidence. However, initiation of injection drug use among early injecting careers remains understudied. While there is growing recognition that contextual factors play a central role in determining youth's high-risk drug using behaviors, little is known about initiation into injecting, early injecting careers, and potential interventions that may help prevent initiation into injecting. Furthermore, our understanding of factors that determine early cessation or predict sustained injecting among recent initiates remains very limited. Therefore, this study proposes to employ longitudinal data analyses to characterize early injecting careers, with a focus on the individual (e.g., childhood trauma, drug use patterns) and social-structural (e.g., homelessness, incarceration) factors that shape injection initiation, early cessation of injecting, and sustained injecting. Findings of this study are essential to developing meaningful and effective policy and program interventions that seek to prevent early injecting careers from progressing to sustained injecting.

column36: Exoskeleton for post-Stroke Recovery of Ambulation (ExStRA)
column37: 400,000 Canadians currently live with disability as a result of stroke, amounting to a staggering economic burden of $2.8 billion annually. Walking ability, or lack thereof, is a key determinant of disability and can impact whether an individual returns home after stroke; individuals who do not regain the ability to walk are more likely to go to nursing homes and develop secondary complications. However not all stroke patients, especially those requiring more physical assistance, have the opportunity for early walking practice due to therapist and safety limitations. A possible solution is the use of a powered robotic exoskeleton in therapy, a new technology which straps to the lower limbs to safely automate walking regardless of leg weakness. This device will afford patients the opportunity to practice walking during the early window after stroke when the greatest recovery of the brain occurs. In this study we will compare the effectiveness of an exoskeleton-based rehabilitation program to standard stroke rehabilitation. We hypothesize that individuals who are able practice walking, by means of the exoskeleton, during the period when the brain experiences the most recovery will experience greater functional improvements than individuals receiving standard care; those receiving standard care will still receive mobility and walking training, though guided by the patient's strength, therapist discretion, and safety regulations. We will also interview therapists and patients who use the exoskeleton for rehabilitation, in order to explore their experience and perception of the device. Using an exoskeleton for rehabilitation has the potential to provide treatment to patients with severe stroke who are not yet able to walk. If the exoskeleton program generates greater recovery of walking, it may become an integral component of physical therapy care. It would also have implications at various levels, from patient health outcomes to the national economic burden of stroke.

column36: Validation The Antigen Presentation Capacity of Human Mesenchymal Stem Cells Overexpressing The Immuno-proteasome Complex
column37: B-cells play a key role in establishing a protective immune response by synthesizing antibody molecules to recognize and neutralize invading pathogens. During their development and maturation, B-cells rearrange their genetic material that encode for antibodies. This process named class switch recombination requires B-cells to undergo programmed DNA double strand break (DSB). DSBs are particularly dangerous as they compromise genomic integrity. In case of a faulty DSB repair B-cells may not elicit a functional immune response and are prone to become malignant. Therefore, B-cells have developed a complex DSB response to ensure that these DNA lesions are properly repaired. It is primordial to fully understand how DNA repair occurs in B-cells to provide genetic diversity while avoiding triggering B-cell malignancies including lymphoma and leukemia. My work will focus on the role of Ubiquitin in the repair of DSBs in B-cells. The dynamic ubiquitin system has an important regulatory role in different cellular functions including DSB signaling/repair. The E3 Ubiquitin ligase RNF168 is critical in signaling DSB. Mutations in RNF168 result in an immunodeficiency syndrome called RIDDLE. Recently, a deubiquitylation enzyme OTUB1 has been identified as an important regulator of RNF168 activity during the DSB response. OTUB1 is overexpressed in several B-cell lymphomas and could be a promising target for their treatment. The goal of my project is to study the role of OTUB1 in B-cells, in particular the repair of DSBs during antibody diversification. In this regard, I will characterize different mouse models where Otub1 has been deleted and determine the impact of its loss for B-cell biology, DSB repair, and the emergence of B-cell lymphoma. This project will provide insight on OTUB1 role in B-cell biology. It will also help elucidate DNA repair mechanisms in B-cells. Finally, it will shed light on the implications of improper DSB repair for the development of B-cell malignancies

column36: Combining mathematical models and machine learning for the identification of novel neuroimaging biomarkers for disorders of neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration
column37: Disorders of brain development and degeneration, including Autism Spectrum Disorder and Alzheimer's disease, cost the Canadian healthcare system billions of dollars every year. The identification of new measures of disease progression or severity using brain scans can enable the development of new therapies, reduce the cost and length of clinical trials, and allow doctors to better track the progression of brain disease. The recent creation of large collections of brain images has provided researchers with access to more medical images than ever before. This creates a challenge because now researchers need to develop new ways to use this complex data. Once new methods are developed, it could allow us to better understand normal brain development and any changes to the brain caused by disease. Recently, success has been made in identifying methods of measuring brain disease progression using machine learning, an approach to artificial intelligence that is good at recognizing complex patterns. In addition, mathematical models have allowed for a better understanding of how diseases progress in the brain. This project will develop new ways to identify measures of disease progression by combining mathematical models and machine learning techniques. This project could contribute to the understanding of the underlying mechanisms of multiple disorders, enable doctors to better monitor patients, allow doctors to better predict how patients will respond to treatment, and lead to the development of new treatment options.

column36: Function of PAI-1 and regulation of its gene expression in human diabetic platelets
column37: Cardiovascular disease is the second leading cause of death in Canada. Patients with coronary artery disease are treated through percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or through bypass surgery. One of the major complications of PCI involves blood clot formation at the site of intervention. To prevent blood clots, two anti-platelet therapies are given in the form of aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor (receptor on platelets) after treatment. However, this dual anti-platelet therapy regime appears to function poorly in diabetic patients. Also, diabetic patients are known to have hyperactive platelets and increased chance of blood clot formation. Currently, the reason why diabetic patients have higher platelet reactivity than their non-diabetic peers is poorly understood. One protein of interest is plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1 or SERPINE1), which is responsible for inhibiting the breakdown of blood clots in the body. Resistance to existing anti-platelet therapy could be due to high levels of PAI-1 in diabetic patients. As a result, this proposal seeks to identify the reason for the elevated level of PAI-1 expression in diabetics. It is of utmost importance to understand why diabetic platelets express more PAI-1 than non-diabetic platelets as this protein may contribute to resistance to current medicine. The goals of this project involves understanding the molecular basis of PAI-1 expression and to develop new potential therapies to specifically target PAI-1. In addition, novel therapies could be developed and tested in diabetic animal models. The knowledge gained from understanding the regulation of PAI-1 expression is important to the research community, as it may serve as a blueprint to develop novel inhibitors. In the future, these inhibitors may be developed into new drugs to decrease hyperactive platelets in diabetic patients undergoing PCI to reduce adverse events after the procedure to reduce mortality.

column36: Can trophic cascades transcend nearshore habitats and link marine and terrestrial ecosystems?
column37: Carnivores can change entire ecosystems through a trophic cascade. A simple, three species trophic cascade occurs when a carnivore affects the abundance of plants by limiting the herbivores that previously grazed the plants. Sea otters are an example of a predator that causes a trophic cascade. On rocky reefs, sea otters limit sea urchins. Because sea urchins eat kelp, when otters are present ecosystems switch from being urchin-dominated to kelp-dominated. Sea otters were once hunted to near-extinction, and their recovery has provided a natural experiment with equivalent areas differing only in whether sea otters are present. Sea otter recovery might also affect terrestrial communities. Kelp growth facilitated by otters might increase the amount of kelp that washes up on shore. This kelp provides a nutrient source to insects, birds, and mammals on land-a boost that could lead to healthier or larger populations. I will test if the presence of sea otters increases the biomass of invertebrates and small mammals on adjacent land by increasing kelp deposits on shore. Such a connection would link marine and terrestrial ecosystems through a nutrient subsidy created by sea otters-furthering our understanding of community ecology. Another way sea otters might affect nearshore communities is by switching their diets. Once otters have eaten the easily available urchins, they eat clams and crabs in sheltered habitats. I will investigate how and when re-colonizing sea otters switch to these sheltered habitats and how this switch affects soft-bottomed ecosystems. Understanding how top predators structure ecosystems is a key component of community ecology. My research will contribute to the advancement of ecological theory and help to evaluate management tradeoffs as sea otters recover in areas they were previously extirpated from. Such studies are increasingly important as humans learn to coexist with recovering apex predators around the world.

column36: Integration du controle a la source et du controle en temps reel comme mesures de reduction des debordements de reseaux d'egout unitaires
column37: Dans de nombreuses villes du Canada et ailleurs dans le monde, l'eau usee et l'eau qui ruissele lors d'evenements pluvieux se jettent dans le meme reseau d'egout. Ce melange d'eaux contaminees est ensuite transporte et traite avant son rejet dans l'environnement. Toutefois, par temps de pluie ou de fonte des neiges, la capacite du reseau peut s'averer insuffisante, ce qui entraine des debordements d'eaux usees dans les cours d'eau. Ce phenomene de debordements de reseaux d'egout unitaires, est associe a de graves problemes environnementaux, la perte d'usages recreatifs et la degradation visible du milieu. Les solutions disponibles pour contrer cette problematique comprennent les mesures de controle de l'eau pluviale a la source telles que l'implantation de surfaces vegetalisees ou la construction de reservoirs. Alternativement, le controle optimal de l'ecoulement de l'eau pluviale au sein du reseau par l'ajustement instantane des infrastructures hydrauliques est un autre type de solution possible. Toutefois, les connaissances sont limitees quant a la maniere optimale de reduire le nombre et la quantite des debordements de reseaux d'egout unitaires, d'autant plus que l'impact des changements climatiques et l'influence du climat continental froid et humide doivent aussi etre consideres dans l'evaluation des solutions disponibles. Pour repondre a ce defi, l'utilisation d'outils de modelisation hydrologique et hydraulique combines a des calculs d'optimisation mathematique permettra d'estimer le potentiel d'integrer a la fois des solutions de controle du ruissellement a la source et en reseau sur un meme territoire. La recherche vise en particulier a proposer des solutions optimales en termes de cout et d'efficacite pour des reseaux d'egout de differentes tailles. Les resultats escomptes appuieront ainsi les municipalites, les gouvernements et les scientifiques dans le developpement d'outils de gestion durable des eaux pluviales et de preservation de l'environnement.

column36: Molecular mechanisms mediating a positive calcium balance during development
column37: Calcium has multiple essential roles in the body including forming the foundation of bone structure. Bone growth occurs rapidly in infancy and continues throughout childhood, with bone mass peaking in early adulthood. It is, therefore, crucial to build strong bones during childhood. Unfortunately, many infants and children are at increased risk of poor bone health due to factors including prematurity, bowel disease, and kidney disease. Calcium balance in the body involves interactions between the intestines, kidneys, and bones. If inadequate calcium is absorbed from the intestine, it is sacrificed from the bones. Unfortunately, mechanisms leading to a positive calcium balance for appropriate growth are not clearly understood. Our first objective is to understand these mechanisms. We use mice at different ages to measure gene expression and protein levels of molecules and hormones involved in calcium absorption in intestines and kidneys. We then directly measure calcium movement across intestine sections of mouse intestine to investigate the role of non-typical intestinal sections during growth. To date, our results suggest the finding of a new pathway of absorption in some sections of the small intestine that only exist in young mice. The results of this research thus far challenge the current understanding of calcium absorption. These studies will have a significant impact on scientists and non-academics in this field. Given the important role of calcium in the body, understanding how it is absorbed from the diet will inform adequate calcium intake for humans and animals, aid in optimising infant formulas, and create potential targets for new therapies to prevent poor bone health later in life.

column36: Broke but not Broken: Examining Agency and Resistance Among Homeless Canadian Youth
column37: By engaging in in-depth interviews, focus groups, and arts-based methods with homeless and street-involved youth in Ottawa, Montreal, Vancouver and Halifax, this doctoral research will explore how homeless Canadian youth negotiate and/or overcome their marginalization through agency, empowerment, and community during their lives on the street. I will explore the following three core questions: (i) In what ways do young homeless and street-involved adults (age 18-30) experience street life as an empowered choice? (ii) How do personal experiences of trauma, stigma, and marginalization shape how young homeless people view, conform to and/or resist pressures to engage in formal education, paid work or traditional living situations? And (iii) how do they speak about and experience past and present challenges to conforming to mainstream societal expectations and authority? Because many youth do not access shelters and other homeless services due to their reluctance to conform to the rules and obligations required, such as sobriety (Finley 2010; Kort-Butler & Tyler 2012; Shillington et al. 2011), they are a difficult population to access. There is an urgent need for scholarly literature that explores their lived experiences and modes of resistance (Marshall et al. 2008) to aid in developing public policy recommendations and improving services for homeless youth. Discovering how youth use agency in their interactions with authorities will help inform policy makers and scholars how to better engage homeless youth and provide services that respect their autonomy, while improving relationships with the police and the broader community.

Enfin, l'analyse de la prise en charge financiere de la gestion de la nature permettra de questionner le developpement d'une nouvelle representation commune de la nature. Cette recherche sera determinante pour la sociologie et la philosophie sociale dans la mesure ou elle permettra de saisir les ressorts concrets du pouvoir de la finance. column36: A mixed-methods analysis of the experience of post-war displacement and psychological resilience in Sri Lanka
column37: Individuals in post-conflict settings have experienced not only direct exposure to violence but also secondary traumatic events associated with displacement such as interrupted school attendance, loss of family and community, lengthy and dangerous journeys, and inadequate resources or shelter (American Psychological Association, 2010). Following a 26-year civil war, Sri Lanka has tens of thousands of internally displaced persons (IDPs), including many born during the conflict (Siriwardhana & Wickramage, 2014). Despite living in adverse circumstances, a growing body of literature points to vital protective factors such as support networks and a sense of community that are important in recovery post-conflict. There is increasing awareness of the importance of social and cultural dimensions of resilience that extend beyond the individual. While some literature exists on risk and protective factors in displaced populations, there has not been an explicit exploration of the intersection between age at displacement, return migration, and resilience in a post-conflict setting. Using a mixed-method design, this study will explore: (1) which factors of the environment in a post-conflict situation are important to the maintenance and promotion of resilience in return migrants, and (2) how resilience is conceptualized in returning IDPs born prior to and those born during the conflict in Sri Lanka. The Conservation of Resources Theory (COR), an integrative model that considers both environmental and internal processes in resilience research (Hobfoll, 1988, 1989, 1998, 2015), will provide a framework for analysis. The theoretical contribution of this study will be adding a cohort perspective to Hobfoll's COR theory in a post-conflict setting. Additionally, understanding how age at displacement plays a role in the development and maintenance of resilience and psychological wellbeing can inform community-based mental health interventions for displaced communities globally.

column36: The Emergence of New Street Level Bureaucrats: How Formal Policy is Re-Shaped and Implemented by Non-State Contracted Agencies
column37: My research will focus on how non-state agencies (private firms and NGOs) and their employees, that are contracted by the state for the purpose of supplying public social services (health, education, employment, etc), re-shape public policy entrusted to them, through the process of policy implementation. I will use the theoretical framework of "Street Level Bureaucracy" approach, used by researchers over the last 30 years to examine actions of public servants (teachers, social workers, school nurses, police officers, public defenders etc.), responsible for implementation and enforcement of public policy. This approach attributes a pivotal role to street level bureaucrats in the process of policy implementation, in virtue of their discretion and autonomy. It has not yet been applied to explore actions of non-state agencies that supply public services. My research will close this significant gap in literature. Understanding ways in which public policy is re-shaped by non-state agencies, will further our knowledge on ramifications of privatization and outsourcing, and will contribute to this on-going public debate. My research will explore comparative case studies - in Israel and in Canada, in areas of public health and employment programs. First stage will explore formal policy (as crafted in government and entrusted to these agencies), through a comprehensive formal policy document analyses (such as cabinet decisions, legislation and public tenders). Second stage will focus on characterizing factors shaping the actions of employees in contracted agencies. For this I will use qualitative methods often utilized in Street Level Bureaucracy research, such as interviews with employees and managers in these agencies. My research will explore how personal, organizational, and professional factors of street level bureaucrats (employment structure, motivation, work ethos etc,), may differ when considering non-state agencies, and effect the process of implementation.

column36: Mentoring new patient-oriented researchers in innovative HIV e-care
column37: HIV medications are getting better but for many HIV-infected Canadians taking their lifelong medication is a serious challenge. Current HIV care insufficiently addresses this. This measure will be filled out on an electronic tablet prior to patients' regular clinic visits and scores will be shared with their doctor so that any difficulties can be discussed and addressed. column36: HIV Risks, prevention and HIV criminalization: Optimizing Continuum of Care to Reduce HIV risks among Black African and Caribbean Communities in Ontario
column37: The overly broad application of HIV-related criminal case laws continues to stifle public health and HIV prevention efforts. Since 1990s, the Canadian Criminal Justice System became involved in cases of perceived HIV exposure and/or transmission, prosecuting persons living with HIV for engaging in behaviors deemed "risky" in terms of possible HIV transmission. Canada continues to enforce these laws despite evolving scientific evidence on HIV transmission and the lack of empirical evidence to demonstrate that HIV-related case laws are effective at preventing HIV transmission. The African, Caribbean, and Black (ACB) communities are disproportionately burdened by HIV and HIV-related criminal laws. Despite the significance of these laws in influencing HIV epidemic, large research gaps still remain in understanding how HIV criminalization impact HIV risks, HIV prevention efforts and healthcare engagement for the ACB Communities. The aim of the proposed study is to examine the impact of HIV-related criminal and public health laws on HIV prevention and healthcare engagement among ACB communities at risk and living with HIV (undiagnosed and diagnosed) in Ontario, Canada. This qualitative research will utilize Community Based Research approach, intersectionality, Syndemics theory, and socio-ecological framework to examine and analyze the contextual, individual, cultural, social and structural factors that currently drive health disparities and HIV risks, and undermine HIV prevention and healthcare engagement. This is a multi-level research project that will employ critical discourse and intertextual analysis, in-depth interview and focused group discussions, and participant observations. Knowledge translation and exchange of the research findings to local and transnational partners will inform the ongoing development of public health policies to reduce health disparities and HIV risks, as well as provide evidence for enactment of alternative approaches to criminal laws.

column36: Examining how patients and providers bridge Indigenous and Western healing paradigms in the Northwest Territories
column37: Indigenous people in Canada experience a disproportionate number of health issues compared with their non-Indigenous counterparts. Although studies show that the quality of health services offered to and taken up by Indigenous patients is negatively impacted when Western approaches to health and healing are prioritized over Indigenous approaches, Indigenous healing paradigms and practices are excluded from institutionalized healthcare in most parts of Canada. In an attempt to improve the quality of care for Indigenous people, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) has called for greater collaboration between Indigenous and Western healers. Currently, however, there are very few hospitals in Canada that work to bridge Indigenous and Western approaches to healing. In the Northwest Territories (NWT), the need is particularly great. Despite NWT's high proportion of Indigenous residents (51%), there are few initiatives in hospitals that incorporate both Indigenous and Western healing practices. Furthermore, there is a gap in knowledge about how patients and providers currently experience Indigenous and Western healing paradigms in practice. In order to address the TRC's calls for action and improve the quality of health services for Indigenous people and communities in the NWT, it is critical to fill this knowledge gap. My PhD research will use community-based qualitative research methods and the 'two-eyed seeing' approach to (1) examine how healthcare providers and patients in the NWT understand and experience the interaction between Indigenous and Western healing paradigms in hospital settings, and (2) illuminate the assumptions and values underlying these paradigms, which inform the quality of health service provision. Working in partnership with Dene Elders, this project aims to inform the creation of government health policies and programs in the NWT and to improve the quality of healthcare for Indigenous patients and communities.

column36: A New Framework for Addressing Aboriginal Health Issues: A Participatory Approach in Two First Nations Communities Using Frontline Worker Input
column37: Aboriginal peoples face multiple health challenges and a significant health gap exists between Aboriginals and non-Aboriginals. Une grande proportion des logements du Nord canadien sont surpeuples et necessitent des reparations majeures. Ces pietres conditions de vie, la promiscuite et le manque d'intimite qui en decoulent engendrent des tensions familiales et peuvent declencher des episodes d'abus et de violence, dont les enfants sont parfois temoins ou victimes. Plusieurs etudes suggerent des liens entre les conditions d'habitation et la sante mentale des familles, particulierement celle des femmes, et le developpement des enfants. Pourtant, un tres petit nombre d'etudes s'est interesse a l'impact des conditions de logement sur la sante des populations autochtones. Mon projet doctoral comprend deux volets. Le 1er volet profite d'une initiative ayant permis la construction de 360 logements au Nunavut et Nunavik. Il vise a evaluer l'impact de demenager dans un nouveau logement sur la sante mentale des meres (evaluee a l'aide de questionnaires avant-apres le demenagement) et sur la dynamique familiale (decrite lors d'entrevues individuelles aupres de 24 meres avec jeunes enfants). Le 2e volet vise a evaluer l'impact des conditions de logement sur le developpement moteur, cognitif et socio-emotif des enfants (0-11 ans). Pour ce faire, j'utiliserai les donnees quebecoises de l'Enquete regionale sur l'education, l'emploi et la petite enfance chez les Premieres Nations (3540 repondants), une enquete developpee par et pour les Premieres Nations. Les deux volets de mon projet seront developpes en etroite collaboration avec les communautes autochtones. Mon objectif au final est de fournir des resultats permettant d'informer les prochaines politiques de logement en contexte autochtone autour d'enjeux juges pertinents par les familles autochtones, permettant d'ameliorer la sante des familles et le developpement des enfants.

column36: The effects of chronic HIV infection and antiretrovirals on cellular aging and mitochondrial health in immune cell subsets
column37: Over 37 million people live with HIV globally. In Canada, there are over 75000 persons living with HIV, with a new HIV infection every 3 hours. HIV is currently treated with combination antiretroviral therapy (cART), a mixture of three different anti-HIV drugs. This allows people with HIV to live longer and prevents death from Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). However, despite successful treatment, people with HIV are still more likely to suffer from diseases that usually occur with old age. These include heart, bone, and liver diseases, as well as certain cancers. A rapidly-aging immune system is suspected to lead to these age-related diseases, but it is unclear whether this results from the virus (HIV) or the treatment (cART). Although people with HIV are known to have older immune cells, it is unknown which types of immune cells are affected. In addition, approximately 1% of people with HIV are "non-progressors", and remain healthy without treatment. We do not know how the virus affects aging in their immune systems. I will separate blood samples from 400 participants into specific types of immune cells, and measure parameters that are related to cellular aging. column36: Improving prescribing practices in primary care: treatment of depression in obese and overweight patients.
column37: People who are very overweight (considered obese) often suffer from depression. Similarly, people with depression are at risk for becoming obese. Both obesity and depression are very common among Canadians. Family practitioners are usually the first health professionals that people visit to help deal with depression. In patients with depression, excessive weight may make the treatment less efficient because fat can interfere with the action of the drug. Yet, it is not clear if family practitioners prescribe drugs against depression differently for obese patients to account for this fact. It is also unclear whether these ways of prescribing may influence a person's general health. The goal of our study is to evaluate how primary care practitioners prescribe antidepressants for overweight and obese people, and to assess how this influences a patient's general health. For our analysis, we will use two data sets: a large healthcare data set based on the primary care-based electronic medical records from several Canadian provinces, and a database on Quebec residents diagnosed with depression. Our study will help us understand if primary care practitioners prescribe antidepressants differently for patients of different weight groups, and whether it affects treatment effectiveness and patients' general health. This study will help improve policies for prescribing antidepressants for obese and overweight people in primary care.

column37: Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) suffer bouts of extreme gut inflammation that disrupt the population of bacteria in their intestines. Thus IBD patients often have fewer beneficial bacteria and suffer an overgrowth of potentially dangerous bacteria. In healthy individuals, such responses are typically prevented by SIGIRR, a protein made by the cells that line the gut. SIGIRR acts by suppressing mechanisms that drive inflammation. We have shown that loss of SIGIRR dramatically increases inflammation and drives bacterial imbalance. The inflammation can become so severe that gut tissue can become necrotic. We do not have a way to promote the beneficial actions of SIGIRR in the gut, but recently, a newly recognized anti-inflammatory compound called interleukin (IL)-37, has been shown to interact with SIGIRR to inhibit inflammatory responses in human cells. In this project, we plan to test whether IL-37 stimulates SIGIRR to: i) control inflammation and suppress bacterial killing responses in the cells that line the gut; ii) protect mice from experimentally-induced IBD; and iii) promote normal gut microbe balance. Ultimately, my studies will explore the potential for IL-37 to act as a new therapeutic for patients with IBD.

column36: Improving Medication PRescribing for Ontario's Vulnerable Elderly High Cost Healthcare Users (IMPROVE-HCU)
column37: High cost healthcare users (HCUs) are a small group of patients that use a disproportionate healthcare resources compared to the average patient. In 2011, 5% of Ontarians used 65% ($19.8 billion) of total measurable public healthcare expenditures. Most HCUs are seniors with multiple chronic conditions taking multiple medications. With costs expected to double in 20 years, the current approach to HCUs has been deemed unsustainable by leading economists and there is an urgent need to design interventions to improve their health outcomes and costs. Our proposed research program seeks to better understand the impact of prescribing quality and drug use in senior HCUs. It is currently unknown whether HCUs are using optimal drugs and whether savings can be found through more cost-effective drug use. In Study 1, we will be using health administrative databases to investigate the current quality of prescribing and drug use in senior HCUs. We will be using the STOPP-START screening tool to look for potentially inappropriate prescribing that should have been stopped or started based on high quality scientific evidence. We will also explore the cost-savings if the government adopted a policy known as "reference-based pricing" for select high cost drugs with cheaper, equally effective alternatives. In Study 2, we will test the feasibility of conducting a large randomized trial to test the effectiveness of a new strategy to optimize drugs for hospitalized seniors HCUs to reduce their risk of death, re-hospitalization and healthcare costs. This project will demonstrate the impact of optimizing medications for Canada's high need, high cost seniors. It is the first of its kind internationally and it will help clinicians, hospitals and government develop new strategies to address the healthcare sustainability crisis. If only 10% of HCU expenses could be avoided or delayed, an additional $1.7 billion would be available in Ontario alone to fund better care for these seniors.

column36: Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies (CEMT)
column37: The term epigenome refers to chemical modifications of DNA and proteins that control the structure and regulation of the "genome", a term referring to all the DNA within our cells. In contrast to the genome, which changes very little if at all over the course of an individual's life, the epigenome is dynamic and changes during normal development, aging, disease challenges and in response to various external stimuli. Such epigenome changes can result in significant differences in how genes, and thus how cells, behave. Thus, an understanding of the epigenome and how it works in different cell types is critically important to understanding many aspects of human health and disease. The Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies (CEMT) has established a track record of leadership in the International Human Epigenomic Consortium; in the generation of reference epigenomes from a broad spectrum of normal and diseased human cell types; in the development and testing of technology for broader future applications; and in making such technology rapidly available to Canadian scientists. The CEMT is designed as an integrated unit composed of internationally leading biologists and clinicians with specialized access to, and knowledge of, the normal and diseased cell types we will analyze. The collaborative team effort described herein will transform our understanding of the relationship between the dynamic nature of the epigenome and how genes are turned on and turned off, and lay the foundation for larger studies to revolutionize our understanding of the role played by the epigenome in health and diseases, and from there how to more effectively manage the health of our populations.

column36: Accessing chromatin interactions by high-resolution analyses of correlated regulatory element variation
column37: Disease and development are reflected in chromatin states and their interactions in regulatory space. As opposed to developmental processes, it is anticipated that the genetic and epigenetic predisposition in disease is based on subtle alterations in chromatin conformation. Translational studies of altered chromatin structure are currently hampered by inflexible technologies. Direct "chromatin conformation association studies" require methodology that is scalable, tunable, and robust to variable quality of biological materials. We have charted CpG methylation variation in high-resolution across hundreds of population samples and observe significant enrichment of allelic and non-allelic methylation variation correlations in genomic regions shown to directly interact by conventional chromatin conformation assays. Preliminary data also points to preferential location of informative CpGs at boundaries of regulatory regions. We now propose the generation of a resource and framework to utilize interacting differentially methylated regions (iDMRs) applicable in large-scale studies to assess phenotypic importance of chromatin looping variation. We leverage methodologies we developed for targeted bisulfite sequencing to allow very high-resolution analyses for iDMRs as well as a unique cellular panel of human mesenchymal stem cells and their differentiated derivatives where standardized reference epigenome maps are generated in parallel. The full spectrum of chromatin conformation variation ranging from inter-individual to developmental differences are represented in this dataset serving as the optimal platform to develop analytical approaches for iDMR discovery. Conventional approaches for detecting and disrupting chromatin conformation in same cells serve to benchmark iDMR specificity and sensitivity. The resource and methods developed here will pave the way for systematic interrogation of chromatin conformation in new areas of population health and complex disease risk.

column37: The health and economic burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) is increasing rapidly worldwide and falls disproportionally on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where almost 75% of the global deaths from NCDs occur. Undernutrition is a very significant problem in India, and low birthweight occurs in ~25% of the 26 million babies born each year. Further, the prevalence of stunting, wasting, underweight and anaemia is very high in children under 5. At the same time, obesity is also increasing in India, with estimates that 19% of children and adolescents and 15% of women of reproductive age are overweight or obese. An estimated 65 million people live with diabetes and a further 77 million are pre-diabetic, making India one of the diabetes capitals of the world. The rising burden of cardiometabolic disease is accompanied by a growing recognition of the burden of neurodevelopmental and mental health disorders in India, with 13% of children aged 1-16 years experiencing mental health problems. column37: The burden of non-communicable diseases in low and middle income countries (LMICs) is significant and increasing due to several risk factors including undernutrition at early age, sedentary behaviour, poor diet, and heredity. South Africa's evolving burden of diseases is particularly challenging due to persisting infant malnutrition that co-exists with high prevalence of obesity notably among women, and rising rates of diseases such as type 2 diabetes. It is recognised that prevention of obesity in women of reproductive age is critical both for their health and for that of their children but efforts to address the paradoxical challenges of stunting in early childhood and escalating obesity have been largely unsuccessful. To date, interventions in overweight pregnant women have not produced appreciable impact on pregnancy and birth outcomes. column36: Investigating the role of microRNA-7 in the hypothalamic control of energy homeostasis
column37: The hypothalamus is a region of the brain that controls food intake, energy expenditure, and utilization of glucose and fats in the body. When the brain senses changes in energy status (e.g. after overeating, fasting, or exercising), the hypothalamus responds by switching specific genes on or off and coordinating brain circuits to tightly manage fuel storage in the body. In obesity and diabetes, the pattern of gene expression becomes disturbed and leads to metabolic dysfunctions. MicroRNAs (miRs) are RNA molecules that control biological processes by shutting off specific genes. MicroRNAs are essential to maintain energy balance, as mice lacking microRNAs in the hypothalamus become severely obese. One microRNA in particular, called miR-7, is one of the most highly and specifically expressed miRNAs in the hypothalamus. It plays a crucial role in brain development, but it remains unknown if miR-7 is also needed for the brain to control metabolism. We are studying gene-edited mice with either a lack of, or excessive expression of, miR-7 in specific hypothalamic cells. We will measure their body weight, lean and fat mass, food intake, and energy expenditure. We will also monitor their blood glucose levels, glucose tolerance and insulin tolerance. If we detect metabolic abnormalities, we will study the cells which lack or overexpress miR-7 to identify the genes being targeted and shut off by miR-7 and causing the dysfunctions. We will also collect hypothalamus samples into a culture dish and manipulate the target genes to study their specific functions. To understand how miR-7 responds to energy status changes, we will measure miR-7 levels in mice after high-fat feeding, prolonged fasting, and exercising, as well as in obese and diabetic mice. This study aims to define a new mechanism involving miR-7 in the brain that may be manipulated as a therapeutic strategy to combat metabolic diseases.

column36: Evaluation of novel cancer immunotherapies that combine the potency of chimeric antigen receptors and the intracellular targeting of T-cell receptors
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada and in many developed countries around the world. Recently, progress in the field of immunology has allowed for the development of "immunotherapies" against cancer. These allow doctors to use a patient's own immune system against their cancer. This can be done in three different approaches. One approach involves 'checkpoint' blockade drugs that decrease immune inhibition, leading to better-activated immune cells throughout the body and allowing immune cell-driven cancer cell killing. This strategy is most effective in tumours with a high number of mutations, such as melanoma, but due to the blanket nature of activation of the immune system this approach often leads to side effects. Another approach involves collecting tumour-associated immune cells surgically, treating them in the lab to strengthen them, and re-injecting them back into the patient. Finally, a third approach involves collecting a patient's immune cells and modifying them with an alternative targeting system, re-targeting them to the cancer. This re-targeting can be done with optimized natural receptors or with synthetic proteins - chimeric antigen receptors (CARs). In addition to re-targeting the cells, CARs also include co-stimulatory components, strengthening their anti-tumour response. This latter approach has so far been very successful in the clinic, and in a relapsed B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia trial at MSKCC, it induced an 88% "overall complete response" rate. A limitation with CARs compared to naturally-occurring receptors is that they must target cell-surface targets and cannot, currently, target intracellular proteins. This makes designing tumour-specific therapies difficult. My project aims to evaluate three different ways of resolving this limitation by combining the intra-cellular scanning ability of naturally-occurring receptors with the higher efficacy of CARs, expanding the number of CAR-treatable cancers.

column36: Defining Synthetic Lethal Genes in YAP/TAZ-Dependent Breast Cancers
column37: Breast cancer, the most common cancer in women worldwide, is the second leading cause of female cancer death in North America. Despite advances in therapy, breast cancer remains a significant cause of mortality, and improved treatments utilizing novel approaches are needed. One characteristic of breast cancer cells that distinguishes them from normal cells is that they are often tetraploid, a condition where cells harbor twice the normal number of chromosomes. Normally, tetraploid cells fail to proliferate. However, our lab recently demonstrated that inactivation of a cellular pathway termed the Hippo pathway restores proliferative ability to tetraploid cells. The Hippo pathway controls cell proliferation by regulating two proteins, YAP and TAZ, which can enter the nucleus of a cell and activate growth-promoting genes. When the Hippo pathway is active, it prevents these proteins from entering the nucleus and thus restrains cell division. Conversely, when the Hippo pathway is inactivated, YAP/TAZ accumulate in the nucleus to turn on pro-growth genes. Breast cancer cells frequently show abnormally high levels of YAP/TAZ in their nucleus. This suggests that a common, and perhaps requisite, feature of breast cancers is that they inactivate the Hippo pathway to drive growth. However, whether these cells are dependent on YAP/TAZ for their survival is unknown. In addition, the genes turned on by YAP/TAZ that are critical for tumour growth are poorly resolved. Our proposal aims to find new drug targets in YAP/TAZ-driven breast cancers. To this end, we will characterize YAP/TAZ dependency across a cohort of breast cancer cell lines and identify key genes that differentially drive the growth and survival of YAP/TAZ-dependent cell lines. These genes represent novel drug targets whose identification holds the potential to enable the selective killing of tetraploid breast cancer cells dependent on YAP/TAZ, while sparing the non-cancerous diploid cells around them.

column36: Targeting microglial Panx1 to treat the adverse effects of repeated opioid use
column37: Chronic pain is pervasive, insidious, and afflicts 1 in 5 Canadians. Treating chronic pain is notoriously difficult and often requires opioids, one of the most powerful and effective classes of drugs used for managing pain. While opioids are potent analgesics for relieving moderate to severe pain, their prolonged use can lead to severe side effects, such as physical dependence (characterized by a withdrawal syndrome upon cessation of opioid use), tolerance (the drug no longer produces the same level of pain relief), and opioid-induced hyperalgesia (a paradoxical increase in pain that develops with repeated opioid use). The risk of these adverse effects has led to concerns by physicians and patients to use opioids for pain management, triggering an emerging issue of under-treatment in chronic pain patients. The goal of my research is to understand how the side effects of opioid use occur, and to find new ways to interfere with these processes. Microglia are key immune cells in the central nervous system that are increasingly linked to the adverse effects of repeated opioid use. As key targets of opioid action, microglia are 'activated' in the spinal cord in response to opioid treatment, yet the underlying mechanisms of how microglia contribute to the negative effects of opioid use remain elusive. This study examines the role of microglial pannexin-1 (Panx1) in opioid withdrawal, tolerance and hyperalgesia. Panx1 channels expressed on the surface of microglia are known to release molecules that modulate neuronal activity. By studying the inner workings of microglia, this research will identify key molecules and processes involved in regulating the negative effects of repeated opioid use, and will improve our current understanding and therapeutic strategies for treating pain. Opioids are the pharmacological cornerstone of pain therapy, and the goal of the proposed research is to decrease the risk of severe side effects that are associated with long-term opioid use.

Within the healthcare system, accurate diagnoses bypass the waste of health care resources on unnecessary treatments and continued diagnostic testing. These experiments will be the first to explore how these molecules can potentially prevent defective communication between brain cells. Resolving the reasons for inappropriate cellular communication within the brain will provide a solid foundation to develop new and effective drug treatment strategies for ASDs.

column36: When rare meets common: burden and impact of rare genetic variants in primary psychiatric populations

Discovery of rare genetic diseases in psychiatric patients would reveal specific treatment options, and give information about the chances of other family members being affected. As well, recent findings show that in one of ten people over the age of 70, at least one of these rare cells will have acquired a mutation that causes it to display some features of leukemic cells (such as increased proliferation). Although these mutant cells can still produce normal mature blood cells, the individuals in which they are found are at a much greater risk of eventually developing a full-blown leukemia. The objective of my project is to determine whether the number of times a normal adult blood stem cell divides predisposes it to developing changes associated with cellular aging and a tendency to become leukemic. I will explore this idea by transplanting normal human adult blood stem cells into a type of immunodeficient mouse strain that can support the growth of human blood stem cells better than any previously available mice. I will then chemically treat these mice to stimulate the transplanted human blood stem cells to divide much more frequently than they normally do in a person. I will also use an approach that marks the DNA of each blood stem cell to be transplanted with a unique DNA barcode. I will then be able to track the number and type of blood cells produced by each transplanted blood stem cell and determine whether forcing them to divide frequently causes one to become dominant and possibly mutated. I will also determine whether increased blood stem cell proliferation accelerates the appearance of other signs of cellular aging and whether the cells are more likely to become leukemic. These studies will provide insights into how leukemias arise, and serve as a foundation for future treatment strategies for these currently incurable diseases which affect thousands of Canadians.

column36: The roles of brain reserve, cognitive reserve, and psychological resilience in the outcomes of paediatric mild traumatic brain injury
column37: Child and youth concussion is a major health concern contributing to rising health care costs in Canada. A variety of post-concussive symptoms (PCS), such as fatigue, headaches, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating, can occur following a concussion and strongly impact a child's ability to return to normal living. These symptoms can persist far beyond expected recovery periods (i.e., 1-3 months) in approximately 10-30% of cases. Prolonged recovery periods place a significant burden on children, families, and the health care system when children seek treatment for their unresolved symptoms. Persistent PCS are best understood from a biopsychosocial perspective, though previous research has failed to incorporate neurobiological and psychosocial factors into one single model to help understand how these differential factors interact to predict PCS over the time course of recovery. Specifically, brain reserve (i.e., brain size), cognitive reserve (i.e., intelligence), and psychological resilience (i.e., personal characteristics that enable positive adaptation following injury) share conceptual similarities (e.g., protective "reserve" factors), and have all been found to be individually associated with PCS in concussion, though how these factors interact together and with PCS over the time course of recovery is not well understood. Thus, the objective of the proposed study is to examine the role of these factors in predicting acute and persistent PCS. This study, the first of its kind, will increase our understanding of the neurobiological and psychosocial complexities surrounding poor outcomes of concussion, with the ultimate goal of guiding interventions towards improved outcomes, which can serve to help alleviate child, family, and health care burden.

column36: Investigating the interaction between nicotine self-administration in adolescence and responding for ethanol-paired cues in adulthood.
column37: Alcohol and tobacco are often taken together and have adverse effects on health and society. Epidemiological studies have shown that tobacco use initiates during adolescence and results in greater alcohol consumption in adulthood, relative to tobacco use initiated during adulthood. Individuals may come to associate environmental cues, such as the sight of a glass of wine, with alcohol consumption. Exposure to alcohol-related cues can increase craving, promote alcohol consumption, and induce relapse in abstinent alcoholics. Consequently, these cues are believed to have acquired motivational properties. Studies to date have yet to investigate whether individuals who initiate smoking during adolescence are more vulnerable to the effects of alcohol-related cues. Using animal models, the proposed study will investigate the interaction between exposure during adolescence to nicotine, the main addictive component in tobacco products, and the motivational properties of ethanol-related cues. Importantly, this study will examine sex differences, as women may be more vulnerable to alcohol-related cues than men. Adolescent and adult, male and female rats will self-administer nicotine and saline (in separate experiments) during adolescence. Once all rats have reached adulthood, they will learn to associate a sensory cue, such as a light, with ethanol delivery. Next, they will respond on a lever that will result in presentations of the cue but no ethanol will be delivered. The pattern of lever-responding will provide an indication of the motivational properties of the ethanol-paired cue. The effects of varenicline and lorcaserin, two drugs that reduce ethanol consumption in animal models, on the motivational properties of the ethanol-paired cue will be examined. Results from this study will contribute to a better understanding of how personal history (i.e. tobacco smoking during adolescence) can influence treatment outcomes for alcohol dependence.

column37: Hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation is used to treat a broad range of cancer and blood disorders, mainly leukemia and lymphomas. This therapeutic approach is effective because HSCs are able to produce all the cell types circulating in the blood, which allows the immune system to recover after chemotherapy. There are many challenges associated with HSC transplantation, in particular, their source. HSCs are a rare occurrence and are mainly found in adult bone marrow or umbilical cord blood; this means a limited supply for medical treatment. The need for compatible donor can also delay transplantation procedures. Several groups have tried to make HSC, but these attempts have failed because our current knowledge is insufficient. The goal of this project is to broaden our understanding of the genes involved in hematopoietic stem cell formation and assist with the production of stem cells for curative strategies. Our preliminary findings reveal that Meis1 gene is highly expressed in cells having the potential to become HSC during development. My data suggests that the absence of Meis1 interferes with the ability to produce stem cells. Therefore I hypothesize that Meis1 plays a key role in promoting hematopoietic stem cell formation. My objectives are to 1) understand the requirement for Meis1 in HSC development and 2) determine which genes are controlled by Meis1 during this process. I will trace and knock-down Meis1 expression with the use mouse models to look at cell fate and gene expression during the normal development of HSC. Ultimately, this study will build knowledge for molecular programming needed to make hematopoietic stem cells for medical treatment, disease modeling, and testing therapies without risking the lives of patients.

column36: Consequences, healthcare utilization and cost of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
column37: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetic disorder with no cure. Patient with ADPKD suffer from a poor quality of life and may require dialysis and/or transplantation. Recently, Tolvaptan has been approved by Health Canada as the first drug to slow disease progression. Tolvaptan and other drugs currently in clinical trials are expensive. We need evidence to guide future healthcare policies on the coverage and reimbursement of these drugs. I aim to: 1) determine the risk of disease-related consequences, healthcare utilization, and cost of patients with ADPKD compared to the general population without ADPKD, and patients with other chronic kidney disease; and 2) determine whether the risk of ADPKD complications, healthcare utilization and costs differ between two mutation-based prognostic classes of ADPKD. I hypothesize that the risk of disease-related consequences, healthcare utilization, and cost of patients with ADPKD will be higher compared to the general population, and lower compared to patients with other chronic kidney disease; additionally, it will be higher for mutation-based classes of ADPKD with an expected poor prognosis. I will conduct several population-based cohort studies using the Ontario's healthcare administrative database held at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) Western and the ADPKD registry, which contains clinical, laboratory, and genetic data on patients seen at the ADPKD clinic in Toronto. Statistical and health economical analyses will be conducted to address my objectives. Key findings from these studies will help to: 1) provide evidence to strengthen policy-makers' decisions of drug reimbursement and coverage; 2) inform screening recommendations for extra-renal manifestation of ADPKD; and 3) assist with healthcare resource allocation.

column36: Phenomic approaches for the functional characterization of drug targets
column37: Drug development is time-consuming and very expensive. One of the solutions to alleviate the problem is the repurposing of approved drugs for new disease indications. Successful examples of such drug repurposing, however, often emerge from coincidental discoveries and there is room for improvement. In this project, we propose to use a novel approach that uses large genetic datasets for the repurposing of drugs. More specifically, we will do this by studying the genes that encode the proteins that are targeted by cardiovascular drugs. Recent studies have shown that individuals with mutations in drug targets can have clinical manifestations that mimic the action of the medication. For example, statins are one of the most prescribed drug classes in Canada for the reduction of cholesterol. Individuals with mutations in the gene encoding the drug target of statins were shown to have lower blood cholesterol levels and lower coronary artery diseases, similar to statin users. Following on this concept, in our study we propose to search for clinical presentations in individuals that have mutations in drug targets of cardiovascular drugs. We will use data from 150,000 individuals to the UK Biobank and over 10,600 participants to the Montreal Heart Institute Biobank, which are observational cohorts that include detailed medical information along with large genomic datasets. We will also develop the informatics tools necessary for such studies and we will make them available to the research community. Replication and validation of our findings will be possible by using data from over 27,000 participants to clinical drug trials that include patients using the tested cardiovascular drugs. This approach leverages a large collection of clinical and genomic datasets to discover new clinical uses for existing cardiovascular drugs.

column37: Deaths due to prescription opioids (PO) are rising dramatically in North America. column36: Defining the biology and therapeutic potential of human T regulatory cells with tissue repair function
column37: Transplantation can be a life-saving treatment for patients in organ failure. Unfortunately, transplant rejection, when the patient's immune system destroys the new organ, is a major cause of illness and death. Patients must take anti-rejection drugs for the rest of their life, which do not always work and have many side effects. Our goal is to replace these drugs with a safer and more effective therapy that will protect the transplanted organs over the long term. One promising strategy is to infuse patients with a dose of a special type of white blood cell, called T regulatory cells (Tregs). Tregs normally balance (regulate) the immune system by stopping unwanted immune responses. Recently, Tregs in mice were found to have a key role in tissue repair, which was needed to recover from infections and injuries. Tissue-reparative Tregs may exist in humans as well, but little is known about how to promote this function in patients. In this project, we will see whether human Tregs in the blood, skin, fat, and lung fluid can also mediate tissue repair, and what external signals are needed for these cells to work. We will also modify Tregs to boost their tissue repair potential, and test whether they can better protect against organ rejection and damage in mouse models. Ultimately, this work will contribute to the application of tissue-reparative Tregs as cell therapy both for transplant patients and others at risk of immune-mediated tissue damage.

column36: Immunotherapy against neuroserpin to correct Nerve Growth Factor metabolic dysfunction and consequent cholinergic and cognitive deficits in a transgenic rat model of Alzheimer's disease.
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an increasing problem in our aging population. Unless new disease-modifying treatments are discovered, the problem may become unmanageable. In AD, cholinergic neurons of the basal forebrain become atrophic or die, and most brain cholinergic synapses are lost. Since cholinergic input from these neurons is critical for cognition, these changes are believed to contribute to cognitive decline in AD. Cholinergic neurons depend on a supply of NGF for their survival. We discovered a metabolic pathway that controls the maturation and degradation of NGF in the brain and we documented its deregulation in AD and Mild Cognitive Impairment (a precursor state to AD). Since these disruptions lead to less support of cholinergic neurons by NGF, they could explain cognitive and cholinergic deficits in AD. The McGill-R-Thy1-APP rat model of Alzheimer's disease closely mimics the early human disease condition and provides a good platform for testing therapeutics for Alzheimer's disease. We have identified a key molecule contributing to the disruption of the NGF metabolic pathway: neuroserpin. We propose to infuse an antibody against neuroserpin into the brains of McGill rats; this will lead to more NGF, more support of cholinergic neurons, and may therefore prevent the cognitive problems associated with cholinergic disruption. We will test the animals' cognitive abilities using behavioural tasks, their cholinergic neurons using microscopy, and their NGF processing by measuring protein and mRNA levels. We hypothesize that our antibody will correct deficits in these domains. This approach may provide a better way to save cognitive function in AD than currently exists; current drugs potentiate remaining cholinergic input but do not prevent the atrophy of cholinergic cells. Ideally, this treatment could offer a five-year reprieve from cognitive decline which would have huge benefit for the Canadian economy and healthcare system, as well as AD patients.

column37: Plusieurs etudes ont montre que l'exposition a la lumiere, particulierement a la lumiere bleue, peut augmenter la vigilance et la performance des jeunes a plusieurs types de taches cognitives. D'ailleurs, les reponses a la lumiere pourraient etre diminuees chez les personnes agees vu le jaunissement du cristallin. Lors de la chirurgie des cataractes, le cristallin affecte est remplace par une lentille intraoculaire qui est aussi claire que celle d'un jeune adulte. Ainsi, l'objectif de cette etude est d'evaluer les effets de la lumiere sur la vigilance et la cognition des personnes agees avec ou sans lentille intraoculaire de remplacement. Nous posons l'hypothese que comparativement a une condition de lumiere blanche tamisee, qui correspond a une mesure de controle, la condition de lumiere bleue ameliorera la vigilance et la performance cognitive des personnes agees principalement chez celles ayant une lentille intraoculaire de remplacement. column36: Methodological Considerations of registry-based cluster-randomized controlled trials in hemodialysis
column37: Dialysis is a life-saving treatment for the 23,000 Canadians and two million individuals worldwide whose kidneys have failed. These patients have very high death rates and are 30 times more likely to die compared to the general population at the same age. There are very few high quality studies that come from randomized controlled trials that test interventions to improve health outcomes for dialysis patients. Randomized controlled trials (RCT) randomly allocate patients to an intervention or control group and are often considered the gold standard evidence. Areas in medicine with the highest number of RCTs have experienced the most improvements in health outcomes (for example, cardiology). One of the reasons traditional RCTs are often not conducted in the dialysis population is because patients cross between the control and intervention groups, thus biasing the results of the study. For example, many patients are treated within the same dialysis centre. If nurses or the patients observe that other patients on the intervention have better outcomes, they may apply this intervention to patients in the control group. This defeats the purpose of randomization, contaminates the control group, and biases the results of the study. In contrast to traditional RCTs, cluster RCTs randomize intact groups (so the entire centre is on the same treatment). For example, for the 82 dialysis centres in Ontario, we would randomly assign 41 centres to the intervention and 41 centres to the control group. By design, cluster RCTs protect against bias from cross-group contamination. But, before we can begin conducting research using cluster RCTs, there are some practical challenges that require further study in the dialysis population. During my doctoral training, I will focus on these considerations and suggest appropriate adjustments to overcome those challenges. These findings can then be applied to future dialysis trials so we can produce high quality research that is free of bias.

column36: The pathogenesis of depression: Identifying links between familial predisposition, stress reactivity, and neural response to rewards
column37: Some four million Canadians will experience depression in their lifetimes; as such, almost every person in Canada will either experience first-hand or will witness the immense emotional, physical, and economic burden associated with the illness. Markers of risk for depression have been well-documented, but effective ways to prevent and treat the disorder remain elusive. Prevention and early intervention are particularly important since once depression takes hold, it is often chronic and recurring. Development of prevention and treatment strategies has been slow, in part, because it is unclear what moves people from being at-risk to being ill. To address this issue, my goal is to identify interactions between known risk factors, such as familial history of the disorder, life stress, and abnormal reward processing, in order to explain why some at-risk people become depressed and others do not. Using a sample of mothers with a history of depression and their never-depressed adolescent daughters, I will determine how intergenerational transfer of abnormal reward sensitivity may interact with life stress to lead to depression. This research will involve biological, behavioural, self-report, and interview measures, and will allow for the identification of factors that lead to depression. I will explore how having a mother with depression impacts neural responses to rewards in psychologically healthy adolescent girls, if experience of life stress deteriorates neural responses to rewards even further, and whether this deterioration leads to increased symptoms of depression two years later. Identifying causal pathways to depression through this research program will open up new avenues for effectively preventing and treating this costly and debilitating disorder.

column36: Linking Inactivating Mutations in Chromatin Remodeling Complex Subunits to Aggressive Dedifferentiated Endometrial Carcinoma
column37: Most recently, cancers of the ovaries, endometrium and even lungs have been hypothesized to originate from the unchecked growth of dedifferentiated cells that most closely resemble embryonic stem cells. Specialized cells constituting these organs revert back to a simpler stem cell-like state and this dedifferentiation process is triggered by the switching of various protein signaling pathways. The end result is that the cells gain oncogenic properties, acquiring the ability to adapt to a changing environment, which confers resistance to current therapies, and showing self-renewing potential, allowing them to re-establish the tumor post- treatment. Regardless of the size of the dedifferentiated portion of these ovarian and endometrial tumors, the poorer the survival of patients is compared to those suffering with high-grade carcinomas. Despite its aggressive nature and link to patient survival, the exact molecular mechanisms by which cancer cells acquire and maintain stem-cell like properties is not clear. Although some factors that participate in this cancerous cellular event are known, the role of proteins that expose genetic material by remodeling chromatin still remains to be discovered. It has been demonstrated that the mutations that inactivate proteins comprising the chromatin remodeling complex are often found in these aggressive forms of dedifferentiated cancers. column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that is characterized by multiple pathologies of abnormal aggregates of misfolded proteins: amyloid beta (Ab) and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT). Also, they did not meticulously identify where the clearance of Ab was localized in the brain. At various stages of AD, Ab abnormality spreads from local brain regions to the global level. Here, my project will examine the efficacy of a novel drug, Kal-ABP, developed by National Research Council selectively targets Ab aggregates. My project will quantify the Ab load and neuroinflammation using positron emission tomography (PET) and structural and functional changes using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) before and after the therapeutic treatment. This is a unique opportunity and first preclinical study to profile the efficacy of the drug under multi-modal translational neuroimaging platform. This will allow better understanding of the target engagement and regional association to improve cognition.
