column36: Vascular Imaging as a Barometer for Early Detection of Cardiovascular Disease (VIBE Study)
column37: Atherosclerosis, a disease characterized by fatty deposits in the blood vessel wall, is a progressive, silent, and deadly disease. It is the primary cause of heart attacks and strokes, costing Canadians $20.9 billion each year. Early detection of atherosclerosis is essential in order to relieve its enormous societal burden. Atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries, known as coronary artery disease (CAD), is the leading cause of death in North America. A procedure known as an angiogram, used to visualize these arteries, remains the clinical standard for the diagnosis of CAD. However, its invasive and costly nature prohibits its use as a routine screening tool. Ultrasound is an inexpensive, radiation and pain-free method to monitor the progression of atherosclerosis. Our lab has previously determined that using ultrasound to detect the amount of plaque in the carotid arteries (neck vessels) can predict cardiac risk factors, such as blockages, in the heart vessels. My objective is use a safe, non-radioactive contrast agent to enhance ultrasound images and determine if it can more accurately predict heart disease. I hypothesize that establishing cut-off criteria for certain plaque characteristics will serve as a low-cost screening method to identify patients at risk for cardiac events. I will address this by performing carotid ultrasounds on patients scheduled for an angiogram and determining if there is a relationship between carotid plaque characteristics and the degree of atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries. This novel approach to plaque assessment has the potential to become an important tool for the early detection of cardiovascular disease.

column36: Mesenchymal Stromal Cells to Treat Lung and Brain Injury in a Novel Triple-Hit Neonatal Mouse Model of Chronic Lung Disease
column37: An estimated 29 000 infants are born premature (<37 weeks) in Canada each year. Infants born extremely premature (<28 weeks) have lungs that are too weak to support their own breathing. The only life-saving option available is to administer oxygen and mechanically ventilate their lungs. Close to 40% of premature infants receiving this treatment develop a life-threatening disease called bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Infants with BPD have underdeveloped, weak lungs compared to healthy full-term babies. Babies with BPD are also at a high risk of brain damage, which can lead to difficulties walking, seeing, hearing, and learning. The most common brain injury occurs around the ventricles, one of the main areas where brain stem cells are found after birth. Brain stem cells are important because they can make new brain cells. It is unknown whether brain stem cells are damaged in BPD. To date, there is no treatment for BPD. Our lab has shown that stem cells from human umbilical cord can protect the lungs in a BPD rodent model. The purpose of this project is to determine whether brain stem cells are injured in a BPD mouse model and if so, to test whether human umbilical cord stem cell therapy can protect not only the lungs, but also the brain. To this end, we will compare the brain stem cells from our BPD-like mice with those from normal, healthy mice. We will also investigate whether brain stem cell injury correlates with deficits in learning and motor function by using mouse behavioural tests. In the final set of experiments, we will test whether umbilical cord stem cells prevent lung and brain injury in our BPD mouse model, so as to preserve normal behavioural function. This study will be the first to examine brain stem cells to explain the link between BPD and brain damage. Further, this work may provide a strong rationale for testing umbilical cord stem cell therapy in the clinic to reduce the life-threatening complications of extreme prematurity.

column36: Patient perceptions of the effectiveness of oral hydromorphone for long-term opioid dependence
column37: Opioid dependence (e.g., heroin) is a chronic illness that poses harms to the individual, their family and the wider community. Oral methadone is the most widely used treatment for opioid dependence. For patients continuing to inject street opioids, evidence suggests that injectable diacetylmorphine (active ingredient in heroin; [DAM]) is an effective alternative. Access to DAM poses regulatory and logistical challenges in Canada and worldwide; thus, there is a need for alternative medications that could attract and retain long-term street opioid injectors not benefitting from conventional treatments. For such contexts, SALOME (Study to Assess Long-term Opioid Medication Effectiveness) tested if hydromorphone (a licensed pain medication; [HDM]) could be an alternative to DAM in a two-stage, randomized, double-blind clinical trial. In Stage I, participants with long-term opioid dependence were randomized to either injectable HDM or DAM. In Stage II half of the participants randomly switched to the oral route of their Stage I medication to test if the oral formulation is as effective as the injectable. Stage II of SALOME was stopped prematurely because of evidence that oral was not as effective as injectable. Despite this, some participants were retained to oral medications and stopped using street opioids. Moreover, some have continued on oral medications since the end of the trial. To determine the effectiveness of these alternative oral medications, this study will analyze the relationship between participant's characteristics and oral treatment access. This study will also meet with a sub-group of participants to collect their perceptions of the effectiveness of oral treatments. This evidence is essential to understand the effectiveness of alternative oral treatments, an approach that could be beneficial for those willing to stop injecting street opioids and not reached by conventional opioid-dependence treatment.

column36: Investigating the role of amyloid beta, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction in pre-symptomatic Alzheimer's disease
column37: There are currently no cures nor preventative therapeutics for Alzheimer's disease (AD) which is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly. Clinical symptoms of AD including memory loss, appear late in the disease progression. Therefore, it is critical to study the earliest, pre-symptomatic stages of AD and enable the development of preventative therapeutics that halt AD before memory loss occurs. In humans, the earliest stages of AD are difficult to study because they occur decades before clinical symptoms appear, thus transgenic (Tg) AD animal models have been developed. During these early stages of AD there is a build-up of the protein amyloid beta (Abeta) that at late stages, causes damage to neurons by producing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and disrupting mitochondrial function. The exact location and time-frame when Abeta begins to build-up, and how it initiates damage to neurons at the earliest stages of AD is not understood. The aim of my project is to understand the earliest, pre-symptomatic stages of AD by studying the role of Abeta, ROS production, and mitochondrial dysfunction in AD progression. Based on these findings, I will assess the efficacy of therapeutics that prevent these disease aggravating processes. The project will determine when, where, and how disease aggravating processes start during the earliest stages of AD. Using novel probes available through an interdisciplinary collaboration, and innovative methods, the ROS levels and mitochondria function will be measured in the brains of both Tg (AD) and healthy rats. Areas of the brain that are the initial sites of Abeta build-up will be assessed in order to understand the earliest disease processes of AD. These results will help determine promising therapeutic interventions for AD and a time-frame for when treatments would be most effective. By interrupting the early disease progression of AD, patients can be helped before any memory loss or irreversible damage occurs.

column36: Cannabis use and opioid-related health outcomes among people who use drugs
column37: Canada is facing a growing public health crisis marked by increased opioid (i.e., prescription painkiller and heroin) dependence and opioid-related morbidity and mortality. In British Columbia, opioid overdose has been declared a public health emergency; the problem is particularly pronounced among Vancouver's Downtown Eastside (DTES) neighbourhood, home to a large population of people who use illicit drugs (PWUD). In an effort to tackle this emerging public health challenge, experts across North America have called for innovative prevention and response strategies. Meanwhile, in light of the imminent legalization of cannabis in Canada, there is a push to understand how increased cannabis access and use will influence a range of public health outcomes. Compelling evidence from research of medical cannabis legalization in the United States suggests that cannabis legalization may help reduce opioid use and related morbidity and mortality, possibly through increased use of cannabis over opioids to treat chronic non-cancer pain conditions and/or substitute higher risk drug use, including opioid use. Among illicit drug using populations, the relationship between increasing cannabis use and opioid-related health outcomes has not been fully explored. Using health data from two long-running studies of over 2000 PWUD recruited from Vancouver's DTES, this work will examine relationships between access to/use of cannabis, use of opioids (including prescription opioids), health service utilization, and drug-related morbidity (e.g., overdose and injury). It is hypothesized that increased access to and use of cannabis will be associated with subsequent reduced opioid use, and consequently reduced opioid-related overdose and drug-related injury. Findings from this work will help shape adaptations and evaluations of the framework for cannabis legalization in Canada, and inform clinical guidelines and practices related to opioid and cannabis prescribing among drug using populations.

column36: Measuring G protein-coupled receptor signaling in vivo with resonance energy-based biosensors
column37: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are proteins that modulate cellular function in response to being activated by hormones, neurotransmitters or drugs. The intracellular signal produced by a given GPCR is highly context dependent. Different physiological outputs can be produced by the same GPCR in response to different drugs or hormones, or depending on the type of cell the receptor is expressed in. Fluorescent biosensors are common research tools that can be used to detect signaling events that occur within cells. However their use has typically been limited to cells in culture due to a variety of technical limitations. While much can be learned from such in vitro studies, it is also necessary to study drug action in the complex biological conditions that affect cell signaling in a living organism. My project thus aims to extend the use of fluorescent biosensors to application in the brains of living animals. To this end we will target the expression of our biosensors to specific cell types in the brain using a viral vector, and we will then use surgically implanted fiber-optic probes to monitor signaling in real time from freely moving animals. The ability to monitor receptor signaling in real time while simultaneously measuring behavior would represent a novel way to study neuropsychiatric diseases and to evaluate potential drug treatments.

column36: Contribution of social determinants of health on infectious diseases in Latin America: the burden beyond biological facts
column37: Sometimes, identifying the cause of the disease and providing medicines is not enough. Dengue, chikungunya and zika are diseases transmitted by mosquitoes, for which the treatment is challenging and effective vaccines are not yet available. Therefore, constituting major public health problems in the Latin American region. Although it is known that the health of individuals and communities is patterned by gender, ethnicity, education, income and access to health care, among various other social determinants of health, it is still not well understood how those factors relate specifically to mosquitoes' transmitted diseases. Moreover, this lack of understanding leads to a lack of efficient disease control and therefore to a greater number of avoidable deaths. Hence, in order to contribute to a better understanding of the role of social determinants of health and social inequalities in the burden of these important infectious diseases, we will quantify their relationships estimating health outcomes, such as incidence of disease and mortality rates, by each of the social determinants in the region. We consider that besides biological factors, those social determinants are contributing to increase the burden of those infectious diseases, and therefore providing only medicines to treat the cases and send them back to the social and environmental exposure to the mosquitoes is not enough. Consequently, using national and regional databases and implementing epidemiological models we would like to estimate the differences observed (if any) and to estimate determinant-specific inequality indexes. We will also analyze the implications of these four diseases for health equity within countries across the region and evaluate what has been done to prevent and control them. Finally, we expect to provide recommendations to improve modifiable factors and decrease avoidable health outcomes (mortality and morbidity) associated to inequalities in the region.

column37: Prescription opioids (POs) misuse has become an emerging public health concern globally. Data will be collected from three ongoing CIHR- and U.S. National Institutes of Health-funded prospective cohort studies comprised of over 3200 illicit drug users in the Greater Vancouver area, Canada. The research findings will contribute to the development of more effective harm reduction interventions, health care and disease management strategies.

column36: "Breathe into Pain" - The Role of Parasympathetic Activation in the Development of Chronic Pain 3 Months After Thoracic Surgery
column37: STUDY SIGNIFICANCE Significant numbers of patients undergoing major surgeries develop chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) every year. CPSP can be so severe, stressful, and intractable that it can require extensive medical care long after the initial surgery. Since stress intensifies pain, many nonpharmacological pain interventions involve eliciting one's relaxation response to "turn down" pain signals. However, pre-existing difficulties in eliciting one's relaxation response to cope with pain-related stress may be a risk factor for developing CPSP. Previous research has shown that breath-focused mindfulness meditation is effective for reducing pain symptoms and eliciting relaxation. Using an innovative, hospital-integrated assessment protocol, my proposed dissertation research will test the relaxation response as a risk factor for developing CPSP. STUDY METHODS The relaxation response is primarily activated by the vagus nerve, a major parasympathetic nerve involved in decreasing heart rate and pain signals. Patients undergoing thoracic surgery at the Toronto General Hospital will be assessed for vagus nerve activity using non-invasive heart rate variability measures during rest, pain-induction, and mindful breathing. The assessments will take place ~1 week before and 3 months after surgery on a total of 60 patients; n = 30 with CPSP, and n = 30 without CPSP. We will test whether vagus nerve activity predicts the onset of CPSP 3 months after surgery, and also examine differences in vagus nerve activity between patients with and without CPSP. IMPACT ON PATIENTS & HEALTHCARE Thousands of Canadians undergo surgery yearly to treat major illnesses and ~10% will develop moderate-to-severe chronic postsurgical pain. Results from this study will promote future research on how relaxation response data can be used to predict CPSP, and inform preventive treatment strategies for CPSP and other pain conditions to be implemented into perioperative and outpatient care settings.

column36: Identification of bioactive molecules that target acute myeloid leukemia stem cells
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive form of blood cancer characterized by the uncontrolled expansion of the number of myeloid white blood cells. When left untreated, this can ultimately lead to death by uncontrolled bleeding or infection. The disease can be forced into remission by using very aggressive treatments such as chemotherapy or stem cell transplants. Unfortunately, many patients relapse and succumb to the disease resulting in a poor 5-year survival rate of approximately 30% in adult patients. Relapse is thought to be caused by unique cells called leukemic stem cells (LSCs). These LSCs are often resistant to the standard treatment because they do not reproduce extensively; the trait of cancer cells that chemotherapies typically target. In addition, these cells have the ability to turn into all the various cancer cells found in an AML patient and thus if left unattended can completely restore the disease. Therefore, it is clear that a successful therapy would need to target and destroy all LSCs to more effectively prevent relapse and cure a higher proportion of AML patients. We hypothesize that we will be able to identify drugs that specifically target LSCs in AML by screening molecules predicted by computational analysis to be harmful to LSCs. Through this method we have already identified 152 drugs and through further screening found 12 drugs that target the LSCs without harming the healthy blood stem cells. We hope to further characterize and understand the effects of these drugs against AML samples as well as test them in animal models of AML. The identification of drugs that can eliminate these therapy-resistant LSCs will result in the development of novel therapies that can eventually lead to improved survival in AML patients.

column36: Investigating the Lipidomics of Oligodendrocyte Differentiation in the Multiple Sclerosis Lesion
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurological disease with no known cause and limited treatment options. In this disease, the myelin sheath, which is the protective insulation surrounding the nerves, is damaged. Oligodendrocytes are cells that are responsible for the production of myelin. Identification of a therapeutic option that will promote the ability of these cells to produce myelin may be a beneficial treatment option. However, there are changes to the environment near the damage, including an abundance of molecules that inhibit oligodendrocyte growth. In order to overcome this block, and promote repair, it is crucial to understand how oligodendrocytes communicate with these inhibitors, and the mechanism driving the stalled repair. The basic building blocks of all cells are dominantly proteins and lipids (fats). To date, the effects of the inhibitory environment on oligodendrocyte proteins have been investigated, but the exploration of lipid involvement is minimal. This work aims to understand how the structures of lipids in the oligodendrocyte are altered by cues in the MS brain with the hopes of developing a method to promote repair in such an inhibitory environment. The goal is to develop a method to promote repair in progressive MS and, ultimately, discover novel therapeutic avenues.

column37: Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections that can be serious and in some cases fatal. They have saved countless lives and have extended life expectancy since their discovery in the early 20th century. Unfortunately, their widespread use also contributes to the development and spread of antibiotic resistance in illness-causing bacteria, with the result that antibiotic treatment becomes ineffective. The problem is a serious 21st century global public health crisis and steps need to be taken urgently to preserve the effectiveness of these precious medicines. Many types of antibiotics are used both in humans and animals. While it is known that antibiotic use in food animals can lead to antibiotic resistance, the extent to which this use contributes to resistant bacterial infections in humans is unknown. This research will address this important need by determining the impact of antibiotic resistance in enteric (gut-related) bacteria on human health in Canada and the contribution from antibiotic use in animals, focusing on 3rd generation cephalosporin resistance in Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Salmonella. There are three components to the research: 1) determination of the human health impact of antibiotic resistance in selected E. coli and Salmonella human infections; 2) identification of the proportion of these antibiotic resistant infections involving animal sources; and 3) mathematical modelling of antibiotic resistance selection by antibiotic use in animals, spread of resistant E. coli and Salmonella through contaminated food and environment to humans, and resultant risk of human illness from antibiotic resistant infection with these bacteria. The results from this research are essential for improvement of veterinary antibiotic use policy in Canada and around the globe. All Canadians will benefit from improved and appropriate antibiotic use that will preserve current antibiotic effectiveness and reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistance.

column36: The efficacy of the external artificial pancreas in regulating blood glucose levels in patients with type 2 diabetes who require insulin therapy to manage their disease.
column37: Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) is a lifelong disease with epidemic levels. Glucose control (normal sugar in the blood) is essential to prevent and slow the progression of complications such as blindness, kidney failure and heart disease. At the early stages, most patients are treated with oral medications. However, T2D progresses with time to a state of decreased insulin secretion. It is estimated that up to 50% of patients will need the addition of insulin at some point over the course of their disease. Despite the addition of insulin injections, the majority of patients do not reach the recommended glucose levels, at least partly due to the fear of hypoglycemia (low sugar levels). New advances in technology led to the development of the external artificial pancreas (AP). The AP components are: a continuous glucose sensor (to read blood glucose), a pump to infuse insulin and an intelligent software that commands changes in insulin infusion doses based on the sensor readings. Our team has developed an expertise in and has already tested successfully our AP in patients with type 1 diabetes (insulin deficiency at the onset of diabetes); AP resulted in a better glucose control while minimizing the risk of hypoglycemia from intensified insulin treatment. Only one study has so far been published about the use of AP in patients with T2D who are on oral agents showing 20% improvement in glucose control. We propose to study AP efficacy in regulating glucose in patients with T2D who require insulin in their treatment (at least 3 injections/day). We will start with a pilot project to test AP over 24 hours that the participants spend at the research center. The next step will be to test the AP in free-living conditions home over several days. AP performance will be compared with the regular treatment (insulin injections). The eventual aim is to provide a safer (less hypoglycemia), better (less hyperglycemia) and easier (automated glucose control) treatment option for patients with T2D.

column36: Improving the detection and understanding of metastasis-promoting transient tumour hypoxia.
column37: The treatment of cancer over the past century has been challenged by tumours that grow so fast that they run out of oxygen, and this project will be focusing on a solution - a breath of fresh air for cancer cells. Low oxygen (or 'hypoxia') develops in many tumour types, makes them resistant to radiation therapy and most chemotherapy, and increases the risk for cancer progression. It is possible to detect hypoxia in tumours to some extent, but a major challenge for this field is reliable detection of 'unstable hypoxia' - when oxygen levels in a tumour are constantly changing. Importantly, much laboratory data suggests that unstable hypoxia is more impactful for driving cancer aggression than general hypoxia. This research project intends to improve upon past methods and develop innovative new strategies for detecting unstable hypoxia that will be applicable to further basic science as well as clinical practice, including biopsy analysis and non-invasive imaging. On top of improving detection strategies, we plan to test therapies for the ability to directly address unstable hypoxia. We believe a rational avenue for this application is a group of drugs termed 'anti-angiogenics'. These drugs act to modify the blood vessels in tumours and data from human patients suggest that anti-angiogenic therapies could stabilize tumour blood flow and halt unstable hypoxia. Using the detection techniques developed from the early aspects of this project, we will test if anti-angiogenic drugs do indeed solve unstable tumour hypoxia. The inability to detect unstable hypoxia is a significant limitation to current cancer therapy. This project will improve our understanding of this phenomenon, improve detection methods for basic science and clinical practice, and test strategies to address unstable hypoxia with already approved and in-use therapeutics.

column36: Trajectories of executive dysfunction in youth with pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis: A mixed methods approach to assessing cognitive outcomes
column37: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic disease of the central nervous system that has a prevalence rate in Canada that is among the highest worldwide. MS can also occur in children and adolescents, with up to 10% of patients diagnosed prior to age 18. Cognitive impairment is common for these youth, with particular impact on executive functions. These are a range of skills which play a role in mental control and self-regulation, and allow for engagement in goal-directed behaviours. Deficits in executive function may result in poorer academic function, difficulties in social relationships, reduction in autonomy, greater risk-taking, and challenges in planning to achieve goals. Although these youth fare worse than their peers on executive function tasks, it is not known whether MS leads to slower development, a lack of development, or an actual loss of these functions over time. We also don't know whether children who are younger at their first MS attack are at greater risk of having these cognitive difficulties as the disease progresses. We aim to investigate how executive functions develop differently in youth with MS, and whether one's age at disease onset influences how these functions mature. As performance on typical paper-and-pencil tasks of executive function have not fully mapped on to skills in daily life, we will also explore the experiences of these youth as they encounter real-life challenges that require executive function. This will be done through questionnaires and interviews with the patient and their family. This research will help us to understand cognitive outcomes for patients with pediatric-onset MS. We also hope to gain insight into the real-life consequences of executive dysfunction, to help health care practitioners and families develop strategies for accommodation and rehabilitation around these deficits.

column36: On the Relationship between Neurocognition, Cognitive Biases, and Automatic Thoughts: The Development of Positive Symptoms in Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a severe disorder characterized by hallucinations (e.g. hearing voices) and delusions (e.g. believing others are plotting to harm them), known as "positive" symptoms. Approximately 7 or 8 individuals out of 1,000 will have schizophrenia in their lifetime. The Canadian healthcare system spent $150 million dollars in 2004 on medication for patients with schizophrenia, but only a quarter of patients experienced a complete recovery. Psychological treatments are only moderately effective because what causes the development of positive symptoms is still unknown. This research will test a novel theory that explains the development of positive symptoms. My previous work demonstrated that the theory is well founded. Here, it will be tested for the first time in a patient sample with schizophrenia. Neurocognition refers to skills involved in processing one's surroundings (e.g. attention, memory). Patients with schizophrenia have problems with neurocognition prior to the onset of the disorder, which tend to worsen after its onset. Problems with neurocognition appear to be related to the increased use of cognitive biases (i.e. distorted ways of interpreting things in the environment), but few studies have examined this relationship. Cognitive biases are associated with negative automatic thoughts (i.e. distorted thoughts about the self) and positive symptoms. The relationship between negative automatic thoughts and positive symptoms has not been tested. Thus, this project will test for the first time the relationship between neurocognition, cognitive biases, automatic thoughts, and positive symptoms in patients with schizophrenia. My research brings together a multidisciplinary team of research experts in the field of schizophrenia from the University of Toronto and the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health. It has potential to open new, promising directions for research on early interventions for schizophrenia by allowing us to identify relevant risk factors.

column37: Three similar neurological disorders will be studied: multiple system atrophy (MSA), Parkinson's disease (PD), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). These three disorders are all characterized by aggregates of a protein called alpha-synuclein; however, these aggregates are found in different regions of the brain in each of the disorders. This is thought to contribute to the slightly different clinical symptoms observed in these neurological disorders. I hypothesize that genetic, epigenetic (changes to DNA that do not change the actual DNA sequence), and gene expression differences influence which brain region is affected and, thus, which disorder is presented. Therefore, I aim to compare these genetic, epigenetic, and expression changes across each affected brain region in patients with MSA, PD, and DLB. If there are differences among the three neurological disorders, these results could have a significant impact on the diagnosis and treatment of these disorders. There is currently no biological test to diagnose MSA, PD, or DLB; thus, diagnosis is based solely on clinical features and misdiagnosis is common. Consequently, neurologists cannot easily prescribe medications that target the specific disorder correctly, so prescribed medications may have no benefit and may even be detrimental if they are meant to treat a different disorder. If there are distinct genetic, epigenetic, and expression differences among these three disorders that can be easily measured in a laboratory test, this would provide a more accurate diagnosis and allow for more effective treatment that targets the specific neurological disorder.

column37: Adjuvant endocrine therapy (AET) is prescribed to women with hormone sensitive breast tumours, representing 75% of breast cancer cases. Quantitative and qualitative data will be collected among participating women and health professionals delivering the program. Results from this pilot study will be used to optimize this adherence-enhancing program and plan a multicenter RCT to evaluate cost-effectiveness. column37: Memory problems exist across many forms of mental illness. Patients with depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia all report significant day-to-day memory disturbances and perform more poorly than controls on standardized tests of memory ability. In addition, the region of the brain responsible for forming new memories, the medial temporal lobe, tends to function differently in individuals with these disorders. One way to learn more about dysfunctions in this memory system is to use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine brain activity. This will be the first study which uses fMRI to compare brain activation related to memory encoding across these three patients groups and a group of healthy controls. This study will also take a "transdiagnostic" approach by exploring how these differences may be related to the severity of specific symptoms common to all three disorders. Participants will be presented with pictures of scenes while undergoing fMRI scanning, after which they will complete a surprise memory test on the scenes that they previously viewed. By comparing the brain activity recorded during the presentation of scenes that were subsequently remembered versus those that were forgotten, patterns of brain activity representative of successful memory encoding are revealed. These patterns will be compared across patients groups and controls to explore how disturbances underlying memory encoding may be similar or different across these mental disorders. Depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia are estimated to cost the Canadian economy over $10 billion each year due to losses in productivity. Understanding the origins of the cognitive disturbances related to these disorders is the first step in developing treatment to help improve the functional ability and quality of life of those affected.

column36: Early structural brain connectivity changes in stroke patients: Potential early biomarkers of language recovery and impairment
column37: Every year 62,000 Canadians have a stroke. The loss of language abilities is highly prevalent among stroke survivors and 100,000 Canadians are living with chronic language impairments. The sudden loss of the ability to communicate has a heavy impact on the life quality of patients and their families. While some stroke survivors show good recovery of their language abilities a few days after the incident, others show poorer recovery and will continue to live with language impairments months after the stroke. Previous research seems to suggest that dynamic changes take place in the brain a few days after the stroke. White matter fibers, which are connections between grey matter areas in the brain, can be damaged by the stroke. However, they sometimes spontaneously regenerate. This phenomenon could be behind good early language recovery found in some patients. Moreover, atrophy (i.e. loss of brain cells) can be found in remote regions connected via white matter to the brain area affected by the stroke. However, these early brain changes after a stroke and their contribution to language impairment and recovery are largely unknown. In this project we will examine stroke patients with language impairments within the first 2 weeks after a stroke, in order to assess the patterns of progression of their language impairments and their relation to brain changes using neuroimaging techniques. We will establish the relationship between white matter regeneration and the degree of early language recovery. Then, we will determine whether patients with poorer recovery show atrophy in brain regions connected by white matter fibers to the location of the stroke-induced brain damage. A better understanding of the changes in the brain's connections in the early phases after a stroke and their contribution to the progression and recovery of language impairments can eventually lead to improved diagnosis, prognosis, and rehabilitation of this devastating consequence of stroke.

column37: Following a heart attack, or myocardial infarction (MI), progression to heart failure occurs in 10% of patients even with current surgical and pharmaceutical interventions. Heart failure is incurable and has a 50% five-year mortality rate. Heart failure occurs due to the limited capacity of the heart to regenerate or repair itself after injury, which leads to pathological remodeling of the ventricular chambers that reduces blood pumping efficiency. A key component of this remodeling process is the degradation and modification of the cardiac extracellular matrix (ECM) post-MI. The cardiac ECM is primarily composed of type I and type III collagen protein fibers that support the cardiac tissue and also mediate tissue homeostasis and repair. Collagen-based hydrogels are biomaterials that are produced to mimic the native cardiac ECM and have shown promise to preserve heart function post-MI. However, all of the biomaterial therapies tested to date have not been of human origin, which limits their clinical translation. Our group has produced the first recombinant human collagen type I and type III hydrogels (rHCI and rHCIII). It was observed that rHCI injection post-MI improved heart function after 4 weeks compared to baseline prior to injection, while rHCIII injection maintained heart function and non-treated animals showed a reduction in heart function. My hypothesis is that the mechanical support provided by these hydrogels as well as by-products of their degradation provides both structural support and activates signaling pathways involved in increasing vascular density and improving inflammation resolution in the infarct. For my doctoral work I will focus on the optimization of rHC hydrogel treatment as well as investigating the mechanism of action of this treatment in a mouse MI model. This research is anticipated to direct the clinical translation of the first recombinant human biomaterial therapy for heart failure prevention.

column37: Brain aneurysms can occur in populations of all ages and often go unnoticed until they require medical intervention. With an occurrence of 3.2%, approximately 1.1 million Canadians live with unruptured aneurysms. Brain aneurysms found in almost 2% of all MRI scans, coupled with 22 000 patients with burst aneurysms, lead to a large population seeking medical attention. The best method for their treatment is angiography which uses catheters to access the aneurysm from inside the blood vessels and treat them. These procedures allow the patient to be treated and released the same day, but require extensive training on the clinician's side. As trainees access the blood vessels in the patient through their leg, they need to be able to navigate in 3-D space while twisting a catheter at the level of the thigh, use snapshot x-raying to update their position within the body, and be able to fill an aneurysm in the brain with electrolytic coil. This complicated array of skills is only learned through an operating room-based fellowship program which results in unnecessary patient risks, high healthcare costs and inefficient skill development opportunities for novice fellows. Furthermore, the standard of skill the learner needs to reach is not standardized at all. The goal of my research is to show that these skills can be learned outside of the operating room using modern simulation and, subsequently, be standardized for performance and patient outcome across the board. I have already been able to show that using diagnostic simulation training lowers total operating time and radiation exposure by at least factor of 4. In addition to this, these improvements are a direct result of the trainee's lower number of mistakes. Our upcoming research will provide exciting data on how to better train future interventionalists conducting these procedures and establish concrete expectations for their performance.

Research has also shown that both maladaptive perfectionism and suicide are associated with having difficulties managing emotions. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) is a treatment specifically focused on managing emotions, and it was specially designed for treatment of suicidal individuals. Adapted from DBT, DBT Skills Training (DBT-S) is a short-term and cost effective treatment that effectively treats university students. However, DBT-S has not yet been used to treat maladaptive perfectionists. This study will therefore explore the effectiveness of DBT-S for treating maladaptive perfectionism and suicide-risk amongst university students. Participants will complete measures of maladaptive perfectionism, suicide-risk and difficulties managing emotions prior to treatment, immediately after treatment and 4 weeks after treatment. Statistical tests will explore whether DBT-S results in significant reductions in maladaptive perfectionism and suicide-risk and whether these changes are due to improved ability to manage emotions. This project will be the first to examine a treatment that is easily accessible and cost-effective for this high-need population, as well as inform future research and mental health programming.

column36: Harnessing the mineral-inducing properties of the enamel protein amelotin to remineralize human teeth
column37: Amelotin (AMTN) is a protein that is produced during the late stage of tooth enamel formation. Enamel is the outermost layer of our teeth that protects them from wear and tear and from decay by bacteria and acidic food and drink. Our lab has recently shown that the role of AMTN during enamel development is to properly mineralize enamel. Underneath enamel, dentin is the mineralized tissue that constitutes the bulk of a tooth. It is different from enamel as it contains collagen, but its mineral component is very similar to that of enamel. The loss of tooth mineral, starting usually at the enamel and progressing into the dentin, is the major cause of tooth decay (dental caries) and more serious health problems. In spite of constant improvements to dental hygiene, caries remains one of the major problems in dentistry that affects a large part of the population from a young age. Treatment of dental caries is a major financial burden on the health care system. Currently, synthetic restorative materials are used as "fillers" to replace the lost tooth mineral. However, because these materials are different from the natural tooth mineral, not as hard or not as flexible, these restorations don't last very long. Bacteria can "crawl" into the contact area between resin and tooth and cause further decay. It has become obvious that an ideal approach to circumvent these issues in a minimally invasive manner is to repair or remineralize the dentin/enamel constituents. In this project, we propose using the mineral-inducing properties of amelotin to develop a method to remineralize enamel and dentin. We will do this by incorporating AMTN into a "remineralizing formulation" that we intend to apply to demineralized enamel and dentin in the lab. In the next stage will test these treatments on extracted teeth. We expect this to help us develop a product that can reduce the incidence of tooth decay and improve the longevity and success of dental restorations and root canal treatments.

column36: Laying the foundation for innovative and equitable health systems: integrating critical pedagogy in health professional education
column37: Health professional education (HPE), an upstream element of our health system, is understudied and few effective reforms have been made in recent years. While there are notable pockets of innovation the uptake of health equity perspectives in HPE has been limited. The specific aim of this research project is to address the gap in curriculum and pedagogy for medical and nursing (MedNurs) education in Canada. In the context of recent calls by international organizations for the greater incorporation of equity-oriented perspectives, this project contributes to research on a vital stage of health systems planning. To study this complex issue the project will employ a qualitative design using interview and ethnographic research methods. Interviews will be conducted with a purposive sample of 40-50 key informants and stakeholders across two Canadian universities and inquire about strategies, difficulties, and excellence in health equity, patient-oriented care, and cultural safety in MedNurs teaching and mentorship. Observations in MedNurs classrooms will provide evidence for how these concepts are taken up in practice. The aim of the project is to understand if and how curriculum designers, teachers, and administrators in HPE take up critical advancements in theories of health equity when preparing students for practice. Analysis of the data collected in this study will inform the development of a pedagogical framework, constructed with input from the MedNurs community and practice guidelines from HPE and higher education literature. The findings, framework, and subsequent knowledge translation will impact our collective goal of reducing health inequity experienced by vulnerable populations in Canada and beyond. Policy-makers and educators will use the results of this project to increase the capacity of emerging health professionals to attend to global inequities that cut across race, Indigeneity, socio-economic class, sex/gender, ability and other social relations.

column36: Validation of biomarkers associated with the risk of developing diabetes as well as accelerated weight and lung function loss in a multinational prospective cystic fibrosis cohort
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal recessive genetic disease in Canada. Increased longevity due to aggressive treatments is however associated with the emergence of new complications, including cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD), with a prevalence of above 50% in patients over 30 years. CFRD is associated with a decline in weight and in pulmonary function, increasing the risk of mortality. In order to target patients needing more intensive monitoring and interventions, it is important to establish biomarkers that could predict the risk of CFRD and also the risk of accelerated clinical deterioration. Currently, CFRD is diagnosed using the 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test. Data obtained from our CF cohort in Montreal suggest that glucose and insulin values obtained at the first hour of this test would be good biomarkers because the values (high glucose and low insulin) are associated with a reduction in lung function and weight. These 2 key clinical parameters of the treatment of cystic fibrosis tend to decrease before CFRD diagnosis. To succeed, we will pool our data with a similar ongoing cohort that was established in 2010 in Lyon (France, Rhone-Alpes cohort), which includes more than 120 patients. These two cohorts will provide the largest CF cohort to study the risk of CFRD and relations between blood glucose and insulin levels as well as between lung function and weight. Because CFRD is a major complication accentuating the mortality, targeting patients at risk and establish biomarkers of clinical deterioration are priorities. Those biomarkers will then allow to test intervention studies to reduce glucose excursions, in addition to creating an international Francophone network to improve detection and prognosis of CFRD.

column36: Understanding the Brain's Functional Connections During Lower Limb Locomotion: Towards the Design of Brain Computer Interfaces
column37: Creating a comprehensive computational model of the brain's sensory, cognitive and motor activities has been one of the greatest scientific undertakings of the 21st century. The proposed study contributes to this important field by using both function magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalogram (EEG), to capture multiple sources of temporal and spatial brain activity during the task of walking. Pairing the two technologies is an attempt to overcome the limitations of each system. Specifically, fMRI has excellent spatial resolution but poor temporal resolution, while EEG is plagued by the inverse problem. The primary objective of this study is to develop a model of normal brain activity while participants are engaged in the task of actually walking and simply imagining themselves walking. The data that forms the foundation of the model are based on both fMRI and EEG results recorded in real time. This research will to add to the extant literature in understanding psychomotor brain activity, particularly that associated with thought coordination processes involving in the task of walking in normal persons. The results will help to: 1) assess deviations from normal brain patterns, 2) develop more effective deep brain stimulators, and 3) aid in the creation of devices that will assist motor movements for those with compromised mobility. This includes those with neurological diseases, the elderly, and those who have experienced accidents or injuries.

column36: Comparing Self-reported and Rater-assessed Clinician Fidelity to Cognitive Processing Therapy for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
column37: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a chronic and disabling condition associated with severe negative effects on individuals' emotional, occupational, and social functioning. Approximately 75% of Canadians will experience a traumatic event in their lifetime, and about 9% will go on to develop PTSD. Despite the existence of several supported treatments for PTSD, research indicates that only a small minority of clinicians use these treatments in practice, leaving many patients untreated or inadequately treated. Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) is recommended as a first-line intervention for PTSD and studies indicate that a therapist's competence in delivering treatment is associated with patient outcomes. Another method suggested is to have clinicians rate their own competence, but there is little research examining if this method is reliable. This study will examine how clinicians' ability to rate their own competence compares to expert-rated competence in CPT. The results of this study will indicate if clinicians can accurately assess their own competence in delivering CPT, and determine if they can identify the need to seek additional consultation and resources to support the treatment, which ultimately leads to better care for the many Canadians suffering from PTSD.

column36: Virus-induced Tumor MHC Ligandome Discovery for Cancer Immunotherapy
column37: One of the most promising modern-age cancer treatment options is cancer immunotherapy. It uses the immune system, in particular T cells, to attack existing and reoccurring cancer cells. Many studies so far have shown that this T cell-based anti-tumor immunity increases patient survival. Thus, understanding the activation and role of these anti-tumor T cells is important in generating novel immunotherapies with enhanced capacity to fight cancer. Anti-tumor T cells identify and kill cancer cells when they recognize tumor peptide ligands bound to Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules on the cell surface. Since cancers exhibit proteins with mutations or abnormal expression, they possess a Tumor MHC Ligandome (TML) that is unique compared to "normal" tissues. These TMLs can thus be used to design immunotherapeutics (e.g., T cell vaccines) that promote anti-tumor immunity. Unfortunately, the identification of TMLs has remained challenging mainly due to two reasons. First, tumors have many mechanisms to escape detection by the immune system, such as decreased MHC expression. Second, the precise identification of MHC ligands has been difficult due to technological limitations. Here, we propose an innovative approach that addresses these challenges. We will use reovirus, known for its direct cancer-killing abilities, to overturn impaired TML presentation. Reovirus will promote the display of otherwise inaccessible tumor peptides, resulting in unique virus-driven TMLs. Next, we will use cutting-edge technological advances in mass spectrometry, combined with next generation exome sequencing, to identify TMLs. Ultimately, we aim to determine immune targets that can be used to promote anti-tumor T cell responses. We will apply this knowledge to design immunotherapies that will improve prevention, prognosis, or therapy for various cancers.

column36: Secular Trends in Child & Adolescent Mental Disorders in Ontario: A Comparison of Prevalence and Risk Factors Over the Past 3 Decades
column37: Over 1 million Canadian children (age 4-18) suffer from a mental disorder, severely impacting their quality of life. Research from the UK and US suggest that the prevalence of child mental disorders has increased over the past 30 years, but these secular trends have not been examined in Canada. Substantial economic and demographic changes have occurred in Canada over the past 30 years, including increases in income inequality, poverty, and family dissolution that may compromise children's mental health. The 1983 and 2014 OCHS contain information on 3,294 children and 7,000 children respectively, both using the same, validated measures for assessing mental disorders. The 2014 OCHS was designed to sample a range of SES families and neighbourhoods, allowing to understand the true impact of SES on child mental disorders. The NLSCY provides longitudinal mental health data for 14,000 Canadian youths aged 4-11 years between 1994-2009. The SMHS includes data from over 30,000 Ontario students and the OSDUHS is a survey that contains mental health and substance use data for Ontario students in grade 7-12, repeated every two years since 1977.

column36: Enhancing the Effects of Written Exposure for Generalized Anxiety Disorder via Imagery Training
column37: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a highly prevalent, chronic, and difficult-to-treat condition characterized by excessive worry and anxiety. Research has shown that people with GAD avoid thinking about feared situations in a clear way in an attempt to keep anxiety and other uncomfortable emotions at bay. However, this avoidance is actually counterproductive because it intensifies worry and anxiety. Past research has shown that an intervention called written exposure (WE) improves worry. In WE, people counteract their avoidance by fully imagining and processing clear, vivid thoughts of their worst fear coming true. This is accomplished by writing repeatedly and concretely about their worst fear. This study will examine a way to optimize the WE intervention; specifically, whether the addition of an imagery-training (IT) phase can further enhance WE's beneficial effects. Research in other clinical populations has shown that those who have better imagery abilities show larger symptom improvements within exposure-based treatments. For individuals with GAD, imagery ability may be even more important because these individuals report difficulties generating vivid images of their worst fears. Individuals with GAD will be assigned to one of two conditions: (1) WE with imagery training or (2) WE without imagery training. Both conditions will engage in 20-minute WE sessions on 3 consecutive days, but participants in the IT condition will also receive a 15-minute imagery training each day prior to engaging in WE. During IT, individuals will be trained to engage in imagery through different exercises. We hypothesize that the addition of imagery training to WE will lead to greater improvements in GAD symptoms, worry and worry-related difficulties than WE without imagery training. WE has considerable promise as a brief, inexpensive treatment for Canadians with GAD and the proposed experiment examines a novel enhancement of it.

column36: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Chromatin: the Circadian and Aging Connection
column37: This project is dedicated to understanding of how genes are regulated in the cell's nucleus. We will investigate not only spatial parameters of such regulation but also temporal ones: how molecules surrounding DNA change during the 24 hour period (circadian cycle) as well as over months and years in the aging cells. This interdisciplinary research project combines three loosely associated fields - chromatin architecture, circadian biology, and aging. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study exploring aging- related changes in chromatin architecture from the circadian perspective. Our intuitive and testable hypothesis may help to prove that ageing is, at least to some extent, deterministic. We will generate the first circadian map of interaction of regulatory elements, which will help understanding the 4D regulation of gene expression and other functional aspects of the nucleome. Our effort may show that spatial aspects of nuclear organization are inseparable from the temporal dimension, and that 'spacetime' is a critically important concept not only in physics but also in life sciences. This basic molecular biology study may have innovative translational implications. Establishing a relationship between aging and circadian rhythmicity may allow us to leverage circadian pathways to delay or reverse aging and aging- related diseases, such as cancer, type 2 diabetes, and Alzheimer's disease.

column36: The immune pathogenesis of neonatal infection: Relevance to digestive health
column37: The susceptibility of infants to infection, compared to adults, is a major global health burden and an immunological challenge. A second immunological challenge for the young (0 to 9 years of age) is the increase in immune disorders such as food allergies and inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs). Understanding the immune mechanisms that operate in infants is key to developing new approaches to improve their health around the globe. The challenges of infant infections and immune disorders may be two sides of the same phenomenon. Recently, we have shown that newborns are physiologically enriched with immature red blood cells. These cells are suppressing their immune system and presence of these cells is associated with poor immune response to pathogens, but they play a crucial role in early life for gut tolerance to colonization with good bacteria. My studies will give novel insight into mechanisms that govern the immunological differences seen in early life that result in extreme vulnerability to infections or autoimmune diseases.

column36: Voice Adaptive Training for older adults with Aphasia
column37: Older adults are the fastest growing segment of our society and several common chronic conditions present a risk to older adults' health and wellness. Stroke is a chronic condition, which is the leading cause of disability throughout North America and Europe. Nearly one third of individuals who have a stroke will present with aphasia, a communication impairment that affects the ability to speak, understand, read and write. These persistent language impairments can have a negative impact on all aspects of daily life, and people who live with aphasia often report that this negative impact is worse than is reported even in cancer or Alzheimer's disease. The aim of the project is to empower older people with aphasia to improve their communication abilities. We will do this by developing an app for communication and everyday life support called VoiceAdapt. We will apply innovative speech-sensitive technology to the app in order to develop a system that detects and adapts to the language difficulties of the person with aphasia. The system will have built-in features that personalize and adapt to an individual's communication difficulties in specific locations in order to provide individualized exercises to facilitate therapy and recovery. First, the input and feedback of users, including people with aphasia, speech-language therapists and others, will be incorporated into the design and development of the app. Second, the app will be tested in a trial where one group of people with aphasia will receive the VoiceAdapt app for six weeks and another won't. We expect that the group that practices the individualized exercises in VoiceAdapt will have improved language, communication and well-being compared to the other group. It is hoped that the unique features of this technology will help to improve the communication abilities of people with aphasia.

column36: Building Reconciliation Together: Transformative Intergenerational Mentorship
column37: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) Calls to Action highlight the importance of Canadian post-secondary institutions in increasing the number of Indigenous health professionals and scholars. While several calls urge our institutions to provide culturally appropriate academic mentorship, existing models have not engaged Indigenous partners to any extent. Accordingly, the purpose of the Indigenous Mentorship Network Program (IMNP) is to develop an Indigenous academic mentorship model, with substantive input from Indigenous graduate students, post-doctoral fellows, newer faculty and mid-senior career faculty in the health research domain. Our mixed methodology approach includes the development and circulation of an Indigenous Academic Mentorship Survey, and subsequent semi-structured interviews with a smaller sample of survey respondents. Results will reveal new Indigenous mentorship principles, to be integrated into existing health research mentorship programs across partner universities. Specific knowledge translation avenues will include: annual presentations at a national graduate student and new investigator gathering, development of a graduate e-module seminar series, integration into existing teaching/learning effectiveness and academic mentorship programs, development of a handbook on essentials of Indigenous academic mentorship, and various web-based mentoring activities. The end result will be an expanding cohort of Indigenous scholars with leading edge mentorship experience, appropriate work-life balance, and the capacity to lead future Indigenous health research and other professional initiatives.

column36: Alberta Indigenous Mentorship in Health Innovation Network (AIM-HI Network)
column37: The AIM-HI Network represents a commitment on the part of established Indigenous and non-Indigenous health researchers at distinct stages of their careers, and community partners, to strengthen and provide new and expanded opportunities for (FNMI) mentees to pursue and succeed in health research careers. We have developed an intergenerational, multilayered cascading mentorship program for mentees at all levels-undergraduate through to new investigator stage-and in all health-focused research disciplines, including the health, social and laboratory sciences. The program encourages networking and interdisciplinary gatherings among peers affiliated with six Alberta universities, the oldest tribal college in Canada, the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity, Alberta partner organizations, and between Indigenous Mentorship Network Program nodes. By establishing enduring infrastructure, it promotes sustainability in training by building capacity in Alberta for FNMI health research mentees, and in partnership with Indigenous communities of support, it dynamically reaches future mentees in urban and remote sectors throughout the province and in the Canadian North. We will catalyze a generation of FNMI health researchers, who through participation in the AIM-HI Network, will strengthen their personal resources and resilience to succeed academically and meaningfully apply research knowledge for the improved health of FNMI communities. Finally, we will generate evidence on best practices for Indigenous mentorship, demonstrate the impact of the network, and advocate for systemic change to enable FNMI promotion and success in academia and in health research more broadly.

Support the training and development of the next generation of Indigenous health researchers throughout their respective stages of training and early careers; 2. Leverage the mentoring capacities of our existing network of 60+ researchers and Indigenous community health partners from across the Atlantic region and beyond as well as their expertise in Indigenous health research; 3. Facilitate the implementation of Indigenous knowledge(s) and support for Indigenous health research within institutions of higher learning in Atlantic Canada, thus creating a supportive environment that welcomes, encourages and builds the capacity of Indigenous students and early career researchers. column36: Neuroprotective agents for cerebral malaria
column37: Malaria is the third leading cause of death in children globally. In Canada, we see about 400 cases per year, especially among new immigrants and travellers returning from the tropics. It mostly affects young children in sub-Saharan Africa, who are at risk of severe disease, death, and mental disability following infection. Cerebral malaria is a deadly complication which occurs when the brain is involved. Despite the world's best antimalarial drugs, the mortality rate is still about 20%, meaning that one in five children with cerebral malaria will die of their infection. Furthermore, 25% (one in four) children who survive cerebral malaria will be left with lasting brain problems. New treatment strategies are needed to reduce the number of deaths as well as the long term effects of cerebral malaria on the brain. We think that some newly licensed drugs for cancer and brain disorders can be used for an entirely different purpose: to protect the brain in cerebral malaria. This surprising re-purposing of new medications makes sense because these drugs target molecules which govern the leakiness of vessels and brain swelling. By targeting these molecules, we think that we can improve outcomes in cerebral malaria. We want to test these drugs in 2 ways: a model of the blood brain barrier using cells in a "petri dish," and an animal model of disease. We will test these drugs to see if they can protect the brain by stabilizing the "blood-brain barrier" which separates the brain cells from the bloodstream. If we find promising molecules, this will be significant because it will suggest new treatments that could be tried in clinical trials of children with cerebral malaria.

column36: Early movers: The role of physical activity and sedentary behaviour in the healthy growth and development of infants
column37: The first five years of life are a dramatic period of growth and development. These early years lay the foundation for life-long health. Regular physical activity and minimal sedentary behaviour, such as screen time, strengthens healthy growth and development. I was one of the leaders in developing new Canadian guidelines to support healthy active lifestyles during these first five years. These guidelines will be released in 2017 and include recommendations on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. In developing the guidelines, we found gaps in the information available. For example, we found few long-term studies on young children, especially infants. Few studies looked at how physical activity and sedentary behaviour affect a child's development of motor skills, thinking skills, and social skills. My research study will fill these gaps in information. I will examine the long-term associations of physical activity (tummy time) and sedentary behaviour (screen time, reading, carriers, car seats, high chairs, strollers, swings) in infants with their gross motor skills and their achievement of gross motor milestones in the first 18 months of life. In partnership with Alberta Health Services, 250 parents of infants in Edmonton, Alberta will fill out a questionnaire when their infant is 2, 4, and 6 months old. They will tell us about their infant's physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and gross motor skills. They will also record the gross motor milestones that their infant reaches over the first 18 months of life. A sub-sample of 115 parents will also complete a more detailed questionnaire at 2, 4, and 6 months and their infant's gross motor development will be directly measured at 6 months. Our findings will fill gaps in knowledge and help update Canada's guidelines with the best information. column36: Pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome: determining post-discharge outcomes, the effect of early diagnosis, and identifying inflammatory signatures to better understand disease mechanism
column37: Pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) affects children of all ages with a severe lung injury needing respiratory support in the intensive care unit (ICU). It has a mortality rate of 18-27%. Because children are still developing, long-term consequences of PARDS are highly significant. However, only a few small outdated studies have looked at the long-term outcomes of PARDS survivors. While most of these studies looked at lung function, none focused on issues that may be important to patients and their families such as breathing problems, quality of life, mental health symptoms, and health care resource use. Given that PARDS is a heterogeneous syndrome, clinical and biological data may be used to identify distinct subgroups of children within PARDS, who may have different treatment responses and outcomes. Not only this would be useful in understanding disease mechanism, but importantly, it may also identify subgroups of children with worse outcomes and ultimately allow for the design of targeted treatments. Finally, delays are common in the diagnosis of PARDS and compliance with current management guidelines is poor. Novel techniques such as decision support systems may help physicians in the management of these children. In this study, we aim to better characterize the outcomes of PARDS survivors, to examine whether subgroups of children with PARDS can be identified, and to determine whether an earlier diagnosis of PARDS using a computerized decision support system will improve the care of these children. We will also build a database containing information on children with PARDS linked to biological samples for future research. The results of this study will provide insight into the long-term outcomes of PARDS survivors and the mechanisms underlying this condition, and may change the way PARDS is currently diagnosed. Finally, the creation of a PARDS database will be a valuable tool for future interdisciplinary studies in this field.

column36: Infants born to women with disabilities: Health and health care
column37: In Canada, one in 8 women of childbearing age has a disability. Disabilities can be categorized as physical (e.g., spinal cord injuries), sensory (e.g., vision and hearing impairments), and intellectual and developmental (e.g., fetal alcohol syndrome). Until recently, childbearing rates among women with disabilities were low. With medical advances and better integration of persons with disabilities in the community, more women with disabilities are starting families. Women with disabilities experience high rates of poverty and poor health, and research is beginning to show that these factors increase their risk for poor pregnancy and later child outcomes. However, there is little research examining the health of their infants. Our aim is to compare access to health care, health, and mortality among infants born to women with and without disabilities. We will use data collected from Ontario medical records and documentation on disability support recipients to identify all infants born to women with and without disabilities in Ontario in 2009-2015. We will follow these infants to 12 months of age. In our analyses, we will determine whether infants born to women with disabilities overall and those born to women with physical, sensory, and intellectual and developmental disabilities specifically are at increased risk for missed well-baby visits, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and mortality. We will identify specific maternal social and health factors that worsen these risks, and pregnancy-related factors that explain them. Our findings will improve the health care delivery system: Evidence of increased risk for poor outcomes among infants born to women with disabilities will provide information needed to create specialized supports for women with disabilities and their infants. Because women with disabilities represent a growing maternal population, our research could have a significant impact on the health of Canadian infants.

column36: Integrated view of the preterm birth syndrome
column37: Approximately 8-10% of pregnancies end prematurely with important negative effect on the development of the newborn with increased risk of mortality and morbidities in surviving newborn. These morbidities include neurodevelopmental disorders having life long effects of affected newborns. Inflammation, both in the mother and the placenta, has been strongly associated to preterm birth (PTB). However, the cause of inflammation is still debated. Infections are a well-known cause of inflammation but detectable only in a small proportion of women with PTB. Endogenous inflammatory mediators, known as alarmins, are another important cause of inflammation and they have recently been implicated in the etiology of PTB. There are now some potential anti-inflammatory therapeutic options that were shown beneficial in preclinical studies. It is however very difficult to translate these promising results in the clinical setting without taking into consideration the maternal and placental inflammatory profile. Taking these into account would allow to target specifically women that would benefit from anti-inflammatory treatment and this way ascertain the genuine efficacy of the treatment. It is therefore of high importance to get an integrated view of the PTB syndrome, including analysis of the immune profile in both the mother and in the placenta combined with genomic analysis to get in-depth understanding of PTB and identify groups of women that would benefit from anti-inflammatory therapeutic intervention. We will gather in-depth understanding of the immune activation in the mother and in the placenta in pregnancies with PTB through immune cells population and genomic analysis in order to identify women that might benefit from anti-inflammatory therapeutic intervention. This combination of multiple approaches will fill an important knowledge gap and allow to identify women that could benefits from targeted anti-inflammatory therapeutic intervention.

column36: One year of brain maturation following a preterm birth
column37: Children born very preterm [VPT] (<32 weeks gestational age) are at a greater risk of presenting with lifelong developmental difficulties. One possible explanation for the presence of these difficulties stems from the hypothesis that brain development (i.e. maturation) of VPT infants is delayed. Nevertheless, how much the brain adapts and whether it catches up during its most active period of development that is the first few years of life remains to be determined. A greater understanding of the core brain characteristics of abnormal neurodevelopmental profiles and the identification of critical time periods of brain plasticity could provide specific targets for early intervention strategies tailored to this at-risk group. We therefore propose to characterize and compare in vivo brain maturation using quantitative magnetic resonance imaging techniques during the year that follows corrected term equivalent age between VPT and healthy term-born controls. Understanding how the brain grows and adapts during this active time of maturation will subsequently help us better plan early targeted care for VPT infants throughout this sensitive period. Our long-term goal is to optimize neurodevelopment in this highly vulnerable group.

column36: Perpetually, Potentially Pregnant: The Discursive Construction of "Women of Childbearing Age" and its Effects in Public Health and Biomedical Research
column37: The concept of "women of childbearing age" is ubiquitous in public health initiatives and biomedical research. The understanding that women's reproductive potential can and should make them a site of study is often taken for granted in the name of protecting fetal health. There are, however, many women who are not planning to reproduce, or who are not physiologically capable of conception or pregnancy and who may be of "childbearing age." Furthermore, there are important roles for men, for the state, and for the private sector in the protection of fetal health, although public health initiatives and biomedical research disproportionately focus on women. This research examines how "women of childbearing age" emerged as a category within public health policy and biomedical research. Through document-based analysis and interviews with key actors, I will investigate whether and how describing women's bodies in terms of "childbearing age" has contributed to the idea that women's health is primarily reproductive, and what effects this might have on women's health and autonomy. I will use these findings to develop other approaches to thinking about women's autonomy and fetal health beyond the language of "childbearing age" and women's reproductive capacity. Then, I will make these other approaches available to policy makers, public health agencies, clinicians, and biomedical researchers through decision-making tools (i.e. fact sheets and checklists) to help knowledge users better consider women's experiences and interest in engagements with "women of childbearing age." Overall, this research aims to reorient public health initiatives and biomedical research to understand fetal health as a collective endeavour, and to challenge uncritical use of discourses that reinforce the idea that women's health and decision-making are inherently matters of reproduction.
