column36: Prevention of postpartum hemorrhage: addressing critical knowledge gaps for the use of tranexamic acid.
column37: Canada is one of the few economically developed countries where rates of pregnant women dying during childbirth have increased over the past ten years. Many of these deaths are a result of increased blood loss or postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) at the time of childbirth, which often requires blood transfusion that has its own risks. In 2010, 6.2% of pregnant women in Canada suffered PPH and 5/1,000 pregnant women required a blood transfusion. Reducing PPH and blood transfusions in pregnant women is a major health priority both in North America and worldwide. Tranexamic acid (TxA) is an affordable, safe and widely available medication that has been shown to safely reduce blood loss in trauma patients and those undergoing major surgery. Recently, it has been shown to prevent deaths and reduce blood transfusions if given within three hours to women suffering from PPH. Instead of waiting for women to have PPH before giving TxA, the question now is whether we could reduce PPH and blood transfusions by giving TxA to women planning natural childbirth after the baby is born but before PPH occurs. We cannot however, conduct a trial to answer this question, unless we have addressed three critical knowledge gaps - (1) What dose of TxA should be given after childbirth to reduce PPH? (2) Should we administer TxA to all women or only to those at increased risk for PPH? (3) What are the barriers to conducting a large trial to definitively answer the question on the effectiveness of TxA? Our research will address these knowledge gaps by conducting (1) a TxA dose-finding study, (2) a decision-analysis study and (3) a feasibility trial, thereby making it possible to conduct a large trial that will finally answer the question on the effectiveness of TxA in women planning natural childbirth. In addition, it will directly help women worldwide, by providing information on the dose of TxA that should be given after childbirth and the group of women most likely to benefit from it.

column36: Non primary cytomegalovirus infections in pregnancy
column37: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a frequent cause of congenital infection and an important cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children worldwide. Preconceptional immunity against CMV provides only incomplete protection against intrauterine transmission. Cases of congenital infection have been described in children born to women who were seropositive prior to pregnancy, secondary to CMV non-primary infection . Among non-primary CMV infections, CMV reactivation needs to be distinguished from CMV reinfection, which is infection by a new CMV strain despite the presence of CMV-IgG antibodies. Even though studies have shown that CMV shedding is frequent among pregnant women, there is to date very limited data on the actual rate of non-primary CMV infections in pregnancy. Therefore, our objectives are (1) To evaluate the frequency of CMV reinfections and explore its risk factors, (2) To assess the frequency of CMV congenital infection following non-primary CMV infection in pregnancy and explore its risk factors, (3) To assess the impact of these findings on reassignment or withdrawal from work of pregnant daycare workers for the prevention of CMV congenital infection. We will use the data and samples collected within the existing biobank Grossesse en Sante (Quebec). Improved knowledge of non-primary CMV infection in pregnancy will help identify new targets for the prevention of CMV congenital infection. Moreover, the findings could have direct impact on the policy of preventive reassignment or withdrawal from work of pregnant workers currently in place in Quebec.

column36: Therapeutic and Enhancement Uses of Neuroscientific Knowledge: A Question of Individual Autonomy?
column37: Neuroscientific research is providing novel and promising technologies for diagnosis, treatment and prognosis in the context of neurological and psychiatric conditions. While this research has been aimed at addressing disorders or deficits, the same interventions (e.g. externally applied electrical or magnetic stimulation of the brain) can often be turned toward enhancement uses in people without disorders or deficits, as they are currently conceived. These brain-based interventions may alter our perceptions of the agency and capacity of patients, and accordingly of their responsibility. People may be reproached for untreated problematic behaviours that could be avoided through treatment, or for the unintended behavioural consequences of therapeutic or enhancement uses of brain-interventions where they are applied. At the same time, a complex web of potential responsibility draws together the individual who chooses (or refuses) to use these interventions, the maker, marketer and medical personnel who provide the interventions, third parties who may be benefited or harmed by the use or non-use of the interventions, and the broader society that stands to be affected in more diffuse ways. The Canadian part of this interdisciplinary biomedical ethics project will provide a comprehensive analysis of the complexity of ethical and legal responsibility in relation to brain-based interventions intended to modify human capacities but that may also pose some risks of harm to the individual and to others. In particular, this project will provide patients, clinicians, and health policy-makers (e.g. drug and device licensing authorities) with the careful analysis necessary to understand the potential legal ramifications of these treatment decisions. These issues will form an important part of the context within which clinicians and patients will have to navigate as they consider whether to use the fruits of this neuroscientific research.

column36: FutureBody
column37: Neurotechnologies (NT) evolve and are increasingly used not only within a medical but also consumer product context. The 'early' involvement of people impacted by NT developments in the discussions around the socio-compatible use of NTs is seen as important by many. The FUTUREBODY project aims to explore societal and cultural changes induced by NT developments focusing on three NTs: (1) cochlear implants, (2) deep brain stimulation and (3) brain-computer interface (BCI) technology. The Canadian team concentrates on the contribution of health professionals and disabled students, two under-researched groups, to NT development discussions. Nurses, social workers, occupational therapists and speech-language pathologists/audiologists are health professionals that encounter clients using NTs. As such NT development discussions impact their professional practice. Aim 1 is to better understand the usefulness of lifelong learning processes in place for the health professionals mentioned to learn about NT advancements and their impact in a timely fashion so that the health professionals can contribute in a meaningful way to discussions on the socio-compatible use of NTs. Disabled people are often early adopters of technologies and the first that have to deal with issues raised by technologies which makes disabled people important knowledge producers not only as NT users but also as researchers. Aim 2 is to gain insight from disabled students on NTs and their impact and whether they ever thought of performing research on NTs and their impact. The Canadian project will use podcasts, videocasts, online and face to face workshops, movie screenings, facebook and twitter and a blog page to make their project accessible to the public. The results are seen to be useful to strengthen the life-long learning process of health professionals and the research landscape around NTs which in turn is seen to enhance future discussions of the socio-compatible use of NTs.

column36: Canadian Frailty Network - Technology Evaluation in the Elderly Network (TVN)
column37: Canadian Frailty Network (CFN) is Canada's Networks of Centres of Excellence (NCE) focussed on frailty, a common yet under-recognized health state associated with functional decline, chronic illness, multiple health problems, cognitive impairment and poorer health outcomes in late life. Recognizing the growing prevalence of frailty and the dearth of research evidence to address the complex care needs of frail elderly Canadians, in 2012 NCE awarded CFN (Technology Evaluation in the Elderly Network) a funding mandate to improve the care of frail elderly Canadians and their families within the Canadian healthcare system through the development, rigorous evaluation and ethically-guided implementation of evidence-informed care strategies and practices. The burden of frailty in Canada is steadily growing. Today, approximately 25% of seniors over age 65 and 50% past 85 - over one million Canadians - are medically frail. These individuals are at higher risk for poor health outcomes, adverse events and mortality than would be expected based on their age alone. Frail elderly Canadians are over-represented in all sectors of the healthcare system including primary care, community and residential care, acute care and end-of-life care, and frailty is associated with increased healthcare resource consumption. In 10 years, based on population growth it is estimated that well over two million Canadians will be living with frailty and this growing population is both under-recognized and under-serviced, challenging the healthcare system to improve the quality and quantity of care delivered.

Namely, the system will provide physical activity interventions targetting urinary incontinence, by training the pelvic floor muscle in a functional standing position and achieving better bladder control. Also, specific physical activity interventions will be provided for fall prevention, by focusing on strength and balance training. Mild cognitive impairment causes cognitive changes that are serious enough to be noticed by the individuals experiencing them or to other people, but the changes are not severe enough to interfere with daily life or independent function. Those with MCI have an increased risk of developing Alzheimer's. This new system will provide interventions in the form of cognitive-motor games that will reduce the incidence of mental disorders. The final system will act as an umbrella for these major categories of impairments associated with age and should feature a "basket" of interventions that should be tailored to each users' needs. column37: In recent years, health systems in Canada and other countries have been exploring how to better assist people with complex needs, who account for a large share of system costs, but receive fragmented care. Integrating primary care providers, specialists, and community services is a key strategy for improving their experiences and outcomes. The Canadian Institute for Health Research (CIHR) Strategy for Patient Oriented Research (SPOR) has funded the Primary and Integrated Health Care Innovations Network (PIHCIN) of networks in 11 provinces and territories to address this issue, each co-led by a researcher, clinician, and policymaker. They have supported 4 rounds of funding of new approaches to primary and integrated care, as well as several cross-provincial policy comparisons. There is a Network Leadership Council (NLC) with representation from each network, but there is no structure to engage with national and international partners or coordinate pan-Canadian evaluation initiatives. This proposal describes a Coordinating Office that will act as a secretariat for the NLC, facilitate information exchange internally and externally, set and report on common performance measures, and engage with national and international groups to support transformation of health systems to improve care for people with complex needs. It will do this through information sharing across networks with a shared database of operational documents, a platform for video conferencing, and a website. It will help organize symposia to disseminate new knowledge emerging from the networks and mentor junior researchers in primary and integrated care. It will also raise funds to grow and sustain these efforts. The overall goal of the Coordinating Office is to work with provincial networks, national, and international partners to promote a learning health system to help people with complex needs, and promote the spread and scale of successful primary and integrated health care innovations across Canada.

column36: Mutation-targeted gene and pharmacological therapies for dystrophic and junctional Epidermolysis Bullosa
column37: Translating new experimental therapies for rare diseases to the clinic remains a formidable challenge. New, innovative, safe and efficacious approaches to restore expression of adhesive skin proteins in epidermolysis bullosa (EB) patients are needed. Supported by strong preliminary data, we propose in this project several potential therapies to correct recurrent mutations causing recessive dystrophic EB and junctional EB that will be advanced through in vitro testing and assessed in vivo using skin-humanized mouse models that faithfully recapitulate the human EB skin conditions. The therapies are gene edition to remove and replace mutations; skipping of mutant exons; and new drugs promoting the readthrough of nonsense mutations. The consortium gathers together outstanding research and clinical groups with complementary expertise to jointly attack the disease from several fronts. Together we hope to bring new therapies to the clinic.

column36: IL-18 and MRP neutralization for the treatment of anti-IL-1-refractory autoinflammatory diseases
column37: Autoinflammatory diseases (AID) are a group of devastating systemic inflammatory syndromes characterized by seemingly unprovoked episodes of severe inflammation without signs of classical autoimmunity. The general prevalence of AID is below 1:1,000,000 individuals. As the genes mutated in AID are increasingly being mapped, inflammasome signaling and the cytoskeletal network are emerging as key mechanisms responsible for AID. Excess interleukin (IL)-1beta production has a primary pathogenic role in select AID (exemplified by CAPS), but IL-1 neutralization therapies are ineffective or only partially effective in the majority of AID patients. Thus, there is a high unmet need for development of novel therapies to treat IL-1-refractory AID and devastating AID-associated complications such as macrophage activation syndrome (MAS). Our consortium has classified a subset of AID patients with selective and highly elevated IL-18 and MRP8/14 in circulation. These inflammatory mediators are hypothesized to support a vicious inflammatory cycle in anti-IL-1-refractory AID. The consortium has at its disposal a unique set of preclinical therapeutic agents, as well as cellular and in vivo models of non-classical AID that will be exploited to address the therapeutic potential of IL-18 and MRP neutralization strategies in single and combination regimens. Finally, we will address how cytoskeleton dynamics and immune cell activation contribute to IL-18 and MRP8/14 secretion in AID mouse models using cutting-edge in vivo imaging.

column36: Novel therapies for neuromuscular diseases with altered phosphoinositide metabolism
column37: MTMopathies are a group of childhood rare diseases encompassing severe forms of congenital myopathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and due to mutations in myotubularins (or MTMRs). MTMRs are proteins responsible for dephosphorylating 3-position phosphoinositides (PIs), low abundance lipids found in specific locations inside the cell that have a range of important functions. MTMopathies are perhaps the best understood diseases of PIs metabolism, an emerging group of neurogenetic conditions that include forms of epilepsy, neurodevelopmental disease, peripheral neuropathy, and congenital myopathy. These disorders are caused by mutations in enzymes and regulators that modulate PI levels. Despite their significant morbidities (including wheelchair and ventilator dependence) and potential for early mortality, PI metabolic diseases are uniformly without treatment. The long-term goal of our team is to develop and translate therapies for these devastating disorders. Based on our previous data and preliminary results, we hypothesize that drug based inhibition of proteins that make 3-position PIs will be an effective strategy for treating MTMopathies. In this proposal, we will test this hypothesis using a pipeline that combines drug identification and validation studies in patient cell and zebrafish models with interventional pre-clinical trials in established mouse models. The proposed research is formulated from and fully integrates the synergistic expertise of our collaborative team. If successful, this work will identify novel therapies for MTMopathies suitable for rapid clinical translation and will lay the ground work for treatment development for the broader group of PI metabolism disorders.

column36: Mother Provided Essential Care: The Power of Mothers in Infant Care in Low Resources Countries
column37: The period from birth to one year is highly vulnerable. Nearly three million babies die worldwide within the first month with prematurity, pneumonia, and birth asphyxia as the leading causes. To address this, a newborn care training program targeting health care providers (HCP) called Helping Babies Survive (HBS) was developed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. HBS addresses essential HCP interventions that support the needs of at-risk full term, preterm, and low-birth weight babies. Despite the success of HBS, there remains a limited number of HCPs in many low resource countries to provide the consistent care needed by at-risk babies. Due to low HCP-to-patient ratio, the burden of ongoing assessment and intervention often falls on the mother (e.g., feeding of expressed breast milk via cup, skin-to-skin contact). However, mothers are inadequately trained compared to HCPs, creating a knowledge gap in how to improve their babies' chances of surviving and thriving. The current study will utilize a mixed method approach to explore the feasibility, acceptability, and impact of a complementary HBS module to train mothers in essential newborn care. First, a needs assessment will be conducted using focus groups of mothers and HCPs at an international HBS Center to assist in identifying educational needs and priorities of the module. Once the mothers' module has been created, we will evaluate the acceptability and impact with mothers (n=60) who have recently given birth to a preterm or at-risk newborn in a HBS Centre using a pre-post test design. Mothers and HCPs will provide feedback on the acceptability of the module as well as impact data will be collected on neonatal outcomes (e.g., mortality, temperature, growth) and maternal outcomes (e.g., confidence, knowledge on essential care) before and after receiving the training. It is anticipated that this module will reduce the burden on HCPs and optimize newborn outcomes.

column36: Childhood mental health and future employment in the welfare state: A cross-national comparison of five longitudinal cohorts
column37: Mental illness affects society as much as it does the individuals who experience it. Population health research consistently finds that people who experience symptoms of depression and anxiety in childhood are more likely to have poor academic outcomes and drop out of school, negatively impacting their chances for employment. Poor and disadvantaged children suffer disproportionately. Yet while social inequalities in mental health occurs in all high-income societies, the extent of inequality and its impact on future employment varies substantially. These cross-national differences imply that the children's mental health and their later employment outcomes are not attributable solely to health selection, but are related to the political and economic institutions that define health and labour market entry. This research uses longitudinal data from five countries in North America and Europe to examine how differences in the provision of social protections and labour institutions produce inequalities in health and employment from childhood to early adulthood. Regression methods will be used to identify youth's mental health trajectories and to examine the association with employment. Cross national differences will be examined using comparative methods. The findings will contextualize health selection and youth unemployment within social, political and economic settings, helping governments to identify systematic and context-specific barriers to youth labour market entry.

column36: Women's Reproductive Health and Colombia's Zika Epidemic: A Case Study in Public Health Ethics
column37: In 2016, the Zika virus (ZIKV) was declared a public health emergency of international concern due to the elevated risks of microcephaly in fetuses of infected pregnant women, and the fact that there are presently no cures or vaccines. ZIKV is transmitted through mosquito bites and sexually between humans, which complicates prevention measures. In Colombia, the country with the second highest rates of ZIKV infections, the government issued warnings for women to not get pregnant until further notice. The US Centers for Diseases Control also recommended that at-risk couples use condoms, and is collaborating with Colombia's National Institute of Health on public health surveillance and research initiatives. Colombian women of reproductive age are in a precarious position. They are told to avoid becoming pregnant, but in a country where contraceptives are not readily available and access to abortion is restricted, these women bear an unequal burden in measures to effectively control a major public health emergency. This situation raises challenging questions about human dignity, respect for women's autonomy, and public health ethics. This exploratory research project will examine how women's reproductive autonomy is addressed (or not) in the context of the public health interventions to respond to the Zika epidemic in Medellin, Colombia. This will be done through semi-structured interviews with Colombian women that will have been pregnant at least once before the ZIKV epidemic and once more during the ZIKV epidemic. The primary objective of this project is to examine the ethical issues raised by public health policies aimed at combatting the ZIKV epidemic in Colombia, specifically as they relate to women's autonomy and reproductive health. A secondary objective is to identify potential avenues for developing policy interventions that address these ethical challenges, and to respond to the public health emergency while respecting women's autonomy and dignity.

column36: Deliberative public engagement to inform cancer control decision-making in Canada
column37: The overarching aim of this study is to develop a framework for sustained public involvement to better support priority setting processes in the context of cancer control. column36: Decreasing Cancer Burden: Testing a Proactive Model of Care to Improve the Quality of Toxicity Management through Patient Activation for Cancer Self-Management during the Active Treatment Phase
column37: Cancer incidence in Canada is rising with 2 in every 5 Canadians expected to be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime. Cancer patients generally receive treatment as an outpatient and experience a wide range of treatment and disease-related side effects that can be disabling. While early intervention for side effects is essential, current models of care for managing these in clinical practice are reactive rather than proactive, and the burden of management largely falls on the patient and their caregivers. Poorly managed side effects leave patients at risk for poor quality of life, and result in high rates of potentially avoidable emergency room visits and hospitalizations during treatment. Models of care that include self-management support have been shown to improve patient outcomes and lower the costs of health care in other chronic conditions. However, the cancer system lags behind in providing interventions to help patients understand their role in the care process, or to support them in developing the knowledge, skills and confidence needed to become active and effective managers of their health. As such, we propose the implementation and evaluation of a proactive, personalized model of care that incorporates self-management support for patients being treated for colorectal cancer, lymphoma or lung cancer early during treatment to improve the quality of self-management of side effects and provide patients with the support and skills needed to be a partner in their own care. The model of care includes self-management training for clinicians, and for patients, online self-management education modules together with nurse-led, telephone-based self-management coaching tailored to patient self-management capabilities. Study findings will provide valuable knowledge on how proactive, personalized care can be integrated in real world cancer practices for spread to other cancer programs.

column36: Developing a Framework for the Incorporation of Real World Evidence into Cancer Drug Funding Decisions in Canada
column37: Drug costs represent a rapidly growing expense for health care systems. In cancer care, the emergence of new treatments has become a regular occurrence and easily outpaces budget growth. As a result, provincial funders must use evidence to prioritize and fund selected drugs from the pipeline of new drugs awaiting funding. Our team believes that the prioritization process should not only consider the evidence for the drugs in the pipeline when allocating resources, but also for drugs that are already being funded. Decisions to fund these drugs would have been made based on controlled clinical trials, where the population or environment may not reflect practice in the "real world". Our goal is to develop and test a framework for the generation and use of real world evidence (RWE) of cancer drugs to enable (i) reassessment of cancer drugs by recommendation-makers; and (ii) refinement of funding decisions or renegotiations/disinvestment by decision-makers/payers across Canada. Our project has 4 objectives: (1) to develop an understanding of the current state of RWE in health care; (2) to develop and refine a framework for the generation and use of RWE dedicated to (i) policy/process and (ii) methodological applications of RWE; (3) to conduct multi-province RWE evaluations using the framework developed in Objective 2; and (4) to employ knowledge translation strategies to establish and integrate a working RWE framework into sustainable practice of participating provinces and on a national level. Our team will assemble a national panel of clinical, methodological, and policy experts to create adoptable RWE frameworks for cancer drug funding decisions. The RWE framework will not only support evidence-based policy reform, price renegotiations, and reallocation of funding from low- to high-value settings, but will also drive accountability and sustainability of the cancer system in an innovative way that can be replicated by all provinces and by other areas of health care.

column36: Palliative Care, Early & Systematic (PaCES): Impact on Patient & Health System Outcomes
column37: Living with worsening cancer creates significant distress for patients and their families, especially when care transitions abruptly from a focus on the life-prolonging cancer therapies to a focus on palliative care (supportive care for enhancing quality of life). Patients and their families have told us that to improve these transitions they need: (1) a sense of continuity in their care, (2) opportunities to discuss preferences for future care, and (3) prompt access to specialized palliative care when needed. We know that patients who receive palliative care supports earlier, e.g. while also being treated with chemotherapy, tend to spend less time in hospital, with less invasive treatments when at the end of their lives. This is associated with improved quality of life, reduced family distress and decreased healthcare system costs. Currently, our cancer systems struggle to provide that "early palliative care." Our proposal aims to demonstrate the effectiveness of routinely offering early, community-based palliative care to support people with non-curable colorectal (lower gut) cancer. We will do this by closing current gaps in care by using: (1) A "Pathway" or roadmap to guide clinicians on when and how to identify and address suffering associated with colorectal cancer, developed together by patient and families, family doctor, cancer and palliative clinicians; and (2) Routinely ensuring all patients and families are supported in five key palliative needs. We will measure the impact on patients, their families and healthcare system costs. We will start in one city and compare results with another similar city. Senior health services leaders are involved with the research to ensure that this innovative pathway of care continues after the project. What we learn will be adaptable and spreadable to help people living in rural and other areas across Canada and people with other cancers.

column37: Les patients atteints de cancer ont a faire face a des situations complexes, non seulement au niveau de leurs soins mais aussi en ce qui concerne l'impact qu'a la maladie sur l'ensemble de leur vie. Une des voies pour aider emotivement les patients a mieux vivre cette periode est le soutien par les pairs. Ces personnes, qui ont eu a vivre des episodes de vie semblables, sont pretes a partager leur experience pour aider d'autres personnes a y faire face. L'originalite de ce projet de recherche est mettre en place des patients accompagnateurs comme ressource organisationnelle pour ameliorer l'experience des patients. Ils sont consideres comme des membres a part entiere de l'equipe de soins en offrant un soutien emotif qui peut aider les patients a etre de meilleurs partenaires dans leurs soins et mieux s'orienter dans le systeme de sante. column36: An evaluation of survival, patient-reported outcomes and costs for advanced gastrointestinal cancers
column37: Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers account for nearly 25% of all cancers diagnosed each year. Depending on the type of cancer, between 20-80% of cancers are incurable at the time of diagnosis. Patients with advanced GI cancer may be offered a range of cancer-directed treatments aimed at improving the quality and quantity of life but without the possibility of cure, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation-therapy, as well as supportive care measures such as pain control. While some of these treatments are beneficial for patients, some are ineffective and costly. These treatments can negatively affect the patient's experience, as well as the sustainability of the Canadian healthcare system. Our study aims to use healthcare data collected from a recent cohort of Ontario GI cancer patients, as well as speak directly with patients, physicians, and policy-makers to understand variation in clinical, patient-centered, and economic outcomes, and set priorities for improving advanced GI cancer care. We will pay careful attention to the cancer care provided to patients who may be vulnerable to experiencing worse outcomes, such as the elderly, those with a mental illness, and recent immigrants to Canada. This study will combine newly available province-wide data sources, including a patient-reported symptom screening tool and a novel Cancer Costing Algorithm. Our study will be structured into 3 phases. In phase I, we will conduct focus groups with patients, caregivers, physicians, and policy-makers to define needs and priorities advanced GI cancer care. Phase II will comprise systematic analysis of clinical, economic, and patient-reported outcomes for all advanced GI patients in Ontario from 2010-2016. In phase III we will share Phase I and II output with patients, physicians, and policy-makers in a second round of focus groups to determine how these routinely collected data may be leveraged to improve person-centered, sustainable care provided in the Canadian cancer system.

column36: Mitigating cisplatin-induced ototoxicity in childhood cancer treatment through applied pharmacogenomics
column37: Advances in the treatment of childhood cancer have successfully increased the 5-year survival rate to almost 80%. While this is a dramatic improvement over the 1960s survival rate, it comes at the cost of causing poor long-term health outcomes for the majority of children treated with chemotherapy. Studies that follow childhood cancer survivors into adulthood clearly show that children receiving chemotherapy suffer serious health complications that include major organ and sensory toxicities. These toxicities, known as adverse drug reactions (ADRs), can also occur soon after the completion of chemotherapy, or even during treatment resulting in the withdrawal of life-saving cancer drugs. For example, cisplatin is the chemotherapy of choice for treating solid tumours in children including brain, liver, bone and germ cell cancers. Unfortunately over half of treated children will permanently lose their hearing after receiving cisplatin, which severely impairs a child's ability to develop language skills, social skills and self-confidence. We now know that genetic differences between children can influence whether hearing loss, or other ADRs will develop from chemotherapy treatment. Pharmacogenomics is the study of how genetic variation influences drug response and this understanding can open the door to developing tools to predict and prevent the occurrence of ADRs. We have now completed the first stage of a comprehensive pharmacogenomic study in Canadian patients that has identified a new pathway involved in cisplatin-induced hearing loss. This project will capitalize on this discovery and explore its application towards developing predictive biomarkers and preventative treatments to reduce the occurrence of cisplatin-induced hearing loss in childhood cancer patients.

column36: Novel therapeutics to target leukemia stem cells
column37: The goal of this project is to identify drugs that can target the rare cells that cause treatment failure in leukemia - leukemic stem cells (LSCs). AML is sustained in a patient by LSCs that act somewhat like normal stem cells, although cancerous, in that they are the 'root' of the disease and need to be eliminated to achieve a cure. Therapy for childhood acute myeloid leukemia (AML) involves extremely intense toxic treatment. This can impair the development of children, cause long term cardiac dysfunction, affect fertility and cause secondary cancers later in their life. Even with this aggressive treatment, approximately 40% of these patients do not respond to therapy or the leukemia returns later. Therefore novel treatment approaches are desperately needed to improve outcome and reduce toxicity. We have taken data on the activity of genes in LSCs and regular leukemic cells and combined it with data sets on how drugs cause changes in gene activity to identify 152 compounds that we predict would specifically eliminate LSCs. We have directly tested 83 of these compounds and found that 12 of them do preferentially target LSCs in human leukemia. We propose to examine these 12 compounds in depth and determine how well they work against multiple leukemia samples, what exactly they do, and how safe they are. Our efforts to understand their mechanisms of action and their effectiveness in primary leukemic cells from patients will yield novel insight into the unique functioning of LSC in this type of leukemia. This increase in our knowledge of LSC and leukemia biology will in turn enable additional gains in prognosis, therapy and prevention. Any improvement in AML treatment will benefit children in particular since they are most vulnerable with regard to the long-term side effects of current treatments.

column37: In 2009, the Public health Agency of Canada released the Canadian Maternity Experiences Survey (MES, PHAC 2009). column36: The paternal contribution to neurodevelopmental and metabolic outcomes in the child
column37: This proposal focuses on: (1) how paternal factors can affect brain and endocrine function of the child; and (2) whether the impact of paternal factors extends beyond fetal life up until middle childhood (i.e. 6-8 years of age). Pre-conception paternal factors (factors present before sperm meets egg) may directly cause alterations in the molecular machinery regulating gene expression in sperm, particularly in genes related to both brain and endocrine function. During pregnancy and postpartum, perinatal paternal factors may further impact the child's brain and endocrine function through their indirect influence on perinatal maternal depression and anxiety. Research from our group and others indicates that both pre-conception and perinatal paternal risk factors may lead to permanent changes in brain and endocrine systems during fetal development, and that this effect may last until adrenarche (i.e. a peak in adrenal steroid hormone production around 6-8 years old that represents the 1st step in pubertal maturation). Endocrine disruption during development (e.g. premature adrenarche) significantly increases the risk of impulse control disorders such as attention-deficit hyperactivity (ADHD), conduct and oppositional disorders. This suggests that paternal effects on brain and endocrine function of the child can potentially have long-term behavioral impacts that may extend to middle childhood. Understanding the paternal contribution to the child's brain and endocrine development will help tailor preventative public health interventions to decrease exposure to modifiable paternal risk factors. Paternal lifestyle changes made even a few weeks before conception could make a critical difference down the line in vulnerable children. Hence, anticipated results from this project are likely to have a strong public health impact and can be used to counsel fathers about modifiable risk factors as early as the pre-conception period.

column36: Improving maternal and perinatal outcomes in high risk mothers.
column37: The average maternal age, obesity, multiple pregnancy, and chronic diseases such as diabetes and hypertension continue to increase in industrialized countries. For example, 34% of mothers in Canada are overweight or obese, and about 20% of births are to women over 34 years. These demographic trends highlight the need for increasingly complex obstetric care with careful prenatal monitoring and timely obstetric intervention if necessary. Many studies have shown an increased risk of adverse perinatal outcomes in older women. The risk of maternal death also increases with maternal age over 35 years and is 10 times higher in mothers over 45 as compared with 20-24 years old. As maternal death is a very rare event, preventive efforts need to focus also on potentially life-threatening maternal conditions and identification of women who are at high risk, including those of older maternal age, overweight or obese, and those with twins/triplets or underlying chronic diseases. These risk factors often co-exist, therefore the combined effects and interactions between these conditions need to be addressed and quantified carefully. Some of the severe maternal conditions (e.g., eclampsia or sepsis), are potentially preventable. We propose to examine these specific types of severe potentially life-threatening maternal morbidity in relation to older maternal age, high body mass index and underlying morbidity using data on all births in Canada between 2004 and 2015 (> 4,000,000 births). We will quantify the risk of severe maternal morbidity by developing a score system that will accurately distinguish between high, moderate, and low risk women. This score calculator will help, for example, women in rural areas to decide about transport to higher-level obstetric care, as these women may face geographical barriers to timely transfer. These results will also provide information to women who contemplate to delay childbirth, who are overweigh or obese, or have chronic health problems.

column36: Heterologous stem cell therapy to treat acute liver failure in infants, children and adolescents without the need of immunosuppression
column37: Acute liver failure (ALF) is an extremely severe, progressive syndrome resulting from a sudden insult on the liver exceeding the organ's innate regenerative capacity. ALF in children and adolescents has a poor outcome, with only 50% of patients surviving with their native liver. Infants are at even greater risk of death, with almost half dying before transplantation and 50% of those receiving a transplant dying post-operatively. Therefore, there is an urgent need for effective liver support systems able to replace liver functions for the time needed for the patient's liver to regenerate, or for a suitable donor to be found. We developed a pioneering stem cell-based product to be used as a bridge to liver regeneration or transplantation. Using clinical-grade stem cells, we are able to generate complex 3D cellular microaggregates (organoids) performing the functions of a human liver. We developed an innovative biomaterial to encapsulate such liver organoids to improve their maturation and functions while making them resistant to cryopreservation. Once transplanted to a patient with ALF, such an encapsulated "liver tissue" is expected to purify the patient's blood from toxic substances and to synthesize proteins needed for vital functions, improving survival and preventing complications. Moreover, the biomaterial is expected to protect the embedded organoids from the immune system of the recipient, thus eliminating the risk of rejection and the need for immunosuppression. The aims of this project are: 1) to assess the safety of such a stem cell-derived liver tissue upon transplantation in terms of biocompatibility, risk of rejection and tumor formation; 2) to evaluate the its efficacy to restore lacking liver functions in a mouse model of ALF. This approach will deliver an innovative off-the-shelf, sustainable stem cell therapy with the potential to treat thousands of infants, children and adolescents with ALF worldwide.

column36: Bridging the gap to prevent adverse events between pediatric and adult diabetes care
column37: Background: During the transition to adult diabetes care, youth are at risk for admission to the hospital for life-threatening diabetes complications and for long gaps before establishing adult diabetes care. We don't know the best way to help youth with chronic diseases including diabetes to transition to adult care. The effect of a system-level transition intervention is not known. Improving transition is a key priority of the Ontario Pediatric Diabetes Network and other diabetes organizations. Objective: To optimize care for youth with diabetes and to prevent acute diabetes complications during transition to adult care. Our specific aims: 1)To determine the baseline rate of and risk factors for diabetes-related admissions in early adulthood 2)To determine the effectiveness of a system-level intervention to prevent diabetes-related admissions in early adulthood. Methods: We will follow all youth with type 1 diabetes from their final pediatric diabetes visit at five pediatric diabetes centres in Ontario and measure the rate of diabetes-related hospital admissions every 12 months before and after an intervention on April 1, 2018. The Intervention has three parts: 1) a data platform to collect medical record data and link it to provincial data about physician visits and hospital admissions; 2) performance reports to participating pediatric centres about the rate of diabetes-related admissions in recently-transitioned youth; these reports will inform centre-level quality improvement transition strategies; and 3) an online transition resource center for providers and families. Impact: Our project targets youth at high risk for diabetes-related problems during transition. If our intervention is effective, it can be used immediately by diabetes teams in Ontario and beyond. Our data platform can be expanded in scale to other jurisdictions to evaluate the impact of other quality improvement strategies.

column36: Early Neurodevelopment in the Offspring of Women Enrolled in a Randomized Controlled Trial Assessing the Effectiveness of a Nutrition+Exercise Intervention for Healthy Gestational Weight Gain
column37: Optimal early brain development is vital to health and success in life. Since neurodevelopment begins at conception, maternal health problems, dietary imbalances, and physical inactivity during pregnancy can lead to intellectual and behavioural difficulties in offspring early in life. Many Canadian women consume an unhealthy diet and/or fail to get enough exercise during pregnancy. It is not surprising then that up to 40% of women enter pregnancy overweight and that even more (up to 75%) gain too much weight during pregnancy. Despite these facts, no studies in humans have examined if interventions that optimize maternal diet and exercise during pregnancy can improve the intellectual, behavioural, and/or emotional functioning of their children. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a study that will follow the offspring of 400 women that will be enrolled in an ongoing study of a nutrition+exercise intervention in pregnant women. The nutrition component of this intervention consists of an individualized nutrition plan that is tailored to women's needs, as well as educational sessions with a dietitian. Our exercise intervention involves women engaging in a structured and monitored walking program. In this study, half of the women will receive our nutrition+exercise program and the other half will get treatment as usual from their healthcare providers. The main objective of this study is to determine if fetal exposure to our maternal intervention leads to improved intellectual and/or emotional development in offspring at 36 months of age compared to women who receive usual pregnancy care. If we are able to show that offspring neurodevelopment can be improved via our structured and monitored nutrition+exercise program during pregnancy, it could be used to prevent or reduce the severity of cognitive, behavioural, and emotional problems in their children early in life.

column36: Specialized pro-resolving mediators: A novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe disease characterized by progressive and irreversible muscle wasting. Dystrophic patients display ambulatory dysfunctions in early childhood that quickly degenerates into respiratory dysfunctions and premature death in young adult. The disease is caused by a genetic mutation leading to the loss of expression of dystrophin, a structural protein important for muscle fiber stability. Moreover, we recently showed that dystrophin also regulates the function of muscle stem cells (also named satellite cells), which are responsible for muscle repair. Therefore, muscle wasting observed in Duchenne muscular dystrophy is not only caused by fragile muscle fibers, it is also attributable to poor muscle healing due to impaired muscle stem cell function. Thus, new therapeutic approaches must target muscle stem cells to mitigate the disease. To date, glucocorticoids are the only drugs that can temporarily slow down muscle wasting in Duchenne muscular dystrophy by dampening the chronic inflammatory process; however, they also have detrimental side effects that impair muscle stem cell function and stimulate long-term muscle wasting. Therefore, there is room for improvement and for the development of a more efficient therapy for this severe disease. Our research program investigates the impact of a new class of omega-3 and omega-6 derived mediators for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. These molecules, named specialized pro-resolving mediators, have a potent ability to resolve inflammation, without the harmful side effects, and they could directly stimulate muscle stem cell activity and promote muscle healing. With their ability to dampen inflammation and simultaneously restore muscle stem cell functions, the specialized pro-resolving mediators have the potential to preserve dystrophic muscle function overtime, improve the quality of life and the life expectancy of the patients suffering from Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

column36: Discovering novel biomarkers for juvenile arthritis: focus on platelet signaling
column37: Juvenile arthritis is a very serious disease that affects over 300,000 children and teenagers in North America and causes severe pain, physical deformities and confers a risk of long-term disability. While it is known that juvenile arthritis is characterized by chronic inflammation of the joints, it is currently impossible to accurately identify those children who may be at highest risk for future disease. In chronic diseases such as arthritis, signaling molecules called cytokines are largely responsible for tissue inflammation and destruction. Platelets are tiny cells in the blood that control blood clotting but also release cytokines that can promote inflammation during arthritis. The purpose of this grant application is to study platelet activity in patients with juvenile arthritis in order to determine (1) whether platelet-derived cytokines contribute to juvenile arthritis and (2) if these molecules can be used as markers to predict the clinical course of the disease. An improved understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying juvenile arthritis will eventually lead to improved clinical tools for diagnosing, prognosticating and treating this debilitating disease.

column36: TRajectories Of healthy life using Public Health and primary care Interventions in Canada: The TROPHIC Trial
column37: The "Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD)" hypothesis suggests that a healthy growth and development in pregnancy and early childhood is critical for optimal health and lifetime wellbeing. Yet, Canada's children are falling behind. Nearly 1 in 3 Canadian children are overweight or obese, 1 in 4 is not developmentally ready for school, and 1 in 5 has a mental health problem. Early interventions can improve child health and development. Our study will evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention on child obesity and broader indicators of child development. Our trial, TROPHIC (TRajectories Of healthy life using Public Health and primary care Interventions in Canada), will take a 'cumulative-impact' approach, designed to improve health behaviours and reduce modifiable risk factors across the entire early child developmental period. TROPHIC will randomise pregnancy-planning women to evaluate a 4-phase intervention, from preconceptually all the way through early childhood. Its innovative design will enable the collection of family-level data, by including fathers/partners preconceptionally, and following more than one child within the family. TROPHIC comprises of a pan-Canadian team of 48 established investigators, from 21 institutions, across 6 provinces with proven expertise to successfully undertake this Healthy Life Trajectories initiative (HeLTI) project. The proposed project is aligned with the international HeLTI studies. TROPHIC capitalizes on efficient study recruitment and data collection methods, using existing research initiatives, such as TARGet Kids! The planned linkage of TROPHIC data to provincial administrative health datasets will enable longitudinal follow-up of children past age 5 years. We will leverage existing structures in public health and primary care to recruit participants, and then deliver interventions, if proven effective, to enable scalability at provincial and national levels.

column36: Disease-modifying Drug Safety and Effectiveness in Multiple Sclerosis [DRUMS]
column37: The goal of our research is to determine how safe and effective the drugs used to treat multiple sclerosis (MS) are when used in the real world. Canada has some of the world's highest rates of MS. This chronic disease of the brain and spinal cord often affects young adults and there is no known cure. In the last two decades, over 10 different drugs have been approved to treat people with MS. These drugs are very expensive and can require regular injections as well as frequent blood tests to monitor safety (side effects). We know how well these drugs work in the short-term, but only against certain aspects of MS. In the real world, people with MS may take these drugs for many years but we do not yet understand all their possible benefits and side effects. There have been few studies as large as ours investigating such a range of possible side effects, including cancer, stroke and infections. We will also look at whether the MS drugs have benefits which are often hard to measure, such as MS disability and fewer hospital or doctors' visits. Our research brings together medical data collected for over 2 decades within multiple large health databases in several Canada provinces. No study as large or as comprehensive as ours has ever been done. Our team approach enables findings to be directly relevant to Canadians, including people in poorer communities or those with co-existing medical conditions, who are often excluded from studies. Our research will be independent from the pharmaceutical industry, the manufacturers of MS drugs. This important research will help develop a framework in which to evaluate the benefits and side effects of both the current and future new drugs for MS across Canada. Our study findings will provide much needed information to help treatment-related decision making for both patients and doctors. Ultimately our study findings will directly benefit the outcomes related to treatment and health-related quality of life of people living with MS.

column36: Host microbe interactions in health and disease
column37: Humans have evolved with microbes. Although a subset of microbes have long been known to cause infectious diseases, there is growing appreciation of the critical role they play in health and chronic diseases. This new development also opens up powerful opportunities to find new ways of treating diseases and improving health outcomes. To this end, my lab has been studying how Salmonella and pathogenic E. coli cause diarrhea and related diseases, using new techniques to gain a much more comprehensive understanding of these diseases. Moreover, we have found that normal microbial inhabitants of the gut - the microbiome - can be used to inhibit these pathogens, thus we are pursuing these as potential therapeutics. We have also shown that certain early life microbes can affect the risk of asthma, and these are being explored as potential asthma preventatives. This work is being expanded to related food allergies, especially in the context of very early life gut microbes. A novel mouse model has been developed for malnutrition and an associated intestinal disease (environmental enteropathy). This model will allow us to gain a better understanding of these worldwide problems, as well as to test new products that can then be used to prevent these diseases. Recently, we have begun to explore the gut-brain axis in the context of microbes affecting brain function in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's/dementia. Exciting preliminary data indicate that the microbiomes in these patients are different, and we have new experiments planned to mechanistically probe this initial finding. Important next steps include the development of clinical tools that can be used to decrease these brain diseases. I am proposing a compelling and ambitious program to study these host-microbe interactions. Collectively, this research has significant potential to impact on many major Canadian health issues, including intestinal infections, asthma and allergies, malnutrition and degenerative brain diseases.

column37: Chronic diseases such as diabetes and high blood pressure are increasing around the world. This is a problem because the effective management of chronic diseases require considerable effort by patients and health professionals. Further, these patients also require many healthcare services such as emergency room visits, physician visits and medications to help control their disease. Detailed care plans developed by health professionals in partnership with patients are being encouraged, which cover everything from required medical tests and medications to exercise and diet, with the goal they will improve patients' health. In 2009, in order to improve health care for Albertans with chronic diseases, Alberta Health implemented new health policies to pay physicians to create care plans for patients who have several chronic diseases. Following its introduction, physicians in Alberta were found to be very actively providing and billing for these plans. In 2012, Alberta Health also began to pay pharmacists to develop care plans for patients, given their newly expanded scope of practice in Alberta. However, the success of providing these care plans has not been evaluated to determine whether they are improving patients' health, as well as whether patients are satisfied with the quality of care provided. We aim to study what types of patients have received these care plans, whether their health care and outcomes have improved, and whether patients think they have received good quality care using patient-reported surveys. We will compare their health outcomes and quality of care to patients with similar disease who did not receive these care plans.

column36: Unraveling The Molecular Mechanisms of Cardiomyocyte De-Differentiation During Zebrafish Heart Regeneration
column37: Cardiovascular disease leading to heart attacks represents one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Survivors are typically faced with a lifelong reduction in heart function, as the adult mammalian heart is unable to restore lost heart muscle after injury. Rather, induction of a strong inflammatory response results in replacement of muscle with non-contractile, collagen-rich scar tissue. Prior research focused on delivering the injured heart with various types of stem cells has yielded few meaningful results with respect to achieving significant improvements in cardiac function at the clinical level. Therefore, it is increasingly attractive to consider applying the lessons learned from examples of organ regeneration found in nature to solve this problem. The zebrafish heart can fully regenerate following removal of up to 20% of the adult ventricle, or complete ablation of ventricular muscle in 3-day old embryos. Virtually all regenerated heart muscle derives from pre-existing heart muscle cells that divide after they de-differentiate, or move backwards through development, losing many specific characteristics of mature cardiac cells. Remarkably, the molecular machinery which drives this process in zebrafish is present and competent to respond to the appropriate molecular signals to direct heart repair in mammals. Mechanistically, little is known about what factors are responsible for initiating this process. During my PhD studies, I will use genetic tools to isolate de-differentiating cells in the regenerating zebrafish heart. Cells will be sampled at the onset of injury, during dedifferentiation, and as regeneration ends. Changes in gene expression will be measured at single-cell resolution to identify key factors and the specific cell subpopulations responsible for driving regeneration. This work will reconstruct the molecular events required for heart regeneration, ultimately revealing new avenues of treatment for stimulating self-healing of the heart.

column36: Development and Application of Liquid Skin Substitute for Promoting Wound Healing and Preventing Hypertrophic Scarring in Burn Injuries.
column37: Each year in North America, more than half a million patients receive immediate medical care due to burn injuries. Fifty thousands of these patients need acute hospitalization related to these injuries. The gold-standard treatment for extensive burn injuries is using a healthy part of the patients' skin for covering the wounds area which is called skin grafting. Split thickness skin grafts can be "meshed" to allow them to be used to cover larger areas than would be otherwise possible. This process involves creating a large number of small cuts in the skin graft that allow the sheet to be expanded. Although this process is highly beneficial by allowing smaller skin graft donor sites to treat larger wounds, it requires more of the wound to heal secondarily (without the benefit of a direct skin graft). This results in slower healing and a poorer final outcome in terms of the scar. Specifically, the scar ultimately has a "cobble stone" or "fishnet" pattern. This is an indelible remainder to the patient of their injury, and also produces a poorer quality scar with less mobility and stretch. To address this issue, we propose the use of a novel powdered reconstituteable liquid skin substitute (MeshFill) to fill the splits of meshed grafts. MeshFill is a low-cost, simple chemical product to create an artificial skin composite that can fill a wound bed or skin void, such as in a meshed graft. Prior to potential clinical application, we will examine the outcome of this approach with meshed skin grafts on Red Duroc Pigs. Skin healing in pigs is remarkably similar to humans. If our hypothesis proves correct, the application of this strategy will significantly improve surgical wound care of millions of burn patients. Unlike many potential treatments in this area, the final product is going to be inexpensive and readily produced, which dramatically increases the potential benefit of this approach. The benefits of MeshFill for these patients is faster healing and reduced scar.

column36: Clinical impacts of tumoural spatial heterogeneity
column37: Tumours progression is usually caused by mutations in the genetic code. These mutations can vary spatially throughout the tumour , forming populations of cells that have distinct genetic properties (tumoural heterogeneity). Genetic diversity within tumours allows them to evolve as they grow and respond to treatment, which can impact patient outcomes and obstructs personalized medicine. My doctoral work seeks to better understand the biology of tumoural heterogeneity in prostate cancer and its impact disease severity, outcome, and treatment. As prostate tumours are often driven by large-scale structural mutations, I will use a large prostate cancer patient cohort to develop a method that characterizes heterogeneity in DNA rearragements, which existing methods currently neglect. As heterogeneity can also confound genetic tests that predict outcome based on a single biopsy, I will develop a test that integrates information from multiple spatially distinct biopsy samples to predict recurrence-free survival in a prostate cancer cohort. Finally, I will use a 4000 patient prostate cancer cohort to investigate patterns in tumour evolution and investigate their impact on disease severity and progression. This work will produce clinically applicable tools and insights on tumoural heterogenety leading to improved disease management for prostate cancer patients.

column36: Integrity of Inhibitory Control and Relationship to TMS Treatment Response in Youth MDD
column37: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is one of the most common and severe mental health illnesses reported in youth. There is now growing concern over the prescription of antidepressants, which although may be effective for adults, have not only been found to have modest efficacy in MDD youth, but have also been reported as inducing harmful side-effects such as an increase in suicidal thoughts, creating an urgent need to explore for other potential treatment options. A neurostimulation treatment called repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been found to be effective for adults with MDD, with the added benefit of being associated with little to no side-effects. However, rTMS treatment has yet to be thoroughly investigated in youth MDD. Along with a need to find new treatments, there is also a need to explore for potential biomarkers that can be indicative as to whether a youth MDD will successfully respond to a treatment such as rTMS. Recent studies in MDD adults suggest that one's ability to successfully suppress unwanted thoughts and behaviours, also referred to as inhibitory control (IC), may be an indicator of treatment response, with impairment of this ability at baseline being associated with poor treatment outcomes. However, the potential of IC as a biomarker of treatment response in youth MDD has yet to be explored. Thus, our aims including 1) assessing the efficacy of rTMS for treating youth MDD and 2) assessing whether IC has any predictive value of rTMS treatment response in youth MDD. This project thus not only holds the potential to substantiate rTMS as a treatment for youth MDD, but to also uncover biomarkers of treatment response in this patient population, which ultimately may help prevent further time and costs lost on ineffective therapies by allowing us to make an informed decision as to whether a person is likely to respond to a specific type of treatment or not.

column36: Assessing the impact of lymph node hypoxia on malignant progression and anti-tumor immunity
column37: Almost 90% of deaths due to cancer occur when a tumor spreads (metastasizes) to other tissues in the body. Many solid cancers first spread to regional lymph nodes, and detection of these lesions predicts worse patient outcome. In the past, researchers believed that tumor cells were passively transported through the lymphatic circulation to nearby lymph nodes; however, recent evidence suggests that metastasis to these sites is an active process. For example, the lymph node closest to the tumor undergoes several changes prior to tumor cell arrival, including a shift in the balance between different types of immune cells that creates a more tolerant environment for incoming cancer cells. We have discovered that lymph nodes directly draining the tumor also have regions of low oxygen availability, a condition called hypoxia. A hypoxic environment is known to promote tumor aggression and suppress immune responses that would normally kill cancer cells; therefore, it is important to understand how lymph node hypoxia relates to cancer metastasis, and what effect it has on nearby immune cells. We will first determine whether low oxygen develops in the lymph nodes prior to tumor cell arrival, by labeling tumor cells with a fluorescent marker in order to track their movement. Since lymph nodes play an important role during the development of an effective immune response, we will also determine whether oxygen shortage inhibits the function of certain immune cell populations in the lymph node. The results will have important implications for the development of new therapies to help the immune system eradicate metastatic tumor cells in the lymph node.

column36: High-throughput behavioural neurogenetic characterization and precise structure-function analysis of genes and gene variants associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder using Caenorhabditis elegans.
column37: A primary challenge in investigations of genes associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is the lack of a model system in which to characterize the large number of candidate risk genes in a rapid, cost-effective manner. The time and money constraints associated with modelling psychiatric disease in higher-order organisms necessitates an alternative approach. I propose using Caenorhabditis elegans, a microscopic worm commonly used in neuroscience and genetics research, to characterize ASD-associated genes and mutations within those genes. C. elegans is an ideal genetic model organism with which genetic screens and precise genetic engineering can rapidly correlate genotype to phenotype and determine the biological pathways in which genes function. Also, we have developed an automated machine vision system, the Multi-Worm Tracker (MWT), to collect 15 phenotypic measures of development, locomotion, and habituation - a form of learning that is impaired in ASD. I will use the MWT to rapidly characterize hundreds of ASD-associated genes by analyzing the morphology and behaviour of different strains of C. elegans each carrying a mutation in a different ASD-associated gene. After an unbiased characterization of all genes, I will use multivariate analyses to identify genes that induce strong and unique effects to prioritize them for detailed analysis. I will use CRISPR genome engineering to insert human mutations identified in individuals with ASD to determine how these mutations disrupt normal neurodevelopment and learning. This research will generate a large number of novel genotype to phenotype relationships and detailed mechanistic information of how ASD-associated genes alter a nervous system to disrupt normal development, locomotion, and learning. This data can be used to inform future, targeted studies in higher-order organisms and humans. Importantly, this work will identify novel therapeutic targets for ameliorating the effects of ASD.

column36: Identification of early epigenomic changes produced by oncogenic mutant KRAS in transduced normal human mammary cells
column37: Breast cancers are extremely complex diseases with fatal outcomes in thousands of women annually in Canada and millions worldwide. In any single person, the prognosis is affected by many factors. This is due, in part, to the fact that breast cancers destined to be fatal, even with the best current therapies, have already become very diverse by the time they are diagnosed. It is generally assumed that eliminating all of the malignant cells capable of causing a relapse will require targeting changes that develop in the first cells to acquire malignant properties, regardless of any later changes that appear in their daughter cells. The objective of this proposal is therefore to characterize these initial changes. To make this possible, I will investigate human breast cancer cells that are experimentally produced using a defined protocol. According to this protocol, a special strain of immunodeficient mice are transplanted with normal human mammary cells into which a mutant cancer-causing gene has just been introduced. Our lab has found that within 2 weeks after being transplanted into mice, the genetically altered cells are already exhibiting abnormal growth and protein expression properties. In addition, our lab has obtained a complete description of the molecules that control the genes expressed in the different types of normal human cells from which tumours can be obtained, as well as a picture of how these molecules interact with DNA to control gene expression - like fingers on a keyboard producing different chords of music. I propose to similarly characterize 2-week post-transplant cells from our engineered human breast cancer model and identify how these molecules contribute to breast cancer development by genetically manipulating their activity. The results will provide new information about the identity and role of very early changes that contribute to human breast cancer development and thus set the stage for the discovery of new therapeutic agents.

column36: Unraveling medulloblastoma developmental pathways using single cell mRNA sequencing
column37: Pediatric medulloblastoma (MB) is a brain cancer that is caused by defects in the developing brain. Current therapy for MB involves, surgery, radiation of the entire developing brain and spinal cord, followed by non-specific chemotherapy drugs that kill any cells that are dividing. While survival rates are approaching 70%, the costs to the children that survive are immense due to the damage to their developing brains caused by both the cancer and the therapy used to treat it. In order to identify targets to better direct treatments and decrease the long-term adverse effects, it is critical to study the changes and transformations that occur in the developing brain of these patients. To solve this, we propose the study of the expression of functional gene products at early and later stages in a strain of mice that will develop MB. More specifically we will monitor individual cells from developing mouse brains at different time points using a technique named single-cell mRNA sequencing. Single-cell mRNA sequencing is a powerful method that can provide enough information for accurate cell identification and for detection of changes within individual cells. We will use it to see the changes in tumor cells at different stages and then use bioinformatic tools to provide insight into the origin of the disease. Overall, this study will provide valuable information that will help shed light on critical events that happen in the development of brain cancer. This additional information will help us better understand the roles of mutations in their biology. Our study will provide detailed clues for researchers to verify new cancer genes with focused experiments. It will also help build better tools for doctors to distinguish cancer types and thus provide personalized therapy to each child.

column36: Characterization of bottlenecks during colonization of C57BL/6 mice by attaching and effacing pathogens using sequence tag-based analysis of microbial populations (STAMP)
column37: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, diarrheal disease claims the life of 1 in every 10 children under the age of 5 - that is 800,000 children worldwide each year. The bulk of diarrheal illness is caused by fecal contamination by a group of bacteria called attaching and effacing (A/E) pathogens. A/E pathogens are a major threat to food and water safety in Canada, with an estimated annual cost of $403.9 million to the economy. To establish an infection, A/E pathogens must overcome many environmental barriers including the host immune system and the trillions of microorganisms (such as bacteria, viruses, parasites, and fungi) inhabiting a healthy gut. Recent studies indicate that a 'bottleneck' effect occurs during colonization of A/E pathogens, restricting the sheer number of individual bacteria able to establish a foot hold in the intestine, and effectively decreasing the genetic diversity of the population. For example, in a study using individually tagged Citrobacter rodentium, a mouse A/E pathogen, only half of the tags remained within the population after infection despite equal fitness of the bacteria. The cause of these bottlenecks remains unknown. My research will focus on characterizing the population dynamics of C. rodentium as infection progresses, and on identifying factors affecting bottlenecks across intestinal regions, at different time points post infection. We hypothesize that bottlenecks are caused by a combination of factors from both the host and microbiota such as intestinal integrity and nutrient availability, or chemical signals released by resident microbes. I will then go on to manipulate these factors for their ability to cause bottlenecks. This research is important to help us understand the tripartite interactions between the host, pathogen, and microbiota which influence bacterial infection in the hopes of developing novel therapeutics to combat the rise in antibiotic resistance.

column36: Transcriptional control of cancer metabolism
column37: Cancer cells need specific nutrients and to transform these nutrients using specific biochemical pathways to generate enough energy and building blocks to sustain their growth and rapid division. My research program is centered on understanding how cancer cells adapt their metabolism to favor their proliferation and resistance to therapeutic intervention. More precisely, our team is investigating changes in the expression of specialized genes that modify the metabolic program of cancer cells. These changes in gene expression often result from the aberrant activity of proteins known as transcription factors. The normal function of transcription factors is to respond to cellular needs by modulating gene expression so that the cells have the necessary tools to perform their normal activities during the development and lifespan of the organism. However, cancer cells highjack transcription factors to promote tumour growth and their metastasis to distant organs. The abnormal action of transcription factors in cancer is best-exemplified by a class of proteins known as nuclear receptors, which include the estrogen and androgen receptors that promote the growth of breast and prostate cancer, respectively. In recent years, my research program has been focused on studying the roles played by nuclear receptors and other transcription factors in regulating energy metabolism, notably how cancer cells differentially process nutrients such as amino acids, sugars and lipids to fuel their growth. Our goals are to find differences between the action of transcription factors in normal and cancer cells and to exploit these differences to induce metabolic vulnerabilities in tumours, thus making them more responsive to anti-cancer drugs. The ultimate outcome of this program should be improvement in the treatment and quality of life of cancer patients.

column36: Novel Type 1 Cannabinoid Receptor Allosteric Modulators
column37: The type 1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) is present at high levels throughout the brain and other parts of the body. CB1R is activated by the body's own cannabinoids (anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol), synthetic cannabinoids, and cannabinoids from marijuana (e.g. THC and cannabidiol). CB1R is considered a potential target for the regulation of appetite and the treatment of addiction, pain, spasticity in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, epilepsy, post-traumatic stress disorder, and anxiety. Despite its potential as a therapeutic target, we are still learning how the many naturally occurring and synthetic cannabinoids that exist affect CB1R and how CB1R in turn produces distinct effects in the body. To this end, new compounds known as allosteric modulators are being developed that can increase or decrease CB1R's response to the body's cannabinoids, but lack intrinsic activity and will not, therefore, produce the intoxicating effects associated with other cannabinoids. The goals of my research are: (1) to develop allosteric modulators of CB1R that alter the body's response to its own cannabinoids, (2) test those modulators in animal models, and (3) to apply the knowledge gained from goals 1 and 2 to specific disease states where cannabinoids might be therapeutically beneficial.
