column36: A systematic genome wide effort to identify and validate targetable synthetic dosage lethal interactions of mitotic kinases in colorectal cancer cells
column37: Cancer cells often overexpress specific genes due to the effect of translocations, gene amplification, or other epigenetic modifications. Researchers have thought that directly inhibiting the function of these overexpressing genes could help to eliminate cancer cells. For example, a gene called Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) is overexpressed in multiple cancers including colorectal cancers, indicating that inhibition of this kinase could be a powerful antitumor strategy. However, efforts to inhibit this kinase showed low objective response rates, poor survival and severe toxic side effects in clinical studies. This is because these drugs were not specific enough and often resulted in off-target effects, where they targeted other members of the polo-like family. To circumvent this concern, here we propose to take advantage of a basic biological concept called "Synthetic Dosage Lethality", where cancer cells overexpressing genes like PLK1 could be killed, when another gene is turned "OFF". In other words, rather than directly inhibiting genes like PLK1, we have developed a method that can query every single gene in the genome, in a span of four weeks, and identify those target genes whose loss-of-function can selectively kill PLK1-overexpressing cancer cells. Using this approach, we will execute our investigation in colon cancer cells as it ranks third in morbidity among all other malignancies. In addition, our lab is fully equipped with all the tools and reagents required to test the effect of the target genes that we identify in this cancer. Thus the successful completion of our project has the potential to identify several new druggable targets for colon cancer treatment. Our findings are expected to trigger the development of novel targeted therapies that would improve the survival of colon cancer patients.

column36: Molecular mechanisms underlying the clinical efficacy of inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist combination therapies in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease, characterised by intermittent airways constriction and occurs in up to 10% of individuals. Regular inhaled glucocorticoids are clinically referred to as inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and dampen lung inflammation to control mild to moderate asthma. However, more severe disease and asthma exacerbations are poorly controlled by ICS and clinical guidelines recommend the addition of a long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist (LABA). These drugs enhance the effectiveness of the ICS to a level that is not achieved by increasing the glucocorticoid dose. The glucocorticoid receptor (GR), the protein target by which glucocorticoids act, is responsible for modulating gene expression to mediate beneficial effects in asthma. In the context of LABA, combinatorial effects between glucocorticoid and LABA-activated pathways result in enhanced clinical effectiveness of ICS/LABA therapies. However, the mechanistic basis, and the genes modulated, are not established and therefore cannot be selectively targeted. The current proposal will elucidate mechanisms underlying this clinically important effect. In this context, it is salient that the pharmaceutical sector is currently testing novel drugs that activate GR in ways that are different to conventional glucocorticoids. These compounds enhance some aspects of GR function relative to other activities. While, the objective is to improve the clinical efficacy of GR-based therapies, it is important to stress that we do not know which aspects of GR function are most important for synergy with LABA. There is therefore a risk of failing to identify novel GR ligands that most effectively synergise with LABAs. This will preclude maximising benefit from future combination therapies. The current project addresses this key knowledge gap by identifying mechanisms of GR action that are important for synergy with LABA. Such data will help guide the discovery of improved combination treatments for asthma.

column36: The Role of Small Airways Disease Heterogeneity in Asthma
column37: Asthma is not just a Canadian health issue but a serious world-wide public health problem, with an estimated 235 million people suffering with asthma. This is caused by the structural cells that line the airway tubes which respond to allergen exposure by promoting inflammation and thickening of the airways, termed fibrosis. The goal of our study is to identify the disease drivers that cause airway fibrosis in asthma patients and to identify new therapies to prevent the disease. Our work leverages a unique set of donated human lungs which will be analyzed with new computed tomography (CT) scanning methods to understand how the physical damage and airway fibrosis occurs throughout the asthmatic lung. We will then use lung cells isolated from the patients with asthma to test if the disease-drivers we identify can be modulated with new or existing therapies. This research will allow better understanding of airway fibrosis in asthma, and should lead to improved measures to help Canadians with asthma experience less disease symptoms.

column37: Sexual health is an integral part of physical and mental health, quality of life, and healthy relationships. Sexual arousal and desire problems, however, affect up to one third of women, yet approved treatments do not yet exist. One impediment to effective treatment is poor understanding of how sexual difficulties develop in women. Recently, scientists have reconceptualized sexual desire as being triggered by sexual cues and emerging from sexual arousal, instead of a drive, like hunger, that motivates people to seek out sex. This new model of sexual response more accurately captures women's experiences and may better characterize women's sexual difficulties, but it has not been scientifically tested. Our primary objective is to understand the relationships among neural and cognitive processing of sexual cues, sexual arousal, and sexual desire. One day after completing these tasks, women will complete measures of their experience of responsive sexual desire. Understanding the relationships between sexual arousal and desire will create gender-specific knowledge about women's sexuality and about the causes of women's sexual difficulties, will have direct implications for identifying risk factors for sexual arousal and desire problems, will inform treatment decisions, and will decrease the burden of sexual difficulties and its negative impacts for Canadian women.

column36: TICS: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Intervening in Children with Tourette's Syndrome
column37: Tourette syndrome (TS) is common. TS affects over 80,000 Canadian youth. Tics are the core symptom of TS. These are repetitive, sudden, semi-voluntary movements or sounds. In some children, these tics can be especially bad and require treatment. However, options are limited. Medications for TS carry significant risk of side effects. Behavioral treatments, like habit reversal therapy, show promise and are safe. However, they are difficult to apply to young children. It is only with time and practice that youth with TS are better able to suppress their tics. Finally, neither current treatment approaches target the root cause of the tics in the brain. For these reasons, new interventions are needed. We will target a key brain region involved in tics. It is called the supplementary motor area. Using low frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, we will inhibit the activity of that brain region. This is similar to the tic suppression that develops with age. Brain stimulation can also induce brain plasticity. We think by combining brain stimulation with habit reversal therapy, we can not only provide short-term relief, but also help retrain the brain to be better at suppressing tics at an earlier age than usually expected. (1) We think that the severity of tics will decrease with treatment. (2) We think the tic reduction will be greater in the combined treatment group. (3) We further think that we will see changes in brain function and chemistry in the target area, the supplementary motor cortex. (4) Again, we think the changes will be greater in the combined treatment group. Our team has pioneered brain stimulation in children and adolescents. By developing a way to treat TS, we can reduce the severity of tics and improve their quality of life.

column36: Beyond Transparency in Pharmaceutical Research and Regulation
column37: Making pharmaceutical safety and effectiveness evidence transparent, i.e. accessible, to physicians, researchers, healthcare payers, and ultimately patients is an essential but elusive goal. Consider the drug rofecoxib (Vioxx). It was approved in Canada and elsewhere in 1999 for treating arthritis only to be withdrawn from markets in 2004, before which thousands of patients who took Vioxx are estimated to have suffered cardiac arrest and death. Regulatory officials had prior knowledge of this safety risk but kept it confidential on the grounds that information was the drug manufacturer's property. Following Vioxx and similar cases a variety of new laws and policies were put into place to increase the transparency of pharmaceutical evidence and regulators' decision-making. Most recently, Parliament enacted Bill C-17, "Vanessa's Law", arming Health Canada with several new powers, including the ability to make drug safety and effectiveness information more transparent. However, meaningful improvements in transparency have been slow to arrive; changing the real world practices of regulators and clinical researchers, much less industry, remains a huge challenge. Working with Health Canada and other key knowledge users we will determine: i) how pharmaceutical data can be made more transparent to researchers; ii) what procedural, social, and political factors constrain Health Canada's ability to enforce greater transparency; and iii) how the regulator can communicate and collaborate with key actors such as clinical researchers, research institutions, funding agencies to improve pharmaceutical transparency. With expertise in law, medicine, epidemiology, anthropology, political science, and bioethics, our multidisciplinary team is uniquely positioned to identify and help overcome barriers to pharmaceutical transparency for the benefit of Canadians.

column36: Functional near-infrared spectroscopic measures of coherence as a new bio-marker of injury in mTBI patients
column37: Concussion and brain injury are recognized as a major health issue for Canadians. This problem may be especially severe in pediatric populations where brain injury could have life long implications and since children are more likely than adults to have persistent symptoms. We need better tools to quantify concussion. We have data indicating that regional brain communication may be impaired in brain injury and that we can detect the injury with a portable brain imaging system based on light. This method, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) detects changes in hemoglobin oxygenation as a marker of brain activity. Regions with similar frequency oscillations are thought to be in communication with each other. These fluctuations can be quantified using an analysis called coherence. We have published data, and a new pilot study, showing that coherence is reduced between regions in patients with long term symptoms. This project will collect data on a cohort (75) of mTBI patients over 3 months and compare with controls as well as people with other injuries (to control for pain and other confounding factors). We will determine if measurements at an early point can be used to predict outcome. We will show how these data relate to specific types of cognitive and functional symptoms. We will expand our knowledge of whether damage to regional brain communication is a common problem. The group is the only one in the world with the pilot data, the team and the patient population needed for such a study. This study will provide definitive information on whether this fNIRS protocol could be used for concussion monitoring-in what could be a transformative study.

column36: Progression to Type 2 Diabetes in the 1st Decade after Glucose Intolerance in Pregnancy: Pathophysiology and Clinical Implications
column37: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is defined as high blood sugar that is first recognized during pregnancy. It is a common condition affecting up to 14% of pregnant women. Importantly, women who have had GDM are at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2DM), particularly within the first 10 years after their pregnancy. Indeed, we have previously shown that women with recent GDM have subtle abnormalities shortly after their pregnancy including a reduced ability of the pancreas to secrete insulin. It is not known, however, if further decline in this ability to secrete insulin ultimately leads to T2DM in affected women or if this process can be tracked by following certain factors in the blood (called biomarkers). The aim of our research is to determine whether deterioration of insulin secretion is the key factor that leads to the development of T2DM in young women following GDM. Towards this goal, we have recruited a cohort of women with and without GDM who are undergoing evaluation in pregnancy and at regular intervals for the first 9 years thereafter. At each study visit, we are assessing their ability to secrete insulin, the levels of certain biomarkers in the blood, and whether or not they have T2DM. This study will help to shed light on the early changes in the body that lead to the development of diabetes in young women of childbearing age (who represent the segment of the Canadian population that has had the largest increase in diabetes in recent years). This research may lead to improved ways to treat these early changes and thus possibly prevent the development of T2DM in women.

column37: Spine Osteoarthritis (OA) is a major cause of severe low back pain and long-term disability. Ways to detect or treat spine OA at the onset of disease are not available. Based on these promising findings, we now aim to confirm the reliability/specificity of these biomarkers in a larger set of our spine OA patient blood and tissues (n=500) to justify their use in clinic to detect and determine the stage of spine OA. We will also test the effect of blocking these microRNAs in animal model of spine OA to identify if blocking them can stop spine OA disease.

column37: The Issue: HIV is the leading cause of death for adolescents aged 10-19 years in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Uganda's 2017 HIV prevalence among adolescent girls is three times (9.1%) that of adolescent boys. Only 53.6% of adolescent girls in Uganda know their HIV status, far below the UNAIDS goal of 90% of persons living with HIV knowing their status by 2020. Uganda hosts 1 million refugees/displaced persons, and 98,000 live in Kampala, most in slums. Urban refugee/displaced adolescent girls have increased HIV risks due to poverty, violence, and limited healthcare. Yet we know little of HIV testing and prevention needs with displaced/refugee adolescent girls living in Kampala's slums. Our idea: We plan to develop, implement and evaluate an oral HIV-self testing (HIVST) intervention with displaced/refugee girls aged 15-19 in Kampala. HIVST is acceptable and properly used with adolescents in other SSA regions, yet we do not know the best way to link HIVST to HIV care. We explore how m-health (healthcare delivered on mobile-phones), congruent with how adolescents learn and socialize, can improve linkage to care with HIVST. We will assess changes in HIV testing, HIV status knowledge, and linkage to HIV care between the 3 arms. Phase 3 involves a process evaluation and participatory knowledge mobilization. Impact: We build on our CIHR planning grant that highlights the urgent need for HIV testing and prevention with urban refugee/displaced girls in Kampala. Findings will highlight optimal HIVST delivery approaches that can be expanded to other refugee/displaced adolescents in Uganda, SSA and humanitarian contexts.

column36: Effect of aberrant inflammation during pregnancy on subsequent risk of cardiovascular disease in mothers and their offspring
column37: Conditions during pregnancy can have long-term effects on the health of mothers and babies. Pregnant women who have high blood pressure and their urine contains protein are said to suffer from pre-eclampsia. Women and babies afflicted by pre-eclampsia have a higher chance of getting heart disease later in life. Babies with low birth weight (LBW) also have increased risk of heart disease later in life. Interestingly, excessive inflammation in pregnancy is linked to pre-eclampsia and LBW. We want to determine if and how abnormal inflammation in pregnancy increases the risk of subsequent heart disease in mothers and their children. To accomplish these goals, we developed a rat model of pre-eclampsia and LBW. In this model, inflammation in pregnant rats is induced by administration of a bacterial substance called lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Rats injected with LPS develop a condition similar to pre-eclampsia and their pups have LBW. We plan to monitor these rats and their pups after delivery to look for signs of increased risk of cardiovascular disease. We previously found that certain anti-inflammatory agents and exercise prevent inflammation and LBW induced by LPS. Therefore we will conduct studies to determine if exercise or treatment with anti-inflammatory agents mitigates risk of disease. Higher risk of disease in women and children who suffer from pre-eclampsia and LBW is linked to modifications in the DNA structure or in DNA-associated proteins. These modifications are called 'epigenetic alterations'. We plan to determine if inflammation in pregnancy leads to epigenetic alterations that could predict disease later in life. column36: Interactions between serotonin signalling and autophagy in the context of gut inflammation
column37: Serotonin also known as 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) is an important molecule in the human body that controls many normal and disease processes. Serotonin action is changed in experimental colitis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Recently we showed that serotonin has a critical role in activating immune cells and in generating colitis, in our laboratory experiments with cells and mice. Another normal process that may be disrupted in diseases such as IBD is autophagy, which is the body's process to clear out old and damaged cells. A powerful new research method called Genome Wide Association Studies has identified genes that put people at higher risk for IBD. Identifying those genes also links IBD to autophagy. Both autophagy and changes in serotonin action are connected to IBD. However, we still don't know if serotonin signalling affects autophagy action in IBD. Our research will explore if defective autophagy and changes in serotonin action are pivotal players in IBD. We hypothesize that more serotonin action increases the severity of gut inflammation by reducing autophagy in the key cells involved in the generation and/or perpetuation of inflammation. We plan to pin down three key points: 1) How do serotonin and autophagy interact in gut inflammation? 2) How do serotonin and autophagy interact in affecting production of pro- inflammatory cytokines in key cells involved in gut inflammation? 3) How does serotonin change signals inside cells to affect autophagy in our immune system and gut inflammation? This research will help us understand the roles of serotonin and autophagy in gut inflammation, and how they interact. Our results will point to new targets for treating various health disorders, including IBD, that exhibit dysregulated autophagy.

column36: Systematic profiling of circular RNAs essential for the survival of cancer cells
column37: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) were originally identified in the seventies but were dismissed as splicing errors. The technology used to extract total RNA from the cells also missed identifying these circRNAs because they usually relied on techniques that identify the polyadenylated tails of the RNA molecules. Due to their inherent circularized structures, these circRNAs lacked tail ends and so were never identified. Newly developed RNA sequencing technologies have now re-discovered their abundance within the cells. Although the circRNAs are derived from protein-coding regions of the genome, they do not code for any proteins and are categorized as noncoding RNAs. Understanding their function and mechanism of action will delineate how these circRNAs can be used to treat human diseases such as cancer. Unfortunately, we do not have any methods to systematically query their function, let alone their role in any disease condition. To address this, we have developed a novel lentivirus-based library that can turn "OFF" every single circRNA in the genome. Using this, we screened human cancer cells and have now identified four circRNAs that are essential for the survival of these cells. Here we propose to extend our novel work to additional cancer types and identify which circRNAs are essential to maintain the cancer cell proliferation and explore their mode of action. Completion of our proposal will identify the circRNAs essential for cancer cells and the genes that they regulate leading to the development of a new generation of therapeutic strategies.

column37: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects up to 1% of the adult population and causes fatigue, joint pain, swelling and a reduced quality of life. Fortunately, the treatment for rheumatoid arthritis has advanced, and most patients can now have their disease effectively controlled with medications. After a patient's disease has been successfully treated and controlled, the usual practice is to continue with these medications for life. Emerging evidence suggests some patients may be able to successfully reduce medication once their disease is under control, but this evidence has important limitations, and more clinical trials are needed. In this grant, we will conduct a clinical trial to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a patient-centered approach for treatment reduction in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The study will be embedded within an ongoing national study of over 2000 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. From this study, we will identify patients whose disease has been well controlled for at least 6 months and ask if they would like to participate. Interested patients will be randomized to either usual care or a structured but flexible approach to reduce treatment in a shared decision with their physician. Treatment outcomes, including both benefits (ability to successfully reduce treatment) and harms (disease flares) will be compared over 18 months. Alongside these outcomes, we will also measure patient preferences for the benefits and harms, and other outcomes to evaluate the impact on healthcare costs. The data generated will provide real-world data on a patient-centered approach to treatment reduction in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, a common chronic disease with high drug costs.

column36: Role of lysosomal enzymes cathepsins B and D in neuronal vulnerability: potential implications in Alzheimer's disease pathology
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a brain disease characterized by a gradual loss of memory, followed by deterioration of higher cognitive functions such as language, calculation and judgement. The pathological features associated with AD brain include the loss of nerve cells in selected regions along with abnormal deposits of certain molecules such as amyloid beta (Ab) peptide and tau protein in structures called plaques and tangles, respectively. The brain regions which are severely affected in AD are hippocampus and cortex, whereas certain other regions such as cerebellum and striatum are relatively spared. It is believed that accumulation of Ab peptide can trigger the loss of nerve cells, but why only selected cells die in AD brains remain unclear. There is evidence that leakage of lysosomal enzymes called cathepsins B and D from their storage sites is markedly increased in nerve cells before they die in AD brains, but the role of these enzymes in the death of these cells is not fully understood. In a series of experiments, we will first establish the significance of the leakage of cathepsins in Ab-induced death of nerve cells grown in Petri dishes and the underlying cause of leakage of these enzymes from their storage sites. In parallel, we will measure the levels and activity of these enzymes in affected as well as unaffected regions of genetically modified animal models of AD and in post-mortem human AD brain samples. Subsequently, we will determine whether nanoparticles that have been shown to restore leakage of cathepsins can protect nerve cells against Ab-mediated toxicity in Petri dishes and in animal models of AD. This study will establish the role of cathepsins in the selective loss of nerve cells in AD brains. Additionally, these results could lead to identification of new molecular targets for the early diagnosis and/or development of new therapeutic opportunities such as nanoparticles in preventing the loss of nerve cells in AD brains

column36: Follicle-stimulating hormone regulation of bone physiology and pathophysiology
column37: Osteoporosis is a common and debilitating disorder of bone fragility in aging populations, which is associated with increased fracture rates. In women, the incidence of osteoporosis increases markedly following menopause. As estrogen promotes bone health, it is the postmenopausal loss of estrogen that is usually linked to osteoporosis. Indeed, many therapies target the estrogen receptor to prevent or treat postmenopausal osteoporosis. Recent observations over the past decade challenge this current dogma, attributing bone loss to the actions of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary gland. Estrogen and FSH levels in the bloodstream are tightly linked as FSH stimulates the ovaries to make estrogen. When estrogen levels fall at menopause, FSH levels rise, ostensibly to stimulate more estrogen production. However, the ovaries lack the ability to produce estrogen at this stage of life. Therefore, postmenopausal women have both low estrogen and high FSH, and some researchers have recently argued that it is the elevated FSH that is driving bone loss. In support of their view, they identified receptors for FSH on osteoclast cells in the bone. The normal function of osteoclasts is to degrade bone and FSH has been argued to increase osteoclast activity, and therefore bone loss. As a result of these observations, efforts are being made to develop inhibitors of FSH to treat bone loss in postmenopausal women. This new approach is highly controversial as many investigators question whether previous studies on FSH in bone physiology were correctly interpreted. Here, we propose to resolve this controversy using mouse models unique to our research team. The results of our work will definitely establish whether or not FSH regulates bone.

Seniors in long term care facilities are vulnerable to poor oral health, but they have not been well studied. column36: Novel Drug Targeting of the Circadian Factor REV-ERB Limits Infarct Expansion and Remodelling After Myocardial Ischemia/Reperfusion
column37: Ischemic heart disease leading to myocardial infarction (MI, heart attack) is a leading cause of death worldwide. Studies using broad approaches to reduce inflammation fail to show clinical effectiveness because they act on both beneficial and deleterious immune pathways involved in infarct healing. Specific targets are needed instead. We recently showed that the circadian system is an important mechanism regulating immunocyte recruitment to infarcted myocardium. However, direct targeting of the circadian mechanism to reduce reperfusion injury and benefit treatment of clinically relevant mI/R has not yet been pursued, in large part because we lacked the pharmacology to do so. We will use genetic circadian models to investigate the specificity of this approach. We will also demonstrate that this strategy is vital using a pre-clinical model and state-of-the-art imaging relevant to humans. This is a unique and direct pharmacological approach to limit infarct expansion and remodelling after mI/R, can be given alongside conventional therapies, and is effective for improving outcomes.

column36: Subchondral Bone Properties and their Association with Pain and Joint Deterioration in Postmenopausal Women with Knee Osteoarthritis and Varying Risk for Fractures
column37: According to the World Health Organization, osteoarthritis is 4 times as prevalent as strokes and heart disease combined. Knee osteoarthritis patients develop lesions in the bones of their knees, which have been linked to pain. However, their presence already indicates more advanced disease. One reason why pain is elevated in those with bone lesions is the buildup of pressure in marrow, triggering pain receptors. This phenomenon may be linked to micro damage in bone due to weak bones under normal loads or normal bones under high loads. While knee osteoarthritis has been linked to obesity, a condition associated with high loads, as many as 50% of patients are not obese and have normal loads. Postmenopausal women with elevated fracture risk may be at risk of having micro damage to knee bones. In fact, many non-obese individuals with knee osteoarthritis are postmenopausal women. While no tools have been developed to directly measure pressure in bone, the laws of physics indicate that pressure in a fluid is related to its viscosity and the speed of flow. In the proposed study of postmenopausal women 50-85 years of age diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis, investigators will estimate marrow fluid thickness by looking at its density and by measuring how fast fluids flow in and out of knee bones using imaging. These pieces of information will be linked to knee pain and function measured by questionnaires and examined in the context of fracture risk and osteoporosis. These correlates of bone pressure will also be linked to cartilage volume, bone structure, and other disease-related measures. If these bone pressure-related measures relate to pain and disease features, they may be good candidates for treatment targets and for tracking recovery from knee osteoarthritis in postmenopausal women with elevated fracture risk. This study could also identify a subgroup of individuals with knee osteoarthritis who may need to be treated differently than others.

column36: Cortical contributions to visually-guided locomotion in the cat
column37: This project is designed to determine the contribution of one part of the cerebral cortex, known to be involved in the planning of voluntary movements (the premotor cortex) to the planning of visually-guided gait modifications. While locomotion is sometimes thought of as a relatively automatic behavior in which the major function is to produce rhythmical, alternating movements of the limbs, it is actually a highly complex activity requiring cognitive and voluntary control under natural circumstances. On uneven terrain, for example, decisions have to be made about where to make the next step and frequently one plans a sequence of steps to avoid an obstacle. Walking in the street, one must decide how to walk around objects and people and how and when to step on and off a curb. Even indoors, one must navigate the furniture and objects on the floor. These behaviours require processing of visual information about the environment and a means to integrate this information with the immediate and long-term locomotor goals of the subject and the state of the limbs at the time of making the decision (e.g. which limb is in stance and which in swing and how do I adjust gait to most efficiently. or quickly, step over that obstacle). In the current project, I intend to test the hypothesis that the premotor cortex contributes to several essential aspects of goal-directed locomotion, including: decision processes that determine which limb will step over an obstacle; determining the parameters of the gait modification (trajectory and/or muscle activation patterns); and in more complex circumstances determining the sequence of steps required to clear a series of obstacles (e.g. a boulder field on a walking trail).

column36: Combining bedside neuroimaging monitoring and clinical markers to enhance developmental screening in preterm infants born 29-36 weeks of gestational age
column37: Every year in Canada, 27,000 babies are born preterm between 29 and 36 weeks of gestational age. About a third will have developmental delay at 2 years. It is important to identify infants with developmental delay sooner rather than later so intervention to improve child development can be started as early as possible to maximise benefits. However, developmental delay is difficult to recognize for primary care physicians. Yet, specialized developmental follow-up for all is not cost-efficient. Therefore, the challenge is to target preterm infants at higher risk of developmental delay who will benefit the most from assessment and intervention by a specialized team. We propose a new developmental screening protocol that combines non-invasive clinical markers that reflect brain health from birth to 18 months to identify preterm infants at higher risk of developmental delay. To do so, we will recruit 235 infants born 29-36 weeks of gestational age at Sainte-Justine Hospital neonatal intensive care unit (Montreal, QC). These infants will go through our protocol which includes bedside measures of the brain level of oxygen, blood flow and electrical activity, physical neurological examination and parental questionnaires on child's developmental skills during infancy. These measures along with information on medical complications and socio-economic status will be used to predict whether the child has developmental delay at 2 years. This new developmental screening protocol will enhance the quality and efficiency of developmental follow-up for preterm children.

column36: Real-World Cost-Effectiveness of Direct Oral Anticoagulants in Atrial Fibrillation: A Canadian Health Technology Reassessment Study
column37: For more than 50 years, people suffering from atrial fibrillation (the most common type of cardiac arrhythmia) have been treated with a blood thinner called warfarin. Since 2009, a new type of drugs, called direct anticoagulants, is available to treat these patients. In large randomized controlled trials, those drugs (named dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban) have been shown to be as safe and effective as warfarin and subsequent economic evaluations derived from these trials have shown these drugs to be cost-effective compared to warfarin. Such positive results have led multiple drug insurance plans, both in Canada and abroad, to reimburse direct anticoagulants when prescribed by a patient's treating physician. However, even if these economic evaluations were derived from robust large randomized controlled trials, differences between the randomized controlled trial and real-world settings, mainly the potential for less than perfect adherence and difference in patient populations, could alter (either positively or negatively) the real-world value of direct anticoagulants in the Canadian setting. This proposed project specifically aims to examine this possibility as its main objective. In addition, this proposed project also aims to address significant gaps in knowledge regarding the appropriate methods to use when conducting real-world economic evaluations.

column36: Functional Roles and Therapeutic Potentials of Invariant NKT Cells in Sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening illness caused by a disproportionate host response to microbes. It is characterized by early, severe inflammation followed by impaired immunity to opportunistic infections. Successful treatment of sepsis may thus require a two-step approach, namely to prevent excessive inflammation in the early phase and to boost antimicrobial immunity in the later phase. Natural killer T (NKT) cells are a tiny but powerful subset of lymphocytes with a unique ability to recognize glycolipids (molecules composed of sugar and fat). Promptly after activation, NKT cells secrete large quantities of soluble molecules called cytokines that mediate cell-to-cell communications in the immune system. Importantly, NKT cells can be manipulated to produce cytokines that either promote or suppress inflammation. The proposed research will follow 4 Specific Objectives. Objective 1 will test how NKT cell depletion in mouse models of sepsis may affect host responses, morbidity and mortality. In Objective 2, we will use glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells in a "two-hit" experimental model that simulates early and late phases of sepsis. Mice will be treated sequentially with anti- and pro-inflammatory glycolipids in the above phases, respectively, and will be evaluated for their ability to clear secondary infections. In Objective 3, we will generate mice that harbor either the entire human immune system or human NKT cells. "Humanized" mice will be rendered septic and treated with glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells. In Objective 4, we will obtain blood samples from septic patients shortly after presentation and shortly after resolution of their symptoms. Immune cells will be isolated, exposed to NKT cell stimuli and subjected to functional analyses. Collectively, the proposed studies will reveal the role of mouse and human NKT cells in sepsis, and also importantly hold the promise of introducing new and effective treatments for this dangerous and potentially fatal illness.

column36: Identity and in vitro expansion of human spermatogonial stem cells
column37: Recent research progress has made many types of cancer curable. This development led to a new situation where the post-cancer quality of life became a significant concern for cancer patients. Preservation of the ability to have children draws a particular interest in the patients, and their partners and families. For male patients, the only approach to protect their fertility is currently sperm banking. This approach, however, is not applicable to boys before puberty. Thus, childhood cancer patients face a significant risk of infertility, long before they are ready to make decisions about childbearing and household formation, which also places burdens on their parents. An emerging concept of therapeutic approach to this problem is based on sperm-making stem cells. These cells continuously produce millions of sperm everyday throughout life after puberty. Although sperm production is not fully functional in prepubertal boys, these sperm-producing stem cells do exist from the time of birth. Thus, these cells can be harvested and freeze-stored before cancer therapy, and transplanted back to the patients afterwards when they are ready to form a family. This scheme has been feasible and routinely operational in mice; yet, research on sperm-producing stem cells in humans has seen only a very limited extent of progress. The proposed research addresses the key elements that have been the obstacle to the advancement of our knowledge about sperm-producing stem cells in humans and technical development for their clinical use - what are the cells' markers and how can we amplify these cells?

column36: Pharmacogenetics of Methadone Maintenance Treatment Response
column37: Opioids are commonly used medications for pain but have very high liability for misuse and addiction. There are also street opioids such heroin and the deadly fentanyl and carfentanil. Canada is the second highest opioid consumer in the world and is facing a public health crisis with opioid addiction (opioid use disorder (OUD)) and death. There are relatively few treatment options for OUD and the most common is a substitution with methadone (methadone maintenance treatment, MMT), a synthetic opioid. However, MMT outcomes vary greatly, with the average patient receiving MMT for multiple years and many continuing to use opioids while on MMT. Furthermore, MMT itself carries significant health risks, including high rates of death. There is preliminary evidence that differences in MMT response are partially determined by the individual genetic makeup. Identifying how genes affect the response to methadone has the potential to substantially improve the opioid addiction treatment outcomes via a precision medicine approach. Toward this end, the proposed study will leverage innovations in genomic approaches to systematically examine individual variation in MMT response in a large sample of opioid addiction MMT patients. Our hypothesis is that MMT outcomes are significantly determined by genes that can inform future treatment decisions and the study's fundamental goal is to rigorously test this hypothesis using multiple cutting edge methodologies.

column36: Physiology and biochemistry of small regulatory RNAs
column37: Bacterial resistance to antibiotics has become a global medical concern as shown by recent reports on the rise of highly drug resistant bacterial strains. Although this resistance was predictable, research to identify new antibiotics or cellular drug target has dropped drastically. Furthermore, many of the most commonly used and often last resort antibiotics have debilitating side effects. In stark contrast, we now appreciate that microbes in human microbiomes play crucial roles in maintaining good health. It is now clear that commensal bacteria in the intestine of mammals accomplish many beneficial functions. Although symbiotic bacteria and mammals have co-evolved and adapted to each other, the ecological niche offered by the host is plagued with environmental insults, to which the bacteria need to adapt rapidly and continuously. In response to stressful environment, bacteria express small regulatory RNAs to coordinate gene expression and adapt to various stress. Our recent work with small regulatory RNAs strongly suggest there is a large amount of unknown yet significant RNA-RNA interactions within bacterial cells. These interactions might regulate virulence and pathogenicity as well as antibiotic resistance. We will map the global RNA-RNA interactions quantitatively within the model bacterium E. coli as well as the major human pathogen Salmonella. Concurrently with this long-term goal, we will investigate the most promising RNA-RNA interactions to establish novel mechanisms of gene expression. We already have established the extended interactome of a few specific sRNAs in E. coli using a novel approach that we developed in the lab. Deciphering the most critical RNA-based regulations (including sRNA-mRNA, mRNA-mRNA, tRNA-mRNA), in bacterial cells. New RNA-RNA interactions are creating specific targets to test novel RNA-based therapies for medical doctors, pharmaceutical companies and drug developers.

column36: Access to Recovery with Assistive Technology Devices
column37: There are currently no assistive technology applications (Apps) for culturally-centered substance addiction treatment supports available in Canada. Recent Canadian culturally rooted substance addictions research supports the health and wellness of Indigenous peoples, contributes to cultural renewal, and highlights awareness of the link between colonialism and substance addiction. In addition, quantitative North American evidence has validated that Indigenous culture increases wellness for Indigenous people in the domains of mental, emotional, spiritual, and physical well-being. Thus, this project aims to understand how assistive technology devices (i.e. iPad or smart phone) can be utilized to increase access to culturally-centered substance addiction treatment support for individuals and families, particularly for those who live in rural and Northern areas. This community-based research project that will include qualitative and quantitative data, reflects the principle of two-eyed seeing (draws on strengths of Indigenous and Western knowledge) and prioritizes 'culture' as intervention in substance addiction treatment that promotes a holistic model of health and wellness as outlined in the Cultural Responsiveness Framework (CRF); a framework tool that everyone can access, as the CRF aims to build capacity within mainstream health systems to gain a better understanding of First Nations culture. This project is particularly relevant to the health and well-being of Metis, First Nations, and Inuit and non-Indigenous individuals (and their families) who have both intellectual disabilities and substance addiction issues. Globally, assistive technology device-based mainstream substance addiction treatment interventions have begun to demonstrate to be cost-efficient, when compared with counselor-facilitated substance addiction treatment methods; but also appear to be as effective in the engagement and treatment of patients with substance addiction issues.

column36: Unconventional NMDA Receptor Signalling in Neocortical Plasticity
column37: Few would probably dispute that one of the most important functions of the brain is learning and memory. If you open up any modern neuroscience textbook, you will learn that NMDA receptors are critical for memory formation in the brain. It is therefore perhaps not so surprising that these receptors have been implicated in devastating neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. In recent years, however, its become clear that our understanding of NMDA receptors is incomplete. For example, they are sometimes located on transmitting instead of receiving side of neuronal connections, where they cannot function according to the standard textbook view on how learning in the brain operates. Furthermore, they sometimes signal metabotropically, i.e. in the absence of depolarising neuronal activation, which completely changes how neuroscientists think about their function. This proposal will explore tow unorthodox modes of NMDA receptor signalling: on the transmitting side, and metabotropically. This is a virtual blank on the map, and must be understood to treat major neurological pathologies such as Alzheimer's and epilepsy.

column36: Quantitative ultrasound techniques for diagnosis of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
column37: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is the most common liver disease in Western countries, due in large part to its association with type 2 diabetes and obesity. The more advanced form of this disease is known as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). If left untreated, NASH can evolve to cirrhosis, the late stage of fibrosis. Once cirrhosis is established, patients are at increased risk of developing gastrointestinal bleeding, liver cancer and liver failure that may require transplantation. Fatty liver disease is difficult to diagnose because symptoms can be vague. In some cases, the liver may already be damaged without any symptoms. Furthermore, blood tests cannot be used to definitely establish a clear diagnosis. A liver biopsy is currently needed to diagnose the severity of fatty liver disease but this is usually not indicated in asymptomatic patients. This procedure requires the insertion of a needle inside the liver to remove a small piece of tissue for examination under microscope. Liver biopsy is an invasive procedure with a small risk of major complications such as bleeding in 0.5% of cases. It is also affected by sub-optimal sampling leading to diagnostic errors. Ultrasound is optimum for screening patients with or without symptoms because it is a safe and widely available technology to scan the whole liver. Members of our team have developed advanced ultrasound techniques that provide unique information not possible with state-of-the-art techniques. Unlike liver biopsy, these techniques would be applicable even in asymptomatic patients because it is non-invasive. This research proposal proposes a novel approach for diagnosis of NASH and will be the first study to measure individual components of NASH (fat, inflammation and fibrosis) with quantitative ultrasound (QUS) scores. This study is timely because NASH is the second leading cause of liver transplantation in North America and is predicted to become the leading indication in the near future.

column36: Targeting vulnerabilities in SMARCA4-deficient lung cancers
column37: Cancer is a heterogeneous disease. Distinct subtypes of cancers from the same primary site of origin can be defined by their unique molecular pathological features. Consequently, cancer therapy is shifting towards strategies aimed at genes specific to each patient, where mutated cancer-causing genes in tumors are targeted by highly selective inhibitors. These drugs are often very effective and have minimal side effects as normal tissues do not harbor the cancer-causing mutations, which are being targeted. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer and is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in Canada. NSCLC consists of different subtypes characterized by distinct cancer-causing mutations. For subtypes with mutations activating genes such as EGFR (10-35%) or ALK (3-7%), there are potent drugs that target these activated gene products and have significantly improved patient survival. In contrast, 10-37 % of NSCLCs are deficient in SMARCA4, a known tumor suppressor gene lost in many cancer types and which to this date remains undruggable. Therefore, effective treatment of these patients remains an unmet clinical challenge. In this proposal, we will first exploit a molecular weakness of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs. We have previously uncovered a vulnerability of SMARCA4 loss in an ovarian cancer subtype, which can be targeted using an FDA-approved drug originally developed for treating breast cancers. To extend our findings to NSCLCs, we will use a variety of model systems, including cell culture, mouse preclinical cancer models, and tumor samples from lung cancer patients. Independently, we will use powerful genetic tools to identify novel vulnerabilities of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs that can be exploited therapeutically. Our goal is to provide potential treatment strategies to treat SMARCA4-deficient NSCLCs and provide a clinical benefit for cancer patients.

column36: Interrogation of genome editing applications for the treatment of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a devastating neuromuscular disorder with no cure available. Up to 70% patients carry large deletions in the DMD gene resulting in the absence of dystrophin, an integral muscle protein. Recent advances in genome engineering technologies have the potential to develop into life-saving therapies for this condition. Building on our previous successes we have developed several gene editing strategies applicable for correcting DMD deletions and two mouse models to test these approaches. Specifically, Objective 1 is designed to assess efficacy and safety of repairing a variety of DMD-causing deletions in patient cells using different genome editing systems in order to identify a best candidate for animal studies. The overall goal of the Objective 2 is to perform detailed genetic, biochemical and functional characterization of two novel mouse models with large DMD deletions: del52-54 and del52-55. Finally, in the Objective 3, we will test the hypothesis that disease severity in the newly generated DMD mouse models can be improved via in vivo genome editing using adeno associate virus (AAV) as a delivery vehicle. We anticipate that the development and refinement of therapeutic strategies described in this project will lead to efficient expression of dystrophin to restore muscle strength and function in our newly generated animal models, recapitulating large DMD mutations found in patients. The results of this project will provide data that can be directly translated into large animal models of DMD and subsequently into clinical trials in patients with deletions in the DMD gene. Furthermore, these pre-clinical proof of concept studies will pave the way for development of therapeutic approaches for other inherited conditions caused by large genomic rearrangements.

column36: HIV-1 Nef-Host Interactions Mediating Immune Evasion and Pathogenesis
column37: Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 (HIV-1) is the human virus responsible for Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS). Specifically, the coordinated activity of multiple HIV-1 proteins results in infected patients progressing from the asymptomatic phase to AIDS. Interestingly, the HIV-1 protein Nef has long been considered a major factor contributing to disease progression even though Nef lacks any known enzymatic activity. Instead, Nef binds to human proteins to wreak havoc inside the infected immune cell. This proposal will study interactions between Nef and host proteins. Furthermore, the precise details on how these interactions mediate disease progression and the evasion of the immune surveillance system will be defined. To accomplish this, we will combine our expertise in the movement of proteins within cells and super resolution imaging techniques to define the specific localization of these protein complexes within infected cells. We will also study these molecular pathways in a patient cohort of HIV-1 infected individuals to assess how these Nef interactions mediate immune evasion and disease progression in patients. These studies will provide novel information on new interactions that can be targeted to inhibit HIV-1. Indeed, we believe that performing these studies will lead to the future design of novel drugs and therapeutic agents that will benefit patients infected with HIV-1.

column37: Human chromosome ends are protected from damage by a stretch of repetitive DNA sequence known as telomeres. In healthy mortal cells, telomere DNA is gradually shortened during successive rounds of replication as a cell ages, and ultimately instructs cells to naturally terminate. In cancerous cells the enzyme telomerase ensures maintenance of a stable telomere length and therefore enables the indefinite growth and uncontrolled division characteristic of tumor formation. Active telomerase is diagnostic of cancer progression, as has been identified in the vast majority of malignant cancers. In this proposal, we seek to understand the regulation of telomerase by enzymes known as helicases that exert their effects through prevention of proper telomerase assembly. We will use an integrated experimental approach involving high-resolution structural biology, biochemical analysis, and functional methodologies. Our work aims to provide a template for the rational design of therapeutics to attenuate telomerase activity.

column36: Limiting late effects following pediatric cranial radiation
column37: Recent decades have seen a substantial improvement in the survival of children with brain cancer, the second most common cancer in children. Patients are now living into their adult years. Unfortunately, the side effects from brain tumour treatment frequently affect brain development. Survivors suffer a progressive decline in mental capacity and achieve lower levels of education, household income and full-time employment. These debilitating mental side effects impact quality of life and are strongly linked with radiation therapy. After radiation, the brain experiences loss of cells, inflammation, and reduced capacity to make new cells. We have shown that manipulation of these effects alters impact of radiation on the brain, with the exciting result that brain development can be partially restored. In this proposal, we will determine if it is possible to induce such improvements by drug treatment or lifestyle changes, so that normal brain development can be achieved after radiation. To do so, we will systematically test 11 candidate treatments in a mouse model, measuring brain growth after radiation using magnetic resonance imaging. First, each treatment will be tested individually. Next, we will test the best treatments in combination. Finally, for the most-promising treatments, we will determine how treatment affects tumour response to CRT, and measure the cognitive and behavioural benefits. At its conclusion, this work will establish a strategy appropriate for restoring brain development after radiation in children. Treatments have been selected for ease of translation (9 of 11 treatments are already used in patients for other medical conditions or are in clinical trials), so that promising results can be moved quickly to childhood cancer survivors. Ultimately, our goal is to ensure that cancer survivors have the same opportunities and quality of life as their cancer-free peers.

column36: Age-associated inflammation alters myeloid cell development and function
column37: Our immune system changes as we age. As an example, we begin to produce more of some kinds of white blood cells (monocytes and neutrophils) and less of others (B and T cells). Since monocytes and neutrophils are required to protect us from infection, you might think that this would protect older adults from infections, but what actually happens is that these cells don't mature properly and enter into the bloodstream prematurely. These immature monocytes don't help fight infection but actually make some infections worse. Furthermore, these immature monocytes produce a lot of inflammation which also has a negative impact on our health as we age. The purpose of this proposal is to determine why we start to produce more monocytes as we get older, to determine why these monocytes do not mature properly and to identify ways in which we might be able to restore this process. To do this we will collect blood from young and older adults and assess how maturity decreases with age and determine whether this immaturity correlates with levels of inflammation. Specifically we believe that a molecule called TNF might be involved because when we aged mice that did not have TNF, they did not have any changes in the development or function of their monocytes with age. To determine if this is the case in humans, we have collected samples from humans who are undergoing anti-TNF therapy. We predict that when their TNF is high, their monocytes will be less mature and when their TNF goes down due to their therapy, their monocytes will become normal. We will use our unique colony of old mice (18-22 mo), including old mice that don't make TNF (called TNF knockout mice) to determine which cells make this TNF. The long-term goal of this project is to find novel ways to keep us healthier as we get older. Because monocytes protect us from infections but can also contribute to diseases that increase with age (e.g. cardiovascular disease), we hope these findings will have broad applications.

column36: Inference-Based Cognitive Therapy versus Exposure and Response Prevention for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A 16-Session Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a highly disabling psychiatric illness, characterized by obsessional thoughts that cause patients to perform time-consuming and distressing compulsive rituals. Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is a first-line psychological treatment of choice, which requires patients to face their fears by being exposed to feared stimuli. ERP has been shown to reduce symptoms among those who comply with treatment. However, there is still a significant portion of patients that do not improve, especially those who firmly believe their obsessions are realistic and reasonable (i.e. OCD with Overvalued Ideation). Also, a large proportion of patients refuse the treatment or drop out during treatment due to the distress provoked by ERP. That leaves at most 3-4 out of 10 people with OCD who benefit from ERP, and even then, residual symptoms often remain, or symptoms eventually reappear after treatment. One evidence-based approach to the treatment of OCD, termed inference-based cognitive therapy (IBCT) has been shown to be as effective as ERP with the potential to overcome the limitations of ERP. Since IBCT is a cognitive approach, the treatment does not require exposure to feared stimuli and likely more tolerable for patients with OCD. Also, there is evidence that IBCT is more effective than ERP for those with overvalued ideation, since it directly targets the distorted reasoning that is responsible for the intensity and persistence of the obsession. The current study aims to directly compare ERP with this promising evidence-based cognitive therapy, which is expected to be significantly more effective for those with overvalued ideation, as well as significantly more tolerable with lower rates of treatment refusal, drop-out and higher treatment satisfaction. The project is designed to maximize potential beneficial health outcomes and offer a new evidence-based treatment option for the large proportion of patients unable to benefit from ERP.

column37: Phosphate and vitamin D are critical for many physiological functions including skeletal development, mineral balance, energy metabolism, and proper nerve and muscle function. The kidney is a major player in the maintenance of the body's phosphate and vitamin D balance, by virtue of its ability to regulate: (i) the amounts of phosphorus it reclaims before it gets lost in the urine based on the body's needs, and (ii) the production and thereby the levels of vitamin D in blood, important for the absorption of phosphorus from the intestine. These processes at the level of the kidney are very tightly regulated mainly by two hormones: parathyroid hormone (PTH), and the more recently-identified fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Genetic diseases of phosphate and vitamin D metabolism with have high FGF23 and low vitamin D levels in the blood have been described. For the most common form, XLH, it is estimated as high as 1 in 10,000 newborns are affected. Children with XLH have rickets (bone deformities including short stature and bow or knock-leggedness) that progress to poor skeletal mineralization with soft, brittle bones, and calcification of tendons and ligaments in adulthood. Studies proposed in this application, a continuation of our previous work funded by the KFOC and published recently in a prestigious clinical research journal, aims to use transgenic mice and molecular biology techniques to understand the mechanism by which high levels of FGF23 affects bone development by altering the concentration of vitamin D locally in bone. We aim to show that, whether by genetics or by pharmacotherapy, this process can be altered to allow better bone formation to take place. Findings arising from this work will help uncover previously unrecognized targets and strategies for the treatment of patients with these genetic disorders.

column36: Metformin in Women with Type 2 Diabetes in Pregnancy (MiTy) Trial: A randomized controlled trial
column37: The incidence of type 2 diabetes is rising at a remarkable rate, and with it we see a rise in type 2 diabetes in pregnancy. Insulin is the standard of care for the management of women with type 2 diabetes in pregnancy. However, despite treatment with insulin, these women continue to face high rates of poor maternal and fetal outcomes. Mothers have high blood pressure, preeclampsia, high rates of cesarean section, while infants have preterm birth, low blood sugar, they are large, can get stuck during delivery leading to birth injury, and often require the NICU. Metformin is an oral hypoglycemic agent presently being used in patients with type 2 diabetes outside of pregnancy and in other pregnant populations, with some benefit. Our aim is to see whether the addition of metformin to standard therapy of insulin alone, will improve these poor pregnancy outcomes by conducting a multicentre, randomized trial, randomizing 500 pregnant women with type 2 diabetes to receive either metformin or placebo, in addition to their usual insulin regimen. We hypothesize that metformin use, when added to the treatment with insulin, will improve pregnancy outcomes by reducing high maternal blood sugars, high maternal insulin doses, excessive maternal weight gain and pregnancy-induced high blood pressure, all of which should reduce poor outcomes in the baby. Our primary outcome will be the reduction of a composite outcome, which will include pregnancy loss, preterm birth, birth injury, respiratory distress, low blood sugar, and neonatal intensive care admissions over 24 hours. Our MiTy Kids study (separately funded) aims to follow these children for up to 2 years of age, to see if metformin reduces the risk of childhood obesity. This study will provide critical insight into an important treatment, which will impact standard of care and clinical practice, with the potential to benefit the health of pregnant mothers with diabetes and their children, immediately and in the long-term.

column36: Role of a lipid hydrolase TGH in hepatic fat storage and lipoprotein secretion
column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a major health problem that is caused by extra fat building up in a person's liver cells. Worldwide, this disease affects about 30% of the adult population and over 70% of people with obesity. The health risk for people with NAFLD is that this disease can progress to more serious problems: -inflammation and swelling of their liver, called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) -normal liver tissue being replaced by non-living scar tissue, called cirrhosis -end-stage liver disease and liver failure, the most common reason for needing a liver transplant Having NAFLD or NASH also places people at much greater risk for type 2 diabetes, heart disease and end-stage kidney disease. Today, we have no effective treatments for NASH. My research team has discovered that a protein called TGH affects distribution and storage of fat. Our experiments show that TGH has profound effects on circulating fat in the blood and on development of NAFLD. We showed that reducing the amount TGH in mice protects the liver from developing NAFLD and NASH and improves insulin signaling. Because TGH regulates how fat is stored in the liver, this protein could be a good target for drugs to prevent or treat NAFLD and NASH. My research aims to find out how TGH regulates the amounts of fat that people store in the liver and in the blood. Understanding the mechanisms that this protein uses to regulate fat storage may lead to new treatments for NAFLD/NASH and diseases triggered by NAFLD/NASH.

column36: Medically at-risk drivers: The road to developing evidence-based fitness to drive guidelines
column37: With the aging population also comes an increase in age-related deficits (e.g. decreased vision, slowing of cognitive functions), as well as an increase in age-related medical conditions (i.e. cognitive impairment/dementia, Parkinson's disease, stroke), all of which can affect safe driving. These trends present a significant public health concern given that older adults are disproportionately (per mile driven) involved in collisions resulting in serious injury and death. Hence, determining the most effective means to identify and assess medically at-risk drivers is critical given the rapid growth in this segment of the driving population. Together with the Ministry of Transportation Ontario, the Societe de L'Assurance Automobile du Quebec (SAAQ) and the Saskatchewan Driving Licensing and Registration Office (SGI), this project entails the development of an online, web-based repository (e-repository) where data from comprehensive driving evaluations of medically at-risk drivers are captured and tracked accordingly. By establishing a large-scale database, we will be able to track drivers already referred to a specialized driving assessment centre in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan and use this data to examine the referral process and the relationship between functional abilities, on-road driving performance (i.e., pass/fail), and crashes/violations (from driving records). Ultimately, we will develop evidence based tools to assess fitness to drive which will be translated into policy and practice guidelines for health care professionals and government agencies.

column36: Novel therapies to augment neurological benefits of cellular therapies for traumatic spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a leading cause of permanent neurological disabilities affecting over 2.5 million individuals worldwide. In Canada, there are over 86,000 patients who are afflicted with lifelong consequences of SCI with approximately 4,200 new cases each year. The lifetime medical cost of each SCI patient is estimated at 1.6 to 3 million dollars. Thus, SCI has a profound impact on patients, their caregivers, and the healthcare system. Currently, there is no effective treatment for SCI and new therapies are needed to allow neurological improvement in patients. Extensive research by our group and others show that transplantation of neural stem cells offers tremendous possibility for SCI repair. Indeed, based on these experimental discoveries, neural stem cell transplantation has moved to clinical trials in recent years. Initial outcomes of these trials indicate that while neural stem cells are safe and promising for treatment of SCI, their benefit for neurological recovery of patients is only modest. We have made the same observation in our experimental evaluations, establishing a need for combinatorial therapies to augment the functional outcomes of current cellular therapies. To this end, we have discovered new therapeutic targets with the potential to harness the regenerative capacity of neural stem cells for repairing the injured spinal cord. We have identified that formation of a glia scar around the lesion and increased production of inhibitory molecules in the scar limit the benefits of neural stem cell transplantation. We show that inhibiting these factors facilitates the longterm survival of stem cells and their abilities for tissue regeneration. We are currently investigating several aspects of these strategies and importantly their potential in improving functional recovery in an animal model that clinically reflects human SCI. Our goal is to develop effective regenerative medicine strategies for improving the quality of life in SCI patients.

column36: Altered hepatic retinoid homeostasis in the initiation and progression of alcoholic liver disease
column37: Vitamin A is an essential part of our diet and is used by the body in many ways, including vision, immunity and reproduction. The liver acts as a warehouse for vitamin A: storing it and releasing it for use in other parts of the body. Vitamin A is also important in maintaining liver health, and it has been suggested that a disruption in this role promotes the development of liver disease. Alcohol abuse is a major cause of preventable death and gives rise to a significant disease burden in Canada. The main organ affected by drinking too much alcohol is the liver, with a well-described disease response ranging from fat accumulation (steatosis), to inflammation (hepatitis), scarring (fibrosis and cirrhosis) and ultimately liver failure. According to the Canadian Liver Foundation, approximately 1 in 12 Canadians drink heavily, and thousands of Canadians die every year because of alcoholic liver disease, making it a national research priority. Moreover, heavy drinking rates are double for First Nations people living on Reserves, representing a population at increased risk of alcohol-related disease. The research described in this proposal aims to establish that alcohol disturbs the way vitamin A works in the liver, contributing to hepatic disease. Through a series of complementary experiments, we will determine the mechanism through which alcohol disturbs vitamin A function at two points in the disease process: 1) the initial step of fat accumulation, and 2) the formation of scar tissue, representing the worsening of liver disease. This research will provide a better understanding of how alcohol causes liver disease by disrupting vitamin A function. The new knowledge generated by this research may be translated into improved care for heavy drinkers at risk of alcoholic liver disease by providing ways to prevent its formation, or stop it from worsening. This knowledge will also provide new insight into how altered vitamin A function contributes to other human diseases.

column36: Thermosensitive Liposome Formulation of Vinorelbine in Combination with MR-Guided High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Mediated Hyperthermia: An Innovative Approach to Treatment of Rhabdomyosarcoma
column37: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents, with the majority of cases arising in children under the age of 10 years. Following the successful treatment of the initial disease, recurrence manifests in approximately one-third of patients, with about 80% of recurrences localized at the primary tumor site. Unfortunately, with current treatments, the 5-year survival rate for these patients is only 17-28 %. In addition, due to the characteristic toxicities associated with some anti-cancer drugs for RMS, treatment of these young patients can lead to a series of long-term health complications in adult life including neurological and cardiac disorders. The current research project describes the development of a nanoparticle (termed a liposome) containing the anti-cancer drug, vinorelbine. This drug works by preventing the cancer cells from dividing and ultimately leads to cell death. Liposomes containing various drugs are currently used in the treatment of several cancers. Our liposome nanoparticles have been specially designed such that the drug is released when the temperature exceeds that of normal body temperature. We will achieve localized release of the drug at the tumor site by increasing the temperature of the tumor using an ultrasound machine. This technique will increase the amount of drug delivered specifically to the tumor site and therefore minimize drug exposure to normal tissues. We will also investigate whether the combination of vinorelbine and an increase in the temperature of the tumor has a greater tumor killing effect compared to vinorelbine alone. The potential benefits of this project for RMS patients are a greater killing effect of recurrent RMS tumors and a reduction in the short and long-term side effects, which are commonly associated with exposure of chemotherapy to normal tissues.

column36: Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction and Oxygen Sensitive Cardiac MRI in Women: A Novel Non-Invasive Diagnostic Tool
column37: Although more women than men die annually of coronary artery disease (CAD), nearly one half of women presenting with chest pain are found to have non-obstructive CAD (NoCAD). Historically, these patients were often reassured without consideration for diagnostic or treatment options. More recently, evidence has shown that nearly 50% of women with chest pain and NoCAD have occult disease in the small vessels of the heart, referred to as coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD), which has been shown to carry a heightened risk for future cardiovascular events. Current characterization of patients with chest pain syndromes and NoCAD rely on invasive testing that lack standardized protocols and use pharmacological agents including adenosine, which are often poorly tolerated in patients. This has limited the use of these diagnostic tests in the evaluation of patients with NoCAD, leaving many patients with CMD undiagnosed and untreated. Recently, oxygen sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (OS-CMR) using a combination of breathing manoeuvres has been shown to be capable of identifying microvascular changes in the heart in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Given the less invasive nature of this technique, we intend to study this novel diagnostic tool to assess its ability to detect CMD in women. We will also evaluate whether breathing manoeuvres during OS-CMR can detect CMD as accurately as with the administration of adenosine. We expect that our study will show that women with CMD will have inadequate oxygenation response to breathing manoeuvres that will be identified on OS-CMR. Additionally OS-CMR with breathing manoeuvres will be able to detect CMD as accurately as adenosine. Our results will support the use of OS-CMR as a non-invasive diagnostic tool in the assessment of women with chest pain and NoCAD, which will allow physicians to better identify patients with CMD and provide the foundation for which future treatment can be studied.

column36: Treatment induced changes to bone quality: Impact on the skeletal stability of the metastatic spine
column37: Many malignant cancers can spread (i.e. metastasize) from their site of origin. A very common site of this spread is to the bone. The spine is the most common bone tissue affected. Diseased bones can cause pain and are at a greater risk for breaking (i.e. fracture). Metastatic disease in the bony spine can present as bone destroying (osteolytic), bone forming (osteoblastic) or as a mixture of the two (mixed), but all demonstrate an increased risk of fracture. In the presence of cancer, we have shown that differences exist in the quality of the remaining bone (in both its mineral and organic components) leading to compromised material and mechanical behaviour. This characterization has formed a robust foundation upon which we propose to evaluate the impact of systemic and localized cancer treatments on bone quality in the metastatic spine. This research will elucidate the complex interactions of multimodal cancer treatment on bone quality and fracture risk in the spine using state-of-the-art medical imaging, experimental and computational methods. Our work will link preclinical and clinical data sets to enable translation of this knowledge towards informing clinical practice. The ability to accurately determine the impact of treatments on structural integrity will provide an important foundation upon which to direct new and existing local and systemic treatments for spinal metastatic disease.
