column36: Mechanisms of Deregulated Autophagy in Age-Related Macular Degeneration
column37: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of blindness in adults over fifty. But little is known about the drivers of new blood vessels that invade the retina in blinding AMD. We do know however that abnormal blood lipid levels, oxidative damage, and mutations in mitochondria (the cell's powerhouse) are associated with AMD, as well as disrupted autophagy. Triggered in part by starvation, autophagy helps recycle material inside the cell that can then be used as fuel to produce energy. Although autophagy is abnormal in AMD, we still don't know if it is a cause or a consequence of the disease. We recently provided the first evidence that fuel deficient photoreceptor could drive AMD-like blood vessel formation. We propose to use that model of starved photoreceptors to explore the role of autophagy in AMD. Preliminary data in our AMD model suggest that starved photoreceptors fail to initiate autophagy, pointing to a paradox that will be exploited to investigate how autophagy contributes to AMD. We have identified a retinal lipid receptor that may be involved in the regulation of autophagy in photoreceptors, offering a novel therapeutic target for AMD. Findings may, therefore, confirm a causal role of autophagy as a driving force of AMD and uncover a new therapeutic opportunity.

column36: Of Worm and Man: Using C. elegans to uncover genetic modifiers for rare human disorders
column37: High-throughput sequencing has accelerated the pace at which gene-disease associations are established. However, we need to start addressing the next challenge: why two individuals with the same rare disease-causing variant may have different clinical presentation of the disease? Genetic modifiers are factors that can either alleviate or exacerbate the severity of the disease-causing variants. Identification of such modifiers provides important information about the biological functions of human disease genes and mechanistic role they play in the development of the disease. This in turn allows for better disease outcome prediction, planned prevention protocols and development of targeted treatments. Complexity of human biology makes it difficult to address this challenge effectively; however, fundamental aspects of human disease had been in past and will be in future efficiently addressed through analysis of orthologous genes using experimentally tractable model organisms. The goal of my research is to combine powers of unbiased mutagen-induced modifier screens using Caenorhabditis elegans model and whole genome sequencing (WGS) in order to accelerate discovery of new disease-associated genes, modifiers of known disease-associated genes and potential Orphan drug targets. To reach these goals, I will: (1) isolate modifiers by performing forward genetic screens on orthologous genes implicated in human rare disorders; (2) identify molecular basis of modifiers using WGS, state-of-the-art bioinformatics and molecular genetics techniques, and (3) characterize the phenotypes and mode of action of the genetic modifiers. This research is of high importance as it will establish C. elegans as a model organism for systematic high-throughput heritable genetic modifier screens with high potential for direct impact on diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of rare diseases, in particular the ones with no treatment options (currently >95% of rare diseases).

column36: Modeling gene expression trajectories in the human developing brain: applications to pediatric brain tumors
column37: Brain function and development depend on precise control of gene expression. Thousands of genes must be finely regulated both in spatial and temporal dimensions to achieve proper specialization of brain regions. Moreover, this regulation must be sustained throughout the long lifespan of brain cells, which in many cases is measured in years. Defects in genes affecting this regulation thus, are the basis of a large proportion of brain disease, including, in particular, childhood brain tumors. Using large-scale datasets profiling gene expression in the human developing brain, and novel datasets we will generate at the single-cell level, we will provide a comprehensive map of gene expression switches that may be altered in childhood brain tumors. We will develop computational methods to integrate this data with a large collection of samples derived from patients. This will allow us to identify developmental pathways altered in these aggressive tumors, which may enable identification of novel targets for therapeutic intervention.

column36: CYCLE: An international, multi-centre, randomized clinical trial of early in-bed cycling for mechanically ventilated patients
column37: Background: Critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are the sickest patients in hospital, and need advanced life support. People who survive their critical illness are typically very weak and disabled. Over half of them have severe leg weakness impairing their quality of life for up to 5 years. In-bed cycling uses a special bicycle that attaches to the hospital bed, allowing patients on life support to gently exercise their legs in the ICU. Objectives: The main goal of this research program is to see if patients who need a breathing machine recover faster if they receive early in-bed cycling than if they do not. Methods: Adults who need a breathing machine in the ICU are eligible. Patients will receive 1 of 2 treatments: (1) early in-bed cycling 30 minutes per day, 5 days per week while they are in the ICU or (2) routine physiotherapy. Patients will be assigned to either treatment in a manner similar to flipping a coin. Participants will receive these treatments from physiotherapists for 30 minutes/day, for 5 days/week as long as they are in the ICU. Physiotherapists will also test participants' strength throughout the study. Outcomes: We will measure patients' muscle strength and function 3 days after they leave the ICU. We will ask patients to rate their quality of life after the ICU and at hospital discharge. Finally, we will assess the costs of offering in-bed cycling to these patients. Relevance: By 2026, the demand for ICU services in Canada will increase by 40% compared to 2011. More survivors will have disability after their time in ICU, and there is an urgent need to help them recover faster and be stronger. To-date, early in-bed cycling in the ICU has not been studied in terms of how it affects health issues important to patients (e.g. walking, quality of life). The CYCLE RCT is the largest trial ever done in this field, to help patients get as strong as possible while they are recovering from critical illness.

column36: Regulation and impact of productive AID targeting during antibody responses.
column37: Antibodies are a major component of the human immune system. A large repertoire of specialized cells named B-lymphocytes, each producing a different antibody, are constantly renewed to be able to detect any of innumerable and constantly evolving pathogens. The initial recognition of a pathogen, by the antibody on the surface of a B-lymphocyte, signals the onset of changes in the genes encoding the antibody, which will allow improving its affinity and effectivity to eliminate the infection. Most vaccination strategies rely on stimulating the B-lymphocytes that produce antibodies against known pathogens so that they expand and undergo the AID-mediated antibody improvements before any exposure to the actual pathogen. The genetic mechanisms that shape the antibodies and mediate immunity are initiated by an enzyme named AID. As a side effect of changing the antibody genes, AID can also cause collateral genetic damage. This can predispose to cancer or negatively affect the B-lymphocyte's ability to multiply, which is critical for the process of generating a protective response. We study the mechanisms that balance these beneficial and detrimental effects of AID. We investigate how AID reaches the genome and how much it works once there, which have a direct impact on the antibody response. On one side, these mechanisms need to allow sufficient AID activity to produce useful antibodies. On the other hand, they need to protect the genome from excessive damage. Our results would allow explaining the cause of immunodeficiency when the mechanisms we study do not work and enable manipulations for therapeutic applications. Salient examples would be to treat autoimmune diseases mediated by antibodies, boosting the efficacy of immunization in aged people, or enhancing vaccination to increase the chances of generating infrequent antibodies, such as those that neutralize rapidly evolving viruses.

column36: Practice patterns among early-career primary care physicians and workforce planning implications: a mixed methods study
column37: There are more family doctors in Canada then ever. Yet, patients still have trouble finding a family doctor and getting an appointment when they need one. Changes in how much family doctors work and what services they provide (for example, choosing to practice with a clinical specialty, in a walk-in clinic, or providing care in hospital, rather than traditional family medicine), may help explain the gap between the number of doctors and patient access to primary care. It is widely speculated that new primary care doctors are practicing differently than previous generations. We know there have always been differences between doctors starting their careers and those who are already established, but we do not know if these differences are actually growing. This project will use information from qualitative interviews with doctors, surveys of doctors, and data routinely collected as part of health care delivery in British Columbia, Ontario, and Nova Scotia to achieve several related objectives. First, we will use survey data and interviews to explore plans for practice among doctors training in family medicine and the choices they make as they start out in practice. We want to understand what values and preferences, including the type work, lifestyle, and financial considerations, shape plans and choices. Second, we will use health care data to compare practice patterns among new and established doctors. We will determine if any changes over time are unique to the most recent generation of family doctors, or if there have been changes over time across all family doctors. Finally, we will examine how opportunities available to doctors in each province align with their preferences. We will reach out to doctors and policymakers to explore what other opportunities might be chosen, if available, and consider what policy changes may be needed to make sure that patients can access the services they need.

column36: Understanding of the physiological role of membrane-type I matrix metalloproteinase in lipid metabolism
column37: Cardiovascular diseases are the number one killer in Canada. The current therapy for preventing and treating atherosclerosis (stiffening and blocking of arteries) uses statins to reduce levels of LDL (bad) cholesterol in the blood. Statins reduce cardiovascular events by 20% to 40%. A potentially more effective therapy was recently approved, using antibodies that block the action of the enzyme PCSK9. This enzyme interferes with removing LDL cholesterol from the blood. However, this is a costly strategy that requires injections of large amounts of antibody for clinical effectiveness, limiting the wide use of these drugs. Given that more than 50,000 strokes and 75,000 heart attacks occur in Canada every year, the need for new cardiovascular therapies is clear and urgent. Recently, we found that the protein MMP14 reduces the levels of a protein called the LDL receptor that is critical for clearing LDL cholesterol from the blood. Blocking the action of MMP14 increases levels of the LDL receptor and reduces LDL cholesterol in blood. In this project we will characterize MMP14 and determine how it works when it reduces levels of the LDL receptor. This basic knowledge will open up new opportunities for blocking MMP14 and reducing LDL cholesterol in blood. This knowledge can offer more effective and perhaps less expensive avenues to treat patients with increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

column36: Filamin actin-binding and titin-binding domains fulfill distinct functions in Z-disc cohesion
column37: The major architectural protein in cells is actin, and actin filaments play crucial roles in all cells. Filamin was one of the first actin-binding proteins characterized. It is a rod-like protein with a dimerization (self-association) domain at one end and an actin-binding domain at the other end. Filamin cross-links actin filaments into a loose meshwork in non-muscle cells. In muscle cells filamin function is not well understood, except that it localizes to Z-lines and causes severe muscle disorders when mutated. Here we propose to analyze the molecular and cell biological function of filamin in muscle cells using the fruit fly Drosophila as a model system. Our recent data indicate that filamin mutations have severe, but distinct muscle defects, depending on whether the actin-binding domain or the self-association domain of filamin is mutated. Our proposed biochemical and genetic experiments will provide insight into filamin binding partners and how they function together to enable muscle contractility. This in turn will also provide information on how filamin mutations cause muscle disorders in humans.

column37: More than 50% of women with schizophrenia become pregnant, and birth rates have been steadily rising since the early 1990s. column36: Functional interactions between myogenic factors and REST/NRSF in regulation of heterochromatin during skeletal muscle regeneration
column37: Adult stem cells are the drivers of tissue repair and regeneration. In skeletal muscle a rare population of Muscle Stem Cells, also called the Satellite Cells reside within muscle tissue in an undifferentiated state, poised to enter myogenic program upon injury or trauma. However, in patients with muscle-wasting diseases, such as those with muscular dystrophies and patients with age-related frailty, muscle regeneration and repair is severely compromised. Collectively, muscle-wasting diseases affect more than two million Canadians with elderly population suffering disproportionately due to loss of myogenic recovery with advancing age. Multiple lines of evidence suggest that satellite cells regenerative capacity declines in patients with muscle-wasting diseases. Epigenetic alterations such as histone modifications and DNA methylation play key roles in reprogramming of adult stem cells during disease progression such as those associated with aging. We have recently discovered that maintenance of muscle stem cell pool depends on the functional interaction between Myogenic Regulatory Factors (MRFs) and a chromatin modifier called REST/NRSF. In this project we aim to identify the mechanism by which the interaction between MRFs and REST regulate satellite cell function and skeletal muscle regeneration.

column36: Improvement of ICD Patient Selection Using 4D Cardiac Modelling and Machine Learning-Based Personalized Risk Prediction
column37: Each year 400,000 North Americans suffer sudden cardiac death (SCD), usually from a life threatening heart rhythm. One in five of us will die from SCD, often without any warning and where help is not available. An implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) is a special type of pacemaker that can prevent SCD. However, the current guidelines of who should get an ICD use only one measurement, the "ejection fraction" (EF), to decide if someone should or should not get one. Using this approach only 1 out of 10 patients getting an ICD actually get benefit, and more than 80% of patients who end up suffering SCD are never given one. Therefore, we must find better ways to figure out who should and should not be given an ICD. Our lab has been working for over 10 years to find features on picture of the heart that pick out people at highest risk of SCD. To date we have published 8 features that strongly predict this. We have now made a computer software that can automatically build a 4-dimensional heart model (beating 3D heart) from images taken with an MRI scanner. We believe this can find people at high risk of SCD. To do this we have partnered with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, a group of scientists that use approaches (similar to Google) to solve complex problems. We plan to teach a computer program, using a total of 1,500 MRI studies in patients sent for an ICD, what a "high risk" patient looks like. We will test the ability of this new software to predict if and when a new patient will suffer SCD. If successful, we will make this software available to the community to improve how we deliver ICDs to those patients who need them most. This work could therefore have a major impact by saving a larger number of lives in people with heart disease.

column36: Genome-scale discovery of mechanisms for modulating oncogenic and tumour suppressor microRNAs
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada - nearly one out of four deaths in Canada are due to cancer. Advances in cancer biology and genomics have revealed a wide range of cellular mechanisms that contribute to the development and progression of cancer, as well as mechanisms with the potential to slow down or stop the progress of cancer. Among these are a group of molecules encoded by the genome, called microRNAs. Previous research has repeatedly shown that modifying the activity of some microRNAs can inhibit the growth and even lead to the death of the cancer cell. A promising strategy against cancer, therefore, is to change the activity of such microRNAs so that the cancer cell behaviour is reversed. However, for the majority of these microRNAs, our knowledge of how to manipulate them in the cell is limited. Cellular pathways are highly interconnected, meaning that one component of the cell, for example a particular microRNA, can often be inhibited or activated by manipulating another component of the cell. In recent years, researchers have used genomic technologies such as RNA-sequencing to generate terabytes of data from experiments in which various cellular pathways and proteins are manipulated. Many of these manipulations may affect specific microRNAs - however, microRNA activity is not directly observable from the data generated by these experiments. We have recently developed unique and powerful computational methods that can infer the microRNA activity from the patterns hidden in these data, enabling us to mine the massive body of available datasets to find the manipulations that affect the activity of microRNAs. Using these novel computational methods followed by in-depth analyses and experimental validation, this project aims to provide a map of the cellular pathways and proteins that can be exploited to modify the activity of microRNAs, revealing new strategies for targeting the cancer cell.

column36: Understanding decision making in organ donation: a national study
column37: Transplantation is the only hope for survival for many patients with terminal heart, lung, liver, pancreas and kidney disease and often their only hope for survival. Families of potential organ donors play a central role in the consent process yet little is known about what determines whether or not they consent. Organ donation is a personal decision made by patients and/or their families. As a result, it is expected and appropriate that some families refuse. Amid continuing need for organs and the declining number of organ donors, it is critical that we investigate the factors that influence the decision-making of relatives of potential organ donors. We will investigate relatives of potential organ donor patients' understanding of the process leading to organ donation and their views, beliefs, and motivation for their decisions in regard to organ donation. First, relatives of patients who are potential organ donors will be interviewed to explore their experience, values and beliefs regarding the decision-making leading to organ donation and potential factors viewed to affect their organ donation decision. Second, we will conduct a national telephone survey based on our findings in the first step with patient relatives to test which clinical and behavioural factors are associated with end-of-life decisions in regard to organ donation. This study will identify key factors to help researchers, physicians, decision makers and organ donation organizations develop strategies to support clinicians and families in making informed decisions about organ donation. The project will provide the foundation for developing support to improve family understanding of organ donation process and potentially an improved consent rate that may ultimately lead to a higher number of organs available for transplantation.

column36: Molecular Basis of Quebec Platelet Disorder
column37: Platelets are small blood cells that help control bleeding. Our team is studying an inherited disorder called Quebec platelet disorder (QPD) that alters platelets and causes serious bleeding. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD including its genetic cause. In Canada, about 1:200,000 Quebecers has QPD and each person with QPD has a 50:50 chance of passing on QPD each of their children. QPD causes bleeding because it increases a clot busting enzyme called urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA). Persons with QPD have very high levels of uPA in platelets but not in other cells - we are trying to find out why. QPD is caused by a "duplication mutation" which means that a person with QPD an extra copy of the uPA gene and nearby DNA. In QPD cells that make platelets, uPA production is >100 times normal, which is far more than expected for having one extra uPA gene. Additionally, the overproduction of uPA occurs only in QPD cells that make platelets. We explored why and found that QPD duplicates a gene enhancer ("turn on switch") for vinculin (the next gene) - this switch is active only in cells that make platelets. QPD puts the extra copy of this switch right front of the uPA gene. We suspect this is why the gene for uPA becomes turned on too much in QPD cells that make platelets. We will use special methods, including "chromatic conformation capture methods" to test this "swtich" and if it is the reason that the uPA gene in is switched on in QPD cells that make platelets. We will also use special methods to alter genes to test if we can correct the problem in QPD cells that make platelets. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD. We have exciting new information and the technical skills that are needed to study what causes QPD. The study will give us important new information on how genes are controlled when the body makes platelets and how this is changed by QPD. The study will give us new insights on what causes platelet disorders

column36: A novel role for the breast cancer 1 protein (BRCA1) in prenatal protection against oxidative DNA damage, embryotoxicity and abnormal postnatal brain function
column37: The breast cancer 1 (BRCA1) protein is known to protect against breast cancer. However, we have discovered that during pregnancy BRCA1 also protects fetal mice from DNA damage that can cause birth defects and disorders in brain function after birth. The DNA damage is caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are normal forms of activated oxygen essential for fetal development. However, when the fetus lacks proteins like BRCA1 that prevent and repair DNA damage, or when ROS production is enhanced by drugs like alcohol (ethanol, EtOH), the damage accumulates and causes abnormal fetal development. The developmental disorders in BRCA1-deficient mice may be relevant to children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD), and the exacerbated disorders with fetal EtOH exposure may be relevant to children with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). To elucidate the role of BRCA1 in these disorders, we have developed a genetically altered mouse model lacking only 1 of their 2 copies (+/-) of the Brca1 gene, with a small decrease in BRCA1 protein. The progeny exhibit increased DNA damage and postnatal learning and memory deficits, which are worsened by a single low-level fetal EtOH exposure. We will use this mouse model to determine how both normal and EtOH-enhanced ROS levels and prenatal DNA damage cause birth defects and postnatal behavioural differences, and how BRCA1 protects the fetus from DNA damage. Our studies will establish a biological role for BRCA1 beyond cancer, in protecting the developing fetus from normal and chemically-enhanced ROS levels. This developmentally protective role of BRCA1 is likely important, since both copies of the Brca1 gene must be lost to increase the risk of cancer, whereas the loss of only 1 copy increases the risk of developmental disorders. Our results may identify new mechanisms and risk factors relevant to ASD and FASD, which could help in developing novel predictive and therapeutic strategies for high-risk pregnancies.

column36: Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT): A pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial of a gender-sensitized weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for men who are overweight or obese
column37: About 40% of Canadian men are overweight and another 20% are obese. Approximately 70% of men's staggering health care costs (estimated at $36.9 billion annually) could be prevented if men improved their lifestyles (i.e., got active, ate better, and lost weight); however, few men engage in lifestyle change. The apparent reluctance of men to engage in healthy lifestyle programs may reflect the fact that men with excess weight tend to be less aware or concerned than women about their overweight status. Research has shown that programs situated in a sporting context, where men have a strong sense of affiliation as a fan, are effective and lead to high satisfaction among men. Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT) is adapted from Football Fans in Training and our own HealtheSteps lifestyle prescription program. Hockey FIT is a 12-month (3-month active phase and 9-month maintenance phase) weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for middle-aged, overweight/obese male hockey fans, delivered by trained coaches in collaboration with teams in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL). Across the CHL, there are 52 teams spanning small to large urban centres, located throughout Canada. In the proposed study, 32 sites (affiliated with major junior hockey teams and local YMCA facilities) will be randomly assigned to either the intervention (Hockey FIT program) or comparator (wait-list control). At each site, 40 male hockey fans at-risk for chronic diseases will be recruited to take part in the study. Sites assigned to the comparator will offer the Hockey FIT program to their enrolled male hockey fans after 12 months. Through the Hockey FIT program, our study aims to promote weight loss, increase physical activity levels, and improve other health measures through a cost-effective solution that is acceptable and appealing to men who are overweight or obese. Indeed, findings from our pilot study indicate that Hockey FIT has the potential to achieve these goals.

column36: The effects of reward cues on risky decision making: the role of dopamine and relevance to addiction
column37: In addicted people, exposure to things like drug paraphernalia (known as contextual cues) is believed to trigger cravings, drug use and relapse. Exactly how cues promote such outcomes remains poorly understood. One possibility is that cues influence decision-making and tip the scales in favor of the maladaptive addictive behaviour, making it seem more appealing and worthwhile. Our work in both rats and humans suggests that adding sensory reward cues - similar to the lights and sounds in gambling settings - results in riskier and more disadvantageous choice on gambling-like task. In rats, these effects of cues are dependent on the neurotransmitter dopamine. Our goals are: 1) to study whether problem gamblers are particularly susceptible to risk-promoting effects of sensory reward cues - which are abundant in gambling settings; 2) investigate whether dopamine contributes to cue-driven risky choice in healthy humans and problem gamblers, and dopamine system's responsiveness to cues might be associated with problem gambling. To address these aims, we will use positron emission tomography to look at dopamine levels during decision-making in the presence versus in the absence of sensory reward cues. We will do this in a group of healthy participants and a group of problem gamblers. We expect to find that decisions of problem gamblers will be more influenced by cues than those of healthy participants. We also expect that the presence of cues will result in greater elevation in dopamine levels for problem gamblers than healthy controls.

column36: Understanding molecular control of lipid metabolism in brain aging
column37: While perturbed lipid metabolism has been implicated as a risk factor for aging-related neurological degeneration, it remains unknown how the perturbed lipid metabolism arises during the aging process. Importantly, bioactive lipids have been shown as controllers to regulate neural stem cell function that plays an essential role in learning and memory by producing adult-born neurons. To this end, we are interested in understanding molecular mechanisms that control lipid metabolism to regulate neural stem cell function in the context of aging brain with the long term goal of identifying the molecular target for drug discovery to treat aging-associated cognitive decline. Recently, we discovered a signaling-induced molecular pathway that is required to maintain homeostatic neurogenesis and new memory formation during normal aging. This molecular pathway involves the direct phosphorylation of CBP, a histone acetyltransferase, by atypical protein kinase C (aPKC). We recently identified that monoacylglycerol lipase (Mgll), an enzyme that converts endocannabinoid (2-AG) into arachidonic acid, is a downstream target of the aPKC-CBP pathway. Importantly, we observe that the attenuation of the aPKC-CBP pathway causes upregulation of Mgll expression occurring in both normal and Alzheimer's Disease aging brain of animal models. Thus, we hypothesize that deregulation of the aPKC-CBP pathway in brain aging impairs lipid composition and adult neurogenesis that culminate in the cognitive decline, a phenotype associated with brain aging. Together, our experiments will provide important new information regarding regulation of lipid metabolism and provide fundamental knowledge towards the development of therapeutic strategies fighting against the aging process.

column36: Effects of GPR55 on synapse formation and remodeling during development.
column37: Functional connections between nerve cells (called synapses) are essential to establish the architecture of the nervous system. The modification of synapses is thought to be one of the mechanisms by which learning and memory occur. It has been known for decades that cannabis consumption has a profound influence on learning and memory and that maternal marijuana smoking during perinatal period causes cognitive and social deficits that last in the adulthood of the offspring. For the moment, we do not know if these effects are mediated by the classic CB1 and CB2 cannabinoid receptors or by other receptors such as the GPR55. Altogether, these observations led us to investigate a novel function for cannabinoids (like cannabidiol (CBD)) or other GPR55 ligands in regulating the formation and the maintenance of synapses. We have shown that GPR55 stimulation increases the synapse number and blockade of this receptor decreases it. Therefore, the main objective of this project is to identify the contribution and the mechanisms by which GPR55, and its ligands modulate the synapse number. The identification of a fundamental molecular mechanism regulating the connections between nerve cells will provide important insight into normal brain function and learning process. Furthermore, it will probably permit the discovery of new pharmacological targets and the development of innovative therapeutic strategies aiming at treating congenital or neurodegenerative diseases. This project is timely because Canadians are among the highest consumers of cannabis in the World and its consumption might be on the rise when it will be legalized in 2018. Moreover, the GPR55 system is the target of several compounds in the pipelines of pharmaceutical companies (Sativex(THC+CBD), Epidiolex, and GWP42003(CBD)). Thus, the results obtained from the proposed experiments will potentially explain some of the side effects produced by these drugs.

column36: Real-time Endoscopic Raman Spectroscopy for Improving Dysplasia/Colorectal Cancer Detection in Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
column37: Inflammatory Bowel disease (IBD) affects over 200,000 Canadians. Individuals with IBD have a significantly greater risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC): the risk is 2% after 10 yrs of being diagnosed with IBD, but increases to 30% after 30 yrs of suffering from this disease. Unfortunately, the screening for colorectal cancer that is currently provided to the general population (fecal occult blood testing) is inadequate for this group. White light colonoscopy is currently the gold standard but is challenging, as lesions are sometimes difficult to identify. Thus random biopsies, in addition to targeted biopsies of abnormalities visualized by white light, are often performed. This leads to complications and patients suffering, as well as significant healthcare cost. Our objective is to develop a novel endoscopy approach to improve the clinical management of IBD. An endoscope probe based on a technology Raman spectroscopy will be developed that analyzes the tissue biochemistry before biopsy. We expect that this new technology when successfully developed will greatly improve the accuracy of biopsy, saving health care cost and improve CRC detection in IBD patients.

column36: Hippocampal contributions to approach-avoidance conflict decision-making: a cross-species investigation into the underlying cognitive processes and wider neural circuitry
column37: 'To approach, or not to approach?' Many situations in life induce a state of motivational conflict in us as to whether we should approach a seemingly attractive proposition or stimulus (e.g.,highly calorific chocolate cake), or whether we should avoid the very same stimulus as it may have negative consequences (e.g, weight gain). Very little is known about how the mammalian brain regulates this fundamental process of decision making that can potentially go awry in psychological disorders such as addiction, in which the 'approach' tendency takes predominant control, and others such anxiety, which involve heightened 'avoidance' tendencies. Using both rodent and human subjects, the proposed project will provide evidence that the hippocampus, a brain region more known for its importance in mnemonic processes, and its connection with other areas in the brain that are known to be important in motivational processes, comprise neural circuits that is crucial in approach-avoidance conflict resolution. This will offer a new perspective on the role of the hippocampus in decision-making processes, a capacity that is currently thought to be predominantly mediated by the medial prefrontal cortex. Furthering our understanding of the neural basis of approach avoidance conflict resolution, and the identification of differential neural pathways for the control of approach/avoidance behaviour has the potential to create new therapeutic avenues for psychological disorders in which 'approach' or 'avoidance' tendencies are aberrantly dominant.

column36: Development of Viral Sensitizing Antibody Drug Conjugate and Oncolytic virus Combination Regimens for the Treatment of Breast Cancer
column37: Oncolytic viruses are safe viruses engineered to specifically infect and kill cancer cells, and can also stimulate the immune system to recognize tumors. Although they have the potential to treat a broad range of malignancies, the inconsistency of treatment response remains a major challenge and poor infection of tumors is a recognized issue. We have pioneered the development of small molecules that we termed "viral sensitizers" that are able to sensitize tumors to viral infection and potentiate the activity of oncolytic viruses. However, for these molecules to act at maximum efficacy, they currently need to be injected directly into the tumor, which is often not possible. To overcome this issue, we propose to exploit a technology that allows for targeting chemotherapeutics to tumors by piggy-backing on tumor-targeting antibodies. This strategy has notably led to Kadcyla(R), an approved chemotherapy-conjugated version of Trastuzumab(R) (Herceptin(R)) that targets the tumor protein HER2 expressed in a subset of breast cancers. Coincidentally, we have discovered that the type of chemotherapeutic conjugated to Kadcyla has viral sensitizing properties and we have gathered data in cell lines and in immune-deficient mice carrying human breast tumors that combining an oncolytic virus with Kadcyla leads to improved cancer control. This particular approach could be rapidly tested in humans, but before this, we must gather more data in mice with HER2-expressing breast cancer that have immunological characteristics that more closely resemble what we would observe in a human. Furthermore, we will attempt to modify this strategy to deliver our most promising viral sensitizing molecules, and to bypass the need for tumors to express HER2 in order to be effective. To maximize the likelihood of success and eventual impact on cancer outcomes, we have partnered with antibody-drug conjugation experts at the Centre for Drug Research and Development.

column36: Mechanisms of cell death in inherited retinal degeneration caused by rhodopsin mutations
column37: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a devastating genetic disorder of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. The gene most commonly involved in RP is rhodopsin, which produces a protein that detects light. There are large quantities of rhodopsin protein in the light-sensitive rod photoreceptor cells of the retina. Mutations in the rhodopsin gene result in death of rods. However, it is unclear how rhodopsin mutations kill rods. It is proposed that because rods make so much rhodopsin, even subtle rhodopsin defects can result in drastic consequences. We pioneered the use of genetically modified Xenopus laevis frog tadpoles to study this problem. It is easy to make numerous types of genetic changes (e.g., different disease-causing mutations) in this animal to reproduce and compare different forms of the disease. We demonstrated that there are different types of rhodopsin mutations that kill rods in various ways. Two of these ways kill rods faster if the animals are exposed to light. Although the two light-exacerbated mechanisms are caused by mutations in the same gene, and although to an ophthalmologist, patients with these mutations appear to have the same disease, we find that these are actually two very distinct forms of RP that respond differently to treatment. In fact, certain treatments that benefit one form of RP actually worsen the other form. This has important implications for patient treatment: genetic testing will be necessary to test treatments and establish which treatments to use. We propose experiments that will help us understand how these mutations kill rod cells and key ways these mechanisms differ. Our new knowledge of the underlying cell death mechanisms, the unique genetic aspects of the system, and technical advances in manipulating the X. laevis genome will be of value to the scientific community and patients who suffer from RP.

column36: Mitochondrial dysfunction and reproductive aging in female germline
column37: Due to cultural and societal changes in the developed world, the number of women attempting to conceive in the fourth and fifth decades of life has increased significantly. Since mitochondria, essential cellular organelles, require the vitamin, coQ10, among other substrates, for their efficient function, we are exploring the role of coQ10 deficiency as a cause of poor oocyte/embryo quality in older women. Using animal genetic models as well as patient's cells we will study molecular pathways altered by aging and explore novel treatments that will improve reproductive outcomes.

column37: The deadly mushroom, A. phalloides produces a unique toxin known as amanitin that has a desired property of being able to kill both growing cells (easy) and quiescent cells (more difficult). This uniform toxicity is exciting for use in cancer therapy since not all cancer cells grow at the same rate. It is known that amanitin can be targeted to cancer by using either peptides or antibodies. However there is no viable route to synthetic amanitins and studies have relied on the natural product to develop amanitin drug conjugates. Recently we have published a total synthesis of amanitin and have become experts in its synthesis. This enables us to address the molecular pharamcology of this fascinating toxin and thereby modulate its toxicity to be directed to cancer cells.

column36: Mechanisms of rod and cone disk membrane synthesis and quality control in normal and diseased retina.
column37: Retinal degenerative diseases are genetic disorders of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. Retinitis pigmentosa is a disorder causing death of rod photoreceptors, while other retinal degenerations affect both rods and cones, or primarily cones. Rods and cones are the light sensitive cells of the retina. They are named for the shapes of their light sensitive outer segment organelles, which are modified non-motile cilia. The outer segments contain a highly organized stack of non-contiguous (rods) or contiguous (cones) disk-shaped membranes that contain very high concentrations of the G-protein coupled receptor rhodopsin. The exact mechanism by which these disks form is unclear. However, it is clear that defects in biosynthesis of both the disks themselves, and disk components such as rhodopsin, are responsible for inherited human retinal disease. Disk biosynthesis is proposed to involve the proteins prcad-21 and prominin-1 which form a complex that may be involved in a step such as disk evagination or sealing. We propose to examine the roles of prcad-21 and prominin-1 in disk formation using X. laevis and D. Rerio (frog and fish) knockout animal models, in combination with our newly developed assays for disk membrane synthesis. We will also use transgenic and knockout X. laevis and novel transgene tools to examine the biosynthesis and quality control of the disk component rhodopsin, including the role rhodopsin codon usage in biosynthesis, the roles of different degradation pathways in rhodopsin quality control, and roles of glycosylation and chromophore binding on regulating pathway use.

column36: How Approaches to Care Shape the Pathways of Older Adult Home Care Clients
column37: Home care is increasingly looked to as a means of strengthening the healthcare system by addressing wait lists for residential long term care and supporting older adults to age in place. Although provincial home care policies claim a commitment to "client-centered" approaches to care, there is variation in who delivers home care services, what services are available and for how long, and what the supports are for family/friend caregivers. Regional differences in approaches to care make it difficult to assess the appropriateness of the goals of home care policies, and know if everything is being done that could be done to support clients, caregivers, home support workers and the system in achieving the best possible outcomes. Our multi-method project analyzes how approaches to care shape client pathways within, and potentially out of, the home care system in 2 provinces with similar population size but different service delivery models (Nova Scotia and Manitoba). Our overarching research question is: How do approaches to care shape older adult home care client pathways through the home care system? We will construct typical scenarios of a person's movement over time, by analyzing client data between 2011-2017. We will then interview care groups of clients, caregivers, and care providers at 3 points in time in an 18 month period to understand individual experiences. To gain a systems level understanding, we will examine how regional policies organize approaches to care by analyzing interviews with policy makers and sector representatives, and policy and practice documents. This will create research evidence that can be used to improve home care clients' experiences, and inform care practices, while taking into account individual, provider and system perspectives. We will work with our partners and knowledge users to develop workshops and webinars to share our findings and to support informed decision making at all levels of care.

column36: Innate Defence Regulator (IDR) peptides: Regulatory mechanisms in the control of asthma
column37: Asthma is the most common chronic respiratory disease, characterized by inflammation in the lungs and narrowing of the airways, which makes it difficult to breathe. Nearly 3 million Canadians suffer from asthma. The direct and indirect cost related to asthma in Canada is around $2.2 billion annually. Nearly 10% of patients do not respond to available steroid therapies and have severe uncontrolled asthma. These patients represent the major burden of asthma and associated healthcare costs. Moreover, commonly used steroid therapies can increase the risk of lung infections, which results in worsening of asthma. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new therapies that can control asthma, without compromising a patient's ability to resolve infections. This study focuses on new molecules known as innate defence regulator (IDR) peptides, which are designed from natural molecules that play a critical role in the immune response. IDR peptides can control both inflammation and infection in the lung, with the potential to overcome side effects associated with current therapies. We have shown that IDR peptides improve breathing capacity in an animal model of asthma, and can control cellular processes linked to steroid unresponsiveness. This project is aimed at the development of IDR peptides as a new therapy for asthma. In this project, we will identify the changes that occur in lung cells after they are treated with IDR peptides. We will also study the biological effects of IDR peptides in the control of lung inflammation and fibrosis, in a mouse model of asthma. The results from these studies will allow us to identify new drug targets with the potential to alleviate unresponsiveness to steroid therapies, a condition for which there is currently no effective treatment. This project will directly support the development of a new IDR peptide-based therapy for asthma, which will have the added benefit of countering steroid-refractory asthma and controlling lung infections

column36: Probing the link between amyloid deposition, cortico-hippocampal network dysfunction and cognitive impairment in a second generation of transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a disorder that results in degeneration of the brain which leads to severe memory impairments. This is a devastating disease producing personal and societal costs that are immeasurable and growing as the "baby boomers" age. The common and central feature of AD is amyloid deposition, of which the major component is the amyloid beta peptide (Abeta). As new clinical trials focus on the initial stages of the disease, early diagnosis is now more important than ever. There is growing evidence from human neuroimaging that the preclinical stage of AD is associated with profound functional alterations of specific brain network. Recent studies using transgenic mice model of AD have shown that some brain cells become highly active in the early stages of AD when the animal exhibit normal learning and memory. In the later stages of AD, neurons become less active with an accompanying decline in animals cognitive abilities. Although the relationship between altered neuronal activity, neural network abnormalities and the behavioral consequences are less known, it is fundamentally important to understand these early brain changes as they provide a target for therapeutic interventions early in the progression of the disease before significant and irreversible brain damage occurs. In particular, this work will provide new understanding of how pathogenic forms of Abeta contribute to neuronal activity and network dysfunction and behavioral & cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease. Our hypothesis is that cellular hyperactivity in the early stages of AD is a key driver of changes in the brain that ultimately lead to the descent into dementia. The proposed work will provide evidence of where in the brain and when these changes occur, the cause of these brain changes, and a target for treatments that could halt or slow devastating effects of AD from occurring.

column36: Does traffic-related air pollution reduce the effectiveness of corticosteroids in asthma treatment?
column37: We are all routinely exposed to air pollution derived from transport and power generation, or occupationally in industries that underpin the Canadian economy (forestry, mining, oil & gas), with many Canadians exposed to unacceptable levels. The Government of Canada notes "air pollution costs Canadians and the Canadian economy billions of dollars per year". Much of these costs derive from pollution-induced worsening of respiratory diseases, including asthma (which affects 1 in 10 Canadians at a cost of nearly $3 billion annually). The primary medications for controlling asthma are inhaled corticosteroids, which reduce the inflammation that increases airways muscle contraction, mucus and, consequentially, difficulty breathing. Our preliminary data suggest that exposure to air pollution can reduce the effectiveness of corticosteroids, which then may compromise asthma control and increase the risk of 'lung attacks' that cause hospitalization or even death. The current proposal will validate and build on our early results and, additionally, elucidate the underlying mechanisms therein. To do this, we will conduct a novel, controlled crossover trial of diesel exhaust (DE) and an inhaled corticosteroid in mild asthmatics. We will collect lung samples and assess how air pollution may alter the expression of genes and proteins in the lung. In parallel, we will grow lung epithelial cells and use them to examine mechanisms underlying the effects of air pollution on corticosteroid responsiveness and determine the effectiveness of interventions. This study has the potential to enhance both prevention and therapy for Canadian asthmatics. Our results can inform physician practices and drive regulatory policies to protect vulnerable groups. Additionally, understanding how the effects of corticosteroids on lung gene expression are modified by air pollution could lead to the development of improved medications for the millions of Canadians suffering from airways disease.

column36: Predicting therapy resistance in castration-resistant prostate cancer with circulating tumor DNA
column37: The standard of care therapies for advanced prostate cancer, abiraterone and enzalutamide, are not effective in 20-40% of patients. We currently are unable to recognize this subset of patients up-front, which means they are inevitably treated with a drug that will not work: leading to unnecessary treatment side-effects to the patient and wasted time while their disease worsens. Our unique research team combines cancer bioinformatics expertise with clinical oncology to develop genomic-based strategies that better recognize patients with poor prognoses. Although it has long been known that cancers shed a small amount of their DNA into the bloodstream (known as circulating tumor DNA, ctDNA), the analysis of this DNA is only now possible through advancement of next-generation sequencing technology. Our recent work has shown that changes detected in ctDNA accurately reflect cancer itself and can therefore show the DNA changes occurring in a patient's prostate cancer before, during, and after treatment. In this project we will look at changes occurring in the ctDNA of hundreds of Canadian men with prostate cancer that are being treated with abiraterone, enzalutamide and other therapies. We will determine which changes can predict a patient's subsequent response to treatment. We are uniquely placed to perform this analysis given our strong track record of success in prostate cancer ctDNA profiling, our novel custom (and validated) methodology, and our recent establishment of a province-wide ctDNA profiling program that has rapidly accrued hundreds of patient blood samples. Success with our project will help us understand why some cancers are intrinsically resistant to the most commonly used therapies. Furthermore, we will have developed a clinically-practical framework (requiring only a blood sample, rather than a metastatic tissue biopsy) that may ultimately help prioritize patients for other therapies that have an improved chance of success.

column36: Function of Flaviviridae viral RNAs in the host cell nucleus
column37: Pathogenic RNA viruses of the Flaviviridae family include Zika (ZIKV), West Nile (WNV), Dengue (DV), and Hepatitis C (HCV). ZIKV outbreaks are occurring in more than 80 countries and in 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. DV is endemic in at least 100 countries and WHO estimates that nearly 400 million infections occur yearly, while HCV causes serious liver damage with more than 170 million individuals infected worldwide. A central tenant of Flaviviridae virus biology, and one that guides therapeutic strategies, is that the virus production cycle occurs within the cytoplasm of host cells. However, we recently discovered that the RNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV shuttle in and out of the host cell nucleus. The movement of ZIKV and HCV RNA genomes through the host nucleus has not been explored in the literature, and the functional importance of nuclear viral RNAs remains completely unknown. Critically, altering the transport of ZIKV and HCV RNAs through the nucleus negatively impacts virus production, pointing to a crucial, yet uncharacterized, role for the nucleus in Flaviviridae biology. We hypothesize that the vRNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV enter the host nucleus to (1) engage nuclear pathways that aid in virus production and (2) to regulate host cell gene expression including activition of cell defence mechanisms. column36: Regulation of the intraflagellar transport pathway, a mutational hotspot required for cilium formation and maintenance
column37: Cilia, the antenna-shaped structures found on most human cells, have recently emerged as major hotspots for genetic diseases called ciliopathies. Over 30 different ciliopathies, caused by mutations in nearly 200 genes, are currently known. Defects in the functions of cilia, which play critical roles in physiology and development, result in many clinical ailments. These include blindness, polycystic kidney disease, morbid obesity, skeletal anomalies and brain defects. Since 2003, my group has made seminal contributions to the understanding of cilia and ciliopathies. In particular, we were the first to link a multi-organ genetic disorder, Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS), to defective cilia function. We discovered that several components (proteins) implicated in BBS specifically function in a process termed intraflagellar transport (IFT), which is responsible for the formation and functions of cilia. We also identified and uncovered the functions of novel IFT-associated proteins, all of which are now associated with ciliopathies. The central goal of our research proposal is to establish an experimental system in which we can decipher or 'model' the mechanisms by which different patient ciliopathy mutations cause IFT and ciliary defects. To further enhance our ability to understand how patient mutations affect IFT, we will conduct genetic, cell biology and biochemistry experiments to shed new insights into the functions and regulation of the IFT system. We will accomplish these goals by taking advantage of innovative resources and experimental tools that are either not available for, or not easily applicable to, other researchers using mammalian (e.g., human cells) or vertebrate (e.g., zebrafish) model systems. Collectively, our findings will help unravel fundamental mechanisms of cilia formation and function, and importantly, provide molecular diagnostic tools necessary to understand how IFT mutations can lead to an important and growing class of human disorders.

column36: Reducing HIV target cells in the female genital tract: Determining the mechanism of inducing immune quiescence.
column37: The two basic elements of successful Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) transmission are a viable virus and a susceptible target host cell. Activated immune cells are more susceptible to HIV infection than resting cells and, once infected, they produce up to 1000 times more virus. It is known that inflammation brings activated HIV target cells to the site of irritation. Most of biomedical prevention approaches focus on either keeping HIV away (condom use) or neutralizing it once it is present in the genital tract (antiviral drugs, microbicides, vaccines). However, what has not been a focus of HIV prevention efforts, is trying to limit the availability of susceptible HIV-target cells at the genital tract. We conducted a pilot study to determine if a common anti-inflammatory drug acetylsalicylic acid (ASA or Aspirin) could decrease inflammation among low-risk Kenya women. The results showed ASA reduced the number of HIV target cells in the female genital tract by 35%. In this current study, we build on those finding using detailed molecular studies to determine the molecular mechanism(s) involved in ASA's effect on the recruitment of HIV target cells in the genital tract. We will also determine if daily administration of ASA will reduce HIV target cells numbers at the genital tract Kenyan female sex workers who are at high risk of acquiring HIV. We will also determine which dose of ASA is most effective, the duration of the effect and whether there are any side-effects on the vaginal microbiome. The long-term goal of this study is to provide a novel HIV-prevention approach that is both readily available and non-stigmatizing. If we can demonstrate that ASA is able to reduce HIV target cells among women at high risk of acquiring HIV, then we will be one step closer to a much needed novel HIV prevention.

column37: Stroke is the 3rd leading cause of death and is a leading cause of long-term disability in Canada, with the risk of stroke doubling every 10 years after the age of 55. The Canadian Stroke Network's Burden of Ischemic Stroke (BURST) study has calculated that 50,000 new strokes occur each year. This leads to health-care costs in excess of $2.5 billion. For the most part there is not much we can do to treat or prevent strokes at this time other than encourage patients to develop good lifestyle habits that promote cardiovascular health. The clot-busting drug tPA is used to treat patients who have a large stroke and results in very favorable outcomes. However, the vast majority of strokes are "covert" strokes with no obvious clinical presentation. The cumulative impact of these strokes leads to substantial, irreversible neuronal damage. Our research aims to characterize a new mechanism by which we can protect the brain against these stroke events. In this proposal, we set out a series of experiments to characterize a potential new avenue for stroke therapy. Our preliminary results show that administration of drug that increases brain glycine, called NFPS, leads to a dramatic decrease in stroke size. In our proposed experiments, we will elucidate the molecular mechanism that underlies this phenomenon and also determine the therapeutic window of NFPS as a stroke treatment. NFPS is well tolerated in the clinic and our discovery will open up new avenues for treatment using a drug that is readily available. This will greatly improve the health of Canadians and lessen the economic costs associated with stroke recovery.

column36: Dissecting the neural and behavioural mechanisms of persistent behavioural change
column37: Reducing or eliminating problem behaviours is a critical component to every-day healthy functioning and to the successful treatment of clinical conditions such as drug and food addiction or anxiety disorders. Reduction in unwanted behaviours can be achieved through extinction training. This training consists of the presentation of cues for biologically significant events in the absence of those events. In the laboratory this training is used to better understand the behavioural and neural mechanisms that regulate extinction learning and its diminutive effect on behavior. In the clinical setting, extinction-based therapies such as abstinence or cue exposure, are used to help patients eliminate behaviours that define their psychopathologies. However, the success of extinction-based training strongly depends on the generalizability of this learning to new contexts, across long temporal intervals or upon experience with motivationally or emotionally charged events. This proposal seeks to develop novel, long-lasting and generalizable behavioural routes via which reduction in unwanted behaviour can be achieved. This will be done using two distinct paradigms, which drive extinction learning via two ways: by manipulating outcome delivery (omission of an expected outcome) or by manipulating outcome expectation (generating an inflated expectation of an outcome). We will use these two paradigms to uncover the general or common neural mechanisms of this learning by studying how the brain processes extinction in a variety of settings real-time, and what neural circuits are causally involved in regulating this learning. Our ultimate goal is to use behaviour and neuroscience to develop novel routes that support lasting reduction of unwanted behavior from bench to beside.

column36: Characterization of Traumatic brain injury as a contributor to chronic neuropsychiatric and neurocognitive impairment in a marginally housed population.
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) occurs with an alarmingly high rate and severity in people who are homeless or marginally housed and causes disproportionate damage because brain health is already compromised. Mental illness and addictions are common and are strong risk factors for prolonged symptoms after TBI. For these reasons we believe that TBI may be a primary but underappreciated contributor to chronic impairment in this vulnerable population. As part of a ten-year CIHR-funded study we have been investigating persons at high risk for homelessness. We currently follow over 300 marginally housed persons with monthly assessments for psychiatric symptoms, urine drug screens, detailed substance use history and yearly MRI brain scans. To our knowledge this is one of the most thoroughly characterized large cohort of marginally housed individuals worldwide. Important data we have already gathered indicates that the rate of psychosis is nearly 50% and a history of TBI is the most potent predictor of psychotic illness, strikingly surpassing even stimulant abuse (including methamphetamine). We have also found a synergistic effect of TBI and depression, and a relationship with cognitive impairment. Given the extremely high rate of TBI (31% of this group suffers at least one concussion per year) we expect at least 50 subjects per year who's life trajectory after brain injury can be studied in a uniquely powerful and thorough fashion to accomplish the following aims; (i) Define the relationship between brain injuries and the onset or exacerbation of neuropsychiatric problems and addictions in people who are homeless or tenuously housed and (ii) to discover, with advanced neuroimaging, which brain changes are important in imparting risk for prolonged or poor recovery from TBI. Through our well established links with clinical teams, municipal and provincial government and local police, this data will immediately and meaningfully inform care and social policy.

column36: Ectosteric inhibitors of cathepsin K: their mechanism and in vivo efficacy
column37: Worldwide, 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men over 50 years of age will experience osteoporotic fractures. Current osteoporosis treatments have various shortcomings such as poor bone quality and several skeletal and non-skeletal side effects. Therefore major investments have been made into the development of more effective drugs that are less prone to side effects. Due to efforts of ourselves and many others it has been discovered that bone-degrading cathepsin K (CatK) is a highly suitable drug target whose inhibition led to increased bone quality and reduced fracture rates in clinical osteoporosis trials. Although there is little doubt about the validity of CatK as a drug target, none of the CatK inhibitors have been approved because of various safety concerns. Based on our research, this might be due to the multifunctional character of the enzyme, where total inhibition leads to the observed side effects. However, the osteoporosis relevant activity of this enzyme is limited to its potent collagenase activity, which should be selectively blocked. Based on our previous studies on the mechanism of collagen degradation by CatK, we have developed a strategy to specifically block the collagen-degrading activity without affecting other biologically important actions of this protease. We termed this novel and innovative type of drugs "ectosteric inhibitors" and our proposed project is aimed at characterizing these substrate-specific drugs at their molecular, cellular and in vivo levels of action and efficacy as anti-resorptives. We have identified compounds that have a similar bone-preserving potency in cell assays and in an osteoporosis mouse model similar to the most advanced clinically evaluated CatK inhibitor without affecting non-bone-related pathways. This proposal introduces the novel concept of substrate-selective inhibitors that are superior to all previously developed protease drugs and aims to develop potent, efficacious, and side effect free osteoporosis drugs.

column36: Phylodynamics of HIV within hosts
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infects different parts of the body and types of cells, including cells that play an important role in our immune system. Furthermore, an infected cell can become "latent" so that it does not produce new copies of the virus, making it essentially invisible to the immune system and drug treatments, only to become reactivated months or years afterwards. The existence of these reservoirs of latently infected cells is a key reason why it is so difficult to cure an HIV infection. HIV also evolves rapidly because it makes many mistakes when copying its own genome. This rapid evolution makes it possible to infer how different copies of a virus from the same patient are related. These evolutionary relationships are usually represented by a tree or "phylogeny". Phylodynamics is a new interdisciplinary field where the shape of a phylogeny is used to reconstruct how an epidemic has spread through a human population. Methods from phylodynamics have already made enormous impacts on our understanding of HIV, influenza A virus, and the recent Ebolavirus outbreak in West Africa. Our proposal is a completely novel application of phylodynamic methods to examine the proliferation of HIV within patients. We will extend techniques from pattern recognition being developed in our lab to enable computers to extract information about HIV latency and its spread among different populations of cells from the shapes of phylogenetic trees. The key expected benefits of the proposed research are to inform the development of HIV cure strategies by reconstructing how the virus spreads among different cell types and tissues, and their respective characteristics as potential latent reservoirs.

column37: This project is about helping Continuing Care Aides (CCAs) improve their own health while also supporting the older adults they care for. CCAs serve many clients every day, and the work is often physically demanding with the potential for musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). In our study, groups of older adults together with their CCAs will complete the Home Support Exercise Program (HSEP) 5 days per week for 6 months. The older clients in the CCA's care will follow the proven HSEP version while the CCA may move to the intermediate and advanced versions. Two other comparison groups will be involved - older adults doing the HSEP alone and older adults not doing the HSEP. We will measure physical function and fall risk, and rates of MSDs. The outcome will be measured when the project starts and then at 3 and 6 months. The study will include 150 older adult participants (50 in each group) and 50 CCAs from two health regions in Saskatchewan. All participants in the two exercise groups will be taught the HSEP, and CCAs will be encouraged to do more difficult versions of it 5 days a week for 6 months. The participants in the non-HSEP group will receive usual care and will be treated as a comparison group with friendly visits to examine the stability in the outcome indicators. We think the older adults in the two HSEP groups will show more improvement or at least maintain their current health and that the older adult working together with the CCA will have the greatest benefit, followed by the older adults doing the HSEP alone, and then the no HSEP comparison group. We also think the CCAs participating in the exercise group will show improvement in their health and less MSDs. The dual focus on senior clients and health system staff makes this project innovative and unique.

column36: Enabling Multi-site,Tailored Feedback Interventions to Reduce Low-Value Test Ordering in Critical Care: A Systematic Approach
column37: Laboratory testing of patient blood samples is one of the highest volume activities in health care, but between 20-30% of tests ordered are thought to be low-value or entirely unnecessary. This leads to three major problems: 1) wasted spending on unnecessary tests that could be used for other healthcare purposes 2) increased health risks (e.g. blood loss causing anemia that can be particularly dangerous for the highly vulnerable patients in critical care), and 3) risk of false positive results that lead to further unnecessary testing that can be costly, anxiety-provoking, and invasive. Reducing low-value testing is often difficult, particularly in team-based settings like critical care. A potentially effective strategy is Audit and Feedback, where providers' own practice data (e.g. the number of a specific lab tests ordered over the past month) is provided back to them to spur change. Our overall goal is to develop, test and deliver feedback strategies to reduce low-value test ordering in critical care, a highly complex and team-based environment that is one of the heaviest users of laboratory testing. Our team combines 1) lab testing data, infrastructure, and expertise from the Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association (EORLA), the body responsible for all 13 million annual in-hospital lab tests in Eastern Ontario; 2) world-leading expertise in feedback and healthcare professional behavior change, and 3) critical care clinical expertise from a range of critical care units in Eastern Ontario. This project will 1) develop tools to help organizations identify low-value tests and design feedback strategies to reduce their use; 2) design tailored feedback strategies for several critical care sites, and 3) evaluate the effectiveness of these feedback strategies. This work will enable better test ordering practice, help improve efficiency of a major component of modern health care, and reduce the need for patients to be put at risk by unnecessary testing.

column36: Changing the patient-PCP dialogue: fostering trust through joint clinical decision making
column37: A patient visits their doctor with a set of symptoms hoping for a diagnostic test, a prescription, or a diagnosis. Yet, sometimes doing nothing is better. Unnecessary interventions needlessly expose the patient to harms, lengthen the wait for other patients in need of tests or therapy, and burden the health system with avoidable costs. The challenge is how to have doctor-patient conversations about clinical decisions about tests and procedures in a way that is patient-focused and maintains trust. To change the conversation, we need a better understanding of the doctor-patient interaction. We need to understand how doctors build trust with their patients, and do these strategies change if the doctor feels that the patient before them might face barriers in accessing health services. This is very important when faced with suggestions that "doing more" (tests, procedures) is not necessarily better. We need to understand how different groups of patients perceive their doctor visits, including how these might affect Metis patients compared to other Manitobans. In theory, all Manitobans, including the Metis, have equal access to the health care system, but the reality is quite varied and different. Some, by virtue of education, income, race, gender, language, and other issues might have trouble accessing health services and have poorer health outcomes. It is important to understand if there are aspects of initiatives promoting "more isn't better" that might harm some Manitoba patients, like the Metis, because of their already poorer health status. Equally important, unless the expectations of patients who are able to access the health system are met about what they need to feel assured they are getting the best care, trust in doctor recommendations may be compromised. Using interviews with doctors and focus groups with Metis and other Manitobans in Winnipeg, Brandon and Winkler, we focus on common reasons bringing patients to visit their doctor: pain or infection.

column37: Patterns of gene expression distinguish different cell types (i.e. brain, hair, and muscle cells express different sets of genes to make them different from each other). Misregulated gene expression can lead to developmental disorders, infertility, cancer, and other diseases, thus there are many cellular safety mechanisms that regulate the process. One key mechanism for controlling gene expression involves sRNA pathways that can act in different cellular compartments and at several steps in the process of turning a gene on or off. Small RNA pathways play key gene regulatory roles in a variety of organisms, and rely on conserved Argonaute effector proteins, which utilize sRNAs to provide sequence-specific identification of target genes. Our research focuses on understanding how sRNA pathways regulate gene expression in the nuclei of cells known as germ cells (sperm and egg). The nucleus is where the process of gene expression initiates, and sRNA activities in the nucleus are currently poorly understood, especially in animals. Our studies focus on understanding the molecular mechanisms by which sRNA pathways impact chromatin (how chromosomes are packaged), using the nematode, C. elegans, as a powerful model system, and applying integrated genetic, genomic, molecular and cell biology approaches. Uncovering the molecular mechanisms of sRNA-mediated gene regulation in germ cell nuclei reveals a deeper understanding of basic cellular functions that contribute to development, differentiation, fertility and disease, and provides a more precise means to manipulate gene expression, leading to more effective sRNA-based therapeutics and laboratory techniques.

column36: Role of alternative polyadenylation in Ras-driven cancers
column37: Cancer is a disease of genes, which are blueprints for proteins that carry out the work of cells. Genes make proteins through an intermediate template called messenger RNA (mRNA). Proto-oncogenes can be thought of as gas pedals that drive cell proliferation. Mutations that convert proto-oncogenes into oncogenes push the "pedal to the metal", causing cells to over proliferate and form tumours. Oncogenes drive cell proliferation in simple organisms like worms by same mechanisms as they function in humans. Despite sequencing thousands of cancer genomes we still lack an understanding of how oncogenes drive tumour growth. Taking advantage of the powerful gene manipulation techniques of the tiny worm C. elegans we found that an oncogene called Ras cooperates with insulin signalling to promote tumour growth, which is also conserved in human tumour cells. We show that Ras requires an intact insulin pathway to sustain its oncogenic activity, and that this is achieved by dictating where messenger RNA tails are placed. These tails have sections where specific molecules can bind and put the brakes on to prevent its translation into protein. Cancer cells produce too much protein, which is required to fuel their rapid growth. We hypothesize that inhibiting insulin signalling promotes the formation mRNAs with longer tails containing sites to apply the brakes on activated oncogenes, and suppress tumour formation. To understand how this works we will combine the powerful gene manipulation technologies available in C. elegans, human cells, and mice. By exploiting these models we hope to identify new drug targets that can prevent abnormal tumour cell growth in humans.
