column36: Novel targeted therapeutics against leukemia stem cells
column37: The goal of this project is to identify drugs that can target the rare cells that cause treatment failure in leukemia - leukemic stem cells (LSCs). AML is sustained in a patient by LSCs that act somewhat like normal stem cells, although cancerous, in that they are the 'root' of the disease and need to be eliminated to achieve a cure. Therapy for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) involves extremely intense toxic treatment. Even with this aggressive treatment, approximately 40% of these patients do not respond to therapy or the leukemia returns later. Therefore novel treatment approaches are desperately needed to improve outcome and reduce toxicity. We have taken data on the activity of genes in LSCs and regular leukemic cells and combined it with data sets on how drugs cause changes in gene activity to identify 152 compounds that we predict would specifically eliminate LSCs. We have directly tested 83 of these compounds and found that 12 of them do preferentially target LSCs in human leukemia. We propose to examine these 12 compounds in depth and determine how well they work against multiple leukemia samples, what exactly they do, and how safe they are. Our efforts to understand their mechanisms of action and their effectiveness in primary leukemic cells will yield novel insight into the unique functioning of LSCs. This increase in our knowledge of LSC and leukemia biology will in turn enable additional gains in prognosis, therapy and prevention.

column36: A New Entity of Cardiac Arrhythmia Associated with Loss of Cardiac Ryanodine Receptor Function
column37: In the heart, muscle contraction is triggered by the release of calcium from the internal calcium stores through the calcium release channel, called the ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2). It has been well established that enhanced RyR2 activity as a result of gain-of-function (GOF) RyR2 mutations can lead to irregular heart rhythm and sudden death. An increasing body of evidence indicates that suppressed RyR2 activity due to loss of function (LOF) RyR2 mutations can also cause sudden cardiac death. However, the molecular mechanism underlying sudden death caused by LOF RyR2 mutations is largely undefined. Despite their fundamental differences, unfortunately, patients with LOF RyR2 mutations are currently being diagnosed and treated the same way as those with GOF RyR2 mutations. As a result, patients with LOF RyR2 mutations are often misdiagnosed and mismanaged, which may lead to sudden death. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop effective diagnostic tests and treatments for these patients. The objective of this research proposal is to explore the mechanism, diagnosis, and treatment of heart dysfunction associated with LOF RyR2 mutations. To achieve this goal, we propose to identify and characterize LOF RyR2 mutations and their associated heart defects, to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms of their actions, and to develop novel diagnostic tests and therapeutic strategies for RyR2 LOF mutation associated diseases. These proposed studies will gain new insights into the mechanism of RyR2 LOF-associated heart dysfunction, and may lead to the development of novel diagnostic tests and treatments for this new entity of heart disease.

column37: The human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) has infected more than 70 million people worldwide. column36: Stem cell related genesis and maintenance of glioblastoma
column37: Brain cancers, particularly glioblastomas (GBM), are amongst the worst human cancers. The 5-year survival is <10%, effectively rendering patients with this diagnosis to a death sentence. Patients are desperate for better treatments. A major barrier to finding better treatments has been a poor understanding of the mechanisms of brain tumor initiation and growth. My research group found that GBM growth was dependent on a few cells in the tumour that have stem cell properties, these cells lie at the root of GBM growth and are also resistant to conventional therapies. We have found that human GBM stem cells depend on the Sox2 gene, which is a master gene of stem cells. These findings suggest that the Sox2+ normal stem cells in the brain may be the cells that give rise to glioblastoma, but how, when, and why they do is not known. In this proposal, we will study the role of the brain's normal Sox2 expressing cells in the genesis and growth of glioblastoma, using experimental approaches that cannot be performed with human cells, by creating tumours in the brains of mice. We will test whether normal Sox2+ neural stem cells in the mouse give rise to experimental glioblastomas and how activation or suppression of the growth activity of these cells affects the emergence of glioblastoma. We will also determine if the growth of these tumors, and their therapeutic resistance depends on subpopulations of Sox2+ cells. These studies will complement and extend knowledge derived in research of human cells by allowing us to study all stages of glioblastoma, from the earliest tumors to full-blown cancers both pre- and post-treatment. We cannot easily get access to the first steps of the disease, nor some of its worst forms, so this work in mice will fulfill areas of unmet need in the research of this cancer. We will then use these models to test preventative measures and to develop more effective therapies.

column36: Delineate the Extent of Trophoblast Differentiation in Molar Pregnancies and their Malignancies
column37: Hydatidiform mole is an aberrant human pregnancy with no embryo that has fascinated scientists in all civilizations since its description by Hippocrates more than 2000 years ago. The common form of this condition affects 1 in every 600 pregnancies in western countries. Most of these moles are sporadic, not recurrent, and benign. However, up to 20% of them degenerate into malignant tumors, require single or multiple-drug chemotherapy, and may lead to the death of the patients in the absence of appropriate follow-up and treatment. Today, it is not known why some moles become malignant and not others. I, together with my team, identified a major gene, NLRP7, responsible for a rare form of recurrent moles and have made significant contribution to its current understanding. Because of the contribution of my group, patients with recurrent moles are now tested for NLRP7 and those with recessive mutations counselled that their defect lies in their oocytes and that they can have normal pregnancies and live births from ovum donation. Our most recent and important finding is that the root of this disease in patients with NLRP7 mutations stems from the placenta because it did not complete its full differentiation and that is why it keeps proliferating. This proposal aims at delineating the extent of the undifferentiated state of the placenta of recurrent moles from patients with recessive NLRP7 mutations, investigating whether the identified markers are involved in the malignant degeneration of sporadic moles, and demonstrating the roles of these markers in conferring tumorigenesis. In this application, I am seeking the CIHR support to start understanding the molecular basis of the malignant component of moles and help the most fragile patients with this condition.

column36: Synaptic, cellular and molecular mechanisms of depression susceptibility
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide and existing antidepressant therapies have limited efficacy. It is well known that chronic stress can lead to depression, yet not all those who encounter stress will become depressed. Understanding what makes some people especially vulnerable to depression is essential for developing proper treatment and for possibly even preventing the disorder. Stress experienced in early life is one factor known to increase risk for depression but key questions remain unanswered. What are the enduring changes in brain function that are induced by early life stress to mediate life-long susceptibility to depression? Can neural signatures of aberrant brain function be detected before depression is observed? To answer these questions, we will employ a multi-disciplinary approach integrating advanced neuroscience techniques with robust mouse models to probe the enduring effects of early life experience on neuronal activity and the underlying changes in gene expression in a key brain circuit implicated in depression, the ventral hippocampus projection to the nucleus accumbens. We will use ex vivo measurements of neuronal connectivity, in vivo imaging of neuronal activity and post-mortem assays of genome-wide gene expression to examine how maternal separation in mice, a form of early life stress, shapes neuronal function and gene networks in the ventral-hippocampus to nucleus accumbens circuit to increase susceptibility to chronic stress in adulthood. Elucidating both the alterations in brain circuit function and the underlying gene networks that render an individual susceptible to depression will provide the knowledge necessary to develop treatments to treat and even prevent depression. This research will open the door to new interventions to regulate brain activity to mitigate susceptibility before depression emerges, reducing the enormous societal costs and improving the lives of millions of Canadians struggling with depression

column36: Lipophagy in Reverse Cholesterol Transport
column37: Atherosclerosis, a form of heart disease caused by the build-up of cholesterol deposits in the artery wall, is responsible for one in five deaths in Canada. Meanwhile, existing cholesterol-lowering drugs are only partially effective at reducing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. New therapies are urgently needed to combat this deadly disease. Our research team is looking for new ways to improve the removal of cholesterol from atherosclerotic plaques, stop the plaques from growing bigger, and possibly even reduce their size. We are testing whether increasing a process in cells called "autophagy"-which breaks down lipids and exports them-could achieve this. Autophagy plays a key role in recycling toxic elements from cells and promotes cell survival during periods of cell stress. Through autophagy, cellular components are delivered to organelles called lysosomes (the waste disposal system of the cell), which digest unwanted materials. Our research has already shown that autophagy can also engulf and digest cholesterol that has accumulated in the artery wall. This process helps remove cholesterol, through a process called 'reverse cholesterol transport' providing an entirely new therapeutic target to reverse atherosclerosis. Specifically, this proposal seeks to determine the role of autophagy in digesting accumulated lipid in various cell types found in atherosclerotic plaques (macrophages, vascular smooth muscle cells), and to compare the relative importance of the autophagy pathway in these cells for reverse cholesterol transport and atherosclerosis regression. By shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms of lipid autophagy, our research team hopes to identify pathway components that can be targeted and manipulated to treat heart disease. We are also looking for new targets for developing drugs that can increase cholesterol breakdown and export by cells in the artery wall.

column36: Maternal Iron Nutrition and its Consequences in Pregnant Women and Their Children in the Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition (APrON) Study
column37: IIron is an important nutrient for delivering oxygen to the body and for ideal growth and development. When mother's iron status in pregnancy is either too low (as in iron deficiency) or too high it can lead to complications such as low birth weight, preterm birth, pre-eclampsia. If her iron status is low it can also lead to baby starting life with low iron. There is not much known about iron status of) pregnant women in Canada. However, new research from Canada and Australia suggest that even women who eat right and take prenatal supplements may not have the amount of iron needed for a healthy pregnancy. In this study we will determine: 1.Iron status in a group of pregnant and early postpartum women using different blood markers. 2.Women's iron intake from diet and supplements and how these affect her iron status. 3.Whether women's iron status affects her pregnancy and her child at birth (e.g. are they likely to be born with a LBW). 4.Whether women's iron status in pregnancy affects her child's development. The Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition (APrON) study has already collected information from pregnant women about what they eat, the supplements they take, their pregnancy (such as weight gain or whether they had pre-eclampsia), and about their children's motor and intellectual development (such as IQ) up to 4 years old. APrON has also measured some blood markers of iron status. This study will measure more of the important iron blood markers and will combine this new data with information already collected to answer the questions described above. This study is important because it will tell us about the ranges of iron status of women during pregnancy and postpartum and how this has been affected by her diet and supplement intake. It will also tell us about iron status, pregnancy outcomes and child development in Canada. Results will help to guide help the research and policies needed to improve women and children's health.

column36: Assessing the role of adolescent hormonal contraceptive use on risk for depression
column37: Young women in Canada often use hormonal contraception (HC), and its popularity is increasing. The use of HC is highly effective in preventing teenage pregnancies and has a number of positive societal and economic consequences. However, HC was originally developed as a medication for adults, and much remains unknown about the potential side effects for teenagers of using HC. For example, because adolescence is a life stage during which major brain development is still ongoing, use of HC during this period could have effects on brain development with long-lasting consequences on young women's mental health. Our proposed research builds upon the growing evidence that relationships may exist between the synthetic hormones that are contained in HC, patterns of brain development, and mental functioning. We will conduct a three-year study of young women aged 13-18, documenting their use of HC during this period along with their stress reactivity, social competence, and depression symptoms. Thus, our study is designed to examine not only whether young women who use HC are at increased risk for developing depression, but also why such a relationship might exist, and which women may be particularly sensitive to such side effects of using HC. Women are approximately twice as likely as men to develop depression in their lives. Depression is a leading cause of years lived with disability and reduced quality of life, unemployment and lost wages, and risk for suicide. We expect that our research will advance scientific understanding about why women might be at particular risk for developing these disorders. We also hope that our research will contribute new data relevant to an important ongoing conversation in the medical community and in the public about the prescription of HC to adolescent women, ultimately promoting more informed dialogue and decision-making.

column36: Deciphering the role of DCIR in HIV-1 pathogenesis
column37: Several studies have shown that early or pre-exposure treatments help prevent HIV-1 infection and the consequent destruction of the immune system which is then able to regain some control over the infection. In link with these observations, identification of new targets for HIV-1 involved in the first stages of infection remains the best option to eradicate HIV-1 infection. Dendritic cells (DCs) are the first immune cells which recognize HIV-1 in mucosal tissue. The initial interaction between HIV-1 and DCs occurs through attachment factors and we have identified the dendritic cell immunoreceptor (DCIR) as a key receptor. The binding of HIV-1 to DCIR allows the virus to be internalized, to escape the mounting of an immune response and to be transported to the lymphoid organs, where it gains entry into CD4 expressing T cells (CD4TL) by cell-to-cell transmission from DCs. Subsequent virus replication causes severe and irreversible depletion of CD4TL, bereaving the infected person of an efficient immune response against HIV-1. We are now interested in a possible role of DCIR in the early step of infection that appear to interfere with and ultimately compromise the immune response to HIV-1. We propose to test this hypothesis in vitro and in vivo using well-characterized cell models and humanized mouse models. We hope this novel approach will constitute a springboard for the development of new innovative therapeutic strategies against HIV-1 by blocking HIV-1 binding to DCs via DCIR without affecting the specific immune responses.

column36: Enhancing the Delivery of Novel Chemotherapeutics to Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine Glioma
column37: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, or DIPG, is a devastating tumour that occurs predominantly in children ages 5 - 9 years and is 100% fatal within 2-5 years following diagnosis. The location of these tumours within the brainstem precludes surgical removal because this region controls essential functions like breathing and the heartbeat. In addition, because of the essential importance of this region, a blood brain barrier protects the tissues from toxins, pathogens and drugs present in the circulation, making delivery of chemotherapy to tumours in this region nearly impossible. We have recently successfully demonstrated the safety of using ultrasound waves guided by MRI imaging to transiently open the blood brain barrier, permitting a window of opportunity to adminsiter cancer treatment. In our proposed studies we will first screen libraries of Health Canada and FDA approved drugs for effectiveness on our panel of DIPG tumours and select the best candidates that work well alone or in combination with each other. We will then test these compounds on mouse models of DIPG to determine effectiveness, ensure delivery and evaluate survival benefit for treated animals. Preclinical experiments such as these are essential for the Phase 1 Clinical trials that we are planning for children with this fatal disease.

column36: Roles of Alkali Cation/Proton Exchangers in Organellar Function and Neurodevelopmental Disorders
column37: The human brain has one of the highest rates of consumption of biochemical fuel (i.e., glucose) needed to sustain neuronal electrical activity. This in turn produces significant levels of metabolic ionic byproducts, such as protons (acid), bicarbonate and phosphates (bases) that must be effectively buffered, recycled for other purposes, or removed in order to maintain a suitable acid-base (pH) milieu for optimal brain function. Abnormal disturbances in brain pH balance are associated with the progression of various pathophysiological conditions, including newborn asphyxia, stroke, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and neuropsychiatric disorders - debilitating conditions that have an enormous human and economic impact on society. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that control brain pH levels are not fully understood. This project examines the roles of one major class of pH-regulating ion transport proteins called alkali cation/proton exchangers (i.e., SLC9A gene family), with a specific focus on the SLC9A6 transporter that is located in mobile membrane-bound vesicles located inside most brain cell types. Recent studies have identified mutations in SLC9A6 that cause an increasing diagnosed form of severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and autistic behaviour called Christianson Syndrome. We have isolated the SLC9A6 gene and are currently studying the effects the mutations have on neuronal function. We hypothesize that these defects impair the proper pH and functioning of vesicles that carry neurotransmitter receptors and other proteins to synapses of neurons, which in turn affects brain electrical activity and function. This assumption will be tested using a range of molecular, cellular, genetic and electrophysiological techniques in cultured cells and mouse animal models; thereby shedding new insights into the contributions of SLC9A6 to human health and disease, and identification of efficacious strategies for disease treatment.

column36: CEACAM-1 and TIM-3 interactions in HIV reservoir establishment, persistence and evasion from HIV specific immunity.
column37: No therapy can yet rid the body of HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, thus requiring life-long adherence to drugs. People on effective therapy harbour residual virus in their bodies, which can remain silent or 'latent' for many years, in areas of the body called 'reservoirs'. The main reservoir of hidden virus is within CD4 cells. It has been estimated that there are only about a million of CD4 cells in the body that contain HIV hidden from the effects of the immune cells. An immune cell called the 'cytotoxic killer T cell' can attack this reservoir. This proposal will explore new strategies to allow the immune system to 'see' the latent virus better instead of it being hidden and also improve the ability of the immune system to kill HIV infected cells better and eliminate reliance on drug therapy. Our preliminary findings suggest that two immune molecules called CEACAM-1 and TIM-3 are key to HIV's ability to hide and evade immune attacks. Our grant proposal aims to increase our understanding of the effects of these molecules on the reservoir. If successful, these studies will pave the way to new immune based therapies that can be used so that the immune system can rid the body of HIV. If successful, such treatment would benefit Canadians living with HIV as it will reduce the burden of lifelong treatments and side effects associated with them, thus improving their health and well-being.

column36: The neural basis of cognitive reserve, the brain's principal defense against Alzheimer's dementia and normal age-related cognitive decline
column37: Cognitive reserve (CR) is the principal source of resilience against dementia and normal age-related cognitive decline. Behavioral evidence indicates that CR is related to the degree of knowledge acquisition over the lifespan, but its neurobiological basis is unknown. For a given level of brain pathology, people with higher educational status, occupational achievement, bilinguality, vocabulary, and school grades show fewer symptoms of dementia; but the linkage between enhanced knowledge and CR needs to be experimentally established and the underlying neural mechanisms need to be determined. We will use advanced optical neural activity imaging methods in both normal mice and in an animal model of dementia, to establish the neurophysiological basis of CR and to show that these CR biomarkers are associated with protection from dementia in the Alzheimer's mouse model. The main dependent variables will be the complexity of the brain's spontaneous (resting-state) activity, the efficiency with which the brain encodes and retrieves information, manner in which new and old memories interact in the brain. These measures will be correlated with behavioral & cognitive measures of CR, biological age, and AB load . We expect new and unanticipated insights into how the brain creates CR and will help establish a basis for comparison with abnormal brain dynamics that may underlie or be consequences of several neurological and cognitive disorders, in particular, normal aging and age-related dementia

column36: MR-Guided Management of Occlusive Peripheral Arterial Disease
column37: Occlusive peripheral arterial disease occurs when blockages in blood vessels limit the blood supply to the leg. This disease is widespread and represents a major societal burden. Approximately 20% of those over the age of 59 years suffer from this disease, which results in over 160,000 limb amputations being performed per year in the US alone. Our goal over the next 5 years is to extend the role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to increase the success rates in patients who can have this disease treated using minimally invasive percutaneous techniques using catheters and wires advanced through blood vessels. X-ray fluoroscopy, the imaging modality that is currently used to guide percutaneous procedures, has relatively poor soft tissue contrast. This makes it difficult to visualize blockages and to ensure that a revascularization device stays within the vessel during the procedure. This limits success rates and restricts minimally invasive treatment to short blockages in large arteries (which occur much less frequently than long occlusions further down the leg). Other treatment options include bypass surgery, which has substantial associated risk, and medical therapy, which has been shown to have limited effectiveness. MRI, unlike x-ray, has excellent soft-tissue contrast and with MRI it is possible to develop a detailed picture of blocked vessels and downstream tissue that can greatly aid in guiding revascularization procedures. Through a program of technical developments we plan to advance methods which will improve revascularization of blocked blood vessels. We anticipate this will facilitate less invasive treatment in a significant population that would ordinarily be subjected to more invasive surgery or to less effective treatments.

column36: Implementing an intervention to foster meaningful engagement and shared decision-making among residents, families and healthcare teams in long-term care: A mixed methods approach.
column37: The specific aim of this study is to develop and assess the suitability of a shared decision-making strategy to engage residents of nursing homes, many of whom have Alzheimer's disease or other dementias, their family member (substitute decision-maker), and the healthcare team in a collaborative approach to decisions about resident care. Researchers have shown that resident and family member involvement in care decisions is inconsistent, and their role in decision-making is often unclear. Facilitating meaningful engagement of residents and family members in care decisions is an important part of supporting person-centered, high quality care, and may lead to improved outcomes such as greater resident and family satisfaction with care, staff satisfaction with quality of work life, and resident quality of life. The strategy includes: 1) staff education (communication strategies); 2) leadership coaching; and 3) team huddles (brief meetings) involving the staff, resident, and family that includes an engagement tool (one-page guide) to be used by the resident and family to lead the huddle discussion. The huddle meetings are a modification of current practice of family and resident care meetings and are not meant to replace them, but rather to supplement them. We will use interviews and surveys with staff, residents and families to ask about the usefulness of the strategy. The expected outcome from this study is an increased understanding of how to engage residents and family in care decisions impacting quality of life.

column36: A computational assay for risk and progression in Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting more than 1% of the Canadian population. PD is marked by a progressive spread of atrophy from the midbrain to subcortical structures and eventually, to the cerebral cortex. The motor and cognitive consequences of PD are devastating, yet symptom severity is impossible to predict. Why some patients develop purely motor symptoms, while others develop affective and cognitive symptoms, remains a mystery. Recent discoveries suggest that PD may be caused by neuron to neuron spreading of an endogenous protein, alpha-synuclein, which misfolds and aggregates, causing damage and cell death. An exciting possibility is that an individual's clinical phenotype depends on which large-scale brain networks are targeted by this protein abnormality. Here we propose to integrate clinical measures, neuroimaging and genetics to predict spreading patterns of alpha-synuclein and the emergence of clinical symptoms. Key deliverables include (a) statistical methods to identify atrophy patterns and at-risk patients, and (b) computational methods to infer spreading patterns and predict future atrophy. Currently, little is known about the large-scale network mechanisms driving the spread of neurodegeneration and emergence of symptoms, so the proposed project will offer important insight into designing novel therapies to slow or divert disease progression.

column37: Heart Failure (HF) remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide, representing a major economic burden on the healthcare system. Although the pathophysiology of HF is not fully characterized, the role of prolonged endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in the development and progression of HF is well-established. The ER is the largest membrane-bound organelle that participates in a wide array of cellular processes in eukaryotic cells. Instabilities in its structure and function can lead to activation of ER-dependent cellular pathways ultimately resulting in cardiac dysfunction. Defects in ER formation and function have been shown to result in numerous related diseases including neurological hereditary spastic paraplegia, cardiac dysfunction and eventual heart failure. Therefore, proper ER formation and maintenance of ER homeostasis are critical factors for understanding the pathophysiology of ER-related diseases. While the formation of the ER is not fully understood, an important group of proteins that mediate the formation and maintenance of the ER are receptor expression enhancing proteins (REEPs). Here, we propose to investigate the role of Reep5 in muscle pathologies, including cellular ER stress and heart failure. We aim to examine the physiological role of Reep5 utilizing Reep5 conditional knockout (KO) mice. Ultimately, understanding the role of Reep5 will provide greater insights into ER-related cardiac disease.

column36: Do community-based food security interventions influence use of community services, food security, social integration and health among new users?
column37: In Canada, hunger jeopardizes the health and well-being of one out of eight households. Donations of food banks are a well-known attempt to resolve the problem, but not everyone agrees on their benefit. Some think they are part of the problem, because they undermine the movement to adopt policies to fight against poverty. Others see them rather as a bridge to other community services that help people pull through. Who is right? For now, there is insufficient scientific data available to settle the matter. In a previous study we demonstrated the positive effects of food donation on food safety and on the physical and mental health of those using these community organizations. The results must be confirmed, however, and several questions remain. What is the trajectory of the people who call on these organizations? Do they find the guidance they need to overcome the hardships at the root of their request for food? In what way? On what conditions? Is the situation different in Montreal, in the periphery, or in rural areas? It is in an attempt to answer these questions that our team proposes to meet, three times over two years, 1,800 new users of 180 community organizations offering food donations in four regions of Quebec (Montreal, Estrie, Lanaudiere, and Mauricie-Centre-du-Quebec). Interviews with organization heads and with users with different pathways will help complete the picture. Our team brings together veteran and new researchers, and also 16 organizations intimately familiar with the environments to be studied. Together, they will communicate their results to practitioners, managers, and decision-makers to improve public and community network planning and intervention practices and to guide public policies on food security.

column36: Regulation of stem cell proliferation in the C. elegans germ line
column37: Stem cells provide the source material for development, tissue maintenance and wound repair. They are able to provide these functions because of their unique ability to both self-renew and differentiate. Self-renewal, or the ability to make new stem cells, ensures that a stem cell population is maintained. Differentiation is the process by which these cells form the desired tissue. A balance must be maintained between self-renewal and differentiation in order for stem cells to function properly. If there is too much self-renewal, a tumour may form instead of the desired tissue. If there is too much differentiation, the stem cell population will become depleted, preventing the desired tissue from being formed in the future. We study the genetic and molecular mechanisms that control the balance between self-renewal and differentiation. As a model, we use the germ line of the small nematode worm, C. elegans. This model is one of the best-understood stem cell systems due to the vast array of investigative tools that are available. We have identified a number of genes that, when mutated, cause the balance between self-renewal and differentiation to become compromised. By studying how these genes function, we will determine the molecular mechanisms involved in regulating stem cell behaviour. Importantly, each of the genes we have identified have similar genes in humans, which are also thought to be involved in regulating stem cell proliferation; therefore, our analysis will be directly applicable to understanding human stem cell behaviour. We are also taking the next step in understanding stem cell behaviour by identifying the proteins that are enriched in stem cells. Through this exquisitely sensitive stem cell system, we will determine the proteins that provide stem cells with their unique characteristics. Understanding how specific factors regulate stem cell behaviour will bring us closer to realizing their full therapeutic potential.

column36: Cannabis effects on white matter microstructure and outcomes in early phase psychosis: a 1 year dual site longitudinal study.
column37: Schizophrenia, affecting 1% of the population, causes significant burden to individuals, families and society. Fortunately, specialized early phase psychosis (EPP) intervention programs result in positive long term outcomes. Unfortunately, the high rate of cannabis use in EPP affects these outcomes. Cannabis use results in a higher risk of relapse and severity of symptoms, reductions in individuals following thru with treatment and overall functioning deficits (e.g. work and school) compared to EPP non-cannabis users. Cannabis use can reduce the recovery gains of these young adults. Cannabis, thru its receptors located on the brains white matter (WM) tracts, may be affecting WM development during the critical brain developmental period of young adulthood, resulting in these negative outcomes. Damage to the connections in the brain have themselves been reported in long-term schizophrenia, potentially causing schizophrenia symptoms. The effects of regular cannabis use, on a potentially already damaged brain in early disease, has not been well studied but we suspect that it too reduces the strength of brain connections but in a different way than schizophrenia. Our 2 site study (Halifax, NS; London, Ont), will recruit subjects to four groups: cannabis use disorder (CUD) and non-CUD patients within the first year of entry to the EPP programs, and CUD and non-CUD age and sex matched healthy controls. We will collect detailed information about past and current use of cannabis and clinical measures using established rating scales and methods. We will combine novel brain imaging techniques focusing on WM to generate an understanding of specific WM abnormalities associated with cannabis use in EPP, separate from illness and cannabis effects alone. This research design will allow a pioneer assessment of the potential negative impact of regular cannabis use longitudinally in this population (baseline and 1 year later), allowing for more directed education and treatments.

column36: A prospective study of DNA methylation in women and girls with Anorexia Nervosa: relationship to stage of illness and nutritional status
column37: Anorexia Nervosa (AN) can have devastating effects upon the physical and psychological well-being of its sufferers, and has the highest mortality rate of any mental-health problem. AN can be difficult to overcome, especially when people have had the disorder for a long time. Such realities beg for the identification of factors that cause and maintain this life-damaging disorder. AN is believed to involve the activation of certain genetic tendencies by the environment. For example, social pressures towards thinness induce people to diet intensively, and resulting nutritional factors are believed to affect gene expression. A main process involved is DNA methylation, which is influenced by one's nutritional state, and which can be measured in DNA extracted from blood. Our previous research has shown that women with AN have abnormal DNA methylation patterns, especially when they have been ill for a long time. Furthermore, we have found that treatment helps "reset" DNA methylation in some genes. To learn more about what DNA methylation levels mean for illness staging and recovery, we will study a large group of women and girls affected by AN and test whether: 1) Refeeding and weight normalization "restore" DNA methylation levels to normal. 2) Diet-induced changes in specific nutrient levels in blood underlie some of the methylation changes we see. 3) Someone's DNA methylation levels predict how well they will respond to treatment. 4) Findings differ between teenage and adult patients. We will study women and girls who currently have AN, before and after intensive treatments; women and girls who are recovered from AN for at least a year; and healthy women and girls who have never had an eating disorder. We hope that our study will promote a better understanding of the causes of AN, so as to guide improvements in preventive efforts and treatment.

column36: Deregulation of the anaphase promoting complex in human cancer
column37: The anaphase-promoting complex (APC) is an essential component of the cell that is required for cells to divide. Cancer cells particularly require activity of this complex since cells in tumours are in a constant state of cell division. Work from the lab of Dr. Teodoro has shown that some types of ovarian cancers are driven my mutations that inappropriately activate the APC. One of the goals of the proposed research is to understand how genetic mutations in the APC lead to cancers in humans. Since cancerous cells constantly require activity of the APC, targeting this complex using drugs may be an effective new manner of treating cancer. Inhibition of the APC has been shown by the Teodoro lab to selectively induce death in cancer cells while leaving normal cells unaffected. Another goal of this research project is to identify the pathways that maintain APC activity in cancer cells. It is hoped that inhibition of the APC will be an effective mechanism to arrest the growth of cancer cells that can be translated into novel chemotherapies.

column36: Testing a novel reward processing model of negative urgency in individuals with binge eating
column37: Mental illness is a significant public health concern; approximately 50% of the population will experience a mental health disorder in their lifetime. Research has led to the development of effective treatments for mental health disorders. However, psychiatric disorders commonly co-occur, and it is not always clear which disorder should be treated first. Moreover, treatments have generally been designed based on expressed symptoms rather than the bio-behavioural mechanisms that underlie symptom expression. The proposed research will focus on identifying the bio-behavioural mechanisms that explain negative urgency - the tendency to act impulsively when experiencing negative emotions. This personality trait has been linked to almost all mental health conditions (e.g., eating disorders, alcohol and substance use disorders, major depression, borderline personality disorder) and is thus a prime target for novel trans-diagnostic treatments. We will test the hypothesis that negative urgency is related to increased processing of rewards when an individual experiences negative emotions, and that emotion-enhanced reward processing explains why negative urgency relates to mental health conditions. These hypotheses will be examined in a sample of women with binge eating and eating disorders. Binge eating has a strong, specific relationship with negative urgency, and negative affect is the most common precipitant of this behavioural eating disorder symptom. If reward processing increases under negative mood conditions relate to negative urgency and binge eating, treatments for mental health conditions characterized by high negative urgency should be designed to decrease reward processing and should be administered in the context of a negative mood for maximal benefit.

column36: Identifying Therapeutic Vulnerabilities of Brain Arteriovenous Malformations
column37: Brain arteriovenous malformations (BAVMs) are a tangle of large, abnormal blood vessels within the brain. The resulting high blood flow can cause these blood vessel malformations to rupture and bleed, which may lead to severe illness or even death. BAVMs are a leading cause of bleeding in the brains of children and young adults. The main reason to treat a BAVM is to prevent a rupture. Treatment of BAVMs with surgery or radiation carries significant risk, and is both invasive as well as costly. There are currently no drugs available to treat this disorder and the cause of BAVMs is not known. We have identified spontaneous, non-inherited genetic mutations in a gene called KRAS in the majority of BAVM patients. These mutations occur in the cells that line blood vessels within BAVMs, but do not occur elsewhere in the patient. The KRAS gene codes for a protein that serves as an ON-OFF switch in blood vessel cells. When the KRAS gene is mutated, blood vessel cells are stuck in the 'ON' state and think that they are receiving cell growth and migration signals, even when they are not. In this proposal, we first aim to identify the defective genes in BAVMs that do not have mutations in KRAS, and second to understand how KRAS mutations influence the formation of BAVMs. To do this, we will introduce mutations in KRAS in blood vessel cells of mice and zebrafish; both common animal models to study blood vessel development and disease. In addition to testing whether these animals develop BAVMs, we will also use drugs to block cellular signalling pathways downstream of the 'ON' switch to determine whether we can treat BAVMs in these animal models. This may help us to discover drugs that could be used to treat this disorder in humans.

column36: Signaling and chromatin mechanisms of Paneth cell differentiation in intestinal development and disease
column37: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is one of the most common and deadly gastrointestinal diseases in human infants. With 30% mortality, it is characterized by inflammation and death of intestinal cells. Currently, how NEC initiates is unknown. As newborns become exposed to gut microbiota after birth, intestinal cells begin to differentiate into Paneth cells, a critical cell type controlling immune response. Therefore, we hypothesize that proper gut microbiota exposure is essential for intestinal cell differentiation into Paneth cells, thereby preventing NEC initiation. Indeed, our preliminary work demonstrates that gut microbiota exposure is critical for intestinal cell differentiation into Paneth cells, and its proper differentiation is critical to the prevention of NEC in early postnatal development. Interestingly, antibiotic treatment significantly reduced the number of immune cells. We will investigate further how gut microbiota promotes Paneth cell differentiation through immune cells. During cell differentiation, the chromatin structure, a massive protein complex that organizes and protects DNA, must open to make the DNA accessible to processes that will bring about major changes in gene expression. However, the chromatin mechanisms underlying Paneth cell differentiation are unknown. By analyzing chromatin and gene patterns of Paneth cells and intestinal progenitors isolated from pups treated with antibiotics, we will define the role of gut microbiota in Paneth cell-specific regulation of chromatin. By modifying chromatin, we also aim to restore Paneth cell differentiation, thereby rescuing NEC-like symptoms. Our work will provide important insight into the chromatin mechanisms of Paneth cell differentiation, identifying novel Paneth cell regulators and effective biomarkers for NEC. Additionally, this work will help advance the development of novel therapies.

column36: Contributions of the Ventral Auditory Cortical Pathway to Auditory Cognition
column37: Auditory categorization enables listeners to efficiently identify and respond to auditory stimuli. It is a computational process in which auditory stimuli are classified and grouped into sound categories based on their acoustic features, perceptual representations, or other types of information. For example, when we hear the word "fundable" from different speakers, we can categorize the sex of each speaker based on the pitch of the speaker's voice. On the other hand, to analyze the linguistic content transmitted by speech stimuli, we ignore the unique pitch, timbre etc. of each speaker's voice and categorize it into the distinct word category "fundable". Despite an important literature on the neuronal mechanisms of auditory categorization, many issues remain unknown or have yet to be fully elucidated. First, no studies have identified the sites in the brain that contain the information needed to create categorical representations. Second, and relatedly, there is not a clear understanding of distinct contributions of different brain regions to different types of auditory categorization. Finally, although our world is inherently multisensory, it is not known the degree to which the ventral auditory pathway contributes to multisensory categorization. The accomplish these goals, we combine high-density recordings within and across brain regions, rigorous and quantitative behavioral studies, and causal manipulations in rhesus monkeys to address these issues and identify the mechanisms underlying auditory categorization. These studies will provide important insights into hearing dysfunction and hearing perception. This understanding is crucial for guiding the development of more effective clinical approaches to alleviating hearing difficulties in complex acoustic environments- difficulties which are common in the elderly, the hearing impaired, and in individuals with cochlear implants or certain developmental disorders.

column36: Elucidating a new role for bile acids in protecting against C. difficile toxin pathogenesis: Implications for therapy
column37: Clostridium difficile (C.diff) is the leading cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea in the developed world. This opportunistic bacterium is a major problem in hospitals for three main reasons. The first is that C.diff is able to form highly resilient spores outside of the body that are difficult to eradicate from hospital settings. The second is that C.diff disease is triggered by antibiotics, which deplete most of the normal healthy gut bacteria, with the exception of antibiotic-resistant C.diff itself. Third, C.diff produces toxins in the gut that cause tissue damage leading diarrhea and in some cases death. column36: The risk for premature atherosclerosis in survivors of childhood cancer: A study in the Preventing Cardiac Sequelae in Pediatric Cancer Survivors (PCS2) cohort
column37: Most children newly diagnosed with cancer will survive their illness. Unfortunately, many of these survivors will develop long-term complications from their cancer treatment that can lead significant illness and even early death. Most cardiac research in these patients has focused on heart failure which is a result of some of the common chemotherapies used to treat childhood cancer. Little is known about who is at greatest risk for this life-threatening outcome. We will recruit 250 of these survivors and 250 of their siblings to undergo an assessment of their blood vessels using several innovative imaging tools in our cardiovascular laboratory. These risk factors will inform the design of a tool that can be used by clinicians that care for childhood cancer survivors (during childhood and adulthood) to determine which survivors are at greatest risk of having a heart attack. column37: Stroke occurs when there is a blockage of a brain artery which stops blood flow causing brain damage and disability. Rapid removal of the blockage with micro instruments, a procedure called endovascular therapy (EVT), has been shown to dramatically improve the functional outcome of patients with stroke. MRI will measure early infarct growth by measuring brain damage immediately after treatment and the following day, and the delayed infarct growth that occurs over 3 months. The REPERFUSE NA1 study will provide an important step to establishing whether brain protective treatment NA1 can work together with EVT to help reduce the growth of stroke related brain damage and improve stroke recovery.

column36: Type IV pilins - multifunctional subunits of bacterial virulence factors
column37: Many bacterial pathogens use hair-like filaments called type IV pili (T4P) as mini grappling hooks to stick to their hosts and rapidly spread. T4P are thus potential targets for new antimicrobial therapies such as vaccines. Each filament is made of thousands of small lollipop-shaped proteins called pilins. The "stick" of the lollipop is very conserved and has a number of important functions. It stores pilins in the cytoplasmic membrane; forms the inner core of the pilus; and acts as a recognition domain for sensor proteins that monitor pilin inventories, so more are made only if needed. We will investigate how these monitoring systems recognize pilins, so we can fool them into shutting down even if there aren't enough pilins available. In contrast, the "lollipop" part of a pilin is diverse, making it harder to design a vaccine that will cover all possible "flavours". We are trying to understand the causes and consequences of pilin diversity, to inform the design of new treatments. We study Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), a pathogen designated by the World Health Organization as a critical priority for new therapies due to its high level of resistance to antibiotics. We searched thousands of Pa DNA sequences to find all of its pilin flavours, and constructed a panel of different pilins in a common genetic background. This unique and expandable resource will allow us to ask how the immune system "sees" different pilins - when is recognition lost? We think that diversity arises from attempts to escape from viruses that stick to the pili. Changing a pilin's sequence or hiding it with sugars blocks attachment. Remarkably, some viruses can bind to very different pilins, suggesting they see a non-obvious common feature. We will characterize how those viruses interact with diverse pilins. They are of interest as therapeutics, as they can kill multidrug resistant bacteria. Together, this work will give us an unprecedented understanding of how pilus diversity is shaped.

column37: Cancer develops following increased alterations within DNA, which are usually repaired by complex groups of proteins involved in DNA repair. Defects in one or more DNA repair mechanisms cause the accumulation of changes in DNA, called mutations, that increase the possibility that certain cells become tumorigenic. Paradoxically, once cancer cells emerge they are acutely dependent on certain DNA repair mechanisms, even more so than normal cells, because they proliferate rapidly and their metabolism generates highly reactive DNA-damaging molecules. Hence, to survive cancer cells must adapt by increasing their capacity to repair specific types of DNA damage. As a by-product of this adaptation, cancer cells become more resistant to therapies that cause DNA damage, such as chemotherapy and radiation. We have discovered one strategy that cancer cells use to augment their DNA repair capability. They can increase the expression of proteins that stimulate the activity of DNA repair enzymes. In contrast to DNA repair enzymes, these accessory proteins are not essential to normal cells under physiological conditions, but are required by cancer cells. This provides a therapeutic window to develop new drugs targeting accessory proteins to which cancer cells have become addicted to. Our characterization of the CUT domain family of proteins has established a paradigm in this field. We now have identified a novel accessory factor that stimulates a different DNA repair enzyme. In the current project, we will characterize the activity of this accessory protein, determine which cancers are dependent on it and demonstrate why cancer cells die without it whereas normal cells can survive. We will develop biochemical tests that are amenable to high-throughput screening in order to identify small molecules that inhibit the accessory protein. These studies are expected to target multiple cancers and eventually to provide new mechanisms to treat cancer.

Our research shows that PsA is chronic, severe, and can result in joint destruction, disability, and a poor quality of life. Early diagnosis of PsA in individuals with psoriasis can prevent such poor outcomes. Unfortunately, early diagnosis is difficult and a large proportion of patients with psoriasis and PsA remain undiagnosed. A clinical tool that can help clinicians diagnose PsA is urgently needed. Our first objective is to identify markers in the blood that can help clinicians diagnose PsA in psoriasis patients, and verify the usefulness of these markers in a clinical setting, by rigorously testing them in large populations of PsA and psoriasis patients. We are in a unique position since we have the patients, and are also able to combine a number of techniques to measure these blood markers and how they are regulated. Our second objective is to discover additional markers in the blood that will predict the severity of PsA. We propose to use the most advanced genetic techniques to identify the differences in gene activity between PsA patients with mild and severe disease. These differences will then be measured in large populations of patients to evaluate their usefulness in a clinical setting. A tool that can identify patients destined to develop more severe PsA would also enable clinicians to treat these patients more aggressively and avoid toxic medications for those likely to follow a milder course. Development of clinical tools to diagnose PsA and predict its severity will facilitate earlier diagnosis and treatment, and enable clinicians to make informed treatment decisions based on predicted severity. This project has the potential to improve the lives of thousands of Canadians, and greatly reduce the burden of PsA on the Canadian health care system.

column36: Healthier by doing: Testing the effectiveness of a youth-centred employment/education intervention for young adults with mental illness
column37: Youth and young adults aged 15-24 are typically completing school or job training and laying the foundation for a stable future. In Canada, 20-25% of youth and young adults experience mental health problems. For this group, challenges at school, home, and community are compounded by fragmented resource services, resulting in low graduation rates, high unemployment, and poor health outcomes. Our team has spent the last two years understanding how youth with mental illness develop job skills and enter employment. We identified a lack of youth-specific models of care that comprehensively support youth to concurrently managed their illness and achieve their employment and education goals. In response, we partnered with the YMCA, the Inner City Youth Clinic, and youth leaders to develop and deliver an innovative intervention of employment support tailored for individuals aged 15-24 years. The 16-week intervention is called Y-BEAT (Youth Breaking though Employment And Training). Our preliminary research shows Y-BEAT to be acceptable and feasible for rigorous study. We propose to examine the effectiveness of Y-BEAT in facilitating improved employment/education, health, and quality of life outcomes for youth with mental illness. The intervention involves two elements: (i) in-class health and skills training (5 weeks), and (ii) individualized placements to gain experience (11 weeks) in employment or training settings that match their goals. Intervention staff support participants and employers to develop a workplace Action Plan that outlines training, support and work expectations. Building on preliminary success, we will now test this intervention's effectiveness in a randomized trial. This involves comparing outcomes of the Y-BEAT intervention to usual treatment. If Y-BEAT is shown to improve employment, school, and health outcomes, we expect to reach thousands of youth by subsequently sharing the program with health and social agencies nationwide.

column36: Health, Prevention, and Policy Environments (HAPPEN): Investigating Policy-Maker and Public Knowledge, Attitudes, and Beliefs about the Effectiveness of Healthy Public Policies
column37: Healthy public policies are key strategies for supporting health. While some places have policies that make the healthy choice easier, those policies vary widely. There is little research that helps coordinate policy adoption across places. We need to know which policy options (e.g., taxes, education, etc) are the most acceptable to, and highest priority for, policymakers and the general public. The HeAlth, Prevention, and Policy ENvironments (HAPPEN) project will address this critical gap. Our team will study the knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs of policymakers and the public about policies related to preventing chronic disease and promoting mental health. We have done 5 surveys focused on chronic disease prevention (2009-2016) of the public and policymakers across Canada. Now, we propose to: i) use research and practice expertise to add mental health and substance misuse policies to that survey; and, ii) repeat the survey for two more years (2019 and 2021) in AB and MB to identify trends in policy priorities and to build on other work in those provinces. We will conduct email and phone surveys with school, workplace, municipal, and provincial policymakers and the general public. HAPPEN's research-practice team will gather and share policy evidence and develop practitioner resources. Our past surveys helped partners to act on policy opportunities, evaluate policies, and target advocacy efforts (e.g., smoke-free vehicles, school food strategies). Currently, there is no other survey that asks both policymakers and the public about policies related to chronic disease, mental health and substance misuse. We will share our data to help NGOs and others act on the most promising policies and focus policymakers' attention on policies with strong public support. HAPPEN will create new and much needed evidence on trends in policy priorities over time and place, enhancing policy action and evaluation in Canada.

column36: Cardiovascular disease attributable to nutrition-related causes: Estimating future burden and evaluating nutrition policy options for maximizing population health benefit in Canada
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of mortality in Canada. Studies have shown that individuals who consume excess sodium and sugar-sweetened beverages are more likely to develop CVD. Excess consumption of these dietary factors is common in Canada, leading the Canadian Government to identify sodium and sugar-sweetened beverages as high priority policy targets requiring effective interventions. To help reduce sodium and sugar-sweetened beverages consumption, three population-level dietary interventions are being considered: 1) cutting sodium in processed foods; 2) taxing sugar-sweetened beverages; and, 3) mandatory front-of-package food labels for packaged foods. The project goal is to determine whether three proposed population-level dietary interventions will impact sodium and sugar-sweetened beverage intakes and CVD in Canada. We will explore whether the intervention benefits are equally experienced across social groups (i.e., age, sex, socioeconomic status and food insecurity). To answer these important research questions, we will use the Cardiovascular Disease Population Risk Tool (CVDPoRT), a policy tool that predicts the likelihood of developing CVD based on individual risk factors profiles. This research will describe current sodium and sugar-sweetened beverage intakes using the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) 2015 (the first national nutrition survey since 2004). We will estimate the anticipated change in consumption-levels that would be achieved if the three population-level dietary interventions were implemented. Applying CVDPoRT to CCHS 2015 data, we will predict the number of CVD cases avoided, both in the population and across social groups, by implementing the three population-level dietary interventions. This research will fill a critical gap by providing policy-makers with the evidence to inform the implementation of population-level dietary interventions to reduce nutrition-related CVD in Canada.

column36: Regulation of an ion channel complex in Fragile X syndrome
column37: Fragile X Syndrome is the greatest inherited cause of intellectual disabilities and autism spectrum disorder worldwide and yet has no cure. Fragile X occurs at a rate of 1 in 4000 males and 1 in 6000 females, and 1 in ~200 females are carriers that could pass this disorder onto children. The Fragile X mutation leads to the loss of "Fragile X Mental Retardation Protein" (FMRP). Previous work has shown that FMRP regulates the translation of numerous proteins needed to maintain normal synaptic function and plasticity. Because Fragile X is known to reduce synaptic plasticity in cerebellum, we use the mouse cerebellar mossy fiber-granule cell pathway as a model to explore the basis for synaptic abnormalities in Fragile X. Our preliminary data reveal that FMRP binds to an ion channel complex between calcium and potassium channels (Cav3-Kv4) that potentiates the mossy fiber EPSP and increases granule cell excitability via an ERK kinase pathway. We find that FMRP knockout mice completely lack mossy fiber potentiation and associated changes in granule cell excitability. Importantly, intracellular infusion of an active FMRP fragment into granule cells of FMRP knockout mice in vitro restores Cav3-Kv4 function and potentiation of excitability. In addition, an FMRP fragment attached to a tat peptide to facilitate passage across cell membranes rapidly crosses the blood-brain barrier and enters cerebellar granule cells after injection into the bloodstream, opening the door to reintroducing FMRP in live animals. These exciting results provide important steps to understanding a new role for FMRP in controlling a membrane ion channel complex that sets cell excitability, and to assess tat-FMRP as a therapeutic strategy to reduce abnormal behaviour in Fragile X Syndrome.

column36: Dissecting RNA binding protein-directed control of hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Blood stem cells, because of their ability to remake all blood cell types as well as regenerate themselves, hold the key to a healthy immune system and have lifesaving potential for the treatments of a range of blood cancers and immune disorders. Despite their promise, the lack of understanding of the mechanics that control these specialized cell types has prevented their widespread use, depriving many patients of a potentially curative therapy for their disease. Our work aims to uncover proteins that are required for blood stem cells to carry out regeneration and to perform experiments that will shed light on how they operate. While in the past, much research has focused on defining the molecular players that work on the DNA of these blood stem cells to make their RNA intermediate, we have new evidence that how this RNA intermediate is changed to impact the final step of protein production is of major importance to the regenerative capacity of blood stem cells. Our study will focus on systematically identifying and understanding the players that act on RNA in these rare and clinically valuable cell types in the hopes that we can capitalize on them and on this previously underappreciated layer of control to promote blood stem cell-based regeneration.

column36: iCanCope with Post-Operative Pain (iCanCope PostOp): Development and evaluation of a smartphone-based pain self-management program for adolescents following surgery
column37: The goal of this project is to develop a smartphone app, called "iCanCope with Post-Operative Pain" (iCanCope PostOp). This app will help teenagers to track and treat their own pain after surgery by providing "in-the-moment" advice wherever and whenever they need it. If pain is not properly treated after surgery, teenagers often have a poorer quality of life, use more opioid pain medications, and have a greater risk of developing chronic pain. Currently, few supports are available in the community to help teenagers manage pain after surgery once they leave the hospital. We plan to develop the iCanCope PostOp app in four steps. Step 1 is already complete and Steps 2-4 are the focus of this application. In Step 1 (completed), we spoke with teens who have had surgery and healthcare providers to find out what features they think are important to include in the app. Based on their input, we designed a basic test version of the app to help teens (a) track their pain, sleep, mood and activities, (b) set and try to meet their goals to improve function, and (c) give advice about how to manage pain in the moment. We also brought together a group of pain experts to suggest what pain management advice to include in the app. In Step 2, our team will ask teens who have had surgery and healthcare providers to review the "in-the-moment" advice. We will also show them all of the features in the basic test version of the app so we can make any improvements. Based on their feedback, we will build a more complete version of the app. In Step 3, we will conduct a study to find out whether teens find the completed version of the app easy to use and satisfying. In Step 4, we will conduct a study to determine how feasible it is for teens to use the app after surgery, and whether it improves their pain and other important outcomes. If the app is helpful, it will be made freely available in Canada for use by teenagers who have had surgery.

column36: Neurochemical and behavioural characterisation of a novel Dopamine Transporter Deficiency Syndrome mouse model.
column37: Dopamine transmission in the brain is a tightly regulated process, and alterations in dopamine signaling result in several disease with enormous human and economic burden, including schizophrenia, ADHD, Bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease and dyskinesias. One of the key regulators of dopamine transmission is the plasma membrane dopamine transporter, DAT, which transports released dopamine back into the neuron. In addition to the above prevalent diseases, there is also a rare, fatal disease caused by mutations in the dopamine transporter, called dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. We hypothesize that several disease states could be corrected by increasing the protein levels of the dopamine transporter. Drugs that increase dopamine transporter activity could potentially treat conditions such as such as dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. We have worked to identify drugs that would increase the levels and activity of the dopamine transporter, and have discovered that the prescribed drug bupropion increases dopamine transporter levels and activity. Recently, we generated a transgenic mouse model of dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. Our proposed research is designed to uncover the pathophysiology of this by studying these new transgenic animals. Also, we will measure whether bupropion will be able to have therapeutic effect in this new mouse model. Positive results from our studies could be quickly translated into the clinic, since bupropion is already an approved drug and used in humans.

column36: Mechanism of Microtubule assembly by CKAP2
column37: When cells divide, the DNA in form of chromosomes is pulled into the two new daughter cells. The machinery, that exerts the force necessary for separating the chromosomes and is made out of tiny flexible tubes that we call microtubules. Microtubules have to form and grow very quickly and precisely during cell division. They have to be very stable and very dynamic at the same time and constantly be replenished. To make these microtubules, help them grow, stabilize them and ultimately break them apart again, cells use an army of proteins, called MAPs (microtubule-associated proteins). While we know some MAPs, the large majority of these proteins is still not well characterized or completely unknown. We are investigating a MAP that makes new microtubules and helps them grow extremely fast. The same MAP is involved in causing several types of cancer as well as making these cancers more aggressive. We will attempt to solve how this protein makes microtubules grow, how it is involved in building the machinery that divides chromosomes, why cell division is not working well when the protein is misregulated, and how that can cause cancer. In addition, we will solve the structure of that protein bound to microtubules, which might help developing new anti-cancer drugs.

column36: DCIS-Precise: A Genomics-Driven Model for Predicting DCIS Response to Radiation
column37: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast cancer but some DCIS will progress to invasive breast cancer. DCIS is not life-threatening but women with DCIS require treatment to lower their risk of developing invasive breast cancer. Most women with DCIS receive breast-conserving surgery and whole breast radiation treatment (RT) which is proven to lower the risk of recurrent disease including invasive breast cancer. Our inability to identify which women benefit from radiation results in unnecessary treatment of many women who will not benefit from radiation and inadequate treatment of women with aggressive but radiation-resistant DCIS who will develop recurrence despite receiving radiation. Genomic biomarkers that predict chemotherapy benefit have revolutionized the treatment of breast cancer, but predictors of radiation benefit are unknown. The goal of this study is to develop a biomarker assay that predicts RT benefit in DCIS. This will help reduce unnecessary RT in women who have a low risk of recurrence. However, it will also identify those with aggressive DCIS who will respond (benefit) from radiation and identify those who have radiation-resistant disease in whom alternate interventions are needed to lower their future risk of breast cancer. To accomplish this goal we have established 3 cohorts of DCIS. The Sunnybrook institutional cohort will be used for genomic profiling and assay (termed DCIS RT assay) development. The Ontario population-based DCIS cohort and the Swedish DCIS clinical trial cohort will be used as two independent cohorts for validation of the novel assay. We will also create a nomogram which will help provide women with more accurate estimates of the risks/benefits of RT. We have assembled an international team of experts with a proven track record who have the expertise to accomplish this goal and improvement the management of DCIS by reducing over-treatment and reducing the future burden of invasive cancer worldwide.

column36: Mechanisms of action of antiestrogens: towards improved treatment of relapse in ER+ breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer and second leading cause of cancer death among Canadian women. Estrogens contribute to breast tumorigenesis by acting via a specific effector, estrogen receptor alpha (ER), present in 2/3 breast tumors. Inhibition of estrogenic action is achieved for therapeutic purpose via different drugs that have distinct mechanisms of action, collectively known as hormonal therapies. However, resistance occurs in 30-50% of breast cancer patients treated with hormonal therapies. The mechanisms of action of antiestrogens, a class of drugs frequently used for both first and second line hormonal treatment of ER+ breast cancer, are still not fully understood, preventing their optimal use in patients relapsing after hormonal therapies. The Mader lab has uncovered novel mechanisms of action for antiestrogens that explain the spectrum of clinical profiles displayed by this class of molecules, and has characterized the impact of different antiestrogens in models of resistance to hormonal treatments due to different genetic changes in the estrogen receptor. The current application will further characterize aspects of the mechanisms of action of antiestrogens that remain poorly understood, such as the proteins that cooperate with the estrogen receptor to lead to resistance to these agents. The team will also investigate novel therapeutic combinations that would increase response in progressing patients by suppressing estrogen signalling more efficiently.

column36: Regulation of proteostasis by glycosylation of nucleocytoplasmic proteins.
column37: The cells of all organisms need to adapt to changes in their environment. One mechanism enabling adaptation to environmental changes, including variation in nutrient availability and cellular stressors such as heat, is the ability of cells to tune their levels of specific proteins. This process, known as proteostasis, is of great interest to researchers because it is now well recognized that disruptions in proteostasis contribute to various diseases including various neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson and Alzheimer disease. Further, proteostasis appears to become slowly impaired in processes such as aging. One mechanism that has emerged as a regulator of proteostasis is the modification of a set of proteins, found on the inside of cells, with specialized sugar units. We have recently uncovered that this sugar modification regulates the stability of proteins right at the moment of their creation and extending on to when they are found in large protein complexes that fulfill essential roles in the cell. Because this sugar modification is abundant within cells and depends on the amount of available nutrients, we aim to understand the scope of this modification and its impact on the broad set of sugar modified proteins. We further aim to evaluate the locations of sugar modification and to then determine which of these are physiological important for cell function. These data will help guide more targeted strategies to manipulate this promising but poorly understood pathway that has already delivered compounds into clinical trials.

column36: Frailty assessment for older adults at points of care: Validating the electronic comprehensive geriatric assessment / frailty index (eFI-CGA)
column37: Frailty is characterized by loss of biological reserves across multiple organ systems resulting in an increased risk of death and other adverse outcomes. Mounting evidence suggests frailty may be modifiable and can be prevented and sometimes even reversed. Frailty guidelines recommend the early identification of frailty in "at risk" seniors to address modifiable variables. The Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) is a well-established clinical tool used to determine older adults' medical, psychological, and functional capabilities. It provides key baseline data for identifying degrees of risk and establishing individual care plans. A deficit accumulation based frailty index can be calculated using CGA items (FI-CGA). Key to care planning, the FI-CGA precisely measures the level of frailty. Performing a CGA and calculating an FI-CGA typically requires extra work for front-line clinicians. Electronic healthcare tools offer a more time efficient, cost-effective alternative. In partnership with the world's experts in frailty, our team conducted a pilot study to develop an electronic CGA in the Electronic Medical Records system and to automate the simultaneous calculation of an eFI-CGA in primary care and family medicine. The EMR allows widespread use across the healthcare system, making an eCGA and eFI-CGA an example of how to provide efficient care for older adults. This project aims to establish the reliability and validity of the eFI-CGA for widespread use in the management of older adults (e.g. identifying at-risk individuals and monitoring frailty changes in relation to short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes). Determining the eFI-CGA to be a reliable and valid measurement of frailty may help healthcare providers make more meaningful and comprehensive healthcare decisions; improve patients' clinical outcomes and self-management competence; reducing costly hospital admissions and prolonged stays by providing a better chance to address frailty at an early stage.
