column36: Developing an entirely new anti-vascular therapy approach to treat metastatic cancer by targeting vessel co-option
column37: One in two Canadians will develop cancer in their lifetime and one in four will die, mostly due to tumours spreading to other sites of the body (metastasis). Cancer therapies that inhibit the growth of new blood vessels into tumours have known, but limited effectiveness when treating patients with metastasis. This is partly due to tumour cells bypassing the need of creating their own blood supply and instead hijacking the existing blood vessels in organs with a rich vasculature such as the lung - one of the most common sites of metastatic disease in cancer patients. This process is called "vessel co-option" and in the lung leads to the striking phenomenon of tumour cells filling up the air spaces to exploit the organ's existing blood supply. We propose strategies to target such co-opted vessels in lung metastases. There is a high probability that since co-opted vessels are exposed to many changes brought about by the tumour, they express proteins that are not normally found on healthy blood vessels, and which may be therapeutically targetable. We have developed a mouse model of breast cancer metastasis that mimics cancer observed in human patients. In this model vessel co-option happens exclusively when metastasis occurs in the lung. To determine differences in co-opted versus normal vessels, cells of the co-opted blood vessels will be isolated from lung metastases and undergo gene expression analysis in comparison to vessels from normal healthy lungs. Drugs will be generated that target these differences on hijacked vessels with the goal of destroying them. There are also a number of carefully selected existing drugs and experimental therapies which may have the property of targeting vessel co-option, and these will be evaluated. Such vessel co-option targeting therapies could be used in combination with drugs that stop the growth of new blood vessels to block two major ways a tumour gains a blood supply, in turn starving the tumour and arresting its growth.

column36: Pulmonary MRI to investigate airway inflammation and improve asthma patient outcomes
column37: Severe asthma accounts for a large majority of hospital visits and admissions in Canada and this has enormous costs for the asthma patient, their caregivers and employers and the health care system. Unfortunately, for many patients with asthma, current therapies do not improve their symptoms or their risk of disease worsening, necessitating hospital visits, lost work/school days and poor quality of life. New treatment options are emerging for asthmatics who have a high disease burden. However, currently there is no way to predict those patients who will respond favorably to the different therapies now available and under development. My recent research has shown that our understanding of asthma can be dramatically improved by harnessing the power of medical imaging and computer programs. To decrease the staggering burden on patients and the health care system, we want to develop new imaging measurements of asthma that can be used to improve patient outcomes. Therefore, for the first time, I am developing and evaluating the clinical utility of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based measurements of asthma. We think that MRI can be used to "personalize" treatment selection in individual asthmatics resulting in the correct treatment course, for the right patient and at the right time. Ultimately leading to better patient outcomes. My research will develop, clinically validate and integrate pulmonary MRI into asthma patient care. Our advances are very likely to impact asthma management and how new treatments will be developed, delivered and evaluated. Based on the enormous burden on the health care system, the vastly diminished quality of life, and increased morbidity of patients with asthma, the MRI measurements we develop will have high clinical and economic impact in Canada.

column36: Investigating the structural, biophysical and biochemical properties of large-scale protein association and liquid-liquid phase separation in neurological disorders.
column37: Brain function is poorly understood and there are no effective drugs for major neurological diseases, such as autism, Lou Gehrig's and Alzheimer's diseases, costing many billions of dollars to our society every year. Most of these diseases arise from genetic mutations leading to malfunction of proteins, the molecular machines that perform most biological functions. Some proteins have stable structure but others, called intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), are highly flexible. This extreme flexibility, or disorder, is very abundant in brain proteins, particularly those associated with neurological diseases, as it is advantageous for protein interactions essential for regulating key biological processes. Using unique methodologies developed in my laboratory, I propose to study IDPs and define a new paradigm for protein binding relying on dynamic interactions. This work will change the way proteins interactions are viewed, including those between two, multiple or even huge numbers of protein molecules, which can come together in a process called phase-separation to form liquid droplets involved in organizing the cell. A new paradigm focusing on dynamic interactions of disordered proteins will allow novel approaches to the study of neurological diseases. I propose to study disordered disease-associated proteins, such as caprin1 and G3BP1, which are directly linked to autism and Lou Gehrig's disease. As proteins are never isolated within the cell, I will investigate the disease-associated proteins in large-scale complexes with their cellular interaction partners. I will apply multidisciplinary expertise and powerful methods to key disordered proteins involved in brain function and diseases. I hypothesize that loss of regulation and rigidification of dynamic complexes of these disordered proteins leads to pathology in the brain. This study will yield insight enabling novel therapeutics for a variety of neurological diseases.

column36: Circulating tumour DNA as a precision oncology tool for metastatic bladder cancer
column37: Metastatic bladder cancer is a lethal and under-studied disease. Chemotherapy has historically been the most effective treatment for metastatic disease, but long-term survival has been a rarity. Recently, new drugs including immunotherapies are showing significant promise, but only a small proportion of patients respond to these treatments and we have no reliable way of predicting who the responders will be. During the first three years of my faculty appointment I have worked closely with clinical collaborators to develop a blood test that can identify tumour DNA present in a small blood sample (called circulating tumuor DNA, ctDNA). We can therefore use ctDNA to evaluate the genetic changes (mutations) in metastatic cancers that correspond to treatment response or resistance. Our preliminary work suggests that mutations detected in ctDNA accurately reflect cancer itself, meaning that we can profile a patient's metastatic bladder cancer before treatment without the need for a tissue biopsy. In this project we will identify mutations in the ctDNA of hundreds of Canadians with metastatic bladder cancer that are being treated with chemotherapy or immunotherapy. My research team will determine which mutations can predict a patient's subsequent response to treatment using our rare combination of cancer bioinformatics and clinical oncology. We are uniquely placed to perform this analysis given our strong track record of success in metastatic cancer ctDNA profiling, our novel custom methodology, and our recent establishment of a province-wide ctDNA profiling program that is rapidly accruing hundreds of patient blood samples. Success with our project will help explain why some metastatic bladder cancers are intrinsically responsive or resistant to the most commonly used therapies. Furthermore, we will have developed a clinically-practical framework (requiring only a blood sample) that may ultimately help prioritize patients for therapies with the best chance of success.

column36: Crisis and opportunity: how are social-ecological transformations scaling-up?
column37: Transitioning to a sustainable and equitable planet requires not just incremental improvements but transformational changes at all scales. Yet we know little about how such transformations happen nor how do they scale up. In this postdoctoral project, I will study already embedded solutions found in pre-existing sustainability initiatives - or seeds - that innovate to provide place-specific responses to existing social-ecological challenges. Through a comparative case-study of food-related sustainability initiatives in Athens and Montreal, this postdoctoral project will further our understanding of how social-ecological transformations happen and ways to foster sustainability pathways. More specifically, this project asks: how are small sustainability initiatives - or seeds - affecting wider social-ecological transformations (i.e. scaling up)? And how do these seeds change the way people relate to and manage ecosystem services? This project will integrate a focus on transformations to research on ecosystem services to better assess the sustainability of these emergent sustainability pathways. The first case-study, Montreal, provides an example whereby seeds have managed to institutionalize social-ecological innovation notably by collaborating with formal political structures to create new policies to promote social economy and sustainable development. The second case study, Athens, provides an example of radical new social-ecological innovations that emerged after a major economic crisis in opposition to the state. The project will adopt a mixed methods approach - combining interviews, an online survey, and a social network analysis to an ecosystem services assessment-to assess how seeds in the two case studies scale up and steer (or not) social-ecological transformations. The project will generate a set of lessons learned to aid policy and grassroots efforts and also contribute to advancing theory related to social-ecological transformations and ecosystem services.

column37: Dans le processus judiciaire menant a une decision concernant la garde et les droits d'acces d'un enfant apres une separation, des experts (travailleurs sociaux et psychologues) sont regulierement interpelles afin d'eclairer la Cour. Il est reconnu que les recommandations de ces professionnels sont generalement suivies par les juges ou que l'avis d'un expert incite bien souvent les parents a trouver une entente. Ces professionnels (juges et experts) se trouvent donc a l'origine de decisions cruciales pour le futur d'enfants et de familles particulierement vulnerables, car souvent aux prises avec des conflits chroniques et severes. Durant ce processus, tant les experts que les juges devront avoir le meilleur interet de l'enfant (MIE) pour objectif, car il s'agit du seul critere relatif a la determination de la garde en droit canadien. Or, ce critere a ete maintes fois critique en raison de son caractere subjectif et indetermine. S'appuyant sur la theorie des representations sociales, ce projet a pour objectif d'eclairer la pratique future des juges et des experts en examinant comment le MIE est interprete dans les rapports d'expertise et les jugements concernant la garde (poids accorde aux differents elements presents dans les dossiers, tendances actuelles qui influencent les decisions des juges et des experts et risques de biais). Pour ce faire le contenu de 43 expertises et jugements finaux concernant la garde et les droits d'acces (tires d'un echantillon de dossiers judiciaires de 2000 justiciables dans quatre districts judiciaires au Quebec et en Ontario) sera analyse. A terme, ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre l'utilisation de la preuve psychosociale par les tribunaux et de proposer un cadre d'analyse pour l'interpretation du MIE. Ces avancees sont d'une grande importance pour la prise en charge des dossiers comportant des conflits severes de separation, ces derniers beneficiant d'un arrimage plus fluide entre les services psychosociaux et judiciaires.

column36: "Through the veil": Revealing Mysteries of San Rock Art
column37: Rock art is one of the most ancient expressions of the human mind, and is found across the world, ranging from the Late Pleistocene to the present day. It raises several questions: When was it first produced? How was it made? Who created it? In this project, such questions are intended to be answered for San rock art, also called Later Stone Age (LSA) rock art, one of the longest traditions in the world. Thanks to detailed interpretative work using the extensive San ethnographic studies available, the meaning of LSA rock art is well known. In contrast, little is understood about how the paint itself was made or what it was made from, while the age of these paintings also remains mostly unknown. However, this information is critical to interpreting rock art and apprehending the changes in the art and, by extension, societal and spiritual changes among the San groups that may have occurred when they were in contact with sedentary populations and then Europeans. We aim first at studying San rock art: its representations, the techniques used by the artists, the provenance of raw materials, and detailing its changes through time. Second, we seek to explore changes in San spirituality and to assess whether they are linked to societal changes. To deal with these questions, San rock art will be characterised and dated and the same will also be done for portable art and objects with traces of pigments such as grindstones. This will be the first time that such comparisons are considered in the study of San rock art, though they are crucially needed to assess whether societal changes are linked to changes in the art. The main strength of this project is its interdisciplinary aspect, as it combines chemistry, geology, geochemistry, archaeology, material culture, and the history of art. All of these complementary fields are linked together to give new insights into the San groups, well-known by their art, but still mysterious in their beliefs and aspects of daily life

column36: Cellular senescence in diabetic retinopathy
column37: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most prominent complication of diabetes and the leading cause of severe visual loss. Diabetic retinopathy has largely been perceived as a microvascular disease given its overt vascular phenotype. Yet over the past years, considerable evidence suggests that central neurons in the retina also contribute to disease progression and hence DR presents salient feature of neurodegenerative disease. Current dogma on neurodegenerative diseases dictates that once a central neuron cumulates damage and ceases to transmit sensory stimuli, it degenerates and dies an apoptotic death. Yet, from an evolutionary standpoint, survival advantage would be gained from a mechanism triggered to help weather stressors and preserve nervous tissue integrity, eventually allowing for repair and restoration of function. My host lab (Dr. Sapieha Lab's) has recently identified a new stress response system in DR, where retinal neurons, microglia and endothelial cells enter a state of premature cellular senescence. This state of the retina contributes to disease progression through generation of a series of inflammatory mediators collectively termed the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. On the other hand, why retinal neurons enter a state of premature senescence during diabetes and whether this is a protective mechanism is not understood. In the proposed research program, we explore a novel paradigm of neuronal dormancy, where retinal neurons enter a state reversible senescence to weather diabetic and ischemic stressors. This challenges two dogmas: 1-Cellular senescence is irreversible. 2- Central neurons such as retinal ganglion cells in the retina have the inherent capacity to enter a state of dormancy to activate programs of cellular repair. Understanding the fundamental mechanisms that lead to the induction and reversal of cellular senescence may have broad implications for diabetes, and that beyond the retina.

column36: Integrating person-centered and precision psychiatry in the clinical assessment of depression
column37: Depression is now the leading cause of disability around the world. However, the range of syndromes subsumed under the label of depression remains broad. This heterogeneity has led to a crisis of diagnosis and poor treatment outcomes. In the face of this ongoing challenge, there is an urgent need to develop novel, more specific diagnostic tools and treatments. Assessment of depression is hampered by the growing divide between an increasingly neuroscientific view of this disorder and the importance of affirming the whole person of the patient in light of their individual life history, sociocultural specificity and subjective illness experience. Providing optimal diagnosis and treatment in psychiatry requires addressing individual pathology in all its dimensions: biological, mental, social, and environmental. My research will integrate the latest neuroscientific and sociocultural advances in psychiatric research to tackle this pressing health challenge. With the support of a Banting Fellowship I will develop and evaluate a novel integrative toolkit to assist clinicians in diagnosing and treating patients with symptoms of depression. My research will leverage the conceptual framework of 'precision' psychiatry (which emphasizes individual neurobiology and genetics) to complement recent efforts in 'person-centered' psychiatry (with its focus on experiential and social-cultural context). The project will produce a toolkit that helps clinicians integrate neuroscientific and sociocultural dimensions in their patient assessment. In a second stage, I will study how the implementation of the toolkit impacts clinical practice and treatment outcomes. Ultimately, this project will provide a basis for the continued development of patient-focused research and clinical care that does justice to the neurobiological, psychological and social specificity of individuals.

column36: Defining the Roles of Overgrowth Syndrome Genes in Shaping Developmental Gene Networks in Early Embryos
column37: Human overgrowth disorders such as Sotos syndrome are characterized by pre- and postnatal increased growth, intellectual disability and facial anomalies. These diseases result from mutations in genes that encode enzymes that turn off other genes by changing the structure of DNA. These genes include NSD1, most frequently mutated in Sotos Syndrome patients, and SETD2. Both encoded enzymes chemically modify a specific amino acid on a specific protein associated with DNA called histone H3. Interestingly, the modifications of histone H3 influences the activity of the protein that modifies the DNA, as well as that of another protein, EZH2, which chemically modifies histone H3. The Ezh2 gene is mutated in the related overgrowth disorder called Weaver Syndrome. These observations suggest "cross-talk" between these enzymes and in turn the genes they regulate. However, a systematic study of the consequences of disrupting these regulatory proteins has not been conducted. Here, using the mouse as a model system, we will study the interplay between these enzymes and the marks they deposit, by mutating these "overgrowth syndrome genes" in the mouse and studying the consequences of such mutations in the early mouse embryo, where these genes are first active. This "genome-wide" study, using state-of-the-art sequencing technology and mouse genetics, will lead to a better understanding of the molecular basis of several human overgrowth syndromes including Sotos and Weaver, potentially leading to new avenues for treatment of these diseases.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease is a disabling neurological disorder that is increasing in prevalence and thus having a growing impact on the Canadian population. This disease results from a process called neurodegeneration in which vulnerable nerve cells in the brain die more rapidly than normal. Neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease causes the clinical symptoms referred to as parkinsonism which include tremor, rigidity, slowness of movements, and postural instability. There are therapies which can alleviate these symptoms but they are associated with significant side effects. Furthermore, none of our current treatments for Parkinson's disease can slow or stop the death of nerve cells. This is due, in large part, to our limited understanding of the molecules that cause neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease. The goals of the proposed research program are to elucidate the critical molecules responsible for neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease and to discover drugs that target these molecules. column37: Some individuals have a single mutation within their skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor (RYR1) resulting in Malignant Hyperthermia (MH), a life-threatening complication associated with general anesthesia. The RYR1 is a channel responsible for the rapid, but controlled, release of calcium from internal stores within the cells of our skeletal muscles that triggers muscle contraction. These individuals, only when exposed to general anesthetics, show uncontrolled contraction of their muscles and body temperatures that reach over 40.6 degrees Celsius. While considerable advances have emerged regarding our understanding of RYR1, there is still much to learn about the relationship between the protein's structure and how small molecules like anesthetics can significantly alter their normal function. Our objective is to use techniques from chemistry and biology as well as a novel combined strategy to identify the binding sites for anesthetics within normal and MH mutant RYR1 in order to determine and compare the consequence of binding on RYR1 structure. To accomplish this we will employ photoactive analogs of the anesthetics isoflurane and sevoflurane to 'photolabel' their binding sites within both RYR1s. We will determine the affect of anesthetic binding on the structure of the ion channel using a novel strategy that couples cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) with the photoactive analogs in order to obtain a snapshot of the anesthetic interactions with the channel. Preliminary studies have indicated a potential anesthetic binding site within a unique region of RYR1 that would have long-range effects on the structure within other channel regions. Ultimately this investigation will provide 1) a strategy for the advancement of scientific methods and 2) define the transitions that occur within RYR1 and the impact of anesthetics on the channel's function.

column36: Illuminating the structure and dynamics of the proteasomal Rpn1 protein in unfolded client recognition by methyl-TROSY NMR
column37: Human health relies on the ability to properly degrade old proteins when they are no longer needed. The degradation of proteins is carried out by an enormous protein machine called the proteasome. When protein degradation is impaired, neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) can occur. The proteasome contains two major pieces denoted as the core and regulatory particles (CP and RP respectively). The CP resembles a barrel with pores at each end where proteins enter for degradation. The RP is involved in recognizing and pushing old proteins into the CP to be recycled. Specifically, the RP contains a highly dynamic and multi-functional protein called Rpn1 which is crucial to recognizing and moving proteins marked for degradation into the CP. Rpn1 has been suggested to bind unfolded proteins, acting as a bridge for protein folding and degradation at the proteasome, however the details of this possibility remain unknown. A robust understanding of Rpn1 function, and therefore protein degradation, is predicated on site-specific studies of the interactions of unfolded proteins with Rpn1. We will use solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to investigate how Rpn1 recognizes unfolded proteins. This information will shed new light on the proteasome mechanism and will benefit the development of drugs that prevent neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Moving knowledge to practice: developing, implementing and evaluating in-hospital physical activity practices to enhance health for children during treatment for cancer
column37: Over 80% of children diagnosed with cancer will survive the disease. However, most will experience negative effects that can greatly reduce their health and quality of life. In-hospital physical activity (PA) during treatment is one strategy that can reduce negative physical and psychosocial effects and enhance quality of life in the short- and long-term. Though in-hospital PA practices (ie, recommendations, education, opportunities) are advocated for children during treatment, hospitals in Canada do not provide PA practices as part of usual care. Consequently, most children with cancer are not active enough to receive the health benefits PA can offer. Further, PA remains low for years or decades following treatment. In select countries internationally, in-hospital PA practices are part of usual care. Research suggests improved care and enhanced health and quality of life in the short- and long-term at these centres. To address the gap in childhood cancer care in Canada, this research program will develop, implement, and evaluate in-hospital PA practices for children undergoing treatment for cancer. To do this, healthcare professionals (eg, oncologists, nurses, physiotherapists, child life specialists), childhood cancer patients and their caregivers, and experts (ie, researchers and healthcare professionals who have successfully implemented in-hospital PA practices in their centres) will be consulted. These individuals will help identify strategies for implementing in-hospital PA practices into usual cancer care. Once identified, these practices will be implemented and evaluated in the Alberta Children's Hospital and Stollery Children's Hospital. If successful, the outputs from this project have the potential to improve existing care and enhance health and quality of life in the short- and long-term for children undergoing treatment for cancer in Canada.

column36: Spatiotemporal resolution of the contributions of pre- and post-synaptic mechanisms to synapse-specific transmission variability and synaptic plasticity
column37: Activity-dependent changes of synaptic efficacy are the cellular basis of learning and memory. Synaptic plasticity bidirectionally modifies synaptic strength by enhancing or depressing transmission, effected through a complexity of mechanisms that act pre- and postsynaptically, over different time scales, and in response to different stimuli. Despite decades of intensive research, the fundamental question of how changes in synaptic efficacy are ultimately expressed during plasticity remains to be unequivocally answered; that is, to what extent and over what timescales do plasticity events modify respectively presynaptic neurotransmitter release and the number or function of postsynaptic receptors? This outstanding question represents a fundamental gap in our knowledge about how synaptic plasticity is evoked to modify the function of neuronal networks controlling behaviour. The rapid and dynamic regulation of AMPA-type glutamate receptor (AMPAR) surface mobility constitutes a major mechanism underlying synaptic plasticity. However, it is also apparent that the recruitment or removal of AMPARs by exo- and endocytotic mechanisms postsynaptically, and changes in neurotransmitter release probability presynaptically, are also involved in synaptic modulation during plasticity. Here, I propose to use a multi-level approach combining electrophysiology, genetically-encoded optical reporters, innovative molecular tools to control AMPAR trafficking, and state-of-the-art super-resolution imaging approaches to determine how the dynamics of AMPAR surface mobility postsynaptically, and synaptic vesicle release presynaptically, define the functional properties of synaptic transmission during both basal and plastic states. This work will shed new light on the fundamental mechanisms of synaptic transmission, plasticity and specificity, and advance our knowledge of the etiology of numerous psychiatric, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders that are linked to AMPAR dysregulation.

column36: Mechanotransduction in the central nervous system: elucidation of the role of Piezo1 in microglia
column37: Mechanotransduction consists of sensing and transforming physical tensions on the cell membrane into intracellular signals. Piezo1 and Piezo2 are mechanically-activated ion channels that play crucial roles in sensory transduction as well as cardiovascular and developmental regulation. In the central nervous system (CNS), Piezos haven't been reported. My preliminary data reveal Piezo1 responses in microglia, known as the resident macrophages of the CNS. These highly dynamic cells maintain CNS homeostasis, respond to damage and invading pathogens, and underlie many neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases. Piezo1 may be essential in regulating mechanosensitive processes that characterize microglial function under resting and pathological states. Therefore, we sought to validate the functional expression of Piezo1 in microglia, identify the physiological mechanisms affected by Piezo1, and test the behavioral effects of Piezo1 loss- and gain-of-function in the appropriate animal models. My preliminary results show Piezo1-mediated calcium signals in cultured microglia, a response that is greatly up-regulated in activated microglia. This suggests an important role of Piezo1 in mechanosensitive phenomena that occur under activation, such as morphological alterations, migration, and phagocytosis. The relevance of Piezo1 in these processes will be investigated in vitro and in vivo by comparing control mice to Piezo1 loss- or gain-of-function transgenic models. Once a Piezo1-dependent process is identified, the appropriate mouse disease model will be tested to check for behavioral phenotypes and gain insights on the clinical relevance of microglial Piezo1. This work would present the first evidence of the presence of Piezos in the CNS and may reveal critical roles of mechanotransduction in microglial function underlying neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Neuroimaging Biomarkers for Transition to Mental Illness in Youth
column37: Mental illness is a major cause of disability worldwide, and most of these illnesses develop during adolescence. Like most illnesses, mental health issues are more manageable if they are identified and treated early. However, two issues have prevented the delivery of effective mental health treatment to adolescents. The first issue is that many youths experience symptoms and behavioural disturbances but these symptoms are neither pronounced nor persistent enough to warrant a diagnosis. The second issue is that only some of the youths who experience these symptoms will develop a mental illness. As a result, it is difficult to correctly identify targets for intervention and support. The goal of this project is to use brain imaging, along with psychiatric tests, to create a model that can predict the development of a mental illness. In order to achieve this goal, we are currently recruiting and following youths between the ages of 12-25, the majority of whom are at high risk of developing mental illness, either because they have experienced symptoms, or because of a family history of mental illness. Participants will perform brain imaging experiments and other tests over the course of a year, in order to determine which are best at predicting whom will go on to develop a mental illness. For the brain imaging experiment, we are using a reward task, as this has been shown to differentiate various mental illnesses. The model we propose to develop will allow targeted interventions that can lessen disease impact and foster healthier outcomes.

column36: Multi-regional neuronal dynamics of short-term memory
column37: Short-term memory is a core cognitive function for animals. Imagine solving a Rubik cube, we first recognize the configuration of the cube, maintain the configuration in short-term memory while devising a plan, and then carry out the plan seconds later. In our daily lives, maintaining information in short-term memory is important for reasoning, decision making, and motor planning. Although short-term memory is recognized as a critical function in everyday function, and is impaired in diseases such as schizophrenia, how the brain represents and uses short-term memory is not fully understood. Previous studies only examined single brain areas under one task condition and failed to identify a single area that stores short-term memory. Like almost all brain functions, short-term memory is likely maintained in a circuit across multiple regions of the brain, and we require simultaneous measurement from multiple regions to identify the neuronal substrates. The proposed research aims to use new electrophysiology technology to simultaneously record the activity from hundreds of neurons in multiple regions, and perturb the activity to establish function. We propose to study two different behaviors in mice that involve short-term memory. In the first task, mice need to maintain short-term memory during a delay period. We will record and perturb activity across approximately 50 brain regions, selected based on connectivity data. This will generate a complete functional map of neuronal activity underlying short-term memory. In the second task, the mice must route the short-term memory to the upcoming motor plan to correctly perform the task. The second task will allow us to see how the activity map is used in different behavioral context. The successful completion of the map dynamics for short-term memory will guide the development of computer models of the brain and gives a window into the potential dysfunctions that are responsible for cognitive and motor diseases.

column36: Dentate mossy cell gating of seizure generalization in temporal lobe epilepsy.
column37: It is unclear why some seizures spread beyond the brain region of origin to recruit more widespread networks, a process known as seizure generalization. This is troubling because seizures are not adequately controlled with medication in a third of people with epilepsy and seizure generalization results in convulsions that can cause injury or death. It is important to understand why seizures generalize to treat and avoid these detrimental convulsions whose effects extend well beyond seizure termination. Using cutting-edge techniques, it is now possible to isolate and observe the contributions of distinct cell-types to the function of a larger brain network. Utilizing these techniques to study epilepsy enables me to track the activity of specific cell populations during seizures that either remain within the epileptic network or spread to cause convulsions. Upon understanding how activity patterns of key cell-types lead to seizure generalization, treatments that disrupt these patterns can be selected to prevent convulsions. A basic understanding of this phenomenon could lead to treatments that dramatically improve quality of life and reduce the risk of death in poorly controlled epilepsy.

column36: Deep Cellular- and Immuno-Biology of Alzheimer's Disease Progression - A Framework for Mechanistic Understanding
column37: A continually growing aging population comes with increasing health risks for Canadians. Approximately 750K Canadians are currently living with Alzheimer's disease (AD) or other dementias, and this number is projected to double in 20 years. Current AD research focuses on treatment of patients after development of AD. However, high dimensional neuroimaging will lead to untapped knowledge on disease progression mechanisms of AD, giving us a platform to develop groundbreaking, proactive solutions to AD management. Neuroimaging is critical to better understand the clinical progression of Alzheimer's disease, and understanding processes in the brain and the interplay between pathology and immunology in the onset of AD would better identify: (1) risk factors for AD, (2) therapeutic targets to manage the disease, and (3) understanding of the disease progression mechanisms. The primary aims of this proposal are to understand: (1) what the brain looks like of people with and without AD at a cellular and subcellular level, (2) whether the immune system has a role in disease progression and pathogenesis, and (3) to develop utility of therapeutic targets based on the findings. To answer these questions, we will use multiplexing technologies in order to characterize, phenotype and image the brains of donors. These multiplexing technologies include mass cytometry (CyTOF) and multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI), they will allow us to analyze a large number of proteins (>40) in biological samples at the (sub)cellular level. Current technologies are limited in allowing us to only look at 2 or 3 different proteins that we believe have a role in AD; however, CyTOF and MIBI will allow us to look at >40 proteins which have a potential role in AD, and how they interact with one another. This approach will allow us to understand multiple pathways leading to AD pathology, and potentially identify therapeutic targets for the development of novel drugs to manage AD.

column36: YOUTH WELLBEING IN CHINA AND CENTRAL AMERICA:IMPLEMENTATION OF AN INTEGRATED PREVENTION AND INTERVENTION PROGRAM
column37: High rates of mental illness and addiction (often associated with self-harm) have been reported in China and Central America. Stigma, poor mental health knowledge, and limited awareness and/or accessibility to health services lead to low help-seeking, further compounding the problem. Thus, there is an urgent need for strategies to promote mental health knowledge to enable early identification and treatment and to improve help-seeking behaviour. The aim of this 5-year project is to implement and evaluate a multi-level, integrated mental health education, screening, and intervention program to improve functioning and well-being in youth in China, Honduras and El Salvador. About 5000 students in China, 2000 students in Honduras and 2000 students in El Salvador will be recruited. Participants will receive a 12-week mental wellness and leadership program (MWL) online (at universities) or in class (at vocational/technical schools). Curriculum topics will include mental health education (illness and stigma, help-seeking, stress management), social responsibility (prejudice, violence, gender-based violence), and leadership (values, skills). Students will be assessed on psychosocial function (e.g.distress, coping, stress, academic performance) and physiological measures of stress (saliva and hair cortisol) before and after MWL completion. An open-access phone app will be created to screen for emotional difficulties and addictive behaviours and will be available to MWL and non-MWL students. Those students who screen positive for significant emotional difficulties, as well as those with depression, anxiety and/or addictive behaviours who are referred by health professionals, will receive one of two forms of an 8-week internetbased cognitive-behavioural therapy (iCBT) program. The iCBT emotional well-being program will target mood and anxiety symptoms, and the iCBT addictions program will target substance abuse (including alcohol and tobacco) and problematic internet use. Students will be assessed on symptom and functional improvement as well as on physiological measures of stress before and after program completion. This project offers the opportunity to implement and evaluate the broad benefits of a novel integrated prevention and psychological intervention program for youth in culturally differing regions. The program will be adapted and incorporated into existing postsecondary institutions in the three countries with measurement of cross-cultural acceptability, efficacy, fidelity of implementation, and sustainability. It is proposed that the project will improve the mental wellness of transitional youth with good sustainability in two distinct global regions, and furthermore, it offers an opportunity to objectively evaluate to cost and benefit of this implementation.

column36: Implementation research: community intervention to prevent repeated suicide attempts in Ningxia China and Nunavut Canada
column37: BACKGROUND: Suicide is the most serious outcome of a variety of mental illnesses, including depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, eating disorders and substance abuse. Reducing suicide mortality is an important objective of the World Health Organization's 2013-2020 Global Mental Health Action Plan and the United Nation's 2015-2030 Sustainable Development Goals. A prior suicide attempt is the most important risk factor for death by suicide, but regular brief community follow-up after an attempt can prevent repeated suicidal behavior. AIMS: This 5-year implementation science project will develop methods for adapting the WH0 SUPRE-MISS intervention for suicide attempters in parallel projects in Ningxia, China, and among Inuit in Nunavut, Canada. These methods for adapting SUPRE-MISS will then be promulgated in Inuit and other indigenous populations, other parts of China, other low- and middle-income countries, and other low-resourced settings in high-income countries. METHODS: PHASE 1. Conduct focus groups with local stakeholders to identify local factors that need to be considered when developing a location-specific version of SUPRE-MISS that provides a brief educational intervention about suicide prevention to individuals who have recently made a suicide attempt and periodic social support and access to emergency services to these highrisk individuals. PHASE 2. Pilot-test the adapted intervention in a small number of settings for one year. PHASE 3. Revise and then scale-up the intervention to more settings for 30 months and continuously collect outcome measures, process measures, and resource utilization measures (for cost-effectiveness assessment). PHASE 4. Conduct post-intervention focus groups with stakeholders to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the intervention. Integrate these qualitative results with the quantitative results (e.g., rates of repeated suicidal behavior) to prepare a report on the process of implementing the SUPRE-MISS intervention in low-resource settings. Work with administrators and policy makers in China, Nunavut, and other locations to develop policies that will widely promulgate the use of this approach to suicide prevention. FEASIBILITY: A strong multidisciplinary team with extensive experience in suicide prevention in the target communities has been assembled and the active support of local administrators and policy makers who can provide practical support for the project and develop policies to promote its results has been obtained. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: This project will develop methods that can be widely disseminated to help achieve the United Nation's ambitious goal of reducing suicide mortality by 1/3 by 2030. Combining findings from parallel projects in a low-middle-income country with those from a low-resource setting in a high-income country will provide a unique case example of how implementation science can be used to address complex mental health problems in different low-resource settings.

column36: Enhanced Measurement-Based Care Effectiveness for Depression (EMBED): A Canada-China Implementation Project
column37: Depression affects 300+ million people globally and is now the leading cause of disability and burden of disease worldwide. In China, the National Mental Health Work Plan 2015-20 specifies improving the ability of healthcare facilities to identify depression and increase the treatment rate by 50%. Measurement-based care (MBC) - the routine use of validated outcomes such as the PHQ-9 depression questionnaire to guide clinical decision-making - is a simple evidence-based practice (EBP) that may help meet these objectives. However, there is still a significant care gap in the implementation of MBC in China and elsewhere. In Canada, we have adopted the concept of enhanced MBC (eMBC), in which technology can engage both patients & physicians in using MBC; eMBC enhancements include web and mobile app tools for patients to track their own progress with the PHQ-9, and an evidence-based, lowcost, low-intensity psychological treatment (guided self-management with telephone coaches) that has embedded patient measurement and feedback to physicians. EMBED: a Canada-China implementation project, proposes to develop a novel EBP implementation strategy by adapting, implementing and evaluating eMBC in diverse community mental health clinics in Shanghai, modeled on programs implemented in Canada. EMBED addresses 4 broad aims: 1) identify contextual enablers & barriers to MBC implementation; 2) explore physicianand patient-level factors as mediators for an EBP implementation; 3) provide clinical & health economic outcomes to establish effectiveness of eMBC; and 4) build knowledge & capacity for scale up of eMBC in China and beyond. Our hypothesis is that physician & patient factors that are barriers for implementation of standard MBC will be enablers for implementation of eMBC. To achieve these aims, we will first conduct a Situation Analysis to determine the key barriers & enablers for MBC implementation in Shanghai. We will adapt a Canadian eMBC program for the Chinese context, then will use a hybrid implementation-effectiveness design (an adaptive cluster randomized evaluation) to compare eMBC with standard MBC implementation in 12 community clinics, 240 physicians, and 1200 patients. We hypothesize that eMBC implementation will lead to superior implementation, patient and costeffectiveness outcomes, compared to standard MBC. EMBED will advance the international literature on MBC broadly by focusing on the understudied role of patients in implementation of MBC. EMBED will also further implementation science by creating new knowledge on contextual factors, including mediating effects of physician- and patient-level factors, together, on EBP implementation outcomes. Moreover, the unique partnership of the EMBED team with the APEC Digital Hub for Mental Health will ensure a pathway for integrated knowledge & policy translation so that findings will have significant scale-up and spread potential in other regions in China, the Asia-Pacific and worldwide.

column36: Linking Hearts: Advancing Mental Health Care of University Students Through Interdisciplinary Collaboration (in Jinan)
column37: Young people are vulnerable to the onset of mental illness. Research shows that delayed treatment of mental illness leads to negative outcomes. In China, prevalence of depression among university students is as high as 20 to 30%. However, 9 out of 10 people diagnosed with a mental disorder never sought mental health care. Stigma and low mental health literacy are among the most important help-seeking barriers. Further, mental health services, largely at specialized hospitals only, are overstretched, while community and informal levels of care are underdeveloped. To address this, the study will examine the implementation of an evidence-based intervention, Acceptance and Commitment to Empowerment - Linking Youth and 'Xin' (hearts) (ACE-LYNX), to: (1) decrease stigma (attitude), (2) increase mental health literacy (knowledge), and (3) promote individual well-being (outcomes) and the collective capacity to collaborate (action) to promote mental health and form an integrative network of care for students. ACE-LYNX consists of two components: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a mindfulness-based cognitive-behavioral intervention, and Group Empowerment Psychoeducation (GEP), psychoeducation integrated with principles of equity, empowerment, and social justice. The study will take place in three regions of Jinan, Shandong, China. We will engage one hospital and two universities in each region. We will begin with an assessment of contexts, consisting of a university student survey (n= 600), student focus groups (n=144), and stakeholder and professional focus groups (n=144). The data will inform intervention adaptation. Using a train-the-trainer model, we will train 90 interdisciplinary professionals to become ACE-LYNX-Pro Champions. They will in turn train the "2nd generation" ACELYNX- Pro Champions (n=270) and students to become ACE-LYNX Student Champions(n=360) with a lay version of the intervention. All champions will form a collaborative integrated mental health care network supported by a community of practice through a Learning Management System and Weixin (WeChat). The champions will be followed over 6 months for their outreach and health promotional activities, including using Weixin to form a Student Mental Health Virtual Network. The RE-AIM framework will be used to examine Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance/Sustainability of ACE-LYNX and the integrated network. Psychometric measures will track the intervention's impact on attitude (CAMI), knowledge (MAKS), empowerment (Bulls-Eye, monthly activity logs), and mental health outcomes (DASS-21, AAQ-II), while service volumes and Social Network Analysis will be used to examine the functioning of the real and virtual networks. We will apply an Integrated Knowledge Translation framework to engage key stakeholders throughout the study to ensure maximal impact and dissemination with the aim of system transformation at the micro, meso, and macro levels.

column36: Shared Care for ADHD in Children and Youth: Merging the Canadian and Chinese Experiences
column37: In the context of modern China, children experience a tremendous pressure to perform at high levels. This stressful environment is associated with depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation and attempts in adolescence. Children with a diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are highly inattentive, restless, impulsive, and therefore at high risk, despite a normal intellectual potential. ADHD is easy to diagnose and treat, but difficult to diagnose and treat well. The treatment effects are dependent on the quality of care and on the coordination of different interventions, planned according to individual needs. The first main barrier to treatment is the shortage of qualified clinicians. In response, our main strategy will be to implement a shared care between general practitioners (GPs) and specialists. The second barrier is the lack of training in GPs. We will implement a focused ADHD training targeted to the needs of GPs. A third barrier is the lack referral process. We will implement stepped care in which the patient is treated at the most appropriate level of care, depending on complexity or outcome. We will adapt the Canadian shared care model for ADHD to the Chinese context. To test its flexibility, it will be implemented within the pediatric care system in two districts of Shanghai and within the mental health care system in one district of Beijing. We will first assess how ADHD guidelines are used, and the existing collaboration between GPs and specialists. After a Consensus Conference, we will implement a shared care pathway and we will produce actionable findings in a formative evaluation to improve implementation. At the end of the setup phase, we will assess the use of guidelines, the deviation from the intended protocol, how its members evaluate the care process, examine the effectiveness with regard to ADHD outcome, and functioning of the pathway, in terms of patient flow and timing. Once the shared care model is functionally implemented, we will scale up the care system horizontally by linking it progressively with schools selected randomly in the target districts. Using already established collaborations with the educational psychologists, we will first survey the knowledge and perceived needs of teacher, then implement a screening strategy for ADHD problems in the schools, as well as web-based effective strategies to educate parents and teachers about ADHD and mitigate its impact. We will assess the effectiveness of the intervention, and how it changes the perception of ADHD and the help-seeking process, as well as the rate of referrals into the shared care system. These two steps will allow defining the scalable unit that could be used in further implementation of the model. A costeffectiveness analysis is integrated in the project in order to support its scalability. Beyond ADHD, this shared care model will be able to respond to various mental health treatment challenges, both in children and adults.

column36: Screening and management of perinatal depression within primary care
column37: Depression during pregnancy and after an infant's birth is more common in China than in high-income countries and can harm the mother, infant, and family. Chinese women's mental health needs are unmet given lack of investment in mental health, unequal distribution of mental health services, and few specialized healthcare providers to support mental health issues. Our goal is to create an effective perinatal depression screening and management (PDSM) program that will be sustainable within the maternal and child healthcare system in China. Our implementation strategy is guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and RE-AIM (Reach x Efficacy, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance) and includes 2 Phases: (1) Pilot in Ma'anshan City, Anhui Province during which we will, through stakeholder engagement, adapt current evidence and test the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted screening guidelines and psychosocial intervention (internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy; iCBT) by healthcare providers and women. We will use mixed-methods to (a) identify and evaluate various implementation strategies (e.g., individual, organizational) to promote uptake of the screening guidelines and iCBT; (b) evaluate acceptability (i.e., knowledge, attitudes, and behavior) before and after implementation of guidelines and iCBT; (c) evaluate reach by determining the degree to which the population that is eligible to benefit from the program actually received it; (d) evaluate treatment fidelity by determining the extent to which the screening guidelines and iCBT was implemented as designed by monitoring adherence, dosage of delivery (i.e., the number of weeks completed), and program quality. (2) Scale-up to Hefei (capital and largest city), Bengbu (mid-sized urban city), and Fuyang (urban city) adapting the screening guidelines and iCBT based on Phase 1, and using steps (a)-(d) to promote uptake. Our monitoring and evaluation plan includes evaluating impact, effectiveness, and quality (i.e., public health impact) in both the Pilot and Scale-up phases. column36: Standardizing the treatment, prevention, and management of depression in China: a multi-disciplinary approach
column37: Depression is a common mental disorder affecting approximately 350 million people worldwide and representing the third leading contributor to the global disease burden (World Health Organization [WHO], 2012). However, much of the literature on the depression derives from studies conducted in Western Europe and North America. Consequently, there is a need for novel depression research in low- and middle-income countries, including China. In China, depression is highly prevalent but is not treated in existing community mental health programs, limiting many residents' access to mental health care and contributing to the large treatment gap. Currently, mental health care for depression exists at urban mental health centres; additionally, there is a lack of integration between primary and mental health care and the absence of mental health training for primary care physicians. Collectively, these factors hinder access to mental health care in rural and urban areas, and across communities of various socioeconomic backgrounds, languages and dialects. Thus, the development of community mental health prevention and treatment programs for depression would increase access to mental health care for residents of China in both rural and urban areas. Additional barriers that contribute to the treatment gap include culturally ingrained negativistic attitudes towards mental disorders that contribute to social- and self-stigma, and lack of education about mental disorders and their treatment. Consequently, our research endeavors, involving coordination between Canada and China, are as follows: (1) to help develop community-based mental health services for the early identification of individuals with depressive symptoms and prevention of clinical depression, (2) to improve access to mental health care and the management of patients with depression in community- and hospital-based settings, and (3) to establish international psychosocial networks or systems to monitor the quality of care. In addition, we aim to implement prevention and intervention strategies that address the aforementioned barriers to improve the quality of depression management and increase willingness to seek mental health care. Studies have reported that screening individuals with depressive symptoms and the subsequent provision of psychological therapy to prevent the onset of clinical depression is a cost-effective intervention, compared to treatment after depression onset. If depression prevention strategies become a standard part of mental health services, unnecessary suffering due to depression will be greatly reduced.

column36: Platform technology for blood diagnostics integrating microneedle blood sampling and quantum-dot based multiplexed assays
column37: Blood is the most useful sample fluid for lab medicine and diagnostics. It is most often obtained by inserting a needle in a vein in the arm (venipuncture). In the US, over 2 billion venipunctures are performed annually and is a technique that requires skilled personnel. Venipuncture is often associated with pain, discomfort and bruising, and is most difficult in persons with small, fragile, or "deep" veins (e.g. obesity), in babies, and when repeated sampling is needed. We propose an alternative that will minimize discomfort and bruising, will not require highly skilled personnel, and will be safe and easy. Our project combines an array of tiny needles (microneedles) that can be placed as a "patch" on the surface of the skin to collect small amounts of blood. The microneedles cause little discomfort, have a very low risk of causing bruising, and can be applied by the patient or a non-medical person. As the blood is collected, it will flow into a "lab-on-a-chip-on-a-phone" device, where the blood tests will automatically be performed using new and highly sensitive fluorescent probes. These tests will include immunoassays for protein biomarkers associated with cardiovascular disease, partially in collaboration with our industry partner, as well as assays of the activities of blood coagulation factors. Results from this platform can be immediately and electronically sent to the patient and physician. This research builds on successful preliminary applications with the microneedle arrays and fluorescent probes separately. We will now further develop and combine these innovative methods for a much-needed medical use, make comparisons to the standard venipuncture approach, and ultimately plan to perform many tests simultaneously with the devices. The benefits over current methods will be substantial: a painless, safe and user-friendly way to draw and test blood, with rapid reporting of results to health professionals and patients.

column36: Understanding Diagnostic Pathways of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Towards Improving the Timely Identification and Care of Girls and Women
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is reported to be four to five times more common in boys than in girls. The methods and criteria for diagnosing ASD, however, are largely based on studies with boys, which recent research suggests may overlook girls and women who present differently. Indeed, girls and women with ASD are at a greater risk of being identified at a later age and, as a result, often miss critical opportunities to access early interventions and timely supports. Many women report that they go undiagnosed or are misdiagnosed with other psychiatric conditions (e.g., psychosis, anxiety, personality disorders) before receiving their ASD diagnosis; however, no research to date has systematically examined this issue. The proposed study aims to better understand why girls and women with ASD are often under-recognized, as well as their associated healthcare needs. To do this, I will conduct a two-phase mixed methods study. First, I will use Ontario health administrative and billing data to examine the diagnostic pathways (i.e., the "routes" leading to diagnosis) of women who received their ASD diagnoses as adults. Next, I will compare the health outcomes (e.g., clinical profiles and service use patterns) of women with ASD who received their diagnosis as children with a) women with ASD who received their diagnosis as adults; b) equivalent groups of men with ASD; c) women and men without ASD. Finally, to help contextualize the quantitative results, I will conduct qualitative interviews with front line primary care providers (e.g., family physicians, paediatricians) as well as referral-based specialists (e.g., psychiatrists, developmental paediatricians) concerning current ASD assessment and care practices for females. This research will generate much-needed information to reduce sex/gender diagnostic and care biases and will assist in creating training materials to help clinicians better identify and care for girls and women with ASD.

column36: Identifying the neural correlates of social cognitive performance in schizophrenia spectrum disorders: A dimensional, data-driven approach
column37: Impaired social functioning is often a defining feature of individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). These patients exhibit deficits in social processes such as identifying emotions and understanding things from the perspectives of others. Such impairments are profoundly debilitating and have been linked to the ability to function in daily life. To date, investigations in SSDs tend to compare patients versus healthy individuals, and often include small sample sizes and patients with different levels of impairment, impeding the identification of consistent treatment targets. Indeed, there are currently no approved treatment options for these symptoms. Two circuits in the brain have been implicated in key social abilities affected in SSDs. However, early data from our lab suggests that subgroups of individuals may activate these brain circuits differently, which may result in different profiles of social behaviour and function among these groups. Thus, brain circuit abnormalities may differ in subgroups of people showing different levels of social impairment. In the present study, patients with SSDs and healthy individuals complete social tasks during brain imaging, as well as social and cognitive measures outside the scanner. We will take advantage of the range of social impairment seen in patients with SSDs, determining for the first time whether activation in these social brain networks predicts social performance across a very large sample of patients and healthy individuals. Novel methods will also be used to identify uniquely informative subgroups of participants generated based on these brain-behaviour associations. Critically, these findings should accelerate the identification of treatment targets and inform development of biologically based treatments for social deficits in individuals with SSDs.

column36: Development of a Mobile-based Application for Monitoring Functional Gains and Maintenance After Treatment for Youth at Risk of Psychosis
column37: Mental illness typically develops in adolescence, causing serious disruptions in youth's interaction with peers, family members, and their ability to perform well at school or at work. Current research has already been able to identify early possible signs of psychosis e.g. confusion about what is real or imaginary or feeling suspicious. These youth are considered to be at clinical high risk (CHR) for developing psychosis. Several studies have followed these youth over the years to see how many of them will develop psychosis, and to explore possible reasons for this to happen. One of the major concerns among these CHR youth is a decrease in their ability to function in social situations, at school or at work, and it is important to address them to avoid starting a spiral of loneliness and detachment from peers, discontinuation of hobbies, school, and impairment in work-related activities. To tackle such difficulties, we are currently conducting with CHR youth who have difficulties in social and school or work functioning to participate in a group treatment study that is testing the short-term effectiveness of a specialized treatment to address social functioning. Expert clinicians help youth to practice social skills, improve problem solving and learn new strategies. Given youth's enthusiasm for new technologies, we propose to assess the maintenance of the skills learned in the group through a mobile-based application that will be developed for this treatment and used at the end of the group treatment. This method of follow-up will provide continuously available support to the study participants, and it is anonymous, non-stigmatizing and gives researchers real-time information. One of the features of the tool is the provision of feedback on participants' social and school or work functioning by showing visual charts on a daily basis. We believe the feedback will improve the maintenance of the skills gained through the group intervention.

column36: The role of pericardial macrophages in cardiac repair
column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. 14,000 Canadians die every year from a heart attack, which is 1 person every 40 minutes. Furthermore, the individuals that do survive typically live with a heart that does not function as efficiently and over time will fail. This dramatically impacts the quality of life of these individuals and is also associated with high costs to the Canadian economy. We are trying to understand what goes on in the heart after an injury to find better ways to treat patients. Inflammation, which is driven by our immune system, is known to play an important role in the healing response after a heart attack. Different cells of the immune system can contribute differently to healing in the body, with some promoting while others blocking repair of the injured area. The balance between these two sides during the inflammatory response will ultimately determine how well the heart will function and whether failure will occur. To better understand what is happening at the level of the injury we will be using high-powered microscopes to see the immune system in action within the heart. This will provide us with key information on how different components of the immune cells interact with one another and other cells of the heart to influence the healing process. Our aim is to identify key cells and molecules that are crucial to promoting optimal repair of the heart. This in turn could lead to designing new treatments that will help preserve the function of the heart and ultimately delay or prevent failure in patients who have suffered a heart attack. This collectively will contribute to saving lives and improving the quality of life of Canadians as well as minimizing the financial burden associated with heart disease.

column36: Quantitative imaging of fluorescent Cav3.2 T-type calcium channel biosensor: a novel tool for studying processing of pain signals.
column37: The proper communication between neurons is an important determinant of nervous system function. Malfunction in the communication system between nerve cells can lead to a number of disorders, including chronic pain. Chronic pain is a prevalent problem and it is considered a debilitating condition that affects up to 1.5 Billion people worldwide and bears a tremendous socioeconomic burden. Many chronic pain conditions are not easily treated and new therapeutic avenues are needed. Cav3.2 T-type calcium channels have a key role in regulating electrical pulses in sensing nerve cells and they have emerged as an attractive therapeutic target to treat inflammatory and neuropathic pain. However, to date in vivo studies have been hampered by our inability to record Cav3.2 channel activity at nerve terminals in the spinal dorsal horn. The research outlined in this application explores the contribution of Cav3.2 T-type channels currents to inflammatory and neuropathic pain in vivo using a strategy that combines molecular biology, genetic engineering, electrophysiology, optogenetics and microscopy. We will report, using real time resolution, for the very first time the activity of Cav3.2 T-type channels in the spinal dorsal horn in vivo, thus gaining unparalleled insights into the processing of pain signals. By understanding the regulation of Cav3.2 T-type channels in the spinal dorsal horn, we will shed new light on the cellular mechanisms that give rise to inflammatory and neuropathic pain are present. In the long term, this in turn can be exploited towards new avenues for treatment of chronic pain.

column36: Development and evaluation of a remote robotic ultrasound clinic model to improve access to medical imaging in northern and Indigenous communities
column37: Ultrasound imaging is essential for many medical diagnoses; however, this imaging modality is not available in many northern and remote communities because of a lack of on-site sonographers and radiologists. An emerging solution to increase access to ultrasound imaging is telerobotic sonography. Telerobotic ultrasound systems allow sonographers or radiologists based at a central site to remotely perform ultrasound examinations, allowing patients to receive the care they need in their home community and avoid transport to another facility. The objective of my research is to determine whether a robotic ultrasound clinic is a viable model to increase access to ultrasound imaging for patients in northern and remote communities. I will explore the lived experiences and perceived needs of northern Indigenous community members in accessing ultrasound imaging through interviews. I will then use these findings to inform the design and implementation of a pilot remote robotic ultrasound clinic in a northern Canadian Indigenous community which does not have access to local ultrasound services. I will evaluate the effect of this clinic on patient management and ultrasound imaging utilization, determine best practices for establishing a robotic ultrasound clinic, and conduct a cost analysis comparing a robotic ultrasound clinic and a conventional ultrasound clinic to which patients must travel. Finally, using provincial ultrasound imaging utilization data, I will use spatial analysis and GIS mapping to determine where additional supports for ultrasound imaging are most needed, with a view to scale up the proposed robotic ultrasound clinic model. Findings from this research will inform the development of robotic ultrasound clinics, enabling more patients to receive ultrasound imaging in their home community. This may reduce time to diagnosis and treatment, improve health outcomes and patient satisfaction, reduce strain on major referral hospitals, and reduce healthcare costs.

column36: The Impact of Altered Nutrient Intake or Metformin Treatment on Genome Structure and Function in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) Fibroblasts
column37: Hutchinson Gilford-Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) is a rare premature aging disease affecting 1 in 4 million live births. Children with HGPS exhibit parallel but highly accelerated features of aging, including; hair loss, loss of fat deposits under the skin, arthritis and brittle bones. These children usually succumb to heart attack or stroke at ~14 years of age. HGPS is caused by a mutation in the laminA/C gene, generating the toxic protein Progerin. Progerin accumulates within the cell, disrupting the function and organization of the patient's genetic material (the genome), causing cells to become "old" (senescent) at a faster rate. No effective therapeutic strategies exist for the treatment of HGPS; however, the immunosuppressant rapamycin has been reported to stimulate Progerin degradation. Although promising, potential severe side effects of rapamycin have generated concern over its use as a treatment for HGPS. The aim of this project is to explore alternative treatment strategies that promote Progerin degradation and restoration of normal genome function and organization. Depletion of the essential amino acids leucine and arginine, glucose restriction as well as treatment with the anti-diabetic drug metformin function similarly to rapamycin but with fewer side effects. As metformin is already used to treat type 2 diabetes and is safe in humans, it is a logical choice as a potential HGPS treatment. The aim of this proposed research is to determine if depleted levels of amino acids/glucose or metformin can: 1) stimulate Progerin degradation, 2) decrease rates of cellular senescence and 3) re-establish normal function and organization of the genome within HGPS cells. These findings will not only provide alternative treatment strategies for patients with HGPS, but also -as increased levels of Progerin have been detected in aged cells from healthy humans-provide novel understanding of the underlying biological processes of aging.

column36: Novel 3D bioprinted human cardiac tissue models for drug safety and efficacy testing.
column37: During human clinical trials, a large percentage of candidate drugs fail because they are unsafe or ineffective. Even when pre-clinical cell and animal studies seem positive, problems occur because tests done with drugs on these models are often not predictive of what happens in humans. Much of this is due to significant differences in biology between species. For instance, ion channels (membrane proteins through which heart cells conduct electrical currents) can vary between humans and animals. Many drugs, including non-cardiovascular drugs, target these ion channels in the heart, which can potentially result in lethal arrhythmias. Thus, it is critical to use preclinical models that can closely reproduce what happens in humans to better predict drug safety. To streamline the therapeutic development pipeline, we will develop a novel 3D bioprinted human cardiac tissue model which will improve the translational science process for predicting whether drugs will be safe and effective in humans. The goal is to develop 3D human cardiac tissue structure(s) that closely model the electrophysiological properties of the human heart, relevant to impulse conduction and arrhythmia generation. We will use commercially available human induced-pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes and novel microfluidic based 3D bioprinting technology and methodologies to build the 3D cardiac tissue. Ultimately, these models are expected to replace the use of animals to screen drugs for safety and efficacy. To validate our models, we will evaluate the cardiotoxicity potential of a range of known compounds, and compare the outcome with data obtained using current standard assays. It takes on average over $2.5 billion to develop and gain marketing approval for a new drug. About $100 million is required to complete the pre-clinical studies alone. Using novel bioprinted models of cardiac tissue is expected to significantly cut the cost and time of bringing a new drug to market.

column36: Young adulthood, 'coming of age' in lifecourse epidemiology? Uncovering how transitions towards adulthood contribute to social inequalities in health across age and time
column37: Young adults (ages 18-25) are facing increasingly worrying trends with regard to health-related practices such as smoking, problem drinking, poor diet, substance abuse, unsafe sexual practices, and health care services underuse after adolescence. Their implications are further obfuscated by recent changes in young adults' transition through education, employment, family, and housing arrangements. Better understanding how these current trends intertwine is crucial because we know very little of the consequences that these will play on the rest of these individuals' lives as they become full-fledged adults. The period of young adulthood is, therefore, increasingly understood as a key period in the development of health and health inequalities across the life-course. While an important scholarship addressing these issues has emerged at the crossroads of psychology, sociology, and demography, there is still a paucity of work inside public health developing a comprehensive understanding of the experiences and needs of young adults today. In response, this project seeks to advance our understanding of young adults' transitions and health-related practices during young adulthood and midlife. This project will investigate these issues using four renowned British studies spanning three generations: the (1958) National Child Development Study, the 1970 British Birth Cohort, the Next Steps study and the Understanding Society study. This project will contribute to develop a stronger scholarship able to inform how public health research, policy, and practice should understand young adults and address their needs. This project will start in Fall 2018 in collaboration with Professors Amanda Sacker and Ingrid Schoon at the "International Center on Lifecourse Studies in Society and Health" at University College London (UCL) in London, UK.

column36: The Role of Material Security in Improving Health for People Who Use Drugs

Material security (e.g.,housing, food, and service access) may operate distinctly from income security yet may also be critically important to health.
