column37: Type 2 diabetes in children and youth is on the rise, largely due to increased rates of obesity and unhealthy lifestyle. Prediabetes is defined as abnormal blood sugar levels associated with an increased risk for type 2 diabetes and it affects one in every six overweight adolescents. Prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents are serious conditions which are poorly understood, which limits the development of effective preventive strategies. We aim to study the influence of mothers' diet during pregnancy and childhood dietary quality on adolescent prediabetes and future risk of developing diabetes. Project Viva is a unique study including over 1000 mother-child pairs for whom data is available during pregnancy, at birth, during infancy (6 months), at early childhood (3 years), mid-childhood (8 years), and early adolescence (13 years). Data was collected in both mothers and children and include: lifestyle (detailed dietary information, physical activity and sleep), metabolic profile based on collected blood samples, socio-demographic data (income, education, etc.) and body weight. This project will allow us to gain a comprehensive understanding on the role of diet, both before and after birth, in the risk of diabetes in adolescents. Diabetes in the pediatric population is a growing public health concern because they carry the burden of diabetes for many more years, leading to greater risk of complications and at an earlier stage of life. Identifying individuals at greater risk for life-long diabetes at an earlier stage could contribute to the development of efficient preventive strategies.

column36: Engineering flagellin-specific Tregs to restore intestinal homeostasis in IBD
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of severe, incurable chronic conditions which affect approximately 1/150 Canadians. IBD results from uncontrolled inflammation in the gut, causing symptoms such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bleeding and weight loss. IBD is driven by an imbalance of various types of immune cells which are normally present in specific proportions. I am interested in two cell types: effector T cells (Teff) which help fight infections, and regulatory T cells (Treg) which control Teffs and prevent healthy cells from being accidently attacked. In IBD, too few Tregs are present in the gut thus uncontrolled Teffs end up attacking intestinal tissues. Studies in humans have demonstrated that injecting large numbers of Tregs can help restore the balance of Teffs and Tregs in the gut and inhibit IBD. However, obtaining enough cells to accomplish this is difficult. In this project, I will investigate whether Tregs can be made more potent such that the number of Tregs required to treat IBD is reduced. Research has shown that Tregs which specifically recognise intestinal molecules are better at inhibiting IBD. This is partially because intestine-specific Tregs stay in the gut instead of circulating throughout the body. A molecule often found in the gut which is expressed by E.coli and commonly attacked in IBD patients is "flagellin". In this project, I aim to increase the therapeutic potency of Tregs by genetically modifying them to recognise flagellin. I will investigate whether flagellin-specific Tregs suppress IBD development/progression more effectively than unmodified Tregs in three models of IBD, including a humanised mouse model. I will then re-engineer this approach to be suitable for clinical use. Overall, I expect my findings to critically inform the future clinical investigation of flagellin-specific Tregs for treating IBD. This work can potentially transform how IBD is treated, offering a highly desirable cure with minimal side-effects.

column36: Towards healthy environmental assessment in British Columbia, Canada: Incorporating health imperatives and the determinants of health into natural resource governance
column37: Resource development both positively and negatively influences the determinants of health in resource-dependent communities, many of which are located in rural and remote locations across northern British Columbia. Despite being an identified pillar of environmental assessment (EA) regulation in British Columbia, health is typically analyzed through the lens of biophysical exposure risks and direct health impacts as part of a 'desktop review' of baseline data. Indeed, the limited inclusion of the determinants of health in EA processes has been documented provincially, nationally and internationally due to limitations of capacity and expertise, poor intersectional and disciplinary collaboration, and the need for transparency and efficiency in assessment. This project takes a "health in all policies" approach to consider how the social and ecological determinants of health can be better accounted for in EA processes to promote upstream drivers of health and well-being. Through a combination of policy analysis, surveys, interviews and capacity-building workshops with diverse sectors involved in EA certification (e.g. First Nations Lands officers, industry proponents, EA practitioners, health authority staff, and a variety of other provincial ministerial contacts), this research seeks to promote a new generation of intersectoral engagement in resource governance processes. Specifically, it leverages lessons from across sectors to enhance collaboration during EA certification, bolster monitoring and surveillance of the determinants of health in the EA process, and thereby improve capacity of the many actors examining and responding to population health and health equity impacts of resource development.

column36: HDAC11 as a novel epigenetic regulator of brown fat differentiation and cardiometabolic syndrome
column37: Metabolic diseases including diabetes, high blood pressure, and obesity are strong risk factors for the development of cardiovascular disease and greatly increase the chance of having a heart attack or stroke. High rates of obesity in the western world have made metabolic diseases (and their association with cardiovascular disease) the number one cause of mortality. Current treatment strategies to treat these diseases include lifestyle changes and medications to control high cholesterol and insulin resistance. The application of symptomatic treatments has failed to improve patient outcomes, and the rate of morbidity and mortality remains unacceptably high. Recent research has demonstrated that reactivation of brown fat may protect against the onset of obesity and metabolic diseases by increasing energy expenditure in the body. In this regard, the preliminary data in this proposal provide novel evidence of the involvement of a novel gene regulator in brown fat formation and metabolism. The proposed studies will use cell culture and mouse models to elucidate the mechanisms underlying this observation and evaluate the potential for inhibition of this to reduce diet-induced obesity and to improve cardiac function. From these studies, we aim to facilitate the development of novel drugs for the treatment of obesity and metabolic disease.

column36: Assessing the effectiveness of an online intervention addressing barriers to skin cancer screening behaviours among middle-aged men: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Melanoma can be a deadly disease when diagnosed at an advanced stage, but survival rates are > 98% when detected early and treated. Melanoma often develops with a visible, preclinical phase, hence there are opportunities for early detection via visually inspecting the skin. Skin self-examination (SSE) followed by physician-led clinical skin examination (CSE) are effective means to detect early signs of melanoma1. Middle-age men are often diagnosed with more advanced melanoma, have worse prognosis, and face higher mortality compared to women in the same age groups and younger men. Melanoma early detection interventions targeting men's SSE and CSE behaviours are sparse, primarily because male gender and older age are not generally regarded as risk factors for melanoma. Yet, approximately 60% of all deaths from melanoma occur in men of 50 years of age or older [SEER database; 2013]. Most available melanoma prevention interventions targeting SSE and CSE utilize an in-person educational model, which is time and resource-intensive, and potentially less amenable to men. There is an urgent need for low-cost, effective (evidence-based), and easily accessible interventions targeting middle-age men's SSE and CSE, as part of the overall effort to decrease melanoma-related mortality in this population.

column36: Delineating BRCA1-driven Breast Cancer With Single Cell Genomics
column37: Breast cancer is one of the most prevalent forms of cancer in women worldwide. Despite recent advances in understanding the initiation and progression of breast cancer, prognosis still remains poor. Detection and diagnosis of precancerous lesions and tumors early have the potential to improve treatment and reduce cancer-related deaths. Heterogeneity within the cell population is a striking feature of many tumors. Malignant disease may be mainly driven by rare subpopulations of tumor cells, and tumor cell heterogeneity may complicate therapies due to resistant clones within the population of cells. The goal of this interdisciplinary project is to develop a systems-level analysis pipeline to study cell heterogeneity during early tumorigenesis and advanced stage breast cancer in unprecedented resolution. We will implement a recently developed single cell RNA sequencing platform to reveal the gene expression within individual normal human breast epithelial cells and compare the spectrum of cellular heterogeneity to that of tissue of early stages of breast cancer and in more progressed triple negative breast cancer. We will apply and develop identify distinct ell types and states, their specific markers, and how they relate to each other within their path of cancer development. In doing so, we will unravel early systematic changes that occur in breast cancer. Understanding the systems-level changes during breast tumorigenesis in single cell resolution stages may will lead to the identification of novel biomarkers for early cancer detection and may form the basis for the development of therapeutic approaches to prevent breast cancer from progressing into a life threatening condition.

column36: Contribution to neuroinflammation of immunometabolic reprogramming of resident microglia and infiltrating macrophages
column37: Macrophages are tissue-resident cells that fulfill homeostatic functions, notably in the central nervous system. Following assault, they become activated and secrete mediators that lead to a local inflammation (neuroinflammation). Moreover, large numbers of infiltrating macrophages exert inflammatory effects that contribute to neuroinflammation. Even though resident and infiltrating macrophages may have differing immunological functions and roles, these are dependent on their metabolism (a phenomenon called immunometabolism). As such, metabolic reprogramming can modulate macrophage functions, and subsequently their role, including their inflammatory activities and participation in the development of disease. While controlled inflammation is required to resolve an assault and repair damage, its exacerbation can result in permanent damage and debilitating disabilities. Indeed, exacerbated neuroinflammation is responsible for numerous life-threatening diseases whose burden on human health in Canada is extensive. However, information regarding the contribution to neuroinflammation of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming remains largely unknown. Consequently, the goal of this project is to study this contribution using a mouse model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. Firstly, the metabolic processes of resident and infiltrating macrophages modulated during neuroinflammation, in comparison with homeostasis, will be identified. Thereafter the role of this reprogramming on the immunological functions of macrophages will be evaluated using cells isolated from mice deficient for key metabolic pathways and/or specific checkpoints previously identified. Finally, the contribution of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming to neuroinflammation and the development of and outcome of disease will be assessed using these same deficient mice. In summary, this project aims to dissect the contribution to neuroinflammation of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming

column36: Developing Thermally Stable Dry Powder Vaccine Platforms Via Spray Drying Tailored for Inhalation Delivery
column37: Innovations in vaccine development greatly benefit public health, by pursuing new and improved biologics, and re-envisioning new delivery routes though changes in their formulation and manufacture. The proposed research will advance recent progress made by an interdisciplinary team of scientists in designing new thermally stable vaccine platforms targeted against tuberculosis and influenza infection, where the temperature sensitive biologics will be stabilized by encapsulation in suitable carriers, thereby removing the necessity for costly and often unavailable refrigeration equipment in their storage and transport. The proposed project brings together chemical engineering and biomedical expertise to understand and implement industrially relevant drying techniques that will produce thermostable dry powder vaccines retaining their immune-boosting potency as seen in their original liquid form, yet now can be stored at room temperature for 3 months without loss in activity whereas liquid losses in potency occur in less than 1 week. Spray-drying these vaccine powders under optimized conditions results in a product designed for delivery to the lung by inhalation, boosting their effectiveness against lung-borne infections like tuberculosis and influenza, while avoiding the complex logistics of re-constituting dried vaccines in liquid media prior to administration. The research will produce optimal examples of thermostable dry powder tuberculosis and influenza vaccines, relating their physical and biological properties to engineering principles on particle formation and particle aerodynamics in the human respiratory system. The new knowledge will be transferred to appropriate pharmaceutical experts for the benefit of Canada's public health.

column36: Developing resilience to obesogenic food environments through food literacy
column37: More Canadians now die from diseases caused by poor diet than from smoking-related illnesses, and diets low in fruit and vegetable intake cost Canadians 3.3 billion dollars a year. The food environment profoundly influences diet and is associated with diseases such as obesity and diabetes. This environment has evolved so that children and adolescents are constantly fed cues to consume unhealthy foods. Nutrition "knowledge" may come from social media or advertisements and slick marketing may shape food preferences. All of these factors affect current and future dietary practices. Food literacy is the foundation of healthy dietary practices and provides youth with an opportunity to build resilience to unhealthy food environments. Yet, we know very little about how food literacy is acquired and the level of literacy needed to make healthy dietary decisions. The proposed research will address these knowledge gaps. The purpose of this study is to examine the connections between food literacy, food environments and health indicators among youth. To address the knowledge gaps, we will conduct 1) an environmental scan of food literacy learning opportunities for children and adolescents (consisting of a scoping review, interviews with practitioners followed by a survey) and 2) a cross-sectional survey on food literacy, food environments and health indicators among youth. Results will be translated to practitioners and policy makers through guidelines for enhancing food literacy to promote optimal health. Food literacy will equip youth with the abilities, knowledge and self-efficacy to make healthy food choices, which will reduce risk for diseases and decrease healthcare costs. This research will strengthen Health Canada's healthy eating strategy to improve healthy eating and protect vulnerable populations by understanding how to improve food literacy and make healthy dietary choices in unhealthy food environments.

column36: Impact of Food Production Compounds on Human Microbiota & Metabolic Health
column37: Obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) impact over 25% of adults in Canada and cost the health care system over $20B annually. The gut flora is involved in all three of these metabolic diseases. Our food supply has been affected by changes in agricultural production, food additives, and food packaging over the past several decades. These toxicants in our food supply may modulation of the gut flora and thus alter metabolic activity and contribute to metabolic disease. I aim to identify and characterize how food production compounds and additives contribute to altered metabolic activity in obesity, T2D, and NAFLD, through regulation of the gut microbiome. I will create a rapid screening system to determine bacterial response to our toxicants library of food additives and contaminants. I will then culture the gut flora and screen for bacteria that respond to our toxicants library. The most responsive bacteria will be used to colonize mice that are initially free of any bacteria (germ-free) with and without exposure to the toxicants. We will measure the metabolic outcomes, allowing me to make the connection from gut bacteria to metabolic disease. We will compare results from these mice to uncolonized germ-free mice that are treated with the same chemicals or additives to concretely indicate a causative role for the microbiome. This research will identify chemical exposures through our diet that may be implicated in metabolic disease. Identifying these compounds will provide necessary information to create change in government policy regarding their use in the food industry. Improving food production and understanding metabolic alterations in response to toxicants will improve public health and spur novel therapeutic avenues for the treatment of increasingly prevalent metabolic diseases.

column36: Early Neurodevelopment in the Offspring of Women Enrolled in a Randomized Controlled Trial Assessing the Effectiveness of a Nutrition+Exercise Intervention for Healthy Gestational Weight Gain
column37: Optimal early brain development is vital to health and success in life. Since development of the brain begins at conception, maternal health problems, dietary imbalances, and physical inactivity in pregnancy can lead to emotional and behavioural problems in offspring early in life. Many Canadian women consume an unhealthy diet and/or fail to get enough exercise during pregnancy. It is not surprising then that up to 40% of women enter pregnancy overweight and that up to 75% gain too much weight during pregnancy. Despite these facts, no studies in humans have examined if interventions that optimize maternal diet and exercise during pregnancy can improve brain development in offspring. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a study that will follow the children born to the 400 women that will be enrolled in a study of a nutrition+exercise intervention in pregnancy. The nutrition component consists of a nutrition plan tailored to women's needs, as well as sessions with a dietitian. Our exercise intervention involves women engaging in a structured and monitored walking program. In this study, half of the women will receive our nutrition+exercise program and the other half will receive treatment as usual by their healthcare providers. Our objective is to determine if fetal exposure to the nutrition+exercise intervention leads to improved emotional and behavioural development in offspring in the first 36 months of life compared to women who receive usual pregnancy care. We hypothesize that emotional and behavioural functioning will be superior in the offspring of women exposed to the intervention and the function of an area of the brain that is very important to the development of emotional coping will be optimized. If offspring brain development and behaviour can be improved via a nutrition+exercise program during pregnancy, it could be used to prevent or reduce the severity of emotional and behavioural problems in offspring with benefits across the lifespan.

column36: Beyond Function: Exploring Participation in Life Roles in People with COPD
column37: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a lung condition that makes it hard for people to breathe. Treatment for people with COPD usually focuses on helping them walk for longer and manage their breathing problems. A patient's ability to participate in life roles by visiting with friends and taking care of loved ones is another important part of health. Unfortunately, this is an area not often considered in people with COPD. In fact, people with COPD often say they feel alone and like they have lost their identity. In order to find ways to increase participation in people with COPD we need to start by finding an accurate and valid tool to measure it. Objective: We will test the ability of a questionnaire to measure participation in COPD. We will also see if our usual treatment has any effect on participation. Method: One hundred people with COPD in Toronto and Hamilton will complete a few questionnaires and physical tests. We will ask some of those people to complete the questionnaire a second time within one week. People with COPD who are starting a rehabilitation program will complete the participation questionnaire and some related tests at the beginning and end of their programs. This will tell us if the participation questionnaire measures what it should, if it can detect any change in participation that happens with rehabilitation and if there is meaningful change in participation during the program. Importance: This will be the first study to show the measurement abilities of this questionnaire in people with COPD. It will also be the first study to show if the usual treatment for people with COPD does anything to change participation. These projects will help us develop new treatments to increase participation in people with COPD. Being able to participate in life roles is important to patients so this will have a positive impact on their lives.

column36: Improved Cancer Immunotherapy for Breast Tumours
column37: Breast cancer is a disease that accounts for almost one quarter of all cancers in women. Though current treatment regimens have shown success with early stage primary tumors, there are few to no treatments that can successfully treat aggressive forms, prevent metastasis or completely cure advanced metastatic disease. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) (a subtype negative for hormonal biomarkers) holds an overall dismal clinical outcome due to lack of expression of targets for therapy and as such, patients routinely undergo aggressive regimens of chemotherapy. These regimens come with a multitude of side effects, including high levels of toxicity and an increased risk of developing other forms of cancer later in life. Immunotherapy, a form of therapy that boosts the immune system to fight cancer cells, has gained increasing prominence in recent years largely due to its safety and astonishing success rates. Some chemotherapies can be classified as immunotherapies when administered at low doses, as they stimulate the immune system. Checkpoint blockade is another form of immunotherapy that uses antibodies to initiate the death of cancer cells. It is clinically approved for various forms of cancer and has become a first line treatment for melanoma. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) are another promising form of immunotherapy that selectively kill cancer cells, showing little to no toxicity in healthy cells. They have exhibited excellent clinical tolerability, even when used at high viral doses. For our work, we propose to exploit and improve upon accumulating clinical knowledge in the development of immunotherapies for TNBC. The proposed studies will focus on clinical relevance and translation in order to generate a new treatment regime that displays minimal toxicity and simultaneously exerts anticancer effects on both primary and metastatic lesions. Although this proposal is specific to breast cancer, the underlying concepts can be applied to many other forms of cancer.

column36: The development and testing of a novel knowledge translation intervention for the prevention of pregnancy-related type 2 diabetes risk factors in Indigenous and South Asian women living in Canada
column37: Introduction: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) accounts for more than one-third of total global deaths. Although there has been a decline in CVD over the last three decades, the rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are expected to rise in high-risk ethnic communities. Also, recent evidence suggests that the development of CVD risk factors is influenced by pregnancy-related factors. To better understand these factors, the Aboriginal Birth Cohort (ABC) and South Asian Birth Cohort (START) are recruiting mother-baby pairs from the Six Nations reserve and Peel region, respectively. In parallel to high quality research, it is vital to create accessible avenues for meaningful knowledge translation. Because pregnancy is a time period where women feel especially motivated to make positive lifestyle changes, it makes for an optimal time for knowledge translation. Objectives: In my PhD program, I seek to develop and test novel knowledge translation tools to improve the knowledge of pregnancy-related T2DM risk factors in high-risk communities (Indigenous and South Asian). Methods: A mixed-methods approach of quantitative and qualitative methodologies will be used to develop and test a knowledge translation intervention. Descriptive statistics will be used to compile existing data from two birth cohort studies (START and ABC, both being conducted by my supervisor) on the causes and consequences of these risk factors. A qualitative approach will be used to thematically explore knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and behaviour change. Participants for the qualitative study will be purposely sampled and recruited via the cohort studies' regular clinic visits. Integrated KT methodology will be used to distill the research data to develop products alongside key stakeholders. Conclusion: Now more than ever, it is imperative to integrate knowledge translation approaches to warrant the application of research results to practice and support the improvement of primary care.

column36: A systems approach for enhancing perinatal care regionalization
column37: Canadians benefit from an excellent perinatal health care system. However, some problems persist as evidenced by disparities in illness and death among mothers and babies. Rates of serious illness/ death among mothers and babies vary significantly by region, socio-economic status, location of residence, Aboriginal status and other factors. The delivery of perinatal health care, particularly in rural and remote regions, faces significant challenges. Challenges associated with regionalized perinatal care include geography, climate, highly variable emergency transport service provision, organizational differences between provinces in the provision of care for pregnant women and newborns at different levels of perinatal risk, and the absence of a national program for evaluating and improving regionalization. Besides developing innovative ways to address existing challenges and financial constraints, Canada requires a systems approach for continuous evaluation of the structure, processes and outcomes of perinatal regionalization in order to encourage knowledge-based improvement. This project will provide an assessment of perinatal health services across Canada using a systems approach. Using indicators of maternal, fetal and neonatal tiers of service, we will evaluate the functioning of hospitals in all provinces/territories. Maternal, fetal and neonatal morbidity and morbidity rates will also be assessed especially in rural and remote communities. The project will identify problems with regionalization of perinatal care and ascertain lacunae in the organization of services. Recommendations will be formulated in collaboration with provincial/territorial stakeholders. This initiative has the potential to significantly enhance the care of mothers and babies in Canada.

column36: The Interplay Between Chromogranin-A and Gut Microbiome in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) includes both Crohn's disease (CD), and ulcerative colitis (UC). These diseases affect approximately 280,000 Canadians and have important repercussions on the quality of life, and both personal and societal direct and indirect costs. The causes are poorly understood, and treatment is largely symptom-based and not curative. Commonly used drugs may have potentially important adverse effects such as cancer or serious infections. Moreover, some patients are resistant to these drugs. Therefore, safer and more broadly effective therapies are needed. The human intestine has trillions of microbes, named gut microbiota, that are essential for the life and maintaining the physiological functions. There is some indication that a group of proteins involved in immune control named chromogranin-A (CHGA) and its derived peptides can regulate inflammation in the gut. I aim to understand how CHGA and its derived peptide (Chromofungin [CHR]) can balance the composition of gut microbiota to reduce intestinal inflammation in IBD states in humans and in animal models. Ultimately, this research will serve to determine if CHGA and CHR are potential therapeutic targets in IBD. In summary, I will explore a new pathway of proteins during intestinal inflammation that will provide a basis for possible new treatments of IBD.

column36: Understanding the mechanistic influence of early colonizing microbes on immune development and disease
column37: Asthma is the most common childhood disease within developed countries. Asthma occurs when the immune system mistakenly targets lung tissue with an inflammatory response. Typically, asthma symptoms do not arise until 3-5 years of age, however, growing evidence suggests that events that happen much earlier in life play a pivotal role. Immediately after birth, infants are colonized by a diverse set of microbes that collectively make up the microbiota, and early colonizers have a profound effect on the developing immune system. Four members of the microbiota, Faecalibacterium, Lachnospira, Veillonella, and Rothia (FLVR), are present within the first 100 days in infants who are protected from asthma. These microbes can also provide similar protection in mouse models of asthma. Introducing FLVR to children at risk of developing asthma has the potential to be an effective preventative treatment, however it is important to first understand how these microbes are influencing the developing immune system. Microbes interact with the immune system by producing proteins and metabolites that act as messages. I aim to determine which messages FLVR are sending to immune cells to prevent harmful targeting of lung tissue. Additionally, children with asthma often develop allergies as well. I aim to determine whether FLVR therapies can be expanded to protect against two common food allergies, egg and peanut. By understanding how FLVR is able to confer lifelong protection against asthma and allergies, we can begin to realize FLVR's potential as a preventative therapy.

column36: Interactions between cilia and folic acid during craniofacial development
column37: This research aims to better understand the relationship between craniofacial birth defects and epigenetic factors, of which folate is one. Birth defects are highly variable, even amongst children with the same genetic mutation, likely resulting from epigenetic modification. These epigenetic changes are changes that affect how genes are expressed, without changing the genetic sequence itself. Folate, a folic acid derivative, was added to the Canadian grain supply in 1998 to reduce spinal cord closure defects such as Spina Bifida. Folic acid appears to change how the DNA is expressed. Fortification has reduced the number of infants born with spinal cord defects. It is not understood how folate prevents these types of birth defects, though it may be due to epigenetic effects. Further, the links between folic acid and other birth defects, such as craniofacial birth defects, remains unclear. Importantly, recent data suggest that in some cases folic acid may actually increase the severity of spinal cord defects in mice. Paradoxically, this may reduce the apparent frequency of defects at birth by increasing mortality in utero, possibly by increasing the kinds and severities of the defects. These specific cases involve a structure called the cilia, which helps transmit signals within and between cells. Our preliminary data show that alteration of cilia in the mouse generates variation in how the embryo grows and develops, and alteration of cilia genes can increase variance in the shape of the face and lead to birth defects. We propose to examine how folate and cilia interact during development of the face and to examine how folate can affect birth defects in the face.

column36: The proteomic and metabolomic characterization of clear cell ovarian carcinoma: towards better management strategies
column37: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death for women from cancers, with about 25,000 women diagnosed in North America each year. Ovarian cancer is divided into subtypes based on molecular characteristics and clinical outcome. Although we have understood ovarian cancer as many diseases, the treatment has remained the same for the past 30 years for all subtypes - untargeted platinum-based chemotherapy. Clear cell ovarian cancer (CCOC) is the second most common subtype of ovarian cancer affecting many women. At late stage, it is more aggressive and resistant to current chemotherapy compared to other subtypes. Although deadly, CCOC is still not well understood and lacks effective targeted therapy. Existing molecular and genomic studies suggest that it is a metabolically driven malignancy, but its metabolic profile has not yet been studied. This research will be the first characterization of a large cohort of clinical cases of CCOC using protein expression in conjunction with global metabolite profiling. Understanding of the altered metabolism in CCOC will revolutionize the ovarian cancer research community and provide strong foundations on which to build further discoveries. Most importantly, we hope that identifying targetable metabolic pathways will guide the development of more effective therapies to help patients with this deadly disease.

column36: Examining the role of sexual relationship power inequity on multi-levelled drivers of HIV vulnerability for young women in an HIV hyper-endemic setting of South Africa
column37: On average 2,000 young women (YW) in South Africa acquire HIV every week, representing the highest new infection rates globally. Emerging research has begun to examine and act upon the multiple-intersecting factors that place YW at increased risk for HIV. High-levels of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and immature vaginal lining make YW more biologically susceptible to HIV. HIV risk for YW is also elevated due to social factors. Our previous work has found that YW experience high-levels of sexual relationship power inequity (SRPI), which compromises their agency to negotiate safe sex, impacts mental health, and heightens their risk of STIs/HIV. Evidence is needed to examine how socio-relational factors intersect with biological risk. As such, this proposed research seeks to examine and explore measures of SRPI and how SRPI influences biological, relational, and structural HIV vulnerabilities for YW growing-up within HIV hyper-endemic settings. Using prospective data from a youth-centered sexual reproductive health study conducted among South African youth aged 16-24 over an 18-month period, the objectives of this proposal are to 1) examine how SRPI influences STI treatment uptake, partner notification and STI incidence, 2) explore the pathway from SRPI to heightened biological susceptibility through it's influence on markers of stress and inflammation and 3) explore how SRPI is measured, conceived and influences the sexual decision-making practices and health-seeking behaviours of young men and women. As international targets aim to achieve an AIDS-free generation by 2030, this research merging biological and socio-behavioural data to examine the factors impacting heightened HIV-risk for YW living at the epicentre of the HIV epidemic is extremely timely. Moreover, the proposed research is in line with and can be used to inform the Canadian governments new feminist approach to international aid that prioritizes advancing and promoting equal rights for women.

column36: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease contributes to a tumour-promoting microenvironment and the development of lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Inflammation is a well-known cause of cancer, and inflammatory lung diseases (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)) have been associated with an increased risk of developing lung cancer. While the two diseases share known risk factors, the reasons why COPD airway damage leads to lung cancer are unknown. This includes the understudied role of inflammation in inducing damage, which could be an important factor in cancer development. We believe that COPD-related damage promotes cancer formation by causing gene expression changes in both airway cells and immune cells. Further, we believe gene expression changes crucial to cancer growth will be shared between the damaged tissues and the tumours themselves. We will test our theories by assessing the lungs of 15 individuals with COPD and lung cancer (rare samples collected at St. Paul's Hospital). We will identify changes in gene expression, along with differences in immune cell content, throughout the lung, and compare them to tumours in order to identify the changes most associated with cancer formation. This will reveal previously unknown gene expression changes and immune cell responses that are most likely driving cancer development. Additionally, we will build off the work our lab has previously conducted on the airways of COPD patients with and without lung cancer. We will first see if gene disruptions observed in the airways of COPD patients with lung cancer are also found in this rare lung tissue dataset. Second, we will determine if these genes can initiate cancer in normal lung cells by using CRISPR and virus-based gene editing techniques. Finally, we will test whether inhibition of these genes in mice can prevent the development of cancer. My project will lead to scientific discoveries that will help explain why COPD predisposes patients to lung cancer, and will reveal new targets for cancer therapy and methods of cancer prevention.

column36: Epigenomic Dysregulation in Synovial Sarcoma
column37: Synovial sarcoma is a highly aggressive soft-tissue cancer that predominantly affects adolescents and young adults. This malignancy, which accounts for 10% to 20% of soft-tissues sarcomas in such a young population, has limited sensitivity to conventional chemotherapies and thus a poor survival rate. Synovial sarcomas are characterized by a unique chromosomal abnormality that ultimately dysregulates critical genes via epigenetic modifications. Epigenetic modifications are essentially changes in the control of genetic material that do not alter the genetic code itself. For example, these modifications include the addition or removal of chemical tags on genetic material and change how the genetic material is regulated. In synovial sarcoma, we believe there are abnormal additions and removals of these tags - abnormal epigenetic modifications. The exact mechanism of how this aberrant process occurs in synovial sarcoma is poorly understood and controversial. To shed light on this mystery, it is prudent to examine what these epigenetic differences are and how they transform normal cells into cancer. To study this, I will use synovial sarcoma tissue samples from patients to profile the epigenetic changes that occur in these tumors, look for patterns using computational techniques, and carry out validation studies using mice. By understanding how epigenetic changes drive synovial sarcomas, we hope to guide the use of emerging epigenetic therapeutic agents in the treatment of this deadly disease. Additionally, synovial sarcoma is closely related to a number of other soft-tissue cancers that affect adolescents and young adults. Like synovial sarcoma, these cancers have limited treatment options, leaving numerous young patients in face of high mortality rates. In the long-term, we hope that a better understanding of synovial sarcoma can also reveal novel therapeutic approaches for these related cancers.

column36: Connecting the Microbiome and Neurodegenerative Dieseases
column37: The microbiome consists of trillions of bacteria, viruses and fungi that co-exist with humans in sites such as the intestines, nose and mouth, and is important to most aspects of health. My project will explore links between the microbiome and Parkinson's (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) and the conditions that often accompany these diseases, such as depression and anxiety. PD leads to loss of motor control and affects 100,000 Canadians. Studies have shown that the intestinal microbiome differs between those with and without PD. Interestingly, most patients experience constipation and loss of smell years before motor symptoms; these early symptoms take place at sites densely populated by microbes. AD is the leading cause of dementia, which affects 400,000 Canadians. Animal studies have found that the microbiome is important in AD; therefore, this is a key area to explore in humans. My first aim is to compare the microbiome of PD and AD patients versus controls. We will see whether a microbial "signature" exists for each disease and associate microbiome findings with disease severity. A second aim is to see whether probiotics improve depression, anxiety and fatigue in PD, as these conditions are also associated with microbial imbalances. As most patients have intestinal problems, we hope that shifting their microbiome to a healthier state could improve these symptoms. Finally, any discoveries will be further explored in the lab to understand the mechanisms connecting microbes to brain diseases. This will include seeing whether different microbial populations can modify PD/AD symptoms in mice, and examining how molecules made by microbes impact cells such as neurons and immune cells. The goal of my research is to provide new understanding of how the microbiome is important in neurodegenerative disease, and ultimately to work towards non-invasive interventions such as diet changes or carefully-designed probiotics that might help treat or even prevent these diseases.

column36: Evaluating the Long-Term Efficacy of Affective Mental Contrasting Interventions for Promoting Physical Activity Behaviour and Psychological Well-Being among New Mothers
column37: The transition to motherhood is typically associated with substantial decreases in physical activity levels. New parents are also at an increased risk of compromised psychological well-being. Since moderate-to-vigorous physical activity reduces symptoms of depression in new mothers, increasing physical activity levels has the added benefit of promoting psychological well-being. This study proposes to test the long-term effectiveness of implementing a novel physical activity intervention for new mothers that is designed to increase their physical activity levels and psychological well-being. Specifically, this study will evaluate the effectiveness of a mental contrasting strategy, which involves having new mothers focus on the best outcome of achieving future physical activity goals, while also identifying their biggest potential barrier that may prevent them from achieving these goals. Since the enjoyable aspects of physical activity have been found to be more motivating than the long-term health benefits, the proposed interventions will focus on the former. It is expected that the goal setting intervention targeting participants' perceptions of enjoyment will result in increased health-enhancing physical activity levels among new mothers six months and one-year following the intervention, compared to an intervention focusing on health benefits or an intervention that focuses on neither enjoyment nor health benefits. Further, it is hypothesised that these increased physical activity levels will result in improvements to participants' psychological well-being. The results of this study have the potential to inform scalable interventions for new Canadian mothers.

column36: The growing crisis of overly big babies: Comparing prevalence, outcomes and risk factors in midwifery v physician care
column37: A bigger than average baby (called macrosomia) is generally accepted as an adverse outcome in maternity care. About 10% of all babies in Canada are macrosomic. This is a significant public health concern as macrosomia has been linked to higher rates of cesarean or forceps delivery, severe birth trauma, excess bleeding, infant birth injury and infant death. Macrosomia is increasingly common worldwide, in part due to increases in obesity, excess weight gain and diabetes among childbearing women. A surprising recent finding indicated that 18% of all midwife-involved births in Ontario were macrosomic babies. Midwifery is a rapidly growing profession in Canada and outcomes are understudied. Reasons for these elevated rates of macrosomia among midwifery clients is unknown. Further, the impact of macrosomia on severe health outcomes is also unknown and it may differ for midwifery vs physician care. This study proposes to address this serious research gap by examining two cohorts of births in BC and WA state who were attended by midwives and physicians. The study findings will clarify the extent of macrosomia and associated severe outcomes among midwife v. physician births. Further, this will identify individual factors, aspects of prenatal or labor (adherence to specific obstetric guidelines from the Society of Gynecologists of Canada), or differences in training of midwives or gestational diabetes screening methods which could reduce severe morbidities among bigger babies and their mothers. Study findings can be used to propose evidence-based interventions, updated guidelines or policies to improve health for larger babies and reduce adverse outcomes such as cesarean delivery, birth trauma, or newborn birth injury.

column36: Cholesteryl ester transfer protein as a novel regulator, predictor, and therapeutic target of sepsis
column37: 1 in 18 Canadians die from sepsis (the body's response to a severe infection), each year. One of the challenges in treating sepsis is that it is very hard to predict which patients with an infection will need intensive treatment versus which patients will recover uneventfully. My research supervisor's laboratory has recently shown that patients' levels of high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (the "good cholesterol") drop quickly during sepsis. Importantly, the greater the drop in HDL levels, the greater the chance that a patient will die or suffer from serious organ failure. What is unknown is what controls the drop in HDL during sepsis, and whether genetic variation (differences in the DNA sequences among people) plays a role. My project is aimed at exploring the genetic mechanisms of HDL levels during sepsis. My preliminary data has identified a new gene variant that appears to play a major role in controlling the drop of HDL levels during sepsis. To complete my work, we will examine the DNA of patients with sepsis whose HDL levels drop very low, compared to patients whose HDL levels do not drop as much. Through my supervisor and his collaborators, we have access to large cohorts of patients with sepsis that have been collected from previous studies. We will also examine the function of the gene variants that we identify by introducing these variants into cells and examining the function of the gene products. This work is important for several reasons. Firstly, this work could lead to "personalized medicine" approaches to sepsis, by predicting which specific patients will develop the most dangerous consequences of an infection based on their genetics. Secondly, this project may lead to new ways to treat severe infections by targeted HDL levels. Ultimately this work will lower the burden of death from sepsis and severe infections among Canadians.

column36: Elucidation of the phosphorylation regulated mechanisms that control kinetochore-microtubule attachment stability by quantitative mass spectrometry
column37: Many established cancer therapies target the process of cell division in order to kill cancer cells. These therapies prevent the separation of chromosomes from the mother cell into the two daughter cells. There have been recent gains in the understanding of how such therapies kill cancer cells, but the processes that regulate the separation of DNA to the daughter cells remain poorly understood. The kinetochore is a large protein structure that attaches the DNA to the mitotic spindle. The spindle then exerts a pulling force to separate the chromosomes into the two daughter cells. During cell division, many of the proteins that comprise the kinetochore are modified by the addition of phosphate to alter their behaviour in response to different stimuli. We intend to use a technique called mass spectrometry to measure and define the phosphate modified proteins at the kinetochore. The objective of this project is to define at a systems level how such changes occur during normal cell division and also in cells targeted with anti-cancer therapies, thus leading to a greater understanding of the process of cell division.

column36: Developing An Unconscious Neural-Reinforcement Therapy for Common Fears
column37: Can 'hardwired' fear responses, e.g. for spiders and snakes, be reprogramed unconsciously in the human brain? Currently, exposure therapy is amongst the most effective treatments for anxiety disorders, but this intervention is subjectively aversive to patients, and rates of premature attrition have been reported to be as high as 70%. We developed a fully unconscious method to bypass the unpleasantness in conscious exposure using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) neurofeedback. Using this method, the similarity between the current brain activity and the brain representation of a feared object is computed in real-time and fed back to participants. Over the course of multiple trials, participants learn to generate brain patterns increasingly similar to the pattern of the feared object. I have previously shown that this intervention leads to a decrease in physiological fear responses without exposing patients to feared objects. Despite these promising findings, we could not observe long-lasting changes in fear reports probably because we did not have the technology to target all the relevant brain regions. Now, recent developments in machine learning allow to target whole-brain representations, which might be necessary to achieve clinically significant changes. I will conduct a randomized control trial with patients diagnosed with 2 specific animal phobias. In a double-blind fMRI neurofeedback protocol, participants will be trained to activate the whole-brain neural representation of one of the two feared animals, while the second animal will act as a control. We hope to observe a specific decrease in clinical symptoms, physiological fear responses and behavioural avoidance of real animals, for at least 6-8 months. Combining our unique unconscious fMRI method with in-scanner virtual reality may eventually extend our approach to other forms of fear, and particularly to post-traumatic stress disorders, which still present a considerable therapeutic challenge

column36: Elucidating the interaction between Ail and vitronectin at the atomic level to determine the mechanism of Yersinia pestis pathogenesis.
column37: Yersinia pestis is the causative agent of the plague, and is responsible for the death of millions of people during massive pandemics. It is highly pathogenic as it can prevent the host's immune response and overwhelm it with massive growth. In combination with easy dissemination and potential weaponization of drug-resistant Y. pestis strains, there is a need to understand the mechanism of infection for medical countermeasures. Ail (adhesion invasion locus) is a membrane protein on the cell surface of Y. pestis and is a key virulence factor. Ail is thought to contribute to the pathogenesis through interaction with Vn (vitronectin), a serum protein that regulates various physiological processes including blood clotting and immune system. Their interaction can enhance bacterial attachment to human cells, suppress host immunity, and inhibit coagulation. Despite being important players of pathogenesis, the exact mechanism of Ail and Vn interaction is unknown. My work will, thus, focus on elucidating their interaction at the atomic level, where I will characterize the molecular structure of Vn then identify Ail-binding motifs on Vn and Vn-binding motifs on Ail through biophysical techniques. All of these interactions will be tested and validated using biochemical assays and cell-based assays. This transdisciplinary project will identify essential binding motifs to provide key targets for drug development and further advance our understanding of mechanisms behind Y. pestis pathogenesis.

column36: Developing and Testing of the Patient Engagement In Research Scale (PEIRS)
column37: Background: Patients who engage in health research are actively involved in decision making at any stage of research, from inception through impact evaluation. Impact: I am leading a strong patient-research partnership to co-develop the PEIRS; to ensure the PEIRS is relevant to patients, and to promote its use. Using the PEIRS to evaluate and identify the best ways of meaningfully engaging patients in research could enhance how patients' perspectives lead to improved applicability and impact of research. Health services research, thus, would provide more effective solutions that improve personal health, population health, and the delivery of healthcare services.

column36: Treating advanced retinal degeneration - rebuilding multiple co-dependent retinal layers with stem cells
column37: Despite dozens of clinical trials (and countless animal trials) to regenerate the retina with stem cell transplants, none have solved the challenge successfully. This is because the retina has many layers, and all layers are necessary in order to permanently restore vision in patients with advanced retinal degeneration - ~1 million patients in Canada and >50 million worldwide. This results in a staggering amount of suffering and considerable global economic burden of 1/3rd of a trillion dollars (USD) annually for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) alone (not including the millions of patients that suffer from advanced, diabetes-related or inherited, retinal degeneration). Current stem-cell suspension transplants can only replace a single retinal layer. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplants can delay further degeneration, but they cannot replace dead photoreceptors. Photoreceptor transplants indeed restore vision, but only briefly since the diseased RPE cannot maintain the new photoreceptor graft. Current scaffold- or sheet-based transplants can be multi-layered. However, they provide limited retinal coverage, result in higher levels of surgical trauma than suspension injection, form inappropriate graft structure, and cause additional cell death - in many cases destroying the layer they were designed to regenerate. Given this, there is considerable need for simple, atraumatic replacement of multiple retinal layers. Here, we propose to continue development of new technology that organizes subretinal graft (including RPE and photoreceptors) into correct orientation and layering with wide coverage. This therapeutic is administered using standard outpatient surgical techniques and infrastructure. We have attained dual-graft stratification in: in vitro, pig ex vivo, and rabbit in vivo models. The next critical step towards the clinic is larger-scale animal trials assessing vision benefit.

column36: Optimizing opioid agonist treatment: Novel therapies and models of delivery in the management of opioid use disorder
column37: Overdose death rates have increased dramatically in Canada in recent years. These deaths have been driven largely by the inadvertent use of powerful opioids, including fentanyl, that have been added to street drugs such as heroin. In British Columbia (BC), a record number of overdose deaths led the provincial government to declare a public health emergency in 2016. Strategies to address the overdose crisis have therefore become an urgent public health priority. One such strategy that has recently been introduced in BC is the expansion of treatment options for opioid use disorder, including injectable treatments. Previous research conducted under idealized clinical conditions has found that such treatments may be beneficial for individuals with opioid use disorder who have not had success with oral treatments such as methadone. However, little is known about the effectiveness of injectable treatments for opioid use disorder under "real world" conditions. This is an important gap in understanding given that medications found to be effective under idealized conditions often perform differently once translated to real world populations and general practice settings. The proposed research will use prospective methods to monitor and evaluate the uptake and impacts of injectable opioid treatments as these are expanded in BC. Specifically, this research aims to identify barriers and facilitators to access to and retention on injectable treatments, as well as how retention in these treatments shapes health outcomes, including reductions in drug use and risk of overdose. This project will also seek to determine how healthcare models of injectable treatment delivery (e.g., pharmacy models; health clinic models) can be best adapted to address the needs of different populations of patients. It is hoped that the proposed research will make important contributions to understanding and improving treatment for opioid use disorder, both in Canada and internationally.

column36: Planned missing data designs for health research
column37: Missing data can create significant problems for researchers throughout the health sciences. Missing data arise when participants drop out of a study before completing it, as in longitudinal studies when people move away or become too busy to continue in a study, or when participants skip questions on a survey or parts of a test, because they are bored, or tired, or do not want to answer sensitive or difficult questions. Traditional statistical analysis methods are designed to be used with complete data, so researchers often delete whole cases (participants) who have missing data points. This practice, however, frequently leads to biased results. As such, unplanned missingness can be a serious problem for research generalization. Planned missingness, on the other hand, has tremendous (and for the most part unrealized) potential. With new statistical methods that produce unbiased results, planned missing data designs are an efficient way to manage cost, improve data quality, and reduce participant fatigue and practice effects. To date, however, there is little guidance for researchers on how to design such studies: how to choose the variables which will have missing values, what percent of data should be missing, how large a sample is needed, and to what extent the model will be able to detect meaningful effects. The present proposal aims to provide comprehensive guidance to researchers for using planned missing research designs in longitudinal research. The results will educate researchers on when, how, and why to use planned missing elements in their research designs. Planned missing data designs will increase the validity, generalizability, and cost-effectiveness of applied health research.

column36: Hypoxia-selective inhibitors of DNA repair
column37: The proposed work involves the development of a drug that will improve the effectiveness of radiation therapy. Since radiation therapy is used to treat about 50% of all cancers this drug could have very wide impact, improving cure rates as well as quality of life. The drug works by preventing the repair of DNA damage induced by radiation. The main advantage of this drug is that it is targeted to tumours due to its limited activity anywhere but in hypoxic cells. Hypoxic cells are rare in the body but are common in cancers, and are responsible for resistance to radiation. We already have lead compounds that work in cells and early animal data, but new chemistry and screening work need to be done to develop these compounds into drugs suitable for use in humans. We will synthesize new compounds based on our understanding of how our lead compound works, and will test them in cells and rodent models of human cancer. We have invaluable guidance to the clinic and eventual commercial opportunities through our partnership with the Clinical Oncology department at the BC Cancer Agency, and with DelMar Pharmaceuticals, a Canadian biotechnology company. The final result of this program will be the nomination of a clinical candidate that can be advanced to regulatory processing and commercial partnership. This outcome will produce excellent academic science, an economic benefit to the BC Cancer Agency, and could impact the approximately half of all Canadian cancer patients who receive radiation therapy.

column36: Repenser l'ergotherapie au soutien a domicile pour favoriser la participation sociale des aines (REPAIRS): vers le deploiement et l'implantation d'un continuum d'interventions innovantes
column37: Les personnes qui ont une vie sociale active sont en meilleure sante et vivent plus longtemps. Or, en vieillissant, une personne sur deux est a risque de vivre de l'isolement social et de la solitude. Heureusement, il est possible d'agir efficacement pour reduire l'isolement social des aines et les aider a s'integrer plus facilement dans la communaute. En effet, les cliniciens, dont les ergotherapeutes, peuvent offrir un eventail d'interventions demontrees economiquement rentables pour ameliorer la vie sociale des aines. Par exemple, les ergotherapeutes peuvent batir des liens avec des ressources de loisirs de la communaute ou offrir aux aines des interventions en groupe, en plus de suivis personnalises pour les aider a avoir une vie sociale pleine de sens pour eux. Cependant, ces interventions sont actuellement peu offertes dans les services d'ergotherapie a domicile aupres des aines, notamment en raison d'un manque de soutien pour les implanter. Ce projet de recherche permettra a des chercheurs, des decideurs, des membres de la communaute et des ergotherapeutes de documenter l'implantation d'interventions qui favorisent la participation sociale des aines. Les chercheurs inviteront d'abord un groupe d'ergotherapeutes a choisir, parmi un eventail de possibilites, les interventions qu'ils desirent implanter. Les chercheurs consulteront egalement les ecrits scientifiques afin d'identifier les strategies a privilegier pour faciliter l'implantation de ces interventions. Grace a ces connaissances, les ergotherapeutes integreront ensuite les interventions a leur pratique reelle. Les participants decriront finalement les conditions qui expliquent l'implantation reussie ou non des interventions choisies et les defis associes. Ces recommandations seront utiles pour guider les cliniciens, les decideurs et les membres de la communaute dans l'implantation de services a domicile qui ameliorent durablement la sante et le bien-etre de la population vieillissante canadienne.

column36: Vulnerable young women in Botswana co-design solutions to improve access to government support programs: a structural approach to HIV prevention
column37: Botswana's HIV prevalence is one of the highest in the world, disproportionately affecting young women (15-29 years). Those who are unemployed and out-of-school are among the most vulnerable and at high risk of HIV infection. Conventional HIV prevention messages that promote abstinence, monogamy, and condom use, have failed to stop the spread of HIV. That is in part due to structural factors, such as poverty, lack of education, and sexual violence. These structural factors undermine the ability of young women to negotiate safe sex. Access to government programs that support small businesses, return to education, or opportunities to gain work experience, could empower young women and decrease their HIV risk. However, designed for private sector development, these programs currently do not reach vulnerable young women. This research project is part of INSTRUCT, the first national-level trial that uses a structural approach to HIV prevention. My research goal is to improve access to government support programs by vulnerable young women in Botswana. I investigate individual and system-related obstacles to program access and delivery. As vulnerable young women and service providers are deeply familiar with these obstacles and their underlying causes, they are best suited to identify ways to overcome them. They will therefore co-design solutions to improve access to support programs. To facilitate policy change, the evidence and co-designed solutions will be presented to national policy makers. The larger INSTRUCT trial will assess the impact of several structural interventions on HIV prevalence. Implemented by Botswana NGO CIET Trust and the National AIDS Coordinating Agency, INSTRUCT is fully supported by the government of Botswana. Within this enabling environment I hope my project will demonstrate that active participation of vulnerable young women in policy design can generate innovative local solutions to reverse the global HIV epidemic.

column36: Depression as a gut feeling: The gut microbiome as a mediating factor in the dysregulation of the gut-vagus-brain epigenome in the context of depression.
column37: We live our lives engaged in a biochemical conversation with trillions of intestinal microbes. It is known that this gut 'microbiota' can modulate the intestines, and that neurons in our intestines can 'talk' to neurons in our brain along the vagus nerve, as part of a larger bidirectional signaling system called the gut-brain axis. Recent research has suggested that microbial signals can be transmitted up the gut-brain axis to modulate mood, and may be a factor in the development of mental illnesses, such as depression. However, the exact mechanisms by which the gut microbiome alters gut-brain signaling and depression risk are still unclear. Depression is strongly associated with disrupted stress response pathways. Gene regulatory processes known collectively as epigenetic mechanisms have been shown to be key mediators in this disruption. Interestingly, gut bacteria produce many of the chemicals that epigenetic processes require, and changes in the levels of these chemicals in mice have been associated with specific epigenetic changes in host cells. Thus, the gut microbiome may be an important epigenetic modulator. In addition, some of the gut microbiota-associated mood alterations disappear in animals if the vagus nerve is severed, suggesting that some moods begin in the gut. I therefore hypothesize that gut microbiome mediated epigenetic processes increase depression risk in humans by altering the gut-vagal-brain axis. My PhD project will identify depression-associated changes in epigenetic regulators in the gut microbiomes of depressed people who died by suicide, and clinically depressed populations. I will test whether specific gut microbe species predict the epigenetic changes in neurons along a gut-vagal-brain pathway. As the first investigation of the gut-microbiome-brain epigenome, this project will further our understanding of microbial-host interactions, which may be a factor in multiple other diseases and an important target for future intervention

column36: The Gut Microbiome as a Key Regulator of Early Life Stress Induced Depression - A Translational Mouse Model
column37: Early life stress increases vulnerability to a number of illnesses, including psychiatric illness such as depression, in adulthood. However, the mechanism for this is unknown. The gut microbiome (the collection of over 100 trillion bacteria and small organisms in our intestinal tract) is an interesting target of research in this regard since it is involved in the development of depression following adult stressors. Indeed, the gut microbiome, on top of its roles in processes such as digestion, interacts with both the central nervous system and the immune system to ultimately modulate stress reactivity and risk for psychiatric illness. However, the effects of early life stress on gut microbiome composition have yet to be explored. Consequently, we hypothesize that early life stress disrupts the composition of gut bacteria to promote the progression of disorders that involve the immune system and the brain, including depression. To test this, we are using mice exposed to early life stress or no stress and measuring gut microbiome composition, intestinal inflammation, brain-immune interactions, and depressive-like behaviours. To determine whether the gut microbiome is causally involved in mediating early life stress induced depression, we are conducting microbiome transplants between stressed and non-stressed mice. In humans, we are examining post-mortem intestinal tissue from depressed suicides or healthy individuals who died of other causes. Through forensic interviews, our lab can assess early life histories of these post-mortem individuals, placing us in a unique position to translate findings from our early life stress animal cohort to a clinically relevant population. The ultimate purpose of this integrative project is to further our knowledge of how different systems (brain, immune, gut) interact to promote the development and progression of depression, a leading cause of disability in Canada.

column36: Investigating the link between mild traumatic brain injuries and aggressive behaviour: an advanced structural neuroimaging study of brain injured children
column37: Mild traumatic brain injuries, or concussions, are a pervasive and exceedingly common condition, affecting up to 600 per 100,000 Canadians every year. A proportion of concussed individuals display aggressive personality changes after their injuries. These changes are associated with several negative outcomes, including impaired social integration and criminality. Concussions in children are especially troublesome, as they are associated with worse outcomes. Research suggests that aggressive behavior is controlled by a circuit of the brain composed of an area called the orbitofrontal cortex, a structure called the amygdala, and a connection between the two called the Uncinate Fasciculus. Current theories suggest that the amygdala is involved in detecting threats and mobilizing the brain for an aggressive response, and the orbitofrontal cortex is involved in suppressing these responses via the Uncinate Fasciculus. However, there are many unanswered questions about the role of concussions in aggressive behaviour. Does damage to one or more parts of this circuit lead to increased aggression, and if so, which parts? Are there any other brain areas involved in aggression? Can post-concussive aggression be predicted through brain scans? The goal of this research is to improve understanding of the links between concussions and aggressive behavior in children by addressing these questions. To do so, we will study concussed children using advanced forms of magnetic resonance imaging capable of detecting the subtle impacts of concussions, and innovative techniques to obtain the most accurate measurements of brain structure. The impact of this research will be to better understand the neural basis of aggressive behaviour, as well as the potential to predict which children will display post-concussive aggression. With the vast number of concussions that are sustained by children every year, being able to predict personality changes has important implications for prevention.

column36: Role of the HNF-1aG319S Polymorphism in Early-onset Type 2 Diabetes in Oji-Cree Youth
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is characterized by high blood sugar due to the reduced ability of the body to respond to insulin and the insufficient release of insulin from pancreatic islets. Youth onset T2D is the fastest growing disease among Indigenous children of Central Canada, the majority being of Oji-Cree heritage. This is a serious concern because 50% of youth living with T2D will develop complications such as kidney failure within 15 years of diagnosis. The combination of a change in the DNA of the HNF-1a gene (HNF-1aG319S) and dramatic dietary changes likely contribute to the recent appearance and immense increase in T2D observed among Oji-Cree youth. As a result, we need to decipher how these environmental and genetic factors interact to affect the development of T2D. HNF-1a is a transcription factor, meaning it works to control the expression of other genes within a cell. We have created the first mouse model reflective of the HNF-1aG319S variant using state-of-the-art gene editing technology. Male and female mice that carry zero, one or two copies of the G319S variant will be fed one of three experimental diets: a standard mouse diet, a diet similar to the traditional Oji-Cree diet, or a diet similar to the modern Oji-Cree diet. We will assess markers of diabetes development including whole-body glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity from birth to old age. The pancreatic islets will be isolated to define the cellular and gene expression mechanisms through which the G319S variant impairs insulin secretion and pancreas development. This will be the first detailed investigation into the relationship between genetics, diet, and diabetes in the Oji-Cree population. Our study will provide an in-depth description of the cellular pathways that are disrupted due to the G319S variant, as well as their functional impact at a whole-body level. This model will serve as a foundation to develop culturally-appropriate therapeutic strategies in the future.

column36: Connectome-based brain biotyping and in-silico network simulation in neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: Accumulating evidence has led to the reconceptualization of mental illnesses as syndromes of 'miswired brain connectivity' during brain development. To transform such insights into clinically useful deliverables, however, we need a precise delineation of disease-specific properties. Unfortunately, the current 'symptom-based' diagnosis fails to explain commonly encountered overlaps in clinical presentations as well as their heterogeneity. The key to address this level of complexity may lie in the creation of an objective, data-driven classification system based on an underlying biology. In the proposed research program, I will develop a novel 'disease subtyping' framework based on the brain network derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). I will conduct my research based on the community-referred 'Healthy Brain Network Biobank', an ongoing initiative that collects multimodal MRI and behavioral data from 10,000 youth who may have psychiatric symptoms. My study targets >680 children affected by mental illness including attention-deficit/hyperactivity, anxiety, conduct, and autism spectrum disorders. Two analyses will be performed: 1) connectome-based disease subtyping and 2) computational network simulation. In the first analysis, I will extract the latent pathological components from functional networks underlying developmental disorders and cluster them to find more homogeneous subgroups. Multimodal profiling will then comprehensively evaluate the differences in behavior and brain organization across the identified subgroups. In the second analysis, a computational network simulation will estimate hidden biophysical features related to neurodynamics in order to probe disease mechanisms. Data-driven disease subtyping will provide objective transdiagnostic boundaries that mirror underlying biological processes. The proposed framework holds promise for the development of effective targeted therapies in multiple developmental conditions.

column36: Engineering immunomodulatory exosomes derived from human mesenchymal stem cells for treatment of acute inflammatory conditions
column37: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and sepsis are among the leading causes of death in Canada, especially for critically ill patients. These devastating conditions are characterized by severe inflammation in response to an insult or infection. In ARDS, inflammation localized to the lungs impairs normal gas exchange, which can lead to respiratory failure. For sepsis, overwhelming inflammation throughout the body leads to failure of vital organs such as the kidney, heart, and brain if not quickly treated. Despite decades of research, there are no specific therapies for ARDS and sepsis and current treatment consists mainly of supportive care. The Stewart Lab has completed the first clinical trial using a stem cell type called mesenchymal stem cells to reduce damaging inflammation in septic shock. However, delivery of cells can potentially cause serious adverse events including formation of tumours and blood clots. I believe that small membrane-bound particles released by mesenchymal stem cells, known as exosomes, may have similar beneficial effects in inflammatory diseases, without the risks of cell delivery. Hence, exosomes represent a potentially safer "cell-free" treatment option. The aims of this project are to evaluate the ability of exosomes to treat ARDS and sepsis in relevant animal models, to identify the biologically active cargo contained in these tiny particles that may be mediating this protective property and, given this insight, explore ways to genetically modify this cargo to enhance the therapeutic effects of exosomes. The findings from this research proposal will be a crucial first step in establishing the therapeutic potential of exosomes for treating acute inflammation. If exosomes are proven beneficial in ARDS and sepsis, our research group is ideally positioned to move this potentially life-saving treatment into clinical trials, and provide a novel approach for treating these vulnerable patient populations in Canada and around the world.
