column36: The rise of transnational city networks and the formation of global urban authority: Strong Cities and the C40 Climate Group
column37: My research investigates recent political efforts by cities to confront global challenges. It examines the rise of "city-networks" as a response to a range of transnational issues from natural disasters and health pandemics to nuclear proliferation and terrorism. Specifically, it examines the efforts of two city-networks, the C40 City Climate Leadership Group and the Strong Cities Network, which address climate change and violent extremism respectively. It examines why and how these city-networks emerged and the strategies they employ when attempting to influence global politics. It further asks about the conditions under which these networks are successful in achieving their policy objectives. In addition to improving our understanding of how cities are meeting the challenges of climate change and violent extremism, this examination provides insight into the changing nature of the global political order. Are cities in these networks becoming more influential, in the sense that they are writing new rules and commanding legitimacy in these issue areas? And if cities are making rules and influencing global politics beyond the state, what does this mean for our traditional system of international authority? By analyzing how contemporary global politics is functioning, we can better understand which political strategies are effective and which are not, and with that knowledge, learn more about how to overcome political gridlock on pressing global issues.

column36: Sex-specific functional and transcriptional contributions of the cortico-striatal and -tegmental pathways in mediating stress susceptibility and resilience
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a sexually dimorphic condition affecting millions of men and women every year. Despite its highly heterogeneous aetiology, chronic stress is a recurring factor interfering with the establishment of cognitive strategies required to deal with daily-life stress. While being a major member of complex neuronal circuits involved in mediating the effects of stress, the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is known to project densely to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA). These mutually exclusive projections are involved differently in the regulation of stress susceptibility in males although their impact in females has not been studied yet. We recently showed that the transcriptional organization of gene networks in the brain differs significantly in males and females with MDD and stressed mice. Importantly, our data suggest that these changes interfere with the activity of individual neuronal populations in a sex-specific fashion. So far, it is unclear whether these populations are projecting preferentially to the NAc or the VTA and whether the activity of these projections differ in stressed males and females. Furthermore, the sex-specific transcriptional programs regulating the activity of these cells are unknown. Here, I propose a multidisciplinary approach combining viral approaches with Ca2+ imaging in behaving animals to monitor projection-specific activity following stress in males and females. I will use pharmacogenetics approaches to modulate these projections and determine their behavioral impact in males and females. Finally, I will sort out these cells and use RNAseq combined with advanced bioinformatics approaches to identify male and female-specific gene networks controlling the activity of both projections differently in males and females. Ultimately, these approaches will lead to the development of better therapeutic strategies for the treatment of mood disorders in males and females.

column36: Etude des modulations de l'expression des genes et de l'epissage des ARNm cellulaires dans le cadre d'une infection par differents Flavivirus: le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune et le virus Zika
column37: Les Flavivirus, tel que le virus Zika, le virus du Nil occidental, et le virus de la fievre jaune, sont des virus transmis par les moustiques auxquels plusieurs milliards de personnes sont exposees au niveau mondial. Ces virus sont etroitement apparentes, mais ils causent des maladies distinctes. De facon generale, tous les Flavivirus peuvent infecter le systeme nerveux et causer des inflammations du cerveau. Par contre, seulement certains Flavivirus, dont le virus de la fievre jaune, peuvent causer des fievres hemorragiques. De plus, le virus Zika est le seul Flavivirus associe au developpement de microcephalie, soit une croissance anormalement faible du cerveau chez le foetus, lorsque la mere est infectee durant la grossesse. Il est connu que les virus deregulent un grand nombre de processus cellulaires de l'hote dans le but de favoriser l'infection. Par contre, les mecanismes par lesquels les virus causent ces changements restent a etre elucides. Dans cette etude, nous investiguons l'infection de cellules avec trois differents Flavivirus, soit le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune, et le virus Zika, dans le but de comprendre comment ces virus interagissent avec l'hote. En effectuant les infections dans les memes conditions, il est egalement possible de comparer les differents virus et leurs effets sur les cellules, en plus de determiner des deregulations communes aux trois virus ainsi que des deregulations uniques a chaque virus. Ces resultats permettront de mieux comprendre comment ces virus affectent l'hote et pourquoi ils causent des maladies differentes.

column36: Quantifying the drivers of animal migration - an integrative approach
column37: Migration is the seasonal movement of animals between two distinct ranges, and is a strategy used by a variety of species worldwide to maximize reproductive success. Migration is critical for populations to thrive in changing environments. Despite this, it is among the most threatened processes on the planet, with declines in migratory behaviour attributed to climate change and habitat loss. We know little about what shapes individual differences in migratory behaviour and the relative roles of genetics, physiology (e.g., body condition), and environmental heterogeneity in shaping migration in a changing landscape. My objective is to develop a complete understanding of migration by untangling the effects of environmental conditions, physiology, and genetics on this fundamental process. Using data collected from three migratory species: moose, mule deer, and mountain goat, I will measure individual variation in migratory behaviour within each species and test multiple hypotheses about the drivers of migration. Using recent advances in technology, I will screen the DNA of all three species to determine if the same genes that control migratory behaviour are shared across species. I predict that while environmental factors will be the main factor controlling migration across species, the remaining variation in behaviour can be explained by a few genes of large effect that are shared across all three species. My project takes an original approach to understanding the drivers of migration behaviour and combines ideas and techniques from multiple disciplines in biology, including ecology, genetics, and physiology. My results will contribute to the understanding of migration behaviours in three species that are important for food security, tourism, and culture in Canada, and whose populations are at risk as their migration routes become threatened due to climate change and habitat loss.

column36: Enhancing and Expanding the "Know Your Status" Initiative in on-reserve Indigenous Communities in Saskatchewan: A Community-engaged Intervention to Increase Diagnosis, Linkage to Care and Prevention of HIV, HCV and STBBIs
column37: First Nations people living on-reserve in Saskatchewan have the highest rates of HIV infection in Canada, with an incidence approximately 7.3-times higher than the national average. They also have the least access to care and to life saving antiretroviral therapy. To address this need, a comprehensive on-reserve HIV testing and treatment initiative called "Know Your Status" (KYS) was launched in 2011. KYS is a community-designed and community-managed program based on partnerships and collaborations between First Nations communities and care providers. Key components of KYS include: community involvement and leadership, education, prevention, specialized nursing support, support for mental health and addictions, lab testing and accessible and culturally-safe clinical management that meets clients where they are located. Culturally supportive services, such as mentorship from Elders and traditional teachings, are also integrated within the program. Thus far, KYS has been primarily implemented to care for HIV and sexually transmitted infections on a few on-reserve communities. However, there is a need to expand the program to include hepatitis C testing, linkage and treatment, as a result of similarly high on-reserve rates. The research team, in close partnership with First Nation communities, intends to refine, adapt, and expand the KYS intervention to communities with the greatest need. Traditional experimental designs to evaluate the KYS initiative cannot be used for various reasons. Instead, the team will use practical, though rigorous, methods to evaluate the effectiveness, acceptability and sustainability of the expanded KYS program, while ensuring that community needs are met. First Nations leaders and communities, policy makers and other physicians will be engaged throughout the project to build community and provincial capacity to treat on-reserve HIV and hepatitis C, and to ensure program sustainability for years to come.

column36: ATTEMPT: Adolescent Type 1 diabetes Treatment with SGLT2i for hyperglycEMia & hyPerfilTration Trial
column37: Despite how far along we have come in advancing diabetes care, many teenagers with type 1 diabetes still struggle to meet blood sugar and HbA1c targets, which is a measure of diabetes control. In fact, over 80% of teenagers do not meet recommended Canadian guidelines for HbA1c. High blood sugar levels or HbA1c is known to affect other parts of the body causing long-term health issues. Recently, a group of medications, called sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have been used in adults with type 2 diabetes and shown to improve diabetes control and prevent long term kidney and heart issues due to high blood sugars. This study, called the ATTEMPT Trial, will look to see if the SGLT2i called Empagliflozin benefits teens with type 1 diabetes. This study was designed to include the perspectives of parents and teens with type I diabetes so the researchers can learn more about what is important to them as well as the safety and acceptability of taking these medicines as part of their diabetes care. Given that the teenage years are a challenging time, it is important that we study these new medicines early on to see if they may improve blood sugar levels and protect against future diabetes related problems, such as kidney and heart disease, in teens with diabetes.

column36: Evaluating Innovative Health Care Solutions to Improve Outcomes for Persons with Type 1 Diabetes using a Novel Electronic Data Repository
column37: Living with type 1 diabetes (T1D) is challenging in many ways. People with T1D are expected to fit self-management and regular clinic appointments into busy lives, balancing short- and long-term risks of low and high blood sugar levels. Our research aims to improve the lives of people with T1D by testing an innovative health system intervention to help patients achieve better diabetes control in a way that places less burden on individuals and is more patient-oriented. Specifically, the intervention will involve electronic delivery of health care and related support services to people living with T1D in addition to usual care, including 1) frequent, brief virtual visits with their diabetes care team to share and discuss blood sugar patterns, diabetes self-management, coping strategies, personalized goals and action plans and 2) structured online educational courses, tools and supports. Virtual visits will use videoconferencing technology that can be securely accessed free of charge from any personal device (PC, tablet, smart phone). We will test the intervention's impact on diabetes control, patient-reported experiences and outcomes, and heath care use and costs. The intervention will be tailored to two age groups: young adults 17-24 years of age and adults 25 years of age and older. It will enable "high frequency, low touch" care to patients with poorer diabetes control and at times in their lives when they are at high risk for diabetes complications. This approach will allow patients to receive more education and support than is feasible in traditional health care models based solely on in-person clinic visits, in a way that is more seamless (fewer disruptions to daily life) and tailored to individual needs (by offering an array of online educational classes, tools and resources) based on stage of life. We hypothesize that the intervention will improve diabetes control, patient experience and access to self-management education and support for patients with T1D.

column36: Improving breast cancer treatment using a combination of oncolytic vaccinia virus immunotherapy with image-guided radiation.
column37: We are studying a breast cancer treatment strategy using viruses modified to selectively kill tumours. These oncolytic ("cancer lysing") viruses both directly kill tumours and also educate the immune system to target cancer cells, helping to prevent tumour recurrence. We have modified vaccinia virus to preferentially grow in cancer cells, killing them, while leaving healthy tissues intact. In breast cancer models, our virus slows tumour growth and extends survival, however, mice still eventually succumb to disease. We aim to increase the effectiveness of virus treatment by combining it with radiation therapy (RT). RT is often used to treat solid tumours such as breast cancer. For patient treatment, sophisticated machinery exists to precisely target RT to tumours and reduce damage to adjacent tissue. One drawback is that cells at the tumour margins, or cells that have spread to distant sites (metastatic cells), evade RT, leading to the return of the cancer. We anticipate that combining RT with an oncolytic virus will allow us to achieve better control of breast cancer in mouse models. To study this, we have access to a specialized image-guided RT machine, the only one of its kind in Western Canada, which allows us to deliver RT to mice with similar precision to that used in humans. We anticipate that RT will clear the bulk of the tumour, while our virus will infect and kill any remaining cancerous cells at the tumour margins, or which have spread to other sites in the body. We also expect that when our virus is combined with radiation it will improve stimulation of the immune system to target the cancer. In this way, the virus will function as a cancer vaccine and prevent metastasis and recurrence. We anticipate that this targeted approach will offer a more effective way of treating breast cancer, while also causing fewer side effects compared to traditional approaches. This will improve the quality of life and long-term outcomes for cancer patients in Canada.

column37: Wait-lists for mental health services in First Nations' communities often make services inadequate to meet community needs. The use of transdiagnostic treatments could serve to reduce these wait-times by allowing individuals who are experiencing a wide array of difficulties (e.g., depression, anxiety, substance use) to receive services that address underlying symptoms at the same time. These treatments also provide a new framework for evidence based culturally appropriate services within First Nations' communities by incorporating strategies that align with cultural values. Working in collaboration with a community based organization serving First Nations communities in North Western Ontario, a skill based transdiagnostic group intervention will be developed and implemented. This treatment will target community specific needs through consultation with organizational staff and community members. Culturally appropriate skills, concepts, and examples will be identified and integrated into the treatment. This is the first project to adapt and assess the effectiveness of a transdiagnostic mental health treatment for First Nations children. Following an initial pilot group of the treatment, approximately 50 children aged 7-12 years will complete a revised version. It is anticipated that these group interventions will reduce difficulties in emotion regulation, repetitive negative thinking, behavioural avoidance, and self-care of the children while developing positive coping strategies.

column36: Developing a Conceptual Framework for Measuring the Unmeasurable: Exploring How Structural and Systemic Racism Impacts Chronic Disease in First Nations Communities in Canada
column37: First Nations people in Canada experience higher rates of chronic disease than the rest of Canadians including heart disease, cancer, diabetes and other conditions. Understanding the root causes of these high rates is complex as it requires examining known risk factors. Racism was identified as an influential, yet under-recognized, determinant of health by First Nation leadership in the province of British Columbia. While social determinants of health have been important in understanding the root causes of poor health, racism and its impact on chronic disease is still heavily underexplored. The specific aim of this research is to examine how racism impacts chronic illness in First Nations communities. This study will analyze data from two Canadian health surveys along with conducting interviews with First Nations people living with a chronic health condition to better identify the complex ways that racism can influence risk factors, prevalence, access to treatment and health outcomes. The findings of this study will be used to inform the first provincial heart health and wellness strategy aimed at reducing cardiovascular disease within First Nations in British Columbia. The knowledge generated will enable the identification of key gaps in healthcare delivery, treatment, and screening which can be used to inform the development of innovative and culturally-safe interventions to improve the First Nation health outcomes and the patient-oriented care journey.

column36: Effect of cumulative exposure to antiretroviral therapy on cancer risk in people living with HIV
column37: Background: Cancer has been a major feature of the HIV epidemic, with Kaposi sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma being the first reported manifestation of AIDS-defining cancers. With the arrival of antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV has become a chronic disease and studies have shown an increase in non-AIDS defining cancers. Additionally, people living with HIV have a higher risk of developing cancer than the general population. There are 75,500 Canadians living with HIV, with the highest proportion in Ontario. In Canada, there is a lack of research assessing the cancer burden and the effect of ART on cancer risk in people living with HIV. Objectives: 1) Determine the incidence and prevalence of site-specific cancers in adults living with HIV in Ontario between 1995 to 2016; 2) Determine whether specific ART regimens show protective cancer effects; and 3) Quantify the extent to which cumulative exposure to ART lowers the risk of infection-related cancers via controlled viremia and improved immune function. Methods: Study objectives will be achieved using data from Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences, Ontario Cancer Registry, Ontario HIV Treatment Network Cohort study, and Canadian HIV Observational Cohort Collaboration. We will calculate incidence rates of site-specific cancers after HIV diagnosis using count modelling techniques. Period prevalence before HIV diagnosis, at HIV diagnosis, and short-term and long-term ART exposure will be calculated. We will quantify relationships between ART use, cancer risk, immune suppression, viremia, demographic, socio-economic and behavioural factors using mediation analysis techniques. Significance: This study will bring forward the need for comprehensive HIV care and cancer control. By understanding the cancer burden and the additional hardships of this key population, medical practice and policies can be adapted to offer better long-term care, plan for resource allocation, and optimize treatment to improve health outcomes.

column36: Implementing the Chronic Care Model to improve the care of people living with HIV: The role of self-management
column37: People with HIV are living longer in Canada, mainly due to advances in care and treatment. The success of antiretroviral therapy means that people with HIV are also experiencing more diseases of aging and require ongoing care for multiple chronic conditions. These complex needs may be best addressed through primary care or community-based settings that include integrated health and social services. Care for people with chronic illnesses involves many elements, and one of these elements is support for self-management. There is evidence that self-management programs improve the confidence, knowledge, skills, and motivation people require to take care of their chronic diseases. However, it remains uncertain whether and how these programs similarly help people with HIV to manage their health. In addition, HIV infections in Canada more often affect groups who already must deal with other disadvantages (e.g., poverty, racism), thus requiring an equity lens in research conducted with this population. To address such concerns, I will engage disadvantaged groups (e.g., people who inject drugs) in all phases of this work, and attend to sex- and gender-based issues. In the first part of my research, I will review and describe the literature on the role of self-management in improving health among people with HIV. Second, I will conduct qualitative interviews with diverse individuals, including people with HIV, community-based organizations, and care providers. Results from the literature review and interviews will inform the implementation and evaluation of a sustainable chronic disease self-management program to determine its impact on physical and mental health outcomes. By using existing community partnerships and networks at the local, provincial and national levels, my research is expected to improve health care for people living with HIV. Lessons learned from this research can also be extended to community-focused care for people aging with other chronic conditions.

column37: Around the world, it is estimated that about 37 million people live with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In Canada alone, between 63,000 to 89,000 individuals live with HIV/AIDS and there are thousands of new infections each year. In the absence of an efficient vaccine against HIV and treatments still far away from eradicating the virus, we need to find new approaches to fight this virus. Recent studies have shown that our immune system already possess potentially effective protective mechanism against HIV infection, the antibody-dependant cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) response. The findings of this study will help us to progress in finding a functional cure for HIV-infected patients by sensitizing specifically HIV-infected cells to a strong ADCC response. Moreover, some of these results might be useful at designing new immunogens able to elicit a protective response and thus decrease HIV-1 transmission.

column36: Impact of HPV-induced Immune Changes in the Anal Mucosa on HIV Transmission
column37: There are approximately 37 million people currently living with HIV in the world which, if left untreated, leads to AIDS and death. HIV infection is also a significant public health concern in Canada, particularly when it comes to at-risk populations including men who have sex with men. For instance, in Toronto, almost 1 in 4 men who have sex with men are estimated to be infected with HIV. Therefore, it is important to understand what factors are driving increased HIV risk in this population. One of the factors that have been suggested to play a role in increased HIV risk is infection with Human Papillomavirus (HPV) that can sometimes lead to anal cancer. We believe that HPV infection can increase HIV risk, because when the immune system becomes active in order to respond to HPV infection, this active immune status actually makes it easier for HIV to infect the body. Our goal is to describe this active immune status in detail, so that if HPV infection does increase HIV risk, several methods including HPV treatment and HPV vaccine can be explored to reduce HIV transmission.

column36: ACHRU Community Partnership Program for Diabetes Self-Management for Older Adults - Canada
column37: Living with diabetes and other chronic (ongoing) conditions is common in older adults. These individuals have poorer health and higher use of health services compared to older adults with diabetes alone. Programs that help older adults self-manage their diabetes and other health conditions benefit both individuals and the healthcare system. The McMaster University Aging, Community and Health Research Unit developed and tested a new patient-centered, community-based program to improve the delivery and outcomes of care for older adults with diabetes and other chronic conditions. This 6-month program was developed in partnership with patients, caregivers, primary and community care providers and researchers. The program is delivered by nurses, dietitians and community providers. It involves in-home visits by nurses and dietitians, monthly group wellness sessions at community centers, and monthly team meetings. Wellness sessions include exercise, education, shared meals, and social support. Caregivers are invited to be active participants along with patients. The program was successfully implemented in Ontario and Alberta. Participants who received the program had better quality of life, self-management, and mental health at no additional cost compared to those receiving usual care. To determine how the program can best help people, more testing is needed with different communities and groups of people. We will partner with primary healthcare teams (e.g., family doctors' offices) in three provinces to adapt and test the program in a variety of real-world settings. We will assess how to best put this program into practice and measure outcomes important to patients and caregivers so study results are relevant to them. Study findings will guide the development of a plan for expanding the program to reach and benefit more older adults with diabetes and other chronic health conditions. Patients and caregivers will be involved as key partners in all aspects of the research.

column36: SPIDER-NET, A Structured Process Informed by Data, Evidence and Research-Network: An approach to support primary care practices in optimizing the management of patients with complex needs
column37: Health care costs are increasing quickly. About half is spent on a small number of people with complex health problems. We need to address this. Built on a successful model for improving care by working together, the Structured Process Informed by Data, Evidence and Research (SPIDER) contains 3 parts: 1) Build teams with family physicians, nurses, pharmacists, medical staff and patients. These teams will learn together, from each other and from experts about improving quality in practice; 2) Use information from Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) to discover what the issues in each practice are, and decide together what could be done; and 3) Start making the practice changes that were agreed to with the help of coaches. Repeatedly test, measure and improve care. We will test SPIDER to see if it helps older patients taking many medications (polypharmacy), some of which may not be necessary or may even be harmful. More drugs often mean more side effects and this is even worse as people age. The risks of side effects like confusion, dizziness and falls increases in elders. Older patients taking ten or more medications are especially complex and high risk; we can do better for them. We expect SPIDER to help family doctors and their teams deliver better care by reviewing and reducing riskier drugs for these patients. We will test SPIDER in seven centres, in five provinces. We expect that it will improve patients' quality of life and their heath; it may also save money by reducing the number of times people are admitted to hospital. Our team is made up of experts and leaders in quality improvement, audit and feedback, pharmacists, physicians, patients and researchers. All of us have experience in the parts that make up SPIDER, so we are able to do this; we will now work together to improve care for elders in our communities by reducing and improving medications, to support their health and help them reach their goals for quality of life.

column36: Screening for Poverty And Related social determinants and intervening to improve Knowledge of and links to resources (SPARK) Study
column37: The social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions and processes at an individual, family, neighbourhood, community and societal level that impact on health. Numerous studies have confirmed the central role that SDOH play in creating and maintaining health inequities. While much is known about SDOH, we lack the individual-level data necessary to target interventions, and lack rigorously evaluated interventions to meet social needs in health settings. Sociodemographic data collected at the individual level, paired with interventions to meet social needs when identified, could address this problem. Further, robust sociodemographic data linked to electronic medical records (EMRs) can support quality improvement and new care pathways at the organizational level, planning and resource allocation at the system level, and advance research on health inequities. The SPARK Study is a cluster randomized controlled trial that will rigorously evaluate a "modest" versus "intensive" intervention to help address poverty when identified. While the primary outcome of this intervention is change in income attributable to the poverty intervention, we will capture data on additional impacts, including linkage to community resources, psychological stress and quality of life. To prepare for the trial, we will develop and validate a standard tool for sociodemographic data collection and social need identification, building on our previous research. We will also pilot test our tool, EMR integration, recruitment processes and study instruments before launching the full trial. Finally, we will collect qualitative data alongside the trial to evaluate implementation and better understand how the intervention to address poverty impacts on participants. This program of research will advance the ability of health providers, organizations and systems to collaborate with patients and communities to "go upstream" and address SDOH.

column36: Personalized Risk Assessment for Prevention and Early Detection of Breast Cancer: Integration and Implementation
column37: Breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women. A woman faces a one in eight chance of developing the disease in her lifetime. Currently, women aged 50 to 74 are recommended to have a mammogram every 2 to 3 years. To maximize the benefits and reduce harms, women should be screened based on their personal risk of the disease. More precise risk assessment combining data on genomic profiling and other BC risk factors has the potential to markedly increase the proportion of identifiable high risk women. This project will provide evidence that can significantly expand the benefits of current age-based population screening programs by supporting the transition to a risk-based approach. It will also improve counseling of women with a family history of BC who are seen in cancer genetic clinics. Earlier detection of BC will allow more cancers to be detected while they are still small and curable, which in turn will save lives and bring significant health and socio-economic benefits. By studying very large cohorts of women using high throughput genomic technologies together with statistical and epidemiological methods, this project will develop a validated multi-gene panel test including genetic variants reliably associated with BC risk. This will enable individualized risk assessment and improve the counseling process by health care providers for women with and without a known BC family history. To support a framework for future implementation of a risk-based screening approach, a large population-based cohort will be assembled to evaluate the acceptability and feasibility of using a new comprehensive risk prediction web tool and a genomic profiling test within the existing health care system. The cohort will be followed to determine behavioural, psychosocial and clinical outcomes. Policies will be developed to address the socio-ethical and legal challenges for women, health professionals and decision makers associated with implementing risk-based breast screening. By providing this evidence, this project will change breast screening practice and ensure better use of human and financial resources. Women will face less invasive BC treatment with fewer complications and improved quality of life and survival, thereby reducing both the clinical and economic burden for a large proportion of Canadian women.

column36: Reducing the global burden of infectious diseases through precision population health
column37: The global rise in the prevalence of antibiotic resistant bacteria is a problem so serious that it threatens all modern medicine. We have already reached the point where half of the common bacteria that cause infections are resistant to our front-line drugs. Moreover, new superbugs have emerged that cannot be cured with any drug. Once these multiple-drug resistant organisms take hold in our healthcare setting, many of the benefits of modern medicine, including hip replacement surgery, chemotherapy, and organ transplant, will become too risky due to the chances of acquiring a deadly infection. Finding an immediate solution to this global health crisis is our moral imperative to ensure that future generations will benefit from modern medical practices. One of the primary reasons for the increasing levels of antibiotic resistance is the one-size-fits-all approach we take to treating infections, which encourages the over use of these drugs. The one-size-fits-all approach also causes unnecessary sickness and deaths. Different strains of bacteria can be dramatically different in the risks they pose to our health. However, we do not consider these risks when treating infections because of technological limitations. To solve this problem, we have assembled an international team of infectious disease experts, microbiologists, database experts, and analytical chemistry experts to develop a new approach to treating infections. Our solution is to 1) identify every significant biochemical trait that is found in the most dangerous bacteria, 2) create an automated analytical system and database for predicting the potential risks posed by each individual infection, and 3) implement a new Precisions Infection Management (PIM) strategy that will allow clinicians to match each patient to the exact level of antibiotic therapy necessary to cure infections without unnecessarily selecting for antibiotic resistant bacteria. PIM will reduce overall antibiotic use and may preserve the lifespan of our critical front-line drugs. In addition, it will help ensure people suffering from dangerous bacterial infections (e.g. "flesh-eating" strains) get aggressive therapy faster. Likewise, PIM will ensure that people infected with non-dangerous strains receive milder therapies and minimize the risks of medical complications (e.g. kidney failure). PIM allows these significant health improvements without increasing costs to our healthcare system: we predict that PIM will actually save money because of the reduced time people will need to spend in the hospital, and more importantly, it will save lives.

column36: Care4Rare Canada: Harnessing multi-omics to deliver innovative diagnostic care for rare genetic diseases in Canada (C4R-SOLVE)
column37: There are about 7,000 rare genetic diseases (RDs) that affect more than one million Canadians. RDs have a devastating impact on Canadians: two-thirds cause significant disability, threequarters affect children, more than half lead to early death, and almost all have no treatment. The cause of more than one-third of the 7000 RDs is currently unknown. Care4Rare Canada Consortium leads the world by using genomic sequencing (decoding a person's DNA) to identify the genetic cause of RDs. However, more than one third of patients seen each year in Canada with a suspected RD remain undiagnosed and can spend years visiting specialists and undergoing unnecessary testing to explain their disease. Contributing to this gap in care is that genomic sequencing is not available as a clinical test anywhere in Canada. Thus, building on the success of Care4Rare, the goal of the C4R-SOLVE project is to identify the genetic cause for the remaining unsolved RDs while making genomic sequencing available as a clinical diagnostic test in Canada. To understand the remaining unsolved RDs, C4R-SOLVE will explore new sequencing technologies and improve data sharing world-wide, enabling the discovery of new causes of RDs. To improve access to clinical diagnostic testing, C4R-SOLVE will work with provincial ministries of health to determine the best way to include genomic sequencing as a clinical test to diagnose RDs. By achieving its goal, the C4R-SOLVE project will more than double our ability to diagnose this one third of RD patients, while building the infrastructure and tools needed to improve RD diagnosis around the world. An accurate diagnosis will benefit patients and their families as a genetic diagnosis leads to optimized care, improved family wellbeing, and new disease insights. Further, optimal delivery of clinical genomic sequencing has the potential save at least $28M per year, benefiting the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: Silent Genomes: Reducing health care disparities and improving diagnostic success for children with genetic diseases from Indigenous populations.
column37: Indigenous populations face unique health challenges, inequities, and barriers to healthcare in Canada and around the world. As such, they typically have poorer health outcomes than do non-Indigenous groups. While genomics (the study of the complete set of human genes) has advanced health care by allowing medical treatments to be tailored to the specific needs of individual patients ('precision medicine'), this 'genomics revolution' is also contributing to health inequities. In particular, compared to what is becoming routinely available to other Canadians, Indigenous populations often have little or no access to genomic technologies and the research that drives them. This has created a 'genomic divide', a key component of which is the lack of background genetic variation data for Indigenous populations. This prevents accurate diagnosis because the reference data are needed when multi-gene and exome (entire genome) testing panels are used. Notably, these genomics resources are silent with respect to First Nations (FN), Inuit and Metis peoples (collectively our Canadian Indigenous populations). Silent Genomes will address the genomic divide by reducing access barriers to diagnosis of genetic disease in Indigenous children. With our First Nations, Inuit and Metis partners we will: 1) Establish processes, through an Indigenous lens, for safe governance of biological samples and genome data in the Silent Genomes project, which will lead to broader policy. 2) Address barriers to accessing genetic/genomic health care and bring genomic testing to at least 200 Indigenous children with suspected genetic disorders. 3) Develop an Indigenous Background Variant Library (IBVL) of genetic variation from a diverse group of 1500 FN Canadians and assess improvement in diagnosis for referred children. 4) Assess effectiveness of the IBVL to lower health care costs and plan for long term use of IBVL for Canadian Indigenous children and adults needing genetic/genomic health care.

column36: PEGASUS-2 - PErsonalized Genomics for prenatal Abnormalities Screening USing maternal blood : Towards First Tier Screening and Beyond
column37: The discovery that DNA of fetal origin is present in maternal blood during pregnancy has led to a new genomics-based maternal blood test called non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS), which is very reliable at screening for Down syndrome. Currently, public healthcare systems pay for this expensive NIPS test only as a second-tier screening for women who have first screened positive on less costly and less accurate biochemical and ultrasound tests. Hence, only after an initial screen has delivered a positive result is NIPS currently used to help women participating in prenatal screening programs avoid a diagnostic amniocentesis. If NIPS were used as the entry-level test for Down syndrome screening, it would benefit women by providing a higher chance of detecting an affected pregnancy and a lower chance of providing a false positive result. It would also enable women to have their final diagnostic result sooner than the current standard of care permits. As well, because NIPS can also detect other fetal chromosome anomalies, its use could enable screening for more conditions. This project aims to provide highquality evidence to inform decisions by health care organisations about using first-tier NIPS to replace traditional screening tests for Down syndrome, and potentially to screen for other fetal chromosome anomalies. We will compare the current screening approach of second-tier NIPS with the use of first-tier NIPS in a large cohort of pregnant women. We will also study the costeffectiveness of expanding screening to other conditions, and the ethical, social and legal implications of doing so. As well, we will provide strategies for scaling up shared decision making processes between couples and their health care practitioners. Finally, we will further develop the NIPS technology to lower its costs, expand the detection of other anomalies, and ensure the quality control of clinical-grade NIPS testing in Canada and worldwide. While taking into account the values informing couples' decisions about participation in prenatal screening, this project will enable publicly funded access to a promising genomics technology for all pregnant women in Canada. Further, it will ensure that couples have access to web-based tools to help their decision making, and that all health care professionals are trained in shared decision making for prenatal screening.

column36: Tackling Childhood Brain Cancer at the root to improve survival and quality of life
column37: One in every 285 children will suffer from a cancer before the age of 15 years. While overall survival and quality of life for child survivors have improved substantially over the last 3 decades for cancers of the blood (leukemia), brain cancers are still lethal and disabling. For some aggressive forms of brain cancer barely 10% of children and young adults survive 3 years after diagnosis, despite enormous efforts and costs to families and to the health care system. Those who do survive often have severe disabilities resulting from their treatment (which can include surgery, radiation therapy to the brain and the use of toxic drugs), with consequent limitations to their social and professional lives. Through previous research our team discovered that many paediatric brain tumours are driven by mutations in genes essential for regulating the development and growth of all body tissues, but which have specific roles in brain development. These findings have enabled more accurate diagnosis of the specific subtype of each paediatric brain tumour, and partly explain why these cancers are unresponsive to existing treatments. This new research aims to fast-track the use of targeted therapies against some of the mutated proteins, while continuing to identify new therapeutic targets for children whose tumours do not yet have a clear molecular diagnosis. We will do this using novel ways of interrogating the genome on the single cell level, determining how the genome is rearranged in childhood cancers, and identifying specific vulnerabilities of the cancer cell compared to the normal cell from which it originated. We will validate proposed therapies in reliable models and accelerate translation to the bedside through our network of care providers. As well, we will assess how to assign children rapidly to a personalised treatment strategy early in the disease course, based on the molecular diagnosis of each tumour. These goals will be pursued by engaging relevant stakeholders and developing an innovative business model enabling drug discovery even for rare disease sub-types. Our project promises to improve survival and quality of life for all children and young adults with brain tumours. By leading to more efficient drugs tailored to specific patients, it will enable health care providers to increase success in treating children with brain tumours, while also decreasing the burden of survivorship on patients, their families and Canada's health care system.

column36: Precision Medicine CanPREVENT AMR: Applying Precision Medicine Technologies in Canada to Prevent Antibody Mediated Rejection and Premature Kidney Transplant Loss
column37: Chronic kidney disease affects 1 in 10 Canadians with estimated costs of over $2 billion/year. Transplantation is the treatment of choice for those whose kidneys fail: it improves survival (>85% vs <50% at 5yr), optimizes quality of life (85% vs 70% of normal) and decreases health-care costs ($15,000 vs $55,000/yr) compared with dialysis. But severe graft rejection (known as "antibody-mediated" rejection or AMR) occurs in up to 30% of transplant patients causing premature graft loss, return to dialysis, and early death. We will develop a program to prevent AMR and promote lifetime survival of the transplanted kidney. Our program will employ genetic technologies to: (a) reduce the risk of rejection through better donor-patient matching; (b) monitor the immune response after transplant to predict AMR; (c) enable personalized treatment with powerful drugs to prevent rejection while avoiding infection or cancer; and (d) study the legal, ethical, societal and economic considerations of introducing these strategies into clinical practice to improve quality of life and reduce health-care costs. The program builds on our highly successful national transplant program coordinated through the Canadian Blood Services (CBS) and links 16 major transplant programs, 9 leading universities, and 14 provincial transplant organizations and laboratories. It is led by an experienced Canadian and international team of genome experts, transplant immunologists, clinical scientists, legal scholars, ethicists, and health economists, working collaboratively with patients, members of the public, health providers, provincial health organizations, national coordinating bodies and commercial partners. Our program seeks to reduce the frequency of AMR by at least 50%, with the expected benefits from preventing rejection commencing quickly and increasing annually due to increased survival of transplanted kidneys. The benefits of this program will consequently occur at three levels: (a) the patient and family, with a gain in survival and quality of life, reduced caregiver burden, and personal health expenditures; (b) the healthcare system, with reduced dialysis care and re-transplant needs; (c) and society, due to increased workforce productivity and decreased kidney management costs.

column36: Genomic and Outcomes Databank for Pharmacogenomic and Implementation Studies (GoPGx)
column37: The vision of Go-PGx is to save lives and improve the quality of life for patients through the prevention of serious adverse drug reactions (ADRs) - often called 'side effects'. The treatment of childhood cancer is particularly impacted by ADRs. ADRs in children are 3-fold more likely to be life-threatening and a staggering 75% of childhood cancer patients develop chronic health conditions and 42% develop disabling or life-threatening ADRs from cancer treatment. It is increasingly evident that genetic differences in patients affect one's likelihood of experiencing an ADR - studying the variability in response to medication is called pharmacogenomics (PGx). Go-PGx is an integrated pipeline of innovative research and the development of tools to facilitate these findings (usually referred to as knowledge translation) into clinical practice by implementing lab tests to predict a patient's likelihood of suffering from an ADR in pediatric cancer treatment. Go-PGx builds upon over 14 years of experience in studying ADRs with research collaborators integrated in 10 pediatric hospitals across Canada. We have collected over 6,125 DNA samples and have corresponding reports of medication use and ADR outcomes recorded in a clinical database. We will build upon this with four linked research activities: (1) We will make new research discoveries of genetic susceptibility to ADRs and (2) develop tools to educate and inform physicians and patients beginning with a prioritized focus on five severe pediatric oncology ADRs. We will generate a comprehensive ADR database of linked clinical and genetic information to provide an accessible resource for to help researchers around the world. (3) At the same time, we will start providing PGx testing in 10 pediatric oncology centers across Canada, (4) while studying important components to the uptake of ADR screening in the health care system, such as understanding what the barriers and facilitators are to making this kind of testing successful; what the perceptions of clinicians, patients and families are to this kind of testing; and understanding the economic implications of introducing this kind of testing into clinical practice across Canada. Go-PGx wants to provide this much-needed access to pharmacogenomic testing in pediatric oncology and lay the foundation for accessible pharmacogenomic testing in Canada.

column36: Deciphering the genome biology of relapsed lymphoid cancers to improve patient management
column37: Collectively, lymphoid cancers are the 5th most common cancers in men and women and affect patients of all ages. In Canada alone, 16,000 patients are newly diagnosed, and 6,000 patients will die of the disease each year. The mortality of the disease is almost exclusively linked to disease relapse when the current standard of care fails to cure the cancer. Therefore, successful treatment and symptom control of relapsed disease represents the single most important need for patients suffering from lymphoid cancers. Unfortunately, the causes of treatment failure are mostly unknown and, as a consequence, no clinical tests are available to inform on the individual prognosis of patients, likely treatment outcomes of salvage therapy, and to guide physicians and patient to use alternative therapeutic choices, such as small molecule drugs or modern immunotherapy. Moreover, treatment relapse and associated treatment cost is a major burden for the health care system with over $315 million attributed to relapsed disease in Canada alone. This means that often times expensive, but ineffective treatments are applied without guidance by adequate clinical testing. In this project, we will focus on the most common forms of lymphoid cancer, namely follicular lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia that together account for approximately two thirds of all lymphoid cancers. The main goals of our research are to develop clinical tests, alongside modern treatments available at relapse, to improve patient outcomes, quality of life, and to make tests widely available in the Canadian, publicly funded health care system. We will achieve these goals by applying state-of-the-art sequencing of patient biopsies taken at the time point of clinical relapse, performing detailed economic analyses, and engaging patients into joint decision making with their treating physicians. Our project will provide novel clinical tests in diagnostic laboratories, access to cutting-edge scientific progress, produce decision aids for patients, and help policy makers in the process of implementing personalized treatment approaches into the health care system.

column36: LARGE SCALE GE3LS PROJECT: GenCOUNSEL: OPTIMIZATION OF GENETIC COUNSELLING FOR CLINICAL IMPLEMENTATION OF GENOME-WIDE SEQUENCING
column37: Genome-wide sequencing (GWS) is a powerful new genetic test that analyzes a person's entire genetic make-up to diagnose the cause of genetic disorders. GWS generates unique genetic counselling issues, as it may diagnose disorders or disease risk factors that are unrelated to the original reason for testing. In addition, it can generate complex results that are difficult for nonexpert health providers to interpret. Currently, this technology is not routinely available in Canada, but because of its diagnostic capability, GWS will soon be available for most Canadian patients who need it. This means that many more families will be considering GWS as a test option, further increasing the demand for genetic counselling. Genetic counsellors are specialist healthcare providers with the expertise to lead the integration of genomics into patient care across all areas of medicine. They represent the "front line" of medical genetics. By providing education, emotional and decisional support to patients and families, guiding them to make informed decisions regarding genetic testing, they help prevent inappropriate decision making that can have devastating health and /or emotional consequences for patients and families. In Canada, there is limited access to genetic counselling. Factors such as cost of time and travel, language and cultural barriers exist for many Canadians. Furthermore, the lack of legal recognition of genetic counsellors in Canada means they work primarily in clinical genetics units at academic centres, rather than in the community. GenCOUNSEL, led by international researchers in genetic counselling, genomics, ethics, health services implementation and health economics will determine the most effective socio-ethical, clinical, legal and economic methods to provide genetic counselling with clinical GWS implementation. GenCOUNSEL aims to: understand the current and future need for genetic counsellors, investigate and develop best practices for delivery of genetic counselling, improve access to genetic counselling, in particular for underserved patient populations, and develop a framework for the legal recognition of genetic counsellors. These activities will result in increased access, patient satisfaction, and cost-efficiency through provision of effective and professional genetic counselling for all Canadians who need it.

column36: Noninvasive diagnosis of tuberculosis through point-of-care detection of cell-free DNA in plasma and urine in HIV-positive and negative patients
column37: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis that causes significant suffering worldwide. It remains a challenging condition to diagnose, especially in patients infected with HIV, as they often have forms of disease with few bacteria to detect. In addition, children who have difficulty producing phlegm, and patients who have tuberculosis outside the lungs, also pose diagnostic difficulty. In these cases, invasive sampling (typically a needle-based procedure such as biopsy, or a sample from the lower back to obtain cerebrospinal fluid) is often required. To address this need, we have developed a simple and non-invasive laboratory test to diagnose tuberculosis from blood and urine samples. More specifically, this test is a multiplexed nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis cell-free DNA. The assay has thus far been tested on 126 blood samples from adult patients with tuberculosis in the lungs, and Stanford Hospital patients with tuberculosis outside the lungs and patients without tuberculosis, with an overall sensitivity of 74% and specificity of 100%. The proposed study aims to comprehensively assess and optimize the test performance characteristics of this assay in HIV-positive and negative patients, with the aim of developing it into a point-of-care test. This new test shows potential to improve timely diagnosis of tuberculosis, and thus reduce transmission of the infection to other people. It also may improve targeted anti-tuberculosis therapy by limiting treatment to those who test positive, and avoid unnecessary side-effects in those who test negative.

column36: Couple-based intervention for HIV treatment and prevention in South Africa
column37: This study seeks to develop and evaluate a couple-based intervention targeting antiretroviral (ART) medication adherence for HIV-infected South African women and their male partners. South Africa is a country with one of the highest rates of HIV infection. Since HIV is primarily transmitted through stable heterosexual contact in South Africa, working with both members of a couple is recommended. This intervention has the potential to simultaneously improve HIV-infected women's adherence to life-saving ART (used to suppress HIV) as well as bring men into care. Men's disengagement from HIV testing and treatment is a major barrier to meeting global goals of eradicating new HIV infections by 2030. Therefore, in order to work with both members of the couple and be maximally effective, one intervention must target women's ART adherence and men's disengagement from testing and subsequent treatment. To date, however, this has not been done. The proposed study will develop a couple-based intervention that targets the needs of both women and men by building off existing individual interventions (separate interventions have been developed for ART adherence and enhancing motivation for HIV testing and treatment). The study will then use focus groups with South African men and women to ensure the proposed intervention is culturally appropriate. The intervention will then be pilot-tested with 20 South African couples to evaluate whether it has the intended effect on women's ART adherence and men's HIV testing and subsequent treatment. Overall, this study seeks to test a unique intervention that has the potential to simultaneously meet the needs of South African men and women as an opportunity to both prevent and treat HIV.

column36: Efficacy of Viral RNA Processing Inhibitors in Controlling HIV-1 Replication in vivo
column37: Antiretroviral therapies (ARTs) for HIV-1 infection target the viral lifecycle and delay the progression of those infected to AIDS. However, the effectiveness of these ARTs are plagued by a rise in drug-resistant HIV strains present in over 7-24% of newly infected people in the US and Europe. This issue calls for new approaches in combating HIV-1 infection. Several studies have demonstrated that delivering agents towards this stage, which is not targeted by current ARTs termed HIV-1 RNA processing, can successfully inhibit HIV-1 growth. Two of these inhibitors (digoxin and chlorhexidine) are already FDA-approved drugs for other purposes. Although chlorhexidine is not suitable for systemic use, concentrations of digoxin required to inhibit HIV replication in T cells cultured from HIV-infected patients are within accepted dosage levels used to treat heart conditions. Furthermore, I discovered that one digoxin derivative (digitoxigenin) and compound 191 are both potent inhibitors of HIV-1 RNA processing with improved safety profiles over digoxin. All of these studies, however, were performed in cell culture and these findings may not be transferable to patients. Whether this approach can become a novel ART for treating HIV-1 infection remains to be determined. In this proposal, I plan to investigate if these HIV-1 RNA processing inhibitors are effective against HIV-1 infection in an environment that mimics humans known as "humanized mice." These mice will be infected with HIV-1 and treated with inhibitors to test their ability to inhibit HIV-1 growth in comparison to current ARTs. Successful generation of a humanized mouse model could complement drug screening efforts by supporting their validation in animal models, bringing discoveries one step closer to potential clinical trials. Moreover, this model could also support global efforts in combating other deadly diseases, particularly ones involving human immunodeficiencies, and viruses, such as Zika and Influenza.

column36: Can nutrition care be optimized within an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol for colorectal cancer patients? The effect of pre-operative N-3 fatty acid supplementation on surgical outcomes
column37: Cancer is one of the diseases most commonly associated with malnutrition. Surgery is a main treatment for cancer. When surgical patients also have malnutrition it takes them longer to recover, they stay longer in the hospital and cost the health system more. Specialized surgical programs known as Enhance Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) help to minimize the negative effects of malnutrition with standardized nutrition care protocols. ERAS programs screen patients for malnutrition before surgery, but there are no specific nutrition therapies offered before surgery to treat specific nutrition problems. Muscle depletion and the development of fatty muscle are specific nutrition problems caused by malnutrition. The aims of this study are to: 1) teach registered dietitians to identify patients with muscle abnormalities using CT and 2) determine if pre-surgical supplementation with N-3 fatty acids (fish oil) will treat muscle abnormalities resulting in a shorter hospital stay. column37: The development of medications to safely promote B-cell replication would be ground-breaking for the treatment of all forms of diabetes. GABA, a neurotransmitter, was shown to facilitate B-cell regeneration in mice. However, GABA exerts unspecific effects, mainly due to the activation of its various receptors, leading to cellular events unrelated to proliferation. Specific positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of GABA offer increased specificity and are currently in clinical use. I hypothesize that GABAA-R PAM will increase B-cell mass in both normal mice and those with experimental diabetes (prediabetes and type 2 diabetes [T2D]), being more effective than GABA itself. Repurposing GABAA-R PAMs to treat diabetes is theoretically appealing due to their safety profile and potential to enhance the ability of GABA to promote B-cell replication. Part 1 of the study will focus on the PAM-mediated effect(s) on B-cell proliferation. Pancreatic islet expansion and B-cell regeneration will be evaluated in mice treated with GABAA-R PAMs. To explore the potential use of PAM drugs as an anti-diabetic tool, prediabetic and T2D mice models will be used; thereafter, B-cell proliferation and islet mass will be assessed. I will also verify whether hyperglycemia and glucose intolerance was corrected with PAM administration. Part 2 will focus on the functional and mechanistic effect(s) of PAMs on B-cell function and expansion. I will measure insulin release, insulin granules and the gene levels of proinsulin and preproinsulin in mice and human islets. The mechanism of PAM-mediated B-cell expansion will also be rigorously assessed through a variety of ex vitro experiments. In the end, I will determine the PAMs' 1) effectiveness to expand B-cell mass; 2) ability to correct hyperglycemia in prediabetes and T2D; and 3) functional and mechanistic effect(s) on mouse and human pancreatic B-cells. This study could usher in a new class of drugs for diabetes treatment.

column36: Understanding the role of a4beta7+ Tregs in the development and treatment of inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Canada has some of the highest rates of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in the world. The causes of IBD are complex, but one likely factor is an imbalance in gut immune responses. Immune cells, specifically the subset of immune cells called T cells, are of particular importance. There are two types of T cells that have competing functions: effector cells, which generally cause inflammation, and regulatory cells (Tregs), which suppress inflammation. Under healthy conditions the effector cells are kept in-check by the regulatory cells. Evidence suggests that shifts in this equilibrium between regulatory and effector T cells may contribute to the pathogenesis of IBD; when there is an imbalance, inflammation flares up and damage to the gut can occur. T cells secrete a molecule called integrin a4B7 that helps T cells migrate to the gut; therefore, a4B7 is thought to have a role in IBD. Clinical trials of a commercial antibody called Vedolizumab (which binds to a4B7, rendering it dysfunctional) have shown a reduction in IBD symptoms after treatment. It is not known how Vedolizumab works, but it is likely related to control of inflammatory effector T cells and the function of regulatory T cells in the intestine. Both effector and regulatory T cells express a4B7, but how Vedolizumab affects their homing in the gut is unknown. The primary goal of my proposal is to study how Vedolizumab affects the homing and function of effector versus regulatory CD4+ T cells in the gut of IBD patients. In addition, I will determine if human Tregs that express a4B7 can cure IBD in a mouse model. Understanding the mechanism of action of Vedolizumab is key to understanding more about the pathogenesis of IBD and optimizing the use of this therapy to treat IBD patients. This project will also determine if the use of a4B7+ Tregs to treat IBD patients is a suitable option to reduce the symptoms of IBD.

column36: Enhancing Evidence-Based Practice for Youth and Emerging Adults with Early Psychosis: Implementation and Evaluation in Diverse Service Settings
column37: In this study, we aim to implement a type of coordinated multidisciplinary care, known as 'NAVIGATE' in Ontario to help youth and emerging adults (YEA) suffering from a first episode of psychosis (FEP). Although Ontario already has early psychosis intervention (EPI) programs, our team's recent work has identified major challenges of delivering coordinated care, particularly those elements of care that enhance recovery. These challenges also exist nationally and internationally. By building on the already existing EPI community of practice through the Early Psychosis Intervention Ontario Network, we will implement NAVIGATE with the help of CAMH's Provincial System Support Program facilitators. The use of tele-videoconferencing through ECHO Mental Health Ontario, and the processes and protocols that ECHO provide us with an opportunity to ensure sustainability. Using Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) data, i.e. health administrative data, we can compare hospitalization and emergency department visit rates of YEA suffering from an FEP in Ontario regions where NAVIGATE is implemented compared to regions where NAVIGATE is not implemented. In addition, we can also evaluate health care costs. Prior to initiating this project, we obtained the input of YEA with an FEP and family members. We will also continue to measure engagement across the study. This work fulfills the innovative clinical trial mandate through its implementation and measurement plan, along with the strategy for patient-oriented research through the involvement of patients, family members, and policy makers as equal partners.

column36: Ontario Healthcare Implementation Laboratory: A Learning Health System Approach that Leverages Data to Improve Quality in Primary Care
column37: When clinicians do not have the supports in place to help them follow best practices, patients may not reliably receive the ideal tests and treatments. As a result, they are less likely to achieve the best possible health outcomes. Providing clinicians with data on how often they follow best practices helps improve healthcare quality. This strategy is known as 'audit and feedback' and it can play an important role in directing the efforts of clinicians to improve in areas where improvement is most needed to make sure that patients have the best possible outcomes. Our team is working with provincial organizations using audit and feedback and additional supports to help primary care providers like family doctors improve patient care and outcomes in two important areas: opioid prescribing and antibiotic prescribing. Our patient partners and other stakeholders have endorsed these areas as high-priority for action. Our innovative trials will test how audit and feedback can help primary care practices improve in these areas. Conducting experiments in each area will help us learn about how to better deliver evidence-based, patient-centred primary care across a range of acute and chronic conditions. Patients will be involved in governance and will be on steering committees at every level of this research. Patients will also help co-design interventions (including educational materials that primary care providers can share with their patients). By providing education and orientation to our patient and researcher partners and evaluating our patient engagement strategy, we will build capacity in patient engagement and patient oriented research in innovative trials and implementation science. Our partnerships with provincial health care organizations will help us achieve large-scale impact during this project and beyond, ensuring the results of this research will benefit large numbers of patients.

column36: CoMFORT (Cow's Milk Fat Obesity pRevention Trial)
column37: Childhood obesity is a looming healthcare crisis with 1 in 3 Canadian children now living with overweight or obesity. The long term consequences of childhood obesity include increased risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and stroke which reduce quality of life and longevity. Cardiovascular disease currently costs Canada's health systems $7 billion annually and is forecasted to triple in the next 30 years. Since 1992 Health Canada has recommended that children older than 2 years consume reduced fat milk (i.e. 1% milk fat) rather than whole milk (3.25% milk fat) to prevent childhood obesity. Unfortunately, childhood obesity has tripled since then and whole cow's milk intake has halved leading many to wonder whether the reduction in whole milk consumption is leading to childhood obesity. New research from our group and others supports that reduced milk fat intake early in life may be promoting rather than preventing childhood obesity. Although several biological mechanisms have been proposed, the leading theory is that children may feel more 'full' after consuming whole milk and less likely to seek calories from unhealthy foods. This innovative clinical trial will compare the effect of primary healthcare recommendation for whole milk (intervention) vs. reduced fat milk (control) in early childhood in optimizing childhood growth development and nutrition at 4-5 years of age. We will use new cohort trial methods leveraging Canada's largest childhood cohort study (TARGet Kids!) to conduct this trial which will minimize cost and maximize feasibility. This trial must be conducted now to ensure that primary healthcare providers are delivering the correct nutritional recommendation and to protect the next generation of Canada's children from the long term consequences of childhood obesity.

column36: De-implementing low value care: a research program of the Choosing Wisely Canada Implementation Research Network
column37: Up to 30% of tests and treatments given to patients are not needed. This can lead to significant inconvenience and harms for these patients without any benefit. It also wastes money for patients and the health system. Choosing Wisely Canada (CWC) is engaging patients and health professionals to fix this problem. CWC has made 280 recommendations about tests and treatments that should be avoided in certain situations. But these are still happening because it is not an easy thing to change health care processes. Implementation science aims to understand the underlying reasons for health care processes and to develop and test potential solutions to improve them. This project links CWC, patient and health system partners in three provinces with leading Canadian implementation scientists to develop and test solutions for two important topics: x-rays/CT/MRI scans that are not needed for patients with low-risk back pain; and pre-operative tests that are not needed for patients having low-risk surgery. In each province, we will do preliminary studies to make sure we fully understand the different reasons for unnecessary care. Then we will develop targeted solutions using insights from behavioural and system science that support both health professionals and patients to make informed decisions about whether these tests are needed. We will test these solutions in experiments. Some health organisations (either family practices for low back pain imaging or hospitals for pre-operative testing) will receive the solution and some will not. We will determine who gets the solution using an approach similar to flipping a coin to ensure that health organisations that receive or do not receive the solution are similar. We are working with the Canadian Institute of Health Information to use the data already collected routinely to measure whether the solution worked. If our solutions work, we will engage our partners to spread and scale them across Canada.

column36: ENCOMPASS: ENhancing COMmunity health through Patient navigation, Advocacy and Social Support
column37: Some patients who have multiple long-term health conditions have significant challenges in accessing needed services despite available primary care and social services resources. Patient navigation programs may help those with complex health conditions improve their care and outcomes and if delivered by community health workers (CHWs) who have close community ties, these programs have the potential to reduce barriers to care and increase access to coordinated, person-centred care. The University of Calgary's ENCOMPASS program aims to improve the care and health outcomes for high-risk patients by linking patients with chronic disease with a CHW to help them navigate the health system, facilitate communication between patients and providers, improve patients' understanding of their conditions and treatment plans, and support patients in their self-management. In Canada, patient navigation programs have not been well studied or broadly implemented in patients with chronic disease, making a comprehensive evaluation of ENCOMPASS important. This program has great potential to improve care for patients with chronic diseases in Alberta's primary care system. A key element of ENCOMPASS is that patients have been involved in all stages from planning, to pilot testing, to implementation. Given the increasing popularity of patient navigation/CHW programs in other Canadian provinces as well as in the United States, the results of the proposed research will have value outside Alberta.

column36: Canadian Adaptive Platform Trial in Intensive Care (CAPTIC) Program
column37: More than 250,000 Canadians are admitted to an ICU each year. While most survive, the mortality rate of 10% remains high, and survivors often experience severe long term disability and a reduced quality of life. Improved ICU care has come largely from using available treatments more effectively, than from the development of new drugs. But the questions are many, and available funding is limited. We will introduce a new model of a clinical trial - the platform trial - to Canada. Platform trials study several different questions at a time and use adaptive techniques to increase the odds that patients in the trial receive the interventions that are performing better. They are potentially more efficient and cost-effective than traditional trials, but they are new and untested. We will assemble groups of key stakeholders - patients, clinicians, researchers, and policy-makers - to study the opportunities and threats of the platform trial model. We will recruit 300 patients to an ongoing international platform trial that is building pandemic research capacity. We will use these experiences to design a Canadian platform to support the research activities of the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group - the oldest and most productive ICU research group in the world. The insights gained, and the research capacity created, will affirm Canadian research leadership in critical care, and lead to better patient outcomes in a learning health care system.

column36: Reducing Diabetic Foot Complications through a Multidisciplinary Chiropodist Based Intervention
column37: Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is a major complication of diabetes and can be a significant physical, social, financial and emotional burden. About 25% of persons with diabetes develop DFUs. If poorly managed, DFUs can lead to amputations, 1 of the 2 most feared complications of diabetes. The risk of DFUs can be reduced with simple preventative measures yet DFUs and DFU relapses have not declined as there is no high-quality data supporting proactive DFU treatment. Chiropodists are experts at managing foot disorders. A small study linked chiropodist care with markedly less leg amputations in people with diabetes and on dialysis. This led us to think that an intensive, structured, chiropodist-led strategy will lower amputation-related hospitalizations in those with diabetes and their need for medical, social and financial resources. In consultation with persons with diabetes, amputees and representatives from health agencies, and diabetes and DFU professional groups, we designed a novel trial to study if chiropodist care will lower amputation-related hospitalizations in those with diabetes undergoing dialysis since this group is deemed to have the greatest need and is one that administrators are most likely to effect change in funding allocation and health care systems delivery. Our study will include 2200 participants from 40 sites in Ontario, Alberta and Manitoba. The 2-year study will record amputation-related hospitalizations, deaths, cost effectiveness and perceived quality of life. Our committee includes persons with diabetes, amputees, chiropodists, a nurse, a family doctor and specialists. We have trial experts, a health care economist and statisticians who will assist in data interpretation, and individuals in the government and professional groups who will provide guidance on rolling out the findings (if positive) into clinical practice. Finally, the trainees will receive hands on experience to enrich their expertise as they carve out their career paths.
