column36: Regulation of gonadotropin action by Slit/Robo signaling in the mammalian ovary
column37: Oocytes develop and mature in the ovary within structures called follicles. Follicles are recruited from a reserve and grow under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) produced by the pituitary gland. Once terminally developed, the follicle ruptures to release the (now mature) oocyte at the moment of ovulation. Ovulation itself is triggered by a second pituitary hormone, luteinizing hormone (LH), which also causes the reorganization of the ovulated follicle into a new glandular tissue termed the corpus luteum, which secretes the large amounts of progesterone necessary for the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy. Whereas we have long known FSH and LH to be major players in ovarian follicle development, how exactly they exert their effects remains incompletely understood. Ourselves and others have shown that a class of secreted signaling molecules called SLITs, along with their receptors called ROBOs, are expressed in the ovary in a pattern suggesting their involvement in follicle development. Our preliminary data indicate that, when follicle cells are treated in vitro with SLIT ligand, gonadotropin signaling and action is suppressed. This proposal will seek to confirm these preliminary results, in part by studying mice that lack Slit1, Slit2, Robo1 and Robo2, which we expect to be hyperfertile due to augmented FSH- and LH-mediated signaling processes. We will also study the molecular mechanisms whereby Slit/Robo and gonadotropin signaling interact. Together, our studies will uncover new information regarding how FSH and LH act, and about the biological roles of Slit/Robo signaling in the ovary. Importantly, this research may also identify new and valuable pharmacologic targets that could be exploited in the clinical context, in fields of application as wide-ranging as the treatment of fertility disorders, contraception, and recovery of fertility following chemotherapy.

column36: Cortical Plasticity Following Deafness
column37: In Canada, hearing loss is the most common sensory disability in adults and deafness is the most common congenital sensory abnormality in children. A 2006 Australian study estimated that costs to that nation's economy from hearing loss amounted to $10.6 billion per year. On a per capita basis, this translates to a Canadian equivalent of almost $18-billion annually. Although we hear with our brains little is known about what occurs to the brain as a consequence of deafness. In this proposal we will be studying what happens inside the brain following the onset of deafness shortly after birth or in adulthood. Specifically, we will be studying the regions of the brain that normally process sounds in hearing individuals. To do this we will examine deafness in an animal model. This approach will permit us to examine the activity of individual neurons, to examine changes in brain circuitry and activity, and to examine how changes in the brain affect perception and behavior. If the part of the brain that normally processes hearing is not receiving sound, then what is it doing? Is it processing visual information? Is it processing information concerning touch? If it is processing sight, then it may very well help explain the increased visual abilities of deaf humans. Changes in the brain such as this are known as "plastic" changes, or simply "plasticity". These changes are also called "compensatory" because they help the subject enhance their ability to use their remaining senses. Therefore, the goal of this study is to examine the natural plasticity of the brain. Knowing how the brain responds to changes in its inputs in this way will help us develop appropriate therapeutic strategies to help increase brain plasticity and help patients to overcome conditions such as deafness and blindness.

column36: A novel form of alternative polyadenylation
column37: Controlling the protein content within the cell is important for normal homeostasis and is often dysregulated in many cancers. Cancer cells often modify the protein content. Obviously, understanding protein content, particularly the regulation of factors that could act as effectors of the cancer phenotype, is important. Traditionally, it is thought that mutations or changes in the DNA code lead to the altered complement of proteins found in cancer cells. We study how changes in the protein complement can occur in the absence of these mutations. We found that a protein called eIF4E alters the protein complement by changing the chemical modifications to the RNA, the intermediary between DNA and protein. We identified novel specific chemical modifications that can modify how well the RNA can be converted into its active protein form. Here, we dissect the biochemical foundation for this novel activity and will study how it becomes dysregulated in cancer.

column36: A Randomized, Parallel-Group, Open Label, Non-Inferiority, Pragmatic Trial Comparing Random AND Targeted Biopsies to Targeted Biopsies Alone for Neoplasia Detection During Screening Colonoscopy in Adult Persons with Colonic Inflammatory Bowel Diseases: A Pilot Study
column37: Persons with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are at increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) and require frequent CRC screening with colonoscopy. Colorectal tumours can be more difficult to visualize in persons with IBD than in persons without IBD. Therefore, IBD experts have long recommended a strategy of taking 30 to 40 random biopsies to help detect these lesions during screening colonoscopy. Oddly, there have never been high quality studies demonstrating the usefulness of this practice. Recent literature suggests that random biopsies have an exceedingly low rate of detecting tumours in persons with IBD and that improved technology and practice have made 80 to 90% of colorectal tumours visible. Since random biopsies pose potential risks, such as lower gastrointestinal bleeding and bowel perforation, and substantially increase procedural time and costs, it is important to determine whether this practice is still merited. We ultimately wish to conduct a large, multi-center randomized controlled trial to evaluate whether the practice of taking random biopsies during colonoscopy can be avoided without increasing the risk of developing CRC faced by IBD patients. However, we first propose a smaller-scale pilot study that will evaluate our ability to recruit patients, the rate at which colon lesions are detected, and adherence to the study protocol by investigators, which will inform the capacity and requirements to conduct a full-scale trial. The pilot study aims to recruit 400 patients at 12 academic IBD centers over one year. If we are able to proceed with the full-scale trial, based on the pilot study findings, it could lead to a major advance in IBD patient care. If avoidance of random biopsies during colonoscopy screening is not found to be harmful to patients in the full trial, it would enable practitioners to abandon this practice, which could substantially reduce the risks, time and costs associated with screening colonoscopy in persons with IBD.

column36: Correlates of Healthy Aging in Geriatric HIV: CHANGE HIV STUDY
column37: The population of persons living with HIV (PLWH) is aging due to effective HIV therapy and new infections occurring in older individuals. Much needs to be learned about what it means to age with HIV. Although organ diseases (like heart and brain) are increased in PLWH, aging is more complex and health evaluations must consider the impact of these conditions on a person's ability to function well. We propose to bring together this new interdisciplinary team and the CHANGE HIV (Correlates of Healthy aging in Geriatric HIV) STUDY. We will invite men and women living with HIV >65 years of age from primary care and hospital HIV clinics in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver to join. At regular clinic visits we will add tests of physical, cognitive, mental, social function and quality of life and collect data on external factors like housing, behaviors and stigma that might influence health. We will analyze the way the factors interact to identify the ones that contribute most to healthy aging well if these differ by sex or gender. From the data, we will calculate a healthy aging score that can inform care and research by assessing a person's overall health status and track changes with time or therapy. The knowledge gained will inform interventions and strategies to improve healthy aging and help us know which ones are the most important, feasible and acceptable to those aging with HIV. Our data can be used to advocate for changes to health and social policies and appropriate allocation of resources for services for aging PLWH. A program strength is to train and stimulate new academic and community investigators building future research capacity in HIV and aging. Community members will be meaningfully involved in all stages ensures our research is feasible, ethical and relevant and supports the development of knowledge that is useful to key. Our learning's will advance understanding of aging in PLWH and ultimately lead to improved clinical and community practice and policy.

column36: Healthy Living for HIV-exposed Uninfected Children - cognitive, behavioural, neuroimaging and animal studies to assess the impact of in utero exposure to HIV and antiretrovirals.
column37: The use of HIV medications in pregnancy has enabled a radical reduction in the rate of vertical HIV transmission. As a consequence, there is now a large and growing number of HIV-exposed uninfected children (HEU)-children born to women living with HIV that are not HIV infected. While most HEU children are in good health, some studies suggest that these children may experience developmental delays compared to their peers, including learning difficulties, issues with their memory, and behavioural problems. We know that the environment the child is exposed to during pregnancy (the in utero environment) can influence their long-term health. However, we don't know how HIV and HIV medications change the in utero environment and whether these changes affect the long-term health of HEU children. Our team will investigate how exposure to HIV and various HIV medications during pregnancy affects brain development and mental health in HEU children. We will perform cognitive and behavioural tests and brain imaging studies in a cohort of HEU and HIV unexposed children of similar age and background. column37: Scientists have made extraordinary advances in understanding and treating HIV infection over the past 20 years. Even with antiretroviral therapy, HIV-1 is still able to infect and damage the nervous system. This continues to be a major problem for people who are living with HIV/AIDS. We have also discovered new disease processes and used that knowledge to develop and test new approaches to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. For example, we uncovered new biological markers for people who have cognitive problems and pain from NeuroHIV. We found new possible treatments for these cognitive problems and pain, and we are testing those treatments in clinical trials. We have also identified specific sex and gender factors that make some people with NeuroHIV more vulnerable to thinking problems and pain from damaged nerves. NeuroHIV causes other problems that need research. These problems are linked to sex and gender diversity, and to how aging affects people with NeuroHIV. Our team of researchers from different areas of science and health will map basic pathways in the biology of NeuroHIV. Discovering these pathways can help us to analyze symptoms and risk factors for NeuroHIV. Understanding the pathways will also lead to new ways to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. column37: Older people living with HIV worry about their memory, and with good reason. A third or more have problems with thinking or concentration, despite good control of their HIV infection. Rates of depression, anxiety and poor motivation are also high. Separately or together, these brain health problems affect function and quality of life. Our team has developed new ways to assess these problems in the clinic, identified the factors that relate to poor brain health in a large on-going cohort study, and provided preliminary information about whether these symptoms can be treated. We will extend the existing cohort study to provide crucial information about whether brain health worsens over longer follow-up. We will add a second wave of participants, including more women, to help us provide personalized brain health recommendations suited to a wide range of people. We will implement the assessment tools that we have developed in our current study as easy-to-use apps. We will work closely with the HIV clinicians and community partners on our team to ensure these are user-friendly and clinic-ready. We will test an innovative, two-phase intervention to help people with brain health challenges pursue health goals tailored to their own priorities and risks, to improve their memory, mood and quality of life. This study will provide the knowledge and tools that people living with HIV need to take charge of their brain health now.

column37: The debilitating and lethal consequences of severe adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are a striking failure of modern medicine. The consequences for patients who experience severe ADRs are catastrophic. In Canada, there are an estimated 200,000 severe ADRs, claiming 10,000-22,000 lives, and costing $14-18 billion each year. To tackle this complex problem requires a multi-faceted collaborative linking of scientists, clinicians and regulators sharing complementary expertise in an environment that promotes teamwork. The Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) Active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare (SEARCH) initiative was first funded in 2011, with the overarching goal of conducting active surveillance to identify important drug risks, reduce the occurrence of severe ADRs and improve drug safety in Canadians. In close collaboration with the Drug Safety and Effectiveness (DSEN) Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team (PREVENT) the work of SEARCH is strengthened through the discovery of pharmacogenomics biomarkers - that is understanding the genetic variation between patients that affects their individual drug response. This inter-individual variation acts as key predictors of ADRs for many drugs in clinical use today. Our team will build on its broad experience in active surveillance methods, pharmacogenomics expertise and its established network of ADR surveillance clinicians in Canadian health centres. These surveillance clinicians are located at 13 pediatric academic health centers and 13 adult academic health centers and their role is to identify and report ADRs, and collect DNA and the detailed clinical information that is needed to evaluate potential drug risks. This will allow SEARCH & PREVENT to continue active surveillance in areas of importance to the CIHR Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network, Health Canada and other pertinent stakeholders.

column36: Role of type I interferon in B cell dysfunction associated with chronic viral infection
column37: Persistent viral infections such as those caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), the hepatitis C virus (HCV) or the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are a major global health problem. It is estimated that more than 500 million people in the world are infected with at least one of these viruses. Currently, only HBV infection can be prevented through vaccination while the development of vaccines against HCV or HIV is still a long-term goal. Although a number of highly effective antiviral drugs were recently developed against all three viruses, these are not able to cure HIV infection or have variable success rates against HBV and HCV infections. In Canada, HCV infection constitutes the most frequent indication for liver transplantation and together with HBV, these pathologies account for 1000 deaths annually while the number of people living with HIV continues to rise. There is therefore a great need for further research aimed at better understanding the fundamental mechanisms employed by these chronic viruses to escape the host immune response and establish persistence. One common feature between these three infections is the appearance of dysfunctions in the B cell response with important pathological consequences. The main objectives of this research program are therefore to better understand the mechanisms that contribute to these dysfunctions and to develop clinical interventions to restore normal B cell responses during chronic viral infections. This knowledge will prove very useful for the rational design of vaccines or improved antiviral drugs.

column36: Rhinovirus induced modulation of epithelial phenotype in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic airway disease that affects 300 million people worldwide. Although all children get multiple infections with human rhinovirus (HRV - the "common cold virus") in early life, only a subset get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, and are far more likely to develop asthma by age 6. It is not clear why only some children get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, but the interaction of HRV and development of allergies may play a role. Human airway epithelial cells (HAE) are the main site of HRV infection and it is thought that HRV affects asthma by changing HAE biology. The characteristic features (phenotype) of HAE are altered in asthma, and these altered HAE interact with nearby structural and immune cells to help cause asthma. Despite the central role of HAE in regulating airway diseases, the effects of HRV infection on HAE phenotype have not been well characterized. We have found that HRV infection of HAE from normal people causes transient changes in cell biology. In this proposal, we will fully characterize the effects of HRV on epithelial phenotype and will define the mechanisms by which HRV causes these changes. We will determine if repeated infections with HRV cause greater effects in HAE than a single infection. In addition, we will test the idea that HRV infections (single or repeated) in the setting of an "allergic" environment produce more profound alterations in HAE that mimic the phenotype seen in asthma. We will compare HAE from asthmatic children to those from normal children to see if they have greater responses to HRV. Finally, we will experimentally infect normal and asthmatic volunteers with HRV to test the idea that HAE in asthmatic patients show greater response to HRV in vivo. By understanding how HRV infections alter epithelial responses, alone and in an allergic setting, we may be able to develop ways to prevent or reduce the effects of HRV in asthma in order to improve the well-being of patients with asthma.

column36: The functions of mammalian TRAPP complexes and their role in disease
column37: The Transport Protein Particle (TRAPP) complexes were first discovered in yeast. Subsequent work identified related, conserved complexes in humans. These complexes function in moving proteins between various intracellular compartments within a cell. Although they share a core of common proteins, there are unique proteins that are associated with the core to form the various complexes (three complexes in yeast, two in higher eukaryotes). While the functions of the complexes in yeast are better understood, the functions of the mammalian complexes are less clear. In addition, several of the subunits that associate with the complex in humans have been shown to have functions independent of the complex. Furthermore, recent work has led to the identification of individuals that have mutations in TRAPP proteins. Curiously, these individuals all have different phenotypes depending on which TRAPP protein is mutated. Thus, understanding the functions of the mammalian TRAPP proteins and their role in disease is a necessary next step in our understanding of these complexes. This present application seeks to understand the functions of two specific subunits called C11 and C2L. In order to facilitate this work, we are developing a simplified in vitro assay that reconstitutes transport in the secretory pathway. We will use wild type TRAPP complexes as well as complexes harboring mutations in the aforementioned proteins to assess their ability to reconstitute membrane traffic in this pathway. The results of these studies will provide insight into specific human disorders that are linked to TRAPP mutations and will allow clinicians to more quickly assess new disorders that may be linked to these complexes.

column37: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin in biphasic manner, an initial peak phase (~15 min) followed by a sustained phase (several hours), to ensure continuous assimilation of circulating nutrients into tissues. In type-2 diabetes, both phases are perturbed resulting in deficient insulin release causing hyperglycemia. Half of initial peak phase is attributed to secretory granules (SGs) predocked on calcium channels (Cav1.2/1.3) on the plasma membrane where calcium influx induces SG fusion to release insulin. Newcomer SGs (NSG) are a newly discovered SG population that account for the entire sustained phase and half of first-phase secretion. We discovered the SNARE (syntaxin-3, VAMP8) and associated proteins responsible for NSG fusion; but unlike predocked SGs, little else is known about the NSG secretory machinery. Our first hypothesis (Aim 1) is that NSGs specifically land on and undergo fusion at a new set of calcium channels (Cav2.1/2.3) which bind syntaxin-3. An undefined reserve pool must exist to continually replenish NSGs after depletion from stimulated release. We found potassium channel (Kv2.1) clusters on plasma membrane that bind NSG-syntaxin-3. Our second hypothesis (Aim 2) is that syntaxin-3/Kv2.1 clusters form complexes that serve as an accessible reserve pool for NSGs to park prior to their relocation to adjacent calcium channels. This provides a unique architecture that couples the reserve pool (Kv2.1 clusters) of SGs to SG release sites (Cav), a process that has long eluded previous investigation. This work has broad application to many endocrine cells that exhibit sustained secretion required to meet varying metabolic needs. Insights into these novel fundamental steps of secretion are a basis for development of treatment strategies to improve secretion. As proof, we will express (with virus) Cav and Kv2.1 into pancreatic islets of diabetic humans (in vitro) and rats (in vivo) to improve the deficient insulin secretion and restore glucose homeostasis.

One of the most prevalent examples of chronic inflammation is obesity, which affects over 1/3 of adults in Canada/USA. The objective of this study is to provide a translational framework for understanding how overweight/obesity affects breast cancer metastasis, with the goal of identifying blood-based prognostic markers and new therapies. This could improve treatment methods for a large proportion of breast cancer patients, and contribute to a broader understanding of the relationship between the immune system and cancer. We hypothesize that breast cancer progresses differently in obese patients compared to lean patients, and therefore, obese patients will require different treatment considerations.

column36: The GLP-1 Receptor & Myocardial Glucose Oxidation
column37: Diabetes, which can be described as high blood sugar due to the body not being able to produce insulin, or a failure of insulin to lower blood sugar, is an enormous worldwide health issue. Currently, there are over 3 million Canadians living with diabetes, and treating these Canadians costs our healthcare system over 10 billion dollars annually. Despite our current medicines being very effective at controlling blood sugar levels in our diabetic patients, they do not reduce their increased risk of heart disease. However, recent evidence indicates that liraglutide, a drug that treats diabetes by mimicking the actions of a gut hormone known as glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), decreases risk for death by heart disease in diabetic patients. The main goal of our research is to discover how the drug liraglutide reduces risk for death by heart disease in patients with diabetes. We hypothesize that liraglutide improves heart health in diabetic patients by boosting the heart's ability to burn sugar for energy. We have recently generated a unique genetically modified mouse strain in our lab, in which the ability of the heart to burn sugar for energy has been eliminated. We will carry out our plan by placing normal mice and these unique mice on a fat-enriched diet that causes diabetes. column37: More than 3 million people were treated for skin cancers in North America in 2015. Approximately 40% of all skin-cancer cases occur on a person's nose. When cancer is diagnosed on the face, and in particular on the nose, treatment options often lead to loss of function and significant disfigurement. We have demonstrated the know-how to make nose cartilage from a small biopsy of cartilage taken from the nose. However, the quality of the made-cartilage varies from patient to patient. In this proposal, we plan to improve the quality of nose cartilage we make for the future surgical treatment of skin cancer patients.

column36: A randomized controlled trial of symptom screening by children with cancer and feedback to providers
column37: Most children with cancer survive because they are given intensive treatments. Unfortunately, these treatments are associated with distressing symptoms. Poor symptom control occurs because children do not have a way to report and track their symptoms, healthcare providers are not aware of these symptoms, and guidelines for symptom management are not easy to access. To address these gaps, we developed the Symptom Screening in Pediatrics Tool (SSPedi) specifically for children receiving cancer treatments. We also created evidence-based guidelines to help providers know how to manage symptoms. To bring identification and management of symptoms together, we created a web-based application called Supportive care Prioritization, Assessment and Recommendations for Kids (SPARK). SPARK consists of two components: (1) Symptom screening component centered on SSPedi and (2) Supportive care guideline component. The next step is to establish that these tools improve the lives of children with cancer. We will conduct a randomized controlled trial which evaluates the effectiveness of daily symptom screening by children seen in hospital daily for 5 days and feedback of symptom reports to healthcare providers with links to guidelines for symptom management. Participants in the control arm will receive the standard of care in which symptom screening with feedback is not performed. We will include English-speaking children and adolescents 8-18 years of age expected to be in hospital daily for 5 days. The primary endpoint will be the day 5 total SSPedi score which ranges from 0 to 60 (higher means more bothersome symptoms). We plan to enroll 345 children across 7 Canadian institutions over 4 years. This research will enable children to report symptoms and will help providers know how to manage symptoms using the best available evidence. Ultimately, SPARK implementation will lead to better symptom control and quality of life for children receiving cancer treatments.

column36: Characterization of quality control pathways that target cytosolic misfolded proteins with missense mutations for proteasome degradation
column37: Gene mutations that cause diseases often do so by causing misfolding and degradation of the mutant proteins. Protein misfolding occurs when a protein does not attain its so-called native structure, which is reached when the protein is properly folded to perform its function in the cell. Our goal is to better understand how mutant proteins that misfold are recognized by elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system. The ubiquitin proteasome system consists of groups of enzymes that first mark proteins targeted for degradation by attaching to them a small protein tag called ubiquitin. These ubiquitin-tagged proteins are then recognized by the proteasome, which eliminates them from the cell. Our main hypothesis is there are several degradation paths for different groups of proteins that misfold due to mutations. To test this idea, we will analyze using different cell-based assays a large panel of mutations that have been associated to genetic disorders or diseases. More specifically, we will focus on missense mutations that induce the change of single amino acids. First, we will identify which mutated cytosolic proteins are degraded by the ubiquitin proteasome system from a large panel of known disease-associated mutations. We will then determine which known elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system target these misfolded mutant proteins. A major question is how E3 enzymes that attach ubiquitin recognize misfolded proteins. To address this question, we will employ the identified mutant proteins as model substrates to better identify which regions or domains on E3 enzymes recognize the misfolded proteins. Finally, we will set up a screen to identify novel genes involved in targeting misfolded proteins for degradation. By better understanding how misfolded proteins are triaged within the cell, we will gain fundamental knowledge of disease mechanisms, leading to potential novel therapeutic approaches.

column37: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity" (World Health Organization, 1948). Most importantly the project will include a poverty reduction intervention that connects participants with short-term work and volunteer opportunities. The work and volunteer opportunities' will be made possible with the support of local business owners and networks that support the study's poverty reduction and community building elements. column36: The "Weaving Our Wisdoms" Study: Using a Land-Based Approach to Optimize Whole-istic Health among Indigenous People Living with HIV
column37: Lamouche (2010) notes that "break with the land is the single most important factor in health problems among Indigenous peoples". This study, designed by Indigenous People living with HIV, focuses on the potential for land-based approaches to promote wellness. During this phase, we will investigate research questions about the impact of land-based approaches, the role of "HIV olders" in building the capacity of others, and about land-based research methods. In the final phase, we will "weave our wisdoms". That is, we will build on existing and new relationships with First Nations, Metis and Inuit communities across the country to explore land-based approaches to wellness. This study will be housed at the Canadian Aboriginal AIDS Network, which has a long track record of successfully implementing research that is meaningful to Indigenous People living with HIV. The study is guided by four complementary approaches to research: (1) community-based research, (2) Indigenous knowledge, (3) decolonizing methods, and (4) two-eyed seeing. column37: Over the past two decades, with the advent of modern HIV treatment and a robust provincial HIV strategy across British Columbia (BC), people living with HIV (PLHIV) are now living longer, healthier lives. Home and community care (HCC) services, such as in-home nursing services, community care, and case management, that are responsive to the unique needs of older PLHIV have the potential to appropriately address the evolving landscape of age-related health concerns while simultaneously ensuring a high standard of care. We also aim to identify potential strategies to overcome barriers to accessing HCC services. To employ this knowledge, we will work alongside community partners and healthcare stakeholders to develop interventions that will improve health outcomes and support older PLHIV.

column37: In Canada, as in other high resource countries, preterm birth (<37 weeks gestation) is the most important cause of disability. column36: Multi-centre Temporal Ultrasound Image Analysis for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common cancer diagnosed in Canadian men, with about 25,000 new cases per year. The gold standard for PCa diagnosis and prognosis is ultrasound (US)-guided needle biopsy with pathologic grading. The biopsy procedure is not patient specific; rather, it involves taking "blind" biopsy cores, leading to frequent re-biopsy or over diagnosis of insignificant cancer. There is an acute need for patient-specific targeting techniques that have higher chance of detecting early aggressive PCa. Aggressive PCa must be diagnosed early and accurately to appropriately treat patients at higher risk of morbidity and mortality. Meanwhile, it is critical to balance against over-treatment of indolent PCa, of which is more appropriately managed using an active surveillance approach. The best biopsy technique today is to localize PCa with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and use its fusion with US to improve the detection rate of aggressive PCa. However, this method alone is not able to accurately differentiate indolent PCa and cannot reliably detect small lesions of aggressive PCa. In this project, we propose a turnkey technology, where subtle variations of backscattered US signals from a tissue location over a short time span, i.e., temporal enhanced US, are used to detect physical properties of the underlying tissue using a machine-learning framework. column36: Role of autophagy dysregulation in pancreatitis caused by alcohol and glucagon-like peptide
column37: Acute pancreatitis (AP) causes high morbidity and mortality, and at considerable financial costs to health care in Canada. The most common cause of AP is alcohol, affecting 10% of alcoholics. There is still no effective specific treatment directed at the pathogenesis of alcoholic AP in part because the postulated disease mechanisms could not be directly tested on human pancreatic tissue. Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-based therapies, which potentiate glucose-mediated insulin secretion, is the new panacea for treating diabetes; now a multi-billion dollar pharmaceutical market. However, GLP-1 drug treatments exhibited six-fold increase in AP, the basis is totally unknown. Our overarching hypothesis is that alcohol and GLP-1 drugs can cause perturbations in autophagy, the cellular 'self-eating' process that normally gets rid of cellular garbage. Autophagy involves a series of vesicle formations that involve distinct SNARE proteins (Aim 1), which when pathologically activated (alcohol - Aim 2, GLP-1 - Aim 3), causes inadvertent protease activation (instead of physiologic degradation) which can damage and destroy acinar cells (i.e. AP). To mechanistically address these conditions in a clinically-relevant manner, we've developed the method of preparing fresh human pancreatic slices to assess autophagy processes and how their perturbations contribute to acinar cell injury. We will assess whether manipulation of autophagy SNAREs expression in rat pancreas can modify alcohol- and GLP-1-mediated pancreatic injury. This work may identify novel treatments for AP and impact current diabetes management in patients taking GLP-1 drugs.

column36: Equity in Mental Health Care for Children and Youth
column37: Mental health problems and suicide are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality for children and youth. Yet access to mental health care for children is an ongoing challenge. The principle of equity in access to healthcare is reflected in the Canada Health Act. However, equity in access to MH care is ill-defined and has rarely been examined in relation to child/youth mental health services (CYMHS). The current study will conduct a systematic review of how equity has been evaluated with respect to MH care for children and youth. Equity can be defined as equal access to services. Within Ontario and across Canada, specialized MH and psychiatric services for children and youth are delivered mainly through publicly-funded agencies and psychiatrists. Private providers (psychologists and social workers) also play a role; we have little information on the role that private providers play in the systems that care for this population. The present study will also examine the distribution of publicly-funded agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers, and the extent to which sociodemographic factors (e.g., family income) are related to the distribution of child and youth MH services. If the distribution of agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers varies by regions, this would likely result in inequity in access to care for individuals in regions with fewer agencies/providers. Second, if the distribution of agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers varies by region as a function of sociodemographic factors, it would also reflect inequities in access to care. Identification of inequity is the first step to addressing those inequities and ultimately improving the systems in place to care for children and youth with mental health problems.

column37: Cryptococcus neoformans is an environmental fungus found throughout the world that causes serious disease of the lungs and brain in over one million humans each year. To identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms that control the development of severe cryptococcal disease, we use a mouse model of infection that closely resembles the human disease. We will apply cutting edge technology to analyze the function of lung cells, tissues, and organs and determine how the underlying cellular pathways and genes influence immunity. The knowledge we derive through this project will be translated into improved prevention and clinical management of serious human fungal infections.

column36: Understanding mutagenic replication-transcription conflicts in cancer-initiation
column37: Mutations in DNA are a driving force in cancer initiation, progression and therapy resistance. Some mutations arise from normal functions involving DNA. These functions include copying DNA during cell division, and transcribing DNA into RNA messages that control the production of proteins in the cell. These two independent processes, termed DNA replication and transcription, must occur at the same time on the same DNA, and therefore they can interfere with one another. Our hope is to find new ways to selectively eliminate breast cancer cells experiencing high levels of replication-transcription collisions.

column36: Establishing the importance of diet and insulin resistance in modulating immune function in obesity
column37: Obesity is associated with several risk factors (for example, high blood sugar, poor insulin response and inflammation) that increase the risk of developing cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes (T2DM). Obesity is also associated with abnormalities in the immune system and an increased risk of infection. Specific components of the diet such as high dietary intake of fat and sugar influence not only the development of obesity but also the immune system. Therefore, it is still unclear if the immune dysfunction associated with obesity in human are attributable to 1- the excess of body fat per se and/or 2- the metabolic complications also often associated with obesity such as elevated blood glucose and/or 3- the overall poor diet quality of an individual. We are proposing a study where we will characterize, in controlled feeding conditions, the functionality of the immune system by investigating a panel of makers of the immune system (inflammation in the blood and the response of immune cells). At the end of a 4-week feeding period where participants will all consume the same standardized diet, we will compare the immune system of three groups of adults with obesity: a. obesity with normal blood glucose concentrations; b. obesity with marginally elevated blood glucose concentrations; and c. obesity with T2DM. All groups will be matched for age, sex and body mass index, and compared to a group of healthy normal weight subjects. By comparing these four groups, we will be able to gain an understanding of the immune complications associated with obesity alone (e.g. excess of body fat per se) and the association of blood sugar and diet in modulating these immune complications. This is essential to subsequently identify dietary interventions to counteract the immune dysfunctions associated with obesity.

column36: Mechanisms of REM sleep behaviour disorder
column37: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) affects 2-6% of the elderly population and is characterized by excessive movement during REM sleep. These movements are typically so violent that they result in patient injuries, which often require medical attention. However, the most alarming aspect of RBD is that 80-90% of patients eventually develop a brain disease like Parkinson's disease or dementia after being diagnosed with RBD. During healthy REM sleep, most of the body's muscles are paralyzed. However, in RBD muscle paralysis is lost, which causes RBD patients to actively move during REM sleep. Because RBD is tightly associated with brain degeneration and this degeneration begins in brain regions that cause REM sleep paralysis, it is hypothesized that RBD is caused by degeneration of the brain regions that control REM sleep paralysis. However, it still remains unclear which cells in the brainstem control REM sleep paralysis and if damage to these cell circuits underlies RBD. This medical research will be of importance to Canadians because it identifies the brain mechanisms that cause healthy REM sleep and it determines if degeneration of these regions causes RBD.

column37: Protein degradation constitutes a major cellular function that is responsible for maintenance of the normal cellular physiology by breaking down proteins. The regulation of protein stability by this pathway is critical in the molecular basis of carcinogenesis, as it is involved in the regulation of cell growth and preventing abnormal accumulation of proteins. Additionally, ubiquitin modification of target proteins signals many cellular processes other than proteolysis that are also important for the development of cancer. Deregulation of ubiquitin ligases, which are proteins involved in many biological processes including protein degradation, results in uncontrolled proliferation, genomic instability and cancer. Attempts to develop general protein degradation inhibitors for cancer therapy have been questioned because it is highly toxic, and could results in long-term effects from the accumulation of misfolded proteins that is the hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases. Thus, there is great interests in identifying specific proteins involved in this process that could be targeted instead. We identified UBBP4, a gene encoding novel ubiquitins that could be involved in such specific ubiquitination of proteins. The main goal of studying ubiquitin and ubiquitin ligases is to develop drugs that specifically target these enzymes. Thus, it is crucial to identify the substrates of these ubiquitin ligases and understand their cellular functions. We will be using different innovative approaches to identify the proteins modified by UBBP4, as well as functional role for this new modification. The results obtained from the experiments proposed in this application will allow us to better understand the molecular mechanisms regulated by ubiquitin.

column36: Integrated phylogenetic, molecular and functional analyses of the within-host latent HIV reservoir
column37: Thanks to the advent of combination antiretroviral therapies, HIV infection is now considered a chronically manageable condition. These drugs however do not completely eliminate HIV from the body; as such, an HIV cure is actively being pursued. HIV is able to persist in the body because the virus establishes "latent HIV reservoirs", long-lived cells that harbor a dormant copy of the HIV genome within them. HIV can persist for decades within these cells, but the virus may reactivate at any time to produce infectious particles. It is for this reason that HIV therapy needs to be maintained for life. Establishment of latent HIV reservoirs is a continuous process that begins shortly after infection. Moreover, HIV is continually evolving within a given host. Thus, by the time an individual reaches chronic infection, their latent HIV reservoir is expected to comprise a genetically diverse pool of viral sequences that constitute a "fossil record" of HIV evolution in that individual. Importantly, latently-infected cells are likely to differ in key respects including their ability to reactivate to produce infectious HIV particles and their susceptibility to recognition by the immune system. Methods to study HIV reservoir diversity and to identify key characteristics that associate with reservoir reactivation would greatly aid efforts towards an HIV cure. Our interdisciplinary team, comprising molecular biology, bioinformatics, and clinical experts, has developed an innovative genetics-based method for determining when a given HIV sequence "went dormant" within a host. We now seek to apply our method to address foundational gaps in our understanding of HIV persistence. We believe that our integrated approach will provide a versatile and potentially transformative addition to the growing armamentarium of tools in HIV cure research, towards the ultimate goal of developing strategies for HIV reservoir elimination.

column36: Unravelling the contribution to the hypoxic ventilatory response of purinergic and glial signalling in the preBotzinger Complex
column37: The mammalian brain depends on a constant supply of oxygen to meet its energy needs. If this supply fails for even a few minutes permanent brain damage or death can result. A host of adaptive responses have evolved to protect brain oxygen. Prominent among these is the biphasic hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) in which a fall in blood oxygen (hypoxia) supplying the brain triggers an initial increase in breathing. If this increase does not restore oxygen levels, breathing falls in what is called the secondary hypoxic respiratory depression. Release of the excitatory neurochemical ATP in breathing centers of the brain helps maintain the increased breathing. However, this ATP is degraded to adenosine; brain hypoxia also causes widespread release of adenosine. Adenosine causes widespread depression of neuronal activity. This depression is highly adaptive in most brain regions because it reduces metabolic demand and hypoxic brain injury. However, depression of breathing is highly maladaptive because it is only through increases in breathing that oxygen levels can be restored. The net result is that the initial hypoxia-induced increase in breathing is followed by a secondary depression that is potentially fatal in premature infants who suffer from apnea of prematurity; it is also problematic in adults with sleep-disordered breathing where repeated, cyclic falls in oxygen exacerbate cardiovascular disease. Thus, there is great clinical interest in understanding the mechanisms underlying the HVR. The interaction between ATP excitation and adenosine inhibition of breathing is emerging as key in determining the magnitude of the hypoxic depression. The aim of this proposal is to use rodent models to determine the factors that control the balance between the excitatory actions of ATP and inhibitory actions of adenosine during hypoxia and develop strategies to shift the balance in favor of excitation to counteract the life-threatening hypoxic respiratory depression.

column36: Role of APOBEC3 deoxycytidine deaminases in somatic mutagenesis
column37: Cancers are caused by mutations and genetic alterations. Conventional origins of mutations from chemicals in the environment or inherited mutations are known, but we have just begun to understand that some mutations that contribute to cancer originate from within our own cells. There are enzymes that exist in our cells that can alter the DNA sequence. Usually these enzymes act for our benefit and use their activity to alter the DNA sequence of viruses to make the viral DNA nonfunctional. However, sometimes when the levels of these enzymes are not kept in check, they can become too high and they can alter the DNA sequence of the human cell. If these mutations occur in genes that contribute to cellular replication, they can induce the formation or propagate maintenance of a cancer cell. This research is focused on the internal origins of these mutations caused by a specific family of enzymes, called the APOBEC3 enzymes. If we can identify how their activity becomes unregulated we can design inhibitors to limit their function to slow cancer progression or use their unregulated activity as an early risk factor for cancer development.

column36: Genetic instability of the haploid male germ cells
column37: Genetic diversity is provided by de novo transmittable mutations and it is now known that most new mutations are male- driven. During the formation of spermatozoa, the final steps involves a major change in the way DNA is packaged and we demonstrated that this is accompanied by the formation of transient DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in spermatids of both human and mouse pointing to an evolutionary-conserved mechanism. These DSBs arise in haploid cells where there is a single set of chromosome. The repair process cannot therefore proceed using the homologous chromosome as template as in normal somatic cells and must rather rely on a end-joining process. These end-joining repair processes are less reliable and known to induce DNA deletions and insertions. Our hypothesis is that mutations can therefore be induced when the DSBs are repaired in the subsequent steps of the spermatid's differentiation process. Our goal is therefore to confirm whether this process is indeed genetically unstable and if specific regions are involved in the ethiology of genetic diseases since our first screen suggest that neurodevelopmental genes are targeted with high significance. DSBs are also observed during yeast gamete formation emphasizing the conserved nature of this transition and providing a powerful genetic tool to decipher the DSBs mechanism. These investigations may confirm the discovery of a novel mechanism contributing to genetic diversity, evolution and possibly to neurodevelopment disorders such as autism.

column36: Amylin Receptor: A potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease and diabetes mellitus, two of the most serious public health concerns of our times share many commonalities. In Alzheimer's disease, abnormal deposition of a protein in the brain referred to as amyloid is linked to destruction and death of brain cells involved in learning and memory. In a similar manner, the presence of another protein, human amylin, discovered in the pancreas of diabetic patients, renders insulin-producing cells dysfunctional. Work from our laboratory has shown that both amyloid and amylin exert their damaging effects on cells through the same receptor or "keyhole". We have therefore been working with compounds, which block the amylin receptor/keyhole in the brain, and thus can protect brain cells from toxic effects of amyloid. More recently, we have used such amylin receptor blocking drugs to improve the memory and learning deficits in mice, which are genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's disease. In this project, we plan to #1) genetically reduce the amylin receptor (keyhole) in Alzheimer mice thus preventing the amyloid from damaging brain cells, and in the process delay or prevent the development of Alzheimer-like symptoms, #2) develop compounds that can easily penetrate the brains of Alzheimer's mice, block the amylin receptor/keyhole and thus alleviate the memory problems. At present there is no treatment for AD other than for its symptoms. Studies such as those contained in this proposal may identify newer therapies based on protecting nerve cells from the deleterious effects of amyloid-beta in the brains of AD patients and thus slowing or preventing the disease altogether.

column36: Mechanistic studies of cell-free DNA and histones in sepsis: At the interface of innate immunity, coagulation, and inflammation
column37: Sepsis (ie. blood poisoning) is triggered by harmful microorganisms or their toxins in the blood or tissues. These harmful agents can cause a vicious cycle of blood clot formation and inflammation, which may lead to multiple organ failure and death even after the microorganisms have been cleared with antibiotics. In Canada, there are approximately 90,000 patients with sepsis each year. Of these, 30% to 50% of these patients will die. Many anti-sepsis drugs have been tested in humans, but all of these clinical studies have failed. This suggests that some fundamental knowledge is lacking in our current understanding of why sepsis kills patients. In recent years, neutrophils (a type of white blood cells) have been shown to release web-like structures (called NETs) to capture and kill microorganisms. NETs consist of DNA, histones, and neutrophils enzymes. However, NETs can also cause collateral damage to the body. We have previously shown that the DNA and histone components of NETs can trigger blood clotting and prevent blood breakdown. We have also shown that high levels of DNA in the blood of septic patients is a strong predictor of death. In a mouse model of sepsis, injection of DNAse (an enzyme that breaks down DNA) results in improved organ function and improved survival rates. In the current proposal, we plan to further study how DNA and histones triggers blood clots and inflammation in sepsis. We will perform studies of blood cells and blood molecules in test tubes. By comparing blood samples from septic and non-septic ICU patients, we can identify the precise biological pathways that lead to high levels of DNA in septic patients. We will also perform studies in a mouse model of sepsis to see if removal of DNA and/or histones from the blood can improve survival in septic mice. Our research thus has the potential to identify new anti-sepsis strategies that will improve the lives of septic patients.

column36: Understanding the Impact of Legal Cannabis Access on Health: A Large, Prospective Cohort Study of Canadians Obtaining Medical Cannabis Authorization
column37: Although legal access to medical cannabis has been available in Canada for many years, our society has yet to fully understand the important health impacts surrounding the use of medical cannabis or recreational users. However, the current availability of medical cannabis in Canada means that researchers have access to a large number of individuals who are cannabis users. This is an important group of people as understanding their health outcomes can help identify future health concerns and guide the implementation of policies, programs, practices, and/or resource distribution that would be needed to address potential health arising amongst non-medical cannabis users. The urgency of obtaining this information is emphasized by the proposal to legalize cannabis in Canada and the subsequent projected increase in cannabis users to as high as 7 million by 2021. Thus, without understanding the risks or benefits of cannabis consumption for such a large number of Canadians, we will not know the range of potential health outcomes of these individuals until too late. As a result, researchers must initiate immediate strategies to understand the benefits and risks associated with cannabis use in a real world context. To assist with this, our team of experts will work with one of the largest known databases of patients seeking cannabis as a medical therapy in order to understand the benefits and the risks associated with their cannabis use. We will use this information to determine how medical cannabis influences other health related factors such as use of other medications, hospitalizations, doctor appointments, accident claims, etc. By studying the real-world health outcomes of our group of patients using medical cannabis, we will be able to better understand the potential long-term health impacts of medical cannabis consumption. This information has the potential to have a substantial impact on the overall health of Canadians using cannabis.

column36: Overcoming drug resistance in gonorrhea through metabolic network analysis
column37: The human-specific pathogen, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ngo) is responsible for the sexually transmitted infection, gonorrhea. There are over 100 million new cases of this infection in the world each year, and it causes significant morbidity in both genders, often with serious complications such as infertility. Untreated infections in women can result in scarring of the reproductive tract that leads to chronic pelvic pain and dangerous ectopic pregnancies. Critically, Ngo has recently attained 'superbug' status because it has acquired resistance to all clinically relevant antibiotics, making the threat of untreatable gonorrhea a reality. This has led to a global urgency to develop new antibiotics and other intervention strategies. Our aim is to identify Ngo enzymes involved in producing the molecules the pathogen requires to persist and survive in reproductive tract. Through sophisticated computer modeling we will construct detailed models on Ngo metabolism to systematically interrogate the impact of targeting enzymes for drug inhibition. Comparisons between different Ngo strains will reveal which enzymes are the most effective to target to minimize the emergence of resistance. Where we observe inhibition prevents Ngo growth, we will attempt to validate the essential role of the enzyme using an established animal model developed in the Gray- Owen lab. Our ultimate goal is to deliver the next generation of Ngo-specific therapeutics to fight its global threat.

column36: Nuclear-targeted X-ray activated photodynamic therapy of pancreatic cancer
column37: Ineligibility for surgery and the failure of conventional treatments to control primary pancreatic cancer, PanCa, contribute to its high fatality rate and short survival time. We propose a novel, minimally-invasive modality, NL-XPDT, to destroy primary and local-regional spread of PanCa that will be applicable also to other tumors. This will combine the advantages of photodynamic therapy (PDT), that uses light-activated photosensitizing compounds, with the deeply penetrating capability of high-energy X-rays delivered at well-tolerated low doses to minimise damage to normal tissues. The concept is to generate the activating light within the tumor cells, rather than using optical fiber delivery of laser light, which is complex, invasive and limits the size and location of tumor that can be treated. This will be achieved by incorporating the photosensitizer and X-ray absorbing, light-emitting nanocrystals into polymer-based nanoparticles that will be localized to the highly-sensitive tumor cell nucleus (NL). In this research phase, we will carry out systematic preclinical studies of NL-XPDT using patient-derived PanCa tumor cells, both in culture and grown as solid tumors in mice. We have set quantitative "success targets" for NL-XPDT as a stand-alone treatment, either to destroy tumor completely or down-stage it to enable effective surgery. If these targets are not met, then these nanoparticles may have significant value as a novel class of radiation sensitizers to enhance conventional high-dose fractionated radiotherapy. We have assembled a multidisciplinary team to carry out the tasks of synthesizing the nanocrystals and nuclear-localizing nanoparticles and then to optimize and evaluate the effectiveness of NL-XPDT to kill patient-derived PanCa tumor cells and tumors in mice. Success here will lead to subsequent optimization and translation to first clinical trials. We will patent the technology to ensure its wide dissemination into clinical us

column36: Streptococcus pneumoniae glycan-processing enzymes: understanding and targeting their roles in virulence
column37: Streptococcus pneumonia (the pneumococcus) is a bacterium that often lives in the nose and throats of humans. This relationship is most often benign but this microorganism is also an accomplished disease-causing germ that can cause mild ailments, such as earaches, to lethal illnesses like pneumonia, blood poisoning, and infections of the brain and central nervous system. There are effective vaccines and medicines (antibiotics) to treat infections caused by the pneumococcus; however, this germ is constantly adapting to avoid both of these medical interventions. The importance of S. pneumoniae as a disease-causing germ dictates intense research efforts be directed to understand how it causes infections with the aim of using this knowledge to guide new treatment strategies. The human body has large amounts of carbohydrates with complex structures, termed glycans, displayed on the surface of cells and coating the surfaces of tissues (e.g. mucous). Remarkably, the pneumococcus relies on its ability to attack these glycans to colonize humans and ultimately cause disease. Our research is aimed at determining how this happens. What glycans does the germ attack? What pneumococcal factors do this? What is the outcome of destroying a host sugar? Armed with the fundamental insight from examining these questions we plan to develop and study molecules that can be used to prevent S. pneumoniae from attacking host glycans; such molecules are proving useful as research tools but may also provide a platform for developing new treatments to combat S. pneumoniae infections.

column36: Replication of guanine-rich DNA
column37: The broad goal of the research proposed here is to improve our understanding of how DNA, the hereditary information that determines the development and functioning of all living organisms, is maintained over a human lifetime. Specifically, I propose to focus on the replication of DNA that is enriched for guanine, one of the four DNA bases, in normal development and genome instability. The proposed research is a logical extension of earlier, published work from my laboratory. Following studies on the purification and self-renewal of blood forming stem cells, we focused on the role of telomeres, the normal ends of chromosomes, in normal and malignant cell proliferation. This work led us to studies of the pathways that ensure proper replication of the guanine (G)-rich DNA. In the course of this work, we discovered several genes including DOG-1 (FANCJ) and RTEL that are required for replication of G-rich DNA. Interestingly, both these genes encode for proteins with helicase activity: that is they are capable of unwinding secondary DNA structures of G-rich DNA, called guanine quadruplex (G4) structures. Recently we found that the Bloom helicase protein, deficient in patients with the cancer-prone Bloom syndrome, is required to suppress recombination at G-rich DNA. Here we propose further studies on the pathways required to resolve G4 structures and faithfully replicate Grich DNA at telomeres and at genes. The goal of these studies is to better understand the nature of the lesions that cause problems during replication of G-rich DNA and the pathways that different cells have available to solve such problems. Our studies will generate new knowledge about DNA replication and DNA repair and pathways that prevent genome instability. A better understanding of these pathways has broad potential for our understanding of normal development and aging as well specific disorders linked to DNA repair defects including specific types of cancer.

column36: Mechanisms of long-term change to neuronal activity and secretion
column37: My research focuses on nerve cells from the brain. I am interested in how the bio-electrical properties of nerve cells are controlled. These properties are governed by minute holes in nerve cells called channel proteins, which pass ions (like calcium, sodium or potassium) in and out of the cell. Because ions are charged, their movement through channels results in the flow of electrical current. Nerve cells harness currents to receive sensations, code information, and signal other nerve cells, muscles, or glands. Signalling involves the release of either small chemicals or specialized proteins, termed neuro-peptides, from a nerve cell. My objective is to examine how nerve cells use channels in a coordinated fashion to release neuro-peptides and initiate behaviour. Taking a reductionist approach, I employ the brain of a sea snail, called Aplysia, which has large and identifiable nerve cells. In particular, I study the bag cells, which are motivational cells that evoke reproduction, a behaviour essential to all animals. My work concerns how, after only a very short stimulus, the action of certain channels allows these nerves cells to respond with a prolonged episode of neuro-peptide release to trigger reproduction. I will investigate the mechanisms that allow channels to remain open for lengthy time periods. This includes interactions with structures inside the bag cells, known as mitochondria, which normally act as an energy source, but in this case regulate channel function. Long-term responses are found in nerve cells from many animals, and are essential for handling sensory information, learning, movement, and controlling drinking, eating, ovulation, birth, or breast feeding. Thus, my findings will apply to processes such as perception, memory, and fundamental behaviours. Furthermore, because the channels permit a nerve cell to be active on its own, there may be implications for epilepsy, where bio-electrical properties are inappropriately adjusted.

column37: Nociceptors are sensory nerves activated by harmful stimuli such as thermal changes, mechanical force and chemical insults. They are located in all organs; however, the lungs are densely innervated by sensory nerve fibers. Although we understand how nociceptors trigger cough, sneezing and pain, it has become apparent that sensory nerves might also directly detect pathogens and modulate immune responses. The neuroinflammatory system in the lung remains ill defined. My overall hypothesis is that lung sensory nerves can detect infection and through the selective release of neuropeptides alter the neutrophil response, thereby changing the clinical outcome. To test my hypothesis I have developed mouse models that are deficient in sensory nerves and I am using sophisticated lung imaging to interrogate how these nerves regulate inflammation during homeostasis and during pneumonia. Furthermore, we can now turn on and off nerves using light to demonstrate the function of nerves during infections. Understanding the interplay between the neuro and immune systems is essential to understanding pulmonary diseases.

column36: Behavioural profile matching: A precision medicine approach to concussion rehabilitation
column37: Concussions are very common. Although many people recover well from concussion, at least 1 in 5 will have persistent symptoms and difficulties with daily activities. How people cope with their symptoms following concussion powerfully influences their recovery. We have recently identified two unhelpful coping styles following a concussion - (1) avoidance, where people perceive activity as unnecessarily dangerous and take great care to avoid overexertion, and (2) endurance, where people engage in high levels of activity despite worsening symptoms until they "crash," requiring recuperative rest. These same unhelpful coping styles are seen in other health conditions, such as chronic pain. We believe that individuals who engage in avoidance behaviour benefit from a different type of concussion treatment than those who engage in endurance behaviour. If our belief is true, the current one-size-fits-all approach is not likely to work for everyone who suffers a concussion. We will evaluate whether assigning individuals to a specific treatment tailored to their coping style is practical, acceptable, and beneficial for their recovery. In the proposed study, patients will be recruited from concussion clinics and offered one of two treatment programs based on random assignment (like a coin toss). Both programs will be delivered by an occupational therapist and psychologist over eight weeks, using a videoconference system. We expect that the majority of patients who we approach will choose to join the study and that most of them will attend regularly, do their therapy assignments, and complete a final assessment. We will also check that the therapists are providing the treatments as outlined in a treatment manual. The information collected in this study will inform the development for a larger trial involving additional clinics across Canada, so that we can learn more definitively whether our matching approach can speed up recovery and reduce the burden of concussion.

column36: Ecological Momentary Assessment of Simultaneous Cannabis and Alcohol Use
column37: Cannabis and alcohol are widely used among young adults in Canada and both substances are often used at the same time. Rates of simultaneous use of alcohol and cannabis may increase as a result of legalization and increased access to cannabis in Canada. Combining cannabis with alcohol can increase risk for harms such as psychological and physical symptoms, social problems, and risk for substance use disorders. However, little is currently known about real-time patterns of simultaneous use of cannabis and alcohol, or how these contribute to risk for harms above and beyond using either substance alone. This study will use real-time mobile data collection to examine patterns of simultaneous cannabis and alcohol use in individuals' daily lives. Young adults who regularly use cannabis and alcohol will be asked to track their use of both substances using a smartphone app for three, 21-day periods spaced 6 months apart. On mornings following alcohol and/or cannabis use, participants will complete measures of substance use consequences. Data will be used to examine patterns of simultaneous use, including the frequency of co-use, the overall quantity of each substance used, and the temporal ordering of each substance (e.g., cannabis before alcohol or vice versa). Contextual influences on simultaneous use and the subjective effects of combining cannabis with alcohol will also be investigated. Further, the unique risks of combining cannabis and alcohol (e.g., risky behaviours, hangovers) will be examined relative to the use of either substance alone. Finally, changes in patterns of simultaneous use will be examined over a one-year period in relation to health outcomes such as symptoms of substance use disorders. The findings will improve our understanding of the unique health risks of cannabis and alcohol co-use, which will have direct implications for public health policies as cannabis becomes legal in Canada.

column36: Quantifying Brown Adipose Tissue Thermogenesis in Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Brown fat is the only organ able to burn energy to directly produce heat. This tissue allows small animals to live in cold environments without having to rely on muscle shivering. Brown fat is present in adults and can be seen using 'positron emission tomography' imaging (or 'PET imaging') with injection of a radioactive sugar label (or 'sugar tracer') that is taken up by brown fat when it is activated upon cold exposure. PET imaging with a sugar tracer is currently the standard method to measure brown fat. We have found that brown fat in adults burns energy mostly by utilizing its own fat content. We have demonstrated that PET imaging with a sugar tracer underestimates the total contribution of brown fat to energy expenditure, especially in people with type 2 diabetes. The contribution of brown fat to energy balance cannot be precisely determined using the current methods we have. As brown fat is currently viewed as a promising target for the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes, it is essential to quantify its role in energy expenditure in people without and with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes. We propose here to develop and validate new methods to quantify brown fat energy expenditure by measuring its own fat utilization with a combination of PET imaging with a novel fat tracer and magnetic resonance imaging techniques. We will apply these novel techniques during cold exposure and stimulation with a drug known to activate brown fat in people. Our laboratory has made outstanding contributions to the field of brown fat research through the imaging innovations we made and our integrated approach to the study of energy metabolism directly in people. This project will lead to new standard methods to measure brown fat energy expenditure and will provide essential knowledge on brown fat as a target to prevent and treat obesity and type 2 diabetes.

column36: PARP inhibition in PAH: A Phase 1 clinical trial
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a progressive condition characterized by the chronic elevation of pulmonary artery (PA) pressure leading to failure of the heart. In spite of recent advances in approved therapies, PAH remains a serious disease with significant mortality. In contrast to the earlier belief that contraction of pulmonary vessels played a key role in PAH, it is now established that excessive proliferation of the cells within the pulmonary artery wall is a pivotal component of pulmonary vascular obliteration, a currently irreversible feature of PAH for which available pharmacotherapies have no/limited efficacy. In recently years, it has become increasingly appreciated that, contrary to normal cells, these cells are exposed to stressful conditions, jeopardizing their survival. To deal with these insults, these cells have developed pathways, allowing them to survive and proliferate and leading to intense remodelling of pulmonary vessels. Central to these strategies are the activation of the mechanisms that repair DNA. We recently documented that pharmacological inhibition of PARP1, the most important mechanism involved in DNA repair, reverses PAH in human cells and animal models of PAH. Very recently, Olaparib, an orally available PARP1 inhibitor, was shown to be safe, well tolerated and effective in treating cancers and was approved by Health Canada for the treatment of ovarian cancer. The time is thus right to translate our findings in human PAH. This proposal addresses a very novel and promising therapeutic avenue to treat and is one of the first step of personalized medicine in PAH. We propose an early phase clinical trial to determine whether: 1) PARP1 inhibition with olaparib is safe and effective; 2) patients' genes can predict the efficacy and the side effect profile of olaparib in adult patients with symptomatic PAH.

column36: Systematic Analysis of Post-transcriptional Regulatory Mechanisms and Functions in Drosophila
column37: DNA is copied into messenger RNAs (mRNAs), which in turn encode proteins. For most of the second half of the 20th Century it was thought that the regulation of which proteins are made in any particular cell of the body or stage of development is at the level of transcription (production of mRNA from DNA). However, it has become clear in the last decade that a great deal of this regulation occurs post-transcriptionally via control of mRNA stability, localization within the cell and/or in the translation of the mRNA into protein. These processes are regulated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), which together with their bound mRNAs and other associated proteins, regulate these processes. In order to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms of post-transcriptional control and how the compendium of proteins in each cell type is assembled, we will use the powerful model organism, the fruit fly Drosophila, to systematically identify the mRNAs bound to each of 68 RBPs in the early embryo together with other associated RNAs and proteins. We will use experimental and computational methods to identify the binding sites for each of these 68 RBPs. Finally, we will assess the molecular functions of these binding sites in control of the post-transcriptional processes listed above. Together these studies will provide the first insights into how the 'post-transcriptional code' is read out as the compendium of proteins present in a cell. Given that RBPs and their binding sites tend to be highly evolutionarily conserved and that 90% of the closely related human RBPs have been associated with a variety of diseases, our results will lead directly to insights into the components and functions of post-transcriptional processes in other organisms, including humans.

Our preliminary evidence indicates that sex differences in brain communication patterns may play a role in depression susceptibility. Therefore, we will evaluate sex differences in the innate and stress-induced functionality of brain electrical output and communication, and responsiveness of these neural network activity patterns to various therapeutic drugs using animal models of depression. We will identify the impact of fluctuating female hormones on these physiological processes, and additionally, discern a role for the protein GSK-3 in their regulation. Importantly, we will identify how the efficacy of antidepressants to normalize these electrical patterns in depression model systems is influenced by cyclic changes in female hormone levels.
