column36: Functional Mechanisms of Adult Neural Stem/Progenitor Cells during Post-stroke Recovery
column37: Stroke is caused by an impairment of blood flow to the brain resulting in death and dysfunction of affected tissue. Millions of stroke survivors worldwide are afflicted with significant disabilities in day-to-day function. Unfortunately, the brain's ability for repair and recovery is somewhat limited and impairments caused by stroke are often permanent. However, stem cells in the brain, especially in a region called the subventricular zone, offer a potential source for endogenous brain repair. It is understood that these stem cells proliferate after stroke and other brain injuries, sending newborn progenitor cells towards the injured area in order to aid recovery, but the precise functions of these new cells are unclear. Using a mouse model of stroke, we will investigate how neural stem and progenitor cells influence various recovery and repair processes. These processes include: reorganization of blood vessels to re-establish blood flow and promote recovery of tissue surrounding the infarct, formation of scars that surround the damaged tissue to limit the spread of injury and protect surviving cells, and synaptic plasticity of surviving neurons, which is crucial for recovering lost functions. Importantly, these processes will be related to functional recovery using sensitive behavioural assays in order to identify which are best predictive of functional improvement. This research will define the functional mechanisms of newborn cells after stroke. In addition to revealing fundamental aspects of brain repair, findings may aid efforts directed at exploiting the benefits of stem cells in order to improve recovery from stroke.

column36: Enhancing motor recovery in a non-human primate model of chronic stroke by inhibiting pro-death neuronal signaling
column37: Stroke is a disorder with staggering emotional and socioeconomic impact. It is a leading cause of death in Canada and leaves the majority of survivors with long-term disabilities that significantly diminish their autonomy and quality of life. Motor recovery following a stroke is critically dependent upon the survival of mature and newly born neurons in brain areas adjacent to the injury. In fact, the degree reallocation of motor function to adjacent areas has been shown to be related to the proficiency of motor recovery. Recovery can be hindered by the fact that in the days to weeks following a stroke, neurotoxic signaling resulting from physiological stress from the initial injury increases and can cause neuronal death. Classes of molecules that inhibit neurotoxic signaling pathways may have neuroprotective properties and promote pro-survival signaling. The drug NA-1 is one such inhibitor and its administration in the days following a stroke could promote neuronal survival and improve motor recovery. We will assess the motor function of Cynomolgus macaques using behavioral tests and determine baseline brain connectivity using functional imaging. The animals will undergo a transient medial cerebral artery occlusion to induce a stroke and will be given injections of either NA-1 or placebo during recovery. We will continuously assess motor function and brain connectivity throughout recovery to determine whether NA-1 can significantly improve neuronal survival, functional connectivity, and motor control. The findings of the proposed research has important implications for the efficacy of such drugs in improving stroke recovery which can lessen the socioeconomic burden and the emotional and physical strain of stroke related disabilities.

column36: Etude des hyperactivations cerebrales dans le prodrome de la maladie d'Alzheimer par le biais de l'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle
column37: Le diagnostic de la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) se fait a la phase de demence, c'est-a-dire lorsque l'autonomie au quotidien de la personne atteinte est compromise. Ceci dit, les recentes decouvertes dans le domaine nous ont montre que certains changements cerebraux surviendraient plusieurs annees avant l'apparition des premiers symptomes. La presence de mecanismes cerebraux compensatoires pourrait expliquer cette periode ou les symptomes sont minimaux, voire absents. Des hyperactivations cerebrales, c'est-a-dire des niveaux d'activation superieurs a ceux d'individus cognitivement sains, ont ete observees dans le trouble cognitif leger, une phase qui precede generalement le stade demence. Ces hyperactivations pourraient etre un marqueur precoce de la maladie et sous-tendre de tels mecanismes compensatoires. Toutefois, le moment d'apparition de ces hyperactivations est meconnu, puisque la plupart des recherches ont etudie des individus trop atteints par la maladie. L'etude d'individus presentant une plainte de memoire pourrait fournir des indices precieux pour repondre a cette question. Ensuite, on ne sait pas comment ces hyperactivations changent avec la progression de la maladie, puisque la plupart des etudes n'ont pas evalue leurs sujets a plusieurs reprises dans le temps. Aussi, peu d'etudes ont examine la relation entre les hyperactivations et les pertes neuronales dans les stades precoces de la MA, ce qui limite les connaissances sur la relation entre ces types d'alterations. Enfin, on ne sait pas s'il existe des facteurs individuels (education, style de vie) pouvant favoriser la mise en place de mecanismes cerebraux compensatoires, ce qui pourrait guider le developpement d'interventions cognitives. Ce projet vise donc a etudier les hyperactivations cerebrales chez des individus ayant soit un trouble cognitif leger, soit une plainte de memoire en examinant leur relation avec les dommages neuronaux, la progression de la maladie, et les facteurs individuels.

column36: Integrated Knowledge Translation in Child Health: Advancing Evidence and Contributing to Pediatric Readiness of Canada's Emergency Departments
column37: Not using the best available evidence is common in the field of child health. Past research has found that as many as 4 in 10 children receive care that is not based on latest evidence and that 1 in 4 may receive care that may even be harmful. Knowledge Translation (KT) is often used to help move this research into practice. Yet, in child health and beyond, we still experience challenges to close this gap between what we know and what we do. It has long been thought that developing partnerships between those who produce and those who use research is the solution, as it ensures we ask research questions that are important to those who have to apply it. This joint way of conducting research, called integrated KT, is in its early scientific days with several important gaps that remain. No studies have looked at whether integrated KT efforts are working or not. Also, many of these studies measure and report differently on their interaction with end-users, making it difficult to compare and summarize the effects of research. The long-term goal of this project is to improve our understanding of how well integrated KT projects have worked to date in the field of child health, understand researchers and end-users experiences with practicing integrated KT, and to engage in and learn from an applied integrated KT project. The secondary goal of this research will be to measure baseline pediatric readiness of facilities across Manitoba and assess barriers and facilitators to achieving readiness status using an applied integrated KT approach.

column36: Les symptomes de trouble de stress post-traumatique, de trouble de stress post-traumatique complexe et de trouble de la personnalite limite chez les adultes ayant vecu des traumas interpersonnels durant l'enfance : le role des representations cognitives
column37: Les traumas durant l'enfance peuvent avoir de graves consequences sur la sante mentale a l'age adulte. Trois principaux troubles mentaux semblent etre etroitement lies a un vecu traumatique : le trouble de stress post traumatique, le trouble de stress post traumatique complexe et le trouble de la personnalite limite. Toutefois, certaines questions demeurent sans reponses dans les recherches actuelles. Premierement, il existe un debat dans la communaute scientifique quant a savoir si ces trois troubles sont distincts, ou s'ils referent a un meme phenomene. Deuxiemement, les facteurs permettant de predire si les survivants de traumas developperont l'un ou l'autre de ces troubles sont inconnus. Une avenue interessante a explorer est celle des perceptions de soi, des autres et du monde, qui sont modelees par les traumas et peuvent etre des facteurs de risque au developpement de ces troubles. Les objectifs de cette etude sont donc de 1) confirmer que les trois troubles sont bien distincts et de 2) explorer le role des perceptions de soi, des autres et du monde comme mecanismes pouvant expliquer l'apparition de chacun de ces troubles chez les survivants de traumas. Mille participants ages de 18 a 25 ans et representatifs de la population quebecoise completeront des questionnaires en ligne mesurant leurs antecedents de traumas, leurs perceptions d'eux-memes, des autres et du monde, et leurs symptomes de trouble de stress post traumatique, de trouble de stress post traumatique complexe et de trouble de la personnalite limite. D'une part, leurs resultats seront analyses pour determiner si on retrouve dans l'echantillon des participants qui n'ont aucun symptome correspondant aux troubles, ainsi que des participants presentant des symptomes de chacun des troubles distinctivement. D'autre part, des analyses statistiques seront faites pour verifier quelles perceptions (sur soi, les autres et le monde) expliquent le lien entre les traumas et lesquels des trois troubles

column36: The Kusamala Program: an interactive counselling program for primary caregivers of children hospitalized with severe acute malnutrition in Malawi
column37: Kusamala means "to take care" in the native language of Malawi, a Southern African country with a high burden of malnutrition. When children have severe malnutrition and an illness, they require hospital treatment and have a high chance of dying during or after their treatment. Fortunately, due to advances in research and healthcare, the mortality rate is decreasing. This means that we have to turn our attention to what happens when these vulnerable children leave hospital. How can we ensure that children grow and develop properly once they return to their homes? We believe that the answer is to teach and empower caregivers, who are mainly mothers, with specific messages of how to take care of their children. There is a valuable opportunity to do this while caregivers wait in the hospital during their children's treatment. With this in mind, we developed an interactive counselling program called the Kusamala Program. The program is four days long, with one and a half hour sessions each day taught by hospital nurses. It covers three different topics which could improve growth and development of children: 1) nutrition and feeding; 2) water, sanitation, and hygiene; and 3) play. The first topic is important to help children to gain weight and grow. The second topic is to reduce the chance of children getting sick again. Finally, past studies have shown that play is necessary to improve development of the brain and motor skills. Play is commonly forgotten as a component of care of children in Malawi, where caregivers often have many other essential priorities like making money for their families, looking after several children, and tending to the home. However, if caregivers are made aware of the significance of playing with their children, we believe it is possible for caregivers to add play to their day. Ultimately, the Kusamala Program for caregivers could have profound impacts on their children's future by allowing children to reach their potential.

column37: There is increasing evidence that early-life stressors (either before or after birth) are an important risk factor for the development of eating disorders later in life. There is also evidence that children and adolescents with weight-related concerns, such as being overweight, have a greater risk for developing eating disorders, and lower chances of recovery. Children who are victim of bullying based on their physical appearance are at particular risk for developing an eating disorder. However, little is known about the specific mechanisms through which these risk factors may increase vulnerability to disordered eating. Also, since most of the research has been done in individuals with advanced cases of eating disorders in clinical settings, it is unknown whether these factors predict an even greater amount of eating disorder symptoms in the general population. In our first study, we will investigate how early stressors predict risk for eating disorders in adolescence. We will also look at how childhood weight and eating behaviors (such as over-eating, picky eating and irregular eating) influence this association. In our second study, we will specifically look at how bullying based on physical appearance affects the brains of victims who have lived such experiences. We will perform brain scans in young adolescent girls with and without a history of bullying. While in the scanner, they will look at stimuli (words) relevant for eating disorders. We will then compare both group's brain reactivity to this information in specific brain regions that are involved in emotional regulation. We will also assess the activity of specific genes in both groups. With these studies, we hope to better understand specific behavioral and biological pathways that might explain risk for disordered eating in the general population. This will help the development of prevention and intervention strategies aimed at reducing the impact of weight concerns on risk for eating disorders.

column36: Assessing and improving the use of online information about child development, health and well-being by parents with low socioeconomic standards and their children
column37: RATIONALE Low education low income parents (parents with low socioeconomic status, hereafter SES) usually have a low level of literacy and health status. This study is born from a partnership between online information provider, 'Naitre et grandir' (N&G) and researchers who developed the Information Assessment Method questionnaire (IAM). N&G produces a website and a newsletter providing free, independent and trustworthy information about child development, health and well-being, to parents of 0-8-year old children. N&G is funded by the Chagnon Foundation which seeks to reduce poverty. The IAM allows parents to evaluate N&G information and provide feedback to N&G editors. High quality online consumer information improves health, quality of life, and participation in healthcare, for low SES parents. However, our previous work shows that low SES parents underuse N&G and IAM. Yet, it is these very parents who are more likely to report decreased worries and increased confidence as outcomes of using N&G information. Thus, our previous work clearly indicates a need to improve N&G and IAM. METHODS I will conduct my study in three phases. Phase 1. I will interview 30 low SES parents to identify barriers and facilitators to using N&G information and to interacting with N&G editors via IAM. We will use Phase 1 findings to implement a new version: the IAM+N&G+. Phase 2. I will compare the use of the original (IAM/N&G) and new (IAM+N&G+) versions. Phase 3. I will interview 30 parents to understand what outcomes they experienced after using N&G+. IMPACT Results will directly benefit low SES parents and children. In addition, results will lead to develop a free toolkit for all Web editors that will help improve health interventions to better support and empower low SES parents. AboutKidsHealth (information providers at SickKids Hospital in Toronto) will be the first other resource to implement our results.

column36: Discovering Novel Blood-Based Biomarkers to Identify a Patient's Risk of Cancer and Cancer Prognosis.
column37: In many cases early detection of cancer results in a favourable prognosis. There are several blood-based measures (or biomarkers) such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) which predict future cancers and can also be used as screening tests for existing cancers. In some cases these biomarkers can be used to identify high risk individuals, while in others, they can be used to screen for early cancers. Research to date has shown that fluctuations in certain biomarkers such as serum, iron and platelet counts can predict future cancers. These biomarkers have also been shown to predict a cancer prognosis. The objective of my research will be to identify and validate novel biomarkers for cancer risk and prognosis using recently introduced Ontario laboratory data and novel analytical techniques. We will use data from the Ontario Laboratories Information System (OLIS) which was recently added to a large Ontario health data reservoir at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES). It has been proposed that artificial intelligence applied to electronic databases can be exploited to identify novel biomarkers for cancer risk. We will analyse selected biomarkers using traditional epidemiological methods as well as novel machine learning algorithms. With data from millions of Ontario residents at our disposal we will conduct high powered studies capable of detecting small variations in blood-based biomarkers prior to cancer detection. This study will be the first of its kind in Ontario, and may have implications toward the detection and treatment of certain types of cancers. Variations in blood-based biomarkers could help understand the physiology and etiology of cancer in its earliest phases. Further, biomarkers that predict cancer risk and prognosis could improve patient outcomes through early detection and improved treatment decisions.

column36: Developing comprehensive predictive models of postoperative outcomes to improve surgical performance and perioperative care
column37: Surgery is never without risks. Complications such as wound infections, blood clots and even death are not only possible but still common. The cause of these complications generally falls in three main categories: the patient's medical conditions, the surgeon's skill during the operation, and the care the patient receives after the surgery. Science has come a long way in reducing these risks, but there is still work to be done putting these areas together. In this study, we ask how medical conditions, surgical skill and care after the surgery intersect to cause complications. Currently, before surgery, a patient's risk of complications or death is calculated using a risk score, which assesses their medical conditions alone. Risk scores generally stop at the door to the operating room: they do not take into account the surgeon's performance or the care afterwards. The surgeon, therefore, generally does not know how to tailor her skill or postoperative care to provide her patient with the best outcomes. Programming techniques in the field of machine learning are capable of finding these connections between medical conditions, surgical skill, and care after an operation, to discover ways for surgeons to tailor care and improve their patients' outcomes. We plan to use our large existing database of surgical videos in the field of bariatric surgery and urology to provide insight into surgical skills, and combine this with data from the medical record system at St. Michael's Hospital to get information about patients' health, postoperative care and outcomes. The objective of this project is to build a tool that will teach surgeons how to better care for each individual patient, as certain health conditions may cause their needs to vary. By finding care pathways that are customized to individual patients, this project could change the way surgeons operate on and care for their patients, and in so doing reduce patients' complications and improve their quality of life.

column36: Cytomegalovirus-driven natural killer cell responses in HIV infection
column37: Over the course of our lifetime, we are exposed to many different types of virus infections, and our own healthy cells can transform into cancer cells. Though many viruses only cause transient infection, some viruses (i.e. human cytomegalovirus (CMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis) cause lifelong persistent infection and have great medical and socioeconomic repercussions. Natural killer (NK) cells identify and destroy cancer cells and also fight virus infection. In response to a common herpesvirus infection (CMV), NK cells adapt and become superior killers of infected cells. Our work explores how the pressures of CMV and HIV co-infection affects adaptive NK cell formation and function, and whether we can harness the potential of these adapted NK cells against virus infection or malignancies. One way NK cells recognize and kill infected or cancerous cells is by attaching to antibodies that adhere to cells. We hope to guide these superior NK cells toward infected or transformed targets using specific antibody therapy. Greater insight into the basic mechanism and biology that drives the development of NK cells with heightened activity would facilitate the progress of new strategies for therapeutic targets to control a broad range of infections and malignancies.

column36: Personalizing and improving the treatment landscape of chronic facial pain with machine learning of multimodal neuroimaging data
column37: One in five Canadians will suffer from long-term pain that is no longer tied to potential tissue injuries; however, there is a severe lack of research on chronic pain. This results in a dire shortage in clinical tools to objectively assess and select proper treatments for chronic pain. Chronic pain of the face can be especially severe and damaging to a person's well being. Trigeminal Neuralgia (TN) is so severe that it has historically been described as the "suicide disease." My research uses TN to understand chronic facial pain and surgical treatments for it. By combining state-of the-art brain imaging techniques with machine learning (ML) algorithms, my work seeks to characterize changes in the brain structure and function related to chronic facial pain and develop clinical tools able to personalize treatments. My initial findings have shown that brain imaging patterns can predict treatment success in TN patients. Furthermore, these patterns can be transformed by ML techniques into clinical tools to predict individual, long-term pain relief. I anticipate further studies to lead to more tools that can help monitor long-term treatment outcomes, such as pain intensity and medication use, in TN patients. Additional studies may also identify new brain areas for treating chronic facial pain disorders. My findings may be immediately applicable to clinicians caring for patients with TN. My methods could also be adapted to develop ML-based clinical tools to optimize care for other chronic facial pain disorders. Ultimately, my research will shed light on how chronic pain, especially chronic facial pain, affects the human nervous system and reveal novel tools to create, select, and assess treatment strategies for chronic facial pain.

column36: Marginalizing Migrants: Exploring the Precarity of Migrant Health in Prairie Canada
column37: Within the context of globalization, workers-particularly from the global South-are encouraged to be mobile and flexible in their labour market participation. Over the past few decades, the share of migrants moving from developing countries in the global South to participate in low-wage work in the global North has grown dramatically. Through cross-national trade agreements, the Canadian government supplies a steady stream of transnational workers to Canadian employers who demonstrate labour shortages through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TWFP). In western Canada, Manitoba is a critical hub for a large population of migrant workers. In southwestern Manitoba, aggressive recruitment campaigns by the hog-processing industry (targeting would-be migrants from Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia), have driven population growth in smaller urban centres and towns. The town of Neepawa and the city of Brandon are prime examples of communities that employ a large number of Temporary Foreign Workers (TFWs), usually with limited English or French language ability and possessing limited rights and protections under the current TFWP. In particular, work permits tie TFWs to a single employer, leaving them vulnerable to employer abuse and the under-reporting of workplace injuries and illnesses due to the threat of deportation. As 'non-citizens' of Canada, migrant workers often work under conditions that would be deemed unacceptable to Canadian workers. For this reason, WHO has emphasized the need to draw linkages between migration, health and human rights. This is especially relevant within the context of the Canadian prairies where we know little about the health problems facing transnational migrants. For this reason, I propose to conduct an ethnographic study to explore the health problems and health services utilization patterns of migrant workers in Neepawa and Brandon, Manitoba.

column36: Development of an adjunct behavioural weight management intervention in bariatric surgery
column37: Obesity, defined as having a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m2 or above, is a critical international health care issue with the rates of obesity and morbid obesity increasing worldwide. Morbid obesity (BMI of 40 kg/m2 or above) is associated with an increased risk of multiple serious medical conditions including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, respiratory disease (e.g., asthma) and certain types of cancer. Bariatric surgery is the gold standard of treatment for morbid obesity. While bariatric surgery is associated with important reductions in body weight, weight-related health conditions, and mortality, a significant proportion of bariatric patients experience suboptimal post-surgical outcomes, including consistent and rapid weight regain, even in the short-term (e.g., within 6 months after the surgery). There are a variety of interventions which have been used to try and enhance the effects of bariatric surgery on longer-term weight maintenance through changes in lifestyle behaviours (i.e., physical activity, sedentarity, diet). However, many of these have been poorly developed and not well tested. This has resulted in varied rates of success with little knowledge of how to improve the overall intervention package (combination of intervention components or strategies included in the intervention). The ultimate goal of this project is to develop an appropriate trial protocol to assess the efficacy of different behavioural weight management strategies to improve long-term weight maintenance after bariatric surgery (identify the best combination(s) of intervention components and strategies for certain bariatric patients). Central to achieving this objective is working with key stakeholders (patients, health care professionals, health administrators/policy makers, and researchers) to identify the most pertinent behavioural weight management intervention strategies that should be used before and/or after bariatric surgery to enhance outcomes.

column36: Effects of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) on Cannabis Use and Cognitive Outcomes in Schizophrenia
column37: Background: Cannabis is the most commonly used drug in schizophrenia, posing as a barrier to overall quality of life. Cannabis use disorders (CUD) in these patients is associated with earlier onset and worsened symptomatology and cognitive/functional impairments that have been shown to improve with cannabis abstinence. Moreover trending legalization of cannabis in 2018 poses a significant threat to this population for which there is no satisfactory treatment. Brain stimulation techniques like repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) directed to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are well-tolerated and may have potential to address co-morbid CUD in schizophrenia, while improving psychiatric symptoms and cognition. Objective: To assess effects of rTMS as a treatment for CUD in schizophrenia patients. Methods: A total of 40 individuals meeting criteria for schizophrenia and CUD between ages of 18-55 will be recruited from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) in Toronto. Participants will be randomized into either active (n=20) or sham (n=20) high frequency rTMS (20 Hz) groups in a 6-week, double-blind, randomized, parallel controlled trial. All patients will receive contingency management and drug counselling interventions to facilitate 28-day cannabis abstinence trial endpoint, also monitored by THC levels from urine samples. Outcomes: The primary outcome will be trial endpoint self-reported cannabis use assessed by timeline follow-back and confirmed by cannabis urine toxicology. Secondary outcome measures will include cognitive outcomes (verbal learning, working memory and mismatch negativity), cannabis craving and withdrawal, and psychosis symptom ratings (Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale for Schizophrenia, Calgary Depression Scale for Schizophrenia). Significance: The proposed research may improve the health of patients suffering from schizophrenia and comorbid CUD with use of rTMS as a treatment, thereby improving functional outcomes.

column36: Electroencephalographie quantitative en sommeil paradoxal : un marqueur precoce de la neurodegenerescence cholinergique dans le trouble cognitif leger
column37: La maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) est le trouble neurodegeneratif le plus courant qui affecte les personnes agees et constitue un probleme de sante publique croissant. Le processus degeneratif de la MA debute plusieurs annees avant l'apparition de symptomes cliniques. Cette periode longue et progressive se nomme le trouble cognitif leger (TCL), bien que cela ne soit pas tous les individus avec un TCL qui progresseront vers la MA. Le manque de marqueurs fiables pour identifier quels individus avec un TCL progresseront vers la MA represente un obstacle majeur pour le developpement et l'evaluation de strategies preventives et therapeutiques. Plusieurs marqueurs mesurant l'activite cerebrale a l'eveil semblent prometteurs. Nous proposons que le sommeil paradoxal (SP) soit un etat plus sensible que l'eveil pour detecter les changements precoces de l'activite cerebrale dans la MA. En effet, lors du SP, l'activite du systeme cholinergique, lequel degenere a un stade precoce de la MA, n'est pas masquee par d'autres systemes qui sont actifs lors l'eveil. Ceci offre la possibilite d'etudier l'integrite du systeme cholinergique alors que les autres systemes sont plus silencieux. L'objectif de ce projet est d'evaluer, chez 100 patients avec un TCLa et 30 participants en sante (65-85 ans), la valeur predictive de mesures d'activite cerebrale obtenues lors du SP, comparee a celles obtenues lors de l'eveil, pour determiner qui sont les individus ayant un TCL et ceux etant cognitivement sains. Ceci sera accompli a l'aide d'analyses sophistiquees et de techniques de classification avancees. Grace a l'imagerie cerebrale, nous verifierons aussi, dans un sous-echantillon (i.e. 20 TCL et 20 controles), que le SP soit lie a l'integrite du systeme cholinergique. Si nos hypotheses sont confirmees, les caracteristiques du SP ont le potentiel de devenir un outil fiable, non invasif et peu couteux qui pourrait etre deploye a grande echelle pour le depistage precoce de la MA.

column37: Le traumatisme cranio-cerebral (TCC) constitue une cause frequente de mortalite et de morbidite chez les enfants. Meme les blessures cerebrales dites << mineures >> constituent un probleme d'une magnitude importante. A preuve, les TCC legers (TCCL) ont ete qualifies <<d'epidemie silencieuse>>. Selon de recentes etudes, les troubles de sommeil seraient parmi les sequelles les plus frequentes d'un TCCL et seraient susceptibles de compromettre le retablissement. Malgre le nombre croissant d'etudes sur les difficultes de sommeil post-TCC pediatrique, tres peu ont cible les enfants d'age prescolaire. Par ailleurs, le TCC est bien connu pour ses atteintes executives, et celles-ci sont susceptibles d'etre exacerbees par des problemes de sommeil. La presentera etude evaluera le sommeil et le role de celui-ci dans le fonctionnement executif chez l'enfant d'age prescolaire post-TCCL. Cent enfants ayant subi un TCCL accidentel entre 18 et 60 mois seront evalues 6 mois post-blessure. Leurs resultats seront compares a ceux de cent enfants ayant subi une blessure orthopedique mineure. Leur sommeil sera evalue via le port d'un actigraphe et un questionnaire de sommeil complete par les parents. De plus, des taches d'inhibition, de flexibilite cognitive et de memoire de travail seront administrees a titre de mesures de fonctions executives. A ce jour, les etudes sur les problemes de sommeil engendrees par un TCC ont omis d'inclure des enfants d'age prescolaire, se sont concentrees principalement sur le TCC modere-severe et ont utilise des mesures du sommeil principalement subjectives. La presente etude permettra de remedier a ces lacunes et de dresser un profil plus detaille du fonctionnement nocturne suite a TCCL en bas age. De plus, une meilleure connaissance des problemes de sommeil consecutif a un TCCL, conjugues a des atteintes executives, offrira aux cliniciens l'information necessaire a la mise en place de mesures d'intervention appropriees.

column37: Colorectal cancer is the 2nd most common cancer in Canada and many who are diagnosed progress to advanced disease. The use of targeted agents to treat advanced colorectal cancer has improved patient outcomes. Cetuximab is one of the first of these drugs to be approved in advanced colorectal cancer treatment. A series of tumour mutations have been identified that can help health care providers determine the chance of controlling the disease using cetuximab. However, these predictive mutations are only useful in approximately half of patients. The hypothesis motivating this study is that it is the genes that a person inherits that influence favourable response or failure of this drug in controlling colorectal cancer. We will take a novel, comprehensive approach that simultaneously investigates many inherited genetic variants in the molecular pathways involved in how cetuximab is handled by the body and its mechanism of action, using information gathered from cellular, animal, and human sources. We will then determine which of these genetic variants are linked to either how well the drug works, resulting in longer time before the cancer starts to grow again as well as longer overall survival times, and which are associated with its side effects. Instead of evaluating each side effect separately, we will use innovative statistical techniques to look at groups of symptoms together. We have access to a unique repository of blood and tissues samples from two Canadian-led international trials. In fact, we have already identified one important genetic marker in the gene FCGR2A that helps inform on the effectiveness of cetuximab for an additional 8% of patients. These early results suggest that using a comprehensive approach will further divide these colorectal cancer patients into those who are most versus least likely to respond favourably to cetuximab, such that patients least likely to benefit from cetuximab therapy can be offered an alternate therapy or clinical trial.

column36: Novel strategies to target HER2-positive breast cancer cells while circumventing anti-HER2-induced cardiotoxicity
column37: Breast cancer is the leading form of cancer in Canadian women. About one third of breast tumors are referred to as HER2-positive. This means that the cells in the tumor have abnormally high levels of a protein called HER2. A diagnosis of HER2-positive breast cancer is associated with poorer prognosis, increased metastasis, and lower overall survival rates compared to HER2-negative breast cancer. Strategies to block HER2 in tumor cells do exist; they are commonly used in HER2-positive breast cancer patients and they can help. Unfortunately, HER2 is also found in the heart, where it has important functions. Therefore, when HER2 blockers are used to block HER2 in tumor cells, they might also block HER2 in the heart. This leads to undesirable side effects that sometimes cause the heart to fail. This project is designed to find new ways to block HER2 in breast tumor cells, while still leaving HER2 intact to function properly in the heart. Our research partners have designed new therapies to specifically block breast tumor HER2, and here, the effects of these new therapies on healthy and diseased heart muscle cells will be compared to the older HER2 blockers that are currently used in clinic. This study will also investigate whether abnormal mechanical forces experienced during high blood pressure, for example, put heart muscle cells at risk for HER2 blocker-induced damage. It is hoped that this research will contribute to the body of knowledge that will improve the care of patients diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer.

column36: Pharmaco-epigenetics as a Novel Approach to Personalized Medicine
column37: Epigenetics is an innovative and rapidly emerging field that can be applied to psychiatric disorders in order to decrease the erratic nature of treatment outcomes that so many patients continue to experience. This project will use a large discovery data set to determine the role that the epigenetic modification known as DNA methylation plays in anxiety disorder symptoms, as well as poor response to and increased side effects of antidepressant medications. Epigenetic analyses are at the cutting edge of genomic studies and allow us to gather information beyond the sequence of DNA to examine the small chemical modifications that attach to the DNA. DNA methylation can significantly alter how a gene works. In the context of this project, the genes that are turned on (or turned off) can lead to increased risk for failure to respond to a medication, or to development of serious side effects. As mood and anxiety disorders are closely connected to the function of our stress response system, it is also important to discover how the epigenetic differences of our stress system genes may influence the effectiveness of antidepressant treatment. The project will be expanded to examine many epigenetic sites across the entire human genome to discover new targets involved in treatment outcomes of anxiety disorders, in addition to determining how DNA methylation may change over time with medication treatment. As 50% of all antidepressant treated patients fail to ever reach remission, shortening the trial-and-error process of finding effective medications for patients will significantly improve each individual patient's quality of life, reduce the costly side-effect burden, and offer substantial socioeconomic benefits to the Canadian health care system.

column36: Evaluation of an Alternative Model of Care for Stable Rheumatoid Arthritis Patients: Collaborative Nurse-Led Shared Care Model
column37: Today, one out every 100 Canadians lives with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a debilitating disease, which has a devastating impact on patients' lives and, in Canada, is associated with an annual economic burden over $5B. Currently, there is no treatment for RA. However, the disease can be controlled with medical therapy. For the best outcomes, patients require diagnosis and therapy within four weeks from the first symptoms of the disease. Next, patients require life-long monitoring for adverse effects of medications, disease flares and increased risk of comorbidities. Currently, follow-up of patients in remission (stable RA) consumes most of the rheumatologists' time and limits their ability to see newly onset and urgent patients. The follow-up of stable RA patients can be managed by non-physician care providers. For example, in nurse-led shared care clinics (NLSCCs) for RA patients, nurses take primary responsibility for stable patients' follow-up while allowing rheumatologists to focus on newly onset and urgent patients. In such clinics, besides RA management, patients receive holistic chronic disease care, which includes co-morbidity screening, education, lifestyle management, and ongoing communication between the patient, nurses, rheumatologists and primary care providers to ensure continuity of care. My research will evaluate the quality of care at the first NLSCC for stable RA patients in Alberta compared to a traditional rheumatologist-led clinic. Next, using computer simulation modeling, I will explore the effects of province-wide implementation of NLSCCs on waiting times for new onset and urgent RA patients and cost to the health care system. This research is important, as it will determine whether the use of NLSCCs for RA patients improves quality of care for stable RA patients and whether widespread implementation of this model of care has the potential decrease waiting times for new onset and urgent patients in local Alberta settings.

column36: Functional Characterization of Regulators of p53 Gain-of-Function Mutants
column37: Tumour suppressor p53 is the most commonly mutated gene in all cancers. It encodes for a protein termed p53, which is at the centre of a comprehensive regulatory network that protects our cells from becoming cancerous. More than 22 million cancer patients today carry mutated p53. Nearly half of them are caused by a single mutation in its DNA sequence, leading to a single amino acid substitution on the p53 protein. The resulting mutant proteins, termed point mutated p53 protein (mutp53), not only abolishes its original tumour suppressive function, but also gains novel oncogenic functions (gain-of-function, GOF), promoting tumour formation, growth, invasion, and chemoresistance. Therefore, to improve and tailor therapies for patients carrying mutp53, it is paramount to understand how tumours acquire these GOFs via mutp53. Through earlier work, we observed that mutp53 is preferentially stabilized in tumours but not in normal tissues; in addition, upon reducing mutp53 protein level inside the tumours, these tumours collapse. Therefore, if we can find out what are the factors that stabilize or cause the accumulation of mutp53, we could destroy these tumours. My project therefore aims at finding out these factors that regulate the mutp53 and its associated regulatory networks. To this end, I shall employ a unique gene targeting technique developed in our lab to screen and analyze the role of hundreds of genes in cancer development within a single mouse, in just five weeks. Through these functional genomics and proteomics screens, we can characterize the physiological regulatory and interaction network that is specific to mutp53. Among these regulators, I shall prioritize to validate and functionally annotate those that can be targeted by available drugs. Therefore, my overall goal is to elucidate the genetic network that drives mutp53 oncogenesis, and devise and improve therapies to treat these cancers in a more personalized manner.

column36: Exploring the shared multi-omic architecture of late-life depression and cognitive decline: Discovering and predicting biologically-defined patient subtypes using machine learning
column37: Late-life depression (LLD) in adults over the age of 60, is a highly debilitating mental illness affecting up to 16% of older adults in Canada. More than 50% of patients do not achieve remission which is associated with progressive cognitive decline and a 2-3 times increased risk for dementia. In addition, antidepressant treatment is highly variable and might also depend on cognitive functioning in LLD. Given the aging population with 937,000 Canadians expected to develop dementia in the next 15 years, we need to understand the joint biology underlying depression and cognitive decline to inform treatment and reduce the public health burden currently totalling $10.4B dollars/year. The clinical complexity of depression, cognitive decline and dementia requires that advanced statistical methods, such as machine learning, be applied to develop predictive biomarkers based on biologically-informed subgroups of patients. The proposed investigation will have three major aims which will use machine learning models and multiple types of genomic data, including: (1) exploring the existence of cognitively-different subgroups of depressed patients; (2) predicting the discovered subgroups using genomic data; and, (3) understanding whether the cognitive subgroups respond differently to antidepressant treatment. For these aims, I will be using publicly-available data from large studies of older adults including, as well as, well-characterized clinical sample of older adults treated with antidepressants. By leveraging genomic data and large samples, we will be able to discover subgroups of patients which will have different risks for cognitive decline and dementia, which may affect their response to antidepressants. Furthermore, these findings will allow us to develop genetic tests which could be used to personalize and optimize treatment of depression, as well as, to slow the progression of cognitive decline

column36: Investigating the Role and Therapeutic Potential of Neurolysin in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
column37: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is an aggressive blood cancer with a 2-year survival rate of 35%. Despite aggressive chemotherapy, the majority of patients relapse. AML's poor prognosis is largely due to the existence of treatment-resistant cells, called leukemic stem cells, which cause cancer reoccurrence. New therapies that specifically target leukemic cells and stem cells provide a promising and more effective alternative to the harmful effects of chemotherapy. Mitochondria are important components of the cell that produce energy. It has been shown that AML cells and stem cells have unique mitochondrial characteristics compared to normal blood cells, highlighting a potential therapeutic vulnerability. Mitochondrial function and structure is maintained by a group of enzymes called mitochondrial proteases. We have recently discovered that a specific mitochondrial protease called neurolysin (NLN) is highly expressed in a subset of patients with AML. We have also shown that reducing NLN levels inhibits leukemic disease propagation and disrupts mitochondrial function. However, the role of NLN in the mitochondria is unknown. Moreover, the effects of inhibiting NLN to stop the progression of leukemia have not been studied. The impact of this project is to understand NLN's function in the mitochondria and investigate its potential as a novel therapeutic target in leukemia. Specifically, it will expand our knowledge on targeting the unique metabolic properties of cancer cells and stem cells, with the goal of developing more effective treatments without the toxicity of chemotherapy.

column36: Masters Athlete Screening Study (MASS): Evaluation of Pre-participation Screening and Cardiovascular Risk in Masters Athletes
column37: Middle-aged individuals are exercising more and living longer. Underlying coronary artery disease is the primary cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in Masters athletes (> 35 years) with symptoms preceding the event in only 12-36% of cases. The risk of SCD during vigorous exercise is transiently increased in those with underlying heart disease. Pre-participation screening (PPS) can detect heart disease and prevent SCD but the optimal screening method is undefined. The Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire for Everyone (PAR-Q+) and the AHA Pre-participation Questionnaire are currently used; however, a more comprehensive risk assessment is needed. The percentage of Masters athletes that undergo current recommendations to detect heart disease is modest with the primary driver for a healthcare provider to refer an athlete for PPS is increasing age and participation in long distance events, rather than the presence of traditional risk factors. Our pilot study in 286 Masters athletes suggests that they are not immune to cardiovascular risk and 12% have significant heart disease. This present study will assess the prevalence of heart disease and risk in 800 Masters athletes. We will follow the cohort for five years to determine the incidence of, and the most effective tool for detecting significant heart disease. Study participants diagnosed with heart disease will be invited to participate in a psychological impact evaluation survey to determine the impact of a heart diagnosis through PPS to ensure optimal support in those diagnosed. This research will guide physicians and sporting organizations to determine which athletes are at risk and how to screen to prevent SCD and ensure safe sport participation. This will be the first prospective, longitudinal, large-scale (800 athletes) study in Canada examining cardiovascular risk, incidence of heart disease and examination of comprehensive screening tools in recreational and competitive athletes.

column36: Motives for Desired or Compliant Sex for Young Adult Women with BPD Symptomology
column37: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a prevalent and serious mental illness. Symptoms of BPD include intense and rapid mood swings, unstable relationships, and engagement in self-harm or suicidal behaviors. Effective psychotherapeutic treatments for BPD have been developed, such as dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). There is still, however, much room for improvement when it comes to alleviating key interpersonal problems in BPD. Therapeutic interventions that increase self-compassion (reacting to one's own suffering with kindness and understanding) may improve the treatment of these interpersonal difficulties. This study will evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of adding self-compassion training to DBT skills groups and will explore whether the added self-compassion training impacts interpersonal functioning. Participants diagnosed with BPD will be randomized to complete either thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training, or thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training modified to include self-compassion training. Feasibility and acceptability of the programs will be assessed post-treatment and compared between the two groups. Outcome variables, including interpersonal functioning, will be measured pre-treatment, immediately post-treatment, and at follow-up thirteen weeks later. It is anticipated that there will not be differences in acceptability and feasibility between groups, and participants that receive self-compassion training will show greater improvement in interpersonal functioning. This research will determine whether self-compassion training is a potentially useful addition to evidence-based care for BPD. Furthermore, this research has the potential to reduce the significant personal suffering and healthcare toll of BPD by informing improvements in treatment.

column36: Defining the role of ArpC1b and the actin cytoskeleton in macrophage migration, phagocytosis, and immunoregulation
column37: Macrophages are cells present in virtually every organ, where they play an important role in both the short-term (innate) and long-term (adaptive) immune responses. They can engulf foreign pathogens as well as clear the millions of dead cells produced by our body each day. To reach these targets, macrophages must migrate through the tissues and degrade their way through dense matrix. Following particle engulfment (a process known as phagocytosis), they can interact with lymphocytes, components of the adaptive immune system, and release pro- or anti-inflammatory substances called cytokines. Together, these reactions maintain homeostasis and can regulate the production of antibodies. Many macrophage functions require the activity of the cellular skeleton, particularly the actin-nucleating arp2/3 complex. Recently, patients have been identified with a mutation in ArpC1b, a subunit of this complex. The condition presents with recurrent infections, autoimmunity, and autoinflammation. To understand the source of these abnormalities, I propose to investigate the role of ArpC1b in the context of macrophages. We hypothesize that ArpC1b is critically required for optimal macrophage function and cannot be rescued by the analogous protein ArpC1a present in other tissues. To better determine the impact on macrophage function I will perform migration, matrix degradation, and phagocytic capacity assays. I will also compare the cytokine profile of macrophages isolated from patients and from healthy donors, to determine how the mutated protein may modulate the remainder of the immune system. This research will help us better understand the patients' condition and the role of the macrophage cytoskeleton in autoimmunity and autoinflammation.

column36: Understanding the integrative body composition and metabolic changes of older adults during two weeks of reduced ambulation and following six week of exercise rehabilitation
column37: Beginning around the 4th to 5th decade of life, we typically observe a loss of skeletal muscle tissue and a gain in fat mass. These age-related changes in our muscle and fat tissues predispose many individuals to developing health related impairments (i.e. diabetes, loss of strength, difficulties in performing daily activities). Recent evidence suggests that brief periods of inactivity, such as reducing the number of steps taken in a single day (<1500/day - which may occur from minor injuries or illnesses), accelerates these negative changes in body composition and development of impairments. What must be appreciated, is that following these periods of reduced activity, older adults may not recovery their muscle mass or reduce their fat mass. A key strategy to aid recovery is exercise. However, the extent of recovery in older adults following an exercise program, compared to returning to daily activities, after these periods of reduced activity are unclear. My research aims to determine the extent of muscle loss and fat mass gains during reduced activity (2 week of reduced steps taken in a single day) and assess the role of an exercise program on recovery of pre-inactivity health status in older adults. Alongside assessing changes in muscle health and fat mass, we will also examine how these changes alter our ability to regulate blood sugar and fat levels in our blood and perform functional tasks such as standing up from a seated position. This research will be critical for describing the extent and negative effects that periods of inactivity have on muscle mass, fat mass, and physical health of older adults. In addition, this work will be key in informing strategies to promote exercise programs for older adults following these periods of inactivity. Ultimately, this work will aim to improve independence and quality of life for older adults and promote healthy aging.

column36: Influence of mental health disorders and their management on adult functioning outcomes among emerging adults with a history of out-of-home care: a quantitative and qualitative study.
column37: As youth transition out of foster care at age 19 in British Columbia they are expected to live independently with little or no support from the government or their families. The extreme vulnerability of this population has been brought to the public's attention by several high-profile deaths of youth who had recently aged out government care. A consensus has been reached across the province about the need to reform the services that support youth as they age out of care; the planning of these reforms has been initiated by relevant government agencies. Research has confirmed that youth who have been in foster care have a high risk of suffering from mental illnesses. They also struggle more than their peers to transition successfully into adulthood; for example, they are more likely to not graduate from high school, have unstable housing and employment, have low incomes, and be involved in criminal activity. Although many negative impacts of foster care have been established, there is a lack of research on how mental illnesses influence the transition into adulthood in this population. My thesis project will look at the impact of mental illnesses and how they are treated on key indicators of a successful transition into adulthood among youth (18 to 29 years) who have been in foster care. For this analysis, I will use linked databases that include indicators for the entire population of Manitoba. I will also interview youth living in Vancouver who have a diagnosed mental illness and have been in foster care. We will discuss how they think the treatment of their illnesses (or lack thereof) influenced their transition into adulthood and how the system of care could be improved to better support this transition. The evidence generated by my thesis will serve to inform the reform efforts that are currently being undertaken in British Columbia, and has the potential to significantly impact the long-term outcomes of youth who age out of care in the province.

column36: Exercise Response: Is Irisin a Novel Factor that Explains the Metabolic Adaptation?
column37: Over the past few years, the prevalence of obesity and Type 2 diabetes (T2D) has drastically increased, and is expected to continue to rise. This is unfortunate, as it has led to extreme costs to our health care system. Exercise has been recognized as a first line of treatment to prevent and manage these two chronic conditions; but, not everyone benefits from exercise in the same way. For example, some individuals may lose weight from an exercise program, while others who participated in the same program will not see any results. A number of factors may lead to this variation, including a hormone released from your muscles during exercise, called irisin. Irisin is a recently discovered hormone that has the potential to provide a multitude of health benefits for individuals living with obesity and T2D. However, as irisin is novel, it is not clearly understood how different forms of exercise (intensity or duration) impact the typical health outcomes usually observed with exercise. First, our study will investigate whether irisin is released at a greater extent during high intensity aerobic exercise (e.g.: vigorous bike ride) compared to moderate intensity aerobic exercise (e.g.: jogging) in adults living with obesity. Second, we will study the release of irisin in a group of individuals who did not get any health benefits from a 12-week exercise program. Then, we will see if they get exercise benefits after an additional, more challenging, exercise program that lasts 12 more weeks. This will tell us what form of exercise best stimulates irisin release and whether these changes are related to meaningful clinical outcomes in individuals living with diabetes/pre-diabetes. Results of this study will be of great importance for health research, as they will provide a better understanding of the link between irisin, exercise, and health outcomes. Furthermore, they will provide us with further insight regarding the right amount of exercise needed to optimize health benefits.

column36: Exploring AAA+ unfoldase conformation and interaction landscapes
column37: Proteins are the basic building block of the cell. The ability of proteins to carry out different jobs depends on their 3D shape. The basic unit of proteins is a single string-like molecule that folds in on itself, like yarn knit into a sweater, to form a specific 3D structure. In order to recycle protein components when they are no longer needed or have lost their proper 3D shape, cells have developed specialized machinery, known as unfoldases, that unravel proteins by pulling them through a narrow opening. In this project we will use electron microscopy to see snapshots of one of these molecular motors in action. We can then identify how these unfoldases recognize which proteins need to be recycled. We will determine how the unfoldases co-operate with other helper proteins to recognize and stimulate unfolding activity. This knowledge will help us understand how these unfoldases function in the cellular environment. It will also lend insight into cancers where unfoldases are overactive, and genetic diseases like familial ALS and Paget's disease of the bone, where these systems are underactive due to genetic mutations. Just like looking at a blueprint for a car motor, seeing the structure of this protein can help us to identify why mutations cause the machine to break down, or help design ways to slow down overactive versions.

column36: Advancing physical activity recommendations and their implementation among individuals with osteoporosis
column37: One in three women and one in five men will experience a fracture due to osteoporosis in their lifetime (Osteoporosis Canada, 2016). Regular physical activity, including strength and balance exercise, is often recommended for people with osteoporosis which has been shown to maintain bone mass and reduce falls (Giangregorio et al, 2014). Although physical activity recommendations exist, new research on the optimal type and level of exercise is still emerging. Furthermore, people with fractures, especially in the spine, have been underrepresented in most exercise studies, leaving a gap in our knowledge about the effectiveness and safety of exercise in this population. There are no established guidelines on how to move safely after a recent osteoporotic spine fracture. Health care providers need guidance on what to tell patients - what movements to avoid, how to complete daily activities and leisure activities safely, and what exercises might be helpful during recovery, or to reduce pain. My research has three aims: 1) to complete a comprehensive review and meta-analysis to identify the effects of different types of exercise on outcomes important to people with osteoporosis; 2) to establish expert consensus on safe movement and exercise after a recent spine fracture due to osteoporosis; and 3) to develop and pilot test a community-based program to help implement physical activity recommendations among individuals with osteoporosis. column36: Maximizing colorectal cancer screening strategies to reduce burden and influence provincial and national prevention and screening efforts.
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second most common cancer in Canada. Despite this, screening participation remains low. In addition, it is becoming increasingly difficult in our fiscally restrained environment to provide safe, high-quality, and affordable healthcare. Ontario's provincial screening program, ColonCancerCheck (CCC), recommends that those aged 50-74 at average risk for CRC be screened with an at-home stool test. This test is less invasive and less costly than other tests like colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy, which involve the use of a thin tube to view parts of the colon. For the proposed research, my objectives are to identify interventions or strategies that will improve participation in the provincial screening program. I will work with a team of individuals with diverse expertise in epidemiology, population-health, health services research and economic evaluation in order to identify effective strategies to increase participation in CRC screening given that current screening rates remain below the national target of 60% in Ontario and many other Canadian provinces. In collaboration with my team members, I will disseminate my findings at the local, national and international level in order to maximize CRC screening policy and service delivery.

column36: Development and evaluation of a brief online motivational interviewing intervention for clients who lack motivation to engage in Internet-delivered cognitive behaviour therapy for anxiety and depression
column37: Anxiety and depression are common and disabling conditions that are associated with large economic costs. Traditionally, these concerns are treatable with face-to-face cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT); however, Internet-delivered cognitive behaviour therapy (ICBT) has emerged as an equally effective method of disseminating care while also improving access to services and reducing therapist time and costs. ICBT involves delivering treatment material to manage anxiety and depression online using structured web-pages. While the impact of CBT and ICBT is impressive, clients experience varying responses to these treatments. Opportunities exist though to further enhance outcomes in order to maximize the effect of CBT and ICBT. For instance, motivational interviewing (MI) has been incorporated into the initial sessions of CBT and has been shown to significantly improve symptoms of anxiety and increase treatment completion relative to CBT alone. MI is a clinical tool used by therapists to help facilitate clients' motivation to change. Client motivation is important in therapy and has been shown to predict greater treatment adherence and symptom improvements. Yet due challenges associated with adapting key components of MI over the Internet, this clinical method has not been offered alongside ICBT. Developing a brief online MI treatment that requires no therapist time has the potential to serve as a cost-effective method to bolstering ICBT completion and recovery rates. The goal of the proposed study is to, therefore, develop and evaluate a brief online MI intervention aimed at increasing client motivation to engage in ICBT for anxiety and depression. The development phase will involve adapting the original MI protocol for anxiety over the Internet. The evaluation phase will involve using mixed methods to determine the value of supplementing ICBT with MI for clients who lack motivation to participate in therapy. Results will inform next steps for efficacy testing.

column36: Elucidating the molecular mechanisms that permit sustained interferon gamma signaling to potentiate breast cancer metastasis
column37: Introduction: Metastatic breast cancer (BC) remains incurable. The spread of breast cancer to other organs such as the lungs, liver and brain occurs through a complex set of steps, our understanding of which remains incomplete. Our immune system has mechanisms to target and control early cancer development. In order for tumors to progress and metastasize they must first overcome this anti-tumor immune response. We know that while acute inflammation is a necessary component of the anti-tumor immune response, chronic inflammation can instead contribute to tumor progression and metastasis. Interferon gamma (IFNG) is a very important inflammation molecule that drives anti-tumor immunity. Yet, its role in later stages of BC remains unclear. Using a well-studied mouse model of BC, we recently revealed that IFNG, while important for delaying BC onset, actually increases BC spread to other organs. We hypothesize that this novel and unexpected finding is the result of chronic exposure to IFNG during BC development that improves the ability of these BC cells metastasize. The aim of this research project is to understand how IFNG promotes metastasis. Research methods: We will determine the specific step(s) of the metastatic process that IFNG acts upon to promote metastasis using transgenic mouse models available in our lab. Based on this we will then interrogate which of known and potential effects of IFNG signaling are responsible for promoting metastasis in our mouse model. Finally, we will screen human breast tumors from a large biobank with matching clinical follow-up data, to determine whether increased IFNG levels or signaling in these tumors is associated with increased risk of metastasis in patients. Impact: We have identified a novel role for IFNG in breast cancer. This research will provide insight into the dual and opposing roles immune molecules can play during different stages of cancer. Ultimately, this research will improve our understanding of metastasis.

column36: Deep learning-based study of the endogenous retroviral-derived immunopeptidome in ovarian cancer.
column37: Vertebrates have evolved from primitive life forms with a strategy of survival that bases itself on longevity instead of high reproductive rates. Indeed, while our specie does not produce many offspring, it has a remarkable immune system, that enables it to efficiently combat disease and therefore prolong its lifespan. At the heart of our adaptive immune system are T lymphocytes, that transit through our bodies and scan cells for indications of infection. In fact, all cells display at their surface molecules that present short protein fragments (or peptides) collectively referred to as the immunopeptidome. The immunopeptidome mirrors the processes that are happening in the cell itself. Since T lymphocytes are trained to recognize peptides that indicate infection or abnormal activity, they should be able to recognize and eliminate infected cells but also pre-cancerous cells. However, we still do develop cancers, which suggests that this recognition process is not perfect. In our laboratory, we believe that if we use the right peptides as anti-cancer targets, we could train the immune system to efficiently recognize and destroy tumors. We know that those ideal targets must generate a powerful and prolonged immune response. These targets arise from many genetic differences between tumors and the healthy tissue. Therefore, our study aims to identify tumor-specific peptides and understand their nature.

column36: Determining the mechanism for lung lipid defects in a Mecp2-mutant mouse model for Rett syndrome
column37: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurological disorder that almost exclusively affects females and is caused by mutations in the gene methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2). Girls with RTT reach their normal developmental milestones, but soon lose their ability to speak, use their hands, and walk. Seizures and severe breathing disturbances are also common. These symptoms are progressive, such that most patients require constant supportive care, which is a huge burden on the health care system as well as their families. Although breathing difficulties account for the death of most RTT patients, the lung is rarely studied. Using a Mecp2-mutant mouse model of RTT, our lab showed that MeCP2 bridges a lipid-regulating complex to its DNA targets; when MeCP2 is absent, fat is over-produced. This leads to increased fat content in the brain, liver, and blood of Mecp2-mutant mice. Importantly, specialized cells in the lung also synthesize lipids for lung surfactant and may be affected by the loss of MeCP2 in similar ways. I aim to understand how loss of MeCP2 in the lung contributes to breathing abnormalities in RTT. Surprisingly, I have identified perturbed lung lipid synthesis pathways in the lungs of Mecp2-mutant mice that lead to profound fat accumulation. Additionally, breathing defects in these mice improve following treatment with lipid-lowering statin drugs, implicating a role for lung lipids in RTT respiratory symptoms. Elevated fat in lung surfactant has previously been associated with respiratory distress and breathing disturbances. Therefore, a better understanding of how MeCP2 regulates fat in the lung will shed light on how and why these breathing difficulties manifest in RTT patients. Respiratory impairment is a severe and life-threatening hallmark of RTT. My findings will support the repurposing of lipid-lowering therapeutics to treat this devastating disease and greatly improve the quality of life of patients with RTT.

column36: The impact of prenatal malaria exposure on the susceptibility of offspring to psychiatric disorders.
column37: Worldwide, there are ~125 million pregnant women at risk of infection with malaria each year. Malaria infection during pregnancy (MiP) has severe consequences for the health of both mother and child. Studies have revealed a connection between infections in pregnant women and an increased risk of psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia in their children. Mental illness is a growing problem in areas with high malaria transmission, but the impact of MiP on offspring neurodevelopment has not been well studied. We have used an established animal model of MiP to examine whether MiP can prime offspring for mental illness later in life. We found that offspring born to malaria-infected mothers had abnormal psychiatric behavior in adulthood. Furthermore, brain cells from embryos of malaria-infected mice were mislocalized within the developing cortex, and exhibited an increased proportion of newly born neurons compared to unexposed embyros. The next steps of our research include further investigating the effect of MiP on autism spectrum disorder-like behaviours, as well as studying the consequences of MiP on the long-term trajectory of brain development (e.g. adult brain structure and cell types). We will also examine disturbances in other mechanisms of neurodevelopment that may underlie malaria-related psychiatric outcomes, and investigate potential therapeutic strategies to prevent neurological injury in MiP-exposed offspring. Factors that interfere with normal development of children lead to enormous financial and social costs for low-resource countries. This proposal suggests that malaria infection during pregnancy is one such factor, and one that is preventable. Since such a large number of pregnant women are at risk of malaria, this research has broad implications for global maternal-child health, as well as the potential to reduce the burden of mental illness in low-income countries.

column36: Investigation of PNP-3, a natural product antibiotic effective against multi-drug resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
column37: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multi-drug resistant bacterial pathogen deemed a top threat by both the Center for Disease Control and the World Health Organization. A. baumannii causes pneumonia, blood infections, wound infections, and meningitis in humans. To address this problem, over 100 strains of a group of bacteria called Pantoea were surveyed for antibiotic activity against A. baumannii, and two strains were identified. The purpose of this research is to attempt to isolate and characterize these antibiotics to assess their potential for therapeutic development. My objectives are to: 1) identify and characterize the genes responsible for antibiotic production in each Pantoea strain, 2) extract the antibiotics and identify the structures, 3) evaluate the antibiotic properties, and 4) explore the regulation of antibiotic production. To date, I have identified the genes responsible for antibiotic production in each Pantoea strain and found them to be identical, indicating that the same antibiotic is produced by both bacteria. The group of genes encode proteins that function to synthesize the antibiotic, transport the antibiotic, and regulate its production. I also found the antibiotic to be effective against a wide-range of human pathogens, including several multi-drug resistant A. baumannii strains, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and members of the bacterial group Enterobacteriaceae, all of which are on the World Health Organization's critical threat list. So far, several attempts to extract the antibiotic have been made; however, none have given clear results. Currently, I am attempting to overproduce the antibiotic in E. coli, which will hopefully allow for easier isolation of the antibiotic. Overall, my research highlights not only Pantoea as an antibiotic source, but also an antibiotic with potential to treat multi-drug resistant A. baumannii infections.

column36: Comorbidity and TBI in older adults: A population-based analysis
column37: Traumatic Brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability. While incidence among older adults is steadily increasing, we know very little about factor affecting outcomes this fastest growing segment of the population. To address this research gap, the purpose of this study is to examine how co-existing medical conditions affect older adults with TBI and their subsequent demand for healthcare services. This would be achieved in two phases - (1) a review of current literature and (2) an analysis of existing healthcare data. Specifically, Phase I comprises of a review of current research on the topic are to examine the link between co-existing medical conditions and outcomes in patients with TBI. Based on the review findings, Phase II will involve a population-based analysis of existing healthcare data of approximately 15,000 older adults (age>65) entering the hospital with a TBI in the province of Ontario, Canada. Through statistical tests and models, we will examine the health conditions older adults with traumatic brain injury have when they are hospitalized and how these conditions affect outcomes (healthcare resource utilization, physical functioning and discharge destination). As the first study of its kind to our knowledge, findings can assist in the development of more accurate assessments of the nature and impact of co-existing medical conditions in this vulnerable population. In particular, healthcare providers will be more aware of the different common medical conditions experienced by older adults with TBI, which will guide the planning of treatments and services targeted towards these individuals. On a policy level, the findings will help address the recognized need to inform future projections regarding which interventions might be most needed for which patients, in which settings, and at what time since injury, and highlight a systems approach necessary for the management of chronic disorders such as TBI.
