column36: Transforming Nurses' Work Environments Through a Strengths-Based Leadership and Management Training Program
column37: CHALLENGES: The current healthcare system is fragmented, depersonalized, disease-centric, and costly. Patients and families often feel powerless, disconnected, and voiceless, as do the nurses who care for them. Nurses report that dissatisfaction with the work environment is sufficient to make them want to leave nursing. Nurses often experience systemic sex and gender discrimination expressed in bullying, verbal abuse, and devaluing of their contributions, impacting their physical and mental health. What is needed is a paradigm shift from the current deficit-based management approach to a strength-based approach. Strengths-Based Nursing (SB-N/C) is both a philosophy and value driven-approach to guide the actions of clinicians, leaders, and managers. SB-N/C enhances, develops, and works with peoples' existing and potential strengths to bring out the best in the person and to contain, minimize, and/or circumvent what is not working. This shift requires re-training clinical managers and leaders to work through a strengths-based lens to build communities of caring and create safe workplaces for nurses ensuring that nurses can then provide safe, quality care to patients and families. GOALS & OBJECTIVES: The overall objective is to transform nurses' work-life environments from deficit-focused to strengths-focused through developing leaders/managers who are guided by a strengths-based approach to improve their health and productivity. To achieve this, we will refine a Strengths-Based-Leadership and Management (SB-L/M) Integrated Training Program for clinical leaders and managers with 3 components: 1- create and use innovative, multi-media teaching materials for story-sharing and sharing circles; 2- refine a 12-module course that integrates the best practice of healthcare with a SB-N/C approach paying attention to sex and gender issues in the workplace; 3- develop mentorship with situated coaching to ensure implementation and sustainability. Using a mixed-methods design, we will evaluate the processes and impact of this program on clinical leaders/managers, point-of-care nurses, and quality of patient/family care. PARTNERSHIP: To accomplish the objectives requires a multi-disciplinary Partnership. Partners continuing from Stage 1 (PDG) are: McGill University, Ingram School of Nursing, the birthplace of SB-N/C and SB-L/M; Concordia University's Center of Oral History and Digital Storytelling, with considerable expertise in multi-media story-sharing, collecting and analyzing oral histories and their impact on bringing about social change; and two clinical hospitals in Toronto, SickKids and Holland-Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital. Both hospitals have robust family-centred care, a developmental approach underpinning their pediatric care, and a commitment to SB-N/C in their strategic plans. Added to Stage 2 (PG) are: Two newclinical partners in Quebec, the Jewish General Hospital, Department of Nursing and CIUSSS-Ouest-de-L'Ile-de-Montreal, both of whom are committed to SB-N/C and strengthening their nurse-managers who directly supervise point-of-care nurses; the Canadian Nurses Association, the national voice of Canadian nursing profession that advocates on policy and legislation; and Concordia University's John Molson School of Business, bringing their experience and expertise in teaching operations, management skills, and in evaluation of the program. Our team continues collaboration with an award-winning visual anthropologist, and a knowledgeable scholar in sex and gender issues. Ultimately, this Partnership will contribute to a deeper understanding of the factors that create improvements to or obstacles in nurses' work-life environments, so that we can then inform policy and legislation at local, national, and international levels.

column36: Neuroimmune guidance cues, MicroRNAs & Inflammatory responses: Sex differences in cardiovascular diseases (MISs-CVD)
column37: Atherosclerotic vascular disease continues to be a leader of morbidity and mortality. Although sex hormones are known to play a role in this lipid- and inflammatory-driven disease, the underlying mechanisms are largely unclear. Neuroimmune guidance cues (NGCs) are key regulators of cell movement and positioning, and have emerged as significant players in inflammation. We have previously reported a role for Netrin-1 on macrophage emigration from plaques as well as key regulation of lipid metabolism by microRNA (miRNA)-33. Recently, we have uncovered sex-biased miRNAs targeting NGCs and hypothesize that these miRNAs provide missing mechanistic links in the endothelial-monocyte interactions and macrophage retention in the vascular wall during atherosclerosis in women vs men. We now seek to fully characterize the clinically relevant sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs in monocytes, plasma and aorta specimens from healthy subject and patients with atherosclerosis. We will also use primary endothelial cells and assess direct interactions between the sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs and unravel the functional impact of promising miRNAs on endothelial permeability, monocyte and macrophage trafficking and atherosclerosis using an innovative 3D vessel-on-a-chip platform and in vivo mouse models. This ambitious interdisciplinary project requires combined expertise of molecular cell biology, bioinformatics and physiology to provide crucial understanding of the gender differences in atherosclerosis and may provide novel gender specific therapeutic avenues to combat atherogenesis in both men and women.

column36: Unravelling proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) mechanisms in calcific aortic valve disease: from aortic valve sclerosis to stenosis
column37: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) is a fatal pathology that affects 2-3% of the population. Yet, drug therapies are ineffective, leaving the urgency to fully characterize the aetiology of aortic valve calcification (AVC) to develop innovative therapies. Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) binds to and targets the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). It was recently shown that individuals with loss-of-function genetic variant at the PCSK9 gene have low levels of atherogenic lipoprotein concentrations (LDL and Lipoprotein(a)) and reduced risk of coronary heart disease and CAVS. However, the mechanisms through which altered PCSK9 activity could protect against or cause CAVS is lacking. Our preliminary data suggest that PCSK9 plays an active role in CAVS. We will, therefore, determine whether PCSK9 is a causal risk factor for CAVS using genetic epidemiology. Further, we will shed light on the molecular underpinnings through which PCSK9 causes CAVS in humans using state-of-the-art in vivo as well as in vitro models in combination with next-generation sequencing. As a complementary and potential pre-clinical model, we will determine the role of PCSK9 in the development of aortic valve calcification in mice. The overarching aim of this research program is to provide the required biological evidence using a highly translational approach to support PCSK9 as a therapeutic target for the prevention and treatment of patients with CAVS.

column36: Knee joint function pre- and post-surgery among male and female paediatric patients
column37: It is well understood that adult males and females use different muscle activation and joint loading strategies during a range of movement tasks. It has also been established that females are more at risk, compared to males, of suffering a knee injury in the form of an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. Clinical guidelines have been established to help clinicians determine when a patient is ready to return to physical activity; however re-injury rates remain high,suggesting a need for improved objective assessment criteria. Injury rates are also on the rise in young, active children ages 8 to 18 years old. Each year, approximately 1 in every 20 girls playing competitive soccer or basketball will injure their ACL, or in other terms, one ACL injury per team. These injuries can be devastating to a young individual and there are currently no clinical guidelines specifically tailored to this age group to help optimize their rehabilitation. The overall purpose of my research is to understand how the knee joint is controlled in children who have injured their knee. In order to understand how an injury affects the knee joint differently between boys and girls, I will also evaluate how healthy children control their knee joint. I hope to identify differences in muscle activity and movement strategies between boys and girls that will help create better rehabilitation programs that can be used to improve recovery from a knee injury and prevent other children from having these traumatic injuries.

column36: The Neural Basis of Low-Dose versus Normal-Dose Psychostimulants on Executive Functions in Youth with Attention-Deficit / Hyperactivity Disorder: A Randomised Controlled Trial
column37: Attention-Deficit / Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and deficits in executive functions (EFs). EFs, which are associated with a brain area called prefrontal cortex (PFC), include abilities like attention, self-control, reasoning, and problem-solving. Our brain cells communicate with each other via neurotransmitters. In ADHD, there are lower levels of the neurotransmitter dopamine (DA). Psychostimulants (or stimulants) are often used as treatment as they increase DA. Some 50% of children with ADHD are now medicated with stimulants. Yet, they often struggle in school. At moderate-to-high doses, stimulants block DA's transporters. The striatum (a brain region associated with behavioural problems in ADHD) relies on that mechanism but PFC does not. Thus at those doses, stimulants should help the striatum function better, but not PFC. Recent animal neuroscience studies have now shown that at low doses, stimulants specifically help PFC. Given this, we reasoned that psychiatrists prescribing the right dose to help behaviour in ADHD might be giving too high a dose to help cognition. We just completed a triple-blind study where each youth with ADHD was tested once on their prescribed dose, and once on half that. Whether the full dose was given in the 1st or 2nd session was randomised. Regardless of whether the full dose was given in the 1st or 2nd session, all performed better on EF tasks when on half their dose. For my dissertation I would like to test the neural mechanism underlying this hypothesis. Using fMRI, I aim to show in youths with ADHD that at moderately high stimulant doses, the striatum works more efficiently and performance on a striatum-dependent task is better, while at a low dose, PFC works more efficiently and performance on a classic EF test is better. This is vital as understanding how the brain works on different stimulant doses could help us change the standard of care for ADHD, improving millions of lives.

column36: Identification of converging Molecular Pathways Across Chromatinopathies as Targets for Therapy: IMPACT
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) represent a large and heterogeneous group of disorders. Many NDD risk genes are involved in modification of DNA structure and conformation otherwise known as "chromatin". The end result is that these genes control the production of RNA by a process known as "transcription" which impacts its "translation" into protein in nerve cells. In this proposal we study five distinct NDDs that are grouped together as chromatinopathies: Kabuki, Kleefstra, Gabriele-de Vries, Helsmoortel-Van der Aa, and a syndromic type of Autism Syndrome Disorder. They are caused respectively by mutations in KMT2D, EHMT1, YY1, ADNP and CHD8, which are involved in regulation of chromatin and ultimately transcription. These syndromes share overlapping clinical features, are interconnected by the molecular role of the causative genes, which are further connected by molecular partners. We hypothesize that mutations in these five genes give rise to unique as well as common downstream effects in gene transcription and translation. In brief, we will generate stem cells with mutations in the 5 genes using a method called gene editing; differentiate them into nerve cells to study functional effects on neural connectivity and network circuitry; explore the underlying molecular mechanisms using sequencing approaches that assess chromatin states, RNA transcription and protein translation; and integrate these findings to validate common molecular targets that disrupt neural network activity in NDD. Therefore, the IMPACT collaborative project (featuring labs in Europe and Canada) will reveal common converging disease mechanisms as attractive targets for therapeutic intervention. The development of such knowledge-based therapeutic interventions across individual NDDs can potentially be useful for designing interventions suitable for multiple related rare neurodevelopmental disorders.

column36: Impact of Early life MetaBolic and psychosocial strEss on susceptibility to mental Disorders; from converging epigenetic signatures to novel targets for therapeutic intervention
column37: Each year 38.2% of the EU population suffers from a mental disorder. Extensive research on the biology of stress now shows that healthy development can be derailed by excessive or prolonged activation of stress response systems in the body and brain during fetal life. Such toxic stress can have damaging effects on learning, behavior, and mental health across the lifespan. The consortium has been built to integrate basic researchers and clinicians to work on two very relevant cohorts (offspring of obese or stressed mothers) that will be here combined in a very innovative way to ask specific questions on mental health risk factors and their potential prevention. One main concept is that maternal obesity during prenatal life can trigger similar responses to maternal stress, altering developmental trajectories and increasing the risk for mental health at adulthood. It is hypothesized that maternal stress might be accompanied by inappropriate nutrition patterns which could synergize in activating stress-response systems in the developing organism. These adverse experiences can increase the likelihood of developmental delays and later health problems, including heart disease, diabetes, and depression. This consortium will assess whether common biological signals characterise early exposure to metabolic and psychological stress, affecting the long-term expression of genes involved in brain as well as immune-metabolic function, triggering mental disorders. A special emphasis will be given to long lasting epigenetic modifications, which could alter context- and time-dependent expression of genes relevant for brain function as well as peripheral biomarkers indices of immune-metabolic function that might be used in the clinic for disease prevention and health promotion during pregnancy. The Canadian team will be responsible for mapping epigenetic modifications in human blood and brain samples.

column36: Co-designing dementia diagnosis and post-diagnostic care (COGNISANCE)
column37: Despite many national guidelines for diagnosis and management of dementia, persons diagnosed with dementia and their family care partners are often dissatisfied with the diagnostic process, and receive limited post-diagnostic support. Work packages will: (1) explore through surveys and focus groups current experiences, barriers and facilitators to dementia diagnosis and post-diagnosis support from the perspectives of persons with dementia, care partners and health care professionals; (2) develop internationally-applicable toolkits supporting guideline implementation for the at-risk public and health care professionals; (3) devise and deliver campaigns to produce behavioural change using the aforementioned toolkits in selected regions; (4) evaluate the campaigns using the RE-AIM framework including measuring impact on the diagnosis, post-diagnosis experiences, and practitioner attitudes and behaviour; (5) develop an implementation playbook outlining how to deliver similar campaigns in other countries COGNISANCE will provide a new internationally adaptable set of recommendations and toolkits for persons with dementia, care partners, and health care practitioners on how to make the diagnostic process and post-diagnostic care as positive an experience as possible, and a playbook to assist other countries with implementing their own change campaigns.

column36: Physiologically-based pharmacokinetic modelling of antibody-based drugs in children: Model development and population applications
column37: Children need drug therapies for cancer and other serious diseases, just like adults. However, we cannot use the same drugs at the same doses to treat both adults and children. Children are not just little adults - simply giving a lower dose based on size will not suffice. They are physiologically immature and many of the processes that govern the distribution of drugs in their bodies are not fully developed. We must account for these age-dependent differences in physiology when deriving safe and effective doses. This is especially true for cancer drugs, when side effects can be fatal. I design math models that are based on real physiology to paint a picture of the ways that drugs move and interact throughout our bodies. These models can be used to simulate the impact of certain physiologic differences on drug concentrations in the blood. For most medications, safety is linked to drug concentrations in the blood; higher concentrations lead to more side effects and poorer safety. My models simulate drug concentrations in children and enable us to make predictions about which drugs and doses are safest to use. With a strong prediction in place, fewer clinical trials are needed to explore safety and fewer children are needed to determine the "right dose." I focus on the newest class of drugs called the "monoclonal antibodies." Antibodies are targeted missiles against tumours. Each antibody's mission is to seek and destroy one specific protein that is essential for tumour growth or survival. In my future work, I will be refining a model for antibodies and trying to identify the age-dependent features in children that cause them to process these drugs so uniquely. My goal is ensure the best use of cancer medicines in children. I will strive to make cancer treatment just a small chapter in a child's life, and not the whole story.

column36: Brain-Based Evidence for Exercise as a Treatment for Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Globally, Canada has the highest proportion of people living with multiple sclerosis (MS) - a life-long disorder that damages the brain. Because there is no cure for MS, and people are typically diagnosed in early adulthood, most people require treatment for the majority of their lives. Unfortunately, many continue to experience debilitating symptoms and side effects despite medications, which cost $20,000-$40,000 per person. As a result, there is a strong need for low cost behavioural treatments that help to reduce MS symptoms. So far, there is some evidence that exercise may improve thinking skills, mood, fatigue, and quality of life for people with MS. However, little is understood about how exercise might help protect the brain in order to improve these symptoms. Our study will look at the impact of a cost-free walking exercise intervention on brain structure (using an brain imaging technique called magnetic resonance imaging) and MS symptoms. Specifically, we will look at whether exercise changes the brain in people who have MS and how these brain changes relate to thinking skills, mood, fatigue, and quality of life. This is the first study of its kind. Demonstrating the effectiveness of a free, easy-to-access exercise intervention would have a significant impact in reducing the cost of care and improving the quality of life for people with MS. A better understanding of how exercise affects brain structure and MS symptoms will help doctors better treat MS symptoms. Our ultimate goal is to help people with MS build a better quality of life (with increased thinking skills, and reduced depression and fatigue) by protecting the brain from the degenerative effects of MS through exercise.

column36: Scaling up the Family Carer Decision Support Intervention: A Transnational Effectiveness-Implementation Evaluation
column37: Dementia is increasing across the world. The effect of the disease on families, caregivers and communities is an important global public health challenge. Family carers of dementia patients often make end-of-life decisions for their family members. But, they do not know if these decisions are what their family member would want. Also, staff at care homes do not have the skills and information to speak with family members about end-of-life care decisions. Both of these experiences can put the person living with dementia at-risk for care that they would not want. This project will try to reduce the uncertainty towards end-of-life decision making. It will do this by using a tool called the Family Carer Decision Support (FCDS) intervention. The tool will tell family members about the options for end-of-life care for a person living with advanced dementia. This tool has been used in a study in Northern Ireland. In Northern Ireland, it helped families to make decisions about goals of care at the end-of-life. When this tool was used, family members were happier with the care given to their family member. The goal of this study is to use the tool in homes within different countries and determine if it is helpful for family members to make decisions. When the tool is used in different countries, it will encourage the use of the tool across the world. It will also encourage families to make end-of-life care decisions. This new information about the tool will also help set-up guidelines for the tool's use.

column36: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell dysfunction linked to schizophrenia: from mechanisms towards new therapeutic strategies (project coordinator: Dr. Maria Cecilia Angulo, project acronym: OPCphrenia)
column37: Schizophrenia is a heritable neurodevelopmental disorder affecting 0.5% of the world population. Symptoms include hallucinations, delusions as well as impaired cognition, attention and social interactions. The underlying brain pathology is abnormal function of a particular type of neuron, the fast-spiking inhibitory interneuron. Recent findings also implicate the abnormal integrity of myelin, a fatty substance that coats nerve cell projections and is essential for efficient neuronal signal propagation. Myelin is produced solely by oligodendrocytes, a non-neuronal cell type in the brain. Schizophrenia patient studies suggest myelination impairments could be a critical determinant of the disease. Yet, the mechanisms linking oligodendrocyte lineage cell dysfunction to schizophrenia are unknown. Our team has discovered unique properties of interneuron myelination and critical forms of communication between interneurons and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs). Given their intrinsic regenerative capacity as the cell type responsible for generating oligodendrocytes in the adult brain, OPCs represent a potential therapeutic target for enhancing the repair of myelin deficiencies in schizophrenia. Notably, we recently discovered that OPCs derived from genetically-identified familial schizophrenia patients have impaired function and defective myelination potential. Thus, we propose that schizophrenia is likely to be, at least in part, an OPC disease ("OPCphrenia"), arising from aberrant interneuron-OPC communication. In this proposal, we will dissect interneuron-OPC communication and investigate potential therapeutic rescue strategies for aberrant schizophrenia-related OPC dysfunction by re-balancing the levels of interneuron-secreted factors. We will leverage novel methodological advances, mouse genetics, and human patient samples to advance the understanding of schizophrenia pathophysiology and identify new molecular targets for future therapeutic intervention.

column36: Investigating how mechanosensitive neurons contribute to allodynia in neuropathic pain
column37: Millions of Canadians suffer from chronic pain that severely compromises their quality of life. One of the most debilitating symptoms is mechanical allodynia, wherein gentle touch is perceived to be extremely painful. The fact that current analgesics are not very effective at treating allodynia emphasizes the need for better understanding of how touch becomes painful. While perception of touch occurs in the brain, this perception depends on electrical signals coming from the periphery (usually skin). The skin in innervated by mechanosensitive neurons that have the ability to convert touch into electrical signals. My project will identify changes in how those electrical signals are generated under conditions associated with allodynia. To do this, I will record the electrical activity from mechanosensitive neurons while applying different stimuli to the skin. By making those neurons express a light-sensitive ion channel, I will compare touch and light stimulation. To link the changes in electrical activity to mechanical allodynia, I will then perform behavioural experiments to measure the pain response associated with these changes. Nerve-injured animals will be used as a model of chronic pain. This research will shed light on how neural coding by mechanosensitive neurons is disrupted in chronic pain and how this disruption leads to allodynia.

column36: Understanding Pain Mismanagement in Older Adults with Dementia
column37: The fastest-growing age group in Canada is that of older adults-those aged 65 or older. As individuals age, the likelihood of experiencing painful conditions and procedures increases, as does the likelihood of developing dementia. Despite the fact that pain is more common in older adults, it is often poorly managed in this group, especially among those with dementia. Pain diagnoses are commonly missed in older adults with dementia, and the pain that is diagnosed is often undertreated. This may be because individuals with dementia have difficulty communicating both verbally and nonverbally, or because those assessing their pain are making inaccurate judgments. Though the facial expression of pain in adults is stable and can be used as an alternative method of judging pain when verbal communication is compromised, this expression may change in dementia, possibly affecting communicative ability. In addition, people with negative attitudes about aging and dementia may be less accurate in judging older adults' pain. This study investigates how facial expressions of pain change in dementia, if these changes impair communication, and how observers' negative attitudes affect judgments of the pain of older adults. Initially, we will videotape facial expressions of pain during a physiotherapist assessment in older adults with and without dementia, and compare them to determine whether the facial expression of pain changes in dementia. Next, individuals with varying attitudes toward aging and dementia will rate the older adults' pain, to determine the extent to which negative attitudes about dementia and aging affect the accuracy of pain judgment. This study could improve pain treatment by improving communication and addressing bias in judgments of older adults with and without dementia. If we are able to understand why the pain of older adults is underestimated and undertreated, we can move toward implementing education and training programs to address the problem.

column36: Individualized prognosis and prediction of cognitive decline in cognitively normal individuals at risk of AD
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology is present in the brain 10-15 years before symptoms occur. As in most diseases, early treatment, before too much brain damage has been done, is likely to be more effective. However, accurately identifying people at risk of dementia due to AD early, before symptoms appear, is extremely difficult. We propose to study people with subjective cognitive decline (SCD) - they have issues with their memory or cognition, but not enough to be captured by standard cognitive tests. Such people have significantly increased risk of later dementia and are thus a logical group to study when looking at preclinical AD. Through multiple collaborations, we have built a database of MRI, cognitive and clinical data, with extensive follow up information from 4000+ subjects. We will use this data to develop and validate our DaMoCLES (Decline prediction using MRI, Cognition and LifEStyle) metric. DaMoCLES will combine (1) clinically available cardiovascular risk lifestyle factors known to be associated with cognitive decline, (2) tests of cognition that can be completed quickly in the clinic, and (3) results from sophisticated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis to detect patterns of brain atrophy typical of AD. DaMoCLES will be a clinically useful tool to determine which individual asymptomatic subjects will develop cognitive decline. (DaMoCLES will also be applicable in MCI to determine progression to AD, thus aiding in individualized prognosis in both preclinical and prodromal AD.) The DaMoCLES score will help clinicians to enable optimal treatment for patients. In addition, the DaMoCLES score will enable enrichment of populations studied in clinical trials, so that only people that are likely to get worse are included in the trials, and any benefit of the drug easier to see. This makes clinical trials more powerful, allowing drugs to be properly tested with fewer subjects over shorter durations, bringing new treatments to patients sooner.

column36: Integrated Parkinson Care Networks: addressing complex care in Parkinson disease in contemporary society
column37: Parkinson disease is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder that affects 80,000 Canadians and is expected to double by 2030 worldwide. Care needs are complex. The traditional model of care delivery centred in the physician has strains and limitations. Care Integration has the potential to improve patient quality of life by tailoring the care approach, facilitating the navigation of the patient and caregiver in the complex map of care resources available in the hospital and the community. Informed by the Ontario-developed Framework for Chronic Disease Prevention and Management, we have developed an Integrated Parkinson's disease Care Network in Canada with a significant attention to the participation of patient and care partners in the design of the proposed solutions. Following this model, we are now poised to develop it in other countries partnering with seven reference Parkinson's European centers. We will start by assessing 1) What are the views and needs of people with Parkinson's and care partners in a care delivery model based at home and the community, and 2) How can the implementation of a care delivery model based at home/community be successful in different social geographies and health-economical contexts. We will also develop a novel integrated solution of health technologies to optimize complex care delivery in PD using a patient-center approach throughout its entire development. This solution, the PD virtual coach, will be a powerful tool for empowerment of patients for self-management. Using the knowledge gathered during the early project activities, we will test the real-life feasibility of a patient-centred multi-national integrated care delivery model to set the foundations of its dissemination into national healthcare systems. iCARE-PD care delivery model has the potential to improve the lives of patients with PD and potentially with other neurodegenerative disorders, with optimal use of taxpayer money across a vast geography in Europe and Canada.

column36: Targeting TAO2 and its downstream pathway as critical effectors of Autism spectrum disorders in 16p11.2 microdeletion patients
column37: Atypical brain connectivity is a major contributor to the pathophysiology of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) including Autism spectrum disorders (ASD). TAO2 is one of several genes in the 16p11.2 microdeletion region susceptible to ASD, but whether it contributes to NDDs is unknown. Previously, we performed behavioral analysis on a Tao2 knockout (KO) mouse and found impairments in cognition, anxiety and social interaction. Tao2 KO mice have abnormal brain size and neural connectivity in multiple regions, deficits in dendrite and synapse formation, and reduced excitatory neurotransmission. Whole genome and exome sequencing of ASD families identified three de novo mutations in TAO2. Together, these data provide evidence that TAO2 is a neurodevelopmental disorder risk gene. Therefore, it is imperative to test whether TAOK2 and its downstream effectors are critical for ASD linked to the 16p11.2 microdeletion and whether activation of the TAOK2 pathway can overcome 16p11.2-associated abnormalities. Our proposal builds upon these observations to test the exciting hypothesis that TAO2 is a molecular hub in synapse function and ASD.

column36: Somatic DNA mosaicism of the ADNP gene in cells, ADNP-mouse tissues and tissues of a post-mortem ADNP individual: An indication of how this may affect disease.
column37: Autism, characterized by highly-variable qualitative impairments in social interaction and communication skills, is a poorly understood disorder. In this proposal, we will analyze a form of autism that is caused by mutations in a single gene called ADNP. The high frequency of clustered mutations of ADNP at the stem-loop forming sequence reveal this sequence is a mutation hotspot - somatic mutations of this may account for clinical variations in affected individuals. The potential to form an unusual DNA structure may predispose the sequence to an underlying mutation mechanism involving a DNA repair defect following pausing of a replication fork at these hairpin structures, or during aberrant repair in non-proliferating tissues. It is not known if these de novo mutations in the ADNP gene were incurred in the parental germ line and/or post-natally through the development and growth of the affected individual. The latter might be expected to display some degree of somatic mosaicism for the mutant allele. We developed a novel assay using the ultra-sensitive Digital Droplet PCR (dd-PCR) to assess, with high-sensitivity, the levels of ADNP mutation in DNA extracted from teeth, hair root cells (similar developmental origin as neurons) and ADNP patient-derived iPSCs of autistic offspring. The utility of this assay will permit the assessment of the potential contribution of somatic mutations of ADNP, and other genes, to autism. This could impact our ability to assess the clinical variability amongst affected individuals.

column36: DECODE! Decrypting Cadherin-13 function in cortico-cerebellar circuitry underlying neurodevelopmental disorders!
column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are a group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by deficits in social skills and communication, stereotyped and repetitive behavior, and a range of alterations in cognitive function. ASD shows high heritability and comorbidity with other disorders such as intellectual disability (ID) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), suggesting a strong involvement of genetic and neurodevelopmental elements in its aetiology. The recent progress in human genetics have led to the identification of hundreds of genes associated with autistic-like behaviors, including a growing number of genes encoding synaptic proteins. In particular, genetic variation in Cadherin-13 (CDH13) have been associated with several neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. It is currently unknown how CDH13 dysregulation underlies the pathophysiology of ASD and comorbid disorders. In DECODE! we will develop mouse models to study the cell- and circuit-specific effects of CDH13 deficiency. In addition we will harness the potential of human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) to characterize CDH13 dysfunction in patient iPSC-derived cultured inhibitory neurons at the molecular and cellular level. Understanding circuit-specific alterations caused by CDH13 deficiency in mouse and human models may ultimately help us designing targeted treatment of specific ASD symptoms.

column36: ADORe: TARGETING ADOLESCENT NEUROCOGNITIVE PROCESSES IN DEPRESSION TO PROMOTE INTERVENTION RESPONSE
column37: The World Health Organization "Health for the world's adolescents" report revealed that depression is the predominant cause of illness and disability and among the top three causes of mortality for adolescent boys and girls. Recent studies point to lasting effects of adolescent onset depression, including risk for treatment-resistance in adulthood. There is a need for better prevention, particularly targeted approaches that address the needs of those most vulnerable to depression. The proposed consortium will conduct researches on humans and animals, aiming to provide novel intervention components for at-risk individuals during the critical adolescent period. The researches will be focused on core brain regions and cognitive functions (reward, memory, stress response, and self-referent thinking) developing in adolescence, and relevant to depression risk. Using three exceptional cohorts which have recently completed long-term follow-up of adolescents at varying risk for depression, we will search for deviations of brain and cognitive functions involved in the transition to early-onset depression and subsequent to early onset depression; and we will recruit new samples to determine the role of these deviations in treatment response. Measures will be highly harmonized across experiments in animals and analyses in humans, including complementary intervention approaches. The causal role of cerebral or environmental factors on the deviations of cognitive functions and behaviors, and on intervention response, will be tested in animal studies and using existing databases from at risk youth. In the third year of this project, new brain targets for prevention of depression will be tested in animals. Novel cognitive targets for intervention will be applied in new at-risk adolescent samples: Canadian adolescents who did not respond to previous prevention for depression, and Romanian adolescents exposed to early childhood adversity.

column36: Multi-scale exploration of autoantibodies against synaptic receptors
column37: Psychotic disorders (PDs) encompassing schizophrenia and bipolar disorders, are major health problems worldwide. Growing evidence suggest that these major psychoses have a neurodevelopmental component involving in particular synaptic imbalance mostly between glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurotransmitter systems. However, due to their complexity our understanding of PDs remains limited. It is well-established that several converging factors are involved in these complex PDs, among which immune status, including autoimmunity, are particularly relevant. A role for autoimmune dysfunction in PDs, reported in schizophrenia almost a century ago, is supported by specific autoimmune responses to selfantigens identified in particular in PD. The importance of autoimmunity in major psychosis has been strongly reinforced as a number of syndromes characterized by global encephalopathy and by more focal psychiatric symptoms was found to result from autoimmune dysfunction, caused by anti-neuronal antibodies that alter synaptic transmission, such as NMDARAb in encephalitis. Thus, the role of the autoimmunity against neuronal receptor targets in the pathogenesis of PDs has gained tremendous support over the last years and urgently requires multidisciplinary in-depth investigations to unravel the molecular mechanisms underlying psychosis and offer new therapeutic strategies. We identified that almost 20% of patients diagnosed with schizophrenia are seropositive for these autoantibodies, opening therapeutical options for these patients. Here, we plan to tackle such a major challenge in a unique, complementary and synergistic consortium of clinical and basic research experts, who strongly contributed to our current understanding of autoimmunity in brain disorders. Our objective is to uncover how NMDAR-Ab underliesPDs in seropositive NMDAR-Ab patients, using a unique and multi-scale combination of experimental approaches, from pre-clinical experiments to clinical exploration.

column36: A novel paradigm for effective and safer treatment of schizophrenia: biased (ant)agonists with a characterized polypharmacological profile
column37: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a severe disease affecting 1-2% of the population. Current treatment is associated to side effects such as motor coordination problems, a feeling of the mind slowing down, abnormal electrical activity in the brain, altered heart rhythm, among many others. In addition, a high percentage of patients do not respond (30%) or only partially (additional 30%) to treatment. There is therefore a real need for developing better drugs. The drugs currently used to treat SZ are antipsychotics that act primarily through receptors that belong to a large family of proteins, the G protein-coupled receptors. They are present at the surface of neurons where they recognize and transduce the information of neurotransmitters. One of the main target of antipsychotic drugs is a receptor binding serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood control. However, these drugs are not fully selective and they also act on closely related receptors, the monoamine receptors, resulting in a polypharmacological profile. However, the relative contribution of each receptor to the beneficial and undesired effects is poorly understood. Moreover, each of these receptors control multiple cellular signaling cascades that are differentially regulated by distinct drugs. This phenomenon of 'biased signalling' is an important aspect of drug action. We therefore propose to develop chemical probes with defined biased and polypharmacology profiles to interrogate which signalling activities are responsible for alleviating the different SZ symptoms and which ones underlie the various side effects. For this purpose, we assembled an international team of experts with complementary know-how in computational and medicinal chemistry, molecular pharmacology and cell signalling as well as animal model of SZ. In addition to provide highly original insights into the mode of action of antipsychotics, these studies should open the way to the design of better and safer therapeutics for the treatment of SZ.

column36: INTEGRative multi-OMICs approaches on iPSC-derived 2D and 3D models to elucidate the role of immune and energy metabolism related genes/pathways in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
column37: ALS is the most common motor neuron disease. It is characterized by the death of motor neurons (MNs) in the brain and spinal cord. The disease starts in adult life and causes a progressive paralysis that is typically fatal within a few years, usually due to respiratory failure. The number of ALS cases worldwide is predicted to increase to nearly 400,000 in 2040, largely due to the aging population. Yet, no effective therapy is currently available for ALS. The current lack of treatments that can halt or reverse ALS highlights the need for disease relevant human cell-based experimental model systems to study the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the degeneration of motor circuits in ALS. In this regard, the present application seeks to develop and validate previously unavailable experimental model systems to study ALS pathophysiology based on both neuronal and glial cells derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) obtained from ALS patients or non-ALS controls. This project involves academic partners with solid expertise in ALS, iPSC technology and high-throughput ("omics") approaches. This unique combined international discovery effort will allow the assessment of the roles played by energy metabolism and immune pathways in ALS pathogenesis and their potential as therapeutic targets. Achieving these objectives will lead to new advances into the study of ALS pathophysiology and will contribute to the emerging field of ALS disease modeling based on disease-relevant human iPSC-derived cells. These are both important and timely goals of ALS research.

column36: Multilevel analyses of retinoic acid signaling to understand and treat a rare form of progressive motor impairment. (RAinRARE project)
column37: The main aim of this project is to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying a rare form of progressive motor impairment, called dystonia, associated with mutations in the RARb gene. This gene codes for a regulator of gene expression that is activated upon binding to retinoic acid, an active form of vitamin A. We have already shown that mutations found in the patients with dystonia enhance the activity of RARb in response to retinoic acid in cultured cells. We hypothesize that this increased activity of RARb disrupts the development or the function of a specific region of the brain, called the striatum, which is involved in the control of movements. Using a mouse model of this disease and patient-derived brain cells, we will investigate molecular alterations resulting from the most common mutant form of RARb with the goal of better understanding the mechanisms of the disease and developing rational treatments. The information generated in this project will allow us to build an integrated knowledge database that will provide a comprehensive blueprint of the retinoic acid receptor network function and dysfunction.

column37: Mature T-cell leukemias/lymphomas (MaTCL) are hematologic malignancies of mostly incurable prospects in light of limited efficient therapies. As a heterogeneous group of tumors, single MaTCL types are rare, which impedes large-volume biomaterial and data collections and clinical studies. Hyperactivating somatic mutations in JAK/STAT genes stand out as high-incidence aberrations across MaTCL entities. Particularly the model diseases investigated here, T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) and T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia (T-LGLL), carry those in 50-70% of cases. This interdisciplinary JAKSTAT-TARGET consortium of immunologists, hematologists, structural chemists, and systems biologists capitalizes on unique resources such as clinical registry-linked sample repositories, new high-fidelity mouse models, pipelines of structure-based target design, and in-silico machine learning tools. We propose that targeting the JAK/STAT signalling network in synergistic combinations with drugs inhibiting inter-connected other key driver pathways will improve individualized anti-leukemic efficacy. We will achieve this by three objectives (O): O1 will address the causal T-cell-receptor and cytokine mediated impact on genome integrity and on the occurrence of JAK/STAT mutations. It interrogates the biochemical and functional consequences of the mutated and unmutated clones, and derives actionable differential vulnerabilities. O2 will study the performance of identified synergistic drug combinations using in-house developed optimized STAT-inhibitors in novel animal models and primary samples. O3 will implement drug-screen data from patient material into an ongoing clinical trial. Ultimately, with machine-learning algorithms we will integrate the harmonized data of genomic profiles, drug-sensitivity patterns, and clinical outcomes from all objectives toward multi-omics guided predictions of optimal choices for trial designs and individual-patient based therapy selection.

column36: Violence against women migrants and refugees: Analysing causes and effective policy response
column37: Sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) is a major infringement of women's human rights, and an obstacle to sustainable development as set out in the SDGs. SGBV against migrant and refugee women is widespread, but often remains invisible and under-analysed both in academic research and policy-making. This research will take an intersectional approach to understand SGBV in the context of migration, analysing the ways in which discriminations and inequalities based on gender, race, nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity and age, interact to make certain women more vulnerable to SGBV and less able to access support and services for survivors than others. SGBV may be exacerbated by policies aiming to restrict migration, or to increase control of borders, which can push women into adopting dangerous routes to arrive in their country of destination. Conflict and the risks of migration may also render women vulnerable to trafficking and sexual exploitation. Conditions of reception, and policies for integration in receiving countries may also lead to increased risk of SGBV for migrant and refugee women. But these women are not just "victims", and their strategies and agency should also be explored. In sum while we know that female migrants and refugees are particularly exposed to violence we lack a systematic understanding of the underlying dynamics that (re)produce patterns of violence. It is this gap that the research seeks to fill in order to make policy recommendations for reducing these women's vulnerability to SGBV and increasing their access to services.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases are by far the most prevalent cause of death in developed countries. These diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, often result from atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is a fatty deposit of cholesterol, blood cells and fibres in the wall of arteries. Atherosclerotic plaques develop slowly over time. They gradually encroach onto the interior of blood vessels, and only become symptomatic when a blood vessel is obstructed by 70% or more. A more serious situation arises when the atherosclerotic plaque ruptures suddenly. This happens because the contents of the plaque include fatty deposits that provide poor resistance to daily wear and tear. If a large fatty deposit is accompanied by a thin cap (the cap forms a protective fibrous layer between the atherosclerotic plaque and the interior of the blood vessel), the risk of rupture is enhanced. When a rupture occurs, the contents of the atherosclerotic plaque are exposed to the blood flowing in the vessel, leading to the formation of a blood clot within the vessel. This may completely and suddenly block the vessel, causing heart attack or stroke. Our proposed research will investigate a new treatment option that would reinforce the plaque cap, rendering plaques less susceptible to rupture, based on molecules that influence protein synthesis within cells.

column36: Role, function, and regulation of the delta opioid receptor and its implications for the treatment of pain
column37: Despite the existence of a multitude of drugs with analgesic properties, the treatment of pain often remains problematic. Notwithstanding significant side effects (constipation, nausea, sedation), alkaloid compounds remain the most effective drugs to relieve chronic pain. The best known of all alkaloids undoubtedly remains morphine, belonging to the family of opiates. Morphine and its derivatives bind and activate at least three subtypes of G protein-coupled receptors, the mu (MOP), delta (DOP) and kappa (KOP) opioid receptors. Although these three receptor subtypes possess analgesic properties, the actions of the majority of opioids used clinically target MOP. In contrast to the latter, activation of DOP leads to few unwanted effects. Under normal conditions (i.e. in healthy animals), the analgesic potency of delta selective agonists is lower than that of morphine. In recent years, however, it has been shown that under certain conditions, the activation of DOP can counter the painful sensations with an efficacy close to morphine. In my laboratory we are interested in studying the mechanisms regulating the trafficking of DOP toward the plasma membrane of nociceptive neurons under conditions of chronic pain. A better understanding of these mechanisms could help develop strategies to increase the effectiveness of pain therapies and thus improve the quality of life of patients.

column37: The Cardiovascular Health Awareness Program (CHAP) is a community-based, volunteer-led cardiovascular risk assessment and blood pressure monitoring program with health education/promotion sessions for older adults living in the communities. This region is similar to the setting of other LMIC that has isolated areas, poor roads, several ethnic and linguistic groups, and scarce health resources. The scale-up process will include a team of partners and collaborators from the Philippines and other countries including lay volunteer health workers, researchers, health professionals, public health officials, and politicians. We will conduct several meetings to present CHAP-P; discuss the needs to prepare for its implementation including preparing materials and equipments, personnel training, and cost-sharing; and set-up ways to monitor and evaluate CHAP-P so that the community residents can benefit from the program more. We will document how CHAP-P was scaled up, identify barriers in the process and solutions to overcome them, and produce a guideline on how to scale-up CHAP-P so that other Regions in the Philippines and other countries can use what we learned in this process.

column36: Exercise as a countermeasure for inflammation processes and loss in neuromotor drive following muscle disuse: the SAFE randomized controlled trial.
column37: As evidenced in astronauts returning from a space camp mission, muscle disuse occurs in elderly and frail individuals through the same mechanisms. As the actual scientific research era hinges on patient-centered outcomes, it is equally important to develop tools that are scientifically reliable and of interest and at the patient's benefit. As muscle disuse leads to deleterious and unwanted consequences, there is a momentum to develop countermeasures to initiate prevention. As such, although exercise was proposed as a very efficient strategy to offset the impact of inactivity in those patients, reliable tools to manage its regimen and to evaluate its efficiency are still expected. The SAFE trial focuses on important surrogate outcomes of muscle wasting and loss of function. Eligible healthy participants, aged 55-65 years old, will randomly be allocated to the control (physiotherapy + psychological support) or intervention (physiotherapy + psychological support + 60 min of exercise/day) arms of the study. Trial will be conducted in the context of a bed rest laboratory, where participants will be lying down in bed on a 24/7 regimen during 14 days. Using pragmatic samples (blood and muscle biopsies), to facilitate the future implementation in the clinic, inflammation markers and neuromuscular activity and function will be assessed. Participants will be assessed at 7 days, 4 weeks and 4 months post-intervention. Conclusive evidence that the proposed markers and sophisticated measures accurately monitor neuromuscular changes would certainly change the management of these patients by physicians and therapists during space flight or in context of frailty. The success of the SAFE trial will be secured through the collaboration of a multidisciplary team composed of trainees, young, mid-career and senior researchers with expertise in aging, exercise and muscle function and biostatistics.

column36: Addiction, Health Risks and Recovery in Context of Social Precarity: How to Better Address Complex Needs Taking into Account Gender and Life Stages
column37: Vulnerable populations that experience social precarity tend to have a chronic SUD and require long-term services that are adapted to their complex care needs. Examination of the distinct contexts related to PS use, health risks, and services in France, Belgium, and Canada will help to develop contextualized knowledge that can enhance life-stage-responsive and gender-responsive services locally and internationally, taking into account the needs of specific populations.

column36: Targeting potassium channel to disrupt the cellular hierarchy and suppress malignant growth of pediatric brain tumor
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The conventional treatment, which combines surgery, irradiation and chemotherapy, is toxic to normal brain cells and produces life-long side effects such as lowered intelligence, early aging, and increased chance to develop other cancer. Therefore, identifying the molecules that fuel aggressive MB growth but are dispensable for normal cells is key to develop cancer-specific therapy. Ions, such as potassium and chloride, are essential constituents of human cell. Ion channel proteins form tiny pores to control ion to move in or out of cell. The movement of ions can change the electrical and physical properties of the cells, which control biological processes including tumor growth. We recently found that potassium channel Eag2 is required for MB growth, discovered a drug as a novel Eag2 blocker, and showed that the drug had marked anti-MB efficacy in mice and a MB patient. Therefore, we pioneer in identifying ion channels as novel regulators for MB and developing ion channel-targeting therapy. Brain tumor-initiating cells (BTICs) are rare cells that generate multiple tumor cell types to fuel the malignant brain tumor growth. Since BTICs are insensitive to irradiation and conventional chemotherapy, they are the roots for tumor initiation and recurrence. While Eag2 regulates the growth of non-BTICs, our unpublished study identified that potassium channel Kcnb2 is present in MB BTICs. We discovered that genetic deletion of Kcnb2 reduced the number of BTICs and suppressed MB growth, but it did not overtly alter the normal development of mice. We propose to define the mechanism by which Kcnb2 regulates BTICs and MB growth, and determine the therapeutic efficacy of combining Kcnb2 inhibition and conventional therapy. By completing our studies, we will uncover the unrealized potential of targeting ion channels to treat brain cancer by attacking the root of brain tumor growth and recurrence.

column36: Unitization: a strategy to circumvent memory deficits in aging and amnesia.
column37: Memory is the repository of our personal histories and stored knowledge, and it is essential to planning our futures and maintaining a sense of self. By 2036, almost a quarter of Canadians will be aged 65 and older, and many will experience memory decline. As memory declines, other cognitive functions are affected, as are daily activities. To support our aging population we must develop simple, cost-effective cognitive strategies to alleviate age-related memory declines. We recently discovered that a cognitive strategy, unitization, supports memory function in older adults and even in cases of amnesia who have severe impairments in memory. Through unitization, information about multiple items is represented as a single unit through an interaction between new and existing knowledge. In order to ultimately use unitization more widely to improve cognition in memory-impaired individuals, we must first understand what level of cognitive and neural function is needed for the strategy to be successfully used. We will use neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies to examine the cognitive functions and brain regions that correlate with the successful use of unitization. This will allow us to predict which people would be most likely to benefit from unitization. Additionally, we will examine if unitization can support inference, a cognitive function that relies on memory. The ability to infer information beyond what is directly observed is essential to daily living, as it plays a role in problem solving and in guiding behavior in social interactions. Successful use of unitization to alleviate impairments in inference will show how unitization has broad potential to support declining cognition, allowing older adults to maintain their independence and quality of life for longer.

column37: This fellowship will support the Toronto Rehabilitation Institute - University Health Network (TRI-UHN) in addressing the critical challenge of preventing violence across its diverse rehabilitation sites by optimizing the use of remote monitoring technologies (e.g. video-cameras, motion sensors). While the use of remote monitoring technologies for quality improvement such as fall prevention is becoming more popular, it has yet to be implemented systematically and has yet to be used for the purpose of violence prevention. Little formative research has been conducted on diverse stakeholders' (e.g. patients and families, health care providers and program directors) perceptions of remote monitoring technologies, and policies and guidelines are limited in directing implementation. Safety has recently been identified as a major organizational impact goal for TRI-UHN, along with an interest in expanding the use of remote monitoring technologies to prevent violence and enhance safety. In partnership with the University of Toronto, this two-year experiential fellowship will focus on developing, implementing and evaluating a protocol for use of remote technologies to prevent violence. This will offer the opportunity to develop and strengthen the following enriched competencies: leadership, mentorship, and collaboration; change management and implementation; and analysis and evaluation of health and health-related policies and programs.

column37: Le systeme de sante au Quebec, fait face au defi des soins pour une population vieillissante, soufrant souvent de plusieurs maladies chroniques a l'origine de besoins de plus en plus complexes. column36: Evidence-Based Strategic Directions to Reduce Emergency Department Patient Wait Times within the Hamilton Niagara Haldimand Brant Local Health Integration Network (HNHB LHIN)
column37: Increasing emergency department (ED) patient wait times represent a substantial challenge for health care systems in numerous jurisdictions. In the province of Ontario, there were 5.8 million ED visits in fiscal year 2016-17, a 1% increase over the volume in 2015-16. However, over the same time period, the ED wait times increased by 11% for admitted patients. Over the past few months, substantially high lengths of stay times in Ontario EDs have garnered significant media attention. Longer ED wait times are related to a greater risk of adverse patient outcomes, increased rates of patients leaving without being seen, patient dissatisfaction, ambulance offload delays, and higher levels of stress among ED health professionals. The available research indicates that ED wait times are influenced by factors at three levels: individual patient, hospital institution, and system features. In 2016-17, the HNHB LHIN had the fifth highest ED volumes at 572,770 and the highest ambulance volumes at 116,492 in the province, as well as the worst ED wait times among all 14 LHINs. This project will use a mixed research methods approach to undertake an in-depth analysis of the ED wait time situation within the HNHB LHIN in comparison to five LHINs located in southern Ontario. The findings from the quantitative and qualitative data analyses will be assessed to identify the input and output factors affecting patient throughput and increased ED wait times in the HNHB LHIN in comparison to other LHINs. These factors will be assessed in the context of the Institute of Medicine's aims for the improvement of health care. Based on this, evidence-based strategic recommendations on potential opportunities for alleviating ED pressures will be made to the HNHB LHIN.

column36: Strengthening health system support of caregivers' readiness for engagement in autism care
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is estimated to affect 1 in 66 children, or roughly 350,000 people, in Canada. The impact is far greater when one considers the complex needs of families affected by ASD. Autism Ontario is a non-profit organization whose goal is to strengthen support for caregivers and families of children with ASD, and it works with government to understand the needs and find solutions. More and more, parents or caregivers of children with ASD are being asked to play a role in their child's intervention services and care. While research shows such involvement can be useful, the extra demands can be difficult for some caregivers for a variety of reasons. Health, education and other systems of care need a way to better understand, measure, and support parents' readiness to meet demands of engaging in care. With the right knowledge and measurement tools, such systems can tailor and adjust how they involve caregivers to be more sensitive to their unique needs and strengths. This will prepare such systems to better support family health at a critical time, promoting better outcomes. The proposed fellowship project is a partnership with Autism Ontario, and has two aims. First, the research fellow will conduct a review the literature using systematic methods to summarize what is known about the factors influencing parent involvement in their child's care. Second, the fellow will develop a new measure of parents' readiness and ability to meet these demands for involvement. Information for developing this measure will come from the literature review and from interviewing people on both sides-parents of children with ASD, and professionals that provide ASD services. The measure will then be tested to ensure it works well in a clinical setting. When ready, it will be made available, free of charge, for care providers across Canada to monitor and improve service delivery to families of children with ASD.

column36: Indigenizing harm reduction: Identifying barriers to Western systems and supporting community-driven approaches to reduce opioid-related mortalities among Indigenous people who use drugs in British Columbia
column37: As the opioid crisis in Canada continues, British Columbia is undoubtedly the epicentre with over 1,400 fatal overdoses in 2017. Government statistics indicate that First Nations people are five times more likely to die of an overdose than non-First Nations people in BC, and that this difference is greater for First Nations women and youth compared to non-First Nations women and youth. Despite an array of harm reduction and addiction treatment services in BC, First Nations people encounter several barriers to accessing and completing care and services including, racism and stigma, lack of service availability and anonymity in rural and remote communities, and trauma associated with colonization and the residential school system. In 2013, the First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) became the only province-wide First Nations health authority and since then, has been a primary player in BC's response to the crisis. As such, FNHA has identified key policy challenges that the proposed work will seek to address: prevent fatal overdoses, reduce drug-related harms (e.g., HIV), and increase service access, treatment options and culturally safe support for Indigenous people who use drugs (IPWUD) throughout the province. The proposed work will consist of 3 components with the overarching goal to develop a First Nations-led model of harm reduction that improves access and retention to supports and services, ultimately reducing opioid-related deaths among IPWUD. Part of the work will involve community-based research with 5 of BC's First Nations from each of FNHA's health regions to help articulate 'promising practices' from community harm reduction programs. The other components will identify ways to improve access, retention and cultural safety of harm reduction and treatment services in collaboration with FNHA and the provincially-mandated BC Centre on Substance Use. Findings will inform FNHA policy and programming, and be shared with health system partners in BC and beyond.

column36: Immunization on a budget: Using health economics to inform immunization policy in Alberta
column37: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) causes upper and lower respiratory tract illnesses in adults and children. While generally mild in adults, RSV can result in serious illness, hospitalization and death in infants. To date, the best method to prevent serious RSV infection is the passive immunization of at-risk children with 4-5 doses of the drug palivizumab during the RSV season. Due to the high price tag for a course of palivizumab (~$5,600 per child per season in Canada; totalling $2-3 million per season in Alberta), there is ongoing debate about the cost-effectiveness of this intervention. The Canadian Pediatric Society (CPS) recently updated their recommendations on the use of palivizumab; however, Alberta is not currently following these updated recommendations. The Alberta Ministry of Health is considering more closely aligning their RSV prevention policies with the eligibility criteria currently recommended by CPS; however, prior to making a decision they want to understand the economic and health consequences of applying different palivizumab guidelines in Alberta. To address this issue, we will determine the utilization and cost associated with palivizumab in Alberta. column36: Measuring the impact of current and future harm reduction strategies in the ongoing opioid overdose epidemic in British Columbia
column37: North America is currently experiencing an opioid overdose crisis and this has been particularly pronounced in British Columbia (BC). In this jurisdiction there has been a rapid increase in overdose deaths since 2012, which has largely been driven by an increasing concentration of synthetic and more potent opioids in the illegal drug supply market. Despite a large effort within the province to reduce opioid-related harm, overdose deaths have continued to rise. This includes a scaling-up of BC's Take Home Naloxone program, a non-clinician administered therapy that is highly effective at reducing the effects of an overdose. More novel interventions have also included the introduction of opioid overdose sites, where people who use drugs can be observed and helped if they overdose. There is therefore a greatly urgent and important need to estimate the impact of these interventions and where new resources would be best positioned to have the most impact. In collaboration with the BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions (the Ministry) and with support from BC Centre for Disease Control and the Ministry of Health, I will estimate the impact of the current interventions to date as well as project the impact of future interventions and scale-up. I will combine together cutting-edge mathematical modelling and statistical techniques with provincial administrative datasets to evaluate the current provincial interventions and estimate the number of deaths averted due to current intervention scale-up and proposed novel interventions. The collaboration with both Ministries will ensure modelled scenarios will reflect policy proposals and help to support and inform their decisions.

column36: Economic evaluation and cost valuation of a province-wide quality improvement initiative: a case study of 'Call for Less Antipsychotics in Residential Care' (CLeAR) in British Columbia

column36: Harnessing Health Systems to Optimize Biomedical Prevention for HIV Elimination among Gay, Bisexual, and Other Men Who Have Sex with Men in Canada
column37: Effective biomedical HIV prevention technologies such as Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis and Treatment as Prevention, combined with regular and accessible HIV testing and linkage to care, have the potential to vastly improve the health of people living with HIV and eliminate HIV transmission to HIV-negative individuals. With a cost savings of approximately $300,000 per averted HIV infection, these tools represent an opportunity for significant cost savings to the Canadian health care system. However, access to biomedical HIV testing, treatment, and prevention services remains patchwork across Canada, and HIV incidence among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) remains elevated, with gbMSM being 71 times more likely to acquire HIV than other men. This suggests that further work is needed to ensure health systems are sufficiently equipped to meet the needs of this diverse community. As such, this fellowship leverages the newly-formed Community Alliance project - a collaboration between Canada's leading gay and bisexual men's health organizations - to improve health systems access for gbMSM by (1) by developing a robust evidence base for health systems change through the identification and synthesis of regional and national data sources; (2) developing a monitoring-and-evaluation framework for measuring progress towards programmatic goals; and (3) building research and analytic capacity among community-based partners and researchers to promote ongoing data synthesis, analysis and reporting. Primary data for this project will be drawn from Sex Now - a serial cross-sectional survey of over 8,000 gbMSM across Canada administered by the Community Based Centre for Gay Men's Health (CBRC). Findings will be disseminated through the Community Alliance, which will leverage them to develop strategic partnerships for the betterment of health systems serving gbMSM, resulting in improved quality of life and health outcomes for people living with and affected by HIV.

column36: Informing Policy on School Transitions for Children with Disabilities in Alberta
column37: Children with disabilities face many problems across their lives. On average, they are less likely to go to university and work, and they earn less than others. This research looks at health care problems resulting from transitions across school life and how to decrease these problems. Next, we examine if the use of support programs reduces poor outcomes found during high risk transitions. Finally, we will work with partners in the government and schools to find better ways to support these children during high risk transitions. column36: The social organization of Family Integrated Care (FICare): Mapping coordination of care in NICUs for effective scale and spread
column37: Babies born before 37 weeks of gestation cause serious concerns for their families, care providers, and the health system. These babies are preterm and require care in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) to grow and develop. Admission to the NICU can interfere with early parent-infant relationships and contributes to parental stress. For the most critically ill preterm babies (born before 32 weeks gestation), integrating families into their baby's care (Family Integrated Care or FICare) helps babies gain weight faster and reduces parental distress. We don't know if FICare improves outcomes for babies who are born between 32 and 36 weeks gestation and admitted to a Level II NICU. We do want to know if FICare improves outcomes for babies and their parents, reduces the length of time they are patients in the NICU, and reduces costs. If FICare is effective we want to make this kind of care common practice in all Level II NICUs. If FICare is not effective in reducing length of NICU stay for babies we still need to understand why outcomes were not improved. Therefore, we need to understand how FICare is actually working, and whether it requires adaptation before it is put into practice. Qualitative interview data about health care providers, hospital administrators, and parental experiences of FICare will be analyzed. For this project I will map activities that show how FICare is actually working, and how care is being coordinated by institutional work processes. From this analysis, I will identify the gaps between FICare and how care actually plays out in the NICU. The discoveries will inform how FICare can be adapted and implemented with integrity.

column36: Structural analysis of mycobacterial oxidative phosphorylation and targeting it to treat tuberculosis
column37: Cells use oxygen to convert chemical energy from diverse sources into the universal energy currency ATP before use. This process, called oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos), is performed by a series of large molecular machines that reside in cell membranes. In OxPhos, electrons stripped from fuel molecules ("oxidation") are passed between several of the molecular machines (Complexes I, II, III, and IV) with oxygen serving as the final electron acceptor, reducing it to water. During electron transfer Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from one side of the membrane to the other, establishing a chemical and electrical proton gradient. A final machine, known as ATP synthase, allows protons back across the membrane, using the energy released to make ATP. While example atomic-resolution structures have now been determined for all OxPhos complexes it is still not clear how electron transfer is coupled to the proton pumping that powers aerobic life. Understanding OxPhos has important biomedical implications. Tuberculosis (TB), caused by the organism Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is a leading causes of death worldwide and an important health issue in Canada's indigenous populations. The breakthrough TB drug bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase. Mycobacterial Complexes III and IV form an unusual supercomplex (CIII2CIV2) with a dramatically different structure than the human Complexes III and IV. This structure is both unique and essential, making it an attractive target for developing TB drugs. We will determine structures for CIII2CIV2 and ATP synthase from mycobacteria. The unique CIII2CIV2, which carries out two thirds of the electron transfer pathway in a self contained stable assembly, provides a valuable tool for understanding universal principles of electron transfer. Structures of CIII2CIV2 and mycobacterial ATP synthase in complex with approved and candidate antimycobacterial drugs will provide key insights into how these drugs work and can be improved.
