column36: The role of Rap1 GTPase in coordinating cell adhesion and cytoskeletal rearrangement during epithelial wound healing
column37: Cells move collectively to drive many fundamental physiological and pathophysiological processes. For example, collective cell migration during development ensures the proper formation of different tissues. On the other hand, cancer metastasis occurs when cancer cells migrate together away from a tumour. In all cases, the mechanisms by which cells coordinate their movement are still unclear. Generally, cells interact with each other through cell adhesions, which link cells to each other and their environment, and the cytoskeleton, which provides structure and a means for generating contractility. In this project, I will use the Drosophila embryo to study collective cell migration during wound healing, which is a process conserved across species. Post-wounding, cells at the exposed edge simultaneously rearrange their adhesions and cytoskeleton to facilitate rapid, scarless repair, but it is unclear what mediates this response. I hypothesize that the GTPase Rap1 drives both reorganization of adhesions and the cytoskeleton to mount a collective cell response to wounding. Rap1 has been demonstrated in different contexts to respond to mechanical cues, affect distribution of cell adhesion proteins, and interact with cytoskeletal organizers. I will first track Rap1 localization and activity during wound repair and the effect of removing Rap1 on wound closure dynamics using timelapse confocal microscopy and image processing to determine the role of Rap1. Then, I will quantify the effect of Rap1 activity on the localization and dynamics of adhesive and cytoskeletal structures during wound repair. Finally, I will test the sensitivity of Rap1 activation to mechanical load exerted by the cytoskeleton and across cell-cell adhesions. My findings will elucidate how mechanical and molecular signals are integrated to coordinate cell movements via dynamic regulation of adhesions and the cytoskeleton, contributing to the overall understanding of collective cell migration.

column36: Electroconvulsive Therapy: Analysis of its Safety and Efficacy
column37: Depression affects about 20% of the population in their lifetime and is now the leading cause of illness burden worldwide. It is usually treated with either medications or psychotherapy but a substantial number of people do not respond to these treatments. In this case, a treatment known as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) may be offered. ECT uses electricity delivered under anesthesia to induce a generalized seizure, which is thought to be safe and effective for depression. Numerous clinical trials of ECT have shown it to be effective in treating depression and reducing suicidal thoughts. Furthermore, recent work using administrative health data from Ontario found extremely low rates of adverse medical events (AME) - similar to low-risk outpatient surgeries. Despite this, <1% of depressed individuals receive ECT which may be due to lack of knowledge about ECT's relationship with patient-relevant outcomes for AME (death or hospitalization) and suicide (attempted or completed). We do not currently know the specific contribution of ECT to either of these outcomes as individuals with depression have higher rates for both. Determining the specific contribution of ECT to suicide or AME requires comparing large groups of individuals who receive ECT to a group of similar individuals who do not receive ECT. While there have been previous studies comparing individuals receiving ECT to those not, these have been limited by differences between groups and were conducted in a single location. Therefore, our goal is to compare depressed individuals who receive ECT to a closely matched group of individuals who do not receive ECT using data from the province of Ontario. We hypothesize individuals who receive ECT will have a slightly increased risk of AME (due to the anesthesia required for ECT) but reduced risk of suicide (due to the effectiveness of ECT for treating depression). We believe this knowledge will improve patients' ability to make effective decisions regarding ECT.

column36: Functional Connectivity Biomarkers of Remission and Relapse in Patients with Psychotic Depression
column37: Psychotic depression is a severe psychiatric disorder in which psychotic symptoms (e.g. delusions, hallucinations) emerge during a major depressive episode. Compared to non-psychotic depression, psychotic depression is associated with longer recovery times and an increased risk of suicide. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (R-fMRI) has been used to examine functional connectivity in brain networks and previous studies have demonstrated relationships between functional connectivity and treatment outcomes. The default mode network (DMN) refers to a set of brain regions that demonstrate functional connectivity with each other. The DMN has been studied extensively in non-psychotic depression and a recent study from our group is the first to specifically examine the DMN in psychotic depression. This preliminary study demonstrates that patients who remit from psychotic depression have replicable patterns of abnormal functional connectivity between the DMN and other brain regions involved in sensory processing. This abnormal functional connectivity may be associated with sustained remission (when patients remain well and are symptom free) or relapse (when patients become acutely ill again with a new episode of psychotic depression). We propose to extend our preliminary findings into the full neuroimaging dataset and examine longitudinal DMN functional connectivity. This novel R-fMRI project will also assess whether changes in functional connectivity are associated with the subgenual cingulate, a brain region that has been consistently implicated in severe depression. The discoveries made in this project will directly impact the lack of neurobiological knowledge about psychotic depression. This study will also allow biomarkers to be associated with treatment outcomes with the goal of advancing clinical practice by using neuroimaging to guide treatment decisions.

column36: Identifying the neural correlates of cognitive reserve in late-life depression: A dimensional, data-driven approach
column37: Late-life depression affects approximately 20% of older adults in Canada, though the rates can be as high as 40% in hospitals. Chronic, or treatment-resistant late-life depression (TRLLD) escalates the risk for both Alzheimer's and vascular dementia by as much as 33%. As Canada's population ages, the increasing number of older adults suffering from dementia represents a massive drain on social and healthcare resources. Lifestyle factors such as exercise, education, challenging jobs and learning a second language are collectively known as cognitive reserve (CR) and extend the amount of time a person can cope with Alzheimer's-related degeneration. Two brain circuits involved in cognitive ability and memory are both decimated by TRLLD and dementia, while CR actively strengthens brain regions involved in these functions. Does having higher CR allow people with TRLLD to recover faster and perhaps avert the conversion to dementia? In the present study, we will assess the impact of CR on cognitive ability and memory in older adults with TRLLD at first visit and across time through the course of novel drug treatments. We predict that higher CR accrued over the lifetime will strengthen brain circuits involved in cognitive ability thus allowing these individuals to better resist the devastating effects of TRLLD. Additionally, novel work from our group shows that patient subgroups can be identified using optimal combinations of brain imaging and behavioral data. These subgroups likely represent more biologically plausible groupings than clinical labels afford. We propose to use this technique to identify subgroups of individuals with TRLLD and varying amounts of CR. People with higher CR should respond to novel treatments faster and have a lower risk of converting to dementia. Conversely, these findings also represent a novel way to identify those individuals most at risk of converting to dementia which will allow for intervention far in advance of cognitive impairment.

column36: Investigating the lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG-3) exhaustion marker and its associated defects in invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) immune cell function in HIV infection
column37: Background: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a global health issue, with 36.9 million HIV-infected people in 2018. HIV exhausts the infected person's immune system to the point where it cannot properly fight infections. Despite treatment with anti-HIV drugs to stop virus replication, immune system exhaustion still occurs. Understanding how to reverse this exhaustion is critical in enhancing long-term well-being of HIV-infected people. We have shown that a protein, lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG-3), inhibits immune cells from functioning in HIV infection. LAG-3 is like the handbrake of a car. If you leave the handbrake on while driving, the car will never reach its full-speed. So, with LAG-3 present, the immune system cannot reach its full potential and fight infections. Our lab has shown there is more LAG-3 on immune cells called invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells of HIV-infected people. iNKT cells are essential to a strong immune response; if iNKT cells do not function properly due to LAG-3, the immune system cannot work optimally to protect individuals. Hypothesis: I will determine if by blocking LAG-3, we will remove its handbrake-effect, allowing iNKT cells to work properly, helping to restore the immune system in HIV-infected people. Approach & Importance: In the lab, immune cells from HIV-infected participants will be exposed to a protein, called an antibody, which binds LAG-3 and prevents its handbrake activity. Once LAG-3 is blocked, we determine if iNKT cell activity returns back to normal by measuring how well the iNKT cell now functions. LAG-3 blockades are already in clinical trials to reverse cancer-related immune exhaustion, but LAG-3 research in the HIV field is limited. My project is highly feasible and future applications are very relevant, as the goal is to provide data to ultimately move the LAG-3 exhaustion marker blockade into HIV treatment clinical trials. If successful, this opens doors to transformative approaches in HIV therapy.

column36: Developing a Genome-Wide Platform to Profile Antibiotic Targets and to Identify Novel Bioactive Scaffolds Effective Against Antibiotic-Resistant Pathogens
column37: The ability of drugs to treat many deadly diseases is decreasing due to antibiotic resistance. This is especially worrisome for Gram-negative bacteria, which have high natural resistance to many currently used antibiotics. Pharmaceutical companies rarely invest in creating new antibiotics because it can cost up to 1 billion dollars and take as long as 15 years to make a single new drug. Much of the work in developing effective antibiotics for doctors to prescribe now falls on academics. From decades of work on antibiotic development, there is much to be learned to guide future advances. To leverage these discoveries, I will examine how a large set of antibiotics affects cellular processes essential for bacterial life. My approach applies to many bacteria that cause life-threatening infection. How bacteria respond to these antibiotics will be extracted and used to develop an artificial intelligence system. This program will scan chemical databases of millions of compounds and predict new antibiotic structures, which I will test for their ability to kill bacteria resistant to current antibiotics. Ultimately, my goal is to develop new antibiotics that will be used in the clinic to treat bacterial infection and save lives.

column36: Development of a Magnetic Resonance guided High Intensity Focused Ultrasound Therapy Platform for Perinatal Applications
column37: Congenital abnormalities are complications of pregnancy that can lead to heart failure of the baby and loss of pregnancy. These are diagnosed by ultrasound and can be treated if the risk of fetal death outweighs the risk of surgery. Current therapies all involve minimally invasive access into the uterus and comes with a risk of preterm birth. Magnetic resonance guided high intensity focused ultrasound (MRgHIFU) is a noninvasive therapy that is clinically approved in Canada for thermal ablation of uterine fibroids, and bone metastasis. MRgHIFU transmits ultrasound energy from a transducer located inside a dedicated MRI table that is below the patient, and focuses that energy into the body, producing a thermal lesion as small as a rice kernel. This focus is steered to cover a large treatment volume without repositioning the patient. Since the absorbed energy is nonionizing and incisionless, the risk of infection and long-term side effects are minimal, making it an ideal modality for fetal interventions. However, in the approved devices the energy source is located in configurations that are not adapted for a pregnant mother, and this is not amenable to a safe and ergonomically feasible treatment. The objective of this project is to develop a new modular MRgHIFU robotic platform that brings a HIFU transducer to a patient inside an MRI scanner in a configuration that provides a novel, safe and noninvasive therapy technology for some of our most vulnerable pediatric patients.

column36: Utilizing high resolution physiological data and artificial intelligence to develop a pediatric cardiac arrest prediction tool for integration into bedside clinical practice
column37: Critically ill children are at risk of cardio-pulmonary arrest (CPA). These devastating events occur 300-700 times per year in Canadian pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) and are associated with high mortality (45 to 85%), disability and higher costs of care. Effective management of CPA requires immediate reaction from clinicians. However, changes in a patient's state that precede the CPA are subtle. If these were appreciated, interventions would be possible, potentially preventing CPA and the associated poor outcomes and costs. The objective of this project is to use artificial intelligence to develop and implement a tool to predict CPA in critically ill children. We have been collecting and storing continuous physiologic signals in our PICU since April 2013. We have undertaken preliminary work using machine learning to analyze these data in patients who suffered a CPA. Our results indicate that earlier prediction of CPA is possible. We will use funding from this grant to: 1) Further validate, train and test the model predicting CPA, utilizing multidisciplinary expertise in a team that includes clinicians, engineers, computer scientists, and 2) Translate the model to the bedside using a visualization platform and implementation plan developed with human factors engineers and ethicists. This project is part of the new field of predictive, personalized medicine, and is associated with novel ethical dilemmas related to communicating the significance of predictions to patients and their families, which we will explore and define. An accurate model for CPA will save the lives of critically ill Canadian children and reduce the burden associated with these events. Its development will create opportunities for Canadian researchers to extend predictive modelling and redefine the healthcare team. This initiative will reduce healthcare costs, and positions Canada as a leader in using artificial intelligence to solve crucial healthcare problems.

column36: Self-management in the age of complexity: An eHealth tool to support people experiencing problem gambling, poverty & homelessness
column37: The prevalence of problem gambling (PG) among low income persons in Canada is up to 9 times higher than within the general population. PG is associated with other health and social needs such as homelessness, disability, substance use and mental illness. There is a lack of services available to provide PG care either as a standalone service or as part of an integrated care approach. Previous work by our team identified self-management as an important element of treatment, including the potential of technology in self-managed care. In response, a team of experts is co-developing a free and first-of-its-kind Smartphone/web app to help persons in vulnerable populations self-manage their PG and other complex needs. By collecting client information the app will be able to detect potential crisis situations and push supportive content to the user, such as an option to connect with social supports, a reminder of a PG-related goal or other resources such as self-help materials, gambling facts and motivational quotes. The app will be introduced to clients within the context of existing PG programming/case management as a way to encourage uptake, and then used by clients independently to self-manage post-treatment. It is expected that the technology will facilitate client self-management, improve client outcomes relating to PG and other complex needs and enhance client-provider communication. Lastly, we will work with commercial, service and technical partners towards delivery of a robust and fully substantiated product, with high quality data to support use of the app within target populations and more generally in those affected by problem gambling. There is ample opportunity for the app to be commercialized and incorporated into the Canadian healthcare and social service systems and applied to the treatment and self-management of PG and related health/social problems; a necessity in a sparse treatment environment marked by long wait lists.

column36: Evaluation of an Online Tool to Reduce Unnecessary Antibiotic Prescribing Among General Practitioners
column37: Infections are rapidly becoming resistant to the antibiotics we use to treat them. These resistant infections are responsible for a growing number of deaths and place a tremendous strain on the healthcare system. The World Health Organization has called this issue "one of the biggest threats to global health, food security, and development today." And yet, few new antibiotics are being developed, making it critical to safeguard the efficacy of existing antibiotics. The overuse of antibiotics is recognized as the leading causing of antibiotic resistance, as these medications are often prescribed unnecessarily. While campaigns to improve antibiotic prescribing practices in hospitals have been effective, progress has been slower outside of hospitals, where the vast majority of antibiotics in Canada are prescribed, mainly by family doctors. OPEN Stewardship is an international collaboration to implement a simple, web-based tool to empower family doctors make the right decision about when to prescribe antibiotics and which antibiotics to prescribe. OPEN Stewardship works by providing automated feedback to doctors on their prescribing practices and comparing them to an anonymous sample of their peers. The tool assists doctors by connecting them to information about local guidelines and antibiotic resistance rates and allows the exchange of relevant information. The first phase of the study will test the tool with family doctors in Toronto and Southern Israel. My role will be to develop and apply the statistical methods to analyze how the tool changes each doctor's prescribing practices. The way we use antibiotics is unsustainable and threatens our ability to treat deadly infections. OPEN Stewardship empowers doctors to make the best antibiotic prescribing decisions and has the potential to become an important tool in the fight against antibiotic resistance. As a standardized, low-cost tool, OPEN Stewardship offers a global solution to a global problem.

column36: The Shaky Scalpel: Evaluating a Novel Surgical Stress-regulation Protocol for Optimizing Patient Outcomes and Surgeon Wellness
column37: Physician stress is a serious, unaddressed issue crippling the Canadian healthcare system. This stress is damaging to physician mental and physical health, and contributes to physician burnout, costing our healthcare system $213 million. Patient safety is also compromised; physician stress contributes directly to the over 800,000 serious, highly-preventable adverse events (injuries or complications causing death or harm) inflicted on hospitalized patients in Canada every year. The problem is most severe in surgery, where stressors are frequent and most adverse events occur. Currently, it is simply assumed that surgeons will learn to manage stress through experience, or worse, through trial and error in the operating room. Given that stress in surgical practice is inevitable, it is imperative that we equip surgeons with the most evidence-based tools and training strategies to manage stress. Our lab has been studying surgeon stress for 10 years, and although we have a better understanding of its nature, as a field, we are lagging far behind other high-performance domains such as aviation and elite sport who have established reliable training methods. Therefore, I am collaborating with an expert sport psychologist to establish a stress management training protocol for surgeons which combines evidence-based, best-practices from elite sport with our own knowledge of stress in surgery. The protocol combines two validated training components: psychological skills training (such as visualization, relaxation, and positive self-talk) and biofeedback (where electronic monitoring of the heart is used to show surgeons their physiologic stress levels in real-time, providing a means for surgeons to learn how to control their stress response). This combined approach has not been tested in the surgical domain, yet shows great promise in improving surgeon wellness and patient safety. Ultimately, we propose an expanded program for healthcare professionals more broadly.

column36: Combining genome-wide CRISPR screens and microfluidics to discover genetic regulators during the differentiation pathway towards transplantable hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Stem cells have the ability to become nearly any cell type in the human body. Therefore, they have tremendous potential to be used in the treatment of disease. For example, stem cells can be used to generate healthy blood and bone cells for cancer patients. Currently this is done using bone marrow transplants. However, there are outstanding issues with this treatment. These include difficulties finding a suitable donor and complications such as rejection of the new cells, infection, or reoccurrence of the disease. In fact, nearly 30% of transplant patients die within one year of the treatment. My research aims to provide a better alternative -- turning a patient's own skin cells into stem cells and then blood. This would eliminate the need for a donor and reduce the likelihood of complications resulting in death. To do this I am leveraging a new gene-editing tool, called CRISPR, to search for genes that control the differentiation of stem cells. I am also engineering a platform based on micro-scale fluidic chips which can sort billions of cells using magnetic nanoparticles. This platform allows the search to cover more of the human genome, take less time and be less expensive. This approach has the additional potential to treat other diseases by identifying genes that could tell stem cells to become heart or brain cells.

column36: Vaccine effectiveness against persistent human papillomavirus infection in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal
column37: Gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are recommended to get the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. Most Canadian provinces have introduced publicly funded HPV vaccination programs for boys and high-risk males such as MSM, but we do not know how well the HPV vaccine works in these populations outside of a clinical setting. MSM have higher rates of HPV-associated diseases like anal cancer compared to the general population. In part, this is because they have higher rates of HIV. Based on clinical studies, we know that the HPV vaccine protects against infection about 75-78% of the time in healthy MSM who have had relatively few lifetime sex partners. However, less information is known about how this translates to vaccine protection in a real-life setting or in higher risk groups, such as those who have multiple sex partners or prior HPV infection or in those living with HIV. My PhD will study how well the HPV vaccine protects against ongoing HPV infection in MSM over a one-year period. I will estimate the percent of MSM infected with HPV at the beginning of the study and 12 months after enrollment; identify patient characteristics, such as sexual behaviours or HIV status, associated with infection; and measure the amount of protection from HPV vaccine. I will use data from a community-based study of MSM aged 16-30 years in Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal known as Engage-HPV. At each study visit, men answered questions about their sexual health, including self-reported HPV vaccination status. They were also asked to self-collect oral and anal specimens for HPV testing. This research will fill an important knowledge gap about ongoing HPV infection in this population and will provide a real-world measure of HPV vaccine effectiveness. My findings will help evaluate targeted HPV vaccination programs recently implemented in three Canadian cities with large populations of MSM and contribute to the design of optimal HPV prevention strategies.

column36: Differentiating Suicide Attempters From Suicidal Ideators: A Multimodal Investigation of Impulsivity
column37: Suicide is a public health epidemic. The World Health Organization estimates that suicide is attempted every 1-2 seconds. Though extensive resources are invested in suicide prevention, our ability to predict suicide attempt is only marginally better than chance. Addressing the root of this problem requires that we answer why some people only contemplate suicide while others actually attempt it. To do so, the ideation-to-action framework offers a novel approach to suicide research that emphasizes the importance of separately understanding the origin of suicidal thoughts (i.e., ideation) and the transition from thoughts to suicide attempt (i.e., action). Within this framework, difficulty with impulse control is a risk factor that has been linked to suicide attempt but is poorly understood. Impulse control is a complex process with numerous constituent parts that have not been concurrently analyzed within the context of suicide. In my proposed research, I will apply the ideation-to-action framework to determine which aspects of impulse control differentiate people who have attempted suicide from those who have only contemplated it. I will investigate this research question using multiple measures of impulse control (i.e., personality traits, cognition, and neural systems) in patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD), a group of people that frequently think about suicide, often have a history of suicide attempt, and are highly impulsive. Future public health strategies to prevent suicide require that we discriminate between suicidal thought and suicide attempt to better focus prevention efforts and improve risk assessment tools for health care professionals. Thus, this research informs these efforts by contributing to a comprehensive risk profile of suicide attempt and inviting the exploration of specific treatment and intervention targets related to impulse control.

column36: Cellular exit of Salmonella Typhimurium by an exocytosis mechanism: implications for cell-to-cell spread of infection
column37: Our bodies are bombarded on a second-to-second basis with foreign materials and microorganisms that attempt to take up residence and disrupt our daily functions. Central to the bodies' defense is the immune system which recognizes materials that do not belong, localizes tools of the immune system to the site of the invader, and clears the threat. However, one class of human pathogens, termed intracellular bacteria, are specialized at avoiding the bodies ability to protect itself. These bacteria do so by living and growing directly within human cells. This makes recognition and clearance by the immune system and treatment with medications difficult. Some of the most dangerous bacteria to global health can adopt this intracellular lifestyle to sustain their infection. One example, Salmonella enterica, is a major threat to human health. It is a leading cause of infection in low- and middle-income countries affecting mainly children and young adults. Commonly known as a foodborne pathogen, certain types of Salmonella also cause severe fever and poor recovery rates after it has established itself within the cells of the body. Many studies have worked toward understanding how these bacteria survive within these cells. However, how Salmonella spreads from this environment throughout the body is poorly understood. Here, I propose a novel way that Salmonella escapes its environment within cells and suggest that this explains the spread of bacteria in the body. We aim to understand the bacterial and human factors that promote this process. Understanding this portion of the bacterial lifecycle may provide important insight into diseases caused by these bacteria, their treatments, as well as other bacteria that cause similar human diseases.

column36: Targeting metabolic-epigenetic regulation for lymphedema treatment
column37: Lymphedema is a disease of a damaged lymphatic system, a fluid drainage system that runs parallel to the blood circulatory system in the human body. The disease is associated with abnormal metabolism and metabolism-induced gene activity changes may have an important role in lymphedema development and progression. Why and to whom the research is important: One in five cancer survivors will develop lymphedema as a side effect after surgery and/or radiation treatment. This disease causes a greater than 70-fold increased risk of infection and chance of developing of another lethal cancer. Lymphedema is incurable and there are currently no effective therapies. Nature of the work: Cells break down nutrients, like sugars or proteins, to build chemicals that can modify gene activity without changing the genetic code (i.e. epigenetic changes). To understand how metabolism uses epigenetic modifications to produce lymphedema, high-throughput methods will be employed to profile epigenetic changes induced under lean and obese metabolic conditions, which have been associated with mild and severe lymphedema disease outcomes respectively. The importance of the gene activity changes in impacting lymphedema outcomes will be confirmed in cell and mouse experiments. Anticipated outcomes: Epigenetic data will improve our understanding of the biological mechanisms contributing to this disease and help guide identification of new drugs to be used for lymphedema treatment. How the research will contribute to the field: With more than 1 million new Canadian cancer survivors expected in the next decade, many people will be affected by lymphedema, a disease that causes poor quality of life and life-threatening medical complications. New and effective treatments for lymphedema are urgently needed to improve health outcomes, minimize harm to patients in the long-term, and reduce financial burdens on the health system from ongoing treatment for this incurable disease.

column36: Cardioprotective benefits of combination treatment with a sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitor and a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist.
column37: Heart disease remains a leading cause of death and disability, and heart attack due to blockages in the heart's major arteries remains the dominant mechanism. Optimal treatment requires rapid relief from such blockages, and thus restoring blood flow to minimize heart tissue damage. However, substantial tissue damage also occurs after restoration of blood flow, known as ischemia-reperfusion injury. As such, pharmacological or technical approaches that limit these complications are of interest. Indeed, ischemia-reperfusion injury accounts for ~50% of the final scar size following a heart attack, which is the strongest contributor to the patient's risk of subsequently developing heart failure. This research project seeks to address the unanswered questions and unmet needs for a condition for which there remains no clinically approved therapy, namely ischemia-reperfusion injury and the heart failure that follows such injury. We will be testing the beneficial actions of two distinct drug classes recently shown to reduce risk of major cardiac events in patients with type-2 diabetes, namely (i) the SGLT2i dapagliflozin and (ii) the GLP-1RA exenatide, a.k.a. exendin-4, in a pre-clinical mouse model of ischemia-reperfusion injury and heart failure. These studies will help us better understand and tailor drug therapy to a large patient population (with and without diabetes) at high risk of cardiac events, namely the clinical conditions of heart attack, ischemia-reperfusion and subsequent heart failure.

column36: Defining the pre-leukemic stem cell state through transcriptional and epigenetic interrogation at single cell resolution
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia is a deadly blood cancer with only 1 in 3 patients surviving 3 years beyond diagnosis. Most AML patients are diagnosed only after they present with acute complications of bone marrow failure, highlighting the importance of early detection and intervention. While great strides have been made recently in identifying pre-leukemic stem cells and predicting the risk of AML developing in asymptomatic individuals, we lack a sufficient understanding of the underlying biology of these pre-leukemic stem cells and consequently have no means of intervention to halt AML development. To address this gap, I will work with blood samples collected from AML patients years before their diagnosis and isolate the pre-leukemic stem cells in these samples. I will use single cell sequencing technologies and employ computational methods to identify gene regulatory networks that capture the essence of the pre-leukemic state. I will then examine these networks to identify targets that we can exploit therapeutically in order to eliminate the pre-leukemic stem cells while sparing healthy blood stem cells. The results from this study will inform efforts to understand and target pre-leukemia and bring us closer to introducing early detection and intervention into the clinic towards preventing this devastating disease.

column36: Cost-effectiveness of the geriatrician-led comprehensive geriatric assessment: an economic evaluation in using public health care payer perspective
column37: Older patients are prone to functional decline because of normal aging, disease processes, and social vulnerability. The complex interaction is best addressed by a comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA), which delivers integrated treatment plans for older adults. The CGA can be delivered in various settings, including acute care, rehabilitation, ambulatory clinics, community outreach, and long-term care. It can also be done by geriatricians or other healthcare providers. Geriatricians are physicians who have training in internal medicine and geriatric medicine, allowing for specialized care for older patients. A geriatrician for older patients is like a cardiologist for patients with heart disease, the highest level of expertise for a field. Ongoing research from my supervisor's group showed that a geriatrician-led CGA is more effective than a non-geriatrician-led CGA at improving memory, functional status and preventing nursing home admission. However, the comparative cost-effectiveness of a geriatrician-led CGA across different clinical settings is unknown. Knowing which clinical setting (e.g. acute care, clinics, or rehabilitation) is most cost-effective would allow policymakers to decide how geriatricians should be distributed. This has important implications because there are very few geriatricians across Canada (fewer than 1 for every 10,000 people aged >65 years), and optimal resource management is needed to provide care to older patients across the country. I will systematically review the literature for existing evidence on the cost-effectiveness of CGA done by geriatricians. I will then conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis of the geriatrician-led CGAs across clinical settings in Ontario. I will also conduct a qualitative study engaging policymakers, patients, caregivers and knowledge users to determine the barriers and facilitators of delivering a CGA in different settings. This will help policymakers implement CGAs in the most cost-effective settings.

column36: Probing T-Cell Response in a Hypoxic Pancreatic Tumour Microenvironment using TRACER
column37: Pancreatic cancer is set to surpass breast cancer as the third leading cause of cancer deaths in Canada. Currently, only 7% of patients with pancreatic cancer will survive five years after diagnosis. The disease is often diagnosed too late for surgery, and it is generally resistant to chemotherapy and radiation. As such, new treatment options are desperately needed. Immunotherapy - treatments which recruit a patient's immune system to eliminate cancer cells - has been successful for some cancers but has fallen short in pancreatic cancer. This is partly because pancreatic cancer actively suppresses the immune system, preventing it from killing cancer cells. Investigating the interaction between the immune system and cancer cells using traditional 2D or living animal models has not yielded effective ways to solve this problem. Now, a 3D platform developed by our lab called "Tumour Roll for Analysis of Cellular Environment" - TRACER - is creating new opportunities to study these interactions. TRACER is an engineered 3D tumour model. Cells are grown on a paper strip wrapped around a metal cylinder to create a tumour in a dish that is similar to what would be in a patient. Unlike in a patient, TRACER can be unrolled to look inside the tumour to examine cell interactions up-close. This allows us to understand why immune cells are not functioning properly. Using TRACER, we will create tumours using patients' cells to investigate cellular interactions and identify molecules in the environment that affect the immune system. We will then engineer immune cells to function in the tumour environment and kill cancer cells. In knowing which engineered cells are successful, we can highlight the gene and protein targets which may be important to enhancing immunotherapy in pancreatic cancer and pass these targets along to those developing new drugs. In doing so, we will potentially create treatments that improve the quality of life and survival of pancreatic cancer patients.

column36: Conceptualizing Learning Health Systems from an Indigenous Perspective: A Multiple Case Study in Northwest Territories
column37: This research involves Indigenous Peoples. If you go to the doctor with a problem and the doctor tells you there is nothing wrong, you might feel rejected and misunderstood. Maybe in your community there is no other doctor to go to, so next time you are ill you decide not to go to the doctor at all, making things worse. Unfortunately, this situation is common in many parts of Canada. Our health care system assumes disease is the cause of illness. However, there is more than one way to understand health. This study will help to build a health care system that learns from our different understandings, and constantly improves to provide better care. Many Indigenous peoples do not see health as an absence of disease, but as the result of good relationships with their family, community, environment, and spirit. The differences between these beliefs and the beliefs of our health care system mean that Indigenous patients often receive unhelpful, and even harmful, care. One idea is to build "learning health systems" that continuously improve care by learning from a variety of information sources, including patients. To improve care for Indigenous patients, learning health systems must know what to learn, how, and from whom. This research will take place from 2019 to 2022 in Northwest Territories, where 51% of the population is Indigenous. We will use sharing circles and interviews with Indigenous Elders and communities to find answers to two questions. First, in the eyes of Indigenous community members, what is a learning health system? Second, in what ways can a health system learn from the Indigenous communities it serves? These questions have not been studied before. Our results will indicate how the Northwest Territories health system can improve care for Indigenous patients, but will also benefit places across Canada and the world that have many cultural groups with different beliefs about health.

column36: Genomic and Pathological Consequences of Obesity on Prostate Cancer
column37: More than 1 in 3 Canadians are living with obesity and half will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetimes. Obesity increases the risk of prostate cancer, and in particular aggressive disease that is not cured by standard treatment. It is still unclear what influences obesity is playing on prostate cancer risk and aggression. My project seeks to answer this question by applying new DNA sequencing techniques and state-of-the-art machine learning to study the prostate tumours of obese and non-obese men. In each cell, the information that passes down from parents to child is encoded in the DNA. Some genes (pieces of DNA) that are passed down increase a person's risk for obesity or cancer, and during a person's lifetime genetic changes can make cells turn cancerous. My first question is: Compared to non-obese men, do obese men carry unique genetic changes in their cancers, or do they have changes that are more frequently found in aggressive cancers? Second: What patterns in inherited genes are shared between people who have high risks for both obesity and prostate cancer? Finally: How different do tumour cells appear in men with and without obesity? I will link these questions to clinical outcomes to understand their importance to prevention and patient care. The answers to these questions are critical for better predicting outcomes of patients with both obesity and prostate cancer, for helping doctors make better treatment decisions, and for more cost-effective diagnosis through microscopes. This study will be the first to look at the relationship between obesity and the genetic features of prostate cancer. By understanding how and why prostate cancer differs in obese men, scientists can better understand how prostate cancers develop and how to better match obese patients to the targeted therapy most likely to cure their disease. This research will be vital for improving the care and treatment of thousands of Canadians affected by both obesity and prostate cancer.

column37: Bone marrow transplant (now called Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation) is a life-saving procedure for patients with certain blood cancers. Blood cancer is becoming more common as our population is ageing. With increase in experience with transplant and medication safety, this procedure is being offered to more patients, and is expected to increase in the near future. After the transplant, however, patients temporarily develop a severely weakened immune system. During this time, up to a third of patients can develop serious infections or breathing failure requiring admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) for life support. With increasing number of transplants, more patients are at risk of ICU admissions. Historically, given the extremely poor prognosis of these patients with blood cancer, ICU admissions were generally discouraged. However, recent developments have improved prognosis. The effect of ICU admission on our patients' long-term survival, quality of life and symptoms is still unknown. To better inform clinical practice, the evaluation of up-to-date Canadian data describing their outcomes is required. During my thesis work, I will evaluate medical practice and disease outcomes of patients who received a bone marrow transplant and ICU admission in the past 10 years in Ontario. Describing the epidemiology, patterns of care, mortality, and long-term prognosis of these patients will provide valuable information. This will allow to better inform patients, families, treating physicians, and health policy makers. I expect that this will be the largest existing study addressing this important clinical problem to date. All in all, my work will help laying the groundwork for a better understanding how the survival of these patients can be beneficially influenced.

column36: L-arginine supplementation for the prevention of adverse birth outcomes in pregnancies complicated by malaria
column37: L-arginine is part of a normal protein diet, and an important building block for a growing fetus and developing placenta during pregnancy. Certain infections, such as malaria, can cause L-arginine levels to fall. Millions of women who live in parts of the world with high rates of malaria infection also suffer from dietary protein deficiencies in L-arginine. These women are at high risk of having poor pregnancy outcomes such as still birth, preterm and growth-restricted babies. Infants who are born preterm are at risk for death early in life. In this study, our goal is to develop a safe and effective L-arginine supplement that can be used by women who have poor access to nutritious food and are at high risk of malaria infection pregnancy in order to help them have healthy pregnancies and healthy babies. To do this, we have defined two key goals: 1. To assess L-arginine levels in blood samples taken from women in subSaharan Africa during their first trimester of pregnancy and determine if low levels early in gestation predict poor pregnancy outcomes and, 2. To conduct a large randomized, double blinded placebo control trial in Tanzania using an L-arginine supplement that we will develop for use by pregnant women. The goal of this study will be to see if L-arginine supplementation improves the pregnancy outcomes of women who are likely to have poor protein intake as part of their regular diet and are at high risk of contracting malaria in pregnancy If our intervention is successful, it will hold great promise for the millions of pregnant women who live in low-resource countries in places such as subSaharan Africa. L-arginine is readily sourced from groundnuts and could be made affordably, locally and sustainably to support the health of women during pregnancy, and help them have healthy children.

column36: Practice Patterns and Long Term Adverse Health Outcomes of Bilateral Oophorectomy: A Population-Based Cohort Study
column37: Hysterectomy, or surgical removal of the uterus, is the most common major surgery performed on non-pregnant women in North America. At the time of hysterectomy, women are also offered the option of oophorectomy, or surgical removal of the ovaries (BSO). This is in order to prevent the possibility of developing ovarian cancer, a deadly disease, later in life. However, BSO causes early menopause, which may lead to serious health problems like heart disease/stroke, dementia, and osteoporosis. The data on this are unclear and of poor quality. We also have very little information on how frequently this surgery is performed by Canadian doctors, and what types of patients are most likely to receive it. Our study will use a large repository of data on Ontario residents held at the Institute of Clinical Evaluative Sciences, a non-profit research institute, to answer important questions on BSO. First, we will describe how often BSO is performed. We will determine what types of patients receive BSO, and what types of surgeons perform BSO. Second, we will measure the chances of dying from any cause or from a cancer after BSO. Third, we will measure the chances of developing heart disease/stroke, dementia, and osteoporosis after BSO. We will analyse how these rates change based on the age at which the surgery is performed. Our study will be the largest of its kind and will address many of the weaknesses of earlier studies. It will provide information that women and doctors need to make the right treatment decisions. If women who undergo BSO have a high chance of developing health problems after surgery, then the procedure should no longer be offered. By determining which patients and surgeons are most likely to choose BSO, we will know who to target if education or interventions to stop this practice are required.

column36: Evaluating the Impact of Multi-Site Drug Checking Services on Overdose Risk in Toronto, Ontario During a National Opioid Overdose Crisis
column37: Opioid overdose is a primary public health concern in Canada. There is growing evidence that the rising number of overdose deaths is related in large part to the presence of highly potent opioids, such as fentanyl, in street drugs. Against the backdrop of a national opioid overdose crisis, drug checking services (DCS) have emerged as part of a comprehensive approach to preventing overdose deaths with Health Canada committing to approve and fund pilot projects providing DCS at supervised consumptions sites, including in Toronto, Ontario. Available throughout Europe since the 1990s, DCS provide people who use drugs with information on what is in their street drugs and how strong they are. This information can allow for more educated choices about drug use and enable people who use drugs to avoid consuming lethal amounts of toxic substances. Since DCS in Europe have traditionally targeted people who use drugs recreationally in nightlife settings, little is known about whether DCS can prevent overdose deaths among a high-risk population. In Toronto, DCS will target people who use drugs accessing frontline services, many of whom use drugs chronically and by injection. Evaluating the impact of DCS tailored for this subpopulation of people who use drugs is critical in order to expand the policy responses available to address the opioid overdose crisis in Canada and elsewhere. As evaluation lead on the implementation of DCS in Toronto, I will produce three thesis manuscripts, including: 1) a systematic review of existing evidence on the influence of DCS on people who use drugs; 2) a quantitative analysis of survey data from consenting clients of DCS in Toronto before and after receiving their analysis results to determine whether accessing DCS impacts overdose risk behaviours among a novel subpopulation of people who use drugs; and 3) a qualitative analysis of perceptions of the effectiveness of DCS and barriers to accessing DCS in Toronto among consenting clients.

column36: Seasonal Transmission Dynamics of Influenza and Avian Influenza in Bangladesh: identifying pandemic risk and opportunities for control
column37: Influenza viruses are a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Avian influenza viruses in particular have generated global health concern because of their ability to cause severe disease in humans. Avian strains are also capable of combining with human strains, which allows new influenza viruses to evolve. The emergence of a new influenza virus with improved human-to-human transmission is of concern because it could cause the next global pandemic. The public health risks posed by avian influenza are particularly high in Bangladesh, where high population densities and expanding poultry production industries are bringing humans and animals in closer contact. Despite these risks, there is limited understanding of the seasonal transmission patterns of influenza in human and poultry populations in Bangladesh. To address this research gap, my PhD aims to evaluate human and avian influenza transmission to better understand risk of pandemic emergence and opportunities for control in Dhaka, Bangladesh. This project will bring together routinely collected datasets from laboratories, hospitals, and veterinary programmes in Bangladesh. Using these data, I will implement innovative statistical, mathematical, and epidemiological techniques to characterize the seasonal patterns of influenza in human and poultry populations, as well as simulate the impact of influenza control strategies. column36: A population health- and policy-based evaluation of cannabis legalization in Canada: The effect of recent federal policy change on cannabis and alcohol use and related substance use disorders
column37: Canada will legalize the sale and possession of cannabis in October 2018, marking a foundational shift in national substance use policy as cannabis joins alcohol as a legal psychoactive drug. Research studying recent events in the United States has shown that cannabis legalization has led to increased cannabis use and cannabis use disorders; however, the simultaneous effect on alcohol use and alcohol use disorders is not clear. It is important to study these two now-legal substances in parallel as alcohol is used more widely and is responsible for greater health harms than cannabis in Canada. This program of research, completed as a collaboration between the Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and the National Drug Research Institute (Australia), will evaluate the effect of cannabis legalization on alcohol and cannabis use and associated mental health disorders. Will cannabis legalization lead to an increase in the prevalence of use of cannabis and alcohol among Canadians? Will Canadians experience higher rates of alcohol use disorders and cannabis use disorders after legalization? Or may Canadians substitute cannabis use for alcohol use and therefore experience fewer negative health consequences overall? Changes in prevalence and patterns of cannabis and alcohol use resulting from legalization will be studied using Canadian survey sources. Health records will be analyzed to estimate the rate of cannabis use and alcohol use disorders, for a period before and after legalization. Time series methods will then be employed to study the unique effect of legalization, using Australian states as control groups where legalization did not take place. This proposed research will provide answers to important questions regarding recent substance use policy change in Canada. The results will be both relevant and timely, providing critical information to policymakers in Canada, Australia and around the world regarding the health impacts of cannabis legalization.

column36: Studying the single-neuronal representation of higher-order cognitive processes in the human brain
column37: Despite ongoing progress in our understanding of brain areas involved in human cognition, the underlying single cellular mechanisms remain almost completely unknown. Here, I aim to use unique access to acute neuronal recordings in subjects undergoing planned intra-operative neurophysiology to evaluate human cognitive processes that cannot be evaluated by other study modalities or animal models. A core foundation of human social behavior is "theory of mind", or the capacity to infer another's beliefs, thoughts or desires and recognize that others may have different beliefs than one's own. This ability is a fundamental milestone in human development and is broadly disrupted in psychiatric conditions such as autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. Its single neuronal and population based underpinnings, however, are not known. Building upon extensive experience in the Dr. Williams lab, I aim to record from individual neurons in the dorsal prefrontal cortex as participants perform a structured task that presents them with short narratives about real-world scenarios. The task requires them to formulate an idea about the hidden state-of-mind of individuals in the narratives and demonstrate understanding of another's beliefs even when they differ from one's own. This project will allow me to test, for the first time, a number of core hypotheses about how individual neurons in the human prefrontal cortex processes information about basic events, their relation to other social agents and internal beliefs. It will also allow me to construct an explicit neuron-based model of how beliefs are represented within the human brain and determine the degree to which the semantic features describing the information is encoded in the prefrontal cortex. This proposal will provide insight on a foundational human cognitive process at the single cellular level and will dramatically advance our understanding of pathologic conditions such as autism spectrum disorder.

column36: Mapping the Human Apoptosis Genetic Interaction Network
column37: Despite great advances in genetic research, we cannot fully explain how traits and diseases are inherited. Studies in organisms with simple genomes have indicated that genetic interactions, i.e cooperating genes, play a role in how genetic information encodes appearance and function of cells. With the new precise and efficient CRISPR genome editing technology, such interaction studies can now be carried out for human genes. We will utilize CRISPR to map genetic interactions in human cells. Due to the large number of human genes, it is not possible to test all of them for their pairwise interactions. We will thus focus on genes that regulate programmed cell death (apoptosis) and map their interactions with all other genes. Apoptosis is a tightly regulated process that is essential for the balance of cell growth and death. If it is misregulated, cancer and other diseases can arise. The crosstalk between different apoptosis components is not fully understood, and not all genes involved in this process are known. Our preliminary experiments have identified interesting candidates for novel apoptosis genes, confirming the feasibility of our approach. We will determine the genetic interactions for other apoptosis genes, enabling us to assemble a network, because genes with similar functions are expected to have similar interactions. We can then classify genes into functional groups and predict the functions of uncharacterized genes when they are found connected to well-studied genes in the network. Our approach will also identify interaction partners of genes that are involved in diseases, which could allow indirect treatment through targeting of their interaction partners. In summary, this project will generate a genome-wide map of how apoptosis genes work together with their interaction partners in health and disease, which will benefit fundamental biology as well as medical research aimed at identifying the vulnerabilities of cancer and other apoptosis-related diseases.

column37: Le vieillissement est associe a une perte de masse musculaire et de force musculaire (dynapenie [DYN]) ainsi qu'a une augmentation de masse grasse (obesite [Ob]), ce qui entraine une deterioration des capacites fonctionnelles (CF). Les personnes DYN-Ob (~ 20% de la population) presentent des CF inferieures a celles ayant une seule de ces deux conditions. En relatif, les hommes sont plus touches par ce phenomene. L'activite physique et plus specifiquement l'entrainement en puissance (EP) est une solution efficace pour contrer ces effets deleteres. Malheureusement, plus de 50% des aines sont sedentaires et une des raisons est le manque de temps. De ce fait, l'entrainement par intervalle (EI) plus court a emerge comme une alternative. Neanmoins, les effets de EI et EP sur les consequences de la DYN-OB restent meconnus. L'objectif de ce projet post-doctoral est de comparer via un essai randomise et controle mene en double aveugle, les effets d'un EP vs. un EI sur la CF d'hommes ages DYN-Ob a court (post-intervention) et moyen (6 mois apres) terme. Pour ce faire, 90 hommes DYN-Ob (65 ans et +) seront repartis aleatoirement en 3 groupes d'intervention (12 semaines) soit : 1) EP (type resistance - explosif: 1 heure/seance, 3fois/sem) vs 2) EI (type cardiovasculaire - intense : 30 min/seance, 3fois/sem) vs. 3) controle (sans intervention). La composition corporelle, les capacites fonctionnelles, la force et la puissance musculaire, le volume et l'infiltration du gras dans le muscle, les habitudes de vie et les depenses energetiques, seront mesurees avant, a la fin et 6 mois apres l'intervention. Considerant l'evolution demographique de notre population et sa trajectoire en terme de prevalence de l'obesite, definir si une de ces modalites d'AP s'avere plus benefique pour les personnes DYN-Ob est une priorite pour notre systeme de sante pour maintenir la qualite de vie des aines.

column36: Dynamique du repertoire des lymphocytes T CD4+ infectes par le VIH
column37: Almost 37 millions of people are living with HIV (PLWH) worldwide, including 75,000 in Canada. HIV infection is characterized by a progressive destruction of the overall immune defenses. Actual HIV treatments help PLWH to live almost as long as people who are not infected by HIV. However, the virus persists and hides within their body and exhausts their immune system. Recently, a population of human immune cells, called "regulatory T-cells" (Treg) has been identified to contribute in cancer and chronic viral illnesses progression. It has also been demonstrated that the levels of Tregs are higher in PLWH than general population in line with disease progression as these cells are able to inhibit anti-HIV immune responses. Besides Tregs, another type of immune cells, Th17 cells, plays a pivotal role in the maintenance of mucosal immunity and imbalance between Th17 and Tregs results in HIV disease progression. We hypothesize that changes in cellular metabolism contribute in Tregs increased frequencies, which in turn, help HIV to hide in viral reservoirs of PLWH. Specifically, we aim to understand (1) what is the status of Th17/Treg balance in PLWH with different clinical outcomes; (2) what are the metabolic mechanisms involved in Th17/Treg balance during HIV infection; and, (3) how Tregs contribute in HIV persistence and the immuno-deficiency. In this regard, our laboratories will use different well-established experiments on biological specimens from PLWH with different clinical and therapeutic outcomes. This research will help to develop new therapeutic approaches aimed at modulating deleterious functions of Tregs. Targeting of Tregs with appropriate immuno-therapeutic interventions in PLWH, could lead to a better immune recovery and might help to find an HIV cure.

column36: A systems biology approach to understand the determinants of protein robustness to mutation
column37: All humans carry mutations, both inherited and acquired during their life, making every genome unique. Some of these changes can significantly impact human health, for example causing genetic diseases or increasing the risk of cancer in those who carry them. Since it is impossible to perform laboratory experiments to test the impact of all known and possible mutations, scientists have worked to develop tools that help predict their effect. These methods are not perfect and could be improved by the integration of more experimental data. Many of these mutations alter proteins, the molecular machines responsible for the survival of the cell. Organisms from bacteria to human have developed specialized proteins called chaperones to help them ensure proteins remain functional in periods of stress, but their ability to protect the cell from harmful mutations remains misunderstood. The objective of this project is to generate new reference information to better predict the health impact of mutations, as well as understand the influence of cell mechanisms such as chaperones in buffering or aggravating their effects. By integrating this data, we will gain a better understanding of how a person's heritage influences disease risk and make significant progress towards personalized therapies adapted to the individual.

column36: Targeting mRNA translation to effectively treat metastatic breast cancer
column37: Current treatments for metastatic breast cancer are ineffective for disease that has spread (metastasized) to other organs. Moreover, while new immunotherapies are promising for other cancer types, their effect in breast cancer is limited. Therefore, when laboratory scientists uncover promising new leads, it is imperative to determine how they can be applied to benefit patients. We have also shown that these drugs can unleash immune responses suppressed by tumor cells, potentially stimulating the immune system to attack metastatic breast cancer. In this project, we will test these drugs in sophisticated models of metastatic breast cancer and bring them to the clinic for phase I trials in breast cancer patients. Our team unites world-leading Canadian fundamental and translational scientists with breast cancer clinical trials experts. We will carry out a pan-Canadian clinical trial testing our new therapeutic strategy and use unique resources, including extensive banks of tumour tissue and specialized animal models, to determine how these drugs work and how future treatments can be improved. We will identify all proteins whose production is altered by these drugs, identify responsive breast cancer subtypes and therapeutic combinations that allow us to maximize their effects, and determine whether their immunity-enhancing actions can be harnessed to further increase their effectiveness. We will function as a closely-knit multidisciplinary team, sharing data, methods, materials and information on an ongoing basis with advice from dedicated, passionate patient advocates to ensure progress in this innovative project.

column37: Mental illness accounts for a large and growing share of the total burden of disease in Canada. Widespread concern over the mounting social and economic costs of mental illness has prompted interest in research to better identify and prevent the risk factors that contribute to negative mental health outcomes. Evidence suggests that psychosocial aspects of the work environment (e.g. job control and job security) are major factors contributing to the development of mental health problems among Canadians. However, these dimensions likely co-occur and act in combination with each other to produce negative mental health outcomes. The objectives of the proposed research are: (i) to measure the prevalence of psychosocial work factors in the Canadian population; (ii) to examine how these psychosocial work factors cluster together across the labour market; (iii) to examine the association between different clusters of psychosocial work factors and mental health outcomes; and (iv) to investigate whether clusters of psychosocial work factors contribute to inequalities in mental health outcomes across age, gender, and occupational groups. To meet these objectives, the proposed research will use data from a 2016 population-based survey administered to a sample of 5,697 Canadian workers. This unique survey provides the most comprehensive portrait of the psychosocial work environment currently available in Canada. The knowledge gained through this research will aid in the development of effective workplace intervention strategies to promote the mental health of the Canadian workforce.

column36: Proteomic identification of clinically-important subgroups among basal-like breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most common malignancy diagnosed and the second leading cause of cancer related deaths in women both in Canada and worldwide. However, breast cancer is not just a one disease, but actually consists of at least four main types. For each of these, the management, treatment and outcome can be quite different. This classification of breast cancer was established based on molecular research that identified the biological changes in cell function that leads to the development of breast cancer, by measuring RNA expression. As a result, RNA profiling methods are now used to identify breast cancer types, significantly improving the diagnosis and management of breast cancer overall. However, these molecular tests can currently guide effective treatment only for two of the four main types, and there are still improvements needed, particularly in the type known as basal-like breast cancer. This is the most aggressive form of the disease, with a propensity to afflict younger women, and still lacks successful treatments beyond partial benefits from cytotoxic chemotherapy. Thus, new treatments are highly needed for young women with this aggressive group of breast cancers. We plan to address this problem using a new technology that can measure the expression of thousands of proteins in the same routine surgical tissues that are used for patient diagnosis. We propose to analyze 300 tumor samples from breast cancer patients, many with the basal-like RNA type, and link the expression of proteins with patient treatment and outcome. We expect that this study will identify basal-like breast cancers that may prove treatable with new targeted therapies. If successful, this study will guide more specific and effective treatment options for early stage breast cancer patients with the most aggressive type of the disease.

column36: Neuroprotective Effect of Sigma-1 Receptor and Activin A on Synaptic Function and Calcium Handling in Huntington's Disease
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a devastating inherited disease that can be detected before symptoms arise, but which is incurable. In HD patients, neurons involved in motor functions deteriorate, causing motor and cognitive problems. Neurons transmit signals in our brains, relying heavily on calcium for their function. The function impairment of the connections between neurons, known as synaptic function, as well as their ability to control calcium levels, form a common trait of many neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and HD. One level of calcium control is at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a cell organelle playing a significant part in protein production. This calcium regulation is abnormal in HD, leading to a change in protein production and a decrease in synaptic function. Interestingly, activating Sigma-1 receptors (S1Rs) - proteins located on the ER that play an important role in calcium regulation and therefore protein production - has been shown to normalize this calcium handling and restore synaptic function. The purpose of this project is to determine the relationship between S1Rs, protein production, calcium handling, and synaptic function, in order to better understand the disease mechanisms of HD and other neurodegenerative diseases, and to find new potential treatments. To conduct this project, I will utilize electrophysiological, pharmacological, imaging, and behavioral techniques. As there are currently no effective treatments for HD, the results from this study may revolutionize our approach to patients with this debilitating disease.

column36: Evaluation of pertussis immunization in pregnancy
column37: Pertussis, also called whooping cough, is a lung infection caused by the bacteria Bordetella pertussis. It is a major public health concern. Despite high vaccination coverage, we have seen a resurgence of the disease, both globally and in Canada. In Canada, 60-74% of pertussis cases are among infants younger than 2 months, who are too young to be vaccinated. Among infants younger than 2 months and admitted to the hospital with pertussis, 38% are admitted to intensive care and 2.3% die. To protect infants too young to be vaccinated, a number of countries (e.g. the US, UK, Australia) including Canada recommend vaccinating pregnant women against whooping cough. This approach to vaccination relies, at least in part, on the transfer of anti-pertussis antibodies from the mother to the newborn via the placenta. However, there are critical questions that must be addressed before this strategy is widely implemented: (1) we must determine the best time during pregnancy to give whooping cough vaccine; (2) we must show how efficiently anti-pertussis antibodies transferred from the mother to the newborn protect babies; and (3) we must determine whether vaccination against whooping cough in pregnancy suppresses the infant's immune response to the routine vaccines administered during infancy. This project aims to answer these gaps in knowledge. I will assess the function of anti-pertussis antibodies in newborns born to women immunized against whooping cough in different times in pregnancy. I will establish new laboratory tests that will further assess the function of anti-pertussis antibodies produced after vaccination in pregnancy. Lastly, I will analyze antibody levels of all published studies to date that addressed whether vaccination against whooping cough in pregnancy affects the antibody levels in the infants after their own vaccination. Altogether, this project will ensure we use the best strategy possible to prevent whooping cough in young infants.

column36: Profiling sex differences in neuronal network activity and drug responsiveness in an animal model of depression
column37: Depression is a devastating disorder with incidence in women two times higher than in men, however little is known about the mechanisms that contribute to this increased vulnerability. Normal brain function requires coordinated electrical activity of networks for the communication within and between brain regions. Not only has the dysregulation of electrical activity been shown to play an important role in depression, the normalization of aberrant activity relates directly to treatment success. In these studies, sex differences in innate and stress-induced changes in the functionality of brain electrical output will first be evaluated using a rat model of depression. The goal is to assess the capacity of these electrical alterations to associate with and predict subsequent depression behaviours. In a second study, we will evaluate sex differences in antidepressant responsiveness using a specific diagnostic measure: the normalization of brain electrical patterns. column36: Characterizing the roles of synapse organizers in mediating synaptic function and brain-based diseases
column37: The human brain is made up of neural circuits that are thought to underlie all brain function. These circuits are made up of contact points called synapses where individual nerve cells communicate with each other. For many years, scientists have been working to shed light on how nerve cells transmit information to each other, as well as the molecules involved in this process. In order for information to be delivered efficiently, or at all, proper synapse development has to take place. Synapse development is a process mediated by the binding of cell surface molecules located on the outer borders of both the nerve cell transmitting signals, and the nerve cell receiving them. The binding of these cell surface molecules, which have been coined 'synapse organizing molecules', acts as an anchor that physically glues the synapse together. In addition, depending on which synapse organizers are partnered up, certain properties will be conferred to that synapse. For example, certain binding configurations will give rise to synapses that release excitatory signals, whereas other ones will lead to the development of synapses that release inhibitory signals. This is especially important given that aberrant synaptic development has been emerging as a significant factor that underlies altered neuronal function in complex neuropsychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder. Moreover, little was known about mechanisms regulating the functions of these synapse organizers until recently. Our lab has discovered a process essential to the binding between many of these synaptic molecules and in turn, proper synapse development. Thus, my research is geared towards further functional characterization of synapse organizing molecules to develop a therapy to alleviate the brain-based defects in those suffering from mental disorders.

column36: Survival of the fittest: cell competition in cancer progression
column37: Despite decades of research and development of diagnostic technology, cancer is still often diagnosed based on relatively large abnormalities in the tissue - growths, lumps, or bumps visible to the naked eye. The size of the smallest detectable tumor is still approximately a billion cells. Furthermore, it is often only possible to detect cancer cells that have spread from the initial tumor site to distant organs at late stages, when the cancer has progressed past the point of being curable. Thus, being able to identify cancer cells at very early stages and low numbers could enable identification of molecules to mark cancerous and pre-cancerous cells, and lead to development of therapies to kill cancer cells before the cancer spreads. One potential way to identify cancer cells at early stages is by discovering novel mechanisms cancer cells use to promote their own growth and survival. Cell competition is a process by which faster growing ("winner") cells kill the slower growing ("loser") cells around them, in order to enable their own growth. Although cell competition is known to be important for animal development and for maintaining tissue health, it has not been extensively studied in cancer in animals. I will use a zebrafish model of melanoma to investigate if cancer cells use cell competition to promote their own growth by killing the cells around them. I will transplant melanoma cells into transparent fish and use cutting-edge live, whole-animal microscopy to investigate if tumors cause the death of the surrounding normal cells. In parallel, I will induce cell competition in tumors by upregulating the cancer-promoting gene Myc, and perform a drug screen to identify molecules that inhibit competition and tumor growth, to provide insight into signaling pathways that could be driving cell competition in cancer. These studies will detail molecules that promote cancer progression, and describe potential targets for development of drugs to block cancer spreading.
