column37: Background: Falls in people with spinal cord injury (SCI) are common, but we know little about why falls occur and how they can be prevented. Falls can cause fractures, hospital admissions, decreased ability to move and depression. In this project, we would like to find out: 1) what causes falls and how falls impact the lives of those with SCI, and 2) how we can improve fall prevention practices in Canadian SCI rehabilitation hospitals. Methods: This research will happen at Canada's largest SCI rehabilitation hospital in Toronto. We will track the number of falls in 64 people with SCI over six months. Twenty-four of those that have one or more falls will move on to part two, where they will be asked to take photographs of: what increases and decreases their chances of falling, and how the risk of falling affects their day-to-day activities. This will help us learn about how falls impact their lives. Interviews will also be conducted with 10 hospital administrators and 15 therapists working in SCI hospitals to understand what does and does not work well in current fall prevention policies and determine how policies can be improved. Implications: Our research will shine light on prevalence and causes of falls in people with SCI. The information from our study will help develop effective fall prevention initiatives that can reduce the risk of falls and improve life satisfaction for people with SCI. People with SCI often have low education and income. By lowering the risk of falls, people with SCI may participate more in their community, school and workplace. As our research targets people with SCI as well as hospital administrators and therapists, the research findings can be applied in hospitals, rehabilitation centers and in homes.

column36: Generation of Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Left Ventricular Cardiomyocytes for the Treatment of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
column37: The normal human heart has two pumping chambers: the right ventricle and left ventricle. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs (low-pressure system), whereas the left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body (high-pressure system). Some children are born without a left ventricle, a malformation called hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). To survive, these children must undergo surgery to connect the right ventricle to the rest of the body. However, the right ventricle, which is designed to pump blood into a low-pressure system, is often unable to sustain the high pressure of the rest of the body, and gradually starts failing, leading to heart failure and death. Unfortunately, we currently have no drugs to treat this type of heart failure. The goal of our project is to develop a novel therapy for HLHS using human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). These cells are unique in that they can give rise to all the cell types in the body. Our lab has previously designed a protocol to generate heart muscle cells - called cardiomyocytes - from hPSCs. However, all cardiomyocytes are not identical, and there are significant differences between cardiomyocytes in the right versus left ventricle. We hypothesize that cardiomyocytes from the left ventricle are better suited to sustain high pressure and that transplanting left ventricular cardiomyocytes into a pressure-overloaded right ventricle could prevent heart failure. The aims of our proposal are to 1) understand the molecular differences between right and left ventricle cardiomyocytes; 2) elaborate a protocol to make left ventricle cardiomyocytes from hPSCs; 3) transplant left ventricle cardiomyocytes into pigs with a pressure-overloaded right ventricle to see if these cells can prevent failure. If successful, this project could transform the care of children with HLHS. This would have a profound impact on our healthcare system, as HLHS has become the largest driver of cost in pediatric cardiovascular care.

column36: Uncovering how cortical and subcortical inhibitory brain structures contribute to uncontrollable freezing of movement in Parkinson's disease.
column37: Freezing of gait (FOG) is a devastating symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD) affecting more than half of the people in the advanced stages. FOG is characterized as sudden, uncontrollable moments of freezing in place and inability to move. FOG is considered one of the most significant symptoms influencing quality of life, yet notably has a poor and variable response to antiparkinsonian medications. Despite a great deal of empirical research, the cause underlying FOG in PD patients remains unclear. It's hypothesized that the brain areas activated in healthy humans to inhibit or stop movements, may also be responsible for FOG in PD. Overactivity of these inhibitory brain areas due to PD dysfunction may cause the stopping of movement resulting in FOG. This research program will investigate the role of cortical (pre-supplementary motor area & right inferior frontal) and subcortical (subthalamic nucleus & internal globus pallidus) brain structures in the inhibitory network and how modulation of their activity contributes to the uncontrollable freezing of movement. To answer several specific questions regarding the role of cortical and subcortical structures in the inhibitory network we will integrate several state-of-the-art research tools including Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS). DBS will allow in vivo recording of human subcortical brain activity via implanted electrodes to determine whether overactivation of subcortical brain areas that supress movement contributes to FOG. TMS will allow us to manipulate brain activity to determine whether decreasing brain activity in inhibitory cortical structures reduces inhibition and FOG. This knowledge will yield an understanding of the dysfunctional brain areas in PD and define the next generation of therapeutic procedures. Results may guide the targeted modulation of brain activity as an effective treatment option to improve the lives of Canadians impacted by this debilitating PD symptom.

column36: Peripheral and central chemoreceptor reflex regulation of sympathetic activity in heart failure patients
column37: When the heart fails to pump normally, the brain releases into the bloodstream increased amounts of a chemical called noradrenaline. Noradrenaline increases heart rate, causes the kidneys to pass less salt and water and constricts blood vessels. At first, more noradrenaline improves heart function but over time this muscle weakens and can no longer pump enough blood to the bodies organs. This condition is called "heart failure". For older Canadians, heart failure is the most common cause of hospital visits and a major cause of early death. Our long term research goal has been to identify what it is about heart failure that causes more noradrenaline to be released from noradrenaline-releasing (sympathetic) nerves that can be countered with new treatments. In about 50% of heart failure patients, the specialized blood oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors in the blood vessels and brain become very sensitive to changes in these gases. These patients breathe more vigorously if blood O2 is low or blood and brain CO2 is high. This hyperventilation then brings O2 or CO2 back to normal. Importantly, these sensors also connect to brain areas controlling noradrenaline release. We think that: i) if these O2/CO2 sensors are more sensitive they will tell the sympathetic nerves to release more noradrenaline and ii) heart failure patients with the most overactive O2/CO2 sensors will have the most frequent nerve firing. My study will determine: i) if O2 or CO2 sensors are more active in heart failure patients; ii) if this causes more sympathetic firing during blood O2 or CO2 changes; and iii) if more active O2/CO2 sensors contribute to high nerve firing even when patients are at rest and blood O2 or CO2 are within normal ranges. We are confident that these experiments will discover one or more causes of high noradrenaline in heart failure and that this will promote new ways of identifying and treating this important cause of suffering and death.

column36: Study of the mechanisms underlying seizures and epilepsy after traumatic brain injury in a zebrafish model.
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) occurs in 160,000 Canadians yearly, more than the combined number of patients with breast cancer, HIV/AIDS, spinal cord injury, and multiple sclerosis. One of the effects of TBI is seizures or epilepsy, and TBI is the most common cause of symptomatic epilepsy in people ages 15 to 24. There is no treatment to prevent epilepsy after TBI. Animal studies in rodents are expensive and time-consuming. Most of the conducted studies had a small sample size and there is a need to move toward larger and more randomized animal studies. Studies in zebrafish would allow for more rapid screening of potential targets before moving to rodent studies. Zebrafish are widely used in other disease studies because their genomes are 70% similar to humans, they spawn hundreds of eggs per week, they are cheap to breed, and are readily genetically modifiable. The overall aim of this project is to establish a zebrafish model of severe TBI to understand how this leads to seizures or epilepsy. We will confirm that the spontaneous seizures we have seen in this model are due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain and will also determine whether inflammation and abnormal proteins are involved in the development of epilepsy by using genetic studies. This project will apply modern engineering techniques in neuroscience to enhance our understanding of why some TBI patients develop seizures while others do not. Findings from this project are expected to help in developing treatment options to prevent post-traumatic epilepsy.

column36: Structural and functional study of the GNPT protein complex
column37: Cells regulate their metabolism and growth in response to both external and internal cues. One key cellular element that integrates these diverse signals is an assembly of proteins called mTORC1. The function of mTORC1 is disrupted in the majority of cancers and in other diseases. One of the cellular molecules that regulate the activity of mTORC1 is an assembly of three proteins called TSC. Genetic mutations in TSC cause the rare disease tuberous sclerosis. It is not well-understood how these three proteins assemble into a functional complex. This project aims to study the 3D structure of TSC by electron cryomicroscopy, and to biochemically investigate how TSC controls mTORC1. This knowledge could facilitate development of new drugs against cancer and other disorders.

column36: Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) as a Crucial Regulatory Cytokine and Therapeutic Target in Ankylosing Spondylitis
column37: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the most common form of spine arthritis which causes bones in the spine to fuse together, making the spine rigid and leading to severe low back pain (LBP). The main characteristics in AS are inflammation and abnormal new bone formation. Despite biomedical advancements in suppressing joint inflammation, there is no effective treatment to slow down the bone formation. The exact mechanism that links inflammation and spinal bone fusion remains unknown. Therefore, finding the key regulators that control both inflammation and bone formation is critical in AS. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is a molecule plays pivotal roles in inflammation which is also reported as a potential regulator for bone formation. However, the roles of MIF in AS have never been explored. We recently discovered that the expression of MIF is remarkably higher in blood obtained from AS patients compared to healthy individuals. We also determined that MIF has a great potential as a disease progression marker in the prediction of spinal bone fusion. In my preliminary data using a well-established mouse model of AS, I found that the expression of MIF in the both serum and tissue are remarkably higher in mice with AS compared to healthy mice. Mice with enhanced MIF expression clearly showed AS clinical features including severe arthritis and new bone formation in spine and ankle joints. In contrast, MIF deficient mice or MIF suppression with specific blockers dramatically prevented the AS clinical features. I also determined the cell groups that substantially produce MIF in AS disease conditions. Interestingly, injection of these cells into a MIF deficient healthy mouse led to AS clinical features, whereas blocking the function of these cells also blocked the AS clinical features. This proposal aims to comprehensively confirm my pilot studies on the role of MIF in AS disease-onset and progression, and establish MIF as a new therapeutic target in AS.

column36: Identification of novel vulnerabilities and therapeutic strategies for breast cancers with acquired resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors
column37: Improvements in the early detection and drug treatments for breast cancer have led to increased rates of survival and cure. However, metastatic breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body remain incurable and represent a major challenge. The recent development of a new targeted treatments called CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) have substantially improved the ability to control disease in the most common form of metastatic breast cancer. Unfortunately, this therapy does not provide a cure. Despite the initial response to the treatment, resistance to CDK4/6i eventually develops and tumors continue to grow. Since the tumors evolve during this process, finding new strategies for breast cancers that acquire resistance to CDK4/6i is an imperative for improving survival rates. To address this health challenge, I will use cutting edge laboratory tools identify the factors which the drug-resistant breast tumors rely on to survive and grow. Then, blocking the function of these genes by using specific targeted drugs will allow us to tackle the tumor cell vulnerabilities, and develop new approaches to improve the survival of these patients. My discoveries could be tested through clinical trials, and linked to specific markers to permit "personalized" treatment in this setting. The findings from this project have the potential to be rapidly integrated into the clinical management of patients and to ultimately improve breast cancer survival.

column36: Delineation of the molecular heterogeneity underlying patient outcomes in follicular lymphoma
column37: Follicular lymphoma (FL) represents the second most common lymphoma overall. Despite recent advances, FL remains largely incurable and the vast majority of patients experience progression over the course of their disease. The disease outcomes are highly variable, with some patients remaining free of disease for ten years or longer following initial treatment, while others experience early progression followed by death. Although an increasing number of treatment options is becoming available, we are currently unable to tailor treatment to each individual patient's lymphoma due to two main reasons. First, we are unable to accurately predict risk of progression before starting treatment. Second, we do not understand what patients would benefit more from one treatment compared to another. In our research work, we aim to overcome these challenges that currently impede personalized treatment. We plan to accrue 300 samples from FL patients across Canada and perform analyses at molecular, cellular, tumour, and patient levels. Our goal is to identify patterns that are currently hidden, but that can be uncovered by leveraging statistical computational tools. These patterns will reveal that not all follicular lymphoma patients have the exact same disease, but that they can be grouped based on similar molecular and cellular trends. Such subtypes of follicular lymphoma are expected to be associated with distinct risk of progression and susceptibility to specific treatments. We will validate our findings using independent lymphoma datasets. Our project has key implications for the treatment of lymphoma in Canada and beyond. The identification of novel subtypes will allow to adjust our treatment approach for each individual patient. By identification of the mechanisms underlying poor outcome we can propose novel therapies for patients who were previously thought to be at high risk, thereby circumventing adverse outcome.

column36: Molecular Regulation of Dendritic Cell Homeostasis
column37: The immune system consists of a variety of different cell types working together to actively maintain a delicate balance between responsiveness to foreign pathogens while maintaining tolerance to self-tissue, and avoiding autoimmunity. T cells are a specialized cell type of the immune system important for protection from infections, as well as from tumor growth. Dendritic cells are another type of immune cell and play a vital role directing T cell immune responses. Dendritic cells actively survey the periphery, searching for pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, as well as neoplastic tissue. They can then direct the recruitment and activation of other immune effector cells, such as T and B cells to the site of insult, propagating the inflammatory response. Current understanding suggests that dendritic cells exist at a resting, or immature state, and require activation signals before they can initiate an immune response. Immature dendritic cell interactions with T cells results in programmed cell death or anergy, resulting in a regulatory or anti-inflammatory response. Once stimulated with activating or 'danger' signals, such as those produced by bacteria, dendritic cells can mature and lead to activation of T cells and a robust inflammatory response. Our lab has recently discovered a family of molecules that act as the 'brakes' of dendritic cells, and actively maintain them in an immature state. Dendritic cells that lack these molecules are constitutively active and lead to continuous T cell activation without requiring additional activation signals. Our proposal aims to explore this novel concept and further investigate how these molecules keep dendritic cells in an immature state. Understanding the mechanisms that regulate dendritic cell activity could prove invaluable in boosting T cell mediated anti-tumor immune response, as well as help limit inappropriate inflammatory responses.

column36: The Impact of Exposure to Dolutegravir and other HIV Antiretrovirals during Pregnancy: Risks Associated with Neural Tube Defects and Impaired Metabolism
column37: The majority of people living with HIV are women of childbearing age. Dolutegravir (DTG) and other integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTI) are commonly used antiretrovirals (ARVs) in people living with HIV, including pregnant women. While these ARVs are very good at preventing transmission of HIV from mother to child, the secondary effects of ARVs, which include maternal metabolic perturbations and negative effects on early fetal development remain a concern. Higher incidence of neural tube defects (NTD) in women living with HIV receiving DTG from conception was reported by an ongoing NIH-funded observational study in Botswana. These findings highlight the urgent need to improve our understanding of the underlying pathophysiology associated with DTG exposure in pregnancy. Maternal obesity and diabetes are recognised risk factors for NTD. DTG has been associated with hyperglycemia and metabolic complications are common side-effects of ARVs. In this study we will investigate the impact of exposure to DTG and other INSTIs during pregnancy on maternal metabolic health and fetal development - focusing on NTD - using a mouse model. We will examine whether DTG exposure affects maternal liver function and glucose metabolism. We will study the effect of DTG exposure on insulin-responsive tissues and examine the effects on insulin production and activity. Our study will help to determine if DTG exposure increases the risk for NTD and if this risk extends to other INSTIs. We will identify potential biomarkers of NTD in DTG exposed pregnancies, and mechanistically assess biological pathways contributing to NTD, specifically metabolic dysregulation. Our study will address critical knowledge gaps in our understanding of the pathobiology of NTD in the context of ARV use in pregnancy, establish a rational basis for further evaluation of effective interventions, and help inform regimen selection in pregnancy.

column36: Delineating molecular signatures mediating osteoarthritis progression in the synovium by using single-cell RNA sequencing
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a disabling condition targeting joints affecting mobility and quality of life. There are no effective treatments for OA due to the lack of understanding of molecular mechanisms which drive the disease. OA affects all joint tissues but changes to the synovium are integral to disease progression. The synovium can strongly predict cartilage breakdown, as well as perpetuate a vicious feedback cycle between the two tissues fuelling further joint damage. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), is a new robust technique examining which genes are actively expressed on a single cell level. It accounts for individual differences between cells, and gives us a better understanding of the cell in its own environment. Currently, there are no scRNAseq studies profiling molecular changes in the OA synovium, leading to a weak foundation for therapeutic studies and a lack of effective targets. We hypothesize that scRNAseq on synovium from early and late stage OA patients will identify molecular signatures underlying OA progression that can be used to determine effective therapeutic targets. We will accomplish this by performing scRNAseq on synovium from patients (50 per group) with early or late stage OA as determined by x-ray. We will then perform comprehensive computational analysis to identify molecular mechanisms responsible for regulating disease progression. Our comparisons will give us insight into early vs late disease, sex differences, BMI and more. Promising targets will be evaluated in an animal model of surgically induced osteoarthritis to test therapeutic potential. Our approach stems from building a foundation for comparison between early and late stage OA, using this foundation to identify promising, clinically relevant targets, and determining whether these targets are capable of disease modification. If these approaches prove successful in modifying animal disease, we will be able to apply these treatments to impact clinical prognosis.

column36: Overcoming epigenetic therapy resistance to augment immunotherapy in ovarian cancer
column37: High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is the most common and lethal gynaecological malignancy, accounting for nearly 80% of all ovarian cancer deaths globally. Of the nearly 2,800 Canadian diagnosed with HGSOC annually, only 30% survive beyond 5 years. Standard first line therapy consists of debulking surgery combined with carboplatin/paxitaxel-based chemotherapy. While most patients initially respond to this regimen, ~80% relapse within months. Relapse has remained incurable for over 50 years, emphasizing an urgent need to expand treatment options. Treatment of ovarian cancer with immunotherapies known as 'immune checkpoint inhibitors' (ICI) achieves modest response rates of ~15%. ICI resistance in ovarian cancer is characterized by an 'immunosuppressive' tumor micro-environment. A landmark discovery at UHN reveals that epigenetic therapies can promote an inflamed tumor microenvironment that primes tumors to ICI therapy. Unfortunately, emerging clinical trials demonstrate that many ovarian tumors exhibit resistance to epigenetic therapies. The goal of this project is to conduct the first comprehensive investigation into epigenetic therapy resistance to uncover alternate means to circumvent resistance and re-sensitize ovarian tumors to immunotherapy. This project characterizes tumors and tumor-infiltrating immune cells from preclinical models and ovarian cancer patients treated with ICI and epigenetic therapies in several clinical trials at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre. In addition, this project uses CRISPR technology to screen for yet-unidentified therapeutic vulnerabilities in ICI-resistant ovarian cancers. This work will uncover how ovarian cancers evade the immune system and resist epigenetic therapies. The expected impact of this work will establish 'biomarkers' to match patients to the appropriate epigenetic therapy or immunotherapy, and to develop new drugs that target vulnerabilities in ICI and epigenetic therapy-resistant ovarian cancer cells.

column36: An IFN-iron axis reprograms hematopoietic stem cells to generate trained immunity
column37: It has been recently shown that memory capacity of immune response is not limited to only adaptive immunity as innate immune cells present memory-like capacity termed "trained immunity". However, many aspects of this new paradigm in immunity as well as its relevance for vaccine design remain to be determined. One of the major limitation of exploring the concept of trained immunity in vaccines was how we achieve a long lasting memory in innate immune cells, which have hours to days life span. We have recently demonstrated that Bacillus Calmette Guerin (BCG), the only available vaccine against tuberculosis is able to educate the hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) in the bone marrow (BM) to generate long-term protective innate immune memory responses. However, the key regulatory mechanisms that coordinate HSC self-renewal, proliferation and differentiation in this context as well as the mechanisms involved in durability of trained immunity have not been defined. In the current study, we aim to address these fundamental questions by comparing the impact of BCG on imprinting of HSCs to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), which also get access into the bone marrow and reprograms HSCs. The current study is focused to dissect the mechanism acquired by BCG and Mtb in reprogramming of HSCs to generate trained immunity. However, we envision while BCG imprinting of HSCs generates a protective trained immunity, Mtb imprinting of HSCs leads to detrimental immunity. Thus identifying the cellular and molecular signatures of protective versus detrimental trained immunity will allow us to design an effective vaccines against tuberculosis and potentially many other infectious diseases.

column36: Effets d'un blogue base sur les donnees probantes sur la saine alimentation sur les habitudes alimentaires, les comportements alimentaires et le poids des meres et leurs enfants.
column37: L'adoption d'une saine alimentation, integrant notamment une grande consommation de legumes et fruits et de lait et substituts, est reconnue comme une pierre angulaire dans la prevention de nombreux problemes de sante chroniques et est associee a une saine gestion du poids. Or, la majorite des Canadiens n'atteint pas les recommandations quotidiennes minimales pour ces deux groupes alimentaires malgre des actions soutenues du systeme de sante a promouvoir leur consommation. Un nombre grandissant d'evidences suggere la faisabilite et l'efficacite d'interventions transmises par l'intermediaire des nouvelles technologies de communication, tels que les medias sociaux, pour promouvoir l'adoption de comportements sains en sante comme une meilleure adhesion aux recommandations nutritionnelles. De plus en plus utilises par les dietetistes, les recentes etudes sur les blogues en nutrition montrent que ces outils sont des influences emergentes sur les pratiques alimentaires des meres qui les consultent pour trouver des idees de recettes et des strategies pour guider l'alimentation de leurs enfants. L'impact de l'exposition a ces blogues sur l'alimentation des lecteurs est toutefois encore meconnu. L'objectif de cette etude est d'examiner, a l'aide d'un devis experimental randomise et controle, l'effet d'un blogue base sur les donnees probantes sur la saine alimentation, redige par un dietetiste, sur la consommation de legumes et fruits et de lait et substituts de meres. Un objectif secondaire de cette etude qui aura un impact important dans une perspective de sante publique est d'examiner si l'exposition au blogue se traduira en ameliorations de l'environnement familial permettant d'augmenter la qualite de l'alimentation des enfants et les competences culinaires des meres. Cette etude fournira les premieres donnees empiriques sur l'utilisation des blogues comme strategie de prevention ayant un vaste potentiel de diffusion pour aider les Canadiens a mieux manger.

column36: Applying a molecular understanding of the aging process to develop novel treatments for neurodegenerative disease
column37: While aging is the greatest risk factor for the development of neurodegenerative disease, the role of aging in these diseases is poorly understood. In the inherited forms of disease, the disease-causing mutation is present from birth and yet disease onset occurs multiple decades later. This indicates that these mutations are well-tolerated in younger individuals. Based on this observation, we hypothesized that changes that take place during normal aging make the cells in the brain (and elsewhere) susceptible to the disease-causing mutations. If so, then delaying some of these age-related changes may be beneficial in disease treatment. To test this idea, we used a simple model organism, the worm C. elegans, which has been used extensively to identify genes that modulate aging. We found that targeting molecular pathways that have been shown to modulate aging is neuroprotective in C. elegans models of Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease. These experiments provide support for our idea that delaying changes that take place during aging will be beneficial in treating neurodegenerative disease. The current proposal will build upon these exciting preliminary studies by (1) identifying common downstream factors that contribute to longevity in different long-lived genetic mutants, (2) exploring the mechanisms by which these mutations extend longevity, and (3) examining the effect of modulating these aging pathways in animal models of neurodegenerative disease. Overall this work will advance our understanding of the aging process and apply that knowledge to the development of novel treatments for neurodegenerative disease.

column36: Investigating single cell biophysical properties and the basis for the loss of functional diversity in epileptic networks
column37: Epilepsy is a neurological disease where the brain experiences seizures repeatedly over a life-time. Seizures are debilitating states of abnormal and widespread firing of neurons in the brain. Their impact on an individual's life is significant. Given their largely unpredictable nature, epilepsy patients may lose their ability to drive and work in certain jobs, thus suffering from a loss of independence. Furthermore, about half of all epilepsy cases cannot be managed by medication alone. Currently, the only solution for these 'medication-resistant' patients is invasive surgery to excise the region of the brain causing the seizures. I am interested in seizures because they appear to be the result of a "final common pathway" that develops across a myriad of neurological disorders including genetic disorders, stroke, brain tumors, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's. This begs the question, what is this mechanistic "final common pathway", that allows the brain to transition unpredictably to the abnormal neuronal firing seen during seizures? Our hypothesis is that epilepsy develops in the brain when populations of neurons lose their ability to efficiently parse incoming inputs into their various parts, known as de-correlation. When these neurons are not able to sufficiently de-correlate incoming inputs from other brain regions, they begin to fire in a hyper-synchronous manner that defines seizure activity. Our lab's vision is to develop a neuro-electronics platform, precisely analogous to a computer chip, that can be implanted into the brain. This computer chip will have the ability to detect the transition of the brain into the abnormal seizure state and provide electrical stimulation to prevent the seizure from fully taking form. Such a device would routinely stop seizures in a patient's brain without them even knowing it. My doctoral studies will contribute to the development of this device by providing mechanistic insights into seizures and epilepsy.

column36: Overcoming Obstacles in Cancer Nanomedicine Delivery using a Versatile In Situ Ultrasound-Triggered Microbubble-to-Nanoparticle Conversion
column37: Difficult-to-treat solid tumours have long been a problem for the cancer research community. While modern advances in nanomedicine have created smart drugs that are designed to specifically target different cancers, the improvement they provide is limited by the amount of drug that can infiltrate the complex tumour environment relative to normal, healthy tissue. The development of a delivery system that could load drugs and be selectively triggered to release them into the tumour would revolutionize drug design for some of the deadliest cancers. In 2015, researchers discovered that specially designed contrast agents called microbubbles could be converted into stable nanostructures using a particular type of ultrasound. While microbubbles themselves must remain in the blood vessels, these smaller structures have the potential to leave the circulation and enter their surrounding environment. This opens up the possibility of loading a microbubble with therapeutic nanoparticles and initiating the conversion at a tumour boundary, enhancing local delivery at the tumour site. Because the delivery platform would not depend on the drug itself, it could be used to deliver all types of nanoagents in a versatile and consistent manner. This would open new doors for those designing cancer drugs, allowing for researchers to use more specialized nanomedicines at lower doses and with fewer systemic side-effects. This tool and its accompanying shift in the mindset of drug development is necessary in order to produce the next wave of therapies that will help us fight the most lethal cancers.

column37: Despite the availability of multiple therapeutic approaches, diabetes, cancer and atherosclerosis continue to incur significant health risks to many Canadians. In these diseases, endothelial cells, which form the innermost lining of all blood vessels, interact improperly with cells and soluble factors that circulate in the blood, leading to adverse effects. I hypothesize that the arrangement and mobility of their surface proteins directly impacts how well endothelial cells can make specific interactions their environment, particularly during disease. I am therefore studying the mechanisms that govern cell-surface architecture and molecular mobility in endothelial cells. Presumably, targeting these mechanisms will allow us to modify endothelial responses to external factors. The aim is to uncover novel targets for disease-specific treatments that will outperform current therapies. New technology allows us to accurately track the motions of single particles on the surfaces of live cells. I will use this technology in combination with other imaging techniques to describe how important endothelial receptors move in response to different stimuli. The networks that give cells their shape interact closely with the cell membrane and are likely to be important regulators of molecular mobility. For this reason, I will investigate the effects of disrupting these networks on molecular movements, as well as the consequences of these interventions on endothelial responsiveness. My studies will establish important connections between receptor movements and endothelial cell functions. The impact of this study will be to improve our understanding of the biophysical mechanisms by which endothelial cells regulate their functions, especially during disease. By studying these mechanisms, we will accelerate the path to discovery of disease-specific treatments.

column36: The impact of chronic/latent viral infections on aging
column37: Some viruses give us a nasty cold then go away but other viruses stay with us our whole life. Some of these viruses can make us sick, for example HIV or hepatitis C, but others come back intermittently and are very annoying, for example herpes simplex virus (HSV) which recurrently give us cold sores or genital wards. Several of these chronic or persistent viruses (Epstein-Barr virus responsible for "mono" or cytomegalovirus) are quite common in the population. Whether they lead to sickness or not, they keep our immune system busy fighting the virus each time they come back. As we age, we are less and less able to fight against infections, such as the influenza virus, that we could easily beat when younger. A weaker immune system also increase the risk of several cancers linked to these viruses. We hypothesize that these persistent viruses damage our immune system over time, change the type of immune cells we have, and reduce our immune cells' ability to activate in order to fight new infections. Furthermore, we contend that the recurrent on and off activation of the immune system because of these viruses leads to the accumulation of mutations within immune cells, eventually rendering them less functional. We propose to study a group of people of all ages (1-80 years old), half of them living with HIV, the other half not. We will test for 8 chronic/persistent viruses and determine how many each person carries, how these relate to the health of their immune cells, and to their risk of disease. Understanding the effect of these viruses on immune cells and ultimately cellular aging will inform on the potential benefits of treating or vaccinating against these viruses in the future.

column37: Diverse diseases appear during aging and some of the more important ones affect the brain. Specifically, chronological age is the most potent risk factor for the common form of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). This form of AD is not caused by inherited mutations and comprises an enormous challenge for the patients, their families and for public health services. Inherited forms of AD account for only 10% of cases but are heavily represented in research labs by animal models that overproduce mutant protein molecules involved in the disease. We have created such a "low production" model based on the brain protein called Tau, and, of note, we have observed intriguing animal-to-animal diversity in the disease process. This not only offers a parallel to diversity seen in the human disease but also suggests the action of environmental influences as disease evolves late in the lifespan of these mice. As bacterial populations in the gut are more accessible physically and easier to manipulate than protein molecules inside the brain, we believe they comprise a novel and potentially important route towards stopping these brain diseases. intervention.

column36: Linking Inflammation and Metabolism with Frailty in Chronic Cancer
column37: Is 70 the new 60? One of the greatest risks to developing cancer is age. As the average age of Canadians continues to increase, we anticipate a doubling of newly diagnosed cancer patients. column37: Gradual decline of physical functions during aging increases susceptibility to chronic diseases and inevitably lead to increased health expenditures, morbidity and mortality. During the lifespan, cells within the organism undergo numerous stresses that can lead to irreversible damage. Damaged cells, also called senescent cells, lose their ability to properly function within the tissue leading to disruption of tissue integrity due to their secretion of numerous factors promoting inflammation. Recent evidences suggested that targeted elimination of damaged cells delays the onset of numerous age-related pathologies, such as cataracts, muscular degeneration, atherosclerosis, cardiac hypertrophy, kidney dysfunction, and cancer, and significantly extended the longevity of the animals. We recently identified a new drug displaying senolytic activity (the ability to kill damaged cells while sparing normal healthy cells). Here we propose to study the molecular mechanisms leading to the death of damaged cells, and to validate the use of our newly identified senolytic agent in vivo to improve both healthspan and lifespan. The proposed research program will not only define the molecular pathways allowing clearance of damaged cells, but also provide the proof-of-concept of targeting the viability of senescent cells can ameliorate both healthspan and lifespan. Our research in the area of geroscience will directly benefit to all Canadians by identifying therapeutic avenues decreasing morbidity within the population, but also decreasing the economical burden of age-related diseases on the Canadian health system by alleviating physical dysfunction in the elderly population.

column36: Genetic and chemical ablation of senescent cells that result from age-dependent telomere erosion
column37: The question: Major questions remain unanswered as to how and why we age, and whether we can intervene in the aging process. Recent technological advances in molecular biology and genetics have opened new avenues to investigate how genes function to influence aging at the cellular, tissue and whole body level. Remarkably, in certain cases these gene functions can now be manipulated, either genetically or chemically, to induce aged cells within tissues to be selectively removed to improve the function of tissues, and even improve health outcomes in mammals. This emerging new field of research is called geroscience. The approach: In this proposal, we will take advantage of CRISPR-based gene editing technology to understand how individual genes in the human genome contribute to cellular aging. We will focus on a central mechanism by which human cells age, namely through erosion of their chromosome protective caps, called telomeres. The research we propose will address the important question of whether removal of telomere-eroded "old" or senescent cells could also improve health outcomes. Our preliminary result have identified candidate gene functions whose absence appears to selectively impede the growth of cells with eroded telomeres. We have also identified chemicals that mimic this genetic sensitivity. We will extend these exciting preliminary results to comprehensively identify gene functions and chemicals that permit the removal of old cells that arise due to telomere erosion, and to test how the removal of these cells may improve the health of a mouse model engineered to possess human-like telomeres. Significance of the study: Since cellular senescence due to telomere erosion is already known to be critically important in age-associated human disease, our results may provide new clinical approaches to ameliorate the manifold effects of aging on human health.

column36: Investigating the contributions of mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired neuromuscular junction integrity to the aging-related loss of muscle mass and function in humans
column37: One of the most significant changes associated with normal aging is a progressive loss of muscle mass and strength, a biological process called sarcopenia. Sarcopenia can lead to mobility impairment, falls, and physical frailty in the elderly, dramatically impairing the quality of life of afflicted individuals. With the rapid demographic change of the aging population, sarcopenia will soon rank as one of the major financial burdens that our health care system will have to face. There is currently a lack of effective therapies to either prevent or treat sarcopenia, due in large part to the fact that its molecular and cellular bases are poorly understood. In the present research, we will test, directly in humans, the hypothesis that mitochondria, tiny structures essential for the muscle cell functioning, become dysfunctional with aging and that this accumulation of mitochondrial dysfunction results in a deterioration of the integrity of neuromuscular junction (the interface between neurones and muscle cells) and a decline in muscle mass and performance. We will also assess how physical activity protects against these aging-related changes affecting mitochondria and the NMJ. Finally, we will assess the robustness of recently identified biomarkers of sarcopenia. To ensure success, we have assembled a team of experts in mitochondrial biology (G Gouspillou), neurophysiology and the NMJ (R Robitaille & M Belanger) as well as in Geriatrics and Gerontology (JA Morais, M Aubertin-Leheudre, & P Gaudreau). The results of the present research will provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying the aging-related deterioration of muscle function. In addition, they will enable us to better understand how physical activity exerts its protective impact against sarcopenia. This knowledge will be critical in developing novel strategies to prevent or even reverse sarcopenia and might provide medical professionals with robust biomarkers to identify patients at risk.

column36: From orbit to bedside: using space-based bed-rest techniques to study cardiovascular and skeletal muscle-pump orthostatic reflexes with and without a strength and HIIT exercise intervention to prevent falls in older patients after hospitalization.
column37: Many of the changes that occur to astronauts during a six-month time in space appear to mimic an accelerated aging process of a few decades. These include bone and muscle loss, difficulty with balance and walking properly, and an inability to stand without feeling dizzy and about to fall. Scientists have found that bed rest can have the same negative effects on health. CIHR and the Canadian Space Agency are combining resources to use bed rest to examine these effects as they may relate to older persons who are hospitalized or otherwise confined to bed. It is expected that bed rest will have more severe consequences on old compared to young patients. In older persons, falls often result in a fractured hip, and for the frail, the changes caused by bed rest may be irreversible. The impact of these is decreased quality of life and increased occurrence of illness and mortality. The study design will include in-bed strength and high intensity interval training (HIIT) exercises to see if they are effective in preventing bed rest deconditioning. The research team led by Dr. Blaber at Simon Fraser University will be looking at the relationship between posture control and blood pressure regulation. His group has studied the effect of 60-days bed rest on middle-aged participants and found a large reduction of the ability of the muscles in the leg to pump blood back to the heart. This is an important part of the blood pressure control system and could result in increased incidence of fainting and falls. His team will now study the same system in the older participants to see if they are similarly affected after 15 days. The exercise group will be used to examine the effectiveness of in-bed strength and HIIT exercises to stop these changes. The team will also look at reflexes related to skeletal muscle activity and for specific biomarkers related to declines in nerve myelination as well as self-reports of the bed-rest experience and exercise intervention.

column36: Unraveling the mechanisms underlying of bed rest-induced muscle atrophy and of an exercise countermeasure
column37: Inactivity is associated with muscle loss and decreased bone mineral density, conditions seen with aging and during spaceflights. A model of inactivity of musculoskeletal unloading mimicking lack of gravity is bed rest with head-down tilt. Our reasoning is that bed rest leads to reduced fat oxidation and increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) from the mitochondria, the power house of the cell, which stimulates intracellular mechanisms responsible for developing insulin resistance and to decrease muscle and bone masses. These mechanisms involve the activity- and energy-sensing AMPK and the food-sensing mTOR, under which there are many key factors involved in muscle protein synthesis and breakdown. At the bone level, there is decreased production of osteocalcin, a protein shown to promote insulin sensitivity and to be associated with muscle atrophy in rats. We propose to study 24 men and women of 55-65 years of age engaged in moderate-vigorous exercise. Participants will be randomized into two groups for a two-week bed rest with half of them performing one hour of daily exercise while in bed as a countermeasure. At baseline and at 3, 7 and 14 days of bed rest, we will obtain venous blood and perform muscle biopsies of the thigh to measure muscle protein synthesis and breakdown using the deuterated water method. We will also measure mitochondrial respiration and ROS production in fresh permeabilized fibers, and in frozen muscle tissue, fiber type and size and several regulating factors by western blots. We will measure osteocalcin and many hormones regulating muscle and bone mass in blood samples. Participants will undergo an oral glucose tolerance test, assessment of their body compartments and physical performance before and at the end of bed rest. We wish to uncover the mechanisms related to muscle mass loss with inactivity and in response to exercise, which should open the door to future interventions to prevent the consequences of inactivity

column36: Bed rest in older adults accelerates "aging-like" changes
column37: Older adults confined in bed rest with the head tilted down slightly experience unloading of the heart, muscles and bones that cause rapid deconditioning. The changes they experience will be similar to the responses of astronauts during spaceflight. Our research group has measured "aging-like" increases in arterial stiffness and insulin resistance in astronauts who have reduced aerobic fitness because of their extended periods of inactivity while floating in space. In this research, we will monitor changes in physical function and in blood indicators of cardiovascular, muscular, skeletal, and metabolic and nutritional health. We will monitor the effect of bed rest on changes in cognitive function and spiritual well-being. In this study, we will introduce a new concept for bed rest studies by determining the biological age in addition to the chronological age of each participant. We anticipate that persons with an older biological age will have larger decreases in their body health during the bed rest. We anticipate as well that half of the older adults in the study who are asked to complete a specific exercise regime while in bed rest will have fewer changes in their health indicators. The results from our study will provide unique information for astronauts to maintain health while in space. Importantly for us on Earth, our results will inform older adults and health care providers about causes of physical deterioration with bed rest and of the benefits of daily exercise even if confined to bed.

column36: Sniffing around the Issue: investigating the relationship between solvent use and HIV risk
column37: HIV disproportionally affects the indigenous peoples of Canada with an incident rate 3.5 times higher than the national average and is associated with social-health factors such as poverty. Solvent use, the inhaling of substances to get a psychoactive effect, among street-involved individuals in Winnipeg is considerably higher than the population average. As HIV risk and solvent use are both associated with poverty, understanding how they interact with each other is an important question. Inflammation is a major biological risk factor for contracting HIV. Since solvent use is believed to cause inflammation, it may contribute to HIV acquisition risk and disease progression. However, there is a little information about the effect of solvent use on the immune system generally or HIV susceptibility specifically. Following consultations with the community, and in conjunction with our community partner Sunshine House, I conducted a pilot study of 14 HIV- solvent users and 13 community matched controls. When I analyzed their blood, I found that solvent users exhibited higher levels of immune activation. To confirm and extend this observation, we will enroll 100 Individuals with and without HIV who are or are not solvent users. We will perform studies to determine if solvent users have more inflammation than matched non-solvent users and if HIV positive individuals are at greater risk for faster HIV-disease progression. We will assess the impact of solvent use on: bacteria access to the blood, markers of inflammation and the functioning of the immune system. Understanding the effects of solvent use on the immune system and the potential impact on HIV risk and diseases progression is an important step in improving the health of this underserved community.

column36: So Far From Denendeh
column37: I am a Dene woman who was removed from Denendeh before I was born. I am a member of the Deninu Kue First Nation in Northwest Territories. I am an image-based storyteller. I come from generations of translators but I do not speak my language. My translation takes place in a different capacity. I am a translator of images. I situate Dene concepts of wellness in digital images I paint and I extract story from them. In my thesis, I will use Dene land-based systems of knowledge and image-based storytelling as my methodology). Specifically, I will use the arts-based approach of digital painting whereby I will paint images and extract stories to draw out Indigenous experience and perspectives about disability. Paintings give me the ability to confront the colonial indignities my family have suffered while simultaneously illuminating our resilience as Indigenous people. It is important to be truthful about the brutality of colonialism, yet I must honor our strength, spirit and resilience in my thesis. My objective in this thesis is to explore the disabling effects of colonialism by reflecting on and contrasting: (1) my journey as an Indigenous person who has been diagnosed with a disability (i.e., a learning disability) and (2) the journey of my father as an Indigenous person who was diagnosed with a disability (i.e. a mobility impairment caused by polio). I will use arts-based Indigenous research methods to compare our journeys in terms of our educational/academic and healthcare/clinical experiences as 'disabled' individuals. I will also explore the role of healing and 'rehabilitation' in addressing our disabilities and the disabling effects of the academic and healthcare structures. Both were extremely harmful; there was no healing to take place in the academy or through clinical methods of rehabilitation. We rejected colonial constructed identities. Rather, I will explore how rehabilitation took place through reclamation of culture.

column36: Integrating Indigenous Ways of Knowing into overdose responses for urban Indigenous people who use drugs
column37: The overdose epidemic remains one of the most pressing public health issues in Canada. In British Columba (BC), Indigenous people who use drugs (IPWUD) have been disproportionally affected by the overdose crisis. Further, it has become clear that overdose epidemic patterns are different among IPWUD. For example, while non-Indigenous men are overdosing at greater rates than non-Indigenous women, Indigenous women remain disproportionately impacted by the overdose crisis, and are experiencing non-fatal overdoses and overdose deaths at rates similar to Indigenous men. Diverse models of overdose-focused interventions are now being implemented in jurisdictions such as Vancouver's Downtown Eastside neighbourhood. However, research to date has failed to examine the overdose risk environment surrounding IPWUD living off reserve in inner cities. Given the ongoing harms experienced by off-reserve IPWUD, research is urgently needed to improve overdose-focused harm reduction and substance use programs for this population. This study addresses this gap by using ethnographic approaches that center Indigenous knowledges and ways of knowing to examine how social-structural and environmental conditions shape access to and outcomes from overdose-focused harm reduction and substance use treatment programs among IPWUD. Findings from this study will contribute to the overdose response for IPWUD by identifying policy and programmatic changes to improve the public health benefits of overdose response services.

column36: Interplay of diet, bile acid-metabolizing bacteria and bile acid receptors as a gut microbiota-driven immunomodulatory pathway in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) encompasses ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. These are chronic inflammatory conditions involving the intestinal tract. Symptoms include bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and loss of weight. IBD can result in serious medical complications, significant impairment of quality of life, and huge economic burden. Canada has among the highest reported prevalence and incidence of IBD in the world. The cause of IBD has not been elucidated which has prevented development of curative therapies; however, alteration of the composition of bacteria in the gut plays a key role in intestinal inflammation. Bile acids are molecules present in the intestinal tract which have many functions, including absorption of dietary fat. Since the discovery of bile acid receptors about 20 years ago, functions ascribed to these molecules have increased, and currently include modulation of intestinal barrier function and inflammation. Gut bacteria and bile acids have reciprocal effects; while bile acids exert an antibacterial role, bacteria are capable of transforming bile acids, changing their structure and ability to bind to their receptors. These bile acid receptors in turn, could modulate inflammation in the gut. In addition, specific diet compounds can modify the gut bacteria and activate bile acid receptors, adding another element to this axis. The complex interplay of environment, gut microbiota, bile acids, and intestinal inflammation in the process causing IBD has not been explored. We hypothesize that bile acid-dependent interaction between diet, gut bacteria, and the human gut represents an important pathway leading to IBD. Thus, capacity to modify bile acid-metabolizing bacteria, bile acids, or bile acid receptors might prove to be a successful therapeutic strategy for this chronic, incurable, and disabling disease.

column36: Identification of novel single gene variants in the IL-17 pathway leading to early onset Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a condition where someone's immune system attacks their gut and results in damage. Although, in most people, IBD is caused by a mixture of genetics and the environment, there are a subset of patients who get the condition very early on in life and in this subset a damaging change in a single gene is the cause of the disease. We have gathered a cohort of patients with very early onset Inflammatory Bowel Disease (VEOIBD) and used a technology called ' whole exome sequencing' to read the genetic code of all the genes that code for proteins. We looked in this data to see if there were any changes in genes we thought may be linked to IBD. It has been well documented from previous studies that genes involved in a particular immune pathway that involves a messenger molecule called 'interleukin-17' (IL-17) are associated with the risk of developing IBD. We therefore searched for changes in genes involved in this pathway in the gene code data from the VEOIBD patients. We found very rare changes that are not seen at all in the general population in the codes from three candidate genes in multiple families. A gene is made up of DNA and codes for another molecule called RNA, which then forms a particular protein in a cell. This project will use techniques to determine if these rare changes in the gene code of these families are causing problems in the amount of RNA and protein that is produced in the patient's cells. This work will potentially identify new extremely rare single gene causes for IBD happening in young children. This could provide a rationale to try personalized treatments for these children that might help treat their underlying disease.

column36: Can Blending Together Traditional and Western Knowledge Improve Diabetes and Obesity Health Outcomes in Urban Indigenous Communities?
column37: Indigenous peoples in Canada suffer from significantly higher rates of diabetes and obesity, resulting in reduced quality of life. Health, government and community organizations often lack Traditional Knowledge and community ownership, required to decrease healthcare gaps and burden of disease. The limited impact of Western health services on improving health in Indigenous peoples needs to be addressed. Site-specific, culturally safe, and locally-informed interventions will be co-developed/implemented/evaluated within the six FC/MC partner sites. Indigenous methodologies will be used to acknowledge and honour Indigenous knowledge, traditions, and protocols. Two sites will be offered to join a sub-study exploring the effects/outcomes of the community interventions on diabetes and obesity clinical variables (blood glucose, HbA1c, blood pressure, and waist circumference). One to two community interventions will be implemented at each site per year over three years. Diabetes and obesity clinical variables will be measured before, after, and one month following each intervention in the sub-study sites. The goal of the overall project is to reduce diabetes and obesity health inequities in Indigenous communities. Ultimately, the knowledge gained from this project will support change in diabetes and obesity policy, research, and practice in urban Indigenous communities and health systems, and to ultimately improve wellness.

column36: Potential association between inflammatory markers and vitamin D status on cardiometabolic risk factors among Indigenous populations
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are both inflammatory related conditions that disproportionately affect Indigenous people in Canada. Multilevel influences both individual and environmental have been shown to affect Indigenous populations cardiometabolic risk status. Vitamin D is an important nutrient for human health but has also been recognized as having anti-inflammatory properties, downregulating inflammatory pathways. Currently, measures of vitamin D and inflammatory biomarkers (a proxy for inflammatory diseases) data among Indigenous groups are lacking. For the proposed research data from the "Nituuchischaayihtitaau Aschii Multi-Community Environment and Health Study in Eeyou Istchee" will be used to examine the chronic subclinical inflammation on cardiometabolic risk factors. Next, explore if factors such as vitamin D modify these inflammatory characteristics that are shown to contribute to CVD and T2DM. Additionally, assess the importance of time-on-land activities as it related to Cree health and wellbeing. This research will serve to increase the knowledge of how systemic inflammatory pathways contribute to metabolic dysfunctions, and if vitamin D, which is shown to have anti-inflammatory properties mitigates this relationship among high-risk and vulnerable populations. Findings from this research will provide important information on exposures that are increasingly shown to contribute to cardiovascular and metabolic risk in humans.

column36: Cell populations regulating opioid-induced respiratory depression in sleep-wake states
column37: Opioids are used extensively for their analgesic properties but they have a variety of unwanted side effects, including tolerance, dependence, and most signicantly, respiratory depression. According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, there were more than 8,000 apparent opioid-related deaths in Canada between January 2016 and March 2018, an epidemic responsible for thousands of emergency visits every year, therefore causing a severe social, health and financial burden. The analgesic effects of opioids result from activation of classical opioid receptors (MORs) in the central nervous system and no treatments are currently available to prevent respiratory depression without reducing their analgesic proprieties. MORs are expressed in various brain structures regulating breathing including the preBotzinger Complex (preBotC). The preBotC is composed of neuronal subpopulations expressing neurokinin-1 receptors (NK1-R) and the peptide somatostatin (SST). We propose that genetic deletion of MORs in NK1-R and SST cells, pharmacological activation of NK1-R and antagonism of SST as well as optogenetic stimulation of said cells will reduce opioids-induced respiratory depression. My project aims to determine whether NK1-R and SST cells are sensitive to MOR ligands and whether they regulate opioid-induced respiratory depression and sedation To do so, we will use a variety of physiological (electrocortical and respiratory recordings), pharmacological (MORs agonist injection) and genetic (MORs deletion) approaches. My research hypothesis will open a new path towards the understanding of respiratory depression with opioids abuse, an essential step to develop new therapeutic targets to reduce the risk of opioids overdose, hypoxemia, critical care, and mortality. The benefits will be significant both from a fundamental and clinical point of view.

column36: The Process of Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation - A Combined EEG-fMRI study.
column37: Although we all need to sleep, its function is not yet fully understood. A growing domain in sleep research focuses on sleep's link to memory consolidation, which is to say the strengthening of newly formed memories as they become enduring long-term memories. A form of memory known as "cognitive procedural memory" (i.e., learning a new logical strategy to acquire a new skill) undergoes memory consolidation during sleep. Consequently, the proposed study will use simultaneous EEG-fMRI to identify the hemodynamic cerebral correlates of spindle activity in the post-training night, and their association with cognitive procedural memory consolidation in young participants. Immediately following the evening training session (i.e., at 23h00), post-training simultaneous EEG-fMRI will be recorded while subjects are required to sleep in the scanner where their sleep spindles will be subsequently identified for the main analysis of interest. Spindles have been found to be involved in memory consolidation for declarative memory and simple procedural memory, via the reactivation of the same brain structures recruited during learning. We hypothesize that spindles will be involved in reactivation of the same brain regions recruited during learning (e.g., prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and striatum) for cognitive procedural memory. In addition, greater spindle-related activation in these structures will be associated with greater overnight improvements in performance. This will reveal whether spindle-related reactivation supports memory consolidation for cognitive procedural memory.

column36: Development of a user-centred and evidence-based novel eHealth online sleep program for infant sleep problems
column37: About 25% of families have sleep problems with their baby during the first year, which can impact parental health and the baby's development and behaviour. While researchers know what works to improve sleep, families do not have universal access to baby sleep programs that are based on best clinical practices and up-to-date research. Families often turn to unregulated sleep products or sleep-coaching services, which can be expensive and not research-based. Offering research-based sleep programs online (eHealth) could help parents access high-quality service options. To take advantage of eHealth options, we need to know more about the 'active ingredients' to include in a parent-centered online program that helps parents learn how to help their baby sleep better. My fellowship goal is to develop and test an online sleep program to improve parents' access to best available information about how to help their baby sleep better. I will lead three studies to do this. First, I will systematically review existing research to determine what makes baby sleep programs and parent-centered eHealth programs effective. Next, I will gather information from parents, as well as parenting and sleep experts, about factors that may influence the use of an online baby sleep program. Finally, after developing an online baby sleep program prototype, I will test its usability with an online pilot test and survey with parents. These research studies will result in a final version of an online baby sleep program (Better Nights, Better Days for Babies). Following my fellowship, I will test this final version in a multi-centre trial to assess its short- and long-term effects on family sleep and child development. If effects are positive, I will test how well the program scales up for use across Canada and other countries. This program could increase access to research-based advice for families who are struggling with their baby's sleep and support overall child development and family wellbeing.

column36: Correlation between Odds Ratio Product (ORP), a novel, automatic measure of sleep-wakefulness continuum and patient-ventilator asynchronies - a step towards improvement of sleep in critically ill patients under mechanical ventilation
column37: Very sick patients connected to breathing machines have a high mortality and those who survive experience psychological and functional disabilities. These problems might be related to modifiable factors such as sleep disruption and uncomfortable interactions between the patients and breathing machines ("asynchronies"). Previous research proved that "asynchronies" are related to sleep problems in these patients, but what is the exact relation between these factors remains unknown. Adequately evaluating sleep in patients connected to breathing machines was not possible until the recent invention of a new scoring system named Odds Ratio Product (ORP), a numerical scale that ranges from 0 to 2.5. We used ORP in a previous study for the first time in this type of patients and showed that is a useful tool to measure sleep problems in patients connected to breathing machines. I hypothesize that sleep problems measured with ORP will be intimately related with the presence of "asynchronies" and sleep problems measured with ORP will be more frequent in patients with "asynchronies". I will enroll patients with breathing failure connected to breathing machines and measure sleep using ORP and "asynchronies". I will then correlate the two variables trying to understand the relationship between the two. This project will prove what the exact relationship between sleep problems and "asyncrhonies" is and help to design a strategy to modify the settings of the breathing machines to avoid "asynchronies" and improve sleep in very sick patients preventing future psychological and functional disabilities.

column36: Phase Two of the Canadian Consortium on Neurodegeneration in Aging
column37: The Canadian Consortium for Neurodegeneration and Aging (CCNA) is an important response to the urgent health problem of Alzheimer Disease (AD) and other more rare dementias-together termed the neurodegenerative diseases (NDD)- in Canada. Our mission is to create teams and platforms that will do transformative Canadian research, advancing our understanding of AD and other NDD and leading to new therapies and prevention strategies, along with concrete improvements in the lives of People with Dementia (PWD). The first five years of CCNA have had a strikingly positive impact on the Canadian dementia research community, with meetings, workshops and increased synergy, creation of new national teams, and an increased international profile. In Phase II (2019-2024) we will build on these to make significant progress across a series of areas where Canada has specific research strength and expertise. The total budget will be 45.7 million dollars, less than the daily cost of AD and NDD to Canada. There will be 311 researchers working together, including 19 national teams under the headings of Prevention, Treatment of NDD, and Improvement of Quality of Life for People with Dementia (PWD). We will continue teams focussing on the unique needs of Rural and Indigenous communities dealing with dementia To support team research agendas, we are gathering data from a national cohort (entitled COMPASS-ND) of 2,310 individuals with different NDD and pre-dementia states. We are collecting an array of social, clinical, and biological information on each of these individuals. A second platform- CAN-THUMBS UP - will take the initial first steps towards future dementia prevention studies using combinations of novel medications with lifestyle and non-pharmacological interventions. Our overall program is bold, novel, and ambitious, and will lead to major advances on many fronts againts the NDD over the coming five years.

column36: CIHR Centre for REACH in HIV/AIDS (REACH 3.0) - A National Canadian Research and Knowledge Mobilization Network to Connect People to Testing and Care and Reduce Stigma for HIV, HCV and other Sexually and Bloodborne Infections (STBBI)
column37: Since 2009, the CIHR Centre for REACH (1.0/2.0) has been a Canadian leader in collaborative, interdisciplinary, and community-driven HIV/STBBI services and population health research. REACH supports a nation-wide team - with hubs in Atlantic Canada, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia - to engage in innovative research, participatory evaluation, community-based research (CBR), and program/implementation science research in HIV, HCV and STBBIs. REACH has made significant research and capacity-building gains by engaging policy-makers, community-based agencies, clinicians, people with lived experience and researchers to respond to regional/national HIV health issues. REACH 3.0 will continue and advance the work of REACH to date - our vision is to be a broker of pragmatic solutions to end the HIV epidemic in Canada, and in so doing, to influence the course of HCV and other STBBIs. With this vision in mind, our 5-year goals are to contribute to efforts to increase the proportion of people living with HIV who are diagnosed to >95%, ensure that >95% of people who know their HIV status are on treatment, and for those with HIV on treatment, 95% have their virus suppressed. We will also contribute to efforts to ensure that HCV infection is cleared, and that HIV/HCV stigma is reduced so people have fewer barriers to testing, treatment and care. The REACH 3.0 Centre will provide research infrastructure and coordination for regional and national signature projects; provide capacity-building and career development for all team members; ensure that research findings are mobilized into services and policy action; and we will evaluate our outputs and outcomes to ensure we are meeting our goals. National signature research projects include implementation and scale up of innovative HIV, HCV and STBBI testing in Canada, as well as a major national initiative to document and create interventions for HIV and related stigma and discrimination.

column36: A BC wide program for Indigenous patients to Gain Equitable access to kidney transplantation: The BRIDGE to Transplantation Initiative.
column37: Indigenous populations in Canada have a higher risk of developing kidney failure, but are much less likely to get access to the best treatment for kidney failure - a living donor kidney transplant. There are many reasons that may explain this, but one major barrier is that the Indigenous people with kidney failure are less aware of the benefits of transplantation and have a tough time identifying people who may donate a kidney to them. We recently partnered with Indigenous people who have kidney disease and those that have previously donated their kidney to a loved one to better understand the barriers to transplantation and develop a new program which aims to support Indigenous patients better. The BRIDGE to Transplantation Initiative is a program that will be implemented by the Provincial Health Services Authority (PHSA) in kidney care clinics across BC where Indigenous Patient Liaisons (IPLs) will provide targeted and culturally tailored education about transplantation and living donation to Indigenous people with kidney failure. The education will occur outside of hospitals (usually at Aboriginal Friendship Centres) and will include Indigenous patients and prior living donors. The Initiative also will help patients and potential donors to navigate the medical evaluation for transplantation and donation and coordinate any followup needed after donation. As part of the evaluation of this program, we anticipate that the rates of Indigenous people that are referred for transplantation will double and that the entire process around transplantation will become more culturally safe.

column36: Multi-center validation of non-invasive biomarkers of renal allograft outcomes
column37: End-stage kidney failure (ESKF) is common (38,833 Canadians in 2017), increasing (by 35% since 2008) and costly (more than $1.8 billion/year). Transplantation is the therapy of choice for many patients with better survival and quality of life, and provides healthcare savings of $33,000-$84,000 per patient each year after the first year compared to staying on dialysis. When a patient loses their transplant and returns to dialysis, there is a 3-fold higher risk of dying. Therefore, developing new strategies to keep kidney transplants healthy is a key priority for patients and caregivers. We have identified non-invasive urine tests that can predict late kidney transplant results. We showed that two urine proteins (CCL2 and CXCL10) are elevated 6-months after transplant in patients most likely to lose their transplant. The primary goal of these two large multi-center studies is to independently confirm that these new urine tests predict kidney transplant results, as this is the next critical step to bring these new urine tests into clinical practice. These new urine tests could be used to help personalize transplant care based on individual risk profile. For example, identifying low risk individuals can help doctors decide who may be safe to reduce the amount of anti-rejection medications they are taking. Conversely, high risk patients could be enrolled into clinical trials aimed at improving their long-term transplant health. If these new tests are confirmed as strong predictors of transplant outcome (or "surrogate markers") they could make clinical trials more feasible to conduct. This would help new treatments become available to patients sooner. Finally, these tests may identify low/high risk patients who would benefit from less/more monitoring after transplant. Ultimately, the results from these studies may be used to help inform the design and conduct of the next generation of kidney transplant trials, with the goal of improving kidney transplant results.
