column36: Discovering the effects of DRD2 genotype-based variants on D2 receptor distribution in patients with Parkinson's disease: a [11C]-(+)-PHNO PET study
column37: The underlying impairment of mental functioning and motor planning in Parkinson's disease (PD) stems from the dopaminergic signal loss within the striatum and prefrontal cortex. Neurons within these brain regions contain two dopamine D2 receptor isoforms-D2 long (D2L) and D2 short (D2S). The degree of expression for these receptor isoforms are affected by the genotype within two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), rs2283265 and rs1076560 (both are in high linkage disequilibrium; C>A), found in the DRD2 gene. The importance of these SNPs are heightened clinically as PD patients with the CC genotype showed the most clinical improvement in motor and mental functioning to an anti-parkinsonian medication known as rasagiline compared to minor A allele carriers (AC/AA) (Masellis et al., 2016). However, it is fundamentally unclear how these SNPs affect the distribution of D2 receptors in vivo within the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system and its relevance to behavioral and movement impairment in patients with PD. Therefore, we propose to image PD patients and age-matching controls grouped by their genotype using a high-affinity PET radiotracer biomarker-[11C]-(+)-PHNO (PHNO). This agonist probe has properties allowing high sensitivity and specificity in detecting D2 receptors in certain regions of the brain. Through PHNO PET imaging of PD patients and controls, our objectives are: (1) examine genotype group effects on D2 receptor distribution and correlate it with behaviour and movement functioning; and (2) elucidate how the genotype modulates the dopaminergic system in PD patients. Achieving these objectives will (1) reveal a deeper understanding of the genetic impact on the dopaminergic pathophysiology of PD in vivo and its role in mental and movement impairment; and (2) help pave a path towards the improvement and advancement of personalized medicine for PD patients.

column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed prior to age 18 in up to 10% of patients, and cognitive impairment is a consequence in one third of these individuals. Disruption to white matter integrity (i.e., how healthy the white matter is) has been observed as an early component of pediatric-onset MS. The cerebellum is a structure involved in motor coordination, but more recently implicated in cognitive processes, such as memory and attention. This region is particularly vulnerable due to a high propensity for lesions in this area in pediatric-onset patients compared to adults who have had MS for the same amount of time. This study will examine whether white matter of the cerebellum is associated with cognitive functioning in pediatric-onset MS, and if changes in cerebellar white matter can predict cognitive outcomes over time. This research may provide evidence for the utility of examining white matter to detect early degenerative processes in MS, prior to the development of cognitive decline.

column36: Comparing Attention Interventions in Individuals with Generalized Anxiety Disorder
column37: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a chronic illness characterized by excessive and uncontrollable worry. GAD affects roughly 5% of Canadians, and is associated with elevated use of health services, decreased work productivity, and coronary heart disease. Individuals with GAD experience their worry as overwhelming and often report that it makes concentration extremely difficult. It has been proposed that excessive worry is maintained by two attention processes. One is a heightened bias or sensitivity to threatening information. The other is a decreased ability to control attention, or to shift attention away from a worry spiral and back to the task at hand. Attention Bias Modification (ABM) was designed to help people train their attention away from threat and towards neutral information instead. The Attention Training Technique (ATT) aims to train attentional control in worriers. Preliminary evidence suggests that ABM and the ATT are successful in reducing anxiety and worry in people who worry excessively; however, the two interventions have never been compared in such a population. This next step is important so that clinicians can determine which interventions to recommend to clients. This study will be the first to compare the effects of ABM and ATT to a control condition in people with GAD, on worry and attention. It is predicted that relative to control, ABM and ATT will both be associated with a reduction in worry, attention bias, and attention control, with the ATT being more effective. It is also predicted that attention control improvement will be responsible for improvement in worry. These hypotheses will be tested by randomly assigning participants to engage in 12-minutes of ABM, ATT, or listening to a recording of sounds (control condition), once at the lab and then for six consecutive days at home, and monitoring changes before, during, and after the interventions.

column36: Investigating the Mechanisms of Immune Evasion by a Brazilian Zika Virus Isolate
column37: Zika virus (ZIKV) has recently emerged as a major global health burden, causing numerous outbreaks across South America since early 2015. The most concerning characteristic of these outbreaks is that ZIKV has become associated with more severe disease. This includes neurological symptoms like Guillain-Barre Syndrome, which causes paralysis, and fetal microcephaly, a condition that leads to children being born with poorly formed brains and heads. To understand this sudden change, our laboratory has established a mouse model of ZIKV infection, which we will use to study the immune response to various ZIKV strains that have or have not been associated with these complications. Our data indicate that recent strains are able to suppress important aspects of the anti-viral immune response in order to establish longer-lasting infections. We anticipate that recent strains are able to actively suppress the immune response by disrupting the production of a key anti-viral molecule, type I interferon, by the "first responders" of the immune system, innate immune cells. In addition, it has been shown that pregnancy temporarily weakens the mother's immune system to protect the developing fetus. Using our mouse model, we will explore the impact this has on the immune response to ZIKV during pregnancy, and how this relates to the fetal microcephaly seen during recent ZIKV outbreaks. Together, these studies will tell us how the virus has changed over time to evade the host immune response and establish more severe infections. column36: Titrating Mood on the Basis of Functional Networks: fMRI-guided Programming of Deep Brain Stimulation for Depression
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a widespread and debilitating condition that does not respond to medication or psychotherapy in up to 1/3rd of patients. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a surgical treatment for neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders in which electrical stimulation is delivered via implanted electrodes to specific brain circuits. In order to achieve good clinical responses to DBS, physicians must carefully select (i.e., 'program') several electrical stimulation settings, such as contact (which part of the electrode the electricity is delivered through) and voltage. DBS targeting the subgenual cingulate (SGC - a brain structure involved in mood regulation) has shown promising early results for treatment-resistant MDD. However, SGC DBS has been less successful in larger, controlled studies, likely due to suboptimal DBS programming. Compared to DBS for disorders like Parkinson's disease, DBS for MDD is particularly difficult to program because there is no immediate clinical feedback to help indicate which settings are 'optimal'. DBS programming is instead a trial-and-error process that usually requires multiple clinic visits and imposes substantial financial and time burdens on patients. Given the limitations of this current approach, there is a need for more objective, physiological markers of good response to DBS settings that could help guide DBS programming. Building upon extensive experience at my institution using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in DBS patients, I intend to use functional MRI (fMRI) to better understand and individualize DBS for MDD. Specifically, I aim to 1) use fMRI to investigate how DBS interacts with brain networks in MDD; 2) identify a brain connectivity pattern or 'signature' that is associated with good responses to DBS; 3) use this connectivity signature to guide the adjustment of contact settings in MDD patients who respond poorly to DBS in order to hopefully improve their clinical outcomes.

column36: Optimized manufacturing of thymus-derived regulatory T cells for immune cell-based therapy
column37: Blood and bone marrow transplants can be used to treat blood cancers such as leukemia. The transplant can provide a cure when the donor immune cells attack and kill leukemia cells. Unfortunately, the donor cells often also attack the patient's own tissue, causing serious short- and long-term consequences. To prevent these negative immune responses without inhibiting the anti-cancer effect of the transplant, our strategy is to also give patients a dose of the type of immune cell that suppress the negative immune responses. These are called regulatory T cells, or Tregs. Initial studies with Tregs have been promising, but there are many challenges to using Tregs as a therapy. One major issue is that Tregs are very rare - less than 1% of white blood cells - so to obtain enough cells to use in a patient, we must develop methods to isolate and grow Tregs. Rather than obtaining rare Tregs from blood, my goal is to isolate these cells from Treg-rich tissue and increase their numbers in the lab. For this study, the tissue source is the thymus gland, an immune organ located above the heart that is routinely removed during pediatric cardiac surgery. The thymus is a plentiful source of Tregs that are more uniform in their characteristics than Tregs in the blood. I am developing a protocol to grow thymus-derived Tregs that is compatible with clinical standards and will also identify new conditions that can further enhance Treg growth in culture. Ultimately, this work will result in methods to efficiently produce Tregs for cell therapy applications, a crucial step towards the clinical use of thymus-derived Tregs as a therapy to improve transplantation outcomes.

column36: The effect of a viral mimetic on the expression of nutrient transporters: Exploring the link between maternal immune activation and Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects 1.5% of Canadians. Characteristics of ASD include difficulties in behaviour, social interaction, and communication. Being a spectrum disorder, these symptoms can range from mild to severe, depending on the individual. Recent research has shown that women who are infected with a virus during pregnancy are at an increased risk of having a child with ASD. However, the underlying reason for this association is unknown. To help understand this association, we are investigating whether viral infection alters the transport of nutrients from the mother to the fetus. Many of the nutrients transferred from the mother to the fetus are required for the fetal brain to form properly. If viral infection causes physiological changes that alter the ability of nutrients to be transported to the fetus while the brain is developing, typical brain development could be impacted which could possibly result in ASD. To detect these physiological changes, we will use a pregnant rat model; we will mimic a viral infection in pregnant rats and then examine the placenta and fetal brain to identify changes that may alter nutrient transport. We will then identify the molecular pathways involved in these changes to understand how they occur. Identifying these changes and their causes will provide new treatment targets for early intervention in the development of ASD.

column36: Determining the Impact of Osteoarthritis on Mobility and Physical Inactivity in People with Type 2 Diabetes to Identify Opportunities to Improve Diabetes Outcomes
column37: An estimated 30-50% adults living with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) also have osteoarthritis, the most common form of arthritis. However, joint pain in the hips, knees and/or feet from osteoarthritis can result in difficulty walking and limit people with T2DM from being active. Unfortunately, many people (both patients and medical professionals) view osteoarthritis as an inevitable part of aging, and, despite evidence to the contrary, believe that physical activity will make the symptoms worse. We will use interviews to gain perspectives of patients with T2DM on the impact of osteoarthritis on their diabetes care, as well as to understand the perspectives and practices of doctors who treat people with T2DM on how they assess and manage their patients with walking difficulty and physical inactivity. This work will help illuminate important opportunities to improve the care and health of people with T2DM.

column36: Evaluation des effets du reamenagement d'un espace public en milieu urbain sur le jeu libre des enfants et les pratiques de leurs parents
column37: Au Canada, 30% des enfants ages souffrent d'embonpoint ou d'obesite, phenomene en partie attribuable au manque d'activite physique, notamment sous la forme de jeu actif a l'exterieur. La litterature scientifique presente actuellement les parents comme obstacle critique a ce type de jeu en vertu de normes sociales liees a l'education des enfants. Des craintes croissantes pour la securite des enfants, des pratiques de surprotection, et des preferences envers d'autres activites academiques ou culturelles restreignent ainsi la place du jeu exterieur dans le quotidien des enfants. En milieu urbain, le declin du jeu exterieur serait aussi attribuable aux amenagements de moins en moins concus pour les besoins des enfants, releguant ces derniers a des espaces de plus en plus confines. Malgre ces constats, les facons de raviver le jeu exterieur sont peu connues. Depuis 2015, la Ville de Montreal implante son programme de rues pietonnes et partagees, creant de nouveaux espaces publics de proximite. En reprenant une partie de la voie publique existante pour y amenager des espaces actifs, ludiques et securitaires, ce programme a le potentiel de favoriser le jeu libre en milieu urbain. Ce projet vise a mieux comprendre comment une strategie de promotion du jeu libre axee sur le reamenagement d'un espace public, telles que les rues pietonnes et partagees, pourrait contribuer a optimiser les opportunites de jouer a l'exterieur pour les enfants et reduire les pratiques dites "intensives" des parents. Pour atteindre cet objectif, des peres et des meres seront mis a contribution au moyen d'entrevues et de questionnaires en ligne. S'inscrivant dans le secteur prioritaire de la "promotion des villes en sante" de l'Institut de la sante publique et des populations des IRSC, ce projet contribuera a comprendre comment l'amenagement des municipalites contribue a promouvoir la sante, tant pour les enfants que pour leurs parents.

column36: The utility of brain imaging to advance clinical decision-making for trigeminal neuralgia
column37: Chronic pain is one of the most underestimated health care problems in the world today, causing a major burden to the patient and society. In Canada, one in five adults experience chronic pain, with associated costs estimated at $40 billion a year and rising. On top of this, Canada is currently facing an opioid crisis, affecting many chronic pain patients who use opioid medications to manage their pain. Despite overwhelming evidence of the prevalence and impact of chronic pain on our society, research for pain is greatly underfunded. This results in a lack of understanding and treatment of the disease, with only a small percentage of patients achieving full recovery. Chronic facial pain can be especially debilitating, being described as one of the most excruciating pains one can experience. Therefore, technologies and advances that can help improve the care of patients with chronic facial pain is necessary. Towards this goal, neuroimaging and machine learning have the capacity to assess treatment response and help physicians with their clinical decision-making for an individual chronic facial pain patient. Neuroimaging uses various techniques to measure the structure and function of the brain. Machine learning provides a computer with the ability to learn from data, identify patterns, and make predictions on new, unseen data. My research combines neuroimaging techniques and machine learning to elucidate the brain features that distinguishes treatment responders from non-responders. Using this novel approach, physicians can draw on additional information to better evaluate the selection of optimal treatment and assessment of long-term outcome for patients with chronic facial pain. My research will ultimately advance our fundamental understanding of brain mechanisms in chronic facial pain and improve the quality of life for these patients.

column36: Evaluating the Impact of Incarceration and a Transfer in Correctional Healthcare Leadership on HIV Health Outcomes for Women Living with HIV in Metro Vancouver
column37: Women living with HIV(WLWH) are disproportionality represented within correctional facilities worldwide and experience gender disparities and sub-optimal HIV health outcomes related to incarceration. However, despite the disproportionate burden of HIV amongst WLWH and the evident gender disparities, there remains a substantial evidence gap on the health impacts of incarceration among WLWH. With the current shift in leadership for the provision of healthcare within BC's provincial correctional centres, this research will evaluate and explore the impact of incarceration on HIV health outcomes for WLWH throughout the transition. The research will draw on empirical survey data gathered from a larger longitudinal cohort study of WLWH in Vancouver, and will employ advanced epidemiology modelling techniques to make use of longitudinal data and examine the relationship between incarceration and HIV health outcomes for WLWH. This work will be complimented by in-depth interviews with WLWH who have recently been incarcerated as well as peer mentors and service providers within the correctional healthcare system. Given the high rates of HIV among incarcerated women in Canada as well as globally, there is a critical need to translate these findings into health policy and practice. column36: Evaluating the impacts of end-demand criminalization and immigration policies on the health access and human rights of im/migrant women in sex work
column37: Despite evidence that criminalization promotes stigma, violence, HIV/STI burden and labour rights violations among sex workers, in 2014 Canada enacted end-demand sex work legislation (Protection of Exploited Communities and Persons Act, PCEPA) which upholds the criminalization of clients and third party activities while leaving the sale of sex legal. However, selling sex services remains explicitly criminalized for temporary residents and open work permit holders: this additional criminalization may compound documented health and labour inequities among im/migrant workers. Evidence suggests most im/migrant sex workers in Canada are legal immigrants; yet face unique vulnerabilities including racism, stigma, and language barriers resulting in poor healthcare access. Qualitative research suggests im/migrant sex workers may fear jeopardizing their legal status (i.e., work permit) as a result of police interactions, which has been shown to impede reporting violence to authorities and limit health access through fear of disclosing sex work to health providers. Authorities' broad discretion in enforcing sex work and immigration laws, and the conflation of sex work (consensual exchange of sex services) and sex trafficking (forced sexual labour) among racialized women may exacerbate barriers to healthcare and legal protections. Given that punitive PCEPA and immigration enforcement may disproportionately impact im/migrant sex workers, there is an urgent need to assess how such criminalization impacts their health and human rights. As policy shifts impacting im/migrant sex workers in Canada have occurred despite a dearth of evidence on their experiences, and given the PCEPA's stated goal of protecting vulnerable communities, I will evaluate how shifts in criminalized interactions post-PCEPA relate to im/migrant sex workers' health access and human rights to inform national and global policy discussions on end-demand legislation.

column36: Exploring End of Life Nutrition Care Practices for Residents of Ontario Long-Term Care Homes: A Mixed Methods Approach
column37: Eating and nutrition care for residents at the end of life can be challenging in long-term care (LTC). As residents approach death, they will often lose their interest in food and may stop eating altogether. Conditions such as dementia can pose further challenges. The uncertainty of the dying process can be a great source of stress for family and care staff. Current recommendations for nutrition care at the end of life emphasize comfort and meeting personal care goals. However, it is unclear whether these recommendations are applied consistently in LTC homes. Further, the role of several factors (e.g., resources, policies, family wishes) that likely influence nutrition care decisions at the end of life are not well understood. The goal of this research is to explore the current state of nutrition care for LTC residents at the end of life, and to understand the influential factors behind these care decisions. Mixed methods will be used to gather data from residents, families, and care staff to gain an understanding of end of life nutrition care. Data from resident medical charts will be collected in 12 LTC homes from Ontario. The type of nutrition care practices provided will be identified and compared to resident characteristics (e.g., weight loss, swallowing problems). Interviews will also be conducted with residents, families, and staff who will be recruited on a voluntary basis from the same homes. These interviews will explore various perspectives of nutrition care and the associated decision-making processes among LTC staff, family, and residents at the end of life. Working together with residents, families and LTC staff, this research will help to describe current practices around nutrition care for residents at the end of life. Findings will improve the understanding of the current approaches to end-of-life nutrition care in Ontario LTC homes and is a key step towards improving personalized comfort care for residents up to the moment of death.

column36: The role of uncoupling proteins in post-burn wound healing and keloid formation
column37: Burns are responsible for an estimated 300,000 deaths per year worldwide, with approximately 11 million cases requiring medical attention. One of the negative consequences of thermal injuries is aberrant wound healing, such as keloids. Treatment and prevention of keloids is one of the greatest unmet challenges in burns, with no curative strategies at this time. Recent studies link local glucose and glucose transporter levels with wound healing. Specifically, lack of glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) impairs healing of wounds or UV-damaged skin. Conversely, lack of GLUT1 decreases inflammation and excessive tissue production in psoriasis. Therefore, local glucose levels and GLUT1 expression have an integral role in the balance between impaired and excessive healing in conditions like keloids. Elevated generalized glucose levels and inflammation are consequences of increased metabolism seen in burns. One of mediators involved in this increased metabolism are mitochondrial uncoupling proteins. Uncoupling protein 2 (UCP2), which is at many sites including skin, increases GLUT1 expression and facilitates glucose uptake. UCP2 also activates a mediator of inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome, which is elevated in burns. We propose that UCP2 expression is increased in burn skin and has role in normal and aberrant wound healing, likely through NLRP3 and GLUT1 expression. Ultimately, persistent alterations in inflammation and local glucose levels could detrimentally affect wound healing, predisposing patients to keloids.

column36: Understanding the processes that dictate excitatory versus inhibitory neuronal cell fate specification from cortically derived neural stem cells
column37: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are brain cells that have the potential to make all neural cell types in the brain such as neurons or glial cells. The recruitment of endogenous NSCs for neurological repair is a promising area of biomedicine that is currently being investigated as a therapeutic strategy to regenerate damaged tissue following brain injury. The rationale of this strategy is to manipulate NSCs following brain injury and instruct them to produce new neurons to replace any particular neural tissue that would have been damaged from a brain injury such as stroke. One of the main challenges of this strategy is to ensure that the recruited NSCs produce the correct type of neurons to replace the cells that had died following the brain injury. This is challenging because NSCs are known to make different types of neurons in different contexts. For example, NSCs that come from the cerebral cortex have been shown to make two different types of neurons (excitatory neurons which trigger electric impulses and inhibitory neurons which inhibit electric impulses) at different periods of life: excitatory neurons are made prenatally whereas inhibitory neurons are made during adulthood. Our lab has previously shown that the extracellular environment or niche of a NSC plays a critical role in dictating NSC behaviour. The hypothesis of my research project states that the niche of a NSC plays an important role in instructing the NSC to make one type of neuron over another: the prenatal environment of cortical NSCs favours excitatory neuron production and the adult environment favours inhibitory neuron production. I hope to identify candidate factors within the niche that are essential in promoting either excitatory or inhibitory neuronal specification. The elucidation of these novel factors will lead to new insights regarding the mechanisms by which a NSC can be recruited to make the correct type of neuron in the context of endogenous repair following brain injury.

column36: Developpement et mecanismes cerebraux du raisonnement fluide chez les enfants sur le spectre de l'autisme
column37: Le raisonnement fluide est la capacite d'inferer des solutions a des problemes nouveaux en integrant et en manipulant les relations entre les items d'un probleme. Chez les individus au developpement typique, cette capacite se base sur l'activite d'un large reseau neuronal, impliquant le cortex parietal posterieur et le cortex prefrontal. Les personnes ayant un trouble du spectre de l'autisme (TSA) presentent des particularites sur le plan perceptif, avec un traitement preferentiel pour le contenu visuospatial. Ces particularites donnent lieu a des activations cerebrales distinctes pendant le raisonnement, qui se manifestent par une suractivation des aires occipitales et une sous-activation des aires frontales. Il est bien connu que la capacite de raisonner en se basant sur des liens semantiques plutot que perceptifs emergerait vers l'age de 5 ans chez les enfants au developpement typique. column36: Impaired Autonomic Signalling in the Sinoatrial Node During Angiotensin II Mediated Hypertensive Heart Disease
column37: The prevalence of hypertension (high blood pressure) in Canada has increased nearly 2-fold over the past 2 decades. Around 40% of adults suffer from hypertension which substantially increases the risk of life threatening cardiac arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms). A small area of specialized cells located in the upper right chamber of the heart are responsible for controlling the normal heart beat. This area, called the sinoatrial node, is commonly referred to as the heart's pacemaker. However, in diseases such as hypertension, the heart's pacemaker cells can become dysfunctional leading to abnormally low and dysregulated heart rates that can be life-threatening; this is known as "sinoatrial node disease" or "sick sinus syndrome". The autonomic nervous system (ANS) acts largely unconsciously and helps to regulate heart rate and pacemaker function. In individuals with sick sinus syndrome, the diseased pacemaker cells also begin to fail to respond to ANS signals causing a progressive worsening of heart function. Currently, artificial pacemaker implantation is the major treatment approach for sick sinus syndrome. However, this comes with substantial costs and a number of attendant risks including infections and lead dislodgment. This has serious implications as failure to appropriately regulate heart rate has been shown to increase the risk of long term morbidity and mortality. This indicates a clear need for improved treatment options for patients with sick sinus syndrome. Accordingly, my project aims to assess the mechanisms responsible for sick sinus syndrome and reduced ability for the ANS to regulate heart rate in the setting of hypertension. This study will provide critical new insight into why the heart's pacemaker fails to respond to ANS stimulation and may help facilitate the development of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of sick sinus syndrome.

column36: Effect of Gut Microbial Perturbations on Parkinson's Disease Progression
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease worldwide, characterized the death of certain nerve cells within the brain that produce the chemical dopamine. The loss of dopamine leads to movement symptoms such as tremors, problems with balance, and slowed muscle movement. In Canada, PD affects 1 in every 500 people. Genetic and environmental factors play a role, but in many cases the cause is unknown. PD is currently incurable and there is a desperate need for new and better treatment methods. Recently, the bacteria that live in the healthy human gut, or gut microbiota, have also been found to play a role in PD. Studies have found that PD patients have different amounts of certain bacteria present in their guts when compared to people of the same age without PD. Also, many patients report problems with their gut, such as constipation, that start many years before movement symptoms and official diagnosis with PD. This shows that we need to look more closely at what could be causing the early symptoms of PD, and that the gut microbiota might be a good place to start. In my study, I propose to use a mouse model of early PD. Mice are an excellent model for many human diseases because they are similar to humans in many ways, such as the fact that they have a gut microbiota. The model I propose to use has a genetic mutation that produces gut and movement symptoms similar to those in human PD patients. I plan to investigate how changing the gut microbiota influences these symptoms. The gut microbiota will be changed through treatment with antibiotics to wipe out bacteria or through the addition of certain bacterial species that are thought to influence PD. This study will reveal specific changes in gut bacteria that can influence PD and will increase our understanding of how this disease works. This is an important step towards understanding the early causes of PD, and developing better non-invasive treatments and preventative strategies.

column36: Physiological roles of the dark microglia in normal postnatal brain development
column37: One of the cells involved in brain development and maturation, as well as the normal function of adult brain is microglia, the brain-resident immune cells. Microglia can help the brain remain healthy by surveying the environment and clearing any harmful elements (i.e. dying neurons, cellular debris). A new subtype of these cells, named dark microglia, has been discovered by our laboratory led by Dr. Marie-Eve Tremblay. Dark microglia are particularly active around synapses, the structures that mediate the exchanges between neurons. Their interactions with these elements suggest that they could strongly influence the transmission of neuronal messages which could affect the brain's development. Despite their characterization in various conditions, including development, chronic social stress, aging, as well as neuropathologies (Alzheimer's disease), very little is known about the genes and proteins expressed by dark microglia. To this end, we have identified a specific protein to label dark microglia. This protein will allow us to identify and analyze their characteristics using imagery techniques to further deepen our knowledge of the dark microglia and their relevance during development. These cells will be isolated using a state-of-the-art technique known as single-cell RNA sequencing that will allow us to identify in an individual cells the unique set of genes that can become proteins. This study will help us understand the role of this new subtype in brain development. Since the elimination of superfluous synapses is particularly seen in postnatal brain development, we are confident that dark microglia could play a crucial role in this essential process. This knowledge could be essential to target these cells for eventual therapeutic avenues by modulating their interaction with synapses to prevent or limit the extent of pathological neurodevelopment.

column36: What works for whom, how and why? A Realist Evaluation of a Telehealth Heart Failure Disease Management (HFDM) Program
column37: Heart failure (HF) is the most common and costly disease for seniors in Canada. It weakens the heart and has deteriorating effects on patients' breathing, sleep, ability to work, and mental health. It requires frequent hospitalization, which increases suffering and expense. Heart Failure Disease Management Interventions (HFDMIs) are health services that help patients in taking better care of themselves in order to prevent from worsening of symptoms, leading to less frequent hospital admissions , reduced suffering and cost. These services consist of different components such as educating and following up with patients around medicines, diet, exercise, and symptoms; providing support; and improving access to care. HFDMIs are sometimes provided face-to-face during hospital stay, while sometimes these are provided via tele-health (through web, email and smart phone Apps) at home. At times, these are delivered by individual health professionals such as nurses or doctors or physiotherapists, or sometimes by combined teams of various health professionals. As HFDMIs are diverse in the way these are performed; therefore, it requires a sophisticated statistical analysis to compare the various HFDMIs. We will search for, and analyze data from the randomized trials of HFDMIs, published after 1994. This would be the largest and the most specific literature synthesis, which will identify the fine details around HFDMIs and the context in which these are more or less effective. Such as the HFDMIs that are more effective, using a specific mode of communication (in-person or tele-health), in a specific setting (home, hospital, general practice clinic), delivered by a specific or diverse group of health professionals. This will also be the first ever synthesis to identify the effect of patients' sex on the effectiveness of various parts of the HFDMIs. The findings will guide health professionals and policy makers to design and implement the specifically useful HFDMI components.

column36: Distress regulation during toddlerhood: Discerning parental influences.
column37: The term "Terrible Twos" is used to describe the intense and often unpredictable tantrums that many toddlers experience during the second year of life. This period of difficulty may be explained by the fact that toddlers are still developing distress regulation skills, the skills that we use to manage our emotions in stressful situations, such as when we experience a painful procedure, become frustrated, or receive bad news. While difficulties with distress regulation can be challenging for parents and caregivers to manage in the short term, these difficulties are associated with many types of mental health problems for the developing child later in life. Because of this, it's important to understand what factors contribute to children's distress regulation skills early in life so that at-risk children can be identified and supported. Social influences, and in particular, a child's parents and caregivers, are known to be an important factor contributing to the child's distress regulation skills. When a parent experiences stress, their ability to support their child may be negatively impacted. My project aims to understand how parent characteristics and behaviours predict more optimal or less optimal patterns in the child's distress regulation skills. To do this, the study will follow caregiver-toddler dyads at 12, 18, and 24 months, and record the child's physiology (heart rate) and behaviour during low-, moderate-, and high-distress situations. Characteristics of the parent (e.g., soothing behaviours, mental health, sociodemographic background, culture) will also be measured, in order to identify which characteristics might put children at risk of or protect them from less adaptive outcomes. This is the first step toward developing strategies to support parents in need, so that parents can in turn support their child in learning distress regulation skills that will prepare them to deal with stress in a healthy way.

column36: Physical activity and mental health: Does inflammation explain the relationship?
column37: Mental illness costs our health care system $51 billion per year. To address this burden, it is vital that treatments other than medication and therapy are explored. It is concerning that recent research has found that individuals with serious mental illness (SMI) may have higher levels of inflammation, the reactive process of the body's immune system when a threat is sensed (i.e. injury, infection), even if a threat is not present. In addition, in recent years there has been support for the use of physical activity as a treatment and prevention strategy for mental illness. Interestingly, it has been found that physical activity can decrease inflammation, among healthy individuals. This means that physical activity may have the ability to decrease inflammation, and ultimately prevent and treat mental illness. However, this has yet to be tested among individuals with SMI. In my program of research, I am examining the effects of a 12-week walking intervention on levels of inflammation and on mental health outcomes. Specifically, I will be looking at 4 different groups (i.e. individuals with depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and anxiety), and the effects that physical activity has on the inflammation levels of each group, and subsequent changes in mental health outcomes. If it is found that physical activity does exert positive changes in mental health and anti-inflammatory effects on those with SMI, this can provide support for its use as an additional treatment in psychiatric care. This would result in improved health of these individuals, and decreased health care spending. This study would be the first of its kind to assess levels of mental health and of inflammation following a physical activity intervention among individuals with SMI, and the first to assess these immune responses to physical activity by illness, the findings of which may inform the development of future condition-specific physical activity treatment.

column36: Health and Developmental Outcomes Associated with Prenatal Opioid Exposure: A Population-based Retrospective Cohort Study in Ontario
column37: Opioid use during pregnancy is a growing public health concern. Increased rates of opioid-related harm are reflected in maternal opioid use and Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome, a condition where infants exposed to opioids in utero experience withdrawal symptoms after birth. While poor health outcomes in infants have been documented, the developmental and long-term health outcomes associated with prenatal opioid exposure are poorly understood. The objective of this research is to estimate the effect of prenatal opioid exposure on infant health outcomes, developmental health in children and mental health and addiction outcomes among youth in Ontario. We have a unique opportunity in Ontario to explore these relationships through linked health, demographic and educational databases available at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences. This project will enhance our understanding of the long-term ramifications of the opioid crisis on prenatally exposed infants by being the first study to include prenatal prescription opioid exposure for the whole population of Ontario (including type, timing and duration of exposure) that accounts for a range of variables including maternal and family vulnerabilities known to influence child health and development- providing rigorous estimates of the impact in a Canadian context. We will compare the health of children with prenatal opioid exposure to children who were not exposed to estimate the effect of prenatal opioid exposure on child health and development. The opioid crisis and increase in Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome incidence make prenatal opioid exposure a major public health concern. Through rigorous and well-powered analyses this project will address a critical knowledge gap by identifying specific health risks and developmental deficits associated with prenatal opioid exposure. Findings can be used to inform perinatal and maternal care and to develop targeted health interventions to support healthy child development.

column36: A population health economics approach to assessing tuberculosis interventions in Ontario
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) recently surpassed HIV as the world's leading infectious disease. In Canada, TB rates declined between 1940 and 1980; however, annual rates have remained steady since then, with an estimated 1,600 TB cases diagnosed per year. Canada has endorsed the World Health Organization's EndTB Strategy, aiming to eliminate TB worldwide by 2050. To meet the elimination targets, Canada's TB rates must decline by 10% annually. Moving forward, it is essential to address the social determinants that impact TB infection rates, given that TB affects primarily Aboriginal and foreign-born populations. The economic evaluation of interventions is important in priority setting. However, the majority of economic evaluations focus on single biomedical interventions. For TB, where social determinants of health are important intervention targets in conjunction with biomedical interventions such as screening programs and novel vaccines, well-established methods for economic evaluations face several challenges: equity considerations, complexity of interventions, and the measurement of costs and benefits across multiple sectors. My research will expand established methods for economic evaluation by considering health and non-health outcomes in an equity informed economic evaluation approach. My research aims to (1) elicit societal values for non-health outcomes that may result from interventions aimed at social determinants of health using a discrete choice experiment (DCE); (2) estimate healthcare costs attributable to TB; and (3) assess the equity-informed cost-effectiveness of TB interventions considering health and non-health outcomes. My research will culminate in the development of a data-driven decision-analytic model that relies on real-world data and current literature to inform policy priorities for TB. This research will contribute to the understanding of TB in Ontario, and methods development for conducting economic evaluations on population health interventions.

Parents of children with ADHD take on the important role of implementing behavioural treatment for their children, therefore, parent mental health must be considered to maximize treatment benefit and to better support child mental health. By taking the unique approach of supporting parent mental health within the existing structure of parent training, instead of providing additional/separate parent treatment, this research will be an important contribution to the field of child mental health and family functioning.

column36: Investigating the impacts of maternal obesity-associated oxidative stress and intrauterine hypoxia on placental development and function
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) and Type 2 Diabetes are leading causes of health-related disability in Canada and cause more than sixty percent of global chronic disease-related deaths annually. While lifestyle factors contribute to the development of these conditions, recent evidence has shown that adversity during fetal life can increase the risk of developing these metabolic diseases in adulthood. Maternal obesity during pregnancy is one such adverse condition and a strong predictor of childhood obesity, insulin resistance, and hypertension, which precedes diabetes and CVD. Current estimates place nearly half of women as being overweight or obese during pregnancy. While efforts have been made to intervene during pregnancy to reduce offspring disease risk induced by maternal obesity, diet and lifestyle interventions in the second half of pregnancy do little to improve these outcomes. Attention has now shifted towards the period surrounding conception and early embryonic development as a window of intervention. This research aims to understand how obesity alters the earliest stages of development and how this predisposes to chronic diseases later in life. The embryonic period consists of rapid development of the placenta, an organ which principally supports fetal development. Placental dysfunction is a leading cause of pregnancy-related complications and is believed to underlie the connection between maternal obesity and childhood metabolic disease. Obesity has been described as an inflammatory condition, and this elevated inflammation may disturb early placental development with consequences for fetal growth and postnatal health, however this area has remained largely unstudied. Understanding how early placental development is altered in the context of obesity will help to inform strategies to intervene during the periconceptional window and prevent both complications during pregnancy as well as the metabolic disease burden in the next generation.

column36: Role of specific inflammatory cells and mediators in the pulmonary response to cigarette smoke exposure
column37: Cigarette smoking (CS) remains a major contributor to the rising incidence of many pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases, most importantly chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The contents of CS induce damage in the lung tissue, which in turn causes an inflammatory response marked by the activation and recruitment of white blood cells to help initiate repair mechanisms. However, repeated injury caused by years of smoking leads to chronic inflammation and improper remodelling of the lung. Previous research has shown that the response to CS exposure involves mostly macrophages, responsible for the clearance of damaged tissue and debris, and neutrophils, normally involved in the response to bacterial infection. Although the cell types and the mediators involved in the response to CS have largely been identified, the extent to which each element of this network contributes to the healthy and/or pathological response is not well understood. The proposed project involves elucidating the specific and collective contributions of alveolar macrophages and neutrophils in the response to CS in acute and chronic conditions. Firstly, depletion or enrichment of individual cell populations will be assessed in mouse models to assess their impact on the response to short- and long-term CS exposure. Secondly, the effect of blocking specific inflammatory molecules on the development of lung damage and inflammation will be assessed in mice exposed to CS. Thirdly, collaboration with clinicians will allow for the collection of lung inflammatory cells from COPD and healthy patients to determine whether the activity of these cell types correlates with lung function. Elucidating which cell populations and which signaling molecules are involved in the development of lung damage and inflammation in response to CS will help us to better understand how the lung defends itself, how lung diseases like COPD develop and how best to tackle their treatment.

column37: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in the world, primarily due to the heart failure that follows a heart attack. column36: Estradiol and cognitive functioning in the menopause transition.
column37: It is widely recognized that many women experience cognitive difficulties such as forgetfulness and poor concentration when they reach menopause, which begins one year after a woman's final menstrual period. However, it is much less recognized that as many as 50% of women report cognitive problems in the years leading up to menopause, otherwise known as the menopause transition (or 'perimenopause'). Although it has been proposed that the hormonal changes associated with the menopause transition may contribute, very little research has been devoted to studying cognitive deficits during this transition period. The goal of this study is therefore to improve our understanding of both the nature and hormonal causes of perimenopausal cognitive deficits. The proposed study will enroll 50 women aged 45-55 years who are complaining of cognitive difficulties and currently in the menopause transition (defined according to menstrual bleeding patterns). Once every three weeks across a 12-week period, the participants will provide a urine sample for hormone measurements and undergo cognitive testing, including assessments of immediate and delayed memory, attention, language and executive function. We anticipate that weeks characterized by low estrogen levels will also be characterized by deficits in cognitive ability. The results of this study will not only serve to validate and legitimize perimenopausal women's cognitive complaints but will also point to potential treatment options, including estrogen therapy, for women suffering from bothersome cognitive difficulties.

column36: Investigating the niche-dependent regulation of regionally distinct endogenous neural stem cells in the forebrain and spinal cord by myelin basic protein
column37: Myelin basic protein (MBP) is a major protein constituent of the myelin sheath expressed by oligodendrocytes of the central nervous system (CNS). Its canonical function is to enable the adhesion of multilayered compact myelin throughout the CNS for improved saltatory conduction. We have recently demonstrated that MBP inhibits proliferation of two distinct populations of spinal cord derived neural stem cells (NSCs), in a dose dependent fashion without affecting their survival. Interestingly, this inhibitory effect of MBP is regionally distinct along the neuroaxis as revealed by the finding that primary cultures of forebrain-derived NSCs are not inhibited by exogenous MBP unless it is presented in the context of the spinal cord niche. The regionally distinct responsiveness is lost when pure populations of NSCs (i.e. cells derived from passaged neurospheres - cultured in the absence of niche cells) are not inhibited by exogenous MBP, irrespective of where they were derived (i.e. spinal cord or forebrain). The finding that MBP's effect on NSCs is regionally distinct along the neuraxis is consistent with MBP being classified as an intrinsically unstructured protein whereby its structure and function are both dependent on the microenvironment it is presented in, further supporting the finding that the stem cell niche is the key regulator of MBP's inhibitory actions on NSCs. We are currently in pursuit of analyzing possible regionally distinct structural differences in MBP using patented spectroscopic technology. We are also taking advantage of recombinant forms of MBP to try and elucidate the mechanism by which MBP inhibits NPC proliferation. Our current research has implications for understanding the role of the stem cell niche in regulating NPC behaviour and finding potential therapeutic targets for stem cell based regenerative strategies for brain and spinal cord repair following injury.

column36: Microstructure-informed computational model of functional reorganization in childhood brain surgery: towards individualized cognitive prognosis
column37: Brain surgery is among the most effective treatment options to cure childhood diseases such as drug-resistant epilepsy, brain tumors, and stroke. My project therefore proposes to study the effects of childhood brain surgery on cognitive abilities, clinical outcomes, and brain organization. column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide and current treatments remain ineffective for many people. Stress has been linked to the development of depression although not all individuals who experience stress will become depressed. Understanding what makes some individuals more susceptible to developing depression could lead to more effective treatments and new strategies targeting vulnerable individuals to prevent the disorder before it occurs. Early like adversity is a major risk factor for depression, although the mechanisms for its lasting effects are not fully understood. We will investigate how early life stress alters brain function to increase vulnerability to depression in adulthood. We will also test whether we can correct these changes in adulthood to build resilience to stress and prevent depression. To do this we will use cutting edge imaging techniques in a mouse model of depression to uncover the effects of early life stress on brain function. We will probe how maternal separation, a form of early life stress, modulates neural activity in circuits important for emotional behavior to increase susceptibility to later stress. We will then manipulate neural activity to correct these early life stress-induced alterations, essentially normalizing brain function before behavioral changes emerge, to support better stress adaptation in the future. This research will help us to understand how brain circuits are changed in vulnerable individuals and will lay the foundation to develop new preventative therapies to treat depression before it fully emerges.

column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a degenerative brain disorder that affects over six million individuals worldwide. It leads to deficits in movement and cognition that significantly reduce quality of life. Approximately 10% of Parkinson cases have a known genetic cause, but elements explaining the remaining 90% of cases are not fully understood. However, certain lifestyle factors such as stress, diet, pesticide exposure, and exercise have been associated with increased or decreased rates of PD. These factors can alter how genes are regulated, and might help explain why PD develops in some individuals but not others. My project will investigate how pesticides, high fat diet, and stress affect gene regulation in healthy individuals and whether each environment may increase risk of PD. I will also explore whether exercise could prevent PD in individuals that have a known genetic risk for it. To understand how these environments affect the brain, I will use human neurons and brains of mice, that are either healthy or have PD genetic risk. To discover whether we can detect markers of PD before diagnosis, I will also look at blood samples from early-stage PD patients. With information on which patients were exposed to pesticides and how much each person smoked and drank alcohol, I will explore whether indicators of PD are specific to certain lifestyles. This work will enhance our understanding of how disease develops and why it affects some individuals more than others, ultimately leading to identification of early indicators of PD, novel therapeutic targets, and lifestyle prevention strategies.

column36: MicroRNAs as effectors of p53 and BRCA1 in high grade serous ovarian cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer remains one of the deadliest cancers in spite of growing knowledge on its underlying mechanisms. More than 80% of ovarian cancer deaths are associated with high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), a sub-type of the disease that carries alterations in the genes TP53, BRCA1 and BRCA2. TP53 encodes the tumour suppressive (anti-cancer) protein p53, which can become pro-cancer as a consequence of genetic alterations that occur in HGSOC. An important part of the anti-cancer functions of p53 is exerted through a class of short nucleic acids called microRNAs (miRNAs), which exert a widespread control over gene expression, and establish a delicate balance in normal gene functions. Changes in their expression patterns can be used to distinguish types of tumour, reflect the underlying gene defects, and point to sensitivity or resistance to drug treatment. With this project, we will use miRNA profiles to guide our understanding of the genetic defects underlying HGSOC, and determine the interplay of TP53, BRCA1 and miRNAs in response to drug treatments. Towards this, we will develop a panel of HGSOC cell lines bearing very specific genetic lesions in TP53 and BRCA1, using genome edition methods (CRISPR). We will define the impact of these gene defects on miRNA expression with and without treatment with anticancer drugs, and determine their functional importance for treatment sensitivity in HGSOC. This project will provide insight on the synergistic actions of P53 and BRCA1 through miRNAs, and potentially new mechanisms of drug resistance in HGSOC.

column36: Efficacite et implantation du Lifestyle Redesign(R) chez les aines : un essai clinique hybride d'evaluation-implantation a repartition aleatoire
column37: Le vieillissement actif et en sante est une importante cible des societes vieillissantes necessitant davantage d'interventions a visee preventive. Developpe et experimente en Californie, le Lifestyle Redesign(R) (LR) est une intervention d'ergotherapie preventive realisee principalement en groupe et qui a pour objectif de soutenir le developpement de modes de vie sains et signifiants. En raison des evidences scientifiques indiquant une amelioration du fonctionnement, de la vitalite, de la sante mentale globale, de la qualite des interactions sociales de meme que de la satisfaction envers la vie chez ses participants, cette intervention est hautement pertinente pour les aines quebecois et canadiens. Recemment traduite et adaptee au Quebec, la version francophone du LR n'a cependant pas ete implantee en milieu clinique quebecois et aucune etude n'a documente son efficacite et sa rentabilite dans ce contexte. Ce projet de recherche vise donc a evaluer les effets a court terme du LR sur la sante, la participation sociale et les loisirs des aines ainsi qu'a documenter sa rentabilite, tel qu'implante pour une premiere fois en milieu clinique quebecois. Pour ce faire, un essai clinique a repartition aleatoire sera realise dans huit milieux (6 prives et 2 publics). Ces milieux recruteront 19 a 20 participants pour un total de 154 aines (77 par groupe) autonomes ou a risque de perte d'autonomie et habitant dans la communaute. Ces personnes seront reparties au hasard en deux groupes : l'un recevant le LR et l'autre les services sociaux et de sante usuels. Au terme de six mois d'intervention, une analyse des questionnaires, des journaux de bord et des entrevues individuelles aupres des ergotherapeutes sera realisee. Issu d'un partenariat exceptionnel entre la clinique, la communaute et la recherche, ce projet contribuera a soutenir l'integration d'approches preventives innovantes susceptibles d'ameliorer la sante et le mieux-etre des Canadiens vieillissants.

column37: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) is characterized by disobedience, irritability, and hostility directed toward authority figures. Next, the applicant will examine stability and change in ODD subgroup membership over this developmental period. Finally, the associations between longitudinal patterns of ODD subgroup membership and adult outcomes (i.e., antisocial behaviour, mood and anxiety disorders, and substance use) will be investigated. The results will shed light on the possible presentations and developmental courses of ODD and, thus, will have important implications for the individualization of interventions for young people with the disorder.

column36: Improving transferability of clinical decision support systems: estimating bounds for dataset-specific generalization error and rescuing performance with transfer learning
column37: Clinical decision support tools are currently revolutionizing the field of medicine. These tools help clinicians stay on top of their patients' risk for things like sepsis, cardiac arrest, and cancer so when these tools don't work as expected, the results can be devastating. My PhD research will tackle one reason these tools may misbehave known as "dataset shift". Dataset shift occurs when the data you develop your tool in is so different from the data it's being applied to that errors occur more frequently than one would expect. To combat this problem, I will first develop a set of statistics that will let users know if there is the potential for increased errors when using a given tool in their institution (with their own data). I will then test and develop methods to improve tools for specific patient populations, once users identify that a tool will not work in their institution. These methods will be developed and tested on different types of predictive systems using imaging, genomic, streaming, and patient record data to compare their efficacy across these settings. They will also be directly incorporated into predictive systems that are currently being developed so these statistics describing predictive accuracy and methods to improve transferability will be rapidly translated to clinical use. It is important that clinical decision support tools behave as expected since the information they provide can result in life or death. Moreover, having a way to avert large errors that occur when transferring these tools to different institutions will allow more remote populations to safely enjoy the same benefits from clinical decision support tools that major research hospitals are able to.

column36: How do adult cancer patients and their healthcare providers perceive, respond to, and manage uncertainty related to incidental results from genome sequencing?
column37: Genome sequencing is a new type of genetic test that can help diagnosis and manage patients' risk for hereditary cancers. A challenge with using this test is that risks for thousands of other diseases can also be found, called "incidental results." There is a lot of uncertainty associated with these incidental results. It is uncertain if or when the diseases associated with them will occur, and what the impacts of the disease will be on patients' lives. Patients may feel uncertain about what their incidental results mean for their health, or how to act on them. Uncertainty may cause over-diagnosis, over-treatment, and misuse of health services. The impacts of uncertainty related to incidental results on adult cancer patients and their healthcare providers are not known. This study will address the question, how do adult cancer patients and their healthcare providers (primary care and genetics specialists) perceive, respond to and manage uncertainty related to incidental results from genome sequencing? Patients will be participants in a trial (n=260) where they will receive genome sequencing, and half will have the option to learn incidental results. Using survey scales, I will measure perceived uncertainty, psychological distress, and health service use at baseline, 2 weeks, 1 month, 6 months and 1 year after return of results. I will compare perceived uncertainty between patients who receive incidental results and those who do not. Among patients who receive incidental results, I will evaluate the relationship between perceived uncertainty and distress, and between perceived uncertainty and health service use. I will also conduct interviews with up to 30 patients to explore their experiences with uncertainty in more depth. I will interview up to 30 healthcare providers who care for these patients, to explore their experiences with managing their patients' incidental genome sequencing results. This research could inform how genome sequencing is offered clinically.

column36: Les associations entre les caracteristiques et la disponibilite des ressources infirmieres, le rationnement des soins et la survenue de la mortalite et d'evenements indesirables aux soins intensifs.
column37: Introduction : Plusieurs etudes ont mis en evidence des associations ecologiques entre les caracteristiques des ressources infirmieres aux soins intensifs (SI) et l'incidence de la mortalite et d'evenements indesirables (EI). Pour expliquer ces associations, on suppose qu'en situation de manque de ressources, les infirmieres rationnent certains soins importants requis par l'etat de sante des patients. Or, cette hypothese n'a jamais pu etre verifiee empiriquement, faute d'un instrument valide mesurant le rationnement des soins. L'etude doctorale proposee vise a: 1) developper et valider un instrument de mesure du rationnement des soins infirmiers aux SI; 2) decrire la prevalence et les caracteristiques du rationnement aux SI, et; 3) examiner ses associations avec les caracteristiques des ressources infirmieres et l'incidence de la mortalite et d'EI. Methodes : Un devis de recherche mixte en trois phases est propose. Phase 1 : Une analyse conceptuelle permettra de generer une liste preliminaire d'enonces et d'echelles mesurant le concept de rationnement aux SI. L'approche iterative par sondage Delphi sera ensuite employee aupres d'un comite d'experts afin d'en etablir la validite de contenu. Phase 2 : Une enquete provinciale sera realisee aupres des infirmieres des SI afin de decrire la prevalence et les caracteristiques du rationnement dans ce milieu. column36: Decrypting Cryptogenic Strokes using an Integrated Molecular Approach
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, most often caused by a blockage of an artery leading to reduced blood flow to the brain. One in every four stroke patients have no identifiable cause of disease and are considered "cryptogenic". Beyond the frustration of being unable to pinpoint the cause of disease, cryptogenic stroke patients are at greater risk of having additional strokes. No effective treatments to prevent these secondary strokes are currently available, and this is largely due to the fact that so little is known about the biology of cryptogenic stroke. Therefore, there is an urgent need to study the biology of cryptogenic stroke in order to develop effective and safe treatments. We propose to study the genes and proteins that may predispose and help diagnose cryptogenic stroke patients using a systematic and comprehensive approach. More specifically, we will examine millions of genetic variants and thousands of proteins to find those that are most strongly associated with risk of cryptogenic stroke. We hypothesize that some genes and proteins will be highly predictive of cryptogenic stroke. Learning about the specific molecular markers that have a strong role in cryptogenic stroke will hopefully bring clarity to this subgroup of stroke patients and their caregivers who are desperately in need of answers and effective treatments.

column36: Investigating the Regulation of Muscle Stem Cell Polarity during Muscle Regeneration
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a devastating childhood disorder marked by severely debilitating muscle weakness that worsens with age. DMD arises as a consequence of muscular degeneration caused by a genetic mutation that primarily affects boys, with a worldwide incidence of 1 in every 3500 male births. Defects caused by the mutant gene create abnormalities in muscle fibers and muscle stem cells. Because of these abnormalities, the muscles of people with DMD are highly prone to damage. Normally, muscle stem cells are able to easily heal injured muscle; however, the muscle stem cells residing in people with DMD are defective and can't keep up with the muscle damage. Even with current treatments, boys with the disease are wheelchair bound between the ages of 9-12, paralysed below the neck by 21, and usually die in their 20's or 30's due to heart or breathing failure. Previous studies in our lab have shown that treatment with a specific protein (Wnt7a) improves the symptoms of DMD. Wnt7a improves DMD symptoms by stimulating the defective muscle stem cells to multiply and heal damaged muscle more effectively. However, the cellular mechanism behind Wnt7a's ability to improve muscle stem cell function remains unknown. My project aims to identify precisely how Wnt7a improves muscle regeneration by studying the molecular events responsible for making a muscle stem cell divide and multiply. Studying the molecular events within muscle stem cells will allow us to use Wnt7a more effectively for improving muscle regeneration, and potentially reveal new therapeutic targets for treating people suffering from DMD. The ultimate goal of this research is to set the stage for Wnt7a's use as a clinical therapeutic that improves the quality of life and lifespan of people suffering from DMD. Furthermore, it is predicted that this treatment will be used to regenerate muscle in combination with future gene therapies that attempt to fix the underlying genetic mutation that causes DMD.

column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, mainly due to the lack of effective drugs available. column36: Investigating the molecular basis of the Nedd4-FGFR1 interaction and its role in cancer
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada, accounting for 30% of deaths nationwide in 2017. Oftentimes, cancer is associated with detrimental mutations in many proteins, causing them to have altered structures and functions. My project focuses on Nedd4 and FGFR1, two proteins that are often mutated in cancer. FGFR1 is a receptor involved in processes such as cell growth and differentiation, while Nedd4 is an enzyme that regulates FGFR1 degradation. Mutations in either protein may result in uncontrolled cell growth and differentiation, phenomena often seen in cancer. The goal of my project is to determine why a subset of Nedd4 mutations, specifically those located at the FGFR1 binding interface, are associated with cancer. To do so, I will create these Nedd4 mutants and introduce them into cells to study if they can bind FGFR1 and induce its degradation. Moreover, I will introduce these mutants into cancer cells to see how they affect various parameters such as cell proliferation. Finally, I will utilize a technique called nuclear magnetic resonance to solve the structure of the Nedd4:FGFR1 complex. Understanding how these proteins interact at a microscopic level would allow for strategic drug design for future cancer therapy.

column36: Determining Vertebral Stability on Metastatically Involved Vertebrae using Deep Learning
column37: The spine is the most common site of secondary tumour growth for patients with breast, prostate, lung and renal cancers. These tumours can cause osteolytic and/or osteoblastic diseases and in severe cases lead to vertebral compression fracture (VCF). An effective way to treat these tumours is with Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT). However, a complication with SBRT is induced VCF ranging from 10% to 40% occurrence rate. Current evaluation of the risk of SBRT induced VCF is done based on a scoring of six criteria, but this score only provides a qualitative metric to determine risk of fracture. Previous work has shown that the size of the osteolytic tumour compared to overall size of the vertebral body is highly linked to VCF occurring. However, that work did not provide a quantifiable probability of fracture, only a threshold for when it is more likely to occur. The proposed work here is to use deep learning to evaluate both Computed Tomography (CT) images and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to provide a quantitative probability of fracture occurring. This will be done by developing a network that can first isolate a vertebral body from the different images and extract information of the vertebral body including size of the tumour and vertebral body and shape of the spine. This information will then be used to determine the probability of the vertebra fracturing.

column36: Process-specific Cortical Contributions of Olfaction and Memory: A Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Study of Cognitive Decline
column37: Dementia currently affects more than 700,000 people in Canada, impacting both their life expectancy and quality of life. Effects are widespread, with ramifications extending beyond their own life and into the lives of their family, friends, and the larger society they live in. The incidence of dementia is projected to rise over the coming decades, but no system is currently in place to quickly and cheaply screen large populations for risk of dementia. The earliest symptom of Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common form of dementia, is traditionally considered to be the progressive loss of memory and cognitive ability that individuals suffer as a result of the disease. Unfortunately, cognitive decline occurs well into disease progression and is a symptom of significant neurodegeneration. However, an emerging body of evidence strongly indicates that olfactory declines precede the onset of cognitive impairment and dementia by 5-15 years and, significantly, that with early detection, interventions may be more effective in preventing or treating cognitive decline and AD dementia. The olfactory system has rich cortical representation in the brain. To capture this, we will use Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy to examine brain activation patterns in olfactory and memory tests in individuals with and without dementia. We expect that those with a high risk of dementia can be differentiated from normal controls, providing additional information on how to detect and monitor early-stage neurodegenerative disease using inexpensive tests that can scale up to screen populations. Early detection and monitoring could maximize targeted interventions, leading to more preventative measures, personalized care, and better patient outcomes. This study will lay the groundwork for olfactory interventions and aims to take a proactive approach to understanding and addressing cognitive decline via targeting the improvement of health outcomes in the areas of prevention and diagnosis.

column36: Imagining the glass half-full: An intervention to improve negative interpretation bias in GAD
column37: In 2012, 2.4 million Canadians reported suffering from generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) in their lifetime. GAD is a chronic condition characterized by excessive and uncontrollable worry, associated with high medical utilization (e.g., high risk of heart attacks, peptic ulcer disease) and considerable societal and economic burden (e.g., high unemployment). Over 50% of Canadians with GAD report their mental health needs go unmet, which necessitates research on novel interventions for GAD that are effective and easy to disseminate. Cognitive bias modification (CBM) is a computerized intervention that directly targets a process that maintains worry and GAD: the tendency to appraise ambiguous information in a negative or catastrophic way. CBM training repeatedly guides favorable appraisals of ambiguous information. Research in depression has found that the effects of CBM are augmented through the use of mental imagery. The present study is a novel investigation of the therapeutic potential of imagery enhanced CBM (IE-CBM) for GAD. Individuals with GAD will be assigned to one of three conditions: 1) IE-CBM where they will practice generating positive resolutions of ambiguous information using mental imagery; 2) CBM, in which participants will complete the CBM training without instruction to use imagery; and 3) a neutral condition that will determine whether it is the act of reading scenarios alone that improves GAD related processes. All conditions will complete 30 minutes of their respective practice at home every day for 7 days. It is hypothesized that IE-CBM will lead to the greatest improvements in GAD processes, relative to the other conditions, pre- to post-training and at a 2-week follow-up. IE-CBM has considerable promise as an intervention to improve the tendency to assume the worst in GAD, a tendency that maintains chronic worry. PI-CBM is inexpensive, easy to disseminate, and could help meet the high mental health care needs of Canadians with GAD.

Parmi les participants, des sujets en sante sans AOS et des sujets de toutes les severites d'AOS seront representes. Les participants ont ete enregistres pour une nuit de polysomnographie afin d'evaluer la severite de l'AOS. Une evaluation neuropsychologique et une evaluation en neuroimagerie IRMf ont ete completees. Les sujets ont par la suite ete evalues en neuropsychologie avec des versions alternatives des tests 18 mois apres la premiere evaluation.
