column36: Spatial variation in PM2.5 oxidative potential and its relationship with neurodegenerative disease
column37: Exposure to ambient air pollution particles is associated with a wide range of negative health outcomes, ranging from short-term respiratory issues to chronic diseases including cardiovascular disease and cancer. However, assessing a population's exposure to particulate air pollution remains a major challenge in epidemiologic studies of the health effects of air pollution. Individuals are exposed to a complex mixture of particles which vary in size, shape, surface area, chemical composition, and origin and may have differing impacts on health outcomes. The ability of particles to cause oxidative stress in the human body has been identified as a possible mechanism for the health effects associated with air pollution exposure. A new metric, oxidative potential, has been developed as a means to assess exposure to air pollution that reflects the ability of particulate matter to cause oxidative stress. Despite increasing evidence of an association between air pollution exposure and neurological disease, the relationship between oxidative potential and chronic neurodegenerative diseases such as dementia has not been evaluated. In the proposed project, I will characterize the spatial variability in oxidative potential that exists in two Canadian cities, develop models for oxidative potential, and apply these models in cohort studies based on existing databases of administrative data to estimate the association between oxidative potential of particulate air pollution and dementia incidence. By identifying new disease-exposure relationships, this research will inform policy on air pollution regulation in Canada. Ultimately, I hope to enable the development of more efficient risk reduction strategies to improve the health of Canadian urban populations.

column36: Determining the role of peroxisome contact in maintaining mitochondrial health
column37: All cells contain membrane bound compartments, called organelles. There are many different types of organelles in the cell, each with a specific function, that must work together for cells to function properly. One organelle of particular interest is the mitochondria, as they are consistently seen to be dysfunctional in neurological diseases (and thus may be what is causing disease). Scientists are therefore interested in learning more about the mechanisms cells normally use to keep mitochondria healthy, and how these mechanisms may break down and cause disease. The peroxisome, another organelle in the cell, may be one of these mechanisms. Peroxisomes appear to be very important for mitochondrial health as cells that are unable to form peroxisomes have severely dysfunctional mitochondria. While peroxisomes and mitochondria are known to work together in several cellular functions, such as lipid metabolism and oxidative species maintenance, we don't know specifically how peroxisomes keep mitochondria healthy. One mechanism that peroxisomes may use to affect mitochondria health is through membrane contact sites. Membrane contact sites are small areas where organelles come into physical contact with each other. This contact is facilitated by interactions between tether proteins on adjacent organelle membranes, somewhat like an "organelle handshake". Membrane contact sites act as a means of quickly and directly exchanging metabolites and communication signals between organelles, and are very important for organelle function. We hypothesise that peroxisomes and mitochondria connect through a membrane contact site and that this contact is important to maintain normal mitochondria functioning. We aim to identify the tether proteins between mitochondria and peroxisomes, what signals are being exchanged at the peroxisome mitochondria contact site, and how the breakdown of this contact site might be involved in the mitochondrial dysfunction observed in neurological disease.

column37: Le virus responsable du SIDA, le VIH, cause une infection dont il n'est pas possible de guerir a ce jour. Les traitements antiretroviraux, mieux connus sous l'appellation tritherapie, permettent de controler la replication du virus, ce qui freine la progression de la maladie chez les gens vivant avec le VIH en plus d'empecher l'infection de nouvelles personnes. En revanche, cette medication doit etre prise a vie, puisqu'une interruption de traitement provoque inevitablement un retour de la replication virale. Au cours de ce << rebond viral >>, certains virus endormis, dits en latence, se reactivent pour produire de nouvelles particules virales infectieuses. Le virus est alors a nouveau detectable dans le sang du patient. La population de cellules infectees avec des virus inactifs constitue le reservoir viral. La guerison du VIH passe donc par leur elimination. Mais ceci n'est pas simple pour plusieurs raisons. En effet, on retrouve principalement le reservoir latent parmi des cellules appelees lymphocytes T memoires, des cellules de la defense immunitaire qui persistent dans le corps pour toute la duree de la vie. Finalement, aucun marqueur connu ne permet de discerner specifiquement ces cellules reservoirs. Mon projet de doctorat vise donc a identifier des marqueurs caracteristiques de ces tres rares cellules infectees pour pouvoir les eliminer sans endommager le reste du systeme immunitaire. Ainsi nous pourrons developper des traitements curatifs contre le VIH qui elimineront specifiquement ces cellules infectees sans toucher les autres cellules necessaires au bon fonctionnement du systeme immunitaire. Les personnes infectees par le VIH seront ainsi gueries et pourront vivre sans prendre de traitement.

column36: Novel Radiotracers Targeting Proteases Overexpressed in Invasive Cancers
column37: Approximately 1 in 2 Canadians will be diagnosed with a type of cancer during their lifetimes, with a mortality rate of 1 in 4. One key contributor to the higher mortality rate is the spread of cancerous cells throughout the patient's body, called metastasis. Therefore, diagnosing and treating the cancer prior to metastasis would greatly improve the odds of successful treatment. One key player in metastasis are proteases, which are proteins that speed up the normal recycling of other proteins. However, in cancers, they can destroy the tissue around the tumour site, enabling their spread, and participate in other processes that enable tumour tissue growth. There is a significant focus on developing methods to monitor protease activity in tumours to ascertain the degree of aggressiveness and potential for metastasis. One method doctors use to diagnose cancers is called positron emission tomography (PET), where the patient receives a small dose of a radioactive drug, which enters the tumour and sends a signal to a camera, localizing the tumour. Furthermore, these radioactive drugs can be used to detect cancers based on specific traits. Our goal is to develop specific radioactive drugs that target select species of proteases overexpressed in cancers by putting a radioactive tag on chemical structures that bind to the proteases. These radioactive drugs will be investigated in animals carrying different types of cancers. This strategy has shown promise in targeting a family of proteases called matrix metalloproteinases and a protease called matriptase, both of which are highly expressed in aggressive and metastatic cancers. This research will enable the development of the next generation of imaging agents, enabling the diagnosis and differentiation of aggressive types of cancers, improving the prognosis of cancer patients in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Epidemiology of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae infection in hospitals: bridging within-host, between-host and between-hospital scales using mathematical modelling, statistical inference and computer simulation to predict dynamic transmission pathways and inform infection control
column37: A growing number of bacterial pathogens have evolved antimicrobial resistance (AMR), limiting options to treat and contain infections that were once easily managed. Evidence is required to inform investment in the prevention of these infections, particularly in hospitals where the burden of AMR is most dire. Yet understanding AMR control is complicated by the multiple scales at which it operates: within patients, AMR arises through genetic mutation and the sharing of resistance genes between bacteria; between patients, bacterial transmission depends on types and levels of inter-human contact; and across health systems, AMR outbreaks depend on the movement of patients within and between wards and hospitals. These scales have traditionally been studied in isolation, precluding a holistic view of AMR dynamics. The goal of my PhD is to use epidemiological and biostatistical methods to unify these scales into one framework, and to use this multi-scale structure to predict optimal means of AMR control. First, I will develop mathematical models of bacterial evolution and transmission to describe theoretical dynamics of AMR emergence across scales. Second, I will use this model to analyze AMR transmission in a real hospital setting, as informed by analysis of an existing hospital dataset that includes longitudinal samples of patient microbiota to capture within-host dynamics, and inter-human contact patterns to capture between-patient transmission. Third, I will build this within-hospital transmission network into a regional model of patient transfer between multiple hospitals. Lastly, I will use the resulting multi-scale model to conduct simulation studies of hospital outbreaks and potential interventions. This novel bridging of within-host, between-host and between-hospital scales will facilitate improved estimation of optimal AMR control, and resulting estimates of the clinical and cost efficacy of interventions should ultimately inform clinical practice and policy.

column36: Characterization and Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA in Liquid Biopsy for Cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death in Canada and technologies to detect and monitor the disease are sorely needed. Currently, this is done through frequent tissue biopsy, but this is unpractical and challenging if the tumor is too small. Alternatively, cancer mutational targets can be found in the blood and saliva of cancer patients in a concept called liquid biopsy. Recently, the fragment lengths of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has been shown to differ amongst cancer and healthy patients which can explain why current DNA detection technologies such as digital droplet PCR have difficulty finding tumor DNA in biofluids. Electric field-induced release and measurement (EFIRM) technology, however, can detect these tumor fragments accurately in plasma and saliva samples from lung cancer patients. We hypothesize that a combination of shorter circulating tumor DNA and EFIRM's mechanics may explain the detection performance in biofluids. This proposal has three fundamental goals to scientifically underpin the performance of EFIRM liquid biopsy. Firstly, we will isolate DNA from plasma and saliva samples from lung cancer patients to study various characteristics, one being length. Secondly, we will examine and describe how DNA capturing probe design and density impact EFIRM's ability to locate tumor DNA in biofluids. Thirdly, we will use EFIRM to demonstrate a proof of concept of liquid biopsy by measuring the changes of tumor DNA in the saliva and blood samples of lung cancer patients throughout their cancer treatment. The impact of this study is multi-factorial. Learning about tumor DNA characteristic will provide new biological information about these tumor biomarker targets. Understanding EFIRM fundamental mechanics will reveal the scientific rationale of its performance. Third, we will introduce a tool which can reliably monitor and adjust drug selection in patients undergoing cancer therapy.

column36: Identifying Immunological Basis for Bladder Cancer Sex Bias
column37: Bladder cancer incidence shows an enigmatic male bias, as it is the 4th most common cancer in men but only the 12th most common cancer in women in Canada. The bias cannot be fully accounted for by lifestyle factors such as smoking, suggesting that it is likely a consequence of more fundamental biological differences between two sexes. To this end, we analyzed human primary bladder cancers and discovered that immune pathways are more enriched in women than in men, which hinted that sex bias may be driven by sex-specific differences in immune function. To address this possibility, we utilized the preclinical murine bladder cancer models that recapitulate the male bias seen in human bladder cancer. Remarkably, we observed that hormonally mediated differences in T cell immunity are responsible for sexual dimorphism in tumor growth. Our Research Proposal seeks to determine exact mechanisms by which sex hormones regulate T cell immunity. Male-based studies predominate in immunology research despite clear evidence that sex discrepancy exists in the outcome from many infectious and autoimmune diseases, vaccines and malignancies. Erroneous assumption that such results can be generalized to both sexes not only damages the scientific rigor and reproducibility but is also a major barrier to the long-term goal of personalizing treatments for immune-related diseases. Specific study design in our Proposal, explicitly aiming to highlight the immune mechanisms underlying unique protection against bladder cancer in females, presents an innovative approach to identify novel therapeutic targets. Also, completion of proposed research will establish an important insight that anti-tumor immunity may be largely different between men and women, thereby emphasizing sex as a critical biological variable to consider in designing future pre-clinical/clinical immunotherapy studies.

column36: Implementing effective community health worker programs to address health disparities among the urban poor in low- and middle-income countries
column37: By 2050, 80% of the world's urban population will live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with the urban poor experiencing stark health inequities. Innovative strategies are needed to meet the health needs of the growing urban poor. In light of health worker shortages and resource constraints in LMICs, this research seeks to understand how community health worker (CHW) programs - which have been predominantly implemented in rural contexts - can be effectively applied in urban settings. CHWs are lay persons who are briefly trained in specific health tasks, but do not hold formal professional medical certificates. Past experience demonstrates that 'proven' primary health care innovations designed for rural communities are not always well-suited to urban contexts. In urban contexts where community cohesion, safety, employment, and other factors differ significantly from rural settings, CHW program features require adaptation. This research will explore the opportunities and challenges that arise when adapting the CHW model to the urban context, with the intention of providing practical recommendations for the design and implementation of urban-specific programs. A scoping review of urban, LMIC-based, CHW programs will be conducted to synthesize the little evidence available. Interviews with LMIC-based program managers will document lessons on how CHW program design and implementation can respond to urban contexts and challenges. Finally, a case study in Colombia will investigate whether a newly piloted role for CHWs (conducting follow-up home visits for patients with chronic diseases) improves CHW job satisfaction and accountability - two important elements for effective and sustainable urban programming. This study is the first to synthesize evidence from urban CHW programs and generate cross-cutting implementation lessons. The findings will contribute to theory-building and serve as a resource for developing future research and guidelines.

column36: The Effect of Developmental Odour Exposure on the Development of the Olfactory System, Eating Habits, and Metabolic Health
column37: The World Health Organization estimates that 340 million people under 19 are overweight or obese. This is troubling as childhood obesity is the strongest predictor of lifelong obesity, a major health burden worldwide. Strong evidence from the past decade indicates that a strong predictor for childhood obesity is nutritional quality during pregnancy. Maternal diets high in fats and calories correlate strongly with overeating in children, predisposing them to a lifetime of obesity. Separately, the olfactory system has been increasingly shown to influence the metabolic health of individuals. Enhancement or elimination of the olfactory system within mice alters their metabolic health and weight, without changing eating habits. Within humans, the olfactory system has been shown to be sensitive to metabolic hormones, including insulin. As well, a decline in olfactory ability is associated with many metabolic diseases. Currently, there is very little information on how maternal diet alters the development of the olfactory system, and its subsequent effects on metabolic health. Therefore, my project will aim to understand how fat-related odors in the maternal diet alter the olfactory system of the developing child, and if that has lifelong consequences on metabolic health. Pregnant mice will be fed specially designed food enriched in odours common to high-fat foods, but containing identical nutrition. I will then measure the olfactory development, eating habits, and metabolic health of the offspring mice. I will use analytical chemistry, molecular biology, and systems neuroscience approaches to determine possible mechanisms contributing to any changes found. Information from this project will help determine whether the olfactory system may contribute to the modern prevalence of overeating, obesity, and metabolic disease. Additionally, the project aims to begin studying more nuanced aspects of maternal nutrition and its effects on childhood and lifelong metabolic health.

column36: Endogenous retroelements as novel immune escape mechanisms in human cancers
column37: Immunotherapy has drastically changed the landscape of cancer treatment. By retargeting the body's own immune system towards a tumour, immunotherapy has proved effective where more traditional therapies have failed. However, tumours have developed sophisticated mechanisms to evade the anti-tumour immune response, thus rendering such immunotherapies ineffective. The advent of next-generation sequencing technologies has highlighted the importance of the non-coding genome in health and disease. A significant proportion of these non-coding genes comprise endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), remnants of ancient viral infections that have since become a part of human DNA. Given their viral origins, these genes have retained their capacity to modulate immune responses. As ERVs and other retroelements are globally deregulated in cancer cells, we propose that they may promote the immune evasive capacity of tumours. Our preliminary analysis of gene expression patterns from 964 cancer patients comprising 31 tumour types has uncovered a novel subset of immune genes that may be regulated by ERVs and other retroelements. My preliminary findings show a novel mechanism by which a retroelement drives expression of alternative soluble form of PD-L1, a molecule that inhibits antitumour immune responses and is thus a key immunotherapeutic target. We propose that this retroelement-derived PD-L1 may affect patient response to immunotherapy, which we will test using in vitro and in vivo models as well as screening patient samples. We aim to uncover diverse mechanisms by which ERVs can contribute to resistance to immunotherapy as well as potential novel therapeutic targets.

column36: Studies of the structure, function and regulation of the ATR-ATRIP complex
column37: The complete and accurate replication of the genetic information in our DNA prior to each cycle of cell division is critical to our health and survival. Changes to the integrity of our genome can result from ongoing intracellular and environmental sources of DNA damage that, if left unrepaired, could disrupt key cellular processes. Importantly, such damage is often a barrier to the completion of DNA replication, a phenomenon known as replication stress. Human cells have mechanisms of preserving genomic integrity during replication that are controlled by a protein called ATR (short for 'ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related'). ATR sits atop a signaling network known as the DNA damage response that detects, signals and resolves DNA damage and replication stress. Upon recognition of aberrant DNA structures, ATR binds to DNA near affected sites where it gets "turned on" by interaction with other signaling molecules. ATR proceeds to coordinate a number of processes required for repairing the damage and restarting the replication process. This study will address two important aspects of ATR function at the molecular level: its ability to bind to damaged DNA, and how it becomes activated in response to damage. In recent years, ATR has been proposed as a potential anti-cancer drug target for a number of reasons. Cancer cells are prone to replication stress and thus highly reliant on ATR for their survival. The DNA repair capacity of ATR signaling mediates resistance to chemotherapy, a mainstay of cancer treatment whose efficacy is dependent on the ability to cause lethal amounts of DNA damage. Taken together, pharmacological inhibition of ATR can be effective on two fronts: by targeting an essential process on which cancer cells depend, and sensitizing the cells to existing chemotherapeutic agents. A better mechanistic understanding of ATR will allow for the rational design of new drugs and open up new cancer treatment options.

column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of mortality in high-income countries, with 30% of all deaths in the United States (U.S.) and 25% of all deaths in Canada attributable to heart disease and stroke. Food insufficiency is a key public health concern in high-income countries. With this research, we aim to identify the mechanism through which food insufficiency impacts obesity and CVD risk in order to develop targeted prevention and intervention strategies. column36: Unlocking HIV-1 Env Towards a Cure
column37: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infected more than 77 million people since the beginning of the epidemic. In the absence of treatment, HIV causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which has already killed more than 35.4 million people worldwide. Available treatments control viral replication in infected individuals but are unable to eradicate the virus. This is because the virus "hides" in some immune cells and establishes a reservoir from which it can replicate again as soon as the treatment is interrupted. The goal of this proposal is to evaluate the potential of an innovative strategy to decrease the size of the viral reservoir and ultimately eliminate it. We found that the majority of HIV-infected individuals have all the elements required to kill infected cells but fail to do so due to the ability of the virus to cover one of its most vulnerable parts (Env). By using certain small molecules we were able to uncover parts of Env and showed that infected cells can be easily eliminated. In this proposal we will test if this strategy is able to eliminate HIV-infected cells isolated from patients (ex-vivo) and in an animal model (in-vivo). Altogether, this strategy will put us a step closer towards HIV eradication.

column37: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in decreasing mortality for HIV-infected individuals, ART has not cured HIV/AIDS. The failure to eradicate HIV infection during ART stems from the virus' ability to persist in the body in multiple cell types and tissues. Without lifetime therapy, the virus quickly rebounds resulting in accelerated morbidity and mortality. The most commonly studied form of persistence is in memory CD4+ T-cells (CD4+ Tm-cells) that are harboring virus out of view of drugs or from the immune system. However, evidence indicates that other long-lived cells, known as myeloid cells, might contribute to HIV persistence. Cells that allow virus persistence are called viral reservoirs (VRs) and represent the main barrier to an HIV cure. While much is known about HIV persistence, many puzzles remain about the source of persistent HIV, the mechanisms underlying the establishment and persistence of VRs, particularly in CD4+ Tm-cells, and the ways to eliminate VRs. The Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise 2.0 (CanCURE 2.0), a team of leading Canadian HIV researchers, proposes an integrated and innovative research program informed by new knowledge in the field and new findings generated under CanCURE 1.0 (2014-2019) to: 1) Define the role and impact of long-lived self-renewing tissue-resident myeloid cells called macrophages in HIV persistence during ART; 2) Conduct detailed mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the critical role played by myeloid cells in the establishment and persistence of VR in CD4+ Tm-cells; 3) Identify new therapeutic strategies to tackle HIV persistence that capitalize on these discoveries and pursue the preclinical and clinical development of therapeutic interventions aimed at targeting VRs initiated under CanCURE 1.0. These studies are all aimed at finding new effective approaches to curing HIV infection in humans by eliminating persistent HIV infection from VRs in ART-treated patients.

column37: The war against HIV/AIDS is not yet over. Although anti-viral drug cocktails have changed HIV/AIDS to a chronic manageable disease, people living with HIV infection still have an increased risk of drug side effects, heart, kidney, and brain diseases, as well as cancer. In addition, living with HIV infection is associated with stigma. Thus, a cure for HIV infection is needed. A main obstacle to cure is the presence of a persistent reservoir of HIV infected cells in the body, where our current drugs cannot reach. Our project proposes harnessing the immune system, in particular, a cell called a 'killer T cell' to eradicate the remaining reservoir in order to cure the infection. In order to do this, we will first extensively characterize the genetic signatures of the remaining virus hiding in the reservoir from blood samples from persons living with HIV. We will then design a number of strategies, where we can mobilize a person's killer cells to be able to eliminate their remaining viruses. We will use a 'personalized' approach by studying each person's own viruses and their own immune systems. We will also borrow from a recent revolution in the cancer field, to improve the killer cells to kill HIV infected cells better and more efficiently, by using new genetic engineering techniques. All of our work will be done in the test tube or in pre-clinical models as a preparation to design clinical trials to cure HIV infection.follow

column36: A longitudinal study of Correctional Services Canada correctional officers mental health and well-being: The role of prison work in shaping correctional staff health and self over time
column37: Correctional work is challenging, stressful, and can be traumatic, so researchers have tried to understand what makes a correctional officer's (CO) likely to develop mental health problems. To date, no researchers have considered if COs feel prepared for their job and the associated challenges that will arise at recruitment and during training. Or how their experiences on the job shape their mental health and well-being over time. With the support of Correctional Services Canada, the employer of COs, we will first learn about correctional officer recruits (CORs) mental health status, coping skills, views, and experiences when they are first hired during their training. Next, we will follow these officers through deployment to the prison they will work in, and across their career for three years, doing qualitative and psychological interviews each year, to see if we can identify CORs that develop mental disorders or have poor well-being versus those who do not, and work toward preventing negative mental health outcome for all staff. We hope our study can help improve COR training and CO experiences. Our research team come from many backgrounds, this helps us use lots of tools to holistically understand staff mental health and experiences. We will conduct face-to-face interviews and clinical assessment interviews with at least 250 CORs/COs each year. The information will help us understand what CORs/COs need in their job, which exposes them to trauma and adversity. The proposed project also represents a central priority of the Public Safety Stakeholder Committee (PSSC) of the Canadian Institute of Public Safety Research and Treatment. Our study will help frame the needs of COs before and during their jobs in corrections-and generate training to support COs mental health resiliency.

column36: Resiliency training for firefighters: a national implementation evaluation
column37: Firefighters are exposed to traumatic events that can cause mental health problems that have lifelong impacts on work and home life. Firefighters identified that peer-led programs could help them be more prepared (resilient) and developed "Resilient Minds" in collaboration with mental health professionals. This 10-hr training program, co-led by trained peers and mental health professionals, worked well at the first test site in Vancouver and with adaptation for volunteer firefighters in PEI. A CIHR Catalyst Grant helped us compare the implementation barriers, facilitators, and outcomes at the Vancouver site to the PEI site. We identified important issues that will optimize program implementation and effectiveness: health literacy, ongoing supports to trainers and firefighters, fit within the fire service programs and culture, fidelity assessment, outcomes evaluation platforms, and adapting to context. Our team developed a national web-based outcomes database and website (trainer collaboration, training materials, online chat, e-learning videos) so that we are now ready for national implementation. We will now evaluate the broad implementation and outcomes of Resilient Minds in 10 volunteer and 10 career fire departments (>2000 firefighters) across Canada. We will compare the outcomes before and after training, and across sites and subgroups using standardized measures of mental health and work limitations. We will examine prior training, age, sex, gender, ethnicity, location, employment, types of service, and events that might mediate the impacts of traumatic events, and effects of resiliency training. We will interview trainers, firefighters, and employers to understand variations in implementation and adherence. We will develop, test, and share program resources; and provide empirical evidence to ensure the sustainability of an effective and accessible resiliency program. The result will be lower rates and severity of mental health problems in firefighters.

column36: A randomized control trial of a novel approach to cognitive training in public safety personnel with post traumatic stress injuries
column37: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a leading cause of disability among public safety personnel (PSP) and is associated with decreases in workplace productivity, loss of income, and high healthcare costs, impacting adversely Canada's economy. PSP with PTSD are vulnerable to alterations in cognitive functioning (e.g., poor short-term memory; decreased attention) that disrupt their ability to engage in activities such as work and retraining efforts. We will examine the effectiveness of a therapeutic intervention aimed at reducing this cognitive dysfunction and improving functional outcomes (e.g., return to work); stay at work) in PSP with PTSD. This intervention has proven highly effective in other populations (e.g., traumatic brain injury; aging) with impairments in memory, attention, and executive functioning. When we trialed this intervention in a small group of PSP with PTSD, we found promising improvements in short-term memory, processing speed, and executive functioning, as well as in the ability to regulate emotion. The objective of the proposed study is to conduct the first gold-standard randomized-control trial of cognitive remediation in PSP with PTSD using Goal Management Training (GMT). GMT is a remediation strategy with demonstrated efficacy in improving cognitive function in neurological and aging populations. Specifically, the primary aim of this proposed study is to examine whether a standardized full 9-session program of GMT results in durable improvements in cognitive functioning relative to a matched active condition (psychosocial education) with equivalent levels of therapist contact and group support. A secondary aim will be to determine whether participation in the GMT group is associated with better functional outcomes (e.g., return to work, stay at work, family) than is participation in the matched control condition. Finally, we will examine potential changes in brain structure and function among PSP participating in this program.

column36: Red Light, Yellow Light Green Light, Go! Stratifying Risk of Post-Traumatic Stress in Northern Ontario Fire Services
column37: Firefighting is a physically demanding, high risk occupation that also increases firefighters (FFs) to critical event exposure (CIE) which is linked to increasing risk of post-traumatic stress injury (PTSI). Examples of CIE include witnessing a death, removing a recently deceased body and/or managing a call that involves children. Our recent research with a subsample of Thunder Bay Fire Rescue (TBFR) FFs and the Thunder Bay Professional Firefighters' Association (TBPFFA) has identified that 94% of FFs in Thunder Bay experienced exposure to at least one critical event in a 2-month period; 79% were in response to an incident involving 1 or 2 deaths and 40% involved removing a dead body. Although TBFR FFs experience a high CIE burden, anecdotal evidence suggests that they are less likely to report PTSI exposure resulting from CIE; consequently, access to treatment may be limited. The proposed research was developed in collaboration with TBFR, TBPFFA and the Chair of their Critical Incident Response team (CIRT) and aims to: a.) identify physiological and self-report response during critical incident exposures (CIE) where physiological responses have been linked to PTSI risk; b.) develop a screening tool that stratifies physiological and self-report responses during CIE into tiered categories (Red Light, Yellow Light, Green Light) to improve awareness of PTSI exposure and direct access to treatment/intervention and c.) identify effectiveness of the "Red Light, Yellow Light, Green Light, Go!" awareness strategy on PTSI among career firefighters in Northern Ontario. The study findings will help to identify whether this approach assists firefighters in managing CIE, PTSI risk and improving their access to treatment.

column36: An Online Biopsychosocial Intervention (Autonomic Modulation Training) to Relieve Symptoms of Post-Traumatic-Stress Injury and Build Resilience Among Police.
column37: Police officers are exposed to hazardous, disturbing events that are associated with severe stress and trauma. Accumulated stress results in physical and mental health conditions, of which post-traumatic-stress-injuries (PTSI) are central. Considering the CIHR initiative for PTSI awareness and prevention strategies, the objectives of the current proposal are to 1) reduce symptoms of PTSI through a biopsychosocial intervention, 2) and to build wellness capacity (i.e., resilience) among police officers to manage accumulated stress. The intervention is a 12-week training to rewire maladaptive autonomic nervous system (ANS) responses to stress that underlie PTSI symptoms and health conditions. Autonomic Modulation Training (AMT) is tailored to police officers, delivered using leading edge research tools (interactive online platform) and innovative technology (app-based, heart rate variability biofeedback monitors, delivering objective-biological measures to assess changes in psychological and physical wellness and resilience). The interactive, online delivery method addresses the population specific needs of accessibility and stigma reduction (it is not necessary to self-identify publicly). Previous research with police using AMT techniques has garnered high 'buy-in' because the intervention is focused on biological change through the use of tangible tools that provide real-time evidence of resilience and health improvement. In designing the study, we have considered sex as a biological variable and gender as a social determinant of health. Using a pre/post, longitudinal study design, we will assess reductions in PTSI symptoms and increases in resilience using both self-reported and biological measures. This grant will support the development of modular AMT training that is compatible with other learning management systems and can be distributed to interested police services across Canada.

column36: Improving Health Outcomes and Coordinating Care for Children with Complex Health and Social Needs
column37: For children born with medical complexity and their families, fragmentation of service delivery negatively impacts their health outcomes, family functioning and quality of life, and often leads to inappropriate and inefficient healthcare utilization. The majority of children with neurodevelopmental disability (NDD) have some medical complexity and the responsibility for care coordination falls largely to the family. This project aims to address fragmentation of services, utilizing economic evaluation and policy analysis to evaluate, scale and spread of care coordination services for children with medical complexity and NDD. Our team will evaluate the impact of the NDD care coordination project (in Calgary, AB), which uses a care coordination framework (with defined roles, services, activities, processes and strategies) and an established care coordination curriculum to guide project processes and ensure a systematic approach, involving identification, engagement, coordinated service delivery, family empowerment, monitoring, transition and follow up. Using mixed methods analysis and a quasi-experimental pre-post design with a nonequivalent control group (in Edmonton, AB) we will: 1) measure the impact of the care coordination model on care integration and caregiver stress and quality of life; 2) examine health service utilization patterns of the child, out-of-pocket costs and work force opportunity cost for caregivers, and cost-effectiveness of the care coordination model from a health system and societal perspective; 3) obtain perceptions of stakeholders on the role of care coordination in improving access to services and outcomes, to inform the spread and implementation of the model. Evidence-based policy recommendations emerging from this study will inform the design of other coordination systems to ultimately help children with medical complexity and their families thrive.

column36: Encouraging Informed Decisions about Cannabis Use in Pregnancy: Educational Needs of Women and Prenatal Care Providers
column37: Recreational use of cannabis has been legal in Canada since 2018; Medical use has been legal since 2001. More and more Canadians are choosing to use cannabis for both recreational and medical reasons. Some women use cannabis during pregnancy and breastfeeding, especially if they were regular users before pregnancy. There is evidence that using cannabis during pregnancy may cause babies to be born early, have low birth weight, and have some impairments in the way their brain develops. However, the medical evidence on this is uncertain and some studies have found no association with cannabis use and these negative outcomes. For women who are only occasional users, this may be a good enough reason not to use cannabis at all during pregnancy and breastfeeding. However, there are many reasons that other women may struggle with abstaining from cannabis use during pregnancy. Some may not understand the potential harms. Others who used cannabis to treat certain conditions before pregnancy may wish to continue this use. Some may choose to use cannabis as a way to stop using other, more harmful substances like opioids. Others may start to use cannabis during pregnancy in order to treat their morning sickness. Because of the stigmatization of cannabis use in pregnancy, women may not feel comfortable talking with their health care providers about this. Health care providers may be uncertain what advice to offer, since the evidence about cannabis is so undeveloped, and many women have compelling reasons to use. This research considers the question of cannabis in pregnancy from the perspective of the pregnant woman, and from the perspective of the prenatal health care provider counselling this woman. It considers existing clinical evidence and creates new ethical, social evidence to formulate advice for pregnant women, creating educational aids for women and health care providers to facilitate discussions about using cannabis during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

column36: Total liquid ventilation for bronchopulmonary dysplasia prevention in a model of extreme preterm lamb
column37: Modern medical care allows for more extremely preterm-born babies to survive. These patients have immature lungs that tend to collapse and render breathing extremely difficult. Despite efforts to avoid mechanical ventilation, most of these babies will require such support in the first few days of life. The use of a gas ventilator to ensure their survival generates inflammation that damages the lungs. Unfortunately, most babies born before the 25th week of pregnancy that survive will develop chronic pulmonary disease, called bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Altered lung function and neurological development are now clearly associated with this chronic lung disease developed after a preterm birth. Total liquid ventilation, where the lungs are filled and then ventilated with a liquid called perfluorocarbon, has been proven to lower inflammation induced by ventilation and could be useful to prevent lung damage. A ventilator developed by our INOLIVENT team at the 'Universite de Sherbrooke' now allows for the precise control of liquid ventilation parameters. We can thus now refine liquid ventilation techniques in order to use this advanced respiratory support on the premature infant to reduce lung damage and potentially prevent bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Our multidisciplinary team has already put in place the techniques to assess the effect of different liquid ventilation strategies on the heart and lung and to evaluate the inflammatory response using a term lamb model. The aim of the current project is to use a preterm lamb model to evaluate the clinical potential of total liquid ventilation to limit lung inflammation induced by mechanical ventilation when compared to conventional gas ventilation.

column36: Perinatal complications and outcomes in female survivors of adolescent and young adult cancer: a population-based study on the impact of cancer on pregnancy in Canada
column37: Each year, approximately 7,600 adolescents and young adults (AYAs; aged 15-39 years) are diagnosed with cancer in Canada. These individuals fall between childhood and adult cancer care programs, and have complex needs because they were diagnosed with cancer during critical developmental, social, and reproductive years. A primary concern among AYAs with cancer is fertility. Because more women are having children later in life, many AYA patients will not have had a child when they are diagnosed with cancer. Previous research has found that cancer therapies can lead to high-risk pregnancies or infertility, and thus the possibility of having future children after cancer is uncertain for these survivors. To date, limited information is available to guide women and doctors about pregnancy after cancer at a young age. In this study, we will look at the impact of cancer on subsequent pregnancy complications and outcomes. Using a Canadian cohort of AYA cancer survivors, we will assess: 1.the rate of abortions, stillbirths, and live births, 2.the degree of complications in mothers and newborns, and 3.whether risks of these complications and outcomes change with time from diagnosis or treatment period. These points will also be explored using more detailed data from Alberta to establish the effect of radiotherapy and chemotherapy treatment, and develop recommendations for doctors. For all outcomes, we will compare AYA cancer survivors to the general population so that the results can be translated easily and clearly. The results of this study will add to the current understanding of pregnancy after cancer by providing evidence to support a hands-on approach to fertility counselling at diagnosis, as well as greater monitoring of pregnancies and deliveries in this vulnerable group.

column36: Identifying premorbid environmental and neural markers of risk for first lifetime onsets of depressive and anxiety disorders in high-risk youth.
column37: Depression and anxiety are common, disabling, and typically first occur in adolescence. Once a person has had one episode of these illnesses, they are at increased risk for subsequent episodes, and often have a poorer prognosis for treatment. We know that a lack of parental care places youth at risk for depression and anxiety. Despite this, there is relatively little knowledge about brain factors that might put youth at risk for the first lifetime occurrence of depression or anxiety. There is also little knowledge of how parenting influences the development over time of brain functioning that is linked to adolescents' risk for depression and anxiety. The first goal of this study is to examine whether brain functioning in regions that govern how individuals process emotions as well as rewards predicts the whether or not high-risk youth develop an episode of depression or anxiety for the first time in their life. We will also examine whether low parental care predicts the development over time in functioning in these ostensible neural markers of risk for depression and anxiety. Participants will be adolescents with least one parent with a history of depression or anxiety, but who have not experienced such an episode themselves. Thus, this will be a sample of youth at high risk for depression and anxiety but who have yet to develop either. Participants and at least one parent will complete measures of depression and anxiety and parental care towards the adolescent, and the adolescent will complete brain scans, at baseline and again 18 months later. We expect aberrant functioning in emotion and reward processing circuitry to predict the first lifetime onsets of depressive and anxiety disorders by follow-up. We also expect a lack of parental care to predict aberrant development of functioning in these circuits.

column36: Evaluating, refining and bringing to scale the endogenous health-promoting attributes of alternative food networks to address diabetes mellitus and hypertension among Ecuadorian farmers
column37: In Ecuador, rural people, and particularly rural Indigenous people are disproportionately affected by both nutrient inadequacies as well as overweight and obesity. This double burden of malnutrition magnifies their risk of developing diet-related chronic diseases such as diabetes mellitus (DM) and hypertension (Hyp). In parallel, many rural Indigenous people in Ecuador have organized around alternative food networks (AFNs) such as farmers' markets to seek more sustainable livelihoods. These local AFNs support food environments and practices that hold strong potential to prevent DM and Hyp among participating farmers. For example, AFNs have been demonstrated to promote food literacy, favor consumption of fruits, vegetables and whole grains, and to place income in women's hands; these, in turn have all been associated with healthier nutritional status and reduced risk of diet-related chronic disease. Our research aims to evaluate specific AFN attributes for their measurable contribution to DM and Hyp prevention in order to leverage the most effective attributes for a stronger and broader positive impact. To do so, we will use validated instruments for assessing diet and physiological risk factors among AFN farming households and a comparison group of non-AFN neighbouring farmers, and we will use participatory qualitative research to determine the most effective implementation strategy for translating research findings into practice. Our implementing partners run an ongoing intervention for managing communication and knowledge-sharing among an estimated 132 Ecuadorian AFNs, positioning them as the cornerstone for streamlining research findings into practice. Through the implementation of our research findings, we expect to provide strategic and practical guidance for integrating health-sensitive attributes into the regular practices of AFNs as they continue to replicate and evolve in Ecuador and elsewhere.

column36: The role of age of cannabis use onset in the developmental pathways leading to substance use problems by early adulthood: key mediators and moderators.
column37: One in three Canadian youth in the 16-25 years of age group are active cannabis users, with statistics showing that trends in cannabis use (CU) are rising. This is worrying as some studies have shown that CU during adolescence is associated with higher risk for adult cannabis and other substance use disorders. However, it is still unclear whether starting CU earlier in adolescence puts youth at higher risk of developing later substance use problems after accounting for early risk factors or different patterns of substance use. We also don't know what individual and environmental factors place boys and girls who initiate cannabis use during adolescence at higher risk of developing later substance use problems. Thus, the present project aims to examine (1) whether the association between CU initiation and later substance use problems remain when considering important environmental and individual factors; (2) whether the association between early CU initiation and later substance use problems can be explained by CU profiles (how much one uses, how frequently, etc.) and individual and environmental characteristics, and (3) whether the effect between age of initiation and later substance use problems differ for different CU profiles, and individual and environmental factors. For this, we will build on two ongoing longitudinal studies, in which participants were followed from age 5 months to 18/19 years, and we will collect detailed information on their cannabis use and other substance use, mental health, and the youth's environment at 23 and 25 years. This study could provide much needed information about how individual and environmental factors work together to increase the risk of developing substance use problems, potentially helping guide policy and prevention for those more likely to develop substance use problems by early adulthood.

column36: Placental Par Polarity Complex in the Pathogenesis of Preeclampsia
column37: Proper placental function is essential for the health of the fetus and mother during pregnancy. Placental dysfunction, which is when cells in the placenta do not form or function properly, is a characteristic of the common pregnancy complications preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction. Importantly, these complications significantly affect the lifelong health of mothers and their babies. The cell that forms the surface of the placenta, the syncytiotrophoblast (ST), is particularly important in the development of placental dysfunction. Unfortunately, there are large gaps in our knowledge about basic ways that the ST functions. This hampers our ability to understand how we could correct ST function in placental dysfunction in order to treat both mothers and their babies. Here we will examine how the ST establishes and maintains the separated arrangement of proteins and cellular components between the "top" and "bottom" side of the cell. This is known as cell polarity, and it is important for cellular function to allow for delivery of nutrients and waste between the mother and the fetus. We will examine the role of the Par polarity complex, a group of proteins known to control cell polarity that have not been studied in the placenta. The Par complex also controls the arrangement of the cytoskeleton, endocytosis, and response to inflammation. These are critical processes that maintain ST function and are disrupted in placental dysfunction, but how these processes are carried out in ST are mostly unknown. Therefore, these studies will increase our knowledge about fundamental aspects of ST cell biology. The knowledge we gain will help us to understand the unique ways in which the ST functions and in the future will lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets to treat placental dysfunction and improve outcomes for both mothers and their children.

column36: Medical Cannabis Concentrates for Opioid Use Disorder
column37: Nearly 1 in 10 Canadian adults suffer from neuropathic pain with limited hope of relief due to a lack of effective treatments. People with neuropathic pain are often prescribed opioids long-term even though there is little evidence to support such use. 'Medical cannabis' is increasingly popular because it contains cannabinoids, the active ingredients that likely provide medical benefits (e.g., cannabidiol [CBD], delta-9-tetrahydrocansnabinol [THC]). Public perception is that CBD oil is the panacea for all pain related-conditions but there is little supporting scientific evidence. Studies to date have methodological problems that limit conclusions and very few studies focus on the dosage and active ingredients available in cannabis concentrates. Therefore, healthcare providers and patients lack information to make informed decisions about whether and how to use cannabis concentrates. The primary objective of this pilot study is to determine the feasibility of a full study. Secondary objectives are to measure the effect of cannabis concentrates on opioid use and pain. In this single centre randomized controlled pilot study, we will recruit 51 patients with opioid use disorder and neuropathic pain. Patients will be randomized to either receive cannabis concentrate capsules high in CBD (5 mg), high in CBD+THC (5 mg each of CBD and THC), or placebo capsules twice a day for 3 months. We will determine whether a full study is feasible and measure the effect of cannabis concentrates on daily opioid dose, pain interference, opioid weaning, and pain severity. Our project will be one of the first to robustly test whether cannabis concentrates can decrease opioid use for people with chronic pain. Our results have the potential to prevent and decrease long-term use-and associated harms-of opioids and help healthcare providers and patients make informed decisions about dosing and the utility of the active ingredients currently prescribed in medical cannabis.

column36: The impact of participation on body functions among youth with physical disabilities: A pragmatic individual-based study
column37: Youth with physical disabilities experience greater limitations to participation in community-based activities than do their average-developing peers, which can result in poor health outcomes. Emerging treatment approaches aimed at improving activity and participation have shifted from focusing only on impaired body functions towards the performance of functionally meaningful activities within the youth's natural environment. It is unclear; however, whether targeting intervention at the activity/participation level can simultaneously result in improvement of personal functional skills (e.g., reaching) and body functions (e.g., range of motion, balance) - components known to worsen with age and, thus, important to address and maintain within the rehabilitation process. Our team has partnered with key community-based stakeholders including youth, clinicians and policy-makers, and together we plan to examine whether engaging in an 8-week self-chosen community-based activity (e.g., sledge hockey, boccia) can lead to a significant improvement in three key body functions: motor, cognitive and affective. Thirty youth with physical disabilities will take part in the study and engage in an activity program of their choice. Changes in their body functions (e.g., movement, attention, mood) will be measured multiple times before, during and after engagement in the chosen activity/program. Findings of this study can guide clinicians, families and policy-makers to select effective approaches that not only promote participation but also facilitate additional motor and mental benefits from one single intervention. Such treatment approaches may also reduce the burden on the healthcare system as well as on the youth and families. Moreover, findings can advance our understanding of methods for testing complex and unique 'real-life' individual-based interventions that are highly relevant to practice.

column36: Are epileptic seizures linked to memory-like neural pattern sequences?
column37: Reflex epilepsy is defined as epilepsy syndrome in which known stimuli evoke seizures. For example, reflex seizures in some patients may be elicited by flickering lights, certain sounds, specific odors or activities. However, in a vast majority of epileptic patients, seizures do not have identifiable triggers and are classified as spontaneous. Here, we ask whether spontaneous seizures might also have identifiable triggers that are generated internally in the brain, i.e.: they are result of specific 'thoughts'. For example, we propose that 'memory' of specific events or places could be an internal trigger of seizures. To study this, in rats, we will induce seizures in specific spatial locations. We hypothesise that, when a rat will have a spontaneous seizure, even in different location or during rest in a home-cage, the brain activity before seizure will be similar as in the place where seizures were initially induced. This project will give us better understanding of mechanisms generating seizures, which could help to prevent seizures from happening. For instance, as the last goal of this project we will test multiple therapeutic strategies. We will monitor continuously brain activity, and if 'memory pattern' triggering seizure are detected, we will deliver electric stimulation to the brain to disturb this pattern and so prevent the seizure. Our team has proven excellent track record in long-term monitoring of brain activity in normal and epileptic rats, and also in memory research. Thus, we are in unique position to investigate 'memory-like' triggers of spontaneous seizures, and to use this knowledge to test novel therapeutic strategies in epilepsy.

column36: Optimizing nurse staffing practices in acute care hospitals for safer patient care
column37: Adverse events (AEs) are a leading cause of death in acute care hospitals. Recent cross-sectional studies have suggested that several nurse staffing practices (e.g., understaffing, the use of less qualified nursing staff and of high volumes of overtime hours) may be important contributors to the incidence of AEs in these settings. There is also emerging evidence that nurses' levels of education and experience might also be related to AE occurrence. The next step in investigation is to determine the optimal number and composition of the nursing staff, and the optimal volumes of overtime hours that are needed to minimize the risk of AEs. To this end, the temporal associations between these nurse staffing practices and the incidence of AEs, and the thresholds for safe staffing levels need to be determined by conducting longitudinal studies. Until recently, detailed daily patient and staffing data were not readily available to conduct such an investigation. With the advent of electronic health records and the digital capture of payroll and staffing data, an exciting opportunity has emerged to address these important questions in the management of nursing staff in acute care hospitals. The objectives of this multisite study are to determine: a) if and which nurse staffing practices are associated with an increased risk of AEs and, b) if thresholds for 'safe' nurse staffing can be established. The results of this study will likely produce evidence-based information that will assist hospital managers in making the most effective use of the scare nursing resources, and in identifying optimal nurse staffing practices that minimize the incidence of AEs. Such evidence is urgently needed given that the international shortage of registered nurses is expected to worsen in the coming years, and because hospitals are increasingly turning to overtime hours and to hiring less experienced or less qualified nursing workers to maintain the accessibility to health care services.

column36: Bipolar Bridges: A Digital Health Innovation Targeting Quality of Life in Bipolar Disorder
column37: More than half a million Canadians live with bipolar disorder (BD), a long-term and potentially disabling mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings from depression to mania. Suicide rates are disturbingly high - up to 15% of people with BD will end their own lives. This evidence paints a bleak picture. Yet, with optimal support, care and empowerment, people with BD can flourish, and make important and creative contributions to society. Our research network - the Collaborative RESearch Team to study psychosocial issues in BD (CREST.BD) - uses a pioneering participatory approach in which researchers, healthcare providers and, critically, people who live with BD work collectively to conduct BD research, and to move research results into action. CREST.BD has recently produced two flagship websites designed for people with BD and their healthcare providers: a 'Quality of Life Tool' and a state-of-the-art 'Bipolar Wellness Centre.' In this project, we will build on our prior work to develop a new mobile app called Bipolar Bridges. The app will addresses some of the most pressing real-world problems that people with BD currently face when using online technologies. First, it will take advantage of advances in online technologies to provide a secure and safe interface where the user is in control of their own health data. Second, it will empower the user to combine and learn from different forms of online self-management or self-care data (for example, medication use, sleep quality, mood variability, activity levels) in one place. Third, it will be co-designed with diverse (for example, people with different gender identities, or of different ethnic or cultural backgrounds) people with bipolar disorder. At the same time, Bipolar Bridges will provide a new way for researchers to assess the relationship between self-management and quality of life outcomes in diverse people with BD.

column36: A prospective study evaluating complement activation among pregnant patients with obstetrical antiphospholipid syndrome
column37: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disease that can lead to blood clots (thrombosis) or complications in pregnancy such as pregnancy loss, pre-eclampsia or intrauterine growth restriction because of placental insufficiency. The cause of APS is poorly understood, and there is a high rate of pregnancy loss despite standard blood thinner injections and aspirin given during pregnancy. The complement system is a network of proteins and is an important part of the immune system. There is growing evidence that changes to the complement system may play a central role in what causes APS. By better understanding complement activation and which complement proteins are abnormal in pregnant patients with APS, we can research targeted therapies to improve pregnancy outcomes for women with APS. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have recently developed a blood test (the modified Ham test) that can detect complement activation in patients. They have already shown that there is complement activation in a related pregnancy complication called HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets), and that complement activation was present before any clinical evidence of HELLP syndrome started. The aim of our study is to assess if there is complement activation in pregnant patients with APS using the modified Ham test and other complement studies, compared to healthy pregnant women, and if this is related to pregnancy complications. We will also test if there are genetic mutations in complement genes. We will follow pregnant patients with and without APS throughout pregnancy. We will test for complement activation with monthly blood tests until the third trimester, and then every 2 weeks until delivery. By collecting this information over time, we will determine if there is an association with the development of pregnancy complications, and if we can identify changes in complement before those complications happen.

column36: Protecting children from unhealthy food and brand marketing in the digital age: A novel artificial intelligence system to assess food and brand marketing on digital media
column37: Background: Unhealthy food/brand marketing has a negative impact on what children eat and on their health. Canada will soon ban marketing unhealthy foods/brands to children <13 years old on television, the internet and other media. However, very little is known about the amount and types of unhealthy food/brand ads that children see online and the government does not have a way to monitor whether companies are obeying the new law. The problem is that public health has fallen behind technologically. Marketers are using artificial intelligence (AI), but public health is still relying on humans to try to find out what marketers are doing. Goals: We will develop and test the first AI system that can assess the amounts and types of food/brand marketing that is online. We will use the system to assess differences in the amount and type of food/brand marketing that is online from before to after Canada's new marketing ban comes into effect. We will also study whether companies are obeying the new law. Methods: We will use AI to identify food/brand marketing on Canadian websites, gaming applications and YouTube videos. AI will also be used to: 1) rate the healthfulness of the foods/brands that are being marketed; 2) assess the types of marketing strategies that are being used; and 3) determine whether marketing targets children. AI and marketing experts will test our system to make sure it is accurate. We will conduct statistical testing to understand how the amount and type of marketing changes from 12 months before to 12 months after Canada's marketing ban is implemented, and whether companies are obeying the new law. Significance: This AI system will provide the first scientific evidence about the amount and type of unhealthy food/brand marketing that Canadian children may see online. It will also provide a way to study whether companies are obeying the Canadian government's marketing ban. This information can help to understand how to improve child nutrition and health.

column36: Older adults' trajectories of health and social care in two Canadian provinces
column37: Navigating the health and social care system can be difficult, in particular for older adults and their caregivers who may interact with different providers of care over time. This study seeks to create evidence that will support improved integration of care services across the system. We have 4 objectives. First, we will prioritize relevant patient-centred outcomes based on previous international work and in collaboration with our diverse stakeholders. Second, we will explore care trajectories (the sequence of interactions with the health and social care system) and identify factors that may lead to certain types of trajectories, as well as how the trajectories are related to the prioritized outcomes. Third, we will explore how to classify the observed types as trajectories as either preferred or less preferred (still in consultation with our stakeholders). Finally, we will identify innovative programs or policies from Quebec and Ontario and examine their potential to improve trajectories of care. We will achieve these objectives using both qualitative and quantitative methods. We will conduct a deliberative prioritization and validation of the outcome measures with our stakeholders. Then, using a dataset that links responses to the Canadian Community Health Survey to the respondents' health administrative data, we will explore and group trajectories and relate them to the relevant outcomes. We will use an existing registry of innovative programs that was developed with previous CIHR funding support, to identify programs that are beneficial for preferred trajectories. We will conduct a comparative study between Quebec and Ontario. Finally, we will interview patients and practitioners to gain their ideas about how to improve trajectories for everyone. This work is expected to support efforts to better integrate care services with the goal of improving care trajectories, ultimately improving the experience and outcomes of the health and social care system.

column37: Problems and Solution: Pressure ulcers (PU) are among the top five leading causes of re-hospitalization in patients with spinal cord injury (SCI) which frequently leads to infections, low quality of life, depression, and even a risk of death.Treatment of PUs is challenging due to the following problems: 1) They usually are in the form of cavities and void spaces which are very difficult to fill and fix by convectional wound healing products, 2) They are located over bony prominences and weight-bearing parts of the body with a high risk of recurrence and 3) Finally, they are usually exposed to unhygienic environment, have a high chance of getting infection before and during treatment. Research Plan: To address the first problem mentioned above, we have recently developed and successfully tested a liquid nutritional scaffold called MeshFill which can fill all wound gaps and cavities. However, further studies are needed to address other difficulties commonly associated with pressure ulcers. Thus, our goal in this study is to develop and test a new product, referred to as MeshFill-Plus which is composed of: 1) liquid scaffold (MeshFill) containing all nutritional ingredients required for skin cells growth, 2) A cotton-ball like spongy and flexible skeleton and 3) Antibacterial nano-silver particles. As such the proposed components of MeshFill-Plus not only fill up all cavities/ tunnels from bottom up, they increase the physical strength of healed wounds and prevent the growth of any potential germs when applied on PUs. We will initially examine this new product in the laboratory and then in a pig wound model which is very similar to human wounds. Finally, after obtaining regulatory approvals, we will test clinical efficacy of MeshFill-Plus in 12 patients with pressure ulcers. Conclusion: The result of this study makes it possible to assemble the components of MeshFill-Plus in a medical package for treating not only PUs, but also other non-healing wounds.

column36: Baseline brain and behavioural predictors of treatment response in pediatric MSK pain
column37: Chronic pain affects one in five Canadian children. In particular, musculoskeletal (MSK) pain is one of the leading causes of long-term disability. Pain, which normally exists to protect the body, sometimes transitions to chronic pain, a disease state. This transition is poorly understood. Recent studies in adults suggest that two brain regions, the hippocampus (HC) and the amygdala (AM) - usually associated with memory and learning, and fear, respectively - may play a key role in this transition. Abnormal HC/AM structure and function are risk factors for the transition of acute back pain to chronic back pain in adults. In pediatric pain, however, the strongest risk factor for chronic pain is a previous traumatic event. These findings may be related. Previous painful or stressful events predispose children to developing chronic pain in life. Therefore, HC/AM abnormalities observed in adulthood may be related to previous trauma. This connection may be measurable in the HC/AM. Stress and trauma trigger the release of a hormone called cortisol. Prolonged cortisol exposure can damage HC cells, and may alter its development. The current proposal will compare levels of stress hormone levels, and brain structure and function between adolescents with MSK pain and healthy adolescents. We will determine the contribution of traumatic events to these abnormalities. These data will provide the first comprehensive study to understand how trauma, stress hormones and pain can affect how the brain develops.

column37: Oral cancer is a deadly disease with 1 in 2 patients dying within 5 years after diagnosis. The only way to reduce the number of oral cancers and the harm endured by patients from the current treatment is to identify the lesions that have a high likelihood to become cancer and treat them early before they become cancer. The long-term goal of this project is not only to identify the characteristics of these pre-cancerous lesions, but to also find a better way to manage/treat them. In our proposed plan, we will be using four of the best currently available technologies to examine cancer-related changes at both genetic and cell morphology levels. This will be performed on normal, pre-cancerous and cancerous tissues collected from the same patient in order to find changes that are present in the precancerous and cancerous cells but not in normal cells. We then use these identified changes to create a test that can analyze small biopsy samples taken from suspicious changes in the mouth and tell us if there is a high chance for them to become cancer in less than 3 years. We will also be able to identify slow growing lesions that we can manage differently by using less harmful ways. We are confident that our team of leaders in oral cancer studies and these new technologies can analyze the large amount of precancerous and cancerous tissues in our collection of samples that are uniquely to the world. For the first time in decades, we have the opportunity to study and explain the biology behind oral cancer from its precancerous stage through the application of the best DNA technologies. This will allow us to realize our proposed plan to find solutions that clinicians can use for delivering effective and appropriate treatment, ultimately benefiting patients.

column36: New molecular targets in rheumatoid arthritis: focus on TAK1 signaling and neutrophils
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is one of the most prevalent chronic inflammatory disorders in North America; it currently affects about 300,000 Canadians, and costs our economy a staggering 5.8 billion per year in direct and indirect costs. RA is characterized by a chronic inflammation of the joints and a progressive destruction of cartilage and bone. It is painful, incapacitating, and incurable. One of the distinctive features of arthritic joints is their massive infiltration by white blood cells, and in particular neutrophils. The latter have been proposed as a source of several inflammatory mediators (including cytokines) that are present at high levels inside inflamed joints, and that perpetuate the inflammatory state. Recent studies made in animal models strongly support this view. In this proposal, we will focus our efforts on a cellular signaling protein that controls the production of chemokines by neutrophils in response to inflammatory biochemicals in the micro-environment. This protein (the TAK1 kinase) has many unique features in neutrophils, and we aim to identify key molecular partners of TAK1 that can be exploited for future therapeutic intervention. Accordingly, we believe that molecule-driven strategies, such as the ones we propose herein, have the potential to reap important benefits for the health of Canadians, and in particular ageing citizens, who are most susceptible to suffer from arthritic diseases.

column36: Glucocorticoid and insulin control of rhythmic human pituitary growth hormone gene expression
column37: Human growth hormone is released into the circulation with highs (at night) and lows (in the day) on a daily basis. Levels are highest during puberty to help provide the energy from fats and sugars for children going through a growth spurt. Part of the way growth hormone helps maintain energy levels is by helping to make sure there are enough insulin producing cells in the pancreas. If you are not able to make enough insulin you will develop diabetes. Studies of growth hormone production, particularly in children and young adults, are limited as pituitaries are not normally available until after death. Use of animals is not optimal, as human and, for example, rodent growth hormones are not the same. Thus, we generated mice with the human growth hormone gene and showed that overeating in puberty negatively affects chromosome structure and specifically a loop of protein and DNA containing the human growth hormone gene, which is needed for efficient growth hormone production. As a result, daily growth hormone levels decreased to those seen in much older mice on a regular diet. However, if the mice were made to increase physical swim activity, the negative effects of overeating on the loop and growth hormone production were lost. We will now study whether changes in daily growth hormone production that were seen as a result of overeating and forced swimming are related to effects of insulin and glucocorticoid hormones, respectively, and identify the downstream protein factors that help maintain or disrupt the loop, which acts as a control 'hub'. These factors are expected to offer a target to resist or repair the negative impact of overeating and help maintain responsiveness of the growth hormone gene, by increasing or lowering their levels. We will also develop a new mouse model to test whether loss of growth hormone signals to the pancreas in puberty directly leads to increased risk for diabetes.
