column36: Mechanism-Based Therapies of Glomerular Disease
column37: Glomerular podocytes are vital in maintaining the structure and function of the glomerulus, the filtering unit of the kidney. Intact function of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is important for protein homeostasis in the podocyte, including production of components of the slit diaphragm, adhesion complexes and glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Disorders of ER function can contribute to disease. Diseases of the renal glomerulus, especially those initiated by immunological processes ("glomerulonephritis"), account for approximately half of the causes of chronic kidney disease in Canada. Treatment of patients with kidney disease with dialysis and kidney transplantation has resulted in a dramatic improvement in the survival of patients, but at a large cost to the Canadian economy. Fundamental research into the disordered mechanisms that lead to glomerulonephritis is essential to the understanding of these diseases, an understanding that will ultimately lead to therapy and prevention. In this proposal, we will study abnormalities in cellular pathways in the glomerulus involving the ER, and establish how ER function allows podocytes to maintain glomerular function in the normal kidney and in glomerular diseases. We will establish urinary biomarkers of ER diseases. The proposed studies will use a tissue-culture system and animal models of glomerulonephritis to characterize abnormalities contributing to the cause of the disease. The elucidation of basic mechanisms of the causes of disease, and testing of therapies in preclinical (animal) models is likely to be the most productive approach to the development of treatment strategies to human glomerulonephritis. The results of the proposed studies will eventually lead to improved strategies for therapies of kidney disorders.

column36: Value for money: A mixed methods study to investigate the impact of funding expanded midwifery care models in Canada
column37: Birth is costly. About 10% of the money that Canadian health care systems spend on hospitals are to pay for the costs of giving birth or being born in a hospital. Canadian research suggests that midwives can provide birth care at lower cost while still ensuring good health outcomes. Midwives help lower costs because they are less likely to use costly interventions, the people they care for leave hospital earlier, and they attend some births at home. Until recently, almost all Canadian midwives work in models that involve providing prenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum care to every person they care for. The way midwives have been paid has limited the ways in which midwives can work within Canadian health care systems. Our research will take advantage of a natural experiment that involves funding midwives in Ontario to work in new models of care, providing a wider range of services, and working in settings that they have not previously worked in. Programs funded by this initiative include a new hospital-based, midwifery-led birthing unit, and programs that target people who are at risk of poor access to health care and poor health outcomes. Our goal is to understand the value for money that has been achieved through this new funding. Our project will involve three parts. One, we will analyse the costs of the new alongside midwifery unit to learn whether the new funding supports a lower cost model of hospital-based midwifery care for births. Two, we will interview patients, health care providers, administrators, and policy-makers to identify what they see to be the value of the new funding and the programs it funds. This will help us to understand the impact of the funding from different perspectives. Third, we will develop a framework that can be used to examine the costs and cost savings of programs that target people who are at risk of poor access to health care and poor health outcomes, and we will use this framework to evaluate the costs of one of these programs.

column36: Optimizing preterm delivery time: brain health & neurodevelopmental outcomes
column37: Preterm birth is a leading cause of still birth and childhood disabilities in Canada. With advances in medical care, the number of babies being born early has increased significantly. Much of this change is related to medical decision making, where babies are delivered early to minimize birth complications. For fetuses who are restricted in their growth, typically due to a failing placenta, early delivery can prevent serious illness and death. However, placental failure causes decreased oxygen supply to the brain and places fetuses at high risk for brain injury and cerebral palsy. Presently, doctors lack tools to determine when the fetal brain is at greatest risk for injury and which babies need to be delivered early. Developing sensitive medical imaging tools that can predict brain injury in growth restricted babies are needed to inform delivery time and promote healthy outcomes. Presently, the decision to deliver a baby who is growth restricted is largely based on ultrasound. While this technology is inexpensive and can be done at the patient's bedside it can only provide limited measurements about blood flow to the fetal brain. Altered blood flow patterns reflect blood being directed away from major organs in order to protect the brain. Ultrasound may only be able to detect injury when it is too late, when there is a risk that brain damage has already occurred. An alternative to using ultrasound is MRI, which can monitor brain regions vulnerable to injury. The long-term goal of this research program is to address this critical need for obstetricians to use better methods to monitor growth restricted babies at risk for brain injury while still inside the womb, to improve newborn brain health and prevent developmental difficulties in learning and motor skills. Presently, no therapies or interventions are available for growth restricted fetuses, so the focus on prevention of neonatal brain injury is key to improving outcomes in this vulnerable population.

column37: Over 3 million Canadians have type 2 diabetes, a condition where blood sugar levels are too high. High blood sugar damages blood vessels and other organs contributing to disability and early death. Our objective is to test whether a newly invented nutritional drink that contains molecules called "ketones" can lower blood sugar and improve blood vessel function in people with type 2 diabetes. column36: Learning from and enhancing Community Capacity for Climate Change and Food Security (C4FS) action in the NWT
column37: The food systems of Indigenous peoples in the Northwest Territories (NWT) are based on the harvesting of country foods, and form the foundation of spiritual, cultural, physical, and mental well-being for individuals and communities. There is a dual food system in communities in the NWT, with country foods complemented by market foods. The lack of fresh and affordable market foods compounded by changes in country food access and availability fuels alarming rates of food insecurity throughout the NWT. There are documented impacts of climate change for Indigenous peoples' food systems, including: access to, and availability of traditional food species and, changes in harvesting practices (including harvester safety concerns). Understanding climate change impacts and identifying local adaptations in the food systems of Indigenous communities in the NWT is critical for the health and sustainability of communities, the environment and land. The proposed research aims to learn from and enhance community capacity to address place-based priorities to inform climate change and food security action locally, regionally, and territorially. The approach includes cross-cutting themes of Traditional Knowledge, Governance, Youth, and Sex and Gender, and is grounded in Participatory Action Research (PAR). Our multidisciplinary team will work closely with community partners in six case study communities in four regions in the NWT to understand the potential of local actions, and to scale-out and scale-up learning. This research will promote community action and self-determination of local food systems in communities in the NWT and ultimately improve health outcomes. The knowledge gathered, and shared across multiples levels (locally, regionally, territorially, government decision-makers/ knowledge users) will facilitate development of more effective programs and policies to address food security and climate change in the NWT.

column37: The most dramatic and fastest climate change is occurring in Inuit Nunangat, which has led to decreased ice thickness and extent, later ice freeze-up and early ice break-up, and changing snow conditions. These changing conditions also impact the ability of Inuit to access, prepare, and consume country foods (local foods). Climate change impacts on country foods have important implications for Inuit health and wellbeing. The Niqivut Silalu Asijjipalliajuq ("Our Food and Climate Change") research program addresses a significant gap in research. The research program will promote adaptive capacity among Inuit by enhancing local capacity to detect and respond to food-related climate-health outcomes; and evaluate opportunities for food-related climate change adaptation polices, programs, and actions. Four intensive research projects span these themes: Project 1: Stories about Country Food Preparation; Project 2: Stories to Inform Reintroduction of Food Sources; Project 3: Stories of Food for Health and Healing; and Project 4: Sharing Stories and Inuit Self-Determination in Research. This is a Nunavut-led research program. Our Nunavummiut-led approach will offer best practice guidance for other initiatives; will create leaders with expertise in climate change, country food, and Inuit health; and demonstrate the importance of Inuit knowledge and Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit for adaptation, enabling communities to manage the food-related health effects of climate change.

column36: The food and beverage industry's sponsorship of junior sports clubs in Canada: its extent, nature and potential effect on child and adolescent health
column37: "Unhealthy food marketing has been shown to promote poor dietary behaviors and obesity among children. The sponsorship of sports clubs is one type of marketing to which children and youth are exposed. Evidence from abroad suggests that this promotional technique, which allows for extended and repeated exposure to marketing, is frequently used to promote unhealthy foods. To date, no research has documented the extent and nature of food company sponsorship of sports clubs in Canada. Furthermore, little research has specifically examined the potential impact of this activity on the health of children and youth. The purpose of this study is to determine the frequency and healthfulness of food company sponsorship of junior sports clubs in Canada and to examine its potential effect on the dietary behaviors of children and youth. To do so, this study will identify junior sports clubs for the 8 most popular sports among children and youth in 4 cities located across Canada. Sport club officials will be interviewed over the phone to identify all food company sponsors. Focus groups will be held with children and youth to explore their perceptions and attitudes toward food company sponsorship and sponsoring companies, and whether sponsorship influences their food purchasing or requesting behaviors. This research is timely given that the federal government is expected to pass legislation in fall 2018 restricting unhealthy food marketing to children. This law, however, will not prohibit food company sponsorship of children's sports nor will it protect adolescents over age 12 from unhealthy food marketing. A review of this legislation is scheduled for 2025. During this review, the law will be evaluated, and its scope may be expanded should evidence support such action. Considering this window of opportunity, this research will provide critical evidence needed to consider the restriction of food company sponsorship targeting children and the extension of protections to adolescents."

column36: Canadian Epigenetics, Environment and Health Research Consortium Network Phase II
column37: The DNA that makes up the genome (the collection of all the DNA in your cell) is tagged with various chemical marks that are attached either directly to the DNA or to its packaging proteins. These marks, collectively called the epigenome, act as a kind of molecular mark-up language that tells the cell's proteins which genes to turn 'on' and which to turn 'off'. Unlike the genome, which remains largely the same throughout life, the epigenome changes with age, in response to environmental influences, and in many types of disease. As the bridge between environmental exposures and peoples' genomes, the epigenome harbours enormous promise to understand normal development and disorders arising throughout a person's lifespan. Our accelerated ability to 'read' these epigenetic marks is revealing their disruption in most diseases; however, the rapid rate of the emergence of new scientific methodologies coupled with the increasing desire of researchers to incorporate epigenetics into new studies highlights the urgent need for a nationally coordinated approach. The CEEHRC Network Phase II aims to continue to address this gap by developing and strengthening collaborations between basic and applied scientists, clinicians, bioinformaticians, statisticians, and experts in drug development. We seek to address the bench-to-bedside gulf in epigenetics research in Canada, to harness improved understanding of epigenetic mechanisms and the potential improve patient outcomes by altering epigenetic states associated with disease.

column36: Development, Implementation and Evaluation of an Innovative Integrated Supportive Care Pathway by Primary Care across Alberta
column37: Caring for patients with advanced-stage diseases is a growing challenge in Canada. Care is uncoordinated with high rates of hospitalization, and aggressive use of treatments towards the end of life, despite limited benefit. Care often does not reflect patients' preferences and is associated with poor outcomes and quality of life. Integrated community- and home-based care aligned with patients' preferences is essential to improving patient outcomes. The use of clinical pathways is effective in integrating care and optimizing patient outcomes. The implementation of a Conservative Kidney Management (CKM) pathway across Alberta for patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) who were unlikely to benefit from dialysis has improved symptoms, increased patient satisfaction, and reduced costs for these patients. This study aims to build on the success of the CKM Pathway by adapting and spreading the Pathway to include patients with advanced cancer and heart, lung, and liver failure. This newly co-designed interactive, on-line Supportive Care Pathway will have health care provider and patient portals to navigate the pathway and access patient education resources, interactive decision aids, and management strategies appropriate for an individual's needs and preferences. This Supportive Care Pathway will be implemented within primary care clinics across Alberta. The effect of the Pathway on patient outcomes and quality of life will be evaluated along with its cost effectiveness. We anticipate high uptake of the Pathway resulting in care that is more consistent with patients' preferences, improved patient outcomes, greater satisfaction with care, and reduced costs across the health system. We anticipate that health care providers will have greater satisfaction with the care they provide using the Pathway. This project will set a benchmark nationally and internationally and will serve as a model for pathway development for patients with advanced-stage diseases.

column36: Implementing ActionADE to Transform Medication Safety
column37: Adverse drug events (ADEs) are unintended and harmful events resulting from medications. They are an enormous burden to patients, families and the health system, causing 276,000 emergency department visits, and 100,000 admissions in BC each year. Unfortunately, healthcare providers commonly re-expose patients to the same medications as ones that previously caused harm resulting in repeat ADEs. This happens because there are no effective health information technologies to ensure that ADEs are documented and shared between providers in a patient's circle of care. We have designed a software application called ActionADE that allows frontline care providers to document ADEs, and communicate this information between one another and across health sectors (for example, from hospitals to community pharmacies). We have partnered with the Ministry of Health, Vancouver Coastal Health, Lower Mainland Pharmacy Services and the College of Pharmacists of BC to integrate ActionADE with PharmaNet, BC's drug information system, and with community pharmacy information systems. This will allow care providers to share information with one another about ADEs to prevent their recurrence. After completing ActionADE's integration with other health information systems, we will implement ActionADE in acute care hospitals in Vancouver Costal Health. We will then evaluate whether ActionADE can prevent re-exposures to harmful medications, and improve patient and health system outcomes in a randomized trial. We will complete an economic evaluation to assess ActionADE's cost effectiveness. ActionADE has the potential to advance the quadruple aims of enhancing patient care, improving population health, improving health system sustainability, and improving the work of care providers. If beneficial, we plan to scale ActionADE to other health sectors in BC, including to other hospitals, long-term care, physician offices, and to rural and remote locations to transform medication safety for all.

Each innovative clinical trial has been developed with multiple stakeholders including patients. A portion of the economic benefits derived from each trial will be used to conduct further studies that will expand the capabilities of the integrated data platform while addressing Provincial health priorities. The creation of an integrated Health data platform will be a transformative undertaking for Manitoba. The integrated data platform will increase Manitoba's ability to make evidence-informed health decisions, help improve patient-centred outcomes, and will promote the sustainability of our healthcare system.

column36: SurgeCon: An Emergency Department Surge Management Platform
column37: Canadian emergency departments (ED) have some of the longest wait times compared to many other first world countries. Extreme waits mean patients will be in pain or discomfort for hours before being seen which can cause serious harm. To address this healthcare system challenge and improve patient experiences, we propose SurgeCon, a quality improvement initiative to reduce ED wait times. SurgeCon includes an electronic Health component, a training program for ED staff, and a series of quality improvement initiatives. SurgeCon provides ED staff with different tasks to complete to improve efficiency based on real-time information (E.g. bed availability, average wait times, available resources, etc.). We tested SurgeCon in a rural hospital ED and found it reduced the average wait time from 104 minutes to 42 minutes, the total time spent in the ED from 199 minutes to 134 minutes, and the proportion of patients who left the ED without being seen by a doctor from 12.1% to 4.6%. This application aims to determine whether these results can be reproduced in other hospitals. To keep the study relevant to patient priorities, patients selected the outcomes that the team should measure (wait times, patient satisfaction, etc.). column37: The current political and social realities of Indigenous life in Canada (i.e., higher rates of sexually-transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs), ongoing colonization, the need for health policy and programs responsive to Indigenous world views, etc.) requires thoughtful attention to Indigenous health research that effect positive social change. The Feast Centre is focused on reducing the health impacts of sexually-transmitted and blood-borne infection (STBBIs) for Indigenous communities. Let by a team of Indigenous community and scholars, the goal of the centre is to use Indigenous knowledge to shape future STBBI research. Drawing community-based research, and Indigenous and decolonizing approaches to doing research, the following objectives are proposed: (1) support STBBI research that uses Indigenous knowledge to reduce STBBIs in Indigenous communities; (2) support communities, investigators, and trainees through mentorship programs, Learning Institutes, writing retreats, and conference participation; and (3) to focus on interventions and the use of knowledge produced in research to inform health policy and programs. Over five years that the Feast Centre will operate, it is expected: (1) Funding up to (15) research development and pilot projects; (2) Strengthened existing and support the creation of new research partnerships; (3) Attracting, training and mentoring outstanding Indigenous researchers across diverse disciplines, career stages and communities; (4) Sharing research and the new knowledge produced through innovative prevention of STBBIs; and (5) Increasing collaborations across disciplines and regions with national and international Indigenous and allied research partners, community organizations, policy advisory bodies, and Indigenous community stakeholder groups.

column36: Wuniska! Indigenous Centre on HIV/HCV/STBBI Inequities
column37: Wuniska is a Cree and Saulteaux word that means wake up, arise. It's a concept filled with optimism for the new day, which we greet with renewed energy and passion. It's a verb, reflecting that as Indigenous people, our knowledge is action-oriented. It is also known as Waniska (spelling variation) and Waanishka (Metis). Wuniska describes the Saskatchewan Health Authority Patient/Family Advisory Committee for HIV/AIDS, and is a tribute to people with lived experience of HIV. The HIV and HCV incidence rates in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba rank among the highest in Canada. In both provinces, Indigenous people bear the burden of these infections with rates 2-6 times the provincial rates. There exists a critical need for a regional Indigenous-led HIV/HepC/STBBI research centre, grounded in Indigenous philosophies and methodologies. Research on HIV and HCV among Indigenous communities has largely ignored the social, colonial and historical context of HIV-related health problems and the inequitable access to screening, diagnosis, treatment, care and social supports. Furthermore, the research is predominantly led by non-Indigenous researchers, and historically by researchers from outside the SK/MB region. Wuniska will address these gaps by building approaches grounded in Indigenous philosophies and methodologies, and employing the concept of Two-eyed Seeing to take advantage of the best of Indigenous and Western capabilities. Via the centre, we will build innovative land-and culture-based research, develop infrastructure to support Indigenous communities and academics, and train the next generation of Indigenous scholars, practitioners and community members to develop innovative HIV research projects in these geographically connected territories. The Wuniska Centre is led by Indigenous PIs and strong Allies, bringing unique partnerships with Indigenous entities regionally, nationally and globally.

column36: Metabolic therapy of heart failure: which role for B vitamins?
column37: Heart failure (HF) is a complex disease resulting from the incapacity of the heart to effectively contract and unfortunately this pathology is a major leading cause of mortality. There is therefore an urging need to find new therapeutic options to slow down the course of this pathology and reduce the mortality rate. The failing heart might be defined as "an engine out of fuel" where the power station of the cell, named mitochondria, is dysfunctional and where the fuel, namely nutrients, replenishing this power station is not correctly used. Moreover, the calcium, important for this contractility process, is also misused in the failing heart, which again affects heart function. All these disregulated events are closely linked to disease progression. In this regard, efforts are undertaken to fix this power station in HF and propose as a metabolic therapy of HF. We are building on complementarity expertise of all members of the Consortium to validate the relevance of using a metabolic therapy using a cocktail of B vitamins, either alone or in combination with current drugs used to treat HF, first in experimental animal models of HF as a proof-of concept. To achieve our aims, the efficiency of such treatment will be evaluated with animal survival rate, and as secondary outcomes we will examine i) in vivo and ex vivo heart function, ii) mitochondrial function, iii) how nutrients needed for an optimal function of mitochondria are used, in other terms metabolized, by the heart, and iv) how the calcium used to promote contractility is processed by cardiac cells. Through this Consortium, we are confident to validate and propose a relevant metabolic therapy for HF that will correct both the energetic deficiency and the defect in contractility of the heart. This will be ultimately of significant clinical relevance to offer alternative or add-on therapy improving the survival of HF patients.

column36: Inflammation and Metabolism in Pulmonary Hypertension are Linked to skewed chromosome X Inactivation: new therapeutic optiONS
column37: Patients with pulmonary hypertension (PHT; high blood pressure in the lungs) have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. These cells proliferate like cancer cells and create an obstruction of the vessels, making it difficult for the blood to go through. They also have evidence of inflammation in their blood, similar to patients suffering from infections. Finally, in patients with PHT several organs display the same abnormal way to produce energy (metabolism). PHT occurs more often in women than in men and it's an area of ongoing research. Women have 2 chromosome x, and one is normally inactivated to equal gene expression of men that have one X and one Y chromosome. In some diseases like cancer, the inactivated chromosome X is re-activated, resulting in increased expression of genes located on the chromosome X. We hypothesized that this phenomenon also occur in women with PHT. We will study the state of activation of the chromosome x in 30 women with PHT compared to 30 healthy control women, as well as in animal models. We will study the mechanisms responsible for chromosome X reactivation and test whether we can reverse it in cells in culture, lung slices and animal models, using specific inhibitors of factors influencing chromosome X reactivation.

column36: Gut-brain interactions modulate immune response in hypertensive heart disease
column37: Pathogenesis of adverse cardiovascular remodelling in hypertension (HTN) has been extensively investigated. However, the intricate interactions established among different organ systems participating in the process hinder therapeutic advancement. Aberration of the compositions or functions of the gut microbes (dysbiosis) is strongly associated with HTN. However, it is still unclear whether it plays a causative or supportive role, or simply a bystander of HTN and related cardiovascular dysfunction. (1) We aim to address this question through interventions altering microbiome profiles i.e. faecal transplantation or antibiotics treatment. Next, to provide mechanistic insight of dysbiosis-HTN relationship, we will focus our investigation on microbiota crosstalk with the nervous and immune systems. We plan to exploit single-cell whole genome profiling (2) to elucidate the response of diverse immune cell subsets residing in the gut and the spleen to dysbiosis and to address whether immune-modulating function of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) is altered. Moreover, employing a series of multidisciplinary approaches including novel genetic tool, optogenetics, and live imaging (3) we aim to elucidate the neural circuit that communicates microbiota signal from the gut and address how the central nervous system (CNS) can, vice versa, influence the gut barrier function. Finally, (4) we will identify bioactive metabolites with the potential to modulate ANS and dysregulated Immune response, and prevent maladaptive cardiac remodelling in HTN.

column36: Interdisciplinary Canadian Collaborative ME Research Network
column37: Myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME), also known as chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), is a complex chronic multi-systemic disease whose etiology remains poorly understood. It is characterized by unexplained long-term fatigue and post-exertional malaise. Of note, women are more often affected than men although little is known about this sex difference. It is estimated that ME may affect over 600,000 Canadians. ME is life-altering and for its more severe forms can be life-threatening. There is growing recognition that ME is a serious disease rooted in fundamental metabolic dysfunctions that impair energy production, immune functions and physiological response to exertion. We are proposing the creation of a national interdisciplinary collaborative ME research network that will carry-out a patient-centered research program, from discovery to implementation, with the ultimate goal of finding the cause(s) and possible treatments for ME. The complexity of unresolved questions around ME require the coordinated efforts of Canadian and international experts and a wide range of stakeholders. By leveraging our collective knowledge, important health data and pockets of innovation, we will contribute to initiate the transformation of ME research landscape in Canada, and to improve the health of Canadians living with ME.

column36: Co-designing a Patient and Family Caregiver-Oriented Transitions in Care Bundle
column37: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are very sick. When a patient leaves the ICU they may have a change in their health that is new to them and their family members, such as new medical problems or new medications. When a patient leaves an ICU they can move to another part of the hospital or go home. Moving from the ICU to other parts of the hospital can be confusing and stressful for a patient and family because there will be new doctors and nurses and it will look and work differently than the ICU. The only people who remain the same when a patient moves from the ICU are the patient and their family. It makes sense that patients and their family should be at the center of their care as they move from across the healthcare system. The goal of this study is to build a tool that puts the patient and their family at the center and in control of their care. The tool will help family caregivers be involved in the patient's care while they are in the ICU. This tool will teach patients and families about the care a patient got in the ICU, the care the patient needs after the ICU, and medical problems the patient may still have. This tool will encourage patients and their families to reach out to other patients and families for peer support. This tool will improve communication between patients, families, doctors and nurses. These actions will put the patient and their family in control of their care. Once built, this tool will make the care that a patient receives better and more adapted to that patient's needs. The tool will also help patients have better recoveries from their sickness. This tool will be made with and used by patients, families, doctors and nurses. This will make sure the tool is easy to understand and useful for all patients and their families. When patients and families have more knowledge, are involved in the patient's care and can communicate with patients, families, nurses and caregivers, they are put in in control of their care.

column36: CONnecting and Coordinating an Enhanced Network for TRansitions In Care (CONCENTRIC): A New Model for Spinal Cord Injury Care in Alberta
column37: Transition in care (TiC) refers to the complicated processes that help coordinate the continuation of services as people experience changes in their health, care needs and where they receive care. Poor coordination of TiC can cause additional health issues, causing more problems such as trips to the emergency department and/or being re-admitted to the hospital. This is very expensive for the patient, their family, and the health care system, and can lead to more health concerns. When someone has a lifelong condition, they have multiple TiC because their needs change over time. A good example of this are those who have a spinal cord injury (SCI). In Alberta, the provincial SCI community (patients, clinicians, decision makers, community partners, researchers) has been working together since 2016, and has agreed that improving TiC for persons with SCI is most important, knowing that other groups with lifelong conditions face similar challenges. Our provincial research team plans to carry out a 4 year project that will create and test a new model for TiC which will be part of a larger provincial "hub and spokes system". The "hub" sites are Calgary and Edmonton (where the SCI specialty services are) and the "spoke" sites will be Lethbridge and Slave Lake, since many patients are discharged there from the hubs. We will measure the impact this new model has on patient health, experiences and well-being, the use of health care services and associated costs. In fact, early analysis by the Alberta Health Services showed that reducing emergency department visits by persons with SCI by 11% we will save $1M per year! Our plan matches the focus of this funding opportunity, as it includes people who are at risk for poor TiC, such as those living in rural and remote areas, and Indigenous Peoples. We will learn together to find ways to improve TiC for persons with SCI, measure its impact and share and expand the TiC model through provincial and national partnerships.

column36: RECOVER Program: A Care Continuum after Critical Illness
column37: Critical illness is a catastrophic life event for the patient and their family. Over 250,000 Canadians are admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) each year. These admissions cost 0.2% of the Gross Domestic Product, or $4 billion annually. Most of these patients will require mechanical ventilation to assist with breathing and more than 10% will die. Those who survive have substantial morbidity, disability, impaired quality of life and increased healthcare utilization. As well, family caregivers experience new mood disorders that compromise their health and well-being. There is no systematic care pathway for these vulnerable patients and their caregivers to meet these complex health needs. This problem must be addressed with high priority. The CIHR-funded, multi-phase RECOVER Program was initiated in 2007 to establish an innovative longitudinal care pathway for patients and families after critical illness. RECOVER Program: Phase I (published in 2016) contributed a comprehensive description of multimorbidities sustained by patients and their families, a longitudinal needs assessment and disability risk stratification to inform rehabilitation and post ICU care. RECOVER Program: Phase II was developed from this foundational work in collaboration with our patient and family engagement group. The current CIHR proposal evaluates the feasibility of an early entry, risk-stratified, inpatient rehabilitation and concurrent mental health program to mitigate care transitions and an evaluation of barriers to establishing RECOVER in three other provinces. Insights gleaned from this work will further the development of the RECOVER Program and its goal to establish a national practice standard for an integrated and seamless continuum of patient-and family-centred care after critical illness.

column36: Facilitating transitions and access across the pregnancy continuum of care - A Health System Intervention for Indigenous Women Living in Northern Manitoba
column37: Pregnancy is a time of transition. Women and families transition from pregnancy, to birth, to post pregnancy care. Each transition requires a connection to various health care providers, from a nurse, physician or midwife, sometimes to a specialist, and from care in an office setting, to hospital care for birth, and back home. In northern Manitoba one of every three pregnant women does not receive adequate care in pregnancy. Indigenous women and children experience the greatest health inequities in this region and in Canada more broadly. These inequities are compounded by transitions between health care systems. The federal government provides health care in First Nations communities, however, for specialized services and birth, women need to transition to the provincial health care system. Many barriers including, travel, transportation issues, financial constraints, poor communication, different providers, and weak referral links are encountered through those transitions. For many, relocating for care and birth away from home is characterized by insecurity, strange surroundings, and isolation from family. A pregnancy collective impact network of service providers, families and community members led by a patient navigator is proposed to assist with access to care, navigation of complex system transitions, and to improve linkages between the services and across systems. Culturally safe care and promotion of shared-decision making between patients and providers are foundational and will be supported through training. It is not enough to facilitate access and navigation, services need to be inclusive and respectful of Indigenous beliefs and issues faced by Indigenous peoples. Shared-decision making promotes effective participation in care. These strategies are expected to increase use of care, decrease low birth weight and premature birth, increase breastfeeding, increase use of well-child care and vaccination rates, and improve patient experiences.

column36: ED to EPI: Using SMS (Text) Messaging to Improve the Transition from the Emergency Department to Early Psychosis Intervention for Young People with Psychosis
column37: Psychosis, a syndrome characterized by loss of touch with reality, is a disabling and life-threatening condition that typically starts in adolescence and young adulthood, a time of life associated with gaps in mental health service use. Despite the availability of effective treatment through early psychosis intervention (EPI) programs, around half of youth do not access these services. Even when youth with psychosis present in crisis to the emergency department (ED), rates of follow-up care are poor, in large part related to young people not attending EPI services when they are referred. The goal of this study is to improve transitions from the ED to evidence-based EPI services for youth with psychosis using a short message service (SMS) text messaging intervention. We will recruit 186 youth aged 16-29 referred by the ED for consultation in EPI services for a pragmatic randomized-controlled trial of 2-way SMS reminders, psychoeducation and check-ins, with the aim of improving rate of attendance at the consultation appointment. We will review participants' charts and link with provincial health data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences to examine additional and longer-term indicators of service engagement and the effect of health equity factors such as gender and race/ethnicity. We will also perform cost-effectiveness analysis of the intervention and use qualitative methods to explore young people's perspectives on the intervention. The project will engage patient and family representatives, early career researchers and trainees, as well as key team members to champion spread of the intervention to other EPI programs and youth mental health services. Establishing evidence that a low-cost, easily implemented strategy improves transitions from the ED to EPI programs can result in more young people with psychosis getting appropriate treatment earlier, leading to improved long-term trajectories.

column36: Illiap Paanganik Qaujisarniq: Adapting Cervical Cancer Screening Strategies for Inuit Women of Nunavik
column37: Among the Canadian Inuit population, the occurrence and mortality associated with cervical cancer(CC)are higher than the national average. These high rates have led to rising concerns about current CC screening methods. Women in Canada are about to face a radical transition in the provision of cervical cancer prevention, as the current, well-known Papanicolau "Pap test" will be replaced by the new human papillomavirus (HPV) test. Research has demonstrated that the sexually transmitted HPV is the necessary cause of CC, which led to the development of this new cervical cancer screening test, more effective than the Pap test in detecting pre-cancerous lesions. Access to screening may be improved through an innovative HPV self-sampling technique, where women can collect their own cell samples. Self-collected sampling addresses many of the current barriers around screening and improves participation of women who are most at risk for CC. Through community-led collaboration, our goal is to increase participation in CC screening in Nunavik by raising awareness of the importance of CC screening in women as they age, and by implementing a pilot screening program that is based on HPV self-sampling. To do so, we want to evaluate the effectiveness of self-sampling for integration into existing public health and clinical service systems in Nunavik. Combining the perspectives of Inuit women and their service providers we defined the best implementation strategies, barriers and facilitators, as well as ways to monitor the process in terms of appropriateness, feasibility, cost, coverage and sustainability. Established evaluation and implementation frameworks will be used to guide the implementation evaluation. We have formed an Advisory Committee who will be our guide in evaluating the process and results from this implementation strategy, in order to produce a scale-up plan for all Nunavik communities, and to be presented to the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services.

A newly developed virtual care platform called aTouchAway (TM) is now developed. It is sophisticated enough to meet the needs of individuals using ventilators and their care needs. This study will test a virtual care intervention using the aTouchAway (TM) platform for children and adults newly going home with ventilators in Ontario, Canada. We are studying the effect on the following: visits to the Emergency Department, patient and families' experience and if they like using it, the costs on the healthcare system and healthcare provider time and if they like using the intervention. We have worked closely with individuals using ventilators at home and their families to design this study and make sure the results are important to them. Our study is testing a promising virtual care intervention for individuals newly going home with ventilators. Our results will help to improve the quality of life for individuals using ventilators at home by making their healthcare better.

column36: Neurosurgical Transition e-Program (Neuro-STEP): Pilot evaluation of an e-Health program to improve the transition of neurosurgical patients from remote locations to specialist neurosurgical care, across life's trajectory from pediatric to adult, and through dynamic changes in acute or chronic health states.

column36: The Digital Bridge: Using technology to support patient-centred transitions from hospital to home
column37: Older adults who live with multiple chronic conditions are more likely to experience frequent admissions and discharges from hospital. These transitions are often challenging and leave people at risk of readmission. Appropriate, timely and person-centred communication across all health care providers involved in transitions (in and out of hospital) as well as with patients and their families is critical to ensure a smooth and effective transition process. Digital health technologies can play an important role in improving person-centred communication across clinical settings and clinicians. This project will develop and test a Digital Bridge by connecting communication technologies already in use in hospital and primary care/community settings to improve communication between providers in hospital and in primary care, patients and family caregivers from admission to 6 months post-discharge. We will engage with all the technology users to co-design the Digital Bridge, ensuring that how we connect the existing technologies and adopt them into practice will meet the needs of providers, patients and their caregivers. Next our hospital partners will adopt the technology into general medicine and rehabilitation services in hospital systems in Toronto (Sinai Health System) and Mississauga (Trillium Health Partners). We will evaluate the Digital Bridge through a pre-post pragmatic trial, assessing impact on patient experience (quality of transition), patient outcomes (quality of life), transition processes (provider communication and teamwork), and system costs (economic evaluation). This project adopts an implementation science lens, allowing us to collect qualitative data on enablers and barriers to adopting the Digital Bridge to help inform development of a scale and spread strategy.

column36: Keeping in Touch (KiT) with Young Adults as They Transition Through Type 1 Diabetes Care
column37: For young adults living with type 1 diabetes moving from pediatric to adult care can be overwhelming because many feel unprepared and find it difficult to make a meaningful connection with the new adult team. column36: The Impact of an Innovative eHealth Transition Intervention on Self-Management Skills Among Young Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
column37: There have been major advances in the care of children born with heart defects ("congenital heart disease"- CHD) over the past 3 decades. Now over 90% of children with CHD reach adulthood. However, adolescent and young adult "survivors" are at risk of further heart problems. Unfortunately, most have very little understanding of their CHD and they lack confidence communicating with doctors and nurses about their heart. Over half do not attend specialized adult CHD clinics after graduating from their children's hospital, despite being advised to do so. This increases the risk that new heart problems, which may develop in early adulthood, will be discovered too late. Transition is the planned movement of adolescents with lifelong health conditions from child to adult healthcare. The Canadian Pediatric Society and other organizations have published guidelines about how children's hospitals should help adolescents prepare for the move to adult healthcare. Nurse-led programs to help with transition are effective but time-consuming, expensive, and not easily accessible to adolescents living in rural communities. However, smartphone apps are widely accessible and may be helpful in providing important transition information and coping strategies to adolescents as they enter adult health care. The objective of this research is to determine whether a transition app is better than a nurse-led transition intervention in preparing adolescents (age 16-17) with CHD to take on responsibility for their healthcare (self-management). We will enroll 188 participants across 5 children's hospitals. Each participant will randomly (like the flip of a coin) be assigned to either receive the transition app or the nurse-led transition intervention. We will also determine if the transition app results in better knowledge of their heart condition, greater self-efficacy, timelier first appointments in the adult health care system, and cost savings relative to the nurse-led transition program.

column36: Structural Determinants of Family Planning Access for Im/migrant Women
column37: One in five Canadian women is an immigrant or refugee (i.e., an im/migrant) and the number of im/migrants around the world and in Canada is steadily growing. Women need to be able to access family planning services (e.g., contraception, abortion, pregnancy planning) where and when they need them for their own health, the health of their babies, and as a basic sexual and reproductive health right. We do not know much about access to family planning services for im/migrant women in Canada. Limited research has found that refugees may face poor access to needed contraception services, and im/migrant women may be more likely to experience unplanned pregnancy. Work by our team to date with im/migrant women and service providers in Metro Vancouver has shown that this community faces serious concerns regarding barriers to care related to language barriers, racism and discrimination, worries about legal immigration status, and difficulty navigating British Columbia's (BC) health care system. The goal of this study is to understand the experiences of im/migrant women and their service providers with barriers to family planning services for women who recently arrived as im/migrants in Metro Vancouver. Through close collaboration with im/migrant women and community-based organizations, this MSc project will be based on interviews with im/migrant women who came to Canada in different ways (as refugees, for economic opportunity, without legal documentation), as well as their service providers (health, legal, settlement), to learn about their experiences with family planning services. We will use our results to make direct recommendations for policies and programmes that will improve access to family planning services for im/migrant women in BC and beyond.

column36: Analysis of metabolic and immune consequences of host-microbe interactions in diabetic mouse models
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) results from self-destruction of insulin-secreting pancreatic cells, and Type 2 diabetes (T2D) results from insulin resistance and its impaired secretion. The frequency of both diseases has increased significantly over the last 50 years, leading us to believe that they may be influenced by similar environmental factors. One hypothesis to explain these changes is that widespread antibiotic use has changed the composition of human gut bacteria (termed 'microbiome'; Mb) that reside in our intestines and play a significant role in our metabolism. The Mb is highly sensitive to diet and antibiotics, and its disruption (termed 'dysbiosis') is implicated in T1D and T2D risk. We believe that the Mb influences the development of diabetes, and that identifying bacteria that impact insulin-secreting cells and insulin-sensitive tissue can transform approaches to prevent both diseases. We hypothesize that children at risk for T1D and T2D exhibit dysbiosis that impair insulin secretion and action. Our goal is to identify intestinal microbes associated with diabetes and the consequences of their metabolic output. We will isolate and identify gut microbes from children at high risk for T1D or T2D in two prospective studies. We will isolate and cultivate the microbial communities of these pre-diabetic subjects, analyze their metabolic output, and determine whether they cause metabolic and immune disturbances by transfer into and analysis of specialized mouse models. Results from this study seek to fill a major knowledge gap in defining the cause-effect relationships involved in Mb contributions to disease. The identification of these mechanisms will help to identify human and microbial therapeutic targets for diabetes' prevention and treatment.

column36: Investigating Stat3 dependent and independent mechanisms of immune evasion
column37: The immune system has the ability to recognize and eliminate cancer cells before a tumor arises. But as time passes by, cancer cells develop mechanisms to evade or suppress the immune system, allowing them to proliferate, grow out of control and spread to other organs. There is significant evidence that the Stat3 gene plays a role in suppressing the immune system and promoting cancer progression. When we deleted Stat3 in one of our mouse models, we observed an enhanced immune response that completely eliminated the initial breast tumor. However, some cancer cells escape the immune system and are able to re-establish the cancerous growth. The details and exact mechanism that promote immune evasion are still unclear. Using advanced single cell sequencing technology available at our disposal, we aim to identify target genes required for these tumors to escape the immune system, and utilize that knowledge in order to develop more effective immunotherapies against breast cancers.

column36: Employing Adaptive Interventions and SMART Designs for the Creation of Optimal Post-Stroke Rehabilitation Programs
column37: Background: Stroke is a leading cause of disability in Canada. The probability of stroke reoccurring is high among survivors, and recurrent strokes are associated with increased mortality and disability severity. Although physical activity (PA) is effective in preventing recurrent strokes, adherence to PA programs is inadequate in this patient population. Adaptive interventions (AIs) are a way to increase adherence among patients by adapting treatments regimens based on their characteristics and treatment response (adherence). To create an AI, a Sequential Multiple Randomized Trial (SMART) design can be used where participants undergo multiple stages of treatment, with randomizations at the beginning of each stage. Interventions: Combinations of telephone consultations(TC), group exercise sessions(GS), and personal coaching(PC) will be used due to their demonstrated efficacy in improving PA adherence. Objectives: 1) Is there a difference in the proportion of chronic(>6months) post-stroke patients responding to PA when undergoing 6 vs 12 weeks of TC? 2) For non-adhering participants, is GS+TC+PC more effective than GS+PC for eliciting higher proportion of PA adherence when evaluated at 12 and 18 weeks? Methods: Forty participants from an outpatient rehabilitation program will be recruited. 1st stage: Participants will be randomized to either a 6 or 12 week TC group and proportion of responders will be identified. 2nd stage: Responders will continue with TC for 12 weeks. Non-responders will be re-randomized to either GS+TC+PC group or a GS+PC group for 12 weeks. Proportion of responders will be identified at 12 and 18 weeks. Data analysts will be blinded to groups. Significance: This is the first ever AI intervention and SMART trial created for post-stroke recovery.

column36: Role of gangliosides in the secretion of extracellular vesicles in neurodegenerative disease
column37: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids enriched in the brain with important roles in cell signaling, cell-cell communication and immune-modulation. Their levels are decreased in several neurodegenerative conditions, including Huntington's disease (HD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). Therapeutic administration of ganglioside GM1 in animal models of both diseases results in significant attenuation of neurodegeneration and improvement of symptoms. In HD mice, these beneficial effects are associated with decreased brain accumulation of mutant huntingtin (mHTT), the toxic protein that causes HD. The underlying mechanisms are unknown, but preliminary data in our laboratory suggest that GM1 increases neuronal secretion of mHTT within extracellular vesicles (EVs), membrane-bound cell-derived particles with roles in cell-cell communication and immune modulation. I will test the hypothesis that cellular levels of gangliosides regulate the secretion of EVs containing toxic misfolded proteins, and that increased ganglioside levels and/or altered ganglioside profile on the surface of EVs facilitate their uptake and clearance by microglia and modulate microglia function towards neuroprotection. My studies will uncover a novel role for gangliosides in EV secretion under physiological and pathophysiological conditions, and will provide mechanistic insights on the neuroprotective role of GM1 in HD and in PD. This knowledge may accelerate translation of ganglioside-based therapies to clinical trials.

column36: Regulation des circuits hipppocampiques et de la memoire par la plasticite synaptique des interneurones inhibiteurs
column37: L'hippocampe est une structure impliquee dans la memoire des faits et des evenements. Les reseaux neuronaux de l'hippocampe sont composes de neurones excitateurs et de neurones inhibiteurs (INs). L'activite des INs joue un role determinant dans le transfert d'information dans l'hippocampe. Pour maximiser sa flexibilite, l'hippocampe est dote d'une large diversite d'INs. Parmi ces INs, on trouve ceux qui expriment la somatostatine (SOM-INs). Ces neurones sont caracterises par une augmentation durable de leur force synaptique ou potentialisation a long-terme (PLT) qui constitue le support physiologique de l'apprentissage et de la memoire. Ces INs sont impliques dans la memoire de la peur par le contexte et dans la memoire spatiale. L'activite de ces neurones est alteree dans la maladie d'Alzheimer qui est caracterisee par un declin de memoire. La somatostatine est un peptide qui est implique dans la vision, l'olfaction, la memoire, l'apprentissage ainsi que dans certaines pathologies. A part son utilite comme marqueur moleculaire, le role precis de ce peptide chez les INs qui l'expriment est peu connu. Les SOM-INs jouent un role important dans les phenomenes de memorisation impliquant l'hippocampe, il est donc pertinent d'etudier le role de la somatostatine dans la PLT. L'hypothese emise est que la somatostatine est necessaire pour la PLT chez les SOM-INs. Il est d'autant plus important d'etudier le role de ce peptide dans les mecanismes de la memoire puisqu'il a ete demontre qu'une alteration de la plasticite synaptique des SOM-INs pourrait etre un facteur precoce dans le modele de souris de la maladie d'Alzheimer. Les resultats obtenus pourraient identifier la somatostatine comme une nouvelle cible therapeutique possible.

column36: The Longitudinal Impact of Social Media Use: Disordered Eating and Body Image Disturbance in Adolescents
column37: A new and important factor to study in relation to disordered eating (DE) and body image issues in adolescents is the impact of social media use, which is associated with the development of risk factors for eating disorders. The proposed longitudinal study will be conducted with a sample of approximately 475 adolescents of all genders from several local high schools over two time points. Adolescents aged 13-18 will complete questionnaires related to social media use, DE, body dissatisfaction, appearance comparison, and SC. I expect that greater use of social media will be associated with higher levels of appearance comparison, body dissatisfaction, and DE, especially among adolescents who present with low levels of SC. column36: Characterizing the role of the SWI/SNF Complex in Oncolytic Virotherapy.
column37: Despite extensive research and efforts, cancer remains the leading cause of death among Canadians. Therapeutic advances have led to the development of immunotherapies; treatments that utilize the patient's immune system to help target and eliminate tumors. One such treatment is oncolytic virotherapy, which uses engineered oncolytic or "cancer-killing" viruses (OVs) to specifically infect and kill cancer cells. These OVs subsequently activate the immune system to stimulate durable anti-tumor responses. Despite strong and promising anti-tumor responses by OV in certain cancer patients, tumor diversity presents as a significant hurdle to the development of widespread cures. The SWItch/Sucrose Non-Fermentable (SWI/SWF) complex is a complex that regulates gene transcription thereby controlling numerous biological processes. Previous work in our lab has shown that functional loss of various subunits of the SWI/SNF complex leads to increased viral sensitivity and cancer cell killing of multiple OV platforms in otherwise resistant cancer cell lines. The goal of this project is to engineer an OV that is specifically equipped to target and inactivate components of the SWI/SNF complex. This should improve the infectability and killing of cancer cells, sensitizing tumors to immunotherapy and leading to durable cures. The project will also elucidate the mechanisms by which complex disruption increases tumor sensitivity to virus and assess the SWI/SNF complex status as a potential predictive marker for OV treatment response. This work will generate a novel OV candidate and has the potential to identify a biomarker predictive of tumor response to OV therapy.

column36: Impacts de l'offre de services en physiotherapie au sein d'une urgence quebecoise - Essai clinique randomise
column37: Les delais d'attente a l'urgence sont un probleme preoccupant dans les centres hospitaliers canadiens et quebecois. En reaction a ce probleme, plusieurs pays ont integre une offre de services en physiotherapie dans les urgences, principalement pour des patients se presentant avec une condition neuro-musculosquelettique. Une telle offre a permis de diminuer les temps d'attente et de traitement et reduire le nombre de consultations et de prescriptions de tests diagnostiques non indiques. Au Quebec, l'offre de services de physiotherapie a l'urgence est marginale et son impact n'a pas ete documente. L'objectif de ce projet est d'evaluer les effets de la prise en charge de patients par un physiotherapeute a l'urgence sur leur evolution, l'utilisation des services et des ressources et le temps d'attente. La collecte de donnees est actuellement en cours au Centre hospitalier de l'Universite Laval. Les donnees sont obtenues via le dossier patient, le dossier administratif de l'urgence et des formulaires standardises administres en personne lors du sejour a l'urgence et par telephone ou electroniquement lors du suivi a 1 et 3 mois. Des analyses statistiques seront effectuees en comparant les resultats de patients ayant ete pris en charge par un physiotherapeute a ceux n'ayant ete vus que par le medecin de l'urgence. En evaluant les effets d'une prise en charge par un physiotherapeute a l'urgence, ce projet contribuera a ameliorer l'acces aux soins et l'efficience des services en sante et a reduire les longs delais d'attente et de prise en charge a l'urgence. Les resultats de ce projet permettront aux gestionnaires du CHUL et des autres centres hospitaliers du CHU de Quebec d'ajuster l'offre de services a l'urgence sur la base des resultats obtenus.

column36: Brain nicotinic receptor function assessed in vivo during chronic nicotine exposure and withdrawal
column37: The common consensus is that tobacco smokers smoke to obtain the stimulating effects of nicotine upon nicotinic receptors in the reward pathway of the brain; conversely, withdrawal symptoms are thought to be due to underactivation of these receptors. Therefore, nicotine replacement therapy is based around intending to stimulate these same receptors. However, there is considerable evidence that while nicotine acts to stimulate the reward pathway in the short term, chronic nicotine use actually leads to desensitization of this pathway. Further research has shown evidence that nicotine withdrawal syndrome is linked to overactivation of receptors in the reward pathway, not underactivation as commonly thought. The evidence for supersensitive receptors in withdrawal has almost exclusively been studied in cell culture or electrophysiology experiments. While these studies are helpful, it is also necessary to study nicotine withdrawal syndrome in the complex biology of behaving organisms. This project will therefore investigate the effects of chronic nicotine administration and nicotine withdrawal on the reward pathway in rats using a recently-developed method called fiber photometry. This method allows one to image the activity of selected neuronal populations in real-time, in freely behaving rats. We hypothesize that during chronic nicotine administration the brain's reward pathway loses its ability to respond to nicotine and during withdrawal the receptors in this pathway are supersensitive. The findings from this study will potentially provide the first evidence of a supersensitive response to nicotine in the reward pathway during withdrawal in living organisms. Our results will potentially force a reconsideration of nicotine replacement therapy.

column36: Neural mechanisms underlying negative cognitive bias in at-risk females of depressed mothers
column37: Depression is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide. Women are twice as likely to develop depression compared to men and the daughters of depressed mothers have a particularly high risk. Nevertheless, sex bias in the occurrence of depression is rarely addressed in interventions. Understanding why the daughters of depressed mothers are more vulnerable to exhibit depression is essential to develop appropriate and sex-specific treatments, which are presently lacking. Recent research has identified that negative cognitive bias, the negative interpretation of neutral contexts, occurs more often in females and predicts the onset of depressive episodes in daughters at risk for depression. However, the underlying mechanisms of this risk factor remain largely unknown. This research will investigate if negative cognitive bias is associated with neural markers of depression, such as dysregulated stress hormones, increased neuroinflammation, and decreased neurogenesis. We will employ extensive behavioural and neuroscientific techniques to assess the mechanisms underlying negative cognitive bias in a robust rat model. Thus, it will determine whether daughters of 'depressed' mothers show greater HPA dysregulation, aberrant neurogenesis, and increased pro-inflammatory signaling compared with the daughters of control dams. Elucidating if such alterations correlate with negative cognitive bias, may serve as an important step towards the discovery of interventions for cognitive dysfunctions that predict the onset and maintenance of depressive episodes in at-risk females. Thus, this study targets prevention and health promotion, and importantly, serves as the groundwork for improving the development of sex-specific treatments for depression.

column36: Community-led action to improve wellness within BC First Nations communities: Process evaluation of an engagement process addressing commercial tobacco wellness strategies.
column37: Indigenous populations in Canada smoke commercial tobacco (CT) at a rate three times higher than other Canadians (Elton-Marshall, Leatherdale, and Burkhalter 2011; de Finney et al. 2013). Yet, little is known regarding the relationship between Indigenous peoples of Canada and their uses and consumption of CT. Under Canada's Tobacco Strategy, there is a call for "distinct approaches" to support tobacco control for Indigenous peoples, yet there are no clear guidelines regarding how to effectively address this public health issue in a culturally respectful way; one which fully engages the community. This study will conduct a process evaluation of an Indigenous-led, health engagement strategy for respecting tobacco, namely, A context-specific and comprehensive menu of commercial tobacco control measures for First Nation communities. As part of a larger study, this process evaluation will be informed and supported by a team of Indigenous and non-Indigenous health researchers and a rich data source. A mixed-methods approach will use data from community engagement meetings, key informant interviews, survey data, research logs, and observations of the author. This study, through engagement with 5 BC Indigenous communities will develop an evaluation tool to assess levels of research partnership (consult, collaborate, engage) and will identify strengths and weaknesses in each. This study will describe the process of respectful community engagement and offer future guidance in the form of lessons learned. The purpose of this study is twofold; 1) create a tool researchers can use when engaging in culturally respectful research partnerships with Indigenous communities and 2) Create a tool communities can use when engaging in research partnerships with non-Indigenous researchers.

column36: Cardiac Energy Metabolism in Barth Syndrome
column37: Heart failure presents as the leading cause of infant death in patients with Barth Syndrome, a rare genetic disorder first described by Peter Barth and colleagues in 1983. Fortunately, with current medical strategies, individuals with Barth Syndrome now have a greater likelihood of surviving past infancy, however heart disease remains a constant clinical concern throughout their lifespan. Recently, it has been discovered that the heart of an individual with Barth Syndrome may not be able to produce energy as efficiently as a healthy heart. Because of this malfunction in energy production, the heart is compromised in its ability to effectively pump blood through the rest of the body, thus leading to heart failure. The goal of our research is to determine whether correcting the heart's ability to produce energy may be an effective therapy to prevent the development of heart disease in Barth Syndrome. Our early data has suggested that the Barth Syndrome heart may be impaired in its ability to effectively burn sugar for energy, and that an energy source made by the liver, the ketone body, may be a better substrate for the Barth Syndrome heart to metabolize. Recently, a genetically modified mouse model has been developed with the same genetic mutation that causes Barth syndrome, and these mice also develop heart failure mimicking the human condition. We will treat these mice with drugs that increase sugar (dichloroacetate) or ketone body (empagliflozin) metabolism in the heart, and assess whether these drugs improve heart function and prevent heart failure. If our hypothesis is correct, our research will suggest that increasing the heart's ability to burn sugar and/or ketone bodies for energy, may be an exciting approach to prevent heart failure in Barth Syndrome children.

column36: Dietary and Microbial Metabolites in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), including Crohn disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis, affect 1 in 150 Canadians; 25% of cases are diagnosed in children. IBD manifests with chronic gastrointestinal inflammation and altered microbial composition. Dietary changes impact IBD, including the pediatric CD therapy exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN), which entails exclusive intake of liquid meal-replacement, making adherence challenging. Predicting patient outcomes to EEN requires improved understanding of pathogenesis. Our study examines how intestinal microorganisms are involved in IBD development. We hypothesize that an altered intestinal microbiome in response to dietary or bacterial-secreted metabolites mediates patient response to dietary therapy. I will investigate whether previous diet is a valid predictor of EEN success, using metabolomics to develop biomarkers that will identify candidates for EEN success. Pilot analysis of pre-diagnosis food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) data shows that simple carbohydrates and processed meat are predictors of EEN failure and success, respectively. I will expand the analysis to a nation-wide FFQ database, and correlate results with stool microbiome analysis and metabolomics to identify potential mediators. Significantly altered metabolites will be assessed in vitro: gentamicin protection assays and immunofluorescent microscopy will identify effects on bacterial invasion, transepithelial electrical resistance will indicate epithelial barrier integrity changes, and qPCR with Western blotting and ELISA will determine human cell line inflammatory responses. Understanding diet and microbial interactions in pediatric IBD can guide novel therapies and facilitate identification of patients likely to respond to dietary therapies.

column36: How does bedaquiline kill drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis? A structural investigation with electron cryomicroscopy
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the top ten causes of death worldwide, in Canada largely affecting foreign-born individuals and Canadian-born Indigenous peoples. TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and, like many bacterial infections, can become resistant to antibiotics. A drug approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2012 called bedaquiline (also known as Sirturo), although still requiring long treatment regimens with major side effects, has been shown to be part of an effective treatment strategy for extensively drug-resistant TB. While it is known that the drug affects M. tuberculosis' ATP synthase, the enzyme that makes ATP (the cell's energy source), it is unclear how the drug affects this enzyme. It is also unknown why bedaquiline inhibits other bacterial ATP synthases, but kills M. tuberculosis and its close relatives specifically. Electron cryomicroscopy (cryoEM) can permit us to determine the structure of the bacterium's ATP synthase with bedaquline bound to it with atomic-level resolution. Knowledge of the structure will enable us to understand how the drug works, and how it is able to sterilize a M. tuberculosis infection. This information can be used to develop more effective and faster treatments for TB with fewer side effects.

column36: Role of the tumour microenvironment in medulloblastoma progression
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common childhood brain cancer. Treatment involves surgery, followed by radiation and chemotherapy. These treatments often fail and result in significant loss of brain function. In some cancers, a specific population of stem cells located around blood vessels can become activated, migrate towards the tumour and create a favourable environment for tumour growth. This project will characterize how these cells aid in medulloblastoma development by assessing their activity and ability to increase tumour severity and growth rate. Understanding how non-cancer cells can promote tumour growth can lead to the development of more effective, targeted treatments for medulloblastoma.

column36: Identifying intratumoral transcriptional heterogeneity in BCR-ABL1 lymphoblastic leukemia
column37: BCR-ABL1 acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common form of ALL in adults, contributing to 25-40% of cases. The development of drugs that inhibit BCR-ABL1, such as imatinib, has improved clinical outcomes for BCR-ABL1 ALL patients, yet many patients still relapse for reasons not entirely known. One contributor to relapse in the disease is the persistence of treatment-resistant leukemic subpopulations that are sufficient to restart the disease. Recent research in the Notta lab has demonstrated that BCR-ABL1 ALL patients can be separated into two subgroups, 'core-B' and 'mixed-B', with different molecular profiles and treatment outcomes. To better understand the subgroups and why they feature differences in relapse rates, I will identify the extent of intratumoral heterogeneity in samples from the 'core-B' and 'mixed-B' subgroups and characterize the resulting cell subpopulations using single-cell RNA sequencing. I plan to analyze the single-cell data by applying novel machine learning approaches to cluster cells. I will identify the cell populations we find from this clustering by comparing to known transcriptional profiles of leukemic and normal cells. Finally, I will compare the composition of cell populations between samples from the 'core-B' and 'mixed-B' groups. Identifying the common and unique subpopulations of blast among the two molecularly and clinically different subgroups will help with developing therapies that target all cancerous populations and prevent relapse.

column36: Correlations Between Thalamocortical White Matter Fiber Tracts and Non-Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Electroencephalogram Oscillations
column37: Based on the neural oscillation, muscle activity and movement of eyes, sleep is divided into two major components: rapid eye movement sleep (REM) and non-rapid eye movement (NREM). NREM is further divided into three distinct stages based on the frequency and amplitude of neural oscillation. In addition, there exist micro-events specific to each stage, which facilitates the detection of each stage. One of these micro-events is spindles. Two of the prominent features of NREM sleep are spindles and slow wave activity. A growing number of human neuroscience studies demonstrate that sleep spindles and slow wave activity play an essential role in different cognitive processes. On the other hand, it has been shown that the neural oscillation and electroencephalography (EEG) features of sleep remain unchanged within an individual from one night to the next. However, there is evidence that the amount of sleep spindle and slow wave activity differ between individuals. It is unclear what exactly causes these inter-individual differences. One recent study attempted to discover if macroscopic differences of the volume of grey matter in humans contribute to these inter-individual differences. However, the relationship of these EEG phasic traits of NREM sleep and other anatomical metrics of the brain, such as the volume of white matter fiber tracts projecting from the thalamus to the neocortex is yet to be investigated. Our study's aim is to utilize neuroimaging and EEG technique to investigate the relation of the volume of white matter fiber tracts projected from thalamus to the neocortex in human and examine whether it can explain the inter-individual differences of spindles and slow wave activity in NREM sleep.

column36: Role of Glucagon-Like Peptide 2 in the Treatment of Celiac Disease
column37: Celiac disease is a common condition in Canadians, and occurs as an immune response of sensitive individuals to ingestion of gluten, a molecule found in wheat. Exposure to gluten in these individuals results in damage to the intestines, resulting in pain and an inability to absorb food that, then, causes diarrhea and (in children), failure to grow normally. Over the past 20 years, we have studied a natural hormone that is produced by the intestines, glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2), which not only causes the intestines to grow but, also, promotes intestinal repair after injury. The aim of the proposed study is to develop a mouse model of celiac disease and to determine whether treatment of these mice with GLP-2 can help prevent intestinal damage and/or promote intestinal repair after damage has been caused by adding gluten to the diet. The long-term goal of these studies is to develop GLP-2 as a novel treatment for patients with severe celiac disease that cannot be prevented by gluten avoidance alone.
