column36: Investigating the safety and efficacy of intra-arterial chilled saline following ischemic stroke
column37: Ischemic stroke impacts over 50,000 Canadians each year, costing billions of dollars. Despite recent treatment advances, not all patients benefit. My goal is to benefit all patients - especially those that do not respond to current stroke treatments. To this end, I will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a novel therapy, known as intra-arterial chilled saline that is hypothesized to work in synergy with current treatment methods. Frankly, animal research findings do not tend to translate to patients. This is often due to unrealistic experimental design. For example, it is not uncommon to see small sample sizes, inappropriate stroke models, and impossibly high treatment dosages used in animal research. These design flaws lead to a paradoxical overestimate of treatment effectiveness in animals, and underwhelming results in patient trials. My research will bridge the gap between treating stroke models, and real strokes. This research has been crafted in collaboration with clinicians that are interested in future use of this method. As such, this data will guide future clinical research and trials. Our approach involves the use of a rat model that mimics our target population, and a more realistic treatment protocol than previous studies, with attention to both risks and potential benefits. I have three aims, which will address the safety and efficacy of the proposed treatment through relevant biological and behavioural endpoints. I hypothesize that intra-arterial chilled saline will improve neurological outcomes, with low risk. Multimodal assessment will confer more confidence in our findings. Although early studies using this therapy in rodents and a few patients are promising, more studies are needed to understand this approach before more humans are tested.

column36: The Effect of Antioxidant Supplementation in Intravenous Nutrition on Gastrointestinal Health in a Neonatal Piglet Model
column37: Intravenous (IV) nutrition is a lifesaving tool used by clinicians to treat premature infants. However, the use of IV nutrition presents with adverse consequences including changes to the structure and function of the intestinal tract. This subsequently reduces the infant's ability to absorb nutrients from the diet once normal feeding into the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is resumed. The loss of GI function is due in part to a decrease in blood flow to the intestinal tract during IV nutrition. Blood flow is regulated by a compound called nitric oxide (NO), so greater availability of NO may help sustain blood flow during IV feeding. However, IV feeding introduces pro-oxidant compounds that contribute to tissue damage and cell death. NO is known to react with pro-oxidant compounds and the resultant compound, peroxynitrite, can also cause tissue damage. These negative effects must be mitigated by the infant's own antioxidant system. Glutathione is the compound within the antioxidant system that reacts with the pro-oxidant compounds. In premature infants, this glutathione system is under-developed and unable to overcome the production and presence of these pro-oxidant compounds. In this study, we will be using newborn piglets that are supported with IV nutrition supplemented with glutathione (versus un-supplemented). We predict that the addition of glutathione will enhance antioxidant capabilities which in turn, will protect NO so it can function as a blood flow regulator rather than contributing to oxidative tissue damage. Glutathione supplementation is potentially an innovative method of reducing intestinal injury caused by oxidative damage and poor intestinal blood flow, and could be applied clinically to aid in the survival and growth of premature infants.

column36: L'effet d'un entrainement metacognitif sur les deficits en theorie de l'esprit en schizophrenie
column37: La schizophrenie (SZ) est une psychopathologie qui affecte les cognitions, les perceptions et les comportements. Les individus atteints de SZ presentent souvent des difficultes dans leur fonctionnement quotidien. La medication contribue a diminuer les symptomes positifs de la maladie (idees delirantes, hallucinations), mais n'elimine pas les difficultes fonctionnelles. Un obstacle important au bon fonctionnement en SZ est la presence de difficultes de cognition sociale. Jusqu'ici, les traitements developpes pour cibler la cognition sociale sont principalement des traitements de remediation cognitive visant l'amelioration des processus cognitifs, la durabilite et la generalisation des acquis au quotidien. La Theorie de l'esprit (TdE) soit la capacite a inferer les etats mentaux des autres, est particulierement alteree en SZ. En outre, la performance de TdE est un des meilleurs predicteurs de fonctionnement quotidien. Le Metacognitive training (MCT) est un traitement psychologique ayant pour but principal d'informer les patients sur les difficultes cognitives susceptibles de sous-tendre leurs symptomes et leurs difficultes fonctionnelles. Ce programme cible notamment les difficultes de cognition sociale, mais son effet sur les habiletes de cognition sociale n'a pas ete demontre. L'objectif 1 est de mener une etude pilote afin de documenter si l'effet du MCT est observe sur la performance de cognition sociale en SZ et en particulier sur les deficits de TdE presents chez les patients atteints de SZ. Ensuite, les objectifs 2 et 3 sont respectivement de repliquer les effets du MCT sur les symptomes psychiatriques et sur le fonctionnement social des patients atteints de SZ et d'etudier les liens entre ces ameliorations et celles observees au niveau de la cognition sociale.

column36: Megakaryocyte Engineering to Create Designer Platelets
column37: Platelets are small circulating cells that act as natural delivery vehicles for numerous small molecules and regulate many physiological processes such as blood clotting, immune function, and cancers. Platelets are often transfused to help stop bleeding, but their application in other diseases is limited by challenges to modify and enhance platelet function for therapeutic purposes. For example, there are currently no methods to modify the protein content of transfusable platelets. This project therefore aims to develop novel approaches to engineer platelets by modifying their precursor cells, megakaryocytes (MKs). This will be achieved by using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs)-a recently FDA-approved drug delivery vehicle-targeted to MKs, delivering nucleic acids to alter the protein composition of platelets. Successful implementation of this strategy will therefore create a platform technology to produce platelets with new and modified functions that current transfused platelets do not possess. The technology will enable platelets to locally deliver therapeutics to injured tissues, such as sites of trauma, or potentially to treat diseased tissues and organs where platelets accumulate, such as tumours or the brain for treating Alzheimer's disease.

column36: A Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating an Information Decision Aid for Late-Life Depression
column37: As Canada's population ages, it is important to protect, maintain, and promote older adults' mental health. The ability to live meaningful and enjoyable lives may be reduced when older adults experience a diagnosis of depression. Older adults face many barriers when accessing mental health services, one of which is decreased knowledge about mental health problems. Information decision-aids (IDAs) are a type of tool that can increase and individual's knowledge about mental health problems by presenting unbiased and research based information on health problems and treatment options in clear and concise language. IDAs help patients to be engaged in the treatment decision making process and improve communication between patients and health care providers. The purpose of this study is to (1) evaluate the effectiveness of a web-based IDA for late-life depression that was developed by our research team, and (2) compare its effectiveness to an existing online IDA. Older adults will be randomly selected to be in an intervention group (IDA developed by our research team) or comparison group (existing online IDA), and will be given an assessment measuring general depression knowledge, conflict about treatment decisions and attitudes about seeking mental health treatment. This study will provide new evidence on the effectiveness of web-based IDAs for late-life depression. Highly effective IDAs have the potential to reduce barriers that older adults face in accessing mental health services by improving mental health knowledge and enhancing their ability to participate in the treatment decision-making process.

column36: The role of 2-hydroxyglutarate as a contributor to immune system evasion in cancer
column37: Our body's immune system is responsible for protecting us from infectious organisms and other invaders. The immune system is made up of cells, tissues and organs that work together to fight infection to keep us healthy. Importantly, the immune system must also detect cancerous cells in the body. As tumors grow, they develop different ways to turn off the immune system, allowing the cancer to grow and spread throughout the body. Many types of cancer have alterations in metabolic pathways - the ways by which the cancer cells produce energy. One of these alterations results in the production of a compound called 2-hydroxyglutarate. We are interested in the ways by which 2-hydroxyglutarate suppresses a specific type of immune cell called Natural Killer cells. Natural Killer cells have a critical function in detecting tumors. We hypothesize that 2-hydroxyglutarate produced by tumor cells is secreted in to the surrounding environment and reduces the capacity of the Natural Killer cells to detect the presence of the cancer cells, which allows the tumor to progress. This project will focus on the mechanisms 2-hydroxyglutarate alters Natural Killer cells' efficiency to kill cancer cells.

column16: Bourse a la maitrise : bourse d'etudes superieures
column36: Neoantigens in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
column37: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is a type of skin cancer that presents with red patches on the skin. These patches can develop into tumours, marking advanced disease. The disease can then spread to other organs. MF is considered incurable and once patients develop tumours, they have only a 56% chance of surviving 5 years. There is an urgent need for advances in therapies. Immunotherapies work by using the patient's immune system to fight tumour cells. These therapies can be non-specific, such as exposure to ultraviolet light in photopheresis, however MF tumours show no response to this. Immunotherapies can also be designed specifically to recognize tumour cells. Neoantigens are new, unique proteins produced only due to mutations in tumors and not by healthy cells. Hence targeting neoantigens with immunotherapy, whether specific or non-specific, has been highly effective in other cancers. Neoantigens have never been investigated in mycosis fungoides, and my project will aim to do this for the first time. My hypothesis is that MF has only a small number of neoantigens that stimulate the immune system, explaining its poor response to non-specific immunotherapies. To characterize neoantigens, I will use DNA sequences of MF samples compiled by our lab. I will then apply computer algorithms to detect mutations and predict what neoantigens will result and cause an immune response. Such a discovery could provide the foundation for new immunotherapies to be designed specifically to target neoantigens. I will also compare the MF neoantigen profile to another skin cancer in the same family, Sezary Syndrome. This will provide insight into whether a higher number of neoantigens are responsible for Sezary Syndrome's superior response to non-specific immunotherapies such as photopheresis.

column36: An Investigation into Arresting the Support of Cancer Associated Fibroblasts on Cancer Metastasis
column37: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is one of the most common types of cancers, with a high relapse rate and poor survival. Its growth and spread is heavily supported by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which when activated, provide tumour cells with a continual stream of nutrients and structural resources. Previous work has shown the importance of CAFs to tumour invasive potential and so the goal of my project is to better understand CAF biology and find ways of inhibiting its activity to reduce the rate of cancer metastasis. There are two main components of my project. The first is to make sense of CAF diversity by using machine-learning techniques to categorize CAFs into functional subgroups. I will then analyse the gene expression and methylation profiles of each category to determine 1) from what cells those CAFs were derived, 2) how they became activated, and 3) why they have remained activated in the presence of cancer cells. This work will improve our understanding of CAF lineages and find potential mechanisms by which to prevent CAF formation. The second component is to inhibit CAF activity to reduce HNSCC metastasis. To do this, I will screen a library of small molecule inhibitors for compounds capable of inactivating CAFs. The inhibitors' performance will be assessed via three functional tests: the ability to 1) limit CAF proliferation and change its shape, 2) reduce CAFs' contractibility of collagen, and 3) decrease cancer cell invasion when exposed to treated CAFs. These experiments together will serve as the first step in developing a drug capable of controlling cancer metastasis. Overall, my project will not only further our understanding of tumour biology but also has the potential to improve HNSCC prognosis for all patients.

column36: Investigating the mechanism of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome development.
column37: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS) is a genetic disorder caused by deficiencies in the Liver Kinase B1 (LKB1) protein. Patients experience chronic inflammation and benign tumor growth along their gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and have a 90% chance of developing cancer by age 65. T cells are part of the adaptive immune system, and either promote or dampen inflammation. We previously discovered that T cell-specific LKB1 deficiencies (LT) are sufficient to induce PJS in mice; however, a subset of these LT mice develop no disease and appear normal. This suggests that inflammation and tumor growth are not intrinsic results of an LKB1-deficient genotype, but require an environmental trigger. The proposed research will investigate whether pro-inflammatory gut-microbiome interactions may trigger an immune response that cannot be adequately dampened, leading to a pro-cancerous, chronic inflammatory state. There are 3 proposed study objectives. Firstly, it is well established that changes in gut microbiome composition are strongly associated with intestinal disease. The microbiome compositions of LT mice will thus be determined and compared to elucidate any differences between a diseased and a non-diseased state. Secondly, Th17 (pro-inflammatory T) cells will be over- and under-expressed in LT mice to determine whether their expression drives PJS development. Lastly, if objective 1 shows observable differences in the microbiomes, young LT mice will be inoculated with diseased and non-diseased microbiomes to determine whether their composition directly modulates disease severity. Current therapies for PJS focus on symptomatic treatment, but understanding the disease mechanism would allow the development of preventative therapies that reduce inflammation and improve prognosis.

column36: Investigating the role DNAJC Chaperones in Parkinson's Disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder causing impaired movement, in addition to autonomous and cognitive dysfunction. It is a progressive condition for which there is no known cure. Dopamine neurons in the Substantia Nigra pars compacta are slowly lost during progression of PD, the reason for this remains enigmatic. Genetic studies have revealed mutations in multiple genes which are causative of PD. With this, converging pathways have emerged, allowing researchers to focus on specific cellular activities likely related to PD onset and progression. Recently, mutations in two chaperone proteins, DNAJC12 and DNAJC13, were discovered as causes of PD. Importantly, these discoveries highlight a potential mechanism in PD, as all 5 DNAJC chaperone proteins now implicated in PD are expressed in the brain (including DNAJC5, CSP?; DNAJC6, Auxilin; and DNAJC26, GAK).We have recently made and begun characterizing a DNAJC13 knock-in mouse expressing the human p.N855S mutation and a DNAJC12 knock-out mouse. Research into these models will provide novel insight into: 1) the role of DNAJC chaperone proteins in PD pathogenesis; 2) the coordinated regulation of DNAJC proteins on dopamine cell homeostasis, and; 3) molecular targets for therapeutic drug development. Insights gained will be relevant not only to PD research, but also to many dopamine dis-regulation disorders including addiction, depression, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.

column36: Exploring the Effect of Nutrition on Mortality and Cardiovascular Disease using Linked Population-based Dietary Data
column37: Diet is a major determinant of health and is considered to be largely responsible for the reduction in cardiovascular disease (CVD) in industrialized countries since the 1960s. Dietary recommendations focus on elimination of trans-fat, reduction of saturated fatty acids (SAFAs), and increases in vegetable and fruit consumption. However, recently it has been highlighted that the evidence-base may not be very strong for these recommendations. For example, systematic reviews fail to demonstrate consistent relationships between SAFAs, CVD, and mortality. The most recently published large nutritional cohort study has identified carbohydrates as detrimental, while fats were protective against death and CVD. Then, a meta-analysis published this summer suggested a u-shaped relationship between carbohydrate and mortality, and that fats are only protective if they're plant-based. Given the inconsistencies, a reliance on predetermined nutrient categories may be problematic. I propose applying novel machine learning techniques to both identify the dietary components truly related to health, and to better characterize the complex relationship. I plan to use the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS), which contains the only detailed Canadian population-based dietary data available and has been linked to participants' later healthcare utilization. This will allow development of a model to both predict CVD and mortality and determine their dietary risk factors, applying both traditional and ML techniques. This would be the first time that such a study has been performed in Canada, and could help identify whether ML may be useful. Ultimately, the project aims to better inform decision-makers, clinicians, and individuals about diet-related policy and behaviour impacts on health.

column36: Design of a gradient-generating bioreactor for zonal cartilage growth
column37: Arthritis leads to the progressive degradation of articular cartilage of the joints, resulting in pain and loss of mobility. Affecting 6M Canadians, it is the most prevalent incurable chronic health condition. Current treatments are often surgical, and range from joint replacement to cell-based therapies that produce repair tissue. None of these approaches, however, regenerate the native structural and mechanical properties; the resulting tissue is structurally and chemically isotropic. However, native cartilage is anisotropic, zonally organized along its depth, with each zone comprising a distinct cell phenotype. This affects the composition and organization of the tissue, and thus its structural and functional properties. Biomolecular gradients, such as those arising from avascular cartilage tissue, are known to affect cell responses. It is hypothesized that these gradients, specifically of glucose, drive the zonal organization of cartilage. This work aims to: (I) test the hypothesis that glucose gradients drive zonal specification of cartilage; (II) develop a mathematical model of a continuous flow bioreactor capable of generating nutrient gradients; and (III) design and construct said reactor. To test (I), chondrocytes will be grown in 2D and 3D conditions, with varying glucose concentrations, and the resulting tissues tested for zone-linked markers. The model of (II) will be developed by combining biochemical, reaction engineering, and mass transfer principles, then used to design and 3D print a reactor (III). The resulting cartilage will be subject to similar analyses as in (I). This has the potential to solve a major problem in the field and improve current practices in the regeneration of anisotropic tissues, including but not limited to articular cartilage.

column36: Mechanism of cell-free nucleic acid release and its utility as a cancer biomarker
column37: Cancer diagnosis often requires invasive tissue biopsy procedures that can be risky, painful, and costly. Non-invasive detection methods would make cancer diagnosis safer and more convenient and would allow for monitoring cancer during and after treatment. Since all cancer cells harbor alterations in their genetic material (DNA), detection of these alternations has clinical potential as a diagnostic tool. Free-floating DNA fragments in the bloodstream that is not associated with cells (cell-free DNA, cfDNA) can be used to detect cancer-specific alterations and could potentially be used to replace invasive biopsies. Since blood collection is relatively easy and can be done regularly, researchers aim to use cfDNA as a biomarker for cancer detection and treatment response monitoring. However, it is poorly understood how cfDNA is released into the bloodstream, limiting its clinical potential. Studies have identified multiple mechanisms of cfDNA release, and the relative contribution of each mechanism has been hotly debated. One such mechanism is via exosomes, which are small lipid structures released by cells that can also be found in the bloodstream. Due to the mounting interest in the use of exosomes as a source of cfDNA, there is an urgent need for rigorous study of the cfDNA content of exosomes and their potential as a cancer diagnostic tool. The objective of this proposed study is to investigate how much cfDNA is contained within exosomes in both cancer patients and healthy individuals. This work will resolve controversies in the field and reveal insights that can advance the use of cfDNA as a non-invasive biomarker to replace traditional biopsy.

column36: Education prenatale et l'anxiete liee a la grossesse et a l'accouchement des futurs meres et peres
column37: Une premiere grossesse est un evenement marquant dans la vie d'un couple, qui peut causer de l'anxiete autant chez la mere que le pere. Differentes formations prenatales se sont montrees efficaces pour reduire cette anxiete. Cependant, selon la disponibilite des services dans leur region, les futurs parents peuvent faire appel a diverses ressources d'education prenatale, autant en ligne qu'en groupe. Ce projet doctoral, qui s'inscrit dans une etude plus large sur les services d'education prenatales, propose de verifier 1) si l'anxiete des peres et des meres predit leur recherche d'education prenatale, et 2) si la quantite et la nature des sources consultees predisent le niveau d'anxiete ressenti au troisieme trimestre et a l'accouchement, en considerant que les conjoints peuvent influencer mutuellement leurs choix et experience. L'etude, menee dans les regions de la Capitale-Nationale et Chaudiere-Appalaches fait appel a 795 femmes enceintes de leur premier enfant et leurs conjoints. Tous sont invites a remplir des questionnaires a trois reprises : entre 10 et 20 semaines de grossesse (T1), apres 33 semaines de grossesse (T2) et 6 a 8 semaines apres l'accouchement (T3). Les resultats serviront a clarifier comment l'education prenatale peut aider a attenuer l'anxiete des futurs parents a l'egard de la grossesse et l'accouchement. Ils informeront egalement les intervenants sur les facteurs pouvant motiver la recherche d'education prenatale, de meme que l'influence possible que les futurs peres et meres peuvent avoir l'un sur l'autre.

column36: Changes in gut microbiota and risk of colitis associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors
column37: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are a class of drugs which relieve suppression of the immune system to induce an anti-tumour immune response in cancer patients. Despite the rise in usage and efficacy of ICI in mainstream cancer therapy, many patients still fail to achieve an adequate response towards the drug, and toxicities associated with ICI, such as colitis, remain common in treated patients. Recently, interactions between regular gut bacteria and tumor response have been well studied largely due to the gut microbiome being implicated as a modulator of systemic immune responses. Thus, this project seeks to identify gut bacteria which may be contributing towards the therapeutic efficacy and toxicities associated with ICIs. My hypothesis is that tumor response and risk of colitis can be predicted by baseline differences between gut bacteria in cancer patients, and that changes in bacteria caused by ICI can improve tumor response and/or induce the development of colitis. Using fecal samples obtained from metastatic melanoma patients, we plan on identifying gut bacteria at baseline before ICI treatment. We will compare this to post-treatment bacterial profiles to identify any changes. Additionally, harmful bacteria causing colitis will be identified post-treatment to determine which specific bacteria induced by ICIs contribute to colitis development. This study is important as there are currently inconclusive findings over which bacteria are predictive of tumor responses after ICI treatment. The involvement of patients from separate institutions may provide clarity on which bacteria contribute towards tumor responses. Determining bacteria associated with post-ICI colitis will also help with the identification of patients at high risk of colitis.

column36: Comparing the cognitive effects of outdoor versus indoor walking among healthy older adults
column37: With a growing elderly population, dementia is a critical global health challenge. Lifestyle factors are promising as accessible, low-cost approaches to prevent or mitigate cognitive decline. In particular, physical activity, such as aerobic exercise, can improve cognitive function in older adults, but more research is needed to determine optimal exercise strategies. Recent evidence shows that time spent in nature can also provide a range of physical and cognitive health benefits. In fact, the benefits of exercise appear to be enhanced when performed in outdoor, natural settings, such as parks and forests, as compared to indoor or built settings, such as gyms or urban environments. However, the role of a green exercise environment in promoting cognitive health in older adults requires further investigation. The goal of my research is to compare the effects of outdoor versus indoor walking programs on cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults. Participants will be randomly assigned into two groups for a 12-week walking program: one group will walk on forest trails, while the other group will walk indoors on a treadmill. The main outcome will be a subset of cognitive skills called executive functions, such as self-control and working memory, which are important for maintaining independence while aging. This research will help better understand the potential of outdoor exercise as a lifestyle strategy to support cognitive health throughout the aging process.

column36: Modification of Protein-Nanoparticle Complexes for Delivery of Nucleic Acid Therapeutics
column37: Improved nucleic acid therapy targeting towards cancer cells in vivo would improve efficacy of treatment, reduce off-target effects and subsequently, reduce toxicity. One technique that may improve targeting is the use of nanoparticles as carriers for therapeutics. Studies have shown that nanoparticles can have positive effects on circulation and biodistribution, however few are currently employed as clinical treatments. By developing a nanoparticle that binds to human serum albumin (HSA) we hope to develop a novel therapeutic technique for treatment of different diseases via the implementation of siRNA based gene silencing. Previous work in the Sleiman lab has shown that rigid nanocube scaffolds can be made with control over the spatial orientation of ligands around the structure. One such ligand that has been conjugated to nanostructures is D1, a molecule made of monomeric alkane chains shown to bind HSA and may hold promise as a method to increase viability of nucleic acid therapeutics in vivo. A D1-fluorophore-siRNA strand will be made via solid phase phosphoramidite chemistry with the siRNA strand silencing luciferase. This molecule will be bound to nanostructures through Watson-Crick base pairing and purified using gel electrophoresis and reverse phase chromatography. The binding of the nanoparticle to HSA will be analyzed using gel electrophoresis and surface plasmon resonance. The tumour penetration, internalization and silencing of luciferase will be tested in cell models to probe the efficacy of this method for potential therapeutic delivery. Future studies may look at other factors such as biodistribution and tumor accumulation or the differences caused by changes in geometry via addition of D1 to other DNA nanostructures made in the Sleiman lab.

column36: Explicit and Implicit Cannabis-Related Cognitions in People with Social Anxiety
column37: Social anxiety and cannabis use are both prevalent and often co-occur. Moreover, researchers have found that undergraduates with high social anxiety report greater endorsement of using cannabis to cope with negative emotions (i.e., expectancies). Indeed, such explicit cognitions or "expectancies" are a chief determinant of usage; however, the role of implicit cannabis-related cognition among individuals with social anxiety is unknown. We will examine the relationship between social anxiety and cannabis use by examining the role of implicit automatic associations (concepts that are linked in memory) between social anxiety groups in predicting cannabis-related problems. We need to establish whether level of social anxiety predicts cannabis use, and if certain automatic associations in memory help explain this relationship. We will also investigate if these measures of automatic associations, in addition to self-report measures, help better predict cannabis-related problems than if we were to rely on either measure alone. We will screen and recruit undergraduate students from Trent University to complete an in-person experiment. To be eligible, students must report consuming cannabis within the last year, and report either low or high social anxiety. Participants will complete two computerized tasks measuring their automatic associations related to cannabis, in addition to completing online self-report questionnaires. This study will help improve cognitive behavioural models and evidence-based treatments of social anxiety disorder. Given the recent legalization and increased accessibility to cannabis in Canada, this research is particularly relevant in addressing public health concerns regarding both social anxiety and problematic cannabis use, in youth and adults.

column36: Using neuroimaging and a quality of life measure to assess the impact of physical activity on the pediatric concussed brain.
column37: Concussions are increasingly prevalent among children and youth in Ontario and the rest of Canada, demonstrating the need for effective treatment methods. One potentially effective treatment being put forward is to encourage children to resume light, non-strenuous physical activity soon after being diagnosed with a pediatric concussion. The proposed research will be investigating the impact of early resumption of physical activity and brain functioning on quality of life following a concussion in children and youth aged 10-18. Brain functioning will be measured using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) technology and quality of life will be measured using a validated pediatric quality of life questionnaire. The use of both subjective (self-reported) and objective measures will provide a well-rounded picture of the use of physical activity as a valid treatment method following a concussion. This research will help to shape future guidelines for physicians, schools, and sporting institutions when attending to the needs of a concussed child.

column36: Determining biomarkers of response to docetaxel for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer using circulating cell-free tumour DNA
column37: The primary chemotherapy for late-stage prostate cancer is only effective in 45% of patients. However, there is currently no way of knowing in advance which patients will benefit from treatment, and which patients could avoid the side-effects of chemotherapy and receive a different therapy instead. Herein lies an urgent clinical need for tests that can predict patient response to chemotherapy, thereby helping clinicians select the best cancer treatment for an individual patient. My aim is to identify molecular markers capable of predicting whether a patient will respond to the chemotherapy docetaxel. My approach relies on the fact that cancerous tissues shed a small amount of their DNA into the bloodstream, creating an opportunity to examine the tumour by analyzing DNA isolated from a patient's blood sample. This DNA, termed 'circulating tumour DNA' (ctDNA), provides a molecular snapshot of the tumor. CtDNA profiling is a novel technique that enables capture of information about a cancer via a blood test. This means that breakthroughs can be quickly translated to the clinic to inform treatment decisions. To identify biomarkers predictive of docetaxel response, I have identified 74 eligible patients from a provincial biobank (established by my supervisors) of ctDNA samples from hundreds of metastatic patients. I will profile DNA from these patients using a custom bioinformatics approach, and will subsequently correlate findings to patient clinical history and treatment outcomes. Success with this project will help optimize treatment selection for patients with late-stage prostate cancer, resulting in improved quality and length of life for men with this aggressive disease.

column36: Manipulation of Impulsivity through Optogenetic Stimulation of Serotonergic Neurons in the Dorsal and Median Raphe Nuclei
column37: Impulsivity is a trait defined by a lack of self-control, often as a result of acting before all information has been acquired. Impulsivity can become pathological and contribute to substance abuse disorders. Neurologically, impulsivity has been linked to the neurotransmitter serotonin (5-HT), which is supplied by two distinct brain pathways originating in the median (MRN) and dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN). It is unclear as to which pathway is more important in mediating impulsivity. Accordingly, my main objective is to discover the relative importance of MRN and DRN 5-HT pathways to impulsivity. To achieve this, I will use an animal model of impulsivity. In this model, mice are first trained on a touch-screen task where they must respond to a visual stimulus for food reward while showing low impulsivity. Once mice have learned the task, they are surgically implanted with optical fibres, which allow the use of a laser to selectively activate the MRN and DRN pathways. Mice will then be tested on two varieties of the task where impulsivity is at a higher level. While completing this task, the mice will have their DRN or MRN pathways activated by the laser. This will allow me to measure the effect of selective stimulation of the DRN or MRN pathways on impulsivity. Accordingly, my main hypothesis is that stimulation of either pathway will reduce mice's impulsive behavior on the task. Furthermore, I hypothesize that the selective stimulation of the DRN or MRN will reveal which pathway is more important for the expression of impulsivity. The results of this study may help delineate the neurobiological basis of impulsivity and provide insight into how impulsivity contributes to the maladaptive drug-seeking behaviors symptomatic of substance abuse.

column36: Computational modelling of interplay between histone tail modifications and its effects on chromatin dynamics in human development and cancer
column37: The causes of cancer have long been an important area of research, and recent studies have indicated an under-appreciation of "epigenetic" changes' contribution to the development of cancer, which concern the chemical modifications to DNA or to the proteins around which DNA is wrapped in the cell nucleus. To study such changes, high-throughput technologies are used to generate a profusion of data comprehensively profiling genetic materials. Although very educational, previous models derived from these observations have oftentimes been rather hand-wavy and commonly suffer from a lack of strong quantitative foundation. With recent reports emphasizing the importance of epigenetics in cancer research, grasping the mechanisms underlying these events are ever more crucial. As we have improved our understanding of these reversible epigenetic changes, we have also noticed potential interplays between them in human cancer cell lines. For instance, based on previous reports and our own data, certain epigenetic marks appear to participate in a tug-of-war of sorts, establishing a delicate equilibrium. Consequently, we would like to model and comprehend these types of phenomenon by applying established statistical tools and algorithms to a variety of tumour, normal, and engineered cell lines. We have already been able to recapitulate the behaviour of a set of marks which builds upon one another in a specific manner using a preliminary model. Although studies directly describing tumour cells can be incredibly informative, they often lack information on earlier, casual events. Given the targetable nature of proteins effecting epigenetic changes, the predictive capabilities of our models could allow us to identify and possibly counteract disease-causing changes at an earlier stage.

column36: Mental Health Services in Primary Care: A Review of Ontario, Alberta & Manitoba
column37: The proposed project aims to investigate health system approaches taken to address mental health needs in primary care settings. The nature and structure of primary care teams will be examined and special attention will be paid to studying the impact of mental health workers within primary care teams. This project will employ a comparative policy analysis in reviewing mental healthcare within primary care settings in Ontario, Alberta and Manitoba. Mental health services in Canada can be a complex system to navigate for patients and to study for health services researchers. The proposed research project could be informative regarding mental health system reform and serve as a foundation for further research.

column36: The effects of exercise therapy on the cognitive functions of patients with chronic low back pain
column37: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is the most prevalent and problematic of all chronic pain syndromes. In addition to enduring persistent excruciating pain, they also experience a constellation of symptoms that further contribute to their disability, including a reduction of cognitive abilities. This is because patients with CLBP have more difficulty summoning the cognitive resources necessary to meet professional and personal responsibilities, often providing them with a major obstacle in every day functioning. Despite this, these cognitive deficits are rarely the focus of therapeutic interventions for CLBP since they are widely viewed as a secondary side effect of chronic pain. Thus, an effective treatment for them is still unknown. Fortunately, research shows that physical exercise is beneficial throughout the lifespan by optimizing overall physical and cognitive health and is one of few interventions that reliably improves pain management in CLBP. The proposed study aims to test the impact of a physical exercise intervention on CLBP and its associated cognitive deficits. It is hypothesized that the physical exercise intervention will affect the cognitive deficits seen in CLBP by either having a direct impact on those cognitive symptoms or having an indirect impact through a reduction in pain experience. To prove this, we will assign CLBP patients to a 14-week physical exercise program of high intensity aerobic and muscular exercise and examine pre- and post-levels of pain intensity and disability, and cognitive performance on a series of neuropsychological tasks. This study will provide insight into a feasible intervention that can enhance the cognitive health as well as the functionality and quality of life of chronic pain sufferers.

column36: Effect of Parental Support on Child Cognitive Reappraisal: A Transition into Adolescence Study
column37: Cognitive reappraisal is an emotion regulation (ER) strategy which involves cognitively altering one's emotional response to an event through reinterpretation (Gross, 1998; Giuliani & Gross, 2009). Findings suggest that adolescents use less adaptive ER strategies and as such may be more at risk of development of mental illness as a relationship has been found between poor ER strategies and depressive and anxiety symptoms in adolescents (Schafer, Naumann, Holmes, Tuschen-Caffier, & Samson, 2017). Thus, it is important to identify factors in the development of adaptive ER. Two factors that influence ER development in children are parent's ER strategies and how they support their children's use of adaptive ER strategies (Lunkenheimer, Shields, & Cortina, 2007; Thompson, 1994). What remains unknown is how the relationship between cognitive reappraisal and parental support unfolds for children transitioning into adolescence and when using experimental methods and objective measures of ER. The current study seeks to rely on brain imaging to measure emotional arousal in children, in an effort to determine how parent's support might affect the relationship between parent ER and child ER through the child's ability to make use of cognitive reappraisal strategies. This research contributes to the goals of the CIHR by directly identifying how parental support influences ER strategies in those transitioning into adolescence through the utilization of experimental methods and imaging technology in support of pen-paper questionnaires/measures. Further, this research has the potential to inform the development of interventions that seek to teach adaptive ER strategies to children and adolescents in an effort to reduce poor ER use, and thereby the risk of development of mental illness.

column36: The Effect of Supervised Consumption Services on Overdose Rates, Infectious Disease Complications, and Opioid Agonist Therapy in Ontario
column37: The opioid overdose crisis has resulted in the death of thousands of Canadians and has been declared a public health emergency by the Government of Canada. As part of Canada's public health response to the crisis, several new Supervised Consumption Services (SCSs) have been approved and are operating across the country. At minimum, SCSs provide people who use drugs with sterile injection supplies, observation after injection, and, as needed, administration of an overdose reversal agent. Prior studies have shown that SCSs reduce overdoses and infectious disease risk behaviour while remaining cost effective. Much of this evidence comes from British Columbia prior to the current epidemic, however little is known this may differ in Ontario and in the current context. Given the important geographical, social, and political differences across provinces, this thesis study aims to evaluate the impact of the implementation of SCSs in Ontario on three primary outcomes: rates of (1) overdose, (2) infectious disease complications, and (3) prescribed opioid agonist therapy. Data will be obtained using Ontario-wide administrative health data. Analyses will be performed to determine the rates of the primary outcomes within defined neighbourhoods surrounding an SCS in the year before and after its implementation. The results of this study will contribute significantly to our understanding of the impact of SCSs on important morbidity and mortality outcomes. It also represents one of the first studies to examine the effect of SCSs on the treatment of opioid use disorder. Overall, an accurate understanding of the role of SCSs in different geographical settings is critical in guiding ongoing harm reduction health policy in Ontario, nationally, and internationally amidst this crisis.

column36: PHASE-SPECIFIC EVALUATION OF COST-EFFECTIVENESS FOR LUNG TRANSPLANT AND EX-VIVO LUNG PERFUSION
column37: Patients with lung disease not responsive to medical therapy may undergo lung transplant as a definitive surgical therapy. Lung transplants have been shown to improve quality of life for patients with severe lung disease, and has been shown to extend length of life. However, the frequency with which donor lungs are determined to be of inadequate quality for transplant and the increasing enlistment of patients on the transplant wait-list means that the demand for lung transplant exceeds the available organ supply. Close to 20% of patients die while waiting for donor lungs. Ex-vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) is a promising new technology which allows for rehabilitation of donor lungs prior to transplant in a recipient. This technology has been shown to be safe and effective. However, the effect that EVLP may have on rates of lung transplant are yet to be determined. Lung transplant and EVLP may offer improved survival and quality of life for patients with severe lung disease, but these technologies come at significant cost to the healthcare system. Few studies have investigated the cost-effectiveness of lung transplant programs, and none has done so in the Canadian context. It remains unclear how cost-effective lung transplant programs are, and what impact, if any, EVLP may have on program efficiency. Further implementation of EVLP in transplant programs must be supported by data that reflects a value-added to patients as well as to the healthcare system. We propose to use health technology assessment principles to study cost-effectiveness of lung transplant and EVLP at one of the world's largest lung transplant centers. This project aims to demonstrate that EVLP may increase the number of potential organs for transplant and improve patient outcomes following transplant.

column36: Comparison of costimulatory domains in combined GD2 chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy and oncolytic vaccine therapy for neuroblastoma
column37: Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer with a poor prognosis in advanced or relapsed disease. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells is a promising new treatment for neuroblastoma. In this treatment, immune cells called T cells are engineered to selectively recognize and kill cancer cells. In the case of neuroblastoma, these CAR T cells recognize a molecule on the surface of the tumour cell called GD2. One important component of the CAR T cell is the costimulatory domain, which consists of either the molecule CD28, 41BB, or both in combination. It has been found that 41BB leads to a longer duration of CAR T cells in the body (persistence), which is associated with a better outcome for the patient. However, CD28 leads to improved killing initially. The combination of CD28 and 41BB appears to lead to enhanced function of the CAR T cell. Initial studies of CAR T cells in solid tumors have encountered some challenges, including insufficient numbers of T cells and poor trafficking of the CAR T cells to the tumor. Our laboratory is interested in using viruses that specifically target tumor cells (oncolytic viruses) to overcome these challenges. We have found that by delivering the oncolytic virus after transfer of CAR T cells, the CAR T cell product is expanded, known as a viral boost. What remains unknown is which costimulatory domain leads to persistence and better function of the CAR T cell product after viral boost. I propose to study GD2-CAR T cells with different costimulatory domains (CD28, 41BB or combined CD28/41BB). I hypothesize that 41BB will lead to improved persistence and function of the CAR T cell against GD2-expressing tumour cells.

column36: Access to Post-Discharge Care for Transgender and Gender-Expansive Individuals After Psychiatric Hospitalization in Ontario
column37: Transgender (trans) individuals, estimated to be 0.5% of the population, are people whose gender identity differs from their sex assigned at birth. Gender-expansive (GE) refers to gender identities not necessarily male or female, such as genderqueer and non-binary. Trans people carry a very high mental health burden, with estimates of five times the rates of depression and ten times the suicide attempts compared to the general population. The time after discharge from a psychiatric hospitalization is known to be high risk for suicide and re-hospitalization. Follow up with a physician after discharge has been shown to reduce those risks. The high mental health burden in the trans population suggests an even greater need for post-discharge care in this population. We will study post-discharge care for trans and GE (TGE) individuals using health administrative data. We will collect data for every adult Ontario patient with a discharge after psychiatric hospitalization between 2012 and 2016 to form the discharge group. From within this discharge group, we will identify all individuals identified as TGE by four clinics in three Ontario cities to create the TGE group. We will select non-TGE individuals from the discharge group to form the comparison group, matching individuals to the TGE group on age and where they live. We will study how many in the TGE group versus the comparison group had a post-discharge visit with a family doctor, a psychiatrist, neither, or both within 7 days of discharge. We suspect TGE individuals have reduced access to post-discharge care due to transphobic health providers and systems not meeting their needs. Findings from this study can guide how to improve mental health policy for TGE individuals post-discharge.

column36: The Role of Microvascular Function in Bed Rest Induced Insulin Resistance and the Countermeasure Potential of High Intensity Interval Training
column37: Physical inactivity and muscle disuse, particularly bed rest, induces insulin resistance from which recovery is prolonged and often incomplete in persons of middle age. As such, along with change in glucose concentrations, the impact of vascular changes on insulin signaling should be considered in characterizing bed-rest induced insulin resistance. Insulin is a peptide hormone critical in the regulation of energy availability. Delivery of insulin to muscle tissue requires dense networks of blood vessels and movement from circulation to tissues via transcytosis, or movement, across the endothelium lining blood vessels. This research addresses the hypothesis that bed rest induced alterations in microvascular function are attenuated by the countermeasure of high intensity interval training (HIIT). I hypothesize muscle disuse will reduce microvascular flow responses to an insulin stimulating challenge involving meal tolerance testing, and that the exercise countermeasure will mitigate these reductions. I also hypothesize an increase in circulating microvesicles with bed rest, and that this increase will depress insulin transcytosis suggesting microvesicle involvement in insulin resistance resulting from bed rest. To assess the skeletal muscle microvascular function, contrast enhanced ultrasound imaging will be used. Subsequently, extracellular vesicles in the blood stream will be assessed using several instruments. The effect of microvesicles on insulin transcytosis by endothelial cells will be assessed using fluorescently labelled insulin. This research will aid in the characterization of bed rest induced changes to microvascular function and role of microvesicles. Additionally, the efficacy of the countermeasure HIIT to mitigate insulin resistance will be determined.

column36: Investigation of breast cancer cell dormancy
column37: The majority of cancer-related deaths are caused by the spread of cancer cells to secondary sites in the body. These cells are difficult to kill using current cancer therapies due to their ability to stop dividing, allowing them to hide from chemotherapy. Months or years later, dormant cells may start growing again and cause cancer to return; therefore, dormancy is an important area of study. DREAM (DP, RB-family, E2F4/5, and MuvB) is a complex of proteins known to induce dormancy and allow ovarian cancer cells to survive as they spread. My proposed work aims to determine if DREAM behaves similarly in breast cancer and if it could be used as a drug target to reduce breast cancer spread. I have already identified conditions that stop breast cancer cells from growing and used gene-editing technology to create cells that no longer form DREAM, which will allow me to identify processes normally controlled by this complex in breast cancer. I will also observe how these cells spread in mice to investigate whether DREAM loss improves cancer prognosis. Overall, this project may identify mechanisms that contribute to breast cancer relapse and lead to development of new therapeutic tools to prevent cancer spread and reduce mortality rates.

column36: Mutual Antibody T cell Engagers (MATEs): A safe, flexible alternative to Chimeric Antigen Receptor T cell therapy for leukemia and lymphoma
column37: Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is a revolutionary treatment delivering complete response rates up to 90% for CD19+ B cell leukemias and lymphomas, yet problems with response durability and toxicity remain. CARs are engineered receptors expressed in T cells that contain an extracellular Antibody Domain (AD), targeting a known antigen, and an intracellular Signaling Domain (SD), which initiates proliferation, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity. Despite impressive efficacy, CAR T cells exhibit unpredictable expansion, ranging from inadequate, which allows tumor escape, to excessive, resulting in life-threatening side effects including cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity. To resolve this, our lab is developing a novel strategy called Mutual Antibody T cell Engagers (MATEs). The MATE strategy splits the CAR AD and SD into two separate proteins, utilizing a leucine zipper to connect them in a non-covalent fashion. In this way, the MATE behaves like a CAR only when the AD is present, providing physicians with exquisite control over T cell activity. My research aims to test the activation, proliferation, and target cell cytotoxicity of T cells transduced to express the MATE SD (MATE T cells) in the presence of varying doses of the MATE AD. We expect these activities to increase with escalating doses of the AD, defining the dose-dependent relationship between it and MATE T cells. In summary, the MATE strategy offers control not previously afforded by CAR T cell therapy, improving safety and flexibility. In future, this strategy could also be used to target several antigens simultaneously using multiple ADs and a single SD, thereby reducing the risk of tumor escape as seen with about one-third of patients after they receive CD19+ CAR T cell therapy.

column36: Updating the Evidence on the Use of Age Adjustment in the Assessment of Preterm Infants' Growth
column37: Preterm birth is defined as an infant born alive before 37 weeks of gestation. The Canadian rate of preterm birth was 8% is 2012 and has shown to be increasing, accounting for over 50% of neonatal mortality and for the majority of all infant deaths. Optimal growth assessment strategies are necessary to support the growth and wellbeing of preterm infants. Clinicians have previously used either the infant's chronological age or the adjusted age in the assessment of preterm infant growth. The adjusted age is the age that corrects for the infant's prematurity by subtracting the number of weeks of prematurity from the infant's chronological age. The chronological age neglects the fact the infant was born early, which can lead to misclassification of infant growth as the infant is expected to grow similar to term infants of the same chronological age. Age adjustment can ensure the accurate assessment of preterm infant growth. Nonetheless, the limited use of age adjustment may be due to the fact that the available evidence is over 20 years old. Also, there remain critical gaps in the literature on the appropriate period for age adjustment, specifically with regards to the various degrees of prematurity: early (< 28 weeks of gestation) moderate (28-32 weeks) and late preterm infants (33-36 weeks). In this retrospective cohort study, preterm infant growth will be assessed using both the chronological and adjusted age. Potential differences in growth assessment will be explored using recent preterm growth reference charts and the World Health Organisation Growth Standard. This study may alter or reinforce the 20-year-old advice about age adjustment for prematurity, providing evidence-based guidance on the optimal strategies for the assessment of preterm infants' growth.

column36: Fast characterization of multiple prion strains in cultured murine neuronal organotypic slices
column37: Prion diseases are a group of fatal diseases that affect both humans and animals. They result in death of brain cells and a decline in the mental capacity of affected individuals. The disease causing agent is called a prion, which is a misfolded form of a normal protein found in the brain of all mammals. Prions convert additional normal protein into the misfolded shape. Prions can sometimes spread from animals to humans, as was the case for mad cow disease, and so pose a public health concern. Human prion diseases vary widely in terms of the symptoms, age of onset, and patterns of damage seen within the brain. These differences are thought to be related to the shape of each prion version. Different prion shapes are referred to as strains and each has distinct properties that can be studied in laboratory assays. Very little is known about the stains that cause human prion diseases for a number of reasons. Human diseases are rare and so the amount of infected tissue available for research is limited. Also, human prions cannot be grown in the laboratory. Characterizing them would help us understand more about the ways in which prions cause disease as well as the origin of infectious prions. I aim to develop a model system that could be used to grow human prions in the laboratory for the first time, and to rapidly characterize many different prion strains. This will be achieved by exposing thin slices of genetically engineered mouse brain tissue to different prion strains, resulting in infection of the brain tissue with the corresponding prion strain. A model system such as this will allow for the comparison of a multitude of different prion strains and provide a new tool to further our understanding of how different prion strains cause disease in both humans and animals.

column36: Advanced Trial Design in Critical Care Medicine
column37: I am an academic critical care physician proposing a program of research focused on evolving clinical trial design. Randomized trials yield the highest level of evidence for therapies, however many clinical questions are unsuitable for classical trials due to costs, sample size, and patient heterogeneity. This is apparent in critical care medicine where patient populations are small and heterogeneous. One mechanism to address these limitations is to explore innovative designs such as adaptive trials. Adaptive trials may answer clinical questions with more efficiency and patient-level resolution but uptake has been limited by the unfamiliarity and complexity of the design and its strengths and limitations are not well known. My graduate work will use a Bayesian analytic framework to evolve adaptive trial designs and facilitate their application to critical care medicine. During the CGS-M award we will conduct reanalyses of prominent critical care medicine trials with simulation to demonstrate principles of adaptive trial design. My supervisor will be George Tomlinson (Professor, Faculty of Medicine, Bayesian statistics expertise) and my mentor Rob Fowler (Faculty of Medicine, Director of Clinical Epidemiology and Health Care Research, critical care physician) will be closely involved. Potential committee members include Peter Juni (Professor, Faculty of Medicine, clinical trials expertise) or Marzyeh Ghassemi (Professor, Faculties of Medicine and Computer Science). Our research in adaptive trial designs for critical care medicine will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and limitations of adaptive trials with corresponding improvements in efficiency and applicability of research that will benefit patients, clinicians and health systems.

column36: The role of embryonic-derived macrophages in cardiac inflammation and disease caused by viral infections
column37: Cardiac disease is one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Although recent advances in cardiac care have greatly improved treatment outcomes, the prevalence of chronic disease is still significant, and is a major contributor to morbidity. Previous studies have demonstrated that viral infections of the heart are linked to chronic inflammation. Fortunately, immune cells, including macrophages (MFs), have roles in the clearance of virus from the body. In the past, cardiac MFs were believed to originate from a single cell type, like what is observed in other tissues. With the recent use of innovative experimental approaches, the Epelman lab has defined two distinct lineages that exist in adults, known as embryonic-derived and adult monocyte-derived MFs, whose roles differ greatly in response to injury. Embryonic MFs form from early development and tend to promote cardiac recovery (and regeneration) in the heart. On the other hand, adult derived MFs are recruited to tissues in adulthood and tend to promote inflammation. The role of these cells in the heart has never been investigated. In order to assess the role of embryonic MFs, we will use a mice strain that lacks embryonic-derived MFs and determine the effects after viral infection of heart tissue. We predict to see that the absence of embryonic-derived MFs will lead to greater disease due to its expected protective role. Then, we will look at the gene expression profile of these cells as well as their ability in cardiac regenerative processes, in order to assess their functional role after viral injury. The ability to determine the exact cell types responsible for reparative processes provide the potential for new treatment options that target such cells in order to promote better health outcomes.

column36: Determination of the initial aging-associated molecular events in the development of sporadic Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD), as the most common form of senile dementia, is a heavy burden to the health care systems worldwide. AD is frequently attributed to protein misfolding and aggregation; one such trouble-prone protein is Tau. AD often does not run in families and is described as 'sporadic' (sAD), which is typically encountered in late adulthood. Although chronological age has been reported to be the greatest risk factor of sAD, little is known about how aging gives rise to sAD pathology at a molecular level. In the experimental realm, the lack of plausible sAD animal model adds another layer of complexity to sporadic Alzheimer's disease research. The overarching goal of my research is to visualize the initial aging-related molecular events that result in sAD pathology, such as Tau misfolding, in sAD models expressing low levels of the human Tau protein (low-expresser). The mutated gene causing the Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) proves to be a powerful tool to construct a molecular environment that mimics natural aging. I will first express the HGPS gene in both a low-expresser sAD cell culture model via transfection and in a transgenic mouse model via stereotaxic injection. Once the HGPS phenotype and sAD pathology are both observed, misfolded Tau proteins will be purified and analysed using biochemical techniques that help determine their folding state. By assessing initial aging-related protein misfolding events in the development of sAD, we may tease apart the complexity in AD's sporadic nature, which may provide insights into the development of new AD models and early disease intervention.

column36: L'impact des calcifications aortiques sur le risque de rupture d'anevrisme de l'aorte abdominale
column37: Les anevrismes de l'aorte abdominale (AAA) sont un probleme de sante publique vu que 20 000 Canadiens en sont diagnostiques chaque annee. Bien qu'ils constituent souvent une atteinte asymptomatique, les patients dont l'AAA rompt ont une mortalite de 90%. Au jour d'aujourd'hui, les deux principaux facteurs pouvant stratifier le risque de rupture d'un AAA sont le diametre dudit AAA ainsi que la vitesse a laquelle son diametre croit. Le probleme est que ce modele a une sensitivite d'environ 60%, ce qui laisse place a un nombre de faux negatifs tres important. En d'autres mots, il est encore trop difficile d'exclure le risque de rupture chez les patients atteints d'AAA. Recemment, un projet de recherche a demontre l'existence de trois formes de calcifications aortiques : << strip, stone et flake. >> Nous voulons donc savoir si la forme des calcifications aortiques pourrait devenir un parametre de prediction de la rupture d'AAA. A l'inverse, nous pensons que les AAA contant de grandes proportions de calcifications <<flake >> pourraient etre moins a risque de rupture. column36: Stress, Parenting Behaviors, and Cortisol's Impact on Maternal Mental Illness and Child Psychopathology
column37: Children who grow up with mothers with mental illness (MI) are more likely to develop their own mental health and behavioural problems. Similar to other difficulties such as neglect or being separated from a parent, exposure to maternal MI is a 'toxic stressor' for children, with preliminary research in infants linking this experience to the excess secretion of stress hormones (i.e. cortisol). Despite established links between maternal MI and higher levels of cortisol secretion in children, there are gaps in understanding how mothers' parenting behaviours underlie this link. I will explore how parenting skills of mother's with MI, toxic stress, and cortisol levels all relate to the early-life mental health and behaviour problems of children. They will be recruited from flyers, community postings and local agencies such as the Seven Oaks School Division and The Manitoba Crisis Response Centre. I will collect information on parenting behaviours using questionnaires and standardized observations of parents interacting with their children. Children's stress levels will be measured through cortisol that is built up in their hair. This research will help to understand the parenting mechanisms that place children of mothers with MI at elevated risk for intergenerational psychopathology. This research may facilitate the development of specific interventions to support well-being in children at-risk for early mental health and behavioural problems.

column36: The Role of Notch Signaling in the Pathogenesis of Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that is characterized by the destruction of myelin in the central nervous system (CNS) by immune cells recognizing self-antigen. The main driver of the demyelination activity are subtypes of T helper (Th) cell, particularly Th1 and Th17 cells, which recruit other immune cells to cause damage to the CNS. There is some evidence that Notch signaling regulates the differentiation and proliferation of Th1 and Th17 cells during multiple sclerosis. However, the exact role that Th1 and Th17 cells play and the disease progression stage at which Notch signaling is critical for Th1 and Th17 cells development are still unclear. Thus, the aims of my project are to identify the role that Th1 and Th17 cells play in multiple sclerosis, what other populations of immune cells also cause damages to the CNS, and when does Notch signaling play a critical role in disease establishment and relapse. My hypothesis is stage-specific modulation of Notch signaling in T cells will lead to different disease severities or amelioration in combination with the local immune microenvironment. To address my hypothesis, I will analyze the impact of Notch signaling in Th1 and Th17 cell responses in the development of multiple sclerosis. I will also determine the role Notch signaling plays in the activation of other immune cell populations during disease development. By answering these questions, my project aims to provide a better understanding of disease development and immune cell functions in the establishment of the disease, which will ultimately provide further insights for more selective and effective therapies for multiple sclerosis.

column36: Does implementation of a comprehensive school health program improve self-esteem among students in Indigenous and northern communities?
column37: Mental health concerns affect at least 20% of youth in Canada, making it a major public health challenge. Poor self-esteem and lack of optimism are early signs for depression and poor mental health in children. column36: Validity and Reliability of a Food Frequency Questionnaire for the Characterization of Toddlers' Diets and their Determinants
column37: During the early years of life, the brain develops rapidly and is particularly sensitive to the nutrition provided. The intake of specific nutrients including zinc, vitamin B-12, choline and omega-3 fatty acids have been associated with cognition and brain development in toddlers. In addition, there is growing literature indicating that the nutrition provided during the first two years of life has a lasting effect on long-term health outcomes. Despite the impact of the early life diet, there is a lack of information on what a toddler's diet is comprised of in Canada. Reliable and validated dietary assessment tools are essential for accurately describing the dietary intake in the early years. As toddlers' diets are dynamic, food frequency questionnaires (FFQs) may represent the most accurate dietary assessment tool as they provide information about nutrient intake over a longer period. The goals of this study are to evaluate the validity and reliability of a toddler FFQ and to characterize the dietary intake and patterns in healthy toddlers at 18 months of age. Gender differences and sociodemographic determinants of dietary intake in toddlers will also be explored. The validated novel tool will allow the characterization of the dietary intake of Canadian toddlers and the identification of nutrients associated with cognitive outcomes, with the overall goal of optimizing child development and reducing the risk of adverse long-term health outcomes.

column36: Are eyes more than just windows to the soul? Exploring the link between age-related macular degeneration and Alzheimer's disease.
column37: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and Alzheimer's disease are both degenerative conditions primarily affecting the elderly population. One type of AMD, "wet" AMD, is characterized by an increased number of leaky blood vessels within the retina, similar to what has been reported in the brains of Alzheimer's animal models and patients. We propose that these two diseases may have similar underlying pathologies via the development of leaky vessels that result in the disruption of the tight barriers protecting the eye/brain. We will further investigate this possible link by using the Tg2576 mouse model and human retinal cell cultures to determine whether leaky vessels and inflammation link these two conditions. The purpose of these experiments is to understand the cause and progression of both conditions and whether the detection of AMD can lead to an early prognosis of Alzheimer's disease. There are currently no cures or even treatments to slow down the progression of Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's disease medications have one of the highest failure rates in clinical trials: 99.6% of drugs tested between 2000-2015 failed. It is believed that the primary reason so many drugs fail is because the medication needs to be administered before cognitive symptoms arise. If a link is discovered between AMD and Alzheimer's disease, this can lead to a new, painless and non-invasive way of diagnosing or detecting early signs of Alzheimer's by simply examining the eyes. Furthermore, it may be possible to test current AMD medications, that are already FDA-approved, as potential therapeutics for delaying the progression or preventing Alzheimer's disease. Ultimately, through our research we plan to demonstrate that the eyes are more than just windows to the soul.

column36: Identification and Characterization of Host Proteins Hijacked by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) currently affects 37 million people worldwide and has led to over 35 million deaths. Although antiretroviral treatments (ART) can control viral replication, they cannot cure infection. As nascent virions bud through the cellular membranes of the CD4+ T cells that they infect, they can acquire cellular host proteins which become embedded in the viral envelope. Key host proteins are selectively incorporated by virions that can alter viral homing and infectivity. Integrin ?4?7 is an adhesion protein on CD4+ T cells that facilitates homing to the gut through interactions with gut-resident mucosal adhesion molecules. Virions that incorporate ?4?7 effectively hijack the homing mechanism used by T cells to migrate to the gut. This allows HIV virions to rapidly infect and deplete CD4+ T cells, as the gut is the largest reservoir for CD4+ T cells, likely leading to accelerated disease progression in HIV-infected individuals. Primate studies highlight the importance of the integrin during infection by showing that blocking ?4?7 homing with an anti-?4?7 antibody can delay disease progression and provide persistent control of viral infection, even in the absence of ART. The mechanism(s) behind these findings is unknown and is the topic of my proposal. My research aims to investigate how ?4?7 integrin becomes selectively enriched in HIV virions, with a goal of characterizing the viral determinants underpinning ?4?7 incorporation. I also plan to characterize new unidentified host proteins in the viral envelope that may also impact HIV infectivity and homing. Collectively, these findings may help identify new targets on virions that can be used for novel drug and vaccine designs, which may help reduce the burden of HIV in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Protective Effects of Akkermansia muciniphila on Intestinal Barrier Function and Inflammation
column37: The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is inhabited by trillions of microorganisms that play a crucial role in digesting food, protecting the gut from harmful bacteria and developing the immune system. These microorganisms are also implicated in various GI disorders including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). According to the Crohn's and Colitis Foundation of Canada, the prevalence of IBD in Canada is one of the highest in the world and over 270,000 Canadians deal with these lifelong conditions for which there is currently no cure. Akkermansia muciniphila is a bacterium that accounts for approximately 3% of fecal microbes and has been shown to stimulate intestinal mucus production and strengthen the GI barrier. Studies have illustrated that lower levels of A. muciniphila are associated with higher levels of inflammation suggesting that A. muciniphila may have anti-inflammatory effects. Though several studies have linked IBD to decreased levels of A. muciniphila, the precise role and mechanism of A. muciniphila in the initiation and progression of IBD is yet to be determined. Based on recent findings, we believe A. muciniphila provides protective effects on intestinal inflammation by strengthening the epithelial barrier of the gut. Thus, the aim of this research study is to investigate the role and mechanism of A. muciniphila in intestinal inflammation and its protective effects on the gut barrier. This research has the potential to enhance the understanding of the development of IBD and the role that microbes play in intestinal inflammation. In addition, this research has the potential to lead to the development of new treatments by utilizing A. muciniphila to alleviate the symptoms experienced with IBD.

column36: The Role of Streptolysin O and Streptolysin S in Streptococcus pyogenes Nasopharyngeal Infection
column37: Streptococcus pyogenes is a human-specific bacterial pathogen that contributes to the global burden of disease. Although S. pyogenes acts primarily as an asymptomatic colonizer of the upper respiratory tract and skin, it may cause mild infections such as strep throat, or more serious diseases such as flesh-eating disease and toxic shock syndrome. S. pyogenes has two toxins, streptolysin O (SLO) and streptolysin S (SLS), which promote disease progression by initiating cell death. The streptolysins have been extensively studied in mouse models of soft tissue infection; however, their role in acute nasopharyngeal infection is unknown. Preliminary data has demonstrated that SLS is a key toxin during acute nasopharyngeal infection. An SLS-deficient strain exhibited a significant reduction in nasopharyngeal colonization in mice, while an SLO-deficient strain did not exhibit reduced colonization. We hypothesize that SLS contributes to disease progression through the destruction of the mucosal membrane and by causing inflammation during nasopharyngeal infection. We will evaluate the role of SLO and SLS on tissue damage and cell death, and tissue analyses of mouse nasal passages will be done to evaluate the role of these toxins in membrane damage and inflammation. We will also assess the immune response to the bacteria, including inflammatory responses and determining the immune cell populations. Pharyngeal carriage represents the predominant state of S. pyogenes colonization, yet initial molecular strategies used by the bacteria are not well defined. Understanding the mechanism of streptolysin activity during acute nasopharyngeal infection is essential to thoroughly understand how S. pyogenes establishes infection and causes disease.
