column36: Ensuring screening quality in a complex governance system: A vision for Prenatal Screening Ontario
column37: Prenatal screening is offered to all pregnant women to determine if a pregnancy is at risk for specific health problems. To maintain a high quality program that is up to date with new technology, health care providers, laboratories and policymakers must work collaboratively. Prenatal Screening Ontario (PSO) is responsible for overseeing and coordinating health care providers (e.g. sonographers, physicians, midwives, radiologists, genetic counsellors etc.) laboratories, and policymakers, in an effort to ensure care is of high-quality and accessible to all women across the province. This is a challenging task because the relationships among the stakeholders are complex, and decision-making authority is not always clear. Motivated by this challenge, the proposed project seeks to understand how program organization impacts quality of care, within the context of a population screening system. Through fieldwork and a range of qualitative data collection strategies, this project will explore and define the specific quality challenges Ontario is facing (e.g. inaccurate tests, inappropriate spending/testing, poor access to care). This work involves describing where and how various stakeholders are interacting, and whether and how that impacts quality. Building from the Ontario case, a scoping review will identify approaches to ensuring prenatal screening quality in other jurisdictions and settings. Three cases will be selected for comparison to Ontario. The purpose of this research is to identify barriers and facilitators to achieving a high-quality prenatal screening system. Finally, in consultation with screening system experts, the findings will be developed into a quality improvement framework that PSO can implement and use to enhance care delivery.

column36: Predicting treatment response with machine learning from clinical notes: Informing clinical decisions and improving the representation of clients with depression at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health
column37: The Major Depressive Disorder Care Pathway (MDD-ICP) is a standardized pathway of care for clients with depression at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH). In the MDD-ICP, psychiatrists write detailed notes about their meetings with clients. Analyzing these notes can help improve our understanding of clients with depression and inform decisions about their care. However, these notes are challenging to analyze because they are unstructured. Advancements in language modelling and machine learning offer solutions to this issue. In the first stage of the Health Systems Impact Fellowship (HSIF), we will use these methods to analyze the MDD-ICP clinical notes. Specifically, we will predict clients' responses to treatment using machine learning models. We will train our models based on clinical notes from intake assessments, as well as questionnaire data available in CAMH health records. According to previous research, the ability of our models to predict treatment responses may depend on client demographics (like sex or income), as well as the writing style of psychiatrists. We will also assess for these biases in our models, by stratifying our analyses according to these characteristics. In the second stage of the HSIF, we will use our findings to develop support tools and workshops that help psychiatrists make clinical decisions and improve the quality of their notes. We will implement these interventions in small groups of MDD-ICP psychiatrists. To evaluate whether the interventions are useful, we will compare outcomes from these psychiatrists to groups of control psychiatrists. This HSIF advances a goal of CAMH's Krembil Centre for Neuroinformatics to gain insights into mental health using innovative technologies. By using these insights to inform clinical decisions, it addresses the MDD-ICP's aim to optimize treatments for clients with depression.

column36: Patient Engagement Toolkit for Health Information Technology Initiatives
column37: Health information technology have a tremendous potential to improve the quality and efficiency of our healthcare system. Despite the potential benefits, there are many policy and practical challenges to implementing health information technology. Several experts and research studies suggest that engaging patients throughout the development and implementation of health information technology is critical in ensuring its success. The purpose of this project is to develop a toolkit to guide healthcare organizations in developing and integrating patient engagement activities in their health information technology implementations. This project will be conducted in three stages. The first stage will focus on understanding the the dynamics of engaging patients through a survey and interviews with patients and healthcare providers. Based on the findings of the first stage, a prototype toolkit will be developed in the second phase. The content of the toolkit will be validated by patient engagement experts. The toolkit will also be tested with patients and healthcare providers to determine its usability and ease of use. The prototype toolkit will applied to a patient portal implementation to understand how the toolkit will work and ways to improve it. The final product of this project is a finished toolkit for healthcare organizations to use in supporting their patient engagement plans when implementing health information technology.

column36: Evaluation of the Neighbourhood Care Team Model: Providing a rigorous evidence base to inform integrated health care policy
column37: The Neighbourhood Care Team Model (NCTM) is a model of integrated care that builds on the strengths of local services and coordinates health care provided in the community to meet local population health needs in densely populated urban neighbourhoods in Toronto, Ontario. Integrated care is an approach to the organization and delivery of health services that is intended to improve continuity of care across services. Continuity of care means better consistency of information sharing between health care providers, relationships between people and their specific health care teams, and the overall approach to managing peoples' health and illness over time. It is widely considered to be ideally suited to serve people with complex health and social needs, which can lead to downstream challenges in the health system, including inappropriate emergency room visits and growing system costs. The NCTM is meant to address these challenges by combining efforts across primary care, home and community care, social support services, and community housing. The objective of this project is to evaluate the program effectiveness of the Neighbourhood Care Team Model (NCTM) being implemented in Toronto. The NCTM will be evaluated according to the Triple Aim framework of improved patient outcomes, steady/reduced health system costs, and improved patient/provider experience to provide evidence to inform policy decisions. If evidence is found in support of NCTM achieving its goals and alleviating downstream challenges in the health care system, it could be considered for implementation more widely across the province and country.

column36: Building Capacity for Food Security Surveillance in British Columbia's Public Health System
column37: Food security is a critical challenge that requires a complex, coordinated population and public health response. Recent calls have indicated the need to monitor the full range of intersectoral public health actions to address food security. The British Columbia Centre for Disease Control (BCCDC) provides health promotion and prevention services, analytical and policy support to government and health authorities across BC. As part of this mandate, the food security portfolio of BCCDC has developed an evidence-based framework and novel indicators to support food security monitoring within and beyond public health. This presents a timely opportunity to examine the capacity of the public health system in BC to fully implement the revised food security indicators. The proposed program of work will assess readiness for implementation, determine the feasibility, usability and relevance of the indicators through pilot implementation, and evaluate the sustainability of the indicators for ongoing monitoring and decision-making. This work adopts a multi-method approach including interviews, workshops and participant observation with with senior decision-makers and practitioners to document and analyze the indicator implementation process. Improving the surveillance of food security in BC will provide accurate, timely and actionable intelligence about the impact of food security policies, practices and programs within and beyond the public health sector.

column36: Using Evidence to Inform Health Policy: Supportive Housing as a Case Study
column37: Government health policies rooted in evidence and collaboration are essential for safe and effective health care delivery. While the steps in policy development and the use of evidence to guide this process are well documented, the ways in which policy cycles work in 'real-world' and complex government settings are less well defined. This is especially the case for supportive housing (SH) services in Canada, where current policies inadequately describe the program purpose and recipients of care. Using SH as a case study, the purpose of my fellowship is to (i) understand how policy cycles 'work' in a complex government setting, (ii) explore how evidence can be used more effectively to ensure that policies achieve their intended goals, and (iii) investigate ways in which other stakeholders (e.g., regional planners, SH clients and their families) can contribute meaningfully to policy development. From these activities I will establish an enriched understanding of government context and the ways in which policies are developed, create synergistic partnerships with key government personnel and health service researchers, develop additional core competencies to help ensure my short- and long-term career success, and produce several publications and related knowledge translation activities (e.g., showing how evidence and intersectoral collaborations can be used to improve policy cycles). My fellowship will occur at Manitoba Health, Seniors and Active Living (MHSAL; Brie DeMone as primary supervisor) and the University of Manitoba (Dr. Malcolm Doupe as academic supervisor). These organizations and preceptors have a rich collaborative history through previous grants and government initiatives designed to train graduate students in applied health services research. Building on their experiences, my preceptors will meaningfully combine the research and policy aspects of the fellowship in ways that help to enrich my training experience and foster a learning health system.

column36: Combining behavioural sciences and user centred design methodology to improve the surveillance of childhood cancer survivors at high-risk of late effects
column37: There are over 14,000 survivors of childhood and adolescent cancer in Ontario. Unfortunately, the treatments used to cure their cancer in childhood leads to a high risk for severe health conditions during adulthood, including the development of new cancers and heart problems. Working with survivors, clinicians, and health-system partners, we will design a province-wide intervention to deliver personalized reminders and supports. We will engage survivors and their doctors to ensure the planned strategy is user-centred while incorporating the science of behaviour change. By the end of this project, we will be prepared to work with our provincial partners on implementing and evaluating a province-wide scale-up of the intervention. This fellowship will enhance my academic training, and expand my skills using patient engagement and patient-centred methods in the design and delivery of health care, as well as my capacity to conduct applied research in partnership with health system organizations. column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes paralysis which affects the person's ability to feed, bathe, or dress themselves and affects their ability to move about their home/community. The second phase will use the products of phase one to inform the creation of a continuing education model specific to SCI rehabilitation providers. This project is the result of a partnership between the Ontario Neurotrauma Foundation (ONF) and the University Health Network allowing knowledge produced in an academic setting to be incorporated into the partner organization's processes. We envision creating a platform for interprofessional groups of clinicians to share their expertise and identify the best pathway of care for SCI rehabilitation. This fellowship will support the creation of a continuing education model. The model will enable the initiatives of ONF related to advancing the SCI Quality Consortium (i.e. measuring and improving quality of SCI rehabilitation care in Ontario) and the Care Pathways (i.e. appropriate care for people with motor vehicle injuries), to achieve ONF's mandate of improved access to quality care across Ontario.

column36: Investing wisely: using economic modelling to optimize public health strategies to reduce harm from alcohol, tobacco and cannabis and optimize benefits in British Columbia
column37: Substance use costs British Columbia $4.9 billion in 2014, of which 70% was due to alcohol and tobacco. These estimates include costs related to the use of health care resources, productivity losses, criminal justice, and other direct costs such as accidents, research and prevention. Broader societal costs not included in these estimates relate to inequities, marginalization and hindered social development. This project aims to develop a model to evaluate the economic and social impact of legal substance use harm prevention in British Columbia. Evidence on economic consequences and how public health programs can minimize costs and harms from substance use is important for policy makers, who need to consider the health system priorities against efficiency, scalability and sustainability of interventions. The challenges to developing comprehensive economic evaluations in public health are well known. In the area of substance use, these pertain to the multitude of the socioeconomic determinants that influence use - such as employment, income, social exclusion, and hopelessness - and the difficulty of measuring broader benefits including family wellbeing, community development and equity gains. This fellowship will facilitate collaboration between knowledge users and academics with the aim of optimizing investment in the area of alcohol, tobacco and cannabis harm prevention in BC. It will provide the Ministry of Health with tools to implement efficient priority setting that aligns with the institution's values and development goals. This will be achieved through important methodological advances to allow evaluations to account for the broader societal impact of preventing harm from legal substance use in BC. As a result, this fellowship will sustain future research in health economics with an increased ability to respond to policy makers' needs when it comes to priority setting.

column36: Fairness: An institutional ethnography to identify risks, benefits and mediation strategies for AI/machine learning in mental healthcare delivery
column37: A strategic priority for the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), the host organization, is evidence based care. The heart of this initiative is the Krembil Centre for Neuroinfomatics (KCNI), which employs state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) techniques to identify, manage and treat mental illnesses, while shaping policy at national and global levels. KCNI manages and curates patient data to create algorithms capable of modelling disease pathways, predicting adverse effects, and facilitating personalized treatment interventions. Concerns about AI applications systematically discriminating against specific populations have spearheaded an urgent conversation about notions of fairness. Namely, who will/should benefit the most from these techniques and why? Thus, the primary objective of this project is to examine how fairness is defined, managed and produced along an Integrated Care Pathway (ICP) for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). We ask: what makes training datasets "fair" and how are principles of "fairness" incorporated into decision-making by human (patients, clinicians, data curators) and non-human (AI) care teams? We anticipate that the concept of fairness is not fully developed, thus a key health system impact objective is to develop guiding principles for incorporating fairness into hospital-wide efforts to engage with AI/ML techniques for health equity. To achieve these objectives the fellow will conduct an institutional ethnography to analyze how concepts of fairness are used to inform the ICP for MDD. Patients, clinicians, and data curators who use and interpret data for recovery will be interviewed and observed. This project will foster the responsible interpretation of knowledge derived from AI/ML and is essential to ensure that policy uptake is relevant and beneficial for all.

column36: Applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and supervised Machine Learning (ML) for immunization programmes in Ontario
column37: Vaccine hesitancy is the phenomena of the delay or refusal of receiving vaccinations. For public health professionals and immunization experts, vaccine hesitancy poses significant challenges to immunization delivery because a successful immunization program is reliant on public's confidence in vaccines. One of the ways vaccine hesitancy spread is through social media platforms. These social media platforms allow user-generated content, with the inclusion of vaccine misinformation, to be passed on. The spread of vaccine misinformation on social media results in observable decreases in the public's confidence in vaccines, as well as an increase in vaccine-preventable outbreaks in Canada and abroad. Three complementary studies will be conducted at the Ontario Agency of Public Health Protection and Promotion (also known as Public Health Ontario, PHO), a Crown corporation dedicated to protecting and promoting the health of all Ontarians. The three studies are: (1) Interviewing stakeholders and decision-makers in key organizations to identify areas in immunization delivery where AI can be applied to address vaccine hesitancy, (2) using AI to explore the linguistic differences among the vaccine-hesitant, the anti-vaccine, and the vaccine supporters, and based on these findings, deploying a surveillance dashboard to monitor the surges of misinformation on social media in real-time, and (3) classifying vaccine information/misinformation using AI to improve the function of the dashboard and explore novel methods to deploy accurate vaccine information that will spread wider, deeper, and farther on social media. The studies address issues of distributive justice pertaining to immunization information on social media. The findings will strengthen PHO's capacity to foster a sustainable and collaborative project-oriented platform for future researchers to conduct AI research for public health.

column36: Leveraging implementation and behavioural science to support laboratory stewardship
column37: Blood samples taken in hospitals are sent to a laboratory, analyzed, and results used to diagnose and treat patients. However, many tests ordered are not needed. This leads to wasted healthcare spending and negative effects on patients, such as false positives (test results which incorrectly indicate that a person has a condition). Researchers have designed strategies to support hospital staff to reduce unnecessary testing. However, these strategies don't work all the time, which prevents widespread uptake. We need to know more about what influences hospital staff to order these tests, and what they think about these strategies, so that we can develop strategies that best suit their needs. The Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association (EORLA), a group of 18 laboratories connected to 16 hospitals in Eastern Ontario, have been testing various different strategies to support hospital staff to reduce their orders of these tests. column36: Building an Integrated Health Delivery System in Burlington, Ontario
column37: In Canada and internationally, the demographic is aging and increasingly faces challenges with leading a strong quality of life while managing chronic conditions. While technological advancements have made it possible to care for many of these conditions outside of hospitals, the fragmentation of traditional models of care delivery does not meet patient needs or expectations and often leads to suboptimal outcomes. The Burlington sub-region, co-facilitated by Joseph Brant Hospital, seeks to establish an Integrated Health Delivery System (IHDS) that will provide comprehensive, integrated 24/7 care to a defined population of approximately 250,000 residents in the City of Burlington and surrounding communities. In the first year, the IHDS will focus on integrating primary care, acute care, and home care for patients affiliated with two family health teams and two family health groups (approximately 60,000 patients). In the second year, there will be a plan to expand the patient population and to phase in the full continuum of care, with a focus on community mental health, palliative care, and COPD care. As a member of the IHDS steering committee, the Fellow will contribute to the planning and implementation of the care pathways (including the development of a shared dashboard), and lead the program's evaluation. Recently, the Government of Ontario released its vision for the creation of local health teams that will advance population health and access to care, improve outcomes, and enhance the patient experience. With established relationships and commitments from partner organisations already in place, learnings from the IHDS will provide emerging insights that are relevant for informing the development, sustainability, and spread and scale of future integrated care models.

column36: Interpreting and addressing barriers impeding effective care transitions for women diagnosed with breast cancer in British Columbia
column37: The number of Canadians diagnosed with cancer is rising with a growing and aging population and we need to ensure our healthcare system is equipped to meet this growing demand. As the most common female cancer worldwide, breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in Canadian women. In recent decades, advancements in breast cancer screening and treatments have resulted in approximately 87% of Canadian women diagnosed with breast cancer surviving 5 years after diagnosis. Increased survival rates are due in part to adjuvant endocrine therapy (AET) (e.g., tamoxifen), which is used to treat early-stage, hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, representing the large majority of breast cancer diagnoses. Women prescribed AET are recommended to take this medication everyday for 5-10 years depending on their diagnosis, which results in the need for increased follow-up care over a long period of time. Previous research, however, has shown there are many issues associated with transitions in care, particularly as breast cancer survivors move from receiving care from their oncologist back to seeing their family physician or nurse practitioner in the community. The objective of this project is to improve transitions in care to better support women diagnosed with breast cancer and also the healthcare providers that deliver care to these women. The goal is to meet the supportive care needs of breast cancer survivors as they transition through the healthcare system to support them in living well beyond their breast cancer diagnosis.

column37: The aim of this research project is to better understand and address the health needs and service requirements of people with multiple, complex needs under the purview of Community Living British Columbia (CLBC). The first is to better understand the health-related needs of this population, which includes an analysis of health-related contacts (type and frequency), outcomes, and costs associated with this population. In BC, much is not known about the health-related needs of this group. The second objective is to identify and learn from promising practices in BC - specifically, what is being done that works for this population and why, with particular attention to issues of sustainability and scalability. Although findings from CLBC's qualitative research highlight the need for significant systemic change in the delivery of services for people with multiple complex needs, it also identified "pockets of excellence" in BC where local or regional solutions have emerged as examples of practice excellence. Through this objective, I will focus on services that directly intersect with the healthcare system (e.g., acute care, residential detox/treatment, etc.) and address underlying social determinants of health, including, for example: homelessness, poverty, and issues of gender and race (indigenous people). The research will include an evaluation of selected services. In addition, an inventory of services for the multiple, complex needs people in BC will be developed.

column36: Early Mechanistic Biomarkers for late Epilepsy and long-term Brain Injury Outcome Jens P. Dreier EBio2
column37: Stroke and traumatic brain injuries (TBI) in humans are common causes of mortality and impose a poor quality of life on the affected individuals and their families. Life-saving treatments after brain injuries improved patients' survival but long-term severe complications, such as motor and cognitive disabilities and epilepsy, still lack preventive treatments. Our studies indicate that specific structural and functional alterations involving neurons, glia and brain vessels underlie the progressive evolution of brain injuries and contribute to the late onset of epilepsy. The unmet need for early identification of these pathologic events in injured patients with clinically applicable approaches is the basis for the current project. Our ultimate goal is to improve current treatment interventions in brain-injured patients by discovering mechanism-driven biomarkers that will permit early preventive treatments for neurological complications. Through a combination approach based on improved and novel analyses of electrophysiological signals, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and selected blood molecules, we will search for common fingerprints of brain network dysfunctions reflecting disease progression using (1) our existing database of brain-injured patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage who underwent intensive neuromonitoring, serial MRI scans, blood collection, and were evaluated for epilepsy after 3 years, and (2) clinically relevant animal models of brain injury that are associated with late epilepsy development and allow neuromonitoring in a similar manner as in the ICU. We envision that monitoring of post-injury brain dynamics will allow us to develop biomarkers that identify patients at high-risk for developing a disease progressive course and epilepsy, thus permitting novel treatments to be applied timely following the concept of Personalized Medicine.

column36: Biomarkers of ANTidepressant RESponse : early indicators and novel targets
column37: Antidepressants (AD) are for now, the best treatment we have for major depression (MDD) a severe mental disorder. AD are one of the most commonly prescribed drugs in the western hemisphere, however their trial-and error nature combined with unwanted side-effects, leave a lot to be desired. More than 60% of patients suffering from MDD fail to respond to the first AD they are prescribed. For those that respond, full response is only observed after several weeks of treatment, and, in case of failure it can take too long a time before alternative options are explored. To be able to predict clinical response at an early-stage of AD treatment is an important aim for the clinician and the potential impact for patients suffering from MDD and for the health system is very high. However, up to date there are no early biomarkers that could help therapeutic decision while this is already true in cancer and other fields of medicine. We recently described the involvement of ELK1 in depression, particularly how ELK1 gene expression in blood may help follow treatment response and will further characterize ELK1 and related genes, and other regulators of cell machinery associated with early clinical improvement. First we aim to identify peripheral "early post-treatment biomarkers" in a novel multicentre human cohort of patients with MDE. Then, we want to validate "early post-treatment biomarkers" in animal models of depression, in the blood. Last, we want to explore the plausibility of our blood biomarkers by studying our biomarkers in the brain. We will focus our analysis on both long and small RNA, by using cutting-edge approaches. These results will constitute the necessary first step to develop new biomarkers predictive of AD response. Such biomarkers, would reduce time to change medication and help avoid unnecessary side effects for patients, inform therapeutic decisions and reduce stress for clinicians, and reduce personal and public health costs.

column37: The gut lining is replaced every 3 to 5 days by rapidly dividing cells. Specialized cells known as stem cells have the longevity and capacity to continually renew all the other cell types. Unfortunately, this unique longevity of stem cells is also what predisposes them to acquire mutations that lead to cancer. Hence, the recent identification of intestinal stem cells has created excitement for both regenerative medicine and the discovery of the cellular origin of colon cancer. More recently, we have identified a radioresistant stem cell population present in the normal (non-mutated) colon and demonstrated that they can contribute to the cellular origin of cancer. The goal of this research is to determine whether a secretory (non-stem) cell can also give rise to colon cancer. My lab has considerable expertise in intestinal stem cells and colon cancer, and we have developed innovative models to help determine the cell of origin for these tumors. column37: Lymphocytes, also known as white blood cells, defend the body against microbes, viruses and cancer by circulating throughout the body. Aside from lymphoid tissues (spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow, etc), a small number of lymphocytes can be found in all other tissues, including the pancreas. Entry of lymphocytes in tissues such as the brain, the eyes, the muscles or the pancreas is regulated by specific proteins and processes. Aberrant or facilitated entry of lymphocytes into these non-lymphoid tissues can lead to severe immune pathologies. Notably, lymphocyte infiltrates in the pancreas have been documented in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Blocking immune cell entry in the pancreas would certainly provide therapeutic benefit to diabetes patients. Our overall objective is to identify the proteins that allow both normal and aberrant lymphocyte infiltration in the pancreas. We will use two complementary non-targeted approach to identify key pathways facilitating lymphocyte entry into pancreatic tissue. First, by a novel molecular biology approach, namely ProCode, we will test the role of over 200 proteins in inhibiting or facilitating lymphocyte entry in the pancreas. Second, we will screen over 200 strains of mice from the Collaborative Cross and determine which of these mice present with more or less lymphocytes in the pancreas. As the genome of the Collaborative Cross mice is known, this unbiased approach will reveal genes that influence lymphocyte entry in the pancreas. Altogether, these complementary approaches will unravel the specific molecular pathways that need to be targeted to prevent lymphocyte entry in pancreatic tissue.

column37: Integrins are the main molecules in the human body that link cells to the extracellular matrix (ECM), a mixture of complex sugars and proteins that forms the base upon which tissues are built. column36: Contribution of the NKG2D pathway to multiple sclerosis
column37: Several studies showed that the immune system contributes to the development of multiple sclerosis (MS). Normally, the immune system defends the body against foreign elements. However, in the case of MS, the immune system attacks the protective sheath surrounding our neurons, called myelin and impairs several essential functions of brain cells. Our team investigates how immune cells hurt brain cells of MS patients. Stressed brain cells can put on their surface alert molecules that are subsequently detected by white blood cells carrying a receptor called NKG2D. The NKG2D-bearing immune cells can recognize and kill cells carrying these alert molecules. We observed that white blood cells from MS patients carry a greater amount of NKG2D compared to those from healthy donors. We will investigate whether these immune cells from MS patients can cause more damage to brain cells. We also observed that some human neurons but also other cells called astrocytes (which are important to maintain neurons' health), express these alert molecules. Our project will evaluate whether blocking the detection by immune cells via NKG2D could prevent harmful attack on neurons and astrocytes. We will also evaluate whether neurons and astrocytes carry these alert molecules in postmortem brains from MS patients.

column37: Pulmonary fibrosis occurs when the lung becomes scarred and stiffened, leading to death from respiratory failure. The average survival of an individual with pulmonary fibrosis is only 3-5 years, worse than many types of cancer. One of the reasons is that it is very hard to diagnose pulmonary fibrosis. Furthermore, there is no biomarker that tells if you have pulmonary fibrosis. Although the cause of pulmonary fibrosis is not known, risk factors include genetic susceptibility and cigarette smoke. There is no cure for pulmonary fibrosis and remarkably few effective therapies. This research will investigate a novel protein- called human antigen R (HuR)- that has never been studied in pulmonary fibrosis. However, HuR may control protein expression associated with pulmonary fibrosis that leads to respiratory failure. Based on what we know about HuR in cancer, we predict that HuR will promote pulmonary fibrosis when it does not behave in a normal fashion. Some things that cause HuR to behave improperly include cigarette smoke and radiation- risk factors for pulmonary fibrosis. The localization of HuR within a cell shows that someone with cancer will progress very rapidly. It is not known where HuR is found in the lung in fibrosis conditions, but we predict that in a person with pulmonary fibrosis, HuR levels and location in the lung may be very different compared to someone without the disease. Determining this may be one way to tell who has the disease and who does not. Finally, inhibiting HuR with a drug would be one way to prevent its function from being irregular. Using animal models of fibrosis, biological samples from individuals with IPF as well as cell and molecular biology techniques, we will test the therapeutic and prognostic utility of HuR in pulmonary fibrosis. In essence, HuR represents an unexplored and innovative pathway that will ultimately serving as a catalyst for future experiments to explore novel drugs and the utility of HuR as a biomarker.

column36: Targeting global programs of gene expression to promote axon regeneration
column37: Numerous neurological conditions and traumatic injuries disrupt connections between nerve in the adult mammalian central nervous system (CNS). Damaged CNS neurons have a limited capacity to repair themselves leading to motor, sensory and cognitive impairments. Promoting axon regeneration could support neurological recovery from a variety of conditions and serve as an adjunct for cellular transplantation approaches. There are currently no approved treatments to stimulate CNS axon regeneration. An exciting advance in the CNS regeneration field is that specific changes in gene expression in injured neurons can trigger extensive axon regeneration; however therapeutic translation of these findings is limited by off-target effects associated with these particular genes. An alternative attractive strategy to positively regulate the repair of injured neurons is through targetting a family of molecules called miRNAs that affect the expression of many genes simultaneusly and may thus have robust effects on axon regeneration. We are using a combination of cell based and animal models to identify miRNAs with robust axon regeneration promoting activity and are identifying the molecular targets of these miRNA that may be therapeutically targeted to promote axon regeneration following injury.

column36: Preventing pathological protein spread in Huntington's disease: relevance to pathology and treatment.
column37: To date, the problem in Huntington's Disease (HD) has been thought to result from a genetic mutation which leads to the production of an abnormal protein - called mutant huntingtin - within brain cells. Over time, this protein causes the cells to slowly stop working and die. In recent years, new evidence has emerged which suggests that other factors may also contribute to the death of these nerve cells but these factors were thought to be of only minor significance for the disease. However, we found that this may not be the case as we detected the abnormal mutant huntingtin protein in healthy transplanted tissue implanted in the brains of affected individuals. This indicates that mutant huntingtin had spread and entered the implanted healthy graft tissue. These findings have been repeated in both cell and animal models and it is now accepted that mutant huntingtin can be transported between cells. We now seek to explore how mutant huntingtin spread relates to disease presentation and how prevention or reduction of this spread by vaccines could diminish disease burden. If true, the theory that we propose would both improve our understanding of what goes wrong in HD and, more importantly, potentially lead to new treatment options.

column36: Prenatal exposure to chemicals in plastics can cause epigenetic variation in genes associated with neurodevelopment in girls and boys
column37: The healthy development of children is very sensitive to exposure to environmental chemicals during pregnancy. Prenatal exposure to chemicals in plastics, specifically phthalates, is substantial due to their widespread use in food packaging, household cleaners, cosmetics and personal care products. Phthalates can cross the placenta and affect the activity of genes critical for brain development. This in turn could influence the development of children's thinking and reasoning abilities and behaviour. Prenatal exposure to phthalates has been associated with adverse effects on children's development, including lower levels of intelligence, poorer motor and language skills and a higher risk for autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. The effect of phthalates on genes is poorly understood and may be different for girls and boys. This could explain the greater proportion of boys who are diagnosed with developmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Our team is comprised of researchers with expertise in child development, epigenetics, environmental toxicology and public health. We will use already collected data on mother's prenatal exposure to phthalate chemicals and children's cognitive, motor and behavioural outcomes at 2, 3-4 and 5-9 years of age. This data comes from two studies that recruited women during pregnancy, one in Canada and the other in Australia. These studies have biobanked DNA samples that will be used to identify genes that change due to phthalate exposure. We will investigate the relationship between these genes and intelligence, language and motor skills, and behaviour in girls and boys. Our results could be used to update recommendations on exposure to chemicals in plastics during pregnancy. They could also be used to design interventions to prevent or reverse the potential negative effects of exposure to these plastic chemicals on children's brains and behaviour.

column36: A role for the regulator of purine biosynthesis at the host-pathogen interface
column37: The bacterium Staphylococcus aureus is one of the most common causes of human infections. These infections range from mild (minor wound infections and carbuncles, for example) to more serious, and often fatal illnesses (e.g. endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septicemia, and toxic shock syndrome). S. aureus is also the most common source of hospital-acquired infections and is frequently found as the cause of surgical wound and indwelling medical device infections. However, efforts to control this bacterium with antibiotics are becoming increasingly difficult due to its multi-drug resistance. This research is centred around a new discovery in my laboratory that has profound implications on the pathogenic potential of S. aureus. We have discovered that mutations in a regulator of purine biosynthesis, as yet uncharacterized in S. aureus, occur in response to stress. These mutations lead to upregulation of proteins on the S. aureus cell surface that bind fibronectin, a host protein. The upregulation of fibronectin-binding proteins results in bacterial cell clumping, massive aggregation in the presence of fibronectin and, during systemic infection of rodents, occlusion of the vasculature resulting in a hypervirulent S. aureus phenotype. The goal of this research is to characterize these mutants and identify targets that when perturbed curtail virulence. Our studies will provide novel information on how serious human pathogens, like S. aureus, have the potential to cause such a wide array of infections, or severity of infection. It is envisioned that uncovering these essential processes will lead to the rational design of successful next-generation drugs and therapeutic strategies to treat patients suffering from S. aureus infection.

column36: Molecular mechanisms that promote cardiac cell survival and heart health
column37: In Canada, approximately 1.6 million people suffer from cardiovascular diseases, and someone dies from these diseases every 7 minutes. The heart is made of different cell types that work together to generate a heart beat. These cells share a common mechanism to handle cellular stress in response to unfavorable conditions, but the outcome of the stress coping strategy depends on the type of heart cell. A condition called cardiac fibrosis results from malfunction of the cell stress coping response, which eventually results in heart failure. We found that long-term stress coping response in cardiomyocytes, (the cells responsible for contraction and relaxation of the heart) and in cardiac fibroblasts (the cells responsible for repairing damage to heart tissue) is instrumental to development of cardiac fibrosis. On the other hand, we found that a drug called TUDCA is effective in preventing cardiac fibrosis in animal models. The proposed research aims to understand how the malfunction in cardiomyocyte and cardiac fibroblasts stress coping response mechanism promotes cardiac fibrosis, and how TUDCA prevents cardiac fibrosis. We will apply the new knowledge generated to guide therapeutic interventions that can prevent or treat the development of heart disease in humans.

column36: Sensory processing impairments in autism
column37: Sensory processing disruptions are common in autism spectrum and some other neuro-developmental disorders. Sensory input is the sole neural input into the brain; in this context, it is debated to what extent changes in sensory processing throughout development is a root cause for brain alterations resulting in autism symptoms. At the very least, sensory processing pathways in the brain might be affected by the disorder in the same way as other brain areas. On a positive note, sensory processing pathways are highly conserved, well described, and relatively easily accessible - they therefore offer a unique window of opportunity for translational studies on sensory processing disruptions and their impact on brain development and function using an animal model. From our previous work we learned two important things: 1) increased reactivity to sound is NOT necessarily due to increased sound sensitivity, as it is often wrongly interpreted in kids with developmental disorders and 2) early disruptions in sensory processing lead to compensatory changes that might be the real problem for the developing brain. We here propose a study in an excellent animal model showing the exact same sensory symptoms as observed in kids with autism, in order to further understand how these compensatory mechanisms work and how we can avoid or reverse them. The animal model will also allow to test the efficacy of early intervention either with drugs or occupational therapy in order to avoid these detrimental compensatory changes induced by sensory processing disruptions. Our results will have a huge impact on clinical assessments and intervention for all people with autism and other disorders that are associated with altered sensory processing, e.g. schizophrenia, obsessive compulsive disorder, or Tourett's syndrome.

column36: Dietary Interventions in psoriatic arthritis (DIPsA): A Randomized, controlled, pilot trial
column37: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis that affects 1 in 400 Canadians and can lead to significant joint damage and disability. Patients often seek information about diets to assist with improving their symptoms. However, little is known about the effect of different dietary patterns on disease activity in PsA. We aim to perform a large study to evaluate the effect of two dietary interventions: 1) Mediterranean Diet; and 2) Low Fat/Low Calorie Diet compared to usual diet on disease activity in PsA. In this pilot study we will assess the feasibility of performing such study in a smaller sample of 90 patients from three large PsA clinics in Canada and the US. We will randomly assign patients into one of the three dietary intervention groups and follow them for 6 months. We will assess changes in their joint and skin disease activity as well as measure variations in relevant biomarkers in their blood and stool which will clarify the role of diet in PsA. Ultimately, our pilot study will provide the necessary information to successfully conduct a subsequent larger study that will define the role of dietary interventions for patients with PsA.

column36: Development of a peptide-based membrane mimetic for solution studies in membrane protein research.
column37: Membrane proteins are a vital component of cells. Until recently, membrane proteins were not studied as extensively as cytosolic proteins. This is due to the propensity of membrane proteins to aggregate outside a membrane environment during their isolation using detergents. Therefore, in recent years, several membrane mimics have been developed in order to facilitate interrogation of membrane proteins by rigorous biophysical and analytical techniques. However, stabilization of membrane proteins in these mimetic remains laborious, costly and difficult to perform. To overcome these limitations, our laboratory has developed a simple method to stabilize membrane proteins in aqueous solution. Called the "peptidisc", the method uses multiple copies of a unique peptide that wraps around membrane proteins to make them feel like they never left the membrane environment. The end result is membrane proteins that are perfectly stable, soluble and free of detergent effects. The peptidisc technology will allow us to better study membrane proteins, yielding a better understanding of their structure and activity, which ones associates and how they interact in the cell and with their environment. Since the peptidisc approach is both simple and easy to apply, more membrane proteins can now also be included in high-throughput searches for new drugs that target medical conditions.

column36: Improving School Food: Universal Integrated Healthy Lunch Intervention Research
column37: The diet quality of Canadian children across the socio-economic spectrum during school hours is poor, yet school settings can be important to promote health behaviours that can last a lifetime. Once children reach school age, they spend more of their waking hours in school than in any other environment. Children's eating habits may be easier to influence than those of adults. In Canada, households with children are more likely to experience food insecurity, and school food programs that are universally available to all children can support the development of healthy eating patterns across groups of varying socioeconomic status. There is a significant gap in rigourous community-engaged academic research on the impact of school meal programs, especially universal ones. The purpose of this population health intervention research is to study the impacts of a two-year universal, curriculum-integrated healthy school lunch program in elementary schools in Saskatoon on food consumption, dietary quality and food and nutrition-related knowledge, attitudes and practices. This study will take place in two intervention elementary schools matched with two control schools. We will compare pre, during and post intervention parameters in intervention and control schools in partnership with a local school board, a school food community-based organization and national school food collaborators. The opportunity we have to systematically and comprehensively study a curriculum-integrated school lunch program, as well as the promising practices for school food programs across Canada is without precedent and can inform ongoing government planning and consultation.

column36: CETP Inhibition as a novel treatment to remove pathogen lipids and improve survival in sepsis
column37: Sepsis, or the severe inflammation in response to an infection, is one of the leading causes of death of Canadians in the hospital. Sepsis occurs when the immune system is activated by lipid molecules from invading bacteria. These "pathogen-associated lipids", or PALs, are transported through the bloodstream by lipoproteins, the same particles that also transport cholesterol. Of the different lipoprotein particles, HDL (also called the "good cholesterol") plays a particularly important role in transporting PALs. HDL levels are known to drop acutely during sepsis, and we have recently shown that the degree of drop in HDL during sepsis is a very strong predictor of whether or not a patient will survive sepsis, with a lower HDL level predicting a worse outcome. How and why HDL levels drop during sepsis is unknown. The major goal of this project is to investigate genetic mechanisms that determine HDL levels in sepsis. We have discovered a gene, called CETP, that appears to play a very important role in determining HDL levels during sepsis, and thereby contributes to whether or not a patient will survive the episode of sepsis. The goals of this proposal are to explore whether inhibition of CETP may represent a new treatment strategy for sepsis. To do this, we will use an existing drug that inhibits CETP to examine its effects in mouse models of sepsis. We will also investigate the role of genetic variation in HDL-related genes on HDL levels and survival from sepsis in large population cohorts. This research will provide new insight into the important role of HDL and CETP in sepsis. The results of this research could lead to new ways to treat sepsis, for example by altering the function of CETP. Ultimately these results will improve the health of Canadians by leading to new approaches to treat sepsis, one of the leading causes of death in Canada.

column36: Allosteric Modulation of the Urotensin Receptor with Small-Molecule Peptide Mimics
column37: The urotensin II receptor (UT) plays important roles in the heart, kidneys, pancreas, adrenal gland, and central nervous system. The receptor is known to bind to two endogenous cyclic peptide ligands: urotensin II (UII) and urotensin II-related peptide (URP). These ligands and the parent receptor have been implicated in heart disease, metabolic syndrome, and kidney failure. For example, in the cardiovascular system, UII acts as a potent endothelium independent vasoconstrictor and endothelium-dependent vasodilator; however, in disease states, this constriction-dilation equilibrium is disrupted. Their specific influences on UT have been difficult to decipher due to a dearth in molecules that can selectively block the activity of UII and URP; however, it is suspected that their functional selectivity leads to differential participation in specific cardiovascular disease pathology. Our collaborative research has identified novel small-molecule receptor modulators that can differentiate the effects of UII and URP. Di- and triazepin-2-one peptide mimics have been conceived based on the side chain orientations and backbone conformation of a biologically relevant tripeptide motif common to both endogenous urotensin receptor (UT) ligands. Contingent on structure the diand triazepin-2-ones can modulate selectively and differentially the contractile effects of UII and URP ex vivo. Considering the importance of UT and its ligands in cardiovascular diseases, these modulators offer unique potential for dissecting the different biological pathways mediated by UII and URP in normal physiology and during disease pathology. A plan is proposed for improving ligand potency to develop probes and ideally therapeutics to treat cardiovascular diseases by an interdisciplinary approach featuring organic synthesis, in vitro and ex vivo screening, and animal models of atherosclerosis.

column36: Audit & Feedback Module Targeting Low-Value Clinical Practices in Injury Care: an Economic Evaluation
column37: In Canada, injury leads to more potential years of life lost and to greater costs than heart and stroke diseases combined. Furthermore, more than 50% of patients hospitalised following injury do not receive optimal care, 20% of injury deaths are estimated to be preventable and significant variations in injury mortality and morbidity have been observed across trauma centers in Canada, the UK, Australia and the USA. Over the past decades, emphasis on adherence to evidence-based processes of care (rewards for doing more) and rapid innovation in imaging and therapeutic techniques has led to an exponential rise in unnecessary tests and procedures. Whole body CT scan for minor trauma is just one example. Low-value clinical practices, defined as "the common use of a particular intervention when the benefits don't justify the potential harm or cost" consume up to 30% of healthcare budgets. They expose patients to physical and psychological adverse events and put enormous pressure on healthcare budgets, thereby threatening accessible, universal health care. According the Canadian Institute for Health Information, 1 in 4 Canadians were recommended a test or treatment that they did not feel was necessary in 2015. The objective of this research project is to evaluate the cost-benefit of an intervention targeting reductions in low-value clinical practices for injury admissions. The results of this study should directly lead to improvements in trauma systems across Canada. Medium and long-term advantages include an increase in the availability of resources for patients who need them and a reduction in adverse events for patients hospitalized following injury.

column36: Ferroptosis-mediated damage in Chronic EAE: implications for Progressive MS
column37: There are limited treatments options for progressive MS, with only one approved drug. Unlike relapsing-remitting MS, progressive MS is not responsive to anti-inflammatory drugs. This suggests that progressive MS is not mainly an inflammatory disease but could be a neurodegenerative disease caused by 'oxidative stress'. 'Ferroptosis' is a newly discovered form of oxidative stress, triggered by excess iron which causes damage to lipids (or fats) found in cells. Ferroptosis can cause damage to myelin which is rich in lipids. It can also cause damage to cells in the brain that produce myelin as well as to nerve cells (neurodegeneration). We have preliminary evidence from a mouse model of MS called experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) that ferroptosis occurs in a chronic form of EAE (CH-EAE), which models aspects of progressive MS. Once ferroptosis starts, it can take off like "wildfire in the hot, dry summer". The good news is, that there are drugs that can "quench this fire" and stop damage to lipids. We already have evidence that certain biomarkers of ferroptosis are produced more highly in CH-EAE. We propose to treat CH-EAE mice with a drug that blocks ferroptosis. We have preliminary evidence that such treatment works. We will confirm this by assessing if this treatment improves weakness and paralysis in these mice and also analyze improvement in pathology. We also plan to study a combination-treatment with a ferroptosis inhibitor and an iron chelator to block ferroptosis-mediated damage to lipids, and other iron-mediated damage to proteins and DNA. We hope this will act like a "one-two punch" to stop progression. In addition, we will also assess various ferroptosis biomarkers in human MS brain autopsy samples of secondary progressive and primary progressive MS. This work could open the way for the development of novel therapies for progressive forms of MS for which there is currently no effective treatment.

column36: Immunogenic wheat protein metabolism by gut bacteria.
column37: Celiac disease is a common food sensitivity triggered by gluten in cereals like wheat, rye and barley and its incidence is rising at an alarming rate. The reasons for this are not fully understood but suggestions are that they relate to changes in the composition or function of gut microbes. We discovered that some pathogens present in the gut use gluten and other non-gluten proteins, as a source of food, but this digestion is partial and generates peptides that cause more inflammation in celiac disease patients. Thus, the metabolic activity of certain bacteria within the gut could increase the chances to develop wheat sensitivity and targeting this function could prevent or treat it. The proposal will study the capacity to digest wheat proteins by the microbe community that resides in the upper gut of celiac patients or controls without the disease. We will then apply these communities to mouse models that express celiac risk genes, and thus are relevant to human disease, to study the inflammation induced. The gluten-free diet is the only available therapy for celiac disease, but it is difficult to follow, expensive and not always effective. The knowledge learned here will guide us in identifying groups of bacteria with optimal capacity to detoxify wheat proteins to prevent or treat food sensitivities, such as celiac disease.

column36: Optimizing patient adherence to stroke rehabilitation treatment: a telerehabilitation trial
column37: Stroke impacts nearly 400,000 Canadians annually. Three quarters of stroke survivors will live with minor to severe impairments or disabilities; which require rehabilitation care representing >$3.6 billion for the Canadian economy. Enhancing stroke rehabilitation care delivery can reduce those costs while optimizing patient outcomes and allowing patients to return home earlier following the stroke event. Strong evidence supports initiating rehabilitation as soon as the patient's medical status has stabilized; however, the need to travel to access rehabilitation, the lack of interprofessional communication among service providers, and the failure to engage the patient/families in the decision making process, limit access to optimal services. This intervention will entail participants receiving rehabilitation care through remote, live treatment sessions with an interdisciplinary group of clinicians (called telerehabilitation). The aim of this application is to evaluate whether telerehabilitation could provide patients who have had stroke the opportunity to return home safely after their acute hospital stay, encourage patient (and family) engagement in rehabilitation care, and overcome challenges of access to interprofessional rehabilitation care. The process of care, clinical outcomes and costs will be captured for 296 patients, half of whom will be offered telerehabilitation. Through qualitative interviews, the research team will uncover and describe contextual factors (both personal and environmental) that will facilitate the delivery of stroke rehabilitation care using a telerehabilitation platform (for whom and how does it work). Given stark contrasts between the Canadian stroke care recommendations and actual rehabilitation practice, and little robust data to support change, this study represents a unique, highly relevant, and innovative opportunity to minimize gaps in both knowledge and practice.

column36: Novel Interplay between the Apelin Pathway and Neutral Endopeptidase in Heart Disease
column37: The overall objective of this proposal is to develop new drugs for heart failure and we have identified the apelin pathway as one potential target. We plan to test the importance of the apelin pathway by studying apelin receptor signaling in heart disease. We have designed and tested novel apelin analogs including their pharmacokinetics (ie. how stable these analogs are) in human plasma. We will demonstrate the beneficial effects of these analogs on human endothelial cells and adult cardiomyocytes. We have identified a key enzyme, neutral endopeptidase (NEP), which cleaves apelin peptides in vitro and we will test the in vivo importance of this enzyme by using pharmacological and genetic inhibition of this enzyme in mice. Interestingly, NEP degradation of apelin peptides may explain the therapeutic effects of EntrestoTM, the newest therapy approved for the treatment of HF. We have identified two optimized stable analogs of apelin 17, the most potent apelin peptide. We will use a combination of in vitro and in vivo approaches, and experimental models of human HF to elucidate the therapeutic potential of novel and stable potent apelin analogs. In order to establish the therapeutic potential of our novel apelin analogs we will study these analogs in male and female pre-clinical models of heart failure, post-myocardial infarction and pressure-overload models of HF. Our success to synthesize novel potent apelin analogs with significantly prolonged stability in vitro and in vivo, puts us in a unique position to elucidate and propose a practical approach to using apelin analogs as novel therapeutics for HF. We will also translate our findings to patients with heart failure and measure plasma apelin peptide levels in heart failure patients in response to sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto), a new heart failure therapy which inhibits this enzyme.

column36: Targeting Translational Control in Retinal Ganglion Cell Degeneration
column37: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, afflicting over 70 million people, and nearly one in ten elderly Canadians. Although glaucoma is often associated with increased eye pressure, it is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the death of retinal ganglion cell neurons to compromise vision. Yet we still do not understand the molecular mechanisms that drive this damage, and there are no neuroprotective treatments. In studying the degenerative process we have identified a gene family, the MNKs, that function to influence protein production in retinal ganglion cells. However, this process has not been previously linked to ganglion cell death or glaucoma. Based on our preliminary evidence we propose that the actions of MNKs have an important role in glaucomatous neurodegeneration. Our research program will generate new insights into how changes in this mechanism contributes to retinal damage, and provide proof of principle for targeting this process as a new therapeutic strategy.

column36: Circadian regulation of host-pathogen interactions in vector-borne parasitic infections
column37: Vector-borne diseases (e.g. parasites or other pathogens transmitted to humans by insects) are major public health concerns for billions of people in tropical and subtropical regions. Of utmost importance, with global warming, the spreading of these vector-borne infections is predicted to reach temperate latitudes within the next decades. Recent research has shown that immune responses, including against pathogens, vary across the day-night cycle and are controlled by biological clocks located in most tissues, including immune cells. Very little research has been performed on the influence of circadian clocks on parasitic infections or any other vector-transmitted diseases. We propose that vector-borne parasitic infections represent ideal models to study circadian regulation of host-pathogen interactions. As a model for the study of circadian rhythms in parasitic infections, we study leishmaniasis, a debilitating and often mortal human disease affecting millions of individuals in tropical and subtropical areas. It is caused by infection by the parasite Leishmania sps., which is transferred by sandflies that are active at dusk and dawn. We previously found that the magnitude of Leishmania infection vary according to the time of day at which the host meets the parasite. We will now aim to determine the mechanisms involved in this circadian rhythm and the involvement of immune cell clocks in controlling the infection, and on the other hand, the effect of the parasitic infection on the circadian rhythms of the host. A better understanding of the timed regulation of host-parasite interactions will allow developing better prophylactic and therapeutic strategies to fight off these vector-borne diseases.

column36: A personalized dynamic blood pressure control plan for cardiovascular disease prevention among patients with hypertension at low cardiovascular disease risk.
column37: Hypertension is a common condition characterized by high blood pressure (BP). It is well established as an important risk factor for heart attacks, strokes, and other heart diseases. It affects approximately 23% of Canadian adults. There is an ongoing debate regarding the most beneficial approach to treat patients with hypertension, with some recent treatment guidelines advocating for a more aggressive approach (defined by a lower target BP level) while others maintaining a more conservative one. There is clear evidence supporting the use of an aggressive approach among patients at high risk of heart disease. However, little evidence is available regarding those at low risk. To address this knowledge gap and facilitate the practice of personalized medicine, we will investigate varied BP control plans using real-world data extracted from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink. This database contains the medical records of over 13 million patients seen by general practitioners in the United Kingdom. We will include all patients who started any drug used to treat hypertension between 1998 and 2019. We will first describe the treatment patterns over time and identify potential factors that may lead to a treatment change. We will investigate whether following a lower target BP decreases the rate of heart diseases compared with a higher target BP among patients at low risk of heart diseases. Finally, a personalized BP control plan will be investigated using sophisticated statistical approaches. Heart disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide. Through its use of big data and a personalized medicine approach, this study will identify the optimal approach to the management of hypertension for the prevention of heart diseases in patients at low risk, a large yet understudied population. In doing so, it will prevent heart attacks, strokes, and other heart disease, and it improve the health of patients in Canada and elsewhere with hypertension.

column36: Polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase: its role in DNA strand break repair and a potential therapeutic target to enhance radio- and chemotherapy
column37: A problem frequently encountered in cancer therapy is that of tumour cell resistance to therapeutic agents, so that although the majority of cells in a tumour will be destroyed, a small fraction will survive, and have the potential to metastasize. At present our ability to predict tumour response to treatment or diminish the resistance to radiation or drugs is very limited. Such methods are only likely to be developed when we have a clearer understanding, at the molecular level, of how cells respond to these agents. For many of these agents, DNA is considered to be the main target leading to cell death. It is known that cells have the capacity to repair much of this damage. Uncovering all the enzymes responsible for repair and learning how they operate is still a major task. This proposal focuses on a particular type of damage, DNA strand breaks, and on the role of a particular enzyme, polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), in carrying out the repair of these lesions. We intend to learn how PNKP interacts with other proteins required to mend strand breaks and if it plays an important role in making cells resistant to a variety of anti-cancer drugs. Almost all cancer cells lack specific proteins called tumour suppressor proteins. We have recently found that cells that have lost specific tumour suppressors either die or become very weak if PNKP is also lost. This is a process called synthetic lethality and it presents an opportunity to target cancer cells rather than normal cells. In order to make full use of this opportunity we will investigate the mechanism(s) responsible for synthetic lethality involving loss of PNKP.

column36: Physiological and pathophysiological roles of renal intercalated cells
column37: Kidneys in our bodies regulate how much and which waste products are eliminated in the urine. Key cells in this process are called intercalated cells, which regulate blood acid-base balance and urinary acidification. Defects in these cells caused by mutations of the kidney anion exchanger 1 (kAE1) result in distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA), a disease where patients experience an acidic blood, kidney stones, increased risk of kidney failure, and urinary loss of salts. Studying the mechanisms of this disease is therefore important as it may identify new therapeutic targets relevant to the millions of Canadians who suffer from chronic kidney disease. Our preliminary results show that kAE1 interacts with another protein called claudin-4, and that altering one or the other results in the disease symptoms. In this funding period, we will dissect the relationship between these 2 proteins, verify our findings in vivo and alter their functional and physical interaction using drugs or genetic engineering as a lead towards development of therapeutic approaches to not only treat dRTA patients but also patients with chronic kidney disease.

column36: Elucidating the role of the IL-1 system in the pathogenesis of CNS autoimmunity
column37: This project is at the crossroads of neuroscience and immunology. It aims at understanding the role of the cytokine interleukin (IL)-1B, a molecule that allows immune cells to communicate with each other, in multiple sclerosis (MS). Because of the availability of transgenic mouse lines lacking key molecules of this signalling system or having fluorescently labeled neurons, glia and immune cells, we have decided to focus our work on an animal model of MS called experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Up to now, these transgenic animals have allowed us to demonstrate that IL-1B has early detrimental effects, causing loss of neurons and their projections (termed axons), myelin sheaths and neurological function. Our results show that the negative effects of IL-1B are mediated by a subclass of innate immune cells called neutrophils and macrophages, and involve stimulation of the IL-1 receptor (IL-1R1) present at the surface of certain veins draining the central nervous system (CNS). More specifically, we showed that IL-1B production by innate immune cells is a critical step for their mobilization inside the CNS. Furthermore, we found that the subsequent activation of IL-1R1 signaling in CNS blood vessels induces a communication loop that drives neuroinflammation and the recruitment of autoaggressive (termed effector) lymphocytes into the CNS, eventually leading to immune attacks and demyelination. In this grant proposal, we aim at identifying the exact molecules involved in the production of IL-1 by both subclasses of innate immune cells involved. Since IL-1 can influence many types of immune and CNS cells (e.g. blood vessels, neurons, T lymphocytes, etc.), we also want to better understand their interplay in the attack phase. Finally, we want to determine whether we can use anti-IL-1 therapies (many are currently approved for arthritis) or downstream molecules to prevent EAE development and/or progression and to offer an additional therapy for MS patients.

column36: Mechanisms by which hyperinsulinemia promotes pancreatic cancer
column37: High levels of the hormone insulin are a cardinal feature of obesity and early type 2 diabetes, and are induced by unhealthy 'Western diets' high in sugar and fat. It has been suggested that excess insulin contributes to cancer initiation and/or progression, but this has never been tested directly in a way that can address cause and effect. Over the past 5 years, we tested for the first time the hypothesis high levels of insulin play a causal role in pancreatic cancer initiation using new mouse models. Remarkably, our data show a clear reduction in the early stages of pancreatic cancer in the mice that with only a relatively modest reduction in insulin. We now want to know how excess insulin has this cancer promoting effect. Specifically, we want to know whether the effects of insulin are direct on the cancer cells, or indirect by altering something else in the body or the cells that are nearby to the tumours. These studies have the potential to further clarify the known links between insulin and many forms of cancer, as well as uncover the exact mechanisms by which excess insulin influences cancer risk. Our findings will have major implications for both cancer prevention via nutrition/lifestyle modification and for cancer treatment by inhibition of insulin signalling in tumours.

column36: Determining the role of the nuclear basket protein Mlp1/TPR in mRNA homeostasis
column37: Regulating the expression of its genes is an essential task for any living organism. In eukaryotic cells, a membrane impermeable to large molecules separates the site where the genetic information is stored (the nucleus) from the site where the information is translated into protein (cytoplasm), the functional molecules executing all cellular processes. After the genetic information stored in the DNA is copied into a messenger molecule, called RNA, RNA has to exit the nucleus and reach the cytoplasm to get translated. The only path to reach the site of protein synthesis is through the nuclear pore complex (NPC), large macromolecular complexes embedded in the nuclear membrane. In this project, we will use different molecular biology, genetic, proteomic and microscopy based approaches to study the mechanism by which the nuclear basket, a substructure of the NPC, regulates the transport of some RNAs, but not all RNAs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Understanding this process is important to gain a better understanding of many diseases, as mutations in the proteins involved in this process have been found mutated in patients suffering from various diseases such as cancer or Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).

column36: The implication of the adaptive arm of the integrated stress response in KRAS lung cancer.
column37: Mutations in KRAS gene are found in deadly forms of cancer like colorectal, lung and pancreatic cancers. In lung cancer, 30% of adenocarcinomas possess mutations in KRAS gene, which render this type of cancer refractory to anti-tumor therapies. Mutant KRAS gene produces a protein that has the capacity to reprogram the functions of normal cells and establish stressful conditions that disrupt normal proliferation. Under these conditions, cells employ mechanisms that help them survive and adapt to stress. However, these adaptive mechanisms act in favor of mutant KRAS to maintain the abnormal proliferation and cause cancer. We have identified that adaptation of cells to the function of mutant KRAS requires a protein known as eIF2. In stressed cells, eIF2 is modified by a process named phosphorylation, which reorganizes key cellular functions to promote the expression of genes and synthesis of proteins that further enhance the oncogenic function of mutant KRAS. In this proposal, we investigate the mechanisms utilized by eIF2 to promote the formation of lung cancer through the action of mutant KRAS. We employ mice, which have been genetically engineered for the disruption of eIF2 function, to examine the effects of eIF2 inhibition on the formation of lung tumors containing mutant KRAS. Also, we will examine the function of proteins that assist eIF2 in the development of lung cancer through the action of mutant KRAS. Moreover, we will test the effects of newly developed eIF2 inhibitory drugs to assess their anti-tumor effects on lung cancer in mice. Our work reveals new mechanisms of lung cancer formation by mutant KRAS, which will help the design of better approaches to treat one of the deadliest forms of cancer like lung cancer.

column37: Roughly 6 million Canadians report a form of chronic pain, yet half of the sufferers do not get enough pain relief from their medications. This severely affects their quality of life and has significant social and economic burdens. Dr. Li will lead a team to produce a new, effective, and safe drug for chronic pain relief. This new drug will improve pain relief options and access for patients who suffer from chronic pain.
