Genetic approaches will investigate if physical activity plays a causal protective role against PCOS, and association studies will help determine the components of physical activity that are associated with specific PCOS features in adolescent girls. The results of our research will better characterize a modifiable factor associated with PCOS to inform public health strategies that promote healthy lifestyles in order to prevent adverse health outcomes.

column36: Reprogramming HSCs to generate protective trained immunity against TB
column37: Ever since German scientist Robert Koch first discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) to be the infectious agent of tuberculosis in 1882, it has defied efforts by scientists to prevent or cure the disease. The presence of Mtb DNA in ancient Egyptian mummies (dated 1550- 1080 BC) suggests a long-standing evolutionary relationship between this bacterium and humans. Despite the world-wide application of BCG vaccination and other anti-Mtb interventions, Mtb remains one of the deadliest human pathogens killing annually two million people. Eight to ten million new cases of active tuberculosis occur each year due in large part to asymptomatic people chronically infected with Mtb. The ability of Mtb to persist in individuals with apparently normal immune systems implies that Mtb has developed strategies to avoid, evade, and even subvert our host defense system. Considering Mtb also desires to be a "residence" of the bone marrow, which is home to stem cells that produce all immune cells, Mtb potentially hijack the control centre of the immune response. Although we know a great deal about the immune response to Mtb in the lung, our understanding of BM immunity to Mtb is extremely limited. The tropism of Mtb for the bone marrow may also explain why it is an incredibly successful pathogen, as the vast majority of our efforts have been dedicated to controlling its growth in the lung while the root of the disease is seeded in the bone marrow. Thus the major objective of this proposal is to define the cellular and molecular signatures involved in HSC activation/function during infection with virulent strains of Mtb or vaccine with the ultimate goal of developing a roadmap of protective versus detrimental immunity to this devastating disease.

In fact, most influenza related deaths result from an unregulated host immune response to the virus rather than the cytopathic effects of the virus itself. column37: Severe infection can lead to many complications within the human body including low blood pressure, which is called septic shock. Some preliminary and limited research in the field has suggested that one specific electrolyte, called chloride, may be harmful when given to patients in high concentrations. The investigators plan to study the impact of giving patients with septic shock intravenous fluids with either a high chloride concentration or a low chloride concentration. If there is benefit seen using low chloride concentration fluids this would be easy to initiate across the world leading to a dramatic and relatively inexpensive improvement in patient care.

column36: Emotion regulation and treatment-based change in children with neurodevelopmental disorders: A diffusion spectrum imaging tractography study
column37: Between 40 - 70% of children with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) such as autism, ADHD and specific learning disorder experience complex emotional problems. Few accessible treatment options are available and current approaches are limited by their focus on one diagnostic category despite frequent overlap of symptoms across disorders; currently over a third of children with NDDs are non-responsive to cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). Emotion regulation - a child's ability to appropriately adapt the intensity of their behaviour - may play a critical role as a moderator of treatment efficacy, modulating symptom expression across a range of emotional difficulties and diagnoses. Additionally, research has identified shared brain-based impairments between groups of children with autism and ADHD, but not OCD, suggesting that these impairments may be common across only the first two disorders. Currently, no research exists using advanced neuroimaging techniques to investigate common neural targets for emotion regulation and treatment-based change in children with NDDs. Further, females are severely underrepresented in clinical pediatric neuroimaging research, limiting the generalizability of current findings. This study has three aims: First, using diffusion spectrum imaging, to identify shared neural biomarkers predicting response to emotion-focused CBT for children with NDDs. Second, to examine the relationship between parent and child-reported emotion regulation and transdiagnostic biomarkers of treatment change; and third, to evaluate findings according to a biological sex and gender-based lens. Greater understanding of the biomarkers related to emotion regulation and treatment responsiveness is critical to ensure a greater number of youth with NDDs are able to access quality care that effectively meets their needs; ultimately, results of this study have the potential to reduce the significant relational and economic costs associated with ineffective treatment.

column36: The Initial Development and Validation of the neuroCognitive Bias Scale for Depression
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide. While many factors may contribute to disability, the extant literature suggests that impairments in thinking abilities (e.g., attention, memory, concentration, decision-making, etc.) that are the primary factors leading to impairment in the day to day functioning. Our research has suggested that it is the perception of these impairments that a patient experiences that lead to disability; not the organic, neurological deficit, per se. As such, I have developed a theory that extends Beck's (1979) seminal research in cognition and depression. I posit that patients with depression have a unique perception (i.e., biased thinking) related to their neurocognitive symptoms. As such, my dissertation will seek to validate a novel construct in the depression literature - 'neurocognitive bias'. Neurocognitive bias is defined as the flawed, or distorted thinking style unique to depressed patients that leads to the perception that one has organic, actual neurocognitive deficits. These deficits can, therefore, lead to disability and impairment in the day to day functioning. It is, therefore, necessary to develop a valid and reliable test to measure neurocognitive bias to accurately diagnose these challenges and to identify treatment targets. My dissertation will 1) develop this tool - the neuroCognitive Impairment Bias Scale (CIBS); 2) validate the CIBS in a patient and control sample; and 3) examine how neurocognitive bias can be targeting in a psychological treatment (i.e., cognitive restructuring), and examine how targeting this bias can improve real-world functioning. Validating this construct, and creating an instrument to measure it will equip clinicians and researchers with an empirically derived method to better understand functional impairments related to depression. Further, treatment targets can be identified to plan and promote the successful return to premorbid levels of social and occupational functioning.

column36: Testing the Efficacy of an Online Self-Help Treatment for Alcohol Misuse and Emotional Problems in Young Adult Manitobans: A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
column37: Nearly half of individuals who struggle with alcohol use also experience emotional problems (i.e., depression and anxiety), especially in Manitoba. The combination of these challenges can have devastating consequences such as more severe symptoms of each disorder, disease, and early death. These combined difficulties also place a financial burden on the healthcare system. The highest rates of these problems are seen among young adults, especially those living in Northern and remote communities. This is concerning as there are often barriers to accessing health services in these areas (e.g., stigma, lack of resources, distance). Considering the high co-occurrence between alcohol use and emotional problems, there is a critical need to develop accessible, cost-effective, self-guided treatments in order to reach the thousands of struggling Manitobans. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to examine the benefits of an online, integrated (i.e., treatment for alcohol use and emotional problems together), self-guided program. Currently, for young adults, no intervention like this exists in Canada that targets the full spectrum of negative emotions (i.e., depression and anxiety). A total of 214 young adults experiencing issues with alcohol use and depression and/or anxiety will be recruited through the treatment website. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either an 8-week online intervention (i.e., integrated cognitive behavioural therapy and motivational interviewing) or to the control group (i.e., education about mental health). This research stands to provide a user-friendly, cost-effective, and feasible option in order to improve the mental health of young adults struggling in the community.

column36: Advancing the Science of Knowledge Translation: Measuring Context
column37: Context is important to the success of interventions aimed to promote use of best available research evidence by healthcare providers in clinical practice. Context refers broadly to social, physical, structural, political, and relational influences on society, organizations, groups, and individuals. Context differs between settings (e.g., between units within hospitals) and changes over time. As a result, context assessment is essential to the design and delivery of interventions to increase the use of research evidence in healthcare. However, information about how to best measure context is lacking. Our previous research focused on obtaining a well-developed and clearly articulated definition of context and resulted in the development of a comprehensive framework (Implementation in CONtext (ICON)) of context domains, defining attributes and their features. Now that we have conceptual clarity on context, the purpose of this project is to advance its measurement. The study will be conducted in two phases. In Phase 1, we will conduct a living systematic review to identify and evaluate measures of context used in knowledge translation and quality improvement studies in any healthcare setting. In Phase 2, using our systematic review findings, we will develop a dynamic publicly accessible resource centre for context measurement in knowledge translation. Central to this resource will be a publicly accessible, interactive web-based repository of the context measures identified. In addition to containing an interactive repository of context measures, the resource centre will provide: 1) access to high-quality context measures; 2) micro-profiles of context measures tailored to users' needs; 3) a decision support tool to aid individuals in selecting context measures appropriate for use in their setting and their specific project; and 4) a research agenda on areas of context measurement where future development, research and/or testing are needed.

column36: Regulating chromatin landscape and organization with non-coding RNAs
column37: Recent technological advances have led to a number of important discoveries. Amongst these is the realization that the better part of our genome is read at one time or another to produce RNA molecules that do not encode proteins. Given that the biological function of most of these "non-coding RNA" transcripts is unknown, they currently fall into different categories based mainly on their size and the site from which they are produced in the genome. The "long non-coding RNAs" (lncRNAs) are one such class of molecules. The biological relevance of many lncRNAs has been demonstrated, with family members even considered as promising therapeutic or prognostic tools. Yet, how they regulate gene expression is very poorly understood. In this project, we suggest using four lncRNAs as discovery tools to identify and characterize new mechanisms used by this family of molecules to control gene expression. These lncRNAs are encoded within the HOXA gene cluster and have been linked to human cancers. We previous showed that one of them, HOTAIRM1, regulates the expression of HOXA genes both by regulating what binds and shapes the DNA encoding them. Our preliminary data indicates that HOTAIRM1 regulates many other genes across the genome. To better understand their biological function, we will first identify new gene targets genome-wide. We will investigate how they regulate genome folding and spatial organization using state-of-the-art technologies that yield three-dimensional maps of our genome at very high resolution. This information will then be used to characterize the molecular mechanisms used by the HOXA-encoded lncRNAs to regulate gene expression, and test our hypothesis that given lncRNAs can use different molecular mechanisms to modulate gene expression depending on the DNA context and/or target gene.

column36: Elucidation of bromodomain functions within SWI/SNF complexes
column37: The effective structural regulation and utilization of a cell's genetic material is essential to its fitness. Unsurprisingly, it is now clear that epigenetic regulators, proteins that organize and regulate the accessibility of the genetic material, are commonly altered in human diseases, including cancer. Unfortunately, fundamental understanding of the functions of the ten bromodomains incorporated in SWI/SNF complex components is still lacking. This project aims to provide this knowledge by employing state-of-the-art tools to identify the cellular targets of SWI/SNF bromodomains, examine how they engage these targets, and determine the functions of these interactions. column36: Diagnosis of Aggressive Prostate Cancer Using Key Features of Raman Spectroscopy
column37: The diagnosis of prostate cancer, the most frequent cancer among Canadian men, is fraught with recurrent difficulties in establishing the aggressiveness of the disease (prognosis). In this project, we first aim to verify how each of these key feature can be used clinically to improve the identification of this aggressive variant of prostate cancer. To do this, we will use a special type of Raman spectroscopy, which is based on the targeted evaluation of one key feature at the time. To do this, we will use mass spectrometry, a technique which allows to identify specific molecules according partly to their weight. Overall, this study will not only provide a comprehensive understanding of our previous results, but it will in parallel establish a clinically applicable method and provide a unique opportunity to identify new potential diagnostic and/or therapeutic biomarkers of prostate cancer.

column36: Symptom Screening Linked to Care Pathways for Children with Cancer: a Cluster Randomized Trial
column37: Most children with cancer survive because they are given intensive treatments. Unfortunately, these treatments are associated with distressing symptoms. Poor symptom control occurs because children do not have a way to report and track their symptoms, healthcare providers are not aware of these symptoms, and guidelines for symptom management are not easy to access. To address these gaps, we developed the Symptom Screening in Pediatrics Tool (SSPedi) for children receiving cancer treatments. We also created evidence-based guidelines to help providers know how to manage symptoms. To bring identification and management of symptoms together, we created a web-based application called Supportive care Prioritization, Assessment and Recommendations for Kids (SPARK). In intervention institutions, we will prompt children newly diagnosed with cancer to complete symptom screening three times weekly for 8 weeks. Reports will be emailed to the primary healthcare team. We will also create care pathways that help clinicians know how to best manage symptoms. Participants in control sites will receive the standard of care. We will not facilitate symptom screening with feedback or create care pathways. We will enroll English and Spanish-speaking children 8-18 years of age with a new diagnosis of cancer and a plan for treatment. The primary endpoint will be the week 8 total SSPedi score (ranges from 0-60; higher means worse symptoms). We plan to enroll 444 children across 20 US institutions. This study is proposed for US sites because we are conducting a CIHR-funded randomized trial evaluating 5 consecutive days of symptom screening and feedback among hospitalized pediatric cancer patients in 7 Canadian sites. These studies cannot be conducted at the same site. This study will test an innovative application to improve symptom control and quality of life for children receiving cancer treatments.

column36: Implication of neutrophil extracellular traps in the efficacy of bladder-sparing therapy in muscle invasive bladder cancer
column37: Radical cystectomy remains the standard of care for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). This surgery entails complete removal of the bladder and surrounding organs, leading to a serious impact on the quality of life (QoL) of patients and associated with a 5-year overall survival of only 50 %. Radiation therapy (RT), which preserves the bladder, would be a more appropriate treatment modality if we could improve efficacy, as lack of local control remains problematic. As part from its direct tumor cell killing potential, there is increasing evidence that RT also leads to significant alterations in the tumor microenvironment, which inflammation being one of the most important factors modulating radiation responsiveness of tumors. During the acute phase of inflammation, neutrophils are one of the first-line responders of inflammatory cells to migrate towards the site of inflammation. Recently, it has been shown neutrophils can exhibit dual behaviors and are increasingly being seen as important players in cancer progression. Neutrophils can expel DNA studded with various proteins to form web-like structures known as neutrophil extracellular traps (NET), which has been shown to be associated with tumor progression and metastasis. Our preliminary findings strongly indicate NET are implicated in radioresistance. Determining the NET-related molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying response to radiation will have direct clinical relevance to better select patients who will benefit most from bladder preservation therapy. The novel approach of the proposal herein can bring transformative changes in developing novel strategies in bladder cancer (BC) therapy as it has the potential to transfer from the bench to the patient, an unquestionably, positive impact on survival and quality of life of MIBC patients.

column36: Microbial Causes of Ulcerative Colitis: Looking Outside the Involved Region
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic disease affecting the gut with limited treatments and significant risk of needing surgery to remove the large bowel (colon). It is very concerning that we still don't know what causes UC, especially since it is becoming more common, particularly in children in Canada. Microbes (mostly bacteria) are different in UC but we don't know if they cause the disease or are changed because of the inflammation found in UC. We have recently shown that children with UC have different bacteria in the healthy-appearing small bowel; we have also developed and just published a new method to isolate bacteria that might be virulent (disease causing) by utilizing the patient's immune system to trap bacteria and identified how they might do this. The next step is to combine these findings and find bacteria that might be causing or at least driving damage in UC. To do this we will also take advantage of some of the basic and unexplained features of UC: 1. It only involves the colon; 2. It is a continuous disease; 3. The appendix seems to have an important (but not understood) role. This study will build on these interesting observations to test our hypothesis that bacteria (and molecules/products they make) from unaffected areas travel down the bowel and cause the damage seen in UC. We will test this by collecting samples from different parts of the bowel in children just diagnosed with UC during a colonoscopy test. Three large Canadian centers, that are already working together through a funded National Network, will collect samples during colonoscopy to identify these bacteria. We will find the bacteria that travel down to the sick areas and identify those that can penetrate and injure the bowel and those that activate the immune system. We will then confirm that these bacteria indeed cause damage using cell models and germ-free mice. This will help explain what causes UC and will direct new therapies.

column36: The roles of betaine and its mitochondrial synthesis in oocyte and preimplantation embryo health
column37: There is strong evidence that the mother's nutrition, health, and environment during the earliest stages of pregnancy immediately after conception can significantly affect the health of the embryo and the fetus and placenta into which it develops. Also, the treatment of human infertility by assisted reproduction technologies (ART), in which multiple eggs are obtained from women, fertilized, and cultured for an extended period before being transferred into the uterus, has been very effective and produced millions of babies, but there is increasing evidence that how eggs and very early embryos are handled during ART can damage eggs before fertilization and can cause health problems in the fetus, placenta, and offspring. In this work, we will be investigating mechanisms that may be important in preventing such problems. We are focusing on a molecule called betaine, which is a modified form of the common amino acid glycine. Betaine is supplied in the diet, for example by wheat germ, spinach, and shellfish. It can also be synthesized in the body from the vitamin, choline. We have previously found that betaine has important roles in mammalian eggs and very early embryos. One function is to control cell size, which turns out to be particularly critical for early embryo health. Another role is in supplying the molecules needed for controlling gene activity in later embryos, just before they implant in the uterus. We also have new evidence that betaine is also involved in the normal function of mitochondria, which are the part of the cell that makes energy, in eggs. How betaine is supplied to the egg and embryo, where it comes from, and the consequences of its dysregulation, are still poorly understood. We hope to show that creating the conditions in which these mechanisms can function normally in eggs and very early embryos will produce healthy eggs and embryos.

column36: Perivascular fibroblasts in maintaining blood vessel integrity
column37: Blood vessels are essential to sustain life in humans. Defects in blood vessels can result in serious consequences, such as hemorrhage, tissue ischemia, and stroke. The conventional view is that interactions between endothelial cells, the inner layer of the blood vessel, and surrounding vessel support cells known as mural cells help keep the blood vessel as a stable tube. Loss of these cells result in fragile vessels prone to damage. We will determine where these perivascular fibroblasts come from during embryo development and how they help stabilize blood vessels. Since the organization of the vasculature and underlying genetic mechanisms are remarkably similar between zebrafish and human, our work in zebrafish may provide insights on how to treat patients with fragile blood vessels.

column36: The regulation of mRNA translation by the Nucleoporin RanBP2/Nup358
column37: To express a gene, its DNA must copied into mRNA in the nucleus. This mRNA is then packaged into complexes that contain proteins and known as messenger ribonucleoproteins (mRNPs). These mRNPs are then ferried across the nuclear pore to reach the cytoplasm where they are used by ribosomes to make new proteins. These proteins are functional molecules that impact the development, physiology and homeostasis of the organism. We have uncovered a key step in the gene expression pathway. We have shown that the protein RanBP2, which is part of the nuclear pore, is required for the efficient production of secretory proteins, likely by modifying how mRNAs are packaged into mRNPs. This mRNP maturation event likely impacts how many mRNAs are translated into proteins. Mutations in RanBP2 are associated to Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy 1 (ANE1), a condition where otherwise normal individuals overproduce cytokines in response to influenza infections. This leads to seizures, coma and a high rate of mortality. Four separate dominant point mutations in RanBP2 have been linked to this disease. In cells that lack RanBP2 or that have mutations that impair its ability to modify other proteins, we find that the cytokine interleukin 6 (IL6) is over-expressed, indicating that RanBP2 likely alters the mRNP that contains the mRNA that is used to make IL6 protein. In this proposal we outline our plans to determine the molecular mechanisms by which RanBP2 regulates mRNP maturation. We have also been in contact with families afflicted by ANE1 and we plan to use epithelial nasal swabs and white blood cells (monocytes) from these patients to understand how mutations in RanBP2 alters cytokine production in normal conditions and after viral infection. Our work will not only provide key insights into the pathology of ANE1, but will also provide a deeper understanding of how RanBP2 regulates the expression of cytokines and other secretory proteins.

column36: Hypoxia mimicry for enhancing peripheral nerve regeneration
column37: In the absence of sufficient oxygen (i.e. during hypoxia), cells die. When oxygen levels are low but not lethal, cells can cope by changing how they metabolize nutrients: they use alternate mechanisms that do not depend so heavily on oxygen, and at the same time increase the capacity for oxygen to be delivered (increasing the number of red blood cells and blood vessels, for example). Interestingly, these mechanisms are also partially engaged when nerves are injured, as they are in 2-3% of all injuries to any part of the body. Nerve injury leads to loss of function (sensation and movement, for example), as well as to neuropathic pain, most frequently described as unpleasant burning, electric shock-like, or crushing sensations. Often these consequences of nerve injury fail to resolve, prompting us to ask whether artificially engaging the hypoxia response can improve peripheral nerve regeneration and reduce neuropathic pain. Our cells "know" how much oxygen is present by virtue of oxygen-sensing proteins called PHDs. There are three of these: PHD1, 2 and 3. When these proteins are blocked with a drug (DMOG), or genetically silenced, cells are "tricked" into behaving as they would under hypoxia. We will use DMOG and PHD-deficient mice to ask whether and how mimicking hypoxia can improve recovery, including preventing neuropathic pain, following nerve injury.

column36: Synaptic physiology and structure of human muscle in a 3D cell culture system: Application to Duchenne's Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Duchennes's Muscular Dystrophy is a disease of muscle that affects approximately 1 in 3500 boys. Disease starts early in life when young boys fail to reach key milestones in their motor development and it is progressive; children are soon bound to a wheelchair and most die in their 20s and 30s from cardiac and respiratory complications. Lack of Dystrophin leads to a breakdown of the Dystrophin Glycoprotein Complex and consequently results in muscle membrane fragility, damage, inflammation, and cell death. Recent technical developments in the areas of stem-cell therapy and gene editing have given renewed hope to developing a treatment for DMD. However, we Identify a knowledge gap in our understanding of the effects of DMD mutations on the physiology of human muscle and synapses. Our proposed experiments are designed to fill that gap and will subsequently direct our studies of therapeutic treatments, especially research into existing pharmaceutical approaches To enable this research, we have developed a pioneering 3D muscle cell culture system to analyze the neuromuscular physiology and structure of human muscle cells grown from healthy and DMD-patient stem cells. Such human muscle microtissues (hMMT) will serve as the model system in our studies. By completing this work we will derive new knowledge of the effects of DMD mutations on human neuro-muscular physiology and test therapeutic efficacy of compounds to improve performance of DMD-affected muscle.

column36: Chromatin context of somatic mutations delineate oncogenic drivers in triple-negative breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is a collection of different types of cancer. One of these, known as triple-negative breast cancer, comprises approximately 20% of breast cancers diagnosed each year. It is highly aggressive and the only standard-of-care therapy offered to patients is chemotherapy, which unfortunately fails in over 40% of patients. This leads to disease progression and death. Hence, new approaches are required to treat and cure triple-negative breast cancer patients. To address this need for new therapy we propose to identify what drives growth of triple-negative breast cancer. In the last year, scientists identified thousands of mutations that populate the genome of triple-negative breast cancer, but unlike other types of breast cancer, the "drivers" are not easy to identity due to the diversity of mutations across patients. We argue that the heterogeneity of mutations underlies their convergence toward common targets. We developed in recent years two methods to identify drivers of cancer development based on convergence of mutations towards genes or proteins. Here, we propose to apply these methods to mine mutations found in triple-negative breast cancer and find the drivers of growth. My approaches contrast with standard strategies in the field by comprehensively analyzing each mutation based on the normal function of the DNA sequence they alter, inclusive of genes and the remaining 98% of DNA sequences found in each cancer cell. My ultimate goal is to identify drivers of oncogenesis, based on the genetics of tumours taking into account their epigenetic context, and use this information to precisely find targets for drug treatment against triple-negative breast cancer. Overall, this proposal is at the forefront of personalized cancer medicine and offers a unique opportunity to accelerate the translation of research discoveries into improved clinical care.

column36: Prognostic Biomarkers and Novel Therapies for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Patients
column37: Patients with head and neck cancer have a 50% 5-year survival. Patients are treated with surgery, and may also receive radiation therapy, or combined radiation and chemotherapy. These therapies are very toxic and can have long-term negative side effects. The needs for these patients include: 1) A better way to identify which patients are in need of more aggressive therapy; 2) More effective therapies for those patients with the most aggressive and life-threatening disease. We have been acquiring tumor tissues from HNSCC patients for many years and implanting them into mice with a defective immune system. 2/3 of these samples successfully grow in the mice ("engraft") and they grow at varying rates: some form a 1 cm mass within a short time (<8 weeks; rapid engrafters); others grow more slowly and can take up to 6 months to form a 1 cm mass; and still others fail to grow at all. Our proposal is focused on using these results to identify new therapies, in particular for those patients that have the most aggressive disease. We will do this by: 1) Identifying the genetic differences between patients in the three categories (rapid engrafters, slow engrafters, and non-engrafters); 2) Using the genetic information to identify drugs predicted to target the genetic profile of rapid engrafters. Any drug candidates that we identify can be tested for their efficacy against aggressive, rapidly growing tumors in the engrafted mice. This project will result in "biomarkers", which can be used to predict which patients have the most aggressive form of the disease and thus adjust their therapies appropriately, and also in new candidate therapies for these patients.

column36: Inflammation and LDL transcytosis - implications for early atherosclerosis
column37: Atherosclerosis leads to heart attacks and strokes and is a leading cause of death in Canada. The first step in the disease is the build-up of the bad cholesterol, LDL, in the wall of blood vessels. Specifically, LDL builds up under the innermost layer of arteries, called the endothelium. How the LDL gets under the endothelium is very poorly understood. We have discovered ways to study this process, which is known as LDL transcytosis. We now wish to learn how a big risk factor for heart disease - inflammation - affects LDL transcytosis. We suspect that inflammation causes more LDL transcytosis to occur, accelerating the build-up of cholesterol in the artery wall. Understanding how this happens will help us develop ways to prevent or treat it. If we can prevent cholesterol from accumulating in the blood vessel wall, we will prevent heart disease and stroke. We will use sophisticated microscopes to study the process by which cholesterol builds up under the special cells that line blood vessels, known as endothelium. We will identify the specific molecules that regulate this build-up, especially under conditions of inflammation. We will also prove that our findings from cells hold true in mice, which are the typical animals used in studies of atherosclerosis. We will compare our findings using cells from men as well as women to determine if there is a sex-based difference. We are the only lab in Canada to study this process of transcytosis, by which the bad cholesterol (LDL) gets under endothelial cells. We therefore have the potential to make huge advances in this field of research.

column36: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial of a group self-management support program for anxiety disorders
column37: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental disorders in Canada, and they are responsible for substantial psychological distress, disability, and health service needs. Self-management support (SMS) is an innovative intervention, complementary to usual care, with great potential to support personal recovery of individuals with anxiety disorders. The Revivre community organization has developed a structured 10-week group SMS program for anxiety disorders. This clinical trial aims at examining the effectiveness of the intervention as a complement to usual care at post treatment and follow-up (4, 8, 12 and 24 months). The intervention will be compared to treatment-as-usual in community-based care. Participants will comprise adults with clinically-significant anxiety symptoms that will be recruited through primary care clinics, bulletin boards and social media in four regions of Quebec. The outcome measures will include anxiety symptoms, personal recovery, self-management behaviors and service utilization. column37: Retinoblastoma (Rb) is the most common cancer of the eye in children and accounts for 3% of all childhood malignancies. Yet, despite considerable efforts, persistent or recurrent tumor growing in vitreous cavity is still a major cause of treatment failure in advanced Rb, because they are remote from the blood supply and rely on diffusion of chemotherapy into the vitreous humor from the retina. Several drugs have been developed for the treatment of Rb, but they kill cancer cells as well as healthy cells which leads to excruciating side effects. My lab has a long-standing interest in developing novel anticancer reagents and strategies. Our recent studies have shown that one of the small biomolecules exhibits dramatic effect of inducing Rb cell death. As these molecules are prone to degradation by cellular enzymes, we propose to encapsulate them in biocompatible and biodegradable nano-sized lipid carriers and delivered locally to target vitreous Rb cells, in such a way to minimize the side effects of current Rb therapies and increases the anti-Rb efficiency. In this proposal, we will assess the ability of the nanostructured lipid carriers loaded with the particular small biomolecule to suppress vitreous Rb growth in well-established animal models. In addition, we will investigate the efficacy of combination therapies, as well as their pharmacokinetics and tissue toxicity. Moreover, we will also dissect how this small biomolecule kill Rb cells at the molecular levels in order to develop better strategies and interventions. Cancer research is an intricate process and it is only through multi-pronged approaches that valuable therapies will emerge. We have generated knowledge, tools, and partnerships with other groups and expertise that place us in a unique position to make major contributions to the Rb cancer research field. We expect that efficacious compounds combine with nanotechnology for targeting vitreous Rb will bring enormous benefits to Rb patients.

column36: The Role of Intramuscular Immune Cell Infiltrations in Tumor and Age Related Muscle Wasting
column37: Muscle wasting that occurs with cancer is known as cachexia and with aging is called sarcopenia. Cachexia and sarcopenia are important healthcare issues. Cachexia affects the majority of patients with late stage malignancy, and is thought to contribute to one third of cancer deaths, while sarcopenia is associated with falls, disability, and mortality in the elderly, and costs as high as 1.5% of our total healthcare expenditure. Despite these significant features, cachexia and sarcopenia are relatively understudied entities with poor understanding of their pathophysiology. One common link that could explain how these conditions occur is the immune system. Our research focuses on the idea that both tumors and an aging body release factors that activate some cells of the immune system which, in turn, release other signals that cause muscles to shrink. Our preliminary data suggest that the immune cell at the "heart" of this process is the myeloid derived suppressor cell (MDSC). These cells rapidly rise during cancer, and steadily rise during aging. Using mice with cachexia caused by tumors, and sarcopenia of old age, we have identified subsets of these MDSCs infiltrating hearts and skeletal muscle. On depletion of these cells during mouse models of cancer, we can eliminate muscle wasting, even though the cancer remains. In this grant, we will characterize the nature of the MDSCs infiltrating the hearts and skeletal muscles during cachexia and sarcopenia, and their role in these processes using functional assays and state of the art technologies, including single cell sequencing. Next, we will determine which factors support the generation and activation of these cells. Finally, we determine the mechanisms by which these cells cause muscles to shrink in cachexia and sarcopenia. Understanding how these immune cells tell the heart and muscles to shrink can help us to prevent or revert these processes and improve the lives of people with muscle wasting from age or cancer.

column37: Preschoolers are exposed to many stressful situations at home and daycare. This is especially true for children who manifest disruptive behaviours or live in low-income neighbourhoods. Repeated and prolonged stress may result in unusually high levels of the "stress hormone" cortisol. Chronically elevated cortisol can have damaging effects on the developing brain, affecting later health and social functioning. It is therefore in the public interest to reduce chronic stress in preschoolers while they are learning social skills essential to have harmonious relationships with others later in life. Our project proposes to test whether two interventions can reduce chronic stress in preschoolers and which one is the best. One is the training of daycare educators for a program that uses a puppet to promote social skills and positive relationships between children at daycare. The other is group training for parents promoting positive parenting practices. Each intervention will be provided over a period of one year and 3 months. We will measure cortisol levels in hair before and twice after the interventions. Our study is paired with the already funded I-CARE trial that will be conducted to reduce behaviour problems in 80 daycares in low-income neighbourhoods in the Montreal and Sherbrooke regions (1280 2-4 year-olds). From our pilot study, we expect that the interventions will reduce chronic stress and improve social behaviour. Results will advance knowledge on child development and how prevention programs work. Our findings will also document which intervention works best and for whom, which could help allocating more effectively our limited resources.

column37: Some women without diabetes develop high blood sugar levels during pregnancy. This condition, called "gestational diabetes", is a health risk to the mother during pregnancy, and to her baby at birth. It also increases both her and her baby's risk of developing diabetes or heart disease in the future. People from the Indian subcontinent, called South Asians, are among the largest nonwhite ethnic groups in Canada, and they develop gestational diabetes twice as often as White women. Diet changes during pregnancy may improve her blood sugar levels. It is hard to make diet changes during pregnancy, but many women do because it is good for her and her baby's health. We think that seeing a nutrition coach during pregnancy can help a woman improve her diet, but we are not sure if this will result in important changes in blood sugar levels. We plan to: 1)Test whether a personalized nutrition plan designed for South Asian women, and delivered by a health coach, can improve blood sugar levels during pregnancy. 2)Test whether a personalized nutrition plan designed for South Asian women, and delivered by a health coach, can prevent gestational diabetes. Working with family doctors and obstetricians, we will identify pregnant South Asian women living in the Peel region, and ask them if they would like to be part of the research study. If a woman is eligible and agrees, we will invite her to our clinic, explain the study to her, and collect some health information. We will then assign her, based on a coin flip, to receive usual dietary advice for pregnant women (provided by Health Canada) or our personalized nutrition plan. Women in both groups get text messages encouraging them to walk. Women who see the health coach set nutrition goals, review them with the health coach every other week, and get text messages to support diet changes. At the 24th week of pregnancy, all women will take a test that measures blood sugar control and tells us if the woman has gestational diabetes.

column36: How does insulin interact with the blood-brain barrier? Therapeutic implications for diabetes and Alzheimer's disease.
column37: Insulin is a hormone essential for life. It is best known for its effect on the regulation of blood sugar levels; the reason why it is an essential player in the pharmaceutical treatment of diabetes. It is increasingly recognized that insulin in the blood also affects the brain. For example, insulin is under clinical trial in Alzheimer's disease, because studies show it improves memory. However, between the blood and the brain stands what we call the "blood-brain barrier" or BBB. The BBB is mainly composed of highly active cells called "endothelial cells", which basically control everything that goes in the brain or that goes out. Although small quantities of insulin are generated in the brain, the vast majority is produced by the pancreas and secreted in the bloodstream. Therefore, to interact with brain cells, blood insulin must first interact with the BBB. Surprisingly enough, how exactly insulin interacts with the BBB remains relatively unknown. Although it is clear that insulin must interact with its receptor located on the BBB, we don't know much of what happens next. The purpose of the present grant application is to better understand how blood insulin (i) is transported into the brain, (ii) stimulates BBB endothelial cells to carry metabolic information into the brain, (iii) changes brain function and behavior. We expect that answering these questions will be extremely useful for treating not only diabetes, but also Alzheimer's disease. For example, we recently found that neurotoxic amyloid peptides are washed out of the brain into the bloodstream within minutes after an injection of insulin, suggesting that insulin-related mechanisms can be used to treat this terrible disease. In summary, we hope that the present proposal will contribute to develop new drugs that will benefit both diabetes and Alzheimer's disease patients.

column36: Healthy Aging: The effects of Parenthood and APOE Genotype on Cognitive Decline
column37: Parenthood is a dramatic life transformation that has profound effects on the brain however this has mostly been studied in the short term (during pregnancy and postpartum) and in females. In the long term, multiple pregnancies increase risk for conditions like Alzheimer's disease, stroke, cardiovascular disease, and obesity. Females who have had multiple pregnancies are a higher risk of developing dementia, show worse brain pathological symptoms and an earlier onset of Alzheimer's disease. This suggests that fundamental aspects of female physiology and life experiences contribute to the disease. Females that have not had any children show better memory in middle age compared to females that have had children but not all studies agree. Factors such as genes (APOE, a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease) and female specific factors such as age of menopause, sex of the fetus, and hormone therapies can affect cognition. On the other hand, in the short-term, males show changes in hormones and brain structure in response to fatherhood, but long-term changes on brain, disease and cognition have received very little attention. To better understand the effects of parenthood on cognition later in life, it is important to study large populations and take genes and female-specific factors into account. This study will investigate how parenthood and genes (APOE) along with sociological factors (age and education) affect cognition in older females and males using a large Canadian database (The Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging). These findings will advance our understanding of how parenthood influences brain aging and cognitive decline in older females and males. Isolating specific risk factors and incidence trends could have significant impact on future treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. This work will also address important and understudied physiological aspects of aging in females. We expect our findings will eventually lead to improved outcomes for all patients.

column36: Enabling the Engineering of Vascular Grafts with Human Cells-Appliations to Pulmonary Arterial Grafting
column37: Limited native vessels are available for arterial vascular grafts (AVGs) to address the needs of patients, some requiring many grafts and patient groups with varied vascular conditions, such as the growing adult population with diabetes which may have multiple other illnesses, complicating their condition. There are also many with more specific challenges related to critical vascular conditions, for example patients with complex congenital heart disease (CHD) due to genetic defects at birth or other events affecting heart development, leading to poor heart ejections, and subsequently vascular stenosis and clotting of the pulmonary arteries (PA). Small vessels (less than 10mm) tissue engineering has attracted research interest for generating living blood vessels given the inability to always have access to a patient's own vessels, and the inherent pro-clotting and poor mechanical match of synthetic implants. Our research is advancing the generation of a synthetic tissue engineered scaffold (made of patented degradable polar/hydrophobic/ionic (D-PHI) polyurethane), conceived to harness the body's own wound healing character with white blood cells. column36: Novel animal and cellular paradigms for studying prion formation
column37: Prion disorders are incurable diseases of the ageing brain that affect both humans and animals. Examples include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in humans, scrapie in sheep, chronic wasting disease in deer and elk, and "mad cow disease". In prion disease, a protein (the "prion protein") clumps together in the brain to form aggregates called prions. Prions cause the death of brain cells and are able to spread within the brain. Under certain circumstances, prions can also transmit disease between people or animals. However, most cases of prion disease in humans do not result from infection but instead occur due to the spontaneous formation of prions in the brain. Little is known about the initial events that cause the prion protein to clump together to form prions, and we currently lack the appropriate tools to study this process. In this proposal, we will use genetically-engineered cells and mice to re-create and study the initial events that cause the prion protein to clump together in prion disease. In particular, we will take advantage of the unique properties of the prion protein from the bank vole, a rodent that is especially susceptible to prion disease. These studies will provide new tools for studying prion disease and will uncover new strategies for treating these devastating disorders.

column36: Predicting and preventing brain injury in the antenatal period
column37: An insufficient supply of oxygen and nutrients to the developing fetus impairs normal growth and risks causing lasting and serious injury to the body organs that have the highest consumption of oxygen, especially the developing brain. Growth restriction of this kind affects 5% of pregnancies in Canada and is particularly difficult to diagnose near the end of pregnancy because of limitations of current diagnostic ultrasound methods. Our proposal is to develop a new diagnostic imaging procedure for reliable use late in pregnancy that could aid in identifying these fetuses that have insufficient oxygen and are at risk of either brain injury or death. We will make use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a specialized measurement protocol called BOLD to assess the health of a fetus. While many of the technical aspects of making BOLD measurements have already been established in pregnant women, it is presently not known how to interpret these data to identify fetuses at risk. We propose to overcome this challenge by using experimental mice under controlled conditions to learn specific signatures of fetal distress that could be applied in human pregnancies. Our research strategy makes use of pregnant mice where pregnancy continues too long, such that the needs of the fetus exceed the available supply of oxygen and nutrients. By taking advantage of advances in genetic engineering in mice, specialized 3D optical imaging methods to visualize the smallest of blood vessels, and computational methods that will relate the distribution of oxygen among the fetal organs to BOLD signal, we proposed to gain a clear understanding of how to use this MRI technology to identify fetuses at risk from brain injury. We will also evaluate this approach for guiding an intervention to protect the fetus from brain injury. This work will open a new avenue for anticipating and preventing brain injury that will be translated into improved clinical outcomes.

column36: Mechanisms regulating contribution of pericytes to brain repair after stroke
column37: Stroke constitutes a major cause of death and disability of the adults in Canada, imposing considerable burden on society and economy. Currently, no efficient therapy exists. The cerebral blood vessels form with the nerve cells a functional interface that enables proper brain functioning. The interface comprises multifunctional perivascular cells located between nerve cells and vessels, called pericytes. Emerging reports are suggesting that pericytes contribute to brain repair after stroke by giving rise to other brain cell types, namely nerve and vascular cells. Our findings suggest that the reparative potential of pericytes is regulated by low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms, which are induced after stroke due to blood interruption. Our findings suggest as well that targeting pericytes using pharmacological and cell-based approaches stimulates brain regeneration. The project will dissect how low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms regulate the intrinsic capacity of pericytes to convert to other cells types to compensate for the lost brain tissue. Furthermore, the project will explore novel therapeutic interventions to promote recovery by exploiting the reparative capabilities of pericytes. To achieve these objectives, clinically relevant animal stroke models in which low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms are genetically modified in pericytes will be used. Furthermore, novel cell transplantation approach will be applied by delivering into the brain via the intranasal cavity pericytes modified to convert to nerve and vascular cells. The expected results will provide new fundamental insights into how low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms regulate the reparative capabilities of pericytes, and will highlight new cell-based therapeutic avenues for stroke that can be safely used in patients.

column36: Disc degeneration, back pain and obesity: PPARdelta as a potential therapeutic target
column37: Back pain is the most common cause of disability worldwide, affecting over 80% of Canadians. Though the specific causes of back pain are not well understood, it is often associated with degeneration of intervertebral discs, the cartilaginous structures that anchor adjacent vertebrae along the spine. The exact cause of disc degeneration is unclear, but it is associated clinically with risk factors including age, sex, obesity and genetic variants. The health care and socio-economic burden resulting from the exceptionally high prevalence of disc degeneration and back pain requires research focused on better understanding the biological processes that regulate disease initiation in order to identify potential therapeutic targets. Our recent work has identified a potential novel treatment strategy, by identifying a role for a specific class of proteins called nuclear receptors in intervertebral disc disease. These proteins are metabolic regulators that might explain the link between obesity and disc degeneration. Using genetically modified mice we showed that when the nuclear receptor PPARdelta is removed from the intervertebral disc, mice are protected from disc degeneration. In this grant, we propose to further investigate the role of nuclear receptor activity in the intervertebral disc, using existing genetically modified mice and model systems. We will characterize how loss of PPARdelta alters age-associated and or diet-induced disc degeneration in mouse models. These studies will measure markers of degeneration in disc tissues, as well as pain related behavior in the mice. column37: Traditional chemo- and radiation-therapy, though often effective, has serious side and long-term effects, particularly for children, who face significant life-long health problems and increased risk for secondary cancers. We need to develop new "targeted therapies" that selectively attack cancer cells and leave healthy organs untouched. Targeted therapies are drugs that interfere with a specific molecule, the 'target', in the cancer cell to block its growth or kill it. The most specific targets are 'abnormal' proteins created by mutation or fusion between two genes. These abnormal proteins are found only in cancer cells, and are distinguishable from normal proteins. But they are also rare. Therefore, most targeted therapies are directed at proteins that occur in both healthy and cancer cells, and so they cause side effects. When they are uncoiled, proteins are a long chain of amino acids that have a start and an end, called the termini. The process called proteolysis cuts the protein apart, creating fragments that have different termini. We have shown that we can identify and quantify these termini in healthy and unhealthy cells, and we could show that in cancer proteolysis creates new termini not found in healthy cells. We found that there are more differences between termini than between the proteins. We now propose to study bone marrow biopsies from children with leukemia to identify cancer specific termini that have the potential to work as drug target. In addition, we will test blood and spinal fluid from these children. If we can find the other part of the protein, that has been cleaved off and released from the cancer cell, we may be able to use this fragment as very specific marker, not only for leukemia in general, but for the presence of the specific drug target. We will also investigate the mechanisms leading to the cleavage that generates the terminus and fragment. Our work will help to develop therapies that target only cancer cells.

column36: Novel insights into GnRH regulation of gonadotropin synthesis
column37: Fertility depends on the coordinated actions of many organs in the body that communicate with via hormones. The brain synthesizes and secretes gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which controls production of two pituitary gland hormones, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). The pituitary also secretes FSH and LH into the blood in response to GnRH. FSH and LH act on the ovaries in females and the testicles in males to control the production of eggs and sperm as well as the synthesis of sex steroid hormones like estrogen and testosterone. During female reproductive cycle, there is a surge of GnRH secretion that promotes a corresponding surge of LH release, which triggers ovulation. Though we have a general understanding of where and how each of these hormones acts, fundamental gaps in knowledge remain. In this application, we propose to address three questions about the mechanisms through which GnRH acts in gonadotrope cells. First, does GnRH stimulate the production of protein called activating transcription factor 3 to selectively stimulate the synthesis of FSH? Second, does GnRH activate a novel intracellular pathway to trigger the LH surge? Finally, does GnRH stimulation of LH synthesis depend on a specific class of enzymes in the protein kinase C family? The answers to these questions will greatly advance our understanding of the hormonal control of reproduction, but may also identify potential treatments for human infertility disorders, including polycystic ovarian syndrome.

column36: Effect of Maternal Disease on Placental Transporters and Fetal Drug Exposure
column37: Many diseases require women to be on drug therapy during pregnancy, however there is little information on drug levels in mother and unborn baby. Several transporters are found in high amounts in the placenta and prevent the transfer of drugs from mother to fetus. The total amount of transporter in placenta influences the amount of drug that unborn babies get exposed to and resulting health problems. Many sudden or chronic diseases such as preeclampsia, lupus and arthritis are associated with inflammation. Therefore changes in placental transporters due to these diseases likely contribute to increased fetal drug exposure. The effect of disease, the underlying causes and the overall effect of these changes on the fetus remain unknown. Hypothesis: Altered levels and activity of transporters due to disease will influence fetal drug exposure. Research Strategy: We will examine the effect of preeclampsia and common inflammatory diseases on transporters in human placenta, examine what disease factors are responsible and the process by which this happens. Using experimental animal models we will then examine the impact of changes in transporter abundance and maternal disease on the amount of drug that mothers and their unborn babies are exposed to. Application: Diseases which occur in many pregnant women can alter levels of drug transporters which can affect the amount of drug that gets across placenta. The results from this study will help us to estimate how much drug gets to the unborn baby and will help in selecting drugs and doses for these women.

column36: Novel Roles for Iron Regulatory Protein 1
column37: Life on earth without iron is nearly impossible. Iron is important for many functions in our body, and probably best known for its role in transporting oxygen, allowing us to breathe. Inhaled oxygen is bound by iron, which sits at the centre of a special molecule called heme. The heme molecule itself is docked to a larger structure called hemoglobin, and together, they deliver oxygen to where it is needed via the bloodstream. These heme groups are also important for other processes in our cells, including the removal of harmful substances and the production of steroid hormones, like the famous testosterone. The King-Jones lab uses the fruit fly as a model to study undiscovered aspects of iron biology. When they studied steroid hormone-producing cells, they discovered that these cells have very high levels of iron and heme. Importantly, King-Jones and colleagues learned that they can take advantage of this system to learn new things about how humans regulate their iron "balance sheet". Since both too much and too little iron can cause severe diseases in humans, it is essential that we learn more about how iron handled in our bodies, and how this is regulated. Using a range of genetic tricks, King-Jones and colleagues have recently discovered more than 20 genes with unexpected roles in regulating and balancing appropriate iron levels. Three of these genes shed new light on how the so-called "Iron Regulatory Protein 1" (IRP1) works. Researchers have studied IRP1 for more than 30 years, and know that IRP1 is very important for our health. The new findings in the King-Jones lab show that our current ideas about how IRP1 controls proper iron balance in cells are remarkably incomplete. The study of these new, unexpected aspects of iron regulation helps us to understand better diseases that are caused by too much or too little iron.

column36: Injury Risk to Youth Skateboarders in Skateparks
column37: Skateboarding is gaining in popularity. In fact, estimates show a growth rate exceeding that of any other sport and reaching 166% yearly. With increasing growth of the sport, there has been a dramatic increase in the popularity of skateparks (SP). Municipalities are building SP to move skateboarders away from traffic, to motivate more outdoor play activities in an effort to improve health, and in response to demands from youth and parents for safe-play resources for skateboarders. In Study 2 we will conduct focus group interviews with youth skateboarders, including those who have experienced a fracture on the SP, to understand their perspectives on our findings and suggestions for solutions. These findings will be used to develop a "Guide for Safer Skateboarding for Youth" which will highlight the risk behaviors that increase risk of injuries. These studies can inform future efforts to prevent injuries to youth who skateboard on skateparks.

column36: Defining the peroxisome-lipid signaling network in innate immunity.
column37: Organisms need an efficient and tightly controlled immune system to defend against infections and cancer. Recently, scientists discovered that immune cells change their "font of energy" and the way they use and transform it (metabolism) to augment the fight against an immune challenge. Peroxisomes are structures found in every cell that control important processes in metabolism. We found that peroxisomes are central regulators of an organism's immune system. Knowing how the immune responses function is quintessential to understand the mechanisms of diseases of immune disorders and to find new and more effective cures. We use the fruit fly as a model system in our studies to dissect the mechanisms of diseases. We use the fruit fly because their genes can be easily manipulated and they have basic cellular processes, including aspects of immune defense, that are similar to those in humans. Thus, studies in fruit fly can help us to quickly define the mechanisms by which peroxisomes function during systemic immune responses and then transfer our discovery to human health. Our research program aims to define 1) how peroxisomes contribute to changing metabolism in immune cells to activate their "defense mode' during microbial challenge; 2) how immune cells use "fats" to control an organism's way to fight an infection; and 3) how conserved in mammals are the mechanisms and pathways found in fruit flies, so that we can exploit peroxisomes as a disease marker for immune disorders and as therapeutic targets for new and more efficient drugs to treat patients with immune deficiency, autoimmune disease and cancer.

We will also do a similar experiment using genetically modified mice. These studies will help us confirm that virus-caused damage of the NFAT5 gene can increase viral multiplication and lead to heart muscle cell death. Based on these results, we will have a better understanding on why viral infection can cause heart disease and how we can prevent and treat this disease by enhancing NFAT5 protein production in our body.

column37: Fungi are significant and increasing mediators of pathogenesis; causing serious challenges medically and economically. Candida albicans is the most prevalent cause of fungal infections in people, and can cause life-threatening systemic infections if our immune defenses are compromised. A battery of fitness attributes promote the pathogenicity and drug resistance of this fungus, most of which arise by rapid generation of genetic diversity within a population in response to stressful growth conditions, such as exposure to antifungal drugs, as a means of adaptation. Research has shown that aneuploidy (an abnormal number of chromosomes) accounts for much of this diversity, and that this condition often arises from changes in components of the chromosome segregation machinery. Our findings indicate that some of these changes could be induced or enabled by kinesin motor proteins that regulate the structure of the cell's chromosome segregation apparatus - 'the mitotic spindle'. By addressing central questions about how kinesins control the assembly and function of the mitotic spindle, and how they integrate spindle function with cell division, we will provide insight into an important mutational process generating chromosome aberrations in fungal genomes that lead to drug resistance.

column36: Improving treatment for GRIN disorders
column37: GRIN disorders are caused by mutations in the GRIN genes, which carry the instructions to make NMDA receptors. When children are born with these mutations, they have intellectual disability and often have other symptoms like movement disorders, loss of muscle tone, developmental delays, and seizures. Some patients are able to attend school, while others are non-verbal and must use a wheelchair. We want to understand the reasons why some patients have a milder phenotype than other patients. We also want to determine what the best treatment strategy should be. GRIN disorder is a new diagnosis that has only been made possible because of genome sequencing, and the long-term prognosis and best treatments are still not known. Therefore, we will use mouse models that harbor patient disease-causing mutations, and will study the phenotypes of these mice and test a number of therapeutic interventions. In Specific Aim 1, we study NMDA receptor biochemistry and function in model animals. In Specific Aim 2, we assess behavioural phenotypes to determine whether the severity of phenotypes parallels that of the patients. In Specific Aim 3, we test treatments for their ability to improve neurological impairments caused by mutations in GRIN genes.

column36: Novel treatment to establish spatial hearing in children who are deaf
column37: Over 1 in 1000 children have permanent hearing loss and need early treatment and therapy to help them develop speech and language. We showed that many children hear better with two rather than one hearing device but that they still have a very hard time listening. Normally, the auditory system combines information from our two ears together seamlessly to help us hear each sound around us and to know where each sound is coming from. This "spatial" hearing is very important because this is how we sense the world in all directions around us and how we pick out and focus on one sound at a time to listen to. The problem is that children with hearing loss are not developing spatial hearing properly. We want to fix this by making sure that two hearing aids or two cochlear implants work well together like two normal hearing ears do. We use responses from the auditory brainstem to tell us when sound from both ears is best matched and then reset the devices to send sound in this new way for >100 children with hearing loss (>50 using two hearing aids and >50 using two cochlear implants). We ask each child to use the new device settings for 12 months. After the first 6 months, we measure changes in responses from the auditory system and the children's ability to hear from both ears. Sound localization therapy in half of the group begins at this time. After 12 months, we test whether children can better hear where sound is located and better understand spoken words in a noisy room. We also do the same tests in >100 similar children with hearing loss and >50 children with normal hearing so that we know how well the treatments have worked and how close these children with hearing loss have come to listening normally. We are known around the world for showing that it is important to give children hearing in both ears. We now have to correct the gaps in present treatment so that they can make the best use of their hearing devices to develop the spatial hearing they need.

column36: Altered vitamin A homeostasis and retinoic acid signaling in the development of congenital diaphragmatic hernia
column37: A newborn baby's first breath is driven by the contraction of the diaphragm, a muscle we all use unconsciously thousands of time every day to aid breathing. Try to imagine what happens if the diaphragm does not form properly during pregnancy. If a hole forms in the growing diaphragm, the liver can grow up into the developing baby's chest and prevent the lungs from growing. At birth, their incomplete diaphragm and crushed lungs mean these babies have a very difficult time breathing and they require intensive care - many will not survive the first week of life. Mercifully uncommon, this birth defect is called Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH), and its cause is unknown. The research proposed in this application is intended to answer questions surrounding the cause of CDH, and hopefully improve the health outcomes for these critically ill babies. Vitamin A is an essential part of the diet, while it is widely known for its role in vision, it is also an extremely important signaling molecule with many different roles in the body. This proposal's specific research question is uniquely focused on how problems with vitamin A signaling in the developing diaphragm may cause CDH. We aim to address this question in three novel ways: 1) develop an animal (mouse) model of CDH caused by specifically blocking how vitamin A signals in the growing diaphragm, 2) determine how important a mother's vitamin A status and intake is for susceptibility to CDH in an animal model, and 3) better understand how vitamin A signaling controls specific genes that have been associated with clinical cases of CDH. While we are using experimental models to answer our research questions, our work is guided by clinical observations. This 'bedside to bench' approach means our research is informed by actual cases of CDH, with the ultimate goal of taking new knowledge generated by our research back to the clinic to improve the outcomes of CDH.

column36: Perennial Policy Issues in Directly-Funded Home Care in Canada: An Intersectional, Qualitative Study to enhance Social and Health Outcomes
column37: The organization and delivery of quality home care services for long-term care needs associated with aging and disability is one of today's greatest health policy challenges. Directly-funded (DF) home care provides government funds to individuals to arrange assistance with the activities of daily living. DF, also referred to as 'self-managed' home care, may relieve the strain on home care systems and is expanding across Canada. While promising, emerging evidence suggests DF home care may exacerbate health inequities when scaled up. Our research team proposes the question: How can DF home care programs be designed to enhance social and health outcomes for diverse home care clients, informal supports, and care workers in Canadian contexts? We hone in on three perennial policy issues - that is, areas in which consensus has not been reached and that present challenges to equitable service delivery. First, we consider the role of home care agencies in DF service delivery. The role of non-profit and for-profit home care agencies is unclear and there may be health equity implications compared to a 'hire-your-neighbour' approach historically endorsed in DF programs. Secondly, we consider the implications of expanding DF to a larger portion of home care users in contrast to focusing on specific groups of people. Finally, we explore how to best adapt DF for rural contexts. Framed with the concepts of intersectionality and health equity, our 5-year study will take place in four provinces (Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Newfoundland & Labrador). We will use a variety of qualitative methods, including an environmental scan, focus groups, key informant and lived-experience interviews, and content and discourse analysis. Our study aims to generate insights about how DF can most equitably serve users, their families and supports, and workers.

column36: Effects of added sucrose on hormones, neural circuits, and behaviour
column37: Sugars such as sucrose (table sugar) are extremely common in the diet, in Canada and across the world. The World Health Organization advises that added sugars should make up 5% or less of daily calories for adults, and even less for children under 2 years. However, in Canada, adults and children often greatly exceed these recommendations. Of particular concern, added sugars during early development might have major and long-lasting effects on hormones, neural circuits, and behaviour. This project will use an animal model to experimentally determine how maternal consumption of sucrose during pregnancy and lactation affects the offspring. This project will examine the long-lasting effects on adult offspring, including important hormones, brain chemicals, and behaviours. Overall, this project will help us understand how maternal diet "programs" hormones, the brain reward system, and sugar-seeking behaviour in the offspring. The results will have important implications for the health of Canadians because very little is known about how added sugars affect brain circuits.

column36: The Muscarinic Hypothesis of Schizophrenia: A [18F]-FP-TZTP PET Study
column37: Acetylcholine is a natural chemical in the brain that carries signals between brain neurons. It is released by one set of neurons, called cholinergic neurons, and attaches to muscarinic and nicotinic 'receptors' on other sets of neurons. This is known as the cholinergic system. There are several types of nicotinic and muscarinic receptors (e.g. M1, M2, M3, M4, and M5). Changes in acetycholine levels and a reduction in the number of muscarinic receptors are thought to contribute to the symptoms of schizophrenia. Many medications, including common over-the-counter medications like diphenhydramine (aka Benadryl), act on muscarinic receptors. They can produce symptoms similar to that of schizophrenia when taken at toxic doses, such as confusion and hallucinations. However, little research has focused on the role of muscarinic receptors in schizophrenia. The M2 receptor is thought to control the release of acetylcholine in the striatum, a part of the brain directly related to the symptoms of schizophrenia. M2 is the first muscarinic receptor that can be studied independent of the others using the brain imaging technique PET (Positron Emission Tomography). With the discovery of a compound the binds preferentially to M2 receptors, it is now possible to measure their amount and location within the brain. The current study therefore seeks to quantify the amount of M2 receptors in patients with schizophrenia. To do this we will: (1) compare 20 patients with good response to antipsychotic treatment with 20 healthy controls matched for age, sex, and smoking status, and (2) determine the statistical relationship between the symptoms of schizophrenia and the quantity of M2 receptors. The results of this study may lead to a new diagnostic marker for schizophrenia, increase our understanding of the pathophysiology of the disease, and provide a new target for treatment.
