column36: Optic flow processing in midbrain-cerebellar circuits for the control of locomotion
column37: As we move through the world, we experience optic flow - the motions of surfaces and objects across our retina. Studies of human behaviour reveal that optic flow is used for controlling virtually all aspects of locomotion such as walking, navigating through cluttered environments like forests or airport terminals, and when driving motor vehicles. Despite the importance of optic flow, there is a major gap in our understanding of how these signals are processed in the brain to allow for complex locomotion. Thus, optic flow processing in the brain is one of the most important, but least understood aspects of locomotion control. Disruptions to optic flow processing in the brain are associated with common diseases including vertigo, oscillopsia, ataxias and Alzheimer's disease. For example, Alzheimer's patients require much stronger optic flow signals to be able to navigate through a series of hallways to find their rooms. For other patients, such as those with vestibular deficits and visual neglect, presentations of optic flow are effective rehabilitative tools. Improving our understanding of optic flow is therefore essential. The principal challenge to studying optic flow processing in the brain is that we lack an appropriate animal model for research. Mice and rats are often used for studies of vertebrate neurobiology, but they are crepuscular/nocturnal and use information from their whiskers to guide many aspects of their locomotion. We will investigate how optic flow is used to guide movement in different environments, how optic flow signals are processed along the pathway from the midbrain to the cerebellum, and how selective silencing of neurons in this pathway leads to deficits in locomotor ability. The experiments will be performed on the visually-guided flight of small birds, which can be easily studied in the lab. Because birds have the same optic flow pathways as humans, this research will identify specific neural connections as potential treatment targets.

column36: Targeting Glioblastoma Heterogeneity through identification of subtype-specific genetic vulnerabilities
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. Current treatment for GBM (surgery, radiation and chemotherapy) extends survival but is ineffective at preventing disease recurrence due to the residual presence of tumor initiating "GBM stem cells" that evade therapy and patients will invariably succumb to the disease, on average, just 18 months after initial diagnosis. Genomics studies have identified a high degree of variability in the genetic make-up of GBM cells-both between patients and within the same patient-which has represented a major barrier to the efficacy of new therapies for this cancer. Recently, our group and others have identified two predominant subtypes of GBM stem cells that can both be isolated from patient tumor samples, indicating that curing a patient of all residual disease would require therapies that killed both subtypes. Herein, we propose to use cutting-edge CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology to determine which genes are required for the growth of each subtype, producing a roadmap of candidate therapeutic targets. By performing these genetic screens in a large panel of patient derived GBM stem cell lines generated by our collaborator, we will produce a powerful dataset highly reflective of the heterogeneity observed in the GBM patient population. Using this data, we will characterize the biological basis for subtype-specific gene dependencies, greatly increasing our understanding of the mechanisms of GBM progression. In addition, our screen data will allow us to nominate drugs and small molecules as potential new targeted therapeutic strategies which we will evaluate through both in vitro drug screening and in mouse models harboring human patient derived GBM tumors. In summary, our proposed study will strive to develop new therapeutic strategies that can be applied in combination to overcome tumor heterogeneity and successfully target both cell types and cure GBM.

column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) causes chronic liver infection with life-threatening complications. In order to enhance a broadly protective vaccine, we are investigating the mechanism behind this genotype bias and also how HCV evades antibody control. Our proposed studies aim to improve the immunogenicity of the HCV vaccine by enhancing cross-protective neutralizing antibodies which are one component of an effective global HCV vaccine.

column36: Adapting a Mindfulness-Based Intervention for Depression and Anxiety Symptoms for Use with Indigenous University Students
column37: There are several treatment options for non-Indigenous Canadians suffering from elevated symptoms of depression and anxiety. Unfortunately, the same cannot be said about treatment options for Indigenous people in Canada; despite comparable rates of depression and anxiety to those of non-Indigenous decent, there are very few sensitive and culturally appropriate treatment options for Indigenous Canadians who may be suffering from elevated symptoms of depression and anxiety, as most these existing interventions have almost exclusively been developed by or with individuals of the majority culture (White; middle class; Judeo-Christian). This is problematic, as this cultural mismatch between how the intervention is designed and traditional Indigenous elements and knowledge dissuades Indigenous patients from engaging with said treatments. Mindfulness-based interventions have gained tremendous popularity in the last two decades, and have been shown to improve mild-moderate symptoms of depression and anxiety. Fortunately, Eastern and holistic influences of mindfulness-based interventions make them more amenable for adaptation for Indigenous patients. In this investigation, the research team will use a community-oriented approach to a) adapt a preexisting mindfulness-based intervention for use among Indigenous university students, and b) pilot-test the initial efficacy of this intervention to reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety among a small sample of Indigenous students, and c) outline a model for adapting existing psychological interventions to make them culturally sensitive and specific for Indigenous peoples in Canada. We hope at the end of this project, an additional, efficacious, and sensitive treatment option will exist for Indigenous students who are looking for ways to supplements traditional ways of dealing with distress.

column36: Accelerating Discoveries: The Employment Trajectory of Young Adults with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
column37: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus is a disease in which the body's immune system makes a mistake and attacks healthy tissue in many parts of the body. It is also called lupus or SLE. People with lupus are often very tired, feel pain all over their body and have mental health problems so it can be hard for them to find or keep a job. If young adults (18-30 years of age) cannot start work, they can run into problems later in life. That is why it is important for us to understand the details of how young Canadians with lupus work. We do know a bit about this, but we need more information so that we can help them in the future. Our research study has 3 parts. The first part of our research study will look at how young adults with lupus change in their work. For example, we will look at how they change from being a student to becoming employed or unemployed. We will compare this to how other people of same age and sex change in their work. Young adults can be hard to study. They move around a lot and they go through many changes in their lives. To deal with this problem, we want to collect this information in a new, quicker and better way (second part). We will use what we learn in the first part to test if we can use the new way to collect information so that we can design better research studies in the future. Finally, we will interview young adults with lupus to learn about their work and any problems they had in the past (third part). Our findings will be shared with young people living with lupus, their families, doctors and employers to raise awareness about how hard it can be to work when a person has lupus. column36: Artificial Placenta: A biomimetic approach to support neonates with respiratory distress
column37: Respiratory failure is the major cause of morbidity among low birth weight neonates. Mechanical ventilation has dramatically improved outcome in this condition but can have side-effects that lead to long-term impairment. Over the past few years we have developed a new approach known as the artificial placenta - a device that mimics the natural circulation before birth where the fetus obtains oxygen from the mother. The device is elegantly designed so that it can operate in a pumpless manner, much like the natural placenta. It is designed to use the baby's own heart to perfuse a significant fraction of the blood volume through a microfluidic extracorporeal device and exchange oxygen with the external ambient environment. Being a passive device, it does not require external pumps and has a small internal volume which eliminates the need for external blood transfusion when it is connected to the neonate. We have developed a series of devices with increasing capabilities and are at a stage where initial animal experiments on piglets with the same weight as human neonatal babies have shown that our devices can sustain them even when under respiratory distress like conditions. These initial experiments show the promise of our approach, but further experiments are needed to conclusively validate that they would be suitable to support the piglets over typical operational lifetime of this device (~ 3-4 days). Further research is also needed to confirm whether the internal coating that we provide to the device is active over the intended operational lifetime. In addition to the validation of the device using animal models, we will also simplify the manufacturing process for the device and evaluate new coating technologies to ensure highest reliability of the device operation as well as its manufacturing. The validation of the technology obtained in this project on animal models will be critical to move it to the next stage of human clinical trials.

column36: Neurobiomarkers of FASD for adolescents and adults in the Criminal Justice System: Portable eye tracking and EEG
column37: In Canada, an estimated 1M people live with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), a lifelong neurodevelopmental disability with wide ranging impacts on brain and behaviour that are linked with adverse outcomes. Studies suggest that over 60% of adults with FASD experience contact with the criminal justice system, and they are overrepresented in correctional and forensic settings at rates 30x that of the general population. They experience high rates of re-offending, health, and mental health problems, and have difficulty benefiting from traditional interventions in the justice system. Despite high numbers, there are currently no evidence-based ways of identifying adolescents or adults who could have FASD in the criminal justice system. Failure to identify people with FASD in this context can lead to increased risk of harm to self and others, recidivism, and high health, social, and economic costs. This study proposes to use novel neurotechnologies, including eye movement behaviour and EEG recordings, to better understand how to identify adolescents and adults with FASD, including those in the criminal justice system. Portable technologies such as these may be used to detect people at risk of having FASD with a high degree of accuracy. These tools are non-invasive, precise, cost effective, and portable, and may allow for early identification of individuals in need of more comprehensive and costly clinical assessment, diagnostic, and intervention services. Findings from this research will be used to develop and implement fast, non-invasive, and affordable screening protocols to aid in large-scale screening for FASD in criminal justice settings. Identifying people who may have FASD may lead to effective use of limited economic and health resources to best support their complex needs.

column36: Optimizing care journeys for adults with hip fractures and complexity: A mixed-methods case study
column37: Hip fractures are one of the most common causes of fall-related hospitalizations in adults over the age of 65. Persons with hip fractures are likely to experience poor outcomes and quality of life following their injury. Patients with hip fractures require treatment from a diverse range of health care providers across settings including hospitals, in-patient rehabilitation units, outpatient clinics, home care, assisted living facilities and long-term care homes. They are estimated to undergo many relocations or transfers within six months of incurring the injury. Unfortunately, many patients do not return to pre-injury functional status. These transitions in care are vulnerable periods for patients and families, especially for older adults with hip fractures and complex health and social needs. Our goal in the proposed research is to fill a research gap through in-depth understanding of care journeys across the continuum for adults with hip fractures in urban and rural settings. We will conduct interviews with patients, caregivers, providers and decision-makers within urban and rural areas. We will also use quantitative health administrative data to gain a comprehensive view of care across the continuum. The research team will then summarize the findings and share with patients, caregivers, providers, managers and decision-makers and discuss how we can improve care transitions for person with hip fractures within Ontario and across Canada.

column36: Stepping-Up: Partnering with the Community to Prevent Early Mobility Decline
column37: Background: Older adults need to be able to walk around their community at a minimal speed in order to ensure their safety. Slowing of walking speed occurs with aging in all persons, and has been linked to decreased independence. Preclinical disability is a stage where older adults begin to change the way they complete mobility tasks, like walking. Programs to improve mobility in people with preclinical disability need to encourage participants to be actively involved in managing their mobility (self-management), should be specifically developed for the individual and should include the practice of mobility tasks. In 2016, we conducted a pilot study to measure the impact of a mobility self-management intervention on the walking ability of older adults, but the results were not clear. In this proposal, we have made some changes to improve the study design and the intervention. Goals, Methods, Approach: We plan to study whether community-dwelling adults 55 years and older with preclinical mobility limitations show improvement in walking distance, walking speed, balance, strength, confidence in their walking and health after completing a 12-week program, called STEPPING-UP, that includes mobility exercises and self-management sessions led by a physiotherapist. This program will be compared to 2 control groups, either a 12-week telephone-based coaching walking program or a 12-week stretching program. We will also compare the cost associated with delivering each program. Expected Outcomes: If the results from this study are positive, it will support the importance of identifying those at risk for mobility related disability and will provide a community-based resource for the prevention of mobility decline in older adults.

column36: Enabling Cellular Therapy Biomanufacturing through Integrated Modeling of Fluid Dynamics and Cellular Metabolism in Bioreactors
column37: Regenerative medicine is a rapidly growing billion-dollar multidisciplinary field at the intersection of medicine, engineering and science. It aims to create living, functional tissues that can repair or replace damaged, diseased or aging tissues or organs, as well as providing models for discovery and drug development. Stem cells are critical to the success of regenerative medicine therapies. Pluripotent stem cells are a unique adult-derived stem cell that can be used for both personalized and population therapies, but technologies are needed to bridge the gap between fundamental biology and clinical applications. One of the major obstacles preventing effective use of stem cells is the limited number of available donor cells, and the small-scale, labour-intensive methods for culturing and differentiating them. Stirred suspension bioreactors are emerging as a critical cornerstone of robust bioprocesses to generate sufficient numbers of stem cells and their differentiated progeny for multiple applications. However, there is a significant gap in our knowledge of how the dynamic environment in the bioreactor affects the quality of the final cell product. More specifically, cell metabolism, which can change greatly between stem cells and their differentiated daughter cells, can be modulated within the stirred suspension bioreactor environment. The overall goals of the research project are to a) develop a deeper understanding of the metabolic behaviour of human pluripotent stem cells in bioreactors, b) relate metabolism to the dynamic environment within the bioreactor through computer modeling approaches. The outputs of this research are essential for efficient, cost-effective, safe and reproducible cell manufacturing, which is a critical next step to precision treatments for conditions such as degenerative diseases, burns, fractures, and other ailments. This is an opportunity for Canada to be a leader in biomanufacturing for the regenerative medicine industry.

column36: Sex Differences in Central Nervous System Autoimmunity
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world, with 1 in every 250 Canadians affected. This translates into a considerable societal and economic burden ($1.6M per patient). At present, it is not possible to reverse the neuron damage in MS. Therefore, the best chance of curing this disease is to prevent it from starting in the first place. Thus understanding the risk factors for development of MS and the biology of how these risk factors initiate the disease process is an important area of research. Three times more women than men develop MS, and we still do not understand why this is the case. In addition, if men get this disease, they tend to exhibit more rapid progression. Our goal is to better understand the fundamental biological differences that account for the greater susceptibility of females to develop MS and for men to develop more rapid progression. Here, through studies in mice and in human MS patients, we are trying to better understand the nuts and bolts of why the immune response may be more vigorous in females and can lead to the initiation of autoimmunity. We are pursuing the novel hypothesis that the reason why females are more prone to develop MS is because they have more T cells that can recognize the myelin sheath. We have thus far found evidence of this in the peripheral blood of human patients and in a mouse model of this disease. Further studies are planned in mice to get to the underlying mechanisms for this sex difference in T cell numbers. We are also going to characterize the immune cells in men and women with MS in order to gain new insights into how the disease may be different between the sexes. Understanding this biology will improve our understanding of how MS gets started and may lead to new ways of preventing or treating this disease. .

column36: Youth and E-Cigarettes: A Knowledge Synthesis

column36: Targeting pericytes to restore sensorimotor function after spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury disconnects the brain from parts of the body below the injury, resulting in paralysis, abnormal pain and bladder dysfunction. Unfortunately, treatments to repair the injured spinal cord are still lacking. However, we recently made the unexpected discovery that blood flow is permanently reduced in the entire spinal cord below an injury, suggesting that improving blood flow offers a new approach to treating injury. We found that this low blood flow is caused by an exaggerated activity in specialized cells called pericytes that act like valves on small blood vessels. This then leads to insufficient blood flow and ultimately loss of residual functions like walking. We find that transiently blocking this exaggerated pericyte activity, or supplying oxygen, temporarily promotes recovery of walking in animal models. This is the basis for our current proposal, where we ask three questions. First, how do we best apply treatments to more permanently restore blood flow and oxygen to the spinal cord, and are these treatments safe (e.g. does not enhance abnormal pain)? Second, what causes the excessive pericyte activity following spinal cord injury, and can it be prevented? We have convincing preliminary data that indicate that a lack of activity in the neurons below a spinal cord injury triggers the excessive pericyte activity, since daily nerve stimulation to excite the spinal cord over the first few weeks after spinal cord injury restores normal pericyte function, eliminates hypoxia and markedly improves residual movement. If proven correct, this idea opens up new clinically applicable treatments to restore blood flow, including electrical nerve stimulation and rehabilitation training that promote neuronal activity early after injury. Lastly, we explore whether humans with spinal cord injury also suffer from a lack of oxygen in the spinal cord below the injury and whether restoring blood flow promotes recovery in sensory and motor function.

column36: Using behavioural science to understand and improve participation in clinical trials: A theory-based research project.
column37: Participation in clinical research is an essential element of improving healthcare. Any change in treatment or management should be tested before it is put into practice, and this requires patients (and others) to participate in research, usually on a volunteer basis. Despite its importance, research participation is consistently low across almost all diseases and geographical regions. The costs of low participation are many and varied, including wasted money and other resources, inability to use those resources for other purposes, delayed new treatments, faulty findings, and unnecessary risks to those who do participate. While many studies have explored this problem, they have not been informed by theories from psychology that contain considerable knowledge about how to help people make difficult decisions, and how people change their behaviour. The overall goal for this project is to develop the knowledge and tools necessary to help patient groups, researchers, and trial sponsors optimize both the rate of participation and the experience of clinical trial recruitment. The work will proceed in four phases, including (1) reviewing the scientific literature to understand how recruitment is currently done from a theoretical perspective; (2) interviewing the range of different groups with expertise in these issues (e.g. participants, physicians, trial recruiters, and experts in the infrastructure underlying clinical research); (3) developing tools to help optimize trial recruitment (e.g. standard surveys that can identify problems before a trial begins; more participant-friendly consent forms); and (4) thinking and writing about the ethical challenges posed by these theories, to safeguard public trust in health research. Our international multidisciplinary team is uniquely qualified to do this work, which will help improve the health care system by optimizing the process of clinical trial recruitment.

column37: Detection of a viral infection by the host cells relies on the detection of the viral nucleic acids by receptors present in the cytosol of the cells. One of the central proteins in the activation and coordination of antiviral pathways is a protein called MAVS. The characterization of these mechanisms requires not only molecular and biochemical approaches, but also molecular modeling approaches to understand the impact of redox modifications on MAVS. This study proposes innovative approaches to better understand the regulation of antiviral signaling pathways. The data generated may open the way for the development of molecular screening assays targeting the activation of MAVS.

column36: SGLT-2 Inhibitors and Early Bladder Cancer Events: An International Multi-Centre Study
column37: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors are a new class of drugs used to treat type 2 diabetes. These drugs have been shown to decrease the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular outcomes (such as heart attacks, strokes and death) in patients with type 2 diabetes in clinical trials. Despite their remarkable benefits, there have been concerns that these drugs might increase the risk of important adverse events including bladder cancer. To date, however, no studies have been conducted in the real-world setting to assess this possible association. To address this concern, we will conduct a large, international, multi-centre population-based cohort study using five administrative, primary care, and insurance databases from Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States. At each site, we will compare new users of SGLT-2 inhibitors with new users of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, a class of drugs used at a similar stage of diabetes severity. The results from each site will then be pooled together for an overall estimate of the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors on bladder cancer. As patients with type 2 diabetes are already at an increased risk of bladder cancer, this large international study will provide concerned stakeholders with much needed information on the safety profile of these drugs in a timely and cost-effective fashion.

column36: Mechanisms of B cell-mediated immunity in human cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer is a challenging disease with unacceptably high mortality. Despite this, about 30% of patients "beat the odds" and live for many years after treatment. Why do some patients do so well? In the past decade, it has become well established that many long-term survivors of ovarian cancer exhibit a strong immune response against their tumor, providing a plausible explanation for their favourable outcome. We have shown that the immune response against cancer involves collaboration between several types of white blood cells, including killer T cells and antibody-producing B cells. With better understanding of the immune response, it will be possible to design new treatments that enhance tumor immunity and increase patient survival. In this study, we will investigate the mechanisms by which B cells work with other immune cells to recognize and attack cancer. In Aim 1, we will use state-of-the-art genomics methods to probe the molecular properties of individual B cells and associated immune cells isolated from 50 human ovarian cancer specimens, giving us unprecedented insights into the inner workings of the immune system in patients. In Aim 2, we will isolate the antibodies produced by 200 or more B cells from ovarian tumours and use these to further decipher the mechanisms by which B cells amplify the immune response to cancer. The data, tools and knowledge arising from this study will help us design new immunotherapies that fortify the patient's natural defense mechanisms, leading to increased survival. Through local and national initiatives, our team is exceptionally well positioned to translate our findings into early stage clinical trials of promising new immunotherapy strategies for ovarian cancer patients in Canada.

column36: Ultra-Low Tidal Volume Mechanical Ventilation in ARDS Through ECCO2R (ULTIMATE) Pilot Trial
column37: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a devastating form of sudden lung failure that can occur after common insults such as pneumonia, other severe infections, or trauma. Despite many advances over the past decades, mortality rates remain high and survivors experience significant and prolonged difficulties with physical and mental health. A key advance in the care of patients with ARDS was the recognition that although life-saving in some cases, mechanical ventilators (breathing machines) can worsen lung injury and contribute to death. Intensive care doctors now recognise that giving normal-to-small sized breaths (6 ml/kg) with the ventilator saves lives, compared with the larger breath sizes (12 ml/kg) that were used in the past. However, in a significant number of cases these smaller breaths are still big enough to cause further damage to the lung which is already injured. New technology is now available that may be able to help in this situation - extracorporeal carbon dioxide removal - is a device similar to kidney dialysis, where blood is pumped out of the body and through a type of artificial lung, removing carbon dioxide. This means that the patient's lungs have to do less work, and breath sizes and therefore stress and strain can be reduced further. This may reduce lung injury and reduce the risk of dying from ARDS, but this is also a new technology with costs and potential side effects, which needs careful evaluation. In this study we will randomly assign adults with ARDS to receive either best standard care or to this new technology allowing lower tidal volumes and will determine whether the new strategy is really better.

column36: Quality control and pharmacological rescue of heteromeric long QT mutants
column37: The Long QT Syndrome (LQTS) is an electrical disorder of the heart, which is associated with abnormal cardiac rhythms and sudden death. The QT interval is determined by measuring the interval between the QRS complex and the T-wave on the electrocardiograph. One form of this syndrome, referred to as LQTS2, has been related to mutations of a protein called hERG (Human Ether-a-go-go Related Gene) that reduces the function of the hERG channel in the cell membrane. This channel also binds many drugs readily, which can cause sudden death, and therefore the U.S.A. Federal Drug Administration requires that new drugs are tested against hERG. However, the mechanisms that regulate the levels of hERG channels at the cell membrane are not well understood. The first mechanism is related to the removal of mutated and improperly folded hERG channels at the endoplasmic reticulum. A second mechanism involves the removal of hERG channels from the cell membrane that become destabilized. We discovered that there are two distinct cell membrane quality control systems, the more recent of which we have little information. Also, we screened a library of drugs and small molecules and found two compounds that can stabilize mutant hERG channels at the cell membrane, which could have potential therapeutic benefits. The nature of this mechanism also is not understood and will be the subject of further investigation. In our study, we will continue to evaluate the quality control and pharmacological modulation of hERG channels using a variety of techniques that involve electrophysiology, molecular biology and advanced microscopy. We believe that this quality control mechanism will provide a new explanation for the effects involved in clinically relevant cases of LQTS2.

column36: The Tumor Suppressor Function of CUX1
column37: Cancer develops following increased alterations within DNA, which are usually repaired by complex groups of proteins involved in DNA repair. Defects in one or more DNA repair mechanisms cause the accumulation of changes in DNA, called mutations, that increase the possibility that certain cells become tumorigenic. We work on a gene, called CUX1, that has been implicated in cancer. Normally, each gene has two copies or alleles, however, one allele of CUX1 is inactivated or lost in a fraction of human cancers. This finding suggests that the probability of developing cancer increases in cells that have only one copy of the CUX1 gene. This defines the CUX1 gene as a "tumor suppressor gene" and in our scientific jargon, we say that CUX1 is a "haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene". The goal of our research is to understand why having only one copy of the CUX1 gene increases the probability of cancer. We already know that less of the CUX1 proteins are expressed when one copy of the gene is inactivated or lost. We want to know and demonstrate what molecular function is affected when there is a lower number of CUX1 proteins. Since the CUX1 protein plays a role in DNA repair, our hypothesis is that cells with less CUX1 are not as efficient at repairing DNA damage and therefore they accumulate changes in DNA faster than normal cells. To make a bad analogy, cancer is like winning the lottery. Cells with less CUX1 accumulate more lottery tickets than other cells and therefore they have a higher probability of getting the bad ticket.

column36: TLR3 is an endogenous sensor of cell death and a potential target for induction of long-term heart transplant survival
column37: When a heart is irreversibly damaged and cannot be treated by any other medical or surgical means, organ transplantation is the most beneficial and highly-pursued treatment option for saving the person's life. However, the immune system of the graft recipient usually recognizes the transplant as a 'stranger', leading to organ rejection. The premature failure of transplanted organ is related to both early rejection and chronic injury. Chronic injury and premature loss of transplanted hearts has emerged as our greatest current clinical challenge. Chronic rejection is the leading cause of late morbidity and mortality in transplant patients. Unfortunately, this long-term outcome has not improved over time. Consequently, searching for new strategies to limit the damage caused by unwanted immune responses and to prolong long-term graft survival has become the key objective in the field of transplantation research. Inflammation post transplantation induces different "forms" of cell death and subsequently organ failure. We have discovered that a unique form of cell death termed "necroptosis" differs from more typical cell death (apoptosis) in that it may lead to increased inflammation within the heart and contribute to long term injury. Furthermore, this inflammation is not affected by current anti-rejection drugs. In this grant, we will study how the form of cell death regulate transplant inflammation and rejection. These studies will determine how the form of cell death affects immune responses and chronic transplant injury. These studies will guide future clinical therapy of inflammation and may translate to truly new approaches to preventing transplanted heart graft injury in patients.

column36: Investigating the regulation of ADAMTS13 in hemostasis and thrombosis
column37: Thrombosis is a pathological condition that occurs as a result of unregulated blood clotting that occludes blood vessels, and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Thrombosis can manifest in various organs and can lead to heart attacks or stroke. Despite the availability of drugs that either prevent blood clotting or encourage clot breakdown, thrombosis is responsible for 1 in 4 deaths in Canada and worldwide. Current therapies are limited by the need to balance their effectiveness at treating thrombosis with their risk of causing bleeding. As a result, more research is needed to explore the mechanisms of thrombosis in order to identify new targets for safe and effective therapy. A critical step in the progression to thrombosis is the recruitment of platelets to the injured blood vessel. This is accomplished in part by the protein Von Willebrand Factor (VWF). VWF is a long string-like protein that adheres to the site of vessel injury and captures platelets flowing in blood. Recruitment of too many platelets can lead to thrombosis. ADAMTS13 is a protease that cuts VWF strings, shortening them and reducing their platelet-capturing activity. Changes in ADAMTS13 activity can lead to dysfunctional VWF and cause either bleeding or thrombosis. However, there is currently very little that is known about the regulation of ADAMTS13. ADAMTS13 is known to remain in a folded compact form in circulation that becomes extended when it interacts with and cuts VWF. Whether this folded form of ADAMTS13 contributes to the regulation of its protease activity is currently not known. Therefore, the objective of this project is to explore the biochemical and structural mechanisms that contribute to the regulation of ADAMTS13. Because ADAMTS13 is an important regulator of blood clotting, investigating the mechanisms that control its activity may reveal novel targets for antithrombotic therapy development.

column36: Biophysical control of mesenchymal morphogenesis in the mammalian embryo
column37: The growth and formation of the mammalian embryo is an inherently physical process that is regulated by genes. Although the identity of genes responsible for development is relatively advanced, the physical principles that shape three dimensional embryonic structures such as solid organs including the face and limbs are not understood. It is also not known how genes regulate physical processes that underlie development. Consequences of these knowledge gaps are that we cannot fully explain how birth defects arise and current efforts at regenerating organs are based on trial-and-error methods rather than on recapitulating actual physical events that take place during natural development. The persistence of these knowledge gaps is attributable to the lack of tools to measure the physical properties of mammalian embryos. The Hopyan and Sun lab teams bring together developmental biologists and mechanical engineers with expertise in the manufacture of micro-scale devices to tackle the physical basis of development. Collaboratively, they generated multiple genetic and physical tools that allow precise measurements of the viscoelastic properties and forces of living tissues and cells in the mammalian embryo. Using those tools, they described how 3D tissues such as the developing face and limbs grow at the resolution of individual cells and measured cellular forces and tissue stiffness. They generated hypotheses about how cells move in response to the stiffness of their environment and about how three regulators (WNT5A, YAP and Piezo1) control that response. Mutations of those regulators cause human birth defects. Therefore, the experiments outlined in this proposal will define how molecular pathways regulate physical processes during development and more precisely explain how specific facial and limb defects arise. In the longterm, understanding the physical basis of organ development will accelerate strategies that are focused on organ regeneration.

column36: Microglial fatty acid signalling as a modulator of diet-induced neuroimmune responses in obesity
column37: Obesity poses a major health and economic burden worldwide. Excess consumption of foods high in fat and sugar can elicit inflammation in the brain that contributes to the development of obesity and associated metabolic abnormalities. The last century has witnessed a major increase in the intake of saturated fats along with a decline in essential omega-3 fatty acids that are anti-inflammatory and can protect against metabolic impairments associated with obesity. GPR120 is a receptor activated by omega-3 fatty acids that mediates the antiinflammatory and insulin-sensitizing effects of dietary omega-3 supplementation. In the brain, GPR120 is primarily expressed in microglia (cerebral immune cells) and activation of GPR120 in microglia decreases their inflammatory status. While pharmacological activation of brain GPR120 inhibits feeding, motivation for tasty food and diet-induced hyperglycemia, the role of microglial GPR120 in the neuroimmune and metabolic responses to diet and obesity development are unknown. The proposed project will test the contribution of microglial GPR120 to diet-induced neuroinflammation and obesity susceptibility in mice using a gene intervention approach that will delete GPR120 specifically in microglia. In view of the promising potential of GPR120 agonists to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, it is critical to understand the role of brain GPR120.

column36: Targeting the immune landscape at presentation and relapse of Immune-Related Lobular Breast Cancer
column37: Recently, escape from tumor surveillance by the immune system has been identified as a critical mediator for cancer progression to lethal disease. This creates a challenge with respect to modeling disease for the development of effective therapy, since most studies are based on injecting human cancer cell lines into mice that have a crippled immune system. Indeed, this approach has worked for development of novel anti-cancer drugs, some of which target the same signaling pathways that are mutated in tumor cells, but cannot be used to develop immunotherapy. In contrast, by inserting cancer-causing mutations into the chromosomes of transgenic mice, new models for human cancer can be generated in an immunocompetent setting. The Egan lab (who study human cancer in mouse models) has collaborated with the Guidos lab (an immunology group) to develop and characterize a completely new model for one type of breast cancer (known as Lobular breast cancer or ILC). We have also identified mutations that can be used to model ILC when it becomes resistant to therapy, leading to metastasis and patient death. By working together, Egan and Guidos, can effectively combine immunotherapy with drugs that target cancer-causing mutations in ILC model mice. Using this approach we can develop new combination therapy for the effective treatment of ILC at diagnosis and recurrence. Ultimately, results from this study can be used to inspire and guide clinical trials for the deployment of combination therapy in ILC patients. As ILC represents ~10% of all breast cancer cases, results from this study will have the potentially to positively affect the lives of thousands of Canadian women.

column36: A UK/Canada Collaboration on the genetics of long-term diabetes complications and their risk factors among people with type 1 diabetes
column37: Over 100,000 Canadians have type 1 diabetes. People with type 1 diabetes require lifelong insulin injections to replace insulin synthesized by specialized cells in their pancreas that have died due to an immune process. Currently there are few treatments to prevent or delay the underlying destruction of insulin producing cells. Studies have shown that many people with type 1 diabetes still produce small amounts of insulin. This is important because these people have less severe diabetes: they require lower doses of insulin; have better control of their blood sugar levels; are at lower risk for the development of low blood sugar; and also importantly at lower risk for long-term complications of diabetes, including eye, kidney and heart diseases which are major health problems. However, we have little understanding of the factors that result in differences in insulin production capacity between people with type 1 diabetes. Genetics provides a unique opportunity to identify causal factors for important biomedical measures, such as varying insulin production in people with type 1 diabetes. We already conducted a pilot study where we identified genetic variations at two different locations in the genome that are related to insulin production. In this project we will use data and samples from nine different studies, with a total of ~12,200 people with type 1 diabetes, to allow us to identify the genetic factors that influence residual insulin production. This would be the largest and most comprehensive study of this topic to date. Identifying the genetic factors is the first step to understanding the mechanisms, which could ultimately be used to develop new approaches to help preserve insulin production in people with type 1 diabetes. Since insulin production is also abnormal in many people with type 2 diabetes, which affects over 2 million Canadians, the findings from this work could also ultimately benefit some people with type 2 diabetes.

column36: CHILDhood Asthma and Puberty: Understanding the Sex Shift in Asthma to Female Predominance
column37: It is well known that asthma is more common in boys than girls in childhood, and more common in women than men during adulthood. We do not understand why this "sex shift" (also known as "gender shift") happens, but it may involve changes in body fat, inflammation or sex hormones during puberty. Unfortunately, most asthma studies have not accurately measured body fat or inflammation, and have not focused on the "critical window" of puberty. The CHILD Cohort Study provides an ideal opportunity to study these factors and the sex/gender shift in asthma. We have followed 1000 boys and girls at the Manitoba site of the CHILD Cohort Study (born in 2009-12) from birth until 8 years of age. Now, we will re-assess the same children at 11 years of age (early puberty) to measure their body fat, sex hormones and inflammation, and diagnose asthma. This research will help us understand and explain the sex differences in asthma, ultimately allowing for better prevention and treatment of asthma in all children.

column36: Minimizing Variation In Care Among Critically Ill Patients With Respiratory Failure Through Implementation Of An Evidence-Informed Care Pathway
column37: Lung failure prevents the lungs from delivering adequate amounts of oxygen to the body. It can be caused by severe infections such as pneumonia and is a common reason for patients to be admitted to the intensive care unit. Patients with lung failure often require assisted breathing with a machine. Some patients develop very severe lung failure, referred to as the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). More than half of patients with severe ARDS will die. Thus diagnosing and treating ARDS correctly is very important. Several treatments for ARDS have been shown to improve a patient's chance of survival. Using the breathing machine carefully (protectively with small breaths), using medications to help relax the chest muscles, and prone positioning (nursing patients while they are lying face down) are all treatments that can save lives. When our team and others have studied how well we use these therapies, we have shown that we do not use these treatments as often as we should. It is likely that we could be helping more patients. The goal of this project is to test a simple but organized approach to diagnosing and treating lung failure. To create the best chance for success, many different types of care providers including physicians, nurses and respiratory therapists will be involved. The approach will focus on timely diagnosis as well as using those treatments that have been proven to save lives. We will look at outcomes in patients (how often are they receiving the correct treatment), health care providers such as nurses, physicians and respiratory therapists (how they like using the pathway), families (does the pathway improve the ICU experience), and cost (does the pathway reduce unnecessary treatments). Our goal is to ensure that patients with lung failure and ARDS patients are diagnosed quickly and provided with the correct therapy at the correct time to best improve their outcomes.

column36: Investigating BC200, a long non-coding RNA critical for cancer cell survival.
column37: BC200 RNA is a 200 nucleotide, primate-specific, long non-coding RNA that is produced at high levels in invasive carcinomas, whereas in normal tissue or benign tumors BC200 is not detectable at significant levels. Remarkably, studies of BC200 knockdown by our group and others demonstrate tumour-cell specific suppression of cell growth. We therefore propose to demonstrate the role that BC200 plays in tumour cell proliferation/migration and investigate possible therapeutic approaches to disrupt BC200 function. We will investigate possible protein binding partners of BC200 using mass spectrometry approaches. Protein targets will be validated and pathways that they regulate in cancer investigated through examination of entire regulatory networks. We will also examine BC200 suppression as a novel therapeutic strategy by targeting specific regions of the RNA with nucleic acid/small molecule inhibitors. Inhibitor design will also focus on optimizing delivery by exploiting unique nucleic acid structural features. Based on solid preliminary data and the team assembled, the experiments proposed present a rational, novel and synergistic approach to determine the critical role of an upregulated RNA in cancer and propose plausible therapeutic strategies.

column36: Impact of regional microinfarct load on cortical reorganization and stroke recovery
column37: A stroke is most commonly caused by a blocked blood vessel within the brain, leading to the death of brain cells in the region near the blockage. A major question that scientists have been working on is to determine why some people improve after the stroke, while others do not. Recent studies have shown that in addition to the major stroke, many patients also have a number of smaller strokes, called microinfarcts spread throughout the brain. We predict that these microinfarcts impair brain plasticity and therefore decrease recovery following stroke. Using an animal model, we will study how microinfarcts alter brain plasticity and affect recovery after a major stroke. First, we will study the effects of microinfarcts on normal brain function by mapping out parts of the brain that control movement of the body. Specifically, we will study the part of the brain that can move the forepaw of mice and evaluate how microinfarcts affect the amount of movement produced when this region of the brain is stimulated. Next, we will study how microinfarcts alter recovery after a major stroke. We will measure brain activity as animals perform a reaching task. By imaging the same animals over several days, we can measure the plastic changes that occur in the brain that are responsible for improving motor performance. We will be able to determine if microinfarcts alter the amount of brain plasticity occurring following a major stroke. In our last experiment, we will evaluate if microinfarcts decrease the benefits of rehabilitation after focal stroke. Motor practice improves recovery after stroke, but we predict that microinfarcts will decrease the amount and quality of this motor behavior, resulting in impaired recovery.

column36: Revealing the Omnigenic Genetic Architecture of End Stage Renal Disease: Investigating the Cumulative Effect of Rare and Common Genetic Variants
column37: Purpose: Kidney disease affects 1 in 10 Canadians. 35,000 Canadians currently have kidney failure needing dialysis or a kidney transplant. A cause for kidney failure is unknown in 50% of patients. Kidney disease does not make people unwell until it is advanced. If properly identified, it may be possible to treat people earlier before their kidney disease has progressed. Diet and the environment contribute to kidney disease, but our genes play a large role. Each person has 30,000 genes, and loss of even one gene can cause kidney disease. Over 200 different types of kidney diseases caused by a single gene mutation have been discovered. However, each of these kidney diseases are rare, and together they account for a small proportion of patients with kidney failure. We will look for patients whose kidney disease is due to the total effect of many genes that are working poorly, instead of a single gene that is very abnormal. Procedure: Using the latest genetic testing available, we will test genetic risk factors in 3,700 patients with kidney disease. We will compare these results to more than 500,000 people from the general population. We will then focus on patients who are without a diagnosis to look for new types of kidney disease. Expected Outcome: We will find new combinations of genes that are working poorly that lead patients to develop kidney disease. Relevance to patients: Our research will improve our ability to tell patients what is causing their kidney disease. It will improve our ability to predict who is likely to get worse, even in early stages of kidney disease. We will be able to give better advice to kidney donors about their personal risk of kidney failure. We and others will use our findings to target new treatments for kidney disease.

column36: Improving methods for the determination of minimal important difference estimates for patient-reported outcomes and their application in clinical research and decision-making
column37: In deciding whether to use a particular treatment for conditions such as depression, arthritis, or heart disease, doctors and patients must balance the benefits against the side effects and burden. To make this trade-off, they must understand the likely degree of benefit in symptoms and well being. Researchers typically measure symptoms and well-being using questionnaires that ask patients to describe how they are feeling. We call such questionnaires patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). More and more, researchers use PROMs to test health care treatments. Information that researchers obtain from PROMs can guide clinical decisions and inform shared-decision making between patients and their doctors. However, the use of PROMs involves challenges. The most important of these challenges is deciding if a particular treatment effect is trivial, small but important, or large. For instance, without further information, patients and clinicians may find it difficult to decide if a 3-point difference on a questionnaire is a trivial or large effect. One way to make this judgment is to consider the minimal important difference (MID), which represents the smallest change in a PROM score that is important enough that patients would consider a change in treatment to achieve that benefit. Over the past 3 decades, researchers have developed methods to estimate MIDs for PROMs. However, the studies using these methods are not planned or conducted equally well. Though the MID represents an attractive way of interpreting research results, there is much we are still learning about the methods of measuring MIDs. We plan to lead a series of projects that will further advance MID methods and optimize the presentation and interpretation of results from PROMs in clinical trials, systematic reviews and clinical practice guidelines to inform evidence-based clinical decision-making, ultimately enhancing quality of care and patient outcomes.

column36: Carbapenemase inhibitors for use as adjuvants in treating carbapenem-resistant bacterial infections
column37: Increasingly, bacterial infections, particularly those acquired in hospitals, are being caused by bacteria that are resistant to current antibiotics. In order to ensure that a last line of defense is available in such cases, antibiotics, such as the carbapenems, to which resistance was very rare, are restricted to use in hospitals. This prudent practice has delayed the onset of resistance to these essential antibiotics. Unfortunately, certain bacteria now produce enzymes called carbapenemases that destroy these last- line-of-defense antibiotics. Thus bacterial infections that were once readily managed through the judicious use of carbapenems are now becoming life-threatening, especially for patients whose immune systems are compromised such as cystic fibrosis patients, burn victims, the elderly, AIDS patients, cancer patients and organ transplant patients. The goal of this project is to discover pharmaceuticals that inactivate the bacterial carbapenemases. Such drugs would be co-administered along with the carbapenems in order to block the bacterial resistance mechanism thus making the carbapenems effective against bacteria that are currently resistant.

column36: Hemodynamics of Pediatric Congenital Heart Disease Using Accelerated and Motion-Compensated MRI
column37: Nearly 1% of babies born in Canada have heart disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an essential technology for evaluating this condition. In addition to showing the anatomy of the heart, MRI can also measure blood flow. This information helps doctors decide how serious the heart problem is, and how to treat the child. MRI can then be used again, to see how well the child responds to the treatment. A major challenge of MRI is that patients must remain motionless when pictures are being recorded, which is difficult for young children. In traditional MRI scans, motion will ruin the images. Medical staff must then repeat the scans, which prolongs the MRI examination. If a child is unable to remain still, sedation is necessary. Another significant challenge of traditional MRI scans of heart disease is the need to align the scan plane to the proper anatomy. This meticulous process further lengthens the scan and requires an expert in cardiac imaging. The goal of this proposal is to address these challenges by developing a fast (<5 minute), motion-insensitive MRI method to visualize three-dimensional (3D) anatomy and blood flow throughout the entire chest in children with heart disease. This proposal first focuses on developing new methods to speed up 3D MRI measurements of chest anatomy and blood flow, while also compensating for patient motions such as breathing and shifting within the MRI. Initially, development will be achieved by scanning adult volunteers. The resulting methods will then be applied to children with and without heart disease. This project will enable comprehensive evaluation of heart disease in a practical scan time and avoid the need for tailored scan prescriptions by an expert in cardiovascular anatomy. In addition to serving as a powerful tool for planning therapy, this work promises to transform our understanding and management of heart disease in kids.

column36: Clearance of senescent cells to improve immune functions in aged mice
column37: Senescent cells are induced during chronological aging and by a wide range of DNA damaging agents such as ionizing radiation (IR). These damaged cells accumulate in tissues and are detrimental to the organism in part through their secretion of inflammatory molecules. We and others have shown that exposure of mice and human to IR leads to an increased expression of p16INK4a, a marker and inducer of aging/senescence. Our recent results have shown that the accumulation of p16INK4a senescent cells interferes with immune cell functions in the spleen. In particular, we found macrophages isolated from irradiated mice to express high levels of p16INK4a and to have a reduced activity. We also identify a defect in the capacity of T cells to proliferate, an effect that was largely dependent on the splenic microenvironment. Elimination of p16INK4a expressing cells allowed for the restoration of T cell proliferation and function of macrophages. Moreover, elimination of senescent cells, using a new class of drugs (senolytic) capable of specifically killing senescent cells, was shown to reverse aging in mice. Based on this information we make the hypothesis that elimination of senescent cells through the use of senolytic drugs may improve immune cell functions allowing better cancer immunotherapies in aged and cancer treated patients.

column36: Multi-centre diagnostic performance of dynamic CT perfusion for functional assessment of multi-vessel coronary artery disease with dense coronary calcification
column37: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is a condition in which one or more blood vessels in the heart are narrowed due to plaque formation, and is one of the leading causes of death and disability in Canada and around the world. Diagnosis and management of CAD are both medically challenging and costly, especially when the disease involves more than one blood vessel and the plaques are densely calcified. This research study aims to evaluate the accuracy of a non-invasive and cost-effective imaging technique to safely and rapidly evaluate the risk of life-threatening heart disease in patients that have densely calcified plaques in multiple blood vessels in the heart. This novel imaging technique will be validated against clinical gold-standards. The new imaging technique uses X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) to take pictures of the heart after injecting a small dose of x-ray dye, to assess whether narrowing of the blood vessels will lead to damage to the heart muscle. The results may allow physicians to accurately and rapidly evaluate patients presenting with chest discomfort for life-threatening heart disease versus other benign causes. Furthermore, the results would allow physicians to more quickly deliver proper treatment, avoid misdiagnosis and reduce unnecessary hospitalizations and invasive procedures. Consequently, this test would potentially decrease healthcare costs as compared to present clinical practice.

column36: Lii Zaanfaan: Understanding Health and Well-being Trajectories of Metis Children in Alberta
column37: The Metis are post-contact Indigenous peoples of Canada with a unique combination of identity, values, language, and cultural traditions. They have been referred to as "hidden" Indigenous peoples because of the lack of health research and service policies specific to their needs and experiences. There are not many studies on Metis health and particularly about Metis children's health. Most research on this area groups the experiences of Metis, First Nations, and Inuit children together. The first decade of life is an important period for the influences of key genetic, biological and socioenvironmental factors It is important to understand the ways in which factors that affect the health and well-being of Metis mothers influence the healthy development of Metis children. Lii Zaanfaan means "the children" in Michif, the traditional language of the Metis. From a Metis perspective, the health of children is deeply linked to the health of their families, communities, and the land. This perspective is supportive of broader knowledge on social determinants of health and childhood development. This research results from a long-standing collaboration between the Metis Nation of Alberta and academic partners to develop community relevant knowledge to inform Metis-specific health initiatives. The project has three objectives: 1) evaluate health and well-being trajectories of Metis children during the first 10 years of life and the influences of maternal and social factors on these outcomes; 2) explore perspectives of Metis children and their families on social, environment and cultural factors that influence well-being and healthy development of children, and 3) identify community-led, culturally meaningful Metis initiatives to promote Metis children's health and well-being through cultural healing and self-determination. We will use a variety of quantitative and qualitative research methods that are culturally acceptable within a Metis context.

column37: Heart failure (HF) is a leading cause of death, hospitalization, and healthcare system expenditure in Canada. While care in HF clinics - multidisciplinary clinics that focus on optimal management of HF - improves health outcomes in HF, there are disparities in access to such care across our province. To respond to the needs of patients and our health care system, we propose to develop and implement a 'Virtual HF Clinic' model of care that will enable Canadians with HF to receive outpatient HF care in the comfort of their homes. We will assess the effectiveness of this model of care in a randomized controlled trial, and collect feedback from patients and providers. We hypothesize that virtual clinics will be effective, and that they will improve clinical, patient-reported, and cost outcomes relative to care in routine heart failure clinics.

column36: Using MRI imaging to develop a personalized risk-based breast cancer screening strategy
column37: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can detect breast cancer earlier than mammography or ultrasound. However, because MRI is very expensive and more likely to mistake benign breast structures for cancer, MRI is usually only offered to women with the highest risk of developing breast cancer based on genetic testing, family history, or previous radiation to the chest. The High-Risk Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP) is a unique screening program which provides annual screening with MRI to high-risk women. There is still a lot of variation in this high-risk group. At one extreme are young women with an inherited BRCA1 mutation who tend to develop aggressive, rapidly growing tumours. These women may benefit from more frequent screening or prophylactic mastectomy. At the other extreme are women with a strong family history associated with a currently unknown genetic abnormality who could actually be at average risk and who may not need annual screening. There is, therefore, a need for improved risk prediction methods. We propose to develop new artificial intelligence methods to extract information about breast tissue volume and texture from MRI. With MRI we can also measure how much contrast agent is taken up in normal breast tissue; this is known as background parenchymal enhancement, BPE, and it has been shown that there is a correlation between BPE and risk. We will assess whether a combination of these MRI properties can be used to predict cancer risk. We will also determine whether they are more strongly correlated with breast cancer risk than mammographic density which is already known to be useful in identifying patients at intermediate risk. Our methods will be tested on data from the OBSP which screens thousands of high-risk women each year at 30 different centres in Ontario. A more accurate assessment of risk could allow screening programs to be tailored to the needs of individual women and would also make better use of limited resources.

column36: Fatty acid metabolism in carriers of apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 allele: determining the blood-to-brain link
column37: In Canada, ~17 millions of adults between 30-64 y old could benefit from a prevention strategy to lower the risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although a lot of epidemiological studies reported positive cognitive outcomes in populations eating fish, there is skepticism about the link between docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 (OM3) fatty acid in fish and prevention of cognitive decline. This is largely because there is a disconnect between epidemiological, molecular and animal studies which generally favor a link between higher DHA intake and cognition whereas clinical DHA and fish oil trial data are less consistant. There are several knowledge gaps in this field that might explain why clinical trials were not successful but this proposal will focus on two major gaps: OM3 fatty acid metabolism and the blood-to-brain DHA link. OM3 supplements in cardiovascular disease have faced the same issues for decades but the more recent trials have now generated the clinical evidence supporting primary and secondary cardiovascular events reduction and a better risk to benefit balance of OM3 drugs compared to statins, for instance. What if, for cognitive decline, we just have missed the target because the supplement/drug formulations were not appropriately designed to target the brain? We hypothesize that (i) E4 carriers display a faulty packaging of circulating OM3, leading to reduced available OM3 for brain cells, (ii) The use of new OM3 formulation can direct plasma OM3 into brain compartments more readily available for the brain, thereby increasing brain OM3 concentrations and improving cognition. We will perform studies in mice and humans to test OM3 metabolism and the blood-to-brain OM3 link. Ultimately the information generated in this grant application will help to better design clinical trials in terms of fatty acid formulation, expected level to reach in the plasma and the brain.

column36: Failing to Heal: Impaired Efferocytosis in Osteoarthritis
column37: Normal tissue turnover requires the clearance of dead and dying cells by special immune cells called macrophages. Without clearance, dead and dying cells can cause inflammation and damage to local tissues. We recently discovered that dead/dying cells accumulate in the lining of knee joints from patients with osteoarthritis (OA), suggesting that the process of clearing dead/dying cell clearance is defective. In this proposal, we will conduct experiments using animal models of knee OA and human tissues from patients with knee OA. Overall, our objective is to confirm and investigate why the process of dead/dying cell clearance is defective in OA to determine how best to treat OA. Specifically, we will: 1. Since females are more often affected by knee OA, we will study the impact of female sex and other OA risk factors on the ability of macrophages to clear dead/dying cells. 2. Test the effects of a) blocking cell clearance, and b) stimulating cell clearance on important OA outcomes using a rat model of knee OA. We will look at joint tissue damage and pain outcomes in this model, which has been shown to mimic the symptoms and joint damage seen in human knee OA. 3. Identify the specific molecular mechanisms that cause cell clearance to be impaired. This step is needed to identify the key targets that will be the focus of new OA treatments. In the future, such treatments would be designed to improve the clearance of dead/dying cells as specifically as possible, without causing unwanted off-target side-effects. These studies are critical to understand the role of cell clearance in OA and to set the stage for new treatment targets to be tested. OA is a massive unmet clinical need because it causes significant disability for people with OA. OA also causes significant costs to our health care system in Canada. Currently, no approved disease-modifying OA treatment exists. Therefore, our proposal describes an exciting new way to look at OA treatments and hope for the future.

column36: Strategies to Relieve Suffering at End-of-Life (STRS-EOL): A longitudinal qualitative study of healthcare policy and nursing practice.
column37: Suffering at end-of-life is not new or uncommon. However, what is new in Canada are the options available to address this suffering and how those options are intersecting in end-of-life decision-making. In this grant, we are using the acronym STRS-EOL to refer to these options for relieving suffering at end-of-life and they include medical assistance in dying (MAiD), palliative care (PC), voluntary stopping eating and drinking (VSED), and palliative sedation (PS). Palliative patients often ask healthcare providers to hasten their death, particularly during moments of suffering. In past, however, no legal options were available to address this request. In 2016 that changed. Canadians who meet eligibility requirements can now have MAiD whereby medications are used to induce death. Persons who request MAiD must be given the option of palliative care; however, it is widely recognized that there is a need to improve access to palliative care in Canada. Further, not all clients meet the eligibility criteria for MAiD, and in those cases, patients may resort to VSED or PS. Patients stop eating until they qualify for MAiD or they are sedated. With these evolving changes, there is a need to understand how the interactions between these approaches, and how broader social and demographic factors, are influencing these end-of-life decisions. Building upon research we are currently conducting, our aim in this project is to gain a thorough understanding of the developmental trajectory over an eight year period of policy and practice related to STRS-EOL. We will gather and analyze longitudinal data from policy documents, key stakeholders, and nurses with the goal of creating unique and highly sought after data to track and compare the developmental trajectory of STRS-EOL across English-speaking Canadian health regions over time. Through this knowledge we will support wide-spread uptake of STRS-EOL best practices and improved practitioner well-being and moral development.

column36: Ketone bodies as therapeutic agents to reduce the harmful effects of bed rest on muscle mass and metabolic health in older adults
column37: Bed rest is a common feature of many clinical environments such as hospitals and long-term care facilities. However, the physical inactivity associated with bed rest results in reductions in muscle size, muscle strength, and physical performance (i.e. rising from a chair) that can lead to a reduced quality of life and a higher risk of disease and death. Eating protein-rich foods and exercising normally helps to maintain muscle size by building proteins found in muscle. However, during bed rest there is a reduction in the rate at which proteins found in muscle are made and this leads to smaller muscles. Bed rest leads to problems with blood glucose regulation and insulin resistance which can increase the risk for diabetes. Both the loss of muscle size and insulin resistance are linked to problems with components of our cells called mitochondria. Mitochondria do a lot of important things including keeping our cells full of energy. Bed rest occurs more frequently in older adults and also negatively impacts their health more than in younger adults. Sadly, there are limited options to prevent the problems associated with bed rest. Ketone bodies are molecules that come from fat that are normally produced in the body in response to reduced carbohydrate intake (i.e. a ketogenic diet). Recently ketone supplements have become available, which increase the amount of ketone bodies in the body without the need to limit carbohydrate intake from food. Elevated ketone bodies may help protect muscle size and health during bed rest by enhancing the process of building muscle proteins, improving blood glucose regulation, and helping mitochondria work optimally. The current research project will determine whether ketone supplements can prevent the typical decline in muscle size, protein synthesis, insulin sensitivity, and muscle mitochondrial function that occurs in response to bed rest. This may positively impact the heath of older adults and speed their recovery from bed rest.

column36: Preventable strokes and deaths in atrial fibrillation patients: Understanding the impacts of anticoagulant nonadherence and nonpersistence
column37: Atrial fibrillation (Afib) is a type of irregular heart rhythm that is common in Canada. Patients with Afib are at much higher risk of stroke than those without Afib. Stroke can lead to disability or death, so it is crucial to prevent it in those at risk. A group of medications called "anticoagulants" are very effective for preventing stroke in AFib patients, but they can't work if they are not taken reliably by patients. Our goal is to provide an understanding of how big this problem is so we can help protect Canadians against preventable strokes and deaths. To achieve this goal, we will study health data (e.g. prescriptions, physician billing records, hospital records) of all Afib patients in British Columbia since 1996. We will study their patterns of medication taking to identify how many of the AF patients are early quitters, late quitters, perfect users, and those who miss many of their doses. We will also identify which kinds of patients follow each pattern so we can better know how to provide the right patients with the right kinds of help to improve their medication taking. We will then study how many strokes and deaths are caused by problems with medication-taking (stopping, taking it unreliably) and the resulting costs to the healthcare system. Our research team includes clinicians, researchers and policy makers who have extensive experience working with AF patients and doing this type of research. Our research will provide much-needed evidence to clinicians, patients, and policymakers to better protect patients with AF against avoidable strokes and deaths.

column36: Low Dose Metronomic Chemotherapy as a Combination Strategy to Combat Innate or Acquired Resistance to Immune Checkpoint Therapy
column37: The most significant recent advance in oncology is the remarkable success of new drugs which harness the immune system to treat advanced metastatic disease of a number of different cancers. Foremost among these drugs are "immune checkpoint inhibitor" (ICI) antibodies. However, a dose of reality has set in to temper some of the initial euphoria about these drugs. First, they are enormously expensive, placing a likely unsustainable strain on health care system budgets. Second, only minor subsets of patient (an average of ~15%) benefit from receiving ICIs. Third, they can be very toxic causing a number of immune related adverse events (irAEs). Finally, tumors which initially respond to ICI therapy usually acquire resistance and relapse. A strategy being studied to improve the efficacy of ICIs is by combination with other types of drug. But this approach can exacerbate the problems of both overall toxicity and cost. This proposal is designed to evaluate a strategy to deal with both problems, and using it to combat ICI drug resistance, namely, evaluating the impact of using lower and hence less toxic doses of certain inexpensive off-patent oral chemotherapy drugs, but given in a close regular fashion - known as "metronomic" chemotherapy (MC) - which Dr. Kerbel's lab has helped pioneer; it has shown positive results in some recent phase III clinical trials, especially when used as maintenance therapies after initial induction chemotherapy. There is evidence that certain chemotherapy drugs given as MC can actually stimulate rather than suppress tumor immunity, the latter of which can occur when given at conventional 'maximum tolerated doses'. Finally, the research will involve use of a number of new mouse models that mimic the clinical treatment of metastatic disease, and new tumor models that are either minimally sensitive, or intrinsically resistant to an ICI, or which have acquired resistance after showing major durable tumor regressions.
