column36: Photoacoustic imaging of kidney fibrosis: A tool for assessing pre-transplant organ quality
column37: Transplantation has revolutionized the lives of patients with kidney failure, being the only therapy that prolongs life span and improves quality of life. Donor kidneys, however, are in very short supply, such that patients must wait up to 8 years for a transplant, and in many cases never receive a kidney. With this shortage in mind, doctors are forced to accept kidneys for transplant from sicker donors. While many of these kidneys are suitable for transplant, some unfortunately are already injured when they are transplanted. Ultimately, the end result is that some patients who wait years for a transplant end up receiving kidneys that work less well, and which fail prematurely, forcing patients right back on the long transplantation wait list. Scarring is the most common and important type of injury seen in donor kidneys. Unfortunately, doctors have very limited ways to assess this chronic damage, relying instead on non-specific and insensitive measures that do not reliably measure the degree of kidney scarring. There is a desperate need for accurate tools to assess the degree of injury in potential transplant kidneys, and that predict how well these kidneys will function in the long term. We are working to develop a new cutting-edge technique called photoacoustic imaging to measure scarring in transplant kidneys. Our ultimate goal is to help doctors better select kidneys for transplantation, and thus improve kidney transplant outcomes by better allocating the scarce kidneys available. Our St. Michael's Hospital-based multidisciplinary team, composed of kidney doctors, radiologists, pathologists, and physicists, is uniquely suited to conduct these studies. Most importantly, working with a world leading industry partner with key connections to transplant centres across Canada, we are ideally positioned to translate our research findings into clinical practice.

column37: Respiratory disease such as asthma, tuberculosis and the flu are huge worldwide health burdens. Treatment options for people remain limited and there is a need for new drugs with minimal side effects. A better understanding of the factors that control the immune cells in the lung will be key to making new treatments for these diseases. Further, the effects of gut dwelling protists on triggering lung disease or changing severity are not known. In this proposal, we aim to characterize the changes in immune cell function within the lungs after T.mu colonization in the gut and determine the effects on the severity of allergic asthma as well as influenza and tuberculosis infection in hopes to open new paths for the development of new treatments for respiratory diseases.

column36: Determining the effectiveness of changes in health behaviours for reducing the risk of breast cancer in women at higher genetic risk: the TAIGA-BC study
column37: For some women, their genes place them at a higher risk of breast cancer. Genetic testing for breast cancer risk is now common place among women with a family history of breast cancer. By knowing her genetic risk of breast cancer, a woman can make important choices regarding how to prevent breast cancer or how to detect it early. Having information specific to women at high genetic risk helps these women make these difficult decisions. For example, it is known that mammography and ultrasound are not as good at detecting breast cancer in women with high-risk versions of the BRCA1 and/or BRCA2 genes when compared to women who do not have these high-risk versions. Therefore, women who have these high-risk versions are advised to be screened for breast cancer using MRI additionally. Breast cancer risk can also be reduced through changes in health behaviours such as quitting smoking, drinking less alcohol or losing weight but there is no evidence tailored toward women who are at a high genetic risk of breast cancer to help them make these decisions. This project aims to produce exactly this type of information. For example, this project will look at whether quitting smoking might have a bigger impact on reducing breast cancer among women at high genetic risk of breast cancer than women at lower risk. This information, in combination with being at high genetic risk of breast cancer might make a woman choose to quit smoking. Without the information specific to women at high genetic risk, she may have made a different decision. This project will produce this type of information for smoking, alcohol and weight loss. It will also produce similar information but for policy makers about how much breast cancer rates might be reduced if, for example, the number of people smoking decreased by half. Finally, this project will lay the statistical groundwork so that other researchers can make the same type of information for people at higher genetic risks of other diseases.

column36: Mechanisms for assembly of membrane protein complexes in the endoplasmic reticulum
column37: Cells contain several nano-machines composed of protein molecules that perform most of the molecular functions required to keep a cell alive. For these nano-machines to function properly, their component protein molecules need to be synthesized and delivered to the right place at the right time. Human cells contain a billion different protein molecules and ensuring their correct localization creates a large logistical challenge for our cells. First, cells need to ensure that newly made proteins get to the right part of the cell and assemble into functional machines. Second, cells have to recognize errors in protein maturation and target the defective products for degradation. Both processes are essential to all living cells, and even subtle problems in protein maturation or quality control can lead to many known genetic and neurological disorders such as epilepsy. 50% of all idiopathic-generalized epilepsy is caused by genetic mutations in molecular machines called the GABA A receptors that are one of the major receptors for signal transmission in our nervous system. Fundamental studies in the field of cell biology have shown that multiple pathways exist in cells to target simple model proteins to their correct sub-cellular location. However, we still do not understand the specific pathway used by complex proteins such as the GABA A receptors that can be formed by 19 different proteins in our body. In this study, we propose assays and experiments by which we can identify the factors involved in assembly of GABA A receptors. Many of the assays proposed in this study were developed in our lab and have been made possible due to recent breakthroughs in gene editing and single-molecule technologies. With these tools, we aim to build a detailed map of cellular pathways involved in maturation of GABA A receptors present in our body. The data generated here can provide insights into the pathological basis of epilepsy-causing mutations and guide design of new therapeutics.

column36: Improving Health System Quality Through Better Measurement and Service Delivery Redesign
column37: Poor quality of health care is currently a bigger barrier to reducing mortality than inadequate access in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs). Advanced quantitative analyses will be conducted to populate the Ethiopian quality dashboard with cross-sectional and longitudinal quality data nationally and by regions. Sophisticated modeling approaches will be used to estimate the impact of service delivery redesign in Kenya. This research has the potential to inform efforts to enhance the quality of health care and improve health sustainably in LMICs, including Ethiopia and Kenya.

column36: Untangling the relationship ageing, frailty, and dementia.
column37: As the world's population ages, the number of people living with dementia is quickly growing. Dementia inflicts an enormous burden on individuals, their families and caregivers, and our society. By 2050, over 131 million people globally will be living with dementia, costing more than US$818 billion. Following multiple failed drug trials for dementia, we urgently need to better understand how dementia develops in order to treat and prevent the disease. Interestingly, the brain abnormalities (pathology) that are thought to cause dementia are not related very well to the symptoms- that is some people have brain pathology but no dementia, and some people with dementia have very little brain pathology. Frailty has been associated with cognitive decline and dementia and they share many risk factors. My hypothesis is that frailty affects the level of brain pathology needed to produce the clinical symptoms of dementia. The objectives of the proposed study are to 1) test how frailty, brain pathology, and dementia are related in a collection of studies that accurately represent the population, 2) test the impact of reducing frailty on dementia risk by re-analyzing clinical trial data. This project is important because it has the potential to change our understanding of how dementia develops. By improving our understanding of dementia development we will be better able to target our research, clinical, and policy efforts towards finding effective prevention and treatment.

column36: Turning White Fat into Energy-burning Brown Fat: New hope in the fight against Obesity.
column37: Obesity, a condition characterized by excess fat accumulation and energy dis-balance, is skyrocketing and remains a major health concern worldwide. The study of white adipose tissue (WAT) 'browning' has become a 'hot topic' in obesity, based on the idea that WAT browning might be able to facilitate weight loss and improve metabolic health. Two types of body fat, white adipose tissue (WAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT), exist in humans. WAT acts as an energy reservoir to store excess calories and supplies stored lipid energy when the body is starved or has increased energy needs. An excessive accumulation of WAT over time results in obesity, a medical condition that has been linked to various life-threatening diseases such as cardiovascular diseases and type 2 diabetes. In contrast, BAT burns excess calories to produce heat as a defense against cold temperatures. For a long time, the adipose tissue was categorized into these two distinct types (brown, white), but recently the lines have blurred with the discovery of beige fat. As the name suggests beige fat shares characteristics of both white (fat storage) and brown fat cells (fat breakdown). This unique bi-functional property in which white adipocytes cells store fat in the absence of stimulation, but burn fat in the form of heat production under-stimulation can potentially be exploited in obesity to induce weight loss. Therefore, this project first aims to elucidate the molecular pathways that regulate fat metabolism and remodeling (switch from white to brown fat) and to tease out the signaling pathways involved in macrophage-mediated WAT browning and energy expenditure. The results of this research project will also both characterize the lipidome associated with WAT browning and the associated effects of these lipids on organ and cellular function during obesity. Overall, this research project will allow us to uncover potential strategies for the treatment of obesity and its associated comorbidities.

We will do this for the entire AYA group, and for AYA with specific cancers (e.g. lymphomas, testicular cancer). Our results will be communicated to doctors, nurses, and AYA patients so that they know which symptoms are most relevant to AYA. Our results will help design interventions aimed at controlling the worst symptoms. Our results will show which AYA should be the target of interventions because they are at high risk. column36: HIV prevention altruism among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men. Associations with attitudes and behaviour related to sexual risk-taking.
column37: A growing body of evidence suggests that concern for others (i.e., altruism) influences decision making to reduce HIV transmission and avoid sexual risk. Thus, HIV prevention altruism ranges from preventing passing HIV to one's partners, to concern regarding the impact of HIV on one's community. Given that HIV prevention altruism might affect the behaviour of gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (GBM), we investigated how this factor could be predicted by community involvement, attitudes, and sexual behaviours among HIV-positive and HIV-negative GBM. We recruited 2440 sexually active GBM living in Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver to take part on a multi-city cross-sectional study (the Engage Study). Participants completed a computer-assisted survey that included a measure of HIV prevention altruism (the Sexual Communal Altruism Scale). We found that higher scores on our measure of HIV prevention altruism were associated with lower sexual compulsivity, fewer male sexual partners (in the past six months), a lower likelihood of engaging in condomless sex (in the past six months), and fewer perceived barriers to condom use. However, HIV prevention altruism scores had no association with involvement in the LGBTQ community. These findings offer some insight into how HIV prevention altruism impacts HIV risk behaviours among GBM.

column36: Mechanism of protein translocation across the parasitophorous vacuole membrane of the malaria parasite
column37: Malaria has caused widespread death tolls around the globe. According to the World Malaria Report released in November 2018, the number of malaria cases in 2017 spanned 90 countries and totaled 219 million worldwide. After infecting the human host, the malaria parasite remodels the cell by exporting hundreds of effector proteins that travel from the endoplasmic reticulum to the parasitophorous vacuole (PV). Upon arrival, these proteins are unfolded and cross the PV membrane with the aid of the Plasmodium translocon of exported proteins (PTEX), a membrane protein complex. Despite the progress in understanding the general protein export process, the molecular mechanism and dynamics of protein translocation across PTEX remain poorly understood. Recent crystal structures of the PTEX engaged and resetting states provide useful starting points for simulating and uncovering the translocation mechanism. By combining structural information with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, I aim to uncover the PTEX translocation mechanism in detail. Coarse-grained MD simulations will allow me to simulate the translocation process (including pre-translocation and post-translocation). I will also calculate the free-energy landscape from MD snapshots to identify distinct states and their associated timescales in the translocation processive phase. In turn, this can inform the design of inhibitors that target PTEX and other related parasitic translocons.

column36: Contribution of the microbiome to asthma risk in premature infants
column37: Premature infants are at increased risk of life-long diseases and treatments. Among the most compromised organs of premature infants are the lungs. In Canada and globally, very premature infants (between 28-32 weeks of gestation) and extremely premature infants (less than 28 weeks of gestation) are up to three and four times respectively, more likely to develop recurrent wheeze than term infants. Until now, lung compromise has been an accepted result of developmental delay and lung structural damage caused by medical practices needed to support respiration. However, epidemiological evidence shows that infants who do not develop lung structural damage are nevertheless at increased risk of asthma, indicating that other variables impact this risk. Exciting recent findings from infant studies and animal models implicate the large community of microbes (microbiome) in the human gut as a factor that contributes to asthma. However, despite their heightened risk of asthma and the pronounced microbiome alterations linked to prematurity, no clinical study of the microbiome and asthma has studied premature infants. Leveraging a world class team of microbiome experts and an established cohort specifically designed to capture clinical and environmental exposures unique to the NICU, this team grant will be the first to unravel microbiome-asthma linkages in the highly vulnerable premature infant population. We will apply powerful statistical tools to detect independent associations between microbiome features and asthma risk, and to interrogate the capacity of these species to mediate asthma risk. We will then use animal models to define the mechanisms by which specific microbes contribute to immune and neuroimmune pathways that lead to allergic airway inflammation. Our work will culminate in the identification of pre-clinical microbiome-based therapeutics aimed at decreasing the risk of asthma in thousands of Canadian children born prematurely every year.

column37: Atherosclerosis is a disease that is characterized by hardened deposits of fat (plaque) buildup within arterial walls. When a particular type of white blood cell - termed 'macrophage'; involved in pinpointing & cleaning cellular debris - is unable to perform its functions, gradual formation of a "dead-cell zone" within this plaque ensues, effectively making it weaker and more prone to rupturing. This rupturing may lead to eventual stroke and/or heart attack. The type of cell death that occurs within this zone is scientifically called "necroptosis". Our group has previously shown that in human advanced plaques this type of death is initiated within this area, as proven by an increase in the levels of informational messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) of genes that govern necroptosis (Ripk3 & Mlkl). The use of small micro-ribonucleic acids (miRs) are employed as a manner to control the levels of mRNA in a cell. Thus, linkages between necroptosis and miRs as applied to atherosclerosis forms the basis of this project. Using a series of computer generated algorithms we have determined various miRs that generally target these key genes in the necroptosis pathway. Based on this knowledge, we predict that there may be additional novel miRs, which are minimally expressed serving to control Ripk3 & Mlkl contributing to the progression of atherosclerosis. In order to test this, various techniques are employed ranging from those that serve to pinpoint the specific genes of interest (Ripk3 & Mlkl) which - when complemented with methods to assess the exact composition of these genes - may serve to identify novel therapeutic molecules. Furthermore, once these are identified, functional analysis - both in a petri-dish and in animal models - may ensue in order to provide more information in a more applicable disease model. Together, these techniques and discoveries may pave the way towards using small biological molecules to control the advancement of atherosclerosis.

Smoothelin-like 1 (SMTNL1) protein is a novel regulator of blood vessel function, including vascular tone and blood flow, blood vessel (endothelial) barrier function, inflammatory responses, transendothelial migration of circulating immune cells, and wound repair. We recently showed development of impairment in relaxation of heart with the deletion of SMTNL1 in young male mice. Echocardiographic (ECG) and pressure-volume loop measurements were carried out in 3-, 12-and 18-month old male and female SMTNL1 knockout (KO) mice to study the effect of age and sex on relaxation with SMTNL1 deficiency. The 129S6 wildtype (WT) background strain at each age point served as the control group. ECG analysis of KO mice showed normal contractile function when compared to the WT counterparts with ageing. However, the PV loop data revealed impaired relaxation in male cohort at all age points while female KO group developed it only at post-menopausal age of 18-months, compared to their control WT counterparts. The study will help us to elucidate the sex-dimorphic and pathophysiological role of SMTNL1 protein in the regulation of cardiac hemodynamics in pre-clinical models of heart failure and aid in the development of SMTNL1 based therapeutics or diagnostic markers in the field of HFpEF.

column36: Usability in Blended Learning Programs within Health Professions Education: A Scoping Review
column37: Blended learning, an educational pedagogy that combines both traditional face-to-face teaching methods with technological innovations, is being implemented in training programs worldwide and specifically within the field of health professions education (HPE). Research indicates that usability, a multidimensional concept that is used to evaluate products and services, can be of paramount importance when evaluating the effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction with the use of blended learning programs (BLPs). Despite its importance, knowledge about the concept of usability and its consideration with respect to BLPs within the field of HPE remains lacking. Therefore, the purpose of my research was to develop a foundational understanding of how BLPs have generally been and are currently being evaluated in the field of HPE in relation to the concept of usability and its primary components (effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction). To do this, I conducted a scoping review guided by a well-established framework outlined by Arksey & O'Malley, 2005. This review initially identified 8626 studies of potential relevance. Through a rigorous screening process, 53 studies were included in this scoping review. Results from the quantitative and qualitative analyses of these studies identified a lack in the conceptual understanding of usability and its associated terms across the literature. The results suggest that there is no consensus among researchers regarding evaluation terminology or methodology in this context. This review presents several key findings that help to establish a fundamental understanding of BLP evaluations with respect to usability in the field of HPE. The findings of this study will be of paramount importance to stakeholders that plan on conducting evaluations of BLPs or developing new tools or frameworks to evaluate BLPs using the concept of usability in the context of HPE.

column36: Health Professional Identified Barriers to Living Donor Kidney Transplantation: A Quantitative Analysis
column37: End-stage renal disease is a serious illness with significant health consequences and high-cost treatment options. Living donor kidney transplantation (LDKT) is the most cost-effective treatment and has a better survival rate when compared to both dialysis and deceased donor kidney transplantation. Despite this, LDKT rates in Canada are decreasing and vary widely between provinces: <15%, 30-40%, and 50-60% of total transplants are from living donors in Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia, respectively. Efforts to increase LDKT tend to focus on patient education and training, but are only modestly effective. In addition, they may have created an unfair system favouring patients with the resources and means to find living donors. Less attention has been paid to barriers at the level of the health professional. The role of health professionals in a patient's decision to pursue LDKT is well known, but what is not known is whether health professionals identify barriers to discussing living donation with patients and potential donors. We first conducted a preliminary study to explore these barriers. Using this data, we prepared a 24-question survey and distributed it to health professionals involved in the care of patients with kidney disease in these three provinces of Canada. Our hypothesis was that these barriers are more prominent in provinces with lower rates of LDKT. The goals of this study were to quantify and compare these barriers between provinces, as well as identify targeted and pragmatic interventions in each province. Future work will involve conducting surveys in other provinces of Canada and prospective trials to address barriers to LDKT at the level of the health professional. Our long-term goal is to improve health care delivery to patients with end stage renal disease by increasing LDKT rates.

column36: Is NUCB1/Nesfatin-1-Like Peptide critical for growth and metabolism?
column37: Growth is a multifactorial process regulated by hormones, nutrition (including metabolic status, meal plan, and diet composition), environment (e.g. season), genetic and age, among other factors. Alteration of these factors results in growth disorders, and the regulation of the growth hormone (GH) is the most critical point. GH is produced and secreted in the somatotropes cells located in the pituitary. After its secretion, GH acts enhancing the secretion of insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) in the liver, and all together promoting somatic growth. Recently, two peptides, nesfatin-1 and nesfatin-1-like peptide (NLP), which are encoded in nucleobindins (NUCB), (nucleobindin-2/NUCB2 and nucleobindin-1/NUCB1, respectively) have been identified. In fact, NLP has been discovered in the lab of Dr. Unniappan (supervisor of this proposal). Nesfatin-1 and NLP are involved in different physiological functions including food intake and insulin secretion. Preliminary data suggest that these peptides have also growth regulatory effects in fish, so we hypothesized that a similar function could be exercised in mammals. In the current project (SHRF funded), the results have demonstrated that rodent somatotropes produce nesfatin-1 and NLP. Moreover, data suggest that those peptides, similarly to that found in fish, are very important in the regulation of GH secretion in the mammalian pituitary. Taking into account that a new mice model that genetically lack NLP (NUCB1/NLP-KO mice) will be available next year, together with the interesting results that we are observing, we aim to explore how critical is NUCB1/NLP for both growth and metabolism. We will study whether the absence of NLP affects somatic growth. As a logical extension of the actual project, we strongly believe that the new experiments planned in this project will increase the progress of this research. The expected results will provide important mechanistic insights on nesfatin-1 and NLP actions in health and disease.

column36: Single cell transcriptomic analysis of the mouse aortic intima: Insights into intercellular communication during early atherogenesis
column37: Atherosclerosis is a disease defined by unresolved inflammation in the major arteries. A primary risk factor for CVD is high cholesterol, but despite effective cholesterol-lowering therapies, atherosclerosis remains the principal cause of death in our society. Atherosclerosis develops silently for decades before causing heart attacks and strokes. My research focuses on cells and genes that participate in atherosclerosis. Currently, there are no therapies targeting cells in the artery wall to inhibit the formation and progression of atherosclerosis. These therapies would benefit patients with risk factors, such as high cholesterol. Myeloid cells (MCs) are white blood cells and important components of the immune system. MCs are found in the inner artery wall of healthy humans and animals, residing under a barrier of cells called endothelial cells (ECs). In fact, MCs are found only in areas where atherosclerosis develops. In mice with high cholesterol, arterial MCs engulf lipid and become "foam cells". This is the first step in the formation of atherosclerosis, and is followed by significant accumulation of foam cells within the artery wall. It is widely accepted that macrophages drive this process, however new data from our lab and others suggest a strong role for endothelial cells is the initial stages of disease. We believe that MCs and ECs communicate with each other within the artery wall and that elevated cholesterol disrupts this communication and prevents normal tissue homeostasis. My goal is to understand how cells communicate with each other under normal conditions and how elevated cholesterol and foam cells can alter this communication to initiate lesion development. This is an important endeavor since we believe that if we foster healthy endothelial-myeloid communication we can attenuate lesion development, and develop novel therapeutics to protect against atherosclerosis.

column37: Over the last decade, there has been a dramatic increase in the number of incarcerated Indigenous women within Canada's federal prisons. column36: Strength-based assessment in autism: toward more inclusive methods for the assessment of cognition across the whole spectrum
column37: Many subgroups of the autistic population, such as autistics who have behavioral challenges, or who have minimal or no verbal language abilities, have been overlooked in research. They do, however, represent an important proportion of the autistic population. In clinical or educational settings, many of these individuals are considered to be untestable and are therefore considered to be intellectually disabled. However, through my doctoral research project, we showed that when using tests that call upon autistics' strengths, by adapting them in ways to facilitate the administration process, it is indeed possible to evaluate young or minimally verbal autistic children. We also demonstrated that many of these children showed "unsuspected strengths", which we would not have been able to capture with usual tests. We called our method the Strength-Based Assessment (SBA). The objective of the current project is to test a new version of SBA that includes tests measuring attention, memory, etc. that were adapted using universal design principles, to make them accessible and feasible to all people regardless of their limitations. The goal is therefore to determine to what extend the adapted tests improve our ability to assess autistic individuals and their performance on these tests compared to standard assessment. Using the SBA method will allow a detailed description of strengths and weaknesses, which would have remained unknown with usual tests, and allow them to reach their highest potential. We hope the project will allow SBA to be implemented in clinical and educational settings and, in turn, will lead to intervention plans that are matched to the potential of each individual.

column36: Bioprinted in vitro models of the healthy-cancerous bone environment
column37: Giant cell tumour of bone is a type of cancer that generally affects people between 20-40 years of age. It occurs near the joints and is characterised by large volumes of bone being eroded. Treatments include surgically removing the tumour and filling with healthy bone from other regions of the patient's body (usually the pelvis). The amount of bone that can be transplanted from one site to another in the same patient is limited so when the tumour is too large, joint replacement surgery is required. There is currently a lack of effective therapies to prevent development of this disease beyond surgical intervention. To develop and screen new drugs to prevent bone erosion, we are developing a laboratory-based model using healthy cells as well as tumour samples from patients. This will use 3D printing technology (bioprinting) to place healthy bone cells in a ring-shape with a hole in the centre. The centre will then be filled with patient tumour samples and the effects of the tumour cells on the bone cells will be evaluated. When the model is established, anti-cancer drugs as well as drugs that prevent bone erosion will be added in varying doses. We hope to be able to screen these drugs to see which are the most effective at killing the cancer cells whilst maintaining the viability of the healthy bone cells, allowing them to grown bone-like tissue.

column36: Unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying cerebral blood flow deficits in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Reductions in blood flow within the brain has been identified as an early event in the development of Alzheimer's disease. It was recently discovered that the smallest blood vessels, capillaries, in the brain of Alzheimer's disease mice were being blocked by an immune cell, and this small blockage was responsible for large reductions in blood flow. Amazingly, when the immune cells were prevented from sticking to the inside of blood vessels, brain blood flow was returned to normal, and performance on memory tests also improved. There is a type of cellular stress that is increased in Alzheimer's disease that could initiate the pathway that leads to the adherence of these immune cells in the blood vessels. We hypothesize that there are two types of cells at the root of this problem: One cell found in close proximity to blood vessels that might be responsible for generating too much of this cellular stress, and another cell that lines the inside of blood vessels that is responding to it. We aim to investigate the role of this cellular stress in reducing brain blood flow by targeting molecular pathways in the brain that will remove this cellular stress and bolster the brain's defences against cellular stress, in hopes of restoring blood flow, and memory. We will use experimental methods that target our two cell types of interest so that we can change how the cells respond to certain molecules by adding or removing certain genes to test our hypothesis. We will also deliver drugs to these cells specifically and examine their effects on cellular stress, brain blood flow, and memory. The proposed project seeks to increase our understanding of how cellular stress can lead to immune cell adhesion in brain blood vessels, and thus reduced brain blood flow. Our work will allow us to identify more cell-specific molecular targets for future drug development efforts with reduced drug side effects, aimed at interfering with immune cell adhesion to blood vessels.

column36: Linking microstructure and macroscale function of affective brain networks in health and disease
column37: Emotional experience is a complex process involving the coordinated activity of a network of brain regions, with key contribution of limbic cortices. These regions are characterized by their unique microstructure (i.e. organization of neurons in the cortex), which can be directly related to functional networks underpinning emotion processing using advanced neuroimaging methods. Notably, microstructural changes in limbic areas are a core feature of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). These patients show connectivity alterations grounded in microstructural abnormalities of limbic structures, as well as increased prevalence of impaired mood and difficulties in emotional processing. This population thus offers a unique opportunity to study how altered limbic microstructure relates to changes in connectivity and affective processing. Our goal is to develop a novel framework integrating microstructure and connectivity of limbic regions to understand their role in affective functions. This approach will allow us to study how local microstructure constrains brain connectivity patterns, and how lesions in limbic systems impair affective functioning. Healthy participants and TLE patients will undergo high-resolution neuroimaging to probe cortical microstructure, functional networks, and brain activity associated with emotion processing. Electrophysiological data from intracranial electrodes recorded at rest and during emotion recognition tasks will also be collected in a subset of patients undergoing this procedure as part of their clinical workup. These investigations will extend neuroimaging findings with direct recordings of neural activity in task-free and affective state conditions. This research will shift our conceptualization of affective functioning, and promises to guide predictions of affective impairments. Our findings will also lead to better recognition of affective disruptions in TLE, facilitating access to treatment and improving well-being and quality of life.

column36: Call for Inclusive eHealth: Identification of Empirical Indicators to Achieve This
column37: Do you have access to your digital health record? What mobile applications do you use? eHealth, or any digital tool to take care of our health, is an integral part of our lives. This study will allow developers to use measurement indicators to develop and evaluate their eHealth tool so that it is accessible to all future users and contribute to digital health equity. column36: A life course approach to mental health of older refugees: A community-based participatory research study
column37: Background: The number of civilians forcibly displaced from their homes due to war and political violence reached over 60 million in 2015. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees estimates that older persons make up roughly 8.5% of the total population of displaced individuals. These individuals often receive limited attention from national and international aid providers although they are more likely to experience physical and psychological distress than younger refugees. These experiences, in turn, are associated with poor mental health. Unfortunately, there are few evidence-based health-promotion interventions designed to meet the needs of older refugees. Objectives: The goal of this proposal is to identify risk and protective factors for mental health and well-being of aging refugees residing in North America and develop best practice guidelines for clinicians and other health care providers working with this at-risk population. A collaborative partnership between refugee community stakeholders, researchers, and mental health providers will translate study findings into best practice guidelines for mental health care providers who work with older refugees. Implications and Public Health Significance: Findings from this proposal will increase our understanding of the impact of displacement on long-term mental health and inform clinical and policy interventions to improve mental health and successful aging of older refugees in Canada.

column36: Identification of biologically relevant gene networks and brain functional connectivity changes affected by glucocorticoids exposure in different developmental periods and their relationship with depressive-like state in male and female rats
column37: Depression is the most common psychiatric disorder worldwide with a age-onset peak during adolescence. Despite the genetic influence, depression is strongly influenced by environmental risk factors, such as stress. Usually, patients suffering from depression have higher levels of cortisol, a stress-related hormone, showing the associations between stress exposure and depression development. However, the precise role of this stress hormone, as glucocorticoids, in the development of emotional disorders remains unclear. Depression-like behaviors can be induced in rodents by repeated administration of glucocorticoids. The aim of this project is to evaluate the mechanisms involved in the depressive-like behavior induced by chronic corticosterone (glucocorticoid) administration in male and female adolescent and adult rats. column36: The Predictive Value of Sensitivity to Physical Activity for Disability among People with Back Pain
column37: Back pain is the leading cause of disability in Canada. Although studies show that physical activity can help reduce disability in the long-term, this is hard to achieve in reality. A major challenge is that, for back pain, physical activity often causes increased pain or emotional distress. This is referred to as "sensitivity to physical activity" (SPA). Unaddressed, SPA often discourages patients from consistently doing physical activities for rehabilitation. SPA can also discourage participation in activities of daily living. I recently published an article showing that SPA is associated with disability. Past studies have also found this. However, no study has yet determined if SPA is able to predict disability in the future. Also, different studies tend to measure SPA differently. Therefore, I aim to determine if SPA predicts disability 3 months later, and if this depends on (1) how SPA is measured (by monitoring increases in pain or the emotional reaction) and on (2) how a person deals with physical activity and pain in their daily life. To test this, I will conduct a study on 100 adults with recent back pain (less than 6 months), who will be recruited from physiotherapy clinics. They will come in for an initial visit and for a follow-up visit (3 months later). They will answer questionnaires evaluating their disability and pain. They will also complete a lifting task and rate reactions (pain, emotional distress); the lifting task's difficulty is adapted to each participant, in order to provoke a painful response. Finally, a smartphone app will be used to complete a journal on pain and activity for 7 days to categorize how a person deals with physical activity and pain in their daily life. This data will be analyzed using statistical calculations. Our findings are expected to help improve success in using physical activity to reduce disability among people with back pain.

column36: Investigation of the function of de novo peroxisomal biogenesis
column37: A cell is a highly ordered and compartmentalized place with intracellular organelles that perform a large number of essential biochemical reactions. Mitochondria and peroxisomes are such examples. While, mitochondria are known as the "energy powerhouse" of the cell, there are many other reactions that rely on a second, smaller organelle called the peroxisome to complete the chain reaction to obtain the final product. For example, the breakdown of very long chain fatty acids occurs first in peroxisomes, and the resulting shorter chain lipids are then transferred to mitochondria to be burned as energy. Without peroxisomes this cannot occur and the accumulation of products are toxic, causing cell death and diseases. These include rare disease, with complete absence of peroxisome, such as Zellweger syndrome, associated with dramatic consequences for the patients. There is also more common diseases associated with dysfunction of a specific peroxisomal pathway like plasmalogen generation in Parkinson's disease. The formation of new peroxisome is poorly understood. Our team showed that small vesicles originating from mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum are involved in peroxisome biogenesis. This project aims to unravel the molecular machinery and the signals that carries this process. Understanding in physiology how peroxisome biogenesis is induced and regulated will allow to help design new therapies for diseases associated with dysfunctional peroxisome.

column36: Computer-Aided Discovery of Estrogen Receptor Activation Function 2 (AF2) Inhibitors as the First-In-Class Therapies for Drug Resistant Breast Cancers
column37: 26,000 Canadian women are diagnosed with breast cancer (BCa) and 5,000 die from it every year[1]. All current BCa drugs block estradiol binding to estrogen receptor alpha (ERa) directly or indirectly. While anti-estrogens are very effective in initially controlling advanced metastatic BCa, tumor cells eventually progress to a hormone-resistant state where they no longer respond to conventional treatments. The Activation Function-2 (AF2) site of ERa is a new promising therapeutic target for advanced BCas, as AF2 inhibitors would be effective in hormone-resistant forms, and mutations of the estradiol binding site should not affect their efficacy. We previously developed AF2 inhibitors able to suppress the growth of resistant BCa cells[2,3]. Herein we propose to expand on our preliminary results and identify better drug candidates for BCa. The number of small molecules available for screening has increased exponentially in the last few years, with major chemical databases already exceeding a billion of purchasable entries. Despite the immense potential for drug discovery offered by this surge of chemicals, research has been lagging behind due to the unavailability of methods able to deal with such enormous amount of data. We developed progressive docking (PD), an artificial intelligence method capable to increase the speed of virtual screening by above 50X[4], allowing to evaluate for the first time billions of molecules. We will use PD to screen the entire ZINC15 database, containing 1.3 billion compounds, to discover new potent AF2 inhibitors with optimized drug-like profiles. We anticipate that this study will yeald a class of therapeutics with a novel mechanism of action to improve the outcome of resistant BCa for patients in Canada and worldwide. column36: A dissection of transmembrane signal transduction and downstream signaling response in cytokine receptors
column37: The immune system is of vital importance to maintenance of human health. There are two main branches of the immune system - the innate and adaptive immune systems. While both of these systems are required for proper defence against pathogens and other foreign challenges, it is truly the combined efforts of the two systems that provides the protection seen. At the intersection between the two systems, there are cytokines and cytokine receptors, which allow for intricate crosstalk between these systems. Many cytokine receptors are seen to have one transmembrane helix in their architecture and are thought to function by dimerizing or rearranging upon cytokine binding, resulting in signalling within the cell. Despite the vast efforts applied to the study of these receptors, the nature of how the signal is able to cross from outside the cell, with binding of the receptor, to inside the cell, where proteins will bind and downstream genes will be regulated, is poorly understood. One area of confusion is the notion that these receptors can have varied cellular responses to differential stimulus, which goes against the dogma that simple dimerization is a driving factor in these systems. I aim to fill this gap in knowledge by pursuing the structures of various full-length cytokine receptors with varying stimuli and resultant internal factors. In addition, I will use an existing toolkit of engineered ligands for a specific non-immunological cytokine receptor, EpoR, to modulate the receptor in a tunable way. In addition, we will expand this toolkit to immune cytokine receptors to decipher the differences between various receptor subtypes. Through this structural and protein engineering, we will provide vast insight into the mechanisms for cytokine signals being transduced across the membrane and provide a framework for the development of novel cytokine receptor targeted therapeutics.

column36: Investigating the impact of evolving cannabis access and use on substance use trajectories and drug-related harm in the context of an opioid overdose epidemic
column37: Cannabis is the most widely produced, distributed and consumed illicit drug worldwide. Canada and many other countries are introducing new regulatory approaches to cannabis, including legalization. Although most research has focused on the harms of cannabis use, recent evidence suggests that cannabis use may alter specific high-risk drug practices. This research indicates that cannabis is often used as a substitute for high-risk substances such as cocaine, heroin or prescription opioids. However, these studies have not examined the impact of cannabis use over time and it is uncertain how the legalization of recreational cannabis will influence rates of high-risk drug use, infectious disease risk and addiction treatment. Given the recent legalization of recreational cannabis in Canada and the current opioid overdose crisis, identifying the impacts of cannabis use on high-risk drug use will be important for informing clinical and public health practice, as well as policy. The purpose of this research program is to describe how changing cannabis access and use influences the development of high-risk drug use patterns and addiction treatment. To accomplish these objectives, we will use data from three long-running community-recruited cohort studies in Vancouver, Canada, which will be supplemented by linked administrative data on participation in addiction treatment. These cohorts are operated by the BC Centre on Substance Use and include over 3,700 individuals who use illicit drugs, including high rates of cannabis use (>40%). Importantly, these studies include participants at different points in their drug use career, including at-risk youth at early stages of illicit drug use and older adults who use illicit drugs and tend to be more involved in addiction services. The diverse composition of these cohorts provide the opportunity to study the effects of cannabis use on the trajectory of high-risk drug use across the lifespan of active illicit drug users.

column36: Examining the Ubiquitin Machinery in Genetic Diseases of Protein Misfolding
column37: Proteins are the critical bio-machines that safeguard a cell's survival. They coordinate an array of critical cellular processes including providing energy, monitoring for signs of damage and facilitating crucial biological reactions. However, the DNA that encodes these molecular machines can often be mutated. Such mutations can cause proteins to become misshapen and toxic. This commonly occurs in neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases as well as in genetic diseases like cystic fibrosis. Interestingly, mutations are most likely to alter proteins by changing the shape and assembly of these critical molecules. Indeed, a number of rare genetic diseases are thought to be caused by proteins changing shape or not taking on the appropriate shape at all. To prevent error-prone proteins from accumulating, the cell has a system to cull and recycle them. This crucial quality control pathway utilizes a distinct molecular tag, called ubiquitin, to triage these misfolded proteins. Ubiquitin can decorate proteins in unique ways to tag them for destruction or quarantine. This molecular signal has already been shown to be key in familial Parkinson's disease and is associated with many other degenerative conditions. Understanding the biology of how ubiquitin labels defective proteins and how we can tune this process will allow for new therapeutic targets to be identified in rare genetic diseases. This project aims to understand which players are key to the destruction of errant proteins, how they triage damaged proteins and how this can be applied to new treatments for rare diseases. This project will use cutting edge technologies to visualize this process in live cells and provide a new way to screen and identify new target genes that can turn back the clock on these aging and defective proteins.

column36: Clarifying and modifying the natural history of vascular cognitive impairment - a Canadian cohort study with a paired pilot clinical trial
column37: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is the second largest contributor to dementia, and commonly results from cerebral small vessel disease (cCVD). It often coexists with Alzheimer's disease. There is an urgent need for therapies to prevent the progression of cSVD and VCI, especially those that can be applied early before cognition is affected. However, VCI can be quite variable in terms of risk factors and outcomes, so if we are to reliably test potential therapies, it is important to clearly identify patients who are likely to show measurable decline versus those with more stable disease. This postdoctoral project aims to identify markers of these individuals-at-risk using data from the COMPASS-ND (Comprehensive Assessment of Neurodegeneration and Dementia) cohort study of the Canadian Consortium on Neurodegeneration in Aging (CCNA). This cross-country cohort will include around 2,310 patients by 2020 with various forms of dementia and mild memory loss or concerns, about 600 of whom would have VCI. These patients have received detailed risk factor and brain scan assessments and will be followed for at least 2 years to start. We will look for markers in the blood and in brain scans that indicate higher risk of worsening VCI in COMPASS-ND patients - especially when compared to cognitively healthy or stable participants in the study. In parallel, we will also study measures of progressive VCI over a shorter time period (90-days) as part of TRIC-VCI (Trial of Remote Ischemic pre-Conditioning in VCI), also being conducted in partnership with the CCNA. This trial, which I have co-designed with my supervisor, will also give us an initial sense of whether markers of VCI can be modified by Remote Ischemic Conditioning, a promising treatment strategy. Therefore, this post-doctoral project will help pave the road towards smarter selection of both patients and outcomes for VCI trials, in addition to piloting a treatment for further study within our Canadian dementia network.

column36: Genetic and epigenetic dysregulation caused by transposable elements in pediatric high-grade gliomas.
column37: Pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are lethal brain tumours with no effective therapies. In most cases, the source of genetic damage leading to tumour formation remains unknown. One potential cause of pediatric DNA damage is specialized DNA sequences that can 'transpose' or move to different positions in the genome. Unlike most DNA, transposable elements (TEs) can mobilize by cutting or copying themselves and then reinserting elsewhere in the genome. Each TE reinsertion event may disturb the sequence or regulation of nearby genes. Although there are millions of TEs in the human genome, the vast majority cannot move around due to errors in reinsertion or DNA damage. Hundreds of TEs, however, remain capable of mobilization. TE mobility is normally prevented by various cellular defense mechanisms to limit further DNA damage, however, these defense mechanisms are weakened or disabled at specific times during development, allowing TEs an opportunity to cause damage. Considering that TEs mobilize more frequently in the brain than other tissues, we hypothesise that TEs could be a significant contributor to cancer-promoting genetic mutations in pHGG. We therefore propose to analyze TEs in pHGG by multiple molecular sequencing approaches: Whole genome sequencing to identify TE insertion sites, ATAC sequencing to identify open regions of DNA, RNA sequencing to measure gene expression, and proteomics to measure protein levels. Together, these approaches will allow us to identify genomic changes caused by TEs and their effects on gene regulation. Defining these genetic events will allow the development of targeted therapeutics or genetic screening approaches to identify individuals with increased risk of disease development. Additionally, this work could be extended to other pediatric brain tumour types with potentially similar developmental origins and elevated levels of TE mobilization.

column36: Quantifying Head Impact Biomechanics and Mechanisms of Sport-Related Concussion in Youth Athletes
column37: The immediate health effects of concussion can be catastrophic, but there can also be long-term cognitive consequences associated with the accumulation of sub-concussive impacts over time. An estimated one in ten youth sustain a sport-related concussion each year. Our current understanding of the mechanisms of concussion comes from studying adults. More work is clearly needed to understand the mechanisms of sport-related concussion in youth athletes, especially out in the field rather than lab-based tests. Recent developments in wearable technology have helped create impact monitoring mouthguards that are embedded with inertial measurement units. These mouthguards can directly measure head impact biomechanics in the field and can help us understand the mechanisms of concussion in youth athletes. Therefore, the main goal of this research project is to use the impact monitoring mouthguards to measure head impacts in high school football athletes and identify key features that characterize a sport-related concussion. A second objective is to determine which positions in youth football experience greater head impact exposure. High school football athletes will wear a validated impact monitoring mouthguard during practices and games. Key biomechanical features (i.e., acceleration and velocity) will be recorded for each head impact. Any incidence of concussion will be documented, and predictive analyses will reveal whether the incidence of concussion can be determined from key biomechanical features. A statistical test (Chi-square) will also be used to compare the head impact exposure between different positions. The results from this project will not only provide invaluable information on the concussion biomechanics for youth athletes, but they will also determine whether head impacts can be accurately measured in the field to monitor the risks of accumulated sub-concussive head impact in football and potentially other sports (e.g., rugby, hockey, lacrosse).

column36: Improving the quality of end-of-life care among cancer patients in Alberta, Canada through the development and assessment of a decision support tool for prognostication
column37: More Canadians die from cancer than from any other cause. It is therefore important to study and find ways to improve the delivery of healthcare to cancer patients who are close to death. We plan to address objectives 1 to 2 using existing healthcare data collected by the Alberta government for the purposes of reimbursing physicians and hospitals. Interestingly, the liver secretes small vesicles known as 'exosomes' that carry biological cargo to other cells/tissues and can alter recipient cell function. We will then use these exosomes to identify their roles on whole body and tissue-specific insulin sensitivity and glucose control. Overall, these studies will determine the role of exosomes in NAFLD-driven impairments in blood glucose control, provide novel insights into the mechanisms linking NAFLD and T2D, and may identify new therapeutic targets for diabetes treatment.

column36: Novel measures to investigate listening effort with naturalistic, real-world auditory stimuli
column37: By age 60, around 50% of all adults will report hearing loss. As a result, listeners regularly fail to grasp what is being said. This is especially true in noisy environments, resulting in increased listening effort to understand speech and in extreme cases, anxiety and depression. Clinical tests of speech perception focus on intelligibility, and use brief, isolated sentences that are neither engaging nor meaningful. Two individuals can achieve the same word-report score, with one finding the task unpleasantly effortful, and the other finding it nearly effortless. Clinical measures of listening effort are urgently needed, and any solution to this problem requires a conscious transformation of both diagnostic content (i.e., in the form of engaging narratives that are true to the real world) and test methods. One solution involves the use of intersubject correlation (ISC). ISC captures shared information across brains by leveraging activity in one brain to model another. This approach becomes especially powerful when exploring dynamic, naturalistic scenarios - such as storytelling that occurs over several minutes. Here, I aim to validate a novel metric (ISC) to assess listening effort as people attend to real-world narratives using multimodal experimental methods of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and eye tracking. The advantage of using narratives is that they capture the dynamics of speech processing and can be used to differentiate between those who are struggling and those who are not - something current tests fail to do. fMRI will allow us to examine the simultaneous contributions of different networks in effortful listening. Whereas using eye tracking as a metric of spatial attention will enable us to calibrate more practical, non-invasive measures of listening effort. This will allow audiologists to measure effortful listening and implement individualised hearing-aid fitting, leading to better outcomes for those with hearing loss.

column36: Walk smarter not harder
column37: Knee arthritis commonly begins in the joint behind the kneecap, termed the patellofemoral joint (PF). It affects middle-aged and older adults, this impacts productivity and contribution to society and results in years of knee pain and disability across the lifespan. There is thus an urgent need for research aimed at understanding modifiable risk factors for PF arthritis that can guide treatment approaches. Cadence (i.e., number of steps taken per minute) during walking is one such risk factor. People with knee arthritis who take fewer steps per minute to cover the same distance (i.e., lower cadence) experience more severe PF arthritis in the future. Evidence suggests elevated knee joint loads contribute to development of PF arthritis and pain. Thus, research is needed to understand the relation of walking cadence to knee loading and pain, and whether cadence can be targeted to improve knee loading and pain in people with PF arthritis. Gait parameters such as cadence, joint angles and forces exerted on the ground can be measured very accurately in a research lab, but may not fully represent what happens outside that controlled environment. Wearable devices are relatively inexpensive and have the potential to monitor gait parameters in the 'real-world'. However, research to support the validity of these devices for measuring gait parameters is limited, especially at lower speeds typical of people with PF arthritis. The proposed study will address the following 3 research questions: 1) Is walking cadence related to knee loading and pain? 2) Does changing cadence (without changing waking speed) change knee loading and pain in people with PF arthritis? 3) Can wearable devices accurately monitor gait parameters (e.g. cadence, speed) in people with PF arthritis? My research will generate important new knowledge that will directly inform the development of a walking program for PF arthritis management that could aid in changing the trajectory of this disease.

column36: Central determinants of recovery from upper limb peripheral nerve injury
column37: Peripheral nerve injuries (PNI) affecting the hand can seriously degrade quality of life and self-efficacy. Following injury, peripheral nerves can regrow but successful regrowth does not guarantee the return of healthy hand function. The reasons for incomplete recovery are unknown. We will investigate the role of brain reorganization following peripheral nerve injury in successful and unsuccessful recovery using state-of-the-art brain imaging methods and carefully designed tests of real-world hand function. We will directly address three main shortcomings in previous research on this topic by (1) using imaging techniques with extremely high resolution, (2) using imaging analysis approaches that take into account individual differences in brain organization, and (3) using tests that reflect real-world hand use by incorporating natural sensory and motor functions. We will recruit individuals with peripheral nerve injuries who have been identified as candidates for nerve reconstruction surgery. These individuals will undergo brain imaging and hand function testing before surgery, as well as at 3, 6, and 12 month intervals post-surgery. We will track their functional recovery and its relation to changes in brain organization observed preceding and following surgery. We hypothesize that changes in brain organization improve hand function; however, because surgery also involves significant peripheral reorganization (like injury itself), brain reorganization before surgery could be counterproductive. The proposed study will yield important insights into the role of peripheral nerve regrowth and brain reorganization for recovery of hand function. It could also influence clinical practice such as the timing for surgery following peripheral nerve injury.

column36: Resisting Vascular Cognitive Impairment: The Effects of Resistance Training on Myelin and Blood-based Biomarkers of Neuroplasticity in Older Adults
column37: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) refers to the loss of cognitive and brain function due to blocked or narrowed arteries in the brain. Very often, these blockages are in the small arteries of the brain and are only diagnosed with brain scans. Another feature of VCI is myelin loss; myelin is critical for the proper transmission of signals within the brain. Thus, myelin loss is associated with impaired cognitive function and mobility. Importantly, VCI is the second most common cause of dementia in the world. Fortunately, VCI may be the most treatable form of cognitive impairment as many of its key risk factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol, can be reduced with lifestyle changes. While we know that exercise is effective in reducing these risk factors, little research has been done specifically in persons with VCI to determine whether exercise can slow down the disease progression. Specifically, despite evidence that shows strength training (i.e., lifting weights) can reduce the damage due to blocked small arteries, current VCI research focus solely on aerobic training (e.g., running, walking). Moreover, no study has examined whether exercise of any type can reduce myelin loss over time in persons with VCI. Based on our prior work, we propose that strength training is an effective treatment strategy for slowing down disease progression in persons with VCI. Using a special brain scan, we will evaluate the effects of twice-weekly strength training on myelin over a 12-month period in persons with VCI compared to an active control group. We will also examine how strength training may minimize myelin loss in VCI by examining levels of neurotrophic growth factors in the blood. Our proposal is very practical as exercise may be an effective, inexpensive, and accessible intervention strategy with minimal side effects. Our proposal is also timely as the prevalence and burden of VCI will only increase due to the world's aging population.

column36: Imaging Synaptic Swelling and Lysis in Stroke
column37: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in Canada, with an estimated 50,000 strokes per year and over 14,000 reported deaths in 2009 (30% mortality rate). In 2014 there were 315,000 stroke survivors in Canada, an estimated 90% live with long lasting brain and mental issues, costing our Health Care system $2.5 billion dollars within the first six months post stroke alone. Our aging population is set to increase the number of stroke victims and survivors - many of whom will be affected with dementia and motor deficits. This is projected to dramatically increase the financial and emotional burdens of government and caregivers alike and underscores the importance of stroke research in a modern age of health care. Brain swelling, or edema, is a hallmark consequence of stroke and brain injury and is the leading cause of death in patients who suffer from large strokes. Edema is caused by the movement of water from the blood into the brain in response to a sudden imbalance of naturally occurring ions (e.g., sodium, potassium, and chloride) that are normally in equilibrium. It is well known that chloride ions entering brain cells is the key to causing water entry in edema, however the field is yet to understand how and why chloride levels become unstable in this context. As a result, current medical treatments for edema are over 30 years old and do not address the root cause of cell swelling. This proposal aims to characterize how chloride ions become imbalanced in the connections between nerve cells, called synapses, which are highly susceptible to stroke damage. We have developed a state-of-the-art imaging technique, the first of its kind, to monitor neuronal chloride changes in real time, allowing us to pinpoint precise chloride changes that cause synaptic swelling and death. In this way, we aim to determine how chloride imbalance occurs to identify new drug targets that would reduce post-stroke dementias and motor deficits that are caused by synaptic loss.

column36: Investigating the impacts of alcohol-sales deregulation on emergency department visits and hospitalizations due to alcohol in the province of Ontario
column37: Problematic alcohol use is responsible for a large and growing burden on the health of Canadians. Prior research has identified possible regulations that governments can put in place to reduce problematic alcohol use and associated health harms. One frequently identified regulation is placing limits on the location and number of stores that can sell alcohol. However, several questions about the effect of this regulation exist including its causality, (i.e. whether having more stores cause individuals to consume more alcohol, or if more stores open in response to there being a high demand for alcohol by the individuals living in the region?), and if the number of stores impact the alcohol consumption of important groups differently (i.e. men and women, young and old, low- and high-income). The purpose of this research is to better investigate the relationship between the availability of alcohol stores and health harms. To do so we will take advantage of a change in government policy in the province of Ontario and the availability of high-quality data on health care visits. Starting in December 2015 two successive Ontario governments have made large changes to how alcohol is sold in Ontario including increasing the number of stores and their permitted hours of operation. This research will collect the location and hours of operation of all stores selling alcohol in Ontario before, during, and after these policy changes. We will then link this data into databases containing records of all emergency department visits and hospitalizations in Ontario and see whether individuals who live near a store selling alcohol are more likely to have an ED visit or hospitalization caused by alcohol. We will also examine this relationship for different demographic groups. We plan to work with health and government officials at the local, provincial, and national level to communicate the results of our research and help inform policy related to regulating how and where we sell alcohol.

column36: Effects of a Virtual Reality Exercise Program on Sleep Quality in Assisted Living Residents with Risk of Alzheimer Disease and Related Dementia
column37: Older adults are the largest growing segment of the Canadian population. Th growing number of seniors poses a concern to the Canadian health care system as almost ~50% of people aged > 65 years experience sleep disturbances. Non-pharmacological interventions (e.g. educational programs and exercise) can improve quality of life of older individuals by enhancing sleep quality. Importantly, it has been suggested that other non-pharmacological interventions, such as virtual reality (VR) exercise programs, are effective on improving cognition and physical function by enhancing short-term recall, spatial abilities, and mood in older adults with dementia. Nevertheless, no prior study has examined the direct effect of VR exercises on sleep quality. Therefore, this project aims to (i) understand the association between sleep quality, cognitive performance, and functional capacity in older adults with risk of Alzheimer disease and related dementia, and (ii) quantify the effects of a VR exercise program on the treatment of sleep disturbances in those individuals. Sleep quality, cognitive performance, and functional capacity will be assessed before and after a VR exercise program through subjective (questionnaires) and objective (wearable devices) instruments. It is hypothesized that the combination of VR and exercise will improve short-term recall and mood and help to reduce stress and anxiety by promoting a relaxing experience. Therefore, the novelty of this study will be (i) to identify the role of cognitive impairments and functional capacity decline on the impact of sleep quality in assisted living residents, and (ii) to test the effectiveness of a VR exercise program on the improvement of sleep quality. The expected benefits of this project to the Canadian health care system are the increase in quality of life of assisted living residents and the decrease in operational costs associated with sleep medication and staffing.

column36: Functional Brain Activation during Simple and Complex Walking After Stroke
column37: Traditionally, the therapies used to relearn how to walk after stroke are determined through physical performance and not through assessment of brain function during these tasks. Emerging research has shown success in identifying appropriate rehabilitation strategies based on brain function. This, however, has primarily been investigated for rehabilitation of the upper extremity and further research is needed to determine if a more accurate prognosis of walking recovery can also be determined through brain function. Clinicians commonly use strategies such as walking over different surfaces, walking at different speeds, or walking while performing another task to improve walking ability in the community environment. Despite this, it is unclear if these walking strategies are appropriate for certain individuals with stroke. The purpose of this study is to investigate which areas of the brain are active during various walking situations and to determine if certain characteristics can explain the differences in brain activation. Twenty-five individuals with stroke and 25 age matched healthy controls will participate in this two day study. Participants will be asked to walk over different surfaces (overground, over gravel), at different speeds (slow, normal and fast) and with or without a secondary cognitive task. During these tasks, brain activation will be recorded using a wireless, portable device called functional near-infrared spectroscopy. The brain activation will be compared between these conditions and between groups. We will also assess if stroke characteristics (location and size), motor impairment, cognition, or age can help explain the differences in brain activation. This study will be the first to characterize and relate brain activity to stroke characteristics during rehab appropriate walking tasks.

column36: Indigenous "Communities within Communities": Aging Well and HIV
column37: Standard convention holds that a person has aged when they reach a fixed "age" (e.g. 65). However, Indigenous Peoples face complex health issues steeped in colonial trauma that impact the experience of aging. This includes aging earlier than the general population and facing a greater number of co-morbidities as they age. Across the Western world, People Living with HIV/AIDS (PLWH) have access to effective, well-tolerated HIV treatment, and strategies have shifted towards HIV treatment and management and staying healthy with HIV. However, these same advances can't be said to be occurring for Indigenous PLWH across Canada, where community level testing, treatment, and access are limited and inconsistent. There are significant knowledge gaps and little evidence of what wellness means to Indigenous Peoples living with HIV/AIDS (IPLWH). This gap is all the more significant when trying to determine what wellness and healthy aging means to IPLWH as they become older adults. The main goal of this proposed project is to hold a two-day meeting to bring together Indigenous communities, organisations, IPLWH, and researchers for exploratory discussions and iterative research development around the creation of a community-based research programme grounded in Indigenous knowledges, methods, and the land, so as to ascertain (1) a clear definition of what wellness and healthy aging means and (2) its practical application for Indigenous Peoples living with HIV/AIDS, including how these may differ for Indigenous women, men and non-binary/2SLGBTTIQ+ people. This planning meeting will be essential to kick-starting national efforts to conduct research in aging and wellness among IPLWH.

column36: Health service use by lonely and socially isolated older adults in supportive living settings
column37: As people age, a spectrum of care is required including home care, retirement home, assisted/supportive living (SL), and nursing home (NH). These services are paid for by provincial health plans or privately. Historically in Canada's public health system, when advanced levels of care were required, support was provided in NHs. SL was envisioned as a homelike and less costly alternative to the healthcare system than NHs. It is a residential care setting where people access services through the provincial home care program. Alberta, has made major public investments in SL and consequently, has restricted investment in NHs. While this policy decision is meant to align with older adults' preferences and to reduce health system costs, there is little evidence that SL sector can achieve either goal. SL facilities have limited staff and no registered nurse on site. There is an expectation in SL facilities that residents have family or friends who can provide emotional or task-based support and this is not always the case. Furthermore, little is known about SL residents who are lonely and/or socially isolated. Poor social connections are associated with increased risk of hospitalization and transfer to NH, which SL is intended to avoid. Fewer staff, limited recreation services and an (unmet) expectation for family involvement raises concerns about the quality of care and quality of life for lonely and/or socially isolated SL residents. My postdoctoral research will address these issues by using provincial health administrative data to understand health and service use of residents who are socially isolated and/or are lonely compared to those who are not. I will compare lonely/isolated residents characteristics, number of hospital visits, and length of stay to those that are not lonely or isolated. Given this sector's tremendous growth, it is essential that we understand the impact of these models of care in order to optimize SL resident quality of life.
