column36: Granzyme B: A Novel Therapeutic Target for Bullous Pemphigoid
column37: Bullous pemphigoid - Skin blisters occur when layers of the skin separate and body fluid collects in a pocket formed between the skin layers. While most of us have had blisters caused by friction, sunburns, or infections, some patients suffer from conditions that cause the blisters spontaneously all over the body. Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common blistering disease and often affects the elderly. As our skin forms an important barrier to protect against infection, loss of moisture, temperature changes, and other factors, widespread blisters in BP interrupt these functions and can be life-threatening. Unfortunately, there are currently limited treatment options for BP. Standard treatment with oral corticosteroids is not effective for all patients and can lead to serious side effects, especially in the elderly. Therefore, there is an urgent need to better understand the disease to develop more effective treatments. The role of granzyme B in BP - In healthy people, the immune system produces proteins called antibodies that help fight foreign entities such as bacteria and viruses. In BP patients, the antibodies mistakenly attack the body's own proteins - specifically, anchoring proteins which attach top skin layers to the deeper layers. When antibodies recruit immune cells for the attack, they release "molecular scissors" called proteases that cut proteins. Our laboratory has discovered a protease called granzyme B that is elevated in the skin of BP patients and appears to induce blistering by cutting the anchoring proteins that hold the skin layers together. Based on these findings, I propose that granzyme B contributes to the onset and severity of BP. I will investigate the role of granzyme B in BP using skin cells, animal models, and human patient samples and test the therapeutic efficacy of a granzyme B inhibiting drug in the animal models. Results from this work will support the development of this inhibitor into a treatment for BP and other diseases.

column36: Suicidality among youth with autism spectrum disorder
column37: Adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are nine times more likely to die by suicide and think about suicide 10 times more often than adults in the general population. Despite this knowledge about adults, little is known about suicidality (thoughts of taking one's life, creating a plan, attempts) among youth with ASD (15-30 years) as youth are significantly underrepresented in research. With little research that has examined suicidality in youth with ASD, it is unknown how they perceive, understand and experience suicidality. Furthermore, little is known about the factors that contribute to, and or protect youth with ASD from suicidality, and potential similarities/differences among young men and women. This limited knowledge is an urgent concern as it is unknown how to support suicidal youth with ASD, provide adequate health care, or best ways to prevent suicide in this population. Given these gaps in knowledge, the study aims to: 1)Explore the perspectives, perceptions and experiences of suicidality among youth with ASD. 2)Understand the factors that contribute to or protect youth from suicidality. 3)Work with youth with ASD, families, and stakeholders to share knowledge, and work to inform policy and practice. This research will generate new knowledge to inform how suicidality is identified, examine how suicidality may be similar or different among young men and women with ASD, uncover the individual/social factors which influence suicidality, and illuminate the factors that may protect youth with ASD from suicidality. The research will contribute new knowledge to inform opportunities for prevention, intervention, and ways to promote mental health against the risk of suicide in youth with ASD. Study findings have the potential to uncover barriers to mental health care, and inform health policy to develop best practices aimed at supporting the mental health needs of youth with ASD.

column36: Neuromelanin Signals in the Substantia Nigra of Patients with Treatment Resistant Schizophrenia: A Cross-Sectional MRI Study
column37: Schizophrenia (Sz) is a chronic, progressive mental illness that affects 1% of the population. The current treatment for Sz includes the medications labelled 'antipsychotics (APs)' to block the action of dopamine. Unfortunately, APs do not work in 30% of patients (TRS: treatment-resistant schizophrenia). Clozapine (CLZ) is the only effective antipsychotic for TRS; its earlier introduction is recommended by the national guidelines. However, only 7% of patients with Sz are treated with CLZ and the average treatment duration before CLZ was 9.7 years in Canada. That could be attributable to the lack of biomarker of TRS. Recently, studies using positron emission tomography (PET) have suggested that those who respond to first-line AP treatment (TnRS: treatment non-resistant Sz) showed increased DA synthesis and release in the striatum compared to those with TRS. However, PET is not widely available in clinical practice and limited because of its high costs and the short half-life of radioligands. On the other hand, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more accessible, less costly, and is able to examine the dopaminergic function by measuring neuromelanin (NM), which is a byproduct of the synthesis of monoamine neurotransmitters, including noradrenaline and dopamine. This technique has already been investigated in Parkinson's disease, but not for any psychiatric disorders such as Sz. This study will measure NM signals using neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) in the substantia nigra, which contains the majority of dopamine neurons, and compare among patients with TRS (n=23), TnRS (n=23), and healthy control participants (n=23). We hypothesize that NM-MRI signals will be increased in TnRS in comparison with controls and TRS. Our approach will validate a broadly available biomarker to predict antipsychotic treatment response. NM-MRI scanning can then be included in the criteria of TRS.

column36: Understanding patterns of healthcare utilization of Canadian Armed Forces Veterans living with chronic pain and their experiences, values, and perceived needs related to chronic pain management: A mixed methods study.

We will perform in-depth one-on-one interviews with CAF Veterans living with chronic pain to understand their experiences, values and needs related to chronic pain management. This research will provide valuable information for healthcare providers, educators, policy makers, and CAF Veterans living with pain. column36: Helping the Helpers: Examining the Mental Health and Support Needs of Direct Service Providers Working with People Experiencing Homelessness
column37: The health of service providers plays an important role in providing high quality and effective health and social care. Symptoms, such as burnout, among service providers are linked to lower satisfaction and poorer health outcomes for service users. The health of service providers is especially important in the homelessness sector, where negative experiences can contribute to avoidance of services and extended periods of homelessness. The rates of common mental health problems, such as depression, anxiety, burnout, and trauma, and the support needs of people working in the homeless service sector are largely unknown. This study aims to better understand the mental health and support needs of this population and learn how organizations are or can be supporting the positive mental health of their staff. This study will recruit service providers in three community settings in Canada: emergency shelters, supportive housing, and harm reduction services. Data will be collected in two ways: (1) an online survey of 430 service providers and (2) interviews with 30 service providers and 15 organizational directors. Data will be used to explore two research questions: (1) What are the rates of common mental health problems and the needs of service providers that are not being met? and (2) What factors are associated with common mental health problems among service providers? It is predicted that mental health problems will be more common among service providers who have less social support (colleagues, friends, and family); a higher workload; less supervision; and more experiences with traumatic events, such as violence and overdoses. To ensure that the study findings are easy to access and to facilitate future research, they will be shared publicly. An educational toolkit will also be made available for service providers and organizations in the homeless service sector.

column36: Attacking glioblastoma multiforme with chimeric antigen receptor Natural Killer cells: a novel therapeutic approach
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes narrowing and loss of blood vessels in the lungs, leading to increased stress on the heart and death by heart failure. Treatments for PAH are expensive and provide little benefit to the patient in terms of symptoms and survival. For many years, PAH has been associated with dysfunction in the immune system. Recently we have discovered that Natural Killer (NK) immune cells are reduced in number and impaired in function in PAH. Normally, IL-15 is needed for NK cell function and survival, while TGFb alters NK cell function and blocks the effects of IL-15. However, we and others have found that IL-15 and TGFb signaling is altered in PAH patients and in animal models of PAH. In the pregnant uterus and cancerous tumors, NK cells change their function to help form blood vessels that allow the fetus or tumor to grow. We believe that something similar occurs in PAH lungs, and NK cells are "tricked" into making the diseased lungs worse. To test this hypothesis, we have bred mice with NK cells that either can or cannot produce the main receptor for TGFb, called TGFbRII. These mice will be exposed to low oxygen levels, which will cause symptoms of PAH in normal mice. We will then test our mice for lung and heart function, as well as measure number and function of NK cells. We would expect the mice with NK cells that cannot produce TGFbRII will not develop PAH when exposed to low oxygen, and will have normal heart, lung and NK cell function. Furthermore, we will test a new treatment made by HCW Biologics which both stimulates IL-15 signaling and blocks the actions of TGFb (known as HCW9218). We will induce PAH in rats using two different methods and then treat the rats with HCW9218. We expect HCW9218 treatment will cure the rats of their PAH symptoms. These studies will help to better understand how NK cells contribute to PAH and will further develop a new treatment based on this idea.

column37: Gamma-delta T cells protect the body by directly combating bacteria and fungi in barrier tissues, as well as send out signals to initiate an immune response. The ability of these cells to perform diverse functions is set up during fetal/neonatal life, when these cells develop from blood stem cells. In this proposal, we will define the molecular events that lead to the acquisition of the pro-inflammatory IL-17 programming in gamma-delta T cells. We will focus on the roles of HEB transcription factors that control gene expression, and on the extracellular signals that modulates HEB activity. A better understanding of how these T cells are programmed for function during development will enable us to target and modulate their important immune functions to promote health and combat disease.

column36: Investigating the relationship between apathy and tau burden in patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease
column37: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a brain disorder in which patients have more memory and thinking problems than healthy people their age, often progresses to Alzheimer's disease (AD) where memory abilities and daily tasks are severely impaired. Apathy, characterized by a state of reduced interest, motivation and activity is one of the most common non-memory related symptoms of MCI and AD occurring in about 50%, and 80% of patients, respectively. Furthermore, 60% of MCI patients with apathy progress to AD. Medications which have been studied for the treatment of apathy have shown that only 30% of patients benefit. Understanding the underlying brain changes that occur in patients with apathy may help identify new treatments and delay progression to AD. Apathy has been associated with changes in the frontal cortex; regions at the front of the brain. In patients with memory difficulties, changes in the frontal cortex have been associated with a build-up of AD-related harmful proteins such as tau. Tau is considered a primary biomarker of AD, and is linked to cell death in the brain. However the relationship between apathy and tau is unclear. Fortunately, tau can be measured easily using positron emission tomography, an imaging test that uses a radioactive molecule to detect disease before it shows up on other imaging tests. Understanding the relationship between apathy and tau would help identify which patients can be targeted for early treatment that may delay or prevent progression to AD, and may also identify a new treatment to improve apathy and AD. Specifically, drugs that target tau may be of interest. Therefore, I propose to study differences in tau accumulation in the frontal cortex between cognitively impaired (MCI or AD) individuals with and without apathy, and whether other important characteristics such as size of brain region, presence of other behavioural symptoms, and severity of memory difficulties, affect the severity of tau accumulation.

column36: Understanding how the immune system is important in heart failure
column37: Everyone is aware of the impact heart attacks have on peoples quality of life, and ultimately that death due to heart failure is an all too common event. This is particularly true in people who have obesity and/or diabetes. We now understand much about the complexity of the heart, its structure and how it functions. This has also allowed researchers to identify things which change in the heart before a heart attack to cause this event. Exactly WHY these various changes occur in people with obesity and diabetes has still to be fully understood. Only when we know these details will more effective therapies be developed. My project is designed to understand what causes changes in the structure and function of the heart in individuals with obesity and/or diabetes by focusing on i) the role of the body's immune system and ii) how the function of immune cells is determined by a hormone which is known to change in people with obesity, diabetes and heart failure.

column36: Optical Coherence Tomography in Patients with Basilar Artery Ischemic Stroke
column37: Strokes are one of the leading causes of death and disease in the world. They occur due to blockages of blood vessels in the brain. These blockages are similar to a bathtub drain being clogged with debris. In this analogy, the bathtub drain would be the blood vessel, and the debris would be the blood clot. For a long time doctors used a clot-buster medication to help patients having a stroke, which is like using a liquid drain cleaner to unclog a drain. More recently, researchers have found that removing the blood clot from within the blood vessel works better than using clot-buster medication, and doctors now use a tool similar to a plumbers snake to remove the blood clot. An important step is checking if the blood clot is removed after the procedure, and making sure the blood vessel is open. This is done by injecting dye into the blood stream and taking pictures. Our research team recently started using a new device called optical coherence tomography in stroke patients. This device is just like a good camera that can take pictures from inside the blood vessel. What we found was very interesting. In three patients there was left-over blood clot even though the pictures with dye showed that the blood clot was completely gone. It was very eye-opening that what we once thought about complete blood clot removal may not actually be true. Just like many new scientific findings, the application of a new technology is what made this possible. Although naturally we would think that this left-over blood clot causes new/worse strokes, we don't know this for sure. Therefore, we propose a study at our regional stroke center to characterize the findings using our new device in a larger group of patients. Our objectives are to make sure that using this device is practical, safe, and compare patients with left-over blood to those without left-over blood clot.

column36: A Participatory Design Approach to Develop and Optimize Aquatic Therapy Practice for Stroke Survivors
column37: Stroke is a life-altering event that can leave a person with a significant physical and cognitive disability that affects their ability to be independent in the community. A promising therapy to help people with stroke recover their health and function is aquatic therapy. Aquatic therapy is where people with stroke undergo physical rehabilitation in a pool with a qualified therapist to help them regain their strength, balance, and ability to move independently. Although there are several accessible therapy pools and aquatic therapy instructors across Ontario, it is unknown how much stroke survivors are accessing aquatic therapy to help with their recovery. To help people with stroke get a better understanding about aquatic therapy and to support their ability to access it in the community, I am proposing to work with stroke survivors and clinical staff to develop a web-based tool-kit that will provide important information about aquatic therapy. To achieve this goal, I will first interview people with stroke and clinical staff about their thoughts and understanding of aquatic therapy, what might prevent them from using it, and what supports they need to be able to access it in the community (PHASE I). Using the interview data from Phase I, I will then partner with stroke survivors and clinical staff to develop a list of strategies and resources to help people with stroke become more aware of aquatic therapy and how to better access and use it (PHASE II). Finally, I will work with people with stroke and clinicians to develop and pilot test a web-based tool-kit that will help people be able to access information about aquatic therapy in their community (PHASE III). As a result of this work, people with stroke will be able to learn about aquatic therapy and how to better access it so they can optimize their recovery process.

column36: Improving the early identification of knee osteoarthritis with electronic medical record data in Canadian primary care
column37: Osteoarthritis is a painful joint disease that affects over 6 million Canadians. The knee joint is one of the most commonly affected joints. Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) starts with mild joint pain and stiffness that worsens to extreme pain often requiring surgery if left untreated. Being able to identify people with KOA in primary care at an early stage would help promote best-practice treatment. Yet, primary care clinicians report many barriers to identifying and treating KOA. This study will target this gap by using electronic medical records (EMR) from primary care clinicians who participate in the Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network to identify patients with KOA at an earlier stage. Next, a pan-Canadian KOA registry will be set up to learn about risk factors and health indicators of KOA. Lastly, an online KOA dashboard will be pilot tested in a small group of primary care clinicians. This dashboard will combine the EMR data with patient reported outcome data on pain, symptoms, physical activity, and quality of life to improve the treatment of their KOA patients.

column36: Understanding the interplay between cytosine demethylation and genome integrity
column37: Genes carry the information that determines human inherited characteristics, or traits. These genes are made up of mainly 4 types of building blocks, or nucleotides. Their order is what determines the shape and characteristics of the proteins, which will carry out the biological process in the body. However, not only the type of proteins, but also how and when these are produced is relevant for body functions. How genes are regulated without changing the nucleotide sequence in the genes is known as epigenetics. Importantly, alterations in epigenetics can lead to diseases such as cancer, neurodegeneration or failures during development. For this, is essential to understand the mechanisms by which human cells carry out this process. One of the key steps in epigenetics is the chemical labelling of one of the 4 building blocks of genes, the nucleotide cytosine. A subtle modification known as methylation in the nucleotides along a gene can dramatically change its activity, and therefore, the production of a certain protein. However, while we precisely understand how this labells are generated, the mechanism that erase these marks is not well-defined. This is highly relevant, since devastating diseases such as many blood cancers, are characterized by common alterations in the labelling of cytosines by methylation. Thus, understanding this alterations will open the possibility for the development of better clinical therapies. Through this project, I will dissect the mechanisms for the removal of these epigenetic marks. Moreover, I will find which components are essential for the growth of cells with alterations in this epigenetic process. This will allow the development of therapies to kill tumoral cells with alterations in this pathway. In summary, this project will allow us to understand better how human cells carry out epigenetic changes, and will find novel therapeutic approaches for the treatment of blood cancer.

column36: Dissecting hippocampal-amygdala circuit dynamics to predict depression vulnerability
column37: Depression is a major health issue, but we lack long-term effective treatment. This is partly due to our limited understanding of the disease biology. Recent research suggests that depression patients show abnormalities in interactions between brain regions that can in turn serve as useful indicators for identifying individuals susceptible to the disease. In particular, changes in interactions between hippocampus and amygdala, two regions critical for processing emotional information in the brain, can be used to predict patients' variation in mood. The goal of my postdoctoral research is to explore the mechanisms and neural circuits underlying changes in hippocampal-amygdala interactions in the depressed population. Specifically, I will identify the cells and circuits underpinning hippocampal-amygdala interactions that track with mood and examine how they are altered in population susceptible to depression. In addition, I will test how we can manipulate the neural circuit to reduce susceptibility. The findings will give new insight into the mechanisms by which depression alters the processing of emotional information in the brain and should inspire novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for the disease.

column36: Evaluating the prevention of disordered weight control behaviours among youth: Informing nutrition and mental health-related policy in Canada
column37: Disordered weight control behaviours (DWCBs), such as self-induced vomiting, unhealthy calorie restriction, and the use of non-prescribed diet pills, are common among young Canadians. Youth who engage in DWCBs are at a greater risk of developing eating disorders, obesity, and mental illness in adulthood. As a result, the prevention of DWCBs is an important avenue for improving population health. This research aims to evaluate health policies relevant to the prevention of DWCBs among youth, with implications for eating disorders, obesity, mental health, and chronic disease risk overall. To address this aim, I will conduct three studies to identify and analyse, generate recommendations for, and evaluate DWCB prevention policies in Canada. First, a literature review will be conducted to assess current DWCB prevention policies at federal and provincial levels within the areas of education, nutrition, mental health, and body weight. The review will be used to identify existing DWCB-related policies and their potential effects on population health, and identify policy gaps. To identify strategies to these gaps, Canadian leaders in the fields of eating disorders, obesity, nutrition, and mental health will be asked to provide policy recommendations. Promising policies will be evaluated using a modelling approach that allows us to estimate the impacts on rates of DWCBs, eating disorders, and obesity on youth as they age. Overall, the results of these studies will provide information on existing policies that can be used to evaluate progress on DWCBs prevention and inform concrete recommendations to address gaps. Such policies are critical for reducing the negative impacts of DWCBs on Canadian youth.

column36: Towards Precision Medicine for Violence and Aggression: Neuroimaging Biomarkers and Targeted Treatments
column37: Human violence is a common phenomenon that takes a large toll on individual lives and, indeed, Canadian society overall. Although the majority of individuals with psychiatric illness are not violent, some mental disorders are associated with increased risk of aggression toward oneself and others. Persistent violence may relate to underlying brain abnormalities or changes in brain chemistry that require specific treatment. Hence, research that strives to understand the brain differences of people who engage in repeated aggression could lead to new treatment tools and violence prevention strategies. We previously found using state-of-the-art brain imaging techniques that a brain chemical called fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) is increased in the brains of people with borderline personality disorder (BPD). BPD is a prevalent psychiatric condition that presents high rates of harm toward the self and others. FAAH is part of a chemical pathway in the brain that has been associated with increased aggression. Therefore, agents that block FAAH may be candidates for treating violence in BPD and other conditions. Continuing with this line of research, the current proposal evaluates whether talk therapies can affect brain FAAH levels in BPD and thus influence anger, hostility, and aggression. In addition, we will also look at FAAH levels in other psychiatric disorders, such as depression, which shares some commonalities with BPD and may also have high brain FAAH levels. The knowledge generated by these studies could stimulate new treatments for persistent violence and ultimately lead to improved health outcomes for both perpetrators and victims of violence. This research has the potential to reduce the economic burden of violence on the health care system, as well as the corrections system.

column36: Understanding the Ghost Core Phenomenon: Analysis of CT Perfusion Ischemic Core Overestimation in Acute Stroke:
column37: In an acute ischemic stroke, occlusion of cerebral blood vessels prevents the critical flow of oxygen to the brain. Without rapid revascularization, the death of brain tissue subsequently occurs. Computed tomography perfusion (CTP) can be used to visualize this process in real-time. Ischemic core, defined as tissue that is no longer salvageable, can be visualized alongside ischemic penumbra, tissue at risk of death that may be saved with blood flow restoration. Over the past 5 years, clinical trials have utilized CTP to select patients with severe stroke to undergo rapid revascularization via mechanical clot retrieval. Patients with a small core and large penumbra have been found to benefit the most from these interventions while, in contrast, patients possessing a large ischemic core benefit less and are at an increased risk of life-threatening bleeding. Patients with a large ischemic core are therefore less likely to be offered therapy. There is a growing recognition that in some cases, CTP may actually overestimate ischemic core. This phenomenon, termed Ghost Ischemic Core (GIC), carries the risk of precluding patients from undergoing necessary clot retrieval. Why GIC occurs in some patients, but not in others, is unclear. We aim to explore this particular question by analyzing the prevalence, topography, and natural history of GIC in relation to baseline clinical presentation, interventions utilized, and overall outcomes. In doing so, we hope to identify patients and/or clinical scenarios where ischemic core may be at risk of overestimation and shed further light into why this issue occurs in the first place. With the use of CTP becoming mainstream worldwide, the findings of this study will have the potential to launch new initiatives to improve ischemic core estimation and provide practical information for clinicians assessing patients at the bedside.

column36: Integrating Personalized Brain Simulation, Machine Learning, and Multimodal Neuroimaging for Early Detection of Alzheimer's Disease: A New Data-Driven Methodological Framework
column37: Maintaining a healthy brain through one's lifespan depends on the complex interaction between the brain, genetics, and lifestyle. With a rapidly aging population, the prevalence of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's Disease are significantly increasing, with a projected 107 million cases by 2050. This is now recognized as one of the major medical challenges facing the world in the 21st century. While treatment options are limited, early detection can allow prevention strategies to provide individuals with additional years of healthy living, significantly less burden on their loved ones, and a substantial reduction in healthcare costs. Current early detection methods mainly limited to inherited types of early-onset Alzheimer's Disease. Our goal is to greatly improve early detection of all types of Alzheimer's Disease. This project will, for the first time, integrate personalized brain simulation and the predictive power of artificial intelligence to improve our understanding of Alzheimer's Disease, to predict as early as possible who will develop the disease, and even to forecast what form it will take for each individual. Breakthroughs in personalized brain simulation, a type of mathematical brain modelling that is tuned to each individual, have already been used to show how and why the brain changes when inflicted with Alzheimer's Disease. We will use high-quality clinical databases that follow the development of thousands of individuals through the aging process in research that can lead to new clinical detection methods. We will use brain simulation to model the effects of Alzheimer's other dementias compared to healthy aging on each person's brain, and we will use artificial intelligence to discover changes in the brain that predict a diagnosis of Alzheimer's in later years. With this new data-driven approach, we aim to help add years of high quality of life for the millions of people who may be affected by Alzheimer's in the future, and their families.

column36: Antimicrobial use and foodborne infections in humans from British Columbia: a multimodal approach to assessing associations and impacts.
column37: Each year, >4 million Canadians develop an illness from the food they eat. Commonly, people are given antibiotics to treat their illness. Sometimes the antibiotics are the appropriate treatment and sometimes they are used inappropriately. However, the impacts of taking antibiotics before and after the illness are not well understood. In order to investigate the link between antibiotic use and illnesses from food, my project has five AIMS: 1. Describe the relationship between antibiotic use and illness from food as you move through the stages of the illness; 2. Determine the chance of developing an illness from food after antibiotic use; 3. Determine whether the chance of developing long-term consequences (eg. reactive arthritis) following an illness from food is related to using antibiotics after illness (both appropriate and inappropriate use); 4. Determine whether the healthcare costs and chance of dying are related to using antibiotics after illness (both appropriate and inappropriate use); and 5. Identify specific ways antibiotics are used inappropriately to help inform future antibiotic use guidelines. For the entire ~4M population of British Columbia, for 2005-2014, I will look at information on all antibiotic prescriptions, healthcare costs, infections from food, long-term consequences, and other pertinent factors (eg. age, sex). I will conduct a review of the existing published literature and describe the types and amount of antibiotics used both before and after illness from food. I will test hypotheses to assess the relationships between antibiotic use, and developing illness, developing long-term consequences, healthcare costs and chance of dying. This novel assessment of existing health data from BC will advance our understanding of the link between antibiotic use and illness from food. column36: Eye movements as a sensitive indicator of motion perception in healthy older adults and patients with ophthalmic diseases
column37: As our population ages, an increasing number of Canadians experience difficulties with their vision. Although it is well known that both normal aging and age-related eye disease can affect a person's ability to see fine detail (such as in reading), tests of visual acuity used in regular eye examinations do not provide a complete picture of a person's ability to see in everyday situations, such as exercising and driving, where moving objects are often involved. Moreover, these tests often demand verbal instructions and do not accommodate sufficiently for the multilingual population of Canada with a range of cognitive functions. We propose to develop an instruction-free test that uses an easy-to-use eye-tracking technology to assess vision with moving objects. This new test addresses the urgent need for accessible assessments for the increasing age of our multilingual population. Our research will gather the scientific evidence that is needed to determine if this test is accurate, and whether it is practical to introduce it into clinical practice. This quick and non-verbal method of assessing vision provides a potentially cost-effective vision assessment strategy that addresses an important population health issue.

column36: A pilot study for brain delivery of recombinant glucocerebrosidase in people with Parkinson's disease using MR-guided focused ultrasound induced opening of the blood-brain barrier
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, affecting 1-2 per 1000 people. There's a need for disease-modifying therapy in PD, but many potentially effective therapeutics are limited from the brain by the blood-brain barrier. Glucocerebrosidase is an enzyme that is the standard of care for Gaucher's disease, which recently has been shown to have shared pathophysiological features with PD. Animal studies suggest replacing brain levels of glucocerebrosidase can be restorative and improve motor symptoms in PD. However, glucocerebrosidase does not cross the blood-brain barrier into the brain. An emerging way to deliver drugs past the blood-brain barrier is by creating a temporary opening using MR-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS). MRgFUS effectively enhances the delivery of large molecules without open surgery such as previously through direct intracranial injection. Also, MRgFUS can explicitly target the blood-brain barrier of brain regions afflicted by PD pathologies. Sunnybrook Research Institute has the world's most extensive clinical experience in MRgFUS induced opening of the blood-brain barrier. Leveraging this experience, we are taking the first-in-human step to investigate the brain delivery of recombinant glucocerebrosidase using MRgFUS in six patients with PD. The primary outcome, safety, will be described by adverse events. The feasibility of blood-brain barrier disruption will be measured by MRI with contrast, and drug delivery by cerebrospinal fluid analysis, metabolic imaging, and clinical scores. Results of this pilot study will be vital in evaluating the safety and potential of MRgFUS drug delivery platform for recombinant glucocerebrosidase. This trial will open doors for future studies in PD, neuronopathic GD, and other alpha-synucleinopathies in urgent need of disease-modifying therapy.

column36: Learning Through Dialogue: Effects of Alcohol on Health and Wellbeing in Indigenous Communities
column37: Alcohol is the most commonly used and abused drug among Canadians despite extensive research linking alcohol with negative health outcomes. While Indigenous populations report higher rates of alcohol abstinence, Indigenous people also report higher levels of heavy drinking and among Canadian Indigenous communities, 75% identified alcohol as a community problem. Overall rates of alcohol consumption have generally remained stable; however, alcohol consumption among women is rapidly increasing. In the context of high rates of unplanned pregnancies, and the reality that pregnancy recognition often does not occur until well into the first trimester, increased alcohol consumption among women presents a significant health challenge to Canadians. Indeed, it is estimated that approximately 1% of children born in Canada are affected by Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), and recent population-prevalence studies suggest that this is likely a significant underestimate. One critical barrier to addressing addiction and prenatal alcohol exposure, particularly in the context of Indigenous communities, involves pervasive stereotypes and stigma about alcohol use and FASD. Importantly, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada: Calls to Action specifically recognized addiction and FASD as priority areas, with emphasis on preventative programs developed in collaboration with Indigenous people. To this end, the present proposal aims to engage Indigenous communities in knowledge exchange with the goal of co-creating culturally appropriate educational, hands-on activities to learn about the effects of alcohol on health and wellbeing across gender. Specifically, this proposal includes involvement by key stakeholders such as Elders, school partners, and youth, and will incorporate both science principles and Indigenous knowledge and ways of knowing, with the overarching goal of empowering youth as self-advocates and catalysts of health and wellbeing within their communities.

column36: The development of a theoretical framework to evaluate the sustainability of research-based interventions in child health
column37: Every year billions of tax-payers dollars are invested and researcher time is spent on the development and implementation of research-based interventions to improve child health. Yet healthcare problems and ineffective care practices continue. This problem is in part, due to a gap between research evidence (what we know) and healthcare practices (what we do). This issue has led to a growing body of science that seeks to understand ways to best ensure uptake of research into practice and uses knowledge translation (KT) strategies to improve uptake. Recent developments of research-based interventions have helped to increase the implementation of best available research evidence into practice. These interventions can target healthcare providers and consumers in ways that are meaningful and accessible. Yet there is little research done on how to sustain these research interventions to improve child health. Sustainability is the degree to which a research-based intervention continues to be used in practice after implementation efforts have ended. Sustainability research is a growing field of science that needs further research to understand how to predict and evaluate long-term use of new knowledge in practice. In my postdoctoral research I have systematically searched the existing literature to understand what current approaches exist to evaluate and predict sustainability. In this proposed research I will (a) develop a framework to evaluate sustainability outcomes, and (b) pilot test the framework across child health hospital settings using a research-based intervention for infant pain management practices (i.e., ImPaC research project). This research is important to ensure that the funding provided for these research-based interventions is warranted, and if they are effective, can be maintained and spread to other child health settings. This research on sustainability will inform the uptake and success of new child health research-based interventions.

column36: Cardiovascular stress testing in pregnancy and the prediction of preeclampsia
column37: Pregnancy is a unique period in which a woman's heart and blood vessels, also known as her cardiovascular system, change dramatically to allow her baby to grow. However, some women have unhealthy changes that lead to high blood pressure during pregnancy. This is a serious illness for mom, but it also increases the risk of giving birth early to a small baby. This means that later in life, both mom and baby are more likely to develop cardiovascular diseases. Blood pressure is controlled by the fight or flight part of the nervous system, known as the sympathetic system. We know that in healthy pregnant women, the sympathetic system is more active compared to non-pregnant women, but in pregnant women with high blood pressure, this is even greater. The causes of very high sympathetic activity are not well understood, but this could be identified before a pregnant woman actually develops a serious illness during pregnancy. Short-term stress tests are used in other non-pregnant groups to predict the development of high blood pressure. Short-term stress from placing a hand in cold water or maintaining a constant handgrip increase the demand placed on the heart and blood vessels. How well a mom adapts to this higher demand may allow us to predict the development of high blood pressure during pregnancy. Understanding how stress tests can be used to predict the development of high blood pressure during pregnancy is the aim of this research. We are recruiting ninety pregnant women (between 16-20 weeks of pregnancy) to complete a 2-hour study visit. Measurements of blood pressure and sympathetic system activity are completed at rest and during these short-term stress tests. The outcome of this research is to develop simple tools that can identify women at risk of high blood pressure during pregnancy. Early prediction of this complication could improve the diagnosis, treatment and outcomes for both mom and baby.

column36: Redevelopment and Optimization of an Adeno-Associated Virus Gene Therapy for the Treatment of Lipoprotein Lipase Deficiency
column37: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) catabolizes the breakdown of triglycerides in blood. LPL is a critical enzyme in the determination of lipoprotein profiles and predisposition to heart disease and stroke. A complete or partial LPL deficiency (type I hyperlipoproteinemia) presents during childhood with high triglycerides, pancreatitis, and a high risk of mortality. We have previously developed a gene therapy treatment for the LPL deficiency and phase I-III clinical trials have demonstrated its long-term safety and effectiveness. In 2012, this drug, Glybera(R) (alipogene tiparvovec) became the first gene therapy product to receive regulatory approval. However, commercialization was limited due to the extremely high price of the drug (>$1M/patient), in part due to the high cost of smaller-scale production methods. Since 2017, Glybera is no longer marketed. Drugs and enzyme replacement therapies are ineffective and as of now there is no treatment for LPL deficiency. In collaboration with the National Research Council of Canada, this aim of this proposal is to develop, optimize and validate a more cost-effective AAV-based gene therapy variant of Glybera for the treatment of LPL deficiency.

column36: Childhood disruptive behavioural profiles - improving economic participation through early screening and prevention
column37: Childhood disruptive behaviours - including aggression, opposition, inattention and hyperactivity - underpin the most prevalent and costly psychiatric disorders in youth. They are associated with increased risk of unemployment, low earnings, welfare receipt and poor mental and physical health outcomes. Given the large costs of disruptive behaviors for individuals and society, it is important to identify children who are at risk as early as possible so that they can be monitored and supported. So far, few studies have identified high-risk behavioral profiles in the general population and examined the impact of these profiles on future economic outcomes. Furthermore, it is unclear what precise mechanisms explain the association between risk profiles in childhood and poor economic outcomes in adulthood (e.g. adolescent delinquency, education underachievement) or what factors in childhood protect against these harmful effects (e.g. consequential parenting, good peer relations). This study will use teacher-rated behavioural assessments from age 6-12 years drawn from the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Kindergarten Children (n=3017) and government tax return records from age 18 to 35 years obtained from Statistics Canada, to address four questions: (1) What are the risk profiles at age 6 years that are associated with poor economic outcomes? (2) What is the structure and stability of these risk profiles from age 6-12 years and are they associated with risk profiles at age 6 and with economic outcomes? (3) What social and psychological factors explain the association between risk behavioural profiles at age 6 and poor economic outcomes? (4) What factors protect against the harmful effects of risk profiles at age 6 and poor economic outcomes? Findings will inform the development of prevention programs and policy initiatives designed to reduce the harmful effects of disruptive behaviours on long-term economic and social participation.

column36: Engineering the design of regulatory T cell therapy in transplantation
column37: Solid organ transplantation (SOT) is a curative option for end stage organ failure; however, the success of this procedure depends on life-long use of immunosuppressive drugs which put patients at risk for infections and cancer. Regulatory T cells (Treg) are immune cells that favour the acceptance of the transplanted organ by the recipient's immune system. One way to increase the numbers of organ-protective Tregs is to isolate them, expand them in the lab, and then re-infuse them into patients. A limitation, however, is that it is difficult to isolate Tregs that are specifically able to suppress immune responses to a transplant. Recently, we developed a revolutionary way to overcome this limitation using a genetic engineering strategy in which organ-specific Tregs can be made by introducing a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This project aims to optimize the function of CAR-Tregs by studying how to best design the CAR and to find ways to reduce risks associated with this strategy. My first goal will be to modify the CAR structure trying to find ways so mimic how Tregs would be naturally activated so their function and lifespan are optimal. I will also aim to reduce the risk of using CAR-Treg therapies. We have recently identified that CAR-Tregs which do not express a protein called Helios are prone to lose their ability to favour organ acceptance. We thus aim to engineer CARs in a way that they would only be expressed in Tregs which continue to express Helios. I will carry out these aims using experimental systems that are well-established. Significance: by optimizing CAR structure I will improve the function and lifespan of CAR-Tregs and also reduce their associated risks. The results generated in this study will inform the design of future clinical studies and will also help to facilitate the use of CAR-Treg-based therapies as a new therapeutic tool to diminish transplant rejection.

column36: Improving the utility of polygenic scores to predict and understand disease risk: a foundational resource.
column37: Many diseases are preventable by early detection and/or intervention if we knew who is most at risk. For diseases like coronary artery disease (CAD), risk predictions are made based on age and sex in combination with known risk factors (e.g. family history, cholesterol levels, body mass index, smoking habits). However, there is also a strong genetic component to the likelihood you will develop CAD (~50% of total). My research focuses on Polygenic Risk Scores (PGS), a method that can be used to predict genetic predisposition for a disease by aggregating the effects of variants across an individual's genome. Studies have shown that currently used risk prediction methods for multiple diseases can be improved by including PGS. Despite the benefits of PGS, there is both a lack of standardization and an incomplete understanding of their predictive ability (especially in people of non-European ancestry). This hinders PGS' adoption in clinical practice. To fill these gaps in our understanding, I am creating the PGS Catalog: a foundational resource to distribute the information necessary to apply and understand PGS for a wide range of diseases and traits. I will also perform a systematic comparison of PGS to measure PGS predictive ability and identify the best PGS for each trait (where multiple exist). Through this research I will identify any deficits in generalizability across ancestries and between sexes that need to be corrected. Finally, I will use the PGS to measure their ability to predict disease risk in rare disease patients, measuring how PGS combine with rare mutations. Together my research aims to establish the PGS Catalog as a foundational resource to advance our understanding of disease risk prediction using genetics, while also enabling new research and clinical uses of PGS.

column36: Exploring the actions of autoantibodies in fibromyalgia
column37: Fibromyalgia is characterized by widespread pain and tenderness. Between 1.5 and 10% of the population suffer from fibromyalgia, but despite this high prevalence no diagnostic tests exist and current therapies have limited effect. We know very little about the causes of fibromyalgia, which is partly why fibromyalgia is diagnosed with a list of criteria, rather than tests, and why current treatment strategies are so limited. We recently discovered that injecting antibodies from fibromyalgia patients into mice causes pain-like behaviour and increased activity of pain sensing neurons. These results suggest that some fibromyalgia patients' immune systems produce autoantibodies that attack their own bodies. Therefore, autoimmunity could underlie fibromyalgia in a subset of patients. Our findings have the potential to change how fibromyalgia is viewed and how it is treated. In this project we will build on our findings to better understand how fibromyalgia autoantibodies cause pain. First, we will search for the protein(s) fibromyalgia antibodies recognize. Identifying which proteins antibodies bind to will provide information about how they could drive pain. Additionally, these results can open the door to the creation of diagnostic tests based on the presence of specific antibodies, similar to the tests used in rheumatoid arthritis, rather than on a certain number of symptoms. Second, we will investigate how fibromyalgia antibodies increase the activity of pain sensing neurons. We have already found that fibromyalgia antibodies bind cells called satellite glial cells, which surround the cell bodies of pain sensing neurons. We will examine how fibromyalgia antibodies alter the activity of satellite cells, and how they then alter pain sensing neuron activity. Our expected results will provide the basis to develop diagnostic tests based on autoantibody presence and provide the rationale for using antibody targeting therapies to manage fibromyalgia.

column36: Understanding Pathways to Mental Health Care During and After the Psychotic Prodrome: A mixed methods study
column37: BACKGROUND: Multicomponent early intervention services have undoubtedly improved care for adolescents and young adults experiencing a first threshold-level episode of psychosis (FEP). However, access to such care remains challenging for many-especially since distress, symptoms and impairment begin long before the FEP, during a psychotic 'prodrome' consisting of non-specific and sub-threshold symptoms. Access can be operationalized by measuring 'pathways to care' (PTC) in the form of (a) treatment delays following onset of symptoms, and (b) subsequent attempts at help-seeking. PTC are well known in FEP, yet unstudied in the prodrome-even though most patients appear to seek help for mental health reasons prior to their FEP. METHODS/OBJECTIVES: Through mixed (qualitative and quantitative) methods, we will undertake the first direct examination of PTC during the psychotic prodrome in a well-established, catchment-based service for FEP based in Montreal, Quebec. We will utilize the Circumstances of Onset and Relapse Schedule in 148 consecutive patients, along with a series of smaller focus groups to better understand: 1) Treatment delays and help-seeking during the prodrome versus the FEP 2) When and why individuals, their families, and others delay decisions to seek help during the prodrome; 3) By whom, how, when and why help is eventually sought during the prodrome; 4) Reasons for and experiences of treatment delays and help-seeking before (versus after) the age of 18. SIGNIFICANCE: This study will be the first to fill the important knowledge gap of PTC during the psychotic prodrome; its KT strategy is designed to obtain multi-stakeholder input on how our findings are relevant to future research and service delivery. Finally, applying a mixed-methods lens to PTC during the prodrome permits us to identify which actors or agencies should be targeted in the next phase of our research: future early identification campaigns aimed at reducing treatment delays or simplifying help-seeking.

column36: Identifying data-driven diagnostic subtypes of depression and treatment outcome using big data
column37: Although depression affects approximately 350 million people worldwide, a substantial percentage of patients do not respond to treatment even after trying several different therapies. column36: Uncovering the synaptic and cellular basis of the persistence of long-term memory.
column37: Long-term memories can be highly unstable like in Alzheimer's disease patients or highly stable like in those suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, the development of clinical therapies for these and other debilitating memory disorders has failed because of a lack of a fundamental understanding of how memory persists. How does a memory change with time in the brain? Recently developed methods that can visualize those cells that store a memory, termed engram cells, have shown that engram cells in one brain region critical to memory storage, the hippocampus, are silenced over two weeks after mice acquired a memory whereas those in another brain region, the cortex, are unsilenced. Additionally, recalling memories at these remote time points is known to make the memory transiently labile by reinstating a hippocampal engram. Interventions that block the reconsolidation of this labile memory could erase memory in rodents but failed in human clinical trials. A significant and compelling amount of evidence has been gathered over many decades that the strength of electric signal transmission between brain cells across 'synapses' is adjustable and underlies learning and forgetting. Engram cells might be silenced because a) a fewer number or weakened synaptic connections from pre-synaptic engram cells fail to activate post-synaptic engram cells, or b) the engram cells are being inhibited by other nearby cells, or c) the responsiveness of the engram cells to inputs has decreased. The unsilencing of engram cells could be explained by these effects in the opposite direction. I aim to find mechanisms of hippocampal engram silencing and cortical engram unsilencing and the effects of memory retrieval at remote time points. I will use cutting edge molecular tools, two-photon microscopy and electrophysiological methods to test the above hypotheses in mice that acquired a fear memory 1 day (short-term memory) and 2 weeks (long-term memory) after learning.

column36: Emerging roles of enteric glial cells in homeostasis and disease
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is an umbrella under which live a number of chronic inflammation disorders in the small or large intestine that induce symptoms like pain, weight loss and diarrhea. All of these make everyday life for patients difficult. Canada has one of the highest IBD incidence rates in the world (1/140 Canadians) and an alarmingly increasing prevalence, especially in infants and children. The intestine is the most highly regenerative organ in the human body as it undergoes constant wear and tear while breaking down food, absorbing nutrients, and eliminating waste. This repair is maintained by resident intestinal stem cells that generate all the different cells type of the gut. To function properly, stem cells need to receive appropriate signals from their environment. If those signals are altered, it can lead to disease, including IBD. My research focuses on glial cells, one of the most abundant cell types of the intestine. Glial cells are located in close physical proximity to stem cells, but their potential interactions are currently unknown. I investigate how glial cells can modulate stem cell behavior under normal conditions, during repair (after injury), and in chronic inflammation. Compiling analysis from a model of IBD created in mice, and from human glial cells from healthy and IBD patients, will reveal the role of glial cells in IBD and inform new targets for drug development and treatment. Improving stem cell response, through glial cells, in the early stage of the disease could enhance intestinal healing and thus prevent and/or alleviate the inflammation, especially in children, reducing or eliminating the human and healthcare costs of IBD in Canada and the world.

column36: Cognitive remediation for social cognitive deficits in schizophrenia: efficacy of the program RC2S and determinants of treatment outcomes
column37: Social cognitive deficits are one of the best predictors of functioning difficulties in schizophrenia. Social cognition refers to the mental processes underlying social interactions. Cognitive remediation therapy (CR) is a behavioural intervention that has shown its efficacy to improve social cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. Despite its efficacy, every patient does not benefit equally from CR, depending on individual characteristics. However, no study to date has systematically examined the role of these individual characteristics in CR efficacy for social cognition. Further, very few CR program targeting social cognition have used a personalized approach to tailor the treatment to individual difficulties. RC2S is an integrative and personalized CR program that targets several social cognitive functions and that uses virtual reality to emulate social interactions. However, no study has yet assessed its efficacy. The objectives of this project are to assess the efficacy of RC2S in terms of cognition, functioning and clinical symptoms in schizophrenia and to identify the personal characteristics that promote treatment outcomes. A total of 50 participants with schizophrenia aged between 18 and 65 years old, with a social cognitive deficit will be recruited. They will undergo an initial assessment of cognition, functioning and clinical symptoms and they will be randomized to the treatment group or to the waiting list. Participants in the treatment group will begin RC2S for 7 weeks. Participants in the waiting list will receive their treatment as usual during 7 weeks, will be reassessed and will then begin RC2S. Initial assessments will be repeated at post-test and 3-months post-test. This project will provide the first data regarding the efficacy of RC2S and the first assessment of individual characteristics that promote treatment outcomes in CR for social cognition. Ultimately, these results could help tailor CR and provide cost-effective interventions.

column36: Growth, Eating and Appetite Together (GrEAT) Study: Examining factors associated with the nutritional status of children born premature and at a very low birth weight
column37: Children born at a very low birth weight (VLBW; <1500g) are at high risk of early-onset obesity and cardiometabolic diseases. Causes are unknown, though poor nutrition is a likely contributor. Advances have been made to improve the nutritional status of VLBW infants in hospital, but we know very little about their diets post-discharge. Preliminary findings from our group suggest that poor diet quality at age 5 is associated with higher % fat mass among a cohort of children born VLBW. Eating habits are established early and track into adulthood; poor nutrition during childhood may exacerbate the consequences of VLBW. Research in term-born children has shown that food parenting practices (e.g., modelling and pressure to eat) influence children's dietary intake and weight status. Among those born VLBW, high rates of feeding problems and neurocognitive impairment may challenge the positive interactions necessary to develop healthy eating habits. Less desirable food parenting practices may also unintentionally contribute to or maintain problematic eating behaviours (e.g., using food as a reward). However, the feeding practices used by parents of VLBW children are unknown, and NICU follow-up is generally medical with little anticipatory guidance or support around feeding. This study will address these gaps by examining the association between directly observed food parenting practices and body composition and dietary intake among children born at a VLBW at 5 years of age in comparison to children born at term. Results will help to mitigate the consequences of preterm birth by helping to create anticipatory guidance and interventions to optimize nutrition throughout the early years.

column36: Assessment of the role of circRNAs in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
column37: Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (cALL) is the most frequent pediatric cancer. Despite remarkable improvements in survival, non-responding or relapsing patients still represent one of the most frequent cause of death by disease in children. cALL is a heterogeneous disease comprising multiple subtypes used for prognosis assessment. Although ~75% of ALL cases can be currently sub-classified using standard techniques, accurate patient risk stratification is still an ongoing challenge in cALL treatment and the development of innovative therapies. In recent years, a new type of molecule, termed circRNA, is emerging as a promising biomarker in cancer. However, little is known about the roles of circRNAs in the development and treatment of cALL. Then, the main goal of this study is to investigate the function of circRNAs in the context of cALL. Towards this goal, we are going to analyze these new molecules in a cohort of patients with cALL by Next Generation Sequencing technologies. The most promising findings will be validated in an independent cohort and functionally characterized to determine their role in cALL. Pending positive results, this project will advance the current state of knowledge by directly addressing a remaining challenge in cALL diagnostics, thereby improving the rate of lifelong remissions and the patients' long-term quality of life. The discovery of new factors involved in the etiology, progression and treatment response will not only add a new layer of complexity in leukemogenesis, but may also help identify new therapeutic targets.

column37: Asthma is a lung disease that makes it hard to breathe properly. It is the most common reason why children miss school or end up in hospital. Scientists have already made some exciting discoveries about who gets asthma and why this happens. One of these discoveries was about the importance of our gut bacteria in helping our immune systems to develop properly so that we do not get asthma. This research will help us understand how gut bacteria are linked to asthma and will provide new exciting tools for testing drugs to change the gut bacteria composition in order to prevent asthma in future.

column37: Recently, Dr. Richard Wilson's lab showed that small internal sensors in the neck - the carotid bodies - drive asthmatic attacks by activating the autonomic nervous system. His lab also found that the carotid bodies play an important role in lung inflammation. These observations suggest that the carotid body's influence over the autonomic nervous system may be a driving factor in common, costly and devastating allergy-associated inflammatory diseases such as asthma and irritable bowel syndrome. We know that the carotid body can active both the sympathetic and parasympathetic subdivisions of the autonomic nervous system. Since both of these systems can influence localized inflammation in select organs, they may therefore be crucial in initiating localized allergic responses. My current research has shown, in humans, that the autonomic nervous system can be controlled selectively to different targets throughout the body, a phenomenon known as differential control. Differential control has been shown to be drastically altered in many disease states, but how this mode of control is achieved, even in the healthy state, is unclear and whether it drives allergic disease is unknown. We suspect that the carotid body will have a strong involvement over differential control of the autonomic nervous system in the healthy state and will be responsible for the manifestation of organ-specific allergic responses and inflammation in asthma (lung) and irritable bowel syndrome (gut). We will also investigate whether we can halt the development of allergic disease by manipulating the activity of the autonomic neural pathways. We suspect these findings to be very translatable to other inflammatory disease states, such as hypertension, and will spark a new school-of-thought in how we treat allergy and chronic inflammatory conditions; that being through direct manipulation of dysfunctional neural circuits within the brain.

column36: Exploring the influence and perspectives of older adults in the development and testing of mobile health interventions in airways disease
column37: Internet-enabled mobile technologies are increasingly being incorporated into the healthcare of Canadians. These "mHealth" tools can be used to improve disease monitoring, patient education, and enhance communication between patients and healthcare practitioners. mHealth may be particularly useful in helping to address the needs of older patients, such as medication assistance, and disease self-management and monitoring. However, there are important barriers preventing mHealth from effectively reaching older patients, including decreased access to technology, and sub-optimal usability of current mHealth tools among older patients. These concerns are particularly relevant to a disease like asthma, which affects 8.3% of Canadians and is growing in prevalence in older adults. The goal of my proposed research is to better understand how older patient age affects the use of mHealth tools in asthma. To accomplish this, I am proposing three connected research projects. First, I will analyze a study that tested an asthma mHealth tool in 2 family practice clinics, in order to determine how older patient age affected the use of the tool. Next, I will carry out an extensive literature review looking to better understand how other researchers have considered older patient age when they developed and tested respiratory mHealth tools. Finally, I will conduct and analyze in-depth patient interviews with older patients with asthma in order to understand their perspectives and experiences using mHealth tools. My work will help respiratory mHealth researchers better understand how mobile technologies are used in older patients with respiratory disease, and may identify ways in which current and future tools can be changed to make them more accessible and usable for older adults.

column36: High Flow Nasal Cannula versus Non-Invasive Ventilation in exacerbations of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary disease
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a disease characterized by shortness of breath, cough and sputum production. COPD worsens over time leading to debilitating complications and frequent hospitalizations. In Canada, COPD affects over 2 million Canadians -the number is expected to rise in the coming years. In under a decade, the number of Canadians diagnosed with COPD increased by 82%, now affecting 1 / 116 Canadians. COPD is the 3rd leading cause of death in the United States, causing 120,000 deaths yearly. COPD is characterized by frequent exacerbations with life-threatening breathing problems requiring management in the emergency department (ED) or intensive care unit (ICU). To relieve shortness of breath, non-invasive ventilation delivered via a mask on the face is recommended, but needs expertise, close monitoring and can be poorly tolerated. Another non-invasive device provides a heated and humidified high flow of gas with controlled oxygen fraction through nasal cannula, avoiding the need for face mask. This promising alternative has not been tested yet in this situation. We recently showed that this technique has advantages compared to non-invasive ventilation in patients with cystic fibrosis which leads to similar problems with breathing. The aim of our program is 1) to assess the potential benefits of this technique compared to non-invasive ventilation, and 2) understand the mechanisms of action in order to adapt therapy to the degree of severity. We will compare the physiologic effects and tolerance of high-flow nasal oxygen and non-invasive ventilation in patients with COPD exacerbation admitted to the ED or ICU If high-flow nasal oxygen is at least as effective as non-invasive ventilation, this could be a major advance in the treatment of COPD, potentially reducing health-care resource burden, hospital admissions and optimizing symptom control for patients. It could significantly improve the long-term management of these patients.

column36: Cow's milk fat: which is best for children?
column37: Health Canada and the Canadian Pediatric Society recommend that children over age 2 years consume reduced (i.e. 1%) fat rather than whole (3.25%) fat cow's milk to prevent obesity. New research supports that reduced fat milk early in life may promote rather than prevent obesity. The Cow Milk Fat Obesity pRevention Trial (CoMFORT) is an innovative clinical trial comparing a primary healthcare recommendation for whole vs. reduced fat milk on optimizing growth, development and nutrition among children aged 2-4 years. PhD candidate and clinician scientist Shelley Vanderhout has been the lead trainee on the CoMFORT trial, from the first stages of development to study implementation in primary care practices. As Shelley develops her research program, this fellowship will provide her with the opportunity to fully develop innovative, family-oriented clinical trial skills from start to finish. She will develop written and online media and hold forums with policymakers and families to integrate results into clinical and public health policies and the lives of Canadian families. This Fellowship will equip Shelley to conduct efficient and meaningful research as a leading clinician scientist focused on innovative clinical trials, inform future clinical trial methods, and impact child health policies with the goal of improving child health in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Epilepsy is a nervous system disorder that causes seizures from abnormal brain activity. It is a disease that affects nearly 1% of the population worldwide. Many old drugs are still used to treat epilepsy eventhough several challenges still persist including drug resistant and adverse side effects. These problems address the need to introduce new anti-epileptic drugs for treatment of this complicated disease. Understanding how these drugs work is of great importance for the development and delivery of safe and effective pharmaceuticals. A common cause of Epilepsy is dysfunction of proteins, known as ion channels, that disrupt electrical signaling in the brain. In particular, dysfunction of ion channels that are selective to potassium ions (potassium channels) have been linked to different forms of epilepsy. Targeting these potassium channels has become a promising endeavour for drug companies and scientists. The drug, Retigabine, became the first FDA approved pharmaceutical option in its class. Retigabine targets potassium channels and works by promoting the open state of these channels and preventing abnormal brain activities that lead to seizures. However, due to health and financial reasons, Retigabine has recently been discontinued as a treatment option for epilepsy. While Retigabine is the most recognized drug in this category, several existing and emerging potassium channel targeting drugs, each with very different mechanisms of action, remain to be investigated or completely understood. My research aims to study in detail this new class of anti-epileptic drug, in connection with the pharmaceutical industry, to improve viable treatment options for epilepsy.

Furthermore, from an Indigenous perspective, language is born of a specific place. It serves to describe with powerful accuracy all the particular life existing therein, and all the sacred histories and events that happen thereupon. Place and language thus provide the context and source of knowledge by which a person can identify or communicate social constructs of identity including gender, community and governance. Those who do not know the language of a particular land are impoverished; without knowing place and language they are challenged to fully identify themselves as that land. Interruption of this connection through colonization has profoundly and negatively impacted Indigenous peoples' ability to articulate a healthful, holistic identity. Indeed the disrupted connection has become a general marker of ill health. The purpose of this project is to develop land, language, and community-based activities in an Indigenous context to support reclamation of wellness based in local understandings of identity and health. Developing established relations with three Coast Salish Indigenous partner entities, this project will utilize funds to create meaningful community programs to support the engendering of Indigenous identity for wellbeing.

column36: The Role of Microglia in Chronic Stress-Induced Cognitive Impairment
column37: Chronic stress is associated with cognitive impairment. It is possible that this is due to the brain's immune cells, microglia. Microglia can engulf and chew up neurons, which are the cells in the brain that talk to one another. It is possible that chronic stress makes these immune cells more likely to engulf neurons, which leads to cognitive deficits. To understand this, we will use live imaging to look at how microglia act in the brain of chronically stressed laboratory mice. We will then see if treatments that can reverse chronic stress induced cognitive deficits, such as probiotics, cannabinoids, omega-3 supplementation or ketogenic diet, work through altering these brain immune cells (microglia). Together these data will better inform how chronic stress leads to alterations in cognition and may provide a new target for therapeutics of stress-associated diseases.

column36: Innovations in Indigenous Implementation Science: Working with First Nations and Metis communities to develop and evaluate shared care models for HIV and other sexually transmitted and blood borne infections (STBBI)
column37: This proposed postdoctoral research is situated within the DRUM & SASH team grant project. DRUM & SASH builds on the DRUM1 project, a partnership between First Nation communities, people with lived experience of HIV, the Canadian Aboriginal AIDS Network (CAAN), policy makers, and academics. The DRUM1 team worked with 3 northern Alberta First Nation communities to develop a community-led process of Shared Care Model (SCM) development for HIV and other STBBIs. As a postdoctoral fellow, I will develop and implement a model for Indigenous implementation science (IIS) in collaboration with DRUM & SASH communities and other stakeholders. This model be used to evaluate the DRUM & SASH approach of SCM development. Using this IIS model, I will collaboratively assess the DRUM & SASH processes including the co-learning and community-led approaches to the adaptation and scale up SCM within diverse (different cultures, rural and urban, smaller and larger) participating AB First Nation and Metis communities and the implementation of the SCM initiatives. Overall, this novel postdoctoral research will contribute to the development of innovative Indigenous approaches to implementation science, as well as provide evidence about using community developed SCM to improve access to culturally appropriate health services for STBBI treatment and prevention for Indigenous people on and off reserve. Improving access to culturally appropriate health services for Indigenous people continues to be of the utmost importance as, due to the ongoing effects of colonialism, Indigenous people in Canada continue to be over represented in rates of HIV and other STBBIs.
