column36: The Eniako'nikonhriiohake (One will have a good mind) Project: Building a technology-based resilience curriculum for Indigenous youth
column37: Resilience is an adaptation process supporting the management of acute stress, as well as chronic, daily stressors (Supkoff, Puig, & Sroufe, 2012; Snowshoe et al., 2015). Indigenous youth face unique challenges as they must navigate three worlds: their traditional culture, Westernized society, and the on-line world (Wekerle, Waechter, Leung, & Leonard, 2007; Wekerle, Vakili, Stewart, & Black, 2018). In a 2016 review, technology is identified as a critical forum, given the confidence with which Indigenous youth approach its use to support their representation and content generation, to self-organize, and to access traditional information. In particular, health promotion approaches that utilize social media and digital technologies were identified as relevant and feasible (Rice, Haynes, Royce & Thompson, 2016). This project has two streams toward building a technology-based resilience curriculum for Indigenous youth from a stakeholder group of youth attending Kawenni:io/Gaweni:yo Private Immersion School on Six Nations of the Grand River territory. The school has been operating for the past 30 years, offering full immersion education and culture in Mohawk and Cayuga languages for Junior Kindergarten to Grade 12 students. Our goal is to develop a culturally-relevant resilience curriculum that embeds cultural teachings in gender, health, and wellness and embraces technology (i.e., the JoyPop app) as a facilitative tool for youth resilience, and to work toward an adapted, culturally-relevant (Haudenosaunnee) version of JoyPop to set the stage for further evaluation as a school health promotion initiative. Also, we will address data sovereignty in planning how the app and questionnaire data is managed. Our goal is to apply for grants funds to continue to evaluate this model for other immersion and non-immersion schools for Indigenous youth.

column36: Investigating Macrophage AMPK as a Potential Therapeutic Target for Treating Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease
column37: Rates of Type 2 Diabetes and cardiovascular disease are rapidly increasing in Canada. These conditions often occur together and evidence suggests that they should also be treated together. Unfortunately, current therapies for either condition are ineffective. We believe that the high blood glucose that occurs during the development of type 2 diabetes causes inflammation, which represents the key link between diabetes and CVD. Specifically, macrophages, a type of immune cell, are essential mediators of the inflammation present in diabetes and CVD. Moreover, we have evidence suggesting that activating an enzyme called "AMPK" in macrophages may reduce inflammation and improve symptoms associated with diabetes and CVD. To test this, we will directly expose macrophages to high amounts of glucose and assess the inflammation that develops. We will also directly treat macrophages with a newly developed drug to activate AMPK to see if we can reduce inflammation in macrophages in the presence of high glucose. We will also treat mice with this AMPK activating drug and assess whether AMPK is activated in macrophages and whether this can prevent the development of diabetes and CVD in lean and obese mice with high blood glucose. Finally, we have previously tracked the development of diabetes and CVD in ~1400 humans, and we will use these data together with the current experiments to try and uncover a new marker that can be used to predict the development of diabetes and CVD in humans. Together, these results will provide extremely important evidence on the development of Type 2 Diabetes and CVD and new therapeutic ways of predicting, preventing, and treating these conditions.

column36: Clinical trajectories of patients recently diagnosed with major depressive disorder: a prospective cohort study
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) affects more than 350 million people worldwide. Previous studies showed that a subset of individuals diagnosed with depression present worse clinical trajectories marked by functional impairment. Of note, about 10% of patients suffering from depression are later diagnosed with bipolar disorder (BD), because they developed a manic or hypomanic episode. That is consequential since it changes their treatment, making the early detection an important need in the field of mood disorders. We have preliminary data showing that in Ontario, people who suffer from mood disorder have a higher propensity of developing disabilities and require ongoing support from the government. In addition, we have preliminary data identifying predictors of conversion from MDD to BD. Our goal is to extend these early studies and, for the first time, prospectively examine the predictors of disability and conversion to BD in a population recently diagnosed with depression (within 2 years of diagnosis). We will assess 400 subjects recently diagnosed with depression, and we will follow them for 2 years to identify the factors associated with disability and conversion to BD. Our research will help to identify characteristics associated with the subgroup of patients with worse clinical outcomes and enable preventive interventions for this specific population.

column36: The Family Check-up in a Canadian Context: Testing Novel Emotional and Physiological Mechanisms of Change
column37: Untreated mental illness accounts for 13% of the total global burden of disease (WHO, 2011). It is estimated that by 2030, mental health will pose the greatest global health burden. Early childhood mental health problems (e.g., aggression, oppositionality, anxiety, depression) are highly prevalent and are strong predictors of mental illness later in life. To reduce the mental health burden during childhood and later in life, effective parent-child interventions, which not only target mental health symptoms but also target the underlying predictors of mental health, are needed. The current study will examine the validity of a brief family intervention (the Family Check Up; FCU) and assess how this intervention impacts stress and emotion regulation, key factors that are associated with parenting and mental health and have broad developmental implications. Participants will include 280 children aged 2-4 years old and their caregivers, from the Child and Youth Mental Health Program at McMaster Children's Hospital. Half of the families will receive the FCU and the other half will receive community resources. The FCU is a family-based assessment and intervention that includes a parent-child interaction assessment using a gold-standard observational measures, a check-up session, feedback visit, and parenting training. We will develop a new coding scheme to assess parent, child and dyadic emotion regulation. We will assess how the FCU intervention affects children's developing emotion regulation and stress responses as pathways to improved mental health. Identifying the underlying stress and emotion mechanisms is necessary to further develop targeted interventions, so to improve child mental health and limit continuing mental health problems.

column36: Improving estimates of patient mortality among drug-resistant tuberculosis patients
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacteria that infected more than 10 million people in 2017. Some TB patients have bacteria that are not killed by our standard anti-TB drugs; these bacteria are referred to as drug-resistant. If patients receive the wrong drugs, they are more likely to die. The number of patients who die during treatment is an important indicator of how well a TB treatment program is working so it is critical that we report this number accurately. However, sometimes up to 20% of patients will stop coming to see the doctor during treatment because they moved or did not want to keep taking the drugs because of side effects etc. I will investigate how to accurately report the number of TB patients who died by correcting for patients who stopped coming to the doctor. I will compare two different correction methods using simulated data and then apply the best method to drug-resistant TB patient data from the Philippines. This project will help researchers and TB programs accurately estimate the number of TB patients who died so they can better measure TB quality of care.

column36: CDX and TRIM31: a novel pathway linking chronic inflammation and colorectal cancer.
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cause of malignancy and second most common cause of cancer death. There are a wide range of therapy available for colorectal cancer, but treatment becomes complicated as there are a range of colon cancer subtypes. Subtypes of cancer respond to therapy differently, as a result there is increased risk of recurrence and metastasis. There is a significant reduction of 5-year survival rate for stage-I CRC to stage-IV CRC (90% to 10%). This necessitate to search early biomarkers and improved therapeutic strategy during the early stage of colon cancer progression. Therefore, in cancer research it is crucial to subcategorize the cancer type based on biomarker discoveries which can lead to more effective therapeutic procedures. Chronic inflammation in the form of inflammatory bowel diseases, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are some of the risk factors for tumor progression in colon. Our lab works with a family of protein called Cdx1 and 2.They are present in high load in the gut. These proteins are crucial for gut development and maintenance. Moreover, Cdx2 is considered as a marker for advanced colon cancer. My preliminary work suggests loss of Cdx protein is linked to aberrant inflammation. I have found that Cdx protein directly regulates production of a protein named Trim31, which has anti-inflammatory properties. Thus, loss of Cdx or Trim31 proteins lead to chronic inflammation in the gut which in turn promotes tumor formation. My study aims to identify the cellular functions and pathways that are affected by the loss of Cdx and Trim31 proteins; and to find out the factors and inflammatory cues that are playing important roles in this imbalance., Thus, this study will reveal a novel roadmap that leads to chronic inflammation and colon cancer formation. ; and may serve as a blueprint for developing improved therapeutic strategy for colon cancer.

column36: Developing AMPK activator as therapeutics for treatment and management of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), that is commonly classified into Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease is the condition of inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract. The incidence of the disease has shown a dramatic increase in the last decades in Canada and worldwide. Despite significant progress in developing improved therapies for IBD, many side effects with existing therapies indicate the need for the development of better therapeutic strategies. The Adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) consist of catalytic alpha-subunit and the regulatory beta-and gamma-subunits and is a key regulator of cellular and organismal metabolism, however, the importance of AMPK in the pathogenesis of IBD is not fully understood. In our lab, we have investigated the important role of AMPK in the pathogenesis of intestinal inflammation. Our data suggest that reductions in AMPK activity mediated through genetic deletion of AMPK beta1 in macrophages up-regulates the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and aggravates dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in mice. We will further investigate the mechanism in the cellular level and investigate whether sodium salicylate, commonly used as anti-inflammatory and analgesic and recently an activator of AMPK targeting AMPK beta1, is effective in the amelioration of DSS-induced colitis in mice. The proposed study will prove to be very important in the development of safer and inexpensive therapy in the treatment and management of the condition of intestinal inflammation such as Inflammatory Bowel Disease which will benefit many Canadians and ultimately nations economy.

column36: Age-associated inflammation alters myeloid cell development and function
column37: Recent statistics tell us that 90 percent of Canadians aged 65 and over live with at least one chronic condition including heart disease, respiratory conditions, diabetes, or arthritis. While the cause of chronic disease is complex and multifactorial, age-related changes to the immune system are a major contributor. Stem cells in the bone marrow give rise to two different lineages of immune cells: myeloid and lymphoid immune cells. As people age, these stem cells may acquire genetic mutations that skew the differentiation of immune cells towards the myeloid lineage at the expense of lymphoid cells. In addition to this "myeloid-skewing", the immune cells are often immature and have reduced function. Accumulating evidence suggests that this predisposes older adults to developing health complications, but the genetic changes that occur in the stem cells and the molecular events that underlie these changes remain unclear. The aim of my postdoctoral fellows is to determine the link between myeloid genetic mutations, myeloid-skewing, and immune impairment with age. We hypothesize that mutations in a specific gene called TET2 results in myeloid impairment. This is thought to be driven by the aging bone marrow environment, which has increased inflammatory mediators. To approach this, I will integrate my prior experience in machine learning with a custom next-generation sequencing platform to identify genetic biomarkers in blood of elderly patients. Concurrently, I will use transplantation studies in Tet2 knockout mice to determine if inflammatory mediators in the aging bone marrow results in myeloid-skewing and impairment. These experiments will determine whether modifying inflammatory mediators in the bone marrow is a viable option for reducing myeloid skewing, which we can pursue in subsequent experiments by administering inflammatory blockers. Ultimately, we believe the results of this research will provide avenues for new therapeutic interventions.

column36: Partnering with speech-language pathologists to improve interventions for children with language disorders
column37: Children with language disorders struggle to learn, make friends, and join activities in their neighbourhood and community. Speech-language pathologists provide treatments to help children develop language. For families of these children, the most important and meaningful treatment is one that targets all aspects of their child's life. In other words, families hope that treatments from speech-language pathologists not only improve the ways that children speak or understand certain words, but also improve how they join classroom activities and play with friends. The goal of this project is to improve preschool speech-language treatments. To do so, we will work with speech-language pathologists in the publicly-funded programs in Ontario. We will then check if these tools actually changed treatments. We will also ask speech-language pathologists and families to give feedback on how we can improve these tools. Aside from improving preschool speech-language treatments, this project will impact all Canadians. Learning from speech-language pathologists, we can improve the tools we have for designing treatments for children with other disabilities. For example, these tools can then be used to improve education and healthcare for children with all disabilities (e.g. to improve physiotherapy for children with cerebral palsy or classroom support for children with hearing loss). Families of children with disabilities can use these tools to advocate for better services for their child. Canadians can use these tools to understand the different ways they can help and engage children with disabilities.

column36: The role of NAD synthetase 1 in VACTERL syndrome
column37: VACTERL syndrome is a set of birth defects that affects multiple areas of the body, including the heart, limbs, kidneys, trachea/esophagus, and spinal cord. If a patient has any three of these defects, they can be diagnosed as having VACTERL syndrome. This syndrome occurs in 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 40,000 newborns. Treatment is specific to the type of symptoms but may include surgery along with long-term management. The exact cause of VACTERL association has yet to be identified, although in some people it appears to be a combination of genetic and environmental factors. At the Children's Hospital of Western Ontario, genetic testing of 2 patients diagnosed with VACTERL association and their parents identified a mutation in a gene called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) synthetase 1. NAD is an important molecule found in all living cells which regulates multiple different biological processes, such as metabolism, aging, and DNA repair. Past studies have shown that other defects in the NAD synthesis pathway have also resulted in VACTERL syndrome patients. My project will aim to understand the role of NAD synthetase 1 in early development and why defective activity of this enzyme results in a specific subset of developmental defects called VACTERL syndrome. I will be using stem cells with the same mutation in NAD synthetase 1 as was identified in the 2 patients in hopes of understanding what type of cell lineages are affected by this mutation and why. This work will be part of an international collaboration with Dr. Sally Dunwoodie at the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute in Sydney, Australia, who is developing mouse models to further understand the molecular basis of this association. Overall, our research will contribute to the identification and understanding of the genetic variants that may be associated with VACTERL syndrome in hopes of developing better treatment options and improving family counselling.

column36: Towards breaking the cycle of intimate partner violence in Canada: Technology-based healthcare screening and interventions for women
column37: Up to half of Canadian women experience sexual, physical, and/or psychological violence from their partners, referred to as intimate partner violence (IPV). IPV is a leading cause of death and impairment, and is estimated to cost Canadians >$6 billion each year. Most women do not disclose about IPV and have limited access to support. However, women affected by IPV visit their healthcare providers (HCPs) more often than other women. Therefore, HCPs are in a position to routinely screen for IPV. Routine screening for IPV is considered to be beneficial by patients and HCPs, and improve detection of IPV. My study tests the feasibility of implementing a technology-based IPV screening tool in different clinics across a large multidisciplinary hospital. I will also examine if screening is associated with increased rates of help-seeking behaviour and improved health for women experiencing IPV. Clinics are randomly assigned to use the screening tool or provide usual care. In clinics assigned to screening, HCPs provide women who screen positive for IPV with a "warm handoff" to a national IPV hotline for counselling. Each woman in each condition is called 3 months after their visit to assess help-seeking behaviours (how many times they contacted the hotline or other resources) and mental health symptoms. I hypothesize that the tool will be widely accepted by HCPs and non-burdensome (e.g., not add significant time to visits). I also hypothesize that screening will be significantly associated with improved help-seeking behaviours and mental and physical health outcomes for women who screen positive for IPV in the screening condition compared to women in usual care who endorse IPV. If found to be feasible and effective, my goal is to implement and test this tool across Canadian healthcare clinics, where no such IPV screening systems currently exists. Ultimately, my project will contribute to improving the health of women affected by IPV, a costly and deadly phenomenon in Canada.

column36: Investigating the role and impact of obesity and measures of adiposity on cognitive function
column37: Obesity is one of the most important unmet prevention and treatment health challenges. The high prevalence of overweight and obesity, which has more than tripled since the 1970s, is of serious public health concern since overweight and obesity are often concomitant with adverse complications, including diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Cognitive impairment and depression are also suggested to be associated with obesity and increased measures of adiposity. Given 50 million people worldwide are diagnosed with dementia and more than 300 million people of all ages suffer from depression, it is important to determine and address possible modifiable risk factors if we are ever to alleviate the overall global burden of these diseases. While obesity has been connected to cognitive health the evidence is still uncertain. Dietary factors have long been implicated in non-communicable disease risk. Consumption of specific dietary patterns may lead to decreases in adiposity and hence improve cognitive function and reduce the risk of neurodegenerative diseases. In order to address these concerns a comprehensive research program is proposed which conducts a series of studies investigating the relationship between obesity and changes to body weight with indicators of cognitive function as well as risk of dementia and depression. This will be done using data from the PREDIMED-Plus trial, one of the biggest milestone trials in nutrition research in Europe. Following this investigation a synthesis and comparison of dietary patterns in relation to body weight and risk of obesity will be conducted to determine potential strategies to reduce obesity, as well as potentially improve cognitive function. This research, specifically determining lifestyle related strategies, such as following a dietary pattern, has the potential to have significant local and global impact on health and our health care system.

column36: Pro-inflammatory role of dietary fibers in IBD: defining how microbes mediate diet-associated inflammation and could guide diet-based therapies
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), including ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn disease (CD), are common and severely devastating chronic disorders. IBD incidence rates are on the rise, especially in children, who make up 25% of newly diagnosed cases. What causes IBD remains poorly understood, although evidence shows that gut bacteria and diet are involved. Interestingly, dietary fibers pass through the body undigested and are normally fermented within the large intestine by the gut bacteria, maintaining gut health. We have identified changes in beneficial vs. harmful gut bacteria (called pathobionts) in children with IBD and hypothesize that lack of beneficial bacteria causes significant changes in fiber fermentation, driving gut injury and disease progression. Our initial results have shown that 'bad' gut bacteria use different dietary fibers for their growth when compared to 'good' or 'neutral' bacteria. Further, unfermented fibers in the gut interact with select types of human cells, resulting in gut inflammation. These results suggest the need for altered and individualized dietary recommendations in these patients. We plan to combine bacterial data with food frequency questionnaires and detailed patient history (already available) in order to identify the role that dietary fibers play in IBD. This study provides an excellent opportunity to define key disease features of IBD and also identify new and improved treatment options, such as microbe-altering treatments, and tailored nutritional recommendations. Nutrition remains an almost untapped aspect of IBD with great and safe potential, in contrast to current therapies, offering a novel, non-toxic, and more readily available therapeutic options for patients.

column36: CRISPR-Cas9 genome-wide pooled screen for the identification of unknown glucocerebrosidase modulators
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, yet remarkably, no therapy exists that can slow the disease. The increasing incidence of PD makes improving our knowledge of the mechanisms and factors leading to PD of importance. Mutations in the gene GBA, which encodes the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase), are the greatest genetic risk factor for PD. In addition, it has been shown that augmenting GCase activity in mouse models can reduce disease progression of PD. Therefore, great efforts are made to identify enhancers of GCase activity. The link between GCase and PD however, remains poorly understood. We propose here the use of a novel chemical genetic screening approach to identify new genes that affect GCase activity. We will use a genome-wide pooled screen in order to evaluate the effect of each single gene on the activity of GCase. The readout will be achieved with our new GCase imaging substrates, that allow the measurement of GCase activity directly in living cells and fluorescence-assisted flow cytometry. The resulting hits, meaning genes having a significant effect on GCase activity, will be validated through downstream experiments and assessed in neuronal models in order to understand how they regulate GCase activity. We expect this project to have major outcomes. First, direct monitoring of enzyme activity in living cells has, to our knowledge, never been applied to genome-wide screening. This chemical biology approach would therefore be pioneering. Second, these findings could pinpoint upstream regulators of GCase activity, illuminating the molecular processes that lead to PD and opening new research directions. Third, as augmentation of GCase activity in PD patients is being pursued as a disease-modifying approach, the discovery of GCase regulators could lead to new targets that could be exploited to create small molecule or gene therapies for PD.

column36: The role of ketones in heart failure
column37: Although advancements in therapies to treat cardiovascular disease have reduced the number of deaths of cardiac patients, these treatments have ultimately increased the number of people who eventually go on to develop another clinical condition called heart failure. Simply stated, heart failure is a condition that is defined by poor heart function that prevents the heart from pumping enough blood to the rest of the body. For decades, it has been established that one of the contributing factors of the failing hearts poor performance is the heart's inability to generate enough energy to beat properly. Recent studies have shown that a major fuel for the heart is ketones. Ketones are molecules that are produced by the liver from fats and can be used in the heart to produce energy. Of importance, recent work has suggested that the failing heart increases the amount of ketones used to produce energy in what is thought to be an attempt to increase energy production. However, whether or not this increase in ketone use by the heart is beneficial or detrimental to the failing heart is still unknown. Using two mouse models of heart failure, we will investigate the role of ketones in heart failure and determine if they are good or bad for the heart. We hypothesize that increased ketone use by the failing heart is beneficial and propose that providing even more ketones to the heart can be used as a potential new therapeutic approach for the treatment of heart failure.

column36: Understanding counsellor-client interactions in spinal cord injury exercise counselling: a novel method to explain outcomes of randomized controlled trials by assessing intervention fidelity
column37: Behavioural interventions often consist of conversations between counsellors and clients and can be a successful way to promote a healthy lifestyle. However, these interventions are not always successfully translated to other real-world settings. A possible reason for this variation in outcomes, is that researchers do not always measure how counsellors and clients interact with each other. Recently, a new method, called state space grids, has been developed to study and visualize how a counsellor and client interact with each other over time. This study will use these state space girds to study conversations about health-enhancing exercise between exercise counsellors and clients with spinal cord injury (SCI) to better understand the frequency, sequence, and duration of behaviour change techniques used in the interaction between the counsellor and client. This study is part of a larger trial of the effects of exercise to reduce chronic pain in adults with SCI. Participants in the study will receive tailored exercise counselling from a trained counsellor. Audio recordings of the counselling sessions will be analysed line-by-line by two researchers. This study is the first to use state space grids methods in an exercise behaviour interventions trial. It will provide new insights into how counsellors and clients with SCI interact with each other. These findings will help us to better understand how, when, and why the counselling sessions are successful or not. The findings can be used to develop training guides for SCI exercise counsellors and can improve SCI exercise counselling. In turn, understanding and improving effective exercise counselling will enhance lives of many Canadians with SCI.

column36: Engaging spinal arm and leg networks to improve walking after spinal cord injury
column37: When we walk, we swing our arms in rhythm with our legs. This relationship between the arms and legs is needed to improve our balance and our ability to walk efficiently. This project aims to develop a novel, cost-effective, and widely translatable therapy to improve walking ability after spinal cord injury (SCI). Two thirds (67.3%) of all spinal cord injuries are incomplete (iSCI), leaving some neural connections intact across the lesion site. Nonetheless, the ability to walk is often lost after SCI, leading to multiple secondary complications that reduce quality of life and increase healthcare costs. Current rehabilitation interventions focus on restoring walking through intensive training of the legs, but ignore engaging the arms. We recently demonstrated that simultaneous arm and leg cycling assisted with functional electrical stimulation doubles the improvements in over-ground walking after iSCI compared to leg cycling only or other gait-specific training paradigms. These findings highlighted the importance of neuronal pathways between the arm and leg control regions in the spinal cord during locomotion, and emphasized the need for activating these pathways to improve walking after iSCI. This project will investigate the innovative use of non-invasive spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) to recruit previously inaccessible spinal circuits in conjunction with arm and leg cycling for improving walking capacity of persons with more severe iSCI than currently possible with conventional rehabilitation paradigms.The results of this pivotal study will be crucial for determining the importance of arm and leg networks in the rehabilitation of walking. If successful, arm and leg cycling coupled with spinal cord stimulation could become an intervention that can be readily translated to the clinic as an accessible, inexpensive and effective rehabilitation therapy, benefiting more persons with spinal cord injury than currently possible.

column36: A method to recapitulate early embryonic gut spatial patterning and morphogenesis in hESCs
column37: As an organism develops, simple homogenous tissues undergo successive patterning and morphogenetic events to produce structurally complex heterogenous organs. In vertebrates, these events are primarily driven by reciprocal morphogen and mechanical signals between two or more adjacent cell types. Despite extensive knowledge about the individual nature of the signals and cell types involved, however, less is known about how they come together to create large-scale patterns, sharp boundaries, and the final size and shape of tissues-especially in the context of human development. A marked example of this is the development of the human gut, where despite the ability to create and study human cell types for almost every region in vitro, we still lack basic knowledge about how the embryonic gut tube regionalizes and sets the sites of the future endodermal organs. Such knowledge is not only critical for understanding development, but also for understanding and potentially treating a variety of common congenital disorders. It would also be greatly beneficial for tissue engineers for deriving new strategies to create tissues and organs for regenerative medicine. With a Life Sciences Research Foundation Fellowship, I plan to build on recent progress combining tools from synthetic biology with human embryonic stem cells to create a novel model system for studying the patterning and morphogenesis of the human gut. The system will also be applicable more generally to studying other instances of tubular patterning during human development, and for experimenting with and creating synthetic organ systems for future clinical application.

column36: The use of machine learning and multi-omics to explore the role of diet in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Cirrhosis is the end stage for most liver diseases. It is caused by a build up of scar tissue and results in a gradual loss of liver function. A minority of patients are candidates for liver transplantation. As cirrhosis advances, most patients experience chronic decline, frequent complications, repeated hospitalizations and a high burden of symptoms. Nutrition and exercise have helped patients with other chronic diseases improve or maintain their overall health. This is particularly important in cirrhosis where 80% of patients have dietary issues and muscle loss contributing to physical and mental frailty. In turn, frail patients with cirrhosis have a higher risk of hospitalization and death. By taking in a liver-friendly diet and engaging in regular exercise, studies have demonstrated improvements in frailty, reduced symptom burden and higher health-related quality of life. The benefit of these treatments is not experienced by all patients however, and the reasons for this remain unclear. During my postdoctoral fellowship, I will have access to a large dataset collected across the length of a 6-month randomized controlled trial. The trial compares patients with cirrhosis receiving standard care (control group) versus those in a nutrition and exercise program (experimental group). Unique from anything else that is available, the dataset will contain a broad range of data including not only clinical features and laboratory tests but also gut bacteria (intestinal microbiome) profiles, and metabolomic profiles (small molecules) present in the urine and blood. I will use machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence to predict the response to nutrition and exercise therapy and understand the mechanisms that explain response. Findings will help medical teams and their patients determine how to personalize these treatments in the future to achieve the most benefit for each individual patient.

column36: Exploring RNA splicing regulation using direct sequencing of nascent RNA
column37: Messenger RNAs (mRNA) are copies of genes that contain the information necessary to produce proteins. The formation of the right cell type depends on the production of the correct mRNAs that contain the instructions to make this given cell type. This is achieved in part through RNA splicing, in which certain parts of the premature RNA called introns are removed to form the mature mRNA. Defects in RNA splicing are a common cause of many human disorders, including cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms that control splicing in human cells are not well understood, which is mainly due to a lack of tools to study splicing while it is occurring. We recently developed a new method, nanopore analysis of CO-transcriptional Processing (nano-COP), which relies on direct RNA sequencing and allows us to monitor splicing while new RNAs are being produced. For example, we gained insight into how fast splicing occurs and the order of intron removal in human leukemia cells. The objective of this project is to use nano-COP to better understand how these aspects of splicing are controlled in various cell types. We will first apply nano-COP to measure splicing in 10 different human cell lines, including normal and cancer cells, to determine how splicing dynamics vary across cell types and in cancer. Next, we will use white blood cells from 10 different individuals to examine how splicing kinetics and order are impacted by genetic variants in parts of the RNA that are known to cause abnormal splicing. Finally, we will remove three proteins that play a role in splicing to determine in which aspect of splicing they are most important. We will repeat this experiment in three different cell types to discover whether certain functions of these proteins are cell type-specific. This study will improve our understanding of the control of the splicing process, which is crucial in order to learn how it goes awry in various human diseases.

column36: Can a single bout of exercise improve clinical outcomes in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery? Investigating the effects of acute local (handgrip) exercise on attenuating cardiac and vascular injury to ischaemia-reperfusion
column37: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in Canada and worldwide. While coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery remains the preferred strategy to restore blood flow to the heart in CAD patients, this procedure is associated with peri- and post-surgery complications. The duration and/or severity of cardiovascular tissue exposed to ischaemia is strongly related to morbidity and mortality, hence the importance to minimize tissue injury to ischaemia during surgery. Novel cardioprotective strategies are needed to improve clinical outcomes in patients undergoing CABG surgery. This project will build on exciting research findings in both animal models and healthy participants demonstrating that an acute bout of exercise lowers tissue injury to ischaemia-reperfusion. The goal of the proposed research is to examine the hypothesis that a single bout of handgrip exercise can attenuate vascular and cardiac injury to ischaemia-reperfusion in participants with CAD. Moreover, I hypothesize that these effects can be enhanced through a short period (4-days) of daily handgrip exercise training. These effects of local handgrip exercise on mediating smaller vascular and cardiac injury to ischaemia will ultimately lead to lower post-surgery morbidity/mortality. The simplicity, low cost, and low risk of handgrip exercise makes it highly suitable to implement into clinical care to potentially reduce cardiac and vascular injury to ischaemia. Moreover, this work will contribute to informing and optimizing exercise guidelines prior to cardiac surgery.

column36: Moving past allergy: how histamine impacts infection by a multidrug resistant pathogen
column37: Histamine is a potent chemical mediator that is commonly known for its function in allergy, but also plays an important role in the immune response. Upon exposure to an allergen, injury, or foreign invader, immune cells such as mast cells and basophils are triggered to release histamine and other inflammatory molecules. Histamine has a number of diverse biological effects, many of which are associated with allergy symptoms, including enhancing mucus production and thickness, increasing blood vessel leakage, and inducing airway constriction. Increasing blood vessel leakage is a crucial early step in the immune response, as it allows immune cells to escape into the damaged tissue to directly engage the perceived threat. Interestingly, some bacteria are also capable of producing and releasing histamine during infection. Acinetobacter baumannii is an emerging hospital-associated pathogen that is not only often extensively resistant to antibiotics, but also has been shown to release histamine. In A. baumannii, histamine appears to be produced as a key precursor of acinetobactin, a small iron-binding molecule that helps the bacteria capture this essential growth-promoting metal. The goal of this project is to understand how histamine availability impacts the outcome of A. baumannii pneumonia and bloodstream infections. We hypothesize that histamine may actually worsen A. baumannii infection by enhancing the ability of the bacteria to obtain iron and by allowing them to hijack the local immune response, using congested airways and disrupted blood vessels to avoid clearance and promote spread within the body. By defining the role of histamine in A. baumannii infection, we will not only enhance our understanding of how this bacterium is able to cause disease, but also may uncover a potential avenue for treatment using preexisting antihistamine-based therapeutics.

column36: Lil'wat Lvmlaomen: Assessing the Potential to Enhance Gendered Cultural Resurgence with a Lil'wat Traditional Medicine Shed
column37: In recent years, the Lil'wat First Nation has been experiencing cultural resurgence through strengthening the knowledge and use of lvmlaomen (traditional medicines) within the on-reserve community. Traditionally, all the lvmlaomen that Lil'wat7ul (the Lil'wat people) needed were cultivated and gathered in the territory. Medicine people today hold intimate knowledge about the uses of over 100 plants. Plants are used as both preventative medicines, being taken regularly as part of the diet, and as treatment for illness, disease and injury. The lvmlaomen of Lil'wat have extensive gendered components to them that need to be better understood at a community level in order for knowledge transmission to occur with the next generation. Because of the ongoing legacy of colonialism, including the Residential School System and forced conversion to Christianity, the cultural understandings about gender of the Lil'wat people have been impacted. Though it is known that there were historically always other-gendered Lil'wat7ul, Ucwalmicwts (the Lil'wat language) words and understandings for these identities has been lost at a community level. There is also a need to create advocacy and support for LGBTQI2s+ Lil'wat7ul. This research scoping project will look to assess the feasibility of Lil'wat Lvmlaomen Tsipun (Medicine Shed) to aid in the strengthening and renewal of cultural protocols for creating safe, gender inclusive spaces. The research team, composed of two Lil'wat Nation researchers and a UBC Phd researcher, will host a series of community meetings, interviews with elders and knowledge keepers, and field visits to assess the potential of creating the Lil'wat Medicine Shed. This research will be guided by the S7itsken, the Lil'wat Research Protocol, and use a community-based action research methodology and Indigenous research methods.

column36: Identifying Early Biomarkers and Nutritional Correlates of Future Reproductive Disturbance in Adolescent Females
column37: Abnormal reproductive development in adolescent females may have long lasting consequences on health. Teens often wait two or more years after their first period (menarche) before being evaluated for reproductive disorders, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Early detection and intervention of abnormal reproductive development would help to reduce future health issues, but a major challenge relates to the lack of knowledge about the nature of the adolescent reproductive transition in the years immediately after menarche. In adults, features of the ovary on ultrasound are useful in detecting problems with reproduction. But, reliable data on how the ovary changes during adolescence are not available, limiting the ability of ultrasound to detect problems early in teens. We know that nutrition can impact the onset of puberty and contribute to reproductive problems later in life. However, what role nutrition may play in the years between menarche and the diagnosis of a reproductive disorder is unknown. This research will address these gaps by defining the changes in the ovaries that occur alongside the development of menstrual cyclicity during the first two years after menarche. We expect to see differences in the appearance of the ovary in teens that achieve regular periods versus those with irregular periods after two years. This research will also determine whether specific aspects of nutrition are related with the trajectory towards PCOS in teens. We predict that dietary intake, even at this early stage, impacts reproductive function. These studies will reveal changes in the ovary during adolescence that can be used to develop early diagnostic tools for clinicians when evaluating teens for risk of reproductive disorders. By identifying dietary factors that may influence reproductive development, this research will form the basis for future studies that can evaluate the impact of nutritional changes on reducing risk and progression of reproductive disorders.

column36: Cellular inhibitor of apoptosis 1 (cIAP1) as a novel therapeutic target for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy
column37: The Nuclear Factor-kB (NF-kB) pathways form a signaling complex that is critical for normal skeletal muscle function and is important in promoting recovery in response to muscle injury. Furthermore, there is strong evidence that too much NF-kB activity is detrimental to normal skeletal muscle function and can contribute to diseases such as the common genetic disorder, Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). As such, NF-kB has become an attractive drug target for the treatment of muscle diseases. Our lab has found that the cellular inhibitor of apoptosis 1 (cIAP1) can control NF-kB signaling to benefit skeletal muscle function. This discovery has raised the exciting possibility that cIAP1 may be a potential therapeutic target for a number of muscle diseases that are caused or worsened by over-activation of NF-kB. Since we have several drugs that effectively and specifically remove cIAP1, we will evaluate their therapeutic potential in mdx mice, the mouse model for DMD. We will also clarify the mechanism of action of these drugs by examining how they change NF-kB activity in dystrophic muscle. Our findings have the potential to improve muscle structure and function and thus the quality of life of patients living with DMD.

column36: Solving unsolved neuromuscular diseases: harnessing the power of phenotype and data integration strategies to optimise diagnosis and discovery
column37: Rare diseases are an important issue in Canada and worldwide. They collectively affect 1 person in 17, or as many as 2 million Canadians. Neuromuscular diseases are rare inherited diseases that affect the muscles and nerves and cause significant disability in both children and adults. Even though we now know of over 500 genes causing neuromuscular disease, in around 50% of patients the precise genetic cause can't be pinpointed after the initial analysis. Recent therapy developments are for the first time showing tremendous promise, but if a patient does not have a precise genetic diagnosis they may not be able to receive the best treatment for their condition. New technologies that look across the patient's entire genome are resulting in more diagnoses, but even healthy individuals have many places where their genome differs from others in a way that doesn't cause disease. This means that when we look at a patient's genome, sometimes we don't have enough information to decide which of the many genetic changes we see is responsible for the disease. My research aims to show that by making better use of the data that we have already, we can often bring it together in a way that allows us to reach a diagnosis. This includes information specific to the patient, especially the "phenotype" - the precise characteristics and symptoms the disease causes in the patient - and also data from experiments done in animal models for the disease. By standardising the ways we capture this data and linking different data types, we can more easily establish which is the disease-causing change and also potentially find other patients in other parts of the world with the same condition. I also aim to develop strategies that optimise the way we use, link and share data in order to create a workflow for undiagnosed neuromuscular patients that results in patients receiving a diagnosis more quickly in future.

column36: Mechanisms underlying abnormal uteroplacental vascular adaptations in pregnancies complicated by advanced maternal age
column37: More women are having their first pregnancies at an older age. In Canada, 8% of women have their first child when they are over 35 years of age (also known as advanced maternal age). A woman's blood vessels need to go through large changes during pregnancy, so that the fetus can receive enough blood and nutrients to grow normally. If the blood vessels do not adapt well enough, this can cause problems during pregnancy such as poor fetal growth and preeclampsia. Advanced maternal age is a risk factor for both of these pregnancy problems. Unfortunately, advanced maternal age impacts on how well these blood vessels change in pregnant women. If we can find out exactly how advanced maternal age adversely affects these blood vessel changes in pregnancies in women at advanced maternal age, we can target these mechanisms for treatment. Our lab found that uterine arteries from aged pregnant rats did not function as well as the arteries from young pregnant rats. The differences that we found may explain the increased problems in advanced maternal age pregnancies. We thus need to know more about these poor functioning arteries and why they do not function well. To do this, we will assess the function of vessels from pregnant young (4 months old) and aged (9.5 months old, equivalent to ~35 years in humans) rats. This will allow us to test if the blood vessels from old rats adapt differently than in young rats. At the same time, we will assess this mechanism in vessels from human biopsies taken during caesarean deliveries from young and older pregnant women. This will help develop new treatments for older pregnant women to improve pregnancy outcomes in this high-risk group.

Our team is strongly inter-disciplinary as it comprises experts in Indigenous wisdom and traditional knowledges, women's heart patient experiences, health promotion and public health, evaluation, and implementation science. column37: European contact created unequal relations between men and women within Inuit communities. This has resulted in many problems in achieving the best health for mothers and their babies. We will identify Inuit traditional knowledge. column36: Novel MXene Quantum Dots for Immunomodulation and Prevention of Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy
column37: Heart failure is when the heart becomes injured and can no longer pump blood well. This can become severe enough such that a person may need a new heart called a transplant. However, the body will not see this new heart as a part of itself and the immune system will attack it in a process known as rejection. To stop this, these patients are given special pills to weaken their immune systems. Sadly, these pills are not perfect and after a few years, the new heart will also become injured. The pills can also have lots of side effects that make these people more likely to get sick from other things. When this happens, many of these people will die. To tackle this problem, our group is studying the use of new technologies to stop the body from attacking the new heart. This year, we have taken some big steps towards making this happen. We have made a new small particle that may be able to stop the immune system from attacking these hearts. Unlike the pills, these nanodots do not weaken the immune system but instead makes the new heart invisible to the immune system. To test this, our group has come up with some experiments to test how these particles work in an animal model as a necessary step before introducing the technology to humans. We know that one of the first parts of a new heart to be injured is its blood vessels. That's why we will be transplanting blood vessels treated with our material between animals. If the particles can stop rejection of these blood vessels, we may be able to stop the immune system from injuring these hearts entirely. These particles can then become a new treatment for these people to make their lives longer and better. We are hopeful that this will soon become a reality.

column36: Impact of Vision-Zero Road Safety Plan on road traffic deaths and serious injuries in Canada.
column37: Traffic collisions are a leading cause of premature mortality; and injuries caused by collisions represent a preventable burden in terms of human suffering and cost to the health care system. Starting with Edmonton in 2015, eleven cities in Canada, have adopted the Vision Zero road safety plan to tackle that issue. Unlike the traditional approach of road safety, the Vision Zero approach considers traffic fatalities as preventable, acknowledges that humans make mistakes and roadway system should be designed in ways that those mistakes are not deadly. However, to the best of our knowledge, a rigorous evaluation of the Vision Zero road safety plan in Canada has not been performed. In addition, due to his branding as a "plan to eliminate all road fatalities", Vision Zero road safety plan has received many backlashes in the press, especially following a series of deadly road traffic crashes. There is therefore, a need for a rigorous evaluation of the impact of Vision Zero approach in Canada on road traffic fatalities and serious injuries. Using police collision reports, we will apply quasi-experimental designs to provide road safety professionals and decision makers with evidences to support or modify the actual implementation of Vision Zero approach across Canada.

column36: Characterizing the role of ETFDH on cancer biology
column37: Cancer is a disease defined by uncontrollable proliferation. As part of cancer progression, cells undergo various molecular changes in how they metabolize nutrients and synthesize proteins in order to meet their high growth demands. Most neoplasms display an increased dependence on glucose metabolism and adapt to their surroundings by regulating the two energy pathways: glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. Although the increased reliance of cancer cells on glycolysis is well documented, the role of oxidative phosphorylation in cancer progression is still unclear. Mining of numerous publically available datasets revealed that the electron transfer flavoprotein dehydrogenase (ETFDH) is consistently under-expressed across numerous cancer subtypes. Our preliminary studies identified ETFDH as playing an anti-neoplastic role, as ETFDH loss increased lymphoma cell proliferation, which was accompanied by increased glycolysis and mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) signaling. We propose to follow up on these exciting preliminary findings to determine the metabolic and translational mechanisms underlying neoplastic growth. These studies are anticipated to unravel metabolic and translational vulnerabilities that can be exploited to develop strategies that hinder the development of ETFDH-reduced cancers.

column36: A mixed-methods study to investigate socio-economic inequities in effective coverage of reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health interventions in low- and middle-income countries
column37: Globally, there has been renewed effort to provide public health services to ensure all women and their children survive and thrive. In lower resource settings, access to healthcare services for women, children and adolescent girls has been expanding. However, there is often much variability in the affordability, quality and experiences of care received by different socio-economic groups, and thereby in the level of health-related and financial hardship that families face. This research project will be conducted in India and Tanzania to measure differences in access to health services before, during and after childbirth for women in higher and lower socio-economic groups, the clinical quality of care provided when they access them, and whether this ultimately improves the health of women and their children. It will examine whether this is related to contextual issues like health system inputs, population density, female literacy rates or public policy in each region. The study will also involve in-depth case-studies in regions with varying socio-economic differences in the health of women and children to explore their experiences with and perspectives on healthcare services, and the context-specific reasons for any differences between socio-economic groups. This research will be conducted through established partnerships with academic and public health organizations in Tanzania and India. It will provide new knowledge by applying theories and methods from different disciplines to understand socio-economic differences in the accessibility, quality, and impact of healthcare services, particularly with a focus on the health system, socio-cultural, political, economic, geographic or other contextual factors shaping them. This will provide international partners with specific information to guide their programs, and contribute to Canada's role as a leader and ally in global health research to improve the health and well-being of all women, adolescent girls and children.

column36: Investigating the role of FAM72A in B cell antibody diversification
column37: Antibodies, also referred to as immunoglobulins (Ig), play fundamental roles in our immune system by providing protection against pathogens. Antibodies are "Y" shaped molecules produced by specialized immune cells called the B cells. The tips of the two arms of the "Y", named the variable regions, differ greatly among different antibodies, thus providing the antibodies with the specificity and diversity for binding pathogens. The stem of the "Y" is named the constant region and it determines the functional properties of the antibodies. Antibodies can be further divided into different classes, with different antibody classes adopting different modes of action, such as directly binding to microbes and neutralizing their effect, localizing antibodies to different tissues, and signalling other immune cells to kill the infecting microbes or microbe-infected host cells. Upon exposure to an antigen, antibodies undergo diversification process to strength their abilities to bind and neutralize antigens. Somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination, both initiated by an enzyme named AID, are two genetic mechanisms that enable B cells to produce antibodies with higher antigen binding affinities and different classes. Our current knowledge towards somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination is likely incomplete, as complex and multifaceted molecular events take place during these two processes. Through a genetic screen I have identified FAM72A as a novel gene that functions in antibody class switch recombination, and propose to fully characterize the role of this gene and its product during antibody diversification using mouse models and diverse biochemical and cellular experimentations. My proposed work will advance our understanding on how antibody diversity is achieved, and influence vaccine development or the generation of therapeutic agents that target specific B cell malignancies.

column37: Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes have a key role in elimination of cancer cells by the immune system, but their anti-cancer efficacy is severely hampered by immune checkpoints. Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) can re-activate anti-cancer immunity and provides durable responses in multiple cancer types. Unfortunately, clinical studies indicate that the majority of cancers do not durably respond due to initial or acquired resistance. Loss of TNF signaling was recently identified as a determinant of ICI resistance. Preliminary work by the Moffat lab identified the TNFa-responsive membrane receptor Tnfrsf1a as a top resistance hit in multiple cancer models. Importantly, it is currently unknown how to re-sensitize cancers with resistance mutations like TNFRSF1A to elimination by cytotoxic T-lymphocytes after ICI therapy. Therefore, I aim to uncover genetic vulnerabilities in TNFRSF1A mutant cancers by performing genome-wide CRISPR screens in Tnfrsf1a-knockout cancer cells treated with cytotoxic T-lymphocytes followed by in vitro and in vivo validation of candidate targets. By determining changes in cancer immune infiltration, through various single-cell RNA sequencing techniques, I aim to get a mechanistic understanding of the immunological consequences of TNFRSF1A loss. Collectively, these strategies will provide new therapeutic targets that can aid to re-sensitize patients who developed ICI resistance through TNFRSF1A mutations.

column36: Indigenous Digital Wellness: Indigenous Masculinity, Identity, and Wellbeing in Male Youth
column37: With technology being used now more than ever before, it is important to understand the affects that interacting within the digital world has on young Indigenous men's health and wellness. It is known that Indigenous youth are struggling to create a salient identity in a colonized world, and this is negatively impacting their health and wellness. However, what is not known is the extent to which interactions within the digital world are contributing to this process. In this project, we will be partnering with the Aboriginal Programs and Services center at UBC Okanagan to engage young Indigenous men from the local school district in an Indigenous-led participatory project. The participants will meet as a group in open sharing circle discussions about how interactions in the digital world shape who they are as Indigenous youths and the impacts that this may have on their health and wellness. Specifically, we will be asking the group members to report what they see when exploring the digital world including what types of digital platforms they are using. The group will then critically reflect about what they see, make notes of their encounters, and return to the group the following session ready to discuss their notes. Ultimately, we will be looking to answer the question, how do digital representations of Indigenous masculinity affect their sense of self, health, and wellness? This project will be infused with Indigenous knowledge and traditions to accommodate the worldview of Indigenous peoples, where the information presented by the group members will be assessed in a critical, Indigenous masculinity, and decolonial lens. This project is a preliminary phase of an Indigenous focused community-based participatory program that will look to create guidelines for Indigenous male youth to protect their health and wellness while they use the digital world for educational/recreational purposes.

column36: Investigating Nuclear Organization-Function Relationships
column37: An emerging fundamental mechanism underlying the specificity and organization of nuclear processes, such as transcription and splicing, is the assembly of nuclear condensates into non-membranous organelles or 'bodies'. These condensates are formed by interactions between RNA, proteins and DNA. Different classes of RNA molecules are thought to interact with structural proteins and act as molecular scaffolds to support the assembly of these condensates. Genetic perturbations of factors associated with these bodies are often linked to human diseases. However, the roles of many of these nuclear bodies are poorly understood. Therefore, understanding how the cell nucleus is organized, and which molecules are involved in these processes is critical to understand the underlying causes of many diseases. In this proposal, I aim to use state-of-the-art experimental approaches to comprehensively map and functionally characterize interactions between RNA and protein molecules that shape the sub-nuclear structures, including those involved in splicing, and develop new tools for directed programming of splicing. The findings of the proposed CIHR fellowship research hold a strong potential to: i) identify RNA molecules that shape nuclear architecture, and ii) establish novel technologies to target splicing outcomes. The outcome of this proposal is expected to have a profound impact in nuclear biology, and provide a method to study alternative splicing in normal physiology, aiming to correct splicing defects implicated in human diseases and disorders.

column36: Creating Safe Paths for Indigenous Women, Girls and LGBTQ2SA+ Individuals in Edmonton and Area
column37: Every day at Creating Hope Society, a community-based Indigenous-led non-profit organization, we hear the stories of Indigenous women, girls and sexually- and gender-diverse peoples who experience gender-based violence (GBV) and then are faced with barriers when they reach out for help. The very services put in place to help Indigenous individuals who disproportionately experience GBV may unintentionally cause them further harm through culturally-unsafe practices. Our goal is to understand GBV experienced by Indigenous women, girls, and sexually- and gender-diverse individuals in and around Edmonton as a way to understand health research paths forward. In this development project, we begin by co-developing a research framework to assess and improve the cultural safety of GBV programs and services currently available. column36: Engineering lymphatic vessels to induce anti-cancer immunity
column37: Immunotherapy, whereby the immune system is stimulated to attack a tumor, has emerged as a novel and revolutionary treatment for previously incurable cancers in recent years. Notwithstanding the excitement about the potential of this new treatment, success in clinical trials has been limited to subsets of patients. Tumors often develop ways of avoiding elimination by the immune system, while immunotherapy can cause serious side effects that lead some patients to interrupt treatment. Addressing this problem requires the development of more potent, yet safer forms of immunotherapy. In the past, independent approaches of stimulating the immune system have demonstrated efficacy against cancer, by inducing the growth of lymphatic vessels, treating tumors with radiation, or delivering molecules that activate the immune system specifically in the tumor. Here, I am proposing to explore whether and how these independent approaches can be combined, to develop more efficient immunotherapies. In addition to the potential of directly developing better treatments, my research will glean biological understanding on the interaction of different types of immunotherapy, thus leading to the broader advancement of the field.

column36: Re(connecting) and Re(membering): Gathering Indigenous Women and Two-Spirit Land-Based Educators and Practitioners
column37: Considering how gender operates within land-based and place-based learning is critical as both humans and more-than-human relations and relationships have been heavily shaped and regulated by settler colonialism and settler heteropatriarchy. The deterioration of Indigenous notions of gender and the forceful colonial imposition of a Western gender binary, has served to fracture Indigenous peoples' relationships with Land. This has engendered dire consequences for Land, Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people . Indigenous Feminist theory reveals how colonialism and patriarchy combine and intersect with race, gender, sexuality, location and other factors to create oppressive circumstances for Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people. The effect is to wreak havoc on the ways Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people, are able to culturally mediate their relationships with Land. As we understand culturally and through Indigenous theory, that knowledge comes up through the Land, it is also equally important to understand and act upon re(connecting) bodies with the Land so that these knowledges can be picked up and new knowledges can be produced and shared. This project, "Gathering Indigenous Women and Two-Spirit Land-Based Educators and Practitioners", would fulfill just that by facilitating relationship building and collaboration between twenty Indigenous women and two-spirit people who are both formal and informal land-based educators and practitioners. Doing so will help strength and solidify the network that exists between women and two-spirit Indigenous land-based educators and practitioners, and help to revive and re(produce) knowledges and practices and affirm and facilitate Indigenous women, girls', and two-spirit peoples' relationships to Land.

column37: This development grant will support and demonstrate the ways in which we are reinstating our Secwepemc child wellbeing through parenting and ceremony including everyday acts of resurgence, decolonial love, relationship and kinship. Proposed activities will focus on the planning and development of an Indigenous-led, community-based project using the methodological framework of Steseptekwle-Secwepemc storytelling and Red Intersectionality (Clark, 2016). Previous research (Clark, 2018; Jules, 2016; Michel, 2012; Billy, 2009) demonstrated that family and community structures were and continue to be taught through Indigenous story, mentorship/apprenticeship, and ceremony, thus the current project would further explore these as ways to share concepts of gender and wellness. For example, within Secwepemc communities, gender, puberty and relationships are introduced and discussed through the Story of Sockeye Salmon, first by teaching of the life cycle, then for preparing to become parents, and the role of the parents and taking care of each other to support the healthy development of children. Embedded within this story and other stories are teachings that discuss gender and family roles, as well as roles within the larger environment. Concepts include respect for each other, sharing, and giving back. Through this planning grant there is an opportunity to focus on Secwepemc concepts of gender and wellness through an intergenerational approach that supports healthy transitions across the lifespan.

column36: Advancing a holistic, physical activity-based wellness program for Indigenous women - Knowledge sharing to foster expansion
column37: The rate of type II diabetes is 3 to 5 times higher for Indigenous people compared to the general population, and the rate of obesity is nearly twice as high. Many Indigenous women lack the opportunity to participate in exercise and do not have access to, or engage in, local health programs. A community led, physical activity-based wellness program for Indigenous women has been running for 4 years in three communities in Alberta. Led by a community member, in the program women come together to experience new types of exercise, learn about nutrition and share their personal experiences in a culturally sensitive environment. The program has been well received and there are many new communities across multiple provinces that would like to be able to host a program. This research project would support the following activities: 1) the continued development of the program itself, 2) the establishment of an Advisory Group to guide program development, expansion into new communities and research; this group would be led by participants of the program and champions from the communities involved, 3) regional community events in which program champions would share information about the program and community leaders would share information about their communities, with a goal to support the new communities in adapting a program to meet their needs and finding financial support for the program, and 4) the continued development of an Indigenous women's health promotion 'community of practice' (CoP) - this is a group of individuals from different regions and different disciplines (homemakers, administrators, researchers, elders, healthcare providers, etc.) that come together to share knowledge, who are all working to support and empower Indigenous women in order to prevent ill health.

column37: Indigenous-Black (IB) communities have been recognized in the US for hundreds of years, but despite an over 400-year presence in Canada, they do not hold the same recognition. As a result of colonial legacies, ongoing structural inequities, intersectional oppression, social, and geographic displacement, and the lack of legislated claims to territory, mixed Indigenous and African diasporic communities may be dually hurt and placed at elevated risk for a variety of social and health ills, such as poverty and HIV. More than 70 000 people are living with HIV in Canada and the over-representation of Aboriginal and African, Caribbean, and Black-Canadian communities in the HIV/AIDS epidemic has been well-documented in national HIV statistics. We infer from these trends that mixed IB people experience disproportionate rates of chronic illnesses such as HIV. While there has been a paucity of national work examining the health needs of IB communities, our team's recent work revealed the need for an interdisciplinary, multi-pronged approach to appropriately address the impact of past and ongoing intergenerational colonial trauma on the mental, physical, and sexual health of IB people. As such, our team will employ oral digital storytelling, community mapping, interviews and a questionnaire to explore questions such as: What are the barriers and facilitators to the health service access and overall wellbeing of IB communities? How do IB people experience intersectional oppression along the lines of gender, race, etc. and what are the implications of this on IB people's health and HIV care service access and retention? What does a culturally-relevant health intervention focused on the sexual health needs of IB communities look like? How can narrative and arts-based approaches aid in gathering the experiences of IB communities as they map, draw, write, and speak their realities into being, contributing to national discourse about their identities and health needs?

column36: Optimizing the Health of Indigenous Infants and Toddlers: Identification of Community Strengths, Needs and Priorities to Promote Early Childhood Development through Healthy, Gender Diverse Parenting.
column37: This Community Gathering will bring together the urban Indigenous community in Hamilton, Ontario to identify and prioritize research projects about the health of Indigenous parents and their infants and toddlers. The period of early childhood is very important to growth and development, and children who experience challenges during this time may go on to have poorer health and success as adults. Parents are responsible for meeting their child's needs and they must have the resources and skills they need to provide for their children. This Community Gathering will bring together parents of various identities (including mothers, fathers, adoptive parents, two-spirit parents and other gender-diverse parents), Indigenous leaders and health providers as well as Elders and Knowledge Holders to discuss the strengths, challenges and gaps related to healthy parenting and the early childhood development of young children in Hamilton. Through this Community Gathering we will (a) learn about healthy, gender-diverse parenting models and roles to promote healthy early childhood development and positive parent-child-community relationships; (b) strengthen partnerships and build relationships among Indigenous community members, organizations and researchers; and (c) inform a research proposal created together with members of the Hamilton Indigenous community to submit to a research grant competition. The proposed Community Gathering clearly aligns with the objectives of the CIHR funding opportunity, including: establishing priorities for an Indigenous-led research project related to optimizing child health and wellness through gender-diverse parenting, facilitating relationship building among Indigenous community members and researchers, and knowledge sharing on parenting from Indigenous Elders, Knowledge Holders and community members.

column36: Exploring the needs of Calgary's urban Indigenous youth across the gender-identity spectrum in relation to culturally relevant programming and services to support sexual health, identity and belonging.
column37: This project seeks to explore the programming/services needed by Calgary's urban Indigenous youth across the gender-identity spectrum (18-24 years old) to support sexual health, identity and belonging. Sexual health includes having control over one's sexual and reproductive choices, as well as having access to enjoyable and safe sexual relationships free of shame, coercion and violence. The ongoing impact of colonization on Indigenous peoples has resulted in the loss of traditional teachings and knowledge around intimacy, rites of passage ceremonies, and individual/collective roles and responsibilities which contributed to the development of healthy relationships, the backbone of community resilience. This project acknowledges that cultural and sexual identities are complex processes of identity development, and particularly complex for urban Indigenous youth who may have already experienced life challenges stemming from colonial violence and historical trauma. It is within this context that the project seeks to engage youth across the gender-identity spectrum, which is inclusive of all gender expressions. Through Indigenous storytelling and Youth Participatory Action Research with Indigenous youth across the gender-identity spectrum, Elders, knowledge holders, and front-line workers this project aims to create a wholistic framework for culturally safe and relevant programming that supports sexual health, identity and belonging among urban Indigenous youth in Calgary, addressing a critical gap in the services for urban Indigenous youth across the gender-identity spectrum.
