column36: Understanding and preventing serious bacterial and fungal infections among people who inject drugs
column37: People who inject drugs face extremely high rates of death and disability from severe and invasive bacterial and fungal infections (including infections of the bloodstream, heart valves, and bones) that require hospital admission for treatment with antibiotics and/or surgeries. These infections are devastating for individual patients, and also extremely costly for our health care system. So how can people who inject drugs, and health systems who care for them, prevent these serious infections from occurring? Unfortunately we don't have scientific evidence to inform us. One promising approach to reducing risk in opioid-injectors is medication treatment for opioid addiction (with methadone or buprenorphine) as this helps people to inject less frequency. However risk for serious infections likely reflects multiple factors, including homelessness, use of stimulants or alcohol, and individual injecting practices. Based at the Collaborative Centre for Inclusion Health (CCIH) at University College London, my Fellowship project aims to inform people who inject drugs, clinicians, and health systems on how to prevent serious bacterial and fungal infections. We will analyze a unique large dataset from South London that contains anonymous health records for anyone who has ever been to addiction treatment, linked to their hospital records. We'll assess whether methadone or buprenorphine treatment is associated with decreased risk of infection-related hospitalization or death in people who inject opioids. We'll also assess what other factors are associated with risk (including homelessness, sex work, injecting practices, stimulant or alcohol use), and see whether these change the effectiveness of methadone or buprenorphine. We'll collaborate with groups of people who use drugs in London, UK, and Halifax, Canada to help refine our analysis plan and determine what risk factors may be most important.

column36: Salt inducible kinases: novel therapeutic targets for chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD)
column37: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is characterized by structural abnormalities and impaired kidney function. Inadequate filtration of wastes and minerals (including phosphate) leads to serious disruption in mineral metabolism and bone disorder (Mineral and Bone Disorder; MBD). In CKD-MBD patients, phosphate retention in blood triggers secretion of a hormone called fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) to promote renal phosphate excretion. However, FGF23 blocks the generation of the active form of vitamin D. As vitamin D is essential in calcium absorption, low vitamin D causes low blood calcium level, stimulating the production of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by parathyroid glands. Elevated PTH levels restore blood calcium by bone breakdown, resulting in bone loss and fractures. Currently, no drugs can improve both vitamin D levels and renal phosphate excretion. Although PTH usually accomplishes these tasks, CKD-MBD patients do not show expected PTH effects on mineral metabolism, despite the high level of PTH. Therefore, we hypothesized that targeting the downstream mediator of PTH signaling pathway would bypass PTH resistance, yet still bring PTH-like effects to help CKD-MBD. Recently, a family of enzymes called salt-inducible kinases (SIKs) was reported to participate in the actions of PTH in bone. To test if SIKs participate in renal PTH actions, we will use cutting-edge genome editing and pharmacologic approaches in multiple cell lines, as well as two mouse models. The role of SIK deletion in kidney will be determined in mice using a genetic engineering technique known as Cre-lox system. Then, the effects of a SIK inhibitor will be studied in CKD mouse models with kidney injury to examine its therapeutic potential. Considering high prevalence of CKD worldwide (about 13.4%), and at least 4 million Canadians suffering from this chronic disease, this study will give insight into a novel approach in managing CKD-MBD and understanding PTH/SIK signaling in kidney.

column36: Molecular Dissection of MECP2 Protein Phase Separation in Rett Syndrome
column37: Lipid-lipid phase separation is a physical phenomenon characterized by molecules de-mixing into distinct lipid phases. This process is known to drive the formation of membrane-less compartments in cells that concentrate biochemical reactions. Increasing evidence points to the involvement of aberrant phase separation in neurodegenerative disorders through excessive protein aggregation. Rett syndrome (RTT) is a postnatal progressive neurodevelopmental disease associated with severe mental retardation that primarily affects females. The majority of the clinical cases have been traced to mutations of MECP2, a multi-talented protein that acts as a repressor or an activator of transcription. However, the mechanism underlying the complex role of MECP2 in cellular physiology and RTT particularly remains enigmatic. The Jaenisch laboratory has recently demonstrated that MECP2 can form phase-separated condensates in murine cells. On this basis, I aim to expand the role of phase separation in biological function and disease-causing malfunction of MECP2 to the human system. I will leverage the experimental paradigm established in the Jaenisch lab and use human embryonic stem (ES) cells to generate normal and RTT neurons in both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) culture systems, and explore the molecular properties of phase separation in these human models. The human ES cells will be engineered to carry relevant disease-causing mutations in the MECP2 gene. The goal of this project is to advance the mechanistic understanding of MECP2's function and pave the way for new therapeutic approaches for RTT.

column36: Examining the role of high-intensity interval training on glucose variability and atrial fibrillation symptomatology: A novel approach for patients with atrial fibrillation living with diabetes?
column37: The incidence of atrial fibrillation (AF), the most common heart rhythm disorder, is increasing. The symptoms of AF are severe and include: unpleasant heartbeats; difficulty breathing; tiredness; dizziness; and, reduced exercise capacity. Patients with AF have lower quality of life (QoL), higher mental distress, and higher risk of heart disease and stroke when compared to the general population. Type 2 diabetes increases the risk of developing AF and accounts for about 20% of patients with AF. High blood glucose concentrations and increased blood glucose fluctuations (large and frequent upward and downward blood glucose swings) are commonly seen in type 2 diabetes. Increased blood glucose fluctuations may worsen AF symptoms and QoL in patients with AF by promoting: (1) inflammation; (2) oxidative stress; and, (3) autonomic dysfunction. Exercise improves QoL and mental health and reduces risk of developing heart disease and stroke. However, no clinical guidelines for managing AF include exercise. The absence of exercise in the AF guidelines may reflect a lost opportunity to provide AF patients with effective treatment options. High-intensity interval training (HIIT), a form of exercise that alternates between intense bouts of exercise and less intense recovery periods, is a time-efficient approach to improve blood glucose fluctuations in type 2 diabetes. In healthy individuals and in patients with coronary artery disease, HIIT also improves QoL and mental health. Currently, the effect of HIIT on blood glucose fluctuations, AF symptom severity and QoL in patients with AF living with type 2 diabetes is unknown. Also, the links between blood glucose fluctuations and AF symptom severity and QoL are yet to be investigated. Examining the impact of HIIT on blood glucose fluctuations, AF symptom severity and QoL may lead to the development of a novel therapeutic option for patients with AF living with type 2 diabetes.

column36: Canadian Study of Arterial Inflammation in Diabetes and the Evaluation of Colchicine Effectiveness (CADENCE)
column37: Diabetic patients are at high risk of suffering atherosclerotic disease related events (eg acute coronary syndromes (ACS), stroke, transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)) and have a higher recurrence rate than the general population. Inflammation has been extensively investigated as a promoter of atherosclerosis development and destabilization. Recent trials have revealed outcome benefit in patients with cardiovascular disease who are treated with anti-inflammatory therapy. The LoDoCo trial also showed a reduction in cardiovascular events in patients with known coronary artery disease who were treated with colchicine. Although the LoDoCo trial did show outcome benefit, colchicine's mechanism of action at the level of the atherosclerotic plaque in patients remains unknown. It is not clear at the present time whether colchicine mainly reduces systemic inflammation, thus reducing the likelihood of plaque progression and new lesion formation; or whether it has a direct effect on local "hot" inflammatory cell activity, thus pacifying the inflammatory plaque to reduce events. Insight into colchicine's mechanism of action may help identify the most suitable patients for this novel approach. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging with 18F-fluordeoxyglucose (18-FDG) provides an opportunity to perform molecular imaging of specific components of the atherosclerotic plaque such as inflammation. 18-FDG has been validated and extensively used for this purpose, and it could potentially enable the prospective evaluation of inflammation targeted therapies and the identification of patients at high risk for vascular events. The primary objective of this study is to determine the pathobiological effect of colchicine compared to placebo, on plaque inflammation (measured by 18-FDG PET/CT at baseline and 6 months) in the carotid arteries and thoracic aorta in high-risk patients with diabetes or pre-diabetes and recent vascular events (ACS, TIA, stroke).

column36: Immune mechanisms of influenza A virus-induced susceptibility to myocardial infarction
column37: Cardiovascular diseases including myocardial infarction, or heart attack, continue to claim an increasing number of lives worldwide, while influenza A virus infection, the major causative agent of the flu, is responsible for recurring pulmonary infections and substantial global mortality. Importantly, influenza infection also augments susceptibility to heart attack. Yet, the reasons for this and how it occurs are unknown. Understanding why is of great value, as both influenza and cardiovascular disease are significant threats to human health with limited therapeutic strategies. Even though flu infections are constrained to the lungs, anti-influenza type I IFN signalling can transcriptionally imprint monocytes in the bone marrow to enhance immune responses in peripherally inflamed tissues. Although type I IFN is protective against influenza, it also increases susceptibility to heart attack by promoting detrimental inflammation in the heart. Therefore, it is the goal of this project to investigate a potential link between influenza-induced type I IFN signalling in the bone marrow and detrimental inflammatory monocyte responses during myocardial infarction, which underlies the enhanced severity. The findings of this study will provide better knowledge of the risk factors of cardiovascular disease and could lead to improved clinical interventions.

column36: Fine-grained mapping of hippocampal subregions using 7T MRI
column37: Epilepsy is among the most common neurological conditions and affects 300,000 Canadians. Medial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) is the most common form. In many cases, seizures are thought to originate in the hippocampus, a brain structure critical for memory and a number of other cognitive functions. Removing parts of the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe is an established treatment that effectively relieves seizures. However, there are usually marked postoperative complications, such as memory deficits and psychiatric disturbances. To minimize postoperative cognitive deficits, we propose to develop a method that will localize, or map, subregions of the hippocampus. Such a map will enable us to determine which subregions are crucial for various functions. In doing so, we will be able to advise neurosurgeons in their surgical planning, to avoid removing subregions that would likely result in severe cognitive deficits. The hippocampus is a complex structure that mediate various brain functions. Different parts of the hippocampus display dissociable patterns of functional connectivity to the rest of the brain. We will leverage this varying connectivity to map hippocampal subregions. Importantly, we will use novel neuroimaging analysis techniques that will enable us to generate a hippocampal map that is unique to each individual. We will then assess the relationship between these subregions and several hippocampal functions, including memory, emotion, and topographical processing. Finally, we will validate the hippocampal maps in MTLE patients, in whom we will be able to directly measure hippocampal activity using intra-hippocampal electrodes. This project will significantly impact epilepsy research as it will enable us to identify hippocampal subregions that are functionally different. One day, these individual maps of hippocampal organization could be used to plan surgical procedures and minimize post-surgical cognitive deficits in patients with epilepsy.

column36: The nexus between drug control and public health: a mixed-methods study investigating the impact of police enforcement activities on access and utilization of HIV prevention and treatment among women who inject drugs
column37: Despite their increased risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV, people who inject drugs (PID) are among those with the least access to HIV prevention and treatment. Police enforcement activities have been shown to increase risk of HIV transmission and impede access to life-saving antiretroviral treatment (ART) among PID. Given that women comprise one-third of injectors globally but shoulder a disproportionate HIV burden, interventions must consider how gender shapes the application and impact of police enforcement on HIV outcomes. Women who inject drugs (WID) face multi-level interpersonal, social, and structural vulnerabilities that increase their risk of drug-related harm, but little is known about how police enforcement activities shape HIV risks and health adversity in general among WID. This project will contribute to HIV prevention and treatment expansion efforts by identifying whether gender modifies the link between police enforcement and HIV risk, prevention and treatment outcomes, elucidating how policing shapes key HIV outcomes, and quantifying the potential impact of eliminating punitive police enforcement practices on the expansion of ART among WID. This mixed-methods research will draw on pooled quantitative data from two studies I lead on as PI and co-PI: the Women Speak Out study, the largest representative dataset of WID in Southeast Asia, and the Jakarta Peer-Driven Intervention study, a community-led treatment intervention exploring determinants of HIV among PID. Additional original qualitative data will be collected from WID in urban sites in Indonesia. This study will be the first to explore how police enforcement activities shape access and utilization of HIV prevention and treatment in the region. Employing integrated knowledge translation, this study will shift the research field from identifying gender-related health disparities related to police enforcement towards informing appropriate interventions to reduce them.

column36: Neuronal and synaptic mechanisms underlying the anti-epileptic effects of cannabidiol
column37: Epilepsy and seizures affect 50 million people worldwide, and approximately 30% of these patients do not respond to currently available medication. Cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive component of Cannabis sativa L., is a novel anti-seizure therapeutic and has recently been FDA-approved for the treatment of Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes, two rare intractable forms of epilepsy. However, how CBD acts on neurons and synapses to decrease seizures remains mysterious. To address this gap in knowledge, we will study the cellular, synaptic and network signaling mechanisms of CBD in the hippocampus, a brain region often affected in patients living with epilepsies. Our most recent efforts have revealed how CBD affects different population of neurons in the hippocampus. We find that CBD differentially acts on a subset of inhibitory neurons to dampen the propagation of high-frequency activity. Here, we will investigate the molecular mechanisms of CBD in this population of neuron, and determine how the specific modulation of these neurons can mimic the effects of CBD. Our multidisciplinary approaches will allow to dissect CBD's mechanism of action, and to specifically pinpoint the neuronal targets allowing for the anti-epileptic effects of CBD. The ultimate goal is to bridge how CBD modulates synapses and neurons to its anti-epileptic effects, aiming to stimulate the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

column36: Characterizing the role of stromal cells on hematopoietic stem cell division
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells supply all the blood cells required during life. During development stem cells migrate to vascular niches where they are enveloped by 'cuddling' endothelial cells and contacted by stromal cells. These stromal cells sustain the stem cells by releasing signals that encourage stem cell self-renewal. Contact with stromal cells also controls how the stem cells divide, ensuring that one of the dividing cells remains in the niche, while the other leaves to form mature blood cells. This makes stromal cells essential to the niche and if they are destroyed the stem cells can be lost leading to blood disorders. Despite the importance of these niche stromal cells no study has yet identified what makes them unique and what specific mechanisms they use to regulate stem cell division. This research will characterize stromal cells using zebrafish models which have many of the same cell types and signaling pathways as the mammalian bone marrow niche. Next generation sequencing technologies will be used to examine stromal cells at single cell resolution and identify the cell types that form the niche. Using this data, the genetic factors that specify niche stromal cells will be determined and used to build tools to target the niche. Stem cell divisions will be visualized within the optically clear zebrafish embryos using 4D microscopic imaging. Polarized proteins previously identified in isolated mammalian stem cells extracted from bone marrow will be fluorescently tagged and expressed in the zebrafish stem cells to visualize cell polarity and asymmetric divisions in context within the niche. Genetic ablation of stromal cells will then test the requirements for these cells in blood homeostasis. The results of this research will deepen our understanding of the stem niche and inform therapeutic strategies to improve the expansion of transplanted stem cells for the treatment of blood disorders.

column36: Timing of antiretroviral therapy initiation during pregnancy and child growth and neurodevelopment: quantifying consequences and understanding mechanisms.
column37: The 2015 World Health Organization guidelines recommend all pregnant women who are positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) to initiate lifelong triple-drug antiretroviral therapy (ART) to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV and to improve maternal survival. While it is essential that HIV-positive pregnant women begin ART as soon as possible after learning about their diagnosis, recent evidence from multiple studies suggests that women who begin ART before pregnancy may have a higher risk of having babies that are born too soon (preterm birth) or too small (low birthweight). Such adverse birth outcomes can put these babies at a higher risk of poor physical growth and brain development in early life, which may have a lasting impact throughout the lifespan. Yet, no study has previously evaluated the direct impact of timing of ART initiation during pregnancy on child growth and neurodevelopment. To address this gap, the purpose of this research is: 1) to examine the role of timing of ART initiation on child growth and neurodevelopment in the first year of life; 2) to quantify the role of poor birth outcomes, as mediators, in the pathway between timing of ART initiation and infant growth and neurodevelopment; and 3) to investigate whether some subgroups of women have a higher risk than others (e.g. based on HIV disease stage or maternal nutritional status). To address these objectives, data from a recently completed longitudinal study of 2300 HIV-positive pregnant women in Tanzania will be used. In this study, 50% of women started ART before pregnancy and 50% at variable times during the second trimester of pregnancy. Using advanced epidemiologic methods in causal inference, which overcome common pitfalls of conventional statistical techniques, this research will provide new evidence to understand the potential unintended consequences of ART, and ways in which treatment of HIV during pregnancy may be optimized to ensure all children survive and thrive.

column36: The role of adipose tissue in host defenses to bacterial pneumonia
column37: A clinical entity termed the "obesity paradox" suggests that overweight individuals (BMI>25) are 20-30% more likely to survive hospitalized pneumonia. There are two ways to survive an infection. The first depends on resistance mechanisms that kill the pathogen creating an arms race between the host and pathogen that can lead to pathogen resistance, immunopathology, and mortality. The second is a distinct defense classification called the co-operative defense system. The co-operative defense system encodes disease tolerance mechanisms that prevent or alleviate pathology generated during infection without affecting pathogen number nor fitness. The role of tolerance in the obesity paradox is unknown. Legionella pneumophila (Lp) is a bacterial pathogen that infects and resides in immune cells of the lung. Preliminary data has identified that host utilization of fatty acids is critical for defenses and survival against Lp. These data suggest that an increased abundance of circulating fatty acids may improve host outcome to infection. I hypothesize that fat promotes host defenses during Lp infection through fatty acid release and availability for utilization by the host. This project will determine how host adipose composition and fatty acid availability effects tolerance defense mechanisms toward Lp lung infection. I will identify specific host immune or metabolic pathways that benefit from the increased abundance of fat and fatty acids that promote host health during infection. Discovering new disease tolerance mechanisms is critical for overcoming resistance in pathogens, creating new avenues to treat infectious diseases.

column37: The workplace presents an environment where people tend to sit for prolonged periods of time and do not regularly engage in physical activity (PA), two factors that have negative health consequences, particularly related to obesity and diabetes. Finding ways to increase PA in the workplace can improve health, reduce sick days, and increase productivity. Traditionally prescribed, sustained aerobic exercise ("cardio") is impractical for many office employees who are unfit and low on time. Such barriers can be overcome by adopting high-intensity interval training (HIIT) - short-duration exercise that involves multiple brief, high-intensity efforts, separated by periods of rest. Stair climbing HIIT can benefit physiological health in less time than traditional exercise training. Further, recent studies show promising psychological implications of engaging in HIIT. Given that stair climbing HIIT is time-efficient and can be easily incorporated into one's daily schedule, there is considerable potential for using it in the workplace. Phase 1 of this research will involve office employees undergoing an 8-week HIIT program of either a) one short HIIT session completed during lunch break or b) brief exercise bouts performed throughout the workday as "exercise snacks." The exercise will consist of stair climbing, which is an effective, lifestyle-based form of HIIT. Phase 2 will deliver an 8-week optimized HIIT program designed to be sustainable. We will measure physical and psychological health, work productivity, sick days and PA behaviour during and up to 6-months following the program. This research will be the first to determine the health, work productivity, and PA behaviour benefits of practical HIIT programs delivered in the workplace. This research has important implications for employees who may be at risk for chronic diseases, employers seeking greater output from employees, and for Canadian society - which benefits from healthier and more productive workplaces.

column36: Uncovering the links between atrial stretch and inflammation in atrial fibrillation associated with cardiovascular disease
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained supraventricular arrhythmia worldwide and is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and socio-economic burden. AF affects 1-2% of the general population and with an incidence expected to double by 2060. While AF is tightly linked to aging and cardiovascular (CV) disease (i.e., heart failure, valve disease), its origins are complex, but are fundamentally linked to altered structural and/or electrical remodeling of the atria. Importantly, most conditions linked to AF are associated with elevated atrial pressures and atrial stretch, which is a powerful stimulus for adverse atrial remodeling. It is well-established that the pro-inflammatory and mechanosensitive cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFa) is a critical factor in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, arrhythmias, and inflammation seen in heart disease as well as athletes with AF, and an enhanced inflammatory response is typically observed in AF patients. While previous work from our group established the requirement of TNFa in exercise-induced adverse atrial remodeling and AF vulnerability in mice, the overlap in pathways mediating arrhythmogenesis in exercise and CV disease is undeniable. My research seeks to translate our exercise findings to more clinically-relevant models of heart disease, including a mouse model of aortic regurgitation (AR), which is characterized by cardiac volume overload, dilatation, elevated atrial pressures, fibrosis, and AF. As AR patients have one of the highest risks of AF, AR offers a clinically-relevant model to study atrial stretch-dependent TNFa-mediated AF pathogenesis. This mechanistic link will be assessed by: 1) assessing the molecular and cellular basis for TNFa-mediated adverse atrial remodeling in CV disease; 2) identifying novel pathways involved in the TNFa-dependent differential effects of AR on the atria with a goal towards developing novel interventions; and 3) translating our findings to CV patients.

column36: Role des comportements alimentaires dans certains facteurs de risque d'obesite
column37: L'obesite, dont l'origine est multifactorielle, touche de nombreuses personnes au Canada. En depit des efforts investis, la prevention et le traitement de l'obesite demeurent actuellement peu efficaces. Ainsi, il est primordial de mieux comprendre les mecanismes par lesquels differents facteurs de risque d'obesite influencent le poids corporel. En effet, les mecanismes par lesquels certains facteurs de risque, tels que la predisposition genetique a l'obesite, la faible capacite a reconnaitre ses signaux de satiete et une alimentation importante en soiree, influencent le poids sont meconnus. Toutefois, ces trois facteurs ont ete associes a certains comportements alimentaires, tels que la surconsommation d'aliments associee a une perte de controle ainsi que la susceptibilite a ressentir la faim, qui sont aussi associes a l'obesite. Il a ete demontre que ces memes comportements alimentaires expliquaient de facon plus importante le risque d'obesite que des facteurs plus communs comme l'inactivite physique ou une mauvaise alimentation. Considerant ces resultats, l'hypothese emise est que la presence de comportements alimentaires non souhaitables explique, du moins en partie, l'influence de ces differents facteurs de risque d'obesite sur le poids corporel. L'objectif de ce projet consiste donc a verifier le potentiel de mediation des comportements alimentaires dans les associations de ces trois facteurs de risque avec l'apport en calories et le poids corporel. Des analyses seront effectuees a l'aide des donnees de participants de projets de recherche portant sur l'obesite. Les facteurs cibles ont ete peu etudies en association avec le poids et l'implication des comportements alimentaires dans ces associations n'a pas ete evaluee a ce jour. Ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre les mecanismes impliques dans l'obesite, ce qui favorisera ultimement la conception d'interventions cliniques et de sante publique novatrices et efficaces dans un contexte de gestion du poids.

column36: Modeling blood-brain barrier dysfunctions using induced pluripotent stem cells: new insights into Huntington's disease pathology
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a strictly genetic disease which manifests with movement, cognitive and psychiatric problems. The dysfunctional protein that results from the genetic mutation, referred to as mutant huntingtin (mHtt), is found in all cells of the body, but it particularly affects the brain. Traditionally, it has been thought that the presence of the mutated gene is necessary for the disease to emerge. This view was radically changed by a recent discovery made by the Cicchetti group. When analysing fetal tissue that had been transplanted into patients with HD as an experimental therapy, they uncovered the presence of mHtt within the healthy cells of the graft. Since the fetal tissue did not express the mutant gene, the toxic form of the protein could only have come from the unhealthy tissue surrounding the transplant. This observation has many important implications, including the idea that the gene is not necessary for the initiation of disease. In association with mHtt in the fetal graft, they also found abnormalities in blood vessels. Normally blood vessels in the brain are surrounded by a barrier known as the blood brain barrier (BBB), which prevents toxins and other materials from reaching the brain. For my project, I will study the interactions between the protein associated with HD and changes in the function of the BBB. To do this, I will use a cell culture model of the BBB which closely resembles the BBB in the body in both cell composition and movement of fluids. Using this model, I will first measure how the presence of mHtt changes the function of the different parts of the BBB and second, determine if changes to the permeability of the BBB influences the negative effects that mHtt has on neurons. This project could shed light on new therapeutic targets for HD.

column36: Understanding polygenic nutrigenetic interactions for cardiometabolic diseases using fine mapping of genome-wide association study signals: Optimizing the science of nutrigenomics and its pragmatic application
column37: Individuals respond differently to the same nutrition strategies. For example, some individuals who consume high saturated fat diets develop heart disease, while others do not. Genetic variation can explain some of these different responses. Specifically, nutrigenomics is a science that explores how our genes interact with the foods, beverages and supplements we consume to affect our health outcomes. When it comes to heart health, many different genetic variants have been linked to nutrition-related heart health outcomes. However, most genetic tests available to consumers only look at a single genetic location. Therefore, in order to provide more accurate and effective nutritional guidance to reduce heart disease risks, we need to improve our understanding of all genetic variants involved in individualized dietary responses. The proposed research has two main goals. First, we aim to identify the large number of genetic variants that have been shown to contribute to individualized heart health responses to different nutrition components. The nutrition components that we will be focusing on include: fish peptides, berries and different types of sugar & sweetener. This will be done by summarizing and critically analyzing previous studies that have been completed. Next, we aim to create an algorithm of multiple genetic variants that can be tested to provide accurate, personalized dietary guidance to help individuals reduce genetic-related heart and metabolic risks. To do this, we will apply genomics tools to nutrition research. Briefly, we will identify genetic variants that contribute highly to individual heart and metabolic responses to nutrition. We will be focusing on identifying genetic variants that contribute to insulin, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels, based on consumption of sugar and on type of sugar. This will help clinicians to provide more accurate genetic-based nutrition advice to reduce inherited heart and metabolic risks.

column36: Evaluation of Quebec's diabetic patient's health-care trajectories in a population surveillance perspective
column37: Since 2000, the population of patients with diabetes in the province of Quebec is on the rise; almost 1 individual out of 10 was living with diabetes in 2016. Diabetes is associated with multiple complications such as lower-extremity amputations, which impose an important burden on Quebec's healthcare system. Management of diabetes and its complications requires the involvement of different healthcare specialists, which is also known as healthcare trajectories; yet, the accessibility to optimal care is not necessarily the reality for all patients with diabetes in light of their status of deprivation, location, treating physician specialities or sex. In other words, in the province of Quebec, optimal healthcare trajectories for patients with diabetes and related complications are still largely unexplored. Also, many gaps remain regarding the balance between benefices and risks of drugs used to treat diabetes. Objective: To evaluate the temporal trends of diabetes and to identify optimal healthcare trajectories in diabetes management and its complications, considering deprivation status, physician specialties, location, sex and drugs used to treat diabetes within patients newly diagnosed with diabetes in the province of Quebec. Methods: Using linked data from provincial health administrative databases, we will identify different patterns in healthcare utilization among patients with diabetes and we will study the relationship between these patterns and the incidence of complications, like lower-extremity amputations, and mortality. Relevance: This project will ensure a better understanding of the population of patients with diabetes, incidence of complications, healthcare trajectories and drugs used to treat diabetes within the Quebec's healthcare system and will propose new strategies to optimize healthcare. Ultimately, this project will allow the development of future programs/approaches that will help better prevent and treat diabetes-related complications.

column36: Induction of Cortical Plasticity in Human using Theta Burst Ultrasound Stimulation
column37: Ultrasound is well known for making visible what is hidden, for example, when giving parents a glimpse of their child before birth. But we are now using these high- frequency sound waves - beyond the range of human hearing - for a wholly different purpose: to manipulate the activity of the brain. Conventional brain stimulation techniques use electric currents or magnetic fields to alter brain activity. These techniques, however, have limitations. They can only reach the surface of the brain and are not particularly precise. By contrast, beams of ultrasound can be focused at a millimetre scale, even deep within the brain. Ultrasound thus has the potential to provide new insights into how the brain works. Most studies of ultrasound stimulation have looked at what happens to the brain during the stimulation itself. But could ultrasound also induce longer-lasting changes in brain activity? Changes that persist after the stimulation has ended would be valuable for research. They would also make it more likely that we could use ultrasound to treat brain disorders by changing brain activity. This study is to establish a repetitive ultrasound pattern to induce long-lasting alterations in human brain activity. It can target areas deep within the brain, including those that are out of reach with other techniques. If this procedure shows longer-lasting effects in people, it could yield valuable insights into the links between brain and behaviour. It could also help us develop new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

column36: Targeting protein arginine methyltransferases as a therapy for triple negative breast cancer
column37: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive subtype of breast cancer that lacks targeted therapy and is currently treated with standard-of-care chemotherapy. Hence, curative therapeutic alternatives are urgently needed against TNBC. Epigenetic reprogramming, which impacts gene expression without changing the DNA sequence, is emerging as a critical mechanism in the development of breast cancer. Unlike DNA mutations, epigenetic states of cancer cells are not permanent, making them an ideal target for cancer therapeutic intervention, yet the potential of epigenetic drugs for treating TNBC remains unknown. We aim to fill this gap by studying the inhibition of protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs), a family of enzymes that put chemical "marks" on proteins that regulate DNA and RNA, and are essential to TNBC growth based on our recent discovery. This new insight will allow us a unique opportunity to demonstrate the efficacy of treating TNBC with epigenetic therapy and provide leads for new clinical trials against this deadly cancer.

column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is one of the most common cancers in men; one in seven men will be diagnosed with this disease in their lifetime. It causes >300,000 deaths worldwide annually with most of mortalities resulting from the developments of metastasis and resistance to androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT). While tremendous efforts have been made, the molecular mechanisms of PCa progression remain elusive and effective treatment strategies are still lacking. This is largely due to limitations of current modelling systems such as cancer cell lines and genetic engineered mice in reflecting complexities of cancer in human patients. Patient derived xenografts (PDX) are models of cancer where cells or tissues from patients' primary tumors are implanted into immunodeficient mice and have demonstrated values in simulating human tumor biology and predicting patient drug response. In this proposed research, we will perform high-throughput genetic screens in PDX models of advanced PCa to identify drug targets. The important roles of epigenetic alterations in driving PCa progression and their potential reversibility make them attractive drug targets. Therefore, we will focus on epigenetic regulators and genes that have corresponding drug inhibitors approved by U.S. Food and Drug Administration (termed as drug genes from hereon). With more clinically relevant PDX models and systematic genetic approaches, this study may elucidate the roles of epigenetic regulators and drug genes in advanced PCa and reveal effective treatments for this cancer.

column36: Graph theory analysis of the dynamic pain connectome: understanding the impact of sex differences in brain network organization of patients with chronic pain.
column37: Chronic pain affects millions of Canadians yearly, causing suffering, disability and great financial burden of >$40 billion/year. Chronic pain is not well understood and treatments are effective for only a minority of patients. What distinguishes responders from non-responders is not known, but there are sex differences in the prevalence of many chronic pain conditions. We know that men and women can experience pain differently and can have different sensitivity to noxious stimuli. The Davis lab and others have previously demonstrated that the individual variability and sex differences in the pain experience can be explained, at least in part, by differences in the communication between some brain regions. However, it is not known whether there are sex differences in the large scale organization of brain connections people with chronic pain. Network analysis of brain connections are a new way to examine changes in the relationship between brain regions through graph theory analysis methods. Thus, this project will investigate the connectivity patterns difference in brain networks in healthy participants and those with chronic pain to elucidate how sex differences influence brain network organization in chronic pain. We will use brain imaging from 2 chronic pain conditions: multiple sclerosis more common in women, and ankylosing spondylitis more common in men. We will measure brain region connections in patients before being treated with ketamine or spinal cord stimulation to determine. These data will be used to examine whether pain relief can be predicted by brain network organization. The study findings will provide important insights about sex differences for better preventing and treating chronic pain. Ultimately, this framework will help to identify new potential targets in the brain to help treat chronic pain and to develop personalized pain management.

column36: Defining the tumor immune microenvironment in homologous recombination-deficient tumors using single-cell immunophenotypic and transcriptomic profiling
column37: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are a new class of drugs that unleash the immune system to combat cancer. These agents have achieved remarkable successes in a variety of cancer types, most notably those that harbor many mutations caused by carcinogen exposures or DNA repair defects. Unfortunately, the success of immunotherapy has been more limited in other cancer types, including breast and ovarian cancer, where chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and targeted therapy remain standard-of-care. Nevertheless, in these settings, tumors with higher numbers of certain tumor-infiltrating immune cells (called lymphocytes) tend to respond better to standard-of-care treatment than weakly-infiltrated tumors, suggesting that the immune system can influence clinical outcome in these diseases after all. Here, we propose to profile thousands of individual cells from patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer before and after standard-of-care therapy using systematic high-throughput approaches. In so doing, we hope to capture a comprehensive and dynamic view of the cells that constitute the tumor microenvironment. In parallel, we will develop new CRISPR-Cas9-based experimental animal models that will allow us to study and manipulate how immune cells respond to cancer cells. Collectively, these efforts will enable us to understand how specific genetic mutations in cancer cells influence the immune microenvironment during cancer development and in response to therapy. In addition, these approaches may nominate new immune-based therapeutic approaches that have the potential to delay or prevent the emergence of chemotherapy-resistant tumors.

column36: DNA methylation profiling in cell-free DNA: a non-invasive method to screen for pre-term birth
column37: More than 10% of births are premature, and premature birth kills more Canadian children than any other cause. Babies delivered prematurely have increased risk for both short- and long-term negative health consequences. There is currently no screening method to identify which pregnancies will deliver early. A method to detect pregnancies with a high risk of premature birth is needed to improve health outcomes for both the mother and baby. During pregnancy, a fetus develops an organ called the placenta, which connects it to the mother and delivers nutrients from mother to fetus. DNA from the placenta circulates in the mother's blood, along with the mother's DNA. Many studies have used the sequence of circulating DNA to predict pregnancy complications. In this study, we will look at the chemical changes found between circulating DNA of healthy pregnancies and pregnancies involving premature birth. Specifically, we will look at DNA methylation, a kind of chemical change known to affect which genes are active in different human tissues. We will identify changes in DNA methylation that can determine pregnancies with a high risk of premature birth. Since the test only uses DNA in the mother's blood, we can do this with a non-invasive blood test with little additional risk to the pregnancy. As such, findings from this study can be easily applied to current pregnancy care. This study will result in a noninvasive blood test that can detect pregnancies with increased risk of premature delivery. Use of this test will lead to changes in pregnancy care to try to prevent premature birth. This will lead to better long-term health for both mother and child. It will also decrease the need for the extreme medical care often used on premature infants. Improved health outcomes with decreased interventions will reduce costs to the Canadian health care system.

column36: Promoting functional recovery after spinal cord injury by optimizing the integration of transplanted cells with spared neural networks
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) can seriously impact the body's function and can cause people to experience a variety of issues such as not being able to move, breathe, or feel with their body. SCI affects a person's quality of life, reduces their independence and costs society due to expensive medical care and lost earnings. After leaving the hospital, SCI is usually treated using rehabilitation. Rehabilitation only leads to relatively small improvements, and patients continue to need help with daily tasks. An exciting new strategy to improve recovery is to repair the injured spinal cord using specific stem cells called neural precursor cells (NPCs). NPCs can divide into various cell types in the nervous system and have the potential to replace cells lost in the spinal cord after SCI. This strategy involves injecting NPCs near the location of injury in the spinal cord. Recently, our lab has shown in models of SCI that transplantation of NPCs improves functional recovery. The goal of my project is to improve this treatment by optimizing the way NPCs grow and connect to the rest of the body. To achieve this goal, I will investigate two methods. First, I will study whether a 3-month long intense rehabilitation training program will improve the integration of NPCs with the existing connections of the spinal cord. Second, I will study a new method for engineering effective connections between NPCs and specific areas of the spinal cord nervous system. This method involves electrical stimulation of the spinal cord and is also planned for 3 months. Collectively, this study will investigate the effectiveness of these techniques in guiding the NPCs to form and repair connections in the spinal cord. It will also assess the function of the integrated NPCs in the neural network of the spinal cord. Ultimately, this research hopes to develop more effective stem cell therapies for people with SCI and improve their quality of life.

column36: Pathways to the Request for Medical Assistance in Dying: Identifying Antecedents and Potential Targets of Early Intervention
column37: Background: In 2016, Canada established the legal criteria for Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) for adults with a grievous and irremediable medical condition. There has been relatively little research attention to MAiD or other forms of the desire for death (DD) that emerge in patients with advanced disease, even though the overwhelming majority of individuals who request MAiD suffer from advanced cancer. Furthermore, the support needs of patients who request MAiD are not well understood, and there has been concern that potentially reversible states of depression may contribute to the DD and the request for MAiD. Objectives: This study will examine in both men and women with advanced cancer: 1) the prevalence and correlates of depression in those reporting the DD and requesting MAiD; and, 2) the impact of specialized psychosocial and palliative care services on depression, the DD, and MAID requests. Methods: 400 patients with advanced cancer will be recruited at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto. Data will be extracted from patients' medical records including diagnostic information, medical history, MAiD requests, and the timing and quantity of psychosocial oncology and palliative care interventions. A 30-minute self-report survey will collect data on patients' sociodemographic characteristics, depressive symptoms, death anxiety, the DD, self-perceived burden, social support, and physical symptoms. Research Implications: This study will add importantly to our understanding of psychological and social factors that contribute to the DD. This information can inform the development and implementation of interventions to alleviate depression and the DD in patients with advanced disease and to identify those most likely to benefit from such interventions. The results of this work will also provide an evidence base to inform decisions about eligibility and conditions for MAID and for the development of legislation and policy guidelines.

column36: Investigating the therapeutic potential of modulating lysosomal biogenesis in normal and leukemic human hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Currently, leukemia is treated by hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) and/or chemotherapies; however, there are challenges. Although 50,000 HSCT procedures are undertaken worldwide annually to treat blood disorders and cancers, two thirds of patients who need HSCT lack matched donor tissue. Although cord blood (CB) banks improve the search for matched tissue, hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) number is usually limiting. HSCs maintain lifelong blood production but they are very sensitive to stress and cannot be easily expanded in culture. Thus, expansion of functional HSCs in the laboratory from CB while maintaining their survival and self-renewal properties offers an avenue to increase the number of HSCs for transplant and tap an underused HSCT source. With respect to chemotherapy, in certain types of leukemias, the stress response of HSCs and leukemia stem cells (LSCs) appear to have some differences (although there are also similarities) and exploiting these differences could make LSCs sensitive to chemotherapy. We and others have shown that lysosomes-organelles that act like the janitors of the cell-play crucial roles in adult stem cell adaptation to stress and survival. Here, we propose that modulation of lysosome activity could be a novel two-prong therapeutic approach for treating leukemia patients: 1) Improving the expansion of CB curative hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Here, we propose to test chemical compounds to enhance lysosome activity and maintain survival of HSCs during expansion using our state-of-the-art xenograft models. 2) Targeting LSCs that are resistant to chemotherapy. We will investigate the role of lysosomes in LSC's survival and test the sensitivity of LSCs to treatment with different lysosome modulators. Collectively, we propose that uncovering the clinical applicability of compounds that can either enhance or inhibit lysosome functionality will selectively target LSCs in patients while sparing HSCs.

column36: Disturbances of neurogenic cardiovascular control in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: characterization and modulation
column37: When the heart pumps poorly, nerves in the body start to fire more often. At first, this improves heart function, but over time it increases heart rate, stores salt and water, tightens blood vessels, and makes it harder to exercise. If the heart weakens and no longer pumps blood well throughout the body, heart failure (HF) will occur. However, many Canadians develop another form of HF, with normal pumping function but a stiff heart that does not relax well or fill with blood properly. We know less about this form of HF even though it is an equally common cause of hospitalization and death. There is little we can do to treat this form of HF. Thus, our goal is to learn if the nerves that fire too often in HF due to poor pumping function also fire more in patients with HF due to poor heart relaxation, and if so, determine why and how to stop this. With a sterile electrode, we will record sympathetic nerve firing from a nerve in the leg, plus blood pressure and heart rate, at rest and during two conditions that we know causes the nerve to increase firing in patients with HF due to poor pumping function: 1) increasing the amount of blood in the heart's upper chambers; and 2) 1-leg cycling exercise. One experiment will help us learn what happens to nerve firing when we move blood suddenly from the legs to the heart, which increases the pressure in the heart. The second will teach us if exercise causes more nerve firing in these patients, if this increase is what makes it hard to exercise, and if this can be improved by exercise training. We will study healthy volunteers to learn the normal response, compare their responses to HF patients, and compare what we find in men and women because we know that more women get this form of HF. If we can identify reasons why patients develop HF because their heart does not relax well, even though it seems to squeeze normally, our findings should inspire new ways of treating it so that patients can live longer and more healthy lives.

column36: Achieving the WHO hepatitis C elimination goals: mapping existing gaps in care, determining the economic burden, and identifying areas of investment along the care-cascade that optimize health outcomes among immigrants living with hepatitis C in Canada
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment has been revolutionized by the introduction of extremely effective direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) in 2013. These drugs offer exciting opportunities to eliminate HCV as a public health concern. To this end, the WHO has set ambitious global elimination targets to be met by 2030. However, planning for HCV elimination requires an accurate understanding of the existing gaps along the "HCV care-cascade" (e.g., diagnosis, linkage-to-care, treatment, cure). Further, high-quality data on healthcare resource use and costs along this cascade is also necessary to optimize elimination efforts. HCV-infected patients are highly heterogeneous with a different set of challenges in accessing and remaining engaged in healthcare. For example, in Canada, 35% of HCV infections are among foreign-born individuals. These groups face long delays to diagnosis and are more likely to have advanced liver disease (i.e., cirrhosis and liver cancer). However, the current DAA-era care-cascade and resource use for this high-risk group remains unknown. This project will identify the strategies required to optimally meet the WHO's elimination targets in immigrants to Canada by 1) identifying the current gaps in the "HCV care-cascade", 2) estimating the healthcare costs attributable to HCV, and 3) using these data to identify investment opportunities along the "HCV care-cascade". We will use population-level administrative healthcare data held at ICES and immigration records at Immigration Refugees & Citizenship Canada, to map the "HCV care-cascade" and determine the mean healthcare cost attributable to HCV for immigrants in Ontario. This data will be used to parameterize an existing, validated economic model that projects the health and economic outcomes of various integrated elimination strategies. We will then use multi-objective optimization to determine areas of investment where policymakers should focus efforts to eliminate HCV among immigrants in Canada by 2030.

column36: Deciphering the Implementability of Epigenetic Reprogramming in Hematopoietic Stem Cells as a Novel Vaccination Strategy against Human Tuberculosis
column37: Ever since the German scientist Robert Koch discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) to be the infectious agent of tuberculosis in 1882, it has defied efforts by scientists to prevent or cure the disease. The presence of Mtb DNA in ancient Egyptian mummies (dated 1550-1080 BC) suggests a long-standing evolutionary relationship between this bacterium and humans. Despite the world-wide application of BCG vaccination and other anti-Mtb interventions, Mtb remains one of the deadliest human pathogens killing annually two million people. Eight to ten million new cases of active tuberculosis occur each year mainly due to asymptomatic people chronically infected with Mtb. The ability of Mtb to persist in individuals with apparently normal immune systems implies that Mtb has developed strategies to avoid, evade, and even subvert our host defense system. To date, BCG is the only licensed vaccine against tuberculosis (TB). It protects against disseminated forms of TB in children but not against pulmonary TB in adults. However, after 100 years of its discovery, the protective mechanism(s) of BCG is still unknown. Although initially it was thought that adaptive immunity is responsible for this protection, many studies suggested otherwise. We have recently demonstrated that the systemic administration of BCG expands and reprograms stem cells to generate protective innate immunity in pre-clinical mouse models of TB. In the current study, we aim to investigate the potential translation of this approach to humans.

column36: The role of adiponectin in cholesterol efflux and high-density lipoprotein biogenesis and functionality
column37: Atherosclerosis is responsible for more deaths in Canada than any other disease. This illness is described as a chronic condition that is characterized by cholesterol build-up inside the arteries, called plaques. However, cholesterol can be transported outside the cells (efflux) of the atherosclerotic plaque, which can be beneficial for the cells. There is a protein in the body called apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I) that accepts this cholesterol from the cells and forms particles of the "good" cholesterol (HDL) in the blood that protects against atherosclerosis. Adiponectin, a protein secreted by fat tissue, has beneficial effects by preventing formation of plaques in the arteries. Studies have shown that adiponectin is strongly associated with the level of the HDL in the blood. However, it is not known if adiponectin can directly increase "good" cholesterol production and function, which would be very beneficial against atherosclerosis. Our preliminary evidence showed that adiponectin can interact with apoA-I and stimulate cholesterol efflux efficiently in a human cell model of macrophages. My project will focus on the study of the interaction between adiponectin and apoA-I. I will perform several advanced laboratory experiments to assess if this interaction increases the production HDL and its "good" cholesterol function. In other words, I will determine if and in which manner adiponectin can enhance the ability of apoA-I to accept cellular cholesterol and generate HDL particles. I will also study their interaction by examining where exactly adiponectin binds on apoA-I. Overall, these findings may support the therapeutic potential of combining adiponectin and apoA-I, to increase HDL, the" good" cholesterol. These may prove to be significant discoveries to reduce atherosclerosis and its related diseases, such as stroke and heart attacks, and save lives!

column36: Targeting and optimizing personalized pre-operative risk factors to achieve better colorectal surgery outcomes
column37: Colorectal surgery is a common surgery for the treatment of colon and rectal cancers as well as other bowel diseases. Recovery from colorectal surgery is difficult because of the many potential negative side effects. These side effects include surgical complications, long hospital stays, and slow recovery of pre-surgery fitness. It usually takes several months for colorectal surgery patients to recover the strength required to return to their typical daily activities. Prehabilitation is a new program for surgery designed to help patients experience better surgical recoveries by preparing them weeks before their operation with nutrition, anxiety reduction, and exercise advice to make better use of their waiting time for surgery. We think prehabilitation programs could be improved if targeted to patients' personalized risk factors for surgery. It might not be necessary for every patient to receive nutrition, exercise and anxiety-reduction advice. Some patients might benefit more from help with nutrition than help with exercise or vice versa. It is important that we figure out which patients benefit the most from the different aspects of prehabilitation programs so that we can use healthcare resources wisely, use patients' time wisely, and ensure the right patient receives the right care. We want to develop a tool that identifies patients who are at risk of having bad surgical recoveries and use this tool to develop a better prehabilitation program that truly meets patient needs and helps patients recover well.

column36: Canadian Sepsis Research Network: Improving Care Before, During and After Sepsis.
column37: Sepsis is the life-threatening response to infection. It affects everybody, especially children, seniors and those with other health issues. Sepsis costs the Canadian healthcare system over $1.5 billion every year, and causes more deaths than breast, bowel and lung cancer put together. Survivors may end up with weak muscles and memory problems. They may lose an arm or leg, have to go on dialysis, and still be at risk for more infections. Yet most Canadians have never heard of sepsis. In 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared sepsis to be a world emergency. It asked countries to count their numbers of septic patients, educate the public and healthcare workers on how recognize and treat sepsis, and to develop new treatments. To meet the WHO's strategic plan, Sepsis Canada scientists, patients and families promise to do exactly that. By 2025, our goal is to ensure that every septic patient in Canada is identified and treated. Our slogan is: Suspect sepsis, save lives, support recovery! We will learn which Canadians are at greatest risk of sepsis and the impact on their families. We will create a bank of evidence-based tools to teach the public and health workers and we will study new sepsis treatments. As a result, more Canadians will be alive and well after sepsis, thanks to better and timely access to care. The healthcare system will save money (about $380 million dollars every year within the next 5 years). We will share our knowledge around the world so that every citizen of the planet will benefit.

column36: Is iron supplementation harmful in populations where iron deficiency is not the cause of anemia? A 12 week RCT in Cambodia
column37: The World Health Organization (WHO) set a Global Nutrition Target to reduce anemia in women of reproductive age by 50% by 2025. In 2016, the WHO implemented a global policy recommending oral iron supplementation (60 mg daily for 12 weeks) for all women where anemia prevalence is more than 40%, such as in Cambodia. However, recent studies have shown the prevalence of iron deficiency to be low in Cambodian women. If iron deficiency is not the cause of anemia, then iron supplementation will not be effective at treating it. Further, iron supplementation may be harmful in some individuals, especially those with anemia caused by genetic blood disorders (which are common in Cambodia), as these individuals are already at an increased risk of iron overload. The risks are made greater by the fact that the type of iron that is commonly used in supplements (ferrous sulfate) is poorly absorbed. Typically, less than 20% is absorbed in the gut; the remaining 80% is unabsorbed in the colon where it can increase the risk of pathogen growth and gut inflammation. To investigate the safety of untargeted iron supplementation, we will undertake a new study in Cambodia, where we will evaluate a newer type of iron supplement that may be absorbed better, and thus, safer than the conventional type. We will recruit non-pregnant women (18-45 years) and ask them to take one of the two forms of iron (ferrous sulfate or ferrous bisglycinate) or a placebo for 12 weeks (in line with the WHO global policy). We will measure hemoglobin and ferritin levels, which are markers of anemia and iron status, and markers of gut inflammation and gut pathogen abundance, before and after the intervention. This study will contribute to the evidence for safe and effective iron supplementation for women worldwide.

column36: Structure of human PINK1-TOM complex by single-particle cryo-EM
column37: Most of our body's cells contain mitochondria, small components critical for providing the essential chemical energy for all biological functions. When mitochondria are damaged or deteriorated, a cell must remove them before they contaminate the cell and lead to cell death. It is widely appreciated that mitochondrial damage, which result in decreased energy production, plays an important role in the development and progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). PD is caused by the death or malfunction of specific kind of neurons, which regulate muscle movement and coordination. To do their job properly, these nerve cells require large amounts of energy, provided by mitochondria. In normal subjects, when mitochondria are damaged or deteriorated, an enzyme (protein) called PINK1 (a cellular hero) charges to the scene of a mitochondrial damage. Like a firefighter, the PINK1 protein first receives an alarm signal and then gets itself ready for the call-going through a series of steps to label the damaged mitochondria, so that these mitochondrial are selectively removed for the sake of cellular health. However, sometimes the whole process goes awry, particularly in PD. The cellular hero (PINK1) doesn't perform its function properly. This leads to increase in mitochondrial damage and an increase in cell death. Unfortunately, we don't know much details about how PINK1 protein tags damaged mitochondria. My project will try to understand the details of this process. By knowing the details of this process, we will better understand how PINK1 communicates with damaged mitochondria. Not only will this knowledge help develop treatments for the thousands of Canadians who suffer from PD, it will also shed new unprecedented light on the very specific language our cells use to keep us functioning properly.

column36: Comprehensive analysis of health inequalities in global cities
column37: More people than ever live in cities, a statement that will be as true tomorrow as it is today. Since 1950, the global urban population has grown by over 450% and is currently estimated at 4.2 billion (over half the global population). The physical, economic and social environments in cities have unique impacts on human health. The impacts of urban living on health are not the same for all countries, nor are they experienced equally by those living within cities, where better average health (compared to rural populations) often masks large within-city health inequalities. Cities across all regions bring together the richest and poorest in society with poor health often concentrated in the most deprived neighbourhoods and the lowest socio-economic groups accounting for a disproportionate burden of disease and mortality. My aim is to understand how cities across different settings can be leveraged to improve the health of impoverished residents and improve health equity. Using data from five case study cities, each with unique characteristics and histories and from different world regions: Accra (Ghana), Beijing (China), Dhaka (Bangladesh), London (UK) and Vancouver (Canada), I will address three important questions: 1. What are the health characteristics of the poorest urban groups? 2. What is the variability of health outcomes within the poorest urban neighbourhoods? 3. Which diseases and injuries contribute the most to inequalities in life expectancy between the poorest and richest urban residents? This research will generate novel information crucial to design and implement policies and interventions that suitably target those falling behind in today's cities, and evaluate their impact on population health.

column36: Engineering pluripotent stem cells to provide a renewable source of T-cells for immunotherapy
column37: A bone marrow transplant provides a patient with stem cells that will ultimately produce new immune cells capable of remedying diseases like immunodeficiency and cancer. These transplants can be dangerous because the recipient needs to undergo toxic chemotherapy or radiation to make room in their marrow for the donor's cells. Furthermore, it can be difficult to find a donor that is a close genetic match with the recipient. If the transplanted cells are not a sufficient match, they can attack the patient's healthy tissues. To avoid these risks, the goal of my project is to produce immune cells from pluripotent stem cells in the laboratory. Directly transplanting immune cells circumvents the need for dangerous chemotherapy or radiation. Creating immune cells from pluripotent stem cells also offers other important advantages. Unlike the cells found in bone marrow, pluripotent stem cells can be grown extensively outside of a patient. The ability to efficiently grow pluripotent stem cells in the laboratory makes them a renewable cell source that can easily be scaled up to meet patient needs. This property of self-renewal also means they are considerably more amenable to genetic modifications that can correct disease-causing mutations, improve cancer fighting properties or compensate for genetic mismatches between the donor and recipient. Others have shown that stem cells can be guided to become immune cells in the lab, but these prior methods required mouse cells to shepherd the stem cells down the right path. To avoid the requirement for these mouse cells, which are not compatible with downstream clinical use, I will genetically program the stem cells so that they can guide themselves down the path to becoming immune cells. By providing a renewable and clinically usable supply of genetically engineered immune cells, we aim to reduce the sizeable impact of cancer and immune disorders in Canada.

column36: Dissecting the mechanisms and long-term impact of activation of transposons by gestational stress
column37: Pregnancy represents the most critical period to impact health throughout life. Embryo and fetus are sensitive to environmental factors such as nutritional deficits or exposure to toxins that can have long-term consequences for disease propensity into adulthood. In parallel, malnutrition, environmental contamination, carcinogens, and other stresses can induce jumping genes across the species. Jumping genes, also known as transposons, are DNA sequences that can alter genomes by moving into new genomic locations. Half of the genome is originated from transposons and their activity is the cause of many genetic disorders. In cells, activation of jumping genes is a conserved response to stress. However, whether jumping genes are activated under stress in embryos and contribute to pathogenesis of adult onset diseases is not known yet. I hypothesize that stress activates jumping genes in embryonic cells by regulating the stress response genes and pathways. To test this hypothesis, I will first use the cutting edge high throughput technologies to screen the impact of various stress molecules on transposon activation in human embryonic stem cells. Afterwards, I will find out the genes and cellular pathways that work in response to stress to activate jumping genes. A second approach will take advantage of the humans of the Dutch Hunger Winter Cohort. At the end of the Second World War in the west of the Netherland, there was an imposed calorie restriction on this previously well-nourished population. Children who were conceived and born in this period were prone to various late-onset health conditions. In this cohort, I will assess the activity of jumping genes and how they contribute to disease pathogenesis. Stress is ubiquitous in disease states and is causally linked to diabetes, heart disease, neurological disorders and epithelial cancers. Thus, insights from my research will open new avenues of inquiry on stress-induced transposon activity in a variety of diseases.

column36: Effets de la stimulation transcutanee du nerf vague a l'oreille chez des patients post-coma en alteration de l'etat de conscience secondaire a une lesion cerebrale acquise : une etude pilote randomisee et controlee
column37: Les personnes ayant une lesion cerebrale acquise soit via un traumatisme a la tete soit via une tumeur, un anevrisme cerebral ou une autre atteinte intra-cerebrale non-traumatique peuvent consequemment avoir un etat de conscience alteree. Le plus connu est le coma, mais l'etat deveil non-repondant et l'etat de conscience minimal en sont aussi et font partie d'un continuum vers l'etat d'eveil. La periode de temps necessaire a une personne pour traverser ces stades et emerger de cette alteration est inconnue, meme que certains ne retrouveront jamais un etat de conscience normale. Jusqu'a maintenant, peu de moyens existent pour faire progresser quelqu'un d'un stade a l'autre. Par notre etude, nous esperons pouvoir moduler l'activite cerebrale par la stimulation du nerf vague afin d'ameliorer l'etat de conscience. Ce nerf a une influence sur l'activite des organes internes du corps dont le coeur et le cerveau. Nous esperons qu'en stimulant ce dernier, cela aura un effet positif sur l'activite cerebrale. Pour mesurer cette activite, nous utiliserons une evaluation clinique standardisee des alterations de l'etat de conscience, l'electroencephalogramme et l'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle. Toutes ces techniques utilisent des moyens differents pour mesurer l'activite des cellules du cerveau. Pour y arriver, nous voulons comparer un groupe avec stimulation placebo a un groupe avec une stimulation active afin d'eliminer l'effet de la progression naturelle d'une alteration de l'etat de conscience. Si notre hypothese est confirmee, cela permettrait d'utiliser cette technique non-invasive au chevet du patient, pendant le sejour hospitalier, afin de le faire progresser plus rapidement d'une phase a l'autre jusqu'a l'etat d'eveil.

column36: Spread and Scale of Integrated Models of Team-Based Care for Chronic Disease Management: A Multi-site Case Study
column37: The prevalence of chronic disease represents a significant burden for the Canadian health care system. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a chronic condition that affects lung function and reduces the quality of life for nearly 5% Canadians. Care for patients living with COPD can be improved through the use of integrated models of team-based care. These models involve coordination of services across providers to provide better care for patients, caregivers and families. Integrated models of team-based care involve multiple healthcare professionals working together to provide appropriate care for patients. The aim of this research is to gain a better understanding of how integrated models team-based care are spread to new contexts, to allow more patients to benefit. The objective of this research is to explore the spread of an integrated model of team-based care for COPD. This one-year study will use a mixed methods approach (surveys, observations, and focus groups). The expected outcomes of this study will be a description of how integrated models of team-based care are spread in different contexts along with an in-depth understanding of the barriers and facilitators to this process. Our research will provide guidance of policymakers wanting to improve in chronic disease management. We will also offer a common language for research and practice, and support best care for patients and caregivers.

column36: Spreading the Alongside Midwifery-led Unit to Strengthen Midwifery Care in Hamilton Ontario
column37: Our aim is to spread the innovative and successful model of the Alongside Midwifery Unit (AMU) from Markham to Hamilton, Ontario. AMUs provide 'home-like' care that supports normal birth for low-risk women but in the hospital setting with close proximity to obstetric-led care if needed. The model improves maternal birth outcomes, lowers costs and improves satisfaction. The Markham AMU, the first of its kind in Canada, was created with the intention of spreading to other sites. The Hamilton AMU will include core features of the Markham model like the hospitalist midwife, a built environment that supports physiologic birth and midwifery leadership and autonomy, but will be scaled-up to include new and innovative in-unit clinics for newborn assessment and early pregnancy loss. The anticipated improvements of spreading this model to Hamilton include: better health outcomes such as a reduction in Cesarean section, cost savings through early hospital discharge, and effective use of health services through a reduction in unnecessary transfers of care from midwifery to obstetric services. Our spread plan, based on existing community relationships with underserved and marginalized populations, will ensure equitable access to this model of care. The consolidation of services at the AMU and the role of hospitalist midwife will allow midwives in Hamilton to increase their caseloads and grow midwifery capacity, thereby improving outcomes for a greater number of women. Our spread plan activities examine our readiness, identify community needs, build a team of leaders and champions, map a strategic plan, and secure funds for implementation. Our team is comprised of midwifery faculty and researchers from McMaster University, midwives and healthcare leaders in the city of Hamilton, as well as the current director and innovator behind the Markham AMU. This team will facilitate synergy between researchers and decision-makers that will aid in implementation.
