column36: CPIN-REACH: Spreading and scaling the CPIN automated patient survey system for primary care practices to support regional health system evaluation
column37: Health systems across Canada are trying to better integrate care across sectors to improve patients' experiences. Patient reported experience measures ( PREMs) of navigating the health system and their reported outcome measures (PROMs) such as functional health status, are critical to shaping and evaluating efforts for better integration. A logical place to collect PREMs and PROMs is in primary care. A strong primary care system is the foundation of a high functioning health system. It plays an important role in meeting most of the medical needs of patients longitudinally and across conditions while also ensuring access to and coordination with the rest of the system. Our team developed and tested an automated patient survey system, the Canadian Practice Information Network (CPIN), as a primary care practice tool that addresses the pressing need for infrastructure and mechanisms to engage patients across the small independent primary care practices where they receive most of their care and care coordination. This proposal is to implement the CPIN system to embed early in our scale up model the capacity for practice-based patient experience measurement to align with and inform regional efforts to improve patient experiences across Canada. We will implement CPIN in ten practices across Eastern Ontario and Kootenay BC, to collect PREMs and PROMs and deploy and evaluate a regional data aggregation approach for PREMs and PROMs to contribute to evaluating health system integration. CPIN allows primary care providers to share short messages, such as flu shot availability, by email or text messaging and collect data on patient experience through an embedded survey. Patient data, is anonymized and reported back to the provider. For CPIN to be scaled up to serve as a foundation for learning about how the health system impacts patients' experiences, we need to build it in partnership with regional decision makers and providers.

column36: Outcomes Associated with Direct Rapid Genetic Testing at Time of Breast Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Approximately 11% of all breast cancers are due to a mutation in a cancer predisposition gene, most frequently BRCA1 or BRCA2. These breast cancers should receive different treatments to increase the chance that a woman will survive, including bilateral mastectomy. However, women must know if they have a genetic mutation in a cancer causing gene at the time of diagnosis when treatment decisions are being made (rapid genetic testing). A new model of genetic testing at time of cancer diagnosis is needed to ensure equitable access to genetic testing for Canadian patients. Direct genetic testing offers patients limited to no pre-test discussion with a genetic counsellor, and written documents or other resources are provided. Our overall objective is to evaluate the impact of Direct Rapid Genetic Testing (DRGT) for breast cancer susceptibility genes in newly-diagnosed breast cancer patients on treatment and psychosocial outcomes, compared to women who received rapid genetic testing (RGT) with standard pre and post-test genetic counselling. We will recruit from 1000 women from hospitals throughout Canada, including those which do not have genetic counselling programs. Sequencing will be done on BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, PALB2, PTEN, STK11, TP53, ATM, and CHEK2 genes. We will have one central genetic counsellor (Women's College Hospital) who will provide post-test counselling. Genetic test results will available in 7 days. Outcomes will be compared between those who received RGT with standard genetic counselling to those who received Direct Rapid Genetic Testing. The traditional cancer genetics model is not sustainable with the current volumes of genetic testing. This proposed delivery of RGT at the time of breast cancer diagnosis is responsive to the need for new models. This research has the potential to lead to the development of a sustainable and accessible model of genetic testing at the time of cancer diagnosis, which has a very high potential to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Design and evaluation of a system-wide surveillance system for late effects of treatment in childhood cancer survivors
column37: There are over 14,000 survivors of childhood cancer in Ontario. Unfortunately, the therapy needed to cure their cancer puts them at high risk of developing new cancers and/or heart problems. Most adult survivors of childhood cancer do not complete the recommended tests to check for these problems. There are many reasons for this. One important reason is that once these survivors become young adults, most of them are 'lost' to the cancer system. There is a need to build a system that can ensure that childhood cancer survivors continue to get the follow-up care they need when they transition from the intensive childhood cancer care system to the routine health care system in adulthood. We will develop a sustainable, centralized solution that builds upon our experience conducting similar work. We will use existing data sources to build a provincial registry of survivors that can benefit from early detection of the health problems that are at high risk of developing. We will send these survivors personalized information about the surveillance tests they are due for, based on their cancer treatment history. Before launching this solution, we will work with stakeholders and survivors, to ensure the intervention is user-centred. We will test the solution in a province-wide experiment to determine whether the reminder system leads to an increase in adult survivor screening test completion. If the reminder system is effective, it will be implemented as a program for all Ontario childhood cancer survivors. It will be applicable to other age groups (e.g. young adults) and high-risk groups (e.g. patients with genetic risks for cancer) who can benefit from routine surveillance for new cancers and other long-term side effects of therapy. Furthermore, our national partners have expressed interest in sharing it with pediatric cancer centres across Canada. Let's not save the lives of children with cancer only to have them die from heart disease or a new cancer as young adults.

column36: Variation in G protein expression in bone cells determines bone quality and skeletal responses to catabolic and anabolic stimuli
column37: Poor bone health is a major issue in the aging Canadian population, in which 2 million people (1 in 3 postmenopausal women and 1 in 6 older men)1 have osteoporosis and half will have a fragility fracture. Hip fractures in people over 65 years of age significantly increase mortality and therefore it is important that we understand the factors that contribute to bone fragility. Lack of exercise, insufficient calcium and vitamin D intake, and loss of estrogen and testosterone with age all negatively impact bone health, but there are also genetic differences that make some people more vulnerable to these skeletal stresses. In our previous studies on bone health we have shown a large variability in expression of two proteins, called G proteins, in human cells. These G proteins are important for cell responses to messages from the hormone and nervous systems. To simulate differences in levels of expression of the two major G proteins, Gs and G11, we created two mouse types with high levels of each of these proteins in bone cells. Our two mouse lines look normal but both have weaker bone that fractures more easily. In our proposed research we will now test if these mice respond differently after they eat a diet low in calcium or vitamin D and when we remove their estrogen and testosterone. We will also assess how their bones repair after fracture, and look at the molecular pathways controlled by these G proteins to understand how they cause bone to be weaker. Our studies will help us decide if people with high G protein levels are more likely to get osteoporosis or have bone fractures or have slow healing after a fracture and what we can do to help keep their bones healthy into old age.

column36: Novel mechanisms in diabetic cardiomyopathy
column37: As diabetes reaches epidemic magnitude worldwide, more diabetics face the problems of morbidity and mortality due to chronic complications. Diabetes causes scarring and damage to heart and is one of the leading causes heart disease in Canada. We plan to investigate the mechanisms leading to development of heart damage in diabetes. In diabetes, cells use its fuel differently and such process causes damage to the cell nucleus.The cell's nucleus, in turn, send signals to make additional proteins causing tissue damage. If this processes continues the cells ultimately fails to function. The signal sent out by the nucleus contains some special type of molecules called lncRNA. They are also known as 'dark matter of the genome'. These molecules have been recently discovered and have a major role in regulating protein production. We plan to examine how lncRNA can interact with other RNA molecules and other mechanisms and change the production of abnormal molecules and whether by manipulating these mechanisms, we can prevent damage to the heart in diabetes. The proposed research is based on several aims, each of which will be investigated at multiple levels of complexities. Our experiments will include examinations of various types of cells from the heart and the cells of the blood vessels. We will also use animal with diabetes. We will also use several compounds to block these mechanisms to understand how this can be prevented. Some of our experiment will focus on specific lncRNAs that we have identified in our laboratory. We will further expand our studies to examine tissue removed from patients and examine whether the abnormalities identified in the cells and in the animals occur in humans. This proposal represents a comprehensive set of studies to investigate a specific process, i.e, the heart damage in diabetes. Understanding such mechanisms will help to develop preventive treatment for such conditions.

column36: Molecular Imaging biomarkers of cognition in Parkinson's disease
column37: Cognitive decline in Parkinson's Disease (PD) may occur, anywhere from 20-60%, with an impairment in one or more cognitive domains. Different subtypes of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) have been identified in PD. Single-domain non-amnestic impairments are most commonly frontal-executive in nature, while multi-domain impairments include any combination of deficits in various cognitive domains. Recent studies found that multi-domain MCI is highly associated with conversion to dementia. Today, the lack of information on the biological bases of these cognitive complications in PD has prevented the development of optimal treatments to alleviate these non-motor aspects. While the role of dopaminergic degeneration in cognitive dysfunction in PD may appear obvious, it has become clear that this alone cannot explain the severity of cognitive decline in those patients with multi-domain MCI and dementia. Other factors have to play an important role as well. In support of this, while there is large preclinical data suggesting a potential role of activated microglia, beta-amyloid and tau deposition in neurodegenerative processes, to date the in-vivo evidence of these pathologies in PD manifesting with multi-domain MCI and dementia remains unclear. This grant proposal shifts the focus from neurotransmitter changes to study the relationship between neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau deposition, using a set of new PET radiotracers. This data set will offer a unique multi-modal integrated approach to investigate and correlate clinical and pathophysiological mechanisms associated with more severe cognitive decline in PD.

column36: Using bioengineered human vessels to understand how brain and peripheral apoE affect cerebrovascular functions relevant to Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Genetic variants in apolipoprotein E (apoE) account for most of the risk of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Humans have three genetic types of apoE, called apoE2 (the protective form), apoE3 (the neutral form), and apoE4 (the risky form). Exactly how apoE affects AD is not known. ApoE is made by multiple cell types in the brain, including astrocytes. Although apoE is also made by the liver, peripheral apoE has largely been ignored in AD as apoE does cross the blood brain barrier. As most AD patients have cerebrovascular pathologies including cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), we hypothesize that brain and peripheral apoE may interact at the cerebral vessel. We recently pioneered a novel experimental platform to investigate vascular contributions to AD, where we engineered three-dimensional human blood vessels with both a "brain" side and a "blood side". We showed that addition of Abeta to the "brain side" increased CAA, especially in the presence of apoE4. We also showed that addition of high-density lipoprotein (HDL; good cholesterol) to the "blood side" prevented CAA, even in the presence of "brain" apoE4. Further, we recently found that HDL particles enriched in apoE (HDL-E) are best at preventing CAA. We now propose to use our innovative model to determine the relative contributions of astrocyte apoE and HDL-E on CAA, Abeta transport and monocyte binding in bioengineered vessels. We will first engineer vessels with astrocytes that express apoE2, apoE3 or apoE4 to study how astrocyte apoE genotype affects CAA from the "brain" side. We will then isolate HDL-E from healthy people of different apoE genotypes to study how circulating HDL-E affects CAA from the "blood" side. We will then combine these approaches to test whether HDL-E from apoE3 donors can counteract astrocyte apoE4. If so, this could open up new ways to treat or prevent vascular AD risk factors, as therapies that can work from the inside of the vessel may not need to enter the brain to be effective.

column36: Prediction of multiple sclerosis disability worsening scores using multi-stream deep learning
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a complex neurological disease that disables mostly young Canadians. While therapies are available for many who have a relapsing remitting clinical form (RRMS), >50% of them worsen to a secondary progressive form (SPMS) within 10-15 years of disease onset despite treatment, from which point the disease is hardly manageable. A major current limitation is our inability to identify who worsens rapidly that needs immediate aggressive therapies, and when, as disease course is never the same between RRMS patients. In this project, we will establish a novel deep machine learning method to predict the 5-year risk of disability score worsening in RRMS individuals. This will take a unique approach that simultaneously evaluate patient outcomes from brain pathology, clinical measures, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Deep learning algorithms have shown enormous fascinating data recently in image analysis and paralleled human ability in disease prediction. Based on standard brain MRI, we have now achieved an ~85% accuracy using deep learning to separate RRMS from SPMS. Yet deep learning is better using pathology-directed image feature maps than standard MRI, and far superior using both. We have done pioneering work in assessing the pattern (texture) of MRI scans and are the first to show that MRI texture features detect specific elements of brain MS pathology. Now we have made new advancement in deep learning that integrates image texture, brain MRI, and clinical variables including sex and age that are known to impact MS patient outcomes, and built cutting-edge technologies to uncover how deep learning works. Built on these exciting results, this project will provide a novel objective method to identify the high and low risks of sustained worsening or SPMS onset for RRMS individual so that each will receive the best personalized care. column36: Harnessing exercise epigenomics to protect the brain from neurodegeneration
column37: Can exercise help heal the brain and protect it from degeneration? This is a critical question that not only applies to people who have a neurodegenerative condition like multiple sclerosis (MS) but anyone who wishes to maintain a healthy brain as they age. We think that participation in aerobic exercise can alter the immune system and shift the balance from a state of inflammation towards one that fosters brain repair. We can measure levels of inflammation and markers of brain repair, such as neurotrophins, in the blood. We detect changes to brain networks using a special device called transcranial magnetic stimulation, which provides a window on brain function and integrity. The chemical switch that makes the link between inflammation and restoration is likely a special molecule called a 'microRNA'. MicroRNAs help cross talk between the brain and the immune system. This field of 'exercise epigenomics' is new and could have important implications for MS as well as other diseases that involve neurodegeneration. Beginning in 2016, we created a unique longitudinal MS patient registry and biorepository which includes detailed demographic, clinical, immune, and exercise/rehabilitation profiles. Of the 220+ people recruited, we have complete data on 84 that are eligible for this project (have mild MS). We intend to gather three years of data on at least 100 people. In this project we will investigate potential links between aerobic fitness/physical activity and the balance of inflammation and brain repair on preservation of brain function, and sensorimotor and cognitive deficits in people with mild MS. People with MS, like anyone else, want to live long and productive lives. Using this unique and powerful dataset we will be able to probe the links between lifestyle and brain health like never before.

column36: Could mitotic exhaustion of NG2-glia explain the remyelination deficit in MS?
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the fatty sheaths that are wrapped around neuronal processes and that aid communication between brain cells become damaged. During the initial phase of the disease, the brain is able to repair those damages but this ability is frequently lost as MS progresses. So far the exact cause of this failure has not been pinpointed. Much of the sheath repair is reliant on new sheath-forming cells (called oligodendrocytes) produced by brain cells known as NG2-glia. We propose that the status of these NG2-glia is key to effective repair. Evidence suggest that these cells need to divide to ensure effective remyelination. We aim to determine whether the need of continuous brain repair as in case of progressive MS, eventually wears out the NG2-glia, rendering them successively less effective at restoring brain function after each period of damage. The proposed research may critically contribute to our understanding of the exact causes that lead to the transition to progressive MS disease stages. Based on our findings, future treatment strategies may focus on preventing or slowing down the decline of the repair capacity of NG2-glia thereby helping to prevent or delay disease progression.

column36: Role and therapeutic potential of MicroRNA-34a-5p in knee osteoarthritis
column37: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and among the leading cause of disability worldwide. Ways to detect or treat knee OA at the onset of disease are not available. Current treatments only target pain while early detection methods are absent. By the time of diagnosis, knee OA has usually progressed to a point leading to severe joint damage. Thus, it's critical to identify early detection methods that can allow early intervention and potential therapies to stop knee joint destruction during OA. Our studies have identified a particular molecule called microRNA-34a that is highly present in the blood, synovial (joint) fluid as well as joints tissues of patients with advanced-stage knee OA patients compared to early-stage and healthy subjects. These elevated levels are not only present in humans with knee OA but also in joint tissues of mouse with knee OA. We anticipate that the levels of this molecule can help us detect or predict the extent of joint damage in the patients with knee OA. To do this, we have created a large-scale biobank of patient biospecimens (blood and tissues) with early to advanced stages of knee OA to help us identify the reliability and specificity of this molecule to detect or measure the degree of joint degeneration in patients with knee OA. Our studies further show that this molecule is not only elevated during OA but also promotes joint destructive activities in the knee joint by degenerating cartilage and promoting inflammation. We anticipate that blocking the activity of this molecule will help us stop the degeneration of knee joints. We have now created a blocker of this molecule and we will test if injecting this blocker in animal models can help stop knee OA. This project will help us comprehensively understand: (1) If this molecule can be used a biomarker to detect or measure the presence or extent of joint damage in patient with knee OA. (2) if the molecule blocker can be used as a drug to stop knee OA.

column36: Improving Care for Knee Osteoarthritis by Predicting Who Will Get Worse: Exploring the Interactions of Joint Biomechanics, Inflammation and Immunity
column37: IMPORTANCE By 2041, over 10 million Canadians will have osteoarthritis (OA), with the knee most often affected. Knee OA causes long-term pain and immobility. It damages all tissues in and around a joint. About half of people with knee OA will decline toward disability, some very rapidly. At diagnosis, we cannot predict who will experience steady disease, versus those on a fast path to disability. Our goal is to predict knee OA worsening so that we target treatment to those who need it the most. In-depth movement analysis shows that the torque rotating the lower leg into a bow-legged position at the knee (called the knee adduction moment (KAM)) predicts worsening knee OA - but only people who are obese. The reason why obesity heightened the effect of KAM is unknown. We believe obesity creates inflammation and changes the way our immune system fights off disease. OBJECTIVES To figure out how KAM and obesity work together to worsen knee OA, we will determine if: 1) Obesity-related alterations in tissue quality, inflammation and immunity relate to tissue function for cartilage and muscle. 2) The combination of KAM with poor cartilage function predicts cartilage loss over 3 y. 3) Pain, mobility and function are related with obesity-related inflammation and immune responses. METHOD In 94 people with knee OA, at baseline and 3 y we will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure the quantity and quality of cartilage and muscle. We will use MRI to assess cartilage function (changes in cartilage thickness after walking) and a strength-testing machine to assess muscle function. Every 6 months for 3 y, we will collect blood to measure inflammation and immune function; analyze walking; and measure pain, mobility and function. OUTCOMES By examining how KAM and obesity work together to worsen knee OA, we will understand why some with knee OA remain stable, while others get worse. This work is essential to targeting treatment for those facing rapid decline.

column36: CardiacDOC: Prospective multi-centre feasibility and validation of a unified screening tool for Depression, Obstructive sleep apnea and Cognition (DOC) in heart failure patients
column37: Heart Failure (HF) is very common. Many people die or are disabled by it and it worsens their quality of life. Depression, sleep apnea (problems breathing at night referred to as OSA) and cognitive impairment (memory, thinking problems) are very common in people with HF. We call these "DOC" conditions for short. Finding out if people with HF have DOC conditions may help them improve their quality of life. It can also help them better control their HF symptoms. For example, someone with cognitive difficulties might need different instructions about when to take or change their HF medicines to make it easier for them to manage their HF. Regular testing for these conditions is complicated and time-consuming, so doctors can't test all HF patients for them. A fast way to know if people have any DOC conditions is needed. This study will test how well a short screening test, that's been studied in stroke patients (and shown to work well), can work to screen for DOC conditions in people with HF. The first goal is to see if screening can be done quickly and easily in HF clinics. The second is to see if the screen scores reliably predict the actual conditions. To do this, we are going to screen people in HF clinics and ask them to volunteer for more detailed testing. We'll compare the screening to the detailed testing to see how well it predicts them. If the screening works well, it can help people with HF improve their quality of life by treating DOC conditions. It may also allow us to study new ways of improving HF treatment; for example, by giving more personalized treatment instructions to those with depression or memory problems. The heart and the brain are very closely connected - each affects the other. We hope we can use this approach to improve both the hearts and minds of many of the 600,000 people living with HF in Canada and in doing so, help them to live longer, healthier lives.

column36: Early diagnosis of mortality using Admission CT perfusion in severe Traumatic Brain Injury patients (ACT-TBI study)
column37: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a principal cause of post-injury hospitalization, disability, and death throughout the world primarily afflicting a young, healthy population with a previously excellent quality of life. In addition to being the leading cause of death and disability among people under 45 years of age, TBI represents the bulk of financial expenditure incurred by the different medical insurance companies for rehabilitation in Canada. TBI is predicted to be the most prevalent and costliest neurological condition in Canada through the year 2031. Outcome assessment after TBI is complex. Clinical examination of these patients are almost impossible as they are on life support and sedated at the time of their hospital admission. Roughly half of these patients who die, die in the first 48 hrs of hospital admission, despite receiving the most resource intensive treatment. These patients receive treatment despite lack of a clear understanding of their prognoses. We believe that some patients with severe TBI have a fatal brain injury at hospital admission, which is not recognized because of inadequate clinical examination. An advanced type of CT scan of brain called Computed Tomographic Perfusion (CTP) can establish brain death, when present. In a small pilot study, CTP done at the time of hospital admission, accurately diagnosed brain death in patients with severe TBI. The proposed research is to confirm these findings in a larger, powerful, well designed and a robust multi-center study. This study will directly address the existing lack of a routine robust neuroimaging test to improve diagnosis and prognosis of patients with severe TBI. This will provide a confident prognosis for the patients with severe TBI and optimize the use of health care resources by preventing the use of expensive intense care for potentially dead patients in the emergency room. Thereby this may improve trust and investment in organ donation in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Neuro-immune control of postoperative pain via CCL22:CCR4 signalling
column37: Pain is one of the major complaints of patients suffering from various neurological and non-neurological conditions, such as autoimmune diseases, tissue infection, and injury. Current therapies for pain caused by inflammation, such as after surgical wound or bacterial infection, include NSAIDs and acetaminophen. These drugs often provide inadequate pain relief and are accompanied by serious gastrointestinal and cardiovascular side effects. Opioids are more effective pain-killers but carry a heavy burden to both the patient and society. While treatments targeting the spinal cord or brain can be challenging and carry risks of unwanted side effects, modulating the inflammation that occurs at the site of injury may be more amenable to treatment. Recent work from our lab has found that dendritic cells in the skin, which act as sentinels to injury and infection, secrete specific immune mediators after injury that can directly activate sensory neurons to cause pain. In preliminary studies, we discovered that tissue injury activates a specific molecule (the chemokine CCL22) in dendritic cells located at the site of tissue injury. We also discovered that blocking its receptor, CCR4, substantially reduces pain. Our work also suggests that pain-sensing neurons control the activation state of dendritic cells in response to injury, and may function in a feedback loop. This proposal will examine how these immune cells communicate with pain-sensing neurons to mediate pain, and whether the neurons themselves can alter the dendritic cell response. Understanding why and how pain occurs during inflammation will enable us to develop new health care strategies to prevent or treat pain in patients with bacterial infection and tissue injury.

column36: Social adjustment in survivors of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
column37: Background: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a cancer that affects the white blood cells and is the most common cancer affecting children. Thanks to many advances in treatment, most children diagnosed with ALL will survive. The treatments needed to cure ALL, however, are toxic because they are directed at the brain and therefore negatively impact survivor's health and psychological well-being. Survivors of ALL experience social difficulties. As children, these survivors do not have as many friends because they are more withdrawn. As adults, these survivors are less likely to go as far in school, have a job or be married compared to others who have not had ALL. Social difficulties are a serious health risk that may be comparable to the health risks associated with drinking and smoking. Yet, we do not understand why these survivors may have social difficulties. We need to understand this in order to find the best way to treat these problems. The goal of the current study is to identify some of the risk and protective factors that might be contributing to social difficulties in survivors of pediatric ALL. Methods: One hundred survivors of pediatric ALL and 100 survivors of solid tumours who have not received brain-directed therapy will be invited to participate and complete tests that will assess aspects of their social function. Their parents, teachers and classroom peers will also complete measures designed to assess the social function of survivors of pediatric ALL compared to survivors who have not received brain-directed therapy. Expected Results: This study will identify some of the factors related to the social function in survivors of pediatric ALL. This will help us learn to better identify which survivors may be at greatest risk of social difficulties and to design better treatments to help these survivors.

column36: Antibody-functionalized nanoparticles for HIV prevention
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), cause of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS), affects 37 million of individuals. Development of HIV prevention strategies is a global health priority to help end the HIV/AIDS pandemic. One of the major challenges is that the virus mutates rapidly but maintains its power to cause AIDS. It changes configuration on its surface and escapes detection by the immune system that would have blocked it otherwise. Earlier test vaccines failed to overcome this problem and did not confer protection against HIV. Molecules of the immune system called antibodies have been discovered in some individuals who have been infected with HIV for several years that are unique compared to other antibodies people usually make. These special antibodies are needed before first exposure to HIV to confer protection. These antibodies are produced by cells of the immune system called B cells, and block most of the HIV types around the world that uninfected people could encounter because they block surface portions of the virus that don't mutate. They also recruit other protective immune functions. These special antibodies can confer protection against infection when directly administered into a patient. Also, the unchanged surface areas are ideal targets for vaccines that can quickly teach the body to block correctly. This proposal combines innovations in molecular engineering, nanotechnology and modulation of the immune system. Specifically, we will investigate how to develop nanoparticles into two HIV prevention products: 1) the special antibodies themselves as stable and long-lasting nanoparticles that can be administered to directly protect against HIV, and 2) a mimic of the natural virus surface that can activate B cells to produce these special antibodies by vaccination. Our studies will provide evidence to advance our HIV nanoparticles into future prevention studies in animals and in human clinical trials.

column36: Establishing an International Core Outcome Set in SAH - What and When to Measure in SAH Research
column37: What is the problem?: In research studies, clinicians and researchers measure specific signs of injury or recovery called 'outcomes' to measure success. In bleeds in the brain from a burst artery (called subarachnoid hemorrhage or 'SAH' for short), there is little consistency in reporting outcomes, literally hundreds exist. We use tools that were not informed by SAH patients and made for use in other diseases. No set of agreed upon measures of outcome in SAH research has been established. As a result, we cannot learn from combining study results and research looking at SAH may be misinformed by not looking at the outcomes that make the biggest difference in the lives of those affected by SAH. Who are we and what will we do?: Our team is made up of patients, families, researchers and clinicians from around the world. Our goal is to create a list of outcomes that all three groups value, agree on, and think should be included in all future research in SAH, called a Core Outcome Set (or "COS"). To create a COS for SAH, we will focus on 'what' outcomes, and 'when', are important to patients/families, clinicians and researchers. How will we do it?: We will achieve this by following a standard and established model with three main steps. First, we will generate full lists of outcomes that each group values by reviewing articles, interviewing people from each group, conducting focus groups, and sending out surveys. Next, each group will rank the outcomes that they think are the most important. We will pool these responses together in the third step and host an in-person meeting with equal representation from the groups. In the end, we will have one prioritized list to be used in and guide future SAH research. Why is this important?: Having a core set of outcomes in SAH that is created by these key groups will help ensure consistency and allow comparisons across studies that are planned with the goal of improving outcomes that matter most to those affected by SAH.

column36: Reducing the activity of the phosphatase STEP to improve memory performance during aging
column37: The majority of older adults will experience some deterioration in cognitive function as they age. Unfortunately, the cellular and molecular changes that lead to memory decline during aging are still poorly understood. The striatal-enriched phosphatase (STEP) is a brain-specific protein highly expressed in regions involved in learning and memory, such as the hippocampus. The physiological role of STEP is to oppose strengthening of connections (synapses) existing between cells (neurons) in the brain. It was shown that STEP acts as a tonic brake on the induction of memory formation and needs to be degraded to enable the activation of cellular and molecular pathways important for learning and memory. Recently, we reported an elevation in the level of active STEP in aged memory-impaired mice and rats, aged rhesus monkeys, and individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment. However, we still ignore if lowering the level of active STEP represents a promising strategy to enhance cognitive performance during aging. The main goal of this project is to determine if reducing the level of active STEP ameliorates memory performance during aging and to determine which proteins are altered after STEP-inhibiting treatment used to improve memory capacities of aged mice. To achieve our goal, we will use genetic and pharmacological approaches to reduce and inhibit STEP function in aged mouse model. These animals will be evaluated in various behavioural memory tasks, and molecular mechanisms underpinning the effects of STEP will be investigated using molecular biology techniques. Currently there is no medication to enhance memory abilities of elderly. This research has the potential to uncover the beneficial effects of decreasing STEP function to improve age-related memory deficits. This project could pave the way to human clinical trials targeting STEP or its substrates to enhance memory capacities of elderly.

column36: Towards eliminating viral hepatitis - Addressing hepatitis B using a multidisciplinary approach
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is one of the most burdensome infectious disease and one of the most expensive infectious disease to prevent and treat. In Canada, 0.4% of the population are infected with HBV. HBV infection can cause chronic infection of the liver (i.e. chronic hepatitis B), that is silent for 20-30 years before about one in five infected people develop liver failure or liver cancer. The Government of Canada has endorsed and committed to the World Health Organization (WHO)'s strategy on viral hepatitis, who has called for a 90% reduction in new HBV cases, a 65% reduction in HBV-related deaths, and treatment of 80% of eligible patients by 2030. To achieve these targets, the government has to consider strategies that include vaccination, screening and treatment, which are expensive for Canada's health care system. As a result, research that assesses how to provide the best quality care with limited health care resources is essential for government agencies who make HBV policies and funding decisions. This study will determine the burden of HBV to patients and the healthcare payer, and will assess the value of integrated HBV interventions to inform policy decision-making. We propose to 1) measure the patients' burden of HBV by surveying patients about their quality of life, the effect of HBV on their workplace productivity and out-of-pocket costs at three liver clinics in Toronto, Calgary and Montreal; 2) develop a computer simulation model that can predict future health outcomes and cost of different integrated HBV intervention strategies (vaccination, screening, treatment); and 3) to identify a set of effective integrated HBV intervention strategies and assess the cost-effectiveness and health equity impact of the most effective strategies. Our research will develop method to better assess the burden of HBV and predict the benefit of interventions, and provide needed evidence to help decision makers to improve HBV care and help Canada achieve the WHO targets.

column36: Sexual Health and STI Prevention For Sexual Minority Men In Suburban Cities
column37: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are at an all-time high in Canada. The Greater Toronto Area (GTA) has an active syphilis epidemic and emerging gonorrhea epidemic among men who have sex with men (MSM). They ways we usually stop STI epidemics are not working; maybe because we have been focusing interventions on MSM in Toronto's urban downtown, where infection rates are highest, and have largely ignored MSM living in suburban and rural areas as part of the epidemic. Our goal is to stop these STI epidemics by improving sexual health care services for MSM in suburbs and rural areas. This requires exploring how MSM from these places manage their sexual lives and sexual health. Our objectives are to: 1.Explore how MSM connect with their social, cultural, racial, ethnic, religious, sexual, and health service communities, and protect themselves from discrimination. 2.Explore how MSM in the suburbs take care (or not) of their sexual health, where they access sexual health services, and how to improve local access and services. 3.Expand STI transmission theory beyond urban cities to include suburban and rural areas. 4.Suggest ways to improve sexual health care for suburban and rural MSM, especially in Peel Region. This qualitative study is a partnership between Region of Peel - Public Health and the University of Toronto. We will interview 60 MSM living in Peel Region (Mississauga, Brampton, or Caledon). We will ask these men about their sex lives, their sexual health, and what it is like getting tested for STIs in Peel. We will suggest ways to improve sexual health services that respect the different identities, communities, and relationships MSM in suburbs and rural areas have to manage. We will host workshops online and in-person with community and health care providers to share results, check our interpretations, get feedback, and maximize uptake of results.

column37: Breast cancer survivors (BCS) living in rural and remote communities do not have access to services to meet their unique exercise, physiotherapy, and nutrition needs. In Phase I we will develop the specific content of HEAL-ME ACE for use with BCS. We will conduct a survey and two focus group sessions with rural and remote BCS residents to collect information on needs and preferences for content and delivery of HEAL-ME ACE. For Phase II, we will conduct a roll-out implementation study across Alberta to test the feasibility and effectiveness of the full HEAL-ME ACE program on exercise, physiotherapy, and nutritional outcomes in BCS living in rural and remote communities. column36: Rescuing beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations from resistance against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens
column37: According to the United Nations and the World Health Organization antimicrobial resistance is the largest threat to public health and economic growth. Currently, the greatest threat to human health derives from three multidrug-resistant Gram-negative priority pathogens that include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii and Enterobacteriaceae. These pathogens have become resistant to all or almost all of our antibiotics. Beta-lactam antibiotics are the most widely used class of antibacterial agents to combat bacterial infections. Beta-lactam antibiotics account for 65% of all prescriptions for injectable antibiotics in the United States. Current strategies to cope with beta-lactam antibiotic resistance are limited to inhibit beta-lactamase enzymes that hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring, thereby inactivating the drug. This can be achieved by combination therapy using a combination of beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor. However, this approach does not address other resistance mechanisms that are prevalent in Gram-negative priority pathogens including outer membrane impermeability and efflux. To overcome these limitations we have developed beta-lactam antibiotic potentiators that restore efficacy of beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens. The overall goal of this project is (i) to develop optimized and safe beta-lactam antibiotic potentiators that overcome resistance and extend the life of clinically approved beta-lactam antibiotics/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens and (ii) to demonstrate efficacy by protecting mice infected with beta-lactam antibiotic-resistant pathogens. Successful demonstration of efficacy and safety of the triple component combination in animal models will serve as a proof of principle to attract an industrial partner with the goal to commercialize novel anti-infective therapies.

column36: Roles for mitochondrial adaptation in fatty liver disease and associated liver cancer
column37: Fatty liver disease affects one third of people in North America. The disease has few symptoms, but over time causes irreversible damage to the liver. Fatty liver disease involves both an accumulation of fat and increased inflammation in liver, which combine to cause permanent damage. Having fatty liver disease increases the chance of liver failure and of developing other diseases such as diabetes, heart problems, and cancer since damaged livers release harmful substances (fats, hormones, and inflammatory signals) into the blood. Diets high in fat and/or sugar and low physical activity contribute to the rising number of people afflicted. There is no cure for the disease and diagnosis is difficult, mainly because we do not understand the triggers. We have shown that low levels of a protein called PGC-1alpha in liver may cause or worsen fatty liver disease and our new studies will help to understand how this happens. We will investigate how low levels of PGC-1alpha decrease the ability of liver to repair damage and whether we can improve this by increasing the levels of this protein in liver cells. We are also investigating whether a common gene variant in PGC-1alpha is associated with the incidence or severity of the disease in humans. Identifying the cause of fatty liver disease will help to discover ways to diagnosis patients early and to design more effective treatments.

column37: One in 10 Canadians suffer from kidney disease. Improving the health of people with kidney disease requires effective partnerships between patients, researchers, doctors, and policy makers. Our Ontario-wide research program (ICES KDT) has been building these partnerships for seven years. Together, we conduct research to improve the health and experiences of people living with kidney disease. We are partnering with the Ontario Renal Network to conduct research that will focus on the issues that matter most to people living day-to-day with kidney disease. We will begin by conducting timely and effective research that will inform the effective use of health care resources in four areas: Mental health for kidney disease patients, prescription drug safety, kidney disease in First Nations communities, and kidney transplantation. column36: Heterogeneity in placental pathology leads to pregnancy pathology
column37: The placenta is the essential supporting organ of pregnancy. The placenta transfers nutrients from the mother to the fetus and sends signals to the mother to increase blood flow and glucose levels to support the developing fetus. The placenta is formed by repeating units called lobules. The total number of lobules is variable, but on average there are about 15. When there is a problematic pregnancy, the placenta is malformed. However, some lobules can still be healthy. How some lobules are normal, and other misformed is poorly understood. Additionally, it is not known how many lobules are required to be misformed before the fetus and mothers health is at risk. In this research project, we propose to collect placentas from different diseases of pregnancy, including preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction to understand the relationship between illness and the number of malformed lobules. In our past work, we noted that there are different kinds of malformations and that sometime these may co-occur in the same placenta. We will also measure the expression of genes in malformed regions compared to healthy areas to find genes that may contribute to disease. Additionally, we will make a detailed examination of the placenta's structure in the cotyledons and relate this to changes in the genes. We think that these genes could be used to test pregnancies for disease and to investigate as ways of treating illness.

column36: Ectopic reactivation of normally silenced germ cell programs contributes to genomic instability, carcinogenesis and cancer progression in Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphomas (CTCL).
column37: Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (CTCL) is the most common lymphoma of the skin. Despite recent advances, this lymphoma remains difficult to diagnose (time to diagnosis ~6 years) because it mimics other common skin rashes such as eczema and psoriasis. It is also not possible to predict which patients with early stage CTCL will progress to advanced stages. Furthermore, advanced CTCL remains difficult to treat with a median survival of only 2-4 years. Hence, new diagnostic/prognostic markers and novel therapeutic targets are urgently needed to aid the medical management of this cancer. We showed that a number of programs that are usually only present in germline tissues (testis/ovaries) are abnormally re-expressed in CTCL. We are proposing to study how reactivation of these genes/programs (e.g., LINE-1 retrotransposition, cancer testis/meiosis regulatory genes) arises contributing to genomic instability, CTCL cancer development and progression. Since these programs are usually not expressed in healthy somatic tissues, their upregulation could be used as a diagnostic marker. Also, since these genes likely promote cancer progression, their expression in early stages may serve as a harbinger for an aggressive disease requiring systemic therapy. Finally, activity of several of these genes is likely central to cancer cell division/survival and, hence, targeting them may lead to novel therapies for CTCL patients. In the proposed grant we will study expression/activation patterns for these genes, their regulation and molecular function in CTCL, determine how they could be used as novel diagnostic/prognostic markers and exploited as therapeutic targets. This project will produce a reliable set of markers that will help shorten the time to diagnosis and help distinguish CTCL from other benign skin rashes; select prognostic markers that will identify early stage patients requiring aggressive therapies and define how these important genes/proteins could be targeted to treat CTCL.

column36: Mapping cellular and extracellular white-matter changes in aging using MRI: Towards clinical translation
column37: The white matter is the information highway for the brain. Microstructural degeneration in the white matter has been known to occur in normal aging, and has been associated with cognitive decline and the potential development of dementia. Scientists have mostly been monitor these changes using diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). However, DWI currently does not provide enough details about what type(s) of changes the white matter undergoes, which limits our understanding of the brain-aging process. Specifically, most researchers are still unable to quantify the amount of extracelluar water in the white matter, which can be a useful indicator of early changes in the brain. In this work, we will validate and optimize a new technique for mapping extracellular water noninvasively in humans. In addition, we will apply this technique to the study of aging, made possible by collaborations with large international studies of aging (the US and UK). The proposed work may drive a paradigm shift in clinical assessment of white-matter health and open the possibility for new clinical questions regarding brain health. These questions will be critical for understanding the neuroinflammation process, enabling clinicians to push the limits for early intervention to delay or even prevent neurodegeneration in dementia.

CI includes decline in memory, thinking speed, attention, and planning abilities and can be associated with significant reduction of patient's quality of life and employment potential. Identifying patients with a high risk of CI and those who are likely to have severe CI overtime will enhance the management of the disease and its progression. Ultimately, our project can help alleviate the burden of disease due to CI and improve the overall quality of life among patients.

column36: Pathogenic roles of platelets in sepsis.
column37: Billions of platelets patrol blood vessels on the ready to prevent the loos of blood when a vessel is injured. The prevention of bleedings is the primarily recognized role of platelets, known since their first description in the late 19th century. When microbes such as bacteria enter the blood circulation, it generates multiple reactions such as fever, loss of blood pressure, alteration of heart rate and respiration. During blood invasion by bacteria, called sepsis, it is recognized that the platelet number diminishes dramatically. Moreover, platelets form aggregates in blood vessels during sepsis. However, how exactly platelets contribute to the pathogenesis in sepsis is not fully understood. We recently developed a novel mouse model of sepsis. In this model, we observed the formation of platelet aggregates in lungs and brain, and we noticed a dramatic reduction of platelet number in circulation. Herein in this application, we wish to utilize our model to determine how platelets may contribute to sepsis pathogenesis and we wish to interfere in the process. For this, we will use compelling mouse models of blood infections (sepsis) and we will administer drugs that target platelets. Using genetic and pharmacological approaches, we wish to improve the success of the therapies to combat infections. At the end of this project, we will have identified how platelets modify responses in blood-borne infections and how manipulating platelets can improve success in clinic.

column36: The physiological, molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying lateralization of motor control
column37: Lateralization of motor control refers to the ability to perform asymmetric and unilateral movements, and is essential for activities such as coordinated hand movements and walking. The right and left sides of the nervous system communicate through crossing fibers. Defective lateralized motor control can result in mirror movements (MM), involuntary movements that mirror voluntary ones on the opposite side of the body. In 2010, we reported that MM can result from mutations in DCC, a gene critical in guiding developing axons to the nervous system midline. We have assembled the world's largest cohort of MM individuals (n=90). 60% carry mutations in DCC and 40% are genetically unexplained, suggesting that many more MM genes remain to be discovered. Furthermore, though DCC deficits in animals result in locomotion deficits, the role of DCC in human gait circuitry and motor control of legs has not yet been explored. Our unique MM cohort provides an exceptional opportunity to study the physiological, molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying lateralization of motor control. We will: 1-Identify novel genes important for lateralization of motor control by genetically studying our MM cohort. 2-Functionally assess the role of novel MM gene mutations using in vitro and mouse experiments. We hypothesize that the majority of novel genes will have a role in midline axon guidance and DCC signaling. 3-Investigate the role of DCC in human gait patterning. We will use biomechanical and electrophysiologic approaches to investigate left-right coordination and motor tract lateralization abnormalities in DCC individuals. This study will (1) expand understanding of the physiological and molecular basis of lateralization of motor control, axon guidance and circuit formation, (2) decipher the effects DCC deficits on human gait circuitry, and (3) identify novel MM genes.

column36: Role of neutrophils in liver fibrosis
column37: Chronic inflammation and fibrosis or scarring are the first triggers of cancer in the liver. Liver fibrosis occurs in response to injury like inflammation due to infection or fatty liver disease where high levels of collagen deposits in the liver leading to stiffness or fibrosis and gradual loss of liver function. The immune system, specifically different subsets of white blood cells produce immune mediators (cytokines) that may increase or decrease the inflammation in the liver and the progression of liver fibrosis. We and other groups have identified a cytokine known as IL-17 as a key accelerator of liver fibrosis. We have also identified a subset of white blood cells known as "neutrophils" that produce IL-17 and that are increased in advanced fibrosis. In this proposal we are interested in understanding how these neutrophils go to the liver during different types of injury and whether different subsets or types of neutrophils can have different functions or play different roles during early versus late stages of liver injury and fibrosis. We would also like to know where these neutrophils are located in the injured liver and how they interact with the different liver cells. Finally, we would like to see if blocking the activity of these neutrophils can stop or delay liver fibrosis. To achieve these goals, we will use a combination of imaging techniques and assays to examine these cells in liver tissues from patients at different fibrosis stages as well as mice. We will also use genetically modified mice lacking the capacity to produce IL-17 and to examine whether they will develop fibrosis at the same rate as normal mice or not and what are the other cells implicated. The results obtained will guide the development of new treatments to stop liver fibrosis and prevent cancer.

column36: Targeting 14-3-3zeta to promote human pancreatic beta-cell proliferation
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a devastating disease caused by the death of insulin-producing pancreatic beta-cells by our own immune system. There is no cure for T1D, and current treatment involves daily injections of insulin to keep blood glucose levels with a healthy range. It is generally thought that patients with long-standing T1D do not have any beta-cells, but numerous studies have now identified the presence of residual beta-cells. This raises the question of whether it is possible to coax these remaining beta-cells to expand in number, which would remove the need for daily insulin injections. Ultimately, this could represent an effective treatment for T1D. The pathways that control human beta-cells proliferation are very complex, and they require precise and accurate actions of numerous proteins at specific times and places within the cell. Currently, the identity of factors that coordinate these proteins in the human beta-cell is not known, but specialized proteins called molecular scaffolds are logical candidates, as they coordinate the actions of proteins within cells and have the ability to control cell growth. Previously, we reported that molecular scaffolds belonging to the 14-3-3 protein family are essential for the regulation of metabolism, and they are important in regulating the survival and growth of mouse beta-cells. Mice lacking 14-3-3zeta in all cells have significantly higher numbers of beta-cells, in addition to better glucose control. This raises the question of whether one can specifically target 14-3-3zeta in human beta-cells to increase proliferation and treat diabetes. This will be tested by first determining the precise roles of 14-3-3 proteins in human beta-cells, followed by developing gene-targeting approaches to reduce 14-3-3zeta function in human beta-cells to stimulate their proliferation. Ultimately, it is the over-arching goal of this proposal to see whether it is possible to stimulate the growth of human beta-cells to cure T1D.

column36: Diagnostic and predictive biomarkers for Frontotemporal Dementia with TDP-43 pathology
column37: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a devastating disease, characterized by profound changes in behavior, personality, language and movement. It is the second most common cause of dementia under the age of 70 years, affecting approximately 50,000 North Americans. Almost half of FTD patients have a positive family history, often with a very strong inheritance pattern. Recent advances in our understanding of the genetic abnormalities and pathology that underlie FTD provide a basis for the development of the first disease-modifying therapies. Unfortunately, clinical testing and implementation of FTD treatments are severely hampered by a lack of useful biomarkers and understanding of the natural history of the disease. Over the past decade, we have established the largest, well-characterized cohort of familial FTD subjects in Canada and one of the most extensive collections of FTD genetic and neuropathological material, worldwide. This unique cohort of participants with genetic mutations are at risk of developing the disease, and provide us the opportunity to examine changes in brain scans and body fluid chemistry at the earliest stages of disease when treatment is likely to have the greatest impact. This valuable resource, together with our team of experts in clinical, imaging, and biochemical research, will allow us to develop new diagnostic tests and provide rational therapeutic approaches for this currently untreatable disease.

column36: Criminalization, Public Health and Incarceration - A participatory qualitative and digital storytelling investigation of the experiences of cis and trans women living with HIV
column37: Cis and transgender women living with HIV women living with HIV are over criminalized and overrepresented in Canadian prisons. This is especially true for women living with HIV who face additional health and social inequities, including poverty, housing instability, racism, and illicit substance use. Despite recent advancements limiting the use of criminal laws in governing HIV non-disclosure in Canada, emerging research reveals that coercive public health interventions have the potential to further criminalize women living with HIV. Under public health law, failure to comply with HIV treatment regimens can result in imprisonment. Among the Canadian prison population, women are more likely to report living with HIV compared to men with incarcerated Indigenous women reporting the highest HIV rates. Following release from correctional facilities, women are less likely to be connected to HIV care and experience worse treatment outcomes compared to men. The objectives of the proposed community-based research is to use participatory, qualitative and digital storytelling methods to generate new insights on the gendered impacts of criminalization, public health interventions and incarceration trajectories on the continuity of care and social inequities among WLWH. The ultimate goal is to inform HIV law reform, best practice guidelines for public health authorities and women-specific interventions to reduce the negative effects of criminalization and incarceration among women living with HIV. This work is firmly rooted in Greater and Meaningful Involvement of People living with HIV/AIDS principles.

column36: Defining the role of ER stress in glomerular disease: identification of new therapeutic and diagnostic targets
column37: Glomerular podocytes are vital in maintaining the structure and function of the glomerulus, the filtering unit of the kidney. Intact function of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is important for protein homeostasis in the podocyte, including production of components of the slit diaphragm, adhesion complexes and glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Disorders of ER function can contribute to disease. Diseases of the renal glomerulus, especially those initiated by immunological processes ("glomerulonephritis"), account for approximately half of the causes of chronic kidney disease in Canada. Treatment of patients with kidney disease with dialysis and kidney transplantation has resulted in a dramatic improvement in the survival of patients, but at a large cost to the Canadian economy. Fundamental research into the disordered mechanisms that lead to glomerulonephritis is essential to the understanding of these diseases, an understanding that will ultimately lead to therapy and prevention. In this proposal, we will study abnormalities in cellular pathways in the glomerulus involving the ER, and establish how ER function allows podocytes to maintain glomerular function in the normal kidney and in glomerular diseases. We will establish urinary biomarkers of ER diseases. The proposed studies will use a tissue-culture system and animal models of glomerulonephritis to characterize abnormalities contributing to the cause of the disease. The elucidation of basic mechanisms of the causes of disease, and testing of therapies in preclinical (animal) models is likely to be the most productive approach to the development of treatment strategies to human glomerulonephritis. The results of the proposed studies will eventually lead to improved strategies for therapies of kidney disorders.

column36: Preclinical safety, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and efficiency of microRNA oligonucleotides for Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a severe, progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing dementia and ultimately death. Unfortunately, there is no cure for AD and current medications only provide limited and temporary relief. In recent years, much attention has been focused on micro-RNAs as novel therapeutic agents for complex diseases such as cancer and diabetes. This type of small RNA (like DNA) has a strong impact on protein networks important for brain health. As of yet, however, it remains uncertain if and how micro-RNAs can be used to treat neurodegenerative disorders such as AD. For more than a decade, my research team and others have gathered substantial evidence pointing to one particular micro-RNA, namely miR-132, as a prime candidate to treat, delay, or prevent AD. This is based on multiple studies in cells and mice where the delivery of miR-132 can, for instance, restore disease symptoms, including memory. Our goal now is to perform the necessary pre-clinical tests to advance miR-132 to clinical trials in humans. For this, we have already developed specialized tools and methods to deliver miR-132 molecules directly into the brain of mice and non-human primates (monkeys). The next steps involve the biological characterization of these molecules following treatment (e.g., bioavailability, degradation, target engagement). Of course, we will also perform extensive biosafety (toxicology) tests in both animal models. Overall, these cutting-edge studies will provide an essential basis for the development of micro-RNA therapies for AD and related neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Y-STROKE NEEDS Study: Psychosocial and Occupational Outcomes in Young Adults with Stroke
column37: One third of brain strokes occur in people younger than 65 (working population) and these rates are increasing. Current research suggests that young patients recover well physically, but have challenges with emotional recovery, social relationships and employment after stroke. It is estimated that only ~ 50% of young stroke survivors return to work and that, of these, ~ 25% require modifications in the workplace. There have been very few studies that have focused on patients' experiences in their post-stroke psychosocial and occupational recovery. This is a patient-reported outcome measures study with two specific aims:1. To assess health-related quality of life (emotional, social and work-related functioning) in young stroke survivors; 2. To guide future development of interventions to improve quality of life after stroke; based on patient reported outcome measures, needs and preferences. Our patient-oriented study methodology is innovative and based on two interlinked phases, which combine both quantitative (measured through surveys) and qualitative (measured through interviews with focus groups of young stroke survivors) methods as described above. It focuses on a young stroke population, whose needs are often overlooked in stroke research. The research that does exist suggests that the effects of stroke in younger people are often "invisible", but greatly impact their quality of life and functioning. We know that people's experience in stroke healthcare impacts their treatments, but also the functional outcomes. So, this connection between physical and mental health is unknown in stroke recovery, thus there is a big importance in understanding people's lived experience to be able to improve their post-stroke care. The study is unique because the investigators are from a variety of disciplines including a neurologist and a psychiatrist and other health professionals (rehab, speech) who work together to care for young people with stroke and mental health issues.

column36: Central mechanisms of opioid withdrawal
column37: Opioid medications provide potent pain relief in the short-term, but their long-term use can cause serious adverse effects. A major problem is that chronic opioid users experience debilitating withdrawal symptoms when attempting to stop or reduce their opioid medications. In an attempt to curb withdrawal, these individuals continue to use opioid drugs. A misconception is that only illicit opioid use or "opioid addicts" are susceptible to withdrawal. The careful use of prescription opioids can also lead to significant withdrawal symptoms. Optimal therapies for opioid withdrawal are unavailable. Our team recently discovered that immune cells (microglia) residing within the brain and spinal cord play an important role in opioid withdrawal. These immune cells communicate with other cells through specialized channels (pannexin-1), which are like gates that open and close to allow passage of chemical signals. Blocking these channels in the spinal cord alleviates withdrawal without diminishing the pain-relieving benefits of opioid medications. We have new data that pannexin-1 channels gate activity within the locus coeruleus, an area of the brain that communicates with the spinal cord by sending specialized projections containing a chemical (norepinephrine). This proposal addresses exciting new questions about how pannexin-1 channels modulate specific circuitry in the brain and spinal cord that are important for opioid withdrawal. Using advanced cellular imaging, biochemical, and behavioural approaches, experiments will also deconstruct the machinery by which norepinephrine enhances pannexin-1 activity and its impact on microglia signaling. Finally, we will translate this detailed mechanistic understanding into the development of next generation, more potent pannexin-1 targeted drugs for treating opioid withdrawal.

column36: Understanding Restriction of Herpes Simplex Virus Replication by Upstream Binding Protein
column37: Herpes simplex virus causes not only the common cold sore, but also serious eye infections, and in some cases encephalitis. Furthermore, newborns and those with weakened immune systems are particularly at risk for serious complications. Cells have evolved protection mechanisms to fight against viral infections, and in response, viruses have evolved to produce factors that overcome these mechanisms. We are interested in understanding the intricate relationship between herpes simplex virus and the host cell. We have discovered a new cellular factor that counters herpes simplex virus replication. The object of this study is to understand how this factor works, and also how the virus manages to propagate despite this antiviral system. Herpes simplex virus is the prototypic herpesvirus. Results from this project will not only contribute to our understanding of herpes simplex virus infections, but may also be relevant for infections by other human herpesviruses such as varicella zoster virus, which causes shingles, and the cancer-causing herpesviruses Epstein Barr virus and Kaposi Sarcoma virus.

column36: Host and Viral Determinants of HCV RNA accumulation
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a global health problem that affects 71 million people worldwide, including over 250,000 Canadians. HCV-infected individuals typically develop a persistent infection that leads to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, steatosis and liver cancer. Currently, there is no vaccine available and although effective antiviral treatments exist, cost and treatment accessibility remain barriers to HCV elimination. To establish an infection, HCV commanders many different factors in our cells. In healthy cells, small molecules, called microRNAs, restrict how much our genes are expressed. HCV co-opts a liver-specific microRNA and uses it to amplify itself. Clinical trials using inhibitors of the microRNA, revealed that preventing the virus from accessing this microRNA may be an effective treatment option. We have preliminary evidence that suggests that HCV uses this microRNA to promote viral protein production and genome stability. The focus of this research is to investigate how HCV uses the microRNA to its own benefit and to identify other human factors that the virus uses to amplify itself in the liver. We will also investigate the mechanisms of resistance-associated variants isolated from patients who underwent miR-122 inhibitor therapy. This research will provide us with insight into mechanisms of microRNA-mediated enhancement of viral replication and may reveal novel antiviral targets. Moreover, as more microRNA-targeted therapies enter the clinic, this work will help to reveal mechanisms of drug resistance that could be applicable more broadly to microRNA-based therapies.

column36: Role of the cytoskeletal adaptor protein leupaxin in immune response regulation
column37: Killer cells of the immune system are important for eliminating most virus infections and serve as a natural defense against tumor cells. We want to understand how killer cells crawl through the body to seek and destroy infected cells and cancer cells. We predicted that a particular protein called leupaxin would be important for controlling either the migration or function of killer cells. We showed that leupaxin localizes to the front end of migrating cells and to the contact zone where killer cells bind to their target cell, consistent with a role for leupaxin in these processes. To directly test its role, we generated a model system where the leupaxin was genetically deleted so that we could study immune responses to viruses and to cancer in its absence. Our preliminary data show that deleting leupaxin causes less severe symptoms in response to influenza virus infection. This was surprising as we predicted the response would be worse. Many of the symptoms of influenza infection are related to damage caused by immune cells responding to the virus and not due to the virus itself. While killer cells contribute to the clearance of influenza virus, too many of these cells could cause some of the symptoms associated with influenza infection. Our hypothesis is that leupaxin contributes to the entry or retention of killer cells and other cells that promote damage in the lungs. By having fewer cells, virus may still be eliminated efficiently, but with less severe disease. To test our hypothesis, we will examine numbers of killer cells and relevant cells in the lungs before and after infection. We will also use genetic mechanisms to pinpoint the function that is responsible for the improved recovery from influenza infection. We want to understand how this improved response occurs to potentially translate the results into therapeutics to improve the outcome after influenza infection, and perhaps other inflammatory diseases.

column36: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) vs. Health Enhancement Program (HEP) Active Control for the Treatment of Late-Life Depression: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: In Canada, depression affects more than 300,000 adults over the age of 60, which costs the healthcare system an estimated $5 billion each year. Late-life depression (LLD) is associated with more deaths, more physical health problems, memory and cognition problems, and brain degeneration. What's more, LLD is hard to treat, as many people will not respond to treatment and many will stop taking antidepressant medication due to negative side-effects. Unfortunately, common non-medication treatments like cognitive behavioural therapy are often inaccessible because of long (6-12 months) wait times and high costs. Recently in our previous pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT), we found that an 8-week group mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) program improved depressive symptoms more than regular LLD treatment (i.e. antidepressants and/or support counselling). Now, a larger scale RCT is required to compare MBCT to an active control group. In this present CIHR study, we will compare the effects of MBCT versus an active control group, Health Enhancement Program (HEP), to see if it improves symptoms of depression in older adults. We will recruit 213 patients who will be randomly assigned to 8-weeks of either MBCT or HEP. We will observe whether these treatments improve symptoms of depression as well as brain structure/function and memory/cognition. Currently there is a lack of affordable non-medication treatments for LLD that can be scaled to reach many people. If successful, MBCT may be a potential solution to this gap in treatment options, as it is easily given in groups and is well-tolerated by older adults with LLD.

column36: Role of vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation in beta cell and diabetes
column37: Vitamin K is an essential micronutrient known to regulate the activity of proteins implicated in blood coagulation and mineralized tissues. Recent clinical observations in humans suggest that partial vitamin K deficiency might be linked to the development of diabetes. However, the biological mechanism by which vitamin K may influence diabetes remains unknown. Beta cell is a unique cell type of the pancreas responsible for the production of insulin. Diabetes is caused by a reduction in the number of beta cells or by a decrease in their capacity to secrete insulin. This research project aims at understanding the function of vitamin K-dependent proteins in pancreatic beta cells and its potential link with the development of diabetes. Our approach includes the use of genetically modified mice lacking the components of the vitamin K cycle in pancreatic beta cells. We will analyze these animals to determine the role of vitamin K in protecting beta cells from cell death, and in promoting their proliferation and function. We will also study the interaction between vitamin K and the endoplasmic reticulum stress in human and mouse beta cells. Finally, we will test if vitamin K can improve or prevent diabetes in pre-clinical mouse models. Altogether, these studies will allow us to understand how vitamin K is implicated in the biology of beta cell and how partial vitamin K deficiency contributes to the development of diabetes.
