column36: Resistance to established and new RET oncogene inhibitors
column37: The biggest road block to curing cancer is drug resistance. This phenomenon occurs when a rare cell, among the billions that make up a tumor, randomly acquires an alteration that renders it insensitive to a drug that kills other tumor cells. The resistant cells gradually multiply and the cancer reappears, but is now resistant to first line therapy. It is thus critical to understand mechanisms of resistance to deduce new strategies to kill these recurrent cancers. Through application of cutting edge screening technology we have identified how thyroid and lung cancers develop resistance to drugs that inhibit the RET oncogene. Here, our goal is to deduce the extent to which these findings apply across RET driven cancers, to understand in more depth how these networks cause resistance, and to test drug combinations that we predict should kill cells that now resist first line therapy.

column36: Deciphering Neisseria pathogens cell envelope evolution: optimisation for virulence or Achilles' heel of N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae?.
column37: The Neisseria genus is composed of bacteria that all evolved to colonize the mucosa of many mammals and that are all obligate symbionts of their respective hosts. In humans, the majority of species reside in the oral cavity or the nasopharynx but evolution has also permitted the adaptation of a few species from this oral ecosystem to the urogenital tract mucosae. If the majority of species have strictly developed a commensal type of symbiosis with humans and are rarely implicated in human diseases, two species named Neisseria meningitidis (causing meningitidis resulting in 0.15 million of death/year) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (causing gonorrheae and infecting around 88 millions persons/year), constitute major human threats. Several invasive strains of N. meningitidis (serogroups A, C, W, Y and nowadays B) are the target of vaccination. However, there is no vaccination available for N. gonorrhoeae. In both cases, a limited number of antibiotics are available which help reduce death rates and other complications. Unfortunately, N. gonorrhoeae is evolving rapidly and is generating resistance with a high risk of worldwide emergence of untreatable infections. This serious situation makes research of novel molecules against N. gonorrhoeae one of the twelve priorities of the WHO. It is therefore crucial to understand the factors that led to the emergence of pathogenic strains from a non-pathogenic commensal ancestors but also develop new avenues of treatments to fight these bacteria. In this proposal, we will focus our research on the cell envelope of these two pathogens. We will try to describe the evolutionary events that led to a specialization of this structure for the symbiosis and pathogenesis, dissect the forces that naturally selected these cell-envelope changes in different infectious contexts which will subsequently help the exploration of how we can target this structure to fight these pathogens.

column36: Genetic Determinants of Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a heterogeneous group of disorders that result in irreversible scarring over time. CKD affects more than 750 million people globally, and results in more than 1 million deaths. Large, granular datasets have now been gathered from world leading cohorts in Canada and the United States, with growing expertise to apply novel biomarker combinations collected at different disease time points with clinical traits. In this proposal, we will focus on a leading cause of CKD called Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and genomics, which is emerging as one tool to identify disease subtypes according to mechanism and treatment outcomes. We have recently reported that a series of rare genetic variations account for ~11% of adults with FSGS, leaving the remaining cases unexplained. We also find that within these genetic cases, different gene categories influence disease progression. However, the cumulative effects of common, subtle changes (called single nucleotide polymorphisms or SNPs) in many genes that are important for normal kidney function have not been explored in FSGS. We will address this critical knowledge gap. By bringing together leading investigators in Canada and the US, we aim to uncover the effects of common genetic determinants, in isolation and cumulatively, important for disease progression and study their effects on gene expression in a large cohort of FSGS patients (n=6500). There is a large unmet clinical need for mechanism-based therapy and to achieve this goal, precise definitions of FSGS subtypes are required. Genomics has emerged as one tool to successfully stratify patients with heterogeneous diseases like major depressive disorder, coronary artery disease and cancers such as breast cancer that have, like FSGS, been historically heavily reliant on pathology. We intend to apply these same genomic approaches to identify clinically meaningful FSGS subtypes to inform management.

column36: Exercise as a primer for excitatory stimulation study (EXPRESS): A combined exercise and transcranial direct current stimulation intervention for cognition
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a type of dementia that causes problems with memory, thinking, function and behaviour. Currently, a group of drugs called cholinesterase inhibitors are used to improve memory, but have important side-effects such as loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea and sometimes slow heart rates and fainting. Moreover, benefits from these drugs are modest and AD patients eventually worsen even with continued use. There remains a critical need for treatments focused on early stages of the disease, when quality of life is still potentially excellent. While transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; neurostimulation with a non-painful current to the brain) has been shown to improve memory in some people with mild AD with minimal side-effects, recent evidence suggests that tDCS works better when brain circuits are active. As exercise increases brain activity using mechanisms that may support tDCS response, it may be an effective primer given before tDCS. This study will assess whether combining exercise and tDCS can help improve memory in mild AD, and whether this combination improves memory better than exercise alone, tDCS alone, or neither (exercise education only with non-active tDCS). Patients will be randomly assigned to receive either 1) combined exercise and tDCS, 2) exercise and non-active tDCS, 3) exercise education only and tDCS, or 4) exercise education only with non-active tDCS for two weeks. Memory, mood and behaviour, as well as measures of brain activity, and brain and blood vessel health will be assessed before, during, and after treatment. This study may identify a new, non-invasive therapy that preserves memory in early stages of AD, therefore having major health implications.

column36: Accelerating the Spread of Integrated Community-Based Primary Health Care in Ontario
column37: As health systems across the globe continue to engage in primary care transformation, spreading and scaling up effective models of Integrated Community-Based Primary Health Care (ICBPHC) remains a significant challenge. Addressing this challenge requires a shift in how we think about, and address, the questions of why, how, for whom and in what context, an innovation, such as a model of care, can be effective. Over the past six years, our team has taken a rigorous approach to addressing these questions and generating new evidence to support spread and scale up of ICBPHC. Our work identified key elements that enable implementation of high-performing models of ICBPHC and supports evidence from large-scale primary/integrated care transformation initiatives, which show that effective spread and scale up require greater attention to two critical elements: the interplay between innovations and the contexts into which they spread, and how to promote change readiness in individuals doing change work. Our current work builds on and extends prior findings in a 'pre-spread, comparative testing' of a model of ICBPHC, which advances access to team-based care for individuals with complex care needs. Comparative 'testing and revision' of the model has enabled us: i) to learn from variations in performance across sites and contexts, ii) to build capacity for reciprocal learning, and iii) to generate new knowledge about factors enabling successful adoption and potential spread. We are prepared to proceed to the next phase of our research: designing and testing a program to spread this model to new sites and identifying the supports required for successful spread of ICBPHC innovations. Since 2017, Ontario has invested $248.4 million to expand access to primary care across the province. This study will provide new evidence to capitalize on these investments and support effective primary care transformation across Ontario and other Canadian jurisdictions.

column37: Innovative Models Promoting Access-to-Care Transformation (IMPACT) was a five-year research program to improve access to community-based primary health care for vulnerable populations. column36: Adapting an effective health promotion intervention for scale-up: a focus on older adults in receipt of home and community care services
column37: Health promotion through physical activity can effectively enhance older adults' social connections, physical and mental health. Despite this, only 11% of Canadian older adults are active enough to enjoy health benefits. To positively affect the health of populations, physical activity programs that demonstrate effectiveness on a small scale must be scaled-up to reach diverse populations across a variety of settings. With BC Ministry of Health, we designed and implemented a community-, choice-based, 6-month health promoting intervention for older adults called Choose to Move (CTM). We called upon the science of implementation as a guide to effectively implement CTM at larger scale-- in 26 communities across BC. CTM improved physical activity, mobility, social connectedness and decreased loneliness in community-dwelling older adults (n=458). As a next step, we aim to scale-up CTM to target older adults at greater risk - those in receipt of home and community care services. Home and community care services are a lifeline for older adults in BC (and across Canada), many of whom are unable to perform activities of daily living. Thus, we propose to 'reimagine' home and community care services to integrate strategies that support the physical and social well-being of older adults who wish to stay at home. To do so we will convene established and new partners to adapt CTM and co-create an action plan to reach older adults in receipt of home and community care services. Our objectives for this operating grant are threefold. First, we will adapt the CTM intervention and implementation strategies to 'fit' the home and community care context. Second, we will adapt the current CTM implementation/scale-up action and evaluation plans for the home and community care context. Third, we will describe the CTM adaptation process. What we learn in BC can be applied to scale-up of health promoting interventions across Canada and the world.

column36: Deliberative Public Engagement informing Canadian Cancer Care Priority Setting-A Focus on Facilitation
column37: Expenditure in cancer care has risen faster in recent years compared to other areas of health care. This is due to expensive drugs, new therapies, improved access in rural areas and increased cases in the population. There is a concern that the economic burden of cancer spending is not proportional to patient benefits such as increased survival rates or quality of life. Policy makers are turning to public input to guide and distribute scarce resources. Deliberative public engagement is well suited for this ethical and fiscal challenge and has been used successfully as a democratic approach to other health care challenges. In a process of facilitated small and large group discussions, stakeholders share views and values and work collaboratively towards decision making. Despite the obvious importance of facilitation of such events, little is known about the role, techniques and strategies facilitators use to support participants. The public are often asked to make decisions in contentious areas where lived experiences collide. In charged environments, conversations can be unstructured without a skilled facilitator. This proposal seeks to further understand the role, techniques and strategies used by facilitators within the context of deliberative public engagement informing cancer control priority setting processes across Canada. Using a mixed method approach, a specific focus on facilitation will ensure the quality of group exchange is consistent with the principles of deliberation. It will ensure policy recommendations for decision makers are meaningful and representative of participants and ultimately contribute to a sustainable model of deliberation that can continue to guide priorities in Canadian cancer care.

column36: Aging into the 21st Century: A Longitudinal Evaluation of Facilitators and Barriers to Improved Care and Health Outcomes in those Aging with Disability
column37: As a result of medical and technological advancements, individuals with long-term disabilities are increasingly living to middle and older ages, resulting in a growing number of individuals who are aging with disability rather than aging into disability This population has the potential to be sizable, with 13% of Canadian youth and 20% of working age adults reporting at least one disability. The "normative" aging process is associated with higher disease burden, changing social roles, and more complex care needs. Individuals entering old age with a disability face additional difficulties including accessing regular health care, which can result in poor Continuity of Care (COC). COC is concerned with quality of care received over time and is strongly associated with health outcomes. This may be due, in part, to structural factors within and outside of the health care system (e.g., neighbourhood environment). However, this remains an understudied area and the limited evidence in this population precludes insight into how to support successful aging in this population. The overall aim of this project is to examine how features of the social, physical and built environment influence successful aging outcomes and care continuity for those aging with disabilities. To address this research question, we will identify a cohort of individuals with disability from Medicare & Medicaid data (2002-2016), which is the federal health insurance program that provides free health care to those with disabilities. In addition, we will link contextual measures generated from several data sources, indicators of health outcomes and trajectories of care continuity over follow-up. With this research, we aim to identify the contextual facilitators for positive health and care outcomes in this population. Through identifying potential areas of intervention, results can inform public health and clinical policies and prevention efforts to support successful aging for those with disabilities.

column36: Building Resilience through Integrated Knowledge Transfer in Police Organizations: A Case Study Series
column37: Resilience is an individual's capacity to effectively cope with extreme stress and persist through adversity, and is an important concept for police officers who are repeatedly exposed to potentially traumatic events and at increased risk for psychological injury. The consequences of these occupational exposures can include physical and mental illness, with significant direct and indirect costs. The current project will expand the definition of resilience to conceptualize it as an ecosystem comprising personal, family, and workplace factors, recognizing events in either of the three categories can impact individual officer resilience. Using an integrated knowledge translation case study design, this study will work with police agencies to develop and deliver training, examine organizational policy and procedure, and implement the Canadian Psychological Standards to build resilience. Individual data will be collected concerning shifts in knowledge, attitudes and behavior related to mental health and well-being. Police agencies will be the unit of analysis for case studies that will collect a comprehensive suite of data about each department, including organizational goals and work performed towards their achievement, aggregated information on disability and return to work rates, and mental health support mechanisms, policies and procedures. Machine learning analytics will identify similarities in case studies to determine enabling factors for a psychologically safe workplace. Sex and gender as biological and social determinants of health outcomes will also be analyzed. Development of an organizational culture supporting psychological health and reduced occupational stress are expected; individuals will enhance their resilience through increased knowledge and awareness of personal, family and workplace factors impacting psychological health and well-being. All resources and processes developed will be made open to other public safety agencies.

column36: The risk of multiple sclerosis among users of tumor necrosis factor inhibitors: A Canadian population-based study
column37: Thanks to better understanding of the inflammatory process, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) (i.e., a protein in our body that causes inflammation) and its inhibitors (i.e., drugs that suppress the effect of TNF) were discovered. TNF inhibitors (TNFi) are widely used in patients with moderate to severe inflammatory rheumatic diseases (RD, like rheumatoid arthritis) or inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD, like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease). RD and IBD affect approximately 1 million Canadians in total. Even though TNFi are able to improve patients' quality of life, a number of case reports have linked taking TNFi medication to a higher risk of developing multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is a disease that can cause problems with vision, balance, muscle control, and other basic body functions. MS is also associated with a very high healthcare burden in Canada, as it shortens Canadians' life by 6 years, incurs $2 billion in healthcare costs annually, and is most often diagnosed in young adults aged 20 to 49 during critical years of work life. Nevertheless, this issue has not been thoroughly studied. To fill this gap, I will do the following: 1. Find out how common MS is among RD or IBD patients who used TNFi compared to those who did not use TNFi. 2. Find out if RD and IBD patients with longer use and higher dose of TNFi have a higher risk of developing MS. I will use administrative datasets from British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan, with information routinely collected during clinic, hospital, and pharmacy records. The datasets include all RD and IBD patients (120,000 and 70,000, respectively) who received medical care between 2000 and 2015 from four Canadian provinces. I will conduct the studies for RD and IBD, separately. Findings from this work will identify MS risk factors, potentially prevent MS cases, and will positively impact Canadian public health, global health and new drug discovery.

column36: Carcinogenic Transcriptional Aberrations caused by Epigenomic Misregulation
column37: While the genetic information encoded in our DNA is stable, there is a layer of chemical modifications acting on the DNA's organization that can control transcription, or how genetic information is expressed, called the epigenome. The epigenome can be compared to a series of dimmer switches acting on the genome, "turning up", or "increasing transcription" of certain genes, or "turning down", or "repressing transcription" of genes, through different chemical modifications performed by epigenetic regulators either on the DNA itself or on histones, which are DNA-organizational units that package the DNA into structures called chromatin. Epigenetic malfunctions are often seen in certain cancers, and notably in multiple childhood cancers like pediatric glioblastoma or chondroblastoma. For this reason, understanding the effects of epigenetic dysregulation, like how it affects transcription and triggers aberrant transcription events, is key to understanding how these cancers begin and how to improve the efficacy of the treatment of these cancers. However, very little is known about how epigenetic dysregulation affects transcription, and whatever is known was based on unreliable experimental models. This project aims to improve this situation by using a bioinformatics-based approach to identify aberrant transcription initiation events occurring across the genome and understand the mechanism driving these events using a series of datasets obtained from appropriate models that better reflect what occurs in these cancers.

column37: Obesity among teens has immense impacts on physical, mental and emotional health globally. Home environmental factors like parenting practices, including modeling of healthy eating habits, purchase and preparation of nutrient rich foods like fruits/vegetables impact a teen's food choices. These choices influence the type and amount of different foods teens consume, having a role in preventing or supporting obesity. Diets consisting of a variety of nutrient rich foods, such as fruits/vegetables, offer protective effects compared to diets higher in sugar or excess calories. I intend to consider the role that parenting practices have on a teen's nutritional behaviours by examining the impact they have on a teen's confidence and motivation to eat more nutritious foods like fruits/vegetables compared to less health promoting foods such as sugar sweetened beverages (pop, blended beverages, juices or sports drinks with sugar added). Using data collected for a larger study, I will consider a parent's influence on teen's sugar sweetened beverage intake, fruit/vegetable consumption, motivation and confidence to pursue healthy eating behaviours. Details on parental modeling, control and support for their teen's healthy eating will also be analyzed. Approximately 350 parent-teen (12-17 years) pairs were assessed using an online survey in 2018. Mother and father differences will be examined as well as differences between girls and boys. This work will help future teen obesity prevention programs use parent-teen interactions to help motivate and provide teens with the confidence to choose health promoting foods like fruits/vegetables instead of foods like sugar sweetened beverages.

column36: Characterizing the functional relevance of neuronal PAS domain-containing protein 4 (NPAS4) to inflammatory and neurodegenerative processes in models of multiple sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the leading neurological disease in young adults in Canada, and it is second only to trauma as the most disabling. MS is a neurodegenerative disease where immune cells attacks myelin that protects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. This damages their ability to send information and results in nerve cell loss. MS causes disabling symptoms including vision loss, muscle weakness or paralysis, and problems with thinking and memory. Current MS drugs help people with relapsing MS where disease changes between attacks and recovery, but they do not treat progressive MS where disability worsens significantly. This drives the need to identify pathways that not only limit immune attack but also protect against neurodegeneration. Our laboratory found that levels of neuronal PAS domain-containing protein 4 (NPAS4), a key protein in nerve cell health and signaling, changes over time in a mouse model of MS. Importantly, deleting Npas4 protects against disability. Npas4 also directs other genes, many of which remain to be identified. Our project will study the role of Npas4 in disease development and nerve cell protection. Npas4 will be measured in MS mouse models at each disease stage - onset, progression, and recovery. We will identify immune cells and their products that regulate Npas4 and test how deleting or over producing Npas4 impacts nerve cell survival in a culture dish. We will also delete Npas4 during disease development in the MS mouse model to see when it is most important. Overall, this project will give valuable insight into the role of Npas4 as a regulator of neurodegeneration and disability. The goal is to use these findings to identify Npas4-mediated neuroprotective factors that may be targeted to limit disability for people with MS.

column36: Functional characterization of SMG1 variants associated with pancreatic cancer susceptibility
column37: Pancreatic cancer, specifically pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), is a devastating and aggressive disease that is often diagnosed in the late stages. Identifying and validating genes which may put individuals at risk for pancreatic cancer may help to aid in surveillance and early intervention for PDAC. Approximately 1 in 10 cases of PDAC are familial, and while some predisposition genes have been identified, they only account for a fraction of the familial PDAC cases. Recent research in our lab suggests that SMG1 may be a novel PDAC predisposing gene, and my proposed research aims to validate this finding. Guided by SMG1 mutations which have been identified in patient populations, I will use CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology to introduce targeted mutations into SMG1 into an immortalized pancreatic cell-line. The SMG1 protein product will then be characterized for functional properties and for the ability to drive the formation of a tumour. Overall, my work will help to validate SMG1 as a cancer predisposing gene, which could be implemented into screening programs to identify individuals at risk for pancreatic cancer.

column36: Understanding the role of progranulin in neurodevelopment and neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: There is a clear and pressing need to provide support for Canadians living with neurodevelopmental disorders like Fragile X Syndrome (FXS). FXS is the most common cause of heritable intellectual disability, affecting 1 in 4000 males and 1 in 6000 females in Canada. Beyond symptom management, there is currently no approved treatment for FXS. This is partly due to gaps in our understanding of the root causes of this syndrome. A clue was identified recently when it was demonstrated that mouse models of FXS have elevated levels of a protein called progranulin (GRN). Moreover, by reducing progranulin levels in these mice, some of the FXS symptoms were alleviated. To further investigate the link between high levels of progranulin and FXS, we in the Leavitt lab have developed mice that express an excess of progranulin (GRN+ mice). We are characterizing the behaviour of these mice to see if they exhibit the same FXS-like symptoms as mouse models of FXS. Indeed, both GRN+ mice and FXS-like mice show hyperactivity, reduced social dominance, and abnormal repetitive behaviour engagement. To explore how increased progranulin has come to affect the behaviour of GRN+ mice, we will perform an in-depth characterization of their brains. In comparing the brains of GRN+ mice to those from FXS-like mice we will also gain insights into the extent of progranulin's involvement in FXS. Should increased progranulin expression be involved in causing FXS symptoms, this research will facilitate the development of therapeutics that treat FXS by reducing the levels of progranulin in the brain. Independent of determining the extent of progranulin's role in FXS, this research is expected to improve the current understanding of how this enigmatic gene shapes the mammalian brain during development.

column36: Engineering the HIV-1 gp41 pocket to increase rigidity and enable small-molecule drug discovery
column37: Since the start of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, over 77 million people have become infected with HIV and half of those infected have died of AIDS-related illnesses. The proposed research is focused on addressing the need for new classes of anti-HIV drugs that are resistant to the emergence of HIV-1 mutations. Gp41 is a HIV-1 surface protein that mediates fusion with host cells and contains a highly conserved cavity in its structure, referred to as the "gp41 pocket". Currently, there is only one drug that targets gp41 to inhibit viral entry into human cells. This peptide drug (T-20) has limited clinical utility because it has poor bioavailability and requires two daily injections. Literature reports indicate that efforts to identify a small-molecule drug against gp41 have hitherto been unsuccessful. A potential explanation for this is the observation that the gp41 pocket is highly malleable. Our hypothesis is that (1) it is more difficult to identify small-molecule drug leads for a target that is malleable compared to one that is rigid, and (2) a high-throughput screen (HTS) with a rigid target will yield better hit rates which will potentiate the discovery of a new small-molecule inhibitor of HIV-1 fusion. To test this hypothesis, the gp41 pocket will first be engineered to increase rigidity using protein engineering, and then the rigid pocket will be subjected to an HTS. An HTS will identify small-molecule chemicals, referred to as hits, that bind to the rigid gp41 pocket. By studying the binding mechanism of different hits to gp41 we hope to elucidate critical chemical interactions that are necessary for the design of a potent anti-HIV-1 drug. Since the gp41 pocket is highly conserved across HIV-1 strains, a drug that targets the pocket is likely to be resistant to the development of escape mutations. Thus, this research has the potential to improve the health of HIV infected individuals that develop resistance to the currently available antiretroviral medications.

column36: Incidence and healthcare utilization patterns of undiagnosed subrachnoid hemorrhage: a population-based study
column37: Strokes remain a leading cause of death in Canada, with a reported incidence of 400-500 new cases per 100000 person-years. Non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhages (SAH) due to ruptured intracranial aneurysms represent 5-10% of all strokes. SAH remains a devastating condition as the case fatality is still around 50%. Studies that surveyed survivors of SAH, reported that 10-43% of these patients had experienced a severe headache the weeks preceding the diagnosis. Referred to as "sentinel" headaches, many believe these to be undiagnosed SAHs. Retrospective studies on the topic, however, are prone to recall bias and selection bias. To measure the incidence of missed SAH diagnoses, and gain a better understanding of the clinical context in which the diagnoses were missed, our study aims to analyze healthcare utilization patterns of newly diagnosed cases of SAH the weeks leading up to this catastrophic event. To do so, we plan to use administrative data, from the Regie de l'Assurance Maladie du Quebec database, which encompasses 25% of the greater Montreal region. By using International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-9, ICD-10 and billing codes, we will conduct a population level assessment of when these patients presented, whether they went to the emergency room, to their family doctor, or to a walk-in clinic, and which investigations were performed (e.g. computer tomography scan (CT), lumbar puncture (LP)). This study design will allow the inclusion of patients who passed away, and as the data is collected prospectively, will avoid recall bias. Furthermore, our data would provide an estimate of the incidence of cases that a healthcare professional could have potentially altered by early confirmation of the diagnosis ((LP/CT/history taking) and treatment.

column36: Defining the Interplay Between Fetal Sex, Inflammation, and Immune Cell Function in Pregnancy
column37: The placenta is an organ necessary for healthy pregnancy. Important in forming the placenta are specialized trophoblast cells created by the fetus. These cells perform many functions to maintain pregnancy health. Importantly, trophoblasts regulate the mother's uterine immune system throughout pregnancy. Because the fetus is a genetic mix of mother and father, there should be a maternal immune response against the fetus. However, through unknown mechanisms trophoblasts are able to modulate this response and keep the fetus healthy. Without this trophoblast regulation, maternal immune responses against the fetus may result in pregnancy miscarriage and pregnancy conditions such as preterm birth and preeclampsia. Biological differences may be present in pregnancy as a result of the baby's sex, creating different risks for specific pregnancy conditions. For example, male fetuses exposed to infection and/or inflammation have a higher risk for spontaneous miscarriage or pre-term delivery. Because trophoblasts regulate the mother's uterine immune system, male and female trophoblasts may respond differently to processes initiated by infection and/or inflammation. My research will use trophoblasts and uterine immune cells isolated from male/female placental (fetal) and decidual (maternal) tissue for analysis of genetic differences in male and female trophoblasts. As well, my research will test the uterine immune response to male/female trophoblasts infected by a common bacterial stimulus. My research aims to establish new insight into why pregnancies of male or female babies have greater risk for developing specific pregnancy disorders and set the groundwork for future experimental design aimed at deciphering how biological sex of the fetus influences pregnancy health and outcome.

column36: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis on healthy and diseased human hearts
column37: Heart disease is the second leading cause of death in Canada. Coronary heart disease (CHD), the most common form of cardiovascular disease, refers to the oxygen starvation and death of heart muscle cells due to plaque accumulation in the coronary arteries. Increasing evidence suggests that alterations in cellular composition and function are mechanistically responsible for cardiac remodeling and repair during disease. However, the cellular composition in healthy and diseased human hearts are still incompletely known. To understand the cellular and molecular pathophysiology of CHD, I will be comparing healthy and diseased human hearts using single-cell RNA-sequencing(scRNA-seq) technology. This modern technology allows scientist to generate a gene expression profile of individual cells in the heart. A catalog featuring the molecular signature of individual cells will be built for the healthy and diseased human heart respectively, shedding light on changes in cellular dynamics, cell-cell interactions and biological pathways during disease progression. Together, datasets generated will serve as an important reference for further studies in cardiovascular diseases, promoting the identification of novel therapeutic targets in future.

column36: Cardiovascular Risk and Primary Prevention Eligibility of Patients with Premature Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in British Columbia
column37: Rates of cardiovascular (CV) events such as myocardial infarctions or stroke in young adults (younger than 55 years old) has not decreased over the last 20 years. Effective primary prevention is the best way to change this situation. Primary prevention is a series of actions to reduce risk factors and avoid the disease completely. Current screening algorithms for cardiovascular disease (CVD) are effective in identifying individuals in older populations who are at high risk of CVD and who are candidates for preventive therapy. The first step in all these decision-making algorithms is a calculation of CV risk. However, all current CV risk calculators are highly dependent on age and often underestimate CV risk in young people. Consequently, many young adults remain unaware of their high risk of CVD and do not receive preventive treatment. The main objectives of the proposed research are: 1) To assess the prevalence of major CV risk factors such as abnormal lipid levels, diabetes, high blood pressure, and other risk enhancers in the population of young adults who developed CVD in British Columbia between 2000 to 2017; 2) To evaluate how many of these patients had their risk assessed and received primary prevention treatment prior to developing CVD; 3) To use the medical history of these patients and other available data to estimate how many of these patients could not have been identified by currently available calculators and screening algorithms as being at high risk and will not have met current guideline-based criteria for preventive treatment prior to developing the disease; 4) To discover what other parameters should be added to the current assessment tools to make them more effective in finding young patients at high risk.

column36: Therapy induced hypermutation to stimulate immune responses in recurrent cancer
column37: In the battle against cancer, massive amounts of time and resources have gone towards the development of chemotherapeutic agents that act to kill cancer cells, while leaving healthy cells relatively unaffected. Unfortunately, when these drugs are unable to fully eradicate all cancer populations, recurrence can occur which leads to prolonged treatment, increased costs, and further stress on the patient. Due to this risk, it is vital that initial treatment plans take into account the widely varying characteristics of each cancer and give the best chance for complete remission. One way this can be accomplished is through the process of "synthetic hypermutation", which is a gene-drug interaction that gives rise to an unexpected number of mutations in surviving cells. When hypermutation occurs naturally, it is often indicative of positive clinical outcomes due to the increased response of the host's immune system against the cancer cells. The elevated immune response is due to the presence of neoantigens, which are mutated proteins found in tumour cells but not in normal cells. Considering this, the Stirling Lab (BC Cancer Research Centre) hypothesizes that cells can be hypermutated in response to certain genotoxic chemotherapies, creating more of these neoantigens and thereby stimulating the host immune response. My research will involve screening a multitude of drugs and chemicals to determine which will result in the highest mutation rate and consistent generation of mutant proteins in these cells. Ideally, these results will allow clinicians to make informed decisions when deciding between chemotherapies and ultimately lead to improved treatment outcomes.

column36: Achieving health equity for individuals living with HIV in Manitoba: Identifying potential cancer disparities using population-based data
column37: As Canadians diagnosed with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) live longer due to effective antiretrovirals, there is an emerging focus on the control of chronic illnesses, such as cancer. Individuals living with HIV, in particular sexual minorities, those with low income, newcomers, indigenous Canadians, and injection drug users, may be more vulnerable to cancer disparities as these populations already have a greater risk of delayed cancer diagnoses, advanced stage cancer, and poor survival. Equity is a key priority for provincial, national, and international cancer and HIV organizations but, there is currently little research investigating potential cancer stage and survival inequities for Canadians living with HIV. In a cohort of Manitobans living with cancer I will: 1) investigate the association between HIV status and cancer stage at cancer diagnosis, and 2) investigate the association between HIV status and cancer-specific survival. This study will use population-based, linked, and routinely collected health and social data held at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy. HIV cases will be identified using a combination of laboratory, medication, physician visit, and hospitalization data and then linked to cancer cases identified using the Manitoba Cancer Registry. This will be the first Canadian study linking HIV laboratory tests, prescription data, and cancer registry data to investigate cancer outcomes for this potentially vulnerable population. Examining cancer outcomes for individuals with HIV is an important step to advance equity agendas and reduce barriers to achieving optimal health and wellbeing for Canadians with HIV. The methods from this study could be used as a framework for examining other chronic disease outcomes for individuals living with HIV.

column36: The effect of alternative visceral osteopathic treatment on pain and quality of life in patients with non-specific low back pain: A study protocol
column37: Les lombalgies chroniques sont une cause d'incapacite majeure du point de vue psychologique et social et de pertes economiques considerables. Bon nombre de ces lombalgies ne presentent aucunes anomalies pathologiques reconnues leur conferent un caractere non-specifiques. A l'heure actuelle, il n'existe aucun traitement curatif pour ces patients qui utilisent beaucoup de ressources du systeme de sante. Les manipulations osteopathiques viscerales representent une avenue complementaire interessante, mais aucune etude n'a demontre leur efficacite. Ce projet permettra d'evaluer l'efficacite des manipulations osteopathiques viscerales aupres de personnes atteintes de lombalgies chroniques non-specifiques sur les aspects qualitatifs et quantitatifs percu de leur douleur et leur anxiete. l'objectif secondaire sera d'evaluer l'effet de l'empathie du therapeute, telle que percue par les patients, sur ces meme variables. Un essai randomise controle multicentrique sera utilise pour mener a terme ce projet au sein de cliniques osteopathiques de la region de Montreal. Deux groupes de patients atteints de lombalgies chroniques non-specifiques seront recrutes: 1) groupe temoin avec traitements visceraux non-osteopathiques ; 2) groupe avec manipulations osteopathiques viscerales. La selection des participants remplira des questionnaires sur la qualite de vie, la caracterisation de la douleur, l'anxiete et leur perception de l'empathie de leur osteopathe assigne. Les caracteristiques seront analysees au moyen de statistiques descriptives, puis par des analyses de covariances. Cette etude permettra, dans un contexte de professionnalisation de l'osteopathie au Quebec, de soutenir l'integration des osteopathes dans la prise en charge multidisciplinaire des lombalgies chroniques.

column36: Neural underpinnings of pain and cognition
column37: Pain poses the largest health-related burden on society, costing Canadians billions of dollars each year. Chronic pain patients report forgetfulness and impairments in problem-solving and mental flexibility. The cognitive burden of pain could be due to pain acting as its own task with an inherent value, or by simply distracting from a task. If the former is true, the impact of pain can determine its value. If a task has a high reward, pain will not hinder task performance. In a standard cognitive branching task, two competing tasks are presented, one with a high monetary reward for each correct response, and one with a low monetary reward. The introduction of a third task adversely affects the performance in the low reward task. Our lab has shown that moderate pain reduces task performance on the low reward task but not the high reward task, and that pain acts as its own task with an inherent value. The frontopolar cortex (FPC) is a brain region active during the cognitive branching task that selects the concurrent task of highest reward to complete. The FPC also demonstrates abnormal structure and function in chronic pain, which co-localizes pain and cognitive branching. I plan to elucidate the neural mechanisms behind pain-cognition interactions to identify how pain imposes a burden on cognitive resources. I will recruit subjects to complete the branching task during functional magnetic resonance imaging under a 1) Baseline condition 2) Heat pain condition and 3) salience-matched non-painful electric condition. I hypothesize that 1) pain will adversely affect low reward task performance, 2) the FPC will show greater activity during the painful condition than the baseline and electric conditions, and 3) that activity in the FPC will be related to pain intensity.

column36: Clinical Psychology Master's Level Funding
column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a neurological disorder that is associated with a wide range of symptoms, including diminished cognitive function, emotional dysregulation, and fatigue. Unfortunately, there is no cure for MS to date. Nonetheless, recent evidence shows that exercise may have positive effects on symptoms and disease progression. The problem is that there is a lack of research investigating the effects of exercise in a detrimental, sub-population of MS- Primary Progressive MS (PPMS)- using neuroimaging and clinical measures together. The goal of the proposed research is to examine symptom presentations and microstructural features of neuronal connections in a group of patients with PPMS before and after a weekly exercise intervention. This study could have significant implications for the management of MS symptoms and overall improved quality of life. Given that pharmaceutical treatments to delay progressive neurodegeneration in PPMS have been unsuccessful, the proposed study has the potential to change the first-line intervention for individuals with PPMS. If there is evidence that exercise leads to changes in brain structure, paralleled by symptom changes, the knowledge translation to physicians and other health care professionals could ensure that patients with PPMS are encouraged to implement exercise as part of rehabilitation (thereby providing a no-cost, evidence-based intervention). The ultimate goal is to help individuals with MS to build a better quality of life, for instance with reduced fatigue and depression, and increased cognitive function by protecting the brain from the degenerative effects of MS through exercise. This research has the ability to change lives of individuals with MS across Canada and globally.

column36: Reduction of Pftk1 as a novel therapeutic target for Parkinson's Disease
column37: A New Target for Parkinson's Disease Over 100,000 Canadians suffer from Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disease that causes a number of clinical presentations including rigidity and tremors. There are currently medications to help with symptom management, but a cure has yet to be found. One of the hallmarks of PD are aggregates called Lewy bodies, which are found in the brain, and we've recently learned that Lewy bodies are mostly made up of a protein called a-Synuclein (a-Syn). The levels of a-Syn are directly related to disease severity; with higher levels we see increased severity in both humans and model organisms. Based on these findings, lowering a-Syn levels will likely enable us to treat PD patients much better by stopping or slowing disease progression. It is difficult to suppress a-Syn directly, so we're focusing on a protein that controls a-Syn levels, PFTAIRE protein kinase 1 (Pftk1), which can be targeted with traditional pharmaceuticals. When Pftk1 is inhibited a-Syn levels are reduced. A recently produced mouse model, completely lacking the gene to produce Pftk1, shows no sign of abnormalities which may indicate that chronic loss of Pftk1 would be safe for humans. Our first goal is to study these mice to confirm that chronic loss is safe and effective at lowering a-Syn levels. Our second goal is to determine whether partial loss of Pftk1 is sufficient to improve PD presentation by using a PD mouse model that contains half of the genes that produce Pftk1. This partial loss will be a better representation of what a pharmaceutical inhibition would look like. If these results are promising our next step will be to identify and test pharmaceutical Pftk1 inhibitors, with the ultimate goal of finding a medication for PD patients.

column36: Evaluation of Electrocochleography for the Diagnosis of Hidden Hearing Loss
column37: Hidden hearing loss, as the name implies, is a type of hearing loss undetectable by current conventional audiometry. Some individuals present with seemingly normal hearing despite reporting symptoms such as a phantom ringing in the ears (i.e. tinnitus) or difficulty understanding speech in noise. Consequently, clinicians will deem these individuals as healthy, leaving the debilitating symptoms untreated and ignored. I am proposing a project to investigate the efficacy of electrocochleography (ECochG), an electrophysiological measure for cochlear activity, as an objective diagnostic measure for hidden hearing loss. The proposed mechanism underlying this condition is poor neural activity between the hearing receptors (i.e. inner hair cells) and auditory neurons. My project will use ECochG to record the electrical signals from activated hair cells in response to auditory stimuli (i.e. cochlear microphonic; CM), which has yet to be investigated in the case of hidden hearing loss. I will collect and compare electrophysiological data from musicians with high noise exposure and non-musicians with low noise exposure to assess if ECochG will reliably differ between groups. My hypothesis is that the CM will be enlarged and prolonged in the high noise exposure group compared to the low exposure group.

column36: Understanding the cellular and molecular basis of Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell therapy resistance
column37: Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has been a major breakthrough in cancer therapy, and recent clinical trials indicate that it is a potentially life-saving option for the most common form of pediatric leukemia. These clinical trials highlight one of the key questions in the field: why is this form of therapy so effective in some patients, yet ineffective in others? We hypothesize that early treatment failure to CAR T-cell therapy can be predicted by cellular pathways within the patient's T-cells, whereas treatment failure after initial response can be attributed to the clonal evolution of therapy-resistant cancer cells. To address this clinical challenge, we will use a systems immunology approach, leveraging modern high-throughput molecular assays on tumor and immune cells. We have collected T-cells from 71 patients prior to receiving CAR T-cell therapy and performed whole-transcriptome RNA-sequencing on their T-cell subtypes, providing a rich resource of gene expression profiles across patients. Using this data, we will develop a comprehensive atlas of T-cell pathways in therapy-responsive and therapy-resistant patients, allowing us to pinpoint the cellular pathways within these immune cells that allow for effective CAR T-cell therapy. In order to interrogate the mechanism of tumor evasion of CAR T-cell therapy, we have acquired tumor cells from patients prior to CAR T-cell therapy and at the time of relapse. Using whole-exome sequencing, RNA-Sequencing, and ultra-deep targeted Duplex sequencing, we will characterize the changes that occur within the tumor genomes and gene regulation that allow tumor cells to evade immune killing by CAR T-cells. Together, our approach will provide a comprehensive portrait of T-cell and tumor cell contributors to therapy response, and will inform the improvement of future cancer immunotherapies.

column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an incurable disease with a 50% 5-year mortality rate. In PAH, the walls of arteries in the lung become inflamed and thicken, which effectively means less blood can flow through to become oxygenated. The increased resistance to pulmonary blood flow creates back-pressure on the heart, which hinders its ability to pump blood effectively. Our understanding of what triggers the cascade of inflammation in PAH is limited, and because of this, there are no targeted treatments available. My doctoral work will investigate a new theory that dysfunctional immune cells found in the blood that flows through the arteries of the lung secrete factors that mediate inflammation in PAH. As we age, our cells divide and can acquire DNA mutations. In our white blood cells, the accumulation of certain mutations over time can lead to cancers like leukemia. However, since this is a progressive process, there are individuals whose immune cells have started to acquire DNA mutations but who have no overt cancer. That is not to say that these mutations are benign, however. We now know that some genetic mutations render white blood cells dysfunctional by making them secrete more pro-inflammatory molecules than healthy white blood cells. Our lab has found that it is common for PAH patients to have mutations in two key genes. These genes, dnmt3a and tet2, act as a lock and key, respectively, to control which parts of the DNA blueprint are accessible. With a broken lock-and-key system, DNA access, and therefore protein production, can be erratic - in the case of dnmt3a and tet2 mutations, for example, preliminary data suggests that pro-inflammatory proteins are overproduced. For my PhD research, I will characterize exactly how DNMT3A and TET2 mutations in our white blood cells mediate pulmonary hypertension. We may then be able to develop new targeted anti-inflammatory therapies (or re-purpose existing ones) to address the underlying problem in PAH.

column37: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), often referred to as self-injury, is the act of deliberately harming one's body and can manifest in a variety of different forms (for example, cutting, burning, biting). NSSI affects 13-47% of individuals globally and has severe long-term consequences (e.g., suicide attempts, hospitalizations, permanent scarring), making it a pressing public health concern. Most commonly, people engage in self-injury to cope with or change overwhelming negative emotions. Stress-inducing events (such as academic failures or interpersonal conflict) often cause intense and immediate negative emotions. Without healthier emotion regulation strategies in place, experiencing stressful events may become even harder to manage and, among those at risk for engaging in NSSI, increase the likelihood of self-injury. However, current research is limited in its ability to examine the emotional and physiological processes underlying NSSI after experiencing a stressful event. This study is investigating the relationship between stressful events and emotion regulation, as it relates to NSSI, by using subjective (e.g., participant report) and objective (e.g., physiology [heart-rate], behavioral tasks) measurements in real-time as participants go about their day-to-day lives. By better understanding how emotional and physiological states change after a stressful event among individuals who self-injure, mental health providers can better help people identify warning signs and teach healthier coping strategies that may mitigate this dangerous behavior.

column36: Elucidating the Impact of Allergen-Specific B Cell Frequency and Affinity on Allergic Reactivity Using Patient-Derived Antibody Sequences in Mouse Models of Peanut Allergy
column37: Peanut allergy is becoming increasingly common in Canada with serious consequences for Canadians' health. When a person with peanut (PN) allergy ingests PN, they can experience a range of symptoms from discomfort to anaphylaxis, a potentially deadly form of shock. PN allergy is among the most common and severe food allergies, yet it is unknown what drives its development or severity. Allergic symptoms in PN allergy are caused by antibodies. Antibodies are proteins that bind to specific targets with a particular binding strength. They then direct immune responses against their bound target. Antibodies that tightly bind to bacterial or viral proteins protect against infection. However, there are many types of antibodies, not all of which are beneficial. Allergic reactions occur when immunoglobulin E (IgE) type antibodies bind to allergens. Normally, antibody binding strength promotes immune responses, but we have observed the opposite effect for IgE responses. Antibodies are secreted by a type of immune cell called a B cell. Non-activated B cells have antibodies in a receptor form, but only when B cells are activated can they begin to secrete their antibodies. It is not known what activates PN-binding B cells to begin to secrete IgE-type antibodies. I hypothesize that PN-binding IgE responses are promoted when greater numbers of PN-binding B cells with lower PN-binding strength are present. To test this hypothesis, I will use the latest advances in CRISPR-Cas9 genetic editing technology and sequences of PN-binding IgE antibody genes from real PN-allergic patients to generate mice with different amounts and strengths of PN-binding B cells. These mice will then be put through a mouse model of food allergy and the impact of their B cells' PN-binding characteristics will be assessed. This research could reveal why some individuals develop PN allergy and not others and may one day predict the severity of an individual's PN allergy even before it develops.

column36: Brain imaging as a preclinical biomarker of chronic pain
column37: Chronic pain is a debilitating condition in which patients have ongoing pain and perceive normally innocuous stimuli (e.g. light touch) as painful. A major roadblock to progress in pain research and analgesic drug development is that conventional methods of assessing pain in animals are time-consuming and often monitor withdrawal reflexes. Reflexes are generated by spinal cord circuits and thus do not adequately represent the complex pain experience, which has both brain-mediated sensory and emotional features. Global monitoring of brain activity (fMRI, EEG) in humans has identified distinct brain regions that are critical to the pain experience and there have been efforts to adapt these for animal studies. However, these techniques lack the resolution necessary to probe the activity of distinct neural circuits within the brain, making it impossible to correlate activity patterns with behavioural measures of chronic pain. To address this problem, first, I will use powerful imaging techniques to record the activity of hundreds of individually identifiable nerve cells in the brains of awake and freely-moving mice, before, during and after a chronic pain develops. Second, I will correlate the neural activity of pain-processing regions in the brain with non-reflex-based measures of rodent pain using the Mouse Grimace Scale (MGS). The MGS, developed at McGill University, monitors pain and discomfort by scoring facial expression patterns and provides a more objective way to assay pain in mice. To induce chronic pain, I will use the spared nerve injury mouse model of neuropathic pain, which our lab developed. By combining these imaging and behavioural approaches, I expect to identify unique pain-related neural circuit activity patterns, which may serve as biomarkers for chronic pain. A reliable biomarker will allow us to accurately and objectively assess treatment efficacy in preclinical analgesic drug development studies.

column37: In the Canadian health care system, just under 60% of medical learners report experiencing mistreatment, including physical abuse, verbal abuse, humiliation, gender discrimination, and racism. This mistreatment has been linked to increased stress, hostility, and burnout; factors that can lead to diminished patient care. Despite what is known about health professional mistreatment, little research exists on how this environment of mistreatment may affect patients who occupy the same clinical spaces. To investigate this link, the proposed study will explore the experience of patient mistreatment in the Canadian health care system, the environmental factors that may facilitate this mistreatment, and the alignment of these factors with the factors that engender health professional mistreatment. These questions will be investigated through reviewing the academic literature to determine the factors contributing to both health professional and patient mistreatment. This will be followed by interviews with patients with lived experience of mistreatment, and with relevant health system leaders including Directors of Patient Safety and Patient Complaints and lawyers who have dealt with cases of medical negligence; these interviews will serve to refine what was found in the review of the literature. Finally, past patient complaints will be reviewed to assess the utility of the suspected factors in the identification of contexts in which mistreatment is most likely to occur. If utility is demonstrated, these factors could be used to predict settings with high risk for mistreatment, providing the opportunity for preventative action.

column36: Getting to Zero: Catalyzing Community-based Research capacity in sexual and reproductive health among men living with HIV in rural Uganda
column37: Millions of men and women living with HIV around the world want to have children and an estimated half have HIV-uninfected sexual partners. For the majority, achieving pregnancy involves condomless sex, presenting risks of HIV transmission to uninfected partners and infants. A range of available safer conception strategies can support individuals and couples to meet reproductive goals with minimal HIV risk. These strategies include sustained use of antiretroviral therapy with viral suppression by the partner living with HIV and/or pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) by the HIV-uninfected partner, which can eliminate HIV transmission risk during condomless sex. While increasing attention has focused on improving access to safer conception care for women, much less is known about the needs of men. In 2018, we launched a pilot safer conception clinical program in a rural district of Uganda and recruited men living with HIV who reported wanting to have a child in the next year with an HIV-serodifferent pregnancy partner. Our preliminary findings revealed a strong demand, need, and retention in safer conception care. After sharing preliminary findings, community and government leaders in Uganda emphasized three critical next steps: (1) support and enhance engagement of people living with HIV in the research, consistent with the GIPA and MIPA principles; (2) assess 18-month outcomes of men who enrolled in the safer conception program; and (3) pursue future applications in the area of HIV and STBBI research, grounded in community-based research principles. Thus, the overall goal of this proposal is to foster a collaboration between Canadian and Ugandan research and community stakeholders to catalyze community-based research capacity in male-inclusive safer conception research in rural Uganda. With a commitment to reciprocal learning, we will leverage Canadian expertise and experience in community-based research to inform safer conception research and clinical care in Uganda.

column36: Circulating Progenitor Cells and Cognitive Resilience in Cerebrovascular Disease
column37: Memory and thinking problems are common in older adults.The two most common diseases that cause these problems are Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and Vascular Dementia (VaD).Changes in the small blood vessels in the brain are related to these diseases.But for many people, abnormalities in small blood vessels in the brain do not cause memory and thinking problems.We do not know why some people are protected from these blood vessel abnormalities and do not develop these problems.Some cells in our body, called Endothelial Progenitor Cells (EPCs), help to form new blood vessels and repair damaged blood vessels.A larger number of these cells are found in blood when blood vessels are damaged.Healthy older adults who do not have memory or thinking problems may still have abnormalities in small blood vessels which show up on brain images like MRI.We hypothesize that older adults with blood vessel abnormalities seen on brain images may have a higher number of EPCs (blood-vessel-repairing cells) in their blood, which may be protecting them from memory and thinking problems.To test this, we will measure the number of EPCs in the blood of older adults and obtain an image of their brain using MRI.We will also assess whether they develop memory or thinking problems over 2 years.We will then compare the number of EPCs in the blood of older adults who have blood vessel abnormalities to those who have no abnormalities, and test whether the number of EPCs is related to the development of memory or thinking problems over time.If we find that older adults with blood vessel abnormalities have more EPCs and that more EPCs are related to fewer memory and thinking problems, our study may explain why some people who have blood vessel abnormalities in their brain do not develop memory or thinking problems easily.This study will clarify how EPCs and memory or thinking problems are related and may indicate if EPCs could be used as a treatment to delay the development of diseases such as AD and VaD.

column36: Senescent fibroblasts modulate the immune response to pancreatic cancer
column37: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the most common pancreatic cancer (~93%) and the most lethal solid tumor type in Canada, with a 5 year survival rate of 8%. The Canadian Cancer Society estimated 5800 new cases and 5300 deaths due to pancreatic cancer in 2019. Furthermore, pancreatic cancer incidence continues to rise and is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States by 2030. There remains no effective treatment or detection method for this devastating disease and new strategies are desperately needed. The refractory nature of PDAC has been attributed to its unique fibrotic tumor microenvironment (TME), which comprises 70-85% of tumor mass and is known to protect tumors from the effects of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. The PDAC TME is composed of a dense fibrotic matrix and an abundance of Cancer Associated Fibroblasts (CAFs) within a harsh environment. We believe that this harsh environment likely induces damage in the non-mutated CAFs and activates the stress response of senescence, which includes cell cycle arrest and the secretion of immune mediators. While senescent CAFs have been implicated in immunosuppression of skin cancer, their presence and role in PDAC remains unexplored. We have identified senescent CAFs in the PDAC TME of patient samples and mouse models. We hypothesize that these senescent CAFs contribute to immunosuppression and immunotherapy resistance in PDAC. To test this hypothesis, we will first assess the effects of senescent CAF depletion and co-implantation on the growth and biology of tumors in PDAC mouse models. Second, we will identify cellular, secreted, and transcriptional regulators of the senescent CAF phenotypes, to identify actionable molecular targets that can be targeted in PDAC combination immunotherapy strategies. Our work will provide novel insight into the PDAC TME and contribute to much needed progress in understanding and treating this lethal disease.

column37: The intestinal microbiota and its interactions with the host play key roles in the maintenance of intestinal and systemic homeostasis. In addition to the direct interactions between the microbiota and the intestinal mucosa, metabolites produced through the actions of microbial enzymes can elicit biological effects. Dr. Hirota's overarching hypothesis is that chronic inflammatory diseases are, in part, driven by alterations in the composition and/or metabolic output of the intestinal microbiota, resulting in aberrant expression/stimulation of specific xenobiotic and orphan nuclear receptors.

column37: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a medical condition in females where pelvic organs, such as the uterus, bladder or bowel, fall out of normal position and press into the vagina. POP will affect up to half of Canadian women in their lifetime, usually in relation to older age, higher body weight, and birthing children. Affected women often experience urine leakage, physical discomfort, embarrassment, and decreased quality of life. Surgery to correct POP is common, and approaches can be broadly divided into those that keep the uterus intact and those that remove the uterus from the patient's body. At present, we do not have enough high quality scientific evidence on which approach can best fix POP and restore quality of life, nor on the reasons women prefer to keep or remove their uterus during surgery. Our study will follow over 200 patients at the Pelvic Floor Clinic in Calgary, Alberta from their initial visit to 8 weeks after surgery to evaluate health outcomes and compare decision-making experiences between women who choose to keep versus remove their uterus during POP surgery. Our diverse team of doctors, researchers, and patient partners will collect study data using medical charts, questionnaires, and one-on-one interviews. Data on health outcomes will be statistically analyzed, and data on patient experiences will be analyzed by identifying themes across responses. As the Canadian baby boom generation ages, the number of women with POP is expected to increase and research on POP is needed to guide decision-making. Our study will address this need, and will provide women contemplating surgery for POP and their care providers with trusted information on the risks and benefits of each surgical approach. Our findings will also help care providers understand how patients think about, and decide upon, whether to keep or remove their uterus, which may improve how they counsel and educate patients about surgical decisions.

column36: Preventing unnecessary surgeries for endometriosis with the Central Sensitization Inventory
column37: Endometriosis affects 1 in 10 reproductive-aged women, or approximately 1 million women in Canada. It is defined as tissue from inside the uterus (womb), being able to grow as implants outside of the uterus, in other parts of the body. Endometriosis is a common cause of infertility and pelvic pain, including painful periods, painful sexual activity, and chronic pelvic pain. Treatment consists of hormonal medications or surgical removal of the implants. Historically, the endometriosis implants themselves were thought to be the primary cause of pain. However, recent research as shown that in many patients with endometriosis, the primary cause of pain consists of changes in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) -- known as central sensitization -- rather than the endometriosis implants themselves. In these patients with central sensitization, repeated surgery to try to remove endometriosis implants is unlikely to be helpful. The problem is that research methodologies to measure central sensitization are not practicable for the clinical setting. There is a need for a clinical tool that can easily identify central sensitization, thereby helping clinicians and patients to determine when surgery is not likely to be helpful. Recently, the Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI) -- a patient-reported questionnaire -- has been shown to be validly identify patients with central sensitization. In this proposal, we will use the CSI in an ongoing prospective registry for endometriosis. We will determine whether the CSI can predict whether endometriosis surgery is effective or not. A cut-off for the CSI score will be identified, which can be used by clinicians and patients in their shared decision making about whether to proceed with surgery. The goal will be to reduce unnecessary repeat surgeries for endometriosis in women. This will be achieved by promoting the CSI in the national clinical practice guidelines for endometriosis and for pelvic pain.

column37: La vulvodynie (douleur/inconfort vulvaire) est une problematique presente chez 8 a 16% de la population feminine et affecte donc une proportion importante de femmes au Canada. La vestibulodynie provoquee, caracterisee par une douleur a l'entree du vagin lors d'un toucher et/ou une penetration est la forme la plus frequente de vulvodynie. Elle limite la qualite de vie et les relations sexuelles de ces femmes. La vestibulodynie provoquee est souvent traitee par des applications de creme de lidocaine avec des resultats mitiges. Recemment, plusieurs evidences en recherche indiquent que des mecanismes au sein du systeme nerveux central contribueraient a cette condition. La methode de reeducation sensitive (MRSD) est une approche innovante et prometteuse pour le traitement des douleurs qui vise a influencer les mecanismes de perception sensitive du systeme nerveux central. Plus de quatre-vingt professionnels au Canada sont formes a la MRSD, qui a fait ses preuves avec d'autres clienteles presentant de la douleur. Tout recemment la MSRD a ete utilisee avec succes chez des cas de vulvodynies traites dans une clinique en Suisse. Cette methode recommande de diminuer le contact cutane avec la zone douloureuse et d'appliquer progressivement quotidiennement des stimulations confortables. La presente etude controlee et randomisee vise a comparer les effets de la MRSD a ceux de la lidocaine pour la vestibulodynie. Cinquante-deux participantes seront assignees aleatoirement a l'un des deux traitements pour une duree de 12 semaines pour en valider l'efficacite. Les evaluations, avant et apres l'intervention, documenteront les effets sur la douleur, la fonction sexuelle, la perception de changement, les variables psychologiques et la sensibilite vulvaire. Si les resultats sont concluants, les professionnels de la sante auront un nouvel outil pour ameliorer la vestibulodynie provoquee et ainsi ameliorer la qualite de vie de nombreuses canadiennes.

column36: L'impact de l'hypoglycemie neonatale sur le neurodeveloppement des nouveau-nes prematures
column37: Au Canada, 8% des bebes sont nes prematurement (avant la 37e semaine de grossesse). Ceux-ci sont particulierement a risque de developper des problemes visuels d'origine cerebrale (causes par des lesions au cerveau affectant le systeme visuel). L'une des principales causes de ces troubles visuels est l'hypoglycemie neonatale (taux de glucose sanguin trop faible). Bien que celle-ci affecte plus de 30% des nouveau-nes prematures, le lien entre l'hypoglycemie neonatale et les deficits visuels d'origine cerebrale n'a pas encore ete etudie dans cette population. L'objectif principal de notre etude est donc d'evaluer les effets de l'hypoglycemie neonatale sur le developpement du traitement cerebral visuel des nouveau-nes prematures a l'aide de l'electroencephalographie (EEG; technique utilisee pour mesurer l'activite electrique du cerveau). Nous croyons que plus l'hypoglycemie neonatale aura ete importante (en termes de severite, duree et nombre d'episodes), plus les reponses cerebrales associees au traitement visuel seront affectees chez les enfants nes prematurement. Afin de tester notre hypothese, 80 nouveau-nes a terme (apres 37 semaines de gestation) et 120 bebes nes prematurement (entre 28 et 36 semaines) seront evalues. Les taux de glucose seront collectes des la naissance. Puis, les participants seront vus pour des seances d'EEG a 3, 12, 24 et 36 mois. Les resultats de l'EEG seront compares entre les groupes (nouveau-nes prematures avec et sans hypoglycemie neonatale, nouveau-nes a terme) a chaque temps de mesure afin d'evaluer le developpement du systeme visuel des differents groupes durant l'enfance. column36: Instrumented i-GRASP for the assessment and treatment of upper extremity function after neurological injury
column37: Neurological conditions such as stroke and traumatic brain injury can seriously impair one's ability to use their arm and hands for essential activities of daily living. We have previously developed the Graded Repetitive Arm Supplementary Program (GRASP) which has been shown in a multi-site randomized controlled trial to improve upper extremity function after stroke through hundreds of repetitions of the arm, hand and fingers, as well as strengthening exercises. It is utilized in over 3000 sites and is part of the Canadian Stroke Best Practice Recommendations. Under ideal supervisory conditions, the program is effective, but adherence is problematic as it is difficult to keep track of the many repetitions, can be challenging to know how to continually make the tasks harder, and lacks feedback to motivate individuals to do the exercise. I-GRASP will solve these issues by developing an instrumented platform derived from the evidence-based GRASP program where patients will be able to 1) measure their own upper extremity function, 2) improve their function through progressive exercises and 3) and receive feedback to help motivate their progress. Our team is a collaboration between engineer and health care researchers and our partners include a wearable sensor company, a public sector rehabilitation hospital, and a private rehabilitation clinic to ensure the relevance of our product. The proposed technology to measure, motivate and enhance hand function will improve the lives of individuals with stroke and will be applicable to other populations with hand problems. The project will also advance technologies related to smart materials and wearable sensors. Lastly, the research has great potential for commercialization by the industry partner Texavie and to potentially open new markets for rehabilitation technology that can be accessed by health providers and stroke survivors.
