column36: Roles of HcpE and DsbK in virulence of Helicobacter pylori.
column37: Helicobacter pylori (HP) is a bacterium that infects chronically up to 50% of the world's population and can cause gastric ulcers and cancers. It was estimated that HP colonization increases the risk of gastric cancer approximately 10-fold. In 2012, gastric cancer was the 5th most malignant cancer. Because of its high prevalence and the severity of the diseases, HP significantly burdens the health care system. Effectively treating HP infections is key to prevent these serious diseases but current treatments are cumbersome, poorly tolerated by patients, and jeopardized by antibiotic resistance. Thus, we are looking for alternatives. Upon detection of HP, the patient's immune system is activated and produces inflammatory molecules that are supposed to help eliminate the bacterium but also cause collateral damage to the surrounding gastric tissue. Unfortunately, HP can alter the normal function of the immune system so that, despite activation of the inflammatory response, the bacterium cannot be eliminated from the body. As the immune system persists in trying to eliminate the bacterium, the constant production of inflammatory compounds by the immune system damages the gastric tissue and favors ulcer formation or cancer development. Our approach is to study proteins produced by HP that trigger the inflammatory reaction in gastric and immune cells. Preventing the secretion or activity of these proteins should help the immune system regain control and clear the infection. Our study will determine the role of these proteins in inflammation using different types of cells, and will identify protein(s) from gastric cells that our proteins interacts with to perturb the normal function of gastric cells. This could be used to design new therapeutics that can inhibit the interaction between these bacterial proteins and their gastric cell targets. The inhibitors, used alone or in combination with existing treatments, should significantly improve outcomes of anti-HP therapies.

column36: Host response modulation results in altered Ebola virus replication and transcription kinetics in immune-privileged testis, which facilitates asymptomatic and persistent infections that may affect reproductive health and sexual transmission
column37: The current Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has resulted in more than 2,900 infections and 1,900 fatalities, with no end in sight. This outbreak is already the second largest in history; the largest only ended three years ago after causing 11,000 fatalities in West Africa. It appears that Ebola virus disease outbreaks are occurring more frequently and with increasing complexity, taking longer to resolve and affecting more people than ever before. Improved epidemiological surveillance, community outreach, and Ebola virus vaccines and therapeutics are being implemented to combat the current outbreak, yet new infections continue to occur. Efforts to respond to Ebola virus disease outbreaks are complicated because Ebola virus persists in the reproductive tracts of male disease survivors after recovery. Persistent Ebola virus disease infections can last for years, are not detectable in blood samples, and occur in the absence of disease symptoms. Critically, the virus can be transmitted sexually from these survivors, which leads to new chains of transmission and increases the duration and magnitude of outbreaks. In an era where globalization has enabled rapid mass movement of people over long distances, persistent and undetected Ebola virus infections could lead to global outbreaks. Despite the danger that persistent Ebola virus infections pose to public health, these infections are not well characterized; why are there no associated disease symptoms or abnormalities in the afflicted reproductive tract, how does the virus persist so long, and what danger does the virus pose during persistence? My goal is to determine how Ebola virus persists in the male reproductive tract, what effect this has on reproductive health, and how frequently sexual transmission occurs. This study will aid in development of therapeutics for persistent EVD infections and limit the risk that male survivors pose to their families and community.

column36: Cannabis for symptom management in children with cancer: a demonstration project by the Canadian Childhood Cannabinoid Clinical Trials (C4T) platform
column37: Unregulated cannabis products are currently being used by children with cancer for a variety of reasons including pain, sleep, nausea and as a cancer treatment. In Canada, no cannabis product has received Health Canada licensing approval for use in children. Without research evidence many doctors are hesitant to recommend cannabis products for children with cancer. Parents desperate for effective treatments and armed with anecdotal information from case reports and social media are obtaining cannabis products (e.g. online or storefront clinics). In order for doctors to feel confident in advising parents on the use and dose of cannabis they need better information on whether these products work and if they are safe. To address this goal, we established a national team of researchers, doctors, nurses, pharmacists, policy makers, youth and parents, called C4T. Our goal is to better understand the risks and potential benefits of medical cannabis use in children with cancer. Our diverse study team will determine how parents and youth are currently using cannabis products in cancer and what the reason for use is. C4T will review the literature and conduct a real-world study with children with cancer who are already using cannabis to try and establish a dose-response. C4T will use this information to create educational tools for doctors, youth and parents as well as to develop large scale studies to test the benefits and safety of medical cannabis products for children compared with existing treatments/standard of care. There is a large knowledge gap on if and when cannabis products can be used safely by children with cancer and other chronic health conditions. To ensure people can use our findings, we will create and update an online resource hut that is accessible to the public. Our research team is well equipped to fill this knowledge gap and continue to conduct high-quality research on cannabis for a variety of health conditions in children.

column36: The right care, for the right patient, at the right time, by the right provider: A value-based comparison of the management of ambulatory respiratory diseases in walk-in clinics, primary care physician practices and emergency departments.
column37: Emergency department overcrowding is a serious threat to patient safety and quality of care. It is a well-recognized cause of mortality, delays and increased health system costs. Although controversial, some believe that emergency department overuse and misuse by ambulatory emergency patients (in other words those not requiring a stretcher) is a significant part of the problem. In Canada, provincial governments have invested massively in improving access to primary care practices and walk-in clinics, hoping that these patients will avoid emergency departments and preferably present to these alternate settings. Although this approach seems reasonable, the scientific evidence supporting it is scarce and contradictory. It remains unclear which care environment provides the best quality of care at the lowest cost. Therefore, our study will compare quality and cost of care in emergency departments, walk-in clinics and primary care practices for low-acuity ambulatory emergency patients. In this four-year project, we will recruit patients with respiratory conditions (for example flu) as they represent most of the population thought to be amenable to outpatient clinics. We will assess how the patients are managed in each setting and what happens to them. Among others, we will answer the following questions: Did they need to consult again because the first visit did not answer their needs? What were the expenses incurred by the system or by them to receive care? We will also survey the patients, so they give us their evaluation of their outcomes and experience. The endpoint of our program will be to identify the most appropriate care setting for the management of respiratory ambulatory emergency conditions, based on the quality and cost of care of each alternative.

column36: Role of cardiac lipoprotein lipase in diabetic heart disease.
column37: In Canada, more than 9 million individuals live with diabetes or pre-diabetes with heart disease being its leading cause of death. Traditionally, the management of diabetes has focused mainly on controlling high blood glucose levels. Unfortunately, despite heroic efforts to normalize this blood glucose, poor medication management predisposes these patients to heart failure. This is because, in Type 1 diabetes, multiple finger pricks and daily insulin injections (3-4/day) mean poor patient compliance, and variations in blood glucose management that fluctuate from insufficient to poor control. One instigator for the development of heart failure following diabetes is how this organ utilizes different sources of fuel for energy. During diabetes the heart switches from using both sugar and fats, to only fats. This transformation to using fats as an exclusive source of energy is helpful in the initial stages of the disease. However, over the progression of diabetes this has terrible end results. This is because toxic by-products are produced by overuse of fats, which weaken heart function (heart disease). Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is responsible for regulating fat delivery to the heart, and its function during diabetes has not been completely revealed. In this proposal, the mechanisms by which LPL regulates fuel utilization by the heart during diabetes will be investigated in an attempt to identify new targets for therapeutic intervention. Currently, as treatment options to directly target diabetic heart disease are scarce, data from this project may assist in drug development that exclusively targets fuel utilization by the heart to help delay, prevent, or treat cardiac failure, and provide long-term management of this condition during diabetes.

column36: Role of tissue-resident progenitor cells in vascular disease
column37: Risk factors such as high blood pressure, or hypertension (HTN), lead to changes in blood vessel function & structure, which progresses to harmful cardiovascular disease (CVD). We believe CVD risk factors cause changes in blood vessels by affecting the stem cells that produce their cell components (e.g. vascular smooth muscle cells; VSMC). Using stem cells from skin, our lab showed that stem cells from patients with diabetes (and HTN) produce VSMC that did not function or repair as well as healthy individuals. Now, we study whether this also happens in stem cells found in blood vessels (i.e. tissue-resident stem cells), which can be identified by a protein known as Sca1. We will study Sca1 stem cells and how they are involved in vessel injury and HTN. Early experiments show that some small gene products known as microRNAs (miR), which stop the production of other genes or proteins, are increased when a mouse has HTN. In Aim-1, we will study if vessel injury or HTN disturbs Sca1 cells from producing normal VSMC, and if so, which genes and miR may be causing this. In Aim-2 we will test how much vessel remodeling after injury or HTN actually comes from Sca1-marked & Sca1-derived VSMC. Using mice that label all Sca1 cells and cells they produce, we can track when and where Sca1 cells are going and how many VSMC they produce after vessel injury or HTN. We will isolate Sca1-derived (i.e. marked) VSMC and test their function, gene and miR expression as in Aim-1. In Aim-3, we will use genetically-modified mice, which do not have Sca1, to see how blood vessel respond. Finally, in Aim 4, we will see if healthy Sca1 cells can be 'diseased' by the candidate disease-causing miR identified in Aims 1-3. We will also see if 'diseased' Sca1 cells can be rescued by antagomiR. Together, these studies will help us understand what is happening after blood vessel injury and in HTN, and help us diagnose and treat the problem (possibly using the miR/antagomiR identified in Aim 4).

column36: Requirement of Bone Morphogenetic Protein-Activated Transcription Factors in Chondrogenesis
column37: Chondrogenesis, or the formation of cartilage, is an essential developmental process for formation of bones, joints, and other tissues. Failures in chondrogenesis are linked to both common diseases including osteoarthritis, and rarer genetic conditions including chondrodysplasia, with few available treatments for these diseases. Chondrogenesis is driven by a collection of proteins termed bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), which are currently being investigated as therapeutic factors in bone and cartilage regeneration. However, progress is hampered by a poor understanding of how BMPs regulate their target genes, which comprise the network of genes that control chondrogenesis as a whole. Our lab has recently identified a set of BMP-activated proteins, which have been implicated in chondrogenesis-related diseases through patient sequencing data. None of these proteins currently have any known function in chondrogenesis. This project will identify the roles of these BMP-activated proteins during chondrogenesis by decreasing their expression levels in pre-cartilage cells, and observing loss of chondrogenesis. Our data will provide the first insight into the link between mutations in these BMP-activated proteins and their corresponding chondrogenic diseases, potentially revealing novel mechanisms regulating chondrogenesis, and opening new possibilities in bone and joint therapeutics.

column36: Drinking to cope: A prospective examination of transition-related risk in early adulthood
column37: Rates of alcohol and anxiety disorder comorbidity are high in adult populations. Yet, we know little about how risk unfolds early on. The undergraduate years are a time when alcohol misuse is commonplace, but most people mature out of heavy drinking when they take on adult roles. Evidence suggests that those who drink to cope are less likely to mature out, and this is concerning given that heavy drinking puts individuals at risk for alcohol use disorder. The goal of the proposed project is to examine anxiety as a predictor of impeded maturing out of alcohol misuse during the transition out of university. Behavioural theories offer a useful framework for thinking about anxiety-motivated drinking. The anxiety (behavioural inhibition) system is thought to lead to alcohol misuse, but the degree of this relationship depends on activation of the impulsive (behavioural approach) system. These systems are thought to influence alcohol attitudes (i.e., 'alcohol will reduce my tension'), which in turn promote risk. We hypothesize that young adults high in anxiety, who are also impulsive, will not mature out of alcohol misuse post-university graduation. A 12-month preliminary study, as part of a larger 6-year study, is proposed. One hundred and thirty undergraduates will complete baseline clinical assessments prior to graduation. Following graduation, participants will complete assessments online, three times, at three-month intervals. Transitioning out of university has inherent stressors. For those high in anxiety, this may be a period when patterns of problematic drinking are solidified. This research may have implications for how we think about, and thus intervene in, heavy drinking during periods of transition.

column36: Enterovirus subversion of the autophagy pathway
column37: Enteroviruses (EVs) are common human pathogens associated with a broad spectrum of diseases, including various neurological disorders, such as poliomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and non-polio flaccid paralysis, particularly in infants and children worldwide. Autophagy is a "self-eating" process in cells by which cells recycle damaged proteins and/or cell parts, called organelles. Autophagy is an important cellular response to limit viral growth and further infection. However, increasing evidence suggests that this pathway can be "hijacked" by EVs to ensure their successful infection of host cells. We discovered that EV infection disrupts the normal process of autophagy, resulting in enhanced viral replication/release and impaired clearance of damaged proteins that clump together and are toxic to the cells. We further showed that several proteins involved in the regulation of autophagy are broken down upon viral infection through the action of virus-encoded proteins. Despite the demonstrated importance of autophagy in EV infections, the exact mechanism by which EVs subvert this pathway and the functional significance of the resulting protein breakdown remain largely unclear. In addition, the possible value of autophagy-based anti-EV inhibitors has not been studied. In this project, we propose to: (1) investigate the mechanism by which EVs interfere with the process of autophagy; (2) determine the outcome of impaired function of lysosome (an organelle that contains digestive enzymes required for autophagy-mediated recycling); and (3) develop anti-viral inhibitors based on the mechanism identified in cells that prevent EV-mediated disruption of autophagy. These studies will provide new information and advance our understanding regarding the factors that govern successful viral infection and contribute to disease progression. Results generated from these studies also offer a potential to identify new strategies to prevent and treat EV infections.

column37: In October 2018, recreational cannabis became legal in Canada; before then medical use was legal. Babies are exposed to cannabis their mothers use during pregnancy and through breastmilk. Mothers will report if, when and how they use cannabis. Their sleep, activity, mental and physical health and the baby's birth, development, behavior and health will be monitored, including a formal assessment at 18 months. The family will use an air quality monitor and passive environmental samplers for mothers and babies. They will also complete an environmental assessment. Breastmilk and urine will be tested for cannabis to see if babies absorb cannabis used by mothers. Passive sampler analyses will provide evidence of other exposures that could confuse the picture, like tobacco smoke and air pollution. Sleep and mood are related and impact development, so maternal and infant sleep will be monitored. Cannabis, used medically and for recreation, presents potential risks and benefits to expectant mothers and families. This study will provide valuable information to help families make informed choices about cannabis and set the stage for future research on the long term effects of cannabis exposure on children.

column36: Pan-Canadian network to investigate cannabis use in pregnancy and neurodevelopmental outcomes in children
column37: Even before legalization, cannabis use has been increasing in Canada, including among new and expectant parents. Cannabis use in pregnancy may harm fetal brain development and impact the long-term well-being of children and their families. The existing scientific literature is inconclusive and outdated. We are proposing a Pan-Canadian network of researchers, health care providers, decision-makers and families to lead a contemporary research program that will address knowledge gaps in our understanding of the risks of cannabis exposure to babies, mothers, and their families. Over the next five years, we aim to determine the likelihood of developmental impairments in children due to perinatal cannabis exposure. We will build a national database using existing Canadian pregnancy cohorts, perinatal registries, and novel data collection. Our research will identify "windows of susceptibility" to cannabis for the developing brain by analyzing biological samples collected from mothers and infants in the perinatal period. We will also seek the experiences and perspectives of new and expectant parents, and their care providers to develop reliable, accessible and easy-to-understand public resources that support informed decision-making about cannabis use in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Our proposed Network will be a sustainable platform for ongoing research on cannabis use in pregnancy in Canada. Our results will improve the transmission of knowledge around cannabis in pregnancy and contribute to better care and outcomes for infants, families and Canadian society.

column36: Impact of Cannabis Use on Indigenous Peoples' Oral Health
column37: The legalization of non-medical cannabis in 2018 has raised many questions about the health effects associated with the drug's use. For instance, emerging evidence associates smoking cannabis with several oral diseases, including oral cancers. However, the effects of cannabis use on the oral health of Indigenous youth and adults are unknown. This study addresses stakeholder priorities and the impact increased cannabis use has on the already disproportionate burden of illness borne by Indigenous Peoples. Self-identified cannabis users and non-users, ages 18 to 44 years, will be recruited from partnering Indigenous communities and neighboring non-Indigenous communities, with each group followed for three years. Baseline and yearly comprehensive oral health examinations will be conducted by calibrated dentists. Saliva samples will be collected to monitor salivary constituents. Saliva and urine analyses will assess cannabis exposure. Non-invasive sensory tests will measure pain sensitivity in the orofacial region. Oral health outcomes will include: oral mucosal lesions, periodontitis, dental caries, changes in oral microbial composition, and abnormal sensory function. We hypothesize cannabis use in Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations is associated with: 1) a shift in the oral inflammatory signature that promotes the progression of pre-malignant lesions to oral cancers; 2) a distinctive salivary bacterial fingerprint; 3) a shift in the proteins in saliva reflecting a higher incidence of periodontitis and early-stage oral cancers, and; 4) oral and facial somatosensory changes dependent on drug use. The Indigenous Learning Circle model will be used throughout to share knowledge around the oral health risks of cannabis consumption and the drug's impact on Indigenous communities. The Circles will also be used to evaluate the research outcomes through the lens of the community so as to inform policy and recommend measures that promote cessation and harm reduction.

column36: A prospective translational model of the therapeutic potential of cannabidiol in reducing acute pain symptoms and opioid usage following traumatic injury.
column37: Recreational cannabis is legal in Canada since October 2018. Based on Colorado's experience, the first U.S. state to have legalized recreational cannabis in 2014, effects on Canadians' health are to be expected including: 1) increased recreational cannabis use; and 2) increased risk of traumatic injuries. Traumatic injuries are associated with an increased risk of chronic pain especially when peripheral orthopedic injuries (i.e., bone fracture) are combined with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Following a traumatic injury, opioid therapy is common despite the high risk of addiction/misuse/diversion as there is no other alternative to relieve severe pain. In parallel, cannabidiol (CBD) is emerging as a potent anti-inflammatory agent extracted from the cannabis plant which could promote pain relief and reduce opioid use after traumatic injuries. However, the low quality of clinical evidence on the safety and action mechanisms of CBD along with the lack of knowledge on interactions with opioids contribute to physicians' hesitation to adopt CBD as a regular therapeutic tool to relieve pain symptoms. The ongoing opioid crisis coupled with cannabis legalization in Canada therefore calls for an intersectoral strategy aiming to determine the potential of cannabinoids as co-analgesic agents for the treatment of pain, especially in vulnerable multi-trauma patients. To this end, expertise from 5 Canadian universities and a patient-expert partnership have led to an action plan with 4 main deliverables providing: 1) The first clinical assessment of the therapeutic potential of CBD for acute pain alleviation after multi-trauma; 2) A long-term assessment of CBD treatment effects on pain symptoms and trauma outcomes; 3) Using animal models of multi-trauma, assessment of interaction between CBD treatment and factors contributing to pain symptoms; 4) Scientific & clinical knowledge transfer strategy tailored to the needs of patients, practitioners, and key stakeholders.

column36: Cannabis-based precision medicine for osteoarthritis therapy
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of disability, in part due to a lack of effective treatment options. Cannabis offers a potential treatment for OA, however, little research has been done on this topic. Cannabinoids are the main active components in cannabis. The most abundant cannabinoids are delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and cannabidiol (CBD). There are many causes and types of OA, so it is likely that any therapeutic (or harmful) effect of cannabis will vary based on characteristics of the patient, and levels of cannabinoids in the cannabis strain used. We propose to study the characteristics of the patient and of the cannabis that predict how well cannabis works for treating OA. First, we will do studies in mice that have OA to examine the effect of different cannabinoids on different types of OA. Specifically, we will measure the effect of THC, CBD, and THC+CBD on mice's pain, motor function and cognitive functions. Second, we will collect joint tissue and blood samples from patients undergoing knee surgery to measure whether the tissues respond to each type of cannabinoid. We will also identify traits in the patient's tissue and blood that predict whether their tissue will respond to cannabinoids. Third, we will carry out a study in patients with OA who use cannabis to manage their OA symptoms. We will measure each patient's daily pain scores, OA type, traits in their blood, and the concentration of CBD and THC from a sample of their cannabis. We will test whether each of these pieces of information predict a patient's pain scores. Our research could create evidence for or against using cannabinoids for treating OA symptoms. These results may help physicians and patients to decide whether a patient might benefit from cannabis and the type and dose of cannabis that might work best for the patient.

column36: Canadian Cannabis and Psychosis Research Team (CCPRT)
column37: While Cannabis is considered a relatively safe psychoactive substance, cannabis-related psychosis risk is a significant public health concern, for which no evidence-based screening or intervention strategies exist. Psychosis often follows heavy cannabis use, particularly if use starts early and is sustained during adolescence. Research also suggests that some individuals, those with genetic and psychosocial risk markers, are more susceptible to cannabis-induced psychosis. What is not known is how to identify and protect individuals at risk of cannabis-related psychosis from such harm. The current team joins genetics experts with clinical and pre-clinical researchers to optimise their research on the neurodevelopmental consequences of adolescent cannabis exposure to answer the following questions in relation to psychosis: What features of cannabis exposure (e.g. cumulative amounts used, age of regular use, sex differences) are more or less harmful? Do reliable biomarkers exist that will predict who is most at risk? Is there a role for targeted and/or early intervention strategies to reduce the cognitive and mental health burden of cannabis? What are the most promising intervention approaches to reduce cannabis-induced psychosis? Our research team will collaborate on an integrated research program that spans animal studies, genetics studies, longitudinal developmental and clinical cohorts, big-data analytics and prevention. All participants will mutually benefit from data-pooling activities and a translational research framework, resulting in exceptional data output and knowledge for the public. The databases and knowledge generated by this team will be of high value to the clinical networks represented within the team (e.g., Canadian Consortium on Early Intervention on Psychosis), who currently seek guidance on how to manage potential cognitive and mental health consequences of cannabis use in their patients.

column36: Adolescent Cannabis Exposure, Brain Development and Cognitive-Emotional Outcomes
column37: There is significant public concern over the impact of cannabis use during adolescence on the developing brain and potential subsequent risk for the development of mental illness. Surprisingly, the evidence gathered to date is quite inconclusive with some individual studies showing adverse impacts of cannabis use while many others showing no effect at all. As such, it is likely that there are specific variables that influence how cannabis use during adolescence modulates these outcomes. This study will use a novel, translationally relevant rodent model of adolescent exposure to cannabis vapor we will be able to explicitly test the impact of cannabis exposure on adolescent brain development using a titrated scale of exposure to cannabis during adolescence, ranging from infrequent use to multiple times per day of high potency cannabis. We will employ repeated testing of magnetic resonance imaging of structural brain development, electrophysiology, behavioural tasks and stress reactivity to determine how exposure to varying levels of cannabis during adolescence impacts neurodevelopment trajectories during this window. We will also explore how additional exposure to early life adversity or concomitant social stress during adolescence, influences the impacts of daily exposure to cannabis on structural brain development and behavioural outcomes. The patterns of cannabis use we will be modelling are guided by our collaborative work with our partners in public health who studies adolescent cannabis use to ensure we are modelling realistic and relevant patterns of cannabis use. These rodent studies will be complimented by integrating with a prospective cohort study of adolescents at high risk for mood disorders, to explore the impacts of cannabis initiation on brain development and the development of any psychiatric illnesses. These studies will help us to establish if there are clear harms associated with cannabis use during adolescence on the development of mental illness.

column36: Is cannabis a useful adjunct in the treatment of symptoms of persons with multiple sclerosis? A formal trial of CBD and THC for the control of spasticity and other symptoms: assessing the clinical effects and the basic mechanisms.
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease that manifests as relapses and/or progression. Multiple disease-modifying treatments (DMTs) are available to control the disease process. Lesser progress has been achieved to treat the multiple symptoms that MS can cause. Persons with MS PwMS, especially after 10 or more years of disease course, are frequently afflicted by a combination of leg weakness with spasticity, neuropathic pains, fatigue, sphincteric dysfunction, sleep disruption, and mood and cognition impairment. These are treated by muscle relaxants, neurotransmitter agents, tricyclics, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and CNS stimulants. The efficacy of these agents, which are fraught with side effects and drug-drug interactions, is often partial. Up to 49% of persons with MS (PwMS), have used cannabis, mostly for mood enhancing, to improve sleep, relieve pain and spasticity. A THC-CBD spray has been approved in Canada in 2005 for symptom improvement in adult PwMS with moderate to severe spasticity who have not responded adequately to other anti-spasticity medications. Now that the use of cannabis is legalized in Canada, the patient and medical communities expect the establishment of evidence-based guidelines for the proper use of cannabis. We are proposing to assess the clinical effects of THC and CBD positive and negative, in a carefully selected cohort of PwMS with single or multiple symptoms, enrolled in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, parallel groups trial of four weeks' duration. The main outcomes will be spasticity, with pain, sleep, mood and cognition, fatigue, and sphincteric function as secondary outcomes. The pharmacology of THC-CBD, as well as their effects on neuro-inflammation, will be explored. PwMS will be involved in all phases of the proposed study.

column36: Guideline for cannabis use in chronic pain
column37: Chronic pain is the primary cause of health care resource consumption and disability during adult working years in North America. Use of cannabis as a treatment option for managing chronic pain is increasing in Canada, in part due to pressure to decrease opioid prescribing. There are over 360,000 Canadians registered to use medicinal cannabis, including over 10,000 Veterans; however, use of cannabis to manage chronic pain remains controversial. We propose to develop a clinical practice guideline for cannabis and chronic pain, incorporating all available research evidence, considering patients values and preferences, and adopting current knowledge synthesis methods to develop an explicit, transparent, and evidence-based guideline. Patients, health care providers and policy makers will benefit from having access to recommendations based on the latest research evidence informing the safety and effectiveness of cannabis for chronic pain. This information will be especially impactful among older Canadians, indigenous populations, and Veterans, who are disproportionately affected by chronic pain.

column36: Impact of an advance practice physiotherapy model of care for older adults referred to neurosurgery for spinal pain: a prospective observational study from the CareAxis initiative
column37: Background: With the aging of the population, need for specialized care such as orthopaedics and neurosurgery, are rapidly increasing, resulting in long wait times. New models of care, involving advanced practice physiotherapy (APP) have been proposed as a potential solution. The CareAxis Group, a non-profit organization has developed with the support of several health charities an APP model of care for older adults referred to neurosurgery for spinal pain. In this program, the advanced practice physiotherapists assess and conservatively manage non-surgical patient in a one-hour session. The program was launched in January 2019 and showed promising results. However, the CareAxis group would like to offer a more comprehensive conservative rehabilitation intervention involving multiple sessions with the APP. To our knowledge, APP models comparing single to multiple consultations have not been evaluated. Objectives: The aim of this proposal is to perform a pragmatic randomized controlled trial to compare the effectiveness of the current CareAxis one session APP model compared to a multiple sessions APP model. Methods: This study will take place in nine physiotherapy CareAxis Group clinics in the Montreal region. One hundred and thirty-six older adults (65 years old or more) with neck or back pain will be recruited. Participants will be randomized in two groups: 1- a single session with the APP or 2- a group receiving multiple sessions with the APP (6 sessions over 5 months). Participants will be compared in terms of pain, function and quality of life. Economic analyses will be performed in order to compare the cost effectiveness of the two interventions. Significance: This study will contribute to the advancement of knowledge concerning APP models of care. Evidence-based development of APP models of care has the potential to profoundly impact access and quality of care for Canadians and is a novel model that may efficiently alleviate increasing health care demands.

column36: Primary care shared decision making for addressing painful chronic musculoskeletal conditions.
column37: Joint and muscle pain to the back, neck or knees are among the most common reasons for visiting a primary care physician. However, often patients are sent for several imaging tests, out of place specialist appointments or inappropriate surgery, and are given only pills for their pain with no rehabilitation to improve their mobility and long-term quality of life. Patients are rarely involved in deciding the best choices from among all possible options when they receive care for joint and muscle pain, and their values and preferences are rarely considered. Shared decision making between clinician and patient is known to improve patients' knowledge about their health problems and their confidence in the treatment chosen. Exercise therapy and pain education offered by rehabilitation professionals have proven useful for short- and long-term management of joint and muscle pain, but not all physicians and patients discuss this option or are even aware of it. A better conversation about options could reduce possibly harmful treatments. We will develop PRISM, an education program for physicians, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and psychologists to help them share decisions with patients about the best choices to diagnose and treat joint and muscle pain. We will test the program with a group of clinicians and patients to see if a larger study is feasible. We will assess clinicians' and patients' level of satisfaction with the program. We will assess patients' confidence that the options offered respect their preferences and that the chosen options improve their well-being. This project has great potential to improve communication among clinicians and patients and increase patients' knowledge, satisfaction and confidence about high-quality alternatives to advanced imaging and pills for their joint and muscle pain. This will contribute to a better experience with our healthcare system and improved quality of care for Canadians living with joint and muscle pain.

column36: A multi-level mechanical assessment of osteoarthritic bone and its interaction with joint arthroplasty. Understanding how microstructure influences trabecular-level strain progression within patient excised arthritic/osteoarthritic bone cores with supplemented organ-level analyses of whole joints from patients treated with arthroplasty. Towards improving and ensuring the longevity of joint replacements.
column37: Shoulder arthritis is becoming more prevalent with the aging population. Typically with shoulder arthritis/osteoarthritis, the joint undergoes adaptive changes as cartilage degrades. When the condition becomes symptomatic with functional loss, patients benefit from total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) surgery. Clinical studies have shown that glenoid failure is the most common complication of TSA. Our group conducted a systematic review of revisions performed in North America and Europe, which found that the mean time to a revision surgery is only 3.9 years. This is too short for implants that are expected to last 10-15 years. While many glenoid designs exist, there is no clear evidence supporting one over the other, and evaluation methods are largely limited to computer models, which may not perfectly represent the physical reality. As a result, even though design innovations continue, there is little progress in strategies to reduce glenoid implant failures. In the proposed research, we will acquire bone samples from rheumatoid and osteoarthritis patients undergoing TSA surgery. We will also acquire shoulders from deceased donors who had been treated in life by TSA using two specific types of implants. Using our novel experimental equipment, joint forces will be applied to these specimens while acquiring high-resolution CT scans, in order to measure deformation in the bone's architecture. The micro-level failure characteristics of the implant-to-bone interface will be measured. These methods will be applicable to other joints including the hip and knee. This one year project will result in a well defined criteria of bone failure specific to rheumatoid and osteoarthritis patients, and a novel apparatus to test implants in real physical conditions, while providing the same form of measurements previously available only from computer modeling. These methods will be valuable to improve the implant design process, and to improve arthroplasty outcomes for patients.

column36: A prospective study to define optimum cup orientation in hip arthroplasty accounting for the individual's anatomy and movement patterns
column37: Over 58,000 total hip replacements (THR) are performed in Canada per year to treat end-stage osteoarthritis. Unfortunately, approximately 8.2% of patients sustain a complication and must undergo a reoperation (revision surgery). Revisions are associated with physical and psychological burden to patients and cost the healthcare system a lot of money. The second most common reason for revision is instability (i.e. dislocation) of the implant components. Orientation of the implanted cup (acetabular component) has been shown to improve the articulation's performance and is a key factor to joint's stability. Unfortunately, no research to date has been able to establish a 'safe' cup orientation to eliminate the risk of instability after a THR. This may be because most research has focused on one-dimensional evaluation and has not considered the individual's anatomy and motion patterns. Our group has recently published on two and three-dimensional assessment of the hip and the spine to study individual spino-pelvic dynamics and how that influences outcomes after surgery. Furthermore, we have studied the arthritic patients' spine-, pelvis-, hip- and femur- dynamics before and after surgery and have established protocols of how to best investigate these with radiographs. As such, it is now known that the orientation of the cup is influenced by the individual's anatomy and movement pattern and that the movement pattern does not significantly differ before and after a THR. Through this prospective research project, we aim to (1) determine the optimum cup orientation in patients undergoing a THR and (2) assess what the relative size this optimum zone of cup orientation is, as this would have implications for the patient and the surgeon. Our hypothesis is that for most patients, the relative size for optimum/safe cup orientation is large enough for surgeons to be able to achieve that target without the need for new and expensive technologies.

column36: Thrombelastography-Defined Duration of Hypercoagulability Following Pelvis and Acetabular Fractures
column37: Patients who suffer a major broken bone, such as a broken pelvis or acetabulum (or hip socket), have an increased risk for developing blood clots in their legs (deep vein thrombosis or DVT) and life-threatening blood clots in their lungs (pulmonary embolism or PE). After these major broken bones, patients experience inflammation, which can be made worse by the surgery that they require, which further increases their risk for blood clots. PE is a common cause of preventable death in patients with a broken pelvis or acetabulum, therefore they receive medication to help prevent blood clots. However, these medications can increase bleeding and are expensive. It is unknown how long this medication should be continued and whether patients who are more prone to forming clots should receive longer treatment. In order to help prevent blood clots, doctors need to be able to identify which patients are at increased risk for clotting. Thrombelastography (TEG) technology uses a small sample of blood to evaluate a person's risk for blood clots. Our study will test if TEG can also determine how long each patient should receive medication to minimize their clot risk, based on their individual risk. TEG technology is readily available, cost-effective, and provides valuable information to help doctors treat trauma patients with abnormal blood clotting. Our interdisciplinary research team includes doctors and surgeons with TEG experience. column36: Niikaniganaw (All My Relations) II: Continuing to Build Capacity for Stigma Free and Culturally Safe Care for Indigenous People Living with, Affected by, or at Increased Risk of HIV in Ottawa-Gatineau
column37: The proposed project, Niikaniganaw II, builds on the success of Niikaniganaw I, a 1-yr CIHR Catalyst Grant that brought together Indigenous People Living with HIV or AIDS (IPHAs), Knowledge Carriers, researchers, nursing students and staff members of six community organizations who provide health or related services to IPHAs. column37: Our goal is to establish a sustainable Community of Practice (CoP) - "HIV in Motion" to advance physical activity interventions with patient-reported outcomes (PROs) for people living with HIV (PLWH). In Phase 2, we will administer the SF-HDQ and assess it properties with PLWH in Canada. Standardized PROs that capture health and its fluctuation over time are critical to guide timely and appropriate HIV care. In earlier work, we developed a 69-item PRO, called the HDQ and demonstrated its reliability (consistency) and validity (accuracy) with PLWH in Canada, Ireland and the United Kingdom. As more adults age with HIV, there is a critical need for a brief yet comprehensive tools to inform interventions that can be equitably used by PLWH and providers. column36: Hormones and Healthy Aging in Women Living with HIV: A Study By, With and For Community.
column37: In Canada, a woman's life expectancy is 4 years longer than a man's. However, for women living with HIV, not only is life expectancy 5-10 years shorter than for women without HIV of same age, but it is also 7 years less than that of men living with HIV. The reason for this remains unknown. This may relate to alterations in hormones normally protective of women's health and/or to social and structural factors that impact a woman's access to care. Women living with HIV more often have a history of amenorrhea/menstrual disturbance, and reach menopause earlier than women without HIV. Menopause and amenorrhea are associated with decreased sex steroid levels and accelerated progression of age-associated diseases. Thus low sex steroid states occurring earlier in the lives of women living with HIV may result in earlier and increased comorbidity risk. We herein leverage the expertise, experience, and infrastructure of the CIHR-funded BC CARMA-CHIWOS Collaboration (BCC3)- integrating established research cohorts of women living with HIV in British Columbia - CARMA (Children and Women:AntiRetroviral therapy and Markers of Aging Cohort) and CHIWOS (Canadian HIV Women's Sexual and Reproductive Health Cohort) to examine the relationship between the reproductive health of women with that of comorbidities in this population.

column36: A First Nations Community Response to Support Recovery from Opioids: Integrating Cultural and Land-based Practices with Clinical Approaches
column37: Wikwemikong Unceded Territory is one of the largest and fastest-growing First Nation communities. The community has many thriving Anishinabe people, pristine waters and lands, strong language, culture, and heritage; but the consequences of centuries of colonial oppression are also present. The most serious health issue is the opioid crisis. It has resulted in social problems, chronic drug-related illnesses, mental health issues, family violence, loss of children into foster care, trafficking of women, crime, vandalism, and breakdown of the social fabric and relationships in the community. Tribal police estimate that for each addicted person there are ten family members whose health and mental health is affected by drug-related consequences. The community is proactive in addressing opioid use and there is a strong commitment to move away from a punitive approach. The community offers opioid agonist therapy (OAT) to treat these addictions. In the clinic, patients are supported with culturally based therapies and counseling. Our pilot research shows documented promising results associated with this community-owned, culturally safe approach, but it also emphasizes that more research is needed to identify promising practices. Our community-based, patient-engaged research will involve clients, family and community members in community-based solutions. We will work with Elders, knowledge keepers and clients in recovery to increase our understanding of the role of the land, Anishinabe language and worldview and their relationship to healing from opioid addiction. Research with providers across diverse sectors will create an Indigenous model of essential services for opioid recovery, and support the uptake results into policy, practice and service development. Finally, we will create access to robust health, social, and justice data sets and administrative data-bases in order to evaluate services, in order to empower the community to make knowledge-based decisions.

column36: Type 1 Interferon as a Master Regulator for Tumor Immunosupression
column37: Currently, chemotherapy is the standard for cancer therapies in the health care industry, even with its large array of negative side effects. Immunotherapy has the potential to replace chemotherapy as the primary method of cancer treatment. Oncolytic viral vaccines (OVV) are one such therapy showing promise and undergoing rigorous clinical development. OVVs are viruses that are harmless to healthy cells while targeting and attacking tumor cells. OVVs are made with a specific molecule that is also produced by tumors - because immune cells can recognize the OVV as an invader, they will then be able to recognize the tumor by picking up the commonly shared molecule from the OVV, and denote it as a threat creating a immune response against the tumor. OVVs are also known to induce a molecule known as type I interferon (IFN-I). In non-cancerous conditions, IFN-I induces the maturation of a multitude of immune cells, strengthening an immune response. In cancerous conditions, IFN-I can prevent tumor cell growth by promoting death of said tumor cells. However, it is also seen that IFN-I can also play a negative role during T cell-mediated response. In particular, IFN-I can lead to the creation of a surrounding environment that prevents the immune system from fighting cancer, a mechanism known as immunosuppression and is a significant hurdle in cancer immunotherapy. Recently, it has been demonstrated that IFN-I, despite its role as an immune system mediator, may not be needed during treatment with OVVs and in high concentrations, may be deleterious to the health of the individual. Accordingly, this project will explore the effects of IFN-I on the environment produced by the tumor as well as the effect it has on immune cell function in the context of OVV therapies.

column37: Severe chronic kidney disease (CKD), a significant decline of kidney function, affects many Canadians and cause poor overall health. Doctors prepare these patients for what will happen when their kidneys eventually fail. Most people who have CKD are elderly and are more likely to die before or shortly after their kidneys fail. It is important for patients and their families to know this so they can make choices that are right for them, rather than worrying about complex treatments that they may never need or will need for a very short time. We have two concerns. First, for patients with CKD, we do not have accurate data to inform them of their risk of kidney failure and possible death. Second, we do not know what information patients need or want to make decisions about their care once they know their prognosis. We will use information from health records of Albertans with severe CKD to study the risks of kidney failure and death. We will determine if using data from Ontario health records will result in the same conclusions. We will then present these findings to patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers using vignettes. column36: Development and Characterization of Novel CB1 Allosteric Modulators
column37: Endocannabinoids are produced in neurones and interact with cannabinoid CB1 receptors to modulate a range of behaviours, including mood; the system can be over-active or underactive in certain diseases. The endocannabinoids interact with the cannabinoid CB1 receptor. In 2005, we produced the first evidence that the cannabinoid CB1 receptor contains an allosteric binding site. CB1 allosteric modulators have therapeutic potential with the advantage of only turning up or down an inappropriately balanced endocannabinoid system, rather than affecting normal physiological function. Recently, we have generated a novel CB1 allosteric modulators, that display more drug like characteristics. These compound have an unusual pharmacological profile, blocking some of the downstream effects of CB1 receptor activation. This unique profile has the potential to offer advantages over previous molecules that target the CB1R. Our preliminary studies also indicate our novel CB1 allosteric modulators are highly effective in reducing the behavioural phenotypes in two distinct mouse behavioural models of hyperdopamine states that are related to schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD). Endocannabinoid levels and CB1 receptors are dysregulated in schizophrenia. Taken together, the data suggest that the endocannabinoid system may be a target for the development of new therapeutics for the treatment for psychosis and mania. Here we will characterize the unique pharmacology displayed by our new molecules. We will develop novel analogues that are further optimized for clinical development. Finally, we will examine the effects of our compounds on behaviours in two distinct animal models of hyperdopamine and models of liver injury. This program will allow us to develop, pharmacologically characterize and optimize a unique new class of CB1 molecules to determine the therapeutic potential to facilitate translation in the clinic.

column36: Studying risk factors and striving to increase the efficacy of prevention programs for cutaneous melanoma in Canada.
column37: Melanoma's incidence in Canada is growing at an alarming rate. While recent studies improved the treatment of advanced melanomas, few efforts have addressed the public health implications of the rising burden of this cancer in Canada. Despite the rapid rise in incidence, only limited resources were devoted to target public awareness of melanoma, when compared to the United States or Australia. In a series of our Canadian studies we documented that the rates of increase for melanoma incidence and mortality are much higher in men than in women. Furthermore, we found that in men, melanoma primarily developed on the head/trunk, while in women melanomas appeared on the arms and legs. Finally, we have identified specific regions in Canada with >2-fold higher incidence of melanoma. Our combined research highlights that populations in certain parts of Canada due to a variety of factors are at a higher risk of developing melanoma. Importantly, targeting disease awareness and patient education in men vs. women should be done differently since sun exposure practices and affected body areas differ between genders. Also, it is not known whether existing campaigns in other countries such as Australia might be applicable in Canada. It has not been studied how these campaigns should be implemented in our country considering our cultural and geographic diversity. In the proposed research with the focus on young adults (ages 18-30) we will study why certain communities may have higher incidence of this cancer than others; what types of melanoma prevention programs may be culturally sensitive and effective in the First Nations communities. We will use existing data nationally on precipitation, solar radiation, shade availability, tree canopy density, etc. to correlate important environmental risk factors with the geographic distribution of melanoma. We will use focus groups to develop gender and region-specific recommendations to help change sun exposure practices.

column36: Hemoglobin A1c and risk of severe maternal morbidity and mortality
column37: In Canada, obese women, and women with pre-pregnancy diabetes, are each at higher risk of developing life-threatening conditions in pregnancy, or soon after birth -- what we call "severe maternal morbidity" (SMM). SMM offers a set of signals that a mother may be at high risk of dying. In screening for diabetes in women without diabetes, or for monitoring sugar control in women with existing diabetes, average blood sugar levels are measured using a test called "A1c." It is not known if an elevated A1c -- representing high average blood sugar -- can identify a woman at greater risk of SMM or death. Accordingly, the current study will use existing big healthcare data collected across all of Ontario. In our dataset, 25,000 births will have had an A1c before pregnancy, and 87,000 births an A1c done in pregnancy. We will determine if the preconception A1c, or early pregnancy A1c, are each associated with a higher risk of SMM or maternal death. This will be repeated among women from Sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean, two groups at especially high risk of SMM. We will also investigate whether a drop in A1c, from before pregnancy to that in early pregnancy, confers a lower risk of SMM or death. Working with national bodies in the fields of obstetrics and diabetes, we might adopt the use of a readily available and inexpensive blood test to identify a mother at high risk of SMM or death. Our research aims to save lives in susceptible women, including those of African and Caribbean heritage, to ensure a safe transition from pregnancy to a healthy motherhood.

column37: Obesity is a critical international non-communicable chronic disease which has many bad effects on individuals. For people with morbid obesity, a surgery which reduces the size of their stomach (bariatric surgery) can help people reduce their weight. This project will provide us with a series of health behaviour change programs that patients think are helpful and they would be willing to do, researchers have shown work, and healthcare professions think can be put into practice around bariatric surgery. Ultimately, these programs should help a group of people who currently don't have access to these kinds of important programs and whose health would really benefit from participating in them.

column36: Understanding the levers and barriers towards improved health among South Asians Across the Life-Course: Can we empower women as Agents of Change?
column37: South Asians refer to people who originate from the Indian subcontinent, and are the largest non-white ethnic group in Canada. South Asians have an increased risk of diabetes and early onset heart disease - making them a high risk group. The higher burden of risk factors is present from early childhood and persists into adulthood when usually unexpectedly South Asian men and women suffer a heart attack. Healthy Active living involves regular physical activity and high quality food intake in order to minimize the risk factors and heart disease that South Asians develop. Interventions which can increase (HAL) across the life-course has the greatest potential to reduce the risk diabetes and heart disease among South Asian families in Canada. Our findings demonstrate that women/mothers are the central figures in households, Therefore focusing on supporting the women of the household as "agents of change" in the promotion of HAL for families has the potential to reduce her own and her families risk of diabetes and heart disease The specific research proposed as part of the Catalyst grant will evaluate the social networks of South Asian women for continual re-enforcement of HAL messaging, and broaden our understanding of structural supports in the community. Using these novel research methods we hope to generate enough information to enable the design of a future population health intervention to improve HAL in this high-risk group.

column36: Personalized Medicine for Children: The Early Childhood Obesity (EChO) Clinical Prediction Tool
column37: Childhood obesity tracks through adolescence and adulthood and has been forecasted to become the leading cause of cardiovascular disease in the next century. One in four children in Canada is currently overweight or obese, with children from ethnic minority and low-income households more likely to be impacted. Successful interventions to prevent childhood obesity exist (e.g. family-based interventions), but can be time and resource intensive. A nuanced approach is needed, where obesity prevention interventions can be appropriately targeted according to a child's risk of obesity. 'Clinical prediction tools' are statistical models that help doctors predict future events or poor outcomes. An accurate obesity risk prediction too which considers ethnicity and income will enable preventive interventions to be delivered to children who are most likely to benefit, while avoiding unnecessary interventions and cost for low risk children. The study will develop, test and validate a new clinical prediction tool designed to be used at the doctor's office through existing electronic medical record systems which will identify young children who are at high risk for childhood obesity in the future. We will create the Early Childhood Obesity clinical prediction tool (EChO) which will be used at 2 years of age to predict obesity at 6 years of age using two methods: traditional statistical techniques (EChO-T) and cutting-edge machine learning methods (EChO-M). We will assess how well EChO-T and EChO-M can predict childhood obesity in children across Ontario, and then specifically in children from ethnic minority and low-income households. EChO will help healthcare providers to determine which young children are most likely to benefit from early obesity prevention programs. EChO holds the potential to prevent childhood obesity, and its long term health consequences, minimizing future health care costs, and reducing obesity-related health inequality.

column36: DemoPredict: Using linked accelerometry data to predict incident dementia in older Canadians
column37: Multimorbidity is rising in the Canadian population. According to data from the Public Health Agency of Canada's Canadian Chronic Disease Surveillance System (CCDSS), the proportion of Canadians aged 40 years and over living with three or more chronic conditions increased by 50% between 2001/02 and 2011/12. Many chronic diseases - such as diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease [CVD] and dementia - share the same underlying pathology and modifiable risk factors (e.g., physical inactivity, poor diet, alcohol consumption, cigarette smoking). Despite this, there are currently few existing tools that can be used to inform public health interventions aimed at reducing multimorbidity by targeting individuals' behaviours. Strategies for disease prevention and management centred on common risk factors across related diseases could improve the overall effectiveness of intervention programs. Among the many shared risk factors across non-communicable chronic diseases, diet, alcohol consumption and physical activity are a few of the largest contributors to the incidence of these conditions. However, existing predictive models relying on self-reported exposure to health risks generally results in an underestimation of risk burden and a source of bias in such studies. There are now opportunities to improve interventions centre-around physical inactivity with the use of new technologies and data sources. Fitness technology, including activity trackers and smartphone applications, has become increasingly popular for measuring and encouraging physical activity in recent years. In this project, we will develop a predictive algorithm of multimorbidity using linked survey and administration data; assess the receptivity to and potential use of activity trackers for disease prevention in older adults; and create a web-based tool (called GaitWay) that has the capacity to use individuals' data from activity trackers to predict their risk for multimorbidity.

column36: Exploring Influencers and Cultural Values in Relation to Health Behaviours Associated with Type 2 Diabetes: A Social Network Analysis in the South Asian Communities of Peel
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a chronic and often progressive medical condition characterized by high blood sugars and insulin resistance. Individuals with T2D are at risk of developing heart, kidney, and eye disease. Peel Region of Ontario has one of the highest rates of T2D in Canada, particularly in the South Asian population. Peel is home to a high number of people who have emigrated from South Asian countries and are at a higher risk of getting T2D. T2D risks can be lowered through behaviour changes such as physical activity and diet. Culturally specific strategies are needed to support individuals from diverse populations in making behaviour changes to effectively prevent and manage T2D. This study aims to understand the influence of social and cultural factors on health behaviours related to T2D prevention and management within intergenerational South Asian families. Three community organizations in Peel (Indus Community Services, Punjabi Community Health Services, and Wise Elephant Family Health Team) and one hospital-based organization (Diabetes Management Center at Trillium Health Partners) are collaborating with us by guiding the research questions, study design, and knowledge translation. The sample will include adults aged 18+ who live in Peel, have been diagnosed with T2D or prediabetes, live in the same household as a child/children age 0-18, and whose ethno-cultural origins include Punjabi, Tamil, and/or Hindi, which our community collaborators have identified as key populations for this study. Through surveys and semi-structured interviews, we will generate social network maps and descriptions about participants' social supports, information sources, cultural values, beliefs, and practices. Findings will inform the design of culturally relevant resources for T2D prevention and management that will be applied locally with our collaborators and can be adapted to other South Asian communities in Canada and globally.

column36: Evaluating the use of a smartphone app to increase nutrition knowledge and promote healthier dietary behaviours among an at-risk Canadian population
column37: Poor dietary habits are the leading risk factor for obesity and chronic diseases, indicating that Canadians' eating habits need to change. In today's busy and fast-paced environment, mobile apps can help people make better food choices, especially when grocery stores are crowded and noisy, filled with numerous choices and confusing marketing messages. We developed an app called the FoodFlip(C) to help consumers. Our research will first test to see if the FoodFlip(C) app can help consumers make healthier food and beverage choices and teach them about healthy food and nutrients. Secondly, we will assess whether the FoodFlip(C) app was easy to use and helped consumers make decisions about which foods to buy. Participants for this study will be those who are at a high risk for heart disease or type 2 diabetes (e.g. have high blood pressure, high blood lipid or cholesterol levels, or those taking medications for these conditions). Participants will be given the FoodFlip(C) app to use. Participants will be randomized to see different features within the app, including different ways of displaying nutrition information when they scan or search for a food product with their phone. Some participants will see the Nutrition Facts table; others will see new types of information systems that provides details about specific nutrients in the foods using traffic lights or 'high-in' symbols to help them interpret the healthfulness of the product. As part of this research, we will also see how these different ways of communicating nutrition information impacts food purchases, which will be tracked while participants are using the app. By understanding the factors driving behaviour change, this app has the potential to impact the lives of millions of Canadians by helping them making healthier dietary choices, change food purchasing behaviours and can potentially lead to long-term behaviour modifications in relation to their condition.

column36: The role of the novel R2TP chaperone complex in ciliogenesis
column37: Protein folding and degradation are central to cell biology. An exquisite control of these processes is required to ensure the proper survival of the cell and the health of the organism. Protein misfolding and aggregation have been linked to many diseases including cancer, aging, and neurodegeneration. Maintaining protein homeostasis in the cell is mainly accomplished by a family of proteins termed molecular chaperones that assist in protein folding. My group identified a highly conserved protein complex, which we named the R2TP complex, that interacts with several other chaperones and adaptor proteins. R2TP acts as a scaffold for the assembly of other critical complexes in the cell. Hence, R2TP has a novel cellular activity dedicated to protein assembly. The aim of the proposed project is to determine the structure and mechanism of function of this complex using cell biological, biochemical, and structural approaches. Here, we will concentrate on the function of R2TP in the biogenesis of cilia, which is a critical sensory organelle of the cell. Understanding the function of R2TP should lead to new insights into the mechanisms that regulate cellular protein homeostasis. Importantly, the proposal will also lead to a better understanding of diseases caused by the loss of such regulatory mechanisms.

column36: Targeting mitochondria metabolism to selectively kill leukemia cells
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a deadly disease with few therapy options. Recent work has shown that leukemia cells are metabolically rewired such that compounds targeting mitochondria are able kill leukemia cells without killing normal cells. Thus, identifying new drugs that target these mitochondria vulnerabilities could improve AML patient outcomes. Mitochondria possess four complexes that are responsible for cell respiration and energy production. In leukemia cells, mitochondria complex II activity is higher than the other complexes. This suggests that targeting and inhibiting complex II might be a simple yet powerful way to selectivity target and kill leukemia cells. Indeed, our preliminary research shows that inhibiting mitochondria complex II selectively kills leukemia cells in vitro and in vivo. In this project, the objective is to further validate, and define how, targeting of this complex imparts selective leukemia cell killing. The end goal of this work is to develop new drugs aimed at extending the lives of leukemia patients.

column36: Role of the ATP-dependent Protease ClpXP in Mitochondrial Protein Homeostasis
column37: Protein folding and degradation are central to cell biology. An exquisite control of these processes is required to ensure the proper survival of the cell and the health of the organism. Protein misfolding and aggregation have been linked to a large number of diseases including cancer, aging, and neurodegeneration. Maintaining protein homeostasis in the cell is accomplished by two classes of proteins: (1) molecular chaperones that assist in protein folding and protein complex formation, and (2) proteolytic complexes that lead to the degradation of misfolded and destabilized proteins. The proposed project aims to investigate how protein homeostasis is maintained in the mitochondrion by the highly conserved ATP-dependent protease ClpXP. The mitochondrion is central for energy metabolism and other essential cellular processes such as the control of Ca2+ levels and apoptosis. Many diseases are related to the malfunctioning of the mitochondria caused by mitochondrial proteostatic stress. In this regard, ClpXP plays a critical role in cell signaling in several diseases including cancer. However, the mechanism of function of mitochondrial ClpXP is not known and is the subject of this grant application.

column36: Prevalence, Burden and Reversal of Stringent Response-Mediated Antibiotic Tolerance
column37: Bacterial infections are a leading cause of hospitalization and death worldwide. Antibiotics are central to our ability to treat bacterial infections, but our capacity to cure these infections is jeopardized by increasing antibiotic resistance (where bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic). Added to this, very few new antibiotics with activity against resistant bacteria are being discovered. Therefore, it is essential that we preserve the effective use of the antibiotics we have. Antibiotic tolerance is emerging as a precursor to resistance that also contributes to antibiotic treatment failures in its own right. Tolerance occurs when bacteria are still killed by antibiotics, but die slower than usual. This means that live bacteria remain at the end of a typical course of antibiotics, resulting in infections that are persistent and recurrent. Persistent infections are associated with higher healthcare costs and death rates than resolving infections. While antibiotic resistance is routinely screened for in clinical laboratories, there are currently no appropriate tests that can detect tolerance. Therefore, the prevalence and consequences of antibiotic tolerance in terms of treatment failures are unknown and likely under-appreciated. We propose to develop a simple screen to detect tolerance and apply it to libraries of bacterial isolates derived from patients with persistent infections, thereby illuminating the true magnitude of this threat to effective antibiotic therapy. We will also investigate one of the mechanisms behind tolerance with a view to understanding how we can reverse it and preserve the effectiveness of existing antibiotics. Our research will improve the treatment of persistent infections by providing physicians with a tool to detect tolerance, as well as practical information on which types of antibiotic are most effective against tolerant bacteria. By targeting antibiotic tolerance, we aim to tackle it before it develops into resistance.

column36: Gut microbiota and the etiology of colon cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. Although significant efforts have been employed to understand the etiology of this cancer, the causes of this cancer is still unknown. Recent work has linked bacteria that reside in the gut to CRC, specifically, certain so-called "pathobionts", which are symbiotic members of the gut microbiota that can participate in disease under specific pathological conditions. Indeed, the list of pathobionts that cause CRC is growing, yet their oncogenic mechanisms are only beginning to be understood. To understand the role of the gut microbiota and pathobionts in CRC, we developed mice that harbor genetic mutations commonly associated with CRC. In addition, since inflammatory bowel diseases predispose to CRC, we have also developed mouse models of colitis-associated cancer. Using these mouse models, we show that certain pathobionts promote cancer by interacting with specific dietary factors, the immune system, or by exploiting mutations in specific genes involved in DNA repair. In short, our work is beginning to uncover the mechanisms by which pathobionts interact with specific etiologic factors to promote cancer. Using these animal models, we are now in position to dissect the mechanisms of how different factors promote CRC and develop protocols to reduce CRC incidence in pre-clinical models. We will leverage our expertise on DNA repair, microbiology, diet, and the immune system to explore the role of gut microbiota in CRC development. Our research has the potential to lead to the development of preventative protocols or therapeutics for CRC. In addition, our research has the capacity to develop diagnostics if certain pathobionts are identified to induce CRC under specific conditions. With this new knowledge, we will be in a good position to enable clinical trials to explore the use of antioxidants, or specific dietary interventions to prevent CRC.

column36: How the brain converts memory to knowledge during the resting state: a critical factor in age-related memory impairment
column37: According to a much investigated theory, most memories are initially stored as a set of synaptic links between a pattern of hippocampal (HC) activity (the 'index' code) and patterns of neocortical (NC) activity, which are distributed widely over NC modules that contain the actual 'attributes' of the memory. During quiet rest and slow-wave sleep (SWS), recently stored patterns are spontaneously reactivated in HC and this facilitates coherent reactivation of the NC attributes of the corresponding memory. In theory, during this coordinated 'replay' process, the NC extracts the gist of recent memories and modifies its connectivity weights to build up a knowledge representation structured to capture regularities in experience and to predict outcomes of situations and ones own actions within them. These internal representations subserve categorization of context-modulated inputs and the execution of, often arbitrary, motor acts that are mapped to these inputs. The foregoing provides a potential explanation for at least a considerable part of the effect of sleep deprivation and age-related sleep disturbance on memory function and the fact that disrupted resting state activity in amnesic mild cognitive impairment predicts more serious memory decline. The better the role of memory-related brain-dynamics during sleep is understood the more likely it will be that brain-interface related interventions can be developed to ameliorate learning and memory deficits. We propose to test a theoretically motivated hypothesis about how schema development and adjustment is furthered during sleep. Specifically, we will use closed-loop recording of brain activity and electrical stimulation in rodents to determine whether the association of HC and NC activation furthers encoding of new information, whereas similar activation of NC without HC reflects spontaneous refreshment of already acquired information, which may be necessary to prevent the old data from being overwritten by the new.
