column36: Pulmonary vascular dysfunction and exercise in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a respiratory disorder commonly caused by smoking, and is characterized by breathlessness and exercise intolerance. During exercise, COPD patients are less efficient breathers, requiring them to breath more compared to individuals without COPD. This increased breathing increases the feeling of breathlessness and causes patients to stop exercising at lower intensities. Our grant will help determine why these COPD patients have inefficient breathing and get breathless during exercise. We think that these patients have problems exchanging fresh gas (i.e., oxygen) into the blood stream because of poor pulmonary blood vessel function. We will look to improve pulmonary blood vessel function and see if this improves the matching of blood flow and ventilation in the lung. We will then see if improving blood vessel function leads to better exercise capacity in more advanced disease. Finally, we will test whether an oral medication (sildenafil) can improve pulmonary blood vessel function and breathing efficiency. With this research, we will understand more about breathing efficiency, pulmonary vessel function and gas exchange in COPD patients, and find out whether improving pulmonary blood vessel function helps COPD patients breathe. Understanding the reasons behind the feeling of breathlessness may lead to more effective therapy and improved quality of life in COPD patients.

column36: Patient Engagement Partnerships in Clinical Trials (PEP-CT): Systematic Development and Testing of Patient Partner and Investigator Decision Aids
column37: The overall goal of this 2-year project is to build capacity for sex/gender uptake and patient engagement in clinical trials. A clinical trial is a research study used to compare a new drug to a harmless pill, or placebo. In Canada, we are changing our approach to clinical trial research. We now believe that patients (men and women) should be partners in deciding on the importance of research, designing studies, and sharing study results. However, investigators do not know how to work with patients, and patients do not know how to work with investigators. Our work will refine and test two decision aids to build capacity for sex/gender uptake and patient engagement in clinical trials. Decision aids can assist patients and investigators weigh their own potential benefits/risks of engaging patients as partners in clinical trial research. We have completed Phase 1 (CIHR-funded) of this project. We partnered with Clinical Trials Ontario and collaborated with patients, investigators, health care providers, and health charity and patient organizations to design two decision aids: one for patients and one for investigators. We are now seeking further funding to refine, translate (English to French), and test the decision aids through: 1) alpha (usability) testing (Phase 2), and 2) beta (field) testing (Phase 3). These methods follow International Patient Decision Aid Standards. In Phase 2, we will conduct testing cycles of five patients (men and women) and five investigators (men and women) per testing cycle. After each cycle we will make changes and continue testing cycles until no further comments are received. In Phase 3, we will test each decision aid with English- and French-speaking patients and investigators to ensure they are: 1) clear, 2) acceptable, and 3) easy to use. We have a strong project team that includes patient partners, investigators, and Clinical Trials Ontario who will make the decision aids freely available on their website.

column36: Understanding the Interaction of Acute Myeloid Leukemia with the Bone Marrow Microenvironment: Elucidating New Therapeutic Targets Through In Vivo Imaging
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a disease of the bone marrow (BM) that spreads throughout the bones of affected patients. Interactions between AML cells and its surroundings play important protective and promotive functions in leukemia growth, maintenance, and spread. Current laboratory experimental systems are not yet able to recapitulate this dynamic relationship outside of the body, and animal studies cannot visualize the changes in AML progression until death of the animal. Such methodologies are blind to important aspects of leukemia development and hinder the advancement of AML research. Our lab has developed a new technique, called the femur window chamber (FWC) model, that allows scientists to look directly into the bone of a living mouse and track the movements and/or changes of cells within the BM, over time. Our project will use this innovation to study AML cell biology and test the effect of various new anti-AML drugs. To do this, we will label AML cells with different colours and monitor their behaviour over time in the BM using the FWC. We seek to better understand the biological differences across AML subtypes and identify new treatments. We will also study the proteins that AML cells produce within the BM. If these proteins are found to be linked to certain disease subtypes or aggressiveness, this knowledge could help to better identify patients who would benefit from a specific 'personalized' treatment. Finally, we will use our unique FWC platform to study the effectiveness of various anti-AML drugs in real time and in the living mouse. Our goal is to uncover limitations in current therapies and find new treatment combinations that address vulnerabilities in AML biology to improve patient outcomes in the future. If successful, our project will establish an innovative new technique for leukemia research, uncover new knowledge surrounding AML biology, and help to develop new AML clinical trials.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of adenovirus pathogenicity and host immune evasion
column37: RuvBL1 is a cellular protein that plays an important role in a multitude of cellular processes that are essential for life. We have recently identified RuvBL1 as a protein that interacts with the adenovirus E1A protein. Adenoviruses are a family of small DNA viruses that cause a variety of diseases in humans, and, importantly, were shown to cause cancer in animals. Adenovirus E1A is the first gene expressed after infection and its function is to alter the cellular state to facilitate virus replication. Due to its cell reprogramming properties, adenovirus is an ideal tool with which to study cellular processes. column36: Rescuing beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations from resistance against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens
column37: According to the United Nations and the World Health Organization antimicrobial resistance is the largest threat to public health and economic growth. Currently, the greatest threat to human health derives from three multidrug-resistant Gram-negative priority pathogens that include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii and Enterobacteriaceae. These pathogens have become resistant to all or almost all of our antibiotics. Beta-lactam antibiotics are the most widely used class of antibacterial agents to combat bacterial infections. Beta-lactam antibiotics account for 65% of all prescriptions for injectable antibiotics in the United States. Current strategies to cope with beta-lactam antibiotic resistance are limited to inhibit beta-lactamase enzymes that hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring, thereby inactivating the drug. This can be achieved by combination therapy using a combination of a beta-lactam antibiotic and a beta-lactamase inhibitor. However, this approach does not address other resistance mechanisms that are prevalent in Gram-negative priority pathogens including outer membrane impermeability, efflux and porin suppression. To overcome these limitations we have developed beta-lactam antibiotic potentiators that restore efficacy in beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens. The overall goal of this project is (i) to develop optimized and safe beta-lactam antibiotic potentiators that overcome resistance and extend the life of clinically approved beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens and (ii) to demonstrate efficacy by protecting mice infected with beta-lactam antibiotic-resistant pathogens. Successful demonstration of efficacy and safety of the triple component combination in animal models will serve as a proof of principle to attract an industrial partner with the goal to commercialize novel anti-infective therapies.

column36: Exploring the role of a mitochondrial protein prohibitin in Leydig cell steroidogenesis
column37: Steroid hormones are essential to life. They regulate critical phases of development, such as puberty, and are essential for a number of key physiological functions in our body. Inadequate levels of steroid hormones are associated with a variety of diseases including infertility, hormone-dependent cancers (prostate, breast, ovarian), osteoporosis, and autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. Thus, steroid hormone synthesis (steroidogenesis) in different steroidogenic tissues, such as adrenal glands, ovary, and testis, is finely regulated to ensure adequate amount are produced but also to avoid conditions of hormone insufficiency or excess. The fundamental framework of steroidogenesis across major steroidogenic tissues is very similar. For example, cholesterol is the common starting material for all steroid hormones. Moreover, its transport to mitochondria (a cell compartment where steroidogenesis begins) within different steroidogenic cells and subsequent utilization for the initiation of steroidogenesis, including the male sex steroid hormone (testosterone) production by the testis, is similar. However, our understanding of this essential step of steroidogenesis remains unknown. Unraveling this may open new therapeutic opportunities for a wide variety of diseases that involved impaired steroidogenesis. Recently, my team has found that a protein called prohibitin, plays an important role in testosterone production, including the functional coupling of the crucial steps across mitochondrial membrane for the initiation of steroidogenesis. However, the mechanisms involved remain to be determined, which is the focus of this international collaborative research project. Research outcomes will advance our understanding of testosterone production by the testis, particularly the role that prohibitin plays, which is entirely unknown. The knowledge gained may create new opportunities to treat testosterone deficiency and related comorbidities.

column36: Oxidative stress in the endoplasmic reticulum and its impact on liver inflammation in an aging mouse model
column37: A recurrent theme associated with aging processes is an increase cellular oxidative stress. In addition, a chronic low-grade systemic inflammation occurring in the absence of infection has been defined as "inflammaging" and represents a significant risk factor for mortality in the elderly. There are specific inherited mutations that appear to accelerate aging in humans and Werner syndrome (WS) is an interesting example of premature aging. To understand how oxidative stress causes liver diseases that affects 20% of Canadians with age, we generated a mouse model with a mutation of the mouse Werner gene that recapitulates WS including liver diseases. These mice produce a mutant protein that ends up in the wrong place in cells causing a distress in a cellular component called Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) in the liver tissue. Interestingly, treatments of such mice with vitamin C at weaning reverse all WS anomalies. The liver is an organ that plays a pivotal role in nutrient, drug, hormone, and metabolic waste product processing, thereby maintaining the normal function of other organs in the body. We found that the ER distress is caused by an abnormal increase in oxidative stress in this compartment. We thus hypothesize that a continuous oxidative ER stress causes a low but chronic inflammation in the liver of Werner mice. However, we do not know how exactly a mutation in the Wrn gene causes this oxidative stress in the ER. To answer this question, we propose the following 2 aims: 1) we will determine whether the mislocalized Wrn mutant protein affects the GRP78 interactome in the ER which is an important protein of the ER stress response and 2) we will determine how the Wrn mutant protein induces ER stress and an inflammatory signal. The results generated with our mice will allow us to identify molecular problems (and thus potential therapeutic targets) causing oxidative stress in the ER and inflammation during aging.

column36: Examining the long-term illness experiences of injured older adults to select patient-driven outcome measures in geriatric trauma
column37: Older adults (65 years and older) make up 51% of all injury hospitalizations in Canada. This number is expected to rise as the aging population surges in the coming years. The most common cause of unintentional physical injury in older adults is a fall, followed by motor vehicle collisions. The injuries resulting from these incidents include traumatic brain injury, fractures, broken bones and internal organ damage. Injured older adults receive specialized care in trauma centres that are equipped for injury management. Because of this organized care, many injured older adults will survive their injuries but their health status and quality of life will significantly change. Up to now, very little has been studied about the long-term illness experiences of older adult trauma survivors because most injury care in the past was tailored to a younger population. For this reason we know very little about the experiences of these survivors; we do not know what outcomes they consider to be most meaningful or if the way we currently deliver care to these patients will lead us to achieve these. Our study will examine the experiences of older adult trauma survivors over two years, so that we can, for the first time, describe and understand what a good quality of life after injury looks like from an older adult's perspective. Using interviews and observations, we will gather survivors' experiences from three Ontario trauma centres at 3-, 12- and 24 months after injury. We are especially interested in understanding how their survivorship experiences are influenced by sociocultural factors such as age and gender, and other social dimensions. Our study results will not only help us to understand what older adult trauma survivors experience and how they might want to receive care differently, but it will help in the selection of measures that healthcare providers and policymakers can use to evaluate and improve the overall quality of care to injured older adults in Canada and beyond.

column37: As diabetes reaches epidemic magnitude worldwide, more diabetics face the problems of morbidity and mortality due to chronic complications. Diabetes causes scarring and damage to the heart and is one of the leading causes of heart disease in Canada. We plan to investigate the mechanisms leading to development of heart damage in diabetes. In diabetes, cells use its fuel differently and as such, causes damage to the cell nucleus. The cell's nucleus, in turn, sends signals to make additional proteins that cause tissue damage. If these processes continue, the cells ultimately fail to function. The signals sent out by the nucleus involve special types of molecules called lncRNAs. They are also known as the 'dark matter of the genome'. These molecules have been recently discovered and have a major role in regulating protein production. We plan to examine how lncRNAs can interact with other RNA molecules and other mechanisms that change the production of abnormal molecules. We will also determine whether by manipulating these mechanisms, we can prevent damage to the heart in diabetes. The proposed research is based on several aims, each of which will be investigated at multiple levels of complexities. Our experiments will include examinations of various types of cells from the heart and the cells of the blood vessels. We will also use animals with diabetes. As well, we will use several compounds to block these mechanisms to understand how this can be prevented. Some of our experiments will focus on specific lncRNAs that we have identified in our laboratory. We will further expand our studies to examine the heart tissues removed from patients and examine whether the abnormalities identified in the cells and in the animals also occur in humans. This proposal represents a comprehensive set of studies to investigate a specific process (i.e. heart damage) in diabetes. Understanding such mechanisms will help to develop preventive treatments for such conditions.

Using this system, we discovered that lipid molecules called PIPs are important for sperm head formation. Male flies with mutations in enzymes that affect formation of PIPs have abnormal sperm heads and are sterile. The main goal of our research is to understand how these enzymes and PIPs regulate sperm head formation. To do this, we will use advanced microscopy, proteomics, biochemistry and molecular genetic techniques in flies. Because human sperm form in a similar way, our discoveries will generate novel insights into human male fertility. Understanding this process will eventually lead to new treatments for male infertility as well as novel approaches to developing male contraceptives.

column36: The role of the medial zona incerta in the control of exploratory and escape locomotion
column37: Over the last decade, impressive advances have been made in our understanding of locomotion and the control of movement. column36: Identifying the Cellular Mechanisms by which Inhibiting Ketone Body Oxidation Improves Glycemia in Obesity/Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Our bodies rely on 3 major fuel sources we obtain from the food we eat; fats, sugars, and protein. However, during starvation our livers make a 4th fuel source that our organs (brain, heart, and muscle are the main users) can use to make energy, the ketone body. Past research has heavily focused on understanding the regulation of fat, sugar, and protein metabolism in health, and how they malfunction in various diseases such as obesity and diabetes. The regulation of ketone body metabolism in health and disease has received much less attention. However, exciting data in our lab has shown that decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control in obesity/diabetes. The major goal of our research project is to understand how decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control. In order to test our hypothesis, our lab has generated genetically modified mice that have reduced metabolism of ketone bodies only in their muscles. We have identified a number of potential factors that may explain the improved blood sugar control in these animals, which includes; (1) general increases in a protein modification known as succinylation, (2) activation of a global energy sensor protein, and (3) enhanced sugar metabolism. We will use both drugs and genetic approaches to independently reverse these 3 changes in our animals, in order to determine whether they counteract the improved blood sugar control we have observed during obesity/diabetes. In summary, our research may lead to the discovery of a new approach to improve blood sugar control in obesity/diabetes, while defining how this improvement takes place at the cellular level.

column37: Normally the neurotransmitter glutamate acts at synapses on the cell surface of spinal cord neurons to signal pain. However, glutamate receptors are also found inside these neurons, including at the nucleus of the cell. column36: When Pain Drives you N. U. T. S.: A mixed methods approach to investigating triggers of the stress response and multidimensional pain outcomes in a sample of individuals suffering from chronic low back pain
column37: One in five Canadian suffers from chronic pain. Psychological factors play an important role in the perception, development and maintenance of chronic pain. These factors however are often examined without considering the nature of the pain experience that could influence these psychological responses. In fact, someone experiencing pain that frequently shoots up to an intensity of 10/10 without any warnings (unpredictable) or ability to decrease its intensity (low control) might perceive this pain as more stressful compared to someone whose pain intensity is relatively stable even if on average both individuals' pain are of a similar intensity. From the general litterature, 4 characteristics of situations lead to a physiological stress response: Novelty, Unpredictability, Threat to ego, and Sense of low control (N.U.T.S.). The objective of this study is to examine the N.U.T.S. characteristics of pain-related and unrelated stressors, combined with individuals' vulnerability to these different characteristics and their associations with pain outcomes such as appraisal, interference, and disability. The study will recruit 300 patients with chronic low back pain from a provincial cohort of back pain patients. Participants will be asked to complete questionnaires at baseline and then fill out an electronic diary daily for 7 days and provide saliva samples to analyse basal cortisol levels. Finally, they will complete follow-up questionnaires 4-8 weeks later. A subgroup of patients will also be asked to participate in an individual interview to explore their experience of the stressful characteristics of pain. Study results will identify important dimensions of the stress experience that have been so far studied in isolation in the field of pain. Such knowledge could help improve the evaluation of pain and the treatment approaches that are proposed to patients. This study may thus potentially change the way we assess patients' psychological response to pain.

column36: Health-Related Quality of Life and Aging: Measuring what Matters to Older People
column37: This study addresses a measurement gap related to assessing those aspects of health that matter to the quality of life of older persons, termed health-related quality of life (HRQL). Measures exist for assessing the HRQL impact of illnesses and conditions but these measures are not best suited for older persons who may have many such illnesses and conditions but who are still interested and involved in aging actively. Some of the existing measures use many items to assess all the different illness aspects; others use very few items and capture only an illness snapshot. Often the items are not relevant to the experience of older persons and some of the items ask the same content in different ways, something that many find confusing, if not annoying. The intent here is to develop a brief measure of what matters to older persons as they attempt to get on with their life despite an illness burden. This study will also use modern statistical and measurement approaches to create a scoring method that produces a value that considers the preferences for different combinations of health circumstances from the perspective of the older person: "If I had to have that (pain) then I would also rather have this (many interesting distractions)". The gathering of evidence to support the interpretation of the scores across different groups of people (validation) will also be conducted through this project using a mix of in-person assessments and anonymous surveys using the internet. The methods proposed are consistent with the most up-to-date and rigorous guidelines for developing and testing measures and will result in a measure that can be used to evaluate seniors in their own communities.

column36: Redefining blood pressure: How novel views of the arterial tree can lead to better cardiovascular risk stratification.
column37: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and hypertension, one of its main determinants, are major health problems in Canada. Despite enormous progress in the treatment of hypertension, the principles of blood pressure (BP) measurement has remained largely unchanged in the past century. In recent years, the reliability of standard BP measurements (using a brachial cuff) has been questioned, raising doubts as to the best way to manage hypertension. This, in parallel with a better understanding of how the pressure travels in the blood vessels, results in a new enthusiasm to find improved ways to determine CVD risk using BP parameters. In this regard, the aim of this study is to determine if various novel arterial wave parameters (central BP, arterial wave reflection and reservoir, aortic stiffness) are better at determining the CVD risk compared to traditional brachial cuff BP and other known risk factors. To achieve these goals, we will use data from CARTaGENE, a large Canadian populational cohort with available arterial wave recordings, and follow-up data from governmental databases. Overall, data is available for 17,795 participants. Through a collaboration with the Austrian Institute of Technology, we will isolate and re-analyse each recording, which will provide the arterial wave parameter we wish to study. Then, using various statistical analyses, we will be able to determine if each arterial wave parameter is better at predicting CVD than traditional factors in the general population. This would by far the largest study to investigate the predictive power of these novel BP parameters, and should provide definitive answers as to their utility above and beyond standard cuff BP. This is the necessary first step to determine if we can improve hypertension management and reduce the burden of CVD. Given the recent technological advances, these innovative parameters can easily be incorporated into devices that could be used in clinical practice.

column36: Investigation of novel host-based approaches for the treatment of tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB), is a mycobacterial infection that is one of the world's most pressing health problems. Each day, 5,000 people die from TB globally. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that TB will infect 225 million and kill 75 million people between 2015-2050. TB spreads by aerosol through sneezing and coughing, and each person with TB infects ~15 more people/yr. There is a clear association between the immune status of an individual, the outcome of infection and reactivation of TB disease. It is crucial to find efficient host-based therapies if we are to conquer dreaded MDR, XDR and TDR-TB. Recently, we have discovered a novel immunotherapeutic that significantly reduces mycobacterial loads in mice. In the proposed work we will investigate its antimycobacterial potential in conjunction with modified Mtb antigens to enhance Mtb-specific host immunity, and in combination with the current anti-TB drugs. These studies will contribute significantly to the investigation of new approaches, and identification of new therapeutic regimens to treat active TB, MDR-, XDR- and TDR-TB infections, and will have major impact on the health of Canadians and people worldwide.

column36: Does inflammation in brain cause hypoxia, which then exacerbates inflammation: a multimodal study using the EAE inflammation model of multiple sclerosis.
column37: We have discovered that many people with MS have low oxygen levels in the brain (hypoxia). We have also found brain hypoxia in the mouse EAE model, the most commonly used animal model of central nervous system inflammation. This supports the idea that both inflammation and hypoxia responses are linked in a cycle, where inflammation causes hypoxia and hypoxia stimulates inflammation. This grant proposal will use the EAE model and novel imaging tools that are only available in my lab to determine if inflammation can cause hypoxia, and whether that hypoxia can make MS worse. We can quantify hypoxia using unique implantable oxygen probes, which we helped design, MRI and NIRS. Hypoxia could be caused by inflammation, resulting in blockage of small vessels and reduction in local oxygen delivery. We will look for this with histology. The inflammation and the loss of myelin covering the axons could cause an increase in metabolic rate. With MRI, we can measure blood flow and assess myelin loss, and with a unique light based system (near-infrared spectroscopy or NIRS) we can quantify metabolic rate. Since the imaging methods have potential for translation to patients, this aspect of the proposal will demonstrate how MRI and NIRS might be used to monitor hypoxia in humans. After determining whether there is a correlation between hypoxia, brain damage and loss of function, we will further study the link by blocking either inflammation or increasing oxygen in parallel studies. We already know that there is inflammation in MS, but only recently did we discover that there is hypoxia. This project will be the only one in Canada to have our unique mouse NIRS system and the ability to combine this with MRI to study the link between hypoxia and inflammation. We will create new knowledge on how inflammation and hypoxia interrelate, and provide new evidence on how oxygen therapy can be helpful in a condition of inflammation induced hypoxia.

The methodology to test his hypothesis directly is to use a complex method that obtains three sources of data at the same time to test for direct causality. This method consists of capturing both fMRI data and electrocardiogram data at the same time that TMS is stimulating the brain. Experiments will be conducted in a group of healthy volunteers as well as patients with depression. The results of this study may have profound implications in both our understanding of the causes of depression as well as the mechanism of action of rTMS and pave the way to the testing of reliable, feasible, and easy to access biomarkers of response in rTMS.

column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is the leading cause of disability in the world. MDD is associated with suicide, which is estimated to claim the lives of 800,000 people worldwide each year, accounting for 1-4% of deaths globally. It is estimated that 30-40% of patients with MDD do not improve with medications (treatment resistant depression-TRD). Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a treatment that stimulates specific areas of the brain by means of small currents while the person is comfortably sitting in a chair. rTMS is associated to significant improvement in approximately 50% of TRD patients and is usually well tolerated. Low frequency rTMS (LFR) has also been shown to be an effective treatment for TRD in small studies, but has never been compared to iTBS and is currently not approved by the FDA. The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that LFR works as well as the established iTBS treatment for TRD. In this multi-centre, triple-blinded, non-inferiority trial 420 patients with TRD will be recruited at three academic centres (UBC, CAMH and UHN). Patients will be randomised to receive either iTBS or LFR for 30 sessions. The primary outcome will be the improvement on a depression scale. Secondary outcome will be improvement of on suicidal ideation. A secondary aim is to test the predictive capacity of a novel, easy to implement heart rate based biomarkers (i.e. heart rate variability). The results of this study may lead to the approval of an alternative form of rTMS for depression and suicidal ideation available and ready for widespread use in clinical settings, including the possibility of exploring a home-based treatment with LFR.

column36: Organoids to guide Post-resistance Therapy In driver MutAted Lung cancers (OPTIMAL)
column37: Some types of lung cancer can be specifically targeted by "designer" drugs. Most patients initially respond very well to these targeted drugs with prolonged survival, but eventually they grow resistant and stop responding. Determining which drug to offer next is a major challenge. We have developed a novel model to study drug resistance: 3-dimensional Patient-Derived cancer cell clusters, or "Organoids" (PDOs). PDOs can be rapidly grown from patient biopsies, mimic important properties of patient tumours and are amenable to laboratory characterization. We hypothesize that extensive drug testing and molecular profiling of PDOs can help scientists identify new effective treatments and help doctors to make better treatment decisions for lung cancer patients. We have already shown that our PDO models successfully mirror their original tumours. Our first aim is to optimize PDO model generation and drug testing. Our second aim is to test our PDO model system in patients: we will biopsy patients when their tumours stop responding to a targeted drug and grow these biopsies as PDOs. We will then test a series of clinically-available drugs on these models to determine the most effective treatment for each patient. Tracking the molecular changes in these models will show us how these drugs are working (or not working). Our third aim will explore the use of experimental drug compounds on PDO models to discover new agents for lung cancer therapy. The results of this study have the potential to greatly impact the management of lung cancer: 15% of lung cancers (>4000/year in Canada) are targetable, mostly in younger patients who have never smoked. Targeted therapies have the potential to convert currently fatal cancer into chronic, controllable and manageable disease. The major barrier to this promise is drug resistance. Our research will identify novel resistance mechanisms and methods to overcome this resistance, providing a clinical pipeline to personalize cancer therapy.

column37: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is the term used to describe children who struggle to learn tasks that require motor coordination. In Canada, about 1 to 2 children in every classroom have DCD. Parents and teachers tell us these children have problems learning to do everyday motor activities like tying shoelaces, playing ball, and climbing stairs. Some research has shown that these kids are more likely to be overweight, inactive, unfit, and to have more mental health problems by the time they are teenagers. Unfortunately, many of these children are not identified, and therefore do not get the help they need when they need it. To understand how to help kids with DCD, we need to be able to determine when they begin to be less active and less healthy, both physically and mentally. The goal of our study is to keep observing a large group of children with and without DCD who we have been following since they were 4 or 5 years old. We will continue following them once per year until they are 10 and 11 years old. At each visit, we will keep measuring their motor coordination, how much physical activity they do, how fit they are, their diet, and how much they weigh. We will also start to ask the children questions about how they feel about themselves and if they are feeling anxious or depressed. What makes our study new and exciting is that we will be able to find out when children with DCD start to become less active and less healthy. Working with doctors, teachers, and parents will help us make sure that we recognize kids with DCD as young as possible so that they are able to get the right type of support, at the right time, before they become inactive, obese, or depressed.

column37: Deficient blood supply to the central nervous system (CNS) leads to several debilitating diseases. Examples of such diseases include stroke which is a leading cause of brain injury affecting 800,000 individuals per year in the United States alone and causing upwards of 150,000 deaths. To study the molecular mechanisms of stroke, an easily accessible model system in which to investigate how blood vessels interact with nerve cells is the retina, the membrane of nerve cells at the back of the eye that relays visual information to the brain. The retina is biochemically analogous to the brain and its anatomical location allows for thorough investigation. In addition, findings that are obtained from studying stroke in the retina can be translated to better understand ischemic retinopathies, such as diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity which are the leading causes of blindness in the industrial world. These blinding diseases happen to also stem from compromised blood supply to the neurons of the retina. This proposal seeks to understand how blood vessels degenerate in ischemic diseases of the CNS by using the retina as a model. Furthermore, we propose to investigate the role of cholesterol metabolism in modulating inflammation upon ischemia. Ultimately, we hope to interfere with the disease process and promote regeneration of functional blood vessels.

column36: Molecular imaging biomarkers of cognition in Parkinson's disease
column37: Cognitive decline in Parkinson's Disease (PD) may occur, anywhere from 20-60%, with an impairment in one or more cognitive domains. Different subtypes of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) have been identified in PD. Single-domain non-amnestic impairments are most commonly frontal-executive in nature, while multi-domain impairments include any combination of deficits in various cognitive domains. Recent studies found that multi-domain MCI is highly associated with conversion to dementia. Today, the lack of information on the biological bases of these cognitive complications in PD has prevented the development of optimal treatments to alleviate these non-motor aspects. While the role of dopaminergic degeneration in cognitive dysfunction in PD may appear obvious, it has become clear that this alone cannot explain the severity of cognitive decline in those patients with multi-domain MCI and dementia. Other factors have to play an important role as well. In support of this, while there is large preclinical data suggesting a potential role of activated microglia, beta-amyloid and tau deposition in neurodegenerative processes, to date the in-vivo evidence of these pathologies in PD manifesting with multi-domain MCI and dementia remains unclear. This grant proposal shifts the focus from neurotransmitter changes to study the relationship between neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau deposition, using a set of new PET radiotracers. This data set will offer a unique multi-modal integrated approach to investigate and correlate clinical and pathophysiological mechanisms associated with more severe cognitive decline in PD.

Such molecules could represent a novel class of therapeutics to prevent and control S. aureus infections. The development of alternatives, or complementary therapeutics to enhance antibiotic action, could reduce the severity of the antibiotic resistance crisis.

column36: Estimating the impact of alcohol deregulation in Ontario on future burden of alcohol consumption and harms for the overall population and across vulnerable sub-populations: Evidence to inform the complex relationships between alcohol policy, consumption, and harms.
column37: Alcohol is a leading risk factor for death and disease in Canada. The top alcohol-related conditions include liver diseases, cardiovascular diseases, injuries, alcohol dependence, and cancers. Studies show that despite consuming lower levels of alcohol, lower socioeconomic groups are more likely to experience alcohol-related harms than higher socioeconomic groups. Therefore, alcohol policies aiming to reduce population-level alcohol use and harms have potential to reduce health inequalities. In Canada, policies have been implemented in provinces and territories to moderate alcohol use and minimize its negative consequences. However, over the past two decades, Alberta, British Columbia, and most recently Ontario have deregulated alcohol sales and increased privatization of alcohol retail markets. Few studies have examined the impact of deregulation on alcohol use and health harms in the population, and particularly on "social inequities in health" (i.e., health differences between social groups that are avoidable and unfair). The proposed changes to alcohol policies in Ontario offer a real-world opportunity to examine the relationships between how alcohol is sold across the province and the current and projected burden of alcohol-related harms and costs in the population, and within social groups (i.e., age, sex, and socioeconomic status). The purpose of the proposed research is to use an innovative modelling methodology that combines population surveys linked to health administrative datasets to better understand the extent to which changes to alcohol policy impact alcohol consumption, alcohol-related health harms and healthcare costs in the population overall and among key subpopulations, including youth and young adults, females, and lower socioeconomic populations. Results of the proposed research can be used to directly inform alcohol policies and health equity strategies in Ontario and across Canada.

column36: A novel approach to determine the dietary docosahexaenoic acid requirement of humans
column37: While omega-3 fatty acids are an essential part of the diet one omega-3, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), is very controversial. DHA has been called nutritionally essential, non-essential and everything in between. We believe that a major reason for this controversy is a lack of objective measures to understand DHA status. We have recently discovered that when feeding DHA to animals or humans there is a "backlog" in some of the precursor molecules that can be used to synthesise DHA. This "backlog" is essentially a negative feedback system telling the body to stop making DHA because there is enough. Thus, we aim to test, in people who do not eat DHA (certain vegetarians and vegans) when DHA causes this backlog. We will then test if other omega-3 fats can contribute to the DHA requirement. This work would resolve a more than 30-year old debate and could be used to start setting worldwide requirements for DHA, possibly affecting the health of billions.

column36: A longitudinal dyadic investigation of the role of interpersonal trauma and couple relationships on parents' mental health and child adjustment
column37: Couple relationships are described as the most significant relationship for a majority of adults, and recognized as a key determinant of mental health. The arrival of a child might be a particularly vulnerable period for parental couple relationships (e.g., conflicts, alliance), and in turn have a negative effect on both parents' mental health and their child's adjustment. An important risk factor related to the health trajectory of parental couples might be the experience of childhood interpersonal trauma (CIT; sexual abuse, neglect, etc). CIT is an endemic social problem associated with longstanding and costly mental health problems that can be exacerbated in the years following the birth of a child. Yet, the complex longitudinal associations between CIT, parental mental health and child adjustment remain unclear. Research including both partners is needed to understand how relationship factors can affect parents and their child. In this project, we will gather novel longitudinal data among parental couples to test relationship factors as the mechanism linking CIT to parental mental health and child adjustment. Both parents will complete questionnaires assessing their CIT, mental health (e.g., stress) and child adjustment (e.g., behaviors problems), at four assessments waves. Interactions among the parental couple will also be assessed using naturalistic observations. The longitudinal design will allow the examination of parental mental health and child adjustment trajectories in the years following the birth of a child, while considering relational factors from the perspectives of both parents. This study will help elucidate how CIT relates to health outcomes in victims, their partner and their child, and identify risk and protection factors, to guide the elaboration of efficient interventions aiming to enhance the health of Canadian families.

column36: Investigating the neural basis of motor and cognitive disabilities following childhood stroke
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of neurological disabilities in Canadian children. Children often have better recoveries than adults after suffering a stroke, however they also are more likely to undergo changes in the brain during recovery that can cause cognitive or movement disabilities, such as dystonia. In addition, its prevalence is higher in children under 10 years of age, suggesting that age at time of stroke also plays a role. It is becoming increasingly important to better understand when and why this happens so that health professionals can tailor therapeutic strategies to target the most effected regions of the brain during recovery, especially during critical periods of childhood development. We will measure changes in movement, sensory and intellectual abilities in children between 6 and 18 years of age during recovery from a stroke. We will use advanced brain imaging techniques (magnetoencephalography, MEG and magnetic resonance imaging, MRI), as well as neuropsychological assessments during their recovery in order to track the development of motor or other deficits. We expect that children who develop dystonia and related symptoms after stroke will demonstrate altered activity in sensory and movement regions of the brain, and severity will be related to age at the time of their stroke. We will also determine whether younger children have a higher rate of post-stroke movement disorders and poor outcomes and if these are associated with more widespread involvement of different brain regions. Our goal is to monitor these changes in the brain during recovery from childhood stroke to determine what factors might predict which children are more likely to have undesired outcomes.

column36: Molecular mechanisms controlling maintenance and plasticity of GABAergic circuits in the adult brain.
column37: GABAergic neurons, a particular subset of brain cells, powerfully control the function of brain circuits. Many common neurological disorders, including schizophrenia and autism, are thought to be partially consequence of defects in the development of GABAergic neurons. In particular, such disorders seem to be associated with defects in the way this subset of neurons connects and communicates with other neurons, via specialized loci called synapses. In addition, the maturation of GABAergic synapses is thought to limit brain plasticity in the adult brain. Because of the complexity of brain circuitry, it has been so far very difficult to understand how GABAergic neurons form, maintain and change their synapses and how disturbances in this process may lead to altered cognitive functions. The experiments we propose will use imaging, electrophysiological and gene manipulation techniques to dissect the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the maturation and plasticity of GABAergic synapses in the postnatal brain. This approach will shed light on the factors regulating the function of GABAergic synapses in the normal brain and on the pathological process leading to their disturbance. In addition, a better comprehension of the mechanisms underlying GABAergic synapse plasticity in the adult brain may help developing novel tools to securely foster brain plasticity to aid cognitive rehabilitation in adult patients suffering of different psychiatric disorders, such as post-traumatic stress disorder.

column36: Targeting opioid neurotransmission in borderline personality disorder with self-harming behavior: A [11C]NOP-1A positron emission tomography study
column37: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious psychiatric condition that is very common. Many patients with BPD intentionally hurt themselves by cutting their skin with blades or knives. This self-harming behavior, which is called non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) when there is no intent to die, is thought to reduce stress levels in BPD and may also occur, because individuals with BPD are less sensitive to pain. Some research suggests that the brain opioid system may be dysfunctional in BPD. We propose to study the opioid system and NSSI in BPD by measuring brain levels of the nociceptin/orphanin FQ peptide (NOP) opioid receptor using positron emission tomography, a brain scanning technique. We will be studying participants with BPD who engage in NSSI (BPD+NSSI), BPD patients who do not self-harm (BPD-NSSI), and healthy controls who have no history of NSSI. Each participant will undergo one PET scan. We believe that brain opioid levels will be lower in BPD+NSSI, because this group shows the least sensitivity to pain. These results would offer one explanation for better understanding the role of opioid functioning in NSSI and BPD. Furthermore, these data could also provide the impetus to develop new opioid-based treatments that might prevent NSSI.

column37: Fats are essential molecules for all cells. Fats are key parts of the walls around cells, and cells also use them as an energy source. Too much fat, however, is toxic. Cells have developed strategies to prevent toxicity from too much fat. Cells can transport fats to other cells that are better equipped to make use of the extra fat. This is a particularly important process in the brain. Of all the organs in our bodies, our brains contain the highest percentage of fat. Problems in transporting fats between cells occur in many neurodegenerative diseases. Recovery from stroke is also affected by problems in transporting fats in the brain. This research project will uncover molecular pathways and mechanisms that control transport of fat in the brain. We will study individual brain cells and mice to determine these pathways and mechanisms. With that knowledge in hand, in the future we can examine molecules in those pathways and mechanisms as targets for drugs. Such drugs could be developed to reduce or avoid fat toxicity in neurodegenerative diseases or stroke.

column36: Optimizing resuscitation of the donation after circulatory death (DCD) heart by mitochondrial redox regulation and opioid receptor activation: a protocol for clinical application
column37: Few therapies are available to patients who are suffering end-stage heart failure. Cardiac transplantation remains the gold-standard therapeutic intervention for those patients with end-stage heart failure. Donation after Circulatory Death or DCD means that organ donation happens after the heart stops beating after withdrawal of life support. This is in contrast to donation after brain death where donors have lost brain function, but the heart is still beating and blood circulates in the body. This type of organ donation is currently the standard in Canada and many other countries, but donation after brain death is limited by the availability of suitable donors. In DCD, the "non-heart beating" donors have suffered circulatory arrest and organ retrieval should ideally start as soon as possible after circulatory death. However, for the donated heart to function well as graft in a putative recipient, it has to be supplied with oxygen and nutrients as quickly as possible after circulatory death to resume normal function without irreversible damage. Our research addresses the use of a novel therapy with clinically approved medication and out-of-the-body heart perfusion in a beating state on a specifically designed apparatus to provide optimized heart protection during the bridging time between heart procurement from the donor and transplantation into a recipient. The data generated from our studies will provide the foundations for a clinical program that will expand the donor heart pool for transplantation.

column36: Mechanisms of epigenetic evolution in pediatric high-grade gliomas
column37: Pediatric high-grade gliomas are rare and always lethal brain cancers. Unlike other malignancies, they harbor few mutations in genes. Only some tumors have mutations in established cancer driver genes. These results led us to hypothesize that the biology of pediatric high-grade gliomas may be driven in large part by epigenetic events. Specifically, we hypothesize that DNA regions that that act as switches for genes could be aberrantly turned on or off to maximize the ability of the tumor to grow. These switches are controlled by proteins called transcription factors. In this application, we propose to investigate the role of control regions (the switches) in determining gene expression and functional properties of malignant cells. Our preliminary data indicate that different switches are turned on when the tumor recurs after treatment, and that this phenomenon may contribute to the emergence of properties that are typical of the tumor at relapse. Because tumors at diagnosis and relapse are so different, our data highlight the importance of specifically studying relapse samples, which are the entities that ultimately kill patients. Our studies will focus on rare pairs of diagnostic and relapse samples from the same patients, as well as on patient-derived models for functional validation. In the proposed studies, we will identify the transcription factors that are turning these switches on or off. The ultimate goal of our proposal is to understand how pediatric high-grade gliomas originate and evolve, and to identify strategies to prevent relapses through new and targeted therapeutic interventions.

column36: Mapping and targeting the niche-specific proteomes of glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive adult brain tumor with an expected survival of under 15 months despite aggressive treatment. In the past, traditional models of cancer biology have largely considered GBMs to be a uniform mass of cancer cells. Research, however, has now challenged this notion and instead supports the idea that cancer is "heterogenous" with important regional differences in the biological programs of cancer cells. This includes tumor areas with low oxygen (hypoxia) and regions where the tumor infiltrates through normal brain tissue. These differences appear to that play important roles in cancer growth and therapy resistance. In light of this, there is renewed interest in revisiting our theories and models of cancer and addressing how the different features of GBM, visible under the microscope, affect its regional biology. To answer this intriguing question, our team will use our expertise using a technology known as mass spectrometry to comprehensively survey the regional protein patterns ("proteomes") of well understood GBM compartments from different patients' tumors to understand how they differ from one another. Similarly, we will also use advanced laboratory tools to study these critical features. By growing cancer cells in various amounts of oxygen, we will be able to closely monitor how cancer cells dynamically change their biology in different environments. column36: Novel endothelial engineering and localized immunosuppression approaches for the protection of organ transplants
column37: Organ transplantation is life saving therapy. However, the potential this therapy is diminished by the rejection. Many thousands of patients are waiting for transplantation and the waiting list is growing day by day. Organs are damaged during the current procurement of organs, which lead to the poor performance of the transplanted organs and ultimately immune mediated rejection. Current treatments are suboptimal. Life-long immunosuppressants are required for all transplant patients to prevent the rejection; however, they have major side effects including infection, diabetics and cancer. The root cause of the delayed performance and rejection of the transplanted organs is the initial damage of blood vessel lining during organ procurement and preservation which exacerbated after transplantation. This initial damage recruit cells and proteins in our immune system upon transplantation, and causes massive damage to the organs which cannot be self-repaired. Based on our recent discoveries, we hypothesized that rebuilding the immunosuppressive blood vessel lining will prevent such injuries and could prevent organ rejection (both immediate and delayed). Thus in this project, we will develop a novel organ engineering therapy based on a polymer based cell surface modification. This is anticipated to inhibit the immune damage and thus will prevent organ rejection. We will study the mechanism of this therapeutic approach and apply this technique in the transplantation of arteries and kidneys as proof-of-concept. If successful, this new immune therapy approach will save millions of patients not only undergoing transplantation but also those undergoing surgeries to repair their damaged tissues. Importantly, the new therapy can be applied during the current clinical organ procurement and preservation protocols thus have significant translational potential. The new approach may also minimize or eliminate the use of immunosuppressants, thus increasing the health benefits.

column37: It is estimated that viruses are responsible for about 10% of human cancers. In this respect, viruses are a risk factor for cancer second only to tobacco. column36: Biotherapeutic implications for oncolytic virus-induced MHC class I ligandomes
column37: Oncolytic viruses (OVs) have emerged as a new class of cancer immunotherapeutics. Apart from their direct cancer-killing activity, OVs promote clinically desired immune attack on cancers from CD8 T cells. This OV-induced CD8 T cell attack on tumors can be further potentiated by immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) agents, and as such, OV+ICB combination therapies are becoming routine in clinical testing. Here, OV-induced, ICB-potentiated CD8 T cells can target existing cancer cells at local and metastatic sites, and maintain protection against possible relapse even after the discontinuation of the therapy. Thus, CD8 T cell response is clinically relevant and can be harnessed to enhance the efficacy of OV+ICB therapies. The harnessing of such CD8 T cell response requires information on the MHC-I ligands [MiLs] that drive their biological activity. Unfortunately, the identification of such MiLs, usually 8-11 amino acids long, has remained technologically challenging. We have addressed this challenge by developing the next-generation of applied immunomics and mass spectrometry-based platforms that now streamline the high-throughput discovery and biological validation of MiLs. Interestingly, OVs induce two types of CD8 T cell responses: antitumor and antiviral- which are defined by Mils arising from tumors (TuMiLs) and the virus (ViMiLs), respectively. These MiLs not only shape the clinically relevant biological features of underlying CD8 T cell responses, but also can be harnessed within novel CD8 T cell repurposing therapeutic strategies to attack cancers. In this context, this project is focused on comprehensively understanding the bio-therapeutic implications for TuMiL- and ViMiL-specific antitumor and antiviral CD8 T cell responses, respectively. Our proof-of-concept multi-disciplinary study promises to identify urgently needed information on establishing effective cancer immunotherapies aimed at promoting better outcomes from cancers in clinics.

column36: Signatures of protective immunity against HCV
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is still a public health priority as many remain undiagnosed and increased infections in association with the opioid epidemic. Direct acting antivirals offer complete cure in >95% of infected individuals but do not prevent reinfection. Furthermore, HCV disproportionately affects some populations with limited access to health services and who remain at high risk of HCV infection and reinfection like Indigenous peoples, people who use drugs (PWUD), newcomers to Canada, men who have sex with men and others. Hence, there is an urgent need for vaccines that can protect against this virus. Unfortunately, despite our knowledge about the immune response against HCV, we still do not have an effective vaccine. Recent results from the only vaccine candidate that made it into a large scale (Phase 2) clinical trial did not show any protection in PWUD at risk of HCV infection. This means that we have to understand better the immune factors that protect against HCV. This project will examine what constitutes such a good immune response by studying immunity in a group of PWUD who are constantly being exposed to the virus where some are able to clear it several times and others cannot. We will identify the differences in those who clear the viruses and those who cannot. We will also compare the immune response in individuals who clear the virus spontaneously versus those who clear it post treatment to determine if they are less protected against HCV if they are re-exposed to it. We will use the latest technology to examine the immune response at the functional and genomic level and identify cellular pathways and key molecules that are implicated in the development and maintenance of a protective immune response. We will attempt to use chemical compounds to correct the defects observed in those who are unable to clear the virus. Such compounds can be combined with different vaccine candidates to enhance their immunogenicity and protective capacity.

column37: An estimated 670,000 Canadians suffer from heart failure (HF) with the estimated direct cost of management >$2.8B annually throughout Canada. column36: The Development of Novel Neuroactive Compounds to Combat Parasitic Nematodes
column37: Over one quarter of the world's population is infected with a parasitic nematode. These infections result in over 130,000 deaths each year. The world health organization reports that disability caused by nematode infection is equivalent to that caused by malaria or tuberculosis. Resistance to molecules that kill parasitic nematodes is emerging in human infections. Public health experts warn that it is only a matter of time before resistance blooms in nematode parasites of humans. Consequently, public health experts are asking that new nematicidal drugs be developed now. To develop new molecules that kill parasitic nematodes, we screened for small molecules that paralyze and/or kill the tractable, but non-parasitic, nematode C. elegans. We re-screened lethal molecules in human cell culture to eliminate generally toxic molecules. We then screened the remaining molecules against several parasitic nematode species. We identified a small molecule family called 'wact-45' that inhibits the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT). VAChT functions to package the acetylcholine neurotransmitter within neurons so that they are able to properly communicate with one another. Our data suggests that wact-45 may preferentially inhibit nematode VAChT. We propose to: i) better understand VAChT structure and function, and ii) further develop the wact-45 small molecule structure to optimize its potency and nematode selectivity so that it is safe for use in humans who are infected with nematode parasites. Parasitic nematodes infect vast numbers of people, and especially in poor countries. Children are particularly vulnerable, and infections can lead to disability that lasts a lifetime. Given that resistance to existing anti-nematode drugs is emerging, our work has the potential to lead to new medicines that could have a tremendous global impact on the health of some of the most vulnerable people among us.

column37: A strong concern has been sweeping through Canada that we are falling behind other countries by underestimating inequities - unfair and systematic differences - in health status across race/ethnic groups. This proposal will use Statistics Canada data to produce this evidence. We aim to: (a) determine the extent of inequities (differences) in chances of dying across race/ethnic groups in Canada; (b) determine whether inequities in chances of dying are further influenced by other social and economic characteristics, such as gender and income. We bring a lot of scientific expertise and experience in engaging government and civil society organizations on matters of race/ethnicity and health. Public Health Agency of Canada and the National Collaborating Center on Determinants of Health has endorsed our project, and we will work with them and other organizations to communicate our findings to a wide audience. column36: Bioenergetic control of plasticity by astrocytes in stress
column37: Adapting to external stress is essential for animal survival, but becomes problematic when the stress is intense or unrelenting. In humans, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorders and depressive disorders can all connect to previous stressful experiences. A fundamental aspect of the stress response involves altering body energy metabolism in response to stress hormones released by the adrenal glands. In the brain, support cells called astrocytes provide energy molecules to nerve cells, thereby helping to feed synapses - the communication points between nerve cells. This process is necessary for learning and memory and proper brain health. Importantly, stress interferes with the ability of synapses to store memories, yet a potential role for astrocytes in this well-appreciated phenomenon is not known. A central question driving our research forward is: how does the energetic support of nerve cells by astrocytes participate in the responses to external stress? Using advanced genetic and physiological techniques to study mouse brains after a bout of intense stress, our preliminary findings have discovered that the delivery of energy molecules from astrocytes to nerve cells is compromised, which prevents memory formation. This leads us to test the idea that astrocytes help regulate the brain's response to stress by gating synaptic memory via the supply of energy molecules to synapses. This proposal will reveal a new understanding for how intense or prolonged stress changes the brain. This is important because novel stress related mechanisms will be uncovered and potential therapeutic targets for stress-related disorders will be identified.

column37: Fracture healing is a complex biological process that fails in up to 10% of cases despite appropriate care and/or surgery. Fracture management results in significant financial expenditures by the Canadian healthcare system while also adversely affecting the patient's functionality and productivity during the lengthy healing period. An inexpensive, non-invasive strategy to increase bone healing would not only aim to reduce this burden but also improve quality of life for patients through earlier restoration of mobility and independence. Lithium is a safe and cost-effective drug that has been the standard treatment for bipolar disorder for over 60 years. Although reports in the past demonstrated a positive link between lithium and enhanced bone repair, the actual dose, duration and timing of lithium treatment was unknown. The proposed low dose lithium intervention treatment represents an easily translatable pharmacological approach for managing long bone fractures in patients that could ultimately reduce the tremendous burden of such fractures on the individual as well as the healthcare system to accelerate and/or predictably heal fractures.

Globally, this work will provide in-depth understanding of the mechanisms linking maternal immune changes with endothelium activation in PE as well as how immune cells are being programmed by pregnancy. This work is of high importance to develop new therapeutic target to minimize the impact PE on pregnancy and prevent the long-term impact negative on the mother. column36: Nurse-Led Model of Integrated Care Facilitated by Telemonitoring for Complex Patients at High-Risk for Hospitalization
column37: Caring for complex patients often with multiple chronic conditions is one of the biggest challenges facing our healthcare system. These patients are managed through siloed specialists and other providers, which can lead to suboptimal clinical management, poor outcomes, and poor patient experiences. While 75% of healthcare dollars are dedicated towards the management of chronic illnesses, more than 50% is consumed by complex patients, who make up only 5% of the population. The high costs are mainly due to patients repeatedly getting admitted to hospital after discharge. This project will explore how to best implement a Virtual Integrated Complex Care Clinic and the impact of the Clinic on patient outcomes including rehospitalizations. The Clinic will include a nurse-led model of integrated care, and telemonitoring. A nurse-led integrated care model means a nurse (or nurse practitioner) is the central point person to communicate with the patient and their care team to plan and execute a care plan that accounts for all of the patient's health conditions, thereby breaking down the current siloed care. However, even with a nurse-led integrated care model, the complex patients could get worse between visits to the clinic without the nurse knowing, and frequent visits to the clinic can be hard especially for these who are very sick. Telemonitoring enables patients to track important measurements (for example, blood pressure and weight) and symptoms at home, and to send this information to their clinicians so they know their patients' health status between clinic visits. The nurse can act on the information before patients are so sick that they need to be admitted to hospital again. This will be the first study to combine a nurse-led integrated care model and telemonitoring into a clinic to help complex patients as they transition from hospital to home. It may provide evidence to support a new scalable way to help complex patients stay out of the hospital.

column36: Novel therapeutic targets for Group 3 medulloblastoma stem cells
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Medulloblastoma is really made up of four diseases, of which one type, called Group 3 is highly aggressive and has a very poor outcome. The main tumor 'lump' in the brain is called the 'primary tumor'. The primary tumor can spread (metastasize) to cover other regions of the surface of the brain and spinal cord. When children die from medulloblastoma, it is mostly because the tumor has spread (metastasized). The most damaging therapies (radiation) for children with Group 3 medulloblastoma are necessary to treat the metastases. The dream of curing cancer through precision medicine has entailed sequencing cancers to identify tumor specific mutations, which could in turn be targeted by specific drugs that are lethal to the tumor but harmless to a child's normal cells. While this model is showing early success for some cancers, it holds limited promise for treatment of medulloblastoma. Recent results from the Ogilvie Lab have shown that Group 3 medulloblastomas appear to be driven by "control switches"-the factors that help choose which genes are turned on or off inside the cells. We want to know how one of these factors, called OTX2, controls other genes, interacts with other proteins, and regulates tumor growth both in a dish and when inside a patient. In addition, we also want to determine whether OTX2 plays different roles in medulloblastoma growth vs. normal development. Understanding how these control switches help make medulloblastomas grow, offers fresh opportunities to target Group 3 medulloblastoma, prevent the progression of metastases, and decrease the toxicity of therapy for children with this devastating disease.

column36: Discovery and characterization of novel genetic-exchange and drug-resistance mechanisms in Leishmania parasites
column37: The leishmaniases are a group of life-threatening diseases caused by parasites transmitted by sand flies. Leishmaniases affect millions of people worldwide, leading to thousands of deaths every year. In the absence of vaccines, current control of these diseases is based in chemotherapy, which counts with a very limited arsenal threatened by the emergence and spread of drug-resistant strains. Cases of leishmaniases in Canada have a long history due to arrival of travelers, armed forces personnel, and immigrants from endemic areas. Moreover, dog imports from endemic areas represent an emerging vector for transmission of leishmaniasis to Canada. In the shadow of growing concern and treatment failure due to resistance, our team studies how parasites that have survived to antimicrobial treatments release small vesicles, named exosomes, containing unique signature motifs allowing for a rapid and accurate identification of such resistant parasites. Moreover, experiments proposed in our research project will permit to understand and characterize how exosomes could serve as shuttle vehicle for different genetic factors, some of which would have the power of transforming sensitive parasites in drug-resistant ones. Collectively, knowledge stemming from our research will likely lead to the development of novel diagnostic tools for the rapid and accurate detection, and appraisal, of antimicrobial resistance in the field, as well as better implemented therapeutic approaches against these important infectious agents.

column36: Harnessing exercise epigenomics to protect the brain from neurodegeneration
column37: Can exercise help heal the brain and protect it from degeneration? This is a critical question that not only applies to people who have a neurodegenerative condition like multiple sclerosis (MS) but anyone who wishes to maintain a healthy brain as they age. We think that participation in aerobic exercise can alter the immune system and shift the balance from a state of inflammation towards one that fosters brain repair. We can measure levels of inflammation and markers of brain repair, such as neurotrophins, in the blood. We detect changes to brain networks using a special device called transcranial magnetic stimulation, which provides a window on brain function and integrity. The chemical switch that makes the link between inflammation and restoration is likely a special molecule called a 'microRNA'. MicroRNAs help cross talk between the brain and the immune system. This field of 'exercise epigenomics' is new and could have important implications for MS as well as other diseases that involve neurodegeneration. Beginning in 2016, we created a unique longitudinal MS patient registry and biorepository which includes detailed demographic, clinical, immune, and exercise/rehabilitation profiles. Of the 220+ people recruited, we have complete data on 84 that are eligible for this project (have mild MS). We intend to gather three years of data on at least 100 people. In this project we will investigate potential links between aerobic fitness/physical activity and the balance of inflammation and brain repair on preservation of brain function, and sensorimotor and cognitive deficits in people with mild MS. People with MS, like anyone else, want to live long and productive lives. Using this unique and powerful dataset we will be able to probe the links between lifestyle and brain health like never before.

column36: Examining the Effectiveness of a Critical Time Intervention to Stabilize Trajectories out of Homelessness for Youth
column37: The problem of youth homelessness affects millions internationally and has major impacts from social to individual levels. The outcomes of these challenges are readily apparent in the high rates of distress, declining health, and loss of life amongst homeless youth populations. Addressing youth needs only during the crisis of homelessness is not sufficient. Providing housing in and of itself is not sufficient. There is increasing recognition of the need for well-timed, sequenced, and combined interventions - with a focus on preventing pathways into homelessness and supporting sustained exits from homelessness. This study examines an intervention that supports youth in their transition out of homelessness. The intervention involves the provision of transitional case management, peer and mental health supports to youth who have recently exited homelessness - provided for a period of 1 year in this critical time. The study is a randomized trial comparing the transitional support intervention as it compares with treatment as usual to determine if youth receiving the intervention have better outcomes with respect to sustaining housing and making gains in other important life domains. It is work that builds upon feasibility studies that have suggested that the intervention has the potential to make a difference and is well-received by youth and youth service providers. This work holds the potential to make a substantive contribution to a field in need of evidence-based interventions and to be a part of the larger systemic effort to ultimately prevent youth homelessness altogether.

column36: Characterizing and comparing sleep-related consolidation neurophysiological mechanisms for procedural and declarative memories
column37: Memories are a fundamental part of our identity, as they guide our behavior in everyday activities. For this reason, an abundance of studies using a large arsenal of neuroscience methods has been carried out, not only to understand how memories are formed and maintained overtime (through the process called 'memory consolidation'), but also to uncover factors and conditions that can enhance one's memory capacity. This research, including work conducted in my laboratory, has revealed that the consolidation of declarative (capacity to retain facts and events) and procedural (ability to acquire motor skills) memories can be enhanced by sleep, more precisely by specific oscillatory electrical brain activity that can be observed in deeper sleep stages. Despite significant progress in this field, however, we still do not know whether the consolidation of those two forms of memory on similar or different action mechanisms, and whether it depends on the oscillatory brain activity occurring in the same or different sleep stages. To answer these research questions, we plan to conduct three studies in which we will record the brain activity during task performance and sleep. In two of these studies we will also deliver auditory stimulation during precise sleep phases, in sync with specific oscillatory electrical brain activity, that are expected to enhance memory consolidation. These studies will allow us to compare directly the mechanisms underlying the consolidation of procedural and declarative memories. Moreover, the results and technical expertise developed therein will provide a basis for the development of non-invasive brain stimulation approaches that can improve memory consolidation when this capacity is impaired by aging or neurodegenerative disease, such as dementia.
