column36: An actomyosin-Arf-GEF negative feedback loop for developmental tissue dynamics
column37: We study how animal tissues are built, focusing on sheets of cells called epithelia. Epithelia form our skin and internal organs, and act as regulated barriers to compartmentalize the body for its functions and protection (e.g. containing digestion inside the stomach). Epithelial structure can also be amazingly dynamic. Simple tissues of the early embryo must grow and reorganize to form the body and its organs. Even in adults, the maintenance of organs from resident stem cells requires continual epithelial remodeling. Similarly, these sheets of cells undergo dynamic movements to repair wounds. Moreover, >80% of human cancers originate from epithelial tissues, and cancers worsen with epithelial breakdown and invasive cell migration. Epithelial dynamics are dictated by the behaviors of cell-cell contacts (their constriction, growth, loss and gain). We are studying a molecular mechanism that regulates these cell-cell contacts. We are elucidating how a contact grows, and how contact growth is coupled with contact constriction. Our research relies on the experimental work-horse Drosophila melanogaster (the fruit fly). We visualize molecules, cells and tissues with advanced microscopy and manipulate specific components of the system with genetics. The molecules that organize cells and tissues in Drosophila have counterparts that perform similar functions in humans, and Drosophila has major experimental advantages. Drosophila research provides rapid advances that inform strategies for regenerative medicine and cancer therapies.

column36: Integrating Multi-Omics, Multi-Modal Neuroimaging and Artificial Intelligence for Biologically-defined Staging and Stratification in the Alzheimer's Disease spectrum
column37: Late-onset Alzheimer's disease (late-AD) is a complex neurodegenerative condition with abnormalities in protein accumulation (amyloid, tau), vascularization, inflammation and/or cerebral atrophy. Numerous clinical trials targeting only one of these components have failed to achieve significant clinical benefits, while the treatments have not accounted for the disease's clinical and pathophysiological heterogeneity. In keeping with the tenets of Personalized Medicine, treatments need to be tailored to individual therapeutic needs as opposed to treating all patients with the same approach. In neurodegeneration, however, we currently do not have appropriate methods for pathophysiological patient staging and stratification. Furthermore, because we continue to lack robust tools to characterize each patient's distinctive disease progression, evaluating the effectiveness of different therapies remains challenging. Prompted by the imperative for customized treatment of neurodegeneration, our goal is the implementation and validation of a biologically-defined staging and stratification of the AD spectrum using an artificial intelligence (AI) framework to integrate molecular, biological and neuroimaging data. Consequently, we are integrating a large amount of biological data (including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, neuroimaging) into a simplified and clinician-friendly personalized clinical profile reflecting both disease progression and variant. This framework aims to bridge the Molecular, Neuroimaging and AI fields in order to overcome the major limitations of traditional clinical diagnoses. We will validate its clinical applicability with five different populations in the AD spectrum. Critically, all resulting analytic tools will be shared with the international community via a user-friendly software and popular web-based code repositories, contributing to translate our research findings in daily clinical practice.

column36: Role of Hedgehog Interacting Protein (Hhip) in Diabetic Kidney Disease
column37: Diabetes is characterized by high blood sugar and is often associated with several complications as a result of poor blood sugar control, the most serious complications including heart disease and kidney failure. People with kidney failure may require treatment by artificial kidney (dialysis) or by kidney transplant to survive. Despite the use of currently available medications to lower blood sugar and blood pressure, kidney function continues to decline in most people with diabetic kidney disease (DKD). New alternative treatments are therefore urgently needed. A molecule called hedgehog interacting protein (Hhip) is a key regulatory component of Hedgehog signalling, which controls organ development during gestation (in the womb) and optimizes cell functions in adults. Our recent work led to the discovery that high blood sugar levels turn on the Hhip expression in diabetic kidney, causing kidney damage. Most importantly, we found that urinary Hhip (uHhip) appears to be elevated in early DKD before the development of microalbuminuria (a hallmark of onset of kidney disease) in diabetic mice and humans with type 2 diabetes, suggesting that uHhip might be a novel indicator that could be used for the early detection of DKD, possibly identifying patients who will benefit from more intensive renoprotective interventions at an earlier stage indicator in DKD. However, several key questions regarding Hhip gene regulation, secretion and cell-to cell communication in responding to elevated glucose levels are poorly understood. My research program is to perform studies in kidney cells grown in petri dishes and in diabetic mouse models to answer these questions. Our studies will provide new insights into the processes how does Hhip causing kidney injury in diabetes and should provide new treatment strategies to prevent kidney damage in patients with diabetes mellitus.

column36: Novel Approach to Peptide Therapy for Rheumatoid Arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a painful, chronic autoimmune disease that damages joints and causes disability. RA is the most common autoimmune inflammatory arthritis affecting >300,000 Canadians. There is no cure for RA and its cause is unknown. Currently, the only available treatments for RA are non-specific drugs that modify the immune system. These drugs may improve joint damage but can cause people to get infections or even cancer. Also, RA disease flares are common, requiring life-long treatment and frequent drug changes. New therapies are needed that target immune responses specific to RA. What is known about RA is that the immune system, which normally attacks bacteria and viruses, attacks specific molecules in the patient's own body. This attack leads to joint inflammation, damage and pain. We designed a new therapy for RA that alters these immune responses so that they do not attack the joints. This therapy is mixed with a new cream that penetrates deep into the skin so that injections are avoided. Preliminary tests in mice showed that this cream therapy prevents arthritis. The goal of this study is to test if this new RA cream therapy can reduce signs of arthritis in mice. We will apply the cream therapy onto the skin of arthritic mice and monitor for joint swelling and pain behaviours. Blood samples from the mice will be studied to see if this therapy alters immune responses. We will also collect immune cells from RA patients and compare them to the immune cells from mice to determine if they are similar. We expect that the RA patients with active disease will have similar immune cell characteristics to the arthritic mice. Similarities between mouse and human immune responses to the cream therapy would suggest that it can be tested in humans. This study will identify a new and specific treatment for RA without serious side effects. The RA cream therapy is easy to use, so expanding this study to human treatment trials is achievable.

column36: Running-induced urinary incontinence in females: pathomechanics and conservative options for prevention and intervention
column37: The experience of urinary incontinence when females exercise is very common, affecting between 15 and 80% of those who regularly participate in physical activities, depending on the frequency and intensity of training. This "exercise incontinence" may ultimately lead females to withdraw from their physical activities, and the resultant inactivity can lead to poor health and/or well-being later in life. Little is known about the mechanisms that cause exercise incontinence; damage to the pelvic floor muscles or their surrounding connective tissues and pelvic floor muscle fatigue are plausible explanations. Conservative management approaches such as pelvic floor muscle strengthening exercises and intravaginal support devices (pessaries) are effective for many females suffering from urinary incontinence induced by everyday activities such as coughing or sneezing, yet it is not known whether these approaches are effective specifically when leakage predominantly or only occurs during exercise. Through this study we will (i) investigate anatomical and mechanical properties of the pelvic floor muscles in female runners who do and who do not leak urine during running to determine whether differences are evident at baseline and/or after a single bout of running, (ii) determine whether abdominal pressures or impact forces experienced during running are different between females who do and do not leak urine when they run, and (iii) determine whether pelvic floor muscle training or an off-the-shelf pessary may effectively eliminate urine leakage during running among females who regularly experience exercise incontinence. The results of this study are essential to guide prevention strategies and conservative interventions that will allow females to continue to engage in physical activities without leaking urine, mitigating their ultimate withdrawal from physical activities because of urine leakage.

column36: Supplementation of folic acid or methyltetrahydrofolate to reduce developmental anomalies in a new mouse model for the MTHFR 677C>T polymorphism
column37: Neural tube defects (NTD) are due to inadequate dietary folate. NTD rate has decreased via folic acid (FA) food fortification and consumption of FA-containing vitamins. A common genetic change is a 677C>T mutation in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), which generates the main circulatory folate, methyltetrahydrofolate (methylTHF). We had identified this change, present in ~ 10% of Canadians, as the first genetic risk factor for NTD and showed that it reduced activity and stability in the mutant enzyme. We also showed that methylTHF could stabilize the TT enzyme and improve function. FA reduces NTD incidence overall but it has never been shown that it reduces incidence for 677TT genotypes because clinical trials have not looked at MTHFR genotypes. Recent data suggest that methylTHF may also be useful, or even more useful than FA, to reduce NTD rate, but this has not been tested in any trial. Our goal is to determine if FA or methylTHF reduces NTD or other developmental anomalies in the 677TT genotype, using a new 677C>T mouse generated by our collaborator. We have just shown that the mutant TT mouse enzyme is similar to the human TT enzyme (reduced activity and stability, stabilized by methylTHF). We hypothesize that methylTHF will be more effective since it is the MTHFR product and can stabilize the mutant enzyme. Our aims are to first assess relevant metabolites in male and female mice of 3 genotypes (CC, CT and TT) fed diets with variable folate. We will then provide FA and methylTHF supplements to CC and TT females, mate them with CC males, and examine embryos for delays/defects; these studies will test impact of maternal TT genotype. We will perform the same experiments with CT females, mated with TT males, to examine impact of embryonic TT genotype. MTHFR activity will be measured in all aims. Our work will help to assess whether current strategies to reduce NTD are useful for 677TT women, and whether FA or methylTHF is more effective for all.

column36: The injured peripheral nervous system and aging
column37: Damage to nerves in limbs often results in motor and sensory problems because the fibers (axons) that form the nerves do not regrow in large numbers back to their targets. Some of the ensuing problems that occur, such as motor incoordination and neuropathic pain, disrupt the quality of life for millions of humans worldwide and create significant personal and economic burden. More concerning is that regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves declines with age. This deficit has become a pressing clinical issue with the growing maturing population and humans living longer because older individuals experience more peripheral injuries because of muscle weakness and slower reflexes. Since surgical interventions are limited in their efficacy, new and specific therapies are urgently needed. Schwann cells are the glial cells of the peripheral nervous system. They wrap axons with myelin, a fatty substance that acts like an insulator that allows electrical signals to pass rapidly from one nerve cell to another. After peripheral nerve damage, Schwann cells play a critical role in creating a favourable environment for damaged fibers to regrow. They accomplish this by secreting growth factors, remyelinating regrowing axons and removing inhibitory molecules. However, the functions of Schwann cells decline with age and this contributes to the impaired regeneration and thus poor functional recovery seen in older individuals. My lab is interested in understanding why regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves and functional recovery are worse with age. We will specifically investigate whether a protein called alphaB-crystallin (alphaBC) that is expressed by Schwann cells, and whose expression in peripheral nerves reduces as an animal ages, is responsible for the deficit in Schwann cell function and thus poorer regeneration in older injured animals. This grant will also inform us whether alphaBC is a possible therapeutic agent for improving functional recovery in older animals.

column36: Reducing ovarian cancer risk by regulating age-associated ovarian fibrosis
column37: For most women, the largest risk factor for ovarian cancer is the monthly ovulation. Oral contraceptives prevent ovulation and can reduce ovarian cancer risk by up to 35%, but how ovulation increases risk is not clear. In trying to find an explanation, our lab has found that ovaries from aged mice and post-menopausal women, which have had many ovulations, harbor a population of cells that are known to suppress the activity of the immune system. These cells were not found in young ovaries. We predict that these cells play a critical role in allowing both primary and metastatic cancers to grow in the ovary. The accumulation of immune suppressing cells in the aging ovary is associated with fibrosis. We have created a mouse model that develops ovarian fibrosis and the question we are asking is: Can this process be blocked or reversed? Metformin, a drug used mostly by diabetes patients, has been shown to reduce fibrosis in other tissues, and diabetic women who take metformin have a dramatic decrease in the incidence of ovarian cancer. We therefore propose to determine the contribution of fibrosis to the recruitment of immunosuppressive cells to the ovary, determine how the development of fibrosis is accelerated in women with BRCA mutations, and explore how metformin can prevent or reverse these changes. Our results would open the door to the possibility that metformin could be used for ovarian cancer prevention in women at high risk.

column36: Decoding gene & genome-regulatory functions of the RNA gene CISTR-ACT
column37: Three-dimensional genome organization in mammalian cells is important for gene regulation. Rewiring of gene-regulatory mechanisms can cause rare disease and cancer. Whilst interactions between genes and their regulators on the same chromosome are well characterized, mechanistic insights into contacts between different chromosomes (inter-chromosomal) remain mostly unknown. Moreover, non-coding RNAs are an important layer for gene regulation and genome organization, but their molecular mechanisms remain to be determined. We identified a long non-coding RNA involved in inter-chromosomal contacts which is biologically and clinically relevant. The RNA gene CISTR-ACT on human chromosome 12 interacts with SOX9 on chromosome 17 to regulate cartilage development. CISTR-ACT and SOX9 remain stably associated in normal cells, but disrupting this interaction leads to the rare disease brachydactyly (hand malformation syndrome) in patients with familial translocations. The results support the notion that CISTR-ACT facilitates developmental programs controlled by genes located on other chromosomes. Most importantly, CISTR-ACT is directly involved in the pathogenesis of brachydactyly, but how does defective inter-chromosomal communication cause brachydactyly? Here, we will use a multidisciplinary approach leveraging functional epigenomics, computational biology, and live-cell imaging to determine CISTR-ACT's function. We will show how CISTR-ACT impacts gene regulation and genome organization in brachydactyly to better understand spatial positioning of genes and RNA-mediated gene regulation. Our findings promise a better understanding of these novel epigenomic disease mechanisms and will establish a research discipline with clinical significance for other genomic rearrangements.

column36: Characterization of invadopodia formation in response to local cues and their role in orchestrating metastasis.
column37: The majority of breast cancer patients die from metastatic disease rather than the primary tumor. Metastasis, which is the spread of cancer cells from a primary tumor to other areas in the body, remains the main cause of patient related death, due to organ damage caused by the growing metastases. Awareness of the importance of metastasis and our basic scientific understanding of the metastatic process has improved substantially over the past few decades. However, many aspects of metastasis are still not well defined and our ability to prevent or treat metastasis is limited. In order to improve patient outcomes, a better understanding of metastasis is required. One way that cancer cells are thought to move around the body is by sprouting tiny 'feet-like' structures called invadopodia. We propose that these 'feet-like' structures respond to cues in their environment and this triggers cell movement and invasion at distant organs. Our work aims to study how these environmental cues promote the formation of invadopodia and how this changes the movements and actions of the cancer cells. Results from this work will identify proteins important for the formation and function of these 'feet'. This will help us understand the mechanisms by which cancer cells move throughout the body, seed and grow in distant organs. This could lead to the future development of therapies aimed at impairing the actions of these 'feet' to reduce metastatic spread and improve patient outcomes.

column36: A prospective and longitudinal investigation of concussive and subconcussive mild traumatic brain injury mechanisms in ice hockey
column37: Sports concussion is a major public health concern. Even more alarmingly, recent findings show that repeated subconcussive head impacts in sports may also lead to long-term brain changes. Despite the prevalence of sports-related brain injuries, we still have very limited understanding of how the forces in head impacts result in brain trauma, and even less is known about how trauma accumulates through multiple impacts. In this study, we will instrument ice hockey athletes with wearable sensors to measure impact forces and accelerations, paired with assessments of their brain structure / function using imaging, neurocognitive, and blood testing at multiple time points across three seasons. Novel imaging techniques and blood biomarkers can identify subtle structural changes in the brain that are often missed in conventional brain imaging, and a sensitive neurocognitive test battery can help detect changes in brain function. With these data, we will investigate the mechanisms of acute and long-term trauma from concussions and subconcussive head impacts. Our findings may lead to novel diagnostic technologies for sports brain injury, inform return-to-play decisions, as well as identify the effects of repeated head impact exposure on brain structure and function. This will guide concussion management in sports, and inform rule changes to limit head impact exposure to a safe level.

column36: Maternal Diabetes Induces Perinatal Programming of Chronic Kidney Disease: The Role of Hedgehog Interacting Protein (Hhip)
column37: Pregnancy with diabetes or gestational diabetes (i.e., maternal diabetes) creates elevated blood sugar levels in the womb, resulting in a variety of birth defects. In addition, there are lifelong consequences for the offspring-increased tendency to develop various disorders, such as metabolic syndrome, hypertension (HTN), obesity, cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease (CKD) in adulthood. The exact reasons for this phenomenon, called perinatal programming, are not well-defined. Moreover, this perinatal programming occurring in progeny of diabetic mothers could be further influenced after a 'second hit' during postnatal life-e.g., chronic exposure to factors including smoking, physiological stress, high-salt consumption or high fat diet, excessive alcohol consumption and a sedentary lifestyle, etc.. Therefore, knowledge of how HTN and CKD develop in at-risk people born to mothers with diabetes will lead to improved prevention/treatment strategies. We recently discovered that high blood sugar levels in the pregnant mother turn on the expression of a molecule called the hedgehog interacting protein (Hhip), which is associated with impaired kidney development in young offspring of diabetic dams. This proposal aims to understand the molecular bases of Hhip impact on maternal diabetes-induced renal programming of HTN and CKD in adult offspring. We will perform the studies using Hhip knock-out mouse model and kidney cells grown in petri dishes to define the physiological role of Hhip in maternal diabetes-induced renal programming. We expect the present project to generate a comprehensive understanding of Hhip impact on maternal diabetes-induced renal programming of CKD; facilitate the identification of novel drug targets to prevent/reduce the long-term risks of complications in the progeny of diabetic mothers; and reduce diabetic pregnancy-associated healthcare burdens in Canada and thereby improve the quality of life of Canadians.

column36: The role of the microbiome in chronic visceral pain in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic, debilitating illnesses. At present, the goal of treatment in IBD is complete healing of intestinal inflammation. However, despite achieving this target, over twenty percent of IBD patients continue to experience chronic abdominal pain, which is a distressing and devastating symptom. Previous research has shown evidence of increased expression of the transient receptor potential vanilloid-1 receptor (TRPV1) in IBD patients with complete intestinal healing; TRPV1 is a key nerve receptor involved in abdominal pain sensation. There is early evidence that disruptions in gut microbes can also change TRPV1 on pain-sensing nerves. The goal of our research is to study the role of gut microbes in the development of chronic pain in IBD and the interaction between gut microbes and TRPV1 on pain-sensing nerves. We will examine this by performing stool transplants from IBD patients with/without chronic abdominal pain or healthy controls into a mouse model. We will characterize gut microbes and their metabolites in both patients and our mouse model. Finally, we will study how microbe-made short chain fatty acids, which are increased in our mouse model and change the activity of pain-sensing nerves, interact with TRPV1. Our research may have a broad impact on the health of patients suffering from IBD as it will give us a greater understanding into the role of gut microbes in pain sensation. This may in turn lead to new strategies, such as the use of stool transplants, targeted therapies against specific microbial products or microbes, and/or the use of pro-/pre-biotics to treat pain in IBD.

column37: Neural tube defects are one of the most common congenital anomalies encountered in Canada. They can result in fetal deaths, newborn and child deaths, and life-long disability. column36: Dissection of pathways regulating meiotic crossover formation
column37: Human reproduction requires the fusion of egg and sperm that each contains exactly half the number of parental chromosomes to form a healthy embryo containing a complete chromosome set. Inheriting an abnormal number of chromosomes is the most prevalent and documented cause of miscarriage, and is also associated with sterility and developmental defects. To produce egg and sperm, germ cells go through two specialized rounds of cell division called meiosis. Correct distribution of the parental chromosomes to these cells relies on meiotic processes which pair identical chromosomes along their lengths and physically anchor them to each other through DNA "crossovers" in preparation for segregation; failure to form crossovers results in germ cells containing abnormal chromosome numbers. While the events leading to crossover formation are highly conserved from fungi to humans, the study of meiotic processes in humans is difficult because of technical and ethical issues. In our laboratory, we use C. elegans, a small transparent roundworm that possesses many of the genetic counterparts found in vertebrates to study meiosis. Using the powerful genetic, molecular and biochemical tools of the nematode system, combined with the accessibility of the germline for detailed microscopy, we propose to identify and study new genes required for the critical processes regulating crossing over with the goal of understanding meiosis in humans.

column36: Characterization and treatment of a novel conditional mouse model of pyridoxine-dependent epileptic encephalopathy caused by antiquitin mutations.
column37: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (PDE) is a rare genetic form of epilepsy or seizure disorder that is also associated with abnormal brain development. PDE is characterized by recurrent fits or seizures that begin around the time of birth and are resistant to conventional seizure medications (anticonvulsant treatments), but show remarkable response to the administration of vitamin B6 or pyridoxine. The research plan of this project will be divided to three parts. In the first part, we will study the effects of modified diet on the PDE mouse model for the presence of various disease symptoms such as seizures and cognitive disturbances a well as testing the presence of disease associated chemical compounds in blood and brain tissue. In the second part, we will examine the effects of selective loss of the antiquitin gene in specific types of brain cells or selective loss at a specific ages. The third part of the project will be dedicated to treatment trials to improve the disease symptoms in these PDE mice. These will include manipulation of vitamin levels and administration of drugs that will minimize the toxic chemical compounds.

column36: Structural biology and biochemistry of PARP enzyme regulation in the DNA damage response and in cancer therapy
column37: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) are a diverse class of medically relevant human enzymes, with regulatory roles in virtually all aspects of cell biology. PARP1 rapidly detects DNA strand breaks and then creates the molecule poly(ADP-ribose) to signal the presence and location of the DNA break. Poly(ADP-ribose) recruits other cellular factors to the site of DNA breaks so that the damage can be repaired in a timely and efficient manner. Certain cancers have inherent deficiencies in the repair of DNA strand breaks, and the survival of these cancer cells is dependent on PARP1 activity. PARP inhibitor (PARPi) compounds block PARP1 activity and are thus toxic to these cancer cells with defective DNA repair, whereas normal cells are able to withstand PARPi treatment. The proposed research will provide fundamental insights into the control of PARP1 activity in cells that will improve our ability to regulate PARP1 activity for cancer treatment. PARP1 hyperactivity is associated with other diseases, such as cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders, thus our findings will also impact our understanding of PARP1 regulation in other areas of biology that are important for human health.

column36: Cigarette taxes, prices and tax evasion in Canada: implications for tobacco control
column37: Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable death and illness in Canada. There is overwhelming Canadian and international evidence that increases in tobacco taxes reduce tobacco use, save lives and increase government tax revenue. However, high taxes create an incentive for tobacco users, manufacturers and others, most notably criminal networks, to devise ways to avoid or evade tobacco taxes. From the mid-2000s, the effectiveness of tobacco tax policies in Canada has been hampered by the emergence of discount brands and the resurgence of contraband cigarettes, most notably in Ontario and Quebec. The illegal nature of cigarette tax evasion makes it intrinsically difficult to measure accurately. The scattered and at times conflicting estimates combined with the tobacco industry's narrative that cigarette contraband has been increasing in recent years and that any changes in policies such as tax increases or plain packaging will inevitably lead to large increases in cigarette tax evasion warrant a more systematic, transparent and timely approach to examine cigarette contraband in Canada. We have three research objectives. Our first objective is to estimate the magnitude of and temporal changes in cigarette tax evasion. Our second objective is to use the estimates of cigarette tax evasion constructed in objective 1 to study the relationship between cigarette tax evasion and cigarette prices (licit and illicit) and policy changes. column36: Interplay of Neuroinflammation and Synaptic Plasticity in Neurodegeneration
column37: Microglia are a class of brain immune cells that play an important role in neuroinflammation, a protective response initiated to ward off toxins and pathogens. However, in Alzheimer's disease (AD), this response is subverted and becomes toxic leading to reduced communication between neurons, which is ultimately responsible for cognitive decline. During chronic inflammation, we know that the activity of a protein called PARP-1 is abnormally elevated in microglia. We also know that activation of PARP-1 promotes microglial responses that are detrimental to neurons. However, the mechanisms responsible for activating PARP-1 in microglia are poorly understood. Moreover, how PARP-1 mediated inflammation injures neurons is not known. By defining the mechanisms that activate and sustain this pathway, and in turn the mechanisms responsible for neuronal injury, we will identify prospective therapeutic targets able to prevent the neurotoxic effects of microglia. This would benefit AD patients, where neuroinflammation contributes to disease progression and severity.

column36: Herpesvirus subversion of unfolded protein responses
column37: Proteins synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) need to undergo complex folding events to function correctly. When ER folding capacity is overwhelmed a stress management program called the unfolded protein response (UPR) is initiated in attempt to alleviate this potentially fatal stress. The UPR has evolved to sense the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER and deliver a signal to the nucleus to increase the expression of genes that (i) increase ER folding capacity and (ii) destroy terminally misfolded proteins. If stress cannot be resolved then the UPR initiates a cell death response. There is emerging evidence that the UPR is a node of control subverted by viruses to support viral replication and aspects of pathogenesis, but specific mechanistic details remain unclear. Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the causative agent of the AIDS defining cancer, Kaposi's sarcoma. We discovered that KSHV usurps host UPR processes to promote viral replication. Though this study, we will identify the viral genes responsible for controlling the host UPR system, and we will figure out how they work.

column36: The role of TOR kinase signaling and lipid metabolism in hypoxia tolerance
column37: Our cells and organs need oxygen from the air we breathe in order to survive. However, although air contains twenty percent oxygen, our cells are exposed to much lower levels. In addition, our cells are often deprived of oxygen in diseases such as stroke, heart disease and cancer. This lack of oxygen, known as hypoxia, leads to the tissue damage seen in these diseases. In important challenge in biomedical research is to understand how cells and organs can respond to, and cope, with low oxygen. We use the fruit fly as a model to address this question. Fruit flies naturally live in rotting fruit which is an environment characterized by low oxygen. Hence, they have evolved mechanisms to tolerate this hypoxia. Our work in the fly has identified the regulation of one enzyme - TOR kinase - as a mechanism by which cells adapt to low oxygen. The goal of this project grant is to use the ease and speed of fruit fly genetics to understand exactly how TOR controls the ability of tissues and organs to survive low oxygen. The fruit fly is proven as a 'lead' model system to discover new biological mechanisms that can guide work in other systems including human cells. For example, the TOR pathway is controlled the same way in human cells as in flies. In addition, TOR becomes deregulated in disorders such as cancer and heart disease. Hence our work will help identify how cells and organs can cope with hypoxia, and in doing so, will provide clues about the defects caused by disorders such as cancer and heart disease.

column36: In vivo roles of autophagy in gut homeostasis and impact on IBD
column37: The digestive system is complex, and it interacts directly with a large number of microbes. Consequently, small problems can lead to various types of digestive diseases. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, collectively named inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) affect 1 in 150 Canadians. Although these two diseases are etiologically different, they both are linked to a cellular mechanism called autophagy. Autophagy is the process by which cells degrade and recycle their own constituents. Autophagy can thus be compared to a recycling factory, where non-essential or damaged constituents can be destroyed and reused for other purposes. Autophagy is induced by different signals. In the intestine, autophagy (the recycling factory) also helps to destroy bad microbes and help to maintain the good ones. In an effort to understand how differences in our genes predispose individuals to develop IBD, differences in genes of affected and unaffected individuals were compared to identify mutations linked to an increasing susceptibility to develop IBD. These approaches have identified a large number of genes linked to IBD, and importantly a good proportion of those genes are regulators of autophagy. However, due to the lack of affordable and time-efficient systems to study the role of these genes in digestive health, their roles in the development or progression of IBD are for the most part unexplored. In this proposal, we will characterize, using Drosophila melanogaster (fruit flies) as an innovative in vivo model of gut health, the role of autophagy on gut function and gut/microbes interaction. Moreover, we will also quantify using a powerful new approach how autophagy is regulated in vivo under stress, and finally we will identify novel potential targets that could eventually help IBD patients with impaired autophagy. The identification of new regulators of intestinal health will generate new basic and translational research avenues and identify new targets for therapies.

column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major health problem that affects 350,000 Canadians. AF, an abnormal heart rhythm, increases the risk of heart failure, stroke and death. These risks increase when AF worsens to a level known as persistent AF. AF can be treated with catheter ablation, a treatment that aims to restore a normal heart rhythm. When successful AF catheter ablation improves quality of life, and decreases the risk of death or hospitalization for cardiac causes. Yet, only 50-60% of patients with persistent AF who undergo standard of care (pulmonary vein isolation catheter ablation alone) remain AF-free at one year. The optimal strategy for ablation of persistent AF is not yet known. We know that scar tissue in the atria (upper chamber of the heart) leads to AF. Recently, our group's pilot work demonstrated that catheter ablation of scarred regions in the atria in addition to pulmonary vein isolation has revealed promising results. Recent studies using a similar approach support our findings, yet a synthesis of current available research reveals that it is of variable quality with important limitations. To confirm the findings from these studies, experts in the field have called for a larger, more representative study. We are answering this call. We propose COAST-AF, a clinical trial to determine the safety and efficacy of atrial scar ablation in addition to pulmonary vein isolation versus pulmonary vein isolation alone (standard of care). COAST-AF is the only study that can provide a definitive answer to this crucial question in cardiac arrhythmia care. We anticipate this trial will directly impact the treatment of thousands of patients with persistent AF in Canada and Worldwide.

column36: Spinal interneuron subpopulations and modular circuits in normal locomotor control and after spinal cord injury
column37: Loss of locomotor activity due to accident or disease is devastating to patients and may lead to early death. Currently, we have limited understanding of the neural circuits that control movement, which hampers efforts to devise better therapeutics to treat loss of motor function. The fundamental goal of my laboratory is to reveal the organization of neural circuits that control normal locomotion in order to identify mechanisms that could be targeted when that behavior is disrupted by injuries and diseases. Currently, we focus on interneuron (IN) populations that form the locomotor circuits in the mouse spinal cord, and aim to reveal the organizational logic and functional roles of these circuits in locomotor control. More importantly, we hope to provide insight into the potential roles of spinal INs in neuroplasticity and recovery after spinal cord injury (SCI). Based on our previous and current studies of one specific IN population, designated V3 INs, as a model system, we predict that spinal IN subpopulations could serve as modular components in locomotor circuits, allowing for task-dependent selection of functionally distinct circuit outputs. These individual modules may function in different aspects of locomotor control and respond differently to SCI and subsequent rehabilitation regimens, knowledge that could be crucial for recovery from SCI. To address these issues, we will employ various genetic and molecular tools in combination with advanced anatomical, electrophysiological, optogenetic, behavioral and computational approaches to define functional V3 IN subpopulations; define task-dependent functional modules of V3 INs in locomotor circuits; and investigate their potential functions in normal locomotion and in SCI.

column36: Developing a Patient-Specific Surgical Decision-Assistance Tool to Improve Reverse Shoulder Replacement Outcomes
column37: The human shoulder is a joint consisting of a ball on the arm side of the joint, and a cup on the shoulder blade side. When a person seriously injures their shoulder joint, they can be left unable to lift their arm. For these patients, the only way to regain function is to undergo a shoulder replacement called Reverse Total Shoulder Arthroplasty (RTSA), whereby the above-described joint geometry is flipped; a cup-shaped implant is placed on the arm side of the joint, and a ball-shaped implant is placed on the shoulder blade side. Because of this, the anatomical landmarks that surgeons use to determine the best implant configuration during a traditional shoulder replacement are not effective. Therefore, the goal of this research is to develop the biomechanical understanding necessary to provide surgeons with an objective and quantitative surgical decision-making assistance tool to aid in the optimal planning of RTSA. This objective will be achieved in a number of phases. First, we will systematically analyze how the shapes of RTSA patients' shoulder bones differ from those of other patient groups. We will then develop computer models that can inform us of how RTSA patients' anatomy influences how different RTSA implant configurations affect how well their joint functions after surgery. Results of these computer modelling studies will then be used to develop the desired decision making assistance tool using machine learning techniques that will help surgeons customize their surgical plans to each of their patients.

Ultimately, the identification of molecules capable of suppressing colon CSC's activity would provide a new therapeutic option aimed at selectively targeting cancers, decreasing side effects and increasing patient survival rates.

column37: Opioid medications provide potent pain relief in the short-term, but their long-term use can cause serious adverse effects. Blocking these channels in the spinal cord alleviates withdrawal without diminishing the pain-relieving benefits of opioid medications. We have new data that pannexin-1 channels gate activity within the locus coeruleus, an area of the brain that communicates with the spinal cord by sending specialized projections containing a chemical (norepinephrine). This proposal addresses exciting new questions about how pannexin-1 channels modulate specific circuitry in the brain and spinal cord that are important for opioid withdrawal. Using advanced cellular imaging, biochemical, and behavioural approaches, experiments will also deconstruct the machinery by which norepinephrine enhances pannexin-1 activity and its impact on microglia signaling. Finally, we will translate our findings into the development of next generation, more potent pannexin-1 targeted drugs for treating opioid withdrawal.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a common neurological disease that disables young Canadians. There are 14 approved therapies now for many who have a relapsing remitting form of MS (RRMS). Yet within 10-15 years of disease onset, >50% of RRMS patients develop secondary progressive MS (SPMS), which remains untreatable. While many factors may cause this poor outcome, the inability to optimize therapy based on an individual's risk of worsening is crucial. There is no reliable way to identify the risks but if there is, early aggressive treatment would be possible for those with a greater risk of worsening, which is critical to save the tissue before irreversible damage accumulates. This project will establish a novel deep machine learning method to predict the 5-year risk of disability score worsening in RRMS patients. Deep learning has shown enormous progress recently in disease prediction, especially when combing pathology-directed outcomes, and multiple types of patient data. Using standard brain MRI, our pilot deep learning data is 83% accurate in predicting RRMS and SPMS. By assessing the pixel pattern (texture) of MRI, our pioneer work also discover that the scale and direction of MRI texture detects specific elements of MS pathology. We have now built new deep learning methods using 3 types of outcomes from MRI texture pathology, clinical data, and brain MRI, and cutting-edge techniques to unveil how deep learning works. Built on these solid data and large cohorts of MS patients, this project will establish a novel objective method to identify the high and low risks of disability worsening for individual RRMS patients so that each can receive the best treatment regimen to improve prognosis. This personalized medicine approach will directly benefit MS patients and families, the health care system, and society.

column37: Stroke affects an increasingly large number of individuals in Canada and around the world. Brain damage as a result of stroke can often lead to difficulties in mobility, language production and understanding, and other functions such as memory and reasoning. Though these difficulties lead to serious reductions in quality of life, we still do not know how damage in one location of the brain is related to specific difficulties. This is in part because we do not yet fully understand how the brain is connected and how its connections support our everyday behaviours. Brain damage is typically described based on its location and size, but this completely ignores how the damage may have interrupted some connections between different regions of the brain. For example, damage to the front of the brain will result in different functional deficits depending exactly where it is: if it is more towards the top the patient may experience difficulties with memory (e.g., phone numbers) but if it is lower the patient may experience emotional issues (e.g., understanding facial expressions). We have a fairly good idea of what the processing regions of the brain do (grey matter, made up of cells that do the "thinking") but we know very little about how they are connected through the white matter of the brain (i.e., the "wires" that connect different processing regions together). Without this knowledge, damage to the "wires" is difficult to predict the effects of or, ultimately, treat with clinical intervention.

column36: Modifications to a hybrid beta-hexosaminidase for transcytosis across the blood-brain barrier
column37: Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff disease are severe neurodegenerative diseases caused by the heritable loss of lysosomal beta-hexosaminidase A (Hex A) activity. In severe cases, neurological symptoms occur by 6-12 months of age, followed by rapid decline and death by 1-4 years of age; whereas, in cases where mutations result in residual HexA activity, GM2-ganglioside accumulation is slowed, and disease onset occurs during adolescence or early adulthood. There are no treatments available for patients affected by these diseases. Lysosomal HexA is responsible for the breakdown of GM2 ganglioside, which is a component of the neuronal plasma membrane that is constantly recycled by the cell. When there are insufficient levels of HexA, GM2 ganglioside accumulate to pathological levels in neurons of the central and peripheral nervous system. Only ~10% of normal HexA activity is needed to prevent, and possibly reverse GM2 ganglioside accumulation, making enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) a promising approach to manage Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff disease. To enable the approach, we recently engineered a stable form of Hex (known as HexM) that has addressed issues of HexA instability and production, and it degrades GM2 ganglioside both in cellulo and in vivo. However, intravenously administered HexM must be able to cross the blood brain barrier (BBB) to affect GM2 degradation in the central nervous system. To address this, I aim to fuse HexM to the receptor binding domains of Apolipoproteins B and E to 'trick' the BBB into transporting the enzyme into the CNS, which will be tested using an in vitro BBB model. I have already developed a robust overexpression system for 'wild-type' HexM and will employ the same approach to generate the HexM fusion in quantities sufficient for ERT studies.

column36: Identifying sex differences in the molecular mechanisms of socially-mediated pubertal suppression
column37: Puberty is an essential developmental process in mammals. Puberty marks the onset of sexual maturation and is associated with increased incidence of depression and anxiety. Two risk factors for the development of depression are psychosocial stress and pubertal timing. Importantly, psychosocial stress can itself shift pubertal timing. Puberty onset, susceptibility to stress, and risk of depression all differ between males and females. For these reasons understanding sex specific mechanisms underlying how social stress influences pubertal timing has tremendous importance for human health. The naked mole-rat (NMR) is a unique rodent exhibiting extreme socially-mediated reproductive suppression. NMRs reside in large colonies of adults who remain in a pre-pubertal state due to the presence of a dominant breeding female known as the queen. In addition to the queen, a dominant breeding male (known as a consort) has also gone through puberty. Most NMRs will never go through puberty unless they are removed from the suppressive cues of their colony. By studying NMRs, we have an exceptional opportunity to learn how social cues influence pubertal timing. Here we will identify genome-wide gene expression patterns as well as modifications to the DNA that turn genes on and off (known as epigenetic changes) in the brain, adrenal glands, and gonads of NMRs. We will also manipulate stress-relevant genes to examine how they influence puberty and gene expression in brain. The goal of our research is to discover sex specific genes that are involved in suppressing puberty in NMRs, which may explain associations between age of pubertal onset, stress reactivity, and risk for psychopathology in humans.

column36: Towards the non-invasive, most accurate radiotherapy of mobile tumours in a hybrid linac-MR system
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada and nearly half of the patients receive radiotherapy (RT). RT uses strong radiation to kill tumour cells, and the radiation is typically delivered by a device called linear accelerator (linac). If a tumour is static during irradiation, e.g. brain tumour, modern RT can deliver highly accurate radiation to the tumour without much damage to the adjacent normal cells. Unfortunately, most tumours are mobile and can deform due to respiratory and cardiac motions (e.g. lung tumour), and such accurate RT is difficult due to the lack of sufficient soft-tissue imaging. Most tumours reside in soft-tissue, and soft-tissue is best seen in MRI. However, current imaging devices on linacs are typically X-ray based, which provide poor soft-tissue imaging. Thus, small metal markers that can be seen in X-ray image must be surgically implanted near the tumour to estimate its shape and location during RT. Our laboratory built the first radiotherapy-MRI hybrid device (linac-MR) in 2008, and a human whole-body system in 2014. This MRI on-board linac allows continuous MR imaging during irradiation, providing clear image of moving tumours. Using linac-MR, our objective is to enhance the geometric accuracy of RT treating mobile tumours without the need of invasive surgery. To achieve the objective, we have established a framework of novel RT method, non-invasive intra-fractional tumour-tracked RadioTherapy (nifteRT). The feasibility of nifteRT was verified in 2013 using our prototype linac-MR system. We were able to deliver accurate radiation to a moving target reproducing 1D lung tumour motion in linac-MR. In this proposal, we aim to further improve our nifteRT research to the level of clinically usable technology. We expect < 3 mm error in radiation delivery to mobile tumours in nifteRT. This will allow the escalation of radiation dose only to the tumours without excessive damage to the adjacent normal cells, which is the ultimate goal of RT.

column36: Contribution of endothelial fatty acid metabolism to diabetes-associated heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
column37: Type 2 diabetes is a leading contributor to cardiovascular death, having damaging effects on organs such as the heart as well as blood vessels. One such disease associated with diabetes is 'heart failure with preserved ejection fraction', also known as HFpEF. In this type of heart disease, the heart stiffens resulting in defective relaxation of the heart between beats, meaning the heart has less blood inside it to pump out to the rest of the body. People are often diagnosed at very late, and untreatable, stages of disease as there are no diagnostic tests that can detect early disease warning signs. The reasons why this disease develops are not understood, but recent evidence has suggested that the function of small blood vessels in the heart is defective. Therefore, dysfunction of blood vessels in the heart may be an early warning sign of disease and may also be a target for therapy. We have been seeking for markers in the blood that indicate defective blood vessel function in the heart. Using animal models of HFpEF we found a small RNA molecule, microRNA-30, is increased in the blood at the same time as blood vessels become dysfunctional. It appears that this microRNA is secreted by dysfunctional endothelial cells (the cells that line blood vessels) in the diabetic heart. We found that in the endothelial cells of the heart, microRNA-30 regulates proteins that are involved in fatty acid metabolism. When microRNA-30 is elevated, endothelial cells use more fatty acids, which causes oxidative stress and defective endothelial cell function. We believe this may be an early defect in HFpEF since fatty acids are highly elevated in the blood of diabetics. Our proposal will determine whether the utilization of fatty acids by the endothelium is involved in diabetic HFpEF and whether targeting microRNA-30 can be a potential therapy. We will also test whether measuring microRNA-30 in the blood of human patients with diabetes can be used to detect the earliest stages of HFpEF.

column37: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is one of the most common inflammatory skin diseases and up to 17% of the Canadian population is affected at some point in their lives. This has sparked the interest of pharmaceutical companies to develop inhibitors of TSLP. Tezepelumab is the most advanced drug showing promising results, however it is a protein which means that it must be administered systemically and cannot be applied locally, for example as a cream. However, drugs which can be applied locally offer several advantages such as reduced side effects, targeted drug delivery at the site of action as well higher acceptance rates among the patients. Hence, this project aims to develop effective blockers of TSLP which can be applied topically. To achieve this goal, we combine our expertise in drug development and skin research. First, we will develop and synthesize potent low molecular weight TSLP inhibitors which will then be tested with regard to efficacy and tolerability in 2D and 3D cell cultures. Finally, the most promising compounds will be tested in animal models of atopic dermatitis. The overall goal are new topical treatment options for AD and the prevention of the development of further allergic diseases such as asthma.

column36: Tau pathology and circuit vulnerability in the hippocampal memory system
column37: Alzheimer's disease is the primary form of dementia in old age and rates are increasing due to longer human lifespan and the aging population of baby boomers. It is estimated that prevalence will quadruple between 2006 and 2050, at which point 1% of the worldwide population will have the disease. Despite these bleak figures, it is important to note that patients typically only live with the severest form of Alzheimer's for 1-2 years. Thus, treatments that can delay disease progression have tremendous potential to reduce the burden of Alzheimer's disease. Here, we will identify exactly which brain cells and circuits are initially most vulnerable to the tau pathology that is observed in aging and Alzheimer's disease. Tau is a toxic protein that is first observed in the memory centers of the brain, before spreading and causing irreversible damage. More specifically, the neurons that first harbor tau also connect with another region that produces newborn neurons throughout life. These newborn neurons have an enhanced ability to integrate into neural circuits, suggesting they may be better at forming connections in disease states. However, no one has ever examined whether they less vulnerable to tau, or more capable at repairing circuits that are damaged by tau. Here we will therefore mimic the human pattern of tau pathology in mice, and examine whether new vs. old neurons are more likely to be damaged. We will then use various therapeutic strategies to enhance new cell growth, with the goal of repairing the damaged circuits. Whereas we currently know, at a general level, which brain regions are sensitive to tau pathology and Alzheimer's disease, these experiments will reveal the precise subpopulations of neurons that are vulnerable and capable of being exploited to delay the progress of disease.

column36: Abinoonjees Nikanenim: Delivering Mental Health Services to Youth Living in Island Lake Anishininew Nations
column37: In Canada, approximately 20% of youth experience mental health issues that impact their daily lives. The rate of mental illness and need for access to mental healthcare is especially troubling for First Nations (FN) youth. As a result of colonial processes, FN youth are at higher risk for developing a mental illness, misusing drugs and alcohol, and dying by suicide compared to non-FN youth. Despite this, there remains a lack of mental healthcare services that are both readily available within FN communities and are culturally appropriate. The goal of this mixed-methods study is to conduct an evaluation of an enhanced telemental health services (ETHS) model to examine its impact in delivering mental health services to FN youth living in the four Island Lake Anishininew communities in Manitoba. Telemental health involves the provision of health information and services over a distance via information and communication technologies such as patient-provider videoconferencing. The ETHS model is rooted in Jordan's Principle-a child first principle developed to eliminate barriers to health and social services, including mental healthcare services for FN youth. The ETHS model takes an innovative approach, using both traditional clinical methods of service delivery (e.g., direct intervention and face-to-face interactions with clinicians) as well as novel strategies (e.g., delivery of services using telehealth) to provide care for youth in their FN communities. The model includes building community capacity as well as educating community service providers to develop sustainable mental healthcare services that are rooted in FN communities and responds to the needs of FN youth and their families. The evaluation of the ETHS model will adopt a child/family-centred approach and integrate multiple methods such as a review of available data, qualitative exploration across multiple levels (e.g., youth, family, community), and arts-based methods.

column36: The common haptoglobin phenotype as a predictor of cardiovascular disease and mortality: a re-analysis of four randomized controlled trials of glycemic control
column37: Nobody knows yet why strict blood sugar control (aiming for lower blood sugar levels) prevents heart disease in some people with type 2 diabetes but can cause harm in others. It makes it hard for patients with type 2 diabetes and their doctors to plan their blood sugar goals. Our team has been working to fill this gap, and we think that the answer may include the form of the blood protein 'haptoglobin' that a person has. Everyone's body makes one of two major haptoglobin forms, and the form can be measured by an inexpensive blood test. We just published a major study in which we used this blood test in participants from a large completed study that had tested strict blood sugar control. We re-analyzed the data in the two haptoglobin groups separately and found that strict blood sugar control prevented heart disease in people with one haptoglobin type, but people with the other type had no heart disease benefit and even had an increased risk of death. We now plan to expand our work to include more: (1) diversity in the people we study (more women, ethnicities, ages, and lengths of time having diabetes), (2) variety in the types of blood sugar control (different blood sugar goals, medications, and lifestyle actions like diet and exercise), and (3) different methods to analyze the data. This research unites us with skilled researchers from four different existing studies of blood sugar control to run the blood test in their studies and re-analyze their data. This is a cost-effective and ethical way to learn whether the haptoglobin type blood test can consistently tell which people will benefit from strict blood sugar control and who will not. It will tell us whether we should further study the blood test with doctors and patients in clinics to personalize their blood sugar control goals. Type 2 diabetes is very common in Canada and worldwide, and so research like ours that aims to better prevent heart disease in people with diabetes could impact millions of people.

column36: Role of early childhood viral infection on the development of childhood sleep disordered breathing
column37: Children with sleep disordered breathing (SDB), from habitual snoring to sleep apnea, are more likely to have ADHD symptoms and poor school performance. There are limited resources to identify and treat children with SDB. Canadian children can wait up to 2 years for a sleep study. SDB treatment often includes surgical removal of enlarged tonsils or adenoids. In Edmonton, children wait up to 1 year to see a surgeon and an additional 6 months on the surgical wait-list. Taken together, children with SDB may wait several years for treatment. Our research program will address 2 of the major questions in pediatric SDB: -Can we predict which children will develop SDB? -Can we prevent childhood SDB? Why some children develop SDB is not known. Viral infections of the respiratory tract in the preschool age group are extremely common. We hypothesize that children with SDB are more likely to have a history of a viral infection compared to children without SDB. This research will leverage data from the CHILD Study Edmonton site; the first study with assessments of SDB symptoms from infancy through to 8-years of age. We will use a comprehensive antibody detection method to determine whether the child has had a prior infection from any of over 1000 strains of 206 human viral species at ages 1, 5 and 8-years. Advantages of our proposal are the broad assessment of viral infection, a very large pediatric study population (over 800 children), our ability to determine if the viral infection came before the child developed SDB symptoms, and testing for many other factors that may cause children to develop SDB. Understanding the role of viral infection on the development of SDB will help spur vaccine development and inform vaccine scheduling. Early identification and ultimately preventing childhood SDB will improve childhood neurobehavioral development while optimizing limited sleep testing and surgical resources.

column36: Pragmatic Pediatric Trial of Balanced Versus Normal Saline Fluid in Sepsis (PRoMPT BOLUS)
column37: Sepsis is a medical emergency caused by severe infection. Septic shock is the most severe form. More than 25 million children worldwide are diagnosed with sepsis/septic shock every year. Sepsis is the most expensive hospital condition in North America and for critically ill children is the most common cause of hospital death. The World Health Organization has called for optimized treatments in sepsis. Crystalloid fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of initial treatment of sepsis. However, there is currently no research that clearly shows which is the most effective and safest type of crystalloid fluid in children. Two types of crystalloids are used for resuscitation in sepsis: balanced fluids (BF) and 0.9% "normal" saline (NS). In the absence of high quality, pediatric-specific data, NS resuscitation remains the overwhelming preference among pediatric emergency clinicians. The objective of this large, pragmatic, randomized study is to test the comparative effectiveness of the two most common types of crystalloid (BF vs NS) to improve clinical outcomes in children treated for septic shock. Thirteen pediatric emergency departments in the Pediatric Emergency Research Canada (PERC) network will collaborate with sites in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand to enroll 8,800 children with suspected septic shock. Children will be randomized to receive fluid resuscitation and maintenance fluids with either NS or BF for 24-48 hours, with all other aspects of care (other than fluid type) at the discretion of the managing health care team. Our primary outcome is major adverse kidney events within 30 days from randomization (MAKE30), a patient-centered endpoint that includes persistent kidney dysfunction, initiation of dialysis, or death. An economic analysis will be completed. The PRoMPT BOLUS study will be the largest trial of pediatric-specific, ED-initiated sepsis management to address the important clinical question of efficacy and safety of crystalloid fluids.

column36: Identifying low bone turnover disease in chronic kidney disease in order to guide anti-fracture therapy
column37: It is now well recognized that people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have weak bones. However, in contrast to people with osteoporosis, those with CKD have specific types of bone disease that could contraindicate the use of common anti-osteoporotic therapy. Indeed, up to 50% of people with CKD have what we call low bone turnover (LBT) disease (extremely low bone formation and resorption), in which anti-resorptive therapy is not recommended. In those patients, anabolic therapy (to stimulate bone formation) could be given. Identifying LBT disease is therefore of extreme importance if we want to propose adequate bone therapy in CKD patients. Until today, doing a bone biopsy at the iliac crest (anterior part of the hip) remains the only way to diagnose low bone turnover in CKD but is rarely done. Based on our prior works, we hypothesize that non-invasive markers could be used to identify CKD patients with LBT. Our global objective is to identify non-invasive biomarkers that will help in identifying patients with low vs non-LBT so that adequate anti-fracture therapy coud be offered. Methods We will recruit patients with CKD for iliac crest biopsy. We will compare CKD patients with low vs non-LBT. We will evaluate non-invasive biomarkers in the skin (AGEs) and in blood (AGEs, sclerostin, micro-ARNs) that may differentiate CKD patients with low vs non-LBT. Their predictive capacity will be evaluated alone or in combination. Then, Iliac crest biopsy specimens will be evaluated for bone quality parameters (microarchitecture, bone material composition) to evaluate the effects of LBT on bone strength. Significance Bone fragility is a major health issue in patients with CKD. We have a unique opportunity to conduct a bone biopsy study in this population to identify non-invasive markers that may predict LBT disease. Our results have the potential to change clinical practice so that personnalized bone therapy could be offered to CKD population.

column36: Participation in aerobic exercise during stroke rehabilitation: a mixed-methods study
column37: People are often physically unfit early after stroke, which can make participating in therapy and daily activities difficult. Aerobic exercise improves physical fitness and general health, which reduces the risk of another stroke, and also promotes stroke recovery. Aerobic exercise is beneficial and safe even early after stroke. Clinical guidelines recommend completing aerobic exercise within stroke rehabilitation. Most physiotherapists say that they prescribe aerobic exercise to their stroke patients. However, the number of people with stroke who participate in aerobic exercise during rehabilitation is low. We need to understand the barriers to exercise from patient and clinician perspectives so that we can develop interventions to promote exercise participation during stroke rehabilitation. The purpose of this study is to understand what stops or helps people with stroke participating in aerobic exercise during rehabilitation. This study will collect information about patients with stroke who are undergoing rehabilitation at one of four different hospitals. Information collected will include medical history, social supports, physical and cognitive function, and exercise preferences. We will compare characteristics of those who participate in exercise to those who do not. We will also interview patients and their physiotherapists to find out how they feel about exercise during rehabilitation. We will combine the quantitative (statistics) and qualitative information (interviews) to get a complete idea of the problem of exercise participation in stroke rehabilitation. Knowing what prevents or helps people with stroke to participate in exercise during rehabilitation will allow us to create strategies to increase the number of people who participate. These strategies will increase the number of people with stroke who can benefit from this important therapy (aerobic exercise), and can in turn improve recovery and health of those with stroke in the future.

column36: The impact of amyloid-induced neurodegeneration on sleep features and memory processes
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an age-related neurodegenerative disease that primarily impairs memory for recent facts and events (explicit memory). Loss of connections (synapses) between cells (neurons) in specific brain regions involved in explicit memory, such as the hippocampus, gradually leads to neuronal cell death and induced the progressive cognitive decline that characterises the disease. Since the hippocampus is also involved in other functions such a sleep, some features of sleep are also affected at the onset of the disease, including poor sleep quality, insomnia and early morning wakening. Given the importance of sleep on memory performance, these sleep disturbances have in return a deleterious impact on memory function of AD patients. The main objective of this project is to determine how hippocampal neurodegeneration and sleep disturbances influence each other to impair memory function in the development of AD. We also propose to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying this bidirectional interaction at the onset of the disease. To achieve our goal, we will perform chronic hippocampal injections of amyloid-beta oligomers in animals to mimic cell death and cognitive deficits observed in AD. Electroencephalographic measurements will be performed to determine sleep alterations in these animals. The impact of neurodegeneration and sleep perturbations will be tested on the acquisition and consolidation phases of memory. Identifying the specific signature of hippocampal neurodegeneration on sleep features might serve as a non-invasive marker to refine the diagnosis of AD. A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underpinning the effects of neurodegeneration and sleep disturbances on cognitive decline in AD could be of great interest to develop new therapeutic targets effective at the onset of the illness before neurodegeneration induces severe memory loss that prevents patients from functioning independently.

column37: Gene defects cause cancer. However, most "cancer causing" gene defects are highly context-specific, and are actually impotent in most cells. The reasons underlying such resistance are poorly understood. Understanding such natural cancer-resistance may expose new therapeutic strategies. Loss of the RB tumor suppressor gene causes retinal and lung cancer, but the gene is typically intact in most cancers. Even in the retina and lung, most cell types are resistant to RB loss. When RB is missing, all cell types behave abnormally, and display numerous hallmarks of cancer cells, yet only select cells generate tumors. We have identified critical features of a susceptible cell type. We also identified molecular regulators that may drive these activities. Here, we will extend insight into features that mark susceptibility, ask if they operate in different tissues, and define whether manipulating them prevents cancer.

column36: What works for whom? Individual participant data network meta-analysis of exercise for persistent low back pain
column37: Low back pain is a leading cause of disability in Canada and globally. Almost every Canadian suffers from low back pain at some point in their life. Most of the cost associated with low back pain is generated by a small percentage of individuals with persistent symptoms. Exercise therapy is a commonly recommended treatment strategy. However, there is no evidence to support the use of one type of exercise over another and very limited evidence about individual patient characteristics associated with effectiveness of specific treatments. There are two specific directions of research evidence that are needed to answer, 'what works for whom?' for patients with persistent low back pain. Neither of these directions can be pursued with more randomized controlled trials or traditional evidence synthesis projects: 1.Determine what types of exercise therapy, design or delivery characteristics improve its effectiveness for patients with persistent low back pain, and 2.Determine the persistent low back pain patient characteristics and patient subgroups that have better or worse outcomes with exercise therapy. To identify different types and characteristics of exercise programs that may be more effective we will use an approach called network meta-analyses. To identify patient characteristics and subgroups of individual patients who may benefit more from exercise therapy compared to no treatment, non-exercise usual care, and other conservative treatments, we will conduct an analysis using individual patient data from the best available trials. There are currently more than 350 randomized controlled trials of exercise therapy for persistent low back pain. Individually, these trials provide limited evidence and have not advanced decision-making for back pain patients. This team will advance the low back pain field by combining and re-analyzing trial data using best-practice statistical methods.

column36: Allegory-Based Literacy Empowering Youth to Overcome Unhappiness (ABLE YOU): A Stepped Wedge Trial of a Novel Intervention to Promote Coping and Prevent Suicide in Youth
column37: Suicide rates in youth have been increasing over time in Canada and most evidence-based interventions focus on prevention once suicidal behaviour has already occurred. There is a dearth of universal interventions targeting suicide prevention and promoting coping before periods of high risk. Our group identified that the third book in the popular Harry Potter series functions as an allegory for the author's experience of depression and suicidal ideation as well as how she learned coping skills based on cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) to overcome them. We have created a 3-month teacher-delivered curriculum for middle schoolers imparting mental health literacy and coping skills to youth. In 2019, it was piloted in students in a rural school board in Eastern Ontario (n=78). Before and after data showed a 44% overall reduction in suicide scores and a statistically significant improvement in measures of coping overall with boys also showing significant reductions in depression and anxiety. This study will build on that pilot data to test the impact of the intervention in a more diverse, urban setting using a stepped wedge design such that all youth receive it but in staggered fashion so that the impact of the intervention can be probed. Outcome measures are both quantitative (validated questionnaires) and qualitative (focus groups). Health administrative data will be used to test whether youth who receive the intervention show different patterns of healthcare utilization and fewer emergency visits for self-harm/suicide attempts.

column36: Traumatic Brain Injury and Perinatal Mental Health Outcomes
column37: In Canada, 2% of the population lives with a traumatic brain injury (TBI), and there are 18,000 hospitalizations for TBI each year. One-third of persons with TBI are women, and TBI is common in young women entering their childbearing years. Women with TBI are more likely than men to have mental health problems post-injury. Yet, little is known about their mental health around the time of pregnancy. This is an important issue because women with TBI may be uniquely at risk for new or worsening mental illness in pregnancy and the postpartum period because of stressors related to sleep deprivation and sensory issues, and the impact of hormonal changes on a vulnerable brain. Our goals are to examine the burden of mental illness among women with TBI before, during, and after pregnancy and the risks of medical problems in the mother and baby during and after pregnancy among women with co-occurring TBI and perinatal mental illness. We will use data collected from Ontario health records to identify all women with a livebirth or stillbirth conceived in 2002-2019. We will compare women with a history of TBI before pregnancy, and those with no such history, on their risks of mental illness diagnoses, mental health service use patterns, and risks of severe mental health outcomes such as self-harm or suicide before, during, and after pregnancy. We will also examine the risks of maternal and newborn medical complications associated with having both TBI and perinatal mental illness. Evidence of an association between TBI and mental illness around the time of pregnancy will lead to the development of health care services that address the unique mental health needs of women with TBI. Given that TBI is a leading cause of disability worldwide, these efforts will result in better outcomes for mothers, infants, and families by providing more responsive support to women with TBI.

column36: Mobilizing knowledge-to-action for responsive feeding in early childhood: A theory-based intervention for the early years
column37: Creating healthy food environments for young children can foster healthy behaviours that provide a foundation for lifelong health. Responsive feeding helps to encourage self-regulation in children by allowing children to communicates feelings of hunger and is followed by an appropriate response from the caregiver. Early childhood programs often follow healthy eating guidelines that encourage responsive feeding principles but there are barriers that prevent this from happening. Past interventions that support healthy eating do not typically think about behaviour change across multiple levels. Our study aims to use theory in the development, implementation and evaluation of an intervention to create responsive feeding environments in the early years in the Maritimes.
