column36: Alcohol consumption and change in blood pressure: evidence synthesis of 24 hour trial data and modelling of intervention effects
column37: Screening for hazardous and harmful drinking is rarely done in clinical practice. Health care providers face two major barriers when considering advice and treatment for patients with hypertension regarding their alcohol consumption: knowledge and motivation. First, clear guidance and information on the risks associated with alcohol consumption is missing from most guidelines for clinical practice. Although heavy drinking is causally related to the development of hypertension (raised blood pressure [BP]), less is known about the risk associated with less heavy drinking, such as 1-2 drinks per day. Several trials have reported conflicting results regarding BP changes after acute ingestion of alcohol, ranging from a decrease to no change to an increase. Currently, no systematic review on the immediate effects of different levels of alcohol consumption exists. This project will systematically summarize the evidence for the effect of alcohol consumption on changes in blood pressure within 24 hours after alcohol intake in clinical trials. The review will follow international standardized protocols for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Second, the potential impact of implementing screening and brief interventions for hazardous alcohol consumption on BP in clinical practice is unknown. We will model the reduction in BP on a population level in Canada, and, consequently, cardiovascular deaths and hospitalizations, for different scenarios of alcohol reduction based on the results of our previous work and the findings of the proposed study. The project will provide important evidence for the development of BP-specific low-risk drinking guidelines and policy initiatives to reduce the health burden from both alcohol consumption and raised BP.

column36: TACAN is an ion channel essential for osteoarthritis pain
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) afflicts more than 10% of Canadians. The cardinal symptom of this disease is chronic pain at rest or during movement. Clinical and preclinical research have indicated that OA pain emanates from hyper-responsive pain-sensing fibers (also called nociceptors). Yet the mechanisms underlying this hypersensitivity remain unknown. We have previously demonstrated that a subtype of sensors expressed in nociceptors become sensitized during OA and are responsible for the pain symptoms. However, the identity of these sensors remained elusive. We have now identified a protein, named TACAN, that acts as a sensor for painful stimuli. The current proposal aims at taking a translational approach to determine whether TACAN is responsible for OA pain and could constitute a valuable therapeutic target for OA pain.

column36: Dissecting and targeting SWI/SNF loss in de-differentiated endometrial carcinomas
column37: There exists a group of cancers that are commonly associated with a de-differentiated phenotype. This means that they no longer look like the tissue from which they arise; but rather look more like tissue in an embryo. These cancers include de-differentiated endometrial carcinomas (DDEC), small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) and certain small cell lung cancers (NSCLC). All of these cancers have a very poor prognosis; thus we need to find better treatment options. We and others have determined that de-differentiated cancers commonly lose components of the SWI/SNF complex; a set of proteins that regulate which genes can be expressed by remodeling chromatin (DNA and the proteins around which it is wound). In this study, we will determine the extent to which the loss of SWI/SNF components may promote de-differentiation. We will also determine how we may be able to specifically target and kill cancers wherein these genes are lost.

column36: Social environment and functioning of adolescents born pre-term
column37: Most pregnancies last 40 weeks. Babies born before the 37th week are known as preterm (or premature) babies; in Canada, about 8% children are born preterm. Preterm birth is associated with a number of adverse outcomes varying in severity and onset, such as cerebral palsy (manifesting shortly after birth), autism (developing in early childhood) or bipolar disorder (presenting by early adulthood). On average, individuals who were born preterm function less well than their term-born peers across many cognitive domains, achieve lower levels of education and have lower employment rates. As with other adversities, however, many preterm-born individuals function very well despite the presence of a long-term disability, lower cognitive functioning or behavioural problems. These inter-individual variations may arise at many levels (biological. psychological, social) and developmental periods. Here we focus on identifying features of social environment that may change long-term outcomes of preterm birth with regards to brain maturation, cognition and mental health of adolescents & youth (~12 to 22 yrs). We chose this period of development because of its dynamics with regards to biology (growth, sex hormones) and sociology (friends, romantic partners). We are interested in how psychosocial stress combines with puberty to shape the brain and mental health. To address our questions, we will use two approaches: (Aim 1) A population-based aggregate-level analysis linking "exposures" (preterm birth) and "outcomes" (health) across neighbourhoods; and (Aim 2) A targeted individual-level analysis linking exposures (preterm birth) and outcomes (cognition, brain structure) of adolescents living in a selected subset of neighbourhoods (n=600). The project will be carried out in the City of Toronto that consists of 140 neighbourhoods, with ~275,000 individuals of the target age (~22,000 born preterm). Both approaches build on our previous research in typically developing children.

column36: Regulation of neuronal pacemaker channels by cannabinoids
column37: Cannabinoids are a broad class of molecules that act on nerve cells, affecting pain sensation, appetite, mood, learning and memory. There are 3 classes of cannabinoids: (1) endocannabinoids produced naturally by the body, (2) phytocannabinoids from some plants, and (3) synthetic cannabinoids. Cannabinoids may provide effective treatments for addiction, pain, epilepsy, major mood disorders, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, spasticity in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease. However, to use them, without negative effects on learning and memory, we must understand exactly how they affect nerve function. Cannabinoids bind to Cannabinoid receptors (CBRs). However, activating CBRs cannot directly change the firing of nerve cells, since CBRs do not generate electrical signals on their own. Instead, electrical signals are controlled by ion channels, which allow for the movement of charged "ions" from one side of a membrane to the other. My lab focuses on hyperpolarization-activated cyclic-nucleotide gated (HCN) channels. HCNs are important for nerve function, learning and memory, pain sensation, and vision. The endocannabinoid WIN55,212-2 effects memory by activating CB1R, which leads to changes in electrical currents through HCNs. However, cannabinoids can also bind ion channels directly, or alter their membrane environment. In addition, different cannabinoids (for example, THC and cannabidiol from marijuana) have different effects on people's mood, pain sensations, and memory. Since HCN channels are involved in all of these processes, we are asking, do cannabinoids have a direct effect on HCNs, independent of CBRs? If so, are these effects specific to the type of cannabinoid? These findings will help us to develop therapeutic approaches to the treatment of numerous neuronal disorders. Also, our results will also help in the development of novel nootropics or "smart drugs" that can enhance memory, creativity, or motivation.

column36: Development and Translation of Novel Donor Lung Gene Regulation Strategies for Lung Transplantation
column37: Lung transplantation is the primary life-saving treatment for patients with end-stage lung disease. Since the first successful clinical lung transplant in the world was performed at Toronto General Hospital (UHN) in 1983, we have led a global effort to improve outcomes, ultimately resulting in more lungs being transplanted each year. However, despite this success, median recipient survival has reached only 6.8 years-largely due to detrimental immune responses that result in lung injury and negative early and late effects on the transplanted lung and the recipient. We have developed key innovations in lung transplantation, including the gold standard preservation solution (LPD, Perfadex(R)) and the Toronto EVLP (Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion) System. With EVLP, surgeons worldwide can now perform advanced assessments and treatment of donor lungs, providing the unprecedented ability to determine donor lung function and quality prior to transplant. EVLP also allows surgeons to treat and control the host immune response to the transplanted lung. We will develop EVLP-based advanced gene regulation of the donor lung to improve the immune response. This technique will better manage harmful inflammation, reduce short-term lung injury and prevent long-term transplant rejection. We will use engineered stem cells and a method to change how genes work in the body, called CRISPR/Cas9, to make better therapies and improve the immune response. As a continuation of our successful track record in gene therapy for transplantation, including a planned first-in-human clinical trial as a result of our past CIHR-funded projects, we will work with our established partners to help achieve our goals. Globally, we aim to improve the quality of life for all transplant recipients. Project outcomes match CIHR's goal to strengthen Canada's health care system and serve as world leaders in scientific excellence, as well as CIHR's goal to maximize transformational impacts on the health of Canadians.

column36: Optimizing HIV testing services in sub-Saharan Africa to end the AIDS epidemic by 2030
column37: Ending the AIDS epidemic begins by building efficient HIV testing services. HIV testing has, and remains, a cornerstone of HIV prevention efforts. A positive diagnosis entails that people living with HIV can receive life-saving antiretroviral therapy and, if the test is negative, people vulnerable to HIV acquisition can be identified and linked to prevention services. The Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) put forward the objective of ending the AIDS epidemic by 2030 by strengthening the HIV care cascade. The proportion of people living with HIV aware of their status is a key progress indicator and common bottleneck in the cascade. Tracking this indicator in sub-Saharan Africa is difficult, however, as surveillance systems are often incomplete. Our team has recently developed tailored tools that specifically address these challenges. Yet, current models are agnostic about testing modalities (e.g., opt-in, HIV self-tests, mobile campaigns) and cannot stratify coverage metrics by key populations (e.g., female sex workers and men who have sex with men). Members of these populations represent close to 50% of global new HIV infections and, if the goal of ending AIDS is to be achieved, they need explicit consideration. To fill these knowledge gaps, we will develop methods, build tools, and validate models to inform, strengthen, and optimize HIV testing services. Specifically, we will 1) improve estimates by integrating new data sources, 2) adapt current frameworks to consider key populations, and 3) optimize national HIV testing strategies considering affordability and cost-effectiveness. By drawing on the expertise of an international team of HIV researchers, biostatisticians, economists, modelers, and knowledge users, our project will guide global recommendations on how best to sustainably close gaps in diagnosis coverage among some of sub-Saharan Africa's most vulnerable groups.

column36: Sex differences in preclinical models of sepsis: a systematic review
column37: Many differences exist between men and women when it comes to how diseases affect the body, and how effective treatments for those disease are. Despite this, medical research has demonstrated a lack of gender diversity over the years, even more so in the preclinical animal research setting. Significant evidence exists demonstrating a large portion of animal research is performed only in male animals. In the past, drugs have been approved by regulatory agencies, only to later be taken off the market due to detrimental effects in women. These harms could have potentially been avoided, had the preclinical research been sufficiently performed in both male and female animals. Our team wishes to study differences in treatment effect between sexes in animal models of sepsis . We will identify these potential differences by reviewing the current scientific literature, in order to identify existing research pertaining to sex-dependent responses to treatment in this devastating disease. Sepsis has been chosen as differences in outcomes have been seen between sexes in the human population, and understanding those differences in animal research may lead to more efficient discovery of treatments. Results from this study will also contribute to a nation-wide initiative, as members of our team are currently in the process of developing Canadian network of preclinical sepsis researchers who will conduct experiments together. Elements of biological sex will feature prominently in these experiments, and our review study proposed here will be essential to appropriately plan these experiments. Ultimately, by identifying differences in treatment response between sexes in preclinical studies, we can better identify therapies and drugs to bring to clinical trials in humans.

column36: Rethinking the role of B cells in IgA nephropathy
column37: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is a leading cause of kidney failure yet very little is known about the immune system defects that cause IgAN. As a consequence, there is no available treatment and 40% of patients require dialysis or transplant within 15 years of diagnosis. While it is known that IgA is a central part of the immune response preventing invasion of bacteria from surfaces lining the airways and gut (mucosal surfaces), the trigger and the location of cells responsible for production of disease-causing IgA in patients with IgAN remains unknown. Prevailing dogma is that IgA protein is released into the blood from cells within tissue along mucosal surfaces. We have recently identified that individuals with IgAN have higher levels of IgA targeted against tonsil bacteria (Neisseria) than healthy counterparts. Using a mouse model, we confirmed that infection with Neisseria causes IgAN in mice. Surprisingly, IgA-producing cells typically residing in the mucosal surfaces may be leaving the mucosa and establishing niches inside the kidney, and then produce disease-causing IgA within the kidneys. This is a radical change in our understanding about the origins of IgAN. Our goal is to explore these transformative findings further in both our mouse model and human subjects. By understanding exactly what type of cell is establishing a niche in the kidney, and what is triggering the cells to move there, we can develop new treatments for IgAN.

column36: The impact of cannabis legalization on the illicit cannabis market in Canada
column37: On October 2018, Canada became only the second country to legalize non-medical cannabis. Reducing the illicit market is critical to achieving the public health objectives under the Cannabis Act; however, the extent to which consumers will transition to the legal cannabis market is unknown. The proposed study will examine how cannabis legalization impacts cannabis purchasing and the illegal cannabis market in Canada. First, an environmental scan of cannabis retail sources will be conducted in each province annually, over a 4-year period. The scan will identify the location of legal and illegal cannabis stores, and collect objective measures of cannabis prices and potency. Second, data from the scan will be linked with data from the International Cannabis Policy Study, a CIHR-funded prospective cohort survey of 10,000 Canadians (1,000 per province, 16-65 years of age) conducted over the same 4-year period. The survey includes comprehensive assessments of cannabis consumption and purchasing-including product types, quantities, price paid, and purchase source-as well as household postal code to enable geographic analyses. Analyses will address five primary objectives: 1) to estimate changes in the retail availability and price of illegal cannabis in Canada following legalization; 2) to examine changes in legal and illegal cannabis purchases, including the overall size of the cannabis market in Canada; 3) to examine the impact of provincial retail policies, such as the number of retail stores, on cannabis purchases and market size; 4) to examine individual-level predictors of purchasing illicit cannabis, including geographic proximity to legal and illegal retail outlets; and 5) to examine changes in THC and CBD levels of cannabis products. Overall, the proposed study represents the most comprehensive assessment of the cannabis market to date. The data has the potential to directly inform cannabis policy in Canada and other jurisdictions.

column36: A novel multimodal intervention for surgical prehabilitation of patients with lung cancer
column37: Many persons with lung cancer lose muscle, are fatigued and have more difficulties performing their normal activities. Those who undergo surgery in these conditions suffer from more complications, take more time to recover and have more risk of mortality. Our research group has shown that a moderate exercise and nutrition intervention can improve functional status, not only during recovery but even before surgery. We will take advantage of the 4-week waiting period to engage patients in this intervention that also includes consultation to reduce anxiety and to improve diet, and which will last for 8 weeks after surgery. Patients scheduled for lung cancer surgery will be assigned by chance to one of three groups: 1) receiving the usual care including education on a healthy lifestyle and a placebo, 2) receiving a novel nutritional supplement that combines important nutrients involved in muscle health, or 3) taking the supplement and following an exercise program (with one supervised session per week). All groups will attend anxiety management sessions and counseling with the dietitian. Tests will include walking endurance, muscle strength, scans for body composition, heart-lung-muscle capacity, and questionnaires for the quality of life before and after surgery. Their length of stay in the hospital and complications due to surgery will be recorded. Small muscle samples will be collected during surgery in a subset of participants to study how the supplement influences the muscle quality and its capacity to build new proteins and store lipids. This work has the potential to help persons with lung cancer regain their normal functions and quality of life faster and with lesser complications after surgery. This would benefit the health care system as well.

column36: Activating the piRNA pathway to prevent heart disease
column37: Heart disease (HD) is a leading cause of death worldwide. 1.3 million Canadians are living with HD, and more than 400,000 are living with long-term disability due to HD. When the heart is sick stress stimulates profound changes in the heart's structure and function. Changes in structure include enlargement of heart muscle cells, which cause the whole heart to enlarge. If the heart remains sick for a longer time, the muscle cells start dying and are replaced by cells that make the heart stiff. Loss of muscle cells results in the thinning of the walls of the heart chambers, causing a significant reduction in the heart's capacity to push blood to the body. These alterations eventually cause the heart to fail. Stopping the progressive changes induced by stress to the heart is required for preventing it to fail. Recent studies have found a family of small messengers that protect the heart against the negative effects of stress. This is very promising and prompted researchers to find ways of controlling the production of such messengers in the heart. However, researchers haven't been able to harness their protective properties. My lab has discovered that inactivating a single gene in the mouse heart activates the machinery that produces such small messengers. Moreover, we found that the machinery producing small messengers is depleted in human failing hearts, indicating that our findings are relevant for human disease. Furthermore, we have identified novel small messengers in the heart. To harness the protective properties of small messengers, we have three objectives. 1) We will find the processes that regulate the production of small messengers in the heart. 2) We will test the protective properties of the machinery that produces the small messengers, and 3) Test the protective properties of our newly discovered small messengers in muscle cells of failing human hearts. These studies will provide much needed new strategies to prevent heart failure.

column36: Role and therapeutic potential of MicroRNA-34a-5p in knee osteoarthritis
column37: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and among the leading cause of disability worldwide. Ways to detect or treat knee OA are not available. Current treatments only target pain while early detection methods are absent. By the time of diagnosis, knee OA has usually progressed to a point leading to severe joint damage. Thus, it's critical to identify early detection methods that can allow early intervention and potential therapies to stop knee joint destruction during OA. Our studies have identified a panel of 7 molecules called microRNAs whose levels are increased in the synovial fluid of patients with advanced stage knee OA compared to early knee OA. Out of these 7 molecules, one particular molecule called microRNA-34a is highly elevated in the joint fluid, blood as well as joints tissues of patients with advanced-stage knee OA compared to early-stage and healthy subjects. These elevated levels are not only present in humans with knee OA but also in joint tissues of mouse with knee OA. We anticipate that the levels of this molecule along with other 6 microRNAs can help us detect or predict the extent of joint damage in the patients with knee OA. To do this, we have created a large biobank of patient blood and tissues with early to advanced stages of knee OA to help us identify the reliability and specificity of these miRNAs to detect or measure the degree of joint degeneration in patients with knee OA. Our studies further show that miR-34a-5p molecule is not only elevated during OA but also promotes joint damage. We anticipate that blocking this molecule will help us stop or delay the degeneration of knee joints during OA. This project aims to comprehensively understand: (1) If microRNA molecules can be used a biomarker to detect or measure the presence or extent of joint damage in patient with knee OA. (2) If the microRNA blocker can be used as a drug to stop or reduce joint damage during knee OA.

column36: Early Initiation of Antiplatelet ThERapy In HeArt TranspLantation - AERIAL Trial
column37: Heart transplantation is a life-saving treatment for end stage heart disease. After transplant, narrowing in the heart arteries can cause the new heart to fail and shorten lifespan. This condition is known as cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV). It is very common and affects about half of all transplant patients. There are few treatments to prevent or treat CAV. Platelets are cells in the bloodstream involved in clotting and inflammation. Both mechanisms are involved in the development of CAV. Studies have shown that platelets are more active in heart transplant patients. Medications that interfere with platelets are commonly used to treat patients having heart attacks due to heart artery blockages. Aspirin and clopidogrel are examples of drugs that work differently to block platelets.These drugs may be able to reduce CAV in heart transplant patients. The aim of our research is to determine if drugs that block platelets can be used to prevent CAV after heart transplant. A large clinical trial is needed to answer this question. We will first perform a trial in 3 Canadian transplant centres, and if shown to be feasible, continue to a larger international trial. We will randomly assign patients early after transplant to receive aspirin, clopidogrel or placebo (non-active sugar pill). Neither the patient or the medical team will know which drug the patient is receiving. We will assess if patients have developed CAV by performing an angiogram at 1 and 2 years post transplant and 1-2 years thereafter. An angiogram involves taking x-ray pictures after dye is injected into the heart arteries. Patients will also have special tests to look for early signs of CAV including thickening of the heart artery wall and abnormal blood flow. Blood tests will be used to measure platelet clumping function and assess the response to aspirin and clopidogrel. New treatments for CAV will improve the lives of heart transplant patients and increase life expectancy.

column36: Neuromodulation of Motivated Behavior and Cognition
column37: Our daily tasks regularly involve several cognitive processes. We can attend to our conversation at a noisy cocktail party and retain in memory a telephone number to dial it a few seconds later. These processes of attention and working memory enable flexibility in our behavior. Recent advances suggest that they share some neural circuit and mechanisms. Moreover, their dysfunctions characterize mental disorders, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the most common childhood disorders that can continue through adolescence and into adulthood. In addition, decline in these basic cognitive functions compromises healthy aging and is diagnostic of neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer and Parkinson's diseases. In this proposal, we aim to gain a comprehensive understanding of the effects of drugs used in mental disorders to modulate cognitive functions. We will investigate the multiple facets of these functions in animals trained to perform a task probing attention and memory. column37: Tinnitus is a bothersome noise or ringing in the ears occurring in the absence of external auditory stimulation. It is a common problem affecting approximately 1 person in 4 in Canada and is most often linked to age-related hearing loss. In around 6% of these cases, tinnitus is so distracting that it interferes with several central aspects of their lives including sleeping and working, and in the worse cases can lead to even depression and suicide. There is currently no effective treatment for tinnitus in large part because the mechanisms causing it are mostly unknown. Aberrant rewiring of the sound processing areas of the brain is thought to play an important role in the emergence of tinnitus, but the very nature of this reorganization remains very controversial. The primary goal of this project is to, using a rodent model of the disorder, understand precisely if and how the brain is reorganized in tinnitus sufferers. We propose experiments that will make use of novel neurophysiological techniques we have developed to map the auditory cortex's functional organization using intracortical recording of individual neurons. Furthermore, we will also make use of novel chemogenetic approaches that allow us to manipulate plasticity-regulating neurons to determine whether they are dysfunctional in tinnitus. The chosen methods, all mastered by at least one member of our team, were selected to best answer our research questions and maximize the quality and quantity of the data obtained. The proposed research will shed light on some of the neural mechanisms that underlie the emergence of tinnitus. We furthermore expect that our findings will significantly enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the emergence of tinnitus and will also hopefully provide new therapeutic targets for future research.

column36: Functional analysis of mitochondrial-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites
column37: All cells in the body require chemical energy to carry out their normal physiological functions. The majority of this energy is packaged as a compound called ATP and is produced by the oxidation of carbohydrate and fat in a biochemical process called oxidative phosphorylation. This process takes place in a compartment of the cell called the mitochondrion, and is carried out by several large protein complexes that constitute the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Respiratory chain dysfunction interferes with the normal supply of energy, and this produces a wide variety of different diseases, such as neurodegenerative and heart disease, the nature and severity of which depend on the exact genetic defect. The genetics of respiratory chain diseases is complicated by the fact that some components of the system are encoded in nuclear genes, others in a small genome that is contained within the mitochondria themselves. Mitochondria also rely on intimate contacts with other organelles in the cell, most notably a structure called the endoplasmic reticulum, which, among other things, supplies mitochondria with the lipids required for mitochondrial growth and division, and acts as a reservoir for calcium, which in part regulates mitochondrial metabolism. Several neurological diseases result from disturbances in the contacts between mitochondria and the ER. The proteins that interact across the mitochondrial-ER contact site are referred to as tethers, but the nature of these proteins remains incompletely characterized. Likewise, their roles in neurological disease and in the physiological regulation of contact sites remains relatively unknown. This project is aimed at identifying and characterizing the proteins at ER-mitochondrial contact sites, and investigating their precise molecular functions in healthy cells and in cells from patients with mitochondrial disease.

column36: Anatomically relevant brachytherapy implants by a 3D printing and radiosensitizing approach
column37: In brachytherapy (internal radiotherapy), millimeter-sized radioactive implants are used to treat different types of cancers. Usually very effective, brachytherapy requires precise calculations for the positioning of radioactive seeds, prior to their insertion. Unfortunately, the size, shape, and radiation per seed, allow very limited flexibility to the implants, and this is a strong limitation for further improvement of brachytherapy and more personalised approaches in the field. In this research project, an integrated 3D-priting (additive manufacturing) approach will be developed to allow the fabrication of anatomically-relevant radioactive implants that could be used in the most geometrically and precision-challenging brachytherapy application: eye cancer. First, a "radioactive polymer ink" will be developed, and used as the base material for a high-performance polymer 3D printer. Then, "radioactive eye plates" will be printed, as potential substitutes for eye cancer plates currently used in radiation therapy. The geometrical models for these plates will be provided by the imaging scans of real patients. The personalised 3D-printed radioactive implants will be evaluated through a dosimetric study based on a combination of numerical simulation and 3D radiographic dosimetry with hydrogels. Finally, a new "radiosensitization" approach based on coatings of gold nanoparticles at the surface of the implants, will be demonstrated as a possibility to decrease the overall amount of radioactivity necessary per implant. Overall, this new brachytherapy approach could open the door to a whole generation of 3D-printed high efficacy radioactive implants that could be fabricated directly in hospitals, and perfectly adapted to the anatomy of patients. An increased number of brachytherapy treatments could therefore become a reality, in particular in the case where geometrical precision and radioactivity concentration per volume of radioactive implant, are challenging.

All youth will also receive usual care. We will also determine whether the intervention impacts symptoms of mental illness, family communication, functional impairment, and whether it is cost effective. column36: Overcoming suppressive micro-environments in early breast cancer progression
column37: Drs. McCaffrey, and Muller will investigate how breast cancer cells disrupt tissue barriers to escape the local environment, and how they subsequently evade elimination by the immune system. Project description Breast cancer develops from early stages that are localized and pose little immediate risk tothe patient. However, up to 50% can progress to potentially lethal forms of invasive breast cancer that move into surrounding normal tissue. Some cells in localized cancers are poised to become invasive, and additional mutations are not required. However, the surrounding normal tissue functions as a barrier and represses invasion of these cells. There are currently no tests that can predict which localized cancers will progress and there is concern of overtreatment. We predict that signals from localized breast cancers reprogram the initially repressive adjacent normal tissue to permit the transition to invasive breast cancer. To test this we will characterize how cancer cells alter the behavior of adjacent normal cells as they progress from localized to invasive cancer. We will test if these changes are functionally relevant by modifying cancer cells or normal cells to promote or suppress the invasive transition using animal models that accurately reproduce cancer progression in patients. We will also elucidate how cancer cells promote suppression of the immune system by looking at the types and activities of immune cells present and whether they function in an anti-cancer or pro-cancer capacity. Finally, we will explore approaches that reactivate the immune system to target and eliminate localized cancer cells that try to escape and invade surrounding tissue. Impact and Relevance A better understanding of how cancers initiate and progress is crucial to develop tests that can guide doctors and patients for treatment decisions, as well as to identify new disease biomarkers and therapeutic targets for preventative treatment.

column36: Rescuing Neurovascular Network Function with Transcranial Neuromodulation
column37: Stroke is the leading cause of adult neurological disability with most survivors suffering moderate to severe long-term sensorimotor deficits. These studies will lay the foundation for development of personalized noninvasive transcranial current stimulation for targeting functional deficits following ischemic stroke.

column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) affects 1 out of every 100 adult Canadians. That's about 300,000 Canadians. Anyone can get RA and at any age. column36: Interrogating the structural basis for protein interactions underlying mitochondrial calcium uniporter regulation in cardiomyocytes.
column37: Cancer and heart disease are responsible for almost 50 % of all deaths in Canada annually. In the past ten years these leading causes of mortality in both sexes have accounted for more than 1,250,000 Canadian deaths. Mitochondria are small compartments in our cells that manufacture a chemical store of energy essential for countless physiological processes. Calcium (Ca2+) uptake into mitochondria not only influences this energy production, but can also trigger cell death. Indeed, a high level of mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake drives the tissue damage caused by heart attacks and a low level of Ca2+ uptake permits the uncontrollable cell growth associated with cancer. The mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter (MCU) mediates most of the Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondria after core protein building blocks interact to form a functional channel. At present, a precise understanding of how MCU functions based on these protein interactions remains unclear. Thus, the ability to control mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake with drugs rationally designed to modulate MCU activity is hampered. To increase our understanding of how MCU functions, we plan to map the atoms that promote interactions between MCU proteins and reveal how their relative orientation control these interactions. We will also elucidate atomic level details of MCU regulating protein-1 (MCUR1), a protein that acts as scaffold for MCU assembly, alone and in complex with MCU. Finally, we will study the role these protein interactions play in opening the MCU channel and causing damage to heart cells. The proposed work is an imperative first step toward developing novel modulators of MCU function, ultimately helping to manage the staggering and undiscriminating Canadian mortality associated with heart disease and cancer.

column37: Introduction Bladder cancer (BCa) treatment is rapidly evolving, with hundreds of new therapies and drug combinations in development or being tested. Research that assesses how to effectively distribute health care resources for BCa will be essential for patients and funders. Impact Our final CPM will prioritize the new and emerging BCa therapies that should be selected for funding while balancing effectiveness, cost, ease of administration, and side effects. column36: A wearable technology approach to managing challenging behaviours in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

column36: An analysis of the food environment in Canada: INFORMAS Canada
column37: The food environment has a major influence on dietary choices and is a critical factor in efforts to reduce rates of obesity and diet-related non-communicable diseases. The project will apply a health equity lens to all modules to examine how environments may differentially impact disadvantaged populations. The results of this research will be a comprehensive national report that identifies the strengths, weaknesses and gaps in the food environment in Canada. This research will support policy evaluation, and serve as a marker of accountability for forthcoming changes to the food environment as the Healthy Eating Strategy policies, regulations and programs unfold over the next 3 years. The study will contribute to a national evaluation in a critical policy area, and will further global efforts to improve food environments.

column36: Monocyte activation by energy sensing pathways in atherosclerosis
column37: Healthier nutrition and lifestyle, along with cholesterol-lowering drugs (statins) have lowered the rates of heart disease in Canada, yet it is still a major health concern and the second leading cause of death. Our research is focused on understanding how the metabolism of cells important for CVD might be controlling its onset. The job of a protein called HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR for short, which is the protein that is shut down by statin drugs) is to make cholesterol, but also something called isoprenoid groups, which are small attachments that are added to proteins to help or control how they work. Since HMGCR is such an important protein, it has many layers of control. One of these layers of control is called phosphorylation (which acts very quickly) and we know that a master regulator of cell metabolism (a protein called AMPK) can switch off HMGCR using this type of control. What we don't fully understand is the importance of this control step in cholesterol and isoprenoid production. We have genetically engineered mice so that they have a very specific and small mutation that makes their HMGCR completely resistant to the control that AMPK would usually have. Using these mice, we saw that when the HMGCR protein (cholesterol and isoprenoid production) was not controlled by AMPK, atherosclerosis (what leads to heart disease) is much worse. The current proposal is focused on understanding HOW and WHY this happens. We will build on our early results and experiments to see if having more heart disease is because of something to do with cholesterol or the use of isoprenoids, and also whether this metabolic pathway is important for making the cells that, in the end, form the plaque found in heart disease. It is our hope that by understanding how this pathway controls the early stages of heart disease, and how this might be different in males and females, we can potentially fine-tune or make new drugs that will further help Canadians affected by this disease.

column36: Self-Management for Amputee Rehabilitation using Technology (SMART) program: A peer supported mHealth approach for rehabilitation after lower limb amputation
column37: Lower Limb Amputations (LLAs) are a substantial burden on the Canadian health services with nearly 50,000 cases reported between 2006 and 2011. To address the challenging nature of a LLA (e.g., decreased mobility, pain, depression), patients need to go through extensive rehabilitation programs. Effective self-management programs can help those with LLA to monitor their own condition and improve their quality of life. However, a lack of self-management programs, a limited healthcare budget, and a decrease in quality of services (e.g. shorter lengths of stay for inpatients and rapid movement to outpatient services) pose further challenges for patients with LLA. Self-management programs can be provided to clients through online mobile technologies (e.g., tablet) and offer accessible, low-cost, and potentially augmentative rehabilitation after discharge, in both urban and rural areas. To address these needs, we designed and developed an online educational and training platform for individuals with LLA called, Self-Management for Amputee Rehabilitation using Technology (SMART). SMART focuses on LLA education, prosthetic limb management, and weekly support of peers. It is monitored by a trainer through a website. We aim to evaluate SMART in men and women with LLA aged 50 years and over, admitted to prosthetic rehabilitation throughout Vancouver, BC and London, ON. SMART has the potential to influence a client's post-LLA needs with direct (e.g., individual's health) and indirect (e.g., healthcare utilization) benefits. The purpose of our randomized controlled trial is to evaluate the effect of SMART in community dwelling older adults with unilateral, above or below, knee amputation.

column36: Establishing the epigenetic drivers of aggressive behaviour in meningiomas
column37: Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumor and will become even more prevalent in the future in the face of an aging population. Surgical removal of the tumor followed by possible radiation therapy is the first line treatment for meningiomas. However, even with maximal treatment, nearly a quarter of meningiomas have aggressive behavior with fast tumor regrowth and a mortality rate that is similar to other well recognized brain cancers. The standard clinical systems that are used to determine the risk associated with tumor regrowth only modestly reflect the degree of aggressive behavior in the tumor, and therefore patients are not being appropriately selected for radiation therapy to prevent tumor regrowth. In addition to this, chemotherapy or other medical therapy options are non-existent for patients with meningiomas, and therefore patients often need to multiple high-risk surgeries and rounds of radiation to try and control disease, and this is often unsuccessful. Recent studies from our research team has found that changes to the tumor genes that do not involve the DNA sequence (i.e. epigenetics) are linked to aggressive behavior in meningiomas. We therefore hypothesize that the drivers of aggressive behaviour in meningioma are a combination of epigenetic changes in the tumour that have yet to be fully characterized. We propose to use high-resolution state-of-the-art scientific approaches to comprehensively study the epigenetic changes that are characteristic of aggressive meningiomas in order to accurately identify which patients are at risk for fast tumor regrowth and to develop novel medical treatment options.

column36: Evaluating the Wiiji app to improve Indigenous workplace mental health: a mixed-methods approach
column37: There is a need to tailor mental health interventions to the needs of Canadian Indigenous people. E-health interventions have shown success for several mental health related conditions, including anxiety, depression, sleeping disorders and feelings associated with low self-worth. Results of this project will help us understand the impact of the app and will help us to better understand mechanisms for scale-up. These contributions have the potential to increase Indigenous participation in employment, reduce work disability, and improve the mental health of the Indigenous population. This will return economic and health benefits to Indigenous employers, communities, families, and individuals.

column37: The increasing world population and escalating rates of sexually transmitted infections (STI) have prompted the WHO to promote the development of MPT (multipurpose prevention technology), which involves applying into the vagina single compounds/devices that simultaneously inhibit pregnancy and kill the bacteria and viruses that cause STI. The MPT efficacy of LL-37/17BIPHE2 will provide women with empowerment to protect themselves against unwanted pregnancies and STI.

column37: The Indigenous history of health care in Canada deserves rigorous, dedicated, and collaborative research that centres Indigenous experiences. We will collect information drawn from the research to create a major exhibit and symposium, a medical and professional health education module. This project is in service to now-elderly Indigenous TB survivors, descendants, and communities; the research outcomes of this project benefit Indigenous stakeholders and their health first. column36: COMPLETE-2: A prospective, randomized, multi-centre trial of physiology-guided versus angiography-guided complete revascularization to treat multivessel disease after early percutaneous coronary intervention for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.
column37: Patients suffering a heart attack undergo a life-saving procedure called angioplasty, by which the blockage in the artery that caused the heart attack is opened and a stent is placed. In about half of the patients, additional blockages are found in other arteries. These are incidental findings and doctors have debated for years whether they should be treated with angioplasty or medications. We recently answered this question in a large multinational study called the COMPLETE trial. We showed that opening additional blockages reduced patient deaths or repeating heart attacks. A major concern is that not all of these angioplasties are necessary, but doctors do not know which arteries should be opened and which should be left alone. In the COMPLETE trial, the severity of blockages was estimated by visual inspection which is not a reliable method. Recently, new technique involving a special wire was proposed. It measures the blood pressure before and after a narrowing to estimate its severity. The advantage of this method is it can reduce the number of angioplasties by opening only the most important blockages thereby improving safety and costs. The main problem with using this method today is that doctors do not know of it. We are proposing a first large-scale trial to address this important issue. COMPLETE-2 trial will enroll 5100 patients at 140 sites worldwide. We aim to test whether the use of a pressure wire is as good as visually estimating the degree of narrowing when deciding which additional blockages found during the heart attack need to be treated with stents. We will test the usefulness of both methods and if it will improve patient safety by reducing unnecessary procedures, thereby decreasing bleeding, strokes and kidney injury. This study question is important in Canada because we have an unique health care system and the collaboration of doctors across the country will allow for efficient performance of randomized trials of heart attack patients.

column36: Traumatic stress symptoms in family caregivers of patients with acute leukemia: a longitudinal observational study
column37: Acute leukemia (AL) is a life-threatening cancer of the blood with sudden onset that occurs in individuals of all ages. The diagnosis of this disease typically requires urgent hospitalization for a course of intensive treatment, often for long periods of time. The disease and the treatment are likely to cause substantial distress in those affected and in their family caregivers (FCs). Research has demonstrated that FCs of individuals with solid tumours are equally or even more distressed than patients. However, little is known about the experience of FCs of patients with AL (who may be partners, adult children, or parents), despite the likelihood that they will be highly distressed and have a central role in supporting their family member with the disease. This lack of knowledge about their experience has limited our ability to help FCs to manage their distress and better support their ill family member. The present study aims to reduce this knowledge gap by assessing psychological distress and risk factors for its occurrence in the FCs of patients with AL across the life course. Consenting FCs of newly-diagnosed AL patients will complete questionnaires at the time of admission to the hospital and at 1-, 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-months thereafter. Statistical tests will be used to evaluate distress in FCs, the severity of this distress, its fluctuation over time, and the risk factors for its occurrence. We will also conduct interviews with a diverse group of FCs at 3-, 6-, and 12-months to learn more about their experience of distress over time, and their views about what help is needed for it to be best managed. This research study will help us understand more about distress in FCs of patients with AL and what approaches are needed to help them best manage this problem. Our results will be shared widely, including with FCs, patients, clinicians, and policy makers.

column36: Exploiting genetic vulnerabilities to improve outcomes in small cell carcinoma of the ovary
column37: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) is a rare but very aggressive type of ovarian cancer affecting young women. Its rarity has hampered the development of effective treatments. In 2014, several groups, including ours, discovered that SCCOHT is almost always caused by mutations in the gene SMARCA4. Our goal is to improve outcomes for women affected by this devastating cancer by providing new potential treatment strategies to treat SCCOHT. Part of our research strategy focuses on repurposing drugs already approved for other cancer types to treat SCCOHT. This approach can greatly facilitate clinical studies by bypassing drug development and safety testing. We recently found that SCCOHT cells are highly sensitive to a type of chemotherapy agents called CDK4/6 inhibitors, which are currently approved to treat breast cancer. This already led to a clinical study testing these inhibitors to treat SMARCA4-mutated cancers. Our research results suggest that SCCOHT cells are also sensitive to PARP inhibitors, also approved in Canada to treat another ovarian cancer subtype. In this project, we will fully validate PARP inhibitors as potential treatment for SCCOHT using a variety of model systems, including cell culture, mouse preclinical models, and patient tumor samples. As with all single-agent cancer therapies, drug resistance is expected to eventually arise in patients. To pre-empt this, we will use powerful genetic tools to identify the mechanisms at work in resistance development as well as identify novel drug targets in SCCOHT to develop secondary treatments or combination therapies to overcome resistance.

column36: Improving social justice in observational studies
column37: Population and public health is concerned not just with overall health but also the distribution of health in the population. Observational studies are conducted in real-world settings. Thus, they are ideal to understand the distribution of health inequity and monitor changes in response to policies over time. Observational studies often do not report/analyze sufficient details related to social determinants of health, thus undermining their ability to inform decisions with implications for social justice. This project aims to develop a reporting guideline on health equity in observational studies using an evidence and consensus-driven integrated knowledge translation process. This will extend the well-known STROBE (STrengthening Reporting of Observational studies in Epidemiology) reporting guideline. The project is novel in co-producing knowledge with Indigenous people, people in low and middle income countries and socially excluded people with diverse stakeholders including patients/public, researchers and decision-makers. We will apply an equity and sex/gender lens throughout. Data will be collected on analysis and reporting of health equity and sex/gender in observational studies. Existing journal and funding guidance will be reviewed. We will use an online global survey to seek broad feedback. We will hold a consensus meeting with researchers, patients/public and knowledge users to draft a global reporting guideline on health equity in observational studies. We will assess the applicability of this guideline to Indigenous research in Canada using a parallel process and consensus meeting. We will develop, implement and evaluate an end of grant knowledge translation strategy which will include pragmatic tools for authors and journal editors. Trainees will co-lead studies with mentorship from senior coinvestigators. The long-term vision is to improve transparent reporting of equity to inform policy and practice in reducing health inequities.

column36: Identifying cancer intrinsic immune evasion mechanism for target discovery
column37: Cancer cells can acquire features that allow them to evade recognition and destruction by effector cells of the immune system known as cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). These features or phenotypic changes not only facilitate progressive expansion and dissemination of cancer cells from within the tumor, but also promote resistance to currently employed immunotherapies that harness the potent cytotoxic properties of CTLs, including checkpoint inhibitors and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. The use of traditional genomic approaches (especially genome sequencing) to characterize patient cohorts treated with immunotherapy has provided fundamental insight into several mechanisms that promote immune evasion. Central to these genetic alterations that allow cancer cells to directly escape CTL killing, a form of immune evasion, includes loss of antigen presentation machinery and defects in cytokine signaling (e.g. interferon, TNF). While these landmark studies underscore the need to understand cancer intrinsic CTL evasion, they are limited to detecting only frequently occurring genetic alterations that contribute to this hallmark of cancer. As such, there remains a paucity of data systematically cataloging how individual cancer cell genetic elements act in a coordinated fashion to facilitate cancer intrinsic CTL evasion. Our research proposal aims to chart genetic dependencies that contribute to cancer intrinsic CTL evasion; to understand how core genetic dependencies that contribute to tumor heterogeneity in vivo and the tumor immune microenvironment, including in the presence of immune checkpoint blockade; to determine how our murine results translate to human cancer models; and to map genes that can overcome mutations that promote resistance to CTL toxicity using a combinatorial CRISPR targeting system recently developed in the lab.

column36: Preventing blindness by going to where you are: Culturally-competent tele-retina programs to support newcomers to attend diabetic retinopathy screening
column37: Retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness in Canada affecting people with diabetes. Yearly eye screening is recommended and there are treatments that limit vision loss. However, most people with diabetes in Canada don't get their eyes screened annually, and over 30% never have. Newcomers to Canada with diabetes are at greater risk and are even less likely to get screened. We conducted studies to understand why this may be and what can help. We looked into all other previous studies to summarize what is known about barriers to screening and which strategies work for addressing those barriers. We conducted interviews in Mandarin and French with immigrants to Canada with diabetes from China, Africa and the Caribbean about barriers for them getting eye screening. Access is a key barrier, and a promising solution is tele-retina screening, involving bringing portable screening equipment to a community location rather than requiring people to wait for specialist clinic appointments. However, there are many other barriers: language, knowledge, concerns about harms to eyes, misinformation about cost of screening, family influences and remembering. This project will involve two steps: First, we will work with newcomers from China, Africa and the Caribbean and community centres in Ontario and Quebec to co-develop strategies to support eye screening using tele-retina screening. Next we will launch screening programs in community centres on a small scale to test if the strategies we co-develop are acceptable and feasible to community centres and patients, how many patients attend and whether the screening is delivered as we expect. Results will give us the evidence needed to justify a larger study that would randomly allocate people to receive the intervention and then check if more people get their eyes screened. If that works, this may be a way of making sure groups at greater risk of blindness get their eyes screened to reduce the chance of vision loss.

column36: Discovering the transcription regulatory networks that control uterine contractions
column37: The contractile activity of the smooth muscle component of the uterus, the myometrium, generates the force needed to expel the fetus at birth. To initiate contractions, individual smooth muscle cells within the myometrium turn on a group of genes in response to hormonal, mechanical and inflammatory signals. In many patient cases this cell-coordinated contractile response occurs prior to term; women can consequently enter labour too early, which results in the delivery of underdeveloped infants at high risk of death or complications later in life. There is currently no effective treatment for preterm labour. Recent research has identified activated genes in the myometrium at term and preterm labour; however, the mechanisms that stimulate expression of these genes remain unclear. To understand the basis of preterm labour and develop new preterm labour therapies, we need to find the components involved in activating genes in both term labour and preterm labour. Inside cell nuclei the DNA that makes up our genome is highly organised into three dimensional structures so that regions of the genome that turn genes on or off can contact the genes they regulate. This genome organisation is specific to each cell type which ensures genes are expressed in the correct context. Currently, genome organisation in the myometrium as well as the parts of the genome that regulate gene expression changes during pregnancy and labour are unknown. Out team will identify the three dimensional genome structures specific to myometrial cells and the labour process. In addition, we will identify the proteins that bind to the genome to regulate gene expression during preterm or term labour. Uncovering the suite of genomic regions and regulatory proteins that underlie the labour process will provide new targets for the development of therapeutic treatments for preterm labour, preventing complications that occur when babies are born preterm.

column36: Why aren't we engaging our most at-risk older patients? Developing an in-depth understanding of patient/family engagement across care transitions
column37: Older patients and their family caregivers wish to be involved as much as possible in decisions about their care, but often feel left out of these decisions, especially during points of transitions in care. Phrases such as "patient-centred care" and "patient engagement" are used frequently, but often without any concrete meaning for patients, their family caregivers, or their health care providers. We also know that currently, care transitions are characterized by poor communication and information sharing, and a lack of engagement of patients and families in decision making. Yet, we know that engagement does improve patient experience and health outcomes. We looked carefully at available theories and evidence around engagement of older adults in healthcare decision-making. This work resulted in the "CHOICE" Patient Engagement Framework, however there is still a gap in how this conceptual framework can be translated to practice. We will work with patients, their caregivers and health care providers to develop an in-depth understanding of the factors that facilitate or hinder engagement in care planning and decision-making during transitions in care. We will explore what resources may be needed to support engagement, and how these resources could be implemented to change practice. By talking to all those involved and observing what happens, we will gain a good understanding of how best to develop resources and materials for patient and family engagement during care transitions.

column36: Evaluating the implementation, the process of empowerment, and the influence of context on a community mobilization intervention to reduce dengue infections in Brazil
column37: The proposed study is a series of implementation science evaluations that will be embedded within a funded cluster randomized trial (CRT) to allow us to understand how the intervention brings about sustainable change, the influence of context on the intervention, and the potential for transferability and scaling up. The CRT is measuring the effectiveness of a community mobilization intervention on dengue incidence in children in Fortaleza, Brazil. Studying if community mobilization results in sustainable change and for whom, will improve our understanding of the intervention processes and the potential success of the intervention in other contexts and thus enhancing the transferability of results and approach. Our proposed study is a series of implementation science evaluations in eight of the intervention communities assessing the implementation process, fidelity, and social acceptability of the intervention (Objective 1). We will also examine if and how the intervention empowers communities and if this can be sustained over time (Objective 2). Finally, we will identify the interactions between the context, the mechanism, and the effect of the intervention through conducting a realist evaluation. The data collection for all three objectives will be a mix of documents, field observations, and interviews with key community stakeholders. For Objectives 1 & 2, a deductive-inductive approach will be used for the analysis of each of the domains of interest. For the realist evaluation, the qualitative data will be analyzed using a realist evaluation process. Knowledge translation activities are integrated throughout the study with community stakeholders as well as municipal and state partners. The insight gained from the implementation science evaluations will be crucial for the interpretation of the findings from the CRT and for advancing our knowledge and practice of community mobilization for dengue control.

column36: Targeting immunodominant regions on platelet factor 4 for the diagnosis and treatment of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
column37: Platelets are small cells in the blood that help control bleeding. Heparin is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) used in heart surgery and to manage heart attacks and strokes. Patients receiving heparin may have an allergic-type reaction called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia resulting in low platelets (thrombocytopenia) and can also develop severe clotting causing loss of limbs, heart attacks, stroke and death. So this drug (heparin) that usually helps patients can actually cause more strokes and heart attacks in some patients. In HIT, some patients develop attack proteins (antibodies) once they are given heparin which attack platelets. However, other antibodies appear similar but do not attack platelets. Testing if people have HIT is a major problem because most tests cannot tell the difference between the dangerous antibodies and the antibodies that do not cause HIT. Our first goal is to study the antibodies that cause the disease in HIT patients and what separates them from other antibodies who do not get the disease. Our second goal is to use the information regarding specific characteristics of antibodies to make tests more efficient and accurate. In addition, we will identify drugs that can interfere with the disease-causing proteins and stop them from causing HIT due to the use of heparin. Our group has hundreds of frozen blood samples from patients who received heparin since we are a test centre for many hospitals across Canada. Once we understand why some patients get HIT and others do not, we will be able to provide better tests, resulting in better patient care for many Canadians at risk of getting this disorder.

column36: Human Cytomegalovirus as a Driver of Adverse Health Outcomes among Children Exposed to HIV in Utero
column37: Every year, nearly 1.5 million HIV infected women give birth around the world. Due to the development and use of antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy, the majority of their children will be born HIV free (1.3 million). These HIV exposed but uninfected children, referred to commonly as "CHEU" children, now make up nearly 30% of the newborn population in some countries where there is a very high prevalence of HIV. While these children are not infected by HIV, they remain affected by it, and have a much higher rate of mortality when compared to children who have never been exposed to HIV, are more likely to be hospitalized, and get sick from infectious diseases. Among children living with HIV (CLWH), antiretroviral therapy works well in suppressing the virus, but is not curative due to the immune system's limited ability to attack the remaining HIV viral particles what is known as the viral reservoir. We suspect that co-infection with another common childhood virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV) may play a role in explaining to poor health outcomes of CHEU infants and maintain the HIV viral reservoir in infected children. CMV is a virus also transmitted from mother to child and is even more common than HIV, affecting nearly 1 in every 100 births worldwide. Because the HIV virus facilitates/enables the replication of the CMV virus, women living with HIV are at much higher risk of transmitted the virus to their newborns, However, at the moment, there are no recommendations for routine CMV testing in HIV exposed and infected children. The objective of our study is to assess the impact of CMV infection on HIV exposed, and HIV infected children. This is important because CMV is a treatable virus. If we find that CMV is contributing to their poor health outcomes, as a team, we will advocate for testing of all HIV exposed children.

column36: Epigenetic mechanisms of gastric cancer associated with ARID1A mutations and H. pylori
column37: Gastric cancer (GC) is the third most deadly cancer in the world, ranked within the top ten fatal cancers in Canada. It is known to be highly influenced by environmental factors. Indeed, Helicobacter (H) pylori is a human gastric pathogen that infects half of the world's population and is associated with 70% of invasive gastric tumors, making it the most significant risk factor for GC. However, how H. pylori promotes gastric cancer initiation and progression is still unclear. During cancer initiation and progression, the chromatin structure, a massive protein complex, organizes DNA available for changes in gene expression. Altered chromatin structures are associated with abnormal expression changes in genes that play critical roles in cancer. Consequently, new therapies targeting these chromatin structures in cancer have emerged recently. Notably, mutations identified in a number of chromatin modifier genes appear consistently in GC, implying that chromatin regulation is central to the disease pathogenesis. Among chromatin modifiers highly mutated in gastric cancer, ARID1A is one component of the key chromatin remodeling complex, and it is the second most frequently mutated gene after TP53. However, its role in GC is still unclear. Utilizing our novel mouse models mutated for Arid1a and infected with H. pylori, as well as mini-gut (organ-on-chip and organoid culture) systems, we will define GC-specific chromatin structures and gene expression profiles, and examine novel, chromatin-based therapeutic strategies targeting a key initiating phase of gastric cancer. This work will not only define how H. pylori interacts with altered chromatin structures to promote GC but also form a key foundation for highly innovative GC therapies.

column36: Remodeling of cerebral plasticity by early-life adversity: cellular and molecular mechanisms in the human brain
column37: Child abuse, defined as childhood sexual, physical or emotional abuse or neglect by a parent or caregiver, causes lasting pain and hardship for millions of Canadians. The aim of this research is to understand the nature of lasting changes in the organization of brain circuits in people having suffered from child abuse. We will examine the consequences of early-life adversity on perineuronal nets (PNNs) which are molecular structures embedding certain types of neurons in the brain. PNNs arise as brain regions mature and, as suggested by animal studies, stabilize brain circuitries while limiting their plasticity. Alterations of PNNs by early-life stress could be associated with the rise of maladaptive emotions and behaviors that can predispose to mental illness. Currently, very little is known about PNNs in the human brain. Here, we hypothesize that a history of child abuse associates with a remodeling of cerebral plasticity through the modification of PNNs in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region that has been implicated in depression and found to be vulnerable to early-life adversity. Having a unique combination of expertise and direct access to the well-characterized post-mortem brain samples (Douglas-Bell Canada Brain Bank), we propose to conduct this research by comparing brain tissues from individuals having suffered from severe child abuse to matched controls with cutting-edge microscopy and molecular approaches. This research will provide novel insights regarding the cellular and molecular nature of altered brain plasticity associated with child abuse and may in turn help identify novel therapeutic targets and better inform public policies aimed at preventing child abuse or minimizing its impact on mental health.

column36: To define the role of primary cilia in long-range axon tract formation
column37: Primary cilia are hair-like, signaling antenna protruding from the cell body on virtually all cell types, including neurons. In the past decade, primary cilia have sparked enormous interest due to the discoveries that mutations in over 100 genes that encode ciliary proteins can lead to 30+ human rare disorders collectively termed "ciliopathies". The brain is particularly vulnerable to impaired primary cilia as reflected in a large group of ciliopathies that are characterized by severe axonal defects associated with intellectual disabilities and autism spectrum disorder. However, we know little of how primary cilia function in the brain. Using our ciliopathies disease models and cilia-specific experimental tools, we are uniquely poised to systematically investigate the primary cilia-dependent mechanisms in axonal development. We recently made exciting progress: We found that impaired cilia in neurons result in malformations of major axon tracts such as corticospinal tract (the longest) and corpus callosum (the biggest). Mutant neurons show defects in axonal growth and guidance, as well as dysregulated cilia-PI3K (Phosphoinositide 3-kinase) signaling. These data are important in beginning to unravel the undefined signaling mechanism linking primary cilia to the control of axonal development. Based on our preliminary work, we will test the intriguing notion that primary cilia function as essential signaling centers to convey environmental signals to neurons for axonal development and circuit formation.

column36: Understanding cannabis use and associated long-term recovery and return-to-work outcomes among Ontario workers following a work-related injury or illness
column37: Work-related injuries and illnesses are an important public health concern, with profound impacts on a worker's physical health, mental well-being, and financial security. There is growing interest in the role of medical cannabis for the treatment of work-related health conditions. However, we know virtually nothing about how workers with work-related conditions use cannabis and how their use may relate to recovery. We are conducting a survey of 1,200 Ontario workers 18 months after filing a workers' compensation claim for a work-related health condition. Early results demonstrate that 31% of workers used cannabis in the past year, 43% of whom used cannabis to cope with their work-related condition. Importantly, 96% of respondents agreed to be re-contacted, providing an opportunity to extend the current study to generate new knowledge on cannabis use and associated recovery outcomes over the long-term following a work-related condition. The proposed mixed-methods study will consist of conducting both surveys and in-depth interviews with the same group of workers 30 months after they first filed their claim. The goals of this study are to describe detailed cannabis use patterns in this population, identify the factors workers consider in deciding to use cannabis, seek medical authorization, and workers' compensation reimbursement; examine the factors associated with condition-related use, authorization, and reimbursement; evaluate changes in condition-related use; and examine the longitudinal impact of condition-related use on recovery outcomes. Findings of this project will provide health care providers, injured worker advocates, and workers' compensation authorities with a knowledge base to inform policies, practices, and initiatives around cannabis use in this population, including an identification of the worker subgroups most likely to benefit from guidance around use.

column36: Evaluating tetrahydrocannabinol as an adjunct to opioid agonist therapy for individuals living with opioid use disorder: A Phase II, placebo-controlled, blinded, pilot study to assess safety and feasibility
column37: Communities across Canada are grappling with the opioid overdose crisis. Sparked by the contamination of the illicit drug supply with fentanyl, the crisis has claimed more than 14,000 lives since 2015, many of them individuals living with opioid use disorder. Medications like methadone are the best available treatment for opioid use disorder and have been shown to lower the risk of death from opioid overdose. However, methadone requires daily ingestion and improvements are needed to increase its beneficial impacts and reduce the risk of patients consuming illicit opioids like fentanyl. In preliminary studies, we have observed that people on methadone using cannabis were more likely to stay on methadone and less likely to use fentanyl. In the current study, we propose to test the safety, tolerability, and feasibility of giving people in treatment for opioid use disorder cannabis alongside daily methadone. The study will recruit 24 people on methadone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside who are interested in taking cannabis (specifically, a high THC/low CBD oil taken orally) along with daily methadone. During the study, they will get their daily methadone dose and, at random, either a high THC/low CBD oil or an identical oil without active ingredients (i.e., a placebo.) The study will last for 12 weeks and compare safety, tolerability, between people who received cannabis and those who received placebo. At the end of 12 weeks, participants adherent to the study protocol will be offered another 12 weeks on cannabis. There will be no cost for participating in this trial. This pilot study is an innovative proposal to try and improve treatment for people with opioid use disorder at high risk of overdose. It will not only help patients and care providers better understand cannabis use during methadone treatment, but also advance efforts to address Canada's overdose crisis.

column37: Over 10% of all patients who have surgery (aged 45 and above) will suffer a major complication and over 1.5% of all adults will die within 30 days after surgery. The most common major complications are injury to the heart muscle, bleeding, and infection. These complications happen on the surgical ward or at home, after hospital discharge. We need better ways of monitoring patients so that we know, ahead of time, if they are going to develop complications and so we act early to stop the complications from happening. We will also look for other things that put people at risk such as disease of the veins and arteries. When patients wear the Vitaliti device, it will send constant readings of their vital signs and heartbeat to our hospital monitoring centre. We will use a type of artificial intelligence called machine learning to study these readings. We will look for slight changes in vital signs that may lead to heart muscle injury, bleeding and infection. Once we know what these signs are, we can then develop an alert system to warn us so we can stop the complications before they happen. At present, patients die from infection and other serious complications after surgery. This work is an opportunity to make a real difference in patient care after surgery.
