column36: MYTHO: An uncharacterized FoxO-dependent gene that controls autophagy and skeletal muscle mass
column37: Autophagy is a fundamental cellular process in which cytoplasmic proteins and damaged cellular organelles are recycled by forming double membrane vesicles that surround these organells and take them to the lysosome for degradation and recycling. Several reports indicate that autophagy under normal conditions is important for the maintenance of skeletal muscle size and that autophagy is enhanced and promotes muscle wasting under pathological conditions such as fasting, loss of innervation and sepsis sepsis. Despite major progress in our understanding of how autophagosomes (double membrane vesicles) are formed inside skeletal muscles, many of the proteins involved in autophagy remain unclear. We performed preliminary experiments in mouse skeletal muscles to identify novel genes that are involved in autophagy. These experiments revealed the presence of an uncharacterized gene that we named MYTHO (Macroautophagy and YouTH Optimizer). We named as such because our preliminary experiments revealed that this gene is critical for longevity in worms. These experiments also revealed that MYTHO protein is present in skeletal muscles of humans and mice and that deletion of this gene in cultured cells inhibits autophagy. In this proposal, we will conduct several experiments designed to identify the importance of MYTHO in the autophagy of intact skeletal muscles in humans and mice and to identify the mechanisms through which MYTHO regulates autophagosome formation in skeletal muscles. These objectives will be achieved by using molecular biology tools to visualize MYTHO protein inside skeletal muscle fibers and to either increase its expression or reduce it and measure its contribution to the formation of autophagosomes and recycling of proteins and organelles in normal skeletal muscles and in muscles of mice in which autophagy is induced and contributes to muscle wasting. These conditions include acute fasting, denervation and severe sepsis elicited by bacterial products.

column36: Investigating risk factors for cognitive impairment using precision neuropsychological and neuroimaging measures in a Canadian multi-ethnic cohort
column37: Cognitive impairment (problems with memory and thinking) is on the rise and so is the proportion of visible minority groups in Canada. Risk factors for cognitive impairment have mostly been studied in Caucasians, with much less research carried out in visible minority groups. This is a problem because some ethnic groups may be at higher risk for cognitive impairment. Furthermore risk factors may differ across ethnic groups. Because visible minorities represent 20% of Canada's population, there is an urgent need to study risk factors for cognitive impairment in these understudied groups. Cardiovascular risk factors, like high blood pressure and obesity, negatively affect the blood vessels of the brain. We call these harmful changes vascular brain injury (VBI). Both cardiovascular risk factors and VBI can lead to cognitive impairment. Interestingly, there are striking differences in the vascular health of Canada's two major visible minority groups: South Asian and Chinese individuals. That is, Canadian South Asians are more prone to cardiovascular risk factors, as reflected by earlier disease onset and more severe risk factors. By contrast, Chinese individuals have less severe cardiovascular risk factors, but are at greater risk for brain hemorrhage (bleeding). An important, but unanswered, question is whether Canadian South Asians and/or Chinese individuals are at heightened risk for cognitive impairment due to cardiovascular conditions and/or VBI. This is the first study to use sophisticated brain imaging and comprehensive cognitive testing to investigate risk factors for cognitive impairment among Canadian ethnic groups. Such knowledge is critical for developing and implementing appropriate prevention and intervention strategies for Canada's diverse communities. column36: Patterns of mortality and cancer incidence among adults who live near Canadian nuclear power plants: A population-based longitudinal study of CanCHEC participants between 1991 and 2016.
column37: Nuclear power is used in Canada to provide electricity, with its greatest use in Ontario where 61% of the province's electrical generation is from 18 CANDU reactors. Barriers to increased production of nuclear energy include public concern over the intractable nuclear waste disposal problem and about the possible health impacts of low levels of exposure to ionizing radiation. In Canada, 7% of the population lives within 25km from a nuclear power plant. Ionizing radiation is a carcinogen, and has been associated with other health conditions such as cardiovascular disease. There are uncertainties about the health risks at low levels of exposure. While previous reports support the conclusion there are no adverse health effects from living near nuclear power plants (NPPs), these studies have many weaknesses. These include: small study populations, lack of lengthy follow-up, the inability to account for residential mobility, and to control for other disease risk factors. Our study overcomes these limitations. We propose to examine patterns of cancer incidence and mortality among adults who live close the 5 NPPs in Canada. The study population is drawn from those who completed a mandatory long form Canadian Census between 1991 and 2011. The cohort contains data for 13.4 million adults whose place of residence is tracked annually. Cancer diagnoses and cause of death information for each of these individuals through 2015/16 has been determined by linkage to national registry data. We will investigate differences in mortality and cancer rates between those who live near NPPs to those who don't while accounting for other determinants of health. We will also create exposure surfaces that map differences in ionizing radiation around the NPPs, and we will estimate how health risks vary by these exposures. Our findings will provide important evidence about the population health impacts of exposure to ionizing radiation for both the public, and regulatory agencies.

column36: Structural characterization of lysosomal enzyme trafficking
column37: The lysosome is a compartment in the cell that acts as the waste disposal system. It degrades proteins, fats, carbohydrates and other molecules so that their components parts can be reused. This is accomplished by numerous enzymes in the lysosome that break up the unwanted molecules. The task of directing these enzymes into the lysosome is a critical step that is currently not well understood at the molecular level. It involves the recognition of numerous unrelated enzymes by a series of protein complexes in the endoplasmic reticulum that tags the enzymes with a marker called M6P. This marker guides the enzymes to the lysosome. This proposal is aimed at understand the molecular basis for the process of marking lysosomal enzymes using structure imaging techniques. Specifically, we are interested in how the protein complex called GNPT manages to mark lysosomal destined enzymes with M6P. Deficiency of GNPT prevents enzymes from reaching the lysosome in many cell types and organs, and mutations in the GNPT gene cause several severe lysosomal storage diseases, for which there are no cures. The results from this proposal will help understand how this process works in great detail, which will be important for designing strategies to help treat diseases.

This study will generate real-world evidence to help inform decisions made by government agencies, guideline writing committees, clinicians, and pregnant women. column36: Unravelling regulatory networks of stem cell states using single cell analysis
column37: Cells continuously sense their external and internal environments to both adapt and perform specific functions. They process such information through intracellular networks of proteins, which are often organized into specific structures or circuits, to induce specific responses. One such biological response involves conversion one cell fate (or type) to another. Conversion of cell fate is fundamental to development of an organism - progenitor cells such as pluripotent cells go through series of cell fate decisions to give rise to variety of adult cell types, and is often misrelated in disease. The differences among individual genetically identical cells response to a condition often also generates both molecular as well as cellular heterogeneity allowing them to exhibit diverse cell states. For instance, pluripotent stem cells exhibit such heterogeneous cell states: Totipotent, Pluripotent and differentiation-Primed, each with distinct differentiation capacity. Pluripotent stem cells are increasingly used for disease modelling and regenerative medicine. By introducing multiple sources of differentiation bias, such multiple cell states compromise the effective use of pluripotent cells. Thus, it is highly important to understand the molecular basis of pluripotent stem cell states. What are their potential cell states? What are the key regulatory mechanisms governing their transitions? Can we control and reverse-engineer such mechanisms to modulate the cell states? We propose to address these in the current grant. We will study the cell states of pluripotent stem cells at the single-cell level using our expertise in the interdisciplinary systems biology approach - combining quantitative single-cell experiments in proteomics and genomics with computational biology.

This proposal will examine how these immune cells communicate with pain-sensing neurons to mediate pain, and whether the neurons themselves can alter the dendritic cell response. This research proposal aims to finely study some of the brain circuits involved in regulating anxiety. The brain region called ventral hippocampus (vHP) plays a central role in anxiety; a second region, the raphe, is critical for many aspects of emotional responses. Neurons from the raphe using the neurotransmitter serotonin contact the vHP and can influence the activity of the vHP neuronal network. Therefore, serotonergic neurons are in an ideal position to relay emotion-related information to the vHP and influence anxious behavior. Our research project combines behavioral studies of anxiety in mice with recording of brain rhythms, recording of single cell activity and optogenetics, a technique allowing the control of neuronal activity using light. The goals of this project are to i) characterize the activity of serotonergic neurons that contact the vHP during anxious behavior, ii) control their activity in freely behaving mice to understand their role in anxiety and iii) understand how serotonin influences neuronal activity in the vHP. This research project will give insight into novel brain circuits of anxiety and help understand the neural mechanisms of anxiety disorders.

column36: The Concussion, Exercise, and Brain Networks (ConExNet) study
column37: Children who get a concussion from sports are usually told to rest and not go back to play too soon. But research is now telling us that some exercise even right after getting hurt might be okay. A kid's brain is still developing, so it is very important to figure out how exercise might help kids get better after a concussion. We want to know more about what happens to a child's brain if they exercise shortly after getting a concussion, because after all, a concussion is a brain injury. We will ask 40 kids between the ages of 12 and 17 years who just had a concussion to come to our hospital for 2 visits. The first visit is for us to figure out how fit they are. The second visit is to look at what happens in their brain after they exercise. We will also test 40 kids of the same age who have never had a concussion. Testing these kids will help us know that any differences we might see between the groups are because of the concussion in the other kids. Doctors are beginning to think that having kids who just had a concussion do some exercise right after they get hurt will help these kids. But we don't know what is happening in their brains when they exercise. Our study will be the first to look at this problem. Knowing how exercise affects the injured brain will really help doctors know what to tell kids who want to get back to playing their sport.

column36: Ubiquitin-Dependent Regulation of DNA Replication during Stress
column37: Our cells need to make perfect copies of their genetic material (DNA) in order to divide and proliferate thereby allowing our bodies to stay fit and healthy. Errors that occur during this copying process can lead to diseases such as cancer. To avoid this, our cells possess numerous systems to detect the occurrence problems during DNA duplication. Cancer cells often have defects in these protective systems and therefore accumulate genetic abnormalities more readily than healthy cells. This is leveraged by doctors to destroy tumors through the use of chemo- and radio-therapy which cause unsustainable levels of damage to the genetic material of cancer cells. To better understand the mechanisms that protect DNA replication in human cells, we have focused our attention on RFWD3, an important cellular factor that acts as a protector of our genetic material. We have evidence that RFWD3 enables many important pathways that allow accurate and complete genome duplication. Our work will help us understand how RFWD3 allows our cells to fully and accurately replicate their DNA thereby avoiding potential mutations that may lead to cancer. This new information will improve our understanding of the complex pathways that protect our DNA, and guide us in the elaboration of novel strategies that will improve the efficiency of current anti-cancer treatments.

column37: Little is known about the health perceptions and behaviours of Indigenous youth in Canada, less is known about young Indigenous men, and information specific to Indigenous fathers is virtually non-existent. Community members note the need to build skills that will help young men make positive changes to their own health and wellbeing, as well support changes within their families and communities. In order to develop a clearer understanding of the health and wellbeing of Indigenous young men, it is also essential that recruitment and participation does not hinge on perceived challenges (such as drug addictions, HIV status or criminal activity). Through a series of strengths-based, capacity building workshops on themes related to health and wellness such as hunting and wilderness survival, media and technology, and positive approaches to play and parenting, we will use participatory action and Indigenous methods to develop a baseline about health issues and wellbeing as identified by young Indigenous men (ages 18-34), with recruitment preference given to those who are caregivers/mentors in their families and communities. Data analysis will be conducted using an Indigenous group consensus process, as well as thematic analysis. Process evaluation methods will also be used to ensure that the study remains relevant for participants. Through this work, we will identify challenges related to current health and social supports. We will be able to begin to unpack some of the complexities that young Indigenous men are currently facing, and we will develop culturally grounded, tangible tools people can use to improve the health and wellbeing of Indigenous men.

column36: High-Throughput Analysis of Low Dose, Repetitive Alpha Particle Irradiation as a source of Radon-Induced Lung Cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the highest lethality Canadian cancer. It is overwhelmingly caused by tobacco smoke and/or inhalation of radioactive radon gas. Radon emits ionizing radiation that can cause serious health effects depending on dose and type. Relative to photon radiation (such as x-rays), the alpha particles emitted by radon produces much more disease-causing, complex DNA damage. Radon is very prevalent in our environment and is the main cause of lung cancer in the ~20% of patients who are never-smokers, encompassing >25,000 North Americans per year. Despite this, technological limitations to conveniently deliver alpha particles repetitively, in low doses and in an affordable, high throughput manner have constrained research on this topic. Consequently, our knowledge of why some people, tissues and cell types are susceptible to radiation is mainly derived from high dose, acute exposure photon research. This is problematic, as health protection risk models are being built on data derived from photon studies that have an ambiguous relevance to what we are most exposed to in life, which are alpha particles via radon inhalation. To resolve this, our lab has developed a next-generation, high throughput alpha particle irradiator able to deliver adjustable, low doses that reflects what is happening to Canadians in our environment. We will use this to define - in exquisite molecular detail - alpha particle effects on the stability of our DNA and changes that can lead to cancer. This project will be the first to employ a high-throughput approach to systematically solve key alpha particle biology questions. This is important as, while radon causes thousands of lung cancer diagnoses annually, knowledge to meaningfully intervene before clinical manifestation is unacceptably low. We will be impactful by building the essential knowledge to identify those at risk of radon-induced cancer based on novel, next-generation methods fuelled by expert knowledge of DNA damage repair biology.

column36: Axonal swellings in the cerebellum in health and disease
column37: In many diseases, post-mortem analysis of the brain reveals an abundance of swellings on axons - the wire-like structures that carry information across the brain - in the cerebellum, a brain region involved in motor coordination. This has led scientists to hypothesize that these axonal swellings contribute to the pathology that causes motor coordination deficits. Our results, however, suggest that this may not be true. The overall goal of this grant is to understand how these axonal swellings function in health and disease. We have surprising results from healthy brain tissue showing that axon swellings improve, not impair, the function of axons, and that this causes mice to learn better. Now we want to determine if axonal swellings do the same thing in disease. We hypothesize that axon swellings are something that the brain produces to repair axonal dysfunction. We will study the function of axonal swellings in two different diseases: one, a mouse model of ataxia, and the second a mouse model of Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Both display prominent axonal swellings, and in MS mice especially, axons eventually degenerate profoundly. We will test whether axonal swellings contribute to axonal dysfunction or work to counteract it. We will also unravel the mechanisms by which axonal swellings form, what role they serve in the developing brain, and where they are located and how long they persist in the intact brain. By studying the role of axonal swellings in health and disease, we hope to deeper our understanding of the brain's mechanisms of healing, which may lead to new understanding about disease mechanisms, and perhaps new treatment strategies.

column37: CONTEXT: GABAergic interneurons (INs) are critical regulators of brain networks. They inhibit principal cells and control the plasticity of neuronal circuits. Thus, alterations in the development or function of INs have been postulated to lead to various neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) including autism and epilepsy. We found mutations in multiple genes that encode regulators of Rho-GTPases, small protein that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics, cell shape and motility, in patients with NDD. In particular, we found variants in MYO9B, a RhoA inhibitor, and in TRIO, a RhoA and Rac1 activator. The mechanisms by which these mutations cause NDD are unknown. HYPOTHESIS: I postulate that the loss of MYO9B or TRIO impairs the migration of INs through deregulation of Rho-GTPases, resulting in disinhibition, seizures and autistic behaviours that can be rescued by re-establishing cortical inhibition. Investigate how the loss of Trio affects cortical network development Aim 4. Test the potential therapeutic benefit of GABAergic agonists or IN transplants METHODS: I will combine mouse genetics, INs explants, high-resolution cellular imaging, patch-clamp electrophysiology, EEG recordings and behavioural assays to assess the impact of targeted Myo9b or Trio deletions on the development and function of INs. EXPERTISE: I have strong expertise in modeling NDD in mice. My long-term collaborator, J.-C. Lacaille (UdeM), is a renowned IN physiologist. T. Kennedy (McGill) is an expert in neuronal migration and FRET/FLIM imaging. Together, we have the expertise, material and reagents required to achieve our goals efficiently. IMPACT: This project will clarify the mechanisms by which MYO9B and TRIO mutations lead to NDD, while generating new mouse models relevant to the human diseases to test novel therapies.

column36: In vivo CRISPR screen to identify clinically relevant therapeutic targets for lung cancer
column37: Finding the genes that are essential for a tumor cell to survive is one of the oldest goals of cancer research. Genes that are essential and fall into classes, which allow drug development to suppress their function, lie at the heart of finding novel therapies to combat cancer. Conventional experiments use cells grown in a plastic dish and switch off one gene at a time followed by analysis of a cell's ability to divide and grow. While we have learned a great deal from those studies, cells grown on a plastic dish do not mimic the situation of a tumor within a patient where dozens of cell types interact in a very intricate and sophisticated way. As such, the genes that might be necessary for a tumor cell to grow on plastic might be very different than the genes required for growth in an organ within a living organism. Our first proof-of-concept experiment shows that lung cancer cells grown on plastic behave very differently compared to the same cells grown in an organism such as an experimental mouse. This experiment has taught us that the mouse experiment indeed appears to be physiologically more relevant. As such, we are proposing to establish several physiologically-relevant models of lung cancer in mice and test every gene, for which drugs and therapeutic strategies can conceivably be generated with the goal of finding novel and more potent drug targets to combat lung cancer.

column36: Prevention of persistent pain with LidocAine iNfusions in breast cancer surgery (PLAN): a multicentre randomized controlled trial
column37: Advances in screening and management have improved the lifespan of those diagnosed with breast cancer. However, since patients are living longer, complications of breast cancer management have become increasingly apparent. Chronic pain is a devastating complication of breast cancer surgery and can affect up to half of patients undergoing surgical resection of their disease. It can last for years and is associated with decreased function and quality of life. To make matters worse, there are not many ways to treat this pain disorder and we are not sure how to prevent it. Fortunately, recent studies indicate that infusing a medication called lidocaine to patients while they undergo breast cancer surgery can prevent chronic pain from developing. Two small studies, including one by our own research team, have shown that administering lidocaine during the procedure can prevent chronic pain 3-months after surgery. Intravenous lidocaine is the most promising intervention to potentially prevent chronic pain in breast cancer patients. However, results from these studies are limited by their small sample sizes. We plan to conduct a large randomized controlled trial (highest quality study) of 1,144 patients to definitively identify whether lidocaine during breast cancer surgery can prevent the development of chronic pain. Each patient in the study will be randomly assigned to receive either intravenous lidocaine or a placebo (salt water) during surgery. Patients will be contacted in-hospital, for the first 3 days after surgery, and at 3 and 12 months after surgery. We expect that patients who received lidocaine will experience less pain, improved function, less opioid use, and improved quality of life. This study could reduce long-term pain and suffering in patients with breast cancer. Since intravenous lidocaine is low-cost and easy to deliver, results of this study have the potential to impact breast cancer treatment around the globe.

column36: Psychological and neurobiological determinants of opioid-related problems and opioid tapering outcomes among patients with chronic pain prescribed long-term opioid therapy
column37: Chronic pain is a major health problem that affects approximately 20 % of the Canadian population. There has been an increase in the use of opioid medications for the management of chronic pain over the past decade in Canada, but this has been paralleled by escalating rates of opioid addiction and overdose deaths in these patients. Experts recommend tapering (i.e., lowering) opioid doses among high-dose opioid users to minimize risks of major health problems. Evidence, however, indicates that roughly 25-35 % of patients who are willing to taper opioids are unable to do so. To date, the factors that may influence opioid tapering outcomes have remained largely unexplored. The factors contributing to pain flares, opioid withdrawal symptoms, and opioid craving in patients with chronic pain who are undergoing opioid tapering have also yet to be explored. Aims: The main goal of the proposed research is to examine the psychological and neurobiological factors associated with opioid problems and tapering outcomes in patients with chronic pain on long-term opioid therapy who are undergoing gradual opioid dose reduction. Aim 1 will examine the contribution of psychological factors (i.e., negative affect, catastrophizing) and potential alterations in the brain to the experience of pain flares, opioid withdrawal symptoms, and opioid craving within the first 3 months of opioid tapering. Aim 2 will examine the degree to which these variables contribute to opioid tapering outcomes 3 months after initiation of opioid dose reduction. The proposed research will help better understand the psychological and neurobiological factors that may influence opioid tapering. Our findings might ultimately contribute to improving opioid tapering outcomes and minimizing opioid-related harms in patients with chronic pain.

column36: Unsupervised Learning Methods to Improve Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
column37: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are designed to be used by patients to describe their health, including their quality of life, pain, fatigue, and functional abilities. PROMs can also be used by clinicians, health professionals, and healthcare decision makers to describe the outcomes of care from the patient's point of view. In order to contribute to improving patient care, PROMs must be valid (i.e., measure what they are supposed to measure) and reliable (i.e., measure the same thing over time and for patients with different characteristics). Sometimes, patient responses on PROMs are not consistent with what was expected. These inconsistencies may occur because patients with different characteristics may not understand or interpret questions about their health in the same way (differential item functioning), or their interpretations may change over time (response shift). While these differential interpretations and response shifts in PROMs data could be a result of positive adaptations to health challenges, such as a chronic illness or a healthcare treatment, they are often difficult to detect and, if ignored, could lead to incorrect conclusions about the outcomes of care. Our research focuses on data-driven machine-learning methods to efficiently cluster (i.e., group) patients with similar patterns of differential item functioning or response shifts. We will develop and apply machine-learning item response methods and compare them to model-based item response methods using computer simulation. We will apply the proposed machine-based methods to existing data for patients with specific health conditions to predict healthcare use. The research will be shared with healthcare providers, PROMs developers, and researchers. The overall goal of our study is to improve the ability to accurately interpret patient-reported information when measuring the effectiveness and responsiveness of the healthcare system.

column36: Characterization of typical and atypical brain development
column37: Neuroimaging-based characterization of typical brain development is of utmost importance to form a baseline for understanding cognitive development and its deviations in neurodevelopmental disorders. Many groups including ours have addressed this question by building prediction models of brain development. However, previous studies focused on 'static' brain measures although there is a need for considering trajectories as opposed to static 'final' brain measures. We need to leverage the availability of large-scale open longitudinal datasets to build prediction models of individual variations in brain and cognitive development. Our first aim is to explore whether developmental changes in individual brains can be used to predict future cognition. Using longitudinal data, we will use within-subject developmental changes in brain in prediction models of cognitive outcomes. Although generative models have been proposed for developmental changes in the brain. However, previous studies lack one important component: they have modeled developmental changes in brain connections, but not brain structure. Brain structure also changes during development; as such generative models need to take into account both brain structure as well as connections. Our second aim is to explore models used in complex systems, particularly co-evolving network models that consider changes in both nodes and edges with time. Furthermore, although previous studies indicate the utility of studying brain trajectories, little is known whether social factors such as the socioeconomic conditions influence these brain trajectories. By studying the epigenetic mechanisms behind the influence of children's environment on their neurodevelopmental trajectories, we can gain insights into the biological processes. In collaboration with Dr. Linda Booij, our third aim is to investigate epigenetic mechanisms underlying socioeconomic conditions and deviant neurodevelopmental trajectories in children.

column36: HPV vaccination effectiveness in a Canadian setting, 12 years after implementation: are we on the road to eliminate cervical cancer?
column37: In Canada, screening has helped to reduce the number of cervical cancer cases. However, there were still 1350 women diagnosed with cancer and 410 deaths in 2019. Persistent infections of high-risk HPV types can lead to the development of precancerous lesions that may slowly transform into cervical cancer. Because cervical cancer usually takes several decades to develop, there is time to identify precancers by screening and thus prevent cancer. Vaccination against high-risk HPVs, especially if done through school programs, can lead to more effective and equitable prevention, with less adverse effects. Our research team will evaluate the effectiveness of HPV vaccination against cervical pre-cancers and cancers, to determine if vaccine effectiveness is as good "in real life" as what was found in initial studies. Some studies have attempted to answer this question, with very mixed results, partly because the methods used led to some errors in the estimation of effectiveness in "real life". Between 2020 and 2023 we will contact women aged between 21 and 32 who will receive a diagnosis of cervical precancer or cancer. With their agreement, we will determine which HPV types are present in the lesions. This information will enable us to calculate the effectiveness of HPV vaccination. We will also check whether the effectiveness varies according to the age at vaccination, the number of doses of vaccine received, whether vaccination was started before or after the beginning of sexual activity and by the severity of the lesions. Vaccination against HPV offers the possibility to improve the prevention of cervical precancers and cancers, while using resources efficiently and few adverse effects. The demonstration, in Canada, of a high effectiveness of vaccination "in real life" could foster greater acceptance of vaccination and help plan future screening activities.

column36: Improved Assessment of Disease in Lymphoma Patients using Quantitative PET Imaging
column37: In this work, we aim to improve quantitative accuracy of PET scans used for imaging of patients with lymphoma, a cancer that begins in cells of the lymph system. We aim to measure the volume of tumors in the patients, which is a measure that has potential for much improved assessment of disease, and we aim to achieve this in a fully automated way using artificial intelligence (AI) based methods, and to routinely report this measure to our clinicians in our systems in the clinic. In addition, we aim to extract and study different features from the images in order to demonstrate which features, or their combinations as obtained using AI-based methods, can better predict patient outcomes and enable potentially improved personalization of therapy for lymphoma patients. Our proposed study includes participation of multiple international collaborators with extensive data from lymphoma cancer patients for improved assessment of our developed techniques.

column36: Mitochondrial dynamics and metabolism in muscle stem cell maintenance and muscle regeneration
column37: An estimated 4 million Canadians currently suffer from muscle wasting conditions, manifesting as loss of muscle mass and function. Muscle wasting is the most significant cause of disability in the aging population and individuals with muscle degenerative diseases, including muscular dystrophies, myopathies and cancer cachexia. The decline in muscle function affects mobility, voluntary function and quality of life, often leading to institutionalization and mortality4. This imposes a dramatic burden on individuals and society, costing Canadians several billions of dollars per year. Thus, there is a pressing need for the development of preventative and therapeutic strategies targeting muscle wasting. For many years, muscle wasting was thought to be only a problem of the myofibers, yet recent evidence shows that muscle stem cell (MuSC) dysfunction plays a significant role. Adult skeletal muscle normally has a high regenerative capacity, however, within the context of muscle wasting MuSCs are depleted and muscle regeneration is impaired. Currently, the reason for MuSC depletion is unclear and thus there are no therapies targeting their restoration. Understanding the underlying etiological factors leading to MuSC depletion is instrumental in identifying novel approaches to restore muscle repair and function. The overarching goal of this proposal is to restore MuSC number and function and promote muscle repair in aging and muscle wasting diseases.

column36: vCHAT-HF: a Virtual Community promoting Health literacy, self-cAre, and peer supporT for Heart Failure
column37: International heart health societies advocate lifestyle counseling for chronic heart failure (CHF) to improve quality of life and self-care behavior (exercise, diet, medications, smoke-free living), and to decrease medical events such as hospitalization, emergency department (ED) visits, and death. Current counseling programs require moderate-to-high contact between the health care team and patients, which is a barrier to delivering self-care counseling to the wider population of persons with CHF. This 2-year pilot trial will evaluate the clinical benefit and usability of a new program of digital counseling + social network support (vCHAT-HF). We will randomly assign 162 CHF patients to vCHAT-HF or to a Control group that receives conventional CHF self-care education through our website. All patients will be contacted bi-weekly by email over 12 months. The vCHAT-HF group will have unlimited home access to CHF self-care chat rooms, and they will be invited to join bi-weekly internet presentations by health professionals and patient representatives. Each presentation will have a 30-minute talk, 30-minute question-answer period, and 30 minutes for free discussion. We hypothesize that over 2 years vCHAT will reduce the combined risk of death, an ED visit, or hospitalization due to HF. We also hypothesize that the vCHAT group (vs. Control) will spend more time engaged with online self-care resources and that they'll have improved quality of life. This trial builds on our previous clinical trials for telehealth and digital counseling. It provides a novel program that promotes CHF self-care, quality of life, and heart health through the synergy of natural peer support that is informed by best evidence information. We will present our findings to key stakeholders (patients, researchers, health care professionals). These findings will be applied to support a Canada-wide trial to promote CHF self-care and quality of life, using this patient-centered approach.

column36: The Montfort Postnatal Care at Home Program: How do health outcomes, costs, patient and provider experiences compare with usual hospital-based postnatal care?
column37: Childbirth is the most common reason for hospitalization in Canada. Although most mothers and newborns are healthy, they stay in hospital for an average of two days after birth. A main purpose of the hospital stay is to assist mothers with breastfeeding and newborn care. However, exclusive breastfeeding rates remain very low and many mothers report not feeling adequately prepared to care for their newborns. Therefore, there is a need to improve postnatal care. Our team designed the Montfort Postnatal Care at Home Program (MPCHP) that aims to be more effective in supporting mothers, and at less cost than the usual care. The MPCHP gives low-risk mother-baby pairs the option of early hospital discharge (at 6-24 hours after childbirth) and midwifery care at home during the first postnatal week. In April 2018 we received funding from Ontario's Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to offer the MPCHP at Hopital Montfort in Ottawa, Ontario. Therefore, we have an important opportunity to study whether the MPCHP increases the quality of postnatal care, including improving health outcomes (e.g. exclusive breastfeeding, parental readiness to care for newborn) and reducing the health care system costs. We will collect and compare data between mothers in the MPCHP and those who receive the usual care. We will also conduct interviews with parents and health care providers to learn from their experiences with the MPCHP. This research will provide evidence regarding the quality of an innovative program that moves postnatal care for healthy mother-baby pairs from hospital to home and extends it over seven days after childbirth. Findings will be highly relevant to Ontario's Ministry of Health and Long- Term Care and other policy makers, administrators and clinicians across Canada who endeavor to provide the right care, in the right place at the right time.

column36: Kaiso, Triple Negative Breast Cancer and Women of African Ancestry.
column37: Despite increased awareness, early detection and novel therapies in the past 20 years, breast cancer (BCa) remains the most common cause of female cancer deaths worldwide. Triple negative BCa (TNBC) is a very aggressive type of BCa that spreads rapidly to vital body organs and for which there are no specific treatments. Thus women diagnosed with TNBC are more likely to die than those diagnosed with other types of BCa. Notably, TNBC is most common in young Black women who although less likely to develop BCa, are more likely to die from BCa than Caucasian women. This difference in TNBC prevalence and mortality seems unrelated to socio-economic status and hints at unknown genetic factors or an ancestral genetic predisposition as the cause. Recently our lab found that a protein named Kaiso was highly expressed in TNBC tissues from Black women compared to Caucasian women, and these Black women with high Kaiso expression were less likely to survive. In mouse models of BCa, low Kaiso expression prevented the spread of TNBC cells to the lungs and liver, suggesting that Kaiso plays a role in the spread of BCa. To learn more about Kaiso's role in TNBC, we seek to determine how Kaiso promotes BCa spread and how Kaiso contributes to the racial difference in BCa outcomes. By clarifying Kaiso's role in TNBC features and outcomes, and identifying genetic differences in Black women, we will better understand TNBC and contribute to the development of better tests and therapies for TNBC. Our findings will help decrease the racial differences in BCa outcomes, and help millions of women diagnosed with TNBC worldwide regardless of ethnicity.

column36: Single turnover covalent chaperones for disease related lysosomal enzymes
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a worldwide health problem that has been linked to deficiencies in an enzyme called glucocerebrosidase (GCase). This enzyme plays a critical role in the body by breaking down a particular large molecule into two smaller, more easily metabolized components, a sugar (glucose) and a fat (ceramide). Without a properly functioning GCase, these large molecules are not recycled normally. Genetic mutations associated with GCase often result in an unstable enzyme structure that is easily damaged within the cell. In the case of PD, loss of function of this enzyme may contribute to disease progression. We plan to stabilize various enzyme's structure by using small molecular mimics of the sugar that form a bond to the enzyme. This event allows the enzyme to fold around our molecule. This can be thought of as using a mannequin to make a suit, once made the suit has a function that the cloth did not. However, one must be able to remove the mannequin for normal use of the suit. Our molecules were designed so that the bond to the enzyme breaks the resulting molecule doesn't properly fit the enzyme and so it departs. The analogy would be an inflatable mannequin that can be deflated to allow the suit to be used normally. This type of strategy has been tried before but with a major difference, the chemical mannequin does not change any of its interactions with the enzyme over time. Thus, it is often difficult for it to be removed (mannequin) efficiently from the enzyme (suit) to liberate free enzyme.

column36: Improving epilepsy surgery outcome by mapping high frequency oscillations.
column37: More than 54,000 Canadians have epilepsy with seizures that often occur daily and are poorly controlled by medication. In these cases, surgical removal of seizure generating tissue (which contains the critical seizure onset zone) is their best chance of seizure freedom and relief from psychiatric and cognitive problems associated with epilepsy. Currently, the clinical gold standard for identifying the seizure onset zone is EEG recordings during seizures. Unfortunately, the surgical success rate is <50%, mostly due to imprecise identification and removal of the seizure onset zone. We propose here a strategy to correct this. Mounting evidence indicates that high frequency oscillations (HFOs), detected between seizures using electrodes implanted into the brain (intracranial electrodes), better localizes the seizure onset zone than seizure recordings. However, intracranial EEG only samples a few brain areas. By combining intracranial EEG with functional MRI, which can measure responses across the entire brain, we have observed HFO-associated brain activity both at the conventionally measured seizure onset zone and in nearby regions. We propose that these additional regions are critical parts of the full seizure onset zone. As a result, we predict better surgical outcomes when they are also resected. We also postulate that the degree to which the seizure onset zone is connected to the rest of the brain (measured by functional MRI) predicts clinical outcome: fewer connections, better outcome. We will study 120 patients with uncontrolled epilepsy. We will determine if a better surgical cure rate is associated with i) the extent of surgical removal of the seizure onset zone as defined by intracranial EEG-functional MRI, and ii) fewer pre-operative functional connections of the seizure onset zone. Our study will offer an unprecedented ability to accurately identify the seizure onset zone and improve surgical and neurocognitive outcomes in persons with epilepsy.

column36: Life beyond vulnerability: Using developmental neuroscience to inform child health, life-course well-being and resilience to chronic disease
column37: Early life adversity, such as stress or malnutrition, exerts a sustained influence on health, increasing the risk for common diseases (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression). However, there is remarkable inter-individual variation among children in the response to adversity, some being more susceptible than others. For this reason, we are unable to effectively identify high-risk children solely on the basis of environmental conditions. We aim to characterize children using several biological markers (genetics, salivary cytokine measures, brain function) that in concert with environmental exposures will define vulnerability in early life, when interventions are most effective. This integrative approach to the study of the developmental origins of common disorders will serve to more effectively identify high-risk children and thus contribute to improved intervention/prevention research designs. Such advances in 'Precision Pediatrics' would also enhance our ability to evaluate the efficacy of intervention programs by focusing exclusively on high-risk individuals. These same analyses will inform on the basis of resilience to early life adversity. This research has the objective of informing the best Canadian scenario for healthy growth and development, long-term well-being, and improved human capital.

column36: A behavioural and neural analysis of secondary fear triggers
column37: Tackling fear behaviourally and in the brain holds the key to developing successful clinical interventions for fear and anxiety-related disorders. One way to do this is through exposure therapy, that is, exposure to fear-eliciting cues or triggers with the aim of decoupling them from fear. This approach has been successful for some but many relapse or fail to respond at all. The key to providing a better treatment to sufferers from anxiety is to look beyond the standard approach of targeting primary triggers for fear, that is, triggers have a direct association with a traumatic or aversive event. Our proposal does this. We will understand how fear spreads across a memory network, how it links with cues were never part of the original traumatic memory, thereby proliferating secondary triggers with fear. The present proposal will utilize a multifaceted approach to examine the behavioural and neural profile of secondary fear. Specifically, we will establish how secondary triggers lose their fear eliciting properties, and whether these properties can be restored under specific conditions. We will also examine whether secondary triggers depend on the original fear memory for retrieval by tackling the integrity of the original fear memory behaviourally (through extinction) and neutrally (through deletion of function-specific cells). Finally, we will uncover the neural circuits that support fear triggered by secondary cues. Our ultimate goal is to provide the basic science platform of fear triggered by secondary cues which will serve as a springboard for the development novel behavioural and pharmacological routes for the treatment of fear- and anxiety-related disorders.

column36: Childhood Epigenetic Age Deviations and Developmental Differences (CEAD3)
column37: All humans have two types of age: chronological, or age in years, and biological, or age according to your body that we can measure by looking at marks on DNA. Sometimes in people these two types of ages are the same, but sometimes they are different. Until recently, we couldn't measure the difference between chronological and biological age in children accurately enough, but thanks to a new tool, called the PedBE clock, we can. Therefore, because these two types of age exist, we will look at potential differences between chronological and biological age in children. We want to know which direction this difference is in, and how big the difference is, depending on if and when children are hitting their milestones throughout early life. This might also be affected by the sex or ethnicity of a child or if they have developmental differences like Autism Spectrum Disorder. We also want to know if there is any change in this age difference if we give children different things to eat or have people come in to help parents. We will explore these differences and when they happen in order to help children and families in the future by testing biological ages.

column36: Assessing the Economic Costs of Obstetric Evacuation and Outcomes/Experiences of Indigenous Midwifery in Urban, Rural and Remote Indigenous Communities.
column37: Indigenous women in Canada are at higher risk for adverse pregnancy and infant health outcomes and health disparities are largely attributed to inadequate access to perinatal healthcare. Community-based, Indigenous midwives who provide essential, clinically and culturally supportive healthcare is a sustainable solution. Unlike federal evacuation policies that continue to transfer First Nation and Inuit women to urban hospitals for delivery at 36-38 weeks' gestational age, the goal of Indigenous midwifery is to return birth closer to home. This research aims to examine the costs and benefits of obstetric evacuation and Indigenous midwifery. Through interdisciplinary, Indigenous and mixed methods research, this research will examine the costs of obstetric evacuation and Indigenous midwifery delivered in rural, urban and remote communities. A health outcomes analysis and Indigenous community engagement will provide additional information on best practices on how to support First Nation, Metis and Inuit mothers, infants and communities throughout their pregnancy, birth, postpartum and early months of parenthood.

column36: III Bhagirath Singh Prize: Pseudomonas aeruginosa protease promotes chronic inflammation and immune evasion
column37: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterial pathogen that inhabits soil and water as well as plant and animal tissues. It is an opportunistic human pathogen, causing infections when normal immune defenses are disrupted. Respiratory P. aeruginosa infection is the leading reason for morbidity and mortality in cystic fibrosis patients. Remarkably, P. aeruginosa causes disease in a variety of hosts, including plants, insects, fish, mice and humans. P. aeruginosa infections normally persist in the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients because of the formations of bacterial biofilms. One of the main problems faced by CF patients is inflammation in the lung caused by persistent P. aeruginosa infections. The objective of the proposed research is to characterize how a P. aeruginosa-secreted protease modulates inflammation in the context of chronic infection in CF lungs. The findings of this project may lead to the development of new strategies for alleviating the terrible inflammation in the lungs of these patients that eventually leads many of them to receive lung transplants.

column36: Characterizing mortality rates and associated modifiable determinants among people who inject drugs in a large, urban Canadian city: Implications for future population health interventions
column37: People who inject drugs (PWID) often face profound socio-economic disadvantage and are one of the most vulnerable groups in society, with a global mortality rate nearly 15 times that of the general population. Largely concentrated in cities, PWID are disproportionately exposed to housing vulnerability, with up to 60% of those living in large North American cities reporting recent unstable housing. Access to safe and stable housing is a well-established determinant of health and has gained renewed focus as a structural target for intervention following the limited success of conventional public health approaches to reducing morbidity and mortality in PWID. Data on mortality rates and trends among PWID are particularly scarce in Canada. Further, despite evidence for a broadly deleterious impact on PWID health, relationships between unstable housing and mortality are not well understood. This study seeks to examine mortality rates and refine our understanding of the relationship between these aspects living context and mortality, and ultimately guide policies and interventions that address inequalities related to housing stability and service distribution within our cities. This study will capitalize on data collected as part of St. Luc/HEPCO, one of the largest prospective cohort studies of PWID, having recruited more than 4000 participants since 1992, with detailed assessment of behavioral and service use data, as well as geospatial and laboratory data. Mortality and causes of death among cohort participants will be obtained via record linkage with the Institut de la Statistique du Quebec. This project will improve our understanding of how housing contexts influence this ultimate health outcome. Findings will be relevant to city planners and community organisations seeking to allocate housing solutions and services in a manner that supports our most vulnerable citizens.

column36: Disparities in the management and outcomes in patients with rectal cancer: A Population Based Study
column37: Rectal cancer is common in Canada. Individuals who are diagnosed with rectal cancer require a number of investigations, multiple types of treatments and require long term follow up. Despite being a treatable cancer, only 65% of rectal cancer patients survive 5 years or longer after diagnosis. Due to the complexity in management, clinical practice guidelines have been created to help ensure receipt of recommended e care. Unfortunately, we do not know how many rectal cancer patients in Ontario are receiving appropriate care and how this affects their survival. Thus, the purpose of this study is to identify how many patients are not receiving recommended care in Ontario. We will examine which factors may contribute to not receiving recommended care, and we will examine whether receiving recommended care improves survival. To complete this study, we will use existing data available at Cancer Care and Epidemiology at Queen's University. We have a database of 5000 individuals with rectal cancer treated from 2010 - 2015. This data will be combined (linked) with other databases, which capture all aspects of care along their continuum from diagnosis to follow up. We will report the proportions of patients adhering to recommended care. We will also assess which factors are contributing to not receiving recommended care, including patient factors (age, sex, geographic location, income level) and provider factors (hospital and treating physician). Finally, we will assess whether receipt of guideline adherent care improves long term survival. This study will provide "real world" results on whether patients are receiving recommended care, what is prevented receipt of this care, and whether adherence to recommendations improves survival. This information will allow those in health advocacy and policy to establish targeted intervention to increase adherence and ultimately improve survival for individuals with rectal cancer in Ontario.

column36: Housing needs, neighborhood quality and mental health
column37: In 2016, 1.7M Canadian households were in core housing needs, meaning that their dwelling required major repairs, was overcrowded, and/or unaffordable. While there is geographic variation between cities, the largest variation in housing needs is within cities. International studies suggest that poor housing conditions in neighborhoods can have an impact on population health. Studies also demonstrate the spatial correlation of housing conditions with other neighborhood features associated with health. Quantifying this correlation is needed since interventions designed to build healthy cities may unintentionally widen social and health inequities by increasing housing prices and displacing people. The aim of this project is to understand the spatial distribution of housing needs and its association with population mental health outcomes, and the potential frictions between building healthy and sustainable neighborhood and housing affordability. To meet these objectives, various sources of administrative, environmental, and population data will be merged. We will focus the analyses on Montreal, given the unparalleled breadth of housing data available for this city, both at the neighborhood and individual levels. Specifically, the project will assess the spatial distribution of housing needs, and test association with mental health outcomes for 5000 tenants and with other features of healthy neighborhood environments, such as access to greenness, active living environments, and access to public transit. The type of evidence generated by the project is paramount to inform public health authorities on where, when, and how to intervene. More broadly, the project will provide critical information for laying the foundation for future research assessing housing interventions for their impacts on population health, and for anticipating the potential for healthy city interventions to increase social and health inequities by increasing housing unaffordability.

column36: Childhood cancer and immune dysregulation in siblings
column37: Cancer, autoimmune disease, and allergies all involve problems with a person's immune system. Researchers have long noted that allergies, asthma, and certain autoimmune diseases frequently appear together in the same person or among family members. Yet it is unclear if childhood cancer also appears more or less frequently in families where children have problems with their immune system, such as autoimmune disease or severe allergies. Very little is known about what causes cancer in children and a better understanding how these diseases cluster together in siblings will be helpful in understanding how the immune system is involved in childhood cancer. In this study, we will examine if siblings of children with immune-related diseases, such as celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, severe allergies and asthma, have a higher or lower risk of cancer. We will use a large dataset containing all children born in hospitals in Quebec, Canada. We will identify brothers and sisters, and will see which children were diagnosed with an autoimmune disease or severe allergy. We will compare these children with those whose siblings did not have an autoimmune disease or severe allergy. We will determine if children from families with autoimmune disease or severe allergy have a higher or lower chance of having a sibling with cancer. As this project will help understand how cancer, autoimmune disease and allergies are inter-linked in families, our results will bring us one step closer to understanding the potential genetic and environmental risk factors for these diseases, particularly why some children get cancer and what can be done to prevent it.

column36: Trajectories of physical activity and its impact on health among Canadians
column37: Physical inactivity is becoming one of the most critical public health issues. Accumulating evidence indicates that physical activity (PA) is critical in the prevention of many chronic health diseases, including some forms of cancer. Despite the benefits, statistics show that the majority of the developed world is insufficiently active. In Canada, self-reported data finds that half the population fails to meet recommended levels of PA. One problem is that our knowledge of PA as it relates to health outcomes (including cancer) is largely based on PA assessed at one point only. This is limiting as we know PA measured at one time point is not entirely indicative of future behaviours. Importantly, we have little knowledge of how sustained levels of PA or inactivity relates to health outcomes. Therefore, we are proposing to use a national health dataset to examine how PA patterns over a 20-year period are associated with the health of Canadians. We will use data from the National Population Health Survey that began in 1994/1995 and re-assesses the same person every other year. This study will enable us to discern the different long-term patterns of PA behaviours among different segments of the Canadian population (e.g., there may be some who are active throughout this period, while there may be some that began active but decline in their PA participation over time). Once the patterns of behaviours are established, we will determine (a) what demographic factors are related to these patterns and (b) how these behavioural patterns predict health outcomes of diagnoses of cancers, self-reported health, and mortality. Identifying the different patterns of behaviours among Canadians will make it possible to uncover groups who are most susceptible to physical inactivity, and to gain a better understanding of how PA over time influences the health of Canadians, including the significance of PA health behaviour that can be modified for cancer diagnoses.

column36: Advancing healthy cities intervention research: developing measures for the bicycling environment
column37: The Canadian Public Health Officer's 2017 Report called for greater attention to the built environment to understand how community design can support healthy living. However, research and surveillance on the impacts of built environment changes remains challenging due to huge data gaps in measuring "healthy" environments. In the realm of active transportation, the new Canadian Active Living Environment (Can-ALE) is a national dataset with measures on how supportive communities are for walking and public transit. But there is no analogous data on bicycling environments, despite the fact that bicycling is the primary travel mode for nearly 12% of commuters in some cities (e.g., Victoria, Census 2016) and the fastest growing travel mode nationally. Further, cities from coast to coast are announcing multi-million dollar investments in bicycling infrastructure networks (Victoria in 2016, Halifax in 2019). In this project, we aim to develop measures for bicycling infrastructure for all communities in Canada, at the neighbourhood level. Specifically, we will: develop a dataset with measures of the bicycling environment; validate the measures using existing national administrative datasets, including Can-ALE and Census bicycle journey-to-work data. Our work will directly advance healthy cities intervention research in Canada by providing standardized metrics that can facilitate multi-city studies, as well as those that track change over time. These new measures will be fundamental for evaluating the impacts of future bicycling-related policy and built environment interventions on population health and healthy equity. As a team of health and geography researchers leading applied bicycle research in partnership with cities across the country, we are uniquely positioned to conduct this work. Our project priorities include accessible data that everyone is able to use.

column36: Prenatal maternal physical activity and brain structure and function in young children
column37: Physical activity during pregnancy can be good for both the mother and the baby. Yet fewer than 2 in 10 pregnant women meet the Canadian guidelines of at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week. Children of mothers who were more active during pregnancy appear to have better learning and cognition, but we do not know why. Studies in mice show that prenatal maternal exercise changes the brain, particularly in the hippocampus, an area that is involved in memory and cognitive processing. This goal of this study is to determine how prenatal physical activity is related to the structure and function of young children's brains. We will use data from an existing study that enrolled women during pregnancy and has followed their children since. Women reported physical activity at work and during their free time in each trimester of pregnancy. Children received a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan between the ages of 2-8 years, and their language skills and memory were also tested. We will measure the structure and function of the hippocampus from the MRI scans and compare to the activity levels of mothers during pregnancy. Finally, we will look at whether our findings help explain language and memory function in the children. Evidence showing the impact of prenatal exercise on children's brains is necessary for developing appropriate guidelines that will ultimately improve child health.

column36: FActors of Mothers and Infants in Longitudinal Years (FAMILY) - A maternal and child birth cohort with babies identified from three Ontario existing pediatric cohorts and linked with health administrative data to create a birth cohort of infants and their siblings and mothers to study prenatal, postnatal and early childhood factors associated with maternal and child health and developmental outcomes
column37: Considering the high health burden of asthma in children, the high incidence of asthma exacerbation during pregnancy, and the significant economic burden of poorly controlled asthma, it is crucial to characterise asthma phenotypes and to examine the impacts of this condition on children and mothers. Our team will combine 3 Ontario pediatric cohorts to create a large longitudinal birth cohort, and will use linked population databases to efficiently identify children, their siblings, and mothers. The birth cohort data will come from three existing studies: the Canadian Healthy Infant Longitudinal Development (CHILD) Study, the Toronto Child Health Evaluation Questionnaire (T-CHEQ) Study, and the Applied Research Group for Kids (TARGet Kids!) Study. The children who participated in these studies, their siblings and their mothers will be identified in administrative data housed at ICES. The resulting FAMILY cohort will consist of a birth cohort of 28,000 children (cohort study participants and siblings) and a maternal cohort of the 12,000 mothers of these children. The FAMILY birth cohort will have demographic, clinical, biomarker and health services utilization data, as well as social and environmental data from the Canadian Urban Environmental Health Research Consortium (CANUE) and the Early Development Instrument (EDI). Using the longitudinal cohort, we will conduct 2 studies to: 1) use early life exposures from birth to 3 years (e.g. air pollution) to predict later childhood health and developmental outcomes (e.g. asthma incidence); and 2) determine whether maternal medical history (e.g. asthma attack during pregnancy) is associated with maternal delivery and infant birth outcomes (e.g. low birth weight). Our proposed study will build a large cohort of children and mothers and use big (administrative) and deep (survey and clinical) data to evaluate longitudinal health and developmental outcomes and investigate questions that were not possible to address before.

This study will use existing data sources to understand the how care is delivered, variations in care and outcome for Head & Neck Cancer surgery patients in Alberta. We will link many data sources to generate knowledge on existing healthcare delivery and its impact on patient outcomes. This knowledge will inform decisions about appropriately allocating healthcare resources that best meet the needs of this population in the future.

column36: Injury Risks among Canadian Bicycling and Walking Commuters: A new application of the Canadian Census Health and Environment Cohort (CanCHEC)
column37: Walking and bicycling are healthy and environmentally friendly forms of transportation. Healthy cities encourage active transportation because it has many benefits to cities and their residents. But people walking and bicycling are more vulnerable to road injury and safety concerns may affect the choice to use active transportation. While Canada has good information on the number of injuries and fatalities among pedestrians and bicyclists, this is not enough to tell us about the rates and risks of injury among users of active transportation. For risk and rate calculations, we need to know how many people use each form and how much they use it (how far and how long they travel). This will then allow "apples to apples" comparisons between groups such as men and women, or between provinces and cities, or within cities before and after changes are made to try to improve safety. Our project will help fill this gap in our knowledge. We will use data created by Statistics Canada and Health Canada: the Canadian Census Health and Environment Cohort (CanCHEC). This is a cohort that follows participants in the long form Canadian census and determines health outcomes they experience over follow-up. The long form census collects information on how people get to and from work, which will allow us to isolate bicycling and walking commuters to determine their risk of injury. We will use records of hospital treatment (including cause of injury) to determine who has been injured and death records (including cause) to determine fatalities. We will examine how risk of injury differs between men and women, by age, by measures of wealth, and by scores that measure whether their neighbourhood design encourages active transportation. This project will build new ways to evaluate, compare and monitor risk among active transportation users for cities, city planners, health care providers, injury researchers and road safety advocates.

column36: Development, evaluation, and implementation of a pediatric shared decision making program: a knowledge translation initiative guided by the Knowledge to Action Framework
column37: Shared decision making (SDM) is considered the best approach for making health decisions. In pediatrics, SDM helps parents and children to participate in decision making and can improve the child's health. Unfortunately, SDM is rarely used in pediatrics. The goal of my research is to improve health decision making for children and parents by using proven strategies to move SDM research into practice and policy. This knowledge translation initiative focuses on a SDM program that helps children and parents making difficult decisions within a large children's hospital. The SDM program involves education and training for healthcare providers, patient decision aids (i.e., tools that provide families with medical information and help guide them through the SDM process), and decision coaching (i.e., a trained healthcare provider that coaches families through the SDM process). Before creating the SDM program, we summarized the research evidence, conducted studies to find out what made it easy and hard to use SDM, adapted proven SDM tools for children and families making health decisions, and provided SDM training and education to 186 healthcare providers. Then, we evaluated the impact of the program with children and parents making health decisions. Findings showed that youth and parents were satisfied with SDM and that it improved their decision making outcomes. For the next steps, we will improve our SDM program based on healthcare provider, parent, and child feedback and test it in a larger study.

column36: Use of glycogen synthase kinase-3B inhibitors (GSK3Is) and prostate cancer risk and prognosis
column37: Approximately 4,000 Canadian men die each year from prostate cancer. There is no known way to prevent prostate cancer. In aggressive prostate cancer, the amount of an enzyme called glycogen synthase kinase-3B (GSK-3B) is higher. Lowering the GSK-3B enzyme level reduces tumour growth and prevents the cancer from spreading (metastasis) in laboratory studies. This level can be lowered by using drugs that are called GSK-3B inhibitors (GSK3Is). Some of these GSK3Is are successful in treating epilepsy and bipolar disorder while others are in experimental stages. We would like to study how successful the real-life use of these drugs is at lowering the risk of prostate cancer and/or dying from the disease by using historical data. First, we will look at whether patients had a higher or lower risk of prostate cancer when using GSK3Is and second, we will look at whether patients had a higher or lower risk of dying from the disease when using GSK3Is. If we find a protective effect from GSK3Is being used in treatment, we can design follow-up studies to determine which drugs work best and how to use them to improve patient care. column36: Association of Canada's Provincial Bans on Electronic Cigarette Sales to Minors With Electronic Cigarette Use Among Youths
column37: Background: Banning e-cigarette sales to minors has been a key policy to protect children from e-cigarettes in the US and Canada, but little is known about its impact. Methods: In this study, I used data from Canadian Tobacco, Alcohol and Drugs Survey (CTADS) and Canadian Student Tobacco Alcohol and Drugs Survey (CSTADS) and quasi-experimental methods to assess the impact of banning e-cigarette sales to minors in Canada. Outcomes of interest included recent e-cigarette use among youth, their reported difficulty of access to e-cigarettes, their perception of e-cigarette harm, and their use of social sources of e-cigarettes. Results: Following the bans, e-cigarette use among youth increased in all provinces, but the increase was 79% lower in provinces with a ban than in provinces without. Youth in provinces with a ban were 18% less likely to believe that regular e-cigarette use poses no harm and 16% more likely to self-report greater difficulty in obtaining e-cigarettes. However, youth in provinces with a ban were also 29% more likely to obtain e-cigarettes from social sources. These findings were robust to several sensitivity analyses. Conclusion and Relevance: Banning e-cigarette sales to minors was associated with a significant reduction in the rate of increase in e-cigarette use by youth, but this policy alone could not reverse the overall rise in e-cigarette use. This policy should be supplemented with other measures such as a ban on e-cigarettes with child-friendly flavors to reduce young people's desire to obtain e-cigarettes through social sources.

column36: Sex-Based Disparities in the Hourly Earnings of Surgeons in the Fee-for-Service System in Ontario, Canada
column37: Background: Sex-based income disparities are well documented in medicine and most pronounced in surgery. In salary-based systems, disparities are commonly attributed to differences in hours worked. One proposed solution to close the earnings gap in medicine is a fee-for-service system, where physicians are paid for each service provided (such as the system in Ontario). In theory, such a system should be free from sex bias; however, it is unclear whether fee-for-service systems are truly less prone to sex-based earnings gaps in the real world. The objective of this study was to determine whether male and female surgeons have similar earnings for each hour spent operating in a fee-for-service system Methods: This cross-sectional, population-based study evaluated claims submitted by surgeons in Ontario for surgical procedures performed between January 1, 2014, and December 31, 2016. We compared earnings per hour spent operating between male and female surgeons within and across surgical specialties. We also explored factors potentially associated with earnings disparities, including differences in procedure duration and type between male and female surgeons Results: We identified over 1.5 million surgical procedures claimed by 3,275 surgeons. Hourly earnings for female surgeons were 24% lower than for male surgeons. In some specialties, earnings differences were more than $70/hour. There were no differences in time taken by male and female surgeons to perform common procedures; however, female surgeons more commonly performed procedures with the lowest hourly earnings Conclusion: This study demonstrates that even when equal hours are worked, female surgeons earn less than male surgeons and have fewer opportunities to perform the most lucrative surgical procedures; increasing hours worked will not close the gender-pay gap.These findings call for a comprehensive analysis of drivers of sex-based earning disparities and highlight the need for systems-level solutions.

column36: Targeting neutrophil-exosome regulated changes in tissue stiffness as a promoter of breast cancer liver metastasis
column37: Increased tissue stiffness has previously been implicated as an important driver of cancer metastasis in primary and secondary tumors. However, the biological mechanisms by which tissues stiffen during cancer progression remain unclear. Neutrophils have emerged as important elements of the immune system that regulate metastatic disease progression, and we have recently discovered that under cancer-related conditions, neutrophils spray out sticky molecular webs called 'extracellular traps' that can stiffen the surrounding tissue. In this work, we propose defining the interconnected relationships between neutrophils present in breast cancer-related conditions, their capacity to stiffen the surrounding tissue, and metastatic progression of the disease into the liver. Specifically, we will examine cancer-related neutrophil subpopulations to evaluate their distinct potential to stiffen tissues and promote metastasis. Furthermore, we propose proteomic-based strategies to understand how neutrophil extracellular traps induce mechanical stiffening of the tissue matrix; and anticipate that these experiments will provide us with strategies that reduce or eliminate immune-driven tissue stiffening. Finally, we believe that certain neutrophil subtypes are primed to produce extracellular traps by incorporating tumor-derived extracellular vesicles. We will therefore define the role of these circulating particles in promoting metastasis, which will ultimately provide prophylactic approaches to disrupt this pro-metastatic disease mechanism. Together, these studies will make fundamental and interdisciplinary advances in our understanding of metastatic disease progression, while providing insight into potential therapeutic avenues to target this process and reduce metastatic disease burden.
