column36: Interventions to Mitigate COVID-19 Related Mental Health Risks for Those With Pre-Existing Chronic Health Conditions and Facing Social and Economic Barriers: A Scoping and Rapid Realist Review
column37: There is an urgent need to provide good evidence that will support mental health and substance use care related to COVID-19, especially for those who are at risk of infection. Examples of groups of people who would most benefit from this evidence include those with mental health, cognition, and physical health concerns. In addition, within these groups are people who face different social and financial barriers that are even higher risk for mental health concerns related to COVID-19. There is a lot of different information which is being shared among researchers and health professionals, however, it needs to be carefully evaluated and combined in order to be more meaningful to those who need it. The purpose of our project is to conduct a structured literature search to identify promising programs and policies. The results will be used to develop resources that will help to reduce mental health issues related to COVID 19 infection and recovery for different people. We will work with experts in mental health who develop policies and programs for mental health care in Canada. They will guide our literature search and how to report and distribute the findings. In addition to these experts we will be guided by people who have recovered from COVID-19. We will use a well established approach referred to as a rapid realist review in order to find out what types of program and policies would work for different types of people and in different situations. We will make recommendations to help address the mental health care needs of different at-risk populations and share our information with other researchers, those in health practice, and the general public. The results of this project will help to provide information that is relevant to researchers, health professionals, and the general public. It is one important step that can help manage the COVID-19 pandemic and future effects of similar disease outbreaks.

column36: A rapid review of the effects of epidemics or pandemics on suicide, suicidal behaviours and suicidal thoughts
column37: Suicide remains one of the most important public health challenges worldwide, with more than 800,000 people dying every year. The effect of the pandemic, including physical distancing measures, on suicides and suicidal behaviors remains unclear. This proposal aims to gather and present all available evidence for the effect of infectious pandemics on suicide, suicidal behavior and suicidal thoughts. This rapid review will answer the question "in a population exposed to an infectious epidemic or pandemic, what is the effect on suicides, suicidal behavior and suicidal thinking both during and after the pandemic". The review will consider this question across all age groups; between men and women; within indigenous populations; those in lower socioeconomic classes; those with pre-existing health conditions (including mental illnesses); and those who have been infected with Covid-19. The review will include all articles found in several electronic databases using predetermined search terms and will be continuously updated. These will be studies published in peer-reviewed journals which address mental health outcomes in an epidemic or pandemic. Papers will not include research related to the epidemic of suicide. Using this review, we hope to provide policymakers with high quality evidence for suicide prevention planning during pandemics. We will also use the review to modify existing guidelines on suicide prevention to be appropriate during times of pandemics and physical distancing. Also, we propose to use this review as a first step in creating a suicide prevention rapid synthesis team with our knowledge users to create "evidence on tap". We will create a governance group with our knowledge users to oversee the generation and answering of questions related to Covid-19 and suicide. The review will inform planning for a strategic plan for suicide and Covid-19 research.

column36: Translating Knowledge for Child Welfare Organizations Across the Prairies: Managing the Impacts of COVID-19 on the Mental Health of Children, Families, and Workers
column37: The shifting circumstances surrounding COVID-19 have led to a rapid proliferation of research and resources, but organizations responsible for meeting the urgent needs of children and families in child welfare typically have little time to find, evaluate, and translate knowledge to inform services for vulnerable children and families. The conditions brought on by COVID-19 have increased the possibility of separation, isolation, and reduced social support, as well as education, mental health, and physical health services. Thus, children and families are at heightened risk for trauma reactivation and deteriorating family conditions. Workers are also challenged in their efforts to rapidly change practices to respond to increasing demands and the growing complexity of cases, to ensure the safety and well-being of children and families. Thus, in close consultation with existing and new partners, we will undertake a rapid, month-long knowledge scan, synthesis, and subsequent mobilization initiative related to child welfare and COVID-19, geared to child-serving organizations from across the Canadian Prairies. We will use a variety of mobilization outlets, including an innovative Digital Connections Hub, which will be organized into policy, systems, and best practice responses to meet the mental, physical, and social health needs of children, families and workers. We will focus on the unique needs of Indigenous peoples, females, and others at risk of the compounding effects of COVID-19 on existing inequalities. Through an established infrastructure, affiliation with several research centres, and a well-connected research team, our initiative will contribute significant benefits by providing a forum for access to synthesized, vetted research and accessible resources to increase knowledge and support for child and family services providers. This will in turn improve the physical and mental health and well-being of vulnerable children and families during COVID-19, and beyond.

column36: COVID-19 Physical Distancing and Post-Traumatic Stress Injury: Utilization of Digital Health and Remote Mental Health Services for Military, Veterans, and Public Safety Personnel
column37: Physical distancing arising from COVID-19 has rapidly forced a paradigm shift toward remote mental health (MH) service delivery and a surge in the use of digital health (DH) (e.g., teletherapy/medicine, eHealth, and mHealth). Though limited in use mere weeks ago, DH has become essential for system access, assessment, and treatment. Legal, clinical, cultural, practical, and security considerations, however, remain unaddressed for delivering MH services to trauma-affected populations (TAPs). TAPs include public safety personnel (PSP; e.g., border services, communications officials, correctional workers, firefighters, paramedics, police, etc.), military members, and Veterans struggling with Post-Traumatic Stress Injuries (PTSIs) and other MH concerns that can be associated with or exacerbated by the pandemic. As TAPs may be particularly affected by changes from in-person to digital delivery of MH services, an understanding is needed of: (1) the clinical effectiveness of DH when addressing PTSIs; (2) perspectives of persons with lived experience, MH clinicians, senior leadership and policymakers; (3) the current context, needs, and considerations associated with DH uptake and use; and (4) realistic solutions for effectively delivering DH to TAPs. The HiMARC research team, with its established relationships with PSP, military, and Veteran communities in Alberta and beyond, is well-positioned to conduct a current state and needs analysis through a rapid review and key stakeholder engagements with the aim of synthesizing knowledge of needs, gaps, barriers, and facilitators for DH delivery of PTSI assessment and interventions. A co-designed, multi-phased knowledge mobilization and implementation plan coordinated with national efforts (e.g., CIPSRT and CIMVHR) will be created to deliver safe digital MH services at local, national, and international levels to PSP, military, Veteran, and civilian populations suffering from MH conditions including PTSIs.

column36: Niikaniganaw (All My Relations) II - the COVID-19 Rapid Response: Indigenous approaches to synthesizing knowledge for culturally-safe and stigma free mental health care for under-served Indigenous communities in Ottawa-Gatineau
column37: Developing capacity for stigma free and culturally safe care in health and social service providers is an urgent and critical need in Ottawa-Gatineau. The Niikaniganaw model outlined in Phase 1 (CIHR catalyst grant, 2018) and 2 (CIHR operating grant HIV/AIDS CBR, 2020) is designed to address this need in existing health and social service providers. We are also committed to building capacity for stigma free and culturally safe care in students who will be the future health or social service professionals. In this COVID-19 rapid response grant, we will focus on the following questions: 1) How is COVID-19 affecting the mental health of Indigenous community members in Ottawa-Gatineau who are living with or affected by HIV or related issues, such as substance use, mental illness, poverty, or homelessness? How are they receiving / adapting to the standard public health messaging? 2)What is the effect of COVID-19 on the mental health of health and social service providers who serve these communities? 3)What does culturally-safe and stigma free care in health and social services look like in the age of COVID-19, and by extension, future pandemics or remote / isolated environments? 4)How can we develop capacity for culturally-safe and stigma free mental health care for under-served Indigenous communities in Ottawa-Gatineau in the context of COVID-19? Building from previous experience and existing relationships with university academics, community partners, NGOs, social and health services providers, indigenous and non-indigenous, we will adapt the Niikaniganaw model to the COVID-19 context, and offer 'virtual' sharing circles and ceremonies to answer these questions. These sharing circles will be co-facilitated by researchers and Indigenous Knowledge Carriers. We will document and evaluate the challenges and opportunities of providing virtual sharing circles and ceremonies in real world with indigenous approaches of synthesizing knowledge and healing.

column36: A COVID-19 rapid evidence synthesis service to support Ontario's Mental Health and Addictions Centre of Excellence
column37: Mental health decision makers in Ontario need to have rapid access to evidence to inform decisions during the COVID-19 response. We will initiate a rapid evidence service based on a partnership with Ontario's Mental Health and Addictions Centre of Excellence. In response to questions posed by the Centre and the Ontario Mental Health and Addictions COVID Response Table, we will rapidly produce a mix of two types of synthesis products over the grant period: 1) rapid evidence profiles (completed in three hours, to address emergent questions); and 2) rapid evidence syntheses (completed in three, 10 or 30 days, to address increasingly complex questions). The relative mix of product types produced will be demand driven and responsive to the evolving needs. Rapid evidence profiles will draw on a process piloted by COVID-END and will make use of COVID-END's guide to evidence sources. Rapid syntheses will involve a search of databases of systematic reviews, with longer syntheses also including single studies and key informant interviews, following the McMaster Health Forum's well-established processes. Some high-priority topics will be identified as "living documents" and updated regularly. We will share findings directly with partners at the Centre of Excellence, the Response Table, and with an existing provincial network for COVID-19 evidence synthesis. All products will also be publicly available through our website. We will support other grant recipients through webinars to share tools and tips developed through COVID-END that can help to jump-start their synthesis activities and convene conversations to explore how synthesis products across research teams can be shared with researchers and decisions makers in other provinces or territories. The availability of a flexible synthesis service can ensure that mental health policy in Ontario continues to be evidence-informed throughout the COVID-19 response and can benefit from expertise elsewhere in Canada and globally.

column36: Examining the Efficacy of Evidence-Based Psychosocial Interventions for Schizophrenia-Spectrum Disorders Delivered Through Virtual Care
column37: Schizophrenia-spectrum disorders are the most persistent and debilitating mental health disorders. Individuals with severe mental illnesses such as schizophrenia-spectrum disorders are among those projected to experience the most negative effects to well-being from the COVID-19 pandemic. Ongoing clinical services have largely been discontinued due to social contact restrictions and access to in-person care has been suspended in most regions. In efforts to maintain clinical services, many programs have turned to virtual delivery of mental health services. However, there is little evidence to suggest which interventions can be effectively delivered through virtual care, and which are only effective when delivered in-person. Due to research suggesting that some interventions can actually cause harm when delivered virtually, and the increasing need for virtual services, it is imperative that we understand which evidence-based treatments should be offered virtually and which should not. The proposed project will conduct a rapid scoping review, meta-analysis, and survey of experts and service-users to determine the efficacy of virtual delivery of ten evidence-based interventions for schizophrenia-spectrums. These results will be disseminated to local and national partners to inform priorities for future research and guidelines for providing virtual care.

column36: Developing a Rational Approach Towards Offering Procedural Interventions (ECT & rTMS) for At Risk Populations in Psychiatry During the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Interdisciplinary Evidence Synthesis.
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic will associate with parallel mental health pandemics, one during the pandemic and the other after. The mental health impact of COVID-19 will be disproportionately experienced by at risk populations, with increased prevalence of mental illness such as mood disorders where procedural neurostimulation treatments such as Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) and repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) have significant evidence. However, hospitals across the country have either discontinued or decreased ECT and rTMS offerings, procedural aspects remain arbitrary varying from hospital to hospital putting healthcare providers at risk, and there is a lack of an understanding of the short-term and long-term impact of these changes on the at-risk population. Thus, there is a need to bring together a more systematic approach with a Canadian perspective and adopt best practices from other countries and procedural disciplines. This rapid knowledge synthesis will bring together interdisciplinary teams from neurostimulation programs at three major hospital systems in Toronto who have been at the forefront of responsible delivery of their respective programs since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. The project will be a collaborative effort with Infection Prevention & Control, Anesthesia, Nursing and Ethics across hospital systems. Importantly, the knowledge users will include leaders from academic hospitals across Ontario, pertinent stakeholders nationally & internationally and patients with lived experience. This project will offer a rational framework for decision makers at the hospital, provincial and other levels to offer neurostimulation treatments and mitigate the negative impact of COVID-19 on vulnerable populations. Further, it will form the foundation to develop services/targeted interventions, and delineate critical areas of knowledge gap in the procedural domain which need to addressed from an interdisciplinary perspective.

column36: Palliative Care for People who use Substances During Communicable Disease Epidemics and Pandemics: A Scoping Review
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic and its response efforts magnify the health care challenges encountered by people who use substances. People who use substances are at high risk of life-limiting illnesses such as end-stage organ failure and cancer. Unfortunately, people who use substances encounter barriers to receiving palliative care. People who use substances often have few social supports and lack financial resources. Moreover, delivery of community-based health services may be restricted due to institution and provider concerns that the settings are risky or unsafe. Zero-tolerance policies toward non-medical use of substances also restrict access to palliative care units and hospices. Given these pre-existing inequities to palliative care access and increased demand for palliative care during the COVID-19 pandemic, it is important to understand the impact of COVID-19 on people with life-limiting illnesses who use substances. To address this critical issue, we propose a scoping review that will identify knowledge strengths and gaps about palliative care for people with life-limiting illnesses who use substances during communicable disease epidemics and pandemics. Our project will critically assess the state of knowledge and provide decision support for healthcare providers and policy makers during COVID-19 and future communicable disease epidemics and pandemics. Through our dedicated knowledge translation strategy, we will ensure timely dissemination of our findings to patients, caregivers, healthcare providers, and decision makers. Our project is aligned with a key goal in the Government of Canada's five-year action plan for palliative care (2019 - 2024), which seeks to to improve access to palliative care for underserved populations who experience difficulties in obtaining health care and to improve the quality of care when it is received.

column36: Knowledge Synthesis to Support and Promote Mental Wellness and Resiliency during the COVID-19 pandemic
column37: There are currently no vaccine or cures for COVID-19. As a result, our government recommends isolation, quarantine, and other measures to control the virus. However, when people isolate for a long time, their mental health may suffer. Some people with no mental illness, for example, may develop anxiety or depression, with symptoms that can last a long time. Others who are already living with mental illness may experience worsening symptoms, and at the same time experience difficulties accessing their usual health care or social supports. It is therefore important to support the mental health of the population during a pandemic. In line with this, our team of researchers, mental health professionals, and people with lived experience, propose to conduct a rapid review of the evidence on home activities and resources that can support mental health during times of isolation. We also propose to conduct an online survey to understand what activities or resources people prefer and will most likely use. Upon completion, study results will be shared with the government, CMHA and the CIHR. We will create a public website to share the results, with selected examples of effective home activities or resources. A research paper will also be submitted for publication. The results of our study will complement government plans to address the mental health impacts of COVID-19. It will work well, for instance, with the virtual mental health platforms that the government is planning to fund with $240M. We plan to update the project website with new evidence and examples from the literature as they become available so that the website continues to be a useful resource even long after the pandemic is over.

column36: Acute airway inflammation induced by vaping
column37: Even though vaping was first promoted as a tool to help smokers quit smoking, it is now practiced by large number of the population independently form previous or current smoking. Vaping has also spread quickly among the youth. Unfortunately, it has been promoted commercially and had gained wide acceptance even though we know very little about any detrimental effects it may have on human health. Vaping exposes individuals to a large number of chemicals. Unfortunately many of those have not been tested appropriate before humans are allowed to inhale them. Many of these chemicals would be expected to cause inflammation in human tissues. Over the last few years there have been studies on the pro-inflammatory effects of vaping in cell cultures and in animal models, but very few studies in humans. Additionally, the few existing studies measured inflammation in the blood and not directly in the lung. Our objective is to describe the pro-inflammatory effects of vaping directly in the lungs. We will recruit healthy subjects that vape and others that do not and will expose all of them to an acute vaping session. We will analyze markers of airway and peripheral blood inflammation before and after the vaping session. We will compare differences in inflammatory markers between subjects that vape regularly and those that do not and changes of these markers after vaping. In follow up investigations we plan to study the pro-inflammatory effects of vaping in subjects with respiratory diseases.

column36: Are e-cigarettes really a healthy alternative to combustible cigarettes? Cardiorespiratory, immune and thrombotic responses to smoking e-cigarettes vs combustible cigarettes under conditions of physical and mental stress
column37: Smoking is key to developing heart disease, lung disease, and cancer, with the number of people smoking highest in healthy young adults (20-24 years old). E-cigarettes (e-cigs) have been suggested as potential helping people stop smoking. However, we really don't know how safe e-cigs are and the recent E-cigarette, or Vaping, product use-Associated Lung Injury (EVALI) events in the US and Canada have increased the need for more e-cig safety data. Our study will look at how smoking e-cigs versus regular cigarettes versus nothing affects heart, blood, lung, and immune function during episodes of low intensity exercise and mental stress in young, otherwise healthy individuals who smoke. We will also test non-smokers (who won't smoke but will do the exercise and mental stress task). In total, we will include 105 smokers and 35 non-smokers and we expect that half of these will be women. This will be one of the first studies to assess the acute effects of e-cigs use (compared to regular cigarettes and doing nothing) influences stress induced physiological responses. Findings will generate new data that can be used to inform the safety debate about e-cig use, both in comparison to combustible cigarettes and to not smoking, that may be used to inform stakeholders (legislators, clinicians, patients) about their potential harms (or benefits) of e-cigs, which may lead to appropriate regulation and use.

column36: Vaping Safety: A Knowledge Synthesis
column37: While vaping is rising in popularity, its short- and long-term respiratory safety remains unclear. There are increasing reports of vaping-related changes in respiratory health, spanning from acute changes such as breathing difficulty to chronic illnesses such as asthma. The respiratory safety of cannabis vaping products is particularly uncertain, given their link to the recent outbreak of vaping-related lung illness. In addition, new questions on the respiratory safety of vaping have been raised in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. We will conduct systematic reviews of the literature concerning the respiratory safety of vaping, including short- and long-term vaping-associated changes in respiratory health and vaping safety during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our research will answer the following questions: 1.What are the short- and long-term changes in respiratory health among individuals who vape, and how do these changes differ among vaping subgroups (e.g., people who both smoke and use e-cigarettes, people who use cannabis vaping products)? 2.Does vaping increase susceptibility to and severity of COVID-19? These reviews will include searching databases (e.g., PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO), preprint servers (e.g., medRxiv), and governmental and organizational publications. The full development of this proposal will utilize the co-applicants' technical and content expertise, involving a librarian, epidemiologist, statistician, and content and knowledge translation experts, as well as knowledge users. Our team has extensive previous experience conducting CIHR-funded systematic reviews of smoking, vaping, and cannabis use. Our expected findings will address questions concerning the short- and long-term safety of vaping, especially in relation to vaping cannabis products and vaping during the COVID-19 pandemic, and will ultimately contribute to the larger goal of reducing harms associated with vaping.

column36: The impact of vaping policies on the e-cigarette product market and youth vaping.
column37: In May 2018, e-cigarettes containing nicotine became legally available for sale in Canada under the TVPA, along with increased marketing and retail access for major international brands, such as JUUL. In the following two years, the prevalence of youth vaping in Canada doubled. In response, provinces have announced a range of policy measures to be implemented in 2020-including restrictions on retail access, flavours, nicotine, and product design. The variation in these policies across provinces provides a unique opportunity for a 'natural experiment' research design. The proposed study has two primary objectives: to examine the impact of provincial policies on: 1) e-cigarette product design and retail availability, and 2) vaping behaviour among young people. The study consists of two data sources. First, an environmental scan of the e-cigarette market will be conducted in each province to collect the following information for leading e-cigarette brands in Canada: retail availability, price, nicotine content, flavours, pack design, and device components. Second, data from the environmental scan will be linked with data from the ITC Youth Tobacco and Vaping Surveys, which consists of population-based surveys of youth aged 16-19 in Canada, conducted annual between 2017 and 2021. Analyses will examine pre-post changes within provinces for four primary outcomes: 1) retail access and purchase source of e-cigarettes; 2) use of flavoured e-cigarettes; 3) product type, including nicotine concentration and use of salt-based e-cigarettes; and 4) overall changes in the prevalence of vaping across provinces. The proposed study represents the most comprehensive assessment of the e-cigarette product market in Canada. The study will evaluate how the industry responds to novel policies and assess the impact on youth vaping. Overall, the proposed project has the potential to directly inform e-cigarette policy in Canada and other jurisdictions.

column36: The pathogenesis of vaping-associated lung injury: interactions between the alveolar epithelium and the immune system
column37: Vaping, inhaling aerosolized liquids from an electronic cigarette is being adopted by an increasing number adolescents and young adults. There is very little scientific data on the safety of this practice although it is advertised as being safe and a good alternative to smoking traditional combustible cigarettes. Vaping associated lung injury (VALI) is a disease related to the use of electronic cigarettes which causes severe inflammation and scarring in the lung and sometimes death. We think that the heated substances in the vapor cause injury to the cells lining the airways (alveolar epithelial cells) and to surfactant, a liquid which is secreted by these cells and which is vital to the proper function of the lung. We will use a 'lung on a chip' which is a cell culture system engineered by Dr Mark Gillrie and which takes cells present in the lung and grows them together on a surface that recapitulates the arrangement seen in the human lung. We will aerosolize various types of vaping fluids onto this model and measure the damage to the different cell types and to the surfactant. We will measure the various substances produced by the various cells. We will also take tissue sections from lungs of patients with VALI and look for the same substances produced by the cells in the lung on a chip. In this way we will identify the underlying mechanism of damage by vaping and therefore develop therapies to treat it.

column36: Vaping and asthma - A study on short and long-term health effects of vaping among Ontario youths and young adults with asthma identified in health administrative data and linked to the Canadian Community Health Survey
column37: While it is generally thought that e-cigarette (EC) is a safer alternative to smoking, new research suggests that vaping may worsen pre-existing health conditions and have long-term health effects. Our proposed study will examine the long-term health risks and outcomes among young EC users, by comparing their health outcomes and health trajectories between EC users and non-users. We will conduct 3 studies using 2 Canadian surveys (Canadian Community Health Survey, CCHS: 2015-17 and Canadian Health Measures Survey, CHMS: 2016-2019) and 6 health administrative databases. The CCHS is a cross-sectional survey that collects information through questionnaires about health status, health determinants and behaviours. Linkage of the CCHS with health administrative data will allow us to measure the health outcomes of the study population for the period of 2010 to 2020. The CHMS is a cross-sectional survey that collects health information including physical activity, quality of life, heart rate and blood pressure, blood sugar and lipid profiles through questionnaires and direct measurements. The 3 studies to be conducted aim to answer the following research questions: 1) Do youth and young adults who are current EC users have increased risks of asthma and/or other allergic diseases? 2) Do youth and young adults who are current EC users and have asthma and/or other allergic diseases have more morbidity as measured by health services use for asthma, allergic disease, and related conditions? 3) Are youth and young adults who are EC users and have asthma and/or other allergic diseases less physically active, have poorer physical, mental and social well-being and quality of life? With a significant number of young Canadians reporting EC vaping, it is imperative to examine data on the health effects of vaping. Our population-based research findings will provide the data needed to guide policy and educate young people to make informed decisions to protect overall health.

column36: Cannabis Vaping Experiences and Decisions among Youth and Young Adults in Manitoba (The CaVED Project)
column37: An increasing number of young Canadians are using e-cigarettes, which may pose significant health risks. With the recent legalization of cannabis vape products in Canada, there are concerns that even more youth and young adults may engage in vaping and experience poor health outcomes. In order to develop education and policies around cannabis vaping that reflect the reality of youth and young adults, our proposed study aims to understand, in their own words, their experiences, beliefs, and decision-making associated with cannabis vaping. We will hold focus groups with a total of 40-50 individuals aged 12-25 years and living in Manitoba that will explore their experiences of using vaped cannabis products, their beliefs about the possible risks and benefits of vaping cannabis, and what factors influenced their decision to vape cannabis. Efforts will be made to invite a diverse group of youth and young adults, including those from the Indigenous/Metis communities and living in rural and remote regions of the province. A brief survey will assess individuals' vaping behaviour related to cannabis and other substances and personal information, such as their age, gender, and ethnicity. The survey data will be summarized using descriptive statistics, and the focus group data will be reviewed, compared, and organized into key themes and ideas. A Youth Advisory Committee will meet throughout the study and provide advice about how the study is conducted and help create strategies to share the study findings with youth and young adults in Manitoba and beyond. The results of this study will inform future education and decision support tools related to cannabis vaping and act as a catalyst for a larger national study that will guide public health policies related to cannabis and vaping.

column36: Optimizing the Ageing Brain? Situating Ethical Aspects of Dementia Prevention (BEAD)
column37: Background: Dementia (the most common form is Alzheimer's disease) has for a long time been conceived of as an unpreventable process of mental deterioration. Now, however, researchers claim that one out of three dementia cases can be prevented if at least nine risk factors are man-aged. These risk factors include some that have not been traditionally linked to Alzheimer's, such as diabetes, hypertension, social isolation, and hearing loss, and which require management over the life course, making prevention a lifelong endeavor. Early detection through biomarkers and digital tracking technologies have also become a central feature of what we call 'the new dementia'. This raises a number of ethical questions, such as: should individuals be considered personal-ly responsible for their own dementia prevention? Should we accept extensive monitoring of our cognitive functions through digital technologies? What does dementia prevention entail for our healthcare systems and cultures of care? And, do national or local contexts play a role in how prevention is articulated and lived? Objectives: We propose a research project that studies in three countries the way the 'new de-mentia' is being articulated, and asks what ethical problems are arising, what the impacts are on health-related and everyday practices, and what solutions might be envisioned. Methodologies: We will study the 'new dementia' through complementary disciplinary approaches. We will adopt a comparative perspective looking at differences and similarities between three countries: Germany, Canada and Switzerland. Expected outcomes: Our results aim to make people more aware that preventing dementia is a highly complex issue that needs to be seen in context through an extensive knowledge transfer on multiple levels.

column36: HYBRID MINDS: Experiential, Ethical and Legal Exploration of Intelligent Neuroprostheses
column37: Intelligent neuroprostheses represent the next phase in the evolution of devices integrated with the nervous system to assist, replace or alter human sensory, motor, cognitive, and affective functions. These devices include "read out" or output systems that detect, interpret and translate neural signals for various applications such as to allow a paralyzed person to move a robotic arm or cursor. They also include "write in" or input systems that deliver signals or stimulation to the brain, to alter thinking, emotions, and the ability to move, among other things. The technology is increasingly incorporating Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create neuroprostheses that adapt automatically without voluntary user input. The current rate of development of AI-based neurotechnology systems is outpacing ethical reflections and is challenging regulatory systems. The current technological departure lies in the complexity, unpredictability, and psychological impact of the integration of AI with human brains and minds. Such hybrid minds are characterized by mutual adaptation, in which both user and self-learning algorithm change over time to optimize system output. Such interactions become even more intricate when "write-into" devices generate stimuli that directly influence mental contents and cognitive processes of users. Our project attempts to lay the foundations for a unified theoretical approach to the ethical-legal assessment of intelligent neuroprostheses, informed by the experiences and perspectives of users, and in dialogue with the neuroengineering community and other key stakeholders, culminating in the central questions: Which AI-elements should future neuroprostheses incorporate, or rather leave out? What technical design choices or legal/regulatory measures are required? How can we support patients in clinical decision-making to avoid overblown hopes and to know, to borrow Thomas Nagel's famous phrase, "what it's like to have a hybrid mind"?

column36: Identifying and inhibiting novel signalling pathways involved in the amplification of C/EBPa expression as a means to prevent muscle wasting in cancer.
column37: "Cancer cachexia is a neurological syndrome caused by the presence of tumour cells in the body that leads to a severe wasting of skeletal muscle in patients. The exact cause of this phenomenon is likely to be multifactorial and is currently being investigated by the Wiper-Bergeron laboratory. The most recent findings have shown that CCAAT/Enhancer Binding Protein beta (C/EBPβ) plays a central role in the development of muscle wasting observed in cancer cachexia. Our laboratory has demonstrated that cachexia-inducing tumors (e.g. Lewis Lung Carcinoma) express high levels of C/EBPβ, while non-cachexia tumours have lower expression. Tumour-derived factors promote muscle catabolism and recent evidence suggests that a combination of secreted factors underlies wasting in cancer patients. C/EBPβ is a central factor in regulating proteins secreted by tumours in muscle wasting, highlighting the importance of further inquiry into its mechanism of action. We hypothesize that tumours expressing C/EBPβ produce cachexia-inducing factors that directly cause muscle wasting, but also stimulate the expression of C/EBPβ in secondary tissues, thereby amplifying the cachectic signal. The aims of this project are twofold: (1) To identify the factors regulated by C/EBPβ responsible for induction of cachexia and (2) To determine if induction of C/EBPβ in non-muscle tissues in tumour-bearing animals leads to amplification of the cachectic signal. Our research will significantly enrich the current knowledge on the mechanism behind C/EBPβ-mediated cachectic signal amplification that leads to muscle wasting in cancer patients. The findings will have implications in the identification of drugs for prevention and treatment of cancer cachexia, with the primary goal of increasing patients' survival."

column36: A Possible Association Between Insulin and Alzheimer?s Disease: Examining the Consequences of Altered Insulin Signalling on the Expression of Human Amyloid-Beta in Caenorhabditis elegans
column37: "Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disease that affects millions of people globally. This disease of ageing has been associated with amyloid-beta and tau plaques in the brain, causing symptoms such as confusion, memory loss, and impaired cognitive abilities. It is known that insulin is a key regulator in the ageing process, as well as other processes such as metabolism and fat storage. An association between insulin regulation and amyloid-beta plaque accumulation has been noted in C. elegans. This study uses C. elegans to compare how different mutations in the insulin signalling pathway affect the deposition of human amyloid-beta in a transgenic worm strain over-expressing human amyloid-beta peptide. Previous work in our lab has showed reduced function of the insulin receptor can rescue worms from amyloid-beta induced toxicity in behavioural assays. We now want to study how insulin regulation could affect amyloid-beta toxicity by investigating antagonistic insulin molecules. Worms which over express antagonistic insulin will be tested to see if they can counter the effects of over expression of human amyloid-beta peptide. Chemotaxis behaviour and time to paralyze will be monitored. Additionally, in-situ antibody staining and western blots will be completed to detect the amount of protein present in the worms. Our lab has engineered an insulin molecule which is originally an agonist but is showing antagonistic properties with the alteration of certain amino acids in its coding sequence. This study aims to confirm if this engineered insulin-like peptide acts antagonistically in the AD model. column36: Words on the Brain: Can low vision rehabilitation improve short term and long term memory in adults with age-related macular degeneration?
column37: "In Canada, the aging population is growing and, within the next 10 years, the majority of the baby-boomer generation will be 65 years of age or older. With increased age, memory decline and sensory impairments in hearing and vision become more frequent; however, the Canadian health care system is not prepared to deal with a drastic increase in the number of older adults. Age-related impairments in vision and hearing are associated with an increased risk of dementia, such as Alzheimer's disease. It is expected that more people will be affected by dementia in the coming decades. To date, there is no known cure for dementia. It is thus important to emphasize prevention. Previous studies have shown that age-related macular degeneration, a highly common eye disease causing central vision loss, is associated with cognitive decline and a higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. This could be due to the fact that vision loss reduces visual stimulation. Therefore, the present research project is exploring the prevention of cognitive decline in older adults with age-related macular degeneration. In order to do this, we will evaluate the effects of low vision rehabilitation for reading on cognition. Vision rehabilitation consists of learning new strategies and the use of magnifying assistive devices to cope and to be able to read even with a vision loss. Older adults undergoing vision rehabilitation will be followed for a one-year period in order to assess their changes in vision, reading abilities and cognition. We hypothesize that low vision rehabilitation will be beneficial for cognition in older adults with age-related macular degeneration because it will reduce reading effort, thereby increasing cognitive functioning."

column36: Fan to Face Therapy for Relief of Exertional Breathlessness in People with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: "For people with idiopathic pulmonary disease (IPF), breathlessness is a common and disabling symptom that negatively affects all aspects of daily life. The drugs used to treat IPF do not improve breathlessness. Thus, it is important to identify alternative non-drug therapies to reduce breathlessness in people with IPF. A recent review of different studies found that use of a fan to blow cool air on the face reduced how much breathlessness people with different chronic conditions experienced in normal day-to-day life. One study reported that cool airflow to the face decreased breathlessness experienced during bicycle exercise testing in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. To date, no study has examined whether cool airflow to the face is associated with decreased breathlessness during exercise in people with IPF. The reason(s) why cool airflow to the face decreases exertional breathlessness is also unknown. Our research aims to: 1) test the hypothesis that fan to the face therapy decreases breathlessness during exercise in people with IPF; and 2) identify the reason(s) why fan to the face therapy improves exertional breathlessness. To address these aims, 16 adults with IPF will complete a 3-min constant-rate stair stepping test (3-min CRSST) under each of three experimental conditions, randomized for order: 1) fan to the face; 2) fan to the lower leg; and 3) no fan. Detailed physiological and perceptual responses will be collected at rest and during the 3-min CRSST. Using statistics, these responses will be compared between the three experimental conditions.The anticipated results of this study will support clinical use of fan to the face as a simple, inexpensive and effective non-drug method of decreasing breathlessness in people with IPF. "

column36: "Characterization, care outcomes and costs of the Diabetes Care program for refugees in Lebanon."
column37: "Managing diabetes for refugees in humanitarian settings is challenging. Today, it is not clear how to best care for diabetic refugees in, or around, conflict areas. This presents serious challenges for patients, healthcare providers, and humanitarian organizations who struggle to care for diabetes patients without clear guidelines or well-established care models. Diabetes a leading cause of illness and death globally. The worldwide number of people with diabetes is increasing continuously, with a faster rate of increase in low and middle-income countries such as Lebanon and Syria. Due to Syria's ongoing civil war, since 2011 Lebanon hosts about 1.5 million Syrian refugees, many with chronic diseases such as diabetes. This large and rapid refugee influx places a large strain on Lebanon's already fractured healthcare system. The unmet health needs of Syrian refugees with diabetes in Lebanon motivated innovative programs to fill this care gap. One such program was the refugee-led diabetes care program (DCP). Through this program, 4033 refugees received free diabetes care between September 2016 and March 2019. This program collected detailed patient and program information and provides a rare opportunity to study a diabetes care program for refugees in a conflict area. In this study, we aim to understand the DCP's structure, processes, its costs, and how successful it was. This research will be guided by a group of diabetic refugee patients and refugee health providers. Our research findings will provide urgently needed information to the international community and help others improve refugee healthcare models for diabetes and chronic diseases in conflict areas, as well as for refugees resettled to high-income countries such as Canada. "

column36: Quantitative Measurement of Osteoarthritic Knee Subchondral Bone Perfusion in Postmenopausal Women with Knee-Specific Pain
column37: "Osteoarthritis (OA) is a cartilage and bone disease of joints. Knee OA is the most common form of OA, associated with being overweight. However, this does not fully explain KOA in non-overweight individuals, accounting for up to 40% of patients. KOA is more common among postmenopausal women than men. Postmenopausal women are also susceptible to losing bone due to the loss of estrogen. If this affects bone quality of the knee, it could explain KOA pain symptoms. In the subgroups of KOA sufferers, it is difficult to locate the source of pain (trauma, repetitive activities, being overweight or age-related/non-overweight). In the latter group, pain symptoms have not been well-studied, especially considering the insult from estrogen on bone loss. Bone marrow lesions (areas with fluid inside bones) are evident in patients with KOA, which could be a sign of micro-damage, triggering pain. Scientific tools cannot directly measure the damage; however, it can be measured indirectly by assessing the build-up of fluid using speed of blood flow in the region. It may be possible to detect damage indirectly by measuring blood fluid kinetic changes on contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Few scientists have examined how factors related to possible micro-damage within bone can contribute to knee pain. In the proposed study, 115 postmenopausal, non-overweight women (50 to 85 years of age) presenting with knee pain will be recruited. We will scan patients with MRI to measure the speed of blood flow in the bones of the knee joint. This information will be linked to knee pain and related hallmarks (bone structure). If these knee bone measures relate to both pain and disease features, they may be good candidates for treatment targets and for tracking recovery from knee OA."

column36: Characterization of tumor-infiltrating T lymphocytes expressing PD-1 as a source of anti-tumoral cells for adoptive cell transfer immunotherapy
column37: "Cancer immunotherapy currently shows great promise in the treatment of a growing number of cancers, including melanoma, exploiting the patient's own immune system to fight cancer. A novel immunotherapeutic method involves the transfer of adoptive T cells (ACT) which naturally infiltrate tumors. These cells are expanded ex vivo and reinfused in large number to the patient. This method yields clinical responses in up to 50% of metastatic melanoma patients but is hindered by the low number of tumor-reactive cells in the infused product. column36: Probing the Network Basis of Memory Function and Dysfunction in Children with Epilepsy
column37: "Epilepsy is a serious neurological condition that affects millions of children worldwide. While epilepsy is characterized by seizures, many children also suffer from cognitive impairments. In particular, deficits in working memory - the ability to maintain and manipulate information in the short-term - are commonly reported. While working memory is thought to be dependent on brain waves in the hippocampus, the mechanisms of working memory deficits in children with epilepsy are unknown. The current research aims to fill this knowledge gap by demonstrating the specific mechanism by which epilepsy disrupts the brain activity underlying working memory. The goals of this research are to: (1) understand how brain waves in the hippocampus support memory, and (2) understand how epileptic activity disrupts brain waves in the hippocampus, leading to working memory impairments. This work will enable us to develop treatments to rescue memory function in children with epilepsy and improve their quality of life. column36: Engineered human gamma delta T cells for multiple myeloma immunotherapy
column37: "Adoptive cell therapy using engineered human T cells can, in many cases, produce a complete response in patients with refractory relapsed hematological malignancies who otherwise lack treatment options. However, the current cost of the commercially available engineered T cell therapies begins at the expensive price of $500,000 CAD, and is consequently not financially sustainable within the Canadian healthcare system. I will adapt our existing chimeric receptors for human γδ T cells by augmenting the chimeric receptor intracellular signalling domains to optimize γδ T cell activation and multiple myeloma-specific killing. column36: Generative modelling for de novo design of peptides with specific protein binding affinity
column37: "Peptides are a type of molecule that has been gaining attention as a potential source of therapeutics. column36: Identifying the Quality Indicators of Knowledge Translation Interventions and Tools

Therefore, measuring both fMRI and EEG simultaneously has the benefits of EEG and MRI, excellent temporal and spatial resolution. EEG-fMRI was first used in 1993 to study epilepsy and is now widely used in neuroscience research. Although EEG-fMRI is a remarkable achievement in medical imaging, it presents challenges. Every pulse of blood flow in the head distorts the EEG signal, an effect called the ""ballistocardiogram (BCG) artifact"". This effect is normally negligible in EEG, but it is amplified by the MRI scanner to an extent that makes the EEG signal unreadable. Numerous algorithms have been developed to remove the BCG artifact; however, they need improvement. While the BCG artifact has been analyzed, such attempts used linear (simpler) methods. The BCG artifact requires nonlinear analysis methods to be fully characterized. Therefore, this project sets out to analyze the BCG artifacts with nonlinear methods. These approaches will shed new light on how the BCG artifact differs from neural signal in EEG and will provide new metrics to quantify how well BCG artifact removal algorithms work. It may also inspire new BCG removal algorithms. Given that EEG-fMRI is employed in neuroscience and psychiatry research, it is critical the BCG artifact does not interfere with EEG-fMRI data analysis."

column37: "Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a cancer of the blood characterized by an increase in the number of immature blood cells (blasts) in the bone marrow. These blasts cells are derived from abnormal leukemic stem cells (LSCs) and cause the bone marrow to lose its function. Chemotherapies used for AML have stayed the same for the last 30 years and involve extremely intense toxic treatment, yet approximately 40% of AML is resistant to initial treatment or eventually reoccurs. The survival rate 5 years after diagnosis of pediatric AML patients is poor (60%) and accounts for approximately half of leukemic deaths in children. This is due to the chemoresistant nature of the LSCs that sustain the disease. For this reason compounds that specifically target LSCs while sparing normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which are similar to the LSCs, may significantly improve patient outcome and lower toxicity across a broad leukemia spectrum in adolescent and young adult (AYA) and pediatric patients. After conducting an initial drug screen, our lab has identified corticosteroids as compounds that can target LSCs while sparing HSCs. The goal of this project is to identify other corticosteroids that will target LSCs more effectively than the compounds used for the initial screen, as well as gain insight into the optimal drug design and the mechanism by which corticosteroids target LSCs. Some of the corticosteroids compounds being used for this project have been FDA approved for other treatments and therefore have a high potential to be quickly transferred to the clinic if proven effective."

column37: "Asthma is a chronic lung disease that affects 1 in 10 Canadians and is characterized by abnormalities in lung airway structure and function. column36: Gene Therapy of Type 1C Usher Syndrome using Mouse Models
column37: "Type 1C Usher Syndrome (USH-1C) is a genetic disorder that typically follows a recessive mendellian inheritance pattern, and is characterized by deafblindness and poor balance. It has its highest prevalence, and is the leading cause of deafblindness in French-Canadian and Acadian populations. Because of USH-1C's cosmopolitan rarity there are no human gene therapies as of November 24, 2019. There are however, mouse gene therapies for USH-1C, but they only focus on restoring hearing and vestibular function, and no therapy for vision restoration has been explored. The objective of the proposed research is to use USH-1C mouse models to begin development of potential gene therapies to restore vision, providing a foundation for USH-1C human vision-restorative gene therapy research in the future. This will help solve a public health issue that is endemic to Eastern Canadian populations, where no current treatment besides cochlear implants are available. This study will be an assessment of the effects and success of several gene therapeutic methods, such as adenoviral vectors, viral vectors, stem cells, and others, and use of gene drives such as CRISPR/Cas9. According to past research on related syndromes, it is thought lentiviruses will be most effective; however, finding non-lentiviral vectors would be preferable due to potential mutagenesis. Furthermore, this research can compare effects of gene addition as opposed to gene replacement in USH-1C mice, in order to predict which method would be optimal in humans. This study will contribute towards a Master's Thesis, and is expected to be finished within maximum of two academic years. "

column36: Relationship between Myeloperoxidase and Executive Function in Mild Vascular Cognitive Impairment
column37: "As people age, they may develop difficulties in remembering things, thinking quickly and clearly, and carrying out important tasks. Injury to the blood vessels such as in coronary artery disease (CAD) puts you at a risk of developing these thinking difficulties. The condition involving a small decline in thinking abilities after an injury to one's blood vessels is called mild vascular cognitive impairment (mVCI). Research has suggested that a build up of toxic chemicals in the blood, produced by the immune system which protects the body against harmful germs and bacteria, can also harm blood vessels and in turn, brain function. Immune cells called neutrophils secrete a molecule called myeloperoxidase (MPO), which has been found in high concentrations in the blood of people with CAD and diseases involving severe forms of thinking difficulties like dementia. Importantly, this relationship has not been tested in earlier stages of disease, like mVCI, where intervention may have a big impact. In this study, I want to measure the amount of MPO in the blood of those with mVCI and see if it is related to their ability to think. Thinking abilities will be measured using validated tests involving problem-solving, puzzles and ""connect-the-dots"". I propose that higher MPO in the blood will be associated with more difficulty in thinking quickly and clearly in patients with mVCI. This research will allow us to better understand mVCI in order to develop medications that can stop it. Thinking difficulties increase risk of hospitalization and mortality, and adversely affects quality of life and ability to perform daily activities. Currently there is no treatment for mVCI. Targeting this decline in earlier stages can help us stop its progression into more severe disorders like dementia."

column36: "Genetic biomarkers of serum iron, and their role in the risk of infectious diseases: a Mendelian randomization approach"
column37: "Iron is intrinsically tied to human health. During inflammation, we observe significant anemia stemming from a profound change in its metabolism. This metabolic response is believed to help protect our body's iron from being used by infectious agents. This is supported by increased infection rates in hemochromatosis, a diseases leading to an iron overloaded state. Iron levels being probably related to infectious risks, iron supplementation could lead to significant infectious adverse events on a population scale. Traditional epidemiological studies have shown increased infectious risks from iron supplementation. However, their retrospective nature, their target population already at risk of severe infections (e.g. leukemia ), and the fact that ferritin falsely increases during inflammatory states, all lead to risks of confounding bias and reverse causation. Confounding happens when the exposure and the outcome are associated with a third variable, which is not in the causal pathway between the exposure and the outcome. Reverse causation occurs when the outcome influences the exposure. More advanced statistical methods such as mendelian randomization (MR) are therefore required. MR mimics a randomized controlled trial by using genetic markers to randomize patients to an exposure (iron) and measure its outcome (infections). It bypasses confounding and reverse causation bias through Mendel's laws on random allele segregation at conception. When used with large genetic databases such as the UK Biobank (more than 400 000 indifivuals), its use was shown in multiple fields. We hypothesize that individuals with lower serum iron levels have a lower risk of infections like pneumonia and sepsis. We will use MR and large genotype databases to answer this important question. "

column36: Characterization of small RNAs as ribosomal regulators during gene expression in bacteria
column37: "Since the discovery of penicillin in 1928, antibiotics have been used to treat bacterial infections. Over the past 20 years, only two new categories of antibiotics have been developed, with industry focusing on producing modified versions of existing antibiotics. However, bacteria have developed resistance mechanisms to many antibiotics used today at a much faster rate than we have been able to design new compounds, with the World Health Organization identifying antibiotic resistance as a global threat. Over 50% of currently used antibiotics target a process called translation. Translation produces proteins that are able to perform functions within the cell. The molecular machinery that is used to produce proteins in translation is called the ribosome. Many regions of the ribosome have been identified as being susceptible to antibiotics. Given the precedence of antibiotics working effectively during translation, this is a promising target for developing novel antimicrobial strategies. We are studying a special type of RNA molecule, called ribosome-associated non-coding RNAs (rancRNAs). rancRNAs are capable of directly interacting with the ribosome like antibiotics do. Our aim is to rationally design rancRNAs that target the bacterial ribosome as an alternative to traditionally produced antibiotics. This proposes a new strategy not only for targeting the ribosome, but also provides a platform for researchers to develop traditional antibiotic compounds that target ribosomal regions that were previously unidentified. No RNA-based antibiotics exist on the market, meaning bacteria have not evolved resistance mechanisms. This means this class of antibiotic would be viable to treat any type of bacterial infection, no matter if it has developed antibiotic resistances."

column36: Mitochondrial DNA mutation expansion in a cell culture model of intermittent HIV antiretroviral drug exposure
column37: "Do HIV drugs accelerate aging, and how?Around the world, more than 38 million people are now living with HIV. There is no cure for HIV yet, but there are ways to treat it using HIV drugs. While these drugs do a good job fighting HIV, they might also have side effects for the people who take them. People who have HIV seem to get older faster, and this might be because of the drugs. One way this might be happening is that the drugs are affecting mitochondria. Mitochondria, often known as the powerhouse of the cell, contain their own DNA and produce energy needed for the body to function. Changes in DNA are called mutations. If the mitochondrial DNA is damaged and mutated, the mitochondria cannot work properly to make energy and maintain our bodies. These mutations in mitochondrial DNA are thought to be one of the main reasons behind aging and age-related diseases. To see how HIV drugs are affecting mitochondria and their DNA, I will grow cells and expose them to different HIV drugs. My goal is to use a new sequencing method to find and measure mutations in the mitochondrial DNA and to determine if and how HIV drugs are causing mutations to accumulate. Because so many people have HIV, and given that in North America about half of people living with HIV are over 50 years old, it is important to understand if and how HIV drugs might be causing faster aging. Premature aging in this population may have significant implications in terms of quality of life and healthcare costs. My research project could reveal ways in which the drugs are damaging mitochondria. This understanding may lead to improved treatment and better outcomes. Ultimately, my project may help people that have HIV live longer, healthier lives."

column36: Role of neutrophil extracellular traps in primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation
column37: "Neutrophils, which are the main immune cells in the blood, play a significant role in complications associated to human lung transplant. When possible, we also sample lung tissue to be grafted in order to screen for the presence of NETs.Our preliminary data (based on 20 lung recipients, including 4 deaths within 60 days post-procedure) are indicating that NETs play a major role in postoperative complications. The potential benefits of our research can be significant, considering that a treatment already exists to degrade NETs. This treatment (Pulmozyme) is used in cystic fibrosis patients and can readily be available for use in lung transplant patients. In short term, we may have a possible life-saving, secure and low-cost therapeutic approach to help a great number of recipients with severe complications following lung transplant."

column36: Re-evaluating the Regulation of Human Genome Editing in Canada
column37: "Though genome editing has tremendous potential for the treatment of disease, this emerging technology has elicited much concern in the scientific community and the public at large. The speed of modern scientific progress, such as the refinement of genome editing technology, presents a serious challenge for ethicists and policy makers. Given the pace of development of genetic engineering technology, the Canadian health policy and regulatory framework may not adequately regulate its use in humans nor address its potential risks. There are currently no regulations or guidelines specifically addressing somatic genome editing for the purpose of therapy, though gene therapy drugs must comply with the Food and Drug Regulations. Germline genome editing, on the other hand, is criminally banned under the Assisted Human Reproduction Act, despite its therapeutic potential. I propose to study the social and ethical consequences of employing genome editing technology in humans, and the implications for Canadian law and policy. I will first identify the ethical risks of genetic engineering in humans by reviewing the academic literature on both somatic and germline genome editing. I will then look at the legal and regulatory framework in Canada and examine the current laws and policies relevant to this issue, allowing me to identify any gaps in the Canadian framework. Finally, I will compare our framework to that of other countries to gain insight into how our system could be improved. This study will improve our understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the existing regulatory framework. This knowledge will contribute to efforts to improve the framework such that Canadians may benefit from emerging genome editing technologies while being protected from unnecessary risks."

column36: Unraveling a contributing factor in neurodegenerative disease: Investigating the molecular links between mistranslation and neurodegeneration.
column37: " Protein formation and how it folds into its final structure is critical for its normal function. Incorrect folding (misfolding) of proteins and their build up in tissue is characteristic of cancer, metabolic, and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). A protein is made in a sequence of processes known as the ""Central Dogma"": DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA, which is translated into an amino acid (AA) chain that form the protein. Although vital, errors occur in translation, where an incorrect AA is added in the chain (mistranslation). As the sequence of AAs is critical for how a protein folds, and also its function, mistranslation may lead to misfolding and disease. One of the characteristics of AD, as well as other neurodegenerative diseases, is the misfolding and subsequent aggregation (clumping) of the protein tau. Much research has investigated tau aggregation, but the primary trigger is still unknown. The purpose of our research is to investigate whether mistranslation of the tau protein triggers its misfolding and aggregation. We will use human neuron cell models, which will produce tau, and a mutated Methionine aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzyme which is prone to cause mistranslation by incorrectly adding the AA Methionine into protein chains. Further, it has been shown that oxidative stress, which has high levels in AD, causes a similar alteration of this enzyme. If oxidative stress promotes mistranslation of tau proteins, we will see its aggregation in our cells. column36: Examining the feasibility of implementing a multi-component self-management intervention in low-income diabetic adults in a primary setting
column37: "Globally, type 2 diabetes (T2D) is an increasingly prevalent chronic disease requiring frequent medical attention and devoted self-management. To prevent T2D complications, multi-component interventions incorporating technology have emerged as low-cost, easily accessible alternatives to traditional T2D treatments. Recently, financial health incentives have been successful in health behaviour interventions, especially in low income adult populations. The effects of an incentivized multi-component T2D self-management intervention has yet to be examined in among lower income adults living with T2D.The purpose of the study is to determine whether an incentivized, multi-component T2D self-management intervention is feasible in low income, type 2 diabetic adults. It is hypothesized that an incentivized, multi-component T2D management intervention will be feasible (high recruitment, retention and acceptability) in low income, T2D adults. This will be a 13-week (pre/post) single cohort study using a T2D patient population at a health clinic. Participants will track step count using smartphone accelerometers and blood glucose with a wearable monitor; the data will be uploaded to respected tracking apps. Participants will be given personalized aerobic and resistance training prescriptions and asked to track two blood glucose readings per day. Lottery-based incentives will be used to increase bi-weekly clinic appointment attendance. The first week will serve as a baseline measurement pre-intervention, followed by a 12-week intervention. 13 weeks post-intervention, participant recruitment, retention rates, and intervention acceptability will be assessed. Secondary outcomes will assess weekly mean daily blood glucose levels and step counts, analysed with an independent t-test."

column36: Sex Differences in Canadians Living with Dementia in Urban and Rural Areas
column37: "As the Canadian population ages, challenges have emerged with the quality and utilization of healthcare services for the most vulnerable populations of older adults, namely in persons living with dementia. These challenges may worsen when we consider the inequalities faced by elderly women. An unfortunate trend in sex differences has arisen among older adult women, where they are more disadvantaged compared to older men when seeking and receiving treatment. Moreover, previous research has shown that older adults living in rural areas have more difficulties accessing healthcare compared to older adults in urban regions. There is a critical knowledge gap on the interplay between sex and rurality as it relates to dementia care. It is crucial to fill this gap to identify pitfalls in service provision and secure necessary and ideal health services for patients with dementia. We will use a cross sectional design to examine health service use data (emergency visits, hospitalizations and long-term care admissions) of patients aged 65+ with dementia in a Quebec administrative database (near-exhaustive repository of health surveillance information). We will specifically look at how sex and rurality synergistically impact health service use for these patients. Addressing the gaps in the utilization of health services in men and women living with dementia in rural and urban settings will inform decision-makers for the implementation of policies associated with health care provision to promote equity in dementia care and ultimately improve the health among men and women with dementia."

column36: "Evaluating the inter-rater reliability of HEARTSMAP-U, a psychosocial self-assessment and guidance tool for post-secondary students."
column37: "Young adults in post-secondary education often experience mental health concerns that go undetected and untreated. They are also among the patients most likely to benefit from the increasing integration of digital technologies (such as smart phone apps) into mental health assessments, diagnosis, and treatment: young adults report a preference for self-administered assessments over face-to-face disclosure, and also value the sense of control over managing their well-being. However, digital health tools are rarely used in post-secondary health systems, where the vast majority of students are aged 24 years or younger - the age at which people are most at risk of developing a mental health condition. To address this gap, we developed HEARTSMAP-U, a digital psychosocial assessment and guidance tool aimed at improving students' ability to self-identify their need for mental health treatment, and to connect them with timely care. Students answer questions across ten categories and the answers are processed by an algorithm, which then recommends local health services and suggests a time frame in which they should be accessed. In my project, I aim to evaluate whether HEARTSMAP-U is used similarly regardless of the individual providing the input (this is called inter-rater reliability). In my experiment, which is split into two stages, 39 participants will assess a set of 25 fictional vignettes describing varying degrees of mental health concerns and enter the assessment data into HEARTSMAP-U. We expect to see substantial inter-rater agreement as shown through various statistics. The results of this study are crucial for validating HEARTSMAP-U, and broadly implementing this tool for use in post-secondary populations."

column36: The impact of whole cannabis smoke exposure on immune and transcriptomic profiles of human bronchial epithelial cells ? a cannabis strain comparison study
column37: "We are exposed to pathogens in the air around us everyday yet, we rarely exhibits symptoms of infection. Epithelial cells in a person's lungs function as the primary defence against invading pathogens. It is well known that tobacco smoke impairs the efficacy of this crucial defence line. However, despite the recent legalization and increasing usage of cannabis joints and cannabis-based products in Canada, very little is known about its immunological effects on epithelial cells in the bronchi. Our proposed study will assess the impact of smoking three distinct, commercially available cannabis strains on human bronchial epithelial cells from patient donors in response to a viral mimetic, poly I:C. We will first use a new 3D printed smoke-exposure model developed in our lab to expose cells to smoke from three strains - Purple Sun God, Terra and Equalize - each with different levels of THC and CBD. We will then measure inflammatory agents (IL-6, IL-8), antiviral agents (IP-10, RANTES) and epithelial barrier function in response to a viral stimulus. Proper triggered release/action of these measured parameters are otherwise vital to a healthy functioning lung immune system. However, we hypothesize that cannabis smoke will increase inflammation, decrease antiviral agents and impair epithelial barrier function skewing the delicate equilibrium and leaving us prone to invaders. Finally, we also seek to elucidate the specific molecular pathway(s) through which cannabis impacts epithelial cells to provide the basis for future studies to identify potential drug targets to mitigate against its effects. We hope that our study will provide insight to guide responsible use in consumers, effective policy development by governments and standards of cultivation in commercial entities. "

column36: Relation between hemodynamic and cerebral parameter of dextro-transposition of the great arteries (dTGA) neonates.
column37: "The dextro-transposition of the great arteries (dTGA) condition is characterized by an inversion between the aorta and the pulmonary artery connected to the ventricle. This malformation leads to independent systemic and pulmonary circulation. Oxygenated blood can only circulate through two specific canals present in the prenatal period: the foramen oval (FO), allowing communication between atriums, and the ductus arteriosus, allowing communication between the pulmonary arteria and the aorta. Those physiologic changes are creating an abnormal distribution of the oxygenated blood. The balloon atrial septostomy (BAS) procedure is often performed in newborn with dTGA to create an opening between the two atriums. That procedure allows the mixture of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and results in a better oxygenation of the brain. Subsequently, the arterial switch surgical operation (ASO) is accomplished and, after a transitional time, hemodynamic parameters normalize. Newborns with dTGA suffer from hypoxia during the intra-uterine and preoperative period. This systemic hypoxic state might lead to neurodevelopment problems including motor dysfunction, dysphasia and learning problems. We hypothesize that characterizing the relationship between foetal hemodynamics and neonatal cerebral hemodynamics and metabolism remains critical to understand neurodevelopmental outcome associated with dTGA. AIM 1. Assess foetal hemodynamics via echocardiographic examination during the foetal period and assess its ability to predict neonatal outcome on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). AIM 2. Assess CMRO2 via advanced near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) during the transitioning physiology and postnatal period and assess its ability to predict neonatal outcome on preoperative MRI."

column36: Elucidation of the Signaling Pathways involved in Human Cerebral Cavernous Malformations for the purpose of Therapeutics
column37: "Cerebral Cavernous Malformations (CCMs) are recurrent malformations (lesions) of the brain and spinal cord caused by leaking blood vessels. CCMs have symptoms that mimic neurodegeneration, and predisposes patients to a lifetime risk of stroke and epilepsy. The only available treatment is brain surgery to remove the lesion, but this is high risk and sometimes impossible if the lesions are deeper in the brain, which highlights a need for new treatments that are more effective, lower risk, and potentially preventative. Loss-of-function mutations in the CCM1, CCM2, and CCM3 genes are responsible for the condition, with CCM3 being the most severe: lesions that are both more numerous and larger in size. My primary objective to investigate the reason behind why the CCM3 condition is so much more severe than CCM1/CCM2 by determining the differences between their functions, which can be achieved by identifying the genes that function in the CCM3 pathways, independently of the CCM1/CCM2. To accomplish this, I propose using mutagenesis to look for genetic changes that are capable of either mimicking or suppressing the CCM condition caused by CCM3 loss-of-function. DNA sequencing will identify the genes that were mutated, and yield a list of genes involved in the CCM3 condition. This list represents new therapeutic approaches for drug discovery and/or synthesis specific to the CCM3 condition that should prevent the lesions from forming altogether, and have the benefit of being much lower risk than brain surgery."
