column36: Beat-by-beat neurovascular transduction in individuals with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
column37: "Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a hormonal irregularity experienced by many reproductive-aged women. It is associated with many health consequences including an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. A PCOS diagnosis involves two of the following features: an irregular menstrual cycle, higher levels of testosterone, and ovarian cysts. However, the specific mechanisms responsible for the elevated cardiovascular disease risk in this population have yet to be established therefore limiting the effectiveness of current preventative measures and treatment options. Changes in the function of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS), commonly referred to as the body's ""fight or flight"" system, have been suggested as a potential mechanism that influences cardiovascular regulation. In response to activation of the SNS, the body's blood vessels narrow in diameter which results in increases in blood pressure (BP). Typically, the greater the increase in BP in response to a given input of sympathetic activity, the greater the degree of cardiovascular disease risk. The translation of SNS activity into changes in BP is termed neurovascular transduction. Preliminary evidence has suggested that neurovascular transduction may be elevated in women with PCOS although this has yet to be demonstrated under resting conditions. Thus, this study aims to quantify neurovascular transduction in individuals with PCOS at rest and to compare these responses to healthy individuals. If neurovascular transduction is enhanced in PCOS, this could explain the increased cardiovascular risk factors present in this group of women. Consequently, this would result in better informed treatment options such as those that target the SNS in order to reduce cardiovascular risk factors in this population."

column36: Supplementing Arginine and Citrulline to Parenteral Nutrition to Enhance Intestinal Recovery
column37: "Parenteral feeding is a means by which nutrients are delivered directly to the blood via intravenous infusion and is necessary when infants cannot tolerate oral feedings. Although lifesaving, prolonged parenteral nutrition leads to reduced blood flow to the gut, gut atrophy and reduced protein synthesis. The smaller atrophied gut reduces intestinal synthesis of arginine, a key amino acid required for regulation of blood flow via nitric oxide production, protein synthesis and creatine synthesis. Our goal is to increase arginine availability, which will enhance blood flow to the gut, thereby preventing gut atrophy and increasing protein synthesis and growth. However, supplemental arginine is rapidly broken down by the liver and not available to the rest of the body. Therefore, we propose to use supplemental citrulline, the precursor to arginine, as an alternative means of increasing arginine availability. Unlike arginine, citrulline bypasses breakdown by the liver, thereby enhancing arginine availability to a greater extent than arginine supplementation. The objective of the study is to improve arginine availability via supplemental citrulline, a novel ingredient for parenteral nutrition solutions. A miniature Yucatan piglet model is used as a model for the human infant to investigate the clinical outcomes of parenteral nutrition. The results from the study will aid in optimizing a parenteral feeding regimen that will meet all nutritional needs while minimizing the current repercussions related to parenteral feeding. "

column36: Analysis of Maternal Immune Profiles in Perinatal Depression with Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRI) Exposure
column37: "Approximately 15% of women are diagnosed with perinatal depression (PND), a subtype of major depressive disorder (MDD), that can occur during pregnancy or within the first year after birth. Mechanisms underlying perinatal susceptibility to depression are currently unknown, but recent research indicates inflammation may play an important role. In both pregnancy and depression, increases in immune inflammatory markers diminish with effective selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) treatment of MDD. Ineffective SSRI treatment, where there are persistent depressive symptoms, coincides with elevated inflammation. However, no clinical studies examining depression or SSRI impacts on immune profiles have been completed in the perinatal period. To fill this gap, this study will use maternal blood samples obtained from a CIHR-funded longitudinal study examining prenatal maternal mood and SSRI exposure and infant development (Oberlander PI). Pregnancy blood samples were obtained from 3 groups of women: depressed with (1) and without (2) SSRI treatment, and healthy controls (3). Electrochemiluminescence will be used to measure blood immune markers. Both individual marker levels and immune marker networks will be assessed in relation to group. We hypothesize that the depressed without SSRIs group (2) will have higher levels of inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, TNF?, and IL-1?. Secondarily, the group with SSRI treatment (1) is expected to show attenuation of these pro-inflammatory cytokines in relation to positive maternal mood scores, as reported at various times in pregnancy and after birth. Exploring the relationships between maternal immune factors, PND and SSRI exposure may uncover the mechanisms that contribute to perinatal depression."

column36: Pulmonary Vascular Fibroblasts As Key Drivers Of Vascular Remodeling in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
column37: " Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a clinical syndrome defined by elevated pressure in the pulmonary arteries. A subset of PH, termed pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), is a disease localized to the lung vasculature. PAH is characterized by remodelling and immunological infiltration within the pulmonary vasculature, often leading to right-sided heart failure. Although a relatively rare condition, the problems associated with PAH can lead to 5-year mortality rates as high as 60%. Available therapies focus on pulmonary vasodilation, and while useful, these drugs have not yielded the benefits that were initially desired. As such, researchers are investigating other therapeutic modalities, focusing primarily on the immunological aspects of this disease. My project seeks to further investigate the immunological problems associated with PAH. Fibroblasts, a major cell type found in the outer layer of the pulmonary vessels, are known to be dysfunctional in many forms of PAH. It is believed that these cells are responsible for the recruitment of inflammatory molecules and immune cells to the vessel wall in PAH. My project will involve investigating the response of these fibroblasts to high-mobility group box-1 (HMGB1), an important signalling molecule known to propagate many inflammatory responses in the body. I hypothesize that this molecule is highly important in contributing to fibroblast dysfunction and pulmonary vasculature inflammation in PAH. If successful, this project will help define HMGB1 as an early driver of vascular fibroblast dysfunction in PAH. Such work would help deepen our understanding of the pathogenesis of this disease, and point to potential therapeutic targets (HMGB1, fibroblasts) in the treatment of this life-limiting condition. "

column36: The recruitment of SLX4 to branched DNA intermediates for genome stability
column37: "DNA is the single most important component in our cells as it contains all the information necessary for survival. However, it is constantly under attack from DNA damaging agents that come from both the inside and outside of the cell. This can lead to mutations and ultimately, cancer if left unrepaired. As such, cells have developed ways to repair this damage efficiently which involve proteins that cut DNA depending on its structure. The SMX complex is a complex made up of three of these DNA cutters. This complex is involved in DNA repair but how it finds damaged DNA remains unknown. Interestingly, BRCA1 may be a possible recruiter of the SMX complex to damaged DNA due to its shared involvement in DNA repair. BRCA1 is a well-studied protein often mutated in breast cancer and functions in recognizing broken DNA and recruiting other repair proteins which fix the damage. As such, BRCA1 could act as a guide for the SMX complex to locate damaged DNA to be repaired.Therefore, we aim to determine if these two proteins interact and if so, what allows this interaction to take place. Investigating the BRCA1-SMX complex interaction will improve our understanding of DNA repair, an essential process to maintain healthy cells and prevent disease progression. In addition, mutations in a component of the SMX complex leads to Fanconi anemia, a disease in which patients have bone marrow failure and a predisposition to cancer. Hence, studying this complex could provide clues as to how this disease arises and most importantly, how to prevent it."

column36: "Application of magnetic resonance imaging for the detection of changes in working memory, executive function and flow velocity post carotid artery revascularization in carotid stenosis"
column37: "My proposed research aims to demonstrate the utility of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) technologies to objectively detect changes in working memory, executive function and blood flow velocity post carotid artery revascularization for treatment of carotid stenosis. MRI is a non-invasive imaging technology that allows precise and direct monitoring of brain structure, activation and blood flow changes in brain vasculature. In carotid stenosis, blockage of the carotid arteries leads to decreased blood supply to the brain. It is a major risk factor for stroke and often results in substantial impairments in working memory and executive function. As part of standard clinical care, carotid stenosis is treated by stenting to open the blocked artery. <span style=text-decoration: underline;>However, the effect of the treatment procedure on cerebral perfusion, working memory and executive function is neither well understood nor evaluated at point of care. Previous research studies have relied on only paper-based cognitive tests to quantify the cognitive impact without direct measure of brain activity. To study the problem, patients with carotid stenosis scheduled for stenting will be recruited for research at three time points: baseline before treatment and 2 months and 4 months' post-stent. At each research appointment, patients will have an MRI scan which will measure brain activation during a working memory task, blood flow velocity and perfusion. Brain images before and after treatment will be compared to measure changes in arising from the procedure. The significance of this study lies in 1) Application of multimodal MRI to objectively detect the effect of the clinical procedure in helping patient's brain function; 2) Collaboration with clinicians such that results have great potential to inform clinical care. "

column36: Understanding how Patients with Kidney Failure and their Family Caregivers make Decisions to seek Acute Care Services
column37: " The number of individuals with kidney failure, a complex chronic condition that requires dialysis treatment to continue life, is increasing in Canada. I will explore these experiences to gain a broader understanding of why patients seek emergency care, and the extent to which this care was perceived as avoidable, from both the patient and provider perspectives. These findings will be used to create a foundation of knowledge that can reduce acute care use for potentially avoidable reasons, inform future health services research interventions, and improve patient outcomes and quality of life."

column36: The identification of novel anthelmintic compounds through natural product drug discovery
column37: "Helminths are parasitic worms that infect approximately one quarter of the world's human population. They cause a variety of debilitating diseases called helminthiases that result in long-term health defects if left untreated. This problem is exacerbated by a scarcity of available anthelmintic drugs and inadequate research in the field of novel drug discovery. Resistance to anthelmintics has also been increasing due to their overuse and misuse, which further threatens the effectiveness of the already limited arsenal of therapeutics. Due to the severity and prevalence of these conditions, research efforts targeted towards the discovery of new anthelmintic drugs should be prioritized. One field of study that has been particularly successful in the past is looking for naturally-produced compounds, such as those from bacteria and fungi, that can be optimized to treat infection. Since parasitic worms have complex life cycles, we use Caenorhabditis elegans, a non-parasitic nematode model for helminths, to help identify natural products that can kill, paralyze, or delay the development of worms. The purpose of this study is to purify the bioactive compounds and fully characterize their activity against C. elegans. This work could uncover novel anthelmintic drugs that may be used to treat parasitic worm infections and improve global human health."

column36: Home-based prehabilitation enhanced with telecare for patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)
column37: " Occurrence of aortic valve stenosis (AS), caused by the narrowing of the aortic heart valve and results in decreased and inefficient delivery of blood, widely impacts the Canadian geriatric population as a result of calcium buildup in the aortic valve cusps. Without intervention, the mortality rates of patients approach 50% within two years. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is an effective treatment that lowers mortality rates by replacing a diseased valve with a bioprosthetic one. Limited research has investigated safe and individualized exercise recommendations in benefiting the functional status of severe AS patients. This study will fill the gap in the literature with the prescription of safe exercises, such as aerobic, resistance, and balance training, as patients await TAVI. The purpose of this study is to examine the effect of a 12-week home-based preoperative rehabilitation or prehabilitation exercise intervention, enhanced with Medly (a telecare mobile platform) and several Bluetooth-enabled devices for physiological measurements, on functional status and frailty of 25 participants. Conversely, another 25 participants in the control group will receive ""usual care"" with no routine exercise guidelines. Findings from this study may lead to changes in standard of care for patients awaiting TAVI. Typically, these patients are provided little to no instruction on health maintenance as they are told to stay active as tolerable."" Helping patients find an individualized exercise plan during this transition period is in the patients' best interests. Furthermore, findings related to exercise in valvular patients could be generalized to other cardiac patient populations by optimizing postoperative recovery and facilitate a healthy lifestyle. "

column36: Development and Adaptation of the OPAL Application for people living with HIV
column37: "Background: People living with HIV (PLWH) face daily challenges affecting their overall quality of life and care. These burdens can be managed with the implementation and use of a patient portal, but none are currently available for HIV care. column36: Cognitive Flexibility in the Face of Stress: A Two-Week Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
column37: "Cognitive flexibility is a transdiagnostic factor that has been implicated in a variety of mental health and behavioral disorders. Indeed, research suggests that interventions targeting deficits in cognitive flexibility may potentially be useful in ameliorating depressive symptoms and various high-risk behaviors (i.e., disordered eating, suicide, and substance use). Much of this research, however, is conducted in controlled laboratory settings, which may limit generalizability particularly in situations involving idiosyncratic stressors and emotional pain. In hopes to address this gap within the literature, this study aims to investigate the association between cognitive flexibility, mental well-being (i.e., depressive & anxiety symptoms), and self-destructive urges and behaviours (i.e., suicidal ideation and attempts, non-suicidal self-injury, disordered eating, & substance use) in the context of idiosyncratic daily stressors over the course of two-weeks using ecological momentary assessment. It is hypothesized that cognitive flexibility will be negatively associated with the aforementioned outcomes of mental well-being and self-destructive urges and behaviours. Moreover, it is also hypothesized that cognitive flexibility will moderate the relations between daily stressors and (1) mental well-being, and (2) self-destructive urges and behaviours—such that daily stressors will be more strongly associated with these outcomes among those with low cognitive flexibility compared to those with high cognitive flexibility. The findings of this study may contribute to the development of more cost-effective, efficacious, and time-sensitive interventions for the prevention and treatment of the aforementioned outcomes. "

column36: Assessing the role of neural stem and progenitor cells in the brain following stroke
column37: "Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability in Canada due to a lack of effective treatments available for stroke patients. The brain has its own endogenous mechanisms to try to promote recovery after stroke. Specifically, neural stem cells are known to migrate in the brain to the site of stroke and become astrocytes, a neuro-supportive cell. Work in our lab has recently identified first evidence of a previously unreported response of stem cells migrating to the site of stroke and taking up a neuronal fate. We show that identifying this neuronal-fated population is specific to labelling stem cells after stroke, whereas labelling stem cells before stroke identifies the astrocyte-fated stem cells. The goal of this proposal is to determine if generation of neurons after stroke is due to either intrinsic cellular mechanisms and/or extrinsic environmental niche factors. To identify if different populations of cells are being labelled after stroke, the cells labelled will be assessed at the RNA level using a tool known as single cell RNA sequencing. Too, this tool will allow for assessing if cells labelled after stroke have different gene expression patterns and differences in transitioning between cell states. Additional work is being performed to understand the role of extrinsic cues by transplanting the stem cells labelled after stroke into naïve mice and assessing if these cells will maintain a neuronal fate when a stroke is induced following transplant. This ongoing research comes together to provide new insight into the contribution of neural stem cells in the brain following stroke and opens the door for new studies aimed at harnessing neurogenesis to promote recovery after stroke."

column36: Neurovascular Unit for Studying Alzheimer's Disease
column37: "Alzheimer's Disease is a neurodegenerative disease which affects everyone it touches. To date, animal models have been unsuccessful in replicating Alzheimer's disease based on the physiological difference between humans and animals [1]. This is why there is an abundance of research in the field of modelling Alzheimer's Disease using new methods. In order to mimic the native environment of Alzheimer's Disease, an initial environment of a healthy blood-brain barrier needs to be developed. We aim to develop a model using a microchannel that will be embedded with a needle and a surrounding liquid. Then, through UV curing of the liquid and removing the needle, we will form a hollow, lumen structure. The gel that we are using will be mixed with cells from the brain (astrocytes, pericytes, neurons) to form the ""brain"", and cells found within the lumen (endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells) will form the ""blood"". Together, we will form a model of the blood-brain barrier. We can validate this model through real-time imaging of the cell-cell interactions, since the structure will be made using a clear, oxygen-permeable material (polydimethylsiloxane). Additionally, we will be able to mimic the native flow environment by using syringe pumps to flow nutrients to the ""brain"" side and through the lumen to the ""blood side. Through step-by-step modelling of Alzheimer's Disease, we hope to identify therapeutic strategies that will help in the clinical advancement of accessible, therapeutic drugs. References [1] F. Q. Zhou et al., ""Lack of human-like extracellular sortilin neuropathology in transgenic Alzheimer's disease model mice and macaques,"" Alzheimer's Res. Ther., vol. 10, no. 1, pp. 1–15, 2018. "

column36: Rapid feedback responses to proprioceptive perturbation in idiopathic dystonia
column37: "Dystonia is a movement disorder associated with painful involuntary muscle contractions and abnormal postures. Although dystonia can affect multiple areas of the body, neck and upper limb regions are most frequently impacted. The cause of dystonia is poorly characterized, however, there is evidence to suggest that abnormal sensory feedback (i.e., information) and processing may play a role. In healthy individuals, the brain utilizes sensory feedback during voluntary movement to ensure that movements are smooth and error-free. This occurs through short and long-latency reflex loops, which use sensory feedback to control muscle activity. It is speculated that in dystonia, abnormal gain (e.g., too much volume) in sensory feedback information may lead to the dystonic painful involuntary contractions, although direct evidence of this is lacking. In the present study we will investigate the role of sensory feedback in dystonia by recording muscle activity (e.g., reflex responses) during arm movements controlled by a robotic exoskeleton called a KINARM. Specifically, reflex responses to unexpected arm movements at rest and during voluntary arm reaching will be examined. It is anticipated that dystonia patients will have heightened reflex responses to applied movements, with the degree of abnormality correlating with the clinical severity of dystonia. The proposed research project will increase our understanding of sensorimotor feedback abnormalities in dystonia. Understanding how sensory feedback contributes to the disorder may assist in identifying novel treatment targets and therapies to improve patient outcomes."

column36: Characterizing the role of ependymal cells in MS pathology and neuroinflammation
column37: "Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive, neurodegenerative disease driven by autoimmune attacks on the brain and spinal cord that result in lesions. No curative MS treatments are available, partially due to a lack of understanding of what causes and perpetuates MS. Recently, researchers have suggested that ependymal cells (E cells) become pathological in MS. There is considerable overlap between other neurological conditions related to E cell dysfunction and MS, yet the role of E cells in MS has not been studied. As such, this project will examine the role of E cells in MS. E cells line the spinal canal and fluid-filled, hollow spaces of the brain, functioning as a border between brain tissue and the fluid. E cells have hair-like projections that ensure that the fluid circulates properly, keeping the brain tissue healthy and the fluid balanced. If this system is broken, toxic factors, including infiltrating immune cells, accumulate within the fluid. We believe that in MS, E cells become dysfunctional due to interactions with toxic factors and/or immune cells accumulating in the fluid. E cell dysfunction may result in reduced fluid flow, exacerbating the accumulation of toxic factors and infiltrating immune cells, which could further perpetuate MS and E cell dysfunction. In this study, we will image brain tissue samples from healthy and MS donors to identify E cell abnormalities and the proximity of immune cells to E cells. We will also test if eliminating E cells influences disease severity in an animal model of MS. Finally, we will examine if E cells are sensitive to mechanisms of cell-death driven by immune cells. This project aims to contribute to a comprehensive understanding of MS progression, which may propel the development of more effective MS treatments."

column36: The Role of the Gut Microbiome in Early Childhood Growth in Zimbabwe
column37: "Stunting, a form of chronic undernutrition which affects 22% of children under 5 years of age worldwide, is associated with reduced childhood survival, impaired development, and ultimately decreased adult economic productivity. Currently, stunting is believed to occur as a result of environmental enteric dysfunction (EED), a clinical disorder of the small intestine. Though this disorder is hypothesized to be the result of excessive exposure to pathogens, the role of the gut microbiome or the native group of microorganisms that live within the intestinal tract, in childhood stunting remains largely unexplored. The main objective of this project is to characterize the composition and function of the fecal microbiome of children from a low-resource setting during the first 18 months of life using an available biobank of stool samples from the SHINE trial (2012-2017) which occurred in two rural districts in Zimbabwe. I hypothesize that the microbiome of stunted children will be enriched in pro-inflammatory organisms, which will be associated with EED and linear growth faltering. Whole metagenome sequencing will be performed on DNA extracts from 141 infant samples from SHINE. The composition and function of the microbiome will be determined using bioinformatic pipelines and additionally, statistical analyses will be performed to determine whether the gut microbiome is independently associated with infant growth, accounting for epidemiologic variables collected during the SHINE trial. The results of this research project will provide key insights into potential relationships between the gut microbiome and early childhood growth, with the hopes that future gut microbiome-targeted interventions may be identified to combat and prevent childhood undernutrition."

column37: " Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and is a major cause of disability worldwide. 4.4 million Canadians were living with symptomatic OA in 2010, which is estimated to have cost Canadians $27.5 billion. My research will investigate the biology of inflammation in patients with knee OA to determine how inflammation is controlled by joint overloading. We will do this by examining the biological changes that happen in the knee lining of patients who are undergoing a surgical procedure that evens out weight-bearing loads across the knee to reduce pain and delay the need for knee replacement. column36: Development and Evaluation of a Knowledge Translation Initiative to Improve Pain Management in Older Adults
column37: "Pain is very frequent in older adults, but it is often undermanaged and undertreated. Although evidence-based pain management approaches and information are well-documented, it takes an average of 17 years for findings to make their way into clinical practice. As a result, patients do not receive the benefits of the research in a timely manner. Traditional methods of knowledge translation (KT) (e.g., brochures) have not been shown to be effective in changing long-standing clinical practices. KT initiatives that capitalize on social media's ability to reach millions of people in relatively short periods of time are showing promising results in bridging this gap. However, there is limited research examining a broader KT initiative for older adults. The primary goal of this study is to implement and evaluate a KT initiative aimed at improving the access to health information for older adults in pain. column36: Impacts of electrical cardioversion on cognitive functions in older adults with atrial fibrillation

column36: Impact on quality of life of alleviating carbohydrate counting for patients with type 1 diabetes using a novel insulin-plus-pramlintide artificial pancreas: a randomized controlled crossover trial
column37: "Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of insulin-producing beta-islet cells in the pancreas, requiring people with Type 1 diabetes to received life-long exogenous supplementation of insulin, either in the form of multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion via a pump. The artificial pancreas is a newly developed therapy for people with diabetes involving a continuous glucose monitor that sends blood glucose information to an algorithm, which subsequently modulates the dose of of insulin a patient receives via their pump.A consequence of diabetes is the loss of amylin, a hormone co-secreted with insulin in the pancreas, responsible for increasing satiety, slowing down gastric emptying, and decreasing glucagon secretion (a hormone responsible for increased blood glucose). Pramlintide is an amylin analog which supplements insulin infusion as a treatment for diabetes.An indispensable requirement for insulin therapy is the need for carbohydrate counting when eating meals, to ensure that a commensurate insulin dose will be dispensed, and will adequately control post-meal blood glucose variations. This practice, however, can be burdensome and have a high risk of inaccuracy.I will conduct a qualitative assessment through questionnaires and interviews of the impact on participants' quality of life of an insulin-and-pramlintide artificial pancreas system that alleviates the need for carbohydrate counting. This project aims to demonstrate the system's efficacy in maintaining good glucose control, all-the-while addressing the concerns raised regarding carbohydrate counting. This will be the first qualitative study run by our lab, a necessary step in making this form of therapy available to patients on a wider scale."

column36: Understanding the mechanisms underlying the progression of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to lung cancer
column37: "Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is an inflammatory lung disease that damages the cells in a patient's airway. Developing COPD increases a person's risk of lung cancer by a factor of two to four, regardless of whether they smoke. The reasons for the increased lung cancer risk of COPD patients are not well understood, and as a result, prevention is difficult. In addition, while immunotherapy is a promising new class of cancer treatments, the roles of immune cells have not been well studied in the context of COPD. Past work in our lab has shown that COPD patients have characteristic changes in the DNA of their airway cells. In particular, we have found that alterations to two genes, PLK4 and p53, are common in both COPD airway cells and lung tumours. Our hypothesis is that these changes vary with COPD severity and, along with the inflammation caused by COPD, promote the onset of lung cancer. To test this hypothesis, we will look at the frequency of PLK4 and p53 alterations in lung tumours in comparison to healthy lung tissue, and investigate whether these changes work together to promote the development of cancer-like traits in lung cell models. We will then determine if these modifications increase the rate of DNA damage over time, which could also heighten cancer risk. Finally, we will use gene activity data to identify the prevalence of different types of immune cells in COPD patient airways, and determine if they are associated with COPD severity. Overall, this project will improve our understanding of the factors that put COPD patients at high risk for lung cancer and provide insight into methods of cancer prevention. It will also expand our knowledge of the role that immune cells play in cancer onset and may contribute to improvements in immunotherapy."

column36: Using a high-throughput biofilm-based assay to identify novel antimicrobials
column37: "Antibiotics have played a pivotal role in the development of modern medicine but are becoming increasingly less effective as a result of antibiotic resistance. Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria develop tools to survive exposure to antibiotics, and the overuse and misuse of antibiotics contributes to the spread of resistance elements through bacterial populations. This makes resistant infections particularly difficult to treat, since drugs in the clinic are often ineffective. This is especially true for pathogens like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium responsible for potentially deadly infections in cystic fibrosis, immunocompromised, and burn wound patients. The aim of my work is to find new molecules that can be optimized and used as antibiotics to treat resistant infections. Historical strategies to uncover new molecules are often unsuccessful and likely to miss promising antibacterial candidates. To overcome these challenges, we are using a novel approach by monitoring the way biofilms, communities of bacteria, react when they are exposed to low concentrations of different molecules. Molecules that have antibacterial activity typically provoke the formation of more biofilm, a stress response, when tested at concentrations too low to kill the cells, providing an excellent proxy for antibacterial activity. Using this ""canary in a coal mine"" approach, we will screen a library of 10 thousand compounds to identify suitable antibiotic candidates, then further optimize these molecules to develop antibiotics to treat infections with P. aeruginosa and other resistant pathogens."

column36: Characterization of the Genetic Landscape of High Grade B-cell Lymphoma to Elucidate Molecular Determinants and Identify Therapeutic Targets
column37: "Lymphoma is the 5th most common form of cancer in North America, with ~130,000 new cases each year in the US. High grade B-cell lymphoma (HGBL) is a particularly aggressive form of lymphoma with low survival rates. Efforts to cure HGBL have been limited to using more intense forms of chemotherapy. This strategy has been largely unsuccessful, curing only 20-40% of patients. Additionally, a consequence of this strategy is that intensified chemotherapy leads to increased toxicity, resulting in frequent hospitalizations, which comes at a significant financial cost. Advances in treatment for HGBL is limited by our poor understanding of the underlying biology of this disease. Additionally, HGBL is distinguished from other types of lymphoma using methods established decades ago. These methods fail to identify the true complexity of the disease. Advances in technology have identified that subtypes of cancer are much more complex than initially thought, with no two cancers being completely identical. This has led to the establishment of ""personalized medicine"", where patients receive treatment specifically aimed at targets unique to their cancer. Through revealing the molecular basis of HGBL, this project aims to identify, prior to treatment, the 60-80% of patients in whom chemotherapy will be ineffective. Within this group, we aim to identify therapeutic targets that are specific to these patients, as well as therapeutic targets that are shared with other forms of lymphoma. Precision medicine is the path to improving the dismal outcomes of patients with HGBL - particularly in those who do not benefit from chemotherapy. This research will ultimately reshape how we define HGBL and guide the development of new drugs and treatment strategies."

column37: "Every year, more and more people are diagnosed with diabetes. Among other consequences, patients with diabetes are at higher risk of having blockages in their heart vessels and, ultimately, a higher risk of having a heart attack. In the general population, angioplasty is usually the best procedure to fix the obstructions in the heart vessels after a heart attack, but we are not sure about patients with diabetes. Patients with diabetes usually have multiple blockages in their heart vessels, which may be treated more comprehensively with open-heart surgery. In fact, preliminary data has shown that open-heart surgery may reduce the chances of dying in patients with diabetes after a heart attack.In our research project, we want to clarify which procedure (angioplasty or open-heart surgery) does better for patients with diabetes who experience a heart attack in Ontario. We will be comparing the rates of death, new heart attacks and brain strokes in these patients, according to the procedure they received. We will be using de-identified data housed by the IC/ES in the last ten years, from patients across the whole province of Ontario. This project will help clinicians and patients to make better-informed decisions when choosing between angioplasty or open-heart surgery in patients with diabetes and a heart attack."

column36: Characterization of Gut Bacteria Associated with Depression in Humans Using Mouse Models
column37: "Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) afflicts 11.3% of Canadians at some point in their lives. Despite devastating social costs and an economic burden of 32.3 billion/year (for all types of depression), current antidepressants lack efficacy in many MDD patients and/or fail to confer long-term remission. Mounting evidence implicates the gut microbiota in MDD pathogenesis. Gut bacteria have been shown impact on diverse neuronal processes in the brain by altering activity of the vagus nerve, releasing neuro-active metabolites (i.e. neurotransmitters such as serotonin), and modulating the neuroimmune system. In MDD patients, the taxonomic composition of the gut microbiota, as well as its metabolic output, differs from healthy controls. The objective of this project is to investigate whether specific gut bacteria positively or negatively correlated with MDD in human patients impact on susceptibility to depression-like behavior in mouse models. To test this, we will colonize germ-free mice, which lack a gut microbiome, with a defined consortium of bacteria +/- single bacteria correlated with MDD. To determine whether bacteria modify susceptibility to depression, we will conduct behavioral tests designed to measure depression-like behavior in mice. We will then use metabolomic and metagenomic techniques to elucidate the mechanisms underlying any observed effects. Our work will provide critical insight into how manipulation of the gut microbiota may provide clinical benefit. By mechanistically defining how specific gut bacteria alter depression susceptibility, we aim to identify targets for novel MDD therapies. Such therapies may involve probiotic administration of ""anti-depressant"" bacteria, elimination of ""pro-depressive"" bacteria, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT)."

column36: A multi-country comparison of household food insecurity in relation to dietary intake
column37: "Food insecurity exists when people have inadequate or insecure access to food due to financial constraints. Youth with T1D on the GF diet who rely on these foods can face abnormal glycemic control (GC). column37: "Vision loss caused by the onset of retinal degeneration is the leading cause of blindness in the industrialized world. While recent advances have been made in stem cell transplantation for vision repair, their effectiveness is limited and these technologies have not yet been translated to the clinic. An attractive alternate strategy is to activate resident stem cells for self-repair. Intriguingly, Müller glia, the major glial cell type in the retina, have stem cell properties in cold-blood vertebrates. However, the regenerative properties of Müller glia are latent in mammals. In fish and frogs, where Müller glia have a natural regenerative response, the first step in Müller glia activation is movement of the cell bodies into the layer where photoreceptors reside. This initiating event for regeneration is poorly understood at the molecular level. We previously found that mammalian Müller glia move in an injury-independent fashion in Phosphatase and tensin homolog (Pten) conditional knock-out retinas. Pten is an important signalling molecule that plays a role in cell survival. My hypothesis is that Pten lies at a critical pathway that blocks mammalian Müller glia from undergoing natural self-repair. To test this hypothesis I will be using biochemical and cellular assays to characterize Müller glia in Pten deleted retinas with and without induced injury. The insights form my work will advance our foundational understanding of retinal disease and direct future therapies for self-repair. Notably, targeting Müller glia for gene therapy can allow us to combat all forms of retinal diseases mediated not only by a loss of photoreceptors (age-related macular degeneration) but also by the loss of interneurons (inherited retinal diseases) and retinal ganglion cells (glaucoma)."

column36: Assessment and Evolution of Concussions in College Student-Athletes

Our data will be collected within an existing concussion management program. Approximately 170 student-athletes aged 17-21 will be included in this research and according to data from 2017-2019, about 30 to 40 of them will suffer a concussion. column36: Measuring the Outcomes of Readiness Assessments in Transgender Healthcare
column37: "The aim of this research is to measure the outcomes of an informed consent model of transgender healthcare. The conventional ""gate-keeper"" model of trans healthcare requires a readiness assessment before commencing medical transition, while an ""informed consent"" model does not. Advocates of the gate-keeper model argue that readiness assessments ensure ethical standards in professional practice while proponents of the informed consent model argue that readiness assessments lead to the paternalization and pathologization of transgender communities. Despite the prevalence of requiring readiness assessment prior to commencing medical transition, there are no published studies which explicitly compare the outcomes of an informed consent model with a gate-keeper model of transgender healthcare. To fill this knowledge gap, I will conduct a comparative analysis of the experiences of clients who accessed hormone replacement therapy (HRT) through clinics operating from each of these different models. The first phase of this study will involve a systematic review of patient health files to determine the length of time accessing services, diversity of health professions who provided care, and cases of regret. The second phase will involve data collection from online surveys about patient and clinician sense of preparedness to commence medical transition As a transgender person and registered social worker, I am well situated to draw upon my community connections and professional experience to complete this project. Moreover, the findings from this research will contribute much-needed data to the debate and allow researchers to quantify the effectiveness and necessity of a requiring mental health assessment in the provision of HRT to transgender and gender non-binary clients."

column37: "Nearly 7 years of a female's life is spent bleeding. This means that women have chronic exposure to sanitary products. However, there are many reusable products that claim not to contain these harmful chemicals, resulting in reduced menstrual pain and bleeding. The objective of this research is to assess these claims and determine if there is a difference in the chemical concentrations present in disposable and reusable products through the use of gas chromatography and capillary electrophoresis, after which concentrations will be compared to safe exposure levels according to the Food and Drug Administration. This research addresses the hypothesis that the concentration of harmful chemicals is greater in disposable than in reusable products and that the use of feminine sanitary products with fewer harmful chemical compounds will have a positive impact on the menstrual cycle by reducing pain and bleeding. column36: Intercellular signaling in the developing liver
column37: "My project focuses on a specialized cells called liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, or LSECs, that line blood vessels. When the liver is just starting to form at early stages of human and mouse development, the LSECs have properties that are very similar to the rest of the blood vessel cells in the body. However, as the liver develops, they develop holes and begin to decrease the amount of structural coating they produce. This results in gaps in and between the LSECs. These gaps are important for liver functions such as nutrient storage and blood detoxification because they allow exchange of molecules between the circulating blood and the liver cells. Although researchers assume that the development of LSECs depends on signalling from neighbouring cells, it is not yet clear what these signals are.For this project I will develop software to process gene expression data from single cells obtained from a developing or evolving tissue and predict which signalling interactions control the cell development. My software will rely on a mathematical model that has been proposed, but not implemented, by a leading computational research group.The signaling interactions can be tested by obtaining the LSECs and their neighbouring cells from developing mice and generating a mini model of the liver in a dish. If the predictions are true, removing the signalling molecules from the neighbours will result in a loss of the gaps between the LSEC cells. We expect that the signaling molecules we uncover will help us better understand liver development. But they could also help us treat disease. This is because the gaps in the LSECs are often closed in diseased liver, and researchers have shown that opening the gaps can lead to reversal of liver damage."

column36: Targeting hepatitis B virus covalently closed circular DNA in vitro and in vivo
column37: "Despite the availability of an effective vaccine, still over 257 million people worldwide are chronically infected with the hepatitis B virus (HBV). The HBV targets specifically liver cells and can cause a persistent (or chronic) infection that can lead to severe liver scarring and liver cancer. HBV related liver complications accounts for over 880,000 deaths annually. HBV's ability to cause chronic infection is due, in part, to its highly stable DNA genome (called cccDNA), which enters and remains in the nucleus of infected liver cells. Once in the nucleus, the cccDNA acts as a ""mini-factory"" to produces new virus particles. There is no cure for chronic HBV infection, and current first line anti-HBV treatments block the virus at later steps, but do not affect the formation or destruction of cccDNA. To achieve a cure, the cccDNA needs to be targeted for elimination. We aim to (1) design a drug to stop the production of new cccDNA particles; (2) characterize the drugs effect on cccDNA production; (3) study the anti-HBV drug in mouse models. To complete these aims we have designed a drug to bind specifically to a region on the cccDNA that is responsible for the production of new cccDNA particles. The drug will be tested in HBV infected liver cells for drug toxicity, efficacy, and markers of HBV replication. To study the drug's ability to target HBV infected liver cells, the drug will be labelled with a marker that can be visualized. Similarly, these marked drugs will be injected into mice models to confirm HBV targeting in the liver using technologies that allow visualization of animal organs. This research will provide insight into new cccDNA targeting approaches which will inform development of an HBV cure to improve health outcomes of chronic HBV infected patients."

column36: Investigation of a vaccine against Cryptosporidium parvum using an attenuated Salmonella vector
column37: "Cryptosporidium parvum is a waterborne human pathogen of significant concern. column37: "Human Immunodeficiency Virus-Type 1 (HIV-1) currently infects over 36 million individuals globally. Although HIV-1 transmission potential and symptoms can be reduced by anti-retroviral therapy (ART), there remains a need for new ARTs to treat those resistant to current treatments. Furthermore, there is no cure for HIV and, therefore, ARTs need to be taken for life. Current and potential ARTs include inhibitors of the proteins encoded by HIV-1. HIV-1 produces an accessory protein called Vpu that helps the virus escape from the human immune system. Our lab has recently demonstrated that Vpu decreases the levels of T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing protein 3 (Tim-3) on the surface of infected cells. Interestingly, Tim-3 has recently been shown to inhibit viral release from the surface of infected cells. Therefore, we believe that Vpu functions to prevent this Tim-3-inhibition of viral release. We have shown that Vpu alters the route of Tim-3 in the cell and keeps it in intracellular compartments, away from the cell surface. However, the full itinerary of Tim-3 in the presence of Vpu has yet to be determined. Furthermore, although Tim-3 is known to affect the activation of T cells, it is unknown how Vpu mediated downregulation of Tim-3 affects T cell activation. Lastly, as Tim-3 is also expressed on the surface of macrophages, we will explore the effect of Vpu on Tim-3 in these cells. This research will provide further insight into the mechanisms used by HIV-1 to evade the human immune system. In addition, targeting the interaction between Vpu and Tim-3 may lead to novel therapeutic strategies to treat infected patients."

column36: Regulation of proliferation and the developmental emergence of adult neural stem cells.
column37: "When the mammalian brain sustains injury acutely or chronically, a significant loss of brain cells can result. In the adult brain, the regenerative capacity to repair and replace these brain cells exists by the activation and recruitment of brain stem cells (BSCs). However, the response of BSCs following injury is short-lived, as most of the new-born brain cells they produce die. BSCs are largely dormant in nature, as they undergo cell division infrequently. Some adult BSCs are derived from radial precursor cells (RPs); the neural stem cells of the embryonic brain. How these BSCs emerge from RPs embryonically is not well understood. Recent studies suggest BSCs emerge developmentally from RPs by entering a 'slow-dividing' state where these cells divide infrequently, allowing them to persist and become BSCs in the adult brain. Furthermore, previous work using a method to sequence the messages which encode for cellular proteins (scRNA-seq) has characterized this transition to the 'slow-dividing' state at the molecular level for the first time. These scRNA-seq data suggest the 'slow-dividing' state is not triggered by factors inside RPs, but may be controlled by outside signals in the stem cell environment. Using these data, a protein known as LRIG1, was identified as a candidate molecule which may control the 'slow-dividing' state of in RPs. We hypothesize that LRIG1 may control how frequently RPs go through cell division and the transition to the 'slow-dividing' state by interacting with receptors at the cell surface, which respond to cues in the cellular environment. Revealing how BSCs emerge developmentally and enter into the 'slow-dividing' state holds much promise to enable strategies designed to produce a robust activation of endogenous BSCs following brain injury."

column37: "Overactive bladder (OAB) syndrome is a condition where unintentional contractions of the bladder cause unwanted urine leakage. column36: Discovery and characterization of CD8+ T cell antigens derived from colorectal cancer oncomicrobes
column37: "Recently, two bacteria that colonize the human intestinal tract, Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) and enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis (ETBF), have been found to be related to the development of colorectal cancer (CRC). Fn is able to invade the cells lining the colon and ETBF secretes a toxin called BFT, which can also enter cells. The entry of these bacteria or toxins into host cells causes various alterations that can lead to cancer. Our immune system is typically able to recognize and combat such bacterial infiltrations through antigens. Proteins within cells are constantly being broken down into fragments called antigens. Antigens can then bind to a protein called MHC I and be presented to the cell surface. CD8+ T cells are immune cells that inspect these MHC I-presented antigens on other cells and discriminate normal antigens from non-self, such as bacterial. Once a foreign antigen is recognized, CD8+ T cells activate and kill the aberrant cell. Cells compromised by Fn invasion or BFT toxin entry, and therefore at risk to become cancerous, possess bacterial antigens that the immune system should respond to. However, it is currently unknown why cells with Fn or BFT are not sufficiently killed by CD8+ T cells in CRC, and whether there are differences in these immune responses between people that develop CRC and those who do not. To address this knowledge gap, we aim to firstly identify MHC I-presented antigens from Fn and BFT. We will then assess which of these identified antigens most frequently lead to CD8+ T cell activation. Lastly, we will assess differences in CD8+ T cell responses to these common antigens between healthy donors and CRC patients. The results of this work will provide information to guide future immune-based CRC interventions, such as vaccines."

column36: "Patterns of follow-up care in frail cancer survivors in Nova Scotia, Canada: A needs-based approach"
column37: "More people are surviving cancer due to better screening and treatment. There is a growing need to tailor the required follow-up care to the unique needs of cancer survivors. This rise in cancer survivors has strained the current cancer care system. Our current model of survivor follow-up care is inefficient as it has been provided by specialists rather than more economical primary care providers. This delivery contrasts evidence that follow-up can be safely done in primary care. Cancer survivors are using more health care resources, yet their needs are not being met. This situation is dire, yet it could worsen as cancer survivors are living longer, and often have multiple other health issues. Related to aging, frailty is a health state described as physical and mental decline, and a decreased ability to overcome stressors. Frail people often receive ineffective care. As Canada's population ages, frailty will become more common in the general population and in cancer survivors. We need to design more personalized ways to deliver follow-up care for the growing population of cancer survivors and target high needs groups, such as those who are frail. The goal of my study is to gather evidence to address this issue. The study will examine patterns of follow-up care use by frail breast, prostate, colon, rectal, or gynaecological cancer survivors in Nova Scotia. Data from the Nova Scotia Cancer Registry will be linked to databases that will help us better understand survivor care needs. This research will address an important gap in our knowledge of health care use by a vulnerable group of cancer survivors, which has not yet been studied, and thereby lay the foundation for designing models of follow-up care that improve quality and reduce strain on the health care system."

column36: Sex-specific effects of chronic stress on neurovascular health: implication for sex differences in depression
column37: "Depression is now considered the leading cause of disability worldwide. This mood disorder is more frequent in women, with prevalence of 11% for men vs 16% for women in Canada. Women report higher levels of stress, the main environmental risk factor to develop depression. Cardiovascular diseases are associated with stress and 50% of stroke survivors become depressed within the next 5 years. Stroke is the 2nd leading cause of death but also, with heart diseases, the main cause of premature death in women. Unfortunately, 30-50% of depressed individuals are unresponsive to common neuron-centered antidepressant treatments and only 30% will completely remit and never experience another depressive episode. This lack of efficacy suggests that causing biological mechanisms, such as vascular dysfunctions, are not appropriately treated. Indeed, we recently reported that chronic social stress fragilizes the blood-brain barrier (BBB) in male mice, promoting infiltration of peripheral immune signals and depressive behaviors.. The BBB represents the ultimate frontier between the brain and harmful circulating immune signals or toxins. Protecting the BBB under stressful conditions represents an innovative therapeutic approach, that has yet to be studied in females. My project will investigate how chronic stress affects BBB function and identify molecular adaptations leading to stress resilience vs depression in a sex-specific manner. I use a multidisciplinary and translational approach combining molecular, morphological, behavioral and human post-mortem samples analysis. It is imperative to study depression not only in a neuron-centric manner and consider sex differences to develop adapted and innovative therapeutic strategies to improve men and women's health in Canada and abroad."

column36: Determining the role of transcription factor Irf5 in regulating microglial transcriptional and cellular activities in the demyelinating brain
column37: "Many patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) end up developing a progressive form of MS that is accompanied by chronic damage to the myelin sheath that promotes neuronal functions. Why progressive MS evolves is still unclear, but studies support a role for deregulated inflammation. Of note, the brain has its own immune cells called microglia. However, why deregulated microglial inflammation arises in MS is not well understood.My preliminary data shows that in microglia that are present at sites of myelin damage, a regulator of expression of inflammatory genes called Irf5 appears to be highly active. Notably, in lesions in other tissues, high activity of Irf5 in immune cells consistently impairs the tissue repair process. Therefore, for my Master's project I propose to investigate how Irf5 regulates the inflammatory activity of microglia in a mouse model of MS, in which Irf5 is specifically inhibited in microglial cells. I will first determine the impact of microglial Irf5 activity to the overall burden of brain lesions using high-end techniques in microscopy. Second, I will define the exact role of Irf5 in regulating microglial inflammatory activity. To achieve this, I will leverage techniques in massively parallel DNA sequencing, including ChIP-seq and RNA-seq, to uncover the epigenetic and transcriptional gene programs modulated by Irf5 that underlie microglial cell activity.Overall, this work will provide highly precise knowledge into the mechanisms that regulate damaging microglia activity in brain lesions associated with MS. As such, it will pave the way for novel therapeutic strategies for MS aimed at restricting microglial inflammatory activity and/or recalibrating the functions of these cells towards pro-repair."

column36: The impact of intestinal microbial colonization during pregnancy on Type 1 Diabetes development in the offspring
column37: "Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease with increasing incidence worldwide. Its connection to microbiota has recently been recognized. In fact, although fetal development occurs in a sterile environment, a mother's microbiota during pregnancy can influence the developing immune system of their children. Certain bacterial strains, found in children less susceptible to T1D, protected genetically pre-disposed non-obese diabetic (NOD) mice from developing T1D. I will study the effects of transient intestinal colonization of pregnant mice with Bacteroides dorei on the incidence of T1D in the offspring. I aim to generate a B. dorei strain which cannot replicate in vivo without supplementation of D-alanine and Meso-diaminopimelic acid. I will orally administer this B. dorei to germ-free, pregnant NOD mice and follow T1D incidence in the offspring by measuring weekly blood glucose levels. I hypothesize that transient B. dorei colonization of the mothers will lead to a decreased incidence of T1D in the offspring, due to the transfer of bacterial products that shape the developing immune system and thus protect the offspring from developing T1D. I will characterize the immune cell profile and bacterial metabolite profile of the offspring to determine the outputs of bacterial product exposure in utero. One challenge with T1D is that there are multiple genetic and environmental factors, making it difficult to characterize which microbial species are essential for shaping the immune system. Using gnotobiotic (known colonization status) and germ-free animals, we can determine keystone species with protective effects against T1D development, which will inform us how to maintain or modify a mother's gut microbiota during pregnancy to support the health of their children."

column36: Exploring responsive behaviours during breast- and bottle-feeding of human milk.
column37: "Human milk is the optimal food for infants, and the World Health Organization recommends breastfeeding for the first 6 months. Bottle feeding pumped human milk and breastfeeding are typically considered the same, however recent research has shown differences between the two methods. Breastfeeding mothers tend to be more aware of their infant's signs of hunger and satiation (fullness), allowing the infant frater control during the feed. This is referred to as responsive feeding, which allows the infant to control the feed and teaches them to listen to their own hunger cues, a skill that can shape a child's relationship with food from childhood into adulthood (e.g. poor self-regulation or eating in the absence of hunger). Conversely, feeding from the bottle provides caregivers with visual cues of intake, as well as more control over the timing and duration of the feed For my proposed MSc research, I will assess responsive feeding among a cohort of n=62 women who exclusively feed their infants human milk, but both from the breast and from a bottle. First, I will video-record feeding sessions in order to observe signs of responsive feeding during both bottle- and breastfeeding, including mutual eye contact, gentle rocking, and ignoring distractions. I will also score videos with the validated Nursing Child Assessment Satellite Training (NCAST) Caregiver/Parent-Child Interaction Feeding Scale. This information will help us understand typical similarities and/or differences in behaviours between bottle- and breastfeeding, in hopes of informing future educational materials for health care professionals and families, aiming to increase rates of breastfeeding, and responsive bottle- and breastfeeding, in the Halifax Regional Municipality, Move Scotia. "

column36: Exploring patient perspectives regarding dysphagia following critical illness and artificial airway use
column37: "Many Canadians become critically ill and require breathing tubes and machines for long periods ( 48h) in order to stay alive. Dysphagia (difficulties swallowing) occurs in most of these cases and if untreated, can lead to complications including death. For some patients, dysphagia treatment often requires that they cannot have anything to eat or drink, receiving their nutrition/hydration from tubes. For others, treatment involves changes to their food and/or drink, making it easier for them to swallow. These treatments are often required for weeks, months or even years. Given that eating and drinking are essential for both physical and psychosocial well-being, being restricted from doing so can affect one's quality of life. Understanding patients' perspectives regarding their care and involving them in determining research priorities improves outcomes. To date no research has explored patients' perspectives of dysphagia and its impacts after critical illness and artificial airway use. This study is the first time that these patients' perspectives and related priorities will be investigated in hospitals and a rehabilitation program. Patient interviews will provide data for qualitative analysis, in particular the impacts of dysphagia, patients' opinions of assessment and treatment, and goals for future research. We will explore these data according to sex, setting, and other medical data. Our findings will help give insight on patients' lived experience as well as their needs and priority areas for research. In the long term, this will contribute to identifying ways in which dysphagia can be better managed by care providers, ultimately improving outcomes while reducing care costs. "

column37: "Background:. In Type 1 Diabetes (T1D), the insulin producing beta cells are destroyed by the patient's own immune cells, rendering them unable to regulate blood glucose. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) normally prevent this autoimmune attack, but T1D patients are thought to have dysfunctional Tregs. Mouse models have shown polyclonal Tregs can delay and reverse diabetes, but giving large numbers of non-specific Tregs risks immune suppression. Therefore, a more efficient system would be to infuse Tregs that can specifically prevent beta cell attack. However, naturally-occurring, specific Tregs in blood are rare and so it is difficult to isolate and expand them for infusion. Objectives:. My project aims to engineer specific Tregs by utilizing Chimeric Antigen Receptors (CARs). CARs are derived from high affinity antibodies and when expressed on the cell surface can re-direct T cell specificity. I aim to create CAR-Tregs to use as a therapy for T1D. Aim 1: Generate and validate CARs specific for molecules relevant to T1D. Aim 2: Generate T1D-relevant CAR-Tregs and test their function in vitro. Aim 3: Test if infusion of CAR-Tregs into T1D-prone mice can delay diabetes progression. Methods:. 1. Use molecular biology methods to clone and express new T1D-relevant CARs and flow cytometry to test for their specificity. 2. Use retrovirus to genetically modify Tregs so they express CARs, then cellular immunology assays to test CAR-stimulated proliferation and suppression. Both relevant and irrelevant CAR stimuli will be tested to determine whether activation and suppression occurs in an antigen dependent manner. 3. Infusion of CAR-Tregs into mice using a diabetic mouse model. The mice will be injected with CAR-Tregs and blood glucose will be monitored over several weeks. "

column36: Development of a deep learning algorithm to predict disability progression in progressive multiple sclerosis using baseline clinical information and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain.
column37: "Multiple sclerosis is a neurological disease thought to be caused by the immune system attacking the protective covering around neurons (myelin). Some patients have a type of disease that progresses continuously, called progressive multiple sclerosis (PMS). Only one drug, ocrelizumab, has been approved in Canada to treat PMS, and its effect is unfortunately modest. There is therefore a need to facilitate drug development for PMS. A major bottleneck occurs in phase 2 clinical trials, where a drug's effect must be demonstrated in a very short time-frame (12 to 24 months) in order to be taken to the next phases where it is tested on larger groups of patients. Phase 2 efficiency could be improved by including more patients who are predicted to progress rapidly, but making this prediction has been difficult. Deep learning is a state-of-the-art method in the field of artificial intelligence that can learn complex patterns in data in order to make predictions. We hypothesize that it can predict if a patient with PMS will progress in the time allotted to a phase 2 clinical trial. We will design a deep learning algorithm that uses a patient's baseline clinical information and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to predict progression over 1 year. It will learn to make this prediction from a large database pertaining to 2,724 patients with PMS that was acquired through 4 clinical trials. Once optimized, we will compare our algorithm's prediction accuracy to existing markers of disease progression such as brain volume loss. If successful, this algorithm has the potential to not only improve drug development efficiency, but also to pave the path to precision medicine, where physicians could predict the future course of an individual patient's disease and adjust treatment accordingly."

column36: Understanding the Role of Inflammatory Cytokine Biomarkers in Sight-Threatening Complications of Retinal Detachment
column37: "Retinal detachment is a serious eye disease affecting approximately 1 in every 10,000 people per year and may lead to blindness if left untreated. Although ophthalmologists can successfully repair most retinal detachments, some patients may experience vision impairment postoperatively as a result of complications such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (scar tissue in the retina), epiretinal membrane (scar tissue in the centre of vision), and cystoid macular edema (swelling and inflammation in the centre of vision). Currently, little is known about these postoperative vision threatening inflammatory diseases, which makes them difficult to treat. The purpose of this research study is to determine the impact of inflammatory biomarkers known as cytokines on development of vision impairment. Additionally, our goal is to study means of using cytokine biomarkers early in the disease process to predict which patients will go on to develop complications in their disease course. Samples of ocular fluid are routinely obtained as standard of care during a retinal detachment repair. In this study, the collected samples of ocular fluid will be studied closely to search for presence and expression level of various cytokine biomarkers. Technologically advanced ophthalmic imaging machines that evaluate microstructural pathologies inside the eye will also be used to assist in determining which eyes have disease and how the disease is progressing over time. A better understanding of cytokine biomarkers and outcomes of patients with retinal detachment will enable researchers and clinicians to develop improved treatment options that target those affected earlier than has been possible before and ultimately decrease the burden of vision loss."

column36: Neurophysiological processes underlying the effects of a newly developed treatment for spatial neglect in healthy young adults
column37: "Spatial neglect is a common debilitating attention disorder that prevents stroke survivors from attending to the left side of their body or of their environment. Peg-the-Mole (PTM) is a newly developed home-based, game-like experimental treatment for spatial neglect. PTM uses the principles of prism adaptation (PA) - an experimental treatment that requires individuals to wear rightward-shifting prism goggles while completing a visuomotor task. Following the removal of the goggles, the brain overcompensates for the rightward shift in vision and allows individuals to reorient their attention to the previously neglected left side of space. PTM has shown equivalent behavioural effects to typical PA protocols. The next step is to explore the underlying neurophysiological mechanisms or brain waves associated with these effects. Furthermore, the effects of this treatment on activities of daily living must be assessed in order to understand its clinical applicability. In the present study, 40 healthy young adults will use PTM with 5-degree or 15-degree shifting goggles while their brain activity is recorded. The 15-degree shifting goggles are expected to induce larger effects on various outcome tasks and the brain waves associated with these effects of different magnitudes will be assessed. Understanding the underlying neural mechanisms associated with the effects induced by PTM as well as the functional generalizability of this experimental treatment will clarify who may benefit from this procedure. These results will also be used to optimize the PTM procedure before its clinical implementation."

column36: Maternity Care in Burns Lake; A Feasibility Analysis
column37: "This research aims to understand what it will take for the northern community of Burns Lake in British Columbia (BC) to re-open maternity services. Burns Lake, a community that falls within the jurisdiction of the Northern Health Authority (NHA), lost its maternity services in 2009. Now, individuals must travel from one to three hours to access maternity care. Longer travel distance to maternity care is associated with worse health outcomes for both childbearing individuals and their infants. In partnership with the NHA, this research project aims to brings maternity services closer to home for residents in Burns Lake. This project seeks to answer the following research questions:1. What are the anticipated barriers for site administrators and health care providers in providing maternity care in Burns Lake?2. What system and structure supports are needed to re-open and sustain maternity services in Burns Lake?In order to understand what it will take to re-open maternity services in Burns Lake, I will conduct interviews and focus groups with health care providers and site administrators. I will also work with key stakeholders in the community, including the First Nations Health Authority. Results from interviews and focus groups will contribute to the development of key recommendations. These recommendations will serve as a tool for implementing maternity services in Burns Lake in the future. This research focuses on building sustainable health care services through collaborating with a rural community, recognizing that rural health services work best when developed to meet needs of a specific community. "

column36: Health System Responsiveness in Circumpolar Indigenous Communities
column37: "Working with Dr. Susan Chatwood, Katherine will be completing an international comparative analysis of health care systems in circumpolar nations where experiences related to remote geographies, indigenous values, and health equity are shared features to which health systems must adapt. This study will be grounded in northern communities and completed with community-based, participatory methods. By working with the University of Alberta, the Institute for Circumpolar Health Research, and members of Northern communities, Katherine will be able to understand the needs of those living in Canada's North, how various health care governance models meet or do not meet those needs, and the health policies in place which most greatly affect Canada's Northern populations. Her thesis will focus on health system responsiveness and what that means to various Indigenous groups. In addition to the communities found in Canada's North, Katherine will study the health care structures of other arctic nations with Indigenous populations. Calls to action have been made prioritizing comparisons with communities that have shared values and contexts; Katherine will be completing her thesis on the similarities and differences between health care models of each nation involved in the study, as well as analyzing which aspects work best for the populations they serve and which need reformation. Through this cooperative approach, a deeper understanding of where policy change can be the most beneficial will emerge. Furthermore, by working with indigenous populations, Katherine's research will aide in reconciliation between the Canadian government and the traditional owners of this land. The role of traditional knowledge and how it can be used to inform health policies will be key to the study."

column36: "Sexualized substance use, sexually transmitted infections, and pre-exposure prophylaxis among men who have sex with men: longitudinal analyses of sexual health clinic attendees in Montr,al"
column37: "In Canada, prevention gaps are such that gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) remain a key population vulnerable to sexually transmitted infections (STI) and HIV. For MSM, the overlapping synergistic epidemic (syndemic) of HIV, STI, and substance use are exacerbating HIV and STI transmission and compromising public health efforts. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), a relatively new and highly effective method of HIV prevention, is now available to high-risk populations. column36: Characterization of meningeal inflammation in progressive multiple sclerosis and correlation to clinical and pathological severity
column37: "Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease of the brain and spinal cord in which the protective covering of the nerves is destroyed due to inflammation. While treatment options exist for the less severe, relapsing form of MS, there has been limited success in modulating the progressive, more severe form of MS. Our failure to effectively treat progressive MS is due to the fact that the molecular signals that drive MS progression remain unclear. Further, although immune cells continue to cause pathology, they reside behind a brain barrier that is largely intact and prevents the entry of drugs. I propose that the meninges - the membranous, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) filled lining of the brain - contain a unique composition of immune cells that cause irreversibly injury to the brain during progressive MS. I propose these cells trapped in the meninges secrete molecules that are able to enter the brain and cause pathology. I also expect these secreted molecules to be present in the CSF. To investigate this hypothesis, I will use brains from MS patients to fully characterize the MS meninges and the underlying brain area. By comparing brains from MS patients to brains from non-MS patients with meningeal inflammation (for ex., encephalitis), I hope to pinpoint unique characteristics that are specific to the MS meninges. I will also compare the cerebral spinal fluid between the same MS patients and non-MS patients with meningeal inflammation to identify secreted molecules that differ between the two groups. This project will enhance our understanding of progressive MS and allow us to identify secreted molecules that correlate to clinical and pathological severity. Ultimately, future blockade of the molecules identified by this project could alter MS disease course."

column36: Differential effects of cannabis use on inhibitory control-indexed brain function in males and females.
column37: "Cannabis is a term frequently used to refer to any consumable product obtained from a species of the Cannabaceae family. The primary psychoactive ingredient of this plant, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), acts on the brain through its interaction with CB1 endocannabinoid receptors.
