The neurocognitive changes THC can cause in the brain are alarming, particularly considering the proportion of use in Canada. In 2019 over 16% of Canadians reported using cannabis within the past three months, of these users, a quarter were between the ages of 15 and 24. This age is important as it closely aligns with critical neurodevelopmental stages involving areas with a high density of CB1 receptors. Males and females, however, reach these neurodevelopment milestones at different rates, with females peaking in neurological development earlier than their male counterparts. To determine how cannabis effects the brains of male and female cannabis users, and nonusers; we will recruit 60 cannabis users and 60 non-users (30 male, 30 female per condition). Participants will be assessed on measures of inhibitory control, using electroencephalography (EEG)-derived-event-related-potentials (ERPs). Finally, this study will enhance our understanding of how cannabis may differentially affect the brains of males and females, specifically on measures of inhibitory control; leading to a clear understanding of how the health of cannabis users may be impacted based on their biological sex. This research addresses a significant gap in the existing literature; understanding sex differences is critical given the high usage rates in the Canadian population. "

column36: Optimized Neurotensin Analogues for the Imaging and Treatment of Advanced Prostate Cancer
column37: "Radioactively-labelled drugs that are engineered to bind preferentially to cancer cells over healthy tissue are a powerful and versatile strategy for non-invasively imaging and treating tumors. The biologically active component of the drug interacts with specific markers on the surface of cancer cells, while the attached radioactive tag can either produce detectable signals for imaging tumors or deliver highly localized, irradiative damage. This diagnostic and treatment platform would greatly benefit patients with late-stage prostate cancers that that have progressed to neuroendocrine prostate carcinomas (NEPCs), as they change their expression patterns to be unresponsive to existing androgen-deprivation therapies, reaching an incurable state with poor clinical outcomes. A key biomarker overexpressed in NEPCs is neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1), which binds the 13 amino acid peptide neurotensin (NTS) and facilitates androgen-independent tumoral growth. Several NTS-based radiopharmaceuticals have been developed, but suffer from poor biological stability due to rapid enzymatic degradation as well as high kidney accumulation. Thus, to make them efficacious as imaging agents and radiotherapeutics, our goal is to generate new NTSR1-binding peptides that employ biologically stabilizing modifications to the NTS sequence while retaining high binding affinity. Optimization of the linker region of the drug, which connects the biologically active and radioactive components, will improve tumor uptake that is beneficial for both image contrast and therapy. These candidate drugs will be assessed in prostate cancer mouse models expressing NTSR1 by monitoring their tumor localization and delivery of radioactivity, and may produce novel diagnostics and therapeutics for NEPC."

Looking at time to surgery as one of the markers for distance decay is the first step in investigating interventions that may decrease time to surgery. column36: Organoid models of high grade serous ovarian cancer: investigating the effect of homologous recombination mutations on genomic stability
column37: "High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGS) is the most common and lethal form of ovarian cancer, with 120,000 people a year dying worldwide from this disease. Recently, new cancer-killing drugs called poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors have shown promise in treating HGS. However, not all patients respond equivalently, and HGS mortality rates have seen little improvement in recent years. This underlines the urgent need for biomarkers to predict which patients may benefit from this novel therapy. A large spectrum of mutations affecting proteins involved in DNA damage repair has been identified in HGS. These mutations compromise tumour cells' ability to repair mutated DNA, forcing them to rely on a less reliable mechanism for DNA repair. PARP inhibitors exploit this vulnerability to selectively kill tumour cells. However, which DNA damage repair gene mutations confer PARP sensitivity is largely unknown. My proposed project will use organoids, which model the three-dimensional architecture of organs, to test the effects of different DNA repair mutations on non-cancerous cells. Using gene-editing technology I will mutate DNA repair genes in organoids, monitor the organoids for changes in their ability to repair DNA, and test whether the mutations confer sensitivity to PARP inhibition. Success with my project will identify biomarkers that may distinguish patients more likely to benefit from PARP inhibitor therapy. In addition, my research will develop a novel model system to improve understanding of the biology of tumours with DNA damage repair defects. I expect these findings may have the potential to provide a rationale for clinical trials that could expand the numbers of patients that receive PARP inhibitor therapy."

column36: Characterization of novel viral sensitizers that enhance oncolytic herpes simplex-1 virus (HSV1) and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) infection in cancer cells through polo-like kinase-1(PLK1) inhibition
column37: "The oncolytic herpes simplex virus 1 (oHSV1) is FDA-approved for the treatment of advanced melanoma, while rhabdoviruses (e.g. Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (oVSV)) are undergoing clinical investigation. column36: "Comparison of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest characteristics, processes, and outcomes by urban/rural status in the United States."
column37: "Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) occurs when the heart stops beating unexpectedly and is a leading cause of mortality and morbidity in developed countries. It is estimated that approximately 40,000 Canadian and 350,000 American adults suffer an OHCA each year, with only an 8-12% survival rate. Various time-sensitive therapies, such as cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation, can improve survival, but must be performed effectively and as soon as possible. The Chain of Survival highlights early recognition, CPR, defibrillation, expert cardiac life support, and post-resuscitation care as key elements to optimize outcomes for patients who experience cardiac arrest. Despite improvements in OHCA care and outcomes over time, persistent disparities in care processes and access are evident in rural areas, which has led to reduced survival rates in comparison to urban settings. With almost 20% of the North American population living in rural areas, OHCA remains a prominent public health concern within this underserved population. This project aims to examine the incidence, characteristics, processes, and outcomes of OHCA between urban and rural areas in the United States. Associations between OHCA care processes and survival outcomes will be assessed and compared by urban/rural status. The findings of this project will be transferable to the Canadian setting, informing the development of evidence-based health programmes that target important care processes along the Chain of Survival, thus improving OHCA outcomes across unique geographical settings. Ultimately, this will help drive new guidelines, policies, and programs to improve rural OHCA care in both the United States and Canada, strengthening access to life-saving therapies among rural communities. "

column37: "Melanoma is a form of skin cancer that arises from the uncontrolled growth of melanocytes, the pigment producing cells in skin. An interesting characteristic of this disease is a better chance of survival in women. Our laboratory has identified a gene on the sex chromosomes that could account for this difference. This gene encodes a protein called PR70, which there is generally higher levels of in tumors from female patients. We found that when tumors have higher levels of PR70, patients have less aggressive cancers and better chances of survival. How this protein exerts this effect is not well understood. Recent data from our lab shows that PR70 may improve survival by reducing the production of other proteins through the modulation of mRNA translation. Our data shows that the effect is specific to certain proteins, and that many of these proteins are associated with cancer progression. In this study, we seek to better understand the underlying molecular mechanism of this action and identify specific oncogenic proteins that have their production decreased by the presence of PR70. Doing so will pave the way for the development of treatment strategies and therapeutics that would specifically help patients with aggressive, PR70-low melanomas."

column37: "Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is an umbrella term for a group of diseases that present similar features in patients including severe back pain, and extreme swelling and stiffness of joints in the body such as at the hip, and the spine. These symptoms place a significant physical and mental burden on affected individuals since many cannot engage in leisure or sexual activities, and face a restricted ability to work. SpA diseases affect 1-2% of the American population, majority being young males under the age of 30, and yet there is a poor understanding of why and how they develop. Some researchers have suggested that gut irritation could be triggering the immune system to target and destroy healthy joint tissue leading to the symptoms seen in SpA patients. We believe that the immune cells involved are travelling from the gut to the joints by using adhesive molecules that help these cells reach the joints. However, this has not been experimentally confirmed. We propose that a pathway exists between the gut and the joints. Therefore, by covering the adhesive molecules with blocking agents, we can potentially prevent the movement of destructive immune cells from the gut to the joints and limit their ability to inflict damage. This is an important topic to pursue as currently, we are unable to treat individuals suffering from SpA diseases effectively. Many either do not respond to the treatment, or the medication does not sufficiently decrease the pain or stiffness in the joints. Our studies will be able to show whether blocking the adhesive molecules on destructive immune cells can serve as a potential alternative treatment for SpA diseases. Our studies will also help in understanding how and why SpA develops, and to help identify other methods we can use to manage the disease."

column36: Targeting Translation as a Druggable Opportunity in Breast Cancer
column37: "In the cellular context, both normal and cancerous, information is largely relayed from DNA to mRNA to functional proteins via transcription and translation, respectively. This provides room for regulation at multiple levels of gene expression. Additionally, it was found that dysregulated translation of certain mRNAs supports the cancer hallmarks. A key protein complex involved in translation initiation is eukaryotic initiation factor 4F (eIF4F). When dysfunctional, two signaling pathways that control eIF4F activity, the PI3K/mTOR and MAP kinase pathways, also play a role in the development of cancer. Current drugs target these pathways in an attempt to combat breast cancer; however, they are met with resistance over time due to the ability of cancer cells to shift to other pathways that bypass the drug's original target. To avoid resistance, it makes sense to directly target the common downstream endpoint of these signaling pathways which is the translation machinery, namely eIF4A, a subunit of eIF4F. CR-1-31b (CR) is a rocaglate compound that targets eIF4A and was most characterized by the Pelletier Lab. My project aims are to determine CR's effect on tumor growth and characterize its mRNA target(s) using genetically engineered mouse models of breast cancer and molecular biology techniques with the potential of creating synthetic derivatives pharmacokinetically optimized for clinical studies. This project should offer insight into the consequences and mechanisms of selectively inhibiting translation in breast cancer and hopefully highlight the advantages of rocaglates over currently marketed drugs."

column36: Governance Innovation for Intersectoral Collaboration: A Theoretically-Informed Case Study of an Ontario Health Team
column37: "The term ""integrated care"" (IC) describes an approach to delivering highly coordinated care that is organized around the health and social needs of patients and seeks to improve patient's experience of care and their health outcomes. The goal of many IC models is to achieve open communication, a shared vision of the patient's care goals, and coordination across a range of providers in multiple environments including primary care, mental health, home and community care, housing, justice, and hospitals. Collaboration between providers, managers and organizational leaders from these organizations is therefore fundamental to implementing and sustaining IC models. Such collaboration is heavily influenced by the governance decisions of organizational leaders, including specifically those decisions related to how legislated policies are translated into internal organizational policies. In many instances, these policies can create environments in which collaboration across organizations is inadvertently impeded. Ontario recently legislated a new IC program called Ontario Health Teams (OHTs) and as providers in these teams begin to work together, it is likely that they will face collaboration-related challenges. Based on a preliminary literature review on governance innovation, I will examine a case study of one OHT to identify policy barriers which prevent collaborations between providers that can be used to anticipate the types of policy barriers that other OHTs may experience. This will involve qualitative interviews with relevant OHT stakeholders as well as document reviews of legislation and regulations related to OHTs and organizational policy documents. This data will be synthesized in a concept map to generate potential policy barriers and solutions."

column36: Using intelligent wearable technology to determine response to deep brain stimulation in children with dystonia
column37: "Introduction:.Dystonia is one of the most common pediatric movement disorders, characterized by abnormal muscle contractions or postures. Current management strategies for dystonia are limited by an inability to objectively evaluate its severity and response to treatment, including deep brain stimulation (DBS). Various scales including the Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale (BFMDRS) are used clinically to assess dystonia severity. These are limited by inaccuracy and do not take into account the fact that dystonia can have significant diurnal variation The current proposal will utilize novel, intelligent wearable devices, actigraphy, in order to define an objective biomarker of dystonia severity and a meaningful measure of the effectiveness of treatments, such as DBS. Actigraphy is a small, wristwatch-sized monitor that can register a human physical activity. Previous findings have shown that actigraphy is effective in objectively assessing disease motor symptoms such as in Parkinson's disease. Currently there are no data on using actigraphy in dystonia. Study Rationale:.Despite the fact that dystonia is among the most common movement disorders in children, there are no objective means to quantify its severity or response to treatments. The development of an objective biomarker of dystonia severity will inform treatment outcomes Study Objectives:. 1) to evaluate wearable actigraphy as a novel tool for dystonia scaling, and 2) to apply this tool in pediatric patients who are undergoing DBS for refractory dystonia. Study design:.20 children with generalized dystonia will be asked to wear the actigraphy device for 2 weeks prior to each clinic visit. At each clinic visit we will document the BFMDRS scores, which will be correlated with actigraphy data. "

column36: Assessment of the impact of antegrade enema insertion on health care utilization in pediatric patients with constipation: A population-based cohort study
column37: "Constipation affects approximately 3% of children worldwide. It is the reason for 2% of children's visits to Canadian emergency departments (EDs) and in the United States, leads to an estimated $3.9 billion in health care spending for children each year. When dietary and medical treatments do not lead to improvement, a surgery to allow children to get enema flushes through their abdominal wall to clear the colon of stool, called an antegrade enema, may be offered. Several treatments for constipation have been shown to reduce health care use, however, the effect of antegrade enemas on health care use has never been studied. This project plans to look at how antegrade enemas impact health care use and the costs associated with this in children with difficult-to-treat constipation. We believe that as antegrade enemas have been shown to help up to 80% of children with their severe constipation, the need for unplanned health care use, such as hospitalizations and ED visits, will likely decrease after this procedure. We will use the ICES database, which includes the health records of nearly all 14 million people in Ontario, to identify all patients under 18 years of age who have had an antegrade enema inserted in Ontario in the last 20 years and see how patients' use of the health care system changes after the device is inserted. This project will include the largest group of pediatric patients with antegrade enemas ever studied. It will give us new insights into how many children get antegrade enemas in Ontario each year and the impact of this procedure on individual patients and health care costs. This will help doctors make better informed decisions on how to treat their patients with severe constipation and will have important implications for health system planning."

column36: Cannabis substitution as a component of Managed Alcohol Programs for individuals with severe alcohol use disorder in unstable housing
column37: "Background.: Managed Alcohol Programs (MAPs) are a harm reduction strategy designed for populations with severe alcohol use disorders in unstable housing. Though MAPs are effective at stabilizing alcohol consumption patterns and at reducing alcohol-related harms, there are concerns associated with continuous, daily alcohol administration. Thus, researchers are interested in the efficacy of cannabis substitution (CS) for alcohol in the context of MAPs. The proposed research will inform the development of a clinical trial of CS for alcohol in MAPs. The purpose of the proposed research is to assess patterns of alcohol, cannabis, and other substance use in MAP participants, and to explore how these patterns are associated with harms across different domains. Understanding how cannabis use patterns change during MAP participation will provide critical insight into the potential of CS in MAPs, thus leading to improved harm reduction initiatives for this vulnerable population. Objectives.: (1) To compare patterns of change in alcohol, cannabis, and other substance use of MAP participants and controls; (2) To differentiate groups based on patterns of alcohol, cannabis, and other substance use (using latent class growth analysis); (3) To examine the associations between group membership and harms (using linear regression); (4) To inform the development of a clinical trial. Methods.: Analysis will be conducted using data collected from MAP participants and controls with severe alcohol use disorders in unstable housing. Objectives 1 and 2 will examine participants' substance use data. Objective 3 will examine harms across several domains: housing stability and satisfaction, alcohol-related harms, and quality of life. Objective 4 will use the results to inform a clinical trial."

column36: Identification of Novel Therapeutic Targets for High-Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer
column37: "Ovarian cancer is the sixth leading cause of cancer related death for Canadian women. Cancers of the high-grade serous (HGSC) subtype are the most prevalent and lethal, accounting for 70-80% of all cases. Despite recent improvements in treatment, 75% of patients relapse with chemoresistance and die from this disease. Thus, there is a need for the discovery of novel therapeutics. Our lab has recently published an integrated proteomics strategy in which glycosylated peptides were enriched from tumor and sera of HGSC patient derived xenograft (PDX) models to detect novel serum biomarkers for HGSC recurrence. An unexplored facet of this study was the simultaneous enhancement of plasma membrane proteins observed in the tumor glycoproteome. Plasma membrane proteins make favourable drug targets due to their easily accessible cell surface localization and their role in important biological functions. Hence, the aim of this project is to interrogate the glycoproteome of HGSC PDX tumors to identify and functionally validate novel therapeutic target candidates. Prioritization of cell surface localization and confirmed expression in patient samples has shortlisted 386 glycoproteins from the PDX glycoproteome. Targeted CRISPR/Cas9 screens will be performed to identify which of these glycoproteins are essential for cancer cell survival. Essential candidates will then be functionally validated to investigate effects on 3D tumor growth and invasion. Functional assays will be performed in spheroid models made with HGSC cells and patient-derived cancer-associated fibroblasts to create a more clinically relevant tumor microenvironment. Ultimately, this project will systematically prioritize and evaluate candidates for novel therapeutic targets to help reduce the clinical burden of HGSC."

column36: Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Seizure (rTMS) therapy as a tool to treat cognitive impairment in treatment-resistant depression
column37: "Cognitive deficits are a common symptom in major depressive disorder, are associated with increased rates of disability, and are challenging to treat. Cognitive impairment is associated with poor treatment response, longer disease duration and poorer functioning. Thus, patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), whom do not respond to conventional treatments and experience disease chronicity, are at a higher risk for cognitive deficits. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a non-invasive treatment modality that is effective in treatment-resistant depression. rTMS works by modulating the activity of a localized brain region in order to produce widespread functional changes. The prefrontal cortex is a brain area associated with complex cognitive functions and is also the brain target that rTMS stimulates to treat depression. Therefore, it has been hypothesized that rTMS might improve cognitive impairment in depression. The goal of the proposed master's project is to investigate whether an adequate course of rTMS in depression is associated with improvement of in cognitive symptoms in TRD patients. Cognitive assessments and fMRI brain scans were performed during baseline testing and 12 weeks post-treatment as part of a clinical trial examining differing rTMS treatment protocols in patients with TRD. Changes in cognition in patients will be compared to changes in cognition over the same time course in a sample of healthy volunteers in order to observe potential effects of treatment. If such effects exist, we will investigate the neurobiological underpinnings in the brain that are associated with improvements in cognition.   "

column36: Structural studies of the Clostridium difficile sporulation complex and associated machinery
column37: "Targeting the virulence pathways of bacteria is a promising way to combat infectious disease with minimal risk of inducing antibiotic resistance. Virulence pathways are the mechanisms pathogens use to persist in and damage the host; for example, toxin secretion, adhesion, and sporulation. Sporulation involves differentiating into a dormant spore when conditions are inhospitable for growth and reproduction and is especially important for pathogens like Clostridium difficile. Its spores are unaffected by host immune systems, antibiotics, and sanitation procedures, and are thus known for persisting in the host and spreading quickly amongst hospital patients. The sporulation complex, a multi-subunit dual membrane-spanning protein complex, is responsible for transporting nutrients to the developing spore during sporulation. Interrupting this process is a promising approach to preventing C. difficile sporulation, and thus a potential target for virulence-based drug design. Understanding the molecular structure of the complex is crucial for learning more about the sporulation complex's mechanism of action and strategies for disrupting its function. Thus, my objectives are to characterize the structure of its foundation component, SpoIIIAG, by cryoelectron microscopy before investigating the structure of the assembled complex using both cryoelectron microscopy and/or cryoelectron tomography. Also of importance are related sporulation proteins like the penicillin-binding protein SpoVD, which is responsible for the resistance of C. difficile to a range of widely-used antibiotics. I will use x-ray crystallography to elucidate both its structure and its interaction with antibiotics with the to describe how resistance is conferred, which is vital information for drug design. "

column36: Study of the role of Myc-interacting zinc finger protein 1 on the transcriptional activity of the c-Myc proto-oncogene in B lymphocytes
column37: "The c-Myc proto-oncogene is over-expressed in over 50% of human cancers and blocking its expression leads to tumor regression in animal models. An important partner of c-Myc is the BTB/POZ domain protein Miz-1. Our group has demonstrated that the expression of Miz-1 deficient for its POZ domain (Miz-1dPOZ) is sufficient to delay the development of c-Myc driven leukemia and lymphoma in mice suggesting that Miz-1 is required for the oncogenic activity of c-Myc. The first objective is to study how Miz-1 regulates the B cell receptor (BCR) signaling pathway in pre-lymphomatous B cells from Eµ-mice that overexpress c-Myc and are prone to develop B-cell lymphoma. The BCR pathway controls fitness and survival of these lymphoma cells and our preliminary data suggest that the expression of some genes of the BCR signaling pathway are regulated by Miz-1. The second objective is to assess the phosphorylation of c-Myc when Miz-1dPOZ is expressed, since the kinases Erk and Akt that are responsible for c-Myc phosphorylation and stability are effectors of the BCR pathway. The third objective will be to characterize how Miz-1 and c-Myc co-regulate the expression of their common target genes within the BCR pathway. Our BioID experiments indicated that Miz-1 is part of both the Tip60/TRRAP complex and the Nucleosome remodeling (NuRD) complex. We will determine whether Miz-1 can recruit these complexes to promoters of c-Myc/Miz-1 regulated genes and how they are affected by Miz-1dPOZ. This project will inform us how Miz-1, through its POZ domain, influences the oncogenic activity of c-Myc in lymphomas. Since POZ domains can be targeted by small molecules, this new knowledge could help design new strategies to target c-Myc activity in a large spectrum of human cancers. "

column36: Deconstructing the cellular and molecular pathways of the allergic recall response
column37: "Food allergies, such as peanut or shellfish, persist up to a lifetime in most individuals. Allergic reactivity range in severity from scratching, to anaphylaxis, a lethal form of systemic shock. Currently, food allergy remains a disease without a cure, and allergen avoidance remains as the best treatment. Reactivity is mediated by antibodies, known as IgE; however, IgE and IgE-producing disappear after allergen exposure. Recent studies demonstrate the existence of long-lived memory B cells (MBC) that with allergen stimulation, transition into an IgE-secreting cell. The primary requirements for IgE generation are IL-4, a pro-allergic molecule, and signals from T cells (TC). Despite the importance of IgE and MBCs, the mechanism through which these cells recruit TC help remain largely unknown. We hypothesize that allergic MBCs help TCs transition to an allergic state through distinct stimulatory receptors and BC-derived IL-4. We first will test the ability of MBCs to generate Th2 cells in a murine model of food allergy. MBCs from allergic mice will be transferred into non-allergic mice, followed by oral administrations of peanut. Mice will be assessed for reactivity and the generation of Th2 cells. Next, we will transfer naïve TCs to allergic mice and evaluate if they become Th2 cells. This examines whether allergic TCs prevent MBC-induced Th2 generation. Second, we will culture MBCs with TCs to asses what receptors and allergic molecules are being used for generating Th2 cells. In the future, we will block these molecules and receptors to abolish the allergic response. There has been limited advancement in the treatment of food allergy and defining the mechanism through which IgE-producing cells are generated remains crucial for the discovery of curative therapeutics."

column36: Association Between Muscle Mass and Exercise Physiological and Perceptual Outcomes in People with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
column37: "Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a disease of the lungs and airways that affects roughly 20% of Canadians over the age of 40. In addition to the high symptom burden - impaired exercise tolerance, and low quality of life (QoL) - abnormally low levels of skeletal muscle mass (MM) are often seen in people with COPD. There are few studies that have examined the impact of abnormally low levels of MM on the physiological determinants of exercise tolerance and the symptom of breathlessness during exercise in COPD patients. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the relationships between MM and physiological and perceptual responses to exercise in people with COPD. This study will include people with COPD and varying levels of MM assessed using an x-ray scanner. All participants will perform an exercise test on a stationary bicycle which requires them to exercise as long and as hard they can while simultaneously recording multiple physiological (e.g. heart rate, breathing) and perceptual (e.g. breathlessness, fatigue) parameters. A subgroup of these participants will also undergo 8-12 weeks of rehabilitative exercise training. From the results of the exercise tests, we hypothesize that people with lower vs. higher levels of MM will have lower exercise capacities because of having more abnormal physiological and perceptual responses to exercise. We also believe that rehabilitative exercise training will improve exercise test outcomes by increasing MM. The results of our research are important because they emphasize improving MM as an important goal of therapies designed to decrease symptom burden and improve exercise tolerance and QoL in people with COPD. "

column36: Generating a Novel Transgenic Model and Developing Gene-Editing Therapeutic Approaches for Retinitis Pigmentosa
column37: "Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) is a vision-threatening disorder that is characterized by progressive blindness due to retinal degeneration (RD). According to Fighting Blindness Canada, 1 in 3500 Canadians are affected by this inherited retinal disease. Thousands of mutations in over a hundred genes cause RP, making it impossible to develop a standard routine treatment for diagnosed patients. However, recent advancements in gene therapy provide the opportunity to develop patient-based therapeutics for specific underlying mutations. Rhodopsin is a key photosensitive pigment of rod cells encoded by the RHO gene and mutation-induced misfolding of this protein has been identified to underly RP. In this project, we aim to use the cutting-edge CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing strategy in X. laevis models for RP to prevent RD-associated RHO mutations. In the conventional gene-editing approach carried out by our group, a single edit resulted in desirable curative outcomes in 2/3 of cases, while in the remaining third it led to exacerbation of the RD phenotype or had no effect. By inducing two simultaneous edits and cutting out the start codon for the RHO gene, we aim to completely eliminate the expression of misfolded rhodopsin protein. In order to efficiently and reliably transfer our findings from lab benches into the clinics, we also aim to develop a humanized mouse model that expresses the mutated human rhodopsin gene in a mammalian environment. This novel model will facilitate a better understanding of RP disease mechanisms, while providing an ideal setting to develop gene-editing therapeutics. Given that the mutated human rhodopsin gene will be targeted for treatment development in this mouse, successful approaches can be more directly translated into clinical trials."

column36: Game-based simulation training to help neonatal resuscitation providers save babies at birth
column37: "10-20% of babies worldwide need help to breathe at birth each year. Helping babies breathe is called neonatal resuscitation. Healthcare providers must perform many tasks quickly and correctly, often as a team, to help babies breathe. However even with their help, 1 million of these babies will die. Medical errors by healthcare providers remain common and are responsible for 60% of this mortality. To address this staggering gap, guidelines recommend frequent simulation training for healthcare providers. Unfortunately, this can be resource-draining, requiring access to specialized equipment, manikin, and trained instructors. Therefore, most healthcare providers do not maintain adequate training to safely provide care. Simulation-based serious games may offer a solution to improve access to neonatal resuscitation training. Serious games use elements like competition and emotional design to teach players relevant knowledge or skills. The simulation-based serious game RETAIN (REsuscitation TrAINing, Retain Labs Medical Inc., Edmonton, Canada) fits this description. In RETAIN, players use equipment pieces, monitors, and action cards to stabilize a simulated infant. Players practice their knowledge and communication skills while navigating game scenarios based on real-life deliveries from a tertiary perinatal centre. My research project will investigate if training with RETAIN improves healthcare providers' i) knowledge of the correct steps of neonatal resuscitation and ii) use of directed closed-loop communication. I will examine these outcomes in both the simulation lab and delivery room at the Royal Alexandra Hospital (Edmonton, Canada). Improving training for neonatal resuscitation providers will ultimately lead to better care for our smallest patients and their families."

column37: "Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a prevalent global malignancy with more than 1 million cases diagnosed every year. What is of more concern is that the age of onset is decreasing. Oncomicrobes, including Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), are microbes linked to the initiation/development of tumors. Eliminating these oncomicrobes from the colon may reduce the likelihood of developing colorectal cancer or slow disease progression. Targeting Fn with antibiotics risks damaging the human gut microbiome and the possibility of Fn and other bacteria developing antibiotic resistance. Instead, a biological antimicrobial agent can be explored; Bdellovibrio-and-like organisms (BALOs). BALOs are aerobic, predatory deltaproteobacteria that kill Gram-negative bacteria as a part of their life-cycle. I hypothesize that BALOs can effectively predate on Fn in such a manner that they can be considered for therapeutic use in the treatment of CRC.. I will investigate how BALOs, including Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus HD100, the type strain, are able to remove oncomicrobes from a variety of mixed bacterial communities that are representative of the human colon, restoring the colonic microbiome to a normally functioning state. My main objectives are to 1) isolate BALOs from the environment, 2) compare the predatory effectiveness of BALO isolates under different testing conditions, and 3) evaluate the predatory effectiveness of BALOs within a CRC colonic microbiome community using a bioreactor model. Using BALOs as a bacterial therapy against cancer-promoting oncomicrobes would be novel and could be promising for colorectal cancer research alongside current or other novel treatment methods to better patient outcomes."

column36: STING Activation via Cyclic Dinucleotide: Exploring A Therapeutic Modality for Treating Soft Tissue Sarcoma
column37: "Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are rare cancers derived from the connective tissues. The most common STS in adults is Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma (UPS) which are highly aggressive tumours. Current treatment options for UPS patients include morbid tumour resections and amputations, chemotherapy, and radiation. Immunotherapy is an emerging cancer therapy that has been successfully used to treat melanoma and numerous carcinomas. However, immunotherapies have not been effective against sarcomas due to the lack of immune cells found within UPS tumours. Novel interventions that are capable of recruiting activated immune cells into the tumour microenvironment are desperately needed to effectively combat sarcoma. We are targeting this strategy by using small molecule activator of the STING receptor (STimulator of INterferon Genes). In pilot experiments, a single dose of the murine STING agonist DMXAA yielded full regression in 60% of treated UPS bearing mice. These encouraging results motivated our laboratory to evaluate STING agonists capable of activating both human and murine STING for UPS treatment. To accomplish this goal, we will be assessing the effectiveness of the human and murine STING agonist ML RR S2-CDA (CDA) which has been successfully used as an immunotherapy in other cancer models. To evaluate CDA's therapeutic potential in our mouse model of UPS, we will be optimizing CDA dosing strategies, combining CDA with current checkpoint inhibitor therapies to determine if it will sensitize tumours to the therapy, and finally, we will quantify markers of immune cell infiltration in tumours following CDA therapy. Investigating STING activation as an immunotherapeutic strategy holds the potential to dramatically improve treatment options for UPS patients. "

column36: "Building on Community?-Led Food Initiatives in the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Northwest Territories"
column37: "The food systems of Indigenous peoples in the Northwest Territories (NWT) are based on the harvesting of country foods and form the foundation of spiritual, cultural, physical, and mental health for individuals and communities. Documented impacts of climate change for Indigenous peoples' food systems include access to, and availability of, country food species in a region where alarming rates of food insecurity prevail. Identifying local climate change adaptations in the food systems of Indigenous communities in the NWT is critical for the health and sustainability of communities and the environment. In collaboration with the ""Learning from and enhancing Community Capacity for Climate Change and Food Security (C4FS) action in the NWT"" project, my research aims to learn from and enhance community capacity to address place-based priorities to inform climate change and food security action locally, regionally, and territorially. Grounded in Participatory Action Research and working closely with community partners, I will examine how research and knowledge sharing of local initiatives can inform community-driven climate change adaptation plans to enhance food security. This will be achieved through interviews and focus group sharing circles in two communities in the Inuvialuit Settlement Region of the NWT (Tuktoyaktuk and Paulatuk) to determine 1) opportunities and barriers at local levels to be overcome to achieve community food security goals and 2) how communities in the ISR can learn from each other through knowledge sharing of evolving country food system practices to better adapt to climate change. This research will promote community action and knowledge sharing of local food systems in the two ISR communities, ultimately improving health outcomes. "

column36: Exploring the Role of GBA1 in Immune Regulation in the Context of Parkinson Disease
column37: "Typical Parkinson disease (PD) is thought to arise from a combination of genetic risk factor(s) and environmental trigger(s). With this in consideration, PD development has been hypothesized to be a multi-staged progression that begins with damage to the olfactory and enteric nervous systems via encounter with external factors (i.e. pathogens), eventually progressing towards the brain. Our group has shown that two key PD-linked proteins; alpha-synuclein and LRRK2, confer anti-microbial activity and believe that this is relevant to PD pathogenesis. Mutations in GBA1, a gene that codes for the lysosomal protein glucocerebrosidase, are the largest known genetic risk factor for PD. Several GBA-PD investigations explore the effect reduced activity in GBA1 mutants in progression of the disease. While GBA-PD patients have reduced enzymatic activity, the majority (~90%) of Gaucher Disease (GD) patients, who carry homozygous mutations in the GBA1 gene and significantly lower enzymatic activity, do not develop PD. The expression of GBA1 in macrophages, cells that are impaired in GD patients and are critical in the innate immune system, points to a potential role of this protein in host immune response. This study provides an opportunity to add upon mounting evidence of PD- associated proteins' role in immune regulation. Identification of immune-related therapeutic targets, including in the periphery could lead to the development of novel therapeutics. Ultimately, the role of GBA1 in PD pathogenesis remains unclear. We believe uncovering a role of GBA1 in immune regulation and host defense may lead to a better understanding of GBA-PD pathogenesis. "

column36: Modelling Ischemia Bodywide in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
column37: "Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is one of the most commonly inherited paediatric musculoskeletal disorders affecting 1 in 3500 boys. The disorder is due to a lack of functional dystrophin protein which, in turn, results in a loss of cell membrane integrity in skeletal, respiratory and cardiac muscle and brain of those affected. It is inevitably fatal by patients' mid-late twenties. In DMD, neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) is delocalized to the cytoplasm due to the compromised integrity of dystrophin-associated proteins which link the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Within DMD muscle, necrotic fibers are often observed in groups, and it has been previously hypothesized that this may be due to a reduction in regional blood supply. The deficiency of dystrophin within vascular smooth muscle when combined with the absence of nNOS from the sarcolemma subject DMD muscles and brain to impaired blood flow. Thus, the objective of the proposed research is to non-invasively measure bodywide ischemic changes during disease progression in DMD mouse models, using a leading edge dynamic contrast enhanced computed tomography (DCE-CT) imaging modality. The significance of this research is that by quantifying blood flow and blood volume in dystrophic tissue we will be able to better assess the Pathobiology and disease progression of DMD patients non-invasively. "

column36: Cardioprotective Role of Resident Macrophages in Ischemia Reperfusion Injury
column37: "Role of Immune Cells in Cardiac Tissue Repair Following Injury. Ischemic heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. After a heart attack, the immune system modulates both injury to the heart and also tissue repair. The most abundant immune cell that resides in the heart are macrophages. We have shown that macrophages can be divided into two categories based on origin: embryonic-derived resident macrophages that are present before birth, and recruited macrophages, which are continuously replaced by bone-marrow monocytes. In contrast to adult, the neonatal heart has a remarkable regenerative capacity in response to injury. In neonates, resident macrophages increase in number in response to cardiac injury and are required for cardiac regeneration. Conversely, this macrophage population is diminished in the adult heart after a heart attack, which forms a scar. After a heart attack, patients are admitted to the hospital and blood flow is restored, which both saves vulnerable myocardium, but also exposes the myocardium to reperfusion-dependent inflammatory damage. The role of resident macrophages in this clinically relevant model of cardiac ischemia reperfusion injury has not been explored. Our preliminary data using a surgical model in mice to mimic reperfusion following a heart attack shows that resident macrophages increase in number in the heart. We will assess whether resident macrophages are protective over the course of reperfusion injury and their role in cardiac tissue repair using specific, genetically inducible depletion models. This work will inform novel reparative pathways that may help improve reperfusion treatment after heart attacks. "

column36: The Role of Exosomes in Parkinson?s Disease and Other Synucleinopathies
column37: "Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are neurodegenerative diseases called synucleinopathies, where alpha-synuclein (alpha-syn) forms sticky deposits in brain cells. This misfolded alpha-syn causes healthy alpha-syn to clump and spread throughout the brain years before clinical symptoms appear. Therefore, it is important to investigate biomarkers that allow us to identify these patients before they display symptoms. Small blood-borne vesicles known as exosomes could serve as a potential biomarker. Exosomes carry alpha-syn from the brain to blood where they can be easily measured, and correlate with disease severity, supporting the idea that exosomes could be used as a diagnostic marker. Exosomes from patients with DLB have been shown to spread alpha-syn pathology in mice, but it is unclear whether exosomes from other synucleinopathies can spread pathology as well. We and others have shown that transgenic mice that overexpress a mutant form of alpha-syn can develop clinical symptoms when their brains are injected with material from human MSA brains. These studies suggest that blood and brain exosomes from synucleinopathy mice are responsible for spreading disease. My aims are to 1) isolate and characterize blood and brain exosomes from affected mice and 2) inject unaffected mice with these exosomes to test whether disease is induced. To date, we have successfully isolated and characterized exosomes from affected mice and have injected healthy mice. As hypothesized, the injected mice developed neurological symptoms and will be analyzed for brain pathology. This project will further our knowledge on exosomes and their role in the spread of alpha-syn. It will advance our understanding of utilizing exosomes as a biomarker for synucleinopathies."

column36: Long-term health outcomes in children following neonatal abstinence syndrome from fetal opioid exposure
column37: "The current opioid crisis is an alarming public health concern in Canada and worldwide and the use of opioids among expectant mothers has increased as well. As a result, there has been a seventeen-fold increase in the number of infants born to opioid dependent-mothers in Ontario in the past twelve years. 55% to 94% of newborns with substance exposure during pregnancy experience withdrawal symptoms, called neonatal abstinence syndrome. Immediate harmful effects experienced by infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome are well understood. However, research in health outcomes in this population at risk as they proceed into childhood and youth is lacking and more research is required to address the gap in our understanding. In this study, we aim to characterize the long-term health outcomes in children who were exposed to opioids before they were born. Children who had prenatal opioid exposure and neonatal abstinence syndrome at birth will be identified and they will be compared to children without opioid exposure. Using various healthcare usage databases, we will examine the health outcomes in terms of routine well-child visits and vaccinations, infection, neurodevelopmental disorders, behavioral disorders, and eye conditions. Ontario offers a publicly funded health care system to all residents, and by using Ontario health records, this study will be able to examine all children with a history of neonatal abstinence syndrome or prenatal opioid exposure born in the province of Ontario inclusively. Our study will be able to provide a comprehensive understanding of this emerging public health issue and inform policymakers in developing efficient and tailored public health responses to support this population at risk."

column36: "Identifying barriers and facilitators to dementia post-diagnosis support in Quebec, Canada, from the perspective of persons with dementia, caregivers and primary care providers: a mixed-methods study"
column37: "The World Health Organization has identified dementia as a public health priority. Many national and provincial plans have been developed to better prepare the healthcare system for the screening, diagnosis and management of dementia. However, despite these efforts, persons with dementia and their caregivers have trouble accessing post-diagnosis support, and are often dissatisfied by those services. The goal of this study is to take a look at the current situation in Quebec and to identify barriers and facilitators to post-diagnosis support, as well as satisfaction with those resources. To do so, we will recruit 50 recently diagnosed patients, 50 caregivers, and 50 primary care providers in Laval, Quebec. We will ask them to fill-out a questionnaire on their experience of the support received post-diagnosis. Then, we will conduct one focus group for each participant category (three focus groups total), composed of 6 to 10 participants each, and invite them to talk about their satisfaction and the barriers and facilitators they perceive with regard to post-diagnosis support. This study constitutes the first step in an international project involving five countries (Canada, Australia, Poland, the Netherland, and the UK) with the aim of co-designing and delivering toolkits and campaigns to improve the dementia post-diagnostic support, in partnership with people with dementia, family care partners and health care providers. The Ministry of Health will also use these results to inform the next phases of the Quebec Alzheimer plan."

column36: End-to-end development and validation of a deep learning model for dengue outbreak prediction
column37: "Dengue is a potentially deadly, mosquito-borne disease with a significant impact on global health. In their mosquito control efforts, public health officials rarely have access to models that inform when and where outbreaks are likely to occur. Current models oversimplify the various human and environmental factors known to drive outbreaks. Here, I propose using a form of artificial intelligence known as deep learning to overcome existing limitations and more accurately predict outbreaks within Southeast Asia—a global dengue hotspot. Deep learning allows computers to learn patterns from massive datasets and create predictive models. After interviewing public health stakeholders in Singapore, the Philippines, and Laos to understand their needs, I will create an outbreak prediction model using state-of-the-art deep learning architectures. Groups predominantly only use climate and weather data to create predictive models, but these are not the only factors that drive outbreaks. I will overcome this limitation by leveraging not only meteorological data, but also data capturing mosquito distributions, air and ground travel, historical outbreak case numbers, and urbanization from the region. Once I have tuned model performance in a laboratory setting, I will convene stakeholders to evaluate perceptions of our model in an outbreak simulation exercise. My work will create a dengue outbreak prediction model that overcomes the limitations of traditional methods by using deep learning and involves stakeholders in the design and validation processes. By demonstrating the application of artificial intelligence for timely outbreak response and containment, this translational research will help public health agencies combat a devastating global health threat. "

column36: Breast cancer risk factors and the built environment: a linked British Columbian cohort
column37: "Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer deaths in women, however, many cases are preventable. It is important to understand preventable risks, especially for post-menopausal women. The built environment influences levels of air pollution, rates of physical activity and obesity. The two datasets have been linked using postal code data to allow pre-cancer environmental exposures to be analyzed. This is an advantage as this information has not been available in previous air pollution breast cancer studies. The analysis of risk factors for breast cancer in the built environment linked to data of early environmental exposures, will provide important addition to the literature. The prospective study design with pre-cancer exposure will allow for measure of temporality of risk factors to be assessed in incident breast cancer cases. "

column36: Longitudinal changes in DNAm in preschool children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).
column37: "Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) are considered to be one of the most severe mental health issues today affecting five males to every one female. ASDs affect an individual's ability to understand the world around them and can lead to significant difficulties communicating with others and leading independent, autonomous lives. Until recently, genetic factors have typically been researched in association with ASDs; however, there is an increasing recognition that epigenetic factors are also implicated. Epigenetics regulates gene expression by either activating or suppressing a gene without modifying the DNA sequence. Epigenetic changes, specifically DNA methylation (DNAm), is a process in which a chemical group is added to the DNA at a specific location and in turn either activates or suppresses gene expression; this process is especially critical during development. The aim of this research is to obtain and compare DNAm profiles between typically developing children and preschool children who have been clinically diagnosed with ASD. Children's clinical and biological samples were collected at baseline (diagnosis), six months, 12 months, and 24 months to determine if changes in DNAm over time are influenced by the intervention that the children diagnosed with ASD received. This research has the potential to significantly improve the lives of those suffering from ASDs by identifying epigenetic marks (abnormal DNAm profiles) associated with atypical development and intervention responses. In addition, recognizing these abnormal DNAm profiles during development could be indicative of disease progression and my goal is to help ameliorate and hinder that progression. Being able to identify children who respond positively to intervention can lead to patient-oriented treatment."

column36: "No Fixed Address: An Arts-based, Feminist Exploration of the Modern Nomad Lifestyle in the Context of the Social Determinants of Health"
column37: "In the context of the determinants of health, my research uses art-based practices and first voice, feminist perspectives to examine benefits and barriers of a modern nomadic lifestyle with regard to access or denial of health services as it relates to the possession, or lack, of a fixed address Our society has long marginalized specific groups - women, the poor, elderly and disabled - leaving many struggling to find solutions to inadequate income, housing, and access to healthcare. Many of these marginalized individuals have chosen to live as modern nomads, forsaking tradition and finding liberty. The nomadic lifestyle can bring unexpected benefits which increase the factors necessary in the determinants of health - for example, social connectedness. Often joining small caravans, with living spaces quite small, nomads tend to go outside more often, where they have increased interactions with others. Inevitably, this leads to the formation of more and stronger relationships - a high priority factor for positive health outcomes. However, while the benefits of reduced shelter costs, increased social networks and engaging directly with the larger world may satisfy factors required for positive health outcomes, nomads face a variety of challenges in accessing health services necessary to maintain health, finding themselves functionally invalidated as citizens; their identity in question on the basis of being without a fixed address. Using Interdisciplinary art-based practices - photography, performance, sculpture and site-specific installation, my aim is to build a body of work that focuses on the inequities of the dissemination of health care services as it relates to mobile dwelling and health determinants; giving expression to the experience of the loss of personhood."

column36: Identification of explanatory modifiers for the phenotypic heterogeneity of dominant RYR1 myopathies
column37: "Neuromuscular diseases are known to be highly heterogeneous with a single variant often associated with a large variety of phenotypes. This heterogeneity complicates the diagnostic process leaving many patients without a prognosis or ideal clinical management and may even preclude the development of viable treatments. Mutations in RYR1 (Ryanodine receptor 1) have been previously associated with several diseases including central core disease, multiminicore disease, and malignant hypothermia susceptibility. However, this phenotypic variability remains unexplained, especially among patients with the same variant. We hypothesize that transcriptomic and epigenomic signatures could explain the differences in severity of RYR1 mutations. Our study comprises of 21 individuals from the region of Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean who carry the same heterozygous missense mutation (c.526G A), but present diverse phenotypes within and between families. In order to study this heterogeneity, we will first stratify patients according to phenotypic severity. Next, we will identify transcriptomic signatures that vary between subgroups and controls using mRNA and microRNA sequencing of muscle tissue. Finally, we will perform whole genome bisulfite sequencing to identify epigenetic signatures such as differential methylation that differ between subgroups and controls. This research will provide insight into the genes and biological pathways associated with heterogeneity of RYR1 mutations that may be applicable to other neuromuscular diseases. Furthermore, these signatures will improve the quality of life of affected patients by advancing diagnostic methods, evaluation of prognosis, and management of care and by driving the identification of new treatments. column36: MicroRNA-122 Mediated Protection of the Hepatitis C Virus Genome from Human Pyrophosphatases
column37: "Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infects approximately 71 million people worldwide, including 268,000 Canadians. HCV is an RNA virus that directly interacts with a highly abundant, liver-specific human small RNA, termed miR-122. HCV binds to two miR-122 molecules, which facilitates HCV infection. Treatment of patients with chronic HCV using a miR-122 inhibitor led to significant reductions in viral loads. However, in some patients, upon treatment cessation, HCV levels rebounded and several resistance-associated variants were identified. Until recently, the mechanism(s) of how miR-122 is able to promote HCV RNA accumulation were unclear; however, recent studies from our group have demonstrated that miR-122 protects the HCV genome from recognition by host cell enzymes that would typically degrade the viral RNA. Specifically, miR-122 protects the viral genome from recognition by two cellular pyrophosphatases which can initiate the decay pathway. However, the precise requirements for the activity of these enzymes is not known. Thus, we plan to study these cellular enzymes and determine their substrate requirements and also investigate how the resistance-associated variants of HCV identified in patients are able to prevent recognition by these enzymes, even in the absence of miR-122."

column36: Exosome Mediated Reprogramming of fibroblast cells to hepatocytes for pharmacological study
column37: "Annually, adverse drug reactions account for the deaths of up to 22,000 Canadians and are associated with a cost of up to $18 billion. The prediction of adverse drug reactions can be greatly facilitated through drug screening via hepatocyte-like cells (HLCs). Thus, an efficient method for the generation of HLCs is necessary for drug screening. I am proposing the use of eXosome-Mediated cellular Reprogramming (XMR) to trans-differentiate human fibroblast cells into HLCs, facilitating the study of patient drug metabolism. Exosomes, small membrane-bound vesicles that engage in the delivery of genetic material between cells, have successfully been used in the Rancourt lab to trans-differentiate fibroblast cells to neuronal cells. This process simplifies the current methodology for cellular reprogramming, which relies on a pluripotent intermediate state between both fibroblast and target cell type. In trans-differentiation, fibroblast cells can be efficiently differentiated to target cell types without having to generate induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs). The benefit of using exosomes in this process is two-fold when we consider that their use does not involve the integration of genetic material to target cells, thus significantly reducing the probability that these cells will develop tumours upon implantation. Therefore, this project would allow the safe and efficient generation of high volumes of HLCs for drug screening, and potentially clinical application and transplantation."

column36: Targeted Covalent Pentafluorobenzene Sulfonamide-Based Afatinib Drug for Treating Breast Cancer
column37: "Breast cancer is a common malignancy in Canadian women accounting for approximately 14 deaths daily. Although there have been several advancements in treatments, current drugs are plagued by resistance mechanisms and off-target effects which leads to higher dosing regimens and unpleasant side effects. This is particularly important for a class of drugs, termed covalent therapeutics. Covalent therapeutics, unlike conventional drugs, are very reactive molecules and bind irreversibly to their target which halts its normal function. Although this is a desirable objective in a cancer cell, since covalent therapeutics are very reactive, they can also bind irreversibly to non-cancer targets, which contributes to patient side-effects and toxicity. We have recently developed new technology that allows us to fine-tune the reactivity of a covalent therapeutic thereby limiting off target effects. We are aiming to apply this technology to current breast cancer treatments, such as the current breast-cancer drug afatinib. We will synthesize a large library of afatinib-like drugs based on our new technology. We will use state-of-the-art computer simulations and quantum mechanical models, to predict the reactivity of the different compounds. We will test these compounds against breast-cancer cells in an isolated petri dish to determine their potency and effectiveness. In this strategy, we will gradually funnel our large library of compounds to generate a small number of the top hits with convincing drug profiles. Since afatinib is currently dosed with other drug combinations for breast cancer, we hope this research seeks to find a treatment that not only improve the quality of life for Canadian women but also extend the life span of women diagnosed with breast cancer."

column36: Functional characterization of serine/threonine kinase 19 (STK19) in RAS-mutant cancers
column37: "The Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK) pathway is a critical signaling cascade regulating cellular migration, proliferation and survival following extracellular stimulation. Mutations in RAS genes (H-, K-, N-), which encode key regulators of the MAPK pathway, can lead to uncontrolled signaling and cellular growth. This is a common driving event of many cancers, accounting for 25% of melanoma and 93% of pancreatic cancer. It is imperative to explore new therapies for this subset of cancers, as treatment options for patients are limited. Recently, a novel regulator of NRAS activity was identified: serine-threonine kinase 19 (STK19). An inhibitor for this kinase was also developed, which prevented tumor growth in NRAS-mutant melanoma models. STK19 is a proposed oncogene, due to the presence of a recurrent mutation (STK19 p.D89N) in 5% of melanoma, and was shown to further promote NRAS-mutant tumor growth compared to wild-type STK19. Recent data suggest that the STK19 mutation is in a promoter region regulating the expression of a shorter STK19 isoform, and not a coding mutation. We hypothesize that the shorter STK19 isoform activates H-, K- and NRAS at a conserved residue. We do not believe the STK19 p.D89N protein is expressed; however, we speculate that the promoter mutation may affect STK19 expression and play a role in the development of melanoma. We will validate the presence of the STK19 mutant by measuring transcription and expression levels. We will then test whether the shorter isoform can activate other RAS proteins, performing pull-down assays with Western blotting. Finally, we will determine whether the STK19 inhibitor can target other RAS-mutant cancers, by treating cells harboring different mutations with the inhibitor and measuring cell survival."

column36: Beliefs About Losing Control As a Moderator Between Social Anxiety and Problematic Drinking in Young Adults
column37: "Social anxiety is a significant risk factor for developing alcohol related problems in adults, however, evidence in support of this association in young adults is mixed. For reasons that are currently unclear, researchers have found both positive and negative risk trajectories for developing alcohol related problems in young adults. Our limited understanding of this relationship is particularly troubling given the severe individual and societal consequences associated with alcohol abuse in young adults (e.g., risk of accidents, health issues). If we are to be successful in developing effective treatment/prevention strategies, it is urgent that we are first able to answer the following question: why do some socially anxious young adults develop drinking problems, while others do not?Interestingly, there is evidence that beliefs play a significant role in the development of both alcohol use and social anxiety. Specifically, individuals with social anxiety may believe that alcohol will impair their ability to maintain control of their thoughts, behaviors, emotions, and/or bodily functions. As such, these individuals may avoid heavy alcohol use, fearing that intoxication might result in embarrassing losses of control. Further, individuals with social anxiety may also endorse beliefs about losing control, and fear that if they were to lose control in a social context, they would be harshly judged by others. As such, we predict that young adults with social anxiety will be less likely to experience alcohol related problems only if they endorse negative beliefs about their ability to maintain control while intoxicated. Importantly, it is our hope that this research will help inform prevention strategies for problematic drinking behavior in this at risk population."

column36: Interpreting Infant Emotional Expression: The Role of Cognitive Behavioral Group Therapy for Women with Postpartum Anxiety
column37: " A mother's ability to accurately interpret and respond to her baby's emotional expressions is crucial to the mental and emotional development of her infant. Postpartum anxiety (PPA) has been shown to interfere with this ability. Specifically, women with PPA are more likely to interpret neutral infant faces as sad and are less likely to recognize happy infant faces than women without PPA. This is important because mothers that are overly responsive to negative emotion reinforce the expression of negative emotion in their infants, which increases the infant's risk of developing depression and anxiety later in life. It is, therefore, crucial that mothers with PPA are able to accurately identify infant emotional expression. Cognitive behavioral group therapy (CBGT) is a leading treatment for PPA and, while it effectively reduces anxiety symptom severity in women with PPA, it is unknown whether CBGT can also improve the ability to interpret infant emotional expression. This is the first study to examine if women with PPA who receive CBGT are better able to identify infant emotional expressions than women with PPA who do not receive CBGT. All women will complete self-report measures of anxiety and will review and label various pictures of infant emotional expressions both before and after CBGT, or at baseline and six weeks later if not receiving CBGT. Given that being able to interpret infant emotional expression is crucial to infant development, it is necessary to determine if CBGT can improve this ability or whether additional treatments are required. This study will inform treatment recommendations for women with PPA and will also advance our understanding of mental health and parenting. "

column36: Investigating the role of MBD1 isoforms in myelodysplastic syndrome
column37: "1 in 1000 Canadians over 65 will develop myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), which causes deficiencies in mature blood cells due to malignant hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and may progress to secondary acute myeloid leukemia. The only cure for MDS are bone marrow (BM) transplants which are dangerous for elderly patients, indicating a need for new therapeutics. Splicing factors are mutated in 60% of cases, suggesting that RNA splicing may be a key pathogenic pathway. By analyzing RNA sequencing data from healthy and MDS BM, we identified MBD1, a DNA binding protein that represses gene expression, as a globally mis-spliced transcript in MDS and a candidate therapeutic target. We identified exon inclusion events that add new repressive capabilities, potentially representing therapeutically relevant gain-of-function events. As most causal mis-spliced transcripts in MDS are loss-of-function isoforms, our identification of MBD1 mis-splicing may highlight a novel mechanism through which alternative splicing can contribute to MDS. In this project, my two objectives are to determine whether increased inclusion of exon 10 or 12 promotes MDS pathology, and the associated mechanism. For my first objective, I will use lentivirally encoded dCasRx to perform exon knockdown and overexpression in the MDSL cell line and primary MDS samples to run clonal competitive assays to define whether exon 10 or 12 promote MDS growth. For my second objective, I will use integrative CHIP-seq and RNA-seq on primary MDS samples and healthy human HSCs to determine altered promoter binding and gene repression due to MBD1 mis-splicing. By studying MBD1 mis-splicing in MDS, I will uncover a new and tractable therapeutic target for MDS while uncovering new ways through which splicing can contribute to MDS."

column36: Pathophysiology and treatment of adult somnambulism
column37: "Sleepwalking (also known as somnambulism) is a sleep disorder that occurs during the deepest stages of sleep and that affects up to 4% of adults. It represents one of the most common causes of violence and self-injuries during sleep. This sleep disorder is known for its dramatic nature, particularly because of the aggressive behaviors that can occur during episodes and the dangers of these behaviors for the patients and their bed partner. In fact, adults suffering from sleepwalking often consult following injuries and/or aggressive behaviors during their sleep.Considering that there is currently no systematic prospective study to evaluate the treatment of sleepwalking, evidence supporting treatment recommendations is limited. The most frequently recommended non-pharmacological treatment for sleepwalking is hypnosis. However, most of the data with regards to the treatment are from case studies or are entirely descriptive and retrospective in nature.For this reason, our project focuses on studying the effect of hypnosis treatment on the frequency and severity of nocturnal episodes in the laboratory. Additionally, the effect of hypnosis treatment will be studied at home over 12 months after the hypnosis treatment. Our study will examine sleep data from a group of adult sleepwalkers and controls (a group of the same-age and same-sex people who are non-sleepwalkers). At the sleep laboratory, we will use polysomnography to record each individual's brainwaves during sleep and will examine the differences between polysomnography recordings before and after the hypnosis Intervention. This project will allow us to better understand the mechanism of action of hypnosis and to document the short- and long-term effects of this treatment on sleepwalking."

column36: Helpful or Harmful? Consequences of Cellular Volume Changes Following Stroke
column37: "Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating stroke subtype that is fatal for over 40% of patients. ICH occurs when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures, causing blood to spill into the surrounding tissues and form a clot. The skull is a closed compartment, so a large blood clot takes up essential space in the brain and drives up pressure within the skull, with often fatal outcomes. Interestingly, we recently discovered a novel phenomenon in which brain cells experience a dramatic reduction in volume (up to 60%) in the days following a moderate to large ICH. We believe that this is a regulated process, in which brain cells get rid of compounds called osmolytes, which are low-weight organic molecules that influence properties of cells, such as protein stability, cell size regulation, and cellular health. By doing this, cells are able to reduce their size in attempt to equalize deadly pressure elevations and prevent death. However, by getting rid of osmolytes to reduce their size, cells are ridding themselves of an important protective mechanism essential for survival in a stroke setting. Therefore, we assert that the loss of protective osmolytes in order to maintain cell size reductions is detrimental to the health of brain cells, resulting in the global functional impairments that we observe in ICH patients, rather than local reductions in blood flow as previously thought. We aim to assess whether these cell size reductions occur across multiple brain cell types, examine the impact of stroke severity, and quantitatively determine how extreme cell size reductions impact cellular health and function through gold standard techniques such as electron microscopy and Fourier Transform Infrared Imaging. "

column36: Use of Phage Therapy for the Treatment of Colitis in a Mouse Model
column37: "The inflammation of the colon is a common symptom among many diseases. It stems from a multitude of factors, one of which being the presence of evil bacteria in the digestive tract. These evil bacteria can cause a lot of problems for patients who will experience unnecessary pain for their entire lives. For many issues surrounding evil bacteria, we employ the use of antibiotics to eliminate their threat. A side effect of this, however, is that many antibiotics used to treat inflammation of the colon results in the deaths of both evil and good bacteria, those responsible for maintaining a healthy gut. This often results in secondary infections that are so dangerous that for many patients, the use of antibiotics is not an option and so there is no cure. The solution we propose is the use of good viruses known as bacteriophages (phages). Phages only infect bacteria and not human cells. They are very specific in targeting bacteria and can knock out one type of bacteria in a mixed population while leaving the others intact. In that sense, phages are like directed missiles, they only attack their assigned targets. Previous work in our lab has confirmed that phages do not cause inflammation when present in the digestive tract nor do they impact the healthy bacteria already there. To understand how phages can help cure the inflammation of the colon, we propose to look at their action in an inflamed mouse gut. From studying mice, we will gather the necessary information required to develop phages into an applicable therapeutic treatment for humans who suffer from inflammation of the colon. The knowledge produced in this project could lead to the development of an effective cure that will directly impact the lives of 270,000 Canadians living with inflamed colon related diseases."
