column36: "Utilization of Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Radiomics for the classification of sub-cm lung nodules in early cancer diagnosis"
column37: "Low Dose Computed Tomography (LDCT) screening programs are well known for detecting small lung nodules in at risk lung cancer patients. Predicting the future behavior of small nodules has proven challenging even for expert clinicians. As such, nodules in this category often have a 'wait and see' plan assigned to them. Computer assisted diagnosis (CADx) tools are in high demand as a cost-effective diagnostic approach for predicting the malignant potential of these small nodules. The proposed CADx approach in classifying these small nodules is founded on Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods such as machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms. By providing these algorithms with a large dataset of nodules and hand-generated radiomic features, these data-driven models can determine which features are both statistically relevant and represent malignant behaviors. Moreover, most current AI methods are largely seen as 'blackboxes' to expert clinicians, and thus are not well trusted in the radiologist medical community as of yet. I propose developing further methods to surmount this hurdle of interpretability, while maintaining a high classification accuracy, for clinical deployment as another tool in the radiologist's toolbox. I will perform this task over the next 12 months. First, I will collect an assortment of public LDCT lung nodules. Second, I will monitor, implement, train, and study of state-of-the-art 2D and 3D ML and DL models, then validate these methods on an in-house lung nodule dataset. This CADx tool could effectively remove the 'wait and see' policy, address the cost-effective challenge of LDCT screening programs, stage shift cancerous nodules into earlier more treatable stages, eliminate extra burden on hospital resources, and save patients' lives."

column36: Homeostatic Plasticity in the Pathogenesis of Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: "Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is currently the fastest-growing neurodevelopmental disorder in North America. Approximately 1 in 66 Canadians aged 5-17 are diagnosed with ASD, a disorder characterized by impairments in communication, difficulty with social interaction, and repetitive patterns of behaviour. Given that the diagnosis of ASD has been steadily rising in recent years, there is growing urgency for the development of novel treatments and therapies. Although many previous studies have documented synaptic aberrations present in ASD, less is known about how these neural abnormalities can be restored. In this project, we will explore if certain types of synaptic plasticity can be manipulated to alleviate ASD symptomology. Specifically, we will focus on the interaction between ""Hebbian"" and ""homeostatic"" mechanisms. Hebbian plasticity is a highly specific process dealing with strengthening or weakening of individual synapses, while homeostatic plasticity occurs at a global scale of neuronal activity. The interplay of both forms is required to ensure optimal functioning, where homeostatic processes prevent Hebbian mechanisms from causing increasing extremes of excitatory or inhibitory synaptic strength. ASD is marked by imbalances of excitatory to inhibitory synapses (E/I ratio), and we speculate this is due to lack of homeostatic influence over Hebbian plasticity. Thus, we propose that homeostatic scaling can be utilized to improve Hebbian learning and normalize E/I ratio. Furthermore, we predict that by restoring synaptic composition, homeostatic scaling may prove useful in alleviating other symptoms as well, including deficits in cognition and social behaviour. "

column36: Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid-4 (TRPV4) channel impacts pathological collagen remodeling by regulating focal adhesion assembly
column37: "Fibrosis is a high-prevalence and debilitating disorder that can affect multiple organs in the body, yet its pathogenic mechanisms are not well-understood, and effective therapies are lacking. Fibrosis is characterized by excessive production and stiffening of the non-cellular component of connective tissue (known as the extracellular matrix), which leads to progressive tissue scaring and that results in organ failure. Fibroblasts are the major extracellular-matrix-producing and remodeling cell type in connective tissue. Fibroblasts can be activated by a stiffened matrix to produce more matrix and cause more stiffening, thereby establishing a vicious cycle that leads to relentless fibrosis progression. Accordingly, it is important to understand how fibroblasts sense and translate matrix stiffness into pathological activities, i.e. mechanical signaling in fibroblasts. My project focuses on the molecules that serve as mechanical receptors and promote pathological matrix remodeling and stiffening by fibroblasts. My research will use cultured fibroblasts to study the molecular mechanism by which they interact with and respond to collagen, which is an abundant protein in the extracellular matrix and a key component in fibrous lesions. A better understanding of how fibroblasts sense and remodel collagen abnormally in fibrosis will generate insights on novel opportunities for effective therapeutic development that can halt or reverse fibrosis progression."

column36: Defining the role of MALT1 paracaspase in immune function through novel substrate identification
column37: "Our immune system is our strongest defence against ""foreign invaders"" such as viruses and bacteria. Primary immunodeficiency diseases (PIDs) are a group of genetic disorders in which parts of the immune system are missing, dysfunctional, or poorly regulated. The MALT1 protein is critical for the activation and regulation of immune cells, exemplified by patients without MALT1 experiencing both a weakened immune system, increasing their risk of infection, as well as an overactive immune system. MALT1 is activated after immune cells sense foreign substances in their environment, and functions as a protease, cutting other proteins (substrates) in order to turn on the immune cell's pro-inflammatory functions to fight the foreign agent. This implicates MALT1 as a promising drug target to treat autoimmunity and certain blood cancers where it is overactive. However, directly stopping MALT1 may result in unpleasant side effects without a better understanding of its activity and function. We aim to identify MALT1 substrates using Terminal Amine Isotopic Labeling of Substrates (TAILS), a powerful technique which identifies cut proteins by binding their newly exposed ends and enabling their identification and analysis. Our access to cells without MALT1 allows us to look at the relative amounts of cut proteins compared to cells with normal amounts of MALT1; the cut proteins more abundant in normal cells compared to cells without MALT1 indicates potential MALT1 substrates, since MALT1 would not be there to cut the proteins in the cells without MALT1. This project will provide the foundation for more functional studies of MALT1 substrates and their contribution to normal immune function, eventually paving the way for the production of targeted drugs."

column36: Smell in subjective cognitive decline: a candidate for an early detection of Alzheimer's disease?
column37: "The diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease is currently made when the criteria for dementia are met, i.e. when the cognitive deficits are severe enough to interfere with the person's autonomy. Thus, it is important to find early markers of the disease in order to be able to intervene before the dementia stage, for example, at the subjective cognitive decline stage. This stage is characterized by complaints of cognitive decline with a level of neuropsychological performance remains within normal range. This marker is sensitive, but not very specific. The sense of smell could specify its predictive value. Olfactory impairment is present in the mild cognitive impairment stage, a stage between subjective cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease. However, no studies have evaluated the olfactory system, as well as its neurological links, within subjective cognitive decline.Thus, the objective of the study is to evaluate the olfactory system of people with subjective cognitive decline compared to a healthy elderly group. In addition, the project aims to study the possible associations between olfactory losses and cognitive abilities of this population. Ultimately, using magnetic resonance imaging, the identification of affected brain regions in subjective cognitive decline will allow links to be made between affected regions and olfactory/cognitive abilities. The results of this project will identify specific patterns of cerebral, olfactory and cognitive changes that are the best predictors of the early stages of Alzheimer's disease. This research has the potential to provide a new approach for early detection of individuals at high risk to develop Alzheimer's Disease."

column36: The Association Between Early-Life Threat and Deprivation on Child and Adolescent Executive Function: A Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis

column36: Improving non-operative care for patients with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome
column37: "Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome (FAIS) is a painful condition caused by abnormal bone structure of the hip joint. It is estimated that 10-15% of the population suffer from this condition, most of whom are active people, aged 20-45. Prior work done by our group has established physiotherapy as an effective treatment method for FAIS and derived which types of physiotherapy protocols are most effective based available evidence. Additionally, previous studies have outlined which patient and disease characteristics are helpful in predicting success of surgery, however we have a poor understanding of which patients are most appropriate for non-operative care and what factors might influence their success. Knowledge of which patients are most appropriate for each treatment modality will allow for clinicians to provide individualized care for FAIS patients, and potentially lead patients to be unnecessarily exposed to risks of surgery. We aim to address this knowledge gap. We will assemble a group of patients with FAIS and collect a baseline of characteristics, including impairment scores. All patients will then partake in an evidence-based, core-focused home physiotherapy regimen for 6 months. At the end of the treatment period, we will compare each patient's function to their baseline scores and determine if there are any characteristics that can help predict success of non-operative care. The findings of this study will allow healthcare to be delivered on a more personalized, patient-centred basis for those with FAI, ensuring the right treatment is prescribed to the right patient. "

column36: "The role of palmitoylating enzyme, Zdhhc9, in regulating neuronal connectivity"
column37: "Palmitoylation, the addition of palmitic acid onto a substrate, plays an essential role in regulating cellular signaling by trafficking proteins to membranes. Emerging evidence suggests that, in the brain, palmitoylation has a critical role in mediating the formation and function of synapses. As such, genetic mutations in palmitoylating enzymes are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, including schizophrenia, autism, and intellectual disability. Notably, mutations in the gene encoding palmitoylating enzyme, zDHHC9, have been identified in nearly 2% of all patients diagnosed with X?-linked intellectual disability (XLID), 75% of whom experience epileptic comorbidities. column36: Interpersonal problems in Borderline Personality Disorder: Mediators for change during Dialectical Behavioural Therapy
column37: "Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a serious mental illness that occurs in 2-6% of the population. BPD impacts a person's ability to manage their emotions, behaviour and relationships. It is also associated with high rates of self-harm and suicide. Indeed, estimates suggest that death by suicide in this population is 50 times higher than the general population. The severity and prevalence of BPD makes it one of the most expensive mental illnesses to treat, consequently posing a high economic burden to society. Fortunately, research has found treatments for BPD, of which Dialectical Behavioural Therapy (DBT; a type of cognitive behavioural therapy) currently has the most evidence. Even with DBT, however, relationship problems in BPD are hard to treat and slow to change. Relationship problems have also been linked to suicide attempts and self-harm. As a result, more research is needed to understand how treatment works to improve relationship problems among patients with BPD. The primary aim of this research is to look at the various ways in which relationships improve for BPD patients doing DBT. Understanding how and why relationships change during treatment could help us find better ways to help patients with BPD. Given the high costs of BPD and the link between relationship problems and suicide, efforts to understand and improve relationships in BPD are important and will have large health impacts."

column36: Drug and Alcohol Use - Land Based Treatment Programs
column37: "My master's thesis will utilize a mixed-methods, Two Eyed Seeing approach to develop a culturally competent evaluation framework for a land-based drug and alcohol misuse treatment program with the Tlicho government in the Northwest Territories. My findings will: provide a valuable tool for evaluating the implementation process and outcomes of land-based addiction treatment programs within Tlicho communities and provide information on how this program may be improved to better meet the needs of facilitators and participants. column36: Investigating the role of type-II innate lymphoid cells in allergic asthma
column37: "Emerging evidence suggests that eosinophilic asthma (EA) may be mediated by type-II innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s). Inflammatory cytokines produced by ILC2s promote eosinophil maturation. In EA, eosinophils migrate to the lungs and cause inflammation, driving pathogenesis. Corticosteroids are typically used to treat EA. However, 5-10% of asthmatics are resistant to this treatment and thus alternative therapeutics need to be developed. Recent work suggests that ILC2s can become resistant to steroids in the presence of specific cytokines. Thus, it is hypothesized that ILC2s may be responsible for the steroid insensitivity observed in some EA patients and that targeting of this cell population for inhibition could represent a novel therapeutic avenue for EA treatment.Currently, it is unknown which cytokines may promote ILC2 steroid resistance, and whether these cytokines influence ILC2 surface marker expression. Peripheral blood, sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid collected from human subjects with EA will be analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs), multiplex arrays and flow cytometry. These analyses will identify the specific cytokines present at each of the three locations and identify differences in surface marker expression of ILC2s from each of these locations. Ultimately, by identifying ILC2 surface markers and cytokines which promote steroid-resistance, novel therapeutics which inhibit these markers and cytokines could be developed to treat EA.This work is very significant as asthma represents a significant economic healthcare burden and its incidence is predicted to rise in Canada. Development of novel EA therapeutics will allow for the treatment of steroid-resistant EA patients and improve the quality of life of these individuals."

column36: Social Shift: Social Media?s Effects on Human Connection and Depression
column37: "According to the World Health Organization, depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide and more than 300 million people (4% of the global population) are suffering from it. Empiric research does suggest that social media and depression are linked, but the details of that connection have not been sufficiently researched. Through a digital survey of social media users, a content analysis of these users' posts and their respective engagement metrics, and the creation of an analytics algorithm, I aim to investigate the link between the two. Specifically, I plan to better understand how the human needs of love and belonging (Maslow's hierarchy) are met through social media usage and explore if/how the reliance on these platforms is affecting users' abilities to connect with others and have this need met, since negative effects would lead to varying levels of depression. Ultimately, I aim to provide insightful information that can lead to predictive, management, and/or preventative solutions."

column36: Do neural progenitor cells mature and become integrated in the stroke injured cortex?
column37: "Strokes are caused from reduced blood flow to a region of the brain producing tissue damage that is a leading cause of disability in Canada. The damage has been shown in many species to elicit a natural response from the brain to increase the neural stem and proliferating progenitor cells that migrate to the site of damage. This is remarkable as it suggests that the brain has abilities to repair itself after stroke in the absence of treatment. This has inspired research efforts to find treatments that increase the number of neural stem cells (NSCs) to improve stroke recovery. While many therapies such as running, increase recovery and increase the number of NSCs, it remains unknown if the adult-generated cells that arise after stroke can induce recovery. Our laboratory has used validated animal models of stroke recovery to test whether only increasing NSCs that migrate to the injury site can improve recovery. We found that increasing the number of cells alone was not enough to improve recovery. These findings have led us to this project that tests if the cells can integrate and become mature in the injured environment. If the cells are unable to integrate, we would need to test alternative method to increase integration to improve recovery. Specifically, the project uses preclinical mouse models to test whether the cells that migrate to the site of stroke damage: 1) express protein that are found in functional neurons; 2) whether the cells are activated during behavioural tasks; and 3) if they are able to make connections within the stroke injured brain. This project will provide the first examination of the maturation and integration status of NSCs in the damaged stroke area for us to determine how to harness these cells to improve recovery following stroke."

column36: To characterize the role of primary cilia in astrocytes
column37: "Epilepsy is a disorder that is characterized by frequent seizures, which are a result of disturbances in neuronal activity in the brain. Being a common neurological disorder affecting roughly 65 million people, the mechanisms underlying epilepsy/seizures remain poorly understood. One major contributor recently identified is linked to dysfunctional astrocytes. Astrocytes closely contact neuronal elements to help maintain an optimised neuronal activity by exchanging and clearing up the neuronal signals between neurons. Such function is facilitated by their highly elaborative morphology and specialized gene expression signature. However, the mechanism that regulate astrocyte morphology and gene expression is poorly understood. Here, I propose a novel hypothesis that primary cilia, small structures protruding from the astrocytic cell body, represent one novel cellular mechanism involved in this process.To test this, I will use a mouse model with impaired primary cilia in astrocytes. I will study how the morphology and gene expression of ciliary mutant astrocytes is affected in the brain. Together, these experiments will help to clarify the importance of primary cilia in astrocytes and identify a new pathological pathway that underlies in epilepsy/seizure conditions. "

column36: Building Health Needs into Community Design
column37: "Housing plays an important role in the health of individuals and communities. Poor housing conditions are associated with worse health outcomes. Healthy housing supports physical, mental, and social well-being. As health needs will differ across communities, involving community members in a co-design process may help achieve healthy housing. Support from individuals with various backgrounds, including those working in health care, is needed for healthy housing design. As nurses act on social determinants of health such as housing and work on the frontline within communities, it would be beneficial to include them in the healthy housing design process. No studies have looked at the place of nurses in the community co-design of healthy housing, and this study seeks to fill this gap. There are three objectives for this study. First, to look at tools that are used by community health nurses to collect health needs and consider if they would be helpful for community co-design of healthy housing. Second, to understand how the health needs of two partnering communities relate to healthy housing design. Third, to explore how nurses can participate in community co-design to develop healthy housing. The knowledge gained from this study will be helpful for nurses working in communities who want to take action on the social determinants of health. The results of this study will be particularly useful for nurses working in rural and remote communities where they have more of this responsibility. By supporting the development of healthy housing, this study ultimately contributes to creating a fair chance for all people to reach their full health potential."

column36: A Randomized Controlled Trial Testing the Efficacy of an Insulin-Dose Learning Algorithm in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes
column37: "Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a metabolic disease that results in no insulin production from the pancreas, a hormone required to allow glucose to be used as energy. Despite advances in diabetic treatment technology, maintaining glucose targets is difficult to achieve for most. Therefore, my proposed research will test Dr. Haidar's new personalized learning algorithm (computer-generated decision-making tool) for people with T1D using multiple daily injection (MDI) therapy. This algorithm is designed to estimate optimal insulin doses based on each person's glucose, meal and insulin data over several days. This research is important to Canada because over 300 000 Canadians are currently living with T1D, and the prevalence is expected to rise in the next decade The goal of my master's project is to run a clinical trial to test the efficacy of the algorithm with the fast-growing combined use of MDI therapy and glucose sensor technology (continuously measures glucose levels every five minutes), and examine if the added algorithm will improve glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) (marker of glucose control over the past three months). This trial will consist of a randomized parallel design, where 84 eligible adults will be recruited at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre, alongside five study endocrinologists, and will randomly undergo one of two interventions at home for three months. The expected outcomes are that the algorithm's recommended adjustments will result in a greater reduction in HbA1c compared to MDI therapy with glucose sensor technology alone. To our knowledge, this data will be the first in Canada to highlight the possibility of incorporating personalized algorithms into smart insulin pens for MDI therapy."

column36: "Examining how end-demand criminalization of sex work shapes the occupational health, safety, and labour rights of cis and trans men sex workers"
column37: "In 2014, the Canadian government enacted legislation that criminalized the purchasing of sex and third parties commercially profiting from sex work, known as end-demand criminalization. There is a growing body of literature that has examined the impacts of end-demand criminalization in Canada on the occupational health, safety, and labour rights of sex workers and has shown that the current legislation has contributed to high levels of victimization, violence, and HIV transmission among sex workers. However, this literature has largely focused on women sex workers at the exclusion of cis and trans men sex workers (MSWs), resulting in a gendered gap on what is known about criminalization's impacts on the health and safety of sex workers. The limited evidence shows that MSWs face distinct barriers to their occupational health and likely experience vulnerabilities that are exacerbated under current Canadian legislation. The proposed study will expand on the existing literature to qualitatively examine how evolving Canadian sex work legislation and regional policing practices shape the occupational health and safety among cis and trans men sex workers in Vancouver, British Columbia. This research will use participatory and community-based research methods, centering MSWs and community organizations in this study's design, conduct, and translation of findings."

column36: Protective equipment in high school athletes: Can mouthguards and optimal helmet fit prevent sport-related concussions in youth collision sport?
column37: "Concussion (e.g., sport-related concussion) is a brain injury that affects over 1.5 million North American youth each year. Unfortunately, suffering a concussion can disrupt the physical (e.g., headaches), emotional (e.g., depression), and social (e.g., isolation) aspects of a youth's wellbeing. Therefore, strategies to prevent concussions must be explored. Equipment-based strategies are simple and perhaps effective for reducing concussion occurrence in sport. Specifically, mouthguard use and optimal helmet fit may protect against concussion occurrence; however, evidence is lacking. The 5th International Sport Concussion Consensus suggests a 19% reduction in concussion when athletes wear a mouthguard (not statistically significant). Further, an estimated 52% reduction in concussion is reported when youth ice hockey players wear mouthguards. Moreover, helmet use is effective for reducing head injury in recreational activities (e.g., bicycling). In the context of concussion prevention, helmet fit is an important consideration. Preliminary data in youth ice hockey evaluating helmet mobility and age, chin-strap fit, and other criteria suggests that proper fit is protective against concussion. Unfortunately, the current literature lacks high quality studies that assess equipment-based concussion prevention strategies across multiple collision sports. Therefore, this study will compare mouthguard use and helmet fit (where applicable) at time of injury for concussion (cases) and musculoskeletal (MSK; controls) inured grade 10 high school students playing collision sport (e.g., ice hockey, football, rugby) in 5 Canadian provinces. Understanding the protective effect of equipment will inform concussion prevention policies and strategies to promote lifelong sport participation."

column36: Quality of life in women who carry the BRCA1/2 mutation post-oophorectomy
column37: "I propose to study the quality of life in women who carry the BRCA1/2 mutation post-oophorectomy (ovarian removal) through qualitative interviews. Women who carry a BRCA gene mutation are at an increased risk for breast and ovarian cancer, and consequently, many women elect to have their breasts and ovaries removed as prophylaxis. Post-surgery, women have experienced physical changes, changes to libido, and subjective cognitive complaints. There is a dearth of qualitative research elucidating the experiences of these women in their quality of life post-surgery, and in particular, there is no qualitative study to date that has captured measures of subjective cognitive impairment in women post-oophorectomy. This is particularly critical, because women with oophorectomy are also at a higher risk of developing Alzheimer's Disease, and subjective cognitive impairment is a precursor state to the development of dementia. The aims of the qualitative interviews are twofold: (1) assess subjective cognitive impairment (2) understand the quality of life post-surgery on various indicators: e.g., physically, socially, emotional. This study hopes to address the gap in the literature and provide a better understanding of the cognitive consequences of oophorectomy, and by gaining a general sense of quality of life post-surgery, potentially identify improvements to counselling and support services to this population. "

column36: Metabolic signatures of combined lifestyle factors for prevention of Type 2 Diabetes
column37: "Type 2 diabetes is widely considered a leading public health issue. By 2030, it is estimated that type 2 diabetes will affect 552 million people, amounting to $727 billion USD per year in healthcare costs. Fortunately, however, this chronic illness is largely preventable. In fact, there is a strong body of evidence showing that adopting a healthy lifestyle (i.e. healthy body weight, nutritious diet, ≥30mins/day of physical activity, no smoking, moderate alcohol intake) is the ideal strategy for avoiding it. Previous research has shown that living a healthy lifestyle could prevent type 2 diabetes, although scientists have yet to understand how these factors (i.e. body mass, diet, physical activity, smoking, and alcohol consumption) work in combination with one another to impact a person's overall health. Recent studies have shown the potential to predict patients' health profiles from blood-based biomarkers, although this has yet to be shown for combined lifestyle behaviours. The main objectives to this research are to: (1) discover how adopting several positive health behaviours in combination with one another (i.e. healthy body mass, nutritious diet, sufficient exercise, no smoking, low alcohol consumption) leads to better health outcomes based on blood biomarker profiles and (2) how a combination of these behaviors help prevent type 2 diabetes in various ethnic groups. These aims are designed to provide doctors, nurses, and other health professionals with a better understanding of how adopting a combination of healthy behaviours may maximize health and prevent type 2 diabetes. With this information, health professionals may gain a better understanding of how to provide patients optimal health guidelines, demonstrating the significant impact of this research. "

column36: The neurobiology of approach-avoidance conflict decision-making in rodents
column37: "Abnormal decision-making, seen commonly in mental illness, affects millions of Canadians. However, the neurobiology of decision-making is just being uncovered. An important aspect of decision-making is whether to approach or avoid an event that can have both positive and negative outcomes simultaneously. Studies have shown that the hippocampus and frontal cortical regions of the brain help regulate this behaviour, yet it is not understood how these regions work together to generate decisions. I hypothesize that increasing communication between the hippocampus and frontal cortex will decrease the amount of avoidance of these types of events and decreasing communication will increase avoidance. To test this, I will express artificial receptors in rat hippocampal neurons that target the frontal cortex, and in doing so I can control the activity of said neurons. The rats will next be placed in a task where they must press one of two levers: one lever will give them a small reward with no punishment, while the other lever will give them a large reward paired with a punishment. Increasing this punishment will shift the rats' preference from the large reward (with punishment) to the small reward (without punishment). By administering a drug that specifically targets the artificial receptors, I can increase or decrease neuronal activity. I will then observe whether these changes in activity will alter the rats' preference for one lever or the other. This work is important in identifying new treatments for mental illnesses with abnormal approach-avoidance behaviour, reducing their burden on the Canadian healthcare system."

column36: Cortical responses to median nerve stimulation in acute brain injury: an functional magnetic resonance imaging study
column37: "Cardiac arrest, more commonly known as a heart attack, often leads to coma due to oxygen deprivation in the brain. This requires extensive hospitalization in intensive care units, where treatment decisions are based off of tools that predict a poor outcome: death or a vegetative state. At present, there is a significant lack of clinical tests that can predict if a patient will awake from coma, and to what extent a meaningful neurological recovery can be made. To address this issue, I propose to develop a novel clinical tool that may predict if a patient will awake from coma following cardiac arrest. I will combine passive median nerve stimulation, known as somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP), with functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI). SSEP is a clinical test that assesses somatosensory system functioning. While in an fMRI suite, comatose patients will be electrically stimulated at the median nerve on the wrist, and brain activation will be recorded. I will look at the strength of activation in somatosensory brain regions in response to the median nerve stimulation, and correlate it to long-term outcomes. I hypothesize that the strength of neural activation during SSEP stimulation in comatose patients will correlate to the degree of functional recovery. Specifically, patients with greater brain activity in somatosensory areas will be more likely to make a meaningful neurological recovery, whereas patients with restricted or minimal activation will likely not regain consciousness. This proposed research will have significant impacts in alleviating the uncertainties of outcome in post cardiac arrest comatose patients, providing urgently needed information to health-care providers and distressed families. "

column36: The Impact of Anxiety Sensitivity and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder in Individuals with Chronic Illnesses
column37: "Living with a chronic illness can be debilitating and isolating. Unfortunately, it is a reality that many Canadians must face. Individuals living with chronic illnesses tend to prioritize their physical health and neglect their mental health. Yet, many of these individuals face mental health difficulties, or are vulnerable to developing mental illnesses, which can make coping even more difficult. In particular, these individuals may develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) from events that occur as a result of their illness, such as a heart attack or chemotherapy. Symptoms of PTSD include insomnia and interpersonal problems. One factor that makes the development of a mental illness more likely in addition to chronic illness is anxiety sensitivity (AS). AS is the fear of fear, meaning that individuals with high AS view arousal sensations (e.g., a racing heart) as threatening or dangerous (e.g., thinking you are having a heart attack). People with high AS are also more likely to develop PTSD after a traumatic event. Since individuals with chronic illnesses are already at risk for developing mental health difficulties, if they also have high AS, they are even more vulnerable. Therefore, my project will survey Canadians who have been diagnosed with at least one chronic illness, and will assess AS, quality of life, illness symptoms, and symptoms of PTSD. They will either receive group therapy or receive no treatment, and the treatment will focus on lowering their levels of AS and PTSD (if applicable). After the therapy, they will fill out the same survey again to see if the therapy has helped their mental health and, hopefully, their quality of life overall. This project has the potential to make a big difference in the lives of Canadians living with chronic illnesses."

column36: Investigating the impact of early life adversity on postnatal susceptibility to infection
column37: "Pneumococcal infection is a global health concern that inflicts wide-reaching personal and social costs. Streptococcus pneumoniae (""the pneumococcus"") is the leading bacterial cause of pneumonia (infection of the lungs) and invasive pneumococcal diseases such as bacteremia (bacteria in blood) and meningitis (infection of central nervous system). Despite the development of vaccines and antibiotics, the pneumococcus remains among the deadliest infectious agents worldwide, accounting for 1.6 million deaths a year. People over 65 years old and those with chronic inflammatory conditions are at increased risk of infection; in turn, having had pneumonia increases the risk of developing chronic diseases such as cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, and dementia later in life. It is also known that exposure to maternal obesity is a key-predictor of age-related diseases, including metabolic and inflammatory disorders. Recently, maternal obesity has been linked to immune compromise after birth. Hospitalizations due to infection are more common in children born to obese mothers compared to children born to non-obese mothers. The continuous rise of obesity among women of reproductive age presents a serious threat to the next generation's risk of infectious disease. Without understanding the factors that make certain individuals more susceptible to infection, there is little hope of combating this global health challenge. This proposed research will provide insight into the links between early life exposure to obesity and the risk of infection, which will enable the development of novel interventions to improve health outcomes for vulnerable populations."

column36: Using Cryo-Electron Microscopy to Guide the Design of Novel Histone Deacetylase 3 Inhibitors for Cancer Treatment.
column37: "Cancer is a multi-faceted group of diseases that hijacks the body's cells, causing them to continuously replicate and attack surrounding tissues. In order to control the cell cycle, many cancer cells edit their epigenomes: the pattern of DNA markings that indicate whether or not genes should be actively making protein. The epigenome differs greatly from that of a normal cell due to high expression of epigenetic editor proteins that can interpret, add or remove genetic markings, so called ""readers"", ""writers"" and ""erasers"". In order to edit the epigenome, these editor proteins must be guided to their intended DNA sequence by interactions with other proteins. A guiding protein that tends to be highly expressed in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is BCL6, which guides the eraser protein HDAC3 to silence genes involved in DNA damage responsiveness. The enhanced silencing program by aberrant BCL6 expression locks immature B-cells in a proliferative state, resulting in cancer. Some success has been had in designing drugs to target human HDACs, but they tend to have off-target effects due to the high number of human HDAC proteins. The goal of my project is to understand how HDAC3 interacts with DNA from an atomic perspective in order to design drugs to selectively target it without targeting other human HDACs, reducing drug toxicity. By using cryogenic transmission electron microscopy, I hypothesize that I will be able to determine a high-resolution image of the HDAC3 protein and those it interacts with to guide the design of novel inhibitors of its erasing function. The inhibition of HDAC3 will serve to help patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma by helping to release immature B-cells from their endless proliferation, leading to better, more effective therapies."

column36: Imaging of the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR5) abnormalities in patients with bilateral focal or neocortical epilepsy
column37: "Epilepsy is a neurological condition characterized by recurrent seizures. If those with epilepsy do not respond to anti-seizure medication, surgical treatment may be an option. Successful brain surgery prevents seizures in as many as 90% of operated patients. To achieve that rate of success, patients with a type of epilepsy called temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) usually undergo a comprehensive evaluation. Nevertheless, many TLE patients still cannot have their seizure focus precisely localized. In our study, we will further evaluate the value of a new non-invasive brain imaging scan that looks at a specific receptor previously shown to be abnormal in brain regions that generate seizures. The receptor that we are examining is called metabotropic glutamate receptor type 5 (mGluR5) and it modulates excitability through glutamate. The availability of mGluR5 in the brain can be imaged in vivo by positron emission tomography (PET). Previous studies from our laboratory have demonstrated that mGluR5 PET scans precisely localize the focus in TLE patients with a well-defined unilateral generator of seizures. It remains to be learned if it could be clinically useful for patients who do not always get offered a surgical treatment. Here, we will apply mGluR5 PET imaging to determine whether its specificity for the focus can localize the abnormalities in patients with a suspected bilateral seizure focus or those that affect the neocortical aspects of the temporal lobes. This project has the potential to validate a non-invasive method to localize the focus and to determine surgical candidacy in a broader way. In the long term, this project will also help pave the way for future research that examines and targets glutamatergic neurotransmission to control seizures."

column36: Pseudomonas biofilms in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis
column37: "Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is an inflammatory condition of the nasal and sinus mucosa that affects up to 16% of the population. Biofilm formation by bacteria is common in CRS patients, especially in those with persistent disease refractory to treatment. Pseudomonas aeruginosa-derived biofilms in particular have been associated with resistance to currently available antimicrobial treatments and worse CRS outcomes. The profile of biofilm exopolysaccharides produced by P. aeruginosa in the sinonasal cavities of CRS patients have yet to be determined. Recombinant microbial glycoside hydrolases that target biofilm exopolysaccharides have shown promise in the treatment of microbial biofilms in vitro and in vivo however have not been evaluated for their activity against bacterial biofilms isolated from sinuses of patients with CRS. This study aims to isolate strains of Pseudomonas bacteria from sinonasal cavities of patients with CRS and to characterize their profile of exopolysaccharide expression and biofilm-forming capacities. Recombinant glycoside hydrolases will be tested for their activity against biofilms formed by these CRS-associated strains of P. aeruginosa using standard in vitro biofilm assays. This study is an important stepping stone towards the development of new and effective treatments for CRS."

column16: Bourse a la maitrise : bourse d'etudes superieures
column36: Understanding the pathogenicity of hypervirulent Klebsiella
column37: "Klebsiella pneumoniae is able to cause bacterial infections in humans. Classical Klebsiella pneumoniae (cKp) infections are restricted to specific sites in medically compromised individuals. However, hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp) is able to cause more systemic infections in healthy individuals, and thus the emergence of hypervirulence in K. pneumoniae is a growing global concern. These strains are said to be hypervirulent as they have acquired factors which allow them to grow more rapidly and uncontrollably, and consequently cause more severe infections. These virulence factors can help the strain outcompete other microbes in the population. hvKp has been associated with increased production of siderophores, molecules which allow iron uptake from the host. In doing so, these molecules can help the strain outcompete other strains by sequestering iron which they need to survive. My project will investigate the factors which have given Klebsiella its increased virulence. By comparing Klebsiella genomes, I will identify the factors that hypervirulent strains have gained. I will then investigate the role of these factors in the ability of Klebsiella to outcompete other microbes in a population. The study of these virulence factors will facilitate the development of antivirulence therapy. This is an approach that seeks to disarm virulence factors rather than eliminate the pathogen itself, thereby reducing the risk of drug resistance development. By increasing our knowledge on these virulence factors, we can learn to identify and selectively target these factors in infected hosts, and combat the increasing incidence of more severe, often fatal, Klebsiella infections."

column36: "Characterization of adverse events, health care resource utilization, and real-world survival outcomes with introduction of ibrutinib for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)/ small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) patients in BC"
column37: "Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is the most common leukemia in adults in western countries. A particular drug that has proven to be very effective in newly diagnosed CLL patients and those who have relapsed is ibrutinib. Ibrutinib, however, causes certain side effects which can lead to early discontinuation of treatment and worse outcomes for patients. Most of what we know regarding the side effects of ibrutinib comes from clinical trials, which only accept healthy patients with few other medical problems. Little is known about how patients tolerate ibrutinib in the ""real-world"". It is therefore important that we obtain information from real-world practice, as clinical studies often underestimate discontinuation and survival rates. The goal of this study is to determine the frequency of side effects associated with ibrutinib compared to standard therapy using provincial administrative data obtained through PopData BC. Additionally, we aim to assess the impact of ibrutinib dose interruptions and reductions on survival outcomes, as well as the impact and cost of the side effects of therapy on the public health care system. A population based study will be completed comparing two groups of CLL patients: those receiving ibrutinib for treatment and those receiving an alternate therapy during the same time period. Both groups will be matched based on age, sex, line of therapy and predisposing factors related to the side effects of interest, to ensure the groups are comparable. Results from our study will provide important information to patients and health care providers regarding real-world risks of ibrutinib therapy and to governments and jurisdictions considering funding implications for ibrutinib on a population-basis. "

column36: Cognitive functions and mental health among transgender people
column37: "Cognition refers to the thought processes by which individuals acquire information and knowledge. Men and women differ in their cognitive abilities. In general, men perform better than women at spatial abilities tasks while women show better verbal abilities than men. The cognitive sex differences observed between the sexes are called sexually dimorphic cognition and are partly influenced by sex hormones like estrogen and testosterone. However, cognitive functioning is complex and goes beyond sex hormones. For example, sexual orientation also influences cognition. Socio-cultural variables such as gender identity (self-identification as male, female, or gender diverse) also modulates cognition. In sum, these elements shape individual differences in cognitive performance. Our research aims to understand how sex and gender explain cognitive functions. Moreover, cognitive functioning is also modulated by distress and mental health. As transgender people experience a discordance between their birth-assigned sex and their gender identity, they are at crossroads of sex hormones changes, sexual orientation and gender identity. They therefore experience a lot of changes in their cognitive functions. This project aims to assess cognitive functioning among transgender people while considering sex hormones, gender identity, and sexual orientation. Compared to controls, we expect transgender people to present cognitive performances similar to the gender they are transitioning rather than their birth-assigned sex. We also hypothesize that a group of gender diverse people who are not undergoing hormonal therapies to perform in between the controls and the participants. This study will help us understand the sex and gender correlates of sexually dimorphic cognition and mental health "

column36: Rare but not forgotten: finding the origins of major defects in KBG syndrome
column37: "KBG syndrome is a rare, underdiagnosed disease with severe multi-organ defects, including the heart and brain. It is caused by a mutation in or deletion of gene ANKRD11, which is responsible for regulating gene expression during development. ANKRD11 was previously shown by our lab to directly regulate neuron development in the brain, but its contribution to heart development is not known. Moreover, it is currently unknown whether cardiovascular malformations seen in KBG syndrome children may indirectly affect brain development. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that congenital heart defects in children are often associated with brain anomalies.To ask these questions, I will model KBG syndrome in a mouse that has Ankrd11 deleted only in cells of neural crest lineage. I will focus on the contribution of ANKRD11 to neural crest development because KBG syndrome patients show defects that are found in diseases of the neural crest, an embryonic tissue that contributes to structures like eyes, ears, face, peripheral nervous system, and the heart valves and blood vessels. Furthermore, my preliminary data show embryos with Ankrd11 deletion in neural crest have a severe heart defect with implications for poor blood flow. In this project, I will characterize all defects in embryonic heart structures, specifically in the valves, septa and blood vessels. I will also describe any defects in vasculature. To examine the effects of heart defects on brain development, I will study different cell types in the embryonic brain of the KBG mouse model to detect anomalies in their numbers and location. The results of my project will elucidate the origins of the most severe defects in KBG syndrome, contributing to better counselling, diagnosis and treatment of this syndrome."

column36: Motion correction for volumetric flow-encoded MRI in paediatric congenital heart disease
column37: "Congenital heart disease (CHD), manifesting as structural malformations of the heart and/or major blood vessels, affects ~1% of children born in Canada. Without intervention, CHD can be detrimental to growth, cognitive development, and overall quality of life. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is regularly applied to assess the severity of CHD and monitor treatment outcomes. With the ability to depict vascular anatomy and quantify blood flow, CMR is crucial for accurate evaluation at major stages of treatment plans. Though CMR is a valuable clinical tool, its use in paediatric CHD is limited. A significant issue is that children have a tendency of moving while being scanned, giving rise to corrupted images. As such, general anesthesia (GA) is the current standard-of-care for CMR for immobilizing children under 7 years of age. GA however is unfavourable in children as there are a host of negative consequences associated with its use, including a threefold increase in incidence of anesthesia-induced cardiac arrest compared to adults. To safely assess paediatric CHD patients, an alternative solution for motion correction is required. Recent development in fast volumetric CMR techniques promises to transform cardiovascular assessment, especially in children with CHD, but further work is essential to make such novel methods robust to patient motion. The objective of the proposed research will be to develop a motion correction algorithm that can be used in conjunction with highly accelerated scan procedures and novel image reconstruction strategies to correct for bulk and respiratory motion, allowing radiologists to quickly and accurately visualize cardiovascular morphology and quantify blood flow in non-sedated, free-breathing children with CHD."

column36: Real-time visualization and disruption of fear memory neuromodulation using a novel biosensor
column37: "A review of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in Canada reported that seven out of ten randomly surveyed participants experienced acute trauma associated with the onset of PTSD [1] Despite this high rate of exposure to trauma, very little is known about the underlying biology of traumatic fear memory and how disorders such as PTSD can be treated effectively. I propose to use the imaging of neural activity during fear conditioning and static circuit mapping to understand the cell types involved in order to elucidate the role and pharmacologic utility of a peptide called gastrin releasing peptide (GRP) in fear memory. To accomplish this, I will use a miniature integrated fluorescence microscope to image Ca2+ spiking in fear-memory-associated brain regions in awake, freely moving mice in conjunction with a custom made, novel biosensor for GRP. Finally, I will map the underlying circuitry of the fear-memory-associated brain regions using retrograde modified rabies viruses. This combination of methods allows me to investigate both the static and dynamic states of fear memory; a unique combination of approaches that has yet to be used within Canada Using novel biotechnology and a multidisciplinary approach I will dissect (1) the role that GRP plays in the various stages of fear memory; (2) how fear behaviours change with GRP neuromodulation; (3) its potential for therapeutic application in PTSD. With this approach, I will deliver an improved understanding of the basic biology in fear memory and contain the spatial and temporal windows for potential GRP-based prevention of PTSD. [1] Van Ameringen, M., Mancini, C., Patterson, B., & Boyle, M. H. (2008). Post-traumatic stress disorder in Canada. CNS neuroscience & therapeutics, 14(3), 171-181."

column36: Examining attitudes towards a proposed sugar-sweetened beverage tax among urban Indigenous adults using a decolonizing lens
column37: "Indigenous people residing in Canadian urban centers are disproportionately affected by health inequities, food insecurity, and reliance on non-traditional market foods. Recently, a number of provincial and territorial political parties have expressed their support for the implementation of a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages as a public health measure to reduce their consumption. However, sugar-sweetened beverage taxes are regressive and, as observed with other 'sin' taxes, may be stigmatizing. Indigenous people living in low income areas may be adversely affected given the considerable barriers to food access, which may further exacerbate health disparities. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to examine the acceptability of a proposed sugar-sweetened beverage tax among urban Indigenous people.The study will employ a participatory action research design in partnership with Aboriginal Youth Opportunities and National Indigenous Diabetes Association. Qualitative data will be collected through semi-structured interviews with approximately 20 self-identifying Indigenous adults living in Winnipeg's North End community, a low-income neighborhood with a high prevalence of food insecurity and a large self-identifying Indigenous population. Specifically, participants who self-identify as food insecure and regular consumers of sugar-sweetened beverages, will be recruited with the help of a community research assistant. Interviews will be coded and analyzed utilizing a theoretical thematic approach. Findings will provide a deeper understanding of the social implications of the tax, which our community partners can use for advocacy purposes, and inform policy makers of the acceptability of the tax through the perspective of urban Indigenous people. "

column36: Enhancing Lung Cancer Therapy with Nutrient Supplementation
column37: "Over 29,000 Canadians will receive a devastating diagnosis of lung cancer in 2019; the majority with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Most often diagnosed at an incurable stage, NSCLC is treated with chemotherapy and immunotherapy to slow tumor growth and extend survival. This disease and it's treatments, however, can have difficult side effects including muscle wasting and profound weight loss, negatively affecting quality of life, functional ability, and the ability to tolerate the recommended treatment. This rapid weight loss is known as cancer-associated weight loss, and cannot be prevented or reversed simply by increasing food intake. Often patients express the feeling of 'living in someone else's body' because of the profound physical and functional changes associated with NSCLC and it's treatment. To support optimal quality of life, strength and function, new strategies to prevent or reduce muscle wasting and weight loss are urgently needed. Results from early phase studies suggest that a novel nutrient supplement taken during treatment may slow or stop muscle loss associated with advanced NSCLC. This same nutrient has been shown to enhance the benefit of chemotherapy, resulting in improved tumor response (reduced size or stable disease). However, this nutrient has not been tested with immunotherapy, which is a recent addition to the standard-of-care. Large, well-designed studies are required to confirm previous results and provide evidence for the use of this nutrient supplement in current clinical practice with immunotherapy. My research study aims to evaluate whether supplementation with this novel nutrient can improve the benefit of standard treatment for NSCLC while preserving muscle, physical function and quality of life for patients. "

column36: Ethnic differences in coercive treatment and its influence on help-seeking behaviours among first episode psychosis patients
column37: "Previous literature in the United Kingdom and United States shows that Black patients are disproportionately diagnosed with schizophrenia or psychosis and are likely to be involuntarily admitted to psychiatric hospitals. Little is known if these findings also hold true in Canada, and how these experiences may have influenced Black patient attitudes towards mental health services. Using a mixed-methods design, the objectives of the study are: 1) to determine whether Black first episode psychosis (FEP) patients are at a higher risk for involuntary admission and coercive treatment than non-Black FEP patients, 2) to examine the experiences of Black FEP patients who have been involuntarily admitted and/or coercively treated, and 3) how these experiences may have influenced help-seeking behaviours. Retrospective data from patients referred to a First-Episode Psychosis program (FEPP) from 2015-2018 will be collected via chart review. A sample of nine English-speaking male FEP patients, who self-identify as Black, and are still active to FEPP, follow-up will be recruited to the study. Semi-structured interviews will be conducted and participants will be asked a series of open-ended questions. Multiple linear and binary logistic regression analyses will explore the relationship between ethnicity, diagnosis of psychosis and coercive treatment measures. Thematic analysis will be used to analyze qualitative data. Study findings will provide information on attitudes to care for first episode psychosis and how coercive treatment measures may influence these attitudes. Information from this study can be used to improve clinical interventions and inform policymakers on how to promote patient welfare. "

column36: Immune Modulation by Bioengineered Oncolytic Viruses Promotes Robust Anti-Tumour Immunity
column37: "Cancer is Canada's leading cause of death, accounting for ~30% of deaths; where most are caused by aggressive cancer spread. Current treatments (chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery) cause significant side-effects and still fail many patients. More effective and safer treatments are desperately needed to treat aggressive cancers. Oncolytic Viruses (OVs) are a promising new cancer therapy consisting of viruses that selectively target and kill cancer cells and other cancer-promoting cells, leaving healthy cells unaffected. Additionally, OVs also stimulate the host immune system to produce an anti-cancer immune response, furthering the destruction of a tumour and preventing its spread. Unfortunately, cancers develop ways of evading the immune system, like preventing its activation or turning it off once activated. To overcome this, I will develop OVs armed with additional tools designed to block these ways of evading the immune system, thus bolstering the effectiveness of the anti-cancer immune response. Previous work has shown that these additional OV tools can be transferred to surrounding cancer/cancer-promoting cells through naturally occurring cell-to-cell communication machinery. Our lab has identified the cellular components Fes and Ezrin as two key drivers of cancer spread. Excitingly, these two components have also been implicated in cancer's immune evasiveness; Fes prevents the activation, and Ezrin contributes to shutting off the immune system. Therefore, by using a cancer killing OV armed with tools to block Fes and Ezrin, we create a more effective cancer therapy. This research will result in better understanding of cancer immune evasiveness and a more effective, safer cancer treatment having significant implications for cancer patients in Canada. "

column36: Improving Preventive Health Care in Primary Care by Changing Electronic Medical Record Functionality
column37: "Today many physicians are using electronic medical records (EMRs) in their practices. Although EMRs promise improved clinic efficiency by simplifying and automating tasks, many physicians are spending more time interacting with their computers than with their patients. This is particularly true when physicians need to extract multiple test results to help patients make informed decisions about their health. Preventive care is a common scenario where physicians need to extract many pieces of data from the EMR, which interferes with the patient-physician dynamics.This project assesses a preventive care clinical decision aid that is integrated with the EMR. The decision aid automatically extracts the relevant age and sex appropriate preventive screening data and generates an overview to improve decision-making efficiency and accuracy. A pilot project was previously completed that tested this decision aid in a simulated clinical environment and showed improved decision-making efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. The time that was saved can then be used to spend longer discussing the screening with patients. The next steps will be using and assessing the decision aid in clinical practice, which is the basis of this study. The goals of this study are to: improve patient health outcomes through screening; improve patient experience of care delivery; improve provider experience of care delivery; and to reduced per capita costs."

column36: Dynamic fatigue measurement using smart textile sensors for children post-concussion
column37: "Many children experience fatigue after a mild traumatic brain injury or concussion that can be debilitating, reducing social, physical, and school participation and overall quality of life. Being multifactorial and highly variable across individuals, fatigue is poorly understood and difficult to objectively measure. While self-report measures for assessing fatigue exist, they cannot be administered in non-stationary environments. Wearable sensors have be used for fatigue monitoring by measuring cardiac activity, blood volume chances, eye movements, and brain activity. This challenging in motion, as motion lowers signal quality and makes it harder to find biomarkers of fatigue. Within wearable sensors, smart textiles present an opportunity for low-cost, unobtrusive measurement, and widespread translation. However, textile sensors have not been evaluated for measuring fatigue. This project will answer the question: To what extent can smart textile sensors be used to accurately measure fatigue under dynamic conditions in children post-concussion? This project has three parts: (i) literature review and textile biosensor testing to evaluate textile sensors in dynamic environments, identifying biomarkers that can be reliably extracted in a dynamic environment, (ii) using textile biosensors to characterize fatigue in children during a neuropsychological battery in a stationary environment; and in a (iii) dynamic environment. Using textile sensors to measure fatigue for children post-concussion will serve as the basis for work that could be used to objectively measure, and potentially even diagnose and treat pathological fatigue. Given the prevalence of fatigue and the need for objective fatigue measurement, this work has potential for widespread impact."

column36: Dissecting the Circuitry Governing Temperature-Dependent Fungal Growth and Morphogenesis
column37: "Elucidating the genetic basis of temperature-dependent virulence traits in the human fungal pathogen, Candida albicans.. Fungi infect billions of people and kill at least 1.5 million people per year. Candida albicans is a leading human fungal pathogen that can cause life-threatening disease in immunocompromised individuals, with mortality rates of ~40%. Not only are there very few antifungal drugs available, but the CDC recently declared drug-resistant Candida species as a serious threat to human health. To combat this, a promising therapeutic approach is to target the fungal traits that help it to cause disease. Two key virulence traits of C. albicans are its capacity to thrive at human body temperatures of 37oC and above, and its ability to undergo a morphogenetic switch from yeast to filamentous growth in response to temperatures above 37oC. The genetic circuitry through which temperature influences growth and morphogenesis remains enigmatic, but its identification could reveal a wealth of therapeutic targets The goal of my research is to determine the mechanisms that C. albicans utilizes to grow and filament in response to elevated temperatures. I recently screened a C. albicans mutant library and discovered 92 genes essential for growth at 39oC, and 23 genes required for filamentation at 39oC. I will perform experiments to determine how these genes are involved in sensing and responding to changes in temperature. I will also analyze data from mouse infection experiments to assess the impact of these genes on growth and virulence in a mammalian host. My project will identify the genetic circuitry underlying the complex connection between temperature and C. albicans virulence, which could reveal new therapeutic strategies to cripple this life-threatening disease "

column36: Role of diet in thoracic aortic aneurysms associated with Marfan syndrome
column37: "Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene. Thoracic aortic aneurysms are one of the most detrimental clinical phenotypes of MFS. There is growing evidence that the dietary composition can affect structure and function of various tissues and organs, including the cardiovascular system. A recent pilot study in the host laboratory showed different phenotypes in adipose tissue of male and female mice based on their diet and the specific MFS mouse model (Fbn1mgR/mgR, Fbn1C1039G/+). However, very little is known in regard to the consequences of specific diets on aortic health and function. This proposed project aims to study whether and how high-fat, high-carbohydrate, and high-fiber diets affect aortic aneurysm progression using both mutant male and female mice separately. For each diet, the survival rates, the rate of aortic aneurysm formation, the integrity of elastic fibers, and the expression and secretion level of elastogenesis-related matrix molecules will be analyzed. Since aortic aneurysms are associated with the apoptosis of vascular smooth muscle cells, proapoptotic (cleaved caspase-3, -9) and antiapoptotic (Bcl-2 and Mcl-1) markers will be examined. As increased TGF-β and Angiotensin-II is a hallmark of MFS, these signaling molecules and their receptors will be determined at mRNA and protein levels. The effect of diet on the aortic calcification, a key characteristic of aortic aneurysms, will also be assessed by histological staining. This project will provide the basis of dietary effects on aortic disease in MFS, and possibly reveal insights that help to generate personalized dietary guidelines for individuals affected with MFS to reduce the progression and severity of aortic dilations and ruptures."

column36: Delivery of Therapeutic Nucleic and Protein Structures Using Extracellular Vesicles
column37: "Recent developments in gene therapies offer great opportunities to treat hereditary diseases. Currently, Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs) are being used in hundreds of such clinical trials. These viral particles transport DNA to cells to repair or replace the gene responsible for a disease. While the treatments have achieved remarkable successes in recent years, the exorbitant costs, potential to trigger an immune reaction, and small carrying capacity inherent to viruses such as AAVs prevent them from being an ideal vector for these treatments. As such, my project will attempt to develop a new, more affordable, and safer type of vector based on extracellular vesicles (EVs) isolated from the patients themselves. These structures are normally used to transport proteins, RNA, and DNA from cell to cell and can be found all throughout the body. Since this is the case, they can be isolated in large quantities from a patient's blood and theoretically co-opted for the purposes of creating a gene therapy. Thus the objective of this project is to purify EVs from a patient's serum and introduce within them a Cas9 nuclease protein along with one or two single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) to produce a proof-of-concept EV-delivered gene therapy. These two elements are a part of the CRISPR/Cas9 system which is renowned for its capacity to target and cleave specific nucleic acid sequences. Our hypothesis is that by introducing within the EVs the Cas9/sgRNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex, we will be able to deliver all of the components required to modify a cell's genome initially in cells in a dish and subsequently to mouse cells in vivo. Our results will permit the development of new treatments for diseases like Alzheimer's disease and muscular dystrophy using EVs as the delivery system "

column36: Mindfulness-based protocol: Does treatment description impact adherence in a police population?
column37: "Mindfulness-based interventions are gaining in popularity. Furthermore, mindfulness has been associated with the reduction of symptoms across multiple psychological disorders including anxiety and depression. Police officers are considered to be at increased risk of developing psychological symptoms. A police population may be unwilling to seek help or engage in behaviours that may be considered ""weak"" or ""touchy-feely."" Research on mindfulness and psychological symptoms in police officers is limited and restricted by small sample sizes. The current study will mirror an established 8-week Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction intervention tailored for police officers. All participants are expected to report symptoms reductions associated with adherence, which is expected to be higher for combat breathing enhancement. Higher adherence for combat breathing enhancement would support the development and implementation of an accessible, mindfulness skills intervention tailored for police."

column36: Association of Rare Variants in CYP2A13 with Lung Cancer Risk
column37: "Cigarette smoking remains one of the most important public health problems worldwide. Lung cancer is one of the many serious pathologies associated with smoking; smoking causes nearly 90% of cases of lung cancer. Lung cancer risk in smokers is affected by genetics, because certain gene mutations can affect the processing of carcinogens in cigarette smoke. My work will focus on an enzyme in the lung called CYP2A13 which normally processes some ingredients in cigarette smoke, known as nitrosamines, into cancer-causing compounds. Some more common mutations in the CYP2A13 gene have been studied, and it has been found that they can lower the risk for lung cancer in smokers who carry those mutations. However, rare mutations which may have stronger effects on CYP2A13 have not been studied. In this study, I will find rare CYP2A13 mutations in a group of smokers by collecting their genetic data, and analyze the mutations to discover if they negatively affect CYP2A13's ability to process nitrosamines. We will then do a study to see if there is a relationship between the mutations that affect CYP2A13 and the risk of lung cancer. In the end, this work will allow us to better understand how CYP2A13 and lung cancer are connected, and more specifically understand the role of rare mutations in CYP2A13 in lung cancer risk."

column36: Impact of multifetal pregnancies on maternal mental health outcomes: A Canadian population-based retrospective cohort study
column37: "This study aims to assess the relationship between multifetal pregnancies (including twins and triplets) and post-partum mental illness. Rates of multifetal pregnancies are on the rise, and literature suggests that they pose a risk for maternal mental illness, specifically depression and anxiety, but data from Canadian populations is lacking. We will be using large population-based administrative databases in Ontario, which will enable us to assess for post-partum mental illness in thousands of women. This will allow us to compare rates of mental illness between women with multifetal and singleton pregnancies. The use of large databases will also allow us to investigate rare and severe outcomes including hospitalization and suicide. Lastly, we will assess for additional factors which may modify the mental health risks of multifetal pregnancies including factors related to socioeconomic status, infertility, and birth complications. This research has several potential implications in improving women's health. Maternal mental illness can have devastating impacts on mothers, children and families, and can be effectively prevented and treated. Identifying at-risk populations is therefore crucial. The current study will help assess and quantify the impact of multifetal pregnancies on post-partum mental illness in a Canadian population. Understanding this phenomenon will allow women to make better informed decisions about their reproductive health, including decisions surrounding infertility treatment, and will improve reproductive care for women including obstetrical and post-partum care. Furthermore, maternal mental health is impacted by local social and health policy, and our findings will therefore have direct provincial and national policy implications."

column36: The Role of a Six-Month Structured Cardiovascular Rehabilitation Program to Improve Cardiovascular Health in Female Breast Cancer Survivors
column37: "Breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer among Canadian women, accounting for 25% of all cancers. Despite successes of decreased mortality, adverse treatment side effects still contribute to a sedentary lifestyle and decreased quality of life. One side effect is cardiotoxicity, damage to the heart from chemotherapy drugs or other treatment. Focusing on cardiotoxicity, BC survivors are more likely to die of cardiovascular disease than of BC 9 years following treatment. However, physical activity is an effective therapy for the late effects of cancer treatment, with past research demonstrating improvements in cardio-respiratory health and quality of life for BC survivors who participated in cardiovascular rehabilitation programs.The proposed research will determine the relationships among fitness, vascular measures, and physical activity adherence after 6-months compared to 3-months in an exercise program for female BC survivors. The program would include both aerobic and resistance training over the 6-month period. The primary outcome is fitness measured through oxygen uptake (VO2peak) and the secondary outcome is adherence to physical activity measured through attendance, step counters and physical activity diaries. Additional measures include function and characteristics of the vascular system. It is anticipated that the BC survivors with greater adherence will have greater improvements in VO2peak, vascular function and vascular structure in response to the exercise training program. Furthermore, it is expected that gains in 0-3-months will be inversely related to gains in 3-6-months, with adherence as an outcome mediator.This cardio-oncology research will help to advance our understanding of how to reduce cardiovascular disease in BC survivors."

column36: Circadian Rhythm Typology in OCD Populations
column37:
"This research aims to examine the relationship between sleep chronotype, which indicates a potential phase delay, and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms in order to help enhance future treatment success for those with OCD. Individuals with OCD frequently experience sleep disturbances, such as insomnia; however, the mechanisms responsible for this prevalence have not been examined in-depth. Research suggests that the high prevalence of sleep disturbances in this population may be related to a circadian phase delay, where a person's natural circadian rhythm peaks later than the average person. It has yet to be determined whether this phase delay is a true biological predisposition, or whether it could be behavioral, a symptom of the compulsions and obsessions related to this disorder. In this study, individuals will complete the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), which indicates their sleep chronotype, and the Insomnia Severity Index. In addition, they will complete the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (YBOCS), which is used to determine OCD symptomology and symptom severity. The number of symptoms individuals experience near bedtime will be examined as a potential mediating factor for MEQ scores. A factor analysis of the MEQ will also be conducted to determine whether the three chronotype structure continues to be valid when studying participants with OCD. This research is necessary as sleep disturbances can impede OCD treatment success and cause further distress. In particular, phase delays are highly prevalent in those with various psychiatric disorders, including depression and bipolar disorder, and are associated with a heightened risk for relapse. This may be true of OCD populations as well, and thus this question must be addressed.
"
