column36: Molecular basis to diet-dependent chromatin dependencies in prostate cancer
column37: "Prostate cancer is a heterogeneous disease and the genetic basis for this interpatient heterogeneity remains unclear. The overtreatment of indolent prostate cancers, which causes unnecessary treatment toxicity, and the ongoing development of new therapies for aggressive prostate cancers increases the need for accurate patient classification and stratification. Systemic metabolic alterations associated with increased intake of saturated fat and obesity are linked with higher risk of prostate cancer progression and mortality. Epigenetic alterations are frequently observed in prostate cancer, yet how aberrant epigenetic signatures are established is poorly understood. We hypothesize that epigenetic reprogramming underlies prostate cancer aggressiveness. Recent data from our laboratory suggest that prostate cancer harbour altered chromatin accessibility in response to a high-fat diet and a potential epigenetic mediator of this phenotype has been identified. Our first aim is to determine, using genome editing techniques, if this candidate gene is a driver of high-fat diet-dependent prostate cancer aggressiveness using cellular and mouse models. Moreover, we have recently identified epigenetic modifications specific to aggressive prostate tumours. Thus, our second aim is to determine if these epigenetic alterations are drivers of aggressive prostate cancer using genome editing and multiple sequencing technologies in various models. Altogether, by elucidating the underlying cause to prostate cancer metastatic progression, our research project will lead to new methods and clinical tests to group patients into high and low-risk groups and the development of new treatments to significantly extend the life of prostate cancer patients."

column36: Understanding Second-Line Osteoporosis Pharmacotherapy in Older Men and Women
column37: "Osteoporosis is a brittle bone condition that results in debilitating fractures. Over 2 million Canadians are affected by osteoporosis, and 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men will experience an osteoporotic fracture. Vertebral fractures reduce quality of life and are often accompanied by difficulty breathing and stomach issues related to a forward curvature of the upper spine. Hip fractures are deadly, 5% of patients do not survive their hospitalization and up to 33% die within the year after hip fracture. In addition, up to 24% enter a nursing home for the first time following hip fracture. Thankfully, there are a variety of medications available to strengthen bones and reduce fracture risk. In Ontario, residents over the age of 65 receive drug coverage through the Ontario Drug Benefit program. First-line medication options for osteoporosis include oral bisphosphonates and raloxifene, which are taken by mouth. However, some patients stop taking their medications because they are not working well enough, or patients are unable to tolerate them. As a result, these patients need to switch to more potent therapies, including annual zoledronic acid or the twice a year injectable denosumab which became covered for women only in 2012. Uncertainty about which therapy should be used, an annual infusion of zoledronic acid or the semi-annual denosumab, was a knowledge gap identified in Osteoporosis Canada's Clinical Practice Guidelines that are currently being updated. We are working directly with Osteoporosis Canada to answer questions about second-line therapy for osteoporosis. Results will inform long-term treatment decisions for older men and women and thus significantly advance osteoporosis management world-wide."

column36: The osteocalcin signaling pathway in exercise-induced improvements of brain function
column37: "Exercise is beneficial in improving symptoms related to Alzheimer's Disease (AD), as it enhances learning, memory, and brain health. However, many individuals are unable to exercise due to physical ailments or aging, and the mechanism behind exercise-induced improvements in brain health is currently unknown. A better understanding of this process is needed, as it has potential to be used in treatment of brain-related conditions, such as AD. For example, therapeutic interventions that mimic the biological changes that occur during physical activity could be used to generate similar benefits in those who are unable to exercise. Current research suggests that osteocalcin (OCN), a protein originating from bone, is an important part of this mechanism. OCN is released from bone during exercise and accumulates in brain regions that are important for learning and memory. In the brain, OCN increases other proteins that are essential for brain health, but how it does so is unknown. To determine how this occurs, we will apply OCN to mouse brain cells in culture and measure the resulting changes in molecules that are likely to be involved in this process. We will then measure the same molecules in mice that have either exercised or not, in order to determine whether the identified mechanism is induced by exercise. This project will study the mechanism underlying exercise-induced improvements of brain function in detail. Since exercise generates improvements in learning and memory, this project could identify novel targets to be used in the treatment of AD. Our results may contribute to development of therapeutics that mimic the effects of exercise in order to improve brain function in physically and cognitively compromised individuals."

column36: Impact of disease-induced dysbiotic microbiota on the protective functions of innate T cells during type 1 diabetes
column37: "Type I diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease characterized by abnormal immune responses that attack insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. In addition to genetic susceptibility, alterations in intestinal microbiota composition - called dysbiosis - have been found in children with T1D. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) and mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells, two populations of unconventional ""innate"" T cells, play protective functions during T1D. Recent studies have suggested that the gut microbiota modulates the development and function of these T cells, leading us to hypothesize that the dysbiosis that occurs in genetically susceptible individuals impacts their immunoregulatory functions which induces a breach in tolerance and development of T1D. To address this, we will reconstitute non-obese diabetic (NOD) germ-free (no microbiota) mice with a human microbiota from diabetic and non-diabetic children. We will analyze the phenotype of iNKT and MAIT cells from various tissues such as the pancreas and pancreatic lymph nodes using flow cytometry and advanced genomic approaches. To study the impact of the microbiota on their function, these cells will be stimulated both in vivo and in vitro to analyze their production of cytokines and cytotoxic mediators. We will assess early T1D onset by analyzing immune cell infiltration within the pancreas using flow cytometry and histology, and will monitor long-term disease progression through glycemia measurements and histological pancreatic islet examination. This project will provide a greater understanding of how the interaction between the microbiota and innate T cells influences disease development and progression, and pave the way towards new strategies to manipulate iNKT and MAIT cells to control or prevent T1D."

column36: Maximizing patient engagement through collaborative outcome measure selection and tracking
column37: "After a person has had a stroke, they often receive physical therapy to improve their mobility. Physical therapists regularly measure a patient's progress using standardized outcome measures, such as timing how quickly a person can walk. Currently in Alberta, the way in which these measures are selected is not standardized, so a person may not receive the same type of tests as they move to different facilities or therapists. Patients may not fully understand which outcome measures are selected or how the measures track progress towards their health goals. Soon, patients will have access to their electronic health record through a patient portal. Regularly tracking and reporting outcome measures will provide patients with important information about their progress in therapy. This project will involve talking to people who have received physical therapy after stroke in group interviews, called focus groups. The information gathered will help us to better understand what outcome measures are meaningful to patients and how they would like to be involved in tracking their own progress. The whole project will be guided by a small research team, which will include one to three patient advisors. Patient advisors are former patients who have relevant personal experience and contribute their perspective to the study. Patient advisors help to keep the research team focused on the patient experience. The result of this project will be a set of recommendations regarding how patients and therapists can collaborate to select and track outcome measures in a way that resonates with patients who receive physical therapy after stroke. If put in place, these recommendations could help patients to actively participate in their own care by monitoring progress toward their stated goals. "

column36: Thermoplastic Elastomer Scaffolds for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction
column37: "Close to a quarter of a million anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries occur each year in Canada and the United States. These injuries can have devastating consequences and are associated with long-term clinical conditions that include meniscal tears, cartilage lesions and an increased risk of osteoarthritis. Surgical reconstruction, despite being the gold standard of care for ACL injuries, is costly and associated with high risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis within two decades of injury. Researchers have explored tissue engineering (TE) to address these shortcomings and have developed degradable graft materials that can guide functional connective tissue formation. However, scaffolds fabricated using current TE methods still do not accurately mimic the biomechanical properties of the ACL and experience an important loss of mechanical properties once introduced in vivo. The objective of this project is to leverage computer-aided design tools to develop thermoplastic elastomer scaffolds that will closely mimic the biomechanical properties of native ACL tissue. Such scaffolds could significantly reduce the costs associated with ACL reconstruction surgeries and enable a personalized clinical approach that may lead to lower risks of recurring injuries. "

column36: Defining the link between CDK2 activity and lineage-specific cancer susceptibility to RB loss
column37: "Gene defects that are oncogenic in one lineage are impotent in another. Understanding these dramatic differences in cancer susceptibility could expose new therapeutic vulnerabilities. RB is frequently mutated in retinoblastoma and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Our group found that while murine RB-deficient retina exhibits many cancer hallmarks, only cell cycle length distinguishes the cancer prone lineage. Thus, in cancer-prone amacrine cells it was half that of resistant Müller glia. Remarkably, this was recapitulated in RB-null lung, where cell cycle length in cancer-prone pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (PNECs) was half that of resistant alveolar type II (AT2) cells. Moreover, lowering Cyclin Dependent Kinase 2 (CDK2) activity doubled cell cycle length and inhibited cancer initiation. My goal is to deduce when CDK2 confers cancer susceptibility. In cell lines, CDK2 activity peaks at G2/M, then dips dramatically at the start of G1. Cells with a shallow CDK2 activity trough in G1 re-enter the cell cycle. I hypothesize that higher CDK2 activity in the G1 trough also distinguishes cancer-prone from cancer-resistant RB-deficient lineages.. To test my hypothesis, I am exploiting a live CDK2 sensor. I validated this tool in retinoblastoma and SCLC cells. I will track CDK2 activity both in RB-deficient murine retinal cells, and in human embryonic stem cell derived lung organoids. I predict that the G1 CDK2 trough will be lower in cancer-resistant Müller/AT2 cells and higher in cancer-prone amacrine/PNECs. The systems I develop will expose CDK2 activity throughout the cell cycle, and define models to pursue critical CDK2 targets. By defining the mechanism of cancer susceptibility or resistance my work could lead to new therapies for SCLC and other RB null cancers. "

column36: Peer Support Intervention for Adolescents with Chronic Pain
column37: "Chronic pain affects the lives of many Canadian children and adolescents. Consequently, adolescents with chronic pain often feel lonely and alienated by others who do not have pain. Therefore, the proposed study aims to address the lack of peer support interventions by developing, implementing, and evaluating a PSI for adolescents with chronic pain. Specifically, the proposed study will explore the feasibility and satisfaction of a psychologist-facilitated chronic pain PSI. It is hypothesized that the PSI will be deemed as feasible and satisfactory by adolescents living with chronic pain. The study will be comprised of two phases. The first phase will consist of the development of the PSI and the second phase will consist of the implementation and evaluation of the PSI. The researcher will observe and take notes during the implementation and will conduct interviews following the conclusion of the PSI sessions. The proposed study is significant because it will be the first time a psychologist-facilitated peer support intervention for adolescents living with chronic pain will be investigated. A PSI could provide social and psychological support for the many adolescents living with pain, thereby helping to decrease the loneliness and isolation these adolescents may feel. The results of the proposed study could also inform future research regarding PSIs for adolescents with chronic pain as well as the use of PSIs in multidisciplinary chronic pain clinics."

column36: Using Ketamine to Mitigate Persistent Cognitive Deficits After General Anesthesia
column37: "The number of surgeries performed each year in the world rose from 235 million in 2004 to over 312 million in 2012. Unfortunately, a significant proportion of surgical patients experience deficits in learning and memory that persist for months after the surgery. These cognitive deficits are associated with poor long-term outcomes. Currently, there are no effective treatments for this type of cognitive dysfunction. General anesthetics are a major cause of post-surgical cognitive dysfunction. Most general anesthetic drugs work by briefly enhancing an inhibitory receptor function in the brain, resulting in memory loss and insensitivity to pain for the duration of the surgery. Although this receptor-enhancing effect is supposed to be temporary, in reality there is a sustained increase in the number of the same inhibitory receptor that persists for weeks after anesthetic removal. It is likely that persistent activation of this inhibitory receptor contributes to cognitive dysfunction after surgery, since blockade of the receptor alleviated anesthesia-induced memory deficits in mice. Unfortunately, drugs that target the receptor are not yet clinically approved, due to either lack of efficacy or unwanted side effects in humans. There is, however, a new drug candidate for treating post-surgical cognitive deficits: ketamine. Our preliminary data shows that ketamine can effectively suppress the activity of the inhibitory receptor responsible for cognitive dysfunction after surgery. My project aims to directly test whether ketamine can alleviate memory deficits by reducing the number of the receptor in mice after general anesthesia. Ultimately, we hope to identify a novel, cost-effective approach to prevent cognitive dysfunction in patients undergoing anesthesia and surgery. "

column36: "Effects of Depo-Medroxyprogesterone Acetate(DMPA) on peripheral blood natural killer cells in sex workers from Nairobi, Kenya"
column37: "Background: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) is the most utilized form of contraceptive in Sub-Saharan Africa. DMPA has been shown to alter the epithelial barrier and increase HIV target cells in the vaginal tract. column36: Approach-Avoidance Conflict Processing in Hippocampal Lesion Patients
column37: "Approach-avoidance (AA) conflict processing occurs when a cue (i.e. situation, object or location) is associated with simultaneous possibilities of reward and punishment. In AA conflict situations, individuals must weigh the possibilities of reward and punishment and decide whether to engage with the cue (approach) or not (avoid). The hippocampus (HPC), a brain structure located in the medial temporal lobe (MTL), has been suggested to play a key role in this kind of processing. Specifically, the anterior portion of the HPC is thought to control behaviour by inhibiting the tendency to approach in AA conflict situations. Most of the evidence for this comes from rodent research, with relatively limited research in humans. This study will examine whether the model extends to humans, by working with patients with HPC damage. Participants will complete tasks designed to produce AA conflict scenarios, in which images will signal the simultaneous possibilities of reward and punishment (represented by gain or loss of points in a game, respectively). The rate at which patients either approach or avoid in these AA conflict scenarios will be compared to that of neurologically healthy controls. I predict that patients will show a greater tendency to approach in these scenarios, given the reduced inhibitory control resulting from HPC damage. This study will shed light on the impact of HPC damage on AA conflict behaviour in humans and speak to theoretical models of the HPC and AA processing. Additionally, AA conflict processing is believed to be disrupted in conditions such as anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder. This study could, therefore, provide clearer understanding of these disorders and inform future treatment approaches."

column36: The impact of genetic variation on novel proteins and functional insight from their physical interaction network
column37: "Cells produce proteins in order to fulfill all of the functions that keep them alive. The information necessary to synthesize those proteins is stored in the genetic material of the nucleus. Indeed, all proteins are encoded in DNA by what are called coding sequences. Since many diseases are caused by defective proteins, many research groups are interested in describing the complete set of proteins encoded in human genes called the human proteome. Contrary to what was previously believed some human genes contain more than one coding sequence, encoding more than one protein molecule. This was demonstrated by the work of the Roucou Laboratory at Sherbrooke University who developed an algorithm that predicts all possible coding sequences with the genome. These predictions are however not all protein producing and functionally relevant sequences. This is why my master of science project will have the following objectives: (1) to identify which of the predicted coding sequences are most likely expressed into proteins in the cell and (2) formulate hypotheses on the possible functions of those novel proteins.I will use computational methods to analyse very large data sets containing information on the physical interaction between proteins. This data is from a technique called mass spectrometry and is meant to directly detect and identify proteins. Since most proteins work in partnership with other proteins in order to do their work, novel proteins detected in the physical interaction network of known proteins can yield hints on their potential role within the cell. With this technique, my project could uncover novel proteins involved in pathological processes, thereby offering novel diagnostic tools or novel therapeutic targets."

column36: The Role of Iron Homeostasis in Selective Vulnerability Patterns in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
column37: "Linking Iron and Oxygen Transport Deficits in Neurodegenerative DiseaseNeurodegenerative diseases are a group of age-related disorders severely damaging the brain and its function with no current cures. Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) is one of these diseases, characterized by a build-up of proteins in the brain called tau. The build-up of tau is believed to start in certain areas of the brain that also accumulate iron. Although iron is essential to brain function, small shifts in its level can be very damaging to all types of brain cells. Indeed, there are studies in other neurodegenerative diseases that show evidence of harmful iron imbalance in vulnerable brain regions. However, since regulation of iron levels and its effects are vastly different in each cell type of the brain, it is important to study iron imbalance separately in different cell populations. In addition, how this relates to the oxygen carrier protein in the blood and brain, hemoglobin, is of particular interest. These critical details are lacking from the current knowledge of diseased-state iron imbalance, particularly in PSP.Using human post-mortem brains, we will examine iron levels in different cell types in specific areas of the PSP brain, compared to non-diseased brains. In the same brain regions, we will also look at the level and distribution of proteins associated with iron regulation, including hemoglobin. Importantly, to correlate these elements with disease progression, we will examine these elements in PSP brains of varying disease stages, along with the key disease protein, tau.Our study will provide a deeper and detailed understanding of the relationship between iron and disease progression in PSP. This may open avenues for novel therapies and diagnostic development."

column36: The gut-brain axis in a mouse model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-frontotemporal dementia (ALS-FTD)
column37: " Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal disorder where the cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscle movement gradually break down and die. As a result, ALS gradually leads to paralysis. ALS symptoms are also seen in patients with frontotemporal dementia (FTD), a disorder with a loss of brain cells in the frontal and temporal lobes. ALS-FTD patients not only develop paralysis, but they also display memory issues and language problems. Currently, there is no way to prevent or cure either ALS or FTD. Recent research suggests that the gut-brain axis (the communication between the gut and the brain) may be critical for the disease progression of ALS-FTD. Millions of microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi inhabit our gut and are referred to as the ""gut microbiome"". In ALS patients, the composition of the gut microbiome is significantly different compared to non-ALS individuals. Interestingly, the levels of lipopolysaccharides (LPS), a toxin released from certain types of bacteria, are abnormally increased in ALS patients. Furthermore, LPS is known to alter the gut structure and affect the immune system. However, the link between LPS, the gut, and the brain is poorly understood My research aims to examine the roles of LPS from different bacteria species on the gut-brain axis of a mouse model of ALS-FTD. Specifically, I will examine the effects of different LPS on the immune response, the gut structure, and the brain cells. I hypothesize that different LPS types will have different effects on the gut microbiome and gut-brain axis, thereby impacting how ALS-FTD progresses. I expect that my research will contribute to identifying new molecules for the diagnosis and treatment of ALS-FTD."

column36: Mitochondrial dysfunction and vulnerability to oxidative stress in induced dopaminergic neurons (PD-iDANs) derived from sporadic Parkinson's disease patients
column37: "The causes underlying over 90% of Parkinson's disease (PD) cases are unknown. This results in a lack of understanding of the mechanisms responsible for these non-familial forms of the disease, called idiopathic, preventing the development of cures or treatments to stop its progression. An additional challenge preventing our full understanding of the disease and how to treat it is the high diversity in its clinical presentation. In PD, the dopaminergic neurons are the main brain cell type affected, and their death is responsible for the motor problems associated to the disease. These dopaminergic cells are especially vulnerable in PD patients, but it is currently unknown whether the triggers leading to their death is the same for every patient with idiopathic PD, partly due to the lack of models mimicking this diversity within the patient population. Here, we are using a new technology, consisting in the conversion of skin cells of PD patients to dopaminergic neurons, which offers a promising tool to study such diversity at a molecular level. In this project, we focus on mitochondria, the powerhouse of the cell, which is suspected to be dysfunctional in PD and as we age. Because age is the main risk factor for PD, and the dopaminergic cells generated maintain the age of the skin cells, this allows for the first time to study this aspect of the disease. As such, this project aims at studying the mechanisms leading to dopaminergic cell death in a context that reflects the age and the individuality of each PD patient. In this optic, we hope to identify different types of cellular dysfunctions responsible for dopaminergic cell death in idiopathic PD, and therefore open the door to new therapeutic avenues as well as the development of personalized medicine for PD."

column36: Assessment of Novel Risk Factors for Chronic Lung Allograft Dysfunction after Lung Transplantation
column37: "Breathing is a ubiquitous action that most of us take for granted, but for patients with end stage lung diseases, every breath is a fight. For many of these patients, lung transplantation is the only treatment that can significantly prolong survival and improve quality of life.The most important limiter of long-term survival after this procedure is chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), which describes a range of disease processes in the airways and tissues of the transplanted lungs that lead to a persistent decline in lung function. Unfortunately, therapies for CLAD remain limited in their effectiveness once the disease has set in so a key focus has been prevention.Azithromycin is an antibiotic that can also help with treating lung diseases by reducing airway inflammation. Previous research on a small group of recipients has suggested that this drug decreases the risk of developing CLAD if given shortly after transplant and maintained thereafter. We want to see if this finding holds true in our much larger group of recipients and furthermore, study the direct relationship between preventative azithromycin use and overall survival following transplant.Of course, it is difficult to treat what one does not know, and much remains unknown about the exact mechanisms leading to CLAD. Ventilation-perfusion (VQ) scans show how airflow and blood flow are distributed in the lungs. These imaging studies provide insight on lung abnormalities but there has been little research on their implications specifically in lung transplant recipients. We want to know if any findings on the VQ scans of recipients at 3-months are associated with CLAD development later on. Identifying these early risk factors could shed light on how CLAD develops and allow for earlier intervention."

column36: Saving Young Lives: Derivation and implementation of the Pediatric Rapid Sepsis Trigger clinical model to improve pediatric sepsis treatment in low-resource settings.
column37: "Sepsis, a severe biological response to infection, affects 4.2 million newborns and children in the world every year. It is most common in developing countries, where one out of every four patients with sepsis will die. The best way to maximize survival from sepsis is to give antibiotics within one hour of first assessing a septic child, a common practice in developed countries. However, low-resource settings in developing countries lack enough trained personnel to diagnose pediatric sepsis timely enough to meet this time frame. To address this problem, we aim to develop a mobile application-based algorithm, called the Pediatric Rapid Sepsis Trigger (PRST), which will allow healthcare personnel to more swiftly identify septic children and provide them with antibiotics sooner.We will be collecting data on children in the emergency department of partner hospitals in Kenya and Uganda to develop the PRST algorithm. Our partner hospitals will then use a mobile application containing the algorithm to identify high risk children who will be given priority for physician assessment and treatment. We anticipate that we will increase the percentage of children who receive antibiotics within the first hour, the current standard of care in developed countries, by 20%. Our project is the first of its kind to use a computer algorithm to prioritize antibiotic delivery, a key step towards further reducing child mortality from sepsis. To facilitate future projects, we will share our data with other researchers in pediatric sepsis through an international data sharing collaboration. Our shared data can also benefit Canadians by informing the design of similar projects in rural Canada, where trained personnel to identify pediatric sepsis is likewise at a premium."

column36: Elucidate the link between combinations of mutations and disease heterogeneity of high grade serous ovarian cancer
column37: "High grade serous ovarian cancers (HGSCs) is the fifth largest cause of cancer-related death in women. The mechanisms of the early disease progression are still largely unknown due to late diagnosis at the advanced stages in most patients and lack of animal models. Since HGSCs are driven by copy number alterations, identifying a gene(s) important for tumorigenesis in each deleted locus has been challenging. In addition, the cell-of-origin of HGSCs is debated between the fallopian tube (FT) and the ovarian surface epithelium (OSE). To address these challenges, we have developed a novel strategy to derive HGSCs in mice with CRISPR-mediated genome modification and in vivo FT/OSE electroporation. This strategy possesses the advantages of testing various mutation combinations in a limited region. Our previous study revealed that the combinations of gene mutations control cell-of-origin, latency and pathophysiology of HGSC. To elucidate such variation, I hypothesize that there is a link between mutation combinations and heterogeneity of HGSCs. To test this, we aim to perform a survival experiment with two, three and four genes mutation combinations targeting either FTE or OSE. The survival of mice and the genotypes of developed HGSCs will be monitored to investigate the effect of mutation combinations on tumour aggressiveness. To evaluate the effect on HGSC initiation and progression, we will also study the expression profile and related molecular pathways in the precancerous lesions, primary HGSCs and metastasis tumor from each cohort. Understanding the relationship between mutational profiles and HGSCs' pathophysiology can provide an insight into the origin of HGSCs, the fundamental pathways in tumour development, which could serve as future therapeutically targets. "

column36: Impact of the implementation of a computerized provider order entry on prescribing errors and pharmacist interventions in a pediatric hospital
column37: "Computerized provider order entry (CPOE), defined as the electronic ordering and transmission of prescription data, is a promising technology that could reduce handwritten prescription errors and promote the appropriate use of drugs. CPOEs have been implemented in several hospitals around the world, and there is extensive literature on the added value of CPOEs in terms of productivity and safety of care. However, the challenges of implementing an electronic prescriber can lead to some detrimental consequences, for example, by generating errors due to the system configuration. The impact of CPOEs on prescription errors depends greatly on the healthcare setting and on the CPOE system configuration. The CHU Sainte-Justine (CHU SJ) was one of the first hospitals in Quebec to implement an electronic health record with CPOE, which was gradually rolled out in the care units since October 2019. Given the unique context of the implementation of this technology in a French-speaking hospital dedicated to pediatrics and obstetrics, it is essential to evaluate the impact of this CPOE system in order to optimize the benefits for both patients and users of the electronic prescriber. Children are particularly vulnerable to medication errors because the pediatric doses are often based on the child's age or weight . A study measuring prescription conformity and the pharmacist interventions on medication orders will be conducted before and after the implementation of the CPOE to measure its impact. Interviews with system users will also be conducted to evaluate the user experience. Ultimately, analyses of the impacts of the CPOE on the quality of prescriptions and system ergonomics will enable the elaboration of recommendations aimed at promoting the benefits of this technology."

column36: Identification of Phosphatase Inhibitors for Host-Directed Tuberculosis Therapy
column37: "Tuberculosis (TB) is a top 10 cause of death worldwide. It is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) bacteria, which infects immune cells known as macrophages and has developed many ways of resisting antibiotic treatments as well as our immune responses. Mtb can hijack our own cells' processes and use them for itself to ensure its survival as well as shutting down our antimicrobial defenses for protection. One new form of TB therapy is ""host-directed therapy"" (HDT), in which our own cells are targeted to try and restore these antimicrobial functions so that we can be more efficient at killing the bacteria ourselves. We have previously identified a host protein known as PPM1A which was shown to be essential for Mtb in order to block defense mechanisms and ensure its survival during infection. We also showed that when PPM1A is genetically deleted in cells, these defenses are restored, and the cell regains its Mtb killing abilities. A drug compound that can inhibit PPM1A does exist, but it is highly toxic. This project therefore aims to test new compounds designed to be PPM1A inhibitors and evaluate if they are able to enhance macrophages and allow them to regain their killing abilities. This will be done by assessing things like activity against PPM1A, cellular toxicity, and ability to increase bacterial killing both within cells and mouse systems. Any active compounds will be followed-up by studying potential mechanisms of action so that we can understand what it does within the cell, as well as looking into how it physically interacts with the PPM1A protein. Ideally, these compounds will provide a new way of fighting TB, contribute to better treatment outcomes for patients, and help curb the rise in antibiotic-resistant TB cases."

column36: The molecular mechanisms bacterial transferrin-binding proteins: towards the development of wide-range therapies
column37: "Like all organisms, dangerous pathogenic bacteria that cause diseases in humans such as meningitis and pneumonia require iron for essential biochemical reactions, which they obtain from their host by siphoning iron from iron-binding glycoproteins through receptors on the bacteria surface. These proteins are termed transferrin-binding proteins (Tbps). Due to the differences in physiology of bacterial and mammalian iron uptake and the ubiquity of Tbps in bacteria, bacterial Tbps are an optimal target for antibiotic therapies and vaccines. The design of these targeted therapies would require an understanding of the mechanisms by which these receptors function and interact with their targets which often depend on subtle interactions at the atomic level, for which structural biology is ideal. My research will focus on determining the structure of Tbps from various bacterial pathogens with associated ligands using structural biology techniques such as x-ray crystallography, mass spectroscopy, and cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to characterize the binding interactions of Tbps with host and bacterial ligands at a molecular level."

column37: "Of all the cells in the pituitary - a small organ under the brain that produces many hormones - only a fraction make follicle stimulating hormone (FSH). FSH is vital for puberty and reproduction and is commonly used in treatments for infertility. Women undergoing assisted reproduction receive daily injections of FSH, which is not only inconvenient, but also extremely expensive. Other methods of regulating FSH that do not require daily injections have been proposed, but none have been successful enough to reach the market. FSH is regulated by many other hormones, notably inhibin A and inhibin B, which decrease the amount of FSH made. It has been shown that inhibin B is more effective at decreasing FSH than inhibin A, yet little is known about the mechanisms of inhibin B action. However, our lab has shown that the proposed receptor for inhibin B, through which it acts, is found only in the same cells that produce FSH. The goal of my project is to determine the factors that restrict the production of the inhibin B receptor, and therefore the actions of inhibin B, to these cells. This knowledge will further our understanding of how and when FSH is made, possibly allowing the creation of drugs to modulate FSH."

column36: "Development and validation of a dynamic, microfluidic, blood brain barrier-brain tumor co-culture model for examining regulation of the tumor microenvironment"
column37: "The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is composed of specialized endothelial and support cells1. Contact and cellular communication between endothelial and support cells ensures establishment of homeostatic neurovascular environments. Additionally, the BBB is composed of specific transport proteins and specialized junctions which control the passage of compounds into and out of the brain. However, progression of diseases like cancer play key roles in disruption of BBB2. Therefore, understanding the mechanism of barrier disruption serves as an attractive target for drug design2. However, for in-depth understanding and analysis of BBB vascular environments, we rely on in vitro models that lack the ability to model cell-cell communication, tubular structure formation, and blood flow simulation, all of which are critical to successful BBB formation and maintenance in vivo. Recently, microfluidic technology has been developed in which microfluidic co-culture models consisting of endothelial cells and support cells more closely capture the dynamics of the BBB neurovascular unit observed in vivo. Microfluidic technology provides the advantage of allowing cell-cell communication and contact between brain endothelial cells and other cells, as well as blood flow simulation. This co-culture model can further be developed to model how tumor microenvironments might influence BBB functions. column36: Characterizing the role of YopK as a potential metaeffector in Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
column37: "The Yersinia genus contains bacteria which cause disease ranging from gastroenteritis to bubonic plague. In order to survive within humans, these bacteria have evolved an arsenal of proteins called effectors which allow them to evade the host immune response. Yersinia uses a needle-like complex called the Type III secretion system to inject these effectors into human cells. My research aims to understand the interactions between these effectors and identify metaeffectors, which are effectors that modulate other effectors. Effectors must be tightly controlled so that they inhibit the cellular processes involved in bacterial killing without actually killing the infected host cell. An important function of metaeffectors is to mediate the balance between immune evasion and pre-maturely killing infected human cells. Some metaeffectors do this by degrading effectors that, in high abundance, can kill the infected host cell that the bacteria relies on. Such a function has been observed in the Yersinia effector arsenal by the potential metaeffector, YopK. Previous studies propose that YopK inhibits injection of the effectors it regulates. However, I have generated preliminary data using yeast as a proxy for human cells which indicates that inhibiting injection of effectors is not involved in the regulatory activity of YopK. To further investigate these findings, I plan to conduct in vitro experiments which will further characterize both the interactions YopK is involved in and its function. I will also develop an infection model to further elucidate the function of YopK. This work will contribute to the understanding of Yersinia pathogenesis and exhibit the role of metaeffectors in pathogenic bacteria. "

column36: "Associations between social vulnerability, health outcomes and use of health care resources in community dwelling older adults"
column37: """The world is aging, and so is Nova Scotia"". Home care is becoming an increasingly important cornerstone of the healthcare system by managing chronic conditions, reducing hospital re-admissions and decreasing hospital length of stay. Delivering care services at home is often preferred by the patient and is associated with lower costs. Predictions regarding an individual's health outcomes and health resource utilization can be made from examination of social circumstances alone. For example, people who are socially isolated have worse health outcomes than others who have rich social networks. The term is called ""social vulnerability"". Social vulnerability is particularly relevant in the elderly, who experience shrinking support groups, have poorer health preventing social participation and have an increased need to rely ever more on the home care system. This project aims to understand the context and contributing factors leading to social vulnerability and to examine how social vulnerability influences older adult health care and outcomes in community settings, with particular attention to the relationship between social vulnerability and frailty. A retrospective data analysis will be conducted using the Nova Scotia Home Care interRAI database of older adults over the age of 65 years who accessed Continuing Care resources. Each social variable will be identified and analyzed individually, then aggregated in a clinical social vulnerability index (SVI). This SVI will be analyzed in relation to mortality, morbidity (calculated using a frailty index), number of health care visits, and home care consumption. Relevant outcome variables and subsequent methods of statistical analysis will be done in collaboration with stakeholders from the Nova Scotia Health Authority. "

column37: "Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory disease that can affect people of all ages. It can occur in almost any body part, but most frequently involves the elbows, knees, and scalp, followed by the hands, feet, nails, and trunk. The disease can cause significant discomfort and psychological distress. One in five patients with psoriasis presents with sore joints, which can be a manifestation of psoriatic arthritis.Fortunately, several drugs are very effective for the treatment of moderate to severe psoriasis. However, some of these drugs, which are called ""biotherapies"" or ""biological drugs"" are very expensive. They can be prescribed by a dermatologist (a doctor specialized in skin diseases) to treat chronic severe psoriasis. In the province of Quebec, people who do not have access to a private plan can still take advantage of the Public Prescription Drug Insurance Plan to receive appropriate treatment and care.To this day, we don't know if patients insured under the Public Prescription Drug Insurance Plan in Quebec have similar characteristics to those with a private plan. In other words, do patients covered by the public plan have more severe psoriasis? Do they respond differently to the drugs they receive to treat their skin disease? Is the delay between the drug prescription and initiation longer? Our goal is to improve access to biotherapy treatments for patients with psoriasis. To do this, we believe it is necessary to better understand the factors that contribute to obtaining a biological agent."

column36: The long-term effects of cannabis on attention to motion: An event-related potential study
column37: "With the recent legalization of cannabis in Canada, there are concerns about the long-term effects of regular use. Research shows that heavy cannabis use can impair cognitive functions up to a week after cessation of use. This has implications for safety as attention and motion perception are cognitive functions essential for tasks such as driving. Research has shown that impaired attention can persist even when sober, however, little research has explored the long-term effects of regular cannabis use on attention to motion. A recent study looking at early-onset users showed slower processing and reduced brain responses to moving stimuli suggesting impaired attention to motion. However, how long one needs to regularly use cannabis to elicit such effects is still unknown. The purpose of the following proposal is to explore the long-term effects of cannabis use on attention to motion by comparing non-users, new users, and chronic users in an event-related potential (ERP) study. ERPs look at brain waves that form when exposed to stimuli and can be used to locate brain activity. Participants will complete a visual attention task where they will be asked to attend to moving dots (target) while ignoring distractors. The targets will be presented at two speeds: either slow or fast in either high or low contrast conditions. ERPs will be analyzed in order to compare brain activity of non-users, new and chronic users. It is hypothesized that chronic users will show greater impaired attention than new users and non-users especially in the low contrast and fast conditions. New users are expected to show similar deficits but to a lesser extent. The results of this study will provide a better understanding of the long-term health effects of regular cannabis use."

column36: Characterizing the blood biomarkers of traumatic brain injury in women who have experienced intimate partner violence
column37: "Intimate partner violence (IPV) is defined as ""physical, sexual, and emotional abuse and controlling behaviors from an intimate partner"" and is now considered a major public health issue. It is estimated that one third of women will experience a form of IPV in their lifetime, of which up to 92% will sustain physical injury to their face, head, and neck. It is increasingly recognized that traumatic brain injury (TBI) plays an important role in the many challenges faced by these women. To date, few studies have examined the physiological effects of IPV-related TBI. It was recently shown that women who have sustained an IPV-related TBI demonstrate deficits in different aspects of brain function. While these studies have provided important insights, there remains a need to further evaluate the immediate consequences and potential long-term effects of IPV-related TBI. Blood biomarkers are an attractive option as they may indicate damage to brain structures as well as provide insight into potential mechanisms underlying lasting symptoms of TBI. Studies of sport-related concussion have previously shown increases in markers of inflammation and brain injury. Additionally, such changes may persist years after injury in military veterans. Given the repetitive nature of IPV-related TBI, it is reasonable to hypothesize these abnormalities may also be present in the IPV population. The purpose of this study will be to examine blood biomarkers associated with IPV-related TBI. Markers of inflammation or brain injury have not been previously evaluated in this population and thus will be novel findings. This data will form the basis for future recommendations and resources for health care providers, first-line staff, and criminal justice workers."

column36: An ERP Investigation of Negative Affect and Memory following Concussion in University Athletes
column37: "A heightened incidence of mood disorder following a history of concussion has been documented in a variety of athlete populations, with emotional symptoms being a common consequence of concussive injuries. Current assessments of mood disorder in concussion focus heavily on self-report measures of depression symptoms, and while this provides a useful index, it neglects neural substrates that may be associated with depression. The proposed study will aim to establish biomarkers of mood disorder in concussion through an investigation of event-related brain potentials (ERPs) obtained from electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings. EEG recordings will be conducted with athletes from both contact and non-contact sports before and after their season of competition, as well as following any concussions sustained during the season. Participants will complete a memory task containing positive, negative, and neutral words and a self-report measure of depression, anxiety, and stress. It is expected that, following concussion, participants will display a memory bias for negative stimuli that is associated with a larger amplitude in the P300 ERP component, indexing allocation of attentional resources. Results of the proposed study will also be applied to examine emotional changes following repeat exposure to head impacts that do not result in diagnosed concussions. A similar pattern is expected to emerge following head impact exposure as would be seen in concussion. Thus, it is hypothesized that contact athletes will display a greater negative memory bias at postseason than non-contact athletes, regardless of the incidence of diagnosed concussion. The findings of the proposed study could provide insight into the progression of emotional changes following concussion."

column36: The Path to Next Generation Cancer Therapeutics: A Structure Guided Approach
column37: "Cancer is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells. Normally, cells know when to grow, divide, and stop growing. To know when to start growing, cells rely on certain proteins that act as a switch. This switch recognizes signals in the body and turns ""on"" when the cell needs to start growing to prepare to multiply. A key protein in this switch is called BRAF. BRAF is mutated in many cancers, causing this cellular ""switch"" to stay on, resulting in uncontrolled growth. There are drugs that can deactivate mutated BRAF in cancer cells, preventing it from keeping the cell growth switch on. Strangely, these same drugs cause the opposite effect in normal cells; they activate normal BRAF, which activates the switch which can promote the growth of new cancers. This adverse process is poorly understood, therefore the use of these drugs to treat cancer patients have been limited. The aim of my research is to develop safer and more effective drugs that target BRAF and the cell growth switch, specifically in cancer cells, without having any effects on normal cells. I believe I can achieve this goal by: a) Explaining why this adverse effect is happening in normal cells. b) Understanding the differences in the configuration of the ""switch"" when BRAF is on vs when it is off. With this information, I will be able to design revolutionary drugs to freeze the BRAF protein in its off position within the switch system. I plan to achieve this by using a technique called cryo-electron microscopy which will allow me to view interactions within the switch and drugs at an atomic level. When completed, these drugs will be able to effectively turn the growth switch off, putting a stop to the growth of cancer cells, resulting in a safer, more effective treatment for cancer patients. "

This issue needs to be urgently addressed in Canada for the health of individuals, and for the fiscal well-being of the country. column36: Investigating the role of the unfolded protein response at early and late stages of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
column37: "Pancreatic cancer is a devastating cancer with only 8% of those diagnosed surviving past 5 years. My project wants to answer how the unfolded protein response (UPR), a cellular stress response, functions at both the beginning stages and stage after a tumor has formed in patients with pancreatic cancer. Research from our lab has shown that one molecule within the UPR pathway, Activating Transcription Factor 3 (ATF3), plays an important role in pancreatic cancer formation through multiple cell types. These include both pancreatic cells, as well as cells that surround the pancreas, like cells of the immune system. The immune system sends immune cells to the pancreas when the body detects cancer cells there. We have shown that turning off ATF3 in the whole body lowers pancreatic cancer formation and pancreatic tissue damage in mice. It also lowered the amount of immune cells sent to the site of damage in the pancreas. The goal of my project is to determine if turning off the Atf3 gene only in pancreatic cells will produce the same result. This project also wants to answer how ATF3 and the UPR stress response increases chemotherapy resistance of pancreatic cancer tumors. Our prediction is that if tumor cells have a greater stress response they will have a stronger defence against chemotherapy drugs. To find out if this is the case, I will use tumor cells taken from patients with pancreatic cancer and prevent them from turning on their UPR stress response using specially designed chemicals. I will then treat them with chemotherapeutic drugs to see if they die more easily than cancer cells with their UPR stress response enabled. The results of this project will offer important information on how pancreatic cancer forms and keeps growing despite use of chemotherapeutic drugs."

column36: Assessing the Impact of Genetic Modifications on Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-Cell Proliferation Capacity and Persistence
column37: "Cancer is the leading cause of death across the globe. There is substantial research being done to develop a curative treatment with minimal side effects. However, these efforts are challenged by the complexity of cancer cells. They have mechanisms in place that allow them to adapt to their environment and become resistant to many drugs that are currently on the market. Moreover, majority of currently available treatments have serious side effects. It is therefore imperative for us to find new and improved therapeutics. Our research focuses on immunotherapy with the aim of reinforcing our own bodies' immune system response against the spread of these tumour cells. Of particular importance to this project is Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-Cell therapy. CAR T-Cells are a type of immune cells derived from patients' own blood, which are then genetically engineered in the laboratory to express receptors that recognize the cancer cells specifically and kill them. This therapy has shown great success in clinical trials; however, its efficacy is hampered by poor proliferation and expansion of the CAR T-Cells after re-administration into patients. In order to overcome this challenge, chemotherapeutic agents are administered beforehand to reduce the host immune cells' response against the treatment, but while also risking damage to the engineered CAR T-Cells. Therefore, our objective is to construct chemotherapy resistant CAR T-Cells and assess their proliferative capacity. Successful modifications of these cells will further enhance their expansion and persistence to ultimately improve their efficacy."

column36: The Impact of Restorative Justice as a Response to Sexual Violence on University Campuses
column37: "Students attending university have a lot of stressors. In striving for success students must adjust to the environment, manage personal obligations, and develop new academic skills while becoming responsible for reading a compilation of textbooks that collectively weigh more than they do. One of these stressors should not be sexual harassment. Unfortunately, this is a concern that needs to be addressed. On university campuses, sexual harassment is a prevalent traumatic event that impacts students psychological, physical, and academic well-being. Academic institutions need to become more effective in responding and preventing sexual harassment. I propose an investigation of the University of Toronto's response to sexual violence between university students. This project will involve exploring the survivors' and perpetrators' perceptions and experiences of university responses to internal reports of sexual harassment. This will inform the following stage in which survivors and perpetrators engage in a community restoration process. This process is called restorative justice (RJ). RJ allows survivors to regain control of the situation while engaging the perpetrator in a process of recognizing and taking responsibility for the negative impact he or she has had on the survivor. This process has proven to simultaneously benefit survivors and perpetrators involved in incidents ranging from bullying to first degree murder. I will explore the impact of RJ as a response to sexual harassment within university settings. I predict that RJ will be an effective community-based response and prevention strategy that mitigates the effects of sexual harassment on the survivor's academic performance, while decreasing the perpetrator's recidivism."

column36: Automated functionalization of lipid nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery and in vivo production of CAR T cells.
column37: "Nanomedicine has transformed drug delivery. Rather than relying on the passive distribution of a therapeutic (antibodies, vaccines, enzymes, nucleic acids) throughout the body to eventually reach the targeted tissue, researchers can now load therapeutics into nanoparticles capable of delivering them to a specific target site. However, the scope of nanomedicine is limited by complicated and expensive manufacturing logistics, thus limiting availability of nanomedicines to researchers and clinicians alike. A potential application of nanomedicine is improving chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, a cancer treatment that reprograms a patient's immune system (T cells) to destroy tumours. Much of the work to date has relied on modifying T cells outside of the body: an expensive and risky process. Instead, nanoparticles can be used to target and reprogram T cells in the patient's body, circumventing the need for expensive and difficult T cell isolation. In my research, I aim to overcome these challenges by developing molecular tools for simplified, portable, and on-demand production and incorporation of biological therapeutics in to nanoparticles. To demonstrate the capability of this technology, I will apply these tools to produce nanoparticles capable of generating CAR T cells inside rather than outside the body. By developing tools for inexpensive, portable and on-demand production of nanomedicines, this research has the potential to i) accelerate nanomedicine research by improving availability to researchers and ii) ensure that the therapeutic benefits of nanomedicine can be delivered to all patients in remote and low resource settings in Canada and globally. column36: Elucidating the therapeutic potential of targeting aryl hydrocarbon receptors in macrophages in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to improve immunotherapy
column37: "Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a malignant cancer of the pancreas and has the lowest 5-year patient survival rate of all major cancer types. Cancer immunotherapy is an increasingly popular and promising approach to treating cancer patients. Immunotherapy is founded on our understanding of how cytotoxic lymphocytes (CTLs), a type of cells of our own immune system can recognize and eradicate cancerous cells. Immunotherapy takes advantage of this knowledge by, for instance, boosting our CTLs to kill tumour cells. However, this approach has shown limited success in PDAC, which can be attributed to the immunosuppressive cells that inhibit the CTLs from killing the tumour cells through various mechanisms. One of such immunosuppressive cells are tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), which have found to be associated with poor prognosis in PDAC. To overcome this obstacle in immunotherapy, we can target these immunosuppressive TAMs to enhance tumour eradication by CTLs. Interestingly, we have found that a receptor molecule in TAMs, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), regulates the expression of inhibitory molecules that are inhibitory signals for CTLs to reduce killing of tumours. Thus, this project proposes to investigate how we can target AhR to reduce immunosuppression, enhance eradication of tumour cells by CTLs, and ultimately increase survival in PDAC patients."

column36: Hysterectomy for endometriosis with or without ovarian preservation in British Columbia: surgical outcomes over 7 years of follow up
column37: "Background: Endometriosis is a common chronic disease affecting approximately 10% of reproductive age women and can lead to painful menstrual cramps, painful sexual activity, and chronic pelvic pain. Hysterectomy (removal of the uterus), with or without removal of one or both ovaries, is commonly performed as definitive surgical management. Given that endometriosis lesions are stimulated by ovarian hormones (ie estrogen), removal of both ovaries (bilateral oophorectomy (BSO)) is often performed as a permanent form of hormonal suppression. However, there can be morbidity associated with BSO such as increased risk of cardiovascular events, osteoporosis, and symptoms of surgical menopause. Research question: Do women undergoing hysterectomy and removal of both ovaries (BSO) experience lower re-operation rates for endometriosis related pain, compared to women undergoing hysterectomy with ovarian preservation? Methods: We will utilize PopData BC data, which is already available to our group, to assemble a population-based cohort including all women who underwent hysterectomy in BC between 1985 and 2016 for endometriosis. Using Cox proportional hazards models, we will compare women undergoing hysterectomy with BSO and women undergoing hysterectomy with ovarian preservation according to their post-surgical outcomes. The primary outcome of interest will be re-operation rate. We will also do sub-analyses by indication for re-operation, by duration of follow-up (2, 5, 7 years after surgery), and by age group (19-29, 30-39 and 40). Significance: Given how commonly hysterectomy (either with BSO or ovarian preservation) is performed for women with endometriosis and pelvic pain, more evidence is needed to inform the practice of removing ovaries at the time of hysterectomy. column36: Cannabis and cannabinoid medications for the treatment of chronic orofacial pain
column37: "Cannabis and cannabinoid medications for the treatment of chronic orofacial painPeople suffering from chronic orofacial pain, persistent pain conditions affecting the head, mouth, and neck, often live with severe disability, and reduced quality of life. To compound the issue, current treatments can be expensive, cause unwanted side-effects, and are only modestly effective. Finding an additional means for treating these patients would be of significant benefit to them, and the specialists who deal with their cases.Cannabis and cannabinoid medications offer a promising alternative to conventional drugs used to treat chronic orofacial pain. Historical accounts and current literature support that cannabis has some effectiveness in treating chronic pain. The purpose of this study is to: 1. summarize current knowledge regarding treating chronic orofacial pain with cannabis and cannabinoid medications; and 2. identify clinician attitudes toward using these same medications to treat chronic orofacial pain. To achieve objective 1, a scoping review will be completed, collating current literature on the use of cannabis for treating chronic orofacial pain. To achieve objective 2, a survey regarding clinician attitudes toward using cannabis to treat chronic orofacial pain will be designed and distributed to oral surgeons and oral medicine specialists. The survey responses will be summarized and analyzed using statistical software.This review will create a resource for oral surgeons and oral medicine specialists seeking to inform their practice regarding the use of cannabis and cannabinoid medications. column36: Investigating the role of oncogenic H3.3K27M mutations in pediatric diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma
column37: "Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine Glioma (DIPG) is a devastating disease and is the leading cause of pediatric brain-tumour related death. The median survival rate after diagnosis is less than 1 year, and there is a desperate need for new treatments to be developed. However, efforts to create new therapies are limited by the lack of animal models that develop DIPG tumours genetically similar to those found in humans. To date, our lab and others have discovered a mutation, H3K27M, which occurs in nearly 80% of DIPG tumours. However, its exact role in these tumours is unknown. We believe that this mutation plays a role in the initiating stages of tumour development. To test this, I will determine which neural cells are the most susceptible to becoming tumour cells, and at which stage during normal development are these cells most likely to begin forming tumours. To do this, I will use mice that have the H3K27M mutation, and I will extract cells from different areas of the brain at different stages of development and characterize them. Using this information, I will create mice with the H3K27M mutation in the cell type that is most susceptible to becoming tumour cells, and express this mutation at the stage of development that is most able to form tumours. These mice will also have mutations in other genes, TP53 and PDGFRA. Mutations in these genes have been shown to occur in human DIPG tumours, and therefore this will aid in creating tumours in mice that are genetically similar to humans. The successful completion of these experiments will result in an animal model of DIPG, that creates tumours that accurately represent the human disease. With this model, we can begin identifying and testing new therapies that could potential help treat this devastating disease."

column36: Gamification of eHealth self-care education in a heart failure population
column37: "As rates of cardiovascular disease climb each year in Canada so do the number of people living with, and managing heart failure at home. Heart failure patients have high rates of hospital admissions and readmissions, many of which are preventable through high quality patient self-care. Patient education is a key factor in determining how patients will manage their disease. There has been a shift in patient education through online modes of delivery however little is known about how best to deliver that education in a way that is engaging and effective. There is a growing body of evidence in education research to support the concept of gamification which is the method of using game design methods in a non-game context. The purpose of this study is to investigate the effect of delivering patient education through an online platform that uses gamification mechanisms to enhance patient motivation and behaviour change. The study will take place in three parts: 1) Design and development of the online platform 2) Focus groups conducted from two British Columbian acute care centres with heart failure nurse specialists 3) Test the online platform with patients recruited through two outpatients heart function clinics to determine changes in knowledge level and self-care behaviours. This will be the first study to explore the effects of delivering heart failure patient education using narrative story game design as a technique to enhance patient education.Patients living with heart failure must be actively involved in self-care to successfully manage the condition. A gamified web-application aimed at improving the self-care of patients living with heart failure has the potential to drastically improve the outcomes and reduce hospital readmissions of this population."

column36: Using Delayed Prognostic Scores for Long-term Mortality Prediction in Acute Intracerebral Hemorrhage
column37: "Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is widely recognized as the most devastating stroke subtype, with the highest rates of mortality and morbidity. About half of ICH patients will die by 6 months, and those that survive are often left with severe disability. Despite our best efforts, there is still no effective treatment for ICH. When there is not a treatment for such a common disease, it isn't surprising that my job often entails telling someone their loved one will not get better. Coming to this conclusion can be challenging, and prognostication in ICH is notoriously difficult. For this reason, there have been tools developed to calculate the risk of ICH morbidity/ mortality based on a patient's initial presentation. However, we know that a patient's initial status is not representative of their clinical course, as ICH is a dynamic disease. Early prognostication can result in early withdrawal of care due to initial severity of assessment. Our previous work has shown that the use of delayed imaging can improve prognostic abilities of multiple ICH scores for 90-day mortality. However, we do not know the implications of incorporating delayed clinical information into our prognostic models, or its effect on a patient's functional outcome. Furthermore, we do not know if these results are true when considering 6-month or 1-year mortality, as the natural course of recovery for ICH is much slower than its ischemic stroke counterpart. Our project will be looking at 3 different ICH patient databases, and calculating multiple ICH prognostic models using delayed clinical and radiographic information. These novel findings could be practice-altering for doctors of any specialty caring for ICH patients, and could improve our communication with family members regarding prognosis. "

column36: The impact of systematic assessments and interventions on neurodevelopmental outcomes in school-aged children with congenital heart disease.
column37: "Congenital heart disease (CHD) are the most common congenital anomalies. Children with severe CHD are at high risk of developing developmental delays, including language, intellectual and motor skills (e.g. coordination, dexterity) difficulties. In 2012, the American Heart Association issued a statement recommending regular developmental follow-ups of all children with CHD. The surveillance is meant to promote early diagnosis and individualized treatment and intervention in order to improve the development of these children. In 2013, the Clinique d'Investigation NeuroCardiaque (CINC) was founded at the CHU Sainte-Justine. Professionals at the CINC follow children born with CHD starting 4 months old to assess their needs and provide early interventions. Previous results have shown that the CINC program has a positive impact on the development of 3-year-old children with CHD. Children enrolled in the CINC program had better language and visuoconstructive skills than children with CHD that were not followed at the CINC because they were born prior to its opening in 2013. With increased environmental and academic demands, several developmental issues arise in school-aged children with CHD. The purpose of this project is to assess the impact of the CINC program in 8-year-olds with CHD. We expect that the children who received systematic early assessments and interventions starting at 4 months will have better language, intellectual and motor skills, and fewer learning disabilities compared to children with CHD who have never been enrolled in the CINC program. This project will have significant consequences by providing strong arguments for the need to develop other developmental neurocardiac clinics similar to the CINC and to improve and perpetuate the existing ones."

column36: Statin drugs exploit a metabolic vulnerability in high-risk multiple myeloma
column37: "Multiple myeloma (MM) is a cancer of the antibody-producing plasma cells, a type of white blood cell that is an essential component of the immune system. Nearly 3,000 Canadians are diagnosed with MM every year, with a median survival rate of approximately three years despite current standard-of-care treatments. Statins are a family of cholesterol-lowering drugs, produced off-patent at a low cost and with an established record of safety and efficacy. Recently, certain subtypes of MM have been shown to be selectively killed by treatment with statins, though the mechanism of this response and the genetic factors that cause one patient to respond to statins while another does not remain unclear. This study will reveal the molecular determinants of statin-induced cell death, a quality that may be screened for or amplified in patients to promote the efficacy of statin treatment. Statins will be tested in conjunction with the current standard-of-care therapy, providing pre-clinical evidence for the use of statins in patients. Ultimately, this will advance the use of statins to the oncology clinic, moving one step closer to employing a cheap, safe, and effective family of cholesterol-lowering drugs to treat aggressive forms of cancer."

column36: The Role of Peroxisomes in Innate Immunity Against Microbial Pathogens
column37: "This proposal outlines experiments designed to investigate the role of peroxisomes in innate immunity against microbial pathogens. Peroxisomes are dynamic organelles involved in metabolism of lipids and reactive anionic species. Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders (PBD) result in a class of disorders on the Zellweger's spectrum which display symptoms including poor muscle tone, hearing/vision loss and organ damage. Individuals with PBDs are expected to be highly susceptible to pathogens. Currently, there is no cure or standardized treatment for these disorders. Previous studies have shown that peroxisomes are crucial in the activation of immune response against viruses; however, the role of peroxisomes in immunity against bacteria is currently unknown. Our lab plans to investigate the link between peroxisomes and immunity through studying genetically modified male and female mice with intestinal epithelial cells lacking peroxisomes (intestinal-PBD). We will infect these mice with an enteropathogenic bacterium to characterize the effect PBD on immunity. This will be done by comparing intestine pathology and RNA profiles of infected wildtype versus intestinal-PBD mice. Our current work has shown that there is a significant difference in the infected phenotype of intestinal-PBD mice, such that knockout mice intestines have a delayed and severe immune response. Future work includes comparing the RNA profiles throughout infection to identify PBD affected signalling pathways. This data will be used to characterize the physiology of PBD's immune effects and to identify molecular pathways involved with the PBD phenotype. Through identifying these pathways, we can aid further progress in creating targeted treatments for individuals with PBDs as opposed to symptomatic treatments. "

column36: Response to dual-antiplatelet therapy in patients undergoing cerebrovascular procedures
column37: "Increasingly, cerebral aneurysms, plaque within the carotid artery, and other diseases within the field of vascular neurosurgery are being treated with less invasive procedures. Placing a stent within a blood vessel is a commonly used technique to treat these diseases. The stent resembles a pipe with both ends being open, which ensures that blood continues to flow within the vessel. To make sure the stent remains open, patients are required to take a standard regimen of anti-platelet medications before and after the stent is inserted. However, multiple studies have shown that not all individuals respond to the anti-platelet medications, which essentially means the medications are not working. Therefore, if patients receiving a stent do not respond to the anti-platelet medications, they could be at an increased risk of the stent closing off and developing a stroke. The objective of our study is to assess the risk of developing a stroke in patients who receive an intracranial stent and determining if this risk is associated with the patient not responding to the anti-platelet medications. We will test patient responses to the anti-platelet medications prior to the insertion of the stent and follow the patients for a period of three months to monitor for any complications. The results of this study may lead to changes in the management of the anti-platelet medications administered to patients who are receiving a stent in order to reduce the risk of stroke that is associated with stent insertion. column36: Targeting inflammation to prevent stroke-induced heart injury
column37: "Stroke is the second leading cause of death in the world and the first leading cause of disability; overall, a devastating burden to our society. Approximately 84% of stroke cases are ischemic and can result in both structural and functional damage to the heart, termed stroke-induced heart injury (SIHI). This manifests in the form of cardiac arrhythmias or more severe cardiac complications that can lead to death or stroke recurrence. Other than managing the risk factors, there is no treatment for these post-stroke cardiac complications. When an ischemic stroke occurs, there are both local and systemic inflammatory responses. Work in our lab has shown that post-stroke inflammation may be leading to heart inflammation and fibrosis, which are early markers of SIHI. Therefore, targeting inflammation could be an intuitive approach to prevent SIHI. Since brain microglia activation is an important component of the inflammatory cascade, the use of Minocycline, a microglia activation inhibitor, could be one means of preventing SIHI. Additionally, preliminary data from our lab has shown that pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β) is up-regulated systemically post-stroke. Therefore, targeting IL-1β using specific IL-1β inhibitory peptide, Anakinra, could be another potential way of preventing SIHI. This study will use a permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion model of stroke in both male and female rats which will be treated with Minocycline, Anakinra, or saline post-stroke. The animals will subsequently be analyzed for heart and brain inflammation as well as cardiac damage. Together, this will help determine if reducing post-stroke inflammation can decrease heart injury, as well as determine a drug that may be effective at doing this."
