column36: Attitudes and barriers surrounding uptake of preconception carrier screening among Manitoba Hutterites
column37: "Hutterites have a higher burden of genetic diseases than others in Canada due to their physical isolation and shared ancestry. Many Hutterites carry genetic changes that make it more likely for them to have a child with a genetic disease. There is a test called a carrier screen that was recently designed in Manitoba which can tell whether a person of Hutterite descent carries any of these genetic changes. Although many Hutterites previously stated they would be interested in the test, our clinic has observed that uptake was low, which made us wonder if there were barriers in our health system that prevent access to the test. In this study, we will determine how Hutterites make decisions about carrier screening, and whether there are barriers that make it difficult for them to get screening. We plan on taking a two-pronged approach where we first develop a survey which will ask Hutterites about their experiences with genetic disorders and how they feel about carrier screening. Then, we will conduct interviews with select people who completed the survey to understand their perspectives about carrier screening and what they feel are barriers to getting screening. We would specifically like to interview individuals who are planning on having children to see whether they would be interested in carrier screening prior to becoming pregnant. In addition, we want to interview those who have a genetic disease in their family to understand how this affects their interest in carrier screening. From the results of these two aims, we will develop recommendations for genetics centres on how and when to offer carrier screening and genetic counselling to people from Hutterite communities, which will help to ensure health care equity among Canada's unique populations."

column36: Understanding informant discrepancies within the WHODAS 2.0 across children with mental disorders and their parents
column37: "Mental disorders affect one in five children, the impact of which extends across the life course. Surveys, often completed by parents, are used to understand the health of children with mental disorders. Discrepancies between parent and child reports can impact the effectiveness of care and the supports provided to children with mental disorders. The World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) 2.0 is a 36-item survey that assesses illness severity by considering six categories of functioning. Evidence shows that agreement between parent and child reports of child mental health and quality of life is low, but how this extends to other aspects of children's health is unknown. Considering this knowledge gap, my thesis will: 1. Estimate child-parent agreement on the WHODAS 2.0 in a clinical sample of children with mental disorders, 2. Examine convergent and divergent validity, as well as internal consistency reliability of the WHODAS 2.0 across informants and, 3. Compare whether risk factors for elevated levels of disability are similar for child vs. parent reports. The data includes a sample of over 100 children aged 8-17 years with mental disorders. This work will inform future research by identifying the domains where disagreement is the most apparent. By exploring parent-child discrepancies, health professionals will better understand the strength, direction and factors that influence differences between parent and child reports. Using these results, clinical practice can be improved by better understanding how to assess information about the severity of mental disorders within children, ultimately leading to the appropriate provision of mental health services and improved child health outcomes. column36: Pain Appraisal in Young Breast Cancer Survivors: The role of Pain Acceptance

column36: Physical Activity Together in Multiple Sclerosis: An integrative exploration of the psychosocial implications of a dyadic lifestyle physical activity intervention
column37: "People with multiple sclerosis (MS) experience the significant impact of the debilitating disease on their mental and physical wellbeing. This impact (i.e., increasing disability levels) greatly compromises individuals' ability to accomplish everyday tasks, reducing their independence and forcing them to rely on informal unpaid support partners. These support partners tend to be the spouses of individuals with MS; therefore, this need for care represents an added dynamic within their partnership. It is clear that MS has far-reaching problematic effects on both the individual living with MS and their primary social networks. Fortunately, physical activity (e.g., walking, cycling, resistance training) has been proven to help manage the negative impact of the disease. A physical activity program that uses a dyadic approach is believed to be an effective way to manage the disease by targeting the physical activity levels of both the person with MS and their support partner. Not only will this teleconference program teach participants simple ways to increase their activity levels as a lasting lifestyle change, but it will also work to improve the relationship between the person with MS and their support partner. This goal is important because social support and healthy relationships are also predictive of overall health. In fact, support partners and those struggling with the hardships associated with chronic disease need the health benefits of high-quality relationships and support more than the average population. This research will assess the dyadic experiences of participating in this intervention through interviews and questionnaires to see how it affects perceptions of social support, resilience, relationship quality, self-efficacy related to MS and caregiver coping. column36: Tracking the Dissemination and Implementation of the International Pediatric Oncology Exercise Guidelines
column37: "Exercise is safe, beneficial and feasible in pediatric oncology. However, the lack of guidelines has been identified as impeding knowledge translation. To address this, a team of 120 international experts has created the international Pediatric Oncology Exercise Guidelines (iPOEG; disseminated Spring 2020). column36: Emergence and mechanisms of multi-drug resistant microorganisms in high-risk patients
column37: "Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major threat to clinical medicine. Hospitals serve as prominent reservoirs for AMR, contributing to the development of deadly multi-drug resistant (MDR) pathogens. They will then be asked to use the tool as seen in the video (feedback available) or to observe the tool being used again (no feedback). After a three- week delay a final memory test will be administered for skilled tool use as as well knowledge about tool features in order to assess procedural and declarative memory respectively."

column36: The development of the gut microbiome and the physiology of stress circuitry in premature infants
column37: "The human gut hosts an abundant and diverse population of microbes, termed the microbiota, which perform functions essential to health. The gut microbiota communicates bidirectionally with the brain via the gut-brain axis, which is increasingly recognized as having broad contributions to human development. In animal models, the microbiota has been causally linked to dysregulation of brain regions and biological processes involved in the stress response. In the first few years of life, the gut microbiome and brain undergo a critical period of development, during which time perturbations have the potential to alter our lifelong health trajectories. This is especially true for infants born prematurely, as they exhibit insufficient stress hormone secretion in infancy, and face increased risk of developing neurological, immune and metabolic disorders later in life. Stress response dysregulation is extremely relevant to these outcomes, as it encompasses biological processes that underpin disease progression. Together with the intensified microbiome alterations premature infants experience, these findings suggest a direct relationship between early gut microbial colonization and the maturation of normal stress physiology. This research aims to determine the role of the early-life gut microbiome in stress response dysregulation in premature infants. To achieve this, we will utilize brain magnetic resonance imaging, stress hormone measurements, and microbiome ecological analysis techniques on a cohort of 60 premature infants in a longitudinal clinical study. New understandings generated will facilitate considerable multidisciplinary knowledge advancements, with the potential to reveal novel research avenues critical to the physical and mental health outcomes of this population."

column36: "Initial evaluation of a Screening tool for Complex Regional Pain Syndrome And Neuropathic Pain,the Paediatric Pain SCAN"

column36: Investigating the therapeutic potential of AMP-activated protein kinase in myotonic dystrophy type 1
column37: "Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), the most common form of adult-onset muscular dystrophy in Canada and worldwide, is a hereditary neuromuscular disorder that results in skeletal muscle weakness, wasting and myotonia. Due to its progressive nature, individuals with DM1 may experience difficulties in carrying out activities of daily living, and in severe cases, lose the ability to walk or breathe independently. In addition to skeletal muscle dysfunction, the symptoms of DM1 are multisystemic and can include cataracts, insulin resistance, heart problems, gastrointestinal issues, as well as cognitive impairments. To date, there is no cure for this debilitating disease. Recent work from our lab has revealed that AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling, a key cellular pathway that maintains skeletal muscle mass and function, is repressed in a mouse model of DM1. Stimulation of this pathway using drugs or exercise, has beneficial effects in the skeletal muscles of DM1 mice. However, the methods of AMPK activation used to date are also known to have additional effects on other cellular pathways, thereby confounding the therapeutic role of AMPK in these studies. Here, I propose to treat DM1 mice with novel AMPK-activating compounds designed to specifically target this pathway. The functional, cellular, and molecular characteristics of skeletal muscle tissue will be analyzed in order to evaluate improvements in the DM1 pathology. In addition, I will initiate a combinatorial approach with AMPK-activating drugs and daily exercise to determine if these improvements are further enhanced in an additive manner. These findings will enable us to better understand the therapeutic role of AMPK in DM1 and contribute to the development of novel treatment strategies for DM1 patients."

column36: An examination of sensorimotor function in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using robotic measurement
column37: "When you think of a child with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), you likely think about the social and communicative difficulties they have. While forming relationships is a challenge for many children with ASD, their physical and sensory (known as sensorimotor) difficulties can further limit the opportunities they have for social development. ASD affects 1 in 59 children and although social difficulties are well-researched in ASD, sensorimotor challenges have yet to be precisely described.We will measure upper limb movements with the KINARM, a non-invasive robotic frame that supports the arms. The KINARM will track reaction times, movement accuracy, and body position awareness. We will compare the results of children with ASD to a sample of healthy children to understand where the differences are, then analyze those results alongside clinical data provided to us by the child's parents. The clinical data will include measures of communicative, social, and daily living skills. We expect to see a correlation between children's sensorimotor and social capabilities.It is important to understand the impact of impaired sensorimotor function. Everyday activities such as bathing and crossing the street can be difficult or even unsafe if a child has poor coordination. They could struggle to understand body language and facial expressions, impacting social relationships. Overall, children with ASD have fewer chances to develop social skills, such as through community sports. Our research will characterize sensorimotor deficits at a high level of precision using robotic measurement, which will assist and improve inclusivity programs to allow children with ASD to have more opportunities to grow and interact with their peers."

column36: Characterizing the cellular mechanics of metastatic prostate cancer progression in response to microenvironment stiffness
column37: "Metastasis, a phenomenon accounting for 90% of cancer-related deaths, is characterized by cancer cell migration from a primary tumour to a new secondary site. Regardless of the mutational origin, in virtually all cancers, cells appear to change their biophysical characteristics: malignant cells generate higher traction forces and become softer, and this is hypothesized to facilitate migration through crowded fibrous multicellular environments. Cell contractility is also observed to increase as a function of microenvironment stiffness, however, it is still unclear how microenvironment mechanics impact the metastatic nature of cancer progression. Prostate cancer is a common latent health hazard for men, and we anticipate that its onset may require key mechanical changes such as cellular softening, contractility, and local stiffening of the microenvironment. We hypothesize that substrate-stiffening triggers increased cell contractility, which may contribute to prostate cancer metastatic progression, and that this increased contractility is reflected in mechanical changes in the cell. In this proposal, I will examine this hypothesis by employing a variety of established biophysical tools to quantify cell mechanics: traction force microscopy (contractility and motility), magnetic twisting cytometry (cell stiffness), and magnetic tweezers (cytoplasmic mechanics) on elastic substrates spanning a range of physiological moduli to investigate the influence of microenvironment stiffness on cellular mechanics and motility. The biophysical insight gained here will strongly complement existing biochemical characterization, and offer more comprehensive insight into the mechanisms behind metastatic progression."

column36: "Projecting the future incidence and prevalence of childhood cancer, and burden of attributable cardiac and cancer-related late effects, in Ontario"
column37: "Between 1986 and 2015 there were 10,339 children diagnosed with cancer in Ontario. During this period, the number of children being diagnosed continued to increase by 1% per year. Over 85% of children now survive their diagnosis, but the cancer treatments they receive place them at high risk to develop one or more serious health conditions during adulthood [2]. By age 50 years, 96% of childhood cancer survivors are expected to be diagnosed with or die from a severe health condition. These are also known as ""late effects"". Breast cancer and congestive heart failure are two common but serious late effects that can occur decades after an initial diagnosis. We will create a statistical model that will project the future trends of children who will be diagnosed with cancer and live as a survivor within Ontario between the years of 2020 and 2038. A number of data sources will be used, such as historical population data from Statistics Canada. Historical treatment information from the province's pediatric cancer registry, The Pediatric Oncology Group of Ontario Networked Information System, will also be used. These future trends will then be used to estimate how many survivors in Ontario will be diagnosed breast cancer or congestive heart failure later in their lives. Survivors have complex medical needs that begin in childhood and continue throughout their lives. Preventing and treating late effects in survivors places considerable burden on Ontario's healthcare system, and this burden is expected to dramatically increase as cancer rates continue to rise. Estimating how many children will be diagnosed with cancer and will survive in future decades is important to help inform healthcare service planning and how resources are allocated across Ontario."

column36: Automated facial pain detection for older adults with dementia
column37: "Pain occurs very frequently in older adults, but it is often undertreated. This problem is further exacerbated in older adults with dementia, who typically have more difficulty self-reporting pain due to the cognitive and linguistic impairments that are associated with dementia. Therefore, we are developing a computer vision-based tool that can monitor and automatically detect pain in older adults and send an alert to the nursing staff if a person is in pain. To codify pain, The Prkachin and Solomon Pain Intensity (PSPI) score, which ranges from 0-16, adds the intensities of 4 core action units (AUs), or facial movements, from the The Facial Action Coding System (FACS). FACS is a system that contains 44 AUs, each of which measures a certain distinguishable facial movement. There are datasets coded by certified FACS coders, and validated by self-reports, containing video frames of older adults with and without pain, that can be used to train a system to automatically detect pain. We intend on using deep learning to train a regression-based convolutional neural network (CNN) to detect pain intensity. However, like other current pain intensity estimation models, which are mostly based on supervised machine learning algorithms, we are limited by the scarce amount of FACS-labelled data. As facial expression databases are abundant online, we have obtained more than 30 non-FACS based datasets to perform unsupervised data augmentation (UDA), which utilizes both labelled and unlabelled data. In addition, since we want our pain intensity detection algorithm to be fair to a person regardless of gender, age, or dementia status, we intend to incorporate fairness with respect to these attributes into our algorithm and then study the tradeoff between fairness and accuracy."

column36: GRAFT PRESERVATION SOLUTION IMPROVES ENDOTHELIAL FUNCTION AND MAINTAINS ENDOTHELIAL STRUCTURE OF SAPHENOUS VEIN GRAFTS IN PATIENTS UNDERGOING ISOLATED CABG
column37: "Saphenous vein grafts (SVG) remain the most often used conduits in coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Injury to SVG during harvesting and storage promotes thrombogenesis and neointimal hyperplasia that can progress to atherosclerosis characterized by SVG stenosis and occlusion. The long-term patency of the SVG is limited with an occlusion rate of 15% to 26% in the first year following surgery. DuraGraft® is a one-time intraoperative graft storage solution developed to protect endothelial function. The hypothesis is that DuraGraft® improves endothelial function and structural integrity because it provides a physiological pH balanced environment to the graft during storage time until anastomosis. It also contains agents that stimulate nitric oxide (NO) production and antioxidants to protect endothelial cells by decreasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) adverse effects. This study aims to investigate functional integrity of SVGs endothelium following storage in DuraGraft® vs heparinized saline by measuring SVG rings vascular reactivity when exposed to various agonists in organ chambers. The secondary objective is to identify the mechanisms responsible for endothelial preservation in DuraGraft® by measuring NO, eNOS activity, cGMP, and ROS levels in both solutions. The third objective is to investigate SVGs structural integrity via histological masson trichrome staining, cell viability assay, and immunohistochemical analysis. The current study about this innovative preservation solution is a great contribution to the improvement of clinical outcomes and intraoperative care of CABG patients. The ultimate goal is to offer patients better survival chances and life quality while lightening the burden of reoperation on the health system."

column36: Artificial intelligence to the profit of dietitians: validity and reliability of a smart food diary
column37: "Most chronic diseases could be prevented or improved through lifestyle changes such as modifications in feeding habits. Nutritional assessment is essential to gather detailed information on what people are consuming, but it is currently difficult to collect precise data on the nutrients consumed. This makes it hard for dietitians to help people change their habits. Keenoa is a food diary that integrates artificial intelligence-based food recognition. The mobile application allows the patient/participants to snap pictures of their meals, specify foods and beverages consumed and estimate portion sizes. We believe that Keenoa is as valid as a written food diary but more reliable, more cost-effective and better appreciated from both researchers, dietitians and their patients/participants. A hundred participants, men and women between 18-65 years old, will be recruited for this 3-month study. Every month, participants will write everything they consume for a period of 4 days, by using both Keenoa and a written food diary. Thirty of them will provide urine samples that we will analyze in order to measure their real intake in certain nutrients. We will be testing Keenoa's validity by comparing nutritional intake of multiple days against the results of the urine tests and will evaluate Keenoa's reliability by comparing repeated measures in time. This study's results will confirm the validity and reliability of the Keenoa app. By its novelty and cutting-edge technology, its user-friendliness and if the results confirm its cost-effectiveness advantages, this tool could be used by numerous researchers. It will promote the development of nutrition knowledge as well as wider research on the role of nutrition on multiple health aspects."

column36: Heavy metal and gut microbiota profiles as biomarkers for autism spectrum disorder
column37: "Despite being one of the fastest growing neurodevelopmental disorders in the industrialized world, the exact etiology of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains unknown. Increasing evidence supports the role of both gut microbiota and heavy metal accumulation in the pathogeneis of ASD; however, knowledge of the potential relationship between the two is lacking. This study will investigate the interaction of heavy metal and gut microbiota profiles of Canadian children with and without ASD. It is hypothesized that a link between heavy metals and gut microbiota exists in the pathogenesis of ASD, and further understanding of this link can help identify biomarkers of this neurodevelopmental disorder. The study's sample will consist of 200 children (100 with ASD and 100 neurotypical controls) aged three to seven years old. Hair samples of 100 mg will be collected and analyzed for levels of lead, arsenic and mercury. In addition, fecal samples will be collected and processed to characterize the children's microbiota profiles. Several statistical methods will be employed to analyze the gathered data, and will focus on identifying key metallic and microbial parameters for ASD and screening for high-dimensional biomarkers of disease. These biomarkers have great implications in terms of elucidating the molecular mechanisms of ASD, preventing the onset of ASD, and improving treatments for individuals with ASD. "

column36: The Effects of Cannabidiol on a Tau P301S Transgenic Mouse Model of Alzheimer?s Disease
column37: "Alzheimer's disease (AD) is growing at alarming rates in humans. The diagnosis includes clinical symptoms, such as confusion and memory impairments and the pathological presence of extracellular beta amyloid plaques (Aß) and abnormal tau protein. The formation of abnormal tau protein accumulates prior to Aß. Additionally, tau protein associated lesions (neutrophil threads (NTs) and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs)) are connected to neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation, and overall cognitive decline among AD patients 9. Consequently, treatments that target tau protein should delay symptom onset and improve overall prognosis. Cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive component of the plant cannabis, demonstrates neuroprotective properties, increases neurogenesis, decreases neurodegeneration, and decreases neuroinflammation. More importantly CBD decreases the hyperphosphorylation of tau protein 2, 3. The hyperphosphorylation of tau protein contributes to the formation of NTs and NFTs. Therefore, CBD should decrease the pathology and learning, and memory impairments associated with AD by targeting the previous pathologies. The proposed experiment will chronically treat tau P301S mice, a transgenic mouse model of AD with CBD. Treatment efficacy will be evaluated with various behavioural tasks that assess learning and memory function 1, 8. After behavioural testing, Nissl and immunohistochemistry will assess the levels of different AD-like pathologies. It is predicted that CBD will decrease the pathology and learning, and memory impairments of the tau P301S mice. If CBD decreases AD-like pathologies and impairments in tau P301S mice, this will provide hope for a potential AD treatment, which targets the early symptoms of the disease in a relatively safe and inexpensive manner. "

column36: Forecasting Pediatric Emergency Department Crowding - The Pediatric CrowdED Study
column37: "Pediatric emergency department (PED) crowding is a direct threat to the care of sick children, as it limits the ability of healthcare teams to recognize severe illness early. Moreover, it is associated with an increased risk of medication errors, to which children are particularly vulnerable. It is unsurprising that satisfaction with care is lower in situations of crowding. High patient volumes as well as care processes within the PED are major causes of crowding. Previous studies have described patterns in PED visits, and factors leading to more patients leaving without being seen by a physician. Based on what is already known on PED crowding, we aim to develop a tool able to predict when a PED will experience crowding, and whether patients will be seen within the recommended times. In order to do so, we will use anonymized information on thousands of patient visits over a five-year period. We will include additional information, such as PED staffing, timing of visits, local weather conditions and patterns of infection, such as the flu. We will analyze these factors with advanced statistical models and artificial intelligence tools. The performance of these models will be determined and compared to currently available measures of crowding.Ultimately, our objective is to develop a tool that is usable, accurate, reliable, and adapts to the realities of a given PED. Given the particularities of acute illness in children, and the unique characteristics of the PED, such a tool will contribute to safer and better pediatric care. By enabling hospital administrators and public health officials to proactively allocate resources where they are most needed, the mismatch between PED utilization and available resources could be reversed. "

column36: Characterization and Functional Assessment of Pituitary Adenylate Cyclase-Activating Polypeptide (PACAP) Protein and Receptor Expression at the Stellate and Celiac Ganglia in Male and Female Mice Following Cold Acclimation
column37: "Obesity reduces quality of life for millions of Canadians and costs $6 billion in health care spending annually. An imbalance in energy intake and output contribute to the development of obesity, increasing risk of chronic disease such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, osteoarthritis and some cancers. Identifying ways to correct energy imbalance has proven challenging, as the basic mechanisms that regulate energy burning via hormones is poorly understood. Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) is a hormone shown to be important in the regulation of energy balance. Specifically, it has been shown to regulate adaptive thermogenesis, an energy burning process that produces heat in specialized fat tissue called brown fat. Adaptive thermogenesis is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system (SNS), also known as the ""fight or flight"" response, which is involuntarily activated when our body perceives stress. While PACAP and its receptors are known to be expressed in parts of the SNS, it is not known if PACAP receptors are present on sympathetic neurons that connect to brown fat. We hypothesize PACAP receptors are expressed in sympathetic nerves innervating brown fat and through these neurons PACAP regulates thermogenesis. To test this hypothesis, we will first measure PACAP receptor gene expression in sympathetic neurons isolated from male and female mice exposed to cold stress. Next we will assess the activity of sympathetic nerves that connect to brown fat when exposed to molecules that mimic or block the effect of PACAP. Experimental outcomes will increase our understanding of PACAP's role in regulating energy balance, potentially identifying PACAP as a new therapeutic target to promote energy burning in obesity to reduce body weight. "

column36: Investigation of the Effects of Psychological Stress on Mucosal Immunity and Microbial Dysbiosis
column37: "The prevalence of inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's Disease (CD), is increasing globally, especially within Canada which has one of the highest incidence rates of CD. Currently, 270,000 Canadians are diagnosed with CD, which is characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract resulting in intense abdominal pain and discomfort. CD is attributed to a unique combination of factors including genetic predisposition, lifestyle choices, as well as bacterial species present within the gut. It has been shown that the gut microbiota of CD patients exhibits an increased proportion of specific strains of Escherichia coli (E. coli) compared to healthy individuals. Patients also report a relapse of symptoms following periods of psychological stress. The immune system is responsible for maintaining a delicate balance between commensal bacteria normally found in the gut and being able to respond robustly to invading pathogenic bacteria. Stress hormones can impair immune function and allow for a disruption in this delicate balance. Preliminary data has demonstrated that stress induces a massive outgrowth of CD-associated E. coli in the intestine leading to worsened colitis in mice. My project aims to identify how psychological stress impacts normal immune function, allowing for this dramatic increase in CD-associated E. coli. By evaluating the production of various antimicrobial factors, we will determine how impaired immune function following stress allows for the expansion of CD-associated strains of E. coli, and how this disruption of the healthy gut microbiome impacts the development of inflammatory bowel disease."

column37: "In Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a devastating neurodegenerative disorder, aggregations of ubiquitinated proteins form in affected motor neurons. Our study will improve our understanding of STI1's function in ALS and whether it can directly improve the health of neurons affected by these toxic aggregations. Deepening our understanding of STI1's role in ALS will potentially lead to the creation of novel therapeutic techniques that are effective at treating this neurodegenerative disease."

column36: Conversations with Indigenous Doulas: Learning How to Reclaim Traditional Birthing Practices

Each interview will be recorded and transcribed. The transcriptions will be coded in order to look for common themes. The primary objective of this project is to provide an outlet for Indigenous Doulas to share experiences, in hopes this information can be used to improve supports and education for Doulas and aid future Doulas doing this work. column36: Examining SERCA2a Acetylation in the Diseased Human Heart
column37: "Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Researchers have discovered that during the development of heart disease, a protein in the heart called SERCA2a becomes damaged. This is a problem because SERCA2a moves calcium within the heart and is responsible for relaxing the heart after each time it beats. Researchers have also discovered that SERCA2a proteins may be influenced by a process called acetylation, where an acetyl group is added to a target protein. In fact, we know that SERCA2a can hold 3 acetyl groups. In some cases, the addition of an acetyl group turns proteins on, while in other cases it turns proteins off. Our most recent research suggests that the acetylation of SERCA2a turns it off. However, we still do not know if the acetylation of SERCA2a directly contributes to the development of heart disease. Therefore, this research project will determine the clinical relevance of SERCA2a acetylation in the diseased human heart. To accomplish this, we will work closely with heart surgeons to collect human heart tissue that is removed and discarded as a normal part of surgery. We will also collect human heart tissue from heart surgery patients with type 2 diabetes to determine if SERCA2a acetylation is worse in this condition, which may explain why people with diabetes tend to develop heart disease more often than people who do not have diabetes. Our work will use experimental techniques such as immunoprecipitation, SERCA activity assays, and Western blotting to examine the effect of SERCA2a acetylation. The information gathered from this research may be used to create new strategies to treat heart disease by altering SERCA2a acetylation. This outcome would be a unique therapy for the diseased human heart."

column36: Testing the Impact of Feedback Following a Deliberate Practice Workshop
column37: "Psychotherapists do not necessarily grow in expertise with experience. An obstacle for gaining expertise is a lack of quality feedback. The primary training for therapists is workshops, which involve passive knowledge transfer rather than practice with feedback. A recent study compared the impact on therapist performance of a Motivational Interviewing (MI) workshop with Deliberate Practice (DP; expert feedback with practice) to a standard MI workshop. Therapists in the MI-DP workshop outperformed their counterparts. While this MI-DP workshop is promising for improving performance, research suggests that skills erode after workshops. The goal of this study is to explore the value of feedback in maintaining skills learned in a MI-DP workshop. Participants will consist of practicing therapists who will take the DP workshop. Each participant will conduct 4 sessions with an ambivalent student volunteer. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three groups: the feedback as usual group, who only receive self and volunteer feedback; the expert feedback group, who receive video feedback of trained coders assessing resistance (using the Adapted Client Resistance Code (CRC)) and MI adherence (using the Motivational Interviewing Treatment Integrity (MITI) scale) of each session; the tape review group, who review their session recordings alone. Therapist and client outcomes will be measured across ambivalent volunteer sessions and participant pre and post-study sample tapes using CRC and MITI. This study has implications for the role of feedback in developing therapist expertise and the value of patient versus expert feedback. If clinicians can be trained to recognize empirically supported therapy processes, this lends support for process coding as clinical training."

column36: "Metabolic control of integrin membrane traffic by AMPK drives breast cancer growth, survival, migration and invasion."
column37: "Cancer cells exhibit large differences in metabolism compared to healthy cells, in particular, how certain nutrients are used as fuel by cancer cells. Cancer cells not only have unique demands for specific nutrients, but are exposed to a unique environment within a tumour that provides limited access to many nutrients and oxygen. Through a poorly understood set of mechanism(s), cancer cells are able to adapt their metabolism to the nutrients in this otherwise restrictive environment, to not only survive, but thrive. Both healthy and cancer cells have a metabolic ""fuel gauge"" protein called AMPK that senses the availability of certain nutrients and then dictates the functions a cell is able to perform. How metabolic energy sensors such as AMPK are triggered to allow for this cancer cell nutrient and metabolism adaptation remains poorly understood, and understanding this is critical to reveal new weaknesses in cancer that can be used as targets for new therapies. In addition, cancer cell migration is a key component of cancer cell invasion and metastasis (cancer spreading). The process of cell migration is controlled by proteins known as integrins, and how metabolic sensors such as AMPK regulate integrin function is poorly understood. This research aims to understand how a novel set of signals triggered by AMPK may be a missing link in how cancer cells sense and adapt to otherwise restrictive nutrient and metabolism conditions. Understanding how a cancer cell may uniquely use AMPK to adapt, thrive, and undergo metastasis may lead to the development of novel pharmacological drug targets for cancer therapy."

column36: A comprehensive integrated molecular map of sarcomas
column37: "Sarcomas are a rare group of aggressive soft tissue and bone cancers that disproportionally affect pediatric patients. We will then incorporate these findings into a comprehensive map made up of new, more clinically relevant sarcoma subtypes.We hope this research will ultimately streamline diagnosis and the selection of effective and targeted treatment options for pediatric and adult sarcoma patients. column36: Elucidating the immunological basis of metabolic recovery post-bariatric surgery
column37: "Obesity is a condition that develops when body fat builds up excessively. In Canada, over 50% of people over the age of 18 are obese. Obesity is awfully dangerous as it is linked with several other conditions such as diabetes and heart disease. An unhealthy diet is a contributor to the development of obesity as it can directly cause excessive fat deposition and negatively impact the beneficial bacteria housed in our gut. With poor diet, there is a reduction in the beneficial bacteria that make up the microbiota. To treat obesity, many people resort to bariatric surgery, a procedure that involves re-directing the flow of food from the stomach to the intestines directly, which restricts food intake and usually leads to a reduction in body mass. Recent findings have shown that after bariatric surgery, the gut microbiota changes so that it becomes more like the microbiota seen in healthy individuals and leads to improved metabolism. We believe that these changes to the gut microbiota promotes a change in the immune system which then enables the body to improve metabolically. Previous work has shown how the microbiota impacts metabolism however, few have explained how the immune system is involved and how this can be applied clinically. With our work, we want to bridge this gap, by showing how the gut microbiota communicates with the immune system and leads to improved disease outcome in patients following bariatric surgery. column36: Does Environmental Enrichment Mitigate the Memory Deficits Associated with Chronic Seizures?
column37: "Epilepsy is a condition that is characterized by recurrent and unprovoked seizures. This condition is associated with pronounced memory deficits, which are believed to be the result of dysfunction in the hippocampus - a structure that is critical for long-term memory. The main goal of the proposed project is to examine if promoting increases in plasticity in the hippocampus can mitigate the memory deficits that occur as a result of chronic seizures. Importantly, environmental enrichment (EE) increases brain plasticity and improves learning and memory. Thus, we can use this approach to increase plasticity and assess whether this can resolve the memory deficits that follow chronic seizures. We aim to characterize the memory deficits produced by chronic seizures in rats that have been exposed to EE, compared to rats that have not been exposed to EE. We also aim to assess the hippocampus for markers of plasticity following the treatment. Rats will be exposed to an enriched environment followed by seizure treatment. Memory abilities will being tested in the Morris Water Task, which is sensitive to changes in the hippocampal network. We expect deficits in this task for each rat that has seizures but no exposure to EE. Next, cell staining and microscopy will be conducted to assess markers of plasticity. We expect that the condition of the rats who experience seizures and have exposure to EE will not be as severe as those who do not receive EE, and potentially no different than rats who do not have seizures The goal of this project is to evaluate whether EE can mitigate the memory deficits produced by chronic seizures. If this is the case, the results of the project will be pivotal for research aimed at alleviating the deficits associated with epilepsy. "

column36: Ampk lipidation: impact on monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation in atherosclerosis
column37: "Due to unhealthy lifestyles, heart disease persists as a burden to Canadians. Atherosclerosis defines the hardening of arteries due to plaque accumulation, which directly contributes to heart disease. Plaque is a complex mixture of fats, cholesterol, and cells. Particularly, immune cells play a key role in atherosclerosis. These immune cells, known as monocytes, differentiate into another type of cell called macrophages, which attempt to clear excess cholesterol but become trapped in the plaque instead. Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation can regulate the amount of these retained macrophages. Our lab is interested in the metabolism underlying this differentiation and how it relates to atherosclerosis.As in humans, each cell must regulate the balance between the energy it consumes and produces. For cells, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a metabolic sensor that is switched on when energy (ATP) is low. AMPK works to restore energy balance by turning on processes that produce ATP and shutting down those that consume ATP. In this way, AMPK is needed for monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation. AMPK has an attached fatty acid that acts like a guide in the cell, regulating which processes AMPK turns on or shuts down. To better understand other parts of this relationship, we have genetically engineered mice that do not have this fatty acid binding ability. This mutated AMPK loses its guide and allows us to ask: what else does this fatty acid do in cells? Does this affect plaque buildup in mice?It is our hope that this study will help us unravel immune cell metabolism in atherosclerosis and provide more precise therapeutic targets for future drug discovery to help those Canadians affected by heart disease."

column36: Quantitative modelling of organ-specific Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) MRI signal as a diagnostic tool for chronic fetal hypoxia
column37: "In over 5% of Canadian pregnancies, the placenta is unable to provide adequate oxygen and nutrition to the fetus. This causes restricted growth, and increases chances of stillbirth and severe brain damage in survivors. Currently we screen for Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) disorder with ultrasound, but it's very difficult, so FGR often goes undiagnosed. Some scientists have proposed using a special MRI scan that images blood flow (called BOLD) to look for abnormalities. It works well, but doctors are hesitant to use it because we don't fully understand how to interpret the BOLD MRI signal in fetal imaging. This is in part because we are scanning multiple organs at the same time - the liver, heart, and placenta - which are all contributing to the signal in different ways. I hope to untangle this signal by developing a model of how the organs' vasculature, blood flow distribution, and reactions to being exposed to different concentrations of oxygen affect the BOLD signal we see in MRI scans. Once we understand how these components affect the BOLD signal, we can compare the signals between healthy fetuses and those experiencing FGR to figure out the differences. Armed with this new understanding, we will be able to diagnose FGR in-utero much earlier than before using MRI, and make better clinical decisions to ensure a safe pregnancy and a healthy baby. "

column36: Long-term Cognitive and Neuropsychological Effects of Repeated mild Traumatic Brain Injury
column37: "Moderate to severe brain injury is a top environmental risk factor for development of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease. It has been discovered that even mild brain injuries, like concussions, can significantly increase the onset of Alzheimer's disease. An estimated 1.6 - 3.8 million sport and recreation-related concussions occur worldwide every year, with most symptoms of the injury resolving within a week of injury. While the short-term effects of mTBI are better understood, there is much less known about long-term effects of mTBI and its relationship to more severe neurodegenerative conditions. Adolescents and young adults have one of the highest incidences of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), so often thoughts of how mTBI impacts age-related dementias are not of immediate concern. Memory and attention deficits have been documented in middle-aged individuals with histories of repeated mTBI, but who have not been formally diagnosed with a neurodegenerative condition. Further, these deficits were not observed in the age-matched group without mTBI, nor younger subjects with histories of repeated mTBI, suggesting persistent effects of repeated mTBI that only appear as the aging process progresses. Our lab has evidence that neurocognitive training can persistently enhance cognitive function in elderly adults with subjective memory complaints, and so in addition to identifying any long-term neuropsychological effects of concussion, the proposed study will focus on determining if neurocognitive training has benefits for these individuals. We hope this study will help identify long-term effects of repeated mTBI and determine the utility of neurocognitive training as a therapeutic option for individuals with early neurocognitive decline. "

column36: Examining attitudes toward a sugar-sweetened beverage tax among adults living in a middle-high income area of Winnipeg
column37: "In Canada, at both the provincial and federal level, governments are considering the implementation of a sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) tax to address a rising prevalence of non-communicable disease and generate revenue, though no province has implemented to date. SSBs includes beverages that contain added sugar, typically this includes pop, fruit drinks (not 100% juice), and sports drinks. A growing number of countries and jurisdictions have implemented a SSB tax, including Mexico, the United Kingdom, and Berkley, California. Implementation of SSB taxes globally rose considerably following the endorsement of this policy by the Word Health Organization in 2016, though the policy remains controversial given its regressive nature and growing concerns over mobilizing stigma as a public health tool. The purpose of my research project is to examine the acceptability of a SSB tax among adults living in a middle-class neighbourhood in Winnipeg. I will analyze 18 interviews conducted in 2019. This middle-class neighbourhood was selected to represent a food secure, and primarily white neighbourhood. Participants were interviewed using a semi-structured interview guide; interviews were transcribed verbatim and will be analyzed thematically using NVivo software. I am particularly interested in exploring moralism associated with the consumption of SSBs, especially among people of higher weight, parents (especially mothers), and racialized and Indigenous populations. The results of my project will contribute to ongoing policy discussions in Canada as to the acceptability of this policy. I will translate the knowledge generated through academic conferences, publication, and infographics to be shared with participants and the neighbourhood interviewed."

column36: Characterizing Treponema pallidum-host interactions
column37: "Treponema pallidum is the causative agent of syphilis, a chronic multistage infection that is transmitted by sexual contact. Rates of infection have been growing on a global scale for over a decade, which demonstrates the need for research into the molecular mechanisms behind the infection. T. pallidum is able to persist within a host indefinitely in the absence of treatment and is able to spread through the bloodstream into every tissue within the body. Additionally, T. pallidum is able to cross the blood brain barrier and placental barrier, gaining access to the central nervous system and to the unborn fetus. Unlike many bacterial pathogens, T. pallidum lacks the ability to introduce effector proteins into host cells, which highlights the importance of host-pathogen membrane interactions. These interactions between T. pallidum and host cells remain incompletely understood, thus, further research is required. To investigate the interaction between T. pallidum and host endothelial cells, mass spectrometry will be used to quantify host proteomic alterations in endothelial cells exposed to live T. pallidum. Additionally, flow cytometry will be used to determine the amount and type of immunoregulatory proteins being released by endothelial cells during exposure to T. pallidum. These approaches will mark the first-time mass spectrometry and flow cytometry will be used to investigate host-pathogen interactions of live T. pallidum with endothelial cells on an organismal level. Insight drawn from these studies will improve understanding of host immune responses, identify target host receptors, and inform vaccine design by characterizing immune modulation by T. pallidum."

column36: Implementing supervised consumption services in acute care: a patient-oriented evaluation of a healthcare innovation
column37: "On average, 11 people die every day in Canada due to an apparent accidental opioid overdose. Evidence-informed interventions designed to prevent harm and death are urgently needed to address Canada's and Alberta's overdose epidemics. Supervised consumption services (SCS) are a key strategy to reduce overdose and other negative health impacts of substance use in Canada. They provide a welcoming environment where people who use drugs (PWUD) can consume substances under medical supervision. Research demonstrates that SCS are effective in the community, but they have not been used or studied in hospitals. This is problematic because many PWUD are not ready or unable to stop using drugs while hospitalized. Current evidence suggests that for patients who continue to use drugs hospitals are high risk environments. Formal or informal prohibitions on substance use in acute care can lead to patients using unsanctioned drugs alone or in unsafe areas, reuse and unsafe disposal of syringes, and leaving against medical advice. The Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton became the first acute care facility in North America to offer SCS to inpatients in response to increasing rates of substance-related hospitalizations, and overdose occurrences on hospital grounds. I plan to conduct in-depth interviews to collect hospital staff perspectives of this novel SCS. My goals are to understand how the service is functioning, identify barriers and facilitators to optimal service delivery, and inform quality improvement. Overall, my findings will provide essential information to allow other hospitals to develop their own SCS programs and lead to hospital policy and practice changes that improve patient care at the RAH and beyond."

column36: Effects of polysubstance use on methamphetamine-induced psychotic symptoms
column37: "Methamphetamine is a drug that has become increasingly popular in recent years among young adults in North America. It is commonly referred to as meth or speed, and causes individuals who take it to experience intense feelings of happiness and excitement. Individuals who consistently use methamphetamine commonly experience symptoms that are similar to Schizophrenia. This includes feeling, seeing, and hearing things that are not really there, as well as believing that irrelevant things are related to them, examples of this would include walking into a room and believing that everyone is staring at them, or believing that things on the radio or television are being broadcast to them specifically. These symptoms often result in increased risk of hospitalization and arrest of methamphetamine users, causing an increased financial burden to society. Individuals who use methamphetamine often also use other drugs, which may affect with these symptoms. The goal of this research will be to understand the effects that the use of other drugs has on these symptoms in methamphetamine users. This will help us begin to understand why these symptoms are present, and how to prevent them. "

column36: "Contextual factors in neurocognition: the impact of amotivation, beliefs, and mood on neurocognitive functioning in schizophrenia"
column37: "Schizophrenia affects approximately 1% of the population and is the mental health condition associated with the highest treatment costs. The vast majority of people with schizophrenia do not recover the ability to function well in everyday life. The current treatments available target the psychiatric symptoms, like hallucinations and delusions, but do not treat problems with everyday functioning. Therefore, it is important to develop treatments that effectively treat these problems. Most people with schizophrenia have problems with cognitive abilities, which refer to skills like memory, attention, and decision-making. These skills are very important for everyday functioning in social situations, work, or school. I want to find out how to improve the treatment of cognitive problems in order to improve community functioning.I will do this by testing how certain psychological factors, like a lack of motivation, having negative beliefs about oneself, or even just being in a bad mood, might have a harmful impact on cognitive abilities. In my study, I will test cognitive abilities in people with schizophrenia. Then, participants will perform a task that activates the presence of negative psychological states. The cognitive abilities will be tested again to see if the psychological factors had an effect on cognitive performance. If they do, then treatments for cognitive problems can make sure to account for these factors, thereby improving the effectiveness of the intervention. Finding ways to improve how cognitive problems are treated in schizophrenia will help the millions of people living with this illness lead more healthy, productive lives."

column36: Tryptophan metabolism by intestinal microbiota: Implications for inflammatory bowel disease.
column37: "Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic relapsing diseases characterized by severe inflammation in the digestive tract. Our gut is exposed to a vast number of bacteria and microorganisms, called microbiota, which in combination with food components, are important for maintaining health. There is growing evidence suggesting that when food-bacterial interactions are broken, conditions like IBD can develop. However, the factors underlying this breakdown are unclear. I propose to study how certain bacteria from the human gut metabolise dietary proteins, like tryptophan, to produce molecules which activate a receptor called the ""aryl hydrocarbon receptor"" (AhR). Recent studies have shown that AhR function is abnormal in patients with IBD, who also have an altered microbiota and impaired production of compounds which activate AhR (""agonists""). What is not known is which bacteria are responsible for the defective production of AhR agonists from foods, and the metabolic pathways involved. I will isolate and study bacteria involved in tryptophan metabolism from patients with IBD and from healthy controls. I will study their tryptophan metabolism in vitro and in vivo using germ-free mice colonized with selected bacteria. Finally, I will use models of colitis to study the capacity of these bacteria to activate AhR and decrease disease severity. About 1% of the Canadian population is expected to have IBD by 2030. Additionally, current therapies to induce and maintain remission are dominated by drugs that often lose effectiveness over time, suggesting the need for complementary therapies. Our long-term goal is to develop combinations of bacteria which act on dietary tryptophan to restore AhR function and prevent and treat IBD."

column36: Examining timelines and modifiable factors of hippocampal atrophy in chronic moderate-severe traumatic brain injury
column37: "Moderate-severe traumatic brain injury (m-sTBI) is known to result in long-term physical, cognitive, and emotional impairments. With converging evidence, m-sTBI is now increasingly being conceptualized as a progressive neurodegenerative process. Hippocampus (HC) atrophy is an area of particular concern because this can lead to deficiencies in learning, memory, and emotion regulation, and increase risk of dementia. We have previously demonstrated that progressive HC atrophy occurs in more than 70% of m-sTBI patients during the chronic stages of injury, and that microstructure of the fornix (a white matter tract that connects the HC to other brain areas) is also disrupted post-injury. Work from our group and others have also determined that increasing injury severity, higher levels of anxiety and depression, and reduced cognitive and/or environmental enrichment can lead to greater HC atrophy in various non-overlapping patient populations. However, it remains unknown when these structural brain atrophies begin and peak in the m-sTBI patient population. Here, using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusor tensor imaging (DTI), and various neuropsychological measures of emotion and behaviour, I aim to: (1) identify the timelines and predictors that underlie HC and fornix deterioration at 3, 6, 12, and 18 months post-injury, and (2) determine the extent to which atrophy in these areas weaken memory performance. Establishing timelines and predictors of structural damage will provide insight into therapeutic time windows, and allow better understanding of which modifiable factors should be targeted during m-sTBI treatment and/or rehabilitation."

column36: Changes in dendritic microstructure and clinical improvement with repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for major depression
column37: "Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability world-wide. Though current medication and psychotherapy treatments are effective, many patients do not improve. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a non-invasive neurostimulation treatment for such individuals. rTMS uses magnetic fields to stimulate specific regions of the cerebral cortex and by delivering specific patterns of energy, leads to changes in the cortex. This involves functional and structural changes in neurons, through a process known as 'synaptic plasticity'. <span style=white-space:pre;> I propose to use a drug called d-cycloserine (DCS) to enhance rTMS' effects on synaptic plasticity. DCS has been safely used in other psychiatric disorders to enhance synaptic plasticity-dependent treatments. In addition to the antidepressant effects of combining these strategies, I will use advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques to capture microscopic structural changes as participants receive treatment. This imaging technique is called 'neurite orientation dispersion and density' imaging, or NODDI for short. <span style=white-space:pre;> Using a randomized placebo-controlled design, participants with MDD will receive either a placebo capsule or DCS in conjunction with ten daily rTMS treatments. At the start of the trial, important clinical characteristics will be measured, and participants will have an MRI for NODDI. These will be repeated at the conclusion of the study. My study will directly test a novel strategy for improving patient outcomes in MDD, a common and debilitating illness where currently available treatments are often inadequate. Further, I will learn and apply advanced neuroscience skills to not only test the clinical efficacy of the strategy but understand its mechanism so that it can be further refined. "

column36: A Novel Method of Stromal Analysis Based on Polarized Light Microscopy is Prognostic of Breast Cancer Progression and Outcomes
column37: "Breast cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers and is the leading cause of cancer death among women worldwide. It is a highly heterogenous disease with much variation among patients in terms of disease progression and aggressiveness. Despite this known heterogeneity, personalized therapy based on prognostic markers remains difficult to implement, often leading to over- or under-treatment. The morphologic features of the tumour-associated stroma have recently been shown to contain prognostic information. In response, our group has developed a simple and inexpensive method to evaluate stromal morphology based on polarized light microscopy. By exploiting the birefringent properties of collagen (a major component of the stroma) and its interaction with polarized light, it is possible to visualize the stroma to glean prognostic information. We have also developed a ""stromal architecture signature"" (SAS), a numerical score that quantifies the patterns of stromal morphology. This research will further develop this novel methodology and will examine how the SAS is prognostic of breast cancer progression and outcomes. It will also produce a clinical workflow to facilitate uptake of this method and use of its prognostic data as a step toward making personalized therapy more readily available. An approach that is inexpensive, reliable, and easily used without specialized training will prove particularly useful in locations and settings without high-end advanced capabilities (e.g., genomic tests) due to limited resources."

column36: Characterization of novel bi-specific fusion proteins for the programming of extracellular vesicles for delivery of cytotoxic payloads to hematologic malignancies

column36: Defining the role of BRCA2-deficient mammary stromal fibroblasts in the growth and transformation of mammary epithelial cells.

column36: Adverse drug events related to polypharmacy in older adults: evaluating deprescribing opportunities in HIV patients through the MedSafer study
column37: "Polypharmacy, often defined as the concurrent use of five or more medications, is increasingly common in older adults aged 65-years and older. Physiological changes within the body at this age affect medication sensitivity and elimination and are compounded with an increase in age-related diseases. This makes older adults particularly vulnerable to adverse drug events (ADEs), which are an injury resulting from medical intervention related to a drug. While Polypharmacy may be well-intentioned for the treatment of chronic diseases, older adults may be prescribed potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs), which confer less benefit and expose them to harm. Several large clinical trials are underway to address this growing problem through deprescribing, which is the deliberate action of carefully stopping PIMs in a supervised setting. We aim to expand this research to the HIV population, where older adults are defined as 50 years or older. Due to the success of antiretroviral therapy, the lifespan of people living with HIV is increasing, posing new challenges for physicians as they are more likely to have multiple complicated illnesses and polypharmacy at a younger age. In this case, polypharmacy is defined as the concurrent use of 5 or more non-antiretroviral medications. We aim to quantify the need of a deprescribing intervention in this complex aging population. Patient data will be inputted into the novel Canadian deprescribing software, MedSafer, which will flag PIMs and allow us to describe the prevalence and most common PIMs seen. This research is the initial step to inform the need for a deprescribing intervention in the outpatient HIV clinic, and to prevent future ADEs and life-threatening complications."

column36: Efficacy Trials and Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: "Children and youth with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are far more likely than children without ASD to experience mental health problems, including anxiety, depression and conduct issues (Arim et al., 2015; Strang et al., 2016), and families often seek treatment for these emotional and behavioural problems. Conducting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is an integral component in ensuring interventions are effective for these youth with mental health problems. There is promising evidence for cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), which has been found efficacious in treating affective problems in this clinical population (Weston et al., 2016). However, 20-37% of families involved in clinical research trials are excluded prior to participation as a result of exclusion criteria that often includes aspects of intellectual functioning (Storch et al., 2013; Storch et al., 2015; White et al., 2015). The literature is relatively sparse on identifying factors that may lead to treatment exclusion and lack of service in clinical trials. It is essential to understand why some families are excluded from clinical research, as this may lead to limited generalizability and methodological issues. The Andersen Behavioral Model of Health Services Use (Andersen, 1968), a model widely used to measure access in health care, suggests predisposing (e.g., age, education, ethnicity), enabling (e.g., income, insurance) and needs (e.g., perceived health, clinical symptoms) factors drive access to services. A better understanding of the predisposing, enabling and needs factors that contribute to the exclusion of children with ASD in efficacy trials could help identify barriers in mental health research, improve research methodology in CBT trials and help facilitate health equity."

column36: From hospital to home: Examining health care providers? experiences of transitioning patients and caregivers across palliative care settings
column37: "Palliative care is defined as an interdisciplinary approach to care that addresses the physical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs of patients and families living with life-limiting illness. Given the unpredictable burden of these illnesses, it is not uncommon for individuals who receive palliative care to transition across a variety of health care settings. Done poorly, these transitions can result in a myriad of negative consequences. The transition from hospital to home is particularly pertinent, as evidence suggests that 75% of Canadians express preference to receive care and die in the home setting. To date, resources to facilitate a successful transition between palliative care settings have been largely understudied. As the Canadian population continues to age, the demand for palliative care services is expected to increase. This warrants further inquiry on how to best support transitions across multiple care settings. Given the influential role undertaken by health care providers during transitions of care, it is necessary to understand their experiences to improve this process for all stakeholders. The purpose of this study is to explore health care providers' experiences of patient and caregiver transitions from hospital to home, where palliative care is received in both settings. A descriptive qualitative study will be conducted with providers affiliated with Sinai Health System, Toronto General Hospital, and the Temmy Latner Centre for Palliative Care, as these services provide in-patient palliative care and home-based palliative care for families across the Greater Toronto Area. The outcomes of this study will provide valuable information regarding ways in which we might streamline discharge processes. "

column36: The Synergistic Effects of Co-Treatment with Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 and -2 Receptor Agonists on Glucose Metabolism and Intestinal Growth/Function.
column37: "The gastrointestinal tract secretes substances that regulate metabolic homeostasis. Specifically, the L cells, located within the distal portion of the small intestine and the colon, secrete Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) and -2 (GLP-2) in response to food intake. Exenatide (Ex-4) is a mimic of GLP-1, and is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity due to its positive effects on glucose metabolism and food intake. Conversely, teduglutide is a GLP-2 mimic that is used to treat patients with short bowel syndrome (SBS), who are missing parts of their small and/or large intestines, as it stimulates intestinal growth and food absorption. Interestingly, these peptides have been shown to have overlapping functions, prompting great interest in engineering a new peptide that, by combining both GLP-1 and 2's effects, can drastically improve upon the current treatment regimen for T2D/Obesity and SBS. By combining both functionalities, it is not only possible for the beneficial effects to be additive, but the potential drug may also exhibit synergism- a phenomenon in which both drugs in combination interact to produce an effect greater than what would be expected if their effects were summed individually. This project aims to investigate the potential presence/absence of synergism here by administering GLP-1 and 2 mimics to mice both alone and in combination. As synergism is dependent on doses, various dosing combinations of both peptides will be studied. By investigating the various doses at which synergy may occur in between GLP-1 and 2, this study has the potential to help inform the engineering of combined GLP1/2 mimics tailored for T2D/Obesity and SBS. "

column36: Evaluating the Effects of Olanzapine on Brain Insulin Signaling and Cognitive Outcomes
column37: "Antipsychotic (APs) medications are the cornerstone of schizophrenia treatment. Unfortunately, APs have been associated with serious metabolic adverse effects, including weight gain and type 2 diabetes. These metabolic abnormalities are also associated with poorer cognitive function, and may worsen pre-existing cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia. The mechanisms underlying AP effects on glucose metabolism dysregulation and cognition are largely unknown. Animal studies have shown that an acute dose of olanzapine, an AP with high metabolic liability, can completely abolish the well-known ability of a brain insulin stimulus to decrease hepatic glucose production in rats. This suggests that olanzapine can induce resistance to insulin action in the brain. The concept of brain insulin resistance has recently been proposed to explain the link between cognitive and metabolic disorders. Inducing brain insulin resistance may be a potential mechanism through which metabolic adverse effects and lack of improvement in cognition occur during AP treatment. As such, the objective of this study is two-fold. First, we will examine if intranasal insulin increases glutamate levels in the striatum and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, improves visuospatial task performance, and changes cerebral blood flow to the aforementioned brain regions, compared to intranasal placebo. Second, we will investigate whether olanzapine acutely inhibits intranasal insulin associated changes in brain functioning and cognitive outcomes. This work aims to shed light on the mechanisms behind metabolic adverse effects of AP drugs and their cognitive effects and has the potential to initiate new streams of work in an area of significant unmet need, potentially leading to new therapeutic strategies."

column36: Salt Supplementation in Paediatric Syncope
column37: "Syncope (fainting; transient loss of consciousness and postural tone) is common in children, affecting up to 1 in 3 youth, and has a devastating effect on their quality of life. Many of these disorders are associated with abnormal cardiovascular control, leading to cerebral hypoperfusion, secondary to hypotension and abnormalities in the normal control of heart rate. The burden of syncope on healthcare resources is substantial. Affected children are at an increased risk of fall-related injury and have difficulty attending school, exercising, and participating in daily activities, with frequent hospital visits and an adverse psychological impact. In particular, the optimal management of this syncope in children is unclear. In adults with syncope, salt supplementation is recommended with the rationale that it will improve cardiovascular control, increase plasma volume, and bolster against hypotension. We will perform a randomised placebo-controlled double-blind study considering the effect of salt supplementation alongside usual care on syncope susceptibility and symptoms in pediatric patients. We hypothesize that salt supplementation will improve blood pressure control and minimize symptoms compared to placebo, without significantly increasing blood pressure. Our clinical trial will better inform the current recommendations for the management of pediatric syncope. Rigorous evaluation of the efficacy and safety of salt supplementation in paediatric syncope will enable evidenced-based management of this devastating condition, improving quality of life for affected children and their families, and reducing the burden of this disorder on the Canadian healthcare system."

column36: Investigating the effects on cardiovascular risk factors of the ketogenic diet vs. a moderate carbohydrate diet in type 1 diabetes
column37: "The ketogenic diet (KD) is a very-low carbohydrate (CHO) (50 g/day), high-fat (75% of energy) diet that has gained popular interest in the diabetes community, however its long-term efficacy is unknown. Of particular concern is its safety in type 1 diabetes (T1D) and its effect on cardiovascular (CV) risk factors. Our study aims to establish the short-term effect on CV risk factors of the KD on T1D through a four-phased (18 weeks total) cross-over study which will compare a moderate-CHO diet (50% CHO, 15% protein, 35% lipids) and the KD (10% CHO, 15% protein, 75% lipids). 30 adults with T1D (2 years diagnosis) on insulin therapy will be recruited. In Phase 1, insulin doses will be optimized prior to randomizing participants to one of the two 6-week dietary interventions (Phase 2). Personalized 2-week menus will be developed by a dietitian to increase dietary compliance, who will review daily food journals and pictures taken of their meals bi-weekly to assess adherence. Participants will be followed up bi-weekly by email or phone to monitor for possible hypoglycemia, side effects of the KD, or insulin adjustments. In Phase 3, participants will resume their regular diets for 4 weeks to achieve a ""wash-out"" effect, before switching to the other 6-week diet (Phase 4). At baseline and at the end of each phase, blood cholesterol, general diabetes management (hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C)), blood pressure and waist circumference will be measured and compared using statistical analyses. We propose that when optimizing the lipid profile of the KD, it will reduce HbA1C and waist circumference, and increase HDL-cholesterol, however it will aggravate certain CV risk factors such as total- and LDL-cholesterol, triglycerides, and blood pressure, more than the moderate-CHO diet."

column36: Dynamic CT to determine normal syndesmosis motion and to compare motion after static and dynamic fixation of syndesmotic injuries
column37: "The syndesmosis is a group of ligaments spanning the ankle joint. Injuries to the syndesmosis are a common orthopaedic problem, especially after an ankle fracture. If not anatomically reconstructed after injury, patients have worse functional outcomes leading to pain, stiffness, instability, and ankle arthritis. These problems can severely reduce quality of life and lead to mental and physical disability comparable to end-stage hip arthritis. A syndesmosis injury can be fixed with rigid screws or a flexible method using an internal button and suture, but non-anatomic reconstruction and functional impairment is common with both methods.As the syndesmosis is a dynamic structure, conventional imaging does not provide a complete picture of syndesmosis motion, but rather a snapshot of the syndesmosis in a single, patient-selected ankle position. Reconstructions may be non-anatomic if we do not consider this motion during surgery. Dynamic CT is a technology that can create moving 3-D images that show changes in syndesmosis position as the ankle moves. This study will use dynamic CT to show how the syndesmosis moves in normal ankles as well as after surgery.First, 20 healthy volunteers will have dynamic CT scans of both ankles. Then 40 patients who have had surgery for a syndesmosis injury with either rigid or flexible fixation will have dynamic CTs. We will be able to determine how the syndesmosis normally moves throughout ankle range-of-motion and compare this to motion after rigid and flexible fixation. We predict that flexible fixation of syndesmosis injuries creates more normal syndesmosis motion and better patient outcomes. Understanding syndesmosis motion can help improve reconstruction techniques and recovery after injury."
