column36: The mechanistic logic underlying bipolar cell subtype specification
column37: "Cell fate determination in the central nervous system (CNS) is a highly regulated process in which dividing multipotent progenitor cells differentiate to give rise to post-mitotic neurons. While much is known about how general different cell classes are formed, little is known about development of specific neuronal subtypes that comprise distinct neuronal classes. The extent of the effect of intrinsic and extrinsic factors on cell fate determination is still debated. The retina is an ideal system to investigate neuronal differentiation in the CNS. It is a relatively simple and experimentally accessible tissue comprised of 6 different cell types, all of which originate from retinal progenitor cells and have different but overlapping birth times. Bipolar cells are postnatally-born interneurons that convey information from photoreceptors to retinal ganglion cells. So far, there are 15 different subtypes of bipolar cells but not much is known about how they develop. In my project, I will use various transgenic mice lines, immunostaining and retinal dissociation experiments to visualize the expression of mature bipolar cell markers at different developmental stages and discover how retinal progenitor cells become fully specified bipolar cell subtypes. The implications of neural development on human health issues are important. Defects during development can result in various neurological disorders with highly detrimental effects for those who suffer them. Understanding the mechanisms underlying cell type differentiation is necessary for the rationale design of future treatments and prevention of such disorders. "

column36: Examining the long-term effects of intestinal helminth infection on susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis
column37: "Intestinal helminths are parasitic worms that infect close to 2 billion people worldwide, predominantly in developing countries. Helminths are able to infect people for very long periods of time, in part, through their potent ability to dampen the host immune response. This 'cold-shower' effect on the immune system is problematic for two major reasons. First, long-term infection can result in chronic illness such as anemia. Second, helminths greatly impact how one is able to deal with other, more lethal microbes. A prime example would be Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis. This bacterium is a major problem in regions of the world afflicted by helminths, and co-infection with both Mtb and helminths is very common. As such, it is of great importance to understand how these immunosuppressive parasites could be shaping host immunity to Mtb. Although helminths can be cleared with anthelmintic drugs, it remains unclear whether infection has long-lasting effects, even after the parasites are cleared. Furthermore, infection often occurs in young children, a period in which the developing immune system can still be influenced by environmental factors. Thus, it is highly likely that early life exposure to helminths has a durable impact on subsequent challenges to the immune system. Our proposed research aims to investigate the long-term effects that helminth infection has on host immunity, with a specific emphasis on co-infection with Mtb. Furthermore, we plan to investigate how early life helminth infection, in particular, could impart such long-term changes to the host immune system. The results from this research will inform strategies to mitigate the negative sequelae associated with infection by these pervasive parasites. "

column36: Investigating Ubiquitin Dynamics and its Involvement in Chromosome Instability and Colorectal Cancer
column37: "In Canada, colorectal cancer is the second most common cancer diagnosis and one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths. To develop new therapies to improve patient outcomes a deeper understanding of the events driving colorectal cancer development and progression is crucial. In this regard, preliminary data from the McManus laboratory have recently identified a set of cellular processes (ubiquitination and deubiquitination) that when altered, are suspected to drive cancer development and progression. Conceptually, these cellular processes serve to add and remove specific marks (ubiquitin) onto or from proteins, respectively, to impact their location and function. My project will use genetic, biochemical and microscopy-based approaches to investigate ~700 genes regulating these marks to identify those that when mutated, may drive the development and progression of colorectal cancer. Using relevant cellular models, I will turn each gene off and determine the downstream impact on chromosome numbers (structural bodies of DNA within cells), as abnormal chromosome numbers (chromosome instability) is a driver of many cancer types. These models will be used to determine whether loss of these proteins enables normal human cells to acquire key characteristics associated with cancer development. The results of this study will generate new insight into the abnormal molecular origins (i.e. mutated genes) driving colorectal cancer development and progression. In addition, these findings will reveal new therapeutic targets that can ultimately be exploited to develop the next generation of therapies aimed at improving the lives and outcomes of those living with colorectal cancer, or perhaps many additional cancer types."

column36: Investigating the Effectiveness of MDMA-Assisted Psychotherapy for the Treatment of Race-Based PTSD for Black Canadians
column37: "This study will investigate the effectiveness of MDMA used in conjunction with psychotherapy for Black Canadians living with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) caused by racism and discrimination. Recent research has found promising results for treatments that combine MDMA and psychotherapy to treat PTSD. MDMA is believed to help reduce symptoms of PTSD by reducing fear of traumatic memories while increasing feelings of trust and enabling emotional engagement. Ethnic and racial minorities, however, have historically been underrepresented in psychedelic research, such that the effectiveness of MDMA as a treatment might not generalize to or be safe for a racially diverse population. The current study will prioritize ethnic and racial minority inclusion throughout all stages of the experimental design and implementation. A sample of 40 Black participants, ages 19-65, will be recruited, and participants will be randomly assigned to psychotherapy either with MDMA or with a placebo. This study will use culturally-informed therapy settings and match therapists to participants based on race and ethnicity to ensure participant comfort. Cultural-competency training will be provided for all therapists to promote more accurate, contextually-based assessments and minimize harm to participants. Severity of racial trauma will be assessed using three tests designed to identify trauma due to experiences of racism and discrimination. This research is necessary to understand the effects of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for race-based PTSD. In seeking to understand these effects, this study directly addresses the broader issue of mental health disparities."

column36: Identifying neuronal subpopulations participating in fear memory
column37: "Following a traumatic event, many individuals will experience adverse psychological symptoms which diminish over time. For some, however, these symptoms will persist, resulting in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). This anxiety disorder imposes a significant burden on individuals and society. As such, it is important to better understand the neural mechanisms underlying PTSD so that effective mitigation strategies can be developed. Recent research has shown that classically known neurons of many brain regions - like those involved in fear memory - can be divided into distinct subtypes based on the genes they express. This difference in gene expression often translates to differences in function and connectivity. My project seeks to identify the unique subtypes of neurons participating in the creation and retrieval of fear memories. Using a new, cutting-edge histology technique, I will fluorescently tag important ""marker genes"" - genes uniquely expressed in a certain subtype. This will resolve the spatial organization of subtypes in fear memory associated brain regions. Then, I will perform fear conditioning on transgenic mice that can fluorescently tag neurons active during memory formation (in red), and memory retrieval (in green). By looking at this fluorescent tagging in conjunction with the marker gene ""map"", I can infer the subtype-specific participation in the stages of fear memory. The data will establish which subtypes of neurons are key in the formation and retrieval of fear memory. This not only investigates a basic question of neuroscience, but will also elucidate cellular and molecular targets that may interfere with fear memory - providing a vital framework for future work developing therapeutic interventions for PTSD. "

column36: Determining astrocyte-mediated defects to glutamatergic signalling and metabolism in Fragile X Syndrome
column37: "Introduction. Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), the leading heritable form of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by silencing of the fmr1 gene leading to the inhibition of fmr1 transcription, and the absence of the Fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP). Astrocytes play a major role in synaptic development, regulating glutamate release and clearance, as well as providing antioxidants to counteract increases to reactive oxygen species (ROS) from the increased neuronal metabolic demand in FXS. We hypothesize that dysregulated glutamate signalling by astrocytes in FXS leads to increased metabolic demand, greater mitochondrial respiration, and oxidative stress within the FXS cortex. Thus, correction of metabolic dysfunction may be a feasible therapeutic target. Methodology. We will determine mitochondrial function of astrocytes isolated from P1 wild-type (WT) and Fmr1 knockout (KO) mice via mitochondrial respirometry during oxidative respiration. Additionally, the production of ROS in WT and FXS astrocytes will be assayed in real time. We will also use time-lapse imaging of astrocytes loaded with ROS indicator dyes to determine whole cell genotypic differences in cellular ROS management. Finally, we will use Western blotting to compare expression and enzyme activity of the antioxidant system present in WT and KO astrocytes.Originality and Overall Impact. Preliminary work in our lab suggests that oxidative stress may play a role in the cognitive deficits associated with FXS. Detection of the source of stress and possible deficits in the anti-oxidant system will further both the understanding of the cellular dysfunction in FXS and the work to guide the development of targeted pharmacological treatments to children afflicted with FXS."

column36: Investigating the melodic pitch memory of children with autism spectrum disorder.
column37: "In this study, we investigate whether the musical strength in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly melodic and pitch memory, can be explained by absolute pitch ability. We also investigate the potential overlap between pitch memory strength and visuo-spatial skills in ASD. Perception in ASD is often conceptualized as an impairment in integration of global and local processing. However, recent findings build evidence towards an understanding of ASD as an altered cognitive style with particular strengths, an example being children with ASD demonstrating exceptional long-term musical memory. However, the nature of such strength is yet to be defined. The first step to answer this question is to assess whether the quality of long-term pitch memory differs between children with typical development and children with ASD. Then, by assessing visuo-spatial skills, a correlate of musical strength, we can also investigate a potential overlap between the two in ASD. This will lead to an understanding of the neurological underpinning of the musical memory and visuo-spatial skills. The study includes a group of 30 children with ASD and a comparison group of 30 typically developing children ranging from 7 to 13 years old. Participants will complete two music tasks, a week apart, measuring pitch and melodic memory. Intelligence, music experience, autism symptomology and social communication skills will also be measured. Analysis will compare the two groups' performance. There is an imminent need to understand cognitive strength in ASD to build upon past research with heavy emphasis on deficits. Findings hold the potential of revealing that a strength-based intervention with music could be a strong leverage with educational and clinical implications. "

column36: Understanding KRAS Imbalance as a Mediator of Pancreatic Tumour Aggression and Metastasis
column37: "Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (pancreatic cancer) is predicted to become the second leading cause of cancer related deaths within the next several years. Patients often present with highly malignant disease with limited treatment options. This highlights the need to understand the molecular mechanisms driving disease progression to better understand how to treat these patients. One particular gene imbalance that is highly prevalent in pancreatic cancer is in KRAS, a GTPase that is mutated in more than 90% of pancreatic cancer cases. When genome instability occurs, it creates an imbalance that increases the mutant:wildtype ratio of this gene. Recent work from our laboratory has shown that pancreatic cancer with a copy number imbalance in mutant KRAS are more aggressive and chemoresistant compared to cases where KRAS is balanced (equal number of mutated and wild type). I hypothesize that KRAS imbalances lead to upregulation of genes that mediate a survival/growth and contribute to therapy resistance. This project seeks to identify genes and pathways that are affected by mutant KRAS imbalance, to uncover molecular vulnerabilities that can eventually be targeted or combined with current chemotherapy. To do this I will generate a target genes using bulk RNA-seq from our recent paper (Chan et al., Nature Genetics, accepted) and use CRISPR to knockout these genes in a pancreatic cancer-derived 3D culture system (organoids). By understanding why these tumours are resistant to the current standards of care it is hoped that new therapeutic approaches can be discovered to improve patient prognosis. "

column36: Using planarian single cell RNA sequencing data to find regulators of PNS regeneration
column37: "Planarian flatworms have spectacular regenerative abilities; following decapitation, the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea can regenerate complete head structures in 7-10 days. Furthermore, the species maintains homeostatic turnover of all cell types throughout adulthood. For this reason, S. mediterranea provides a unique opportunity to study regenerative biology and stem cell differentiation. Interestingly, fate specification occurs early in planarian cell lineages during the stem cell stage, and recent evidence has shown that a distinct group of specialized stem cells is required for populating the central nervous system in S. mediterranea. I hypothesize that similarly, a dedicated population of stem cells is required for populating the peripheral nervous system (PNS) in this species. I will be able to examine this question using single cell RNA sequencing data, which I will use to identify patterns of expression required for peripheral neurogenesis through in silico lineage tracing of peripheral neurons. I will then be able to examine the occurrence of unique molecular signatures to predict lineage sources. Currently, only 60% of patients with damage to the PNS achieve full recovery. As injury and disease causing damage to the PNS affects an estimated 20 million people in the United States alone, there is a great need for improvements to treatment strategies to allow greater return of function. The regulatory direction of stem cells to terminally differentiated cell states is a strategy of interest for the treatment of diseases affecting the PNS. Understanding how stem cells are regulated in their progression to differentiated peripheral neurons in planarians will provide knowledge to support the pursuit of this strategy in vertebrate lineages."

column36: Investigating the impact of non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) on BCG-induced trained immunity against TB
column37: "Tuberculosis (TB) is an airborne infectious disease caused by M. tuberculosis (Mtb). Despite the world-wide application of the Bacillus-Calmette Guerin (BCG) vaccine introduced as early as 1921, TB remains one of the top infectious killers across the world. In 2018, the WHO reported approximately 10 million people were diagnosed with TB and among which there were 1.5 million deaths. BCG is the only licensed vaccine for TB and it is known to provide up to 80% protection in cases of childhood disseminated TB, but its protection efficacy is extremely variable (0-80%) in cases of adult TB. One of the current hypotheses to explain this variability is the link to geographic location and environmental exposure to non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM). NTM exposure does not cause disease in healthy individuals, but previous studies have shown that exposure to NTM (e.g. M. avium) blocks the protection of BCG in murine models of TB. column36: Can quantitative susceptibility mapping help diagnose and predict recovery of concussion in children?

Advances in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have shown promise in detecting brain changes associated with concussion. Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) can detect and quantify blood products, and is likely to be sensitive to concussion. Thus, QSM may be both diagnostic and prognostic in terms of duration and severity of concussion symptoms.This study will use the largest imaging dataset of children with concussion in the world to determine whether QSM can identify children with concussion, compared to children with injuries not involving the head. Additionally, the study will examine whether QSM can add to the ability of the 5P rule to predict PPCS. This will help promote advances in the diagnosis of concussion and the identification of high-risk children who can be provided with more aggressive psychological and medical care for optimal recovery."

column36: High Tibial Osteotomy in Knees with Medial Compartment Osteoarthritis: The Ideal Correction Angle
column37: "The knee is one of the most heavily used joints in the body, often making it prone to the rapid development of osteoarthritis. An alternative surgical procedure for young patients that is less invasive and a viable means of preserving the existing joint, is a leg realignment procedure known as the high tibial osteotomy (HTO). In this study, two groups of cadaveric knees (healthy vs. arthritic) will be loaded in a custom designed rig that simulates weight-bearing, while pressure sensitive film will be used to measure pressures in the knee joint. column36: Novel regulatory mechanisms controlling inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) expression
column37: "Nitric oxide (NO) is a gas naturally produced in the human body with many different functions. Nitric oxide is made by an enzyme called inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), and this enzyme is produced during inflammation. Nitric oxide made by iNOS is important, because it helps our bodies fight off bacteria that infect our bodies. Importantly, dysregulation of iNOS and the resultant production of NO is involved in many different inflammatory and immune-related diseases. Studying how iNOS is regulated is therefore crucial, given the important role of iNOS and NO in different diseases. The overarching goal of my project is to identify new mechanisms by which iNOS expression is regulated. My laboratory has shown previously that the levels of iNOS are amplified in human cells, dependent on NO, that prevents iNOS from being degraded. Therefore, I hypothesize that NO must chemically modify iNOS in a way that allows it to avoid degradation. To pursue this hypothesis, I will collect iNOS protein when it is produced normally as well as when its ability to produce NO has been inhibited. I can then study iNOS using a technique called mass-spectrometry, which will identify any possible chemical modifications on iNOS before and after the production of NO has been prevented. I will then study these modifications in human cells to observe their effects on human iNOS expression. Thus, the studies performed here will further our understanding of iNOS in human cell biology and contribute to our knowledge of iNOS in different diseases."

column36: Impact of a tachycardia-associated mutation in the sinoatrial pacemaker channel on its regulation by cyclic AMP
column37: "Our heart rate is controlled by a group of cells in the heart, which contains a protein that makes up the pacemaker channel. When pacemaker channel opens, positive ions flow into the cell, resulting in electrical impulses that enable the heart to beat. During exercise, heart rate increases because adrenaline in the body produces a special molecule, called cAMP, that binds to the pacemaker protein Abnormalities in the pacemaker protein can affect the binding of cAMP molecule, and therefore impact heart rate. My research proposal focuses on the first discovered mutation in pacemaker protein (R524Q) that results in an increase of heart rate, a clinical syndrome called Inappropriate Sinus Tachycardia (IST). The reason for the faster heart rate is because the mutated form of protein needs a smaller amount of cAMP molecules to bind, in order for the channel to open. My research will seek to understand the underlying mechanism, whether this is due to alteration in the way cAMP binds to the protein, or changes in the downstream processes that lead to channel opening and closing. Our results will further knowledge of the role of specific regions of the protein in regulating cAMP binding and in activating the protein, and the mechanism that leads to opening of ion channels in response to cAMP binding. column36: Systematic evaluation and optimization of immune-targeting modalities for glioblastoma
column37: "Glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the most common brain tumors in adults. column36: Investigating the effects of arrhythmia-associated calmodulin mutants on the structure and function of the voltage-gated sodium channel.
column37: "Calcium sensing plays a critical role in regulating physiological processes that are vital to the maintenance of life. A key player in this phenomenon is calmodulin (CaM) which confers hundreds of proteins the ability to detect changes in calcium. One such protein is the voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV1.5) which allows for the passage of sodium ions into the cell, an essential process for heart muscle contraction. Changes in concentration of calcium inside the cell alters the conformation of CaM allowing CaM to bind to NaV1.5 and exert its downstream effects. Dysregulation of NaV1.5 has previously been shown to lead to many life-threatening arrhythmias including Long-QT syndrome (LQT), a disorder that causes deadly, chaotic heartbeats. Past studies have looked at the structural and functional consequences of arrhythmia-associated channel proteins bound to CaM mutants. This however, remains unexplored for NaV1.5. Using a structural biology approach, this project aims to characterize known LQT-associated CaM mutants and its impact on NaV1.5 function. Using X-ray crystallography and various functional assays, we hope to identify mutant CaM-induced alterations in NaV1.5 structure and quantify the associated physiological changes with relevance to the pathogenesis of LQT. As only a fraction of mutations give rise to disease, genetic information alone is insufficient to determine whether a mutation is harmful. It is only when we characterize mutant protein structure and study the accompanying changes in function that causality can be proven. Elucidating the structural changes of mutant CaM-bound NaV1.5 and its functional consequences will provide novel insight on the underlying mechanisms of LQT and new strategies to interfere with the onset and progression of LQT."

column36: Methodological concerns of stepped wedge randomized controlled trials with unequal cluster sizes
column37: "In an effort to bridge the gap between experimental findings and practice, a special type of cluster randomized trial (CRT), the stepped-wedge trial, has gained increasing popularity over the recent years. Such trial is characterized by the sequential enrolment of clusters in intervention, where all clusters start with the control or standard treatment and at regular steps in time, clusters are randomly selected to cross over to intervention, until all clusters are enrolled in intervention. As such, stepped-wedge trials not only facilitate the implementation of practices but also offer a rigorous evaluation of their effects in the real-world. However, the design and analysis of stepped-wedge trials are complicated by additional considerations such as the confounding effect of time and the implications of cluster sizes imbalance when some clusters enroll more patients than others. While few studies have explored the consequences of cluster size variation in the context of stepped-wedge trials, several studies have compared different analysis methods for parallel-arm CRTs with small sample sizes. However, it is unknown whether the same conclusions apply to stepped-wedge trials, since they yield fundamentally different types of information on the intervention effect than conventional CRTs. This project seeks to compare the performance in terms of Type I error, power and bias of various analysis methods for data arising from stepped-wedge trials with few clusters, unequal cluster sizes and a continuous outcome, using analytical approaches and computer simulations."

column36: Identifying and characterizing novel antifungal compounds to combat azole resistance in the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans
column37: "Candida albicans is the leading cause of invasive fungal disease in humans, which are associated with global mortality rates comparable to those of tuberculosis and HIV. Effective treatment of these deadly infections is threatened by the unprecedented emergence of antifungal drug resistance, given the limited number of antifungal drug classes available. As such, there is an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. In addition to discovering new drug targets, a promising approach to overcome antifungal resistance is developing combination therapies which can improve the efficacy of widely used clinical antifungals such as the azoles. Our lab recently identified six novel chemical agents with potent effects against drug-sensitive C. albicans. The goal of my research is to characterize the activity and therapeutic potential of these compounds against azole-resistant C. albicans, as single agents and in combination with known antifungals. I will perform experiments to evaluate growth inhibition and cidality, as well as to define human cell toxicity and fungal selectivity. Moreover, I will employ global chemical-genetic profiling to elucidate the target genes and mechanism of action of these compounds. I will additionally conduct selection experiments and biochemical analyses to further uncover how target inhibition by these compounds influences the evolution of antifungal drug resistance. My project will contribute to increasing the antifungal repertoire and provide insights to enable new treatment strategies against drug- resistant, life-threatening fungal infections."

column36: Functional near-infrared spectroscopic measures of coherence as a new bio-marker of injury in mild traumatic brain injury patients
column37: "Pediatric mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), including concussion, is a public health burden. By the age of 25, over 30% of Canadians are likely to have had a brain injury. Concussion is characterized by a myriad of cognitive and emotional symptoms following a sudden and external force applied directly or indirectly to the head. There is a need for objective imaging metrics to understand the injury and guide clinical care guidelines, especially in adolescent populations wherein mTBI prevalence is high. One candidate imaging tool is functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), which measures changes in brain hemoglobin oxygenation related to activity. Regions that display similar oscillations in hemoglobin oxygenation are characterized as functionally connected. The current study aims to determine if brain functional connectivity can be used as a biomarker for concussion in an adolescent population and to understand post-injury functional changes in the brain over time. The main study hypothesis is that abnormalities in regional brain connectivity, detected using fNIRS, will be predictive of injury severity. Adolescents will be imaged at an acute time point, one month, and three months post-injury. This will enable an analysis of changes up to 3 months after concussion. Three adolescent populations, a control, an orthopedic control to normalize for pain, and a concussion population will be recruited. Changes in functional connectivity over time will be measured to determine if low post-injury coherence is predictive of poor injury outcome and whether connectivity tracks symptom severity. Thus, this study is seeking to provide a quantitative basis for ""return to play"" decision making and treatment evaluation in sports facilities and clinics."

column36: A comparison of supercharged end-to-side and end-to-end nerve transfer in a mouse model of brachial plexus injury
column37: "Peripheral nerve injury is a challenging clinical problem that has a considerable impact on an individual's quality of life and function. Functional outcomes following peripheral nerve injury remain poor despite the use of direct repair, nerve transplant and tendon transfer. Nerve transfer has emerged as a promising technique to support motor and sensory reinnervation. Surgically, nerve transfer involves taking nerves with less critical roles and transferring the proximal cut end to the distal end of an injured nerve. The purpose of this study is twofold. One will be to create a nerve transfer mouse model of brachial plexus injury. The rationale for a mouse forelimb model is based on several advantages over the standard rat hindlimb model. This model is biomechanically more similar to the human upper extremity, where nerve transfers are most often clinically performed. Furthermore, the use of mice enables genetic manipulation for the elucidation of cellular mechanisms of nerve regeneration following nerve transfer. Second will be to compare supercharged end-to-side and end-to-end nerve transfer coaptation techniques. Our surgical model will utilize a median nerve transection where the musculocutaneous nerve is transferred to the distal stump of the median nerve. For 12 weeks following nerve transfer, a grip strength test will be used to assess the functional recovery of the median innervated digit flexor muscles. At the end of this period, retrograde labelling and tissue histomorphometry will be used to quantify reinnervation between the two coaptation methods. We hypothesize that end-to-end nerve transfer will result in superior functional outcomes compared to the supercharged end-to-side, validating this new model of nerve transfer."

column36: The role of sound in multiline slot machine play: does negative sound reduce persistence of play?
column37: "While slot machines are one of the most lucrative forms of gambling, they are also among the most addictive forms of gambling. In multiline slot machines, there is an outcome coined ""losses disguised as wins"", where a player wins back less than their wager. LDWs are paired with dancing animations and positive sounds, cueing to the player they've won when in reality they have lost. Research has shown that LDWs are an addictive feature of these machines, and they have been implicated in continued slot machine play. In this study, we will investigate how the positive sound paired with LDWs changes participant's reactions to LDWs and how the sound impacts how much they want to continue playing the game following study completion. We will be manipulating the sound that is paired with LDWs to be either positive - as they are in commercially available machines - or negative. Participants will play 300 spins on a slot machine in either the positive or negative sound condition. We will be measuring four key variables: how hard participants press the spin button following various outcomes, how long they wait in between outcome presentation and initiating a next spin, and their win estimations. Importantly, we will also measure how many spins participants play voluntarily in each condition after being told they can either continue playing on the machine or leave the study. This will tell us whether sound can impact how long people voluntarily play on slot machines, which is a key indicator of problem gambling. If we can show that sound impacts how long players persist playing on a machine, this research can be used to inform policy decisions to make gambling safer, and less addictive, for everyone."

column36: The impact of personality and brain structure on response to cognitive training in mild cognitive impairment
column37: "Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is the stage preceding dementia, in which older adults may experience cognitive impairments without meeting the full criteria for dementia. Cognitive training may be valuable for these patients. Although response to cognitive training is variable in MCI patients, factors such as brain structure and personality traits may play a role in predicting which patients will respond best to training. The goal of this study is to determine if considering individual differences in personality in addition to brain structure improves the prediction of how well MCI patients will respond to cognitive training. Participants for this study will be patients diagnosed with MCI. Participants will complete a memory test at baseline as well as a brain scan and a personality questionnaire. Half of the participants will complete six weekly cognitive training sessions which will include sessions on psychoeducation, strategies for promoting memory encoding and retrieval, mindfulness training, and tips on how to transfer these strategies into daily life. The remaining participants will not complete cognitive training. Six months after the end of the cognitive training, all participants will complete a memory test again to see if there has been improvement and determine which factors best predicted improvement. Results from this study will contribute to our understanding of what makes some MCI patients more responsive to cognitive training than others. The identification of personality traits which may predict how well MCI patients respond to cognitive interventions may lead to the development of programs targeting the reduction of negative personality traits in patients who would otherwise be less amenable to treatment."

column36: Identifying and defining the molecular characteristics human immunodeficiency virus related diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
column37: "HIV-related diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (hrDLBCL) is one of the most common cancers affecting HIV-infected individuals. DLBCL is an aggressive B-cell lymphoma. This help better understand hrDLBCL and can also serve as knowledge for new potentially druggable targets. This information could also allow for potential molecular risk stratification and the development of novel therapeutic approaches for hrDLBCL patients who do not respond well to standard therapy. column36: Medications in Breastmilk
column37: "Breastfeeding has numerous important health benefits for both mother and child. Support and encouragement for mothers who wish to breastfeed is an important public health initiative. The five most common medications and results from our systematic review will help develop and validate analytical techniques and breastfeeding sampling strategies locally for future prospective studies to quantify the levels of drugs excreted in breast milk collected in Manitoba. column36: Caregivers Of Frail Older Adults With Metastatic Prostate Cancer: A Qualitative Exploration Of Their Needs
column37: "Caregiving for older adults with cancer can be challenging; in fact, it is associated with high rates of anxiety and depression. Since prostate cancer is one of the leading causes of death in Canada and largely affects older men, the burden on the caregivers is a pressing concern. This will also be the first study to explore the potential changes in caregiving needs, burdens, or benefits over time, and across different treatments. For a more holistic description of the caregivers, we will also collect data on socio-demographic characteristics (e.g. age, gender, ethnicity, comorbidity), and measures of perceived needs, burdens, and benefits via structured questionnaires. The findings will help us understand these individuals who are instrumental to the Canadian healthcare system but fail to receive the attention they deserve. It will also inform health policies and programs that will address the unmet needs, and enable both caregivers and patients to receive better care and quality of life. "

column36: Investigating the molecular structure and function of the mammalian ULK1 autophagy regulatory complex
column37: "Autophagy is a conserved cellular process imperative for the degradation and either recycling or excretion of aged macromolecules and organelles. The process begins with the formation of a double membrane bound ""bubble"" known as a phagophore, which is then utilized for the compartmentalization of cellular components destined for deconstruction. The final portion of the process involves the merging of the ""cargo-laden"" auto-phagosome with a lysosome which then allows the lysosomes low pH microenvironment and catalytic enzymes to degrade the cargo into its basic biological building blocks. The key regulator of this pathway is a large complex of multiple autophagy related proteins (ATG) whose post-translational modifications throttle the relative level of autophagy biogenesis. The relative level of these modifications is dependent on cellular stress and nutritional availability. In recent years a human specific sub-unit of this regulator complex, known as ULK1, has been identified. Though it is similar to the yeast ortholog Atg1, it has various structural and functional differences that are only beginning to be elucidated. It is the purpose of this proposed project to create samples of this human ULK1 complex, via a baculovirus-insect cell expression system, in order to generate a working structural model through the use of single particle cryo-electron microscopy imaging. I will then incur various mutations to the different protein sub-units within this complex to determine the biochemical significance of each subunit's interactions with one another. Collectively, this proposed study will improve our understanding of the mechanism-of-action of the ULK1 complex and the molecular mechanism of autophagy initiation. "

column36: The Last Call; Are physicians caring for end-of-life patients at home?
column37: "Patients nearing the end-of-life have increasing health complications and immobility issues making a visit to the clinic unmanageable. Without proper support in the community, patients may be forced to use acute care, incurring high resource expenditures. Palliative care and house calls are associated with known benefits including improved patient health outcomes, higher self-reported quality of life, and lower acute care costs. However, concerns remain that demands for house calls are not being met. Understanding characteristics of physicians delivering house calls in Ontario could focus efforts that aim to improve end-of-life care. OBJECTIVES 1. Describe characteristics of physicians who provided home visits 2. Explore how physician home visit delivery is influenced by system-level enablers or barriers 3. Assess the impact of physician health outcomes on subsequent physician home visit rates METHODS I will use population-based health administrative data housed at ICES to conduct a retrospective cohort study of physicians in Ontario. This study with describe care patterns and will use multivariable regression models to explore the association between physician health characteristics and subsequent home visit delivery adjusting for select covariates. CONCLUSION Receiving physician-led care is shown to improve patients' chances of receiving care within their home could lead to reduced acute care expenditures and improved patients' quality of life. This research aims to understand both patterns and associations of physician house calls. The results will inform policy decisions and healthcare initiatives that direct the provision of care for dying Canadians."

column36: Let?s talk about it: Association between co-rumination and physiological markers of stress in university students transitioning to the workforce
column37: "When experiencing problems and stressful life events, we tend to rely on our friends for support. However, social support can lead friends to co-ruminate, which involves excessive discussion, speculation and focus on negative feelings associated with a problem. Co-rumination has been associated with mental health problems and can lead to the release of cortisol (the main player in human stress). Co-rumination is also more common in girls, though it can occur in boys. In addition, this behaviour is popular amongst young adults because they have more chances to co-ruminate on social media. For my project, 300 recent university graduates will be recruited, ages 18 to 35, who are currently experiencing the stressful life event of transitioning from university studies to the workforce. Even though we know that co-rumination can increase cortisol, it is unclear if the reverse is also possible. In other words, we are unsure if cortisol can make people co-ruminate. The first goal of my master's project will be to explore if the release of cortisol during a stressful event, such as transitioning from university to the workforce, is associated with increased co-rumination in young adults. My second goal will be to see if females are more vulnerable to co-rumination and/or increased cortisol during a stressful life event. My masters' project will hopefully allow us to better understand the negative outcomes of a stressful life event and to see if females and males have the same risk for these outcomes. "

column36: Factors supporting brain maturation and development in premature newborns
column37: "Premature babies are at risk for lifelong disability and challenges affecting their motor skills, communication, and thinking. Complications of premature birth such as brain injury can affect brain development and increase the risk for developmental disabilities. However, babies with similar risk factors may not have the same developmental trajectories, suggesting that there are protective factors we have not yet found. Identifying these factors could point to new treatments. One of these may be to modify the experience of pain in early life. Babies born premature are exposed to many painful but lifesaving procedures as part of their medical care. However, the experience of pain early in life has been linked to changes in brain development. Recently, the medications used to relieve their pain have been shown to have a negative impact on the structure and maturity of specific parts of the brain, making it challenging to understand which pain medications are best for overall brain development. Therefore, we plan to use MRI scans and artificial intelligence to develop a measure of overall brain maturity that can predict their developmental trajectory. We also hope to use this measure to identify factors, including pain management strategies, that promote overall brain maturity and development in premature babies, which could change the way we care for them in the neonatal intensive care unit. Finally, premature babies with brain injury from families of a higher socioeconomic status were found to be less likely to have lifelong disabilities. Similarly, we will study whether premature babies exposed to pain early in life who are from families of a higher socioeconomic status are less likely to have delays in their development, which could lead to changes in public policies."

column36: Improving diagnosis and linkage to care for patients infected with Hepatitis C in the prenatal population of Alberta
column37: "Hepatitis C (HCV) is a detrimental virus that can be transmitted through blood contact or from mother to infant during pregnancy. Currently in Alberta, the prenatal screening panel does not include HCV. However, with the increase in the opioid crisis in the last decade, the prevalence of HCV in women of childbearing age has increased drastically, leading the province of Alberta to consider implementing universal HCV screening in their prenatal panels. In order to do so, universal screening would have to be considered beneficial for prenatal patients and their infants. Our research focuses on determining the current prevalence and epidemiology of HCV in the prenatal population of Alberta through a universal pilot screening project. HCV antibody testing will be added to prenatal screening panels throughout Alberta for the duration of the next two years. Results from all screening tests will be available through ProvLab's Laboratory Information System online. Data will be analyzed monthly using STATA biostatistical software to determine the prevalence and cost-effectiveness compared to the current risk-based screening. If universal screening is overall more beneficial for patients, a recommendation will be made to Alberta Health to implement this strategy in prenatal panels. Moreover, we propose to generate a new referral system, where women and their infants testing positive for HCV will be directly referred to a specialized physician in their corresponding area. We aim to refer 100% of infected women and their infants to physicians for treatment. Effectiveness of direct linkage to care will be assessed by analyzing diagnostic times to patient outcomes. Overall, we expect this will increase the quality of patient care for women and infants infected with HCV in Alberta. "

column36: "Characterizing climate change related health risks facing immigrants and older adults in Edmonton, Alberta"
column37: "Climate change is a global concern and a critical health threat to Canadians. The health of all populations is and will continue to be impacted, but populations such as older adults and immigrant communities, will be disproportionately affected due to intrinsic characteristics like physiology or occupation. The health impacts of climate change will be heavily influenced by local environmental and socioeconomic contexts and adaptations taken to reduce health threats. Still, in Alberta assessments of the associated risk in these populations are scarce and less is known about the climate change impacts and resilience of older and immigrant populations. Combined with population aging, increased immigration and a lack of coordinated local adaptation measures, this represents a key gap in our knowledge that hinders adaptive strategies. This research will assess the increased risk to climate change facing older adults and immigrants, focusing on Edmonton, Alberta. Our hypothesis is that climate related environmental exposures (air pollution, extreme temperatures, and icy conditions) are related to several health outcomes, (cardiovascular, respiratory, mental health, and musculoskeletal outcomes) and that this relationship will be impacted by community-level factors such as demographics, socioeconomic status, social isolation, and health facility availability. Using statistical modeling we will investigate this relationship and generate critical local data about climate change vulnerability and resilience in older adults and immigrants that can be used to inform community level planning activities for effective adaptation measures to protect the health of Edmontonians. Additionally, this work will allow me to obtain my master's degree."

column36: Ethnicity and Cardiometabolic Risk in Adults and Children
column37: "Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) are severe public health burdens. South Asians (SA), living in or out of South Asia, display increased prevalence of these conditions in comparison to other ethnic groups, particularly white Europeans (WE). Further, although age and body mass index (BMI) are strong predictors of these conditions, SAs tend to develop them at much earlier ages and lower BMIs than WEs. Several studies have investigated this distinct relationship among SA adults, but no systematic reviews of the literature have been yet conducted to collate the evidence. Moreover, few studies have explored whether SA children living in Canada display different cardiometabolic profiles at different BMIs in comparison to children of other ethnicities. This work aims to first conduct a systematic review of published observational studies to assess ethnic differences in cardiometabolic risk among adults at different BMIs. Second, it aims to conduct a primary analysis to compare the relationship between BMI and several cardiometabolic risk factors in children of different ethnicities living in Canada. Data for this will stem from an ongoing longitudinal cohort study of 5062 healthy children. I hypothesize that SA adults and children will be at increased risk of CVD and T2D at lower BMIs in comparison to WEs. Findings from this work will help determine whether different preventative strategies and interventions for CVD and T2D are necessary for SAs, and if so, whether these should be implemented as early as childhood. They will also elucidate whether ethnic specific cut-offs for risk assessment should be established in children, similar to those that already exist for adults. Findings from this work are intended to be presented at international meetings."

column36: How much is too much? The impact of chronic/latent viral infections on aging.
column37: "There are currently over 37 million people living with HIV. These individuals experience faster aging compared to their HIV-negative peers, placing them at a higher risk of age-related diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and liver disease. Even though we have HIV treatment available to prevent death and transmission, people living with HIV still experience many burdens, which include side-effects from the harsh HIV drugs and never-ending presence of HIV in their system. They may also house other viruses that are common even among healthy people, but because of their exhausted immune system, these viruses may do more harm to people living with HIV than usual. Examples of these viruses are hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, Epstein-Barr virus, human herpesvirus, and cytomegalovirus. Not only are people living with HIV more likely to be infected with many of these, but each individual virus may also do more harm to their body more compared to healthy individuals. Many of these viruses have been known to impact aging, however, few studies have looked at how having multiple viruses at the same time might affect aging, let alone in people living with HIV. My study will aim to do this because the accelerated aging and age-related diseases experienced by people living with HIV pose a great burden on millions of people and our health care system. My research will contribute to better understanding how specific viruses and their cumulative burden may impact aging and thus benefit crucial advancements in HIV treatment, and will help us understand more about the aging field in general. "

column36: The implication of human adipocyte hypertrophy in systemic lipid metabolism and insulin resistance
column37: "Diabetes is a chronic disease affecting more than 2 million Canadians. There are two types of diabetes: type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes. Almost all patients with diabetes have type 2 diabetes. These individuals have too much sugar in their blood because insulin, the hormone responsible for lowering their sugar level, does not work properly. Some organs of the body, such as the liver, the heart and the muscles, normally contain little fat. It is known that when these organs are exposed to too much fat, insulin is less able to lower blood sugar. The fat beneath the skin, such as the abdominal fat, is made up of millions of small cells filled with fat. The more fat these cells have, the bigger they become. We now believe that when these cells become bigger, more fat can spill over into the blood and travel to other organs. When these organs are exposed to too much fat, insulin would no longer work properly. However, there is no scientific research able to address these questions. Therefore, in my project, I look at the size of cells in the abdominal fat. With sophisticated scans of the body, I am also able to see how organs like the liver and the heart manage fat found in the blood. The results of my project would enable a better understanding of type 2 diabetes and help to prevent this disease. "

column36: Investigating Myeloid Colony-Stimulating Factors (GM-CSF and M-CSF) as Regulators of Opposing States of Macrophage Polarization
column37: "Macrophages are critical immune cells that provide innate defense to help regulate antiviral and antibacterial immune responses. After infections, macrophages are able to modify their phenotype and effector functions depending on the immune mediators being released also known as cytokines. Two important cytokines that can affect macrophage development include the Macrophage Colony Stimulating Factor (M-CSF) and the Granulocyte Macrophage Colony Stimulating Factor (GM-CSF). When present alone, these cytokines can be used to differentiate two different types of macrophages. M-CSF induces a neutral/anti-inflammatory phenotype, where GM-CSF induces a pro-inflammatory phenotype. The relationship between GM-CSF and M-CSF when administered to macrophages simultaneously has not been well studied. My research involves investigating the interaction between GM-CSF and M-CSF during macrophage differentiation. Specifically, to functionally and phenotypically establish if competition or antagonism between the two CSFs occurs during bone marrow macrophage differentiation. We anticipate that GM-CSF will exert dominance over M-CSF in the absence or presence of viral infection. To address my hypothesis, I will differentiate bone marrow-derived macrophages by culturing them in various ratios of the CSFs based on their concentrations and then stimulate them with bacterial substances or expose them to a virus infection. Macrophage functions, cell morphology, and intracellular signalling pathways will be investigated to define the impact of antagonism that M-CSF and GM-CSF can exert on each other during macrophage differentiation. This work will elucidate the mechanisms by how these CSF can affect macrophages' immune functions during infections. "

column36: Lung small-RNA transcriptome in cancer and organ development
column37: "Lung cancer has a survival rate of less than 17%, making it the deadliest form of cancer both in Canada and across the world. Diagnosis and treatment of this disease is difficult because most patients appear with symptoms at a late stage, where the cancer has spread and is less vulnerable to therapeutics. Currently, there is a lack of markers to discover disease early, as well as a lack of treatment strategies for these advanced cancers. Normal fetal development resembles tumour growth in many ways, including increased cell growth and invasion into surrounding tissue. In normal development, the fetal genes responsible for these traits are repressed in normal adult tissues. However, in cancerous tissues these fetal genes have been seen to be re-activated during tumour formation. Since fetal genes are not expressed in normal adult cells, these oncofetal sncRNAs may represent a treatment strategy that may prevent toxicity to normal adult cells. Small non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs) are known to regulate gene expression, and have been harnessed by tumours to drive growth. We will sequence sncRNAs from fetal lung tissues, and using our established sncRNA analysis tools, we will compare these genes in fetal samples to those in lung tumours. This comparison will allow us to assess the prevalence of re-activated fetal sncRNAs in lung tumour development. Further, to understand the consequences of these re-activated sncRNAs in the tumour, we will alter the expression of these genes in lung cancer cell models. Through our analyses, we will discover re-activated fetal genes in lung cancer. These genes may represent promising new therapeutic targets with minimal toxicity to normal human cells, and deepen our understanding of sncRNAs and their role in the development of lung cancer."

column36: User experience of standardized patients with tuberculosis in urban India
column37: "In healthcare, quality matters as much as coverage. Tuberculosis (TB) is responsible for 1.6 million deaths and 3.6 million missed cases worldwide annually. Using secondary data analyses of a dataset of 2,652 simulated patient-provider interactions in two Indian cities, we propose to assess differences between user experiences, subjective impressions of provider-patient interactions, and the quality of TB-specific care delivered by providers. Over the November 2014-August 2015 period, 24 trained adult SPs enacted four ""clinical scenarios"" depicting different stages of TB-specific progression while visiting representatively sampled private providers. column36: Microdamage evaluation of healthy and metastatically involved vertebral bone post cancer treatment therapy
column37: "A metastasis occurs when cancerous cells from a primary cancer site (such as the breast or prostate) travel and attach to a secondary site (such as the spine, lung, liver or brain). Spinal metastasis occurs in up to one third of all cancer patients, which can lead to spinal fractures, pain, neurologic impairment, and reduced quality of life. Spinal stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is the standard of care for treating spinal metastases, but it commonly leads to post-treatment fractures. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a minimally invasive treatment option that uses chemicals sensitive to specific wavelengths of light to kill cancerous cells. PDT can be used in conjunction with SBRT or on its own. The impact that these cancer treatments have on the quality of bone is not well understood. To gain a better understanding of how SBRT and PDT affect bone, mechanical testing of rat vertebrae will be conducted and the microdamage will be analyzed. To accomplish this, healthy and cancerous vertebrae will be treated with either SBRT or PDT and will be loaded to create microdamage in the bone. Barium sulfate will be used to stain the vertebrae at different loading conditions and micro-computed tomography and backscatter electron imaging will be used to visualize the microdamage. The results of this research will evaluate the fracture patterns observed in the vertebrae after SBRT and PDT. The hardness of the bones will also be quantified with nanoindentation. With these results, future machine learning algorithms can be implemented to predict fracture patterns in human vertebrae affected by a spinal metastasis. column36: Investigation of Novel Therapies for Treatment of Alzheimer's Disease
column37: "Alzheimer's disease (AD) accounts for 60 to 80% of dementia cases. It involves a progressive decline in cognitive functions such as memory and cognition. As per the World Health Organization, there are approximately 24 million people with AD, and this number will only continue to rise. There is no cure for AD, and current treatments have been able to reduce the symptoms of AD, but not slow down its progression Major indicators of AD include the accumulation of amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, neuronal damage and reduction in brain size. The most accepted and studied theories for the disease are the cholinergic hypothesis, the tau hypothesis, and the amyloid-beta (Aβ) hypothesis. The Aβ hypothesis suggests that Aβ peptides aggregate to form toxic plaques which lead to neuronal cell death. Additionally, it suggests Aβ peptides promote the generation of reactive oxygen species, molecules that cause cell damage This research project plans to design, synthesize and evaluate new small molecules as amyloid aggregation inhibitors with antioxidant properties. The molecules will be designed using computational chemistry software and synthesized. They will then be tested for their ability to inhibit Aβ peptide aggregation using Aβ aggregation kinetics assays and transmission electron microscopy. Finally, cell culture studies will be conducted to determine if the molecules offer any protection to mouse hippocampal HT-22 neuronal cells exposed to toxic Aβ peptides. This project will attempt to develop drugs with dual anti-Aβ and antioxidant activity with potential to serve as new treatments for Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, this project will provide novel insights in understanding the disease mechanisms of AD by discovering new chemical tools to study it."

column36: The relationship between violence experience and genital inflammation
column37: "Despite global efforts to reduce Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) incidence, 37 million people still lived with HIV as of 2017. Female sex workers (FSWs) are particularly vulnerable. It is known that genital inflammation directly increases the risk of HIV infection, but the source of this inflammation is unclear. Other HIV susceptibility markers will also be measured in cells from the blood that become HIV targets when found in the genital tract. The impact of individual risk factors will be determined by mathematically modelling their relationship to genital inflammation. Identifying factors that place key populations at higher risk of HIV infection will help establish HIV prevention measures that can be integrated into the existing healthcare framework and address the slowing progress on the fight against HIV."

column36: The mechanisms behind the beneficial effects of Dapagliflozin in the failing heart by providing an extra source of fuel as ketones
column37: "Cardiovascular diseases (CVD), especially heart failure, are a leading cause of death in Canadians and have substantial effects on the health care system and individuals' quality of life. Sodium glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), a class of anti-diabetic drugs,, have shown cardioprotective effects in improving heart failure outcomes in both T2D and non T2D patients at high risk for cardiovascular events in clinical trials involving both the SGLT2i Empagliflozin and Dapagliflozin. However, the exact mechanisms responsible for their beneficial cardioprotective effects are not clear, and only few studies have examined this in a non T2D model of heart failure. The failing heart has a 'starved' energy profile with decreased energy production. SGLT2i have been shown to increase ketone body levels in the bloodstream: another energy fuel source, and studies have shown that the failing heart increases ketone body oxidation. Therefore, we hypothesize that ketone body oxidation may be a mediator of the beneficial cardioprotective effects of SGLT2i in the failing heart. Through providing additional fuel, the total energy production in the failing heart would increase, resulting in improved cardiac outcomes. column36: Spy1: A Potential Driving Force of the Breast Cancer Stem Cell Population in Triple Negative Breast Cancer
column37: "Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women. Despite recent improvements in diagnostics and treatment options, the tremendous heterogeneity of the disease often complicates treatment. Triple Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) occurs in 10-15% of breast cancer diagnoses and typically has poorer outcomes. This is largely due to the lack of targeted therapies and the existence of a population of cells known as breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs); a population known to be high in TNBC. BCSCs are more resistant to therapy and capable of driving patient relapse. Cell cycle mediators may play a key role in driving expansion of this population of dangerous cells. Spy1, a cyclin-like protein, promotes cell cycle progression through the G1/S, and the G2/M phase of the cell cycle and has been shown to be elevated in TNBC patients. Additionally, Spy1 is known to expand the brain tumour initiating cell population in brain cancers. Using an in vitro model of TNBC cell lines (For example, MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468), the relative abundancy of the BCSC population can be assessed to determine if increased levels of Spy1 can expand the BCSC population resulting in more aggressive, invasive and resistant cancers. In addition, an in vivo model through the use of a limiting dilution assay can be used to corroborate these results. BCSCs can be identified using markers known to label this population such as the CD44 high/CD24 low, CD133+ and ALDH isoforms which will first be characterized in order to determine the most effective marker of these cells. This work seeks to determine if Spy1 is capable of regulating the BCSC population and may allow for the development of targeted therapy to increase the survival rate of those diagnosed with TNBC."

column37: "Free the Banana! Do you eat bananas? Stop! Eat doughnuts instead. Sounds crazy doesn't it? column37: "Food insecurity, or the lack of reliable access to sufficient amounts of healthy, affordable, and culturally appropriate food, is a major problem across the globe. column36: The Role of Immature Low-Density Neutrophils in Breast Cancer Metastasis
column37: "Breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed among women. Four out of five women diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer, where the primary cancer spread to different organs, die within five year of diagnosis. In order to metastasize, cancer cells need to escape the detection of the immune system. Neutrophils, the most abundant, fastest responding immune cells, play a crucial role in cancer metastasis. Neutrophils release granules and expel nuclear DNA to form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) upon encountering infectious agents, resulting in local inflammation. Rather than killing the cancer cells, the inflammation response elicited by neutrophils facilitates cancer metastasis. Interestingly, neutrophils in cancer patients are phenotypically immature compared to healthy patients. We previously identified a subset of immature neutrophils that promote breast cancer liver metastasis. Currently, very little is known about the mechanism behind how different subsets of neutrophil affect the metastatic process. Our lab has preliminary data that reveals several differentially expressed markers on these neutrophil subsets and we will validate these markers to enable us to better differentiate these neutrophil subsets. We have previously shown that immature neutrophils preferentially undergo NETosis which is required for metastasis. We hypothesize that NETosis can cause tissue stiffening which facilitates cancer metastasis. The objective of this project is to gain insight into how these immature neutrophils are different from normal mature neutrophils and how these differences translate into metastatic functions in cancer. The result of this research will provide therapeutic opportunities to develop anti-metastatic therapy in breast cancer metastasis."

column36: Cell Vibrational Profiling Using Optical Tweezers to Improve Childhood Brain Tumour Diagnosis
column37: "Studies using atomic force microscopy (AFM) have suggested that all living cells and tissues produce unique vibrations (sounds/frequencies). While these studies have observed cellular sounds, none have employed vibrations as potential diagnostic criteria, nor have they recorded cell-specific frequencies. Moreover, to our knowledge, we are the first to suggest that cells and tissues can be grouped and differentiated by their cell line specific frequency patterns. Using optical tweezers (OT), a more sensitive AFM tool that reduces background noise to provide clearer signals of vibratory frequencies, we recently discovered distinctive spectral sequences which led to the differentiation of BT48, BT53, and U251 glioblastoma cell lines. We propose to expand these discoveries and progress our methodology by incorporating multivariate statistical analysis to mathematically characterize the vibratory frequency patterns (VFPs) of childhood brain tumour (CBT) cells. Our improved methodology will provide objective indicators to discover specific frequency patterns that reliably differentiate within CBT cell lines, or between healthy and cancerous cells. Moreover, our project's significance is rooted in its potential to capitalize on previous discoveries and establish a new method, cell vibrational profiling, to provide cell identity and reveal cell function, without extensive sample preparation, labeling, or interference. Based on our previous findings, we hypothesize that each CBT cell line exhibits unique and measurable frequency patterns reflective of basic intrinsic cellular processes. Our project will utilize astrocytoma, brainstem glioma, and medulloblastoma CBT cells (human fetal astrocytes as a healthy comparison) in vitro and record their respective VFPs using OT."

column36: N-type calcium channels as novel molecular targets for preventing opioid-induced respiratory depression
column37: "In Canada, opioid overdose is a leading cause of accidental death, with one life lost every two hours. Since 2016, there have been 12,800 deaths and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research have identified the opioid crisis as a critical health issue. Opioids are powerful pain-relievers prescribed for moderate to severe pain but they can also stop breathing, preventing oxygen from reaching the brain, which can lead to death. The brain circuits that control their breathing and their ability to respond to opioids is similar to humans. Our team has developed a way to measure the effects of opioids on breathing and pain relief in zebrafish. My research aims to use our zebrafish models to investigate how opioids stop breathing at a cellular level to find a way to exclusively block this side effect. One way that opioids may cause death is by closing calcium channels in areas of the brain that control breathing and my experimental data shows that giving zebrafish a drug that opens these channels with an opioid, blocks that effect. Using zebrafish, I plan to further investigate the role of these calcium channels to determine whether they are a good target for new opioid therapies that have no respiratory side effect, without affecting pain relief. Canada is experiencing a serious opioid epidemic, with the number of deaths rising yearly. My research aims to understand how opioids stop breathing at a cellular level to identify potential molecular targets for new opioids therapies that are safe to use, while still relieving pain."

column36: Prebiotic Adjuvants for Cancer Immunotherapy
column37: "Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), which reinvigorate the immune system to attack cancerous cells, have revolutionized treatments in oncology. While these therapeutics work phenomenally well for some individuals, the majority of patients fail to respond to these therapies. One of the causes of this lack of response lies in the gut microbiota, the complex ecosystem of microorganisms in the gastrointestinal tract. Recent investigations have shown that the gut microbiota can be modulated to improve the efficacy of PD-1 inhibitors in mice. Our research program aims to discover and identify prebiotics, which are molecules that are metabolized by the gut microbiota, that change the composition of the microbiota towards that of responders to PD-1 therapy. We hypothesize that prebiotics can favor the growth of immune-stimulating bacteria to improve the efficacy of PD-1 inhibitors in a mouse model of cancer. Plants contain molecules that are known to exert beneficial prebiotic effects in combination with PD-1 inhibitors in cancer models. However, we don't yet know which molecules are responsible for these effects. Our first objective will be to discover the identity of these molecules. In parallel, we will answer the question of ""who eats what?"" among bacteria overrepresented in PD-1 responding patients in order to better identify candidate prebiotics. We will then evaluate the efficacy of these candidate molecules in a mouse model of cancer in combination with PD-1 therapy. Currently, cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada. The combined administration of prebiotics and PD-1 inhibitors represents a novel strategy that would allow a greater proportion of patients to benefit from this revolutionary cancer therapy. "

column36: Evaluation of a Web-Based Information Decision Aid for Perinatal Anxiety
column37: "Many women develop anxiety while pregnant or in the first year after giving birth, known as perinatal anxiety. Perinatal anxiety can be harmful to the health of mom and her baby. Few people know what perinatal anxiety is, how to recognize it, or where to go for help. Many women use the Internet to learn about their health during pregnancy and feel the information they read improves their healthcare. Information in current websites for perinatal anxiety is hard to understand. They also do not include some topics that women care about, like how to treat perinatal anxiety. Web-based Information Decision Aids (IDAs) might fix these problems. IDAs give patient-oriented information that is based on research. My team made an IDA for anxiety that includes perinatal anxiety. Each woman will answer questions before, right after, and one month after using our IDA. The questions will be about their level of anxiety, what they know about perinatal anxiety, and how they feel about seeking help for it. The results may help women spot perinatal anxiety early and get help from healthcare professionals faster, lowering the risk to mom and babies' health."

column36: Targeting ganglioside dyshomeostasis post-stroke
column37: "Strokes are a leading cause of disability and death around the world. Strokes occur when a blood vessel in the brain becomes blocked, causing loss of blood flow to that area. Brain cells require constant blood supply to stay healthy so when blood supply suddenly stops during a stroke, brain cells start to die. This can cause serious disability if they survive, in fact, over 405,000 Canadians are currently living with some degree of physical or cognitive disability due to stroke This disability may be in part due to the breakdown of certain molecules, known as 'complex gangliosides' within the brain following a stroke. These complex gangliosides help form the membrane that separates the inside of a cell from everything outside. Cells still need to communicate through this membrane, and complex gangliosides are believed to help this communication happen. Complex gangliosides have a pro-survival role, that means they particularly like to help communicate everything is going well outside and that the brain cell should stay alive. However, it is believed that after a stroke these complex gangliosides are broken down into 'simple gangliosides'. These simple gangliosides have a toxic effect on brain cells and may cause brain cells to die over a larger area of the brain than just the initial stroke. Following a stroke, the breakdown of complex gangliosides means the loss of signals telling brain cells to stay alive. It also produces toxic simple gangliosides that cause brain cells to die following stroke. The purpose of this research is to look into what effect preventing that breakdown would have. We believe it will protect brain cells from death following a stroke, and that by protecting brain cells we will reduce disability that is common after stroke."

column36: Live Imaging Neutrophils in the Beating Heart: Understanding Mechanisms of Recruitment Following Cardiac Injury.
column37: "Heart disease is the leading cause of mortality globally and is commonly caused by the restriction of blood flow into the heart, leading to heart failure or death. Unfortunately, the heart has limited ability to regenerate dead tissue and so there is a need for new therapies that target early stages of the disease to mitigate or prevent the more serious, later pathologies. Neutrophil accumulation in the cardiac tissue occurs very rapidly after injury and clinical studies have shown high blood neutrophil counts are predictors of heart failure and death in heart attack patients. Several animal studies support this observation as well, suggesting that targeting neutrophils may have therapeutic potential. However, past clinical trials that blocked canonical neutrophil migration molecules have failed to inhibit migration. Neutrophil recruitment in the heart has not been directly investigated before. Furthermore, our lab has previously shown that neutrophil migration in different organs depend on different molecules for migration. We hypothesize that neutrophils utilize non-canonical molecules for the migration into injured heart tissue. We will test this by using high-powered microscopes to examine neutrophils in real-time, within the beating heart of a live mouse. This will directly identify molecules required for migration in a mouse model of pathological heart injury, which will then be inhibited to minimize long-term heart complications. The findings of this study will provide much needed context for previous clinical trials and aid development of novel therapeutic treatment that will expand our current arsenal of tools to combat heart disease."
