column36: "Emergency Department Clinicians? Beliefs, Values and Shared Practice: Uncovering Discursive Position of Suicide"
column37: "Suicide is a serious public health concern that is prominent both internationally and nationally. Stigma associated with mental health and suicide continues to exist and is a major barrier preventing patients from seeking help. The way in which suicide has been personally, socially, and institutionally constructed through particular beliefs and values continues to marginalize patients with suicidal ideation (SI). The emergency department (ED) is a critical place for suicidal intervention. However, EDs are traditionally and socially constructed to pay less attention to mental health than physical health. Extensive literature exists to describe how ED clinicians perceive ED as ill-prepared to provide appropriate mental health care; yet, there has been very little research that specifically examines suicide-related stigma and ED clinicians' beliefs, values, and current practices when providing care to suicidal patients. The primary aim of this qualitative research study is to gain a better understanding of how ED clinicians' experiences of caring for patients with SI are personally, socially and institutionally constructed. Interviews of ED clinicians in Nova Scotia will be conducted. Following data collection, I will conduct a discourse analysis (DA) of the interview transcripts guided by Foucault's philosophical lens, poststructuralism (PS). To help facilitate and contextualize DA process, I will employ thematic coding. The findings of this qualitative proposed study will help identify areas of social change in ED practice and help ED clinicians become aware of the meanings that they ascribe to suicide and patients with SI. This is an important step to understand and address the stigma in EDs and deliver equitable care to patients with SI."

column36: Abortive TCR Rearrangements Suggest ILCs are Derived from T Cell Precursors
column37: "Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) have potent immunological roles in many inflammatory diseases such as allergic asthma, inflammatory bowel disease, and psoriasis. Due to their clinical relevance, the emerging field of ILC biology and development has become the topic of intense scientific investigation. ILCs are broadly categorized into three major subsets (ILC1, 2, and 3), and together, they dictate the outcome of inflammation or tissue repair by shaping the cytokine microenvironment and priming the downstream effector cells such as tissue-resident macrophages or T cells. Although they function in an antigen-independent manner, these innate cells share similar transcription factor and effector cytokine profiles to those of CD4+ T helper cell subsets. Because they lack cell surface T cell receptors (TCR) and their progenitors have been found in adult bone marrow (BM), most ILC studies have focused on the BM niche as a ""dogmatic"" source of tissue colonizing ILCs. This presumption has arisen despite the fact that ILCs and T cells share similar developmental programming and transcription factor requirements for their regulation and effector functions. Thus, the literature has become entrenched in the view that ILCs and T cells develop along separate and distinct pathways. As a result, there has not been a thorough investigation into whether ILCs contain rearranged TCR loci, the hallmark of T cell maturation. Through sequencing and adoptive transfer experiments, my research work will investigate the status of TCR loci in ILCs and redefine their origin and trafficking during development."

column36: Pilot Emotion-Focused Intervention for Parents of Adolescents with Chronic Pain
column37: "Approximately 11 to 38 percent of youth experience chronic pain, lasting for three or more months, which can lead to psychological problems, poor quality of life, and poor family functioning. Parents of youth with chronic pain experience psychological distress and have difficulties responding to their child's pain. Previous studies have found that emotion-focused interventions for parents improved distress in youth with mental health issues, but emotion-focused interventions have not been explored in families of youth suffering from chronic pain The first goal of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness and feasibility of an emotion-focused intervention for parents of adolescents with chronic pain. The intervention will be administered to parents, over a total of eight sessions, by a registered psychologist and clinical psychology graduate trainees. column36: Neurorehabilitation of sympathetic circuits after spinal cord injury using epidural electrical spinal cord stimulation
column37: "Spinal cord injury is a life-changing condition causing autonomic nervous system dysfunction that often results in blood pressure instability and cardiovascular impairment. Blood pressure instability occurs every day in most people with spinal cord injury, and this leads to poor patient quality of life and reduced cardiovascular health. Most spinal cord injured patients prioritize autonomic health to be a greater health priority compared to walking again. Sadly, however, walking-again remains the goal of the vast majority of spinal cord injury research. Current methods of controlling blood pressure after spinal cord injury are slow-acting drugs with side effects. As most blood pressure instability occurs rapidly, these approaches are inadequate for addressing the actual patient priorities in this population. Our team has shown that epidural spinal cord stimulation (eSTIM) below the site of injury activates specific spinal cord circuits and immediately stabilizes blood pressure. I will focus on understanding the mechanisms through which eSTIM stabilizes blood pressure and test the capability of this promising approach to fix damaged spinal cord tissues. The loss of blood pressure control after spinal cord injury is associated with disrupted neural connections between the spinal cord and blood pressure control centers in the brain. I will be labeling spinal cord pathways associated with blood pressure control and characterizing changes after injury. I will analyze these pathways in three dimensions using a cutting-edge computational approach supported by Compute Canada. I will also assess the effects of long-term eSTIM on this three-dimensional neural network to understand whether this approach can restore the neural network underlying blood pressure stability."

column36: Developing epigenetic biomarkers for chemosensitivity in small-cell lung cancer using circulating tumour DNA
column37: "Lung cancer is the most common cancer killer globally. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a particularly aggressive type of lung cancer that represents about 1 in 7 of all lung cancer patients. SCLC patients live on average about 8-12 months and only 7 in 100 patients survive past 5 years. Two chemotherapy drugs called cisplatin and etoposide are given to all SCLC patients. Initially, patients respond well to these chemotherapy drugs as the cancer is sensitive and shrinks after treatment. Unfortunately, for most SCLC patients, the cancer becomes resistant to the two drugs and is no longer responsive to chemotherapy. Also, some patients are resistant to chemotherapy from the get-go. Recent findings suggest that SCLC might be modifying the genetic code through indirect means i.e. epigenetics. Epigenetics is a biological process that can turn genes on and off. However, the main challenge in investigating SCLC epigenetics is the lack of tumour samples as they are difficult to obtain. This project aims to address this limitation by using blood samples collected from SCLC patients. Specifically, the aim is to use blood to understand the epigenetics of SCLC and identify molecular biomarkers that can be used to predict treatment response in patients."

column36: The Role of Rho Signalling in Mast Cell Activation
column37: "Environmental or food allergen exposure can sensitize our bodies through the production of antibodies. These antibodies are able to bind to the surface of mast cells, ""priming"" them for stimulation. Mast cells are immune cells that possess numerous granules containing immune mediators. Subsequent exposure of mast cells to allergens causes release of pro-inflammatory mediators through a process called degranulation, contributing to the development of allergic diseases such as asthma and rhinitis. Rho GTPases are molecular switches that are able to turn on and turn off signalling pathways in cells and are known to be key for successful degranulation. However, little is known about the regulation of these signalling pathways <span class=Apple-tab-span style=white-space:pre;> The purpose of my research is to determine how Rho signalling is regulated during mast cell degranulation by studying Rho guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors (RhoGDIs), which are inhibitors of Rho proteins. I will study the two RhoGDIs (RhoGDI1 and RhoGDI2) that are found in mast cells using RBL-2H3 cells, which are an ideal mast cell model. Using immunofluorescence microscopy and subcellular fractionation, I will observe and compare the localization of RhoGDIs within mast cells. To examine possible differential functions of RhoGDIs in mast cell degranulation, I will decrease RhoGDI expression by shRNA knock-down and measure any changes in enzyme release from the cells. RhoGDIs can also be modified by phosphorylation to change how they bind to Rho proteins. I can express permanently phosphorylated RhoGDIs to study how this modification affects their functions. By further characterizing the individual roles of the two RhoGDIs in mast cell degranulation, we may begin to define new targets for treatment against allergic diseases. "

column36: The Relation of Possible Selves and Self-Concept Clarity to Generalized Anxiety Disorder
column37: "Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a chronic, difficult-to-treat disorder characterized by excessive and uncontrollable worry. Although there are several leading theories of the etiological and maintaining factors of worry within GAD, one component that has been neglected across all theories is the self. Self-related constructs have been proven to provide a fuller understanding of psychopathological processes in other disorders, but for reasons unknown, have received little attention in GAD. The present study will provide the first investigation into the predictive utility of self-constructs, particularly possible selves and self-concept clarity, in the context of GAD and pathological worry. Possible selves are self-constructs that reflect our individual hopes, fantasies, responsibilities, and fears. Preliminary research suggests that perceived discrepancies with one's possible ought self and similarities with one's feared self predict feelings of anxiety. Self-concept clarity refers to the extent to which an individual's self-identity is clearly and confidently defined, internally consistent, and temporally stable. Our own laboratory's research has shown that low self-concept clarity predicts GAD diagnosis. It is predicted that ought and feared discrepancies, as well as low self-concept clarity, will add predictive value over and above pre-existing constructs in predicting severity of pathological worry. Low self-concept clarity is also expected to be associated with greater perceived differences from the ought self and similarities to the feared self. Findings from this study will inform existing theories of GAD which will serve as the foundation for more efficacious cognitive-behavioural interventions."

column36: Evaluating the role of electro-mechanical integration of human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte graft in the treatment of myocardial infarction
column37: "Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Because the human heart has a limited capacity to regenerate, stem cell-based therapies have emerged as exciting treatment avenues. We can generate new cardiac cells from stem cells that mediate an improvement in heart function when injected after a heart attack in animal models. It is unclear, however, whether this improvement is due to new, functionally integrated heart muscle or due to indirect effects such as the release of growth factors or improved heart geometry. This mechanistic uncertainty remains a source of controversy in the field, and hampers progress towards clinical trials (as it, for example, remains unclear what cell dose, type and delivery mode are ideal). This project aims to investigate the roles of the direct and indirect mechanisms underpinning the improved heart function observed after injecting new cardiac cells into an infarct scar. First, we will genetically engineer stem cells such that they have non-functioning channels called gap junctions (GJ). Without GJs, cardiac cells cannot communicate electrically or contract in a coordinated fashion. We will use a variety of lab techniques to confirm that our engineered cells have lost these functions. Second, we will use a pig heart attack model to compare outcomes after the transplantation of normal cardiac cells, our engineered cardiac cells (incapable of synchronous contraction), or placebo. If we find that the normal cells improve heart function (as we have shown in prior work) but that the engineered cells do not, this would provide compelling evidence that the beneficial effects of our cell therapy are direct and are mediated by the formation of electrically integrated new muscle."

column36: Machine Learning to Predict Functional Ability of Patients Following Total Hip Arthroplasty
column37: "Total hip arthroplasty (THA) is a successful procedure performed to treat hip osteoarthritis by replacing damaged bone and cartilage with implanted prosthetic components. The number of THA procedures done in Canada annually is rising, resulting in increased costs for the healthcare system. Improving surgical plans to minimize patient recovery time is required to decrease the related costs. This clinical study of 100 patients analyzes patterns in implant stability and patient recovery between patients who underwent different surgical approaches and received different implant designs. A special x-ray imaging technique, called radiostereometric analysis (RSA), is used to accurately measure the movement of the implant within the body. Early movement of the implant can be associated with a higher risk for revision surgery. Normally, analysis of patient recovery is based on subjective self-reported questionnaires (PROMs) but incorporating wrist-worn activity trackers at home and novel wearable sensors in clinic allows for more objective measurements of patient function. Machine learning methods allow us to analyze the collected data from RSA, PROMs, activity trackers, and wearable sensors to find patterns and make prediction models. Applying machine learning to wearable sensor data collected before THA, for instance, can predict patients that, after surgery, would be at a higher risk of falling. Prediction of patient recovery after THA benefits the multiple parties involved. Patients will have more informed expectations regarding their personal recovery. Clinicians can identify patients who may require more care and precautions. Healthcare systems can improve patient management and efficiency by recognizing patients who are likely to recover quicker and those who are not."

column36: Multi-Systemic Insomnia Monitoring and Potentiation of Slow Oscillations during Sleep
column37: "Insomnia is a heterogeneous disorder, and further work is required to characterise subtypes. One important aspect influencing insomnia profiles is the high comorbidity with depression. Slow wave sleep (SWS) dysregulation is common in both insomnia and depression, and may thus be a prominent feature of the subgroup of insomniacs with comorbid depression. Treating co-occurring sleep problems can help to better manage depression. Studies show that auditory stimulations carefully phase-locked to the ascending part of slow waves may enhance SWS, with encouraging observations of improved sleep in insomniacs. Slow wave potentiation thus represents a promising therapeutic target for insomnia and depression that is aligned with an identifiable physiological feature which may predict treatment response. This study aims to: i) investigate simultaneous EEG, body temperature and heart rate ambulatory monitoring over multiple days in insomniacs with and without depression; ii) validate a novel portable device for SWS detection and closed-loop auditory stimulation; iii) assess the impact of auditory stimulation on sleep, daytime symptoms of insomnia, cognition and mood; and iv) identify potential predictors of treatment response. Ambulatory EEG, temperature and heart rate will be assessed before, during and after each intervention arm. All participants will go through 1 week of active and placebo interventions in a counterbalanced order, with a week of wash out in-between. Sound stimulations will be delivered by an EEG monitoring device with closed-loop processing. In the placebo condition, the stimulation function will be de-activated. column36: Accuracy of 3D printed prostheses for maxillofacial defects of patients disfigured by head and neck cancer.
column37: "Three Dimensional (3D) printing is a process that creates a solid three-dimensional physical object from a digital design by adding material layer by layer. The technology has a particular resonance with dentistry and is being used routinely to print surgical guides, splints, aligners, complete dentures, models for teaching and prostheses for jaw reconstruction in cancer patients. However, this is neither accurate nor appealing aesthetically. It also unnecessarily causes removal of bone from a healthy area. If an artificial material such as resin is used to make a prosthesis, it releases heat and shrinks in size thereby damaging the adjacent soft tissue. To obtain better results, 3D powder printed calcium phosphate prostheses can be used to replace the defect as it is well accepted by the body. Advantages of prefabrication is the ability to plan the surgery well in advance contributing to less uncertainty in outcomes, less operation time, preservation of good bone and aesthetic results. The aim of this research is to test the marginal accuracy and fit of prostheses thus printed. The outcomes will fill the gaps in literature about the best method of fabrication, relevant values of dimensional accuracy and potential future applications for restoring other regions of the lost maxillofacial complex as well."

column36: The Role of Rho GTPases in Regulating Airway Inflammation
column37: "Asthma patients suffer from chronic inflammation in the airways triggered upon exposure to allergens and pollutants encountered commonly. column37: "Cardiovascular disease is the number one cause of death in the USA and Canada. column36: Examining culture as a healing method in a northern Indigenous community
column37: "In the past, cultural methods of healing were not considered for mental health treatment in Indigenous populations. However, more recently, there is an increasing awareness regarding the role that cultural methods of healing have in achieving mental wellness. Although we are becoming more aware of the importance of cultural methods of healing, we still have a lot to learn about how culture is currently being used as a healing method. The objective of this research is to capture how culture is being used as a healing method in a northern Saskatchewan Indigenous community. To do this, I will use a patient-oriented research approach. This approach will allow me to collaborate with an advisory committee comprised of Elders, community members, and the Director of Health. With the help of the advisory committee, we will identify eligible participants to partake in a photovoice project. This photovoice project will allow participants to capture, from their everyday perspective, how culture helps them to achieve mental wellness. We will then conduct sharing circles to generate a discussion that builds upon the images of healing that result from the photovoice project. Community members that are a part of the advisory committee will be provided with training and resources that allow them to participate in data analysis. Additionally, members of the advisory committee will play an integral role in the dissemination of the results. It is my hope that in using this collaborative approach we not only gain a better understanding of culture as a healing method, but that we also foster empowerment for community members to enact change within the community."

column36: Chronic critical illness in children
column37: "Improvements in the care provided in Pediatric Intensive Care Units (PICUs) have led to fewer deaths in children, but also more children surviving with complex and chronic medical conditions. Many of these children will require PICU care multiple times in their lifetime, stay in the PICU for long periods, and/or are dependent on technology to survive (e.g. breathing machines, feeding tubes). This group of children are increasingly recognized as a unique population referred to as children with chronic critical illness (CCI). As we are just beginning to understand and study this group of children, there is no standard definition of ""children with CCI"" in research studies. This has delayed further research and quality improvement initiatives targeted at this high-risk population of children. The goals of this research project are to: 1. Acquire foundational knowledge for defining CCI, and; 2. Develop a definition for children with CCI. The first goal will be accomplished by a detailed review of the literature to identify and describe what types of children have been studied in CCI research so far, followed by a survey of healthcare providers who commonly take care of these children in Canada. The second goal will be accomplished through a rigorous consensus process involving key stakeholders (healthcare providers and families). The ever increasing numbers of children with CCI makes this project of utmost importance. With a proper definition of CCI it will be possible to complete high-impact research in this area addressing important questions about the healthcare needs and long-term outcomes of children with CCI and their families."

column36: Ocular Bandage Contact Lens for Treatment of Corneal Abrasions
column37: "The cornea is the outermost layer of the eye and supplies 75% of the eye's focusing power, making its integrity imperative for vision. Corneal abrasions (CAs) refer to varying severities of physical impairment that disrupt its structural integrity. Healing times can range from days to months, and improper healing can result in increased light-sensitivity, opacity of the cornea, permanent scarring, or at its worst, irreversible vision loss. Corneal blindness, a result of improper healing, is the leading cause of vision loss worldwide and affects more than 23 million people. Encouraging cell repair and reducing inflammation of the eye are essential to avoid scar-tissue formation and other accompanying complications, minimizing the risk of corneal blindness. Current techniques such as ointments, glues and surgeries are not equipped to treat CAs in their entirety. Therefore, there is a need to design a therapy to target all aspects of CAs as well as their side effects for effective treatment and recovery. Ocular bandage contact lenses (OBCLs) use commercial contact lenses in conjunction with medicated eyedrops to minimize infection and discomfort during healing. I propose that an OBCL containing hyaluronic acid, growth factors and vitamin-E would offer extreme benefits over current methods, as it would reduce inflammation, repair tissue, act as a barrier to infection and accelerate healing times. It would also address CA side effects by reducing scar tissue formation and light-sensitivity. This technique would require minimal patient compliance, is easily implementable and would follow pre-established synthesis techniques. Upon success, this approach would allow for a more comprehensive treatment of CAs and could dramatically decrease the prevalence of corneal blindness."

column36: Avoidable blood transfusions in gastrointestinal cancer surgery
column37: "Red blood cell transfusions are common in patients undergoing gastrointestinal cancer surgery, yet they increase the risk of complications, cancer recurrence, and death. Strong evidence has demonstrated that restricting transfusions improves patient outcomes. However, up to half of transfusions given to gastrointestinal cancer surgery patients are unnecessary and potentially avoidable. Addressing avoidable transfusions is essential to improve transfusion practices and better patient outcomes. We propose to analyze avoidable transfusion practices on the population level in order to generate important knowledge and instigate changes in practice. The primary objective of this project is to examine variation in the use of all blood transfusions and avoidable blood transfusions across Ontario hospitals among adult patients who have undergone gastrointestinal cancer surgery. We also aim to identify important patient, provider, and institutional factors associated with the use of avoidable blood transfusions, which will allow us to identify potential areas for improvement. This question will be addressed in a novel way as we plan to link information from healthcare databases with newly available population-level laboratory data Surgery is responsible for half of all blood usage in Canada - understanding the variation in avoidable transfusion use for surgical patients is crucial to positively impact blood utilization across the country. This project has the potential to improve transfusion use, which will lead to improved patient outcomes, lower healthcare costs, and reduced strain on scarce resources. Understanding the variation in transfusion use in surgery on a wide scale is a crucial step in designing population-level interventions to encourage best practices. "

column36: Improving the healing rates of pressure injuries in a homecare setting using a real-time notification system
column37: "Pressure injuries, also known as bed sores, are painful, expensive, and largely preventable; yet, they affect one in four Canadians across all healthcare settings. Pressure injuries form when tissues remain compressed for extended periods of time. The best way to prevent and treat these injuries is to reposition patients when they have not moved for two hours; however, this regular repositioning is unlikely to occur in the home environment. Our team has developed a pressure injury management system that uses data from small sensors (load cells) under the legs of the patient's bed to track a patient's position with 94.2% accuracy. My project will extend this work by creating a prompting system for use in the home environment with real patients who have pressure injuries to evaluate whether prompts from this system can lead to more consistent repositioning and/or faster healing of existing injuries. Twenty patients and their unpaid caregivers will be recruited and randomly assigned to either a control or intervention group of equal size. Our system will be installed under all patients' beds and participants in the intervention group will receive repositioning reminders when patients have not changed position for two hours. The groups will be compared to see if the intervention group had more consistent repositioning and/or faster healing of pressure injuries. This will be the first study to use a repositioning-based intervention at home to help with healing pressure injuries. It will provide researchers with new information about repositioning rates at home, show the potential for a reminder system to speed up pressure injury healing, and help reduce treatment costs, which are currently estimated to be $3000 per month at home or $30,000 if hospitalization is required. "

column36: Validation and Implementation of Polygenic-Risk Prediction Models for Anthracyclines and Cisplatin in Pediatric Oncology
column37: "Advancement in cancer therapy over the past several decades has allowed most children battling cancer today to survive beyond 5 years. With increasing survival, the lasting effects of cancer therapy are becoming a more prevalent issue. Anthracyclines and cisplatin are two widely-used drugs in the treatment of pediatric cancer, however their tendency to cause severe side-effects, or adverse drug reactions (ADRs), limits their use. Thus, efforts must be made to predict the chances that a patient will experience such an ADR prior to beginning therapy. Pharmacogenomics, the study of gene-drug interactions that influence individual variability in drug response, has allowed for identification of genetic variants associated with anthracycline-induced heart-toxicity and cisplatin-induced hearing-loss, and risk-prediction models based on these genetic variants have been developed. However, further validation of these risk-prediction models, as well as incorporation of newly discovered genetic variants improving their predictive capabilities, are needed before wide-spread implementation of pharmacogenomic testing is achieved. Therefore, I aim to evaluate the ability of these risk-models to accurately predict cases of toxicity in an independent patient cohort to demonstrate their utility and generalizability for guiding treatment decision-making. Additionally, I aim to incorporate newly discovered pharmacogenomic variants associated with anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity and cisplatin-induced hearing-loss in order to update and refine these risk-models. Together, these objectives will serve to advance the ultimate goal of facilitating the implementation of pharmacogenomic testing into clinical practice, thus reducing ADRs and improving outcome for pediatric cancer patients."

column36: The Influence of a Self-Compassion Intervention on Physical Activity Behaviour Among People with Prediabetes: A Pilot and Feasibility Study
column37: "Over a third of Canadians have prediabetes, which can lead to type 2 diabetes (T2D). Physical activity (PA) can lower T2D risk, yet people with prediabetes do not engage in enough PA. In the midst of negative reactions about past unhealthy behaviours and fear about their future health, engaging in PA is hard for people with prediabetes. Such negative reactions can interfere with the ability to manage health behaviours. Self-compassion (SC) may help people with prediabetes cope with negative reactions and manage their PA. SC reduces negative reactions and encourages people to care for themselves (e.g., engage in PA) in difficult times. People can easily learn SC and research shows that small increases in SC <g class=gr_ gr_31 gr-alert gr_gramm gr_inline_cards gr_disable_anim_appear Grammar multiReplace id=31 data-gr-id=31>increases</g> health behaviours. It is unknown if SC will help people with prediabetes increase their PA; I will determine this. I will test the hypothesis that teaching this population SC to cope with their risk and PA struggles will lead to greater increases in PA than PA management skills alone. Participants, 80 adults aged 40-74 years with mid-to-high T2D risk will wear a PA tracking device for 10 days and complete SC and demographic measures. In the first of 6 weekly sessions, they will learn about their risk of T2D and will be advised to increase their PA. In the next 5 weeks, participants will partake in weekly group sessions. One group will learn about PA behaviour change and SC (experimental group); the other group about behaviour change and other health information (control group). Group placement will be random. At the end of the intervention and 6 weeks after, participants will complete the SC measure and wear the PA tracking device. This study will offer a first test of whether SC helps people with prediabetes increase their PA and will inform a larger test."

column36: Characterization of SNF2 Histone Linker PHD RING Helicase as a novel tumor suppressor gene in lung cancer
column37: "Lung cancer is the deadliest type of cancer worldwide, with over 1.8 million people dying from it every year. By the time most people find out that they have lung cancer, the disease is already in its late stages where the tumor is growing fast and has started to spread throughout the body. There are only a small number of treatments for late stage lung cancer, which are largely ineffective and expensive. Being able to predict for individuals at high risk for lung cancer would be incredibly helpful for doctors to identify and treat people in earlier stages, but there are currently no tools to do so. The main cause of lung cancer is smoking, yet people who never smoke also get it. This suggests that other factors, such as genetics, can increase one's risk. SHPRH is a protein that helps fix damaged DNA. The genetic code for SHPRH is found in a region of DNA linked to increasing the chance of getting lung cancer passed on through the family. Data from our lab also shows that SHPRH is frequently deleted in people with lung cancer who have never smoked. But, the specific role of SHPRH in lung cancer has yet to be defined. This proposal aims to study the effect of SHPRH on the repair of damaged DNA and the development of lung cancer. We believe that SHPRH may act to help prevent lung tumors, whereby its inactivation increases the build-up of damaged DNA and mutations caused by DNA damaging agents such as those in tobacco smoke. These mutations will ultimately lead to the enhanced formation and progression of lung tumors. This research may highlight the use of SHPRH as a marker to screen for people who are at-risk for lung cancer, and direct early intervention and treatment methods that will improve the survival of those affected by this devastating disease. "

column36: A genome-wide assessment of the transcriptional basis for the bone morphogenetic protein 9 induced endothelial hyperproliferation in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
column37: "Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a deadly disease of the circulatory system that affects thousands of Canadians, PAH is a result of a cancer-like growth of the cells lining the arteries in the lungs. This growth restricts blood flow, putting the heart under increased stress. Ultimately, PAH patients succumb to right heart failure. Present therapies reduce symptoms, but do not target the root of the disease. As a result, 15% of PAH patients die each year. Mutations in the gene BMPR2 are a key contributor to the development of PAH. Our lab has shown that reduced expression of this gene and its protein product changes the response of cells to the signal protein bone morphogenetic protein 9 (BMP9). With the loss of BMPR2, cells lining the arteries multiply when exposed to BMP9. Under normal conditions BMP9 suppresses growth. This project will study the underlying machinery of these cells to understand why this change occurs.Our preliminary investigations have identified several genes that are expressed abnormally when BMPR2 is lost. These targets will allow us to better understand the response to BMP9. We will use two cellular models as part of our experiments. Initial work will use a standard model of the cells lining the arteries (HPAECs) to understand each targets relation to BMPR2 loss. We will also use cells obtained directly from PAH patients and controls (BOECs) to confirm the relevance to the disease. Finally, we will move into animal models of PAH to begin the exploration of these targets for use in potential new therapies.Overall, this project aims to better understand why we see excessive cell growth in PAH. It aims to understand the key contributors to the disease and take the first steps towards finding a treatment that actually cures the disease."

column36: "Examining the Barriers to, Facilitators of, and Recommendations for Adult Day Programs from a Leadership Perspective"
column37: "Adult Day Programs are services offered in the community to people, commonly older people, who need help with activities. Interest in Adult Day Programs is increasing because of their ability to maintain the health of individuals and keep people living at home. These abilities are necessary in a health system addressing the needs of an aging population. Research has shown the positive impacts of Adult Day Programs from the perspectives of clients and unpaid caregivers. It has also considered the impact of Adult Day Programs on health systems. However, application of this research to the Canadian context is limited as this research is rarely conducted in Canada. Past research has also not considered the perspectives and influence of those who lead and manage Adult Day Programs. The proposed research involves interviewing leaders of Adult Day Programs to determine their perspectives on the current barriers to, facilitators of, and recommendations for Adult Day Programs. During these interviews, areas such as access to Adult Day Programs and care transitions will be discussed. The results of these interviews will be disseminated to and discussed with other stakeholders of Adult Day Programs, such as clients, unpaid caregivers, and health service providers. This research is an important stage in a larger program of research that will examine the perspectives of many Adult Day Program stakeholders and the impacts of Adult Day Programs on these stakeholders. The outcomes of this research will be used to adjust Adult Day Programs to the needs of an aging population through strategies such as changes to services, systems, and policies. These changes will strengthen the Canadian health care system and its effectiveness in addressing later life experiences."

column36: Evaluating the Efficacy of using PEER Interactive to Inform the Pharmacotherapy for Depression and Insomnia in Military Personnel
column37: "Individualized medicine for mental health? It's about time! There's an evident lack of objective tools to guide psychiatric treatment. Past projects focusing on the development of these tools have increasingly used electroencephalography (EEG) as it is widely available, easy to acquire and inexpensive. The Psychiatric EEG Evaluation Registry (PEER), an outcomes database, has been studied in the United States of America for ~20 years and the evidence supporting its effectiveness is significantly positive. This study proposal suggests to evaluate, in a Canadian population, if PEER is in fact an effective tool to help physicians prescribe the right medication, from the start. This study will recruit 100 military personnel diagnosed with depression and insomnia. Participants will be randomized to 2 groups: the control group (receiving treatment as usual) and the experimental group (with access to the PEER Report). All participants will undergo an EEG test which records electrical brain activity. The EEG results will be compared to a large database of ~11,000 baseline EEGs, and ~39,000 associated patient outcomes. PEER Interactive will identify which medications worked best (or didn't work at all) for people with similar brain patterns. All participants will be followed for a 3 month period where assessments will be made at each interaction to evaluate the participant's improvement in mental health. We're using big data and machine learning techniques to help provide patients with better, faster outcomes. The ultimate goal is to bypass the frustration of trial-and-error prescribing, ultimately leading to increased health cost-effectiveness for military staff suffering with mental illness."

column36: How can we better deliver tailored exercise programming for cancer survivors with multiple myeloma?
column37: "Multiple myeloma (MM) is an incurable cancer of the bone marrow associated with chronic fatigue, deconditioning, bone pain and high risk of fracture. In fact, most cancer survivors with MM experience broken vertebrae, losing several inches in height as a result. With current treatments extending survival, people are living with symptoms and limitations longer than ever before. Exercise could prove beneficial, and recent exercise guidelines have been released for cancer survivors. It's not clear whether survivors with MM can safely follow these exercise recommendations. Further, patients' and healthcare providers' fear of fracture and infection is a barrier to exercise. This study seeks to determine the feasibility of having individuals with MM exercise at the guideline in level, the barriers they experience meeting recommendations, and what exercise adaptations are necessary to stay safe. 20 participants will complete a supervised 12-week exercise program starting with 10 minutes of light aerobic and 5-6 resistance exercises 2x/week, progressing to the recommendations of 30 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise 3x/week and 7-8 resistance exercises 2x/week. We will perform exercise tests before and after the program to measure changes in fitness. Weekly logs will track symptoms, whether exercise targets were met, what barriers limited meeting the targets, and what adaptations were made to the program. Exercise holds promise in supporting the long-term health and function of cancer survivors with MM. By understanding if this population can meet exercise guidelines, the reasons why they are not able to, and what adaptations are needed to tolerate exercise, exercise professionals can develop and deliver safe and effective exercise programs for this high-risk population."

column36: Distribution of the opioid receptors in dorsal root ganglia neurons of rodents and higher species
column37: "Chronic pain is a common health problem affecting more than one third of the Canadian and American population. Opioids are the most prescribed drugs to treat moderate, severe and chronic pain. Clinically used opioids such as morphine, codeine, or fentanyl exert their effects by activating the mu opioid receptor. In addition to producing analgesia, the activation of this receptor also induces important adverse effects such as respiratory depression, tolerance and dependence which contribute to the opioid crisis. There are three opioid receptors referred to as mu (MOP), delta (DOP), and kappa (KOP) opioid receptors. The activation of DOP has been shown to have potential analgesic effects with fewer adverse effects than MOP. However, its exact role in pain modulation is still a matter of debate. The aim of this project is to study the distribution of DOP in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons in various species (mouse, rat, monkey and human). DRG neurons are the first step in the transmission of pain. These neurons relay the information from the periphery to the central nervous system and are therefore responsible to detect peripheral (including from the viscera) pain signals. DRG neurons are of various types and therefore play different roles. Large diameter neurons detect non noxious stimuli such as touch. Medium diameter neurons mostly detect noxious mechanical stimuli while small diameter neurons (peptidergic and non peptidergic) detect thermal, chemical and mechanical pain. Understanding which DRG neurons express DOP in each species will give us a better understanding of its potential role in pain management. "

column37: "Mental health issues significantly impact police officers, and mental illness is more prevalent in officers than the general public (Coleman, 2018). column36: Development of SARS-CoV-2 Peptide Therapeutics and Point-of-Care Salivary Diagnostics for Rapid Viral Detection
column37: SARS-CoV-2 (the causative agent of COVID-19) poses a generational threat, with no licensed vaccines or effective therapies to date. Further, the scarcity in reliable diagnostics, especially when testing asymptomatic/mildly symptomatic cases, is of grave concern. Accordingly, our proposal tackles 2 of the 3 research areas of this call, and addresses all 5 objectives, by developing and testing SARS-CoV-2 therapeutics and also prototyping convenient point-of-care (POC) COVID-19 diagnostics with scaling-up feasibility. For the therapeutic arm, we will innovatively design and test peptide disruptors of the SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) glycoprotein interaction with the human ACE2 receptor during viral entry, and other peptide inhibitors of viral-human interactions required for SARS-CoV-2 establishment. These will be tested in vitro using cell-based assays, with promising disruptors validated in SARS-CoV-2 hamster models. In addition, we will screen our in-house synthetic compounds targeting chaperones as potential SARS-CoV-2 replication inhibitors in both cell-based assays and animal models. On the diagnostic front, we will develop new diagnostic solutions for effective detection of even mild/asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 carriers at home and/or in remote locations. This POC lab-on-a tip technology will specifically detect SARS-CoV-2 peptides from patient saliva, with our clinician collaborators taking the lead in scaling-up both peptide therapeutics and our POC diagnostic device through ongoing coordination with the federal government and Saskatchewan Health Authority. This proposal brings together leading Canadian scientists and clinicians to fulfill our objectives by generating high-quality data to diagnostically and therapeutically accelerate the detection and prevention of COVID-19 and foster nationwide collaborations, with a clear scaling-up path that will refine decision-making across Canadian jurisdictions for effective and timely containment of the COVID-19 outbreak.

column36: A rapid at-home test for SARS-CoV-2
column37: As governments move toward re-opening Canada, it is critical that we have in place fast and simple tests for COVID-19. Canada needs cost-effective diagnostic technologies that allow for accurate and real-time mass testing in a variety of places, such as homes, airports, doctors' offices, borders, long-term care facilities and remote locations without access to centralized testing facilities. The goal of this proposal is to adapt and optimize existing technologies, originally developed by a team of researchers at McMaster University for bacterial detection, into a rapid point-of-need test for COVID-19. The test targets two classes of unique biomarkers - RNA and proteins - from COVID-19 to increase the test accuracy. It targets the RNA using molecular scissors made of DNA (called DNAzymes) and the proteins using molecular hands made of DNA (called DNA aptamers). These molecular scissors and hands will convert the presence of viral RNA and proteins to a DNA output, which is then massively amplified via an equipment-free room-temperature amplification method, known as "rolling circular amplification" (RCA), making the test highly sensitive. The device for the test is very simple and cheap, resembling a home pregnancy test. The test uses saliva as the sample source and fast chemical and biochemical reactions so that the test can be performed easily within 30 minutes by untrained users at home or any other points of need. Test reagents are contained in tablets for user convenience and high stability. Our team has already obtained proof-of-concept for most of the components of the test and will aim to optimize and integrate these components into a test kit, and validate the test by working with clinicians at the frontline of COVID-19 diagnostics and treatment. We are also working with Canadian industrial partners who can help with manufacturing and distribution of tests and recording of test results.

column36: Development of a Predictive Serologic Test for Cytopathogenic Autoantibodies in COVID-19 Patients
column37: Patients infected with the SARS-COV2 virus experience large variation in their clinical outcome. Most patients are asymptomatic or have mild symptoms while a smaller fraction of individuals develop devastating organ damage with fatal results. Currently, we have little insight into the factors that contribute to these dramatically different clinical outcomes. This proposal seeks to develop a test that will predict patients who may develop poor outcomes by measuring the emergence of antibodies that are destructive to tissues. These "destructive" antibodies are called autoantibodies. Normally our immune system generate antibodies protect us from viral and bacterial infections. We present preliminary data derived from a small cohort of COVID-19 patients that demonstrates the presence of autoantibodies in as many as 40% of infected patients. In some case these autoantibodies are present at high concentration. We will measure the presence of autoantibodies prospectively in a cohort of 150 patients that react against human lung cells, blood vessel cells and heart cells. The presence of these autoantibodies will then be correlated with the clinical course of Covid-19 infected patients. We will use well established mass spectroscopy methodologies to identify the proteins on human cells that are recognized by these autoantibodies. We will determine if purified autoantibodies from patients cause cell damage or death. Lastly, we will raise antibodies in mice directed against the proteins recognized by COVID-19 autoantibodies and determine if they cause injury to lung, heart, or blood vessels in animals. These efforts will allow us to develop a test to identify the emergence of autoantibodies in COVID-19 patients that will aid in stratification and the application of anti-viral therapeutics for those patients predicted to have unfavourable outcomes.

column36: Analysis of Antibody Neutralization Efficiency and Cellular Immunity in SARS-CoV-2-Positive Individuals Identified in At-Risk Individuals
column37: As the COVID-19 pandemic continues its deadly course around the globe, research efforts are closely focused on viral immunity, antibody responses, and vaccine development. Increasing data from multiple reputable international medical sources now indicate that exposure to the COVID-19 virus induces an antibody response in nearly all exposed individuals. However, questions remain about the protective value of these antibodies against repeat exposure to the virus and how long this protection will last. Furthermore, it is unclear whether there are differences in the virus-neutralizing ability of antibodies produced by asymptomatic carriers of the virus and individuals that develop severe COVID-19 infection. Answers to these important questions will enable us to predict the likelihood of additional waves of COVID-19 as well as inform public health efforts and vaccine development. For our study we will recruit a total of 1,000 healthy primary school teachers, daycare personnel, frontline medical workers in hospitals, and elderly people living in retirement homes. We will monitor them every two weeks for the virus and monthly for antibodies. We will regularly report back the data to the participants. The information learned from our laboratory will have five major outcomes: 1) It will enable early detection of infection and thereby greatly reduced the spread of the virus; 2) We will acquire a better sense of the numbers of asymptomatic and symptomatic individuals exposed to COVID-19; 3) Antibodies in the blood of those infected will be tested to see how well it can neutralize the virus; 4) Critical information about immunity to COVID-19 and how long the immunity will last will be shared with the scientific community and local/regional/national health authorities; and 5) This new knowledge will help vaccine developers make the right decisions about how to create their vaccines and how to give them to all of us.

column37: Canadian Blood Services blood donors are healthy people from cities and smaller urban areas in all provinces in Canada except Quebec. Left over blood samples from blood donations will be randomly selected and tested for antibodies to COVID-19. Antibodies are part of the body's response to an infection and are specific for the infecting virus. The presence of antibodies to COVID-19 means that the person previously had COVID-19. They may or may not have immunity to prevent them from getting COVID-19 again (that is, have functional immunity). Over 12 months, 1,500 samples will be tested each month. All samples that test positive for COVID-19 antibodies will have additional testing to measure the antibody concentration (titer) and how effective the antibodies are at binding to COVID-19 virus (neutralization). These will help to understand how likely people who had COVID-19 are to have immunity against re-infection. Tests that can be used for large numbers of samples will be compared to help Canada develop tests suitable for large scale testing. Monitoring functional immunity over the course of the pandemic will help to understand if people start to lose their immunity over time. Monthly data reports will be made available to public health staff (federal and provincial) to inform policy over the course of the pandemic. Mathematical modelling will refine estimates of immunity in the population which is fundamental to public health policy formulation.

column36: COVID-19: Comprehensive biomarker analysis for prediction of clinical course and patient treatment outcomes (COVID-BEACONS)
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has taken the world by storm. In Canada alone, there are more than 60,000 confirmed cases and more than 5,000 deaths. Despite its global impact, there are no specific therapies. While most patients display mild or no symptoms, a significant number result in severe disease, and sometimes death. We do not know what causes some patients to die from the infection. Developing a test that can identify patients who are at high risk of severe disease would help save lives. Early clinical reports noted that COVID-19 patients have a high risk of developing blood clots in the body including in the brain and lungs, thus hinting at how it makes people ill. We believe that this likely stems from a severe immune response to being exposed to the virus, SARS-CoV-2. This inappropriate response leads to a vicious cycle of damage to the blood vessels. Therefore, measuring when and how clotting problems develop may allow us to learn how severe COVID-19 disease progresses, find new treatment targets, and identify the patients that need to be treated earlier to prevent progression. To achieve this, we have assembled a collaborative effort between the largest intensive care hospital networks in Canada with the Thrombosis and Atherosclerosis Research Institute (TaARI), the largest and most comprehensive Canadian facility dedicated to the study of inflammation and blood clotting diseases. We will measure biomarkers from the biological pathways that control inflammation, blood vessel integrity, blood clotting, and blood clot breakdown. We will then identify which markers can predict disease progression. By understanding which pathways are disrupted over the development of severe COVID-19 disease, we may be able to identify those patients requiring aggressive therapy earlier in the course of the disease.

column36: Development of a Microwave Enabled Bio-Nano-Microfluidic Device for Point-of-Care Diagnosis of COVID-19
column37: The COVID-19 crisis has caused over 280k deaths with more than 4 million infections as of May 8, 2020. These numbers are increasing and may peak again with reopening of businesses. This tragedy could be prevented from happening or its impact could be largely minimized if rapid, massive-scale testing can be performed at community level without the need of highly trained professionals and expensive equipment. This is also the highly recommended action among the immediate next steps by World Health Organization (WHO). The proposed project aims to develop such a system for rapid point-of-care (POC) diagnosis of the COVID-19 virus by leveraging the team's expertise in engineering, nanotechnology, viral immunology and clinical medicine. The proposed system is a palm-sized instrument that consists of a battery-powered microwave circuitry and a microwave-microfluidic device with its sensor surface modified by functionalized gold nanoparticles (gNPs) that specifically recognize the COVID-19 virus. The output is a yes/no answer via a light indicator. A test can be done within 30 minutes including the sample preparation, which is completed by simply stirring a nasopharyngeal swab containing a tested person's sample in a buffer solution. The system allows a test to be completed with a small drop of the sample solution (5 microliter) that is filled in the inlet reservoir and drawn to pass the detection chamber towards the outlet by capillary force. If the sample contains the COVID-19 virus, the virus will be captured by the functionalized gNPs coated on the sensor surface resulting in the change in the microwave spectrum. The microwave circuitry will analyze the spectrum and output a yes/no answer. It is expected that the availability of the proposed portable system will enable the test of COVID-19 at the community level such as at a drive-through point or in an ambulance, which will largely expand the testing capacity and thus assist in the control the COVID-19 pandemic.

column36: A central role for the vascular endothelium in COVID-19 pathogenesis
column37: COVID-19 is a respiratory disease that can lead to a severe lung infection and death in seniors and patients with additional illnesses. Recent studies have recognized severe cardiovascular injury mainly in children and young adults even in the absence of the typical lung disease. Importantly, there are currently no validated vaccines or treatments for COVID-19. Serious and life-threatening cases of COVID-19 involve uncontrolled immune responses. One important part of the immune system's first line of defense is the complement system, which typically helps to clear invaders and damaged cells. Recent studies implicated complement as important in COVID-19, as it is known to activate the inner lining of blood vessels, the vascular endothelium. Endothelial activation leads to the attraction of inflammatory cells, which adds to an "inflammatory storm" and increases the risk of blood clotting, together closing a vicious cycle of blood vessel destruction and poor outcome. In a health care system crisis like the current COVID-19 pandemic, identification of patients in highest need for treatment and early determination of likely patient outcomes are urgently needed. We aim to address these needs by (i) investigating the mechanisms, by which complement injures and activates the endothelium, and (ii) identifying the resulting biological markers (biomarkers) reflecting inflammation and endothelial injury, and correlating them with the outcome of COVID-19 patients, thus establishing a COVID-19 risk score. Our study will help to fight the current COVID-19 pandemic in two ways: (i) identifying complement as important mechanism of inflammation and blood vessel injury will allow for trialing available complement blockers in COVID-19 patients; (ii) identifying biomarkers predicting patient outcomes will help determining patients in biggest need for help, and - in a desperate shortage of resources - identifying the ones who might have a chance to survive.

column36: General and Inexpensive Saliva-based Viral RNA Testing by Direct Imaging
column37: Existing nucleic-acid-based COVID-19 tests use enzymes to amplify low-copy number RNA to detectable levels. This adds cost, complexity and time to viral detection. In this proposal we will image fluorescently labeled probes hybridized to individual SARS-CoV-2 genomic RNA strands to enable a robust and highly sensitive test. The detection system involves three key steps: 1. Sample stabilization: As the assay does not require enzymes, robust stabilization of samples derived from saliva or nasal swabs is dramatically simplified. Detergents and mild denaturants will release viral RNA and homogenize any cell debris while serving to minimize virulence. 2. Hybridization and Washing: Probes within the stabilization solution will hybridize to viral RNA, brightly labeling it with quantum dots. Control RNA, such as human 18S RNA, will be similarly labelled but in a different colour channel. Sample preparation will be as simple as spitting into a sealable reagent container and shaking. A glass slide derivatized with viral and control probe oligonucleotides will then be introduced into the container and incubated for a defined time to immobilize the fluorescently tagged RNAs onto the slide as individual molecules. After hybridization, the slide will be rinsed stringently and placed into an imager. 3. Single molecule imaging. An inexpensive (target cost <$50) and easily mass-produced microscope will be designed to attach to a cell phone for single-molecule imaging. Images will be analyzed and uploaded to a medical site for analysis. Additional advantages over conventional tests include long-term storage and shipping for a test that is rapid (<15 min) and simple for point-of-care use. The test can be easily adapted to other RNA viruses, allowing a suite of tests to be rapidly deployed. This technology has the potential to revolutionize viral testing in remote locations, the home, and clinical settings to the benefit of all Canadians.

column36: Early immune predictors of sustained SARS-CoV-2 antibody responses after COVID-19 disease
column37: COVID-19, a disease caused by a new Coronavirus, is an unprecedented global health crisis for which we currently have nor safe nor rapid response. Given the absence of vaccines and effective therapies, it is essential to understand the development, effectiveness and maintenance of antiviral responses against its causing agent, the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The highly variable immune response against SARS-CoV-2 define the severity of the disease, but many critical questions remain: 1) can we predict patients that will experience a severe disease and delayed viral clearance? 2) do survivors of COVID-19 develop durable and protective antiviral immunity? 3) can serology identify convalescent COVID-19 patients who are at high risk of re-infection? 4) does re-exposure to the virus boost their antiviral immunity? We propose the creation of a multi-site consortium composed of 12 scientists (6 women and 6 men) with solid expertise in virology and immunology and from leading academic institutions in Quebec (UdeM, IRCM) and the US (Columbia, NY) to study antiviral immunity in COVID-19 in both sexes to address unresolved issues, as outlined in the CIHR call: in Aim 1 and 2, we focus on early clinical and immunological features of COVID-19 that can predict the emergence of protective and durable antibodies. We will compare cohorts of patients enrolled in the "Biobanque quebecoise de la COVID-19" (BQC19) that experienced mild or severe COVID-19 or COVID-19-like symptoms attributed to another infectious agent. In Aim 3, we will focus on a cohort of health care worker tending COVID-19 patients, therefore at higher risk of repeat exposure to the virus. Using this cohort, we will study the effect of repeat exposure on immunity boosting against the virus and help define the immunological requirements of a successful vaccine. Taken together, our proposal will provide the immunological perspective needed to better prepare and implement a safe exit from the current public health crisis.

column36: Long-term protective immunity against SARS-CoV-2 virus in COVID-19 patients
column37: The current COVID-19 pandemic is caused by a new coronavirus, named severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Current tests are unable to accurately identify patients who are infected or determine the effectiveness of their immune response against the virus. They also cannot identify patients who have produced a protective immune response for combating future re-infection with SARS-CoV-2. There are many question regarding the effects this pandemic has presented our society; however, understanding if individuals are protected against the virus, after being infected, continues to be very important. In this proposal, we will identify how our bodies react to the virus by examining antibodies in the immune system and by studying the memory immune cells that produce antibodies to determine if and how long our bodies are protected against the virus in the future. We will do this by identifying which patients have developed an immune response (antibodies) and then test for their ability to eliminate the SARS-CoV-2 virus, effectively. We will also determine if recovered COVID-19 patients develop memory immune cells capable of fighting re-infections in the future. These tests are important for many reasons, including: 1) accurately diagnose COVID-19 patients by identifying who developed an immune response; 2) identify individuals who mounted strong antibody responses that eliminates the SARS-CoV-2 virus and 3) determine if there is immune memory against COVID-19 that could protect against re-infection. A deeper understanding of the immune response will help fight the current COVID-19 pandemic and better prepare us for future pandemics.

column36: A low-cost, portable, and decentralized microfluidic device for detecting SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies
column37: Serological surveillance provides population-wide immunity status in a timely manner, which is important evidence in directing public health policy during the COVID-19 pandemic. Immunoassays are serological tests that can measure antibody levels to an infectious disease, and are being rapidly employed to identify individuals with potential immunity to SARS-CoV-2. Although immunoassays can quantify antibodies in a sample, they do not directly measure neutralizing antibodies (nAbs). Tests currently available for nAbs are expensive, labour intensive, require high biosafety containment, and are can only be preformed in centralized national laboratories. Low-cost, rapid, decentralized testing for SARS-CoV-2 nAbs will expedite serological surveys and help evaluate herd immunity and vaccine effectiveness. The goal of this project is to develop a fast and cost-effective assay to detect nAbs for SARS-CoV-2 and with reduced biosafety requirements for immediate distribution. This assay will then be integrated into a paper-based microfluidic device for portable testing that uses a one-step assay capable of separating out antibodies from whole blood. The development of new diagnostic tools will be critical for serological surveillance during and after the current COVID-19 pandemic and can help direct Canada's response to prevent further outbreaks. Low-cost and portable serological testing will also enable low- and middle-income countries to perform high-quality serological surveys and these tools will be of immense value to displaced populations (i.e. refugees). Furthermore, rapid and reliable screening of plasma samples for neutralizing antibodies will provide a valuable resource for the evaluation of current vaccination and antibody-based therapeutic approaches towards SARS-CoV-2.

column36: Diagnosing the onset of severe Covid-19 disease
column37: A recent report from China has indicated that many or most individuals who die from severe Covid-19 infections have sepsis. Sepsis is broadly defined as an abnormal host response to infection that causes life-threatening organ dysfunction, and was responsible for 19.7% of global deaths in 2017. Sepsis is a very complex disease, consisting of phenotypic clusters of patients, that constitute distinct endotypes, which are biologically driven and relevant to clinical outcomes. We have defined 5 sepsis endotypes in a large clinical study and propose to extend this here to severely ill Covid-19 patients. We will collect blood from up to 200 patients in BC and Quebec, and analyze the genes that are expressed in these cells (which will enable us to discriminate endotypes). This will allow us to define a set of genes for which the levels of expression correlate with future disease severity. This information will allow the development of a diagnostic that will enable a physician to predict the likely severity of a patient's disease and apply knowledge-driven clinical management. Furthermore, since endotypes operate under distinct mechanisms this knowledge will enable the discovery, by others, of targeted therapies to treat Covid-19 associated sepsis.

column36: Development of a yeast-based immunoassay for SARS-CoV-2 serologic testing amenable to inexpensive local production
column37: To monitor the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic and test individuals for potential immunity, we need antibody detection tests, where a blood sample is checked for the presence of antibodies induced by past exposure to the virus. These tests are often expensive, requiring either a fully-equipped laboratory with highly trained technical staff, or costing many dollars per test for field-deployable "strip tests". Sending tests to a lab or paying a few dollars per test does not perhaps seem like a problem, here in Canada, but in our partner nation of the Philippines, both of these present significant barriers: public health dollars are sharply limited, and remote areas have very limited access to lab facilities and technical staff. Our goal is to create an antibody detection test that can be "grown" locally, here in Canada and in the Philippines. By modifying baker's yeast (S. cerevisiae), we can put antibody-binding proteins (antigens) on their surfaces, able to capture disease-induced antibodies found in blood samples. We test for the presence of these antibodies with an agglutination test: when the yeast cells settle to the bottom of a round well, in the absence of antibodies they form into a tight button that looks like a dot to the naked eye; or in the presence of antibodies they form larger clumps that stay more spread out and look like a flat sheet to the naked eye. A minimally-trained user can thus obtain a positive or negative result with no expensive instruments. The yeast (once designed) can be grown in a simple sugar solution, at a raw material cost that we estimate to be something less than 0.01 cents per test. We have demonstrated lab-bench success at detecting Chagas' disease and dengue fever antibodies, and now we propose to adapt the technique to detect COVID-19 antibodies and develop it in a fully deployable kit for use in under-resourced areas. Our first target is the Philippines, with the help of our collaborators at UP Manila.

column36: Simple assay to assess antibody-dependent enhancement of SARS-CoV-2
column37: Antibodies are one of our main immune defences against invading pathogens. However, for some viruses, under certain conditions, antibodies can provide a means for enhanced virus entry and replication in a number of cell types. This phenomenon, known as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), often exacerbates disease and is a major challenge for prevention of viral disease by vaccination. ADE has been demonstrated for several human and animal coronaviruses, so there is concern that ADE may increase COVID-19 disease during natural infection or following vaccination. The goal of this proposal is to develop a test for human serum samples that will detect ADE of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. This assay will be relatively simple to perform and will allow high-throughput screening of human serum samples in clinical laboratories. It will allow physicians and scientists to assess whether antibodies produced in response to natural infection or vaccination may predispose an individual to ADE, and potentially more severe disease. In addition, to better understand the importance of ADE in SARS-CoV-2 infection, we will further investigate this phenomenon in biologically-relevant circulating human immune cells.

column36: Rational design and standardization of serology diagnostics using immunoaffinity-targeted proteomics assays
column37: Current design of serology antibody tests is driven by convenience, speed of manufacturing, and affordability. Limitations of common serology tests include cross-reactivity and lack of standardization, which decrease diagnostic specificity and make such tests inappropriate to screen the general asymptomatic populations with low prevalence of COVID-19. Viral antigens used in the common tests assume detection of binding antibodies, but not necessarily neutralizing antibodies, further limiting the value of such tests. In our study, we will focus on rational design and standardization of serology diagnostics of SARS-CoV-2. We will utilize immunoassays and quantitative immunoaffinity-targeted proteomics assays to discover, verify and validate combinations of antigens and antibody isotypes which provide the highest diagnostic specificity and sensitivity. Unlike semi-quantitative serology immunoassays, our proteomic assays are quantitative, have no cross-reactivity, and provide "gold standard" solutions for inter-laboratory and international standardization of serology tests. Our study will facilitate improvements of diagnostic specificity of existing serology immunoassays, thus enabling population screening for the acquired immunity.

In addition, the volunteers will have repeat blood antibody testing 3 and 6 months following the initial testing. column36: REinfection in COVid-19 Estimation of Risk (RECOVER)
column37: Studies done with human coronaviruses (hCoV) have shown that antibodies rise on average 12 days after the onset of symptoms, are higher with more severe disease and seem to decrease the risk of reinfection for 1-3 years. Participants challenged with the same virus (hCoV 229E) 8-12 months after being infected with hCoV still developed symptoms and shed virus. Thus, if reinfection, whether symptomatic or not, occurs with viral shedding, achieving natural herd immunity against COVID-19 is unlikely. Awaiting a vaccine that would protect the entire population, there is hope that short-term natural immunity following natural disease can be achieved. However, we do not know at this point in time if COVID-19 positive patients in whom we detect an immune response have a long-lasting response and if this response protects them against reinfection and viral shedding There is a need to know these answers to plan for future actions. If an antibody response is not long-lasting and protective against viral shedding, then herd immunity is not a goal to aim for, as vulnerable patients will remain at risk; individuals having recovered from the disease may get re-infected and be a source of infections for others. In such a case, other non-pharmacological interventions will be necessary until an efficacious vaccine or therapeutic agent becomes available. We aim to estimate the risk of reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 in healthcare workers (HCW) who have already been infected with COVID-19 and aim to study antibody response and levels in asymptomatic and symptomatic HCWs with confirmed COVID-19 reinfection over a 1-year period. Findings from this study will allow public health decision-makers to decide on future strategies for deconfinement/reconfinement and pandemic management. The 6-month results will be shared with public health. Showing that COVID-19 does not protect against mild reinfection or viral shedding will completely change the paradigm under which we are operating currently.

column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has an unprecedented scale of spread. There is urgent need for effective treatments, and research has focused on development of antiviral drugs and vaccines. However, since host immune response is a critical determinant of disease severity for life-threatening infections, interventions that modify deleterious host responses (for e.g. immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, micro-vascular injury and pro-coagulant responses) may also play a critical role in decreasing progression to severe and fatal COVID-19. Micronutrient deficiencies, particularly vitamin D and zinc, have been associated with dysregulation of these host responses and may play an important role in COVID-19. Nutritional status is critical especially in older individuals and those with chronic disease including diabetes and cardiovascular disease, in whom COVID-19 is often more severe. While supplementation is important in other infections, there are no well-designed studies on the potential effect of such supplements in COVID-19. In line with CIHR's call for testing therapeutics for COVID-19, we propose a 2x2 factorial randomized trial to examine the effectiveness of vitamin D and zinc supplements as immune-based therapy among 700 patients in Mumbai, India. We will also examine the immunological response to COVID-19 and the effect of the intervention on specific biomarkers of immune and endothelial activation (e.g. Angiopoietin-2) that are independent and quantitative predictors of severity and mortality in other severe infections (e.g. sepsis, pneumonia).

column36: Contribution of genetic variation of ACE2, the receptor for SARS-CoV-2, to COVID-19 disease expression and development of therapeutics
column37: The coronavirus causing the COVID-19 pandemic infects by binding to a receptor called ACE2 on the surface of cells lining the lung. One reason for the virulence of this new virus is the strength of its binding to ACE2. However, one of the leading mysteries of the outbreak has been the wide range of responses to infection, from a complete absence of disease in some, to life-threatening pneumonia in others. Regional difference across the world in disease expression have also been reported, as has a striking increased severity of COVID-19 in men compared to women. Here, we propose to investigate whether genetic variation in the human ACE2 receptor protein underlies these differences. We will test this by making all possible mutations in the ACE2 gene and testing impact on binding to the viral protein. Results from our study will have important impact on new development of therapeutics by improving computational models of ACE2-virus interactions used to design drugs blocking this binding. Another important outcome from our study would be the identification of genetic variants of ACE2 with heightened binding affinity for the viral protein. Such variants can be used as novel therapeutics by out competing virus in a patient's system, preventing virus from infecting host cells. Critically, once established, our platform will be highly versatile and readily allow testing new strains of the COVID-19 virus for increased or decreased infectivity. This platform will also be invaluable to provide a more rapid response to any new virus that appears in the future that infects cells by binding the ACE2 receptor.
