column36: Are healthcare workers at higher risk of COVID-19 than other working adults?
column37: To date, there have been 69,000 confirmed or probable cases of COVID-19 in Canada. Healthcare workers are assumed to be at increased risk of infectious diseases, including SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2)/CoVID-19 compared to other working adults due to exposure to infective patients. However, no epidemiologic study has examined this assumption. This study is designed to determine incidence of SARS-CoV-2 in HCWs and other, non-healthcare working adults in other frontline service occupations. We will enrol 1640 people working in acute care hospitals (healthcare workers) and 820 people working in non-healthcare jobs from across Canada, including Edmonton, Toronto, Hamilton, Sherbrooke, and Halifax and follow them over 12 months to compare the incidence of SARS-CoV-2 over the 12-month follow-up, risk factors for infection, and several other outcomes in each group. Not only will this allow us to compare and contrast differences in the rates of infection but also in exposures to infective people from all areas of our lives, protective measures taken to reduce infection, and how those measures may affect the risk of infection. We will collaborate with researchers in the US and Puerto Rico, who are collecting similar information on healthcare and non-healthcare workers to determine the similarities and differences between countries and across sites. The results will inform optimal strategies for protecting the workforce, their families, and their patients/patrons.

column36: Uncovering longitudinal patterns of resilience and vulnerability in a pandemic: The All Our Families COVID-19 Impact Study
column37: The psychological and social effects of the COVID19 pandemic are pervasive and are impacting current mental health and relationships, with potential long-term effects, notably in youth. Youth is a developmental period of significant social, emotional, biological, and contextual change, simultaneously associated with a surge in mental health difficulties. Preliminary evidence at the national level is indicating reduced mental health during the pandemic, particularly among youth. High-quality, contemporary data on coping and recovery for families and youth during and after an unprecedented pandemic is crucial to inform further action and resource allocation in any future periods of lockdown, increased or re-infection, and future pandemics. Further, the acute and sustainable costs and benefits of aggressive public health measures such as physical distancing on the well-being of families and communities are unknown. The All Our Families (AOF) study, an ongoing prospective pregnancy cohort in Calgary, will survey families at three times points over one year to capture the discrete and longitudinal patterns of direct and indirect impacts of the pandemic on mental health, social connections, school achievement, sleep, and screen-time. AOF is uniquely positioned to disentangle emerging and sustained vulnerabilities from pre-existing vulnerabilities to development using longitudinal data that reflect the individual, family, and community determinants of health. Longitudinal data analysis will uncover patterns of resilience and vulnerability immediately, and over time for mothers and youth. Identification the factors that influence family and youth health and well-being during a pandemic is critical to the development of public health communications and strategies to improve outcomes.

column36: TARGet Kids! COVID-19 Study of Children and Families: Safe Return to School, Work, and Play
column37: Across Canada and around the world, governments have implemented policies to limit the spread of COVID-19 including physical isolation, school and childcare closures. Many governments are now reducing these measures and returning children and families back to school and work due to a number of economic, social, and political factors. The World Health Organization recommends that governments seeking to relax physical isolation measures do so through two complementary approaches: 1) breaking chains of transmission through testing, isolating, and treating and 2) monitoring disease circulation through surveillance and serological surveys. We propose to pivot Canada's largest ongoing children's study, TARGet Kids, to provide high-quality, real-time data to monitor, quantify and characterize COVID-19 infection among children and parents. We aim to measure the incidence of new infections as well as previous COVID-19 exposure so that we can understand how COVID-19 is transmitted between children and their parents, risk factors for infection, disease severity, and health system use. We will also answer important questions about COVID-19 serological status of children and parents and the impact of physical isolation on child emotional and behavioral health as well as parent mental health and stress. We will provide evidence to support policy interventions to break underrecognized chains of transmission and reduce illness severity which will help policy makers guide children and their parents in safely returning to school, work and play. Key strengths of this proposal include a scientifically rigorous plan with a well-tested rapid implementation strategy that leverages Canada's largest children's cohort study to provide real-time high-quality data on COVID-19 community transmission.

column36: Development of an Implementation Framework to Advance Provincial and National Health System Supply Chain Management of the COVID-19 Pandemic
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrates the current gap in healthcare supply chain in Canada, as healthcare workers struggle to access the products and equipment needed to deliver safe, timely, and quality care to Canadians. The purpose of this research is to examine supply chain processes and infrastructure to create the evidence for strengthening supply chain infrastructure that ensures that products are available to public health teams and health care professionals to protect the health of every Canadian citizen. The research will conduct mixed-method case studies of seven provinces to document how supply chain processes influence COVID-19 health outcomes, and how data, digital tools and analytics can improve health services and public health efforts to manage COVID-19. Cases will examine policy frameworks that ensure health teams have safe and effective products from quality companies, as well as strategies to support effective federal-provincial-territorial supply chain coordination. This research will inform strategies to ensure Canadians have access to public health prevention initiatives and can access care for those who become infected by COVID-19. The proposed research will advance supply chain resilience across Canada to ensure health system capacity, accelerating Canada's pandemic response, and ensuring public health and health care teams have the products and equipment needed to prevent, detect, treat, and manage COVID-19. Improved supply chain infrastructure will create transparency of the effectiveness of COVID-19 interventions, enabling Canada to better coordinate with national and global supply chain networks and strengthen Canada's capacity to proactively manage COVID-19. Evidence of policy frameworks and supply chain infrastructure informs clinical and health system management of this pandemic and will advance planning and coordination across provincial, federal, and global health systems to support effective and timely management of COVID-19.

column36: Weathering adversity: toward mitigating the impact of prolonged school closure and social isolation on mental health and lifestyle behaviours of elementary school children
column37: In early 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic engulfed the world, leading to drastic measures to limit the spread of the virus. These measures included closure of schools and orders to stay home for many weeks. Although these measures are necessary to prevent the virus from spreading, they also created a lot of hardship, particularly among school-aged children. This research builds on our 12 year partnership with a program called APPLE Schools (http://www.appleschools.ca/) which delivers a very successful intervention to promote healthy living and mental health to vulnerable kids from disadvantaged settings and currently operates in 74 elementary schools in northern Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba and Northwest Territories. In 2018 we collected data on lifestyle behaviours and mental health in 16 schools from northern communities. Together with APPLE Schools, we propose research that collects information on children's mental health (mood, feelings, self-esteem), sleep, diet, physical activity, screen time and how these things may have changed after COVID-19 school closures. We will also ask questions about health-related school programming to find out what worked and what did not. This will help us understand what we can do to improve student supports offered by schools. As we are anticipating repeat school closures to contain COVID-19 and other outbreaks, the knowledge from this study has direct links to the re-opening efforts. The findings can be implemented immediately in schools across Canada and beyond.

column36: Improving the care of older adults living with dementia across Canada during the COVID-19 pandemic: a mixed methods study to inform policy and practice
column37: Persons living with dementia (PLWD) are disproportionally impacted by the current COVID-19 pandemic. Not only are they at increased risk of severe COVID-19 disease and mortality, they are particularly vulnerable to the consequences of the pandemic including containment strategies (eg. physical distancing) and disruptions in the healthcare system, especially non-COVID care due to 1) difficulty in recalling public health recommendations, 2) disruptions to formal care channels and support networks (e.g. postponed day program, virtual consultation with physicians, shortage of workers and volunteers in home care and community services) and 3) increase isolation, anxiety and depression due to physical distancing measures. Caregivers are also strongly impacted, with increased stress, anxiety and burden. In order to inform policy-makers, health system managers, clinicians, and community organizations, as quickly as possible, we will conduct a study to measure, describe and identify strategies to address the pandemic as well as its consequences in persons living with dementia. We will conduct this study in four provinces (QC, ON, AB, SK), as well as in France. We will leverage our existing infrastructure, expertise and methods to measure the impact of the pandemic and its consequences on health service use, infection rate and mortality in persons with dementia, with data extracted from health administrative databases. We will describe the lived experiences of persons with dementia and their caregivers, as well as family physicians regarding health and social services based on qualitative interviews and surveys. Finally, we will conduct an online deliberative consultation with key stakeholders (persons with dementia, caregivers, clinicians, managers, and decision-makers), to discuss the research findings, share promising avenues, and generate evidence-based recommendations to mitigate the negative impacts of the pandemic and its consequences on persons with dementia.

column36: Equity in Emergency Department Utilization in Alberta for Priority Populations during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Exploring Impacts of Changes to Healthcare and Healthcare Utilization through Administrative Data Analysis and Nominal Group Techniques
column37: Alberta has seen a marked decrease in emergency department presentations while pandemic control measures have been in place. In addition to public health measures including physical distancing, many patients who perceive hospitals as high-risk environments and may avoid emergency department visits, even when seriously ill. This can lead to health issues becoming worse and harder to manage. Harms associated with decreased emergency department use may be greater for some populations, who rely more heavily on emergency departments for their care. Frequent users of emergency departments are more likely to be low income and to be older. In Alberta and British Columbia, First Nations individuals utilize emergency departments at a much higher rate than non-First Nations individuals. This study builds on an existing emergency medicine research partnership with the Alberta First Nations Information Governance Centre, as well as connections to operational (Alberta Health Services) and research leaders in the areas of emergency medicine, seniors care and population health. Through structured engagement with patients, clinicians and health systems leaders, we will share findings and develop understandings of results. Highlighting harms and inequities arising from pandemic-driven changes in care patterns and systems will allow policy- and decision-makers to reduce the negative consequences of efforts to manage COVID-19.

column36: Engage-COVID-19: A mixed methods study of biomedical, behavioural, and psychosocial aspects of the COVID-19 pandemic among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men in Canada
column37: Gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (GBM) have historically experienced significant disparities in physical, mental, and sexual health, amplified by systemic marginalization and high barriers to healthcare. This context of inequity creates heightened vulnerabilities to COVID-19. Failure to respond to the health and wellness needs of GBM may have significant negative effects on COVID-19 outcomes and exacerbate existing health disparities. We propose the Engage-COVID-19 Study to rapidly respond to current and pressing knowledge gaps concerning the COVID-19 pandemic among GBM in Canada. This study will be embedded within the Engage Cohort Study, which is the only study with comparable biobehavioural data on HIV/STI prevalence and risk behaviours for GBM in Canada. To date, baseline data collection has been completed with 1842 GBM who are enrolled in the Engage Cohort Study (565 in Vancouver, 388 in Toronto, and 889 in Montreal). All of these participants will be invited to have SARS-CoV-2 antibody testing and complete an in-depth survey that will include COVID-specific quantitative questions. We anticipate recruiting a total sample of 1695-1768 participants. In addition, from this group we will recruit 90 GBM participants for qualitative interviews in Vancouver (30), Toronto (30), and Montreal (30) to assess the direct and indirect impacts of COVID-19 on Canadian GBM. These data are necessary both to understand COVID-19 risks, vulnerabilities, and prevention strategies, as well as the impacts of COVID-19 on health service access and different levels of HIV/STI risk across provinces. By making efficient use of available research infrastructure, our proposed study will ascertain the occurrence of COVID-19 by documenting SARS-CoV-2 immunity within both HIV-positive and -negative participants and produce rapid, high-quality evidence for preventing the direct and indirect effects of COVID-19 for this population across multiple jurisdictions.

column36: Gig couriers delivering people, food and packages in a pandemic: Containment strategies to mitigate the occupational and public health impact
column37: Gig courier workers, such as Uber Eats, Amazon Flex, and Lyft drivers, have been busier than ever during the Canadian COVID-19 pandemic as the public attempts to avoid illness by ordering take-away food, shopping online and taking ride-hails rather than public transportation. This places gig courier workers in a unique position to become infected with COVID-19 and transmit it to others as they move people, food and packages from one location to another. Although gig couriers are key vectors between where people live (e.g. homes, care facilities) and the outside world, formal strategies do not exist to protect them from exposure and to mitigate their role in disease transmission. Importantly, this risk is not expected to change anytime soon as the high use of couriers will likely not decline as the economy re-opens. This study will contribute to coronavirus containment strategies by identifying disease transmission risks embedded in gig work contexts and practices, developing clear and tailored interventions for gig courier workers about gig courier disease-related safety and transmission, and widely disseminating results, in live time, as they are identified. Using framework analysis explicitly geared towards generating policy- and practice-orientated findings within limited time periods, we will: document existing courier safety organisational policy; map gig courier worker work, disease exposure and transmission conditions (with attention to gendered dimensions) via social media forums and in-depth interviews with workers and courier firm representatives; and categorise disease transmission risks. Supported by our Strategic Advisory Committee of unions, government municipalities, employers, and vulnerable worker advocates, and using real-time public health communications, this study will create effective national interventions to reduce gig courier disease exposure and protect the public health of Canadians using these courier services.

column36: Wastewater surveillance of SARS-COV2 to enable real-time clinical case-finding in Calgary
column37: We propose to track SARS-COV2 in the wastewater (WW; i.e., sewage) in Calgary, Alberta. The SARS-COV2 virus is excreted in the poop of infected individuals - often before symptoms start. These viruses are no longer infectious, but their genetic material (RNA genomes) can be detected in wastewater samples using molecular biology techniques for RNA quantification. This project will create a pathway enabling mobilized testing of the WW network throughout Calgary. Our project will achieve 3 objectives: 1 develop procedures to collect and analyse SARS-COV2 genetic material in WW samples from regionally diverse parts of Calgary, 2 develop different molecular assays that complement each other and are resilient to the WW chemical matrix, 3 develop genomics and bioinformatics methods for identifying genetic variants of SARS-COV2 in Calgary WW thereby enhancing epidemiological tracking. In Stage 1 we will develop and validate assays with samples from Calgary's three WW treatment plants, accounting for variability in WW chemistry and its effect on molecular biology methods. In Stage 2 we will work closely with Alberta Health Services and City engineers to apply the assays on WW from areas with known active COVID-19 cases to demonstrate proof of principle. In stage 3 we will deploy in real-time sampling teams through the city to collect samples for monitoring new areas where infections are not known to exist, allowing AHS to proactively find and respond to infected people without symptoms. Our team involves AHS, the City of Calgary, engineers, microbiologists, clinicians/public health experts, and University deans from Science, Engineering and Medicine. We will provide real-time, actionable information on SARS-COV2 in Calgary enabling public health officials to perform regionalized case-finding and develop strategies that focus containment efforts in the areas most affected, while minimizing the collateral social and economic consequences of needed public health interventions.

column36: Assessing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on social and health outcomes among young people: A mixed-method comparative analysis in Canada and France
column37: Youth (<30 years) are among the most at risk for longer-term social and health consequences due to COVID-19-related public health measures (e.g., physical distancing) and the associated social and economic impacts, including unemployment, as well as isolation from their social networks and disruption to their education during key periods of the early life course. To advance evidence and to inform adaptive social, economic and public health responses among youth, we are prepared to rapidly launch a one-year multi-site mixed-methods study. Our aim is to generate new context-sensitive and population-specific data to document how policy and program responses can be optimized to improve the lives of youth in two key international settings: Canada and France. While both Canada and France share some commonalities (e.g., high-income countries, publicly funded health care systems), there are many important contextual differences (e.g., severity and evolution of national and regional COVID-19 curves, economic support/employment insurance programs, community-based responses) that will benefit from empirical investigation as they relate to youth population health. We will conduct a multi-site concurrent mixed-methods study that includes: (i) a series of longitudinal qualitative research activities including semi-structured interviews with youth from across different jurisdictions in Canada (n=30) and France (n=30); (ii) interviews with key stakeholders (n=10 in each setting); and (iii) two national online cross-sectional surveys in both Canada and France with youth (at 6-month intervals). Throughout the duration of the proposed study we will engage in integrated knowledge translation and exchange (KTE) activities to systematically engage in rapid-cycle evaluation and advance actionable findings, including findings that are of relevance to national, federal and local policies and programs that can have an impact on youth social and health outcomes.

column36: Indigenous Health Counts in Urban Homelands: Estimating COVID-19 Incidence and Mortality among Indigenous Populations Living in Ontario Cities
column37: First Nations, Inuit, and Metis peoples face many challenges as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. Due to existing social factors such as poor quality, overcrowded housing, homelessness, and lack of clean running water, infections like COVID-19 can spread quickly. There are also big gaps in data about how COVID-19 is spreading among Indigenous peoples, especially in cities. To address this, we will use information from existing studies about the health of Indigenous peoples living in cities to learn more about COVID-19 spread and it's impacts. The Our Health Counts Toronto, London and Thunder Bay studies used social networks to find Indigenous community members living in these cities. These studies were done by the Indigenous community for the Indigenous community. Our methods allowed us to gather information about the needs of the entire Indigenous populations in these cities, even those who don't use services regularly. By linking the Our Health Counts studies to the provincial COVID-19 database at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES), our team will use new statistical methods to accurately estimate the rate of COVID-19 transmission for Indigenous peoples in these cities. We will also check for increases in mortality rates, due both to COVID-19 itself and gaps in access to health care for acute (e.g. heart attack) and chronic (e.g. diabetes) health conditions. In partnership with Indigenous community health services, our research team will improve statistical methods and produce currently unavailable information regarding the burden of COVID-19 and its rate of spreading through the urban Indigenous communities living in Toronto, London and Thunder Bay, Ontario. This information is important as Indigenous Peoples are highly mobile between urban areas and First Nations reserves, and rural and remote Metis and Inuit communities. Improving our understanding of COVID-19 in urban centres can reduce its risk of spreading within and from these cities.

column36: Expression and Purification of COVID19 Virus Spike (S) Protein for Diagnostics and Vaccines
column37: Projects described within this rapid response proposal relate to diagnostics and vaccine production. The reagents generated also have longer term ramifications for studying virus attachment and developing inhibitors that block host cell entry and virus mediated fusion. The work in this proposal focuses on the spike protein (S) of the coronavirus which mediates attachment and entry into the host cell and is the major target of neutralizing antibodies that block infections. The first goal of this proposal is to generate large quantities of the S protein is a mammalian expression system that can be easily scaled up for large scale production. The protein generated in this procedure can be used to produce immune diagnostic kits as well as serve as a component of subunit vaccines or booster shots directed against COVID-19. The second aim describes the generation of recombinant vesicular stomatitis (VSV) viruses that express the Spike (S) protein derived from COVID-19 virus. In the first experiments, VSV genome vector is modified to contain coronavirus S protein in place of its G glycoprotein which normally mediates attachment and entry of the host cell. The S protein changes the tropism of the recombinant virus and provides a new antigen target for the immune system. VSV is highly attenuated in human cells and is tightly controlled by the host antiviral interferon system. It is also the vaccine vector for the highly effective Ebola virus vaccine. The diagnostic and vaccine reagents developed in this proposal will be distributed and tested by colleagues at the Canadian Center of Vaccinology (Halifax) and VIDO-InterVac Vaccine Cenre in Saskatoon. The final aim of this proposal will use the reagents generated in the proposal to study cell receptors for COVID19 coronavirus and study infections in susceptible cells using model viruses of lower risk and pathogenicity.

column36: Development of Vaccines to Prevent SARS-CoV-2 Infection of High Risk Individuals
column37: The physical-distancing strategy currently implemented in the Covid-19 pandemic in Canada has been very effective in preventing the vast majority of Canadians from being infected by SARS-CoV-2. This essential short-term strategy is saving lives, but paradoxically will leave most of our citizens without protective immunity and a recurrent outbreak is both predictable and likely without an effective Canadian vaccine strategy. A global effort has been initiated to identify an effective Covid-19 vaccine, testing a variety of vaccine platforms and strategies. column36: Development of safe and effective vaccines against COVID-19
column37: The current COVID-19 pandemic is a worldwide threat. Moreover, the ability of asymptomatic carriers to transmit the disease is making it very difficult to contain and control. As such, safe and effective vaccines against COVID-19 are urgently needed. The goal of this research project is to develop effective vaccines to combat COVID-19. Combining our expertise in coronaviruses, vaccine development and viral vector engineering, we plan to take novel approaches to develop highly effective vaccines against COVID-19. We will use a helper-dependent adenoviral (HD-Ad) vector to deliver antigens and we will also generate a bacterium-based BCG-COVID-19 compound vaccine. The HD-Ad vectors that we will use offer several advantages over the conventional Ad vectors: 1) they are safer for human use and potent in the delivery of specific antigens, 2) they have a large DNA carrying capacity for expressing multiple antigen genes without the expression of non-specific antigens from the vector and 3) they produce antigens in their native folded form with proper glycosylation and may not require boosting. BCG is an attenuated bacterium and the approved vaccine against tuberculosis in humans. In addition to its specific immune protection against TB, BCG has non-specific benefits as it prevents about 30% of infections with pathogens including viruses. We will construct a recombinant BCG that secretes a fusion protein composed of the bacterial protein antigen 85A fused to the SARS-CoV-2 RBD. This recombinant vaccine will not only retain BCG's nonspecific anti-viral benefits but will also produce specific immune protection against COVID-19. The success of this project will allow us to proceed with the production of the clinical grade vaccines for further testing clinically more than one vaccines while establishing a collaboration with a Canadian biotech that can oversee the licensing and large-scale production of this vaccine for the Canadian market.

column37: The pandemic of Covid-19 caused by respiratory SARS-CoV-2 infection has brought the world to a standstill. The physical-distancing strategy currently implemented in the pandemic aims to prevent the majority of Canadians from being infected by SARS-CoV-2. Our Team has internationally recognized reputation in bench-to-human translational vaccine research. Particularly relevant to the proposal is our strong expertise in advanced viral vector bioengineering, vaccine efficacy testing in small animal models at CL3 facility, clinical-grade vaccine production at GMP manufacturing facility, optimized inhaled aerosol vaccine delivery method, and clinical vaccine trials. We are confident that our project will make available to Canadians a superb, needle/pain-free vaccine strategy capable of potent respiratory mucosal protection against Covid-19.

column37: In December 2019 a novel coronavirus (CoV) was identified as the cause of pneumonia in a cluster of patients in Wuhan, China. Namely, whether it induces antibodies that are capable of blocking infection - called neutralizing antibodies. Finally, we want to demonstrate that this vaccine actually protects the animals from infection and does not cause any deleterious events, so animals will be infected and monitored to determine whether the vaccine stops infection. Subsequent experiments to support this data will be performed at VIDO-InterVac. Together this work will increase the capacity to assess other vaccine concepts that are being worked on across Canada to identify the best approach to stop transmission of SARS-CoV-2.

column36: Towards a comprehensive understanding of adaptive immunity to SARS-CoV-2
column37: The vast majority of people who get COVID19 fully recover from infection. This means that their immune system has successfully eliminated the virus. After we recover from a virus infection, the immune system leaves behind white blood cells, called memory cells, that can remember the previous infection and prevent that infection from recurring upon re-exposure. This is the basis of how vaccines work. After we recover from infection, two kinds of white blood cells persist, T cells and B cells. T cells and B cells have molecules on their surface that allow them to recognize the specific virus they were first exposed to. B cells give rise to antibody producing cells, while T cells can eliminate infected cells. Some antibodies can bind the virus in such a way that they fully block the virus from entering the cell. These are called neutralizing antibodies and these are ideal to fully protect us from being infected again. However, in some infections, weak antibodies, instead of neutralizing the virus, can actually make things worse by promoting uptake of the virus into cells or by overstimulating certain cells of the immune system. Therefore, there is a pressing need to understand the details of the immune response in COVID19 patients. We need to understand what parts of the virus are recognized when we have an immune response associated with a good outcome and what if any aspects of T and B cell responses are associated with a bad outcome. By studying the immune response in asymptomatic, mild and severe cases in depth, we hope to determine the correlates of a good immune response and use this information to design vaccines and to monitor people for the correct immune responses. For some infections T cell and B cell responses last a lifetime, whereas for other infections they do not last as long. Our study will develop the tools we need to follow how long the immune response to COVID19 infection lasts and to help with evaluating the level of protection in the population.

column36: Characterization of Cellular and Humoral Immunity Against SARS-CoV-2
column37: Understanding the role of the immune response against SARS-CoV-2 in recovery from infection is critical for identifying people who have been exposed to SARS-CoV-2 and for determining whether the immune response confers protection against future infection. It is also critical for design and development of effective vaccines and immune-based treatments against SARS-CoV-2. We plan to systematically assess the strength, specificity, nature and durability of antibody and cellular immune responses generated against SARS-CoV-2 in relation to severity of infection. To do this, we will recruit individuals deemed to have recovered from SARS-CoV-2 infection and additionally test their close contacts to identify individuals who had very mild or asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection. With blood samples obtained from these subjects and from persons hospitalized for SARS-CoV-2 infection, we will test and compare how their antibodies and immune cells interact with SARS-CoV-2 proteins how these interactions affect SARS-CoV-2 in cell culture and how these interactions change over time. These experiments should identify parts of the virus targeted by successful immune responses, parts of the virus targeted by detrimental immune responses and the strength required of successful immune responses. Analysis of these data will help guide vaccine design and evaluation. Testing the ability of antibodies from recovered persons to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 growth in cell culture will provide criteria for identifying the best candidates for donation of convalescent plasma to treat SARS-CoV-2-infected persons with severe disease.

column37: Antibiotic overuse is an important contributor to antimicrobial resistance. Over 90% of antibiotic use is in the community, with estimates of unnecessary use ranging from 25%-50%. Audit and feedback (A&F) can be effective in improving prescribing behaviour. Jurisdictions implementing community antibiotic A&F programs will benefit from tools and resources to optimize effectiveness. Research that builds on existing knowledge to advance the field of A&F is needed. Important questions remain surrounding the optimal data to use and methods of data delivery to clinicians, tools to incorporate data into practice, and ensure sustainability over time. We propose assembling an international network of antimicrobial stewardship, primary care, and implementation science (with A&F expertise) experts, which will bring diversity in expertise, geographical locations, career stages, and genders. The network will be coordinated by three co-leads; antimicrobial stewardship (Schwartz), primary care (Lindbeak), and implementation science (Ivers). With overall objectives to provide best practice resources on conducting A&F interventions on antibiotic use in primary care and define research priorities to advance this field. We will employ a modified Delphi method to solicit input, while minimizing bias, from subgroups of experts via video conferencing and 2 multi-day in-person meetings over two years. There is also a contingency plan to host virtual meetings due to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions. We will leverage existing international collaboration with the A&F MetaLab, to facilitate ongoing knowledge translation. Multiple outputs from this network, including a systematic review, best practice resources and toolkits, and a paper outlining research priorities, will be organized into publishable peer-reviewed manuscripts as part of a broader dissemination and knowledge translation plan that leverages existing stakeholder networks among this diverse network.

column36: BRAIN STIMULATION RECONSIDERED - PARTICIPATIVE DEVELOPMENT OF A CODE OF CONDUCT FOR THE EUROPEAN UNION Acronym: TIMCODE Coordinator: Prof. Dr. Martina Schraudner (CERRI)
column37: Nerve cells communicate via electrical processes. Therefore, these can also be influenced by electrical or magnetic impulses or by other physical stimuli (e.g. ultrasound and lights). Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) uses this ability. The most commonly used methods are repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). In recent years, these very effective instruments have been approved in numerous countries for the treatment of various diseases. In this context, the scientific community has developed safety guidelines for the treatment of patients. However, in recent years, in addition to clinical research, a large market has developed in which people buy devices for cognitive enhancement or for selftreatment of neuropsychiatric conditions, and use them at home without medical supervision. This development, inter alia, raises questions that are currently difficult for researchers and governments to answer as the extend beyond their respective communities to larger spectrum of society. For example, where exactly is the border between enhancement (when NIBS is used to perform better in a given task or sport) or recreational (when NIBS is used because itself produces pleasure, e.g. lucid dreaming) and treatment (when NIBS is used to correct a given disease or to ameliorate symptoms)? Should the procedures also be used to treat children? In order to address questions like this in a reflective manner, this project aims to develop a participatory code of conduct for NIBS. To this end, actors from various scientific disciplines, society, business and governments will be involved. The involvement of laypersons and various expert perspectives will provide scientists with a tool to reflect on their own research and governments will be able to use the Code of Conduct for NIBS to create long-term guidelines that are valid EU-wide.

column36: Investigating the metabolic benefits of intermittent fasting-induced ketogenesis in a non-alcoholic fatty liver disease model
column37: Investigating the metabolic benefits of intermittent fasting-induced ketogenesis in a non-alcoholic fatty liver disease model Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most prevalent form of chronic liver disorder in the world. The disease is characterized by the build-up of excess fat in the liver, progressing to liver tissue inflammation and scarring, as well as in extreme cases liver cancer. Currently there are no therapeutic interventions for the direct treatment of NAFLD, rather patients are often advised with lifestyle adjustments (i.e. exercise and diet-restriction), to manage the complications of the disease (i.e. obesity and insulin resistance). Intermittent fasting has become a popular dietary intervention that has shown metabolic benefits against several diseases in both human and animal models. Fasting promotes the upregulation of ketogenesis for the production of ketone bodies. Besides providing an additional fuel source to non-liver tissues, ketone bodies have also been implied in the protection of cardiovascular, nervous system, and liver diseases, through their roles in mediating anti-inflammatory and antioxidant responses. However, the mechanism by which intermittent fasting confers its metabolic benefits in a disease model, such as NAFLD, has not yet been explored. Thus, I hypothesize that intermittent fasting-induced activation of ketogenesis will have therapeutic applications against NAFLD. To test this hypothesis, I will utilize both cell (in vitro) and mouse (in vivo) studies mimicking ketogenesis insufficiency and ketogenesis upregulation, to better understand the underlying mechanism of ketone body-mediated protection and treatment of NAFLD. This information will be crucial in developing successful NAFLD-directed therapeutics.

column36: Uncovering the mechanisms by which early life adversity increases susceptibility to infection.
column37: In addition to our individual genetics and lifestyles, factors linked to socioeconomic status such as income, food security and early life experiences influence health and infection risk. Obesity is unfortunately linked to low socioeconomic status due to difficulty accessing quality food. Children born to obese mothers are more likely to be hospitalized for an infection and current research indicates that this is due to changes in their immune and metabolic systems that occur before they are born. Previous studies in the Sloboda lab have shown that feeding pregnant mice a high fat diet results in changes to their offspring's growth and development. Previous studies in the Bowdish lab have shown that increased inflammation leads to changes in immune cell development. We will study mice whose mothers were pregnant under ideal conditions and those who were fed a high fat diet when they were pregnant. We believe that mice born to mothers who have experienced early life adversity - in the context of a high fat diet - will be more susceptible when we infect them with Streptococcus pneumoniae. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of bacterial pneumonia and kills one million children younger than five years-old annually. Because having had pneumonia as a child is associated with metabolic, respiratory and cardiovascular disease, we will determine whether mice that are fed a high fat diet have more complications after pneumonia. Even though we can treat and recover from most infections, there are long term health consequences that we cannot yet prevent. These studies will help us uncover why children born to mothers who have experienced socioeconomic stress are at higher risk for infection, allowing us to develop new therapies and prevention strategies.

column36: Prevalence and Determinants of Frailty Across Low-, Middle- and High-Income Countries
column37: Frailty is a state of poor health in which an individual experiences weakness and tiredness and often has complex medical problems. Frailty can result from one disease or a combination of multiple diseases but may also be present in individuals with no obvious signs of a particular illness. A frail person with an illness often ends up in the hospital and emergency room more often than a non-frail person with the same illness. Often frail individuals must stay longer in the hospital compared to non-frail individuals because frailty causes them to become very sensitive to medical treatment. This can cause unintended harm and worsen their already delicate condition. Frail individuals usually depend on family or personal support workers to carry out their daily activities such as cooking and cleaning. Frailty is most common among older adults. There will be about 2 billion older adults worldwide by 2050. Despite frailty being a worldwide phenomenon, most frailty research is done in predominantly Caucasian, high-income countries. The aim of this study is to understand how common frailty is among individuals of diverse ethnic, socio-cultural and economic backgrounds. We will measure and compare frailty across 21 different countries and five different continents and compare how different aspects that may lead to frailty, such as income and education, differ among these individuals. We will analyze data that will allow us to measure frailty in two separate ways to enhance the comprehensiveness of our study. Such a study has never been conducted on such a large and diverse group of people. We hope that as our knowledge of aging expands scientifically, the scope and impact of our research also expands globally, helping older adults all over the world.

column36: Etude du role de la sulfurostransferase mitochondriale MPST dans la necrose regulee des macrophages apres infection par le virus de la grippe
column37: La grippe, une maladie respiratoire causee par le virus influenza, tue des milliers de personnes chaque annee, malgre la disponibilite d'antiviraux et de vaccins. Cela tient en partie au fait que l'eradication du virus ne permet pas de determiner si un patient survivra. De fait, une protection insuffisante des tissus contre les dommages causes par la mort cellulaire contribue de maniere importante aux phenotypes de la grippe. Nous savons que les cellules peuvent declencher leur propre mort par necrose via deux voies paralleles dont l'une permet l'assemblage de l'inflammasome et la mort lytique caspase-1 dependante. Mais trop de necroses finit par endommager les poumons. Bien que les mecanismes menant a l'activation de cette necrose soient definis, on en sait peu sur la maniere dont l'inflammasome est desactivee pour arreter la signalisation de la caspase-1 dans les macrophages, permettant un retour a la sante apres l'eradication du virus de la grippe. Le H2S joue un role important dans la regulation de la mort cellulaire programme. En effet, de recentes etudes ont demontre que des donneurs de H2S inhibent les activites de la caspase-1 induites par l'inflammasome. Nous avons decouvert que la proteine 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurostransferase (MPST), qui produit du H2S3, supprime l'activation de la mort cellulaire necrotique caspase-1-dependante suite a une infection avec le mononegavirus parainfluenza de type 1. Je propose donc d'examiner les effets de la proteine MPST sur la survie cellulaire des macrophages apres infection. L'objectif de mon projet de maitrise est donc d'etudier comment l'activite catalytique de MPST sert d'interrupteur biologique pour la necrose induite par le virus de la grippe et d'examiner son role en tant que facteur de survie pour les macrophages.

column36: Reproductive Rainbow: Exploring Fertility Intentions and Family Planning Experiences Within the LGBTQ2S Community
column37: Individuals in the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and two-spirit (LGBTQ2S) community encounter barriers to accessing health care, for example, feeling uncomfortable discussing health concerns and receiving care that is not specific to their needs. Accessing health care in areas that are highly gender-specific - such as family planning and fertility intentions - can be particularly challenging for those in the LGBTQ2S community. Community partners currently engaging with LGBTQ2S individuals highlighted fertility intentions and family planning as often-asked questions; however, limited community supports and answers to these questions currently exist in Saskatoon. This study aims to explore how to best support fertility intentions and family planning for individuals within the LGBTQ2S community. This study will use case study methodology, an intersectionality framework, and arts-based research (ABR) to achieve these aims. ABR allows for the creation of visual art to engage community discussion and participation, and to explore the experiences within this population. column36: Alterations structurelles et dynamiques des vaisseaux sanguins pulmonaires chez le chat
column37: Le projet consiste en une exploration du remodelage vasculaire pulmonaire chez le chat souffrant d'atteinte respiratoire ainsi que de ses consequences sur la circulation sanguine pulmonaire. En effet, ce phenomene implique un epaississement important des arteres pulmonaires qui, en theorie, devrait mener a une augmentation de la pression sanguine pulmonaire et causer une condition appelee l'hypertension pulmonaire. Cette derniere est tres meconnue chez le chat et n'a ete observee que dans de rares cas. Afin d'etudier la relation entre ces deux phenomenes, le projet se deroulera en 3 parties afin de nous permettre de tirer les meilleures conclusions possibles. La premiere, un examen de la portee, sera effectuee afin de faire ressortir le maximum de connaissance relative au remodelage vasculaire pulmonaire chez le chat, ainsi que des valeurs de references pour la taille normale de leurs arteres pulmonaires. Ensuite, une analyse histologique sera realisee afin de mesurer la taille des differentes couches des arteres pulmonaires de chats atteint d'un desordre bronchiolaire, une condition respiratoire grave. Le but etant d'evaluer la prevalence et la severite des lesions vasculaires. Finalement, une etude clinique sera realisee sur des chats demontrant des symptomes de maladie respiratoire afin d'evaluer, via l'echocardiographie, la presence potentielle de signes reliees a de l'hypertension pulmonaire. Les resultats de ces etudes nous permettrons de mieux comprendre l'impact des maladies respiratoires sur la circulation sanguine pulmonaire du chat, et potentiellement, adapter l'approche veterinaire et le plan de traitement des maladies respiratoires en fonction des changements vasculaires.

column36: Elucidating pathogenic signalling mechanisms underlying SCN2A dysfunction in Autism
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a diverse group of brain disorders that exhibit a range of severities between individuals. There are currently no targeted treatments for the disorder because disease origins remain poorly understood. ASD has a major genetic component with large-scale genetic sequencing studies having identified hundreds of risk genes. Studying risk genes in animal models (eg. mice) or human stem cell (hSC)-derived neurons allows us to study how specific mutations impair brain development and lead to ASD. My project will study one of the top risk genes identified to date, SCN2A, which encodes for the Nav1.2 sodium channel, which is important for neuronal communication. The current understanding of how SCN2A mutations impair brain development and lead to ASD remain poor. Studies in mouse models of Scn2a suggest neurons lacking one copy of the gene are less active and have defects in neural communication. We have new work showing reduced neural activity in hSC-derived neurons lacking SCN2A. Therefore, I will study how the loss of SCN2A affects normal neuronal function and communication and restore SCN2A to normal levels to reverse the defects previously observed. Using a combination of transcriptomic and proteomic techniques in hSC-derived neurons of individuals with SCN2A mutations, I will shed light on how SCN2A mutations lead to abnormal brain development in ASD. Furthermore, I will increase the amount of SCN2A levels in patient stem cell-derived neurons using new CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technologies to reverse previously seen neuronal defects. My project will be one of the first comprehensive studies on SCN2A human patient-derived neurons, revealing insight into how SCN2A mutations impair brain development and can lead to ASD symptoms.

column36: Development and preclinical testing in human cell models and transgenic mice of a novel treatment for Schinzel-Giedion Syndrome
column37: Schinzel-Giedion Syndrome (SGS) is a rare disease usually leading to death in the first decade of life. SGS is caused by mutations in a gene called SETBP1, which increases the stability of the SETBP1 protein allowing it to continue carrying out its function when it might otherwise be degraded. While SGS is a multi-system disorder, a major burden on affected children and their families are the intractable seizures (ie seizures that do not respond to any known medication) that occur frequently in any given day. In collaboration with the SGS Foundation which is run by and for families of people with SGS, we have developed stem cell models derived from six children with SGS and their healthy parents, as well as four mouse models of SGS. We have re-purposed an internationally approved drug currently used to treat Multiple Sclerosis (MS) and that is being investigated in other non-MS clinical trials related to brain health. We have discovered that this drug can reverse molecular signatures of SGS in human brain-like cells. The purpose of this proposal is to perform preclinical proof-of-principle studies to develop this drug and to understand its mechanism of action to create a viable treatment for SGS to reduce seizure intensity and frequency. These studies include investigating: 1) protein and lipid turnover in single cells from mouse and human before and after drug treatment; 2) changes in synaptic vesicle release to understand if this is rescued by drug treatment, which is especially relevant for seizure control; 3) drug effects on mouse brain structure and behaviour, as well as bioavailability of the drug in mouse SGS models; 4) the transcriptional effects of the drug in different types of human brain cells and mouse SGS models with the idea of understanding downstream effects on all human genes; and 5) machine learning approaches using data across all research modalities to aid in determining the validity of the drug as a future treatment for SGS children.

column37: GNE myopathy (GNEM) is a rare severely debilitating muscle disease which affects 1 to 9:1,000,000 people among all ethnicities, with elevated carrier rates in populations of Eastern Europe and Asian heritage, including Jewish, Persian, East Indian, Arab and Japanese. There are no approved therapies and research efforts on sialylation-increasing therapies are difficult because of drug absorption and the absence of biomarkers in clinical development. These challenges are the main focus of our project. ProDGNE aims to overcome these obstacles through a unique joint collaboration among European and Canadian experts in clinical GNEM and basic research in sialic acid, organic synthesis, and -OMICS. Our developed prodrug when processed within cells becomes an active therapy, highly increasing sialic acid in GNEM patient cells and demonstrating a higher stability when compared to clinically tested drugs. The ProDGNE consortium will develop proof of principle studies fostering early stage development for innovative therapeutic strategies tested in vitro in patient derived cells and in vivo in GNE animal models that mimic the pathological mechanism in patients. Moreover, post-translational modifications will be explored and the newly identified biomarkers, will be utilized to monitor efficacy.

column37: Essential tremor is a neurological disorder causing involuntary shaking of the hands and arms. It is of the most common movement disorders, affecting 1% of the worldwide population. Currently, there are no cures for essential tremor and available drug treatment only reduces symptoms. The lack of treatment for the disease is mostly due to the unknown nature of the disease. We previously analyzed genes in patients suffering from essential treatment and discovered mutations in a protein implicated in calcium transport in the cerebellum, a brain region associated with essential tremor. The goal of this study is to characterize the function of this protein in essential tremor by studying its interaction with other proteins in the cerebellum. This project will shine light on previously unknown mechanisms implicated in essential tremor and could lead to drug development to treat the disease.

column36: Telerehabilitation with Aims to Improve Lower Extremity Recovery (TRAIL)
column37: Stroke is one of the leading causes of adult disability and death in Canada. As prognoses continue to improve with medical and research advances, more survivors are transitioning back to the community. The current healthcare and rehabilitation systems, however, do not adequately support the hospital-to community transition, especially for those living in rural areas. This disparity in support can lead to a number of different recovery issues following discharge. Telerehabilitation is a plausible solution to support stroke survivors during this critical transition period, as it uses the accessibility and convenience of technology to bring the direct interactions with a physical therapist to the community. While there has been some use of telerehabilitation to facilitate recovery post-stroke, it is highly under-used and there is a gap in knowledge of using this type of service delivery with a trained physical therapist. My current research focuses on a single group pre-post telerehabilitation study to optimize lower extremity recovery among community-living stroke survivors. People who have experienced a stroke within the past 12 months will be recruited to take part in this 4-week telerehabilitation study. Participants will use an iPad and a video-conferencing software to connect with a physical therapist trained in the delivery of a lower extremity exercise program using video-conferencing technology. We will examine the feasibility of this protocol, as well as examine its effects on clinical outcomes in the areas of functional mobility, impairment, quality of life, and self-management. The results of this study will enhance our understanding of how we can better support stroke survivors transitioning back to the community using technology to promote recovery.

column36: Neurocognitive functioning under acute stress in adults with psychosis and early life stress
column37: Psychosis is a common medical condition, affecting 3% of the population, particularly in individuals with a history of early life stress (ELS; i.e., sexual and physical abuse, and physical and emotional neglect). Neurocognitive deficits (NC; i.e., attention and executive functioning) have been identified as a robust feature of psychotic disorders (PD) and are demonstrated to be impaired under stress in healthy individuals and those with PD. The present study will be the first to stratify performance on NC processes under acute stress in individuals with psychotic disorders with and without ELS. This study will test the hypothesize that individuals with a PD and ELS will perform poorer on an NC task testing flexibility of attention and executive functioning after administration of acute stress in comparison to individuals with PD only and healthy controls. A mixed model with repeated measures test will be used to identify group differences in NC performance at baseline and post acute stress. Furthermore, sex, gender and current medication will be controlled in all analysis. Stress is unavoidable but manageable given the right tools. Given that cognitive impairments are associated with poorer outcomes in daily, occupational and social domains, this study will help guide interventions that remediate NC functions in individuals with a PD and history of trauma and equip individuals with the capacity and tools to deal with stress in a health and effective manner.

column36: Modelling Age- and Sex-related Changes in Gait Coordination Strategies in a Healthy Adult Population Using Principal Component Analysis
column37: As we age, the likelihood of experiencing walking impairments increases which can have consequences on overall health and independence. This proposed research is focused on developing an understanding of age- and sex-related changes in gait coordination strategies in a healthy adult population. The current mechanistic understanding of normal gait, as well as the dimensionality of person-to-person variability, is limited. Utilizing a series of principal component analysis (PCA) models to represent inter-joint kinematic coordination and inter-joint force propagation, at the hip, knee and ankle joints respectively, will allow for the investigation of the biomechanics of non-pathological gait. Results will be compared between young and older adults as well as between males and females, to examine if there are any mechanistic differences that are age- or sex-specific. The aim of this project is to identify specific patterns of healthy joint mechanics to be able to inform diagnostic information for early recognition of mobility decline as well as inform mobility management solutions going forward in order to improve longevity and mobility and independence in aging adults.

column37: The SMILE project is an international effort where European countries and Canada are coming together to provide digital solutions that can help people aged 65 - 80 years with brain disorders (dementia), lung disease (COPD) or other complex health conditions. This observational study (VISION-2) will be conducted with 900 patients who have surgery and are at risk for serious complications. We will use a type of artificial intelligence called machine learning to study these readings. We will look for slight changes in vital signs that may lead to heart muscle injury, bleeding and infection. Once we know what these signs are, we can then develop an alert system to warn us so we can stop the complications before they happen. We will then look at how effective this alert system can be in 100 patients who will be assigned at random to wear the Vitaliti (TM) device or not for the first 30 days after surgery. At present, seniors die from infection and other serious complications after surgery- this work is an opportunity to make a real difference. Currently, few structures in current healthcare systems across the EU and Canada support seniors in dealing with unfavorable outcomes related to the ageing process. With SMILE, the hope is to develop age-friendly innovations that are accepted by the ageing population and their care teams. This work is an opportunity to empower older adults and maintain independence and wellbeing to overall improve the quality of life.

column36: Treating inherited blinding disease with a slow released form of the rod-derived cone viability factor protein
column37: Vision relies on two types of photoreceptors in the retina at the back of the eye: rod photoreceptors, which are responsible for night vision, and cone photoreceptors, which are responsible for daylight vision. Rods and cones have an intimate relationship, with rod photoreceptors producing a factor, rod-derived cone viability factor (RdCVF), which is critical to cone viability. When rod photoreceptors die, cone photoreceptors die and all vision is lost; however, if we could find a way to preserve cone photoreceptors, then we could overcome vision loss associated with blinding diseases. Geneticists have shown that one of the most common forms of inherited blinding diseases is caused by mutations in large numbers of genes, some of which are only active in rod photoreceptors. The death of these rods results in the loss of a protein, rod-derived cone viability factor (RdCVF), which then results in the loss of cone photoreceptors and ultimately blindness. In order to stop the progression of this disease, we propose to save cone photoreceptors, and hence daylight vision, by replacing the lost RdCVF with newly delivered RdCVF. Specifically, we propose to deliver a novel slow-release formulation of RdCVF directly to the eyes of patients using a strategy already shown to be safe for patients with age-related macular degeneration. We will study the benefit of our treatment strategy in three models of blinding diseases, starting from the mouse and rat to a novel model in a minipig, a species in which the eyes are similar those of humans. DrEYE is a preclinical study of an innovative treatment that, with success, will restore vision to the two million patients worldwide suffering from inherited blinding diseases and for which there are no other options.

column36: Targeting Sensory Dysfunctions in Autism Spectrum Disorders
column37: Autism and sensory processing challenges often occurred together, and affected individuals might experience 'hyper or hypo' reactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment. These sensory differences can affect behavior and learning. Sensory function is regulated by the sensory nervous system, which is a part of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) in the body. Over the past decades, independent lines of clinical and basic research have supported the hypothesis that dysregulation of the sensory system is part of the core symptomatology of ASD. For a long time, it was thought that sensory issues in autism were due to disruption of the central nervous system. However, there is emerging evidence that sensory processing disorders in autism arise due to the abnormal function of the sensory nervous system. In our study, our team is studying whether 3 established high risk genetic factors for autism cause sensory dysfunction. We believe that mutations FMRP, CYFIP1 and TAOK2 impair sensory nerve cell development by disrupting the production of important proteins required for electrical communication. To study this, our team will utilize a combination of model systems, including genetically engineered flies, mice, and stem cell-derived human sensory neurons. We will perform behavioral experiments to identify the sensory defects (eg. smell and touch). Further, we will test whether the production of proteins in neural cells is abnormal. Finally, we will test whether specific drugs and gene therapies that correct the abnormal protein production defects, will lead to a reversal of the sensory behavioral deficits in our animal models. Together, these studies will reveal a new line of scientific evidence that genetic mutations impair protein production in sensory neural cells, which ultimately leads to sensory deficits. Our study would open up new possibilities for treating sensory abnormalities related to ASD.

column36: Restoring Motor Functions in Parkinson's Disease with Noninvasive Hybrid Transcranial Neuromodulation
column37: The main objective of this consortium is to supplement invasive deep brain stimulation with new non-invasive brain stimulation techniques in the treatment of Parkinson patients. column36: Developing BBB-ASL as non-invasive early biomarker of Alzheimer's disease (DEBBIE)
column37: One of the earliest signs of Alzheimer's Disease is the loss of the Blood-Brain-Barrier (BBB) integrity in the brain's vascular system, which can be imaged with positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). While most methods require contrast agents, arterial spin labeling (ASL) is an MRI technique for non-invasive measurement of perfusion and change in the vascular permeability or BBB integrity. ASL is currently the only technique for mapping local changes in BBB integrity without the use of contrast-enhancing agents or radioactive tracers. However, for BBB integrity measurement it cannot be used reliably in a clinical setting due to often rather long scan times and sensitivity to patient-specific dynamic changes in blood flow. We propose to develop a robust ASL BBB integrity mapping technique by using novel innovative concepts to automatically adapt relevant MRI scan parameters to the patient's dynamic blood flow status at scan time. Combined with standardized image processing, this will provide a sensitive non-invasive biomarker/predictor of cognitive decline. The newly developed imaging technology will be validated against established BBB invasive technique (PET) and evaluated on patients at four clinical sites.

column36: NEURofeedback for self-stimulation of the brain as therapy for ParkInson DisEaSe (NEURIPIDES)
column37: We will develop a new type of treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD) based on neurofeedback. Neurofeedback is a type of treatment that allows people to see their own brain activity in real time, so that they can learn how to control and self-regulate it. Existing PD treatments are not effective for certain symptoms, and can also require brain surgery. Therefore, new treatments that address these problems are needed. Our project will take place over 3 stages: In stage 1, we will find out what the brain activity of people with PD looks like when their symptoms are well controlled. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a type of brain surgery that is able to give many people with PD good symptom relief. Using an imaging tool called functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we will see what the brain activity of people with PD who have successfully received DBS looks like. We will find patterns of brain activity associated with PD patients who have improved their i) motor symptoms (such as tremor, slowness, or stiffness), and ii) non-motor symptoms (such as their mood, memory, or attention). In stage 2, we will develop a neurofeedback system for people with PD. They will be able to see their own brain activity in real time, and will try to match it to the patterns of good brain activity we find in stage 1 in order to improve their symptoms. In stage 3, we will perform a trial - taking place at multiple hospitals in different countries - of our neurofeedback system to see whether it can help improve the symptoms of people with PD. Our hope is that we will develop a new type of treatment for PD that does not require brain surgery. We believe that it will be able to help patients who have never received DBS, and patients who have had DBS but could benefit from more symptom relief.

column36: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange in Septic Shock: A Pilot Study
column37: Septic shock, a life-threatening infection, is among the most common reasons for admission to intensive care units in Canada and is a leading cause of death. Septic shock leads to uncontrolled inflammation and blood clotting abnormalities that leads to death in up to up to 50% of patients. Apart from antibiotics and supportive care, there are few treatments available to improve survival. Therapeutic plasma exchange (a type of blood purification) is a commonly used procedure that, if used in septic shock, could potentially save lives by removing harmful substances and replacing missing blood components serving to restore balance. Plasma exchange appears to demonstrate positive benefit in several published foundational studies. In preparation for a national randomized controlled trial, we are planning a pilot study in Canada. The primary aim of this pilot study is to evaluate our ability to recruit enough patients per month to demonstrate the feasibility of a larger trial designed to answer the question "does plasma exchange reduce mortality in patients with septic shock". Our secondary aims are to evaluate adherence to the protocol, safety of the procedure and to study biologic signals to help understand how plasma exchange might be working.

column36: Matricellular protein CCN5/WISP2 mediates a synergistic stimulation of pancreatic beta-cell expansion by IGF-I and Wnt signaling
column37: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin which controls energy metabolism; lack of beta cells or insulin secretion causes diabetes mellitus. Studies on the regeneration of pancreatic islets, using animal models, represent a major effort leading to a cure of this deadly disease. Insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-I is a peptide hormone mainly produced from the liver. Research of last decade by us and others has established that IGF-I is a potent growth factor for pancreatic islet cells, promotes cell survival and prevents onset of experimental diabetes. In order to explore where and how IGF-I acts on the islet cells, we have screened and identified the molecular targets using the technique of whole genome cDNA microarray. Prominently among the 82 preliminary targets we have discovered, CCN5/WISP2 has never been known to be expressed by the islet cells nor regulated by IGF-I. In 2 recent studies we have shown that CCN5 is normally expressed in islet beta cells, IGF-I directly stimulates its gene expression, and IGF-I overexpression caused increased level in the islets. We further demonstrate that CCN5 overexpression accelerates the proliferation of insulin-producing tumor cells, activates signaling molecules FAK, Akt and Erk1/2 kinases, and CCN5 overexpression prevents cell death. We thus hypothesize that CCN5 is normally expressed by islet beta cells and activated by IGF-I, its increased production promotes islet cell proliferation and regeneration, and survival, in concert to the action of IGF-I itself. Here, we propose to characterize the change in pancreatic beta cells after knocking out the production of CCN5; to establish that CCN5 treatment promotes beta cell growth or expansion in culture; to characterize a cell surface receptor which interacts with CCN5 and mediates its actions; and to test the therapeutic potential of CCN5 in preclinical, rodent diabetes. The findings will provide a fundamental insight into islet cell biology and lead for designing therapies.

column36: Validation of plasma amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, affecting almost half of Canadians over 85 years of age. With the aging of the population, the prevalence of dementia is expected to increase dramatically. This increase will bring major social and economic costs. Accordingly, there is a crucial need to find treatments that can slow or stop the progression of AD pathology before symptoms appear (the time that such treatments can bring greatest benefit). Clinical trials of such treatments require identification of persons with pre-symptomatic AD. At present, we can identify such persons only with very costly and not widely available PET scans of the brain, or by analyzing cerebrospinal fluid from (unacceptably invasive) Lumbar Punctures. Instead, we urgently need inexpensive and non-invasive methods to select trial participants. The obvious source for such methods is blood (plasma), but until now we haven't been able to measure (very low) plasma concentrations of the key elements of AD pathology, amyloid-beta and tau. Newly introduced methods may be able to do this, but we are not sure that their assay results are valid indicators of what is happening in the brain, Our main objective is therefore to assess the validity of plasma amyloid and tau measures as indicators of early AD pathology in cognitively normal individuals with a family history of AD dementia. We propose to use these new measures of amyloid and tau in a cohort of 385 individuals with a strong family history of AD dementia. First, we will compare these blood marker measures to other well-known brain markers of AD pathology. Then, we will test whether they can identify individuals with amyloid-beta and tau early in the course of the disease. Finally we will test if they can track memory decline over time. Success in this work will almost certainly make it much easier and less costly to conduct clinical trials of treatments that can prevent onset of AD symptoms.

column37: Women living with HIV (WLWH) experience high rates of poverty, food and house insecurity, and report low levels of self-reported health-related quality of life. The causes are multidimensional, but social factors, like stigma and isolation, that impede access to care are identified as potential causes. Community and individual programs that directly target WLWH can alter these health trajectories. Investigators on the team for this proposed project consulted WLWH from the Canadian HIV Sexual and Reproductive Health Cohort Study (CHIWOS) Community Advisory Board in the fall of 2018 to determine the focus of a program to improve the health and wellbeing of WLWH. This consultation informed the development of our proposed pilot study. In the current randomized feasibility and pilot trial, we propose to examine the acceptability and uptake of, and adherence to a 24-week aerobic dance program that is led by dance instructors who themselves are women living with HIV. We further propose to examine the effects of the dance program on a marker of immune cellular aging, as a primary health target, and traditional health markers, such as resting heart rate, blood pressure, waist circumference, and hemoglobin A1C. We will also examine changes in mental health and social inclusion that result from the dance program. The long-term goal for this study is to better understand our program and its effects, with the wider aim of fine-tuning a future larger, pan-BC randomized dance program with a larger cohort of women. By completing this project, we expect to enhance the physical, mental, and social health of WLWH.

column36: Chronic Obstructive Bladder Disease: Persistent Smooth Muscle Responses to the Damaged Microenvironment
column37: Bladder obstruction is common. Outflow in males is frequently blocked by prostate overgrowth, in females and children of all ages by neurologic or acquired outlet discoordination, and in male infants from obstructing urethral valves. After relief of obstruction, Chronic Obstructive Bladder Disease (COBD) persists in 50% of patients, causing infection, incontinence, poor emptying & filling, kidney damage, and severely harms quality of life. COBD related costs are approaching US$80 billion/year. There are no treatments to correct COBD. The first and only available drugs, discovered 50 years ago, treat symptoms, but muscle thickening, scarring, and bladder dysfunction persist, and no new drugs for COBD have yet been discovered--this represents a major knowledge gap. Most research has only studied obstruction, which cannot be detected early. Our goal is to find treatments AFTER the blockage is removed; COBD is the relevant human phase of the disease. In addition to muscle overgrowth, COBD bladders show excessive scar proteins called 'matrix'. A breakthough was our development of a sensitive mouse model of persistent disease (COBD) and model of reversible obstruction where the bladder returns to normal. We are now in a position to compare COBD and reversible obstruction to discover what genes and proteins are UNIQUELY present and problematic in COBD. We also discovered that the abnormal 'matrix' powerfully overdrives muscle cell growth even after the damaged 'matrix' is removed. This suggests muscle genes are being upset by 'epigenetic' changes in their genes: a powerful control process that changes gene function but leaves DNA alone. We believe the 'matrix' is epigeneticly driving muscle damage in COBD. We will now determine which COBD bladder changes are controlled by epigenetic processes, which COBD genes are being epigenetically changed, and then block the specific epigenetic changes we detect, expecting to reverse damage in COBD.

column36: Understanding Human Primary Atopic Disorders
column37: Nearly 1-in-3 Canadians have an allergic disease, such as asthma, food allergy, and eczema. Asthma alone affects 300 million people worldwide, with annual costs over $20 billion dollars. Finally, we will analyze data from over 3000 Canadian children who are enrolled in the CHILD cohort to determine if changes in the PADs genes are also associated with common allergic disease. This research is both important and timely. Understanding the causes of PADs will be life changing for the affected patients and their families, and also provides a unique opportunity to understand how changes in the function of the human immune system cause or contribute to allergic disease.

Our new D-lactate trap is a long string (or polymer), which keeps D-lactate in the gut and removes it from the body in the feces. This prevents D-lactate entering the blood. This new therapy is very safe since it is natural, biodegradable and does not to cross the gut barrier. We already know that our D-lactate trap lowers blood glucose and insulin in obese mice. We will now build a better trap by blocking D-lactate production from all bacteria and by forcing beneficial bacteria to eat D-lactate. There are lots of links between gut bacteria, diabetes and fatty liver disease. This work is new because it moves on from naming gut bacteria. Now we can build a trap for a source of fuel from bacteria. Safely trapping and removing D-lactate from gut bacteria can help lower blood glucose and liver fat without the need to make changes in diet.
