column36: Randomized Phase 3 Evaluation of Lower Dose (3-2-1 Strategy) vs. Full Dose of Ibrutinib for the Treatment of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
column37: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is an incurable blood malignancy with a long natural history, typically characterized by multiple recurrences and repeated requirement for treatment. Ibrutinib (Imbruvica(R)) has emerged as an effective novel therapy for the management of CLL. The standard ibrutinib dose for CLL is 420 mg once daily (3 tablets/day in 28 day cycles), with large randomized clinical trials demonstrating superiority over standard comparators. However, use of ibrutinib in the "real world" (outside of clinical trials) has demonstrated that important toxicities do arise, including major bleeding, heart rhythm abnormalities, diarrhea, joint pains, and infections. As such, dose reductions are frequently required to reduce toxicity with ibrutinib administration. Population-based studies of ibrutinib use suggest that this practice is very common, occurring in ~30-60% of patients. In a recent such study, pre-emptive dose reduction (within the first 3 months of treatment initiation) was able to reduce the toxicity of ibrutinib without compromising the effectiveness in the treatment of CLL. Furthermore, a recent study by our group of a pre-emptive dose reduction strategy ("3-2-1" dosing with initial cycle of 420mg/d or 3 tablets, reduced to 280mg or 2 tablets/d in cycle 2, and 140mg or 1 tablet/d in cycle 3 and onwards) confirmed that, at lower doses, the biologic activity of ibrutinib was fully maintained. We propose a randomized phase III study comparing these two common dosing strategies (a pre-emptive 3-2-1 strategy vs. a full dose strategy) to ensure that the lower dose strategy is just as effective and less toxic compared to full dosing. We further anticipate that the lower dose approach will be associated with improved outcomes of importance to patients and caregivers, including reductions in patient-reported side effects, less "financial toxicity" given the high out-of-pocket costs associated with treatment, and improved quality of life.

column36: The characterization and therapeutic targeting of metabolic and inflammatory signaling in chronic lymphedema
column37: The lymphatics are one of two essential circulatory systems present throughout the human body. When the lymphatic vessel system is blocked, fluid accumulates in tissues causing swelling and scarring. Up to 1 in 5 cancer patients have lymphedema as a side effect of cancer treatment because surgery and radiotherapy often unavoidably damages lymph nodes or lymphatic vessels. This disease is chronic, progressive, incurable, and leads to a high risk of infection and an additional risk of developing a lethal cancer. This research will develop the first effective treatment for lymphedema to improve the health and quality of life for patients with this chronic condition. Lymphedema is characterized by progressive accumulation of fibrotic tissue. Until recently, scarring disorders have been assumed to be irreversible. Our group, however, has successfully identified a new strategy that can potentially reverse tissue fibrosis. During scarring, cells accumulate and break down fats abnormally; restoring normal fat metabolism can reduce fibrosis. In lymphedema, we believe that: i) the excess accumulation of fluid and nutrients in tissues may exacerbate the metabolic and inflammatory defects in this condition, which lead to fibrosis; and ii) repairing these defects will reduce chronic lymphedema. This research will investigate the metabolic and inflammatory causes of lymphedema fibrosis (Aim 1), target metabolic and inflammatory causes to stop fibrosis (Aim 2), and even reverse aberrant tissue changes that occur during lymphedema (Aim 3). Our research team consists of scientists in metabolism, inflammation, bioinformatics, and chemistry as well as clinicians in oncology and lymphedema surgery. Based on our expertise, we will deliver new knowledge regarding the causes of tissue scarring in lymphedema. We will also identify and test new drugs to treat lymphedema, an incurable chronic condition affecting up to 1 in 5 Canadian cancer survivors.

column37: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, Canadians are facing newly arising tough health decisions. Research shows that when people are supported in making decisions, they have better outcomes. We propose to identify emergent decisions Canadians are facing and create a series of field-tested decision support tools to address their decision-making needs. We plan to conduct three surveys of Canadians every 6 months to identify emergent decisions they are facing. We will find, adapt, create, and test decision support tools based on their decisional needs. We will use rapid reviews to follow changing evidence and use a secured collaborative writing platform to allow for new evidence to be added into decision support tools in real time. Then study their use by providing them online and linking them into the electronic medical record. We will provide results for best strategies and create evidence-based decision support tools for empowering Canadians and supporting the important work of clinicians within health systems. Our study also fits Canadians' priorities for making informed decisions that match what matters most to them so their values prevail.

column36: Technologies for Home Medication Vigilance and Protection (TEC4Home MVP)
column37: Many patients with one or more chronic diseases, such as heart failure or weakness, need to take multiple medications for their condition. These patients face daily difficulty in following a complicated schedule in taking many medications at different times and dosages. For older patients, especially those with memory loss, taking medications as directed can be very hard if not impossible. One common but avoidable outcome for these patients can be the worsening of symptoms, which requires visiting the emergency department (ED) or being admitted to hospital for treatment. Home-based digital technologies can unobtrusively help patients taking medications regularly, monitor vital signs such as blood pressure and heartrate, and allow patients to connect with health professionals by video. In this project, we will put together the Medication Vigilance and Protection (MVP) platform, combining technologies that patients can use at home to manage their illness. We will: 1) use Spencer, a digital tool to remind patients when to take medications and get refills; 2) use devices for patients to easily measure their vital signs and share results with their doctors, nurses and pharmacists; and 3) analyze their data automatically to forecast their future health condition. We will work with scientific, medical, and technology experts and patient advisors to develop the MVP platform and ensure it meets the needs and preferences of older adults with heart failure. We will test the MVP platform in different communities in BC and Ontario to determine if it improves patients' health. We expect this project will help older adults with heart failure avoid unnecessarily visiting the hospital/ED, better manage their medications at home, and improve their quality of life. We also expect the platform to lower healthcare costs and be useful to caregivers and health professionals managing these patients.

column36: Elucidating the novel roles of a gap junction protein in the spatial arrangement of synapses
column37: In animals, cells exchange information between the neighboring cells in multiple interfaces. Gap junction is one of such interfaces that is formed between the two neighboring cells. Through gap junction, cells exchange small molecules and information to coordinate numerous biological and cellular processes. Gap junctions are composed of a group of proteins called connexins in vertebrates and innexins in invertebrates. In mammals, there is another group of gap junction proteins called pannexins. Interestingly, several works have shown that these gap junction proteins also control several biological processes independent of their function as gap junction components. We recently found that in the nerve cells, one of the gap junction proteins controls the position of synapses, which is a specialized interface that nerve cells use to communicate with their target cells. Nerve cells have to make synapses at the specific location within the cells for proper communication between the nerve cells and their target cells such as muscles. Abnormal synapse position due to the defective gap junction protein could, therefore, lead to serious neurological conditions. We aim at understanding how gap junction proteins control the position of synapses using nerve cells of nematode, Caenorhabditis elegans, as a genetic model system. From our research, we will learn novel mechanisms by which nerve cells form precise neurocircuit.

column36: Outcomes Associated with Direct Rapid Genetic Testing at Time of Breast Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Approximately 11% of all breast cancers are due to a mutation in a cancer predisposition gene, most frequently BRCA1 or BRCA2. These breast cancers should receive different treatments to increase the chance that a woman will survive, including bilateral mastectomy. However, women must know if they have a genetic mutation in a cancer causing gene at the time of diagnosis when treatment decisions are being made (rapid genetic testing). A new model of genetic testing at time of cancer diagnosis is needed to ensure equitable access to genetic testing for Canadian patients. Direct genetic testing offers patients limited to no pre-test discussion with a genetic counsellor, and written documents or other resources are provided. Our overall objective is to evaluate the impact of Direct Rapid Genetic Testing (DRGT) for breast cancer susceptibility genes in newly-diagnosed breast cancer patients on treatment and psychosocial outcomes, compared to women who received rapid genetic testing (RGT) with standard pre and post-test genetic counselling. We will recruit from 1000 women from hospitals throughout Canada, including those which do not have genetic counselling programs. Sequencing will be done on BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, PALB2, PTEN, STK11, TP53, ATM, and CHEK2 genes. We will have one central genetic counsellor (Women's College Hospital) who will provide post-test counselling. Genetic test results will available in 7 days. Outcomes will be compared between those who received RGT with standard genetic counselling to those who received Direct Rapid Genetic Testing. The traditional cancer genetics model is not sustainable with the current volumes of genetic testing. column37: Urologic and gynecologic patients often have problems requiring surgical reconstruction to recreate a normal function, notably for vaginal reconstruction and for the correction of stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Vaginal reconstruction is still a challenge due to the limited availability of suitable tissue for vaginal replacement. Traditional intervention methods have varying degrees of morbidity. More than 200 million people worldwide, 30-40% of all women during their lifetime, suffer from SUI. Synthetic midurethral slings (MUS) are the gold standard treatment for female patients with SUI. They have excellent short-term cure rates even if their efficacy tends to decrease over time. Nevertheless, campaigns against synthetic MUS led to their abolishment in many countries including severe restrictions in Canada. The traditional autologous fascial sling MUS, has then reemerged as a viable alternative. But, the readoption of autologous MUS is slow due to the surgical technical challenge and perceived higher morbidity rates. Interestingly, tissue engineering (TE) aims to replace dysfunctional tissues and organs. We successfully assembled a TE vaginal model (VM) using the patients' own cells. It has great histological organization and excellent mechanical resistance; hence, it would be possible to use it as a VM for reconstruction, or to serve as a MUS to correct SUI. We propose to reconstruct a vaginal substitute using patient's cells: autologous and free of synthetic material. We will also engineer a MUS made only with fibroblasts, to replace the synthetic material causing the actual turmoil. The development of autologous VM and MUS reconstructed by TE would significantly advance urology/gynecology and would have a considerable clinical impact. The expertise gathered in this research program in TE with Drs Bolduc, Germain, Ruel, and collaborators: Drs Bureau and Nadeau, combine strong clinical and basic science skills and gives excellent assurance of success.

column37: Emergency departments (ED) are specialized and costly resources designed to provide care for patients with urgent or life-threatening conditions. However, low-acuity ambulatory patients, that is, those consulting for health issues that do not require being kept on a gurney for observation, still represent 30-60% of all ED visits in Canada. This patient category has been controversially labeled as a source of ED overuse and misuse and hence unnecessary costs, even jeopardizing the mission of Canadian provincial health systems. It is suggested that such patients be directed to other more affordable care alternatives such as walk-in clinics. According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information, more than 2.7 million ED visits each year across Canada could be treated in community-based alternative settings. As Canadian hospitals struggle with ever-increasing expenditures, more efficient care pathways must be identified and strengthened in order to ensure the viability and sustainability of the health system for all Canadians. In our research program, we propose to compare the value of the care received by ambulatory patients presenting with acute respiratory conditions in EDs, walk-in clinics and primary care practices, and thereby provide deciders and policy makers with objective bases for: 1) determining the most efficient care setting for this patient category; and 2) implementing value-centered reforms that allow the best urgent care at the lowest cost for ambulatory patients with unexpected acute needs. We believe that this will constitute a major contribution to improving the cost-effectiveness and sustainability of Canadian health systems and thereby helping them to fulfil their mission of improving the health of the population.

column36: Investigating the role of accelerated neuronal aging in a mouse model of Huntington's disease from a circadian epigenomic perspective.
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a brain disease caused by an expansion of CAG nucleotide triplet in the huntingtin gene. The longer the CAG expansion, the earlier the onset of the disease. However, this DNA mutation does not fully explain the variability in the age-of-onset, nor fully predicts disease severity. There are numerous other important questions related to HD which need to be addressed. For instance, the average age of disease onset is 45 years, which means that there are decades of "healthy periods" in HD patients despite the fact that the "toxic" gene and its protein product are present in the brain all the while. Another mystery is why the disease only affects some brain cells, while other cells in the same brain are spared. All these fundamental HD questions could be explained by epigenetic factors, which are chemical modifications to DNA that regulate genes. Without proper epigenetic "instructions", the genomic "machinery" cannot function properly and could even be harmful. Epigenetic "instructions" are distinct in different brain regions, which could be why problems arise in some regions but not in others. In addition, epigenetic marks can change in aging cells; it may take extended periods for slow epigenetic degradation to reach a critical mass of malfunction resulting in HD symptoms. In the proposed project, we will use a mouse model of HD to investigate the epigenetic "instructions" within brain cells that are sensitive to (and spared from) the disease. We plan to investigate how epigenomes "age" differently in the brains of HD mice compared to normal mice. For the first time in brain disease studies, we will test if pathological epigenetic aging in HD is related to, and maybe even caused by, another major biological regulator - the brain's internal clock. This unique study of HD epigenomes may lead to insights pertaining to the origin and fundamental mechanisms of brain degeneration.

column36: Sexual dimorphism and menopause in the interaction between immune cells and neurovascular coupling
column37: The increase in cerebral blood flow produced by neural activity (neurovascular coupling), a critical mechanism that matches substrate delivery with energy demands in brain is modulated by circulating immune cells in the blood. Because impaired neurovascular coupling increases the vulnerability of the brain, it is important to understand how changes in vascular tone in response to neural activity may be altered. Our preliminary data showed that a molecule derived from immune cells impairs neurovascular coupling in male only. These data are very exciting since there are very few studies that aimed at studying the effects of the immune system on cerebral blood flow and there no data about sexual differences and menopause on these mechanisms. More importantly, impaired neurovascular coupling increases brain vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease and stroke which incidence is higher in postmenopausal women. Accordingly, the major objective of this research program is to study the effect of sex and menopause on the regulation of neurovascular coupling by immune cells. In particular, we will investigate the effect of proinflammatory components of the adaptive immune system on neurovascular coupling. These studies will be conducted in mice and humanized mice which produces human immune cells in vivo using genetic, biochemical, anatomical and pharmacological approaches. These studies will improve our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the effects of sex differences and menopause on the regulation of neurovascular coupling by pro-inflammatory immune cells. This may provide further therapeutic target to reduce premature disability and death from dysfunctional cerebral blood flow.

column36: How Missed Care Occurs in Nursing Homes: A Qualitative Study of Care Aides' Perspectives
column37: Care aides (personal support workers, nursing assistants) provide most of the direct care for older adults (residents) who live in nursing homes. For example, they help residents with eating, taking baths, and other daily activities. However, care aides often leave some of these tasks undone. This is partly because nursing homes do not have enough care aides to complete the tasks. Yet, lack of staff alone does not explain why some tasks are left undone. Researchers found that care aides in well-resourced nursing homes also reported care tasks left undone. Besides a shortage of care aides, we do not know what other factors can cause care aides to leave tasks undone and how these factors cause tasks to be left undone. We also currently do not know what changes can be made to prevent tasks from being left undone. Our study will answer these questions by asking care aides themselves. We will have conversations with about 48 care aides who work in nursing homes in Alberta and British Columbia. We will ask them questions such as: What happened when you left tasks undone? and What could have helped you to complete the tasks? We will use the knowledge learned from this study to develop an intervention to help care aides reduce tasks left undone. Our long-term goal is to improve the quality of care and quality of life for residents in nursing homes.

column36: Growing up trans: An international longitudinal qualitative investigation of trans youth access gender affirming care, affirmation and well-being.
column37: Trans and non-binary youth (TNBY) are young people who feel that their felt sense of gender doesn't match the one that was assigned to them at birth. For many TNBY, body changes brought about by puberty are very distressing because they generate feelings of dissonance between their body and their felt gender. Gender affirming medical care, such as puberty blocker medication and hormone therapy, have been shown to significantly reduce distress. Other factors leading to improvement of TNBY well-being include strong family support and access to a community and inclusive spaces. However, there is a lack of integrative and in dept understanding of the pathways that TNBY are taking, their journey into care, as well as how their social and family contexts affect their experience of affirmation, that is, how gender identity is respected and validated, as well as their well-being, over time, during the crucial period of puberty and early medical transition. This international study will examine how TNBY who wish to access gender affirming care such as puberty blockers or hormones navigate this journey into adolescence, especially with regard to their well-being and their experience of affirmation. We will pay a specific attention to their context. To do so, the team will follow a group of 50 TNBY and their families in order to better understand their experience over time. These youth, who will be living in Canada, England, Switzerland, Australia and the United States, will be just starting puberty at the beginning of the project and will have expressed a desire to start gender affirming medical interventions. Every year, for four years, we'll ask youth to tell us in their own words how they're doing, how they experience care and access to it, how they feel their gender identity is respected and affirmed by people around them. This will allow us to develop a nuanced understanding of their needs and experience as navigate gender affirming medical care.

column36: HIV antiretrovirals and placenta dysfunction - identifying the mechanisms leading to poor fetal growth.
column37: It is recommended that all pregnant women living with HIV, receive HIV medications for their own health and for preventing transmission of HIV to their babies. While this has dramatically reduced both maternal death and HIV infections in newborns, HIV medication use in pregnancy has been associated with more poor birth outcomes, including babies being born too small. It is not yet clear how HIV medications are causing this, or whether some HIV medications are better to use in pregnancy than others. Further, not all pregnant women living with HIV go on to have a poor birth outcome - if we had ways to identify, early in pregnancy, those who would go on to have a small baby, we could provide them with extra care to ensure the best outcome for mother and baby. Our hypothesis is that HIV medications cause changes in the placenta that affect how well the baby grows. In this proposal, we bring together an international team from Canada, USA, Uganda, and South Africa. We will take advantage of placenta and blood samples collected in 3 different studies across the globe to address our hypothesis. We will investigate how 3 different types of HIV medications (the most commonly used HIV medications in pregnancy) affect how the placenta develops and functions. We will also look for factors we can measure in mom's blood that indicate how well the placenta is functioning and can predict if the baby will be small. We will also use an animal model to dig into the mechanisms on how HIV medications affect the placenta and find out ways to prevent them. Our findings will help guide the choice of best HIV medications to use in pregnancy, identify interventions to improve pregnancy outcome, and develop tests that can identify women at risk for having a small baby. Our animal model will also be an asset in the testing of the safety of new HIV medications in pregnancy.

column36: Patient-centered approaches for sleep apnea diagnosis and treatment in marginalized women living in shelters
column37: In Canada, 35,000 people are experiencing homelessness on any night. Compared to the general population, people experiencing homelessness (PEH) sleep less and experience increased daytime fatigue. A common sleep disorder and treatable cause of morbidity and mortality is obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). High prevalence of chronic comorbid disorders of OSA in PEH suggest high prevalence of OSA, but the rate of OSA treatment in PEH is very low. Also, in PEH, individual, social, and systemic barriers lead to a higher rate of underdiagnosed and untreated OSA. Sadly, mortality is higher in PEH than the general population, and OSA remains a potential silent cause of mortality and low quality of life in PEH. Marginalized women may face more barriers than men to receive OSA treatment. Daily responsibilities such as childcare, mixing of sleepiness with fatigue from high workload, depression, and anxiety can mask OSA symptoms. Consequently, failing to treat OSA reduces quality of life and adds extra barriers to overcoming daily challenges. Our goal is to diagnose and treat OSA in marginalized women living in shelters and to examine the effect of patient-centered OSA treatment on their quality of life. We have established a patient-centered and inter-disciplinary team of researchers and people with lived experience of homelessness, and partnered with 51 women shelters in Ontario for patient recruitment. This study can show that in women living in shelters, OSA can be treated and will improve quality of life; thus, empowering them to engage in daily activities such as school, work and assimilation back into society. Thus, like "housing first", sleep health should be considered as a major determinant of health and equitable access to care in these women. This study will help to inform health policy decision makers that home-based diagnosis of OSA and full coverage of OSA treatments in women living in shelters will be cost effective for health care system and increase health equity.

column36: The Th17 Master Regulator RORC2 as a New Target for HIV Immune Therapy and Cure Strategy
column37: Combined antiretroviral therapies (ART) are highly efficient at suppressing HIV replication, therefore improving the life quality of people living with HIV. However, ART does not eliminate HIV and if treatment is interrupted, the virus comes back quickly. The virus cannot be eliminated because it lives in a silent form in long-lived memory CD4+ T-cells, called the "viral reservoir". Thus, life-long ART treatment is currently recommended. Our group and others have shown that certain subsets of CD4+ T-cells called Th17 cells are particularly prone to become infected by HIV-1 and to become viral reservoirs. In these viral reservoirs, HIV-1 can reactivate spontaneously from time to time, starting to express some viral genes. ART cannot prevent this process because it mainly depends on the host cell machinery, whereas current ART only targets viral proteins. Low level spontaneous viral reactivation induces chronic activation of the immune system, which over time damages the heart, bones and the brain. Our objective is to identify new drug targets that reduce the size of the viral reservoir and block HIV reactivation in reservoir cells, especially in Th17 cells, with the ultimate goal of making these viral reservoirs harmless. Among these potential drug targets, we identified the master regulator transcription factor RORC2, encoded by the rorc gene. We found that inhibition of RORC2 prevents HIV-1 infection. Importantly, RORC2 is found in Th17 cells and not in the vast majority of CD4+ T cells. Therefore, this opens the possibility of specifically inhibiting infection of these cells and preventing viral reactivation in the large Th17 cell viral reservoir. In collaboration with the pharmaceutical company GlaxoSmithKlein (GSK) and internationally renowned experts in Virology/Immunology we will test if RORC2 inhibitors can be used to reduce the viral reservoirs, block spontaneous HIV-1 reactivation and eventually eliminate the virus.

column36: Understanding and improving the care experiences of people with mental-physical multimorbidity during and beyond the COVID-19 pandemic
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has led to rapid transformations in primary care settings, including major shifts to virtually delivered care, re-designed clinical workflows and processes for managing urgent/non-urgent care, and adaptations due to staffing issues. The consequences of these transformations on patients' experiences of care are largely unknown. Certain patient populations have been shown to be highly vulnerable to the effects of the pandemic, and may be at particular risk due to sudden disruptions to their care. This is likely the case for patients with co-existing mental health and chronic physical health conditions, i.e. mental-physical multimorbidity. Indeed, these patients have faced major challenges over the past year given their elevated risks for COVID-19 infection and fears of contracting the disease through seeking needed services. To avoid or address deterioration in both their mental and physical health, we must identify and implement evidence-based practices and innovations that will help address their care needs during this evolving, long-term crisis. The aim of this study is thus to understand and improve the care experiences of people with mental-physical multimorbidity, both during and beyond the pandemic. To achieve this aim, we will conduct an integrated knowledge translation study with three main components: 1) A provincial action coalition that brings together key stakeholders that can influence the delivery of care and services to patients with mental-physical multimorbidity; 2) A mixed-methods study to better understand these patients' care experiences and how their care needs to be improved to better meet their needs; and 3) A learning collaborative to support the implementation of evidence-based practices tailored to meet priority patient needs. This study will ultimately address important knowledge gaps related to the care experiences of people with mental-physical multimorbidity and lead to concrete actions to improve these experiences.

column36: Energy poverty in Canada: What are the implications for the health and well-being of Canadians?
column37: Households are considered to be in Energy Poverty (EP) when they are unable to afford or access adequate energy at home to meet their needs and maintain healthy indoor temperatures. While EP depends on household factors such as low income and energy needs and practices, it is also caused by several external factors, such as energy inefficient dwellings and high energy prices. EP is thus not simply a problem of low income. Depending on the measure used, some 8% to 20% of Canadian households are living in energy poverty. In certain areas in Atlantic Canada, up to 35% of households are energy poor. EP is inequitably distributed, with women, older adults, people living alone, those with lower education, rural dwellers, recent immigrants, and racialized communities being at increased risk of experiencing EP. International evidence shows that living in EP is associated with cardiovascular and respiratory diseases and poorer mental health. This project, EPIC, is the first examination of EP as a determinant of health in Canada. EPIC will: 1) map EP at small geographies across Canada, document the scale of the problem, and identify which communities are most at risk, 2) tap into national survey and linked cohort data to provide epidemiological evidence on the health impacts of EP in Canada, and 3) provide an in-depth understanding of what it means to be living in EP. EP is a modifiable risk factor with potential solutions being shared between the public and private sectors. By providing rigorous evidence, EPIC will lay the foundation for research and action to reduce EP and improve health-related outcomes and contribute to national policy discussions at the nexus of public health, housing, and sustainability.

column37: Family and friend caregivers, two-thirds of whom are women, play an essential role in supporting the 500,000 Canadians living with dementia. Interventions are available to improve the quality of life and mental health outcomes (e.g. burden or depression) of family and friend caregivers (e.g. exercise, peer support program, psychotherapy, education, respite care); however, many interventions have not been directly compared in randomized trials. This makes it challenging for caregivers, clinicians, and policymakers to know which interventions will work best to improve these outcomes for family and friend caregivers. We will review the literature and identify all randomized trials describing the efficacy of in person and virtual interventions (e.g. by telephone or videoconference) for improving quality of life and symptoms of burden, distress, depression, anxiety, and loneliness for family and friend caregivers of persons living with dementia. This will be the first study of its kind to understand which interventions for family and friend caregivers of persons living with dementia will work the best and how these interventions might better support caregivers. column36: Improving Communication of Cause of Death and Heritable Heart Disease Risk to Families of Sudden Cardiac Death Victims: A Mixed Methods Study
column37: When a young person's heart stops suddenly ("sudden cardiac arrest"), it's important to know why, because some heart problems can be inherited from parents to children. Doctors need to test these families to find out if they have the same disease as the person who died ("cascade screening"). Cascade screening can help doctors figure out what the disease is and then treat the person to prevent him/her from dying suddenly too. The coroner or the medical examiner is usually the person who tells the family why the young person died, yet there are no rules that state who should tell families, when and how. Unfortunately, there is no standard way for how and when coroners and medical examiners tell families about why their loved one died and if they should go see a doctor to assess their risk of dying suddenly. This means that some families receive the information too long after their loved one died, others too soon, making it difficult to remember, or not at all. This project aims to find out the best method of how and when to tell families about why their loved one died and about their need to get screened. We will survey family members, coroners, medical examiners and death investigators from Nova Scotia, Ontario and Manitoba about who and how many get screened, and the reasons why, or why not. We will also interview about 15 families per province (total 45), and up to 15 coroners, medical examiners and death investigators from these same provinces to understand their experiences with the current ways to communication this information. We will analyze everyone's responses and then propose best strategies to communicate with families that can be used across Canada to help future families of young sudden cardiac death victims.

column37: The multi-drug resistant bacterial pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii has gained global attention as an important clinical problem. Owing to its resistance to front-line antibiotic therapies, its ability to survive on hospital surfaces for long periods of time, and its ability to infect diverse tissues in the human body, Acinetobacter has become a successful hospital pathogen, accounting for up to 10% of nosocomial bacterial infections. Acinetobacter baumannii has been highlighted by the World Health Organization (WHO), Centre for Disease Control (CDC), and Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) as a pathogen in urgent need of attention by the research community. We will use cell biological, molecular genetic, and biochemical techniques to study Acinetobacter's life cycle in respiratory tract cells, and the strategies it uses to evade immune responses in host cells. This research will provide new insight into the virulence strategies of this important clinical pathogen, and important clues as to how we can target it therapeutically.

column37: Stigma is a pervasive barrier to preventing HIV among persons who inject drugs (PWID). Kyrgyzstan is part of the world's most rapidly expanding HIV epidemic is in Eastern Europe and Central Asia region, where HIV is predominantly concentrated among PWID. Improving PWID engagement in needle and syringe exchange programs, methadone to treat opioid use disorder, and antiretroviral to treat HIV (among PWID living with HIV) is essential to ending the HIV epidemic in this region. PWID contend with stigmas related to HIV, drug use, and drug treatment (i. e. methadone), which reduces their access to these key HIV prevention services. Yet, little is known about the specific ways in which these intersecting stigmas impede HIV prevention efforts. The current study will recruit urban (n = 250) and rural (n = 250) adult PWID in Kyrgyzstan. Experiences with HIV, drug use, and methadone stigma and level of engagement in NSP, MMT (primary outcome) and ART (secondary outcome) services will be measured at baseline. A series of four data-driven and community-informed workshops with PWID (n = 20) and key stakeholders (n = 20) will be held to develop stigma reduction intervention strategies tailored to urban and rural regions in Kyrgyzstan. Kyrgyz co-investigators will be substantially involved at every level of this project to build in-country capacities in stigma and HIV science. This will enable our Kyrgyz team to develop the next generation of research scholars in a region where the HIV epidemic is rapidly expanding. This study is highly innovative because it is the first to measure how intersecting HIV, drug use, and methadone stigma impacts the rapidly expanding HIV epidemic in Central Asia, and could lead to effective HIV prevention strategies.

column36: Neuroprotective peptides for treatment of neurological lysosomal diseases
column37: Our major objective is to develop therapies for Sanfilippo disease, a devastating inherited childhood disorder using a novel type of drugs called nootropic peptides. When used in the form of nose drops, these drugs can be effectively delivered to the brain. In the brain they protect neurons, brain cells involved in memory and learning, restore communication between neurons and treat neuropsychiatric problems and dementia. Sanfilippo disease affects the lysosome, a cellular compartment responsible for degradation and recycling of big biological molecules, glycosaminoglycans. This causes rapid mental retardation in infants and children. Most of patients become demented and die before the adulthood. No effective therapies for Sanfilippo diseases are available yet. Previously we identified defects in the patient's genes, that cause the disease, and generated mice that have the same defects in their genes. We found that the mice have defects in synapses, specialized structures by which neurons communicate with each other. We have also discovered that many proteins in synapses, necessary for transmission of signals between neurons, are reduced or do not have a normal localization. To treat these defects, we propose to use nootropic peptide ACTH(4-7)PGP, clinically approved for therapy of brain stroke. We demonstrated that treatment of Sanfilippo mice with peptide can restore defective exchange of signals between neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region implicated in the formation and storage of memory. It also improved memory of these mice, increasing their ability to remember novel objects and their orientation in the maze. We now propose to test if the drug can improve the long-term outcome of the disease. If promising results are obtained, the drug will quickly advance for testing in human patients since the nootropic peptides have been approved for clinical and specifically pediatric applications in many countries and no side effects have been reported so far.

column36: Genetic basis of host adaptability and biogeography of adherent-invasive Escherichia coli
column37: Canada has the highest reported prevalence and incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in the world. Today, there are 270,000 Canadian adults and children living with IBD, equating to 1 in every 140 people. It is now accepted that Crohn's disease, a major form of IBD, is an inflammatory disease driven by microbes in our gut. However, the mechanisms by which pathogenic or commensal bacteria participate in the diseaes are not well understood. What is known is that gut inflammation enriches for a population of Escherichia coli, called adherent-invasive E. coli (or AIEC) that have pathogen-like characteristics and are commonly found in Crohn's disease. Using an animal model that my group established, we discovered that AIEC can overcome our body's natural host defenses and gain access to sites in the gastrointestinal tract that normally exclude bacteria. Open questions remain around the origins and evolutionary history of AIEC, preventing a deeper understanding of the evolutionary trajectories and host environments that select for this bacterium in the gut. To address this, we developed a natural host-to-host transmission model to track how AIEC adapts and evolves in the gut over time. AIEC traits that emerged from this model were linked to human disease using clinical E. coli isolates from CD patients, thereby establishing strong clinical relevance. Using this novel transmission model, population metagenomics, and transposon mutant sequencing approaches, our immediate goals are to understand the genetic requirements for AIEC colonization of the inflamed gut and to track the biogeography of AIEC in the gastrointestinal track at the anatomic and cellular levels. This research is poised to uncover relevant host-microbe interactions in CD that until now have remained enigmatic and hampered progress into the translational domain.

column36: DIalysis Symptom COntrol-Pruritus Outcome Trial (DISCO-POT)
column37: Itching associated with kidney disease affects more than half of patients on dialysis. It is a top research priority because of its negative impact on quality of life. Why itching is so common in dialysis patients is not fully understood but it is likely due to changes in skin and the accumulation of toxins normally cleared by the kidney leading to nervous and immune system dysfunction. Several therapies have been studied to reduce itching in dialysis patients but most clinical trials evaluating these therapies have been small with design issues resulting in bias and uncertainty about how well these drugs actually work. Medications thought to be effective are limited by their side effects which are common even with appropriate dosing. Even with effective treatments, residual, bothersome itch is common. Cannabis has been used to treat other skin disorders such as eczema, psoriasis and chronic itch. It has been shown to decrease skin irritation and swelling by modulating the immune system and inhibiting itch pathways. DISCO-POT will compare oral nabilone and topical nabilone to placebos (non-active drugs that looks, smell and taste the same as their comparators) to determine if nabilone is safe and effective at reducing symptoms of itch in dialysis patients. Nabilone is a synthetic form of cannabis that mimics the actions of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main drug in cannabis. The trial will use a "n-of-1" design in which individual patients are randomly assigned (like flipping a coin) to each treatment regimen multiple times in different orders. Patients and their physicians will not be aware of which treatment they are receiving (i.e. they are "blinded") until the end of the study where their results will be reviewed so a treatment decision can be made (unlike traditional clinical trials). N-of-1 trials will then be combined to estimate population-based treatment effects to inform clinical decision-making for patients outside of the clinical trial.

column36: Establishing Essential Research Tools to Advance the Knowledge of Interrelated Sex Differences in Adipose and Immune Functions in Health and Disease (The SDAI Core Models) and Exploring the Mechanisms Involved in the Sex-dimorphic Role of Prohibitin Above and Beyond Sex Hormones
column37: Fat cell and immune cell functions undergo parallel changes in the body during various stages of life in health and disease. The most notable examples are puberty, pregnancy, and menopause, as well as metabolic and immune diseases. Notably, both cell types display sex differences in their functions and sex steroid hormones are an integral component of this. In addition, genes and other regulatory factors (e.g. micro-RNAs) that are located on X chromosome also appear to be involved. Consequently, men and women display differences in susceptibility and resistance to metabolic and immune diseases. However, the identities of various factors/genes that mediate sex differences in fat and immune cell functions remain largely unknown. Identifying these factors and understanding how they work are crucial because of their importance in sex differences in body physiology, and their dysregulation in metabolic and immune diseases. Recently, my team has discovered that a protein called prohibitin plays important roles in sex differences in fat and immune cells. Manipulating prohibitin levels or functions in fat and immune cells simultaneously in transgenic mouse models lead to amplified sex differences in metabolic and immune diseases similar to humans, signifying its importance. However, the relative contributions of the role of prohibitin in fat cell and immune cell functions in sex-dimorphic metabolic and immune health (and the mechanisms involved) remain unknown. To delineate this, we have developed new mouse models by knocking out prohibitin in fat and immune cells. In this proposal, we will perform an in-depth study of sex differences in fat and immune cells. We anticipate that these new models, in combination with our previously developed models, will create a unique set of research tools for scientists working in this field, which will create new research opportunities, provide new research directions and stimulate research in this understudied area.

column37: The development of chimeric antigen receptor T-cells, or CAR T-cells has transformed oncology treatment, offering the potential to cure certain end-stage cancers including lymphoma. We will use these results to determine the costs and benefits (cost-effectiveness) of the new therapies in patients with lymphoma. column37: Children receiving occupational therapy, physiotherapy, and/or speech therapy for development and rehabilitation deserve care based on the best available knowledge. Sharing this type of knowledge is supported by connections between people and across groups. We will analyze data for each province and territory, as well as the whole country, to create visual maps of these networks. Aim 2. Fifteen participants from each group (researchers, therapists, families) will be interviewed. We will recruit people who differ in how strongly they are connected with others, and who are diverse in gender, (dis)ability level, age, and other factors. Develop recommendations to improve knowledge sharing on a local and national scale, that build on the strengths of enablers and address barriers. Conclusion: We want to understand the strengths and gaps of knowledge sharing networks in child development and rehabilitation in Canada so we can make recommendations to improve them. column37: Postpartum depression (PPD) affects up to 1 in 5 mothers and is associated with costs of $150,000 per case over the lifespan. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has and will continue to fundamentally alter the ways in which mothers access postpartum mental health care. Under normal conditions, just 1 in 10 women with PPD get evidence-based treatment, a situation that has worsened substantially during COVID-19. As a result, innovative interventions capable of overcoming barriers and reaching large numbers of women safely are urgently needed to reduce the adverse effects of PPD on mothers, their families, the healthcare system, and society as a whole. The purpose of this study is to test the effectiveness of a Public Health Nurse-Delivered Online 1-Day CBT-Based Workshop for PPD. We will conduct a Canada-wide randomized controlled trial where 376 women will be recruited to receive either the Nurse-Delivered Online Workshop plus treatment as usual from their healthcare providers (treatment group), or treatment as usual plus an online informational session (control group). We will compare the effect of the Public Health Nurse-Delivered Online 1-Day Workshop on levels of maternal depression, anxiety, and parenting stress, their relationship with their partners and infants, as well as emotional and behavioural problems in their older children in the treatment and control groups at three and six months. We will also assess the cost-effectiveness of the intervention. Only treatments that are safe and that can be rolled out on a large scale can have a significant positive impact on PPD at the population level. To achieve this, a shift is needed toward treatments that can reach large numbers of mothers safely and efficiently. Public Health Nurse-Delivered Online 1-Day CBT-Based Workshops reduce many of the barriers to treatment that currently exist, and can help women and families both in Canada and around the world during the pandemic and beyond.

column37: Despite the extraordinary progress made over the past 40 years in our understanding of HIV disease and the development of increasingly effective therapies to control the pandemic, AIDS remains one of the greatest scientific and public health challenges of our time. Future advances in the field depend on a deeper knowledge of the key molecular mechanisms underlying HIV transmission and pathogenesis. Indeed, the pace of HIV disease progression is a consequence of the level of viral replication, which in turn, is controlled by an intricate network of immune proteins from the infected host. My research describes how the surface of HIV virions can be decorated with a variety of human proteins, resulting in virions with different biological properties, impacting virus infection and disease progression. My recent work has shown that HIV virions can acquire human proteins that are gut-homing molecules, essentially marking the viruses with a "postal address" to travel efficiently to the gut. This is significant because intestinal (gut) mucosal tissue is the central location of HIV target cells and the dominant anatomical site for the initial burst of HIV replication and subsequent viral spread within the body. Our broad research goals are to continue to discover new human proteins that can be incorporated into HIV virions, to identify new targets on the surface of HIV which can guide the development of more effective treatments and/or vaccine designs, resulting in major contributions to HIV prevention and treatment efforts.

column36: Advancing virtual care in stroke rehabilitation: TeleRehabilitation with Aims to Improve Lower Extremity Recovery Post-Stroke (TRAIL)
column37: Leg weakness is very common after stroke. It affects the ability to walk and balance among people who have had a stroke. The first year after stroke is an important time for rehabilitation because it is the best time for recovery. Unfortunately, many people who have had a stroke often feel that they do not receive enough rehabilitation to restore their ability to use their legs. This is especially true for people who live in smaller communities where there are few health services, and more recently due to the COVID-19 pandemic where physical distancing between patients and clinicians has limited the amount of in-person rehabilitation. It is therefore important to develop innovative leg rehabilitation programs that are both cost-effective and accessible. Our team of stroke survivors, clinicians and research scientists from across Canada has recently developed TeleRehabilitation with Aims to Improve Lower Extremity Recovery Post-Stroke (TRAIL). TRAIL is a 4-week program that focuses on exercise to improve leg function. It is delivered using the Internet and computer/tablet by a physical therapist. In this study, we will examine if TRAIL improves walking, balance, leg strength, and quality of life to a greater extent than a 4-week lifestyle coaching program (LIFESTYLE), that focuses on improving physical activity, diet, and stress management. Ninety-two volunteers who have had a stroke in the past year will be randomly assigned to participate in either TRAIL or LIFESTYLE. Volunteers will be asked to complete assessments and questionnaires before and after the programs. Assessments will be conducted using videoconferencing so that volunteers will not need to travel to a hospital to participate in the study. We are working with 5 cities across Canada (Halifax, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Vancouver). We anticipate that TRAIL is an accessible program that will help improve leg function within the important early window of recovery after stroke.

column36: The DEPRESsion Screening Data (DEPRESSD) Project: Continuous Updating of Databases for Individual Participant Data Meta-analyses of Depression Screening Test Accuracy
column37: Depression is present in 10-20% of patients with acute and chronic medical illness and an even higher percentage of patients in long-term care. It is associated with poor prognosis, which can lead to major consequences for patients and caregivers. Effective interventions are available, but most depressed patients in Canada do not receive adequate care. Depression screening, which involves using questionnaires to identify people who may have unrecognized depression, is often recommended. However, Canada's main health care guidelines have expressed concerns about the quality of evidence on screening tool accuracy. Most studies include too few participants to precisely estimate accuracy levels or to examine differences by patient characteristics (e.g., sex/gender, age, medical condition). Often, studies only publish results for cut-off scores that work well in a particular study sample but may not work well more generally. In recent years, we have conducted rigorous and systematic searches for studies that used the Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale - Depression subscale (HADS-D), Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), and Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) as screening tools and compared results to major depression diagnoses from clinical interviews. To date, we have obtained data from 350 collaborators and almost 90,000 participants across the four screening tools. It is important that we continue seeking participant data from studies published since the previous searches. We will use the updated databases to determine more accurate ways to identify patients with depression. The proposed research will provide accurate estimates of diagnostic accuracy for these tools, including the consideration of participant characteristics that inform depression risk. Results will be used to develop and test improved depression screening and management programs and to make better decisions for individual patients.

column36: Personality-Targeted Interventions for Addressing Polysubstance Use among Opioid-Addicted Clients Undergoing Opioid Substitution Therapy: A Feasibility Study
column37: We are currently amid a severe opioid crisis, worsened by the COVID-19 pandemic. In Canada, prescription opioid use and opioid overdoses/mortality were soaring pre-pandemic, reaching epidemic levels, with opioid-related deaths only increasing since the pandemic. Powerful and dangerous synthetic opioids (e.g., Fentanyl) are increasingly being used to cut street drugs given disruptions to the drug supply chain with pandemic border closures. More effective interventions for addressing opioid use disorder are sorely needed. In Canada, an effective mainstay treatment for opioid use disorder is opioid substitution therapy (OST; e.g., methadone, buprenorphine). However, OST clients frequently have other problems that are not well served by OST alone such as high OST drop-out and continued polysubstance use during OST. The latter can include "topping up" with opioids, using substances that are dangerous in combination with OST (e.g., sedatives), and risky routes of administration (e.g., injection). We have recently shown that personality traits that predict risk for mental health/behavioral problems also predict risky forms and routes of substance use in OST clients. We will use our expertise in brief cognitive-behavioral interventions and clinical research methods to test the feasibility of personality-targeted substance use interventions in OST clients. We will use our existing personality model along with interviews already collected and analyzed from OST clients and treatment providers to adapt our personality-targeted interventions. In collaboration with our knowledge user partners, we aim to try 4 personality-targeted interventions with clients across 4 OST clinics, evaluate feasibility, and provide a first test of their impacts on OST clients' polysubstance use and their OST retention. We will examine feasibility from the perspectives of clients, therapists, and clinic directors to see if the personality targeted approach should be pursued further in this population.

column36: Connection to Perinatal Care for the Management of Maternal Non-Communicable Diseases: The CONNECT Project
column37: The rising trend in non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as endocrine, cardiac, and respiratory conditions, is a public health priority that is affecting those of reproductive age, including women during pregnancy. It is estimated that over 10% of pregnant women in Ontario have an NCD that, if unmonitored, can lead to severe maternal morbidity and mortality. The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) recommends that women with NCDs consult a specialist in the preconception, during pregnancy, and postpartum periods, in addition to routine prenatal care, however there is little information on actual care practices in the Canada. The CONNECT Project is a multi-method study using population-level administrative health data combined with individual patient-level qualitative narratives to evaluate current health care for women with NCDs navigating pregnancy. It focuses on six NCDs that represent specific body systems, specialists, and ICES validated derived population-level cohorts, and include: 1) Gastrointestinal (Crohn's & Colitis); 2) Cardiovascular (hypertension); 3) Respiratory (asthma); 4) Autoimmune (rheumatoid arthritis); 5) Renal (kidney disease); and 6) Endocrine (diabetes). It will use health data from the Ontario Birth Registry (BORN Ontario) and administrative databases held at ICES to investigate connection to specialist care during pre-conception, pregnancy, and postpartum, including inter-conception care. A Clinical Working Group and Patient Engagement Group are integrated throughout the project to identify the most clinically relevant indicators for each NCD and the equally important voices of patients, who are experts in living day-to-day with an NCD. This study is designed to inform clinical guidelines and is supported by the SOGC, American Gynecological and Obstetrical Society, Society for Perinatal and Pediatric Research, and locally the Monarch postnatal care Centre.

column36: Statistical Methodology for Prediction Modelling to Improve Depression Screening with Individualized Risk Estimates in the Context of Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis
column37: Depression is a chronic and disabling condition that is the leading global cause of life-years lived with disability. However, most Canadians with depression do not receive adequate care. Thus, the development and implementation of effective depression management programs is urgent. Depression screening has been recommended as a solution. However, when trials have been conducted, they have failed to show benefit from depression screening. One reason is that screening tools have not been accurately calibrated for use with individual patients. The CTFPHC has emphasized the need for high-quality research that generates unbiased estimates of depression screening tool accuracy and considers individual patient risk factors. Individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA), which uses actual patient data from primary studies, can address existing problems and incorporate important depression risk factors. Our team has built three large IPD databases including individual and study level characteristics. However, best practices for developing prediction models in the context of IPDMA are unknown because of a number of statistical challenges. Particularly, accounting for study specific intercepts and slopes, dealing with study level variables, and accounting for missing data have not been studied. The proposed research will advance and validate statistical prediction models in the context of IPDMA and apply the advanced models to generate personalized risk probabilities for MDD based on individual screening scores and depression risk factors in actual individual participant datasets, which has not been done previously. Results will be used to improve individualized depression screening and management programs and to make better decision for individual patients in primary, perinatal, and hospital care.

column36: Virtual primary care: a multi-provincial mixed methods study of access, experiences, and outcomes
column37: Timely access to high-quality primary care is an ongoing problem across most Canadian provinces. Virtual care - consulting with a health care professional remotely using communication or information technology such as telephone, videoconference, or text messaging - has the potential to increase access, improve quality, and reduce costs; however, it has not been widely available in Canada and has not been widely studied. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a rapid move away from in-office visits and towards virtual care, raising significant questions about the impact of virtual care on patients, health care professionals, and the health system more broadly. This project will use information from interviews with health professionals (physicians, nurse practitioners and nurses) and patients; routinely collected, population-based health service delivery data; and provincial policy documents to study access to, experiences with, and outcomes from virtual care provided in the primary care context across four Canadian provinces. Building on existing surveys and interviews being conducted in Ontario and Nova Scotia, the interviews with patients and health professionals will explore experiences with providing and receiving care virtually. The analysis of routinely collected health service data will identify what groups of patients are receiving care virtually, and for what health concerns. We will use these same data to look at downstream health outcomes and to measure the overall impact of virtual care on the volume of services delivered and on health system costs. Ultimately, this project will strengthen our understanding about the impact of the move toward virtual care on patients, providers, and the health care system, supporting the development of coordinating provincial policies. This will help to ensure that patients have access to the primary services they need, virtually or in person, at the right time.

column36: Cardiac DOC: the predictive validity of a simple screen for Depression, Obstructive sleep apnea and Cognitive impairment (DOC) to identify heart failure patients at risk of adverse outcomes in a prospective, multicenter cohort.
column37: Heart Failure (HF) is a common heart condition, which leads to death or disability in many people and also worsens their quality of life. Depression, sleep apnea (problems breathing at night referred to as OSA) and Cognitive impairment (memory, thinking problems) are very common in people with HF. Although these "DOC" conditions lead to worse outcomes in people with HF, they are often not tested for at regular HF clinic visits. We have created a simple, short screening test (the DOC screen) to help identify these DOC conditions during a regular clinical visit and have tested it in over 300 HF patients. We found that patients with HF were able to complete the screen quickly and that doctors could get useful information from the DOC screen that might help improve quality of life. However, it is not known if using this screen can us identify which patients are at higher risk for bad outcomes (like being admitted to hospital with worsening heart failure or another condition, like dehydration, pneumonia, depression and dementia, or death). The main goal of this study is to test if results of the DOC screen can help to predict which patients have these bad outcomes one year after their clinic visits. Our second goal is to see if there are differences in the impact of DOC conditions on potentially preventable hospital admissions. We will also look at the impact of DOC conditions for people in different age groups or for different sexes (male vs. female). We will screen 4,000 HF patients at their regular visit in 12 different clinics across Ontario and collect information on outcomes one year later using hospital records. If using the DOC screen helps to identify those patients at highest risk for bad outcomes, this will help us design better treatments for patients with HF to improve quality of life and lower the risks of dying or being hospitalized from HF.

column36: Healthy Food Rx - Evaluation of a subsidized healthy food prescription program for patients with type 2 diabetes and food insecurity.
column37: Type 2 diabetes is a caused when one's pancreas is unable to make enough insulin to control blood sugar levels. Over time, high blood sugars can cause damage to the blood vessels, leading to heart attacks, kidney failure, amputations, and blindness. In addition to prescription medications, an important part of the management of diabetes is following a healthy diet consisting of fresh fruits, vegetables, fish, and whole grains. Unfortunately, this diet is more expensive than purchasing highly processed unhealthy foods. Many Canadians with diabetes are unable to afford these healthy foods, a condition known as food insecurity. Food insecurity often results in poor blood sugar control in patients with diabetes. Doctors and other healthcare providers have very few resources to help address food insecurity in their patients. We propose the development of a subsidy program, provided through healthcare encounters, which would help make healthy foods more affordable by providing $1.50/day/household member to be spent on a list of healthy foods. Through a carefully designed randomized controlled trial, we will prove that this program leads to improved blood sugar levels in patients with type 2 diabetes and food insecurity. We will then show how these improved blood sugars, will result in fewer complications and save the healthcare system money. Our team includes a number of high-level healthcare decision-makers from the government Ministry of Health, Alberta Health Services, and the largest healthcare insurer in the province (Alberta Blue Cross), who are keenly interested in our findings and willing to implement this program broadly if we find it to be effective.

column36: Nishtohtamihk li kaansyr (Understanding Cancer): Cancer Screening, Outcomes and Experiences among Metis People in Alberta
column37: Indigenous people in Canada tend to have poorer health outcomes than non-Indgenous people, including higher rates of certain cancers. This project will ask Metis Albertans about reasons for accessing/not accessing cancer screening, including what factors affected their choice to go for screening the first time and for the recommended follow-up tests, and their knowledge about cancer screening as part of preventing cancer. It will also ask small groups of Metis men and women in each of the six regions about their cancer screening experiences. These small gatherings will identify barriers and facilitators of cancer screening. Lastly, this project will conduct a data linkage with cancer screening databases to compare Metis Albertans with non-Metis Albertans in terms of screening uptake, effectiveness, timeliness and efficiency. The study has been co-designed to include both Metis and Western principles and perspectives in all phases of the research project. Results will provide critical knowledge about where inequities and challenges exist. Barriers and facilitators of cancer screening will inform cancer screening program changes that will achieve cancer prevention goals for Metis people. This project will also support the cancer prevention goals of the MNA and Metis people in Canada.

column36: The Next Generation Longitudinal Birth Cohort: Early childhood beta cell and renal function in offspring exposed to maternal T2D.
column37: Rationale: T2D in childhood continues to increase worldwide and affects Indigenous children and families more than non-Indigenous populations. Childhood onset T2D is associated with high rates of early onset rapidly progressive kidney disease. Exposure to T2D in the womb is accepted to be a strong risk factor for the development of childhood T2D. A negative impact of exposure to maternal diabetes on the developing beta cells (which secrete insulin) and kidneys may explain the high risk of T2D and kidney complications in these children. The Next Generation Birth Cohort (NextGen) is a unique prospective birth cohort designed to examine metabolic and anthropometric outcomes of offspring in the first year of life, born to mothers diagnosed in childhood. The overall aim of this project is to determine how exposure to maternal T2D and adiposity impact the natural history of the development of T2D and early renal dysfunction in First Nations children by looking at the beta cell function and renal function in the offspring during childhood (ages 5-7 years) before they are diagnosed with pre-diabetes or T2D. To accomplish this we will build upon the current study frame work to extend follow up of the children to age 5-7 years to meet the following goals: 1. To look for early differences beta cell function and whole body insulin resistance in offspring exposed to maternal T2D compared to offspring unexposed. 2.To look for early differences in renal function in offspring exposed to maternal T2D compared to offspring unexposed. 3. To look at how the HNF1a carrier status impacts both beta cell function and renal function in offspring exposed and unexposed to maternal T2D. The information from this study will help us determine when and how to screen these high risk kids for early evidence of metabolic dysfunction and renal dysfunction before they get sick, and suggest novel personalized medication/intervention strategies to prevent overt T2D from developing.

column36: Feasibility of Advanced Consent for ParticipaTION in Acute Stroke Trials (ACTION)
column37: Before a patient can be enrolled into a medical research study, he or she must give permission (called consent) to the researchers to do so. But what happens when someone is too sick to give permission, like when they are having a stroke? Currently, researchers usually try to find a family member to give permission on behalf of the sick person. Often, family members can't be found, don't know what to say, and feel lots of pressure to answer. Othewise, researchers may enroll the patient without asking for permission. We would like to try to involve patients as much as possible in the decision-making. That's why we are trying to develop a new way of gaining permission from patients ahead of time to include them in studies when they might be too sick to give permission at the time. We call this ADVANCED CONSENT. We want to see if we can identify people at risk of having a stroke, ask them about giving consent in advance, and then see if any of the people who agreed to participate would later come back to the hospital in a situation where they were too sick to sign up for a study at that time. If we are able to show that this program can work, we want to share our findings with stroke researchers around the world, and we hope that lots of other studies will also do this and involve patients as much as possible about research in stroke. Our work has 4 distinct steps: 1. We want to ask doctors, ethicists, and patients about what they think about advanced consent, both through giving them questionnaires and asking them questions in groups 2. We want to develop the ethics of advanced consent - why it's better to do this than use other methods of getting patient permission 3. We want to design a plan to approach patients about enrolling in the advanced consent program 4. Finally, we want to ask the patients how they feel about advanced consent, in principle and in relation to a specific trial

column36: SOmNI (Sleep Outcomes mHealth, wearable sensor and Nudging Intervention) randomized controlled trial: an mHealth intervention for sleep promotion in adolescents
column37: Many teenagers sleep much less than the 9 hours a night that are recommended, which puts them at risk for difficulties with mental health and school. We took input from youth and developed an intervention to promote sleep for teenagers called SOmNI (Sleep Outcomes mHealth, wearable sensor and Nudging Intervention). SOmNI uses a wrist-worn sensor to track sleep, and delivers feedback and suggestions for behavior change, along with real-world (e.g. gift certificates) and virtual (e.g. experience points) rewards through an easy-to-use mobile app. We previously received CIHR funding to test SOmNI in a small group and found that those teens enjoyed using the app, increased the amount of sleep they got (an additional 44 minutes on school nights) and improved their functioning at school. We now want to compare SOmNI and a version of SOmNI without real-world rewards to each other and versus usual care (receiving no information or advice about sleep) in a larger study. We want to know if SOmNI with or without real-world rewards increases nighttime sleep on school nights, if they decrease mental health symptoms, and what their effects are on sleep quality, sleepiness and school attendance and if any changes that occur last after real-world rewards are removed. We will also ask parents about their willingness to pay for the SOmNI apps after the study is over. We will include teens who are in high school, sleep less than 8 hours on weeknights, sleep more than 9 hours on weekend nights, and live anywhere in Canada. We will not include teens with any major health or sleep problem. The study will enroll 264 teens and we will measure sleep at the start of the study and 5- and 10-weeks after they are assigned to their group. By giving teens information and advice to change their sleep through an app linked to a wrist-worn sleep tracker we may be able to reach many teens and increase their sleep when they most need its health benefits.

column36: Intergenerational impacts of diabetes among First Nations mothers and their children
column37: Nearly 2 1/2 million people are affected by diabetes in Canada, but rates among First Nations people are much higher compared to other people in Canada. We recently completed a collaborative project between academic researchers and First Nations partners to study the impact of diabetes on First Nations people in Ontario. We found that the rate of diabetes was more than double that of other people in Ontario. In addition, we showed that diabetes was growing especially quickly for First Nations children. As a result of our work, the Chiefs of Ontario identified diabetes in children and young adults as a high priority for ongoing research, so our study team has turned to focus on this issue. First Nations people have experienced historical and colonial policies of discrimination. These experiences continue through intergenerational traumas, such as the residential school system and ongoing high rates of incarceration and child apprehension. The goal of this research study will be to examine the intergenerational impacts of diabetes among First Nations mothers and children in Ontario. We will identify mothers with and without diabetes in pregnancy. We will compare their children for the development of diabetes in childhood or young adulthood. We will focus, in particular, on people living in urban areas, as they represent 30% of the First Nations population in Ontario but less is known about their health status. We will work with the Chiefs of Ontario to establish an Advisory Group of First Nations people selected from different communities with a personal connection to diabetes. This group will help us understand and contextualize the results, and will help us point to approaches to move forward.

column37: As the population ages, it is becoming increasingly important to find ways to support people with dementia to live well in the community. Primary healthcare that is comprehensive, integrated and effective is important to ensuring people with dementia have the support necessary to live in the community, and team-based approaches, where doctors, nurse practitioners, nurses and other health care providers, work together to provide care have been identified are particularly well suited to the needs of people with dementia. To date there has been little research exploring how these teams provide care. It is important to do this work so that effective practices are identified and gaps in service provision can be found. The proposed project will be guided by people with dementia and their caregivers, and will explore the care provided by collaborative family practice teams to people with dementia through case study research. Qualitative methods will be used to ask primary care providers, people with dementia and caregivers about their experience with collaborative family practice teams, and guided appointments-where a research accompanies a person with dementia through the process of attending a primary health care appointment-will be used to understand the perspective of people with dementia. Data will be analyzed by comparing and contrasting multiple data sources and perspectives to develop themes to describe how collaborative family practice teams provide care. Findings will support the development of recommendations for improving primary health care for people with dementia, and provide opportunities for practice development among primary care providers.
